Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhammapiṭake

In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka

Aṭṭhasālinī nāma

The Commentary named Aṭṭhasālinī,

Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī.

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Karuṇā [M 0.0001][P 0.0001][V 0.0001] viya sattesu, paññā yassa mahesino;

Ñeyyadhammesu sabbesu, pavattittha yathāruci.

As was His compassion for beings, so was the wisdom of the Great Sage; it proceeded through all knowable things according to His wish.

Dayāya [V 0.0002] tāya sattesu, samussāhitamānaso;

Pāṭihīrāvasānamhi, vasanto tidasālaye.

With His mind uplifted by that compassion for beings, He dwelt in the abode of the Thirty-three at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle.

Pāricchattakamūlamhi, paṇḍukambalanāmake;

Silāsane sannisinno, ādiccova yugandhare.

Seated on the stone throne named Paṇḍukambala at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, like the sun upon the Yugandhara peak.

Cakkavāḷasahassehi, dasahāgamma sabbaso;

Sannisinnena devānaṃ, gaṇena parivārito.

Surrounded by the seated assembly of gods, who had gathered from ten thousand world-systems in every direction.

Mātaraṃ pamukhaṃ katvā, tassā paññāya tejasā;

Abhidhammakathāmaggaṃ, devānaṃ sampavattayi.

Placing His mother at the forefront, by the power of His wisdom, He set in motion the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the gods.

Tassa pāde namassitvā, sambuddhassa sirīmato;

Saddhammañcassa pūjetvā, katvā saṅghassa cañjaliṃ.

Having paid homage at the feet of that Glorious, Perfectly Enlightened One, having honored His True Dhamma, and having made a reverential salutation to the Sangha.

Nipaccakārassetassa, katassa ratanattaye;

Ānubhāvena sosetvā, antarāye asesato.

By the power of this homage paid to the Triple Gem, having completely eliminated all obstacles.

Visuddhācārasīlena, nipuṇāmalabuddhinā;

Bhikkhunā buddhaghosena, sakkaccaṃ abhiyācito.

Having been earnestly requested by the monk Buddhaghosa, who is of pure conduct and virtue, and of keen, spotless intellect.

Yaṃ [M 0.0002] devadevo devānaṃ, desetvā nayato puna;

Therassa sāriputtassa, samācikkhi vināyako.

That which the God of gods, the Leader, having taught to the gods, then methodically explained to the Elder Sāriputta.

Anotattadahe katvā, upaṭṭhānaṃ mahesino;

Yañca sutvāna so thero, āharitvā mahītalaṃ.

And which that Elder, having attended upon the Great Sage at Lake Anotatta and heard it, then brought down to the earth.

Bhikkhūnaṃ [V 0.0003] payirudāhāsi, iti bhikkhūhi dhārito;

Saṅgītikāle saṅgīto, vedehamuninā puna.

He taught it to the monks; thus it was mastered by the monks. It was recited at the time of the Council, and again by the Sage of Videha.

Tassa gambhīrañāṇehi, ogāḷhassa abhiṇhaso;

Nānānayavicittassa, abhidhammassa ādito.

Of that Abhidhamma, from its very beginning, which is variegated with diverse methods and repeatedly penetrated by profound knowledges,

Yā mahākassapādīhi, vasīhiṭṭhakathā purā;

Saṅgītā anusaṅgītā, pacchāpi ca isīhi yā.

That ancient Commentary which was compiled and transmitted by the masters, Mahākassapa and others, and which was also recited later by the sages.

Ābhatā pana therena, mahindenetamuttamaṃ;

Yā dīpaṃ dīpavāsīnaṃ, bhāsāya abhisaṅkhatā.

This supreme Commentary, however, was brought to the island by the Elder Mahinda and was there composed in the language of the island-dwellers.

Apanetvā [P 0.0002] tato bhāsaṃ, tambapaṇṇinivāsinaṃ;

Āropayitvā niddosaṃ, bhāsaṃ tantinayānugaṃ.

Removing from it the language of the inhabitants of Tambapaṇṇi, and establishing in its place the flawless language that accords with the textual tradition,

Nikāyantaraladdhīhi, asammissaṃ anākulaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, dīpayanto vinicchayaṃ.

Illuminating the definitive interpretation of the residents of the Mahāvihāra, unmixed with the tenets of other schools and free from confusion,

Atthaṃ pakāsayissāmi, āgamaṭṭhakathāsupi;

Gahetabbaṃ gahetvāna, tosayanto vicakkhaṇe.

I shall elucidate the meaning, taking what ought to be taken from the scriptures and commentaries, and delighting the wise.

Kammaṭṭhānāni sabbāni, cariyābhiññā vipassanā;

Visuddhimagge panidaṃ, yasmā sabbaṃ pakāsitaṃ.

All meditation subjects, conduct, higher knowledges, and insight—since all this has indeed been explained in the Visuddhimagga,

Tasmā taṃ aggahetvāna, sakalāyapi tantiyā;

Padānukkamato eva, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Therefore, without taking up that material, I shall explain the meaning of the entire text strictly in accordance with the sequence of the words.

Iti [V 0.0004] me bhāsamānassa, abhidhammakathaṃ imaṃ;

Avikkhittā nisāmetha, dullabhā hi ayaṃ kathāti.

Thus, as I speak this discourse on the Abhidhamma, listen attentively, for this discourse is indeed rare.

Nidānakathā

The Introductory Account

Tattha [M 0.0003] kenaṭṭhena abhidhammo? Dhammātirekadhammavisesaṭṭhena. Atirekavisesatthadīpako hettha ‘abhi’-saddo. “Bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti no paṭikkamanti” (ma. ni. 3.384; saṃ. ni. 5.195) “abhikkantavaṇṇā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.1-2) viya. Tasmā yathā samussitesu bahūsu chattesu ceva dhajesu ca yaṃ atirekappamāṇaṃ visesavaṇṇasaṇṭhānañca chattaṃ, taṃ ‘aticchatta’nti vuccati, yo atirekappamāṇo nānāvirāgavaṇṇavisesasampanno ca dhajo so ‘atidhajo’ti vuccati, yathā ca ekato sannipatitesu bahūsu rājakumāresu ceva devesu ca yo jātibhogayasaissariyādisampattīhi atirekataro ceva visesavantataro ca rājakumāro so ‘atirājakumāro’ti vuccati, yo āyuvaṇṇaissariyayasasampattiādīhi atirekataro ceva visesavantataro ca devo so ‘atidevo’ti vuccati, tathārūpo brahmāpi ‘atibrahmā’ti vuccati, evameva ayampi dhammo dhammātirekadhammavisesaṭṭhena ‘abhidhammo’ti vuccati.

Here, in what sense is it Abhidhamma? In the sense of superior and special Dhamma. Here, the prefix 'abhi' indicates superiority and distinction, as in "Severe painful feelings are increasing in me, not decreasing" (Majjhima Nikāya 3.384; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.195) and "of surpassing beauty" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.1-2), and so forth. Therefore, just as among many umbrellas and banners raised together, the umbrella which is of superior measure and distinguished color and shape is called the 'supreme umbrella,' and the banner which is of superior measure and endowed with various diverse and attractive colors is called the 'supreme banner'; and just as among many princes and devas assembled together, the prince who is greatly superior and more distinguished in terms of birth, wealth, fame, dominion, and other attainments is called the 'supreme prince,' and the deva who is greatly superior and more distinguished in terms of lifespan, beauty, dominion, fame, and other attainments is called the 'supreme deva,' and similarly, a Brahmā of such a kind is called the 'supreme Brahmā'; even so, this Dhamma, too, is called 'Abhidhamma' in the sense of superior and special Dhamma.

Suttantañhi patvā pañcakkhandhā ekadeseneva vibhattā, na nippadesena; abhidhammaṃ patvā pana suttantabhājanīyaabhidhammabhājanīyapañhapucchakanayānaṃ vasena nippadesato vibhattā. Tathā dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, cattāri saccāni, bāvīsatindriyāni, dvādasapadiko paccayākāro. Kevalañhi [P 0.0003] indriyavibhaṅge suttantabhājanīyaṃ natthi, paccayākāre ca pañhapucchakaṃ natthi. Suttantañca patvā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā ekadeseneva vibhattā, na nippadesena; abhidhammaṃ patvā pana tiṇṇampi nayānaṃ vasena nippadesatova vibhattā. Tathā cattāri sammappadhānāni, cattāro iddhipādā, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, cattāri jhānāni, catasso appamaññāyo, pañca sikkhāpadāni, catasso paṭisambhidā. Kevalañhettha sikkhāpadavibhaṅge suttantabhājanīyaṃ natthi. Suttantaṃ patvā ca ñāṇaṃ ekadeseneva vibhattaṃ na nippadesena; tathā kilesā. Abhidhammaṃ patvā pana “ekavidhena ñāṇavatthū”tiādinā (vibha. 751) nayena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā nippadesatova [M 0.0004] vibhattaṃ. Tathā ekakato paṭṭhāya anekehi nayehi kilesā. Suttantaṃ [V 0.0005] patvā ca bhūmantaraparicchedo ekadeseneva vibhatto, na nippadesena; abhidhammaṃ pana patvā tiṇṇampi nayānaṃ vasena bhūmantaraparicchedo nippadesatova vibhatto. Evaṃ dhammātirekadhammavisesaṭṭhena abhidhammoti veditabbo.

In the Suttanta, the five aggregates are analyzed only partially, not exhaustively; but in the Abhidhamma, they are analyzed exhaustively through the methods of Suttanta analysis, Abhidhamma analysis, and question-and-answer. Similarly, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, and the twelvefold causal formula. However, in the analysis of the faculties alone, there is no Suttanta method, and in the causal formula, there is no questioning method. In the Suttanta, the four foundations of mindfulness are analyzed only partially, not exhaustively; but in the Abhidhamma, they are analyzed exhaustively through all three methods. Similarly, the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, the five precepts, and the four analytical knowledges. However, in the analysis of the precepts alone, there is no Suttanta method. And in the Suttanta, knowledge is analyzed only partially, not exhaustively; likewise, the defilements. But in the Abhidhamma, after setting up the matrix according to the method beginning with "knowledge as a single category," and so on (Vibh. 751), knowledge is analyzed exhaustively. Similarly, the defilements are analyzed in many ways, starting from a single classification. And in the Suttanta, the demarcation of the planes of existence is analyzed only partially, not exhaustively; but in the Abhidhamma, the demarcation of the planes of existence is analyzed exhaustively through all three methods. Thus, Abhidhamma should be understood in the sense of superior and special Dhamma.

Pakaraṇaparicchedato panesa dhammasaṅgaṇīvibhaṅgadhātukathāpuggalapaññattikathāvatthuyamakapaṭṭhānānaṃ sattannaṃ pakaraṇānaṃ vasena ṭhito. Ayamettha ācariyānaṃ samānakathā. Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – ‘kathāvatthu kasmā gahitaṃ? Nanu sammāsambuddhassa parinibbānato aṭṭhārasavassādhikāni dve vassasatāni atikkamitvā moggaliputtatissattherenetaṃ ṭhapitaṃ? Tasmā sāvakabhāsitattā chaḍḍetha na’nti. ‘Kiṃ pana chappakaraṇāni abhidhammo’ti? ‘Evaṃ na vadāmī’ti. ‘Atha kiṃ vadesī’ti. ‘Sattappakaraṇānī’ti. ‘Kataraṃ gahetvā satta karosī’ti? ‘Mahādhammahadayaṃ nāma atthi, etena saha sattā’ti. ‘Mahādhammahadaye apubbaṃ natthi, katipayāva pañhāvārā avasesā, kathāvatthunāva saddhiṃ sattā’ti. ‘No kathāvatthunā, mahādhātukathā [P 0.0004] nāma atthi, tāya saddhiṃ sattā’ti. ‘Mahādhātukathāyaṃ apubbaṃ natthi, appamattikāva tanti avasesā. Kathāvatthunāva saddhiṃ sattā’ti.

From the perspective of the treatises, it consists of seven treatises: the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna. This is the common account of the teachers here. However, a sophist says: "Why is the Kathāvatthu included? Was it not established by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa two hundred and eighteen years after the Parinibbāna of the Fully Enlightened One? Therefore, since it is spoken by a disciple, it should be discarded." "Then are the six treatises the Abhidhamma?" "I do not say so." "Then what do you say?" "The seven treatises." "Which one do you add to make seven?" "There is one called the Mahādhammahadaya—together with that, there are seven." "The Mahādhammahadaya contains nothing new; only a few question-sections remain. Only with the Kathāvatthu are there seven." "Not with the Kathāvatthu—there is one called the Mahādhātukathā; together with that, there are seven." "The Mahādhātukathā contains nothing new; only a small portion of the text remains. Only with the Kathāvatthu are there seven."

Sammāsambuddho hi sattappakaraṇāni desento kathāvatthuṃ patvā yā esā puggalavāre tāva catūsu pañhesu dvinnaṃ pañcakānaṃ vasena aṭṭhamukhā vādayutti taṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbakathāmaggesu asampuṇṇabhāṇavāramattāya pāḷiyā mātikaṃ ṭhapesi. Sā panesā “puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti. Āmantā. Yo saccikaṭṭho paramattho tato so puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti. Nahevaṃ vattabbe. Ājānāhi niggahaṃ…pe… puggalo nupalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti. Āmantā. Yo saccikaṭṭho paramattho tato so puggalo nupalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti. Nahevaṃ vattabbe. Ājānāhi niggahaṃ…pe…. Sabbattha puggalo upalabbhati sabbattha puggalo nupalabbhati, sabbadā puggalo upalabbhati sabbadā puggalo nupalabbhati, sabbesu puggalo upalabbhati sabbesu puggalo nupalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenā”ti (kathā. 15-16) evaṃ paṭhamaṃ vādaṃ nissāya [M 0.0005] paṭhamaṃ niggahaṃ, dutiyaṃ nissāya dutiyaṃ …pe… aṭṭhamaṃ nissāya aṭṭhamaṃ niggahaṃ dassentena satthārā ṭhapitā. Iminā nayena sabbattha mātikāṭhapanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapento imaṃ disvā ṭhapesi – mama parinibbānato aṭṭhārasavassādhikānaṃ dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ matthake moggaliputtatissatthero nāma bhikkhu [V 0.0006] bhikkhusahassamajjhe nisinno sakavāde pañca suttasatāni paravāde pañcāti suttasahassaṃ samodhānetvā dīghanikāyappamāṇaṃ kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ bhājessatīti.

The Fully Enlightened One, while teaching the seven treatises, upon reaching the Kathāvatthu, established a matrix in the Pāli for all the paths of discourse, which amounted to merely an incomplete recitation portion, beginning with that eightfold debating method concerning the four questions by way of two sets of five in the section on individuals. This matrix is as follows: “Is an individual found in truth and in the ultimate sense? Yes. Is the individual found in truth and in the ultimate sense from that which is true and ultimate? It should not be said thus. Acknowledge the refutation… The individual is not found in truth and in the ultimate sense? Yes. Is the individual not found in truth and in the ultimate sense from that which is true and ultimate? It should not be said thus. Acknowledge the refutation… In every way is the individual found? In every way is the individual not found? Always is the individual found? Always is the individual not found? In all things is the individual found? In all things is the individual not found in truth and in the ultimate sense?” In this way, the Teacher established the first refutation based on the first thesis, the second based on the second… up to the eighth refutation based on the eighth. By this method, the establishment of the matrix in all cases should be understood. Furthermore, while establishing this matrix, foreseeing this, he declared: “At the culmination of two hundred and eighteen years after my Parinibbāna, a monk named Moggaliputtatissa Thera, seated amidst a thousand monks, will expound the Kathāvatthu treatise, equal in length to the Dīgha Nikāya, combining a thousand discourses—five hundred from his own school and five hundred from the schools of others.”

Moggaliputtatissattheropi idaṃ pakaraṇaṃ desento na attano ñāṇena desesi, satthārā pana dinnanayena ṭhapitamātikāya desesi. Iti satthārā dinnanayena ṭhapitamātikāya desitattā sakalampetaṃ pakaraṇaṃ buddhabhāsitameva nāma jātaṃ. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā madhupiṇḍikasuttantādīni[P 0.0005]. Madhupiṇḍikasuttantasmiñhi bhagavā “yatonidānaṃ bhikkhu purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti, ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ, esevanto rāgānusayāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.202) mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi.

The Elder Moggaliputtatissa too, while expounding this treatise, did not teach by means of his own knowledge, but taught by means of the matrix established according to the method given by the Teacher. Thus, because it was taught by means of the matrix established according to the method given by the Teacher, this entire treatise has indeed come to be considered the word of the Buddha. How so? Just like the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta and the like. In the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, the Blessed One laid down the matrix: "Monks, whatever the source from which a person is assailed by perceptions and notions of conceptual proliferation; if there is nothing there to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to, that is the end of the underlying tendency to lust," and then rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

Dhammappaṭiggāhakā bhikkhū mahākaccānattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dasabalena ṭhapitamātikāya atthaṃ pucchiṃsu. Thero pucchitamattakeneva akathetvā dasabalassa apacitidassanatthaṃ “seyyathāpi āvuso puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī”ti (ma. ni. 1.203) sāropamaṃ āharitvā sārarukkho viya bhagavā sākhāpalāsasadisā sāvakā, “so hāvuso bhagavā jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passati cakkhubhūto ñāṇabhūto dhammabhūto brahmabhūto vattā pavattā atthassa ninnetā amatassa dātā dhammassāmī tathāgato”ti satthāraṃ thometvā punappunaṃ therehi yācito satthārā ṭhapitamātikāya atthaṃ vibhajitvā “ākaṅkhamānā ca pana tumhe āyasmanto bhagavantaṃyeva upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha sace sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ saṃsandiyamānaṃ sameti gaṇheyyātha, no ce mā gaṇhitthā”ti iminā adhippāyena “yathā vo bhagavā byākaroti tathā naṃ dhāreyyāthā”ti vatvā uyyojesi.

The monks who received the Dhamma approached the Elder Mahākaccāna and asked about the meaning of the matrix established by the One of Ten Powers. The Elder, without answering immediately, to show respect for the One of Ten Powers, brought forth the simile of the heartwood, saying: "Just as, friends, a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood..." He compared the Blessed One to a tree with heartwood and the disciples to branches and leaves. Praising the Teacher, he said, "Friends, the Blessed One knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen. He is vision, knowledge, the Dhamma, Brahmā. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata." Though repeatedly requested by the elders, he explained the meaning of the matrix established by the Teacher. Then, with the intention that they should approach the Blessed One himself to ask about this meaning and accept it only if it aligned with the knowledge of omniscience, he said: "You should retain it as the Blessed One explains it," and sent them away.

Te [M 0.0006] satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchiṃsu. Satthā dukkathitaṃ kaccānenāti avatvā suvaṇṇāliṅgaṃ ussāpento viya gīvaṃ unnāmetvā supupphitasatapattasassirikaṃ mahāmukhaṃ pūrento brahmassaraṃ nicchāretvā sādhu sādhūti therassa sādhukāraṃ datvā “paṇḍito, bhikkhave, mahākaccāno, mahāpañño bhikkhave mahākaccāno, maṃ cepi tumhe, bhikkhave, etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyaṃ yathā taṃ mahākaccānena byākata”nti (ma. ni. 1.205) āha.

They approached the Teacher and asked. Without saying that Kaccāna had spoken poorly, the Teacher, as if hoisting a golden standard, lifted his neck, and filling his great mouth, glorious like a fully bloomed hundred-petaled lotus, emitted a Brahmā-like voice. Saying, "Good, good," he gave approval to the Elder and declared, "Monks, Mahākaccāna is wise. Monks, Mahākaccāna has great wisdom. If you were to ask me this meaning, I too would explain it exactly as Mahākaccāna has explained it."

Evaṃ satthārā anumoditakālato paṭṭhāya ca pana sakalaṃ suttaṃ buddhabhāsitaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Ānandattherādīhi [V 0.0007] vitthāritasuttesupi eseva nayo. Evameva sammāsambuddho sattappakaraṇāni desento kathāvatthuṃ patvā vuttanayena mātikaṃ ṭhapesi. Ṭhapento [P 0.0006] ca pana imaṃ addasa –

From the time the Teacher thus approved, the entire sutta became known as the word of the Buddha. This is the same method even in the suttas elaborated by Elder Ānanda and others. Just so, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while teaching the seven treatises, upon reaching the Kathāvatthu, established the matrix in the manner described. While establishing it, he saw this:

Mama parinibbānato aṭṭhārasavassādhikānaṃ dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ matthake moggaliputtatissatthero nāma bhikkhu bhikkhusahassamajjhe nisinno sakavāde pañca suttasatāni paravāde pañcāti suttasahassaṃ samodhānetvā dīghanikāyappamāṇaṃ kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ bhājessatīti.

At the culmination of two hundred and eighteen years after my Parinibbāna, a monk named Moggaliputtatissa Thera, seated amidst a thousand monks, will expound the Kathāvatthu treatise, equal in length to the Dīgha Nikāya, combining a thousand discourses—five hundred from his own school and five hundred from the schools of others.

Moggaliputtatissattheropi imaṃ pakaraṇaṃ desento na attano ñāṇena desesi, satthārā pana dinnanayena ṭhapitamātikāya desesi. Iti satthārā dinnanayena ṭhapitamātikāya desitattā sakalampetaṃ pakaraṇaṃ buddhabhāsitameva jātaṃ. Evaṃ kathāvatthunāva saddhiṃ satta pakaraṇāni abhidhammo nāma.

The Elder Moggaliputtatissa too, in teaching this treatise, did not teach based on his own knowledge, but taught according to the method given by the Teacher and the established matrix. Thus, because this entire treatise was taught according to the method given by the Teacher and the established matrix, it indeed became the word of the Buddha. In this way, the seven treatises, together with the Kathāvatthu, are called the Abhidhamma.

Tattha dhammasaṅgaṇīpakaraṇe catasso vibhattiyo – cittavibhatti rūpavibhatti nikkheparāsi atthuddhāroti. Tattha kāmāvacarakusalato aṭṭha, akusalato dvādasa, kusalavipākato soḷasa, akusalavipākato satta, kiriyato ekādasa; rūpāvacarakusalato pañca, vipākato pañca, kiriyato pañca; arūpāvacarakusalato cattāri, vipākato cattāri, kiriyato cattāri; lokuttarakusalato cattāri, vipākato cattārīti ekūnanavuti cittāni cittavibhatti nāma. Cittuppādakaṇḍantipi etasseva nāmaṃ. Taṃ vācanāmaggato atirekachabhāṇavāraṃ, vitthāriyamānaṃ pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, there are four divisions: the division of consciousness, the division of matter, the summary, and the extraction of meaning. Therein, eight wholesome consciousnesses pertaining to the sense sphere, twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, sixteen wholesome resultant consciousnesses, seven unwholesome resultant consciousnesses, and eleven functional consciousnesses; five wholesome consciousnesses pertaining to the form sphere, five resultant consciousnesses, and five functional consciousnesses; four wholesome consciousnesses pertaining to the formless sphere, four resultant consciousnesses, and four functional consciousnesses; four supramundane wholesome consciousnesses, and four resultant consciousnesses—these eighty-nine types of consciousness are called the division of consciousness. It is also known as the chapter on the arising of consciousness. By way of recitation, it exceeds six recitation sections, but when elaborated, it becomes boundless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ [M 0.0007] ekavidhena duvidhenātiādinā nayena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārena vibhajitvā dassitā rūpavibhatti nāma. Rūpakaṇḍantipi etasseva nāmaṃ. Taṃ vācanāmaggato atirekadvibhāṇavāraṃ. Vitthāriyamānaṃ pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

Following that, the division of matter is presented in detail, having been classified extensively after establishing a matrix according to the method beginning with 'onefold, twofold,' and so on. It is also known as the chapter on form. By way of recitation, it exceeds two recitation sections, but when elaborated, it becomes boundless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ mūlato khandhato dvārato bhūmito atthato dhammato nāmato liṅgatoti evaṃ mūlādīhi nikkhipitvā desito nikkheparāsi nāma. So –

Thereafter, what is called the Summary is taught, having been arranged by way of root, aggregates, doors, planes, meaning, phenomena, names, and characteristics, and so on. That is—

Mūlato [V 0.0008] khandhato cāpi, dvārato cāpi bhūmito;

Atthato dhammato cāpi, nāmato cāpi liṅgato;

Nikkhipitvā desitattā, nikkhepoti pavuccati.

From the root, from the aggregates, and also from the doors, and also from the planes;

From the meaning, from the phenomena, and also from the names, and also from the characteristics;

Because it is taught having been arranged,

It is called the Summary.

Nikkhepakaṇḍantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Taṃ vācanāmaggato timattabhāṇavāraṃ. Vitthāriyamānaṃ pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

It is also known as the chapter on the Summary. By way of recitation, it amounts to three recitation sections; but when elaborated, it becomes boundless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ pana tepiṭakassa buddhavacanassa atthuddhārabhūtaṃ yāva saraṇadukā nikkhittaṃ aṭṭhakathākaṇḍaṃ nāma. Yato [P 0.0007] mahāpakaraṇiyā bhikkhū mahāpakaraṇe gaṇanacāraṃ asallakkhentā gaṇanacāraṃ samānenti. Taṃ vācanāmaggato dvimattabhāṇavāraṃ. Vitthāriyamānaṃ pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

Thereafter, what is called the section of commentary, being an extraction of the meaning of the Buddha’s words in the Tipiṭaka, is set forth as far as the pair on refuge. It is by means of this that monks devoted to the Great Treatise, when not discerning the computational method in the Great Treatise, rectify the computation. By way of recitation, it amounts to two recitation sections; but when elaborated, it becomes boundless and immeasurable.

Iti sakalampi dhammasaṅgaṇīpakaraṇaṃ vācanāmaggato atirekaterasamattabhāṇavāraṃ. Vitthāriyamānaṃ pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti. Evametaṃ –

Thus, the entire Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, by way of recitation, exceeds thirteen recitation sections in extent; but when elaborated, it becomes boundless and immeasurable. Thus it is—

Cittavibhatti rūpañca, nikkhepo atthajotanā;

Gambhīraṃ nipuṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ, tampi buddhena desitaṃ.

The classification of consciousness and matter,

The Summary, the clarification of meaning,

Profound, subtle, the underlying basis,

That too was taught by the Buddha.

Tadanantaraṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ nāma. Taṃ khandhavibhaṅgo āyatanavibhaṅgo dhātuvibhaṅgo saccavibhaṅgo idriyavibhaṅgo paccayākāravibhaṅgo satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgo sammappadhānavibhaṅgo iddhipādavibhaṅgo bojjhaṅgavibhaṅgo maggaṅgavibhaṅgo jhānavibhaṅgo appamaññāvibhaṅgo sikkhāpadavibhaṅgo paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgo ñāṇavibhaṅgo khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgo dhammahadayavibhaṅgoti aṭṭhārasavidhena vibhattaṃ.

Thereafter, the treatise called the Vibhaṅga. It is divided into eighteen kinds: the Analysis of Aggregates, the Analysis of Sense-Bases, the Analysis of Elements, the Analysis of Truths, the Analysis of Faculties, the Analysis of Dependent Origination, the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness, the Analysis of Right Exertions, the Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power, the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment, the Analysis of the Path Factors, the Analysis of Absorptions, the Analysis of Immeasurables, the Analysis of Training Rules, the Analysis of Discriminations, the Analysis of Knowledge, the Analysis of Minor Matters, and the Analysis of the Essence of the Dhamma.

Tattha [M 0.0008] khandhavibhaṅgo suttantabhājanīyaabhidhammabhājanīyapañhapucchakānaṃ vasena tidhā vibhatto. So vācanāmaggato pañcamattabhāṇavāro, vitthāriyamāno pana ananto aparimāṇo hoti. Tato paraṃ āyatanavibhaṅgādayopi eteheva tīhi nayehi vibhattā. Tesu āyatanavibhaṅgo vācanāmaggato atirekabhāṇavāro, dhātuvibhaṅgo dvimattabhāṇavāro. Tathā saccavibhaṅgo. Indriyavibhaṅge [V 0.0009] suttantabhājanīyaṃ natthi; vācanāmaggato panesa atirekabhāṇavāramatto. Paccayākāravibhaṅgo chamattabhāṇavāro, pañhapucchakaṃ panettha natthi. Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgo atirekabhāṇavāramatto; tathā sammappadhāna iddhipādabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgavibhaṅgā. Jhānavibhaṅgo dvibhāṇavāramatto, appamaññāvibhaṅgo atirekabhāṇavāramatto. Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgepi suttantabhājanīyaṃ natthi; vācanāmaggato panesa atirekabhāṇavāramatto; tathā [P 0.0008] paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgo. Ñāṇavibhaṅgo dasavidhena vibhatto; vācanāmaggato panesa timattabhāṇavāro. Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgopi dasavidhena vibhatto; vācanāmaggato panesa timattabhāṇavāro. Dhammahadayavibhaṅgo tividhena vibhatto; vācanāmaggato panesa atirekadvibhāṇavāramatto. Sabbepi vitthāriyamānā anantā aparimāṇā honti. Evametaṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ vācanāmaggato pañcatiṃsamattabhāṇavāraṃ; vitthārato pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

Herein, the Analysis of the Aggregates is divided in three ways: according to the Suttanta exposition, the Abhidhamma exposition, and the catechism. By way of recitation, it amounts to five recitation sections, but when elaborated, it becomes endless and immeasurable. Following this, the Analysis of the Sense-Bases and others are also divided by these same three methods. Among them, the Analysis of the Sense-Bases, by way of recitation, amounts to more than one recitation section, while the Analysis of the Elements amounts to two recitation sections. Likewise, the Analysis of the Truths. In the Analysis of the Faculties, there is no Suttanta exposition; by way of recitation, however, it amounts to more than one recitation section. The Analysis of Dependent Origination amounts to six recitation sections, but herein there is no catechism. The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness amounts to more than one recitation section; likewise, the Analyses of the Right Exertions, the Bases of Psychic Power, the Factors of Enlightenment, and the Path Factors. The Analysis of Absorptions amounts to two recitation sections, while the Analysis of the Immeasurables amounts to more than one recitation section. In the Analysis of the Training Rules, there is also no Suttanta exposition; by way of recitation, however, it amounts to more than one recitation section; likewise, the Analysis of Discriminations. The Analysis of Knowledge is divided in ten ways; by way of recitation, it amounts to three recitation sections. The Analysis of Minor Matters is also divided in ten ways; by way of recitation, it amounts to three recitation sections. The Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma is divided in three ways; by way of recitation, it amounts to more than two recitation sections. All these, when elaborated, become endless and immeasurable. Thus, this Treatise of Analysis, by way of recitation, amounts to thirty-five recitation sections; but by way of elaboration, it is endless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ dhātukathāpakaraṇaṃ nāma. Taṃ saṅgaho asaṅgaho, saṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ, asaṅgahitena saṅgahitaṃ, saṅgahitena saṅgahitaṃ, asaṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ; sampayogo vippayogo, sampayuttena vippayuttaṃ, vippayuttena sampayuttaṃ, sampayuttena sampayuttaṃ, vippayuttena vippayuttaṃ; saṅgahitena sampayuttaṃ vippayuttaṃ; sampayuttena saṅgahitaṃ asaṅgahitaṃ, asaṅgahitena sampayuttaṃ vippayuttaṃ, vippayuttena saṅgahitaṃ asaṅgahitanti cuddasavidhena vibhattaṃ. Taṃ vācanāmaggato atirekachabhāṇavāramattaṃ, vitthāriyamānaṃ pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

Thereafter is the treatise called the Dhātukathā. It is divided in fourteen ways: inclusion and non-inclusion; what is not included by what is included; what is included by what is not included; what is included by what is included; what is not included by what is not included; association and dissociation; what is dissociated by what is associated; what is associated by what is dissociated; what is associated by what is associated; what is dissociated by what is dissociated; what is associated and dissociated by what is included; what is included and not included by what is associated; what is associated and dissociated by what is not included; what is included and not included by what is dissociated. By way of recitation, it amounts to more than six recitation sections, but when elaborated, it becomes endless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ puggalapaññatti nāma. Sā “khandhapaññatti āyatanapaññatti dhātupaññatti saccapaññatti indriyapaññatti puggalapaññattī”ti chabbidhena vibhattā. Sā vācanāmaggato atirekapañcabhāṇavārā; vitthāriyamānā pana anantā aparimāṇāva hoti.

Thereafter is the treatise called the Designation of Persons. It is divided in six ways: the designation of aggregates, the designation of sense-bases, the designation of elements, the designation of truths, the designation of faculties, and the designation of persons. By way of recitation, it amounts to more than five recitation sections; but when elaborated, it is endless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ [M 0.0009] kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ nāma. Taṃ sakavāde pañca suttasatāni paravāde pañcāti suttasahassaṃ samodhānetvā vibhattaṃ. Taṃ vācanāmaggato idāni potthake likhitaṃ aggahetvā saṅgītiāropitanayena dīghanikāyappamāṇaṃ, vitthāriyamānaṃ pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

Thereafter is the treatise called the Kathāvatthu. It is divided by combining five hundred suttas concerning one's own thesis and five hundred concerning another's thesis, thus totaling one thousand suttas. By way of recitation, not taking into account what is now written in books, it is, according to the method established at the Council, of a length comparable to the Dīgha Nikāya; but when elaborated, it becomes endless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ yamakaṃ nāma. Taṃ mūlayamakaṃ khandhayamakaṃ āyatanayamakaṃ dhātuyamakaṃ saccayamakaṃ saṅkhārayamakaṃ [V 0.0010] anusayayamakaṃ cittayamakaṃ dhammayamakaṃ indriyayamakanti dasavidhena vibhattaṃ. Taṃ [P 0.0009] vācanāmaggato vīsabhāṇavārasataṃ, vitthārato pana anantamaparimāṇaṃ hoti.

Thereafter is the treatise called the Yamaka. It is divided in ten ways: the Root Pairs, the Aggregate Pairs, the Sense-Base Pairs, the Element Pairs, the Truth Pairs, the Formation Pairs, the Latent Tendency Pairs, the Mind Pairs, the Dhamma Pairs, and the Faculty Pairs. By way of recitation, it amounts to one hundred and twenty recitation sections; but by way of elaboration, it is endless and immeasurable.

Tadanantaraṃ mahāpakaraṇaṃ nāma. Paṭṭhānantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Taṃ hetupaccayo ārammaṇapaccayo adhipatipaccayo anantarapaccayo samanantarapaccayo sahajātapaccayo aññamaññapaccayo nissayapaccayo upanissayapaccayo purejātapaccayo pacchājātapaccayo āsevanapaccayo kammapaccayo vipākapaccayo āhārapaccayo indriyapaccayo jhānapaccayo maggapaccayo sampayuttapaccayo vippayuttapaccayo atthipaccayo natthipaccayo vigatapaccayo avigatapaccayoti. Paccayavasena tāva catuvīsatividhena vibhattaṃ.

Thereafter is the treatise called the Great Treatise. Paṭṭhāna is also its name. It is divided in twenty-four ways by means of conditions: the root condition, the object condition, the dominance condition, the proximity condition, the contiguity condition, the co-nascence condition, the mutuality condition, the dependence condition, the strong dependence condition, the pre-nascence condition, the post-nascence condition, the repetition condition, the kamma condition, the result condition, the nutriment condition, the faculty condition, the jhāna condition, the path condition, the association condition, the dissociation condition, the presence condition, the absence condition, the disappearance condition, and the non-disappearance condition.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne paṭṭhānaṃ samānetabbaṃ. Kusalattikādayo hi dvāvīsati tikā, nāma hetū dhammā nahetū dhammā…pe… saraṇā dhammā araṇā dhammāti ime sataṃ dukā. Aparepi vijjābhāgino dhammā avijjābhāgino dhammā…pe… khaye ñāṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇanti dvācattālīsa suttantikadukā nāma. Tesu dvāvīsati tikā sataṃ dukāti ayaṃ āhaccabhāsitā jinavacanabhūtā sabbaññubuddhena desitā sattannaṃ pakaraṇānaṃ mātikā nāma.

In this context, the Paṭṭhāna is to be understood. There are indeed twenty-two triads, beginning with the wholesome triad. And these are the one hundred dyads, namely: phenomena that are roots, phenomena that are not roots... and so on... phenomena with taints, phenomena without taints. Moreover, there are forty-two Suttanta dyads, namely: phenomena pertaining to knowledge, phenomena pertaining to ignorance... and so on... knowledge of destruction, knowledge of non-arising. Among these, the twenty-two triads and one hundred dyads are called the matrix of the seven treatises, spoken impromptu, being the words of the Conqueror, taught by the All-Knowing Buddha.

Athāpare dvācattālīsa suttantikadukā kutopabhavā kena ṭhapitā kena desitāti? Dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherappabhavā, tena ṭhapitā, tena desitāti. Ime ṭhapento pana thero na sāmukkaṃsikena attano ñāṇena ṭhapesi. Ekuttariyaṃ pana ekanipātadukanipātasaṅgīti dasuttarasuttantehi samodhānetvā ābhidhammikattherānaṃ suttantaṃ patvā akilamatthaṃ ṭhapitā. Te panete ekasmiṃ nikkhepakaṇḍeyeva matthakaṃ [M 0.0010] pāpetvā vibhattā. Sesaṭṭhānesu yāva saraṇadukā abhidhammo vibhatto.

Now, whence do these other forty-two Suttanta dyads originate? By whom were they established? By whom were they taught? They originate from the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma; by him they were established, and by him they were taught. However, the Elder, in establishing these, did not do so with his own special knowledge. Instead, having integrated them with the Ekuttara, the Ekanipāta, the Dukanipāta, the Saṅgīti, and the Dasuttara Suttantas, they were established for the sake of ease, having reached the Suttanta for the Abhidhammika elders. These, moreover, were analyzed and brought to completion in a single section of exposition. In the remaining sections, the Abhidhamma is analyzed up to the dyad of taints.

Sammāsambuddhena hi anulomapaṭṭhāne dvāvīsati tike nissāya tikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhaṃ. Sataṃ duke nissāya dukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tato paraṃ dvāvīsati tike gahetvā dukasate pakkhipitvā dukatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Tato paraṃ dukasataṃ gahetvā dvāvīsatiyā tikesu pakkhipitvā tikadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Tike [P 0.0010] pana tikesuyeva pakkhipitvā tikatikapaṭṭhānaṃ [V 0.0011] nāma dassitaṃ. Duke ca dukesuyeva pakkhipitvā dukadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Evaṃ –

Indeed, by the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the forward order of the Paṭṭhāna, what is called the Triad Paṭṭhāna was designated, relying on the twenty-two triads. Relying on the one hundred dyads, what is called the Dyad Paṭṭhāna was designated. Thereafter, by taking the twenty-two triads and incorporating them into the one hundred dyads, what is called the Dyad-Triad Paṭṭhāna was shown. Thereafter, by taking the one hundred dyads and incorporating them into the twenty-two triads, what is called the Triad-Dyad Paṭṭhāna was shown. Moreover, by incorporating the triads into the triads themselves, what is called the Triad-Triad Paṭṭhāna was shown. And by incorporating the dyads into the dyads themselves, what is called the Dyad-Dyad Paṭṭhāna was shown. Thus:

Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukatikañceva tikadukañca;

Tikatikañceva dukadukañca,

Cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrāti. (paṭṭhā. 1.1.39);

The excellent Triad Paṭṭhāna and the supreme Dyad,

The Dyad-Triad and the Triad-Dyad,

The Triad-Triad and the Dyad-Dyad—

These six methods in the forward order are very profound. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.39)

Paccanīyapaṭṭhānepi dvāvīsatitike nissāya tikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Dukasataṃ nissāya dukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Dvāvīsatitike dukasate pakkhipitvā dukatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Dukasataṃ dvāvīsatiyā tikesu pakkhipitvā tikadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Tike tikesuyeva pakkhipitvā tikatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Duke dukesuyeva pakkhipitvā dukadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti paccanīyepi chahi nayehi paṭṭhānaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

In the negative order of the Paṭṭhāna too, relying on the twenty-two triads, it is called the Triad Paṭṭhāna. Relying on the one hundred dyads, it is called the Dyad Paṭṭhāna. Having incorporated the twenty-two triads into the one hundred dyads, it is called the Dyad-Triad Paṭṭhāna. Having incorporated the one hundred dyads into the twenty-two triads, it is called the Triad-Dyad Paṭṭhāna. Having incorporated the triads into the triads themselves, it is called the Triad-Triad Paṭṭhāna. Having incorporated the dyads into the dyads themselves, it is called the Dyad-Dyad Paṭṭhāna. Thus, in the negative order too, the Paṭṭhāna is designated by six methods. Therefore, it is said:

Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukatikañceva tikadukañca;

Tikatikañceva dukadukañca,

Cha paccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrāti. (paṭṭhā. 1.1.44);

The excellent Triad Paṭṭhāna and the supreme Dyad,

The Dyad-Triad and the Triad-Dyad,

The Triad-Triad and the Dyad-Dyad—

These six methods in the negative order are very profound. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.44)

Tato paraṃ anulomapaccanīyepi eteneva upāyena cha nayā dassitā. Tenāha –

Thereafter, in the forward-negative order as well, six methods were shown in this very manner. Therefore, it is said:

Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukatikañceva tikadukañca;

Tikatikañceva dukadukañca,

Cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrāti. (paṭṭhā. 1.1.48);

The excellent Triad Paṭṭhāna and the supreme Dyad,

The Dyad-Triad and the Triad-Dyad,

The Triad-Triad and the Dyad-Dyad—

These six methods in the forward-negative order are very profound. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.48)

Tadanantaraṃ [M 0.0011] paccanīyānulomepi eteheva chahi nayehi niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tenāha –

Following that, in the negative-forward order as well, it is designated by these same six methods. Therefore, it is said:

Tikañca [V 0.0012] paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukatikañceva tikadukañca;

Tikatikañceva dukadukañca,

Cha paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrāti. (paṭṭhā. 1.1.52);

The excellent Triad Paṭṭhāna and the supreme Dyad,

The Dyad-Triad and the Triad-Dyad,

The Triad-Triad and the Dyad-Dyad—

These six methods in the negative-forward order are very profound. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.52)

Evaṃ anulome cha paṭṭhānāni, paṭilome cha, anulomapaccanīye cha, paccanīyānulome cha paṭṭhānānīti idaṃ catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānasamodhānaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ mahāpakaraṇaṃ nāma.

Thus, there are six Paṭṭhānas in the forward order, six in the reverse order, six in the forward-negative order, and six in the negative-forward order. This Paṭṭhāna, which is a compilation of the twenty-four comprehensive Paṭṭhānas, is called the Mahāpakaraṇa.

Idāni imassa abhidhammassa gambhīrabhāvavijānanatthaṃ cattāro sāgarā veditabbā – saṃsārasāgaro, jalasāgaro, nayasāgaro, ñāṇasāgaroti. Tattha saṃsārasāgaro nāma –

Now, to understand the profound nature of this Abhidhamma, four oceans should be known: the ocean of saṃsāra, the ocean of water, the ocean of method, and the ocean of knowledge. Among them, the ocean of saṃsāra is:

Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatīti.

The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, proceeding without interruption, is called saṃsāra.

Evaṃ vuttaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ. Svāyaṃ yasmā imesaṃ sattānaṃ uppattiyā purimā koṭi na paññāyati ettakānañhi vassasatānaṃ vā vassasahassānaṃ [P 0.0011] vā vassasatasahassānaṃ vā, kappasatānaṃ vā kappasahassānaṃ vā kappasatasahassānaṃ vā matthake sattā uppannā, tato pubbe nāhesunti vā, asukassa nāma rañño kāle uppannā, asukassa buddhassa kāle uppannā tato pubbe nāhesunti vā, ayaṃ paricchedo natthi; “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya, ito pubbe avijjā nāhosi atha pacchā samabhavī”ti (a. ni. 10.61) iminā pana nayena saṃsārasāgaro anamataggova.

Thus is the round of saṃsāra stated. For these beings, a first point of their arising is not discernible; it cannot be determined that beings arose at the culmination of so many hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of years, or of so many hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of aeons, and did not exist before that; or that they arose during the time of a certain king or a certain Buddha and did not exist before that. No such demarcation exists. As it is said: 'A first point, bhikkhus, of ignorance is not discerned, [with the thought:] "Before this, ignorance was not, and afterwards it came to be."' (AN 10.61) By this principle, the ocean of saṃsāra is indeed without a discernible beginning.

Mahāsamuddo pana jalasāgaro nāmāti veditabbo. So caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīro. Tattha udakassa āḷhakasatehi vā āḷhakasahassehi vā āḷhakasatasahassehi vā pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi[M 0.0012]. Atha kho asaṅkhyeyyo appameyyo mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Ayaṃ jalasāgaro nāma.

The great ocean, however, is to be understood as the ocean of water. It is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep. Therein, the measure of water is not reckoned by hundreds of āḷhakas, or thousands of āḷhakas, or hundreds of thousands of āḷhakas. Rather, it is counted as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water. This is called the ocean of water.

Katamo nayasāgaro? Tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Dvepi hi tantiyo paccavekkhantānaṃ saddhāsampannānaṃ [V 0.0013] pasādabahulānaṃ ñāṇuttarānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ anantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati. Katamā dve? Vinayañca abhidhammañca. Vinayadharabhikkhūnañhi vinayatantiṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ dosānurūpaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ nāma – imasmiṃ dose imasmiṃ vītikkame idaṃ nāma hotīti sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ – aññesaṃ avisayo, buddhānameva visayoti. Uttarimanussadhammapeyyālaṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ nīlapeyyālaṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ sañcarittapeyyālaṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ anantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati. Ābhidhammikabhikkhūnampi khandhantaraṃ āyatanantaraṃ dhātvantaraṃ indriyantaraṃ balabojjhaṅgakammavipākantaraṃ rūpārūpaparicchedaṃ saṇhasukhumadhammaṃ gaganatale tārakarūpāni gaṇhanto viya rūpārūpadhamme pabbaṃ pabbaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā vibhajanto dassesi vata no satthāti abhidhammatantiṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ anantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati.

What is the ocean of method? The Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha. For when noble sons—endowed with faith, abundant in confidence, and supreme in wisdom—reflect upon the two treatises, boundless rapture and mental gladness arise. Which two? The Vinaya and the Abhidhamma. For when monks who uphold the Vinaya reflect upon the Vinaya treatise, [they think:] 'The establishment of training rules according to the offense—that is, for this offense, for this transgression, such-and-such is the training rule laid down—is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Buddhas alone.' When they reflect upon the passage on superior human qualities, the passage on blue, and the passage on acting as a go-between, boundless rapture and mental gladness arise. For the monks versed in the Abhidhamma as well, when reflecting upon the Abhidhamma treatise—the distinctions between aggregates, sense-bases, elements, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, kamma and its results; the analysis of material and immaterial phenomena; the subtle and refined Dhamma—[they think:] 'Our Teacher has indeed shown, analyzing material and immaterial phenomena joint by joint, part by part, as if one were counting the forms of the stars in the expanse of the sky!' and boundless rapture and mental gladness arise.

Evaṃ uppattiyā panassa idaṃ vatthupi veditabbaṃ – mahāgatigamiyatissadattatthero kira [P 0.0012] nāma mahābodhiṃ vandissāmīti paratīraṃ gacchanto nāvāya uparitale nisinno mahāsamuddaṃ olokesi. Athassa tasmiṃ samaye neva paratīraṃ paññāyittha, na orimatīraṃ, ūmivegappabhedasamuggatajalacuṇṇaparikiṇṇo pana pasāritarajatapaṭṭasumanapupphasantharasadiso mahāsamuddova paññāyittha. So kiṃ nu kho mahāsamuddassa ūmivego balavā udāhu catuvīsatippabhede samantapaṭṭhāne nayamukhaṃ balavanti cintesi. Athassa mahāsamudde paricchedo paññāyati – ayañhi heṭṭhā mahāpathaviyā paricchinno, upari ākāsena, ekato cakkavāḷapabbatena, ekato velantena paricchinno; samantapaṭṭhānassa pana paricchedo na paññāyatīti saṇhasukhumadhammaṃ paccavekkhantassa balavapīti uppannā. So pītiṃ vikkhambhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā yathānisinnova sabbakilese khepetvā aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhāya udānaṃ udānesi –

Regarding its arising, this story should also be known. It is said that the Elder Mahāgatigamiya Tissadatta, intending to pay homage to the Mahābodhi, was crossing to the other shore. While seated on the upper deck of the ship, he gazed upon the great ocean. At that time, neither the far shore nor the near shore was discernible to him; only the great ocean was discernible, covered with fine water-spray churned up by the force of the waves, like a spread-out silver sheet and a carpet of jasmine flowers. He then reflected: 'Which is stronger: the force of the ocean's waves, or the opening of the method in the twenty-four-fold Samantapaṭṭhāna?' Then, a boundary became discernible to him in the great ocean—for it is bounded below by the great earth, above by the sky, on one side by the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and on the other by the shoreline. But no boundary was discernible for the Samantapaṭṭhāna. As he contemplated the subtle and refined Dhamma, strong rapture arose in him. Having suppressed that rapture and developed insight, just as he was seated, he eradicated all defilements and became established in the supreme fruit of Arahantship. Then he uttered this inspired utterance:

Attheva [M 0.0013] gambhīragataṃ sudubbudhaṃ,

Sayaṃ abhiññāya sahetusambhavaṃ;

Yathānupubbaṃ nikhilena desitaṃ,

Mahesinā rūpagataṃva passatīti.

There is indeed that which is profound and very difficult to awaken to. Having directly known it himself, with its cause and origin, the Great Sage taught it completely and in due order, so that one sees it as if it were a visible form.

Ayaṃ nayasāgaro nāma.

This is called the ocean of method.

Katamo [V 0.0014] ñāṇasāgaro? Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ñāṇasāgaro nāma. Ayaṃ saṃsārasāgaro nāma, ayaṃ jalasāgaro nāma, ayaṃ nayasāgaro nāmāti hi aññena na sakkā jānituṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇeneva sakkā jānitunti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ñāṇasāgaro nāma. Imesu catūsu sāgaresu imasmiṃ ṭhāne nayasāgaro adhippeto. Imañhi sabbaññubuddhāva paṭivijjhanti.

What is the ocean of knowledge? The knowledge of omniscience is called the ocean of knowledge. For that 'This is the ocean of saṃsāra, this is the ocean of water, this is the ocean of method' cannot be known by any other knowledge; it can be known only by the knowledge of omniscience. Therefore, the knowledge of omniscience is called the ocean of knowledge. Among these four oceans, in this context, the ocean of method is intended. For only the omniscient Buddhas penetrate this.

Ayampi bhagavā bodhimūle nisinno ‘imaṃ paṭivijjhitvā imaṃ vata me dhammaṃ esantassa gavesantassa kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni vītivattāni, atha me imasmiṃ pallaṅke nisinnena diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ khepetvā ayaṃ dhammo paṭividdho’ti paṭividdhadhammaṃ paccavekkhanto sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisīdi. Tato tamhā pallaṅkā vuṭṭhāya ‘imasmiṃ vata me pallaṅke sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭividdha’nti animisehi cakkhūhi sattāhaṃ pallaṅkaṃ olokento aṭṭhāsi. Tato devatānaṃ ‘ajjāpi nūna siddhatthassa [P 0.0013] kattabbakiccaṃ atthi, pallaṅkasmiñhi ālayaṃ na vijahatī’ti parivitakko udapādi.

This Blessed One, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, reflecting on the Dhamma he had penetrated, sat for seven days on that single seat, thinking: 'Indeed, while I was seeking and searching for this Dhamma, four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more passed by. Then, while seated on this very seat, having eradicated the one thousand five hundred defilements, this Dhamma was penetrated by me.' Then, rising from that seat, he stood for seven days gazing at the seat with unblinking eyes, thinking: 'Indeed, on this very seat, the knowledge of omniscience was penetrated by me.' Thereupon, this thought arose among the deities: 'Surely, even today Siddhattha still has some duty to perform, for he does not relinquish his longing for the seat.'

Satthā devatānaṃ vitakkaṃ ñatvā tāvadeva tāsaṃ vitakkavūpasamanatthaṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi. Mahābodhipallaṅkasmiñhi katapāṭihāriyañca, ñātisamāgame katapāṭihāriyañca, pāṭiyaputtasamāgame katapāṭihāriyañca, sabbaṃ kaṇḍambarukkhamūle katayamakapāṭihāriyasadisameva ahosi. Evaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā pallaṅkassa ṭhitaṭṭhānassa ca antare ākāsato oruyha sattāhaṃ caṅkami. Imesu ca ekavīsatiyā divasesu ekadivasepi satthu sarīrato rasmiyo na nikkhantā.

The Teacher, knowing the thoughts of the deities, immediately ascended into the air to allay their thoughts and displayed the Twin Miracle. Indeed, the miracle performed at the Great Bodhi Seat, the miracle at the gathering of relatives, and the miracle at the Pāṭaliputta assembly—all were similar to the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree. Having performed the Twin Miracle in this way, he descended from the sky between the seat and the standing-place, and walked to and fro for seven days. And during these twenty-one days, not on a single day did rays emanate from the Teacher's body.

Catutthe pana sattāhe pacchimuttarāya disāya ratanaghare nisīdi – ratanagharaṃ nāma neva sattaratanamayaṃ gehaṃ. Sattannaṃ pana pakaraṇānaṃ sammasitaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0014] ratanagharanti veditabbaṃ – tattha dhammasaṅgaṇiṃ sammasantassāpi sarīrato rasmiyo na nikkhantā. Vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ dhātukathaṃ puggalapaññattiṃ kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ yamakappakaraṇaṃ sammasantassāpi sarīrato rasmiyo na nikkhantā. Yadā pana mahāpakaraṇaṃ oruyha “hetupaccayo ārammaṇapaccayo…pe… avigatapaccayo”ti sammasanaṃ ārabhi, athassa catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānaṃ sammasantassa ekantato sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ mahāpakaraṇeyeva okāsaṃ labhi. Yathā hi timirapiṅgalamahāmaccho caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīre [V 0.0015] mahāsamuddeyeva okāsaṃ labhati, evameva sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ekantato mahāpakaraṇeyeva okāsaṃ labhi.

In the fourth week, however, he sat in the jewel house in the northwestern direction—the jewel house was not a house made of the seven precious gems. But the place where the seven treatises were examined should be understood as the jewel house. There, even while examining the Dhammasaṅgaṇi, rays did not emanate from his body. While examining the Vibhaṅga, the Dhātukathā, the Puggalapaññatti, the Kathāvatthu, and the Yamaka, rays still did not emanate from his body. But when he took up the Great Treatise and began examining, 'The root condition, the object condition... the non-disappearance condition,' then, as he thoroughly examined the twenty-four-fold all-embracing Paṭṭhāna, the knowledge of omniscience found its opportunity exclusively in the Great Treatise itself. Just as the great Timirapiṅgala fish finds its opportunity only in the great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, so too the knowledge of omniscience found its opportunity exclusively in the Great Treatise itself.

Satthu evaṃ laddhokāsena sabbaññutaññāṇena yathāsukhaṃ saṇhasukhumadhammaṃ sammasantassa sarīrato nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassaravasena chabbaṇṇarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu. Kesamassūhi ceva akkhīnañca nīlaṭṭhānehi nīlarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu, yāsaṃ vasena gaganatalaṃ añjanacuṇṇasamokiṇṇaṃ viya umāpupphanīluppaladalasañchannaṃ viya vītipatantamaṇitālavaṇṭaṃ viya sampasāritamecakapaṭaṃ viya ca ahosi.

When the Teacher, having thus gained the opportunity, was examining the subtle and refined Dhamma at his ease with his omniscient knowledge, six-colored rays emerged from his body in hues of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and radiant. From his hair and beard and the blue parts of his eyes, blue rays emerged, by which the surface of the sky appeared as if strewn with collyrium powder, covered with flax flowers and blue lotus petals, like a revolving jeweled fan, and like an outstretched dark-blue cloth.

Chavito ceva akkhīnañca pītaṭṭhānehi pītarasmiyo [P 0.0014] nikkhamiṃsu; yāsaṃ vasena disābhāgā suvaṇṇarasadhārābhisiñcamānā viya suvaṇṇapaṭapasāritā viya kuṅkumacuṇṇakaṇikārapupphasamparikiṇṇā viya ca virociṃsu.

From his skin and the yellow parts of his eyes, yellow rays emerged; through them, the regions appeared as if bathed in streams of golden liquid, spread out like golden cloth, or strewn with particles of saffron powder and kaṇikāra flowers, shining brilliantly.

Maṃsalohitehi ceva akkhīnañca rattaṭṭhānehi lohitarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu yāsaṃ vasena disābhāgā cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇarañjitā viya supakkalākhārasasiñcamānā viya rattakambalaparikkhittā viya jayasumanapāribhaddakabandhujīvakakusumasamparikiṇṇā viya ca virociṃsu.

From the flesh and blood and the red parts of the eyes, blood-red rays emerged, by which the quarters of space shone as if dyed with fine cinnabar powder, or as if sprinkled with the juice of well-ripened lac, or as if covered by a red blanket, or as if strewn with jayasumana, coral tree, and bandhujīvaka flowers.

Aṭṭhīhi ceva dantehi ca akkhīnañca setaṭṭhānehi odātarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu; yāsaṃ vasena disābhāgā rajataghaṭehi āsiñcamānakhīradhārāsamparikiṇṇā viya sampasāritarajatapaṭṭavitānā viya, vītipatantarajatatālavaṇṭā viya, kundakumudasinduvārasumanamallikādikusumasañchannā viya ca virociṃsu.

From the bones, the teeth, and the white parts of the eyes, white rays emerged, by which the quarters of space shone as if strewn with streams of milk poured from silver pitchers, as if covered with extended canopies of silver cloth, as if fanned by revolving silver palm-leaf fans, or as if covered with kunda, white lotus, sinduvāra, sumana, and mallikā flowers, and other blossoms.

Mañjiṭṭhapabhassarā [M 0.0015] pana tamhā tamhā sarīrappadesā nikkhamiṃsu. Iti tā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo nikkhamitvā ghanamahāpathaviṃ gaṇhiṃsu.

Then, crimson and radiant rays emerged from various parts of his body. Thus, those six-colored rays, having emerged, enveloped the solid great earth.

Catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalā mahāpathavī niddhantasuvaṇṇapiṇḍi viya ahosi. Atha mahāpathaviṃ bhinditvā heṭṭhā udakaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Pathavisandhārakaṃ aṭṭhanahutādhikacatuyojanasatasahassabahalaṃ udakaṃ suvaṇṇakalasehi āsiñcamānavilīnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ahosi. Udakaṃ vinivijjhitvā [V 0.0016] vātaṃ aggahesuṃ. Chanahutādhikanavayojanasatasahassabahalo vāto samussitasuvaṇṇakkhandho viya ahosi. Vātaṃ vinivijjhitvā heṭṭhā ajaṭākāsaṃ pakkhandiṃsu.

The great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness, appeared like a mass of purified gold. Then, breaking through the earth, they seized the water below. The water, four hundred and eighty thousand yojanas in thickness, supporting the earth, appeared like molten gold being poured from golden jars. Having penetrated the water, they grasped the wind. The wind, nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas in thickness, appeared like a mass of piled-up gold. Having penetrated the wind, they plunged downward into the limitless space.

Uparibhāgena uggantvāpi cātumahārājike gaṇhiṃsu. Te vinivijjhitvā tāvatiṃse tato yāme tato tusite tato nimmānaratī tato paranimmitavasavattī tato nava brahmaloke tato vehapphale tato pañca suddhāvāse vinivijjhitvā cattāro āruppe gaṇhiṃsu. Cattāro ca āruppe vinivijjhitvā ajaṭākāsaṃ pakkhandiṃsu.

Having ascended to the upper regions, they enveloped the realm of the Four Great Kings. Having penetrated them, they enveloped the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, then the Yāma heaven, then the Tusita heaven, then the Nimmānaratī heaven, then the Paranimmitavasavattī heaven, then the nine Brahma-worlds, then the Vehapphala heaven, then the five Pure Abodes. Having penetrated these, they enveloped the four formless realms. And having penetrated the four formless realms, they plunged into the limitless space.

Tiriyabhāgehi anantā lokadhātuyo pakkhandiṃsu. Ettakesu ṭhānesu candamhi candappabhā natthi, sūriye sūriyappabhā natthi, tārakarūpesu tārakarūpappabhā natthi, devatānaṃ uyyānavimānakapparukkhesu ceva sarīresu ca ābharaṇesu cāti sabbattha pabhā natthi. Tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuyā ālokapharaṇasamattho mahābrahmāpi sūriyuggamane [P 0.0015] khajjopanako viya ahosi. Candasūriyatārakarūpadevatuyyānavimānakapparukkhānaṃ paricchedamattakameva paññāyittha. Ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ buddharasmīhiyeva ajjhotthaṭaṃ ahosi. Ayañca neva buddhānaṃ adhiṭṭhāniddhi, na bhāvanāmayiddhi. Saṇhasukhumadhammaṃ pana sammasato lokanāthassa lohitaṃ pasīdi, vatthurūpaṃ pasīdi, chavivaṇṇo pasīdi. Cittasamuṭṭhānā vaṇṇadhātu samantā asītihatthamatte padese niccalāva aṭṭhāsi. Iminā nīhārena sattāhaṃ sammasi.

In the transverse directions, they pervaded countless world-systems. In those places, there was no radiance of the moon in the moon, no radiance of the sun in the sun, no radiance of the stars in their forms, and no radiance at all in the gardens, celestial mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, bodies, and ornaments of the devas. Even Mahābrahmā, who is capable of illuminating the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world-system, became like a firefly at sunrise. Only the limited extent of the moon, sun, stars, devas, gardens, celestial mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees was discernible. That entire space was pervaded by the Buddha's rays. This was neither the power of determination of the Buddhas, nor the power born of meditation. But as the Lord of the World reflected on the subtle and refined Dhamma, his blood became clear, his bodily substance became clear, and his skin color became clear. The color element, arising from the mind, stood perfectly still in an area measuring eighty cubits all around. In this manner, he contemplated for seven days.

Satta rattindivāni sammasitadhammo kittako ahosīti? Ananto aparimāṇo ahosi. Ayaṃ tāva manasādesanā nāma. Satthā pana evaṃ sattāhaṃ manasā cintitadhammaṃ vacībhedaṃ katvā desento vassasatenapi [M 0.0016] vassasahassenapi vassasatasahassenapi matthakaṃ pāpetvā desetuṃ na sakkotīti na vattabbaṃ. Aparabhāgepi hi tathāgato tāvatiṃsabhavane pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ majjhe nisinno mātaraṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammāti dhammaṃ desento satabhāgena sahassabhāgena satasahassabhāgena dhammantarā dhammantaraṃ saṅkamitvā saṅkamitvāva desesi. Tayo māse nirantaraṃ pavattitadesanā vegena pavattā ākāsagaṅgā viya adhomukhaṭhapitaudakaghaṭā nikkhantaudakadhārā viya ca hutvā anantā aparimāṇā ahosi.

To what extent was the Dhamma contemplated for seven days and nights? It was infinite and immeasurable. This, for a start, is called the mental exposition. However, it should not be said that the Teacher, having contemplated the Dhamma mentally for seven days and then expounding it by breaking it into speech, would be unable to teach it to completion even in a hundred years, a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years. For on a later occasion, the Tathāgata, seated on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in the midst of deities from ten thousand world-systems, and having made his mother the principal witness, taught the Dhamma—'wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states'—transitioning from one Dhamma-topic to another by a hundredth part, a thousandth part, and a hundred-thousandth part. The teaching, which continued uninterruptedly for three months, flowing swiftly like the celestial Ganges or like a stream of water pouring from an overturned water pot, became infinite and immeasurable.

Buddhānañhi [V 0.0017] bhattānumodanakālepi thokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anumodentānaṃ desanā dīghamajjhimanikāyappamāṇā hoti. Pacchābhattaṃ pana sampattaparisāya dhammaṃ desentānaṃ desanā saṃyuttaaṅguttarikadvemahānikāyappamāṇāva hoti. Kasmā? Buddhānañhi bhavaṅgaparivāso lahuko dantāvaraṇaṃ suphusitaṃ mukhādānaṃ siliṭṭhaṃ jivhā mudukā saro madhuro vacanaṃ lahuparivattaṃ. Tasmā taṃ muhuttaṃ desitadhammopi ettako hoti. Temāsaṃ desitadhammo pana ananto aparimāṇoyeva.

Indeed, for the Buddhas, even when giving the blessing after a meal, if they extend it just a little, their teaching becomes equal in extent to the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas. And when, after the meal, they teach the Dhamma to the assembled congregation, their teaching becomes equal in extent to the two great Nikāyas, the Saṃyutta and Aṅguttara. Why is that? Because for the Buddhas, their mental process is swift, their teeth are well-set, their articulation is smooth, their tongue is soft, their voice is sweet, and their speech is agile. Therefore, even the Dhamma taught in a single moment is of such an extent. The Dhamma taught over three months, however, is truly infinite and immeasurable.

Ānandatthero hi bahussuto tipiṭakadharo pañcadasa gāthāsahassāni saṭṭhi padasahassāni latāpupphāni ākaḍḍhanto viya ṭhitapadeneva ṭhatvā gaṇhāti vā vāceti vā deseti vā. Ettako therassa eko uddesamaggo nāma hoti. Therassa hi anupadaṃ uddesaṃ dadamāno añño dātuṃ na sakkoti, na sampāpuṇāti. Sammāsambuddhova sampāpuṇeyya. Evaṃ adhimattasatimā adhimattagatimā adhimattadhitimā [P 0.0016] sāvako satthārā temāsaṃ iminā nīhārena desitadesanaṃ vassasataṃ vassasahassaṃ uggaṇhantopi matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti.

Indeed, the Elder Ānanda, being deeply learned and a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, could grasp, recite, or teach fifteen thousand verses and sixty thousand lines from a fixed position, as if plucking flowers from a vine. This much is called a single course of instruction for the Elder. Indeed, no one else giving him instruction word by word could keep pace; only a Perfectly Enlightened One could keep pace. Thus, even a disciple with such surpassing mindfulness, surpassing comprehension, and surpassing fortitude, while learning the teaching taught by the Teacher in this manner for three months, would be unable to bring it to completion even in a hundred or a thousand years.

Evaṃ temāsaṃ nirantaraṃ desentassa pana tathāgatassa kabaḷīkārāhārappaṭibaddhaṃ upādinnakasarīraṃ kathaṃ yāpesīti? Paṭijagganeneva. Buddhānañhi so so kālo suvavatthito suparicchinno supaccakkho. Tasmā bhagavā dhammaṃ desentova manussaloke kālaṃ oloketi. So bhikkhācāravelaṃ [M 0.0017] sallakkhetvā nimmitabuddhaṃ māpetvā ‘imassa cīvaraggahaṇaṃ pattaggahaṇaṃ sarakutti ākappo ca evarūpo nāma hotu, ettakaṃ nāma dhammaṃ desetū’ti adhiṭṭhāya pattacīvaramādāya anotattadahaṃ gacchati. Devatā nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ denti. Taṃ khāditvā anotattadahe sarīraṃ paṭijaggitvā manosilātale ṭhito surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā cātumahārājadattiyaṃ selamayaṃ pattaṃ ādāya uttarakuruṃ gacchati. Tato piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā anotattadahatīre nisinno taṃ paribhuñjitvā divāvihārāya candanavanaṃ gacchati.

But while the Tathāgata was thus teaching uninterruptedly for three months, how was his physical body, which is sustained by and dependent on physical food, maintained? By careful tending. For the Buddhas, every single moment is well-ordered, well-defined, and directly known. Therefore, while teaching the Dhamma, the Blessed One observes the time in the human world. Noting the time for the alms-round, he creates an emanated Buddha and makes a resolution: 'May this one's manner of accepting the robe and bowl, his vocal intonation, and his deportment be of such a kind, and may he teach this much Dhamma.' Then, taking his bowl and robe, he goes to Lake Anotatta. Deities offer him a tooth-stick of nāga-creeper. Having chewed it and refreshed his body in Lake Anotatta, he stands on the red arsenic slab, puts on a bright red double-layered undergarment, drapes his outer robe, and taking the stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings, he goes to Uttarakuru. From there he brings back almsfood, sits on the shore of Lake Anotatta, and partakes of it. Then, for his day-sojourn, he goes to the Sandalwood Grove.

Dhammasenāpatisāriputtattheropi tattha gantvā sammāsambuddhassa vattaṃ katvā ekamantaṃ nisīdati. Athassa satthā nayaṃ deti. ‘Sāriputta, ettako dhammo mayā desito’ti ācikkhati. Evaṃ sammāsambuddhe nayaṃ dente paṭisambhidāppattassa aggasāvakassa velante ṭhatvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā dassitasamuddasadisaṃ nayadānaṃ hoti. Therassāpi nayasatena nayasahassena nayasatasahassena bhagavatā desitadhammo upaṭṭhātiyeva.

The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, would also go there, perform his duties for the Perfectly Enlightened One, and sit down to one side. Then the Teacher would give him the method, saying: 'Sāriputta, this much of the Dhamma has been taught by me.' Thus, when the Perfectly Enlightened One gives the method to the chief disciple who has attained the analytical knowledges, the giving of the method is like showing the ocean by extending one's hand while standing on the shore. For the Elder, too, the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One through a hundred methods, a thousand methods, or a hundred thousand methods, would become perfectly clear.

Satthā [V 0.0018] divāvihāraṃ nisīditvā dhammaṃ desetuṃ kāya velāya gacchatīti? Sāvatthivāsīnaṃ kulaputtānaṃ sampattānaṃ dhammadesanavelā nāma atthi, tāya velāya gacchati. Dhammaṃ desetvā gacchantaṃ vā āgacchantaṃ vā ke jānanti ke na jānantīti? Mahesakkhā devatā jānanti, appesakkhā devatā na jānanti. Kasmā na jānantīti? Sammāsambuddhassa vā nimmitabuddhassa vā rasmiādīsu nānattābhāvā. Ubhinnampi hi tesaṃ rasmīsu vā saresu vā vacanesu vā nānattaṃ natthi.

After his day-sojourn, at what time does the Teacher go to teach the Dhamma? There is an appointed time for teaching the Dhamma to the clansmen of Sāvatthī who have assembled; he goes at that time. When he is departing or arriving after teaching the Dhamma, who knows and who does not? The deities of great power know; the deities of lesser power do not know. Why do they not know? Because there is no difference in the rays of light and so forth between the Perfectly Enlightened One and the emanated Buddha. Indeed, for both of them, there is no difference in their rays, their voices, or their words.

Sāriputtattheropi satthārā desitaṃ desitaṃ dhammaṃ āharitvā attano saddhivihārikānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ desesi. Tesaṃ ayaṃ pubbayogo – te [P 0.0017] kira kassapadasabalassa kāle khuddakavagguliyoniyaṃ nibbattā pabbhāre olambantā dvinnaṃ ābhidhammikabhikkhūnaṃ abhidhammaṃ sajjhāyantānaṃ sare nimittaṃ gahetvā kaṇhapakkhasukkapakkhe ajānitvāpi sare nimittaggāhamattakeneva kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbattiṃsu. Ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devaloke vasitvā tasmiṃ kāle manussaloke nibbattā yamakapāṭihāriye pasīditvā therassa santike pabbajiṃsu. Thero satthārā desitaṃ desitaṃ dhammaṃ āharitvā tesaṃ desesi. Sammāsambuddhassa abhidhammadesanāpariyosānañca [M 0.0018] tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sattappakaraṇauggahaṇañca ekappahāreneva ahosi.

The Elder Sāriputta also, having taken the Dhamma taught by the Master, taught it to his own five hundred resident pupils. Their past connection was this—it seems that during the time of Kassapa the Ten-Powered One, they were born as small bats. Hanging in a cave, they took the sound of two Abhidhamma-reciting monks as their object. Without even knowing the distinction between the dark and bright lunar fortnights, merely by grasping the sign of the sound, they passed away and were reborn in the heavenly realm. After spending one Buddha-interval in the heavenly world, they were reborn in the human world at that time. Inspired by the Twin Miracle, they went forth in the presence of the Elder. The Elder, having taken the Dhamma taught by the Master, taught it to them. The conclusion of the Abhidhamma discourse by the Perfectly Enlightened One and the mastery of the seven treatises by those monks occurred simultaneously.

Abhidhamme vācanāmaggo nāma sāriputtattherappabhavo. Mahāpakaraṇe gaṇanacāropi thereneva ṭhapito. Thero hi iminā nīhārena dhammantaraṃ amakkhetvāva sukhaṃ gahetuṃ dhāretuṃ pariyāpuṇituṃ vācetuñca pahotīti gaṇanacāraṃ ṭhapesi. Evaṃ sante therova paṭhamataraṃ ābhidhammiko hotīti? Na hoti. Sammāsambuddhova paṭhamataraṃ ābhidhammiko. So hi naṃ mahābodhipallaṅke nisīditvā paṭivijjhi. Buddho hutvā ca pana sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinno udānaṃ udānesi –

The path of recitation in the Abhidhamma originated from the Elder Sāriputta. The method of enumeration in the Mahāpakaraṇa was also established by the Elder. Indeed, by this method, one is able to easily grasp, retain, master, and recite the Dhamma without confusing it with another teaching, and that is why he established the method of enumeration. Given this, is the Elder the foremost Abhidhammika? No, he is not. The Perfectly Enlightened One is the foremost Abhidhammika. For He realized it while seated on the great Bodhi seat. And having become the Buddha, He sat for seven days in one posture and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,

Ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa;

Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā,

Yato [V 0.0019] pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ.

“When phenomena truly appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin, then all his doubts vanish, since he understands the phenomenon with its cause.”

“Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,

Ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa;

Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā,

Yato khayaṃ paccayānaṃ avedi.

“When phenomena truly appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin, then all his doubts vanish, since he has known the destruction of conditions.”

“Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,

Ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa;

Vidhūpayaṃ tiṭṭhati mārasenaṃ,

Sūriyova obhāsayamantalikkha”nti. (mahāva. 1-3; udā. 1-3);

“When phenomena truly appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin, he stands dispelling Māra's army, like the sun illuminating the sky.”

Idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ nāma. Dhammapadabhāṇakā [P 0.0018] pana –

This is called the first utterance of the Buddha. The Dhammapada reciters, however, say:

“Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ;

Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

“Through many a birth in saṃsāra I wandered, seeking but not finding the house-builder. Painful is birth again and again.”

“Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhataṃ;

Visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā”ti. (dha. pa. 153-154);

“O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build a house again. All your rafters are broken, your ridgepole is shattered. My mind has reached the Unconditioned; the destruction of craving has been attained.”

Idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ nāmāti vadanti.

This, they say, is the first utterance of the Buddha.

Yamakasālānamantare [M 0.0019] nipannena parinibbānasamaye “handa dāni, bhikkhave, āmantayāmi vo, vayadhammā saṅkhārā, appamādena sampādethā”ti (dī. ni. 2.218) vuttavacanaṃ pacchimabuddhavacanaṃ nāma.

The utterance spoken at the time of His final passing away, while He was lying down between the twin sāla trees—“Now then, bhikkhus, I address you: conditioned phenomena are subject to decay; strive on with diligence!”—is known as the last utterance of the Buddha.

Ubhinnamantare pañcacattālīsa vassāni pupphadāmaṃ ganthentena viya, ratanāvaliṃ āvunantena viya, ca kathito amatappakāsano saddhammo majjhimabuddhavacanaṃ nāma.

For forty-five years in between, the true Dhamma, the revealer of the Deathless, was proclaimed, like one weaving a garland of flowers or stringing a necklace of jewels; this is called the middle utterance of the Buddha.

Taṃ [V 0.0020] sabbampi saṅgayhamānaṃ piṭakato tīṇi piṭakāni honti, nikāyato pañca nikāyā, aṅgato navaṅgāni, dhammakkhandhato caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassāni. Kathaṃ? Sabbampi hetaṃ piṭakato vinayapiṭakaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakanti tippabhedameva hoti. Tattha ubhayāni pātimokkhāni dve vibhaṅgā dvāvīsati khandhakā soḷasa parivārāti idaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ nāma. Brahmajālādicatuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho dīghanikāyo. Mūlapariyāyasuttādidiyaḍḍhasatadvesuttasaṅgaho majjhimanikāyo. Oghataraṇasuttādisattasuttasahassasattasatadvāsaṭṭhisuttasaṅgaho saṃyuttanikāyo. Cittapariyādānasuttādinavasuttasahassapañcasatasattapaññāsasuttasaṅgaho aṅguttaranikāyo. Khuddakapāṭhadhammapadaudānaitivuttakasuttanipātavimānavatthupetavatthutheragāthātherīgāthājātakaniddesapaṭisambhidāapadānabuddhavaṃsacariyāpiṭakavasena pannarasappabhedo khuddakanikāyoti idaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ nāma. Dhammasaṅgaṇīādīni satta pakaraṇāni abhidhammapiṭakaṃ nāma. Tattha [P 0.0019] –

All of that, when compiled, becomes three Piṭakas, five Nikāyas, nine Aṅgas, and eighty-four thousand Dhamma-sections. How so? All of it, when divided according to Piṭaka, consists of the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—thus it is threefold. Therein, the two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras—this is called the Vinaya Piṭaka. The Dīgha Nikāya is a collection of thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta. The Majjhima Nikāya is a collection of one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. The Saṃyutta Nikāya is a collection of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta. The Aṅguttara Nikāya is a collection of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta. The Khuddaka Nikāya, which is of fifteen divisions—Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka—this is called the Suttanta Piṭaka. The seven treatises beginning with the Dhammasaṅgaṇī—this is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein:

Vividhavisesanayattā, vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ;

Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto.

Because of its various and distinctive methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, this is called ‘Vinaya’ by those skilled in Vinaya.

Vividhā hi ettha pañcavidhapātimokkhuddesapārājikādisattaāpattikkhandhamātikāvibhaṅgādippabhedā nayā visesabhūtā ca daḷhīkammasithilakaraṇappayojanā anupaññattinayā. Kāyikavācasikaajjhācāranisedhanato cesa kāyaṃ vācañca vineti. Tasmā vividhanayattā visesanayattā kāyavācānañca vinayanato ayaṃ vinayo vinayoti akkhāto. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

Here, indeed, there are various methods, such as the divisions of the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha, the seven groups of offenses beginning with Pārājika, the summaries, and the detailed analyses; and there are also distinctive methods of further enactments which serve the purpose of strengthening and relaxing. And because it prohibits bodily and verbal transgressions, it disciplines body and speech. Therefore, due to its diverse methods, its distinctive methods, and its disciplining of body and speech, this is called ‘Vinaya’. For this reason, for the sake of skill in the meaning of this word, it was said:

“Vividhavisesanayattā[M 0.0020], vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ;

Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto”ti.

“Because of its various and distinctive methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, this is called ‘Vinaya’ by those skilled in Vinaya.”

Itaraṃ pana –

As for the other—

Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato;

Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca ‘sutta’nti akkhātaṃ.

By indicating meanings, by being well-spoken, by producing, by pouring forth, by protecting well, and by having the nature of a thread, it is called ‘Sutta’.

Tañhi [V 0.0021] attatthaparatthādibhede atthe sūceti. Suvuttā cettha atthā veneyyajjhāsayānulomena vuttattā. Savati cetaṃ atthe, sassamiva phalaṃ, pasavatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sūdati cetaṃ, dhenu viya khīraṃ, paggharatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Suṭṭhu ca ne tāyati rakkhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Suttasabhāgañcetaṃ. Yathā hi tacchakānaṃ suttaṃ pamāṇaṃ hoti evametampi viññūnaṃ. Yathā ca suttena saṅgahitāni pupphāni na vikiriyanti na viddhaṃsiyanti evametena saṅgahitā atthā. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

For it indicates meanings in terms of distinctions such as one’s own benefit and the benefit of others. Well expressed indeed are the meanings here, since they are spoken in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained. And it produces meanings, like a crop its fruit—thus it is said to be productive. And it pours forth, like a cow its milk—thus it is said to pour forth. And it protects them well—thus it is said to be safeguarding. Moreover, this has the nature of a thread. Just as a thread is a measure for carpenters, so too is this for the wise. And just as flowers strung on a thread do not scatter or are destroyed, so too are the meanings gathered by this. Therefore, this has been said for the sake of skill in the meaning of its expression –

“Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato;

Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca suttanti akkhāta”nti.

By indicating meanings, by being well-spoken, by producing, by pouring forth, by protecting well, and by having the nature of a thread, it is proclaimed as 'Sutta'.

Abhidhammassa vacanattho vuttoyeva. Aparo nayo –

The meaning of the term 'Abhidhamma' has already been explained. Another method is as follows:

Yaṃ ettha vuḍḍhimanto, salakkhaṇā pūjitā paricchinnā;

Vuttādhikā ca dhammā, abhidhammo tena akkhāto.

Herein, the dhammas that are augmented, have specific characteristics, are honored, and are well-defined, and are spoken of as superior—therefore it is called Abhidhamma.

Ayañhi [P 0.0020] abhisaddo vuḍḍhilakkhaṇapūjitaparicchinnādhikesu dissati.
