Tathā hesa “bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.384; saṃ. ni. 5.195) vuḍḍhiyaṃ āgato. “Yā tā rattiyo abhiññātā abhilakkhitā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.49) lakkhaṇe. “Rājābhirājā manujindo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 558) pūjite. “Paṭibalo vinetuṃ abhidhamme abhivinaye”tiādīsu (mahāva. 85) paricchinne; aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite dhamme ca vinaye cāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Abhikkantena vaṇṇenā”tiādīsu (vi. va. 75) adhike.

For this prefix "abhi" is seen in the sense of increase, characteristic, veneration, distinction, and superiority. Thus, in phrases like "strong painful feelings are increasing in me, not decreasing" (MN 141; SN 56.11), it appears in the sense of increase. In phrases like "those nights well-known and marked" (MN 4), it appears in the sense of characteristic. In phrases like "the king of kings, the lord of men" (MN 92; Snp 3.7), it appears in the sense of veneration. In phrases like "capable of training in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya" (Vin. Mahāvagga 1.36), it appears in the sense of distinction; this means the Dhamma and the Vinaya devoid of mutual admixture. In phrases like "with surpassing beauty" (Vv 5.1), it appears in the sense of superiority.

Ettha [M 0.0021] ca “rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 163 ādayo) nayena vuḍḍhimantopi dhammā vuttā. “Rūpārammaṇaṃ vā saddārammaṇaṃ vā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1) nayena ārammaṇādīhi lakkhaṇīyattā salakkhaṇāpi. “Sekkhā dhammā, asekkhā dhammā, lokuttarā dhammā”tiādinā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 11; dukamātikā 12) nayena pūjitāpi; pūjārahāti adhippāyo. “Phasso [V 0.0022] hoti, vedanā hotī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1) nayena sabhāvaparicchinnattā paricchinnāpi. “Mahaggatā dhammā, appamāṇā dhammā, anuttarā dhammā”tiādinā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 12; dukamātikā 99) nayena adhikāpi dhammā vuttā. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

Herein, the dhammas are also said to be augmented, in the way of the passage: "One develops the path to rebirth in the form realm with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, having pervaded one direction and abides therein" (Dhs. 163, etc.). They have specific characteristics, because they are to be characterized by objects, etc., in the way of the passage: "With form as object, or sound as object" (Dhs. 1). They are also honored, in the way of the passages: "The dhammas of trainees, the dhammas of non-trainees, the supramundane dhammas" (Dhs. Tikamātikā 11; Dukamātikā 12), the meaning being that they are worthy of honor. They are also well-defined, because they are defined by their intrinsic nature, in the way of the passage: "There is contact, there is feeling" (Dhs. 1). Moreover, the dhammas are said to be superior, in the way of the passages: "The exalted dhammas, the immeasurable dhammas, the unsurpassed dhammas" (Dhs. Tikamātikā 12; Dukamātikā 99). Therefore, this has been said for the sake of skill in the meaning of its expression –

“Yaṃ ettha vuḍḍhimanto, salakkhaṇā pūjitā paricchinnā;

Vuttādhikā ca dhammā, abhidhammo tena akkhāto”ti.

Herein, the dhammas that are augmented, have specific characteristics, are honored, and are well-defined, and are spoken of as superior—therefore it is called Abhidhamma.

Yaṃ panettha avisiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ –

As for that which is common herein, that is—

Piṭakaṃ piṭakatthavidū, pariyattibbhājanatthato āhu;

Tena samodhānetvā, tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā.

Those skilled in the Piṭaka say that 'Piṭaka' has the meaning of both the scriptures and a container. Therefore, by combining with that, the three—Vinaya and the others—should be understood.

Pariyattipi hi “mā piṭakasampadānenā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) piṭakanti vuccati. “Atha puriso āgaccheyya kudālapiṭakaṃādāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.228; a. ni. 3.70) yaṃkiñci bhājanampi. Tasmā piṭakaṃ piṭakatthavidū pariyattibhājanatthato āhu.

For 'Piṭaka' is used in the sense of the scriptures in phrases such as 'Let him not be content with the accomplishment of the Piṭakas' (AN 3.66). It is also used for any kind of container in phrases such as 'Then a man might come carrying a spade and a basket' (MN 28; AN 3.70). Therefore, those skilled in the Piṭaka say that 'Piṭaka' has the meaning of both the scriptures and a container.

Idāni tena samodhānetvā tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyāti. Tena evaṃ duvidhatthena piṭakasaddena saha samāsaṃ katvā vinayo ca so piṭakañca pariyattibhāvato, tassa tassa atthassa bhājanato cāti vinayapiṭakaṃ. Yathāvutteneva nayena suttantañca taṃ piṭakañcāti suttantapiṭakaṃ. Abhidhammo [P 0.0021] ca so piṭakañcāti abhidhammapiṭakanti evamete tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā.

Now, by combining with that, the three—Vinaya and the others—should be understood. This means: having formed a compound with the word 'piṭaka' in its twofold meaning, the Vinaya is a Piṭaka both because it is the scriptures and because it is a container for its respective meaning; hence, Vinaya Piṭaka. In the same way as stated, 'the Suttanta which is also a Piṭaka' is the Suttanta Piṭaka, and 'the Abhidhamma which is also a Piṭaka' is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Thus these three, Vinaya and the others, should be understood.

Evaṃ ñatvā ca punapi tesveva piṭakesu nānappakārakosallatthaṃ –

Having understood this, and for the sake of further skill in various aspects of those very Piṭakas:

Desanāsāsanakathābhedaṃ tesu yathārahaṃ;

Sikkhāpahānagambhīrabhāvañca paridīpaye.

Pariyattibhedaṃ [V 0.0023] sampattiṃ, vipattiñcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvaye.

One should clarify the distinctions of teaching, instruction, and discourse within them, as is appropriate, and the profundity of the training and of abandonment. One should also fully explain the distinctions of the scriptures, success, and failure, and how a monk fares with regard to them.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 0.0022] paridīpanā vibhāvanā ca – etāni hi tīṇi piṭakāni yathākkamaṃ āṇāvohāraparamatthadesanā, yathāparādhayathānulomayathādhammasāsanāni, saṃvarāsaṃvaradiṭṭhiviniveṭhananāmarūpaparicchedakathāti ca vuccanti.

Herein, this is the clarification and explanation: These three Piṭakas are respectively called the teaching of command, the teaching of conventional expression, and the teaching of ultimate meaning; the instruction according to the offense, the instruction according to suitability, and the instruction according to the Dhamma; and the discourse on restraint and non-restraint, the discourse on disentangling from views, and the discourse on determining name-and-form.

Ettha hi vinayapiṭakaṃ āṇārahena bhagavatā āṇābāhullato desitattā āṇādesanā; suttantapiṭakaṃ vohārakusalena bhagavatā vohārabāhullato desitattā vohāradesanā; abhidhammapiṭakaṃ paramatthakusalena bhagavatā paramatthabāhullato desitattā paramatthadesanāti vuccati.

Herein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is called the teaching of command because it was taught with an abundance of commands by the Blessed One, who possesses command. The Suttanta Piṭaka is called the teaching of conventional expression because it was taught with an abundance of conventional expressions by the Blessed One, who is skilled in convention. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is called the teaching of ultimate meaning because it was taught with an abundance of ultimate meanings by the Blessed One, who is skilled in ultimate meaning.

Tathā paṭhamaṃ ye te pacurāparādhā sattā te yathāparādhaṃ ettha sāsitāti yathāparādhasāsanaṃ; dutiyaṃ anekajjhāsayānusayacariyādhimuttikā sattā yathānulomaṃ ettha sāsitāti yathānulomasāsanaṃ; tatiyaṃ dhammapuñjamatte ‘ahaṃ mamā’ti saññino sattā yathādhammaṃ ettha sāsitāti yathādhammasāsananti vuccati.

Likewise, the first is called instruction according to the offense, because beings who frequently commit offenses are disciplined herein according to their offenses. The second is called instruction according to suitability, because beings with diverse inclinations, underlying tendencies, conduct, and dispositions are disciplined herein according to their suitability. The third is called instruction according to the Dhamma, because beings who perceive “I” and “mine” in a mere mass of phenomena are disciplined herein according to the Dhamma.

Tathā paṭhamaṃ ajjhācārapaṭipakkhabhūto saṃvarāsaṃvaro ettha kathitoti saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā; saṃvarāsaṃvaroti khuddako ceva mahanto ca saṃvarāsaṃvaro, kammākammaṃ viya ca phalāphalaṃ viya ca; dutiyaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhipaṭipakkhabhūtā diṭṭhiviniveṭhanā ettha kathitāti diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathā; tatiyaṃ rāgādipaṭipakkhabhūto nāmarūpaparicchedo ettha kathitoti nāmarūpaparicchedakathāti vuccati.

Similarly, the first is called the discourse on restraint and non-restraint because it discusses restraint and non-restraint, which are the counterpart to transgression. 'Restraint and non-restraint' refers to both minor and major restraint and non-restraint, like action and inaction, or fruit and absence of fruit. The second is called the discourse on disentangling from views because it discusses disentangling from views, which is the counterpart to the sixty-two views. The third is called the discourse on the delimitation of name and form because it discusses the delimitation of name and form, which is the counterpart to lust and other defilements.

Tīsupi cetesu tisso sikkhā tīṇi pahānāni catubbidho ca gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo. Tathā hi vinayapiṭake visesena adhisīlasikkhā vuttā, suttantapiṭake adhicittasikkhā, abhidhammapiṭake adhipaññāsikkhā.

In these three Piṭakas, the three trainings, the three abandonments, and the fourfold profundity should be understood. Thus, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue is especially mentioned; in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind; in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom.

Vinayapiṭake ca vītikkamappahānaṃ[P 0.0022], kilesānaṃ vītikkamapaṭipakkhattā sīlassa; suttantapiṭake pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ, pariyuṭṭhānapaṭipakkhattā samādhissa; abhidhammapiṭake anusayappahānaṃ, anusayapaṭipakkhattā paññāya.

And in the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is the abandonment of transgression, because virtue is the counterpart to the transgression of defilements; in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the abandonment of obsession, because concentration is the counterpart to obsession; in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the abandonment of latent tendencies, because wisdom is the counterpart to latent tendencies.

Paṭhame [M 0.0023][V 0.0024] ca tadaṅgappahānaṃ kilesānaṃ, itaresu vikkhambhanasamucchedappahānāni. Paṭhame ca duccaritasaṃkilesassa pahānaṃ, itaresu taṇhādiṭṭhisaṃkilesānaṃ pahānaṃ.

In the first, there is the abandonment of defilements by substitution; in the others, the abandonments by suppression and by eradication. In the first, there is the abandonment of the defilement of misconduct; in the others, the abandonment of the defilements of craving and views.

Ekamekasmiñcettha catubbidhopi dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīrabhāvo veditabbo – tattha dhammoti tanti. Atthoti tassāyevattho. Desanāti tassā manasā vavatthāpitāya tantiyā desanā. Paṭivedhoti tantiyā tantiatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodho. Tīsupi cetesu ete dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhā. Yasmā sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo mandabuddhīhi dukkhogāhā alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā ca tasmā gambhīrā. Evaṃ ekamekasmiṃ ettha catubbidhopi gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo.

In each of these, the fourfold profundity of Dhamma, meaning, exposition, and penetration should be understood. Here, 'Dhamma' means the text; 'meaning' refers to the meaning of that very text; 'exposition' is the teaching of the text as mentally determined; 'penetration' is the true understanding of both the text and its meaning. In all three Piṭakas, these are the Dhamma, meaning, exposition, and penetration. Just as the great ocean, with its sharks and other creatures, is difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and has a bottom that cannot be reached, so too are they profound. Thus, in each of these, the fourfold profundity should be understood.

Aparo nayo – dhammoti hetu. Vuttañhetaṃ – “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720). Atthoti hetuphalaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720). Desanāti paññatti, yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpoti adhippāyo; anulomapaṭilomasaṅkhepavitthārādivasena vā kathanaṃ. Paṭivedhoti abhisamayo. So ca lokiyalokuttaro. Visayato ca asammohato ca; atthānurūpaṃ dhammesu, dhammānurūpaṃ atthesu, paññattipathānurūpaṃ paññattīsu avabodho. Tesaṃ tesaṃ vā tattha tattha vuttadhammānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo salakkhaṇasaṅkhāto aviparītasabhāvo.

Another method: 'Dhamma' means cause. For it was said, 'Knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma' (Vibh. 720). 'Meaning' means the result of the cause. For it was said, 'Knowledge in the result of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning' (Vibh. 720). 'Exposition' means designation; the intention is the verbal expression of things according to the Dhamma, or it is the teaching by way of direct order, reverse order, condensation, expansion, and so on. 'Penetration' means comprehension. And that is both mundane and supramundane. It is in terms of its object and its non-delusion; it is the understanding of the Dhamma in accordance with its meaning, of the meaning in accordance with the Dhamma, and of designations in accordance with the path of designation. Or it is the non-perverted nature, known as its own characteristic, of those various phenomena stated here and there, which is to be penetrated.

Idāni yasmā etesu piṭakesu yaṃ yaṃ dhammajātaṃ vā atthajātaṃ vā yā cāyaṃ yathā yathā ñāpetabbo attho sotūnaṃ ñāṇassa abhimukho hoti tathā tathā tadatthajotikā desanā, yo cettha aviparītāvabodhasaṅkhāto paṭivedho tesaṃ tesaṃ vā dhammānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo salakkhaṇasaṅkhāto aviparītasabhāvo – sabbampetaṃ anupacitakusalasambhārehi duppaññehi, sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo, dukkhogāhaṃ alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhañca, tasmā gambhīraṃ. Evampi ekamekasmiṃ ettha catubbidhopi gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo. Ettāvatā ca –

Now, because in these Piṭakas, whatever category of Dhamma or category of meaning there is; and whatever exposition there is that illuminates that meaning in such a way as to make it accessible to the knowledge of the listeners, according to how that meaning is to be made known; and whatever penetration there is here, known as unerring comprehension, or the non-perverted nature, known as its own characteristic, of those phenomena to be penetrated in each case—all this is profound for those of little wisdom who have not accumulated a store of merit, just as the great ocean with its sharks and other creatures is difficult to fathom and its bottom cannot be reached. Thus, in each of these, the fourfold profundity should be understood. And to this extent—

Desanāsāsanakathābhedaṃ [P 0.0023] tesu yathārahaṃ;

Sikkhāpahānagambhīrabhāvañca paridīpayeti –

It illuminates the distinction of teaching, instruction, and discourse among them as appropriate, and the profundity of the trainings and abandonments.

Ayaṃ gāthā vuttatthā hoti.

This verse has the meaning already stated.

Pariyattibhedaṃ [M 0.0024][V 0.0025] sampattiṃ, vipattiñcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvayeti.

It also clarifies the division of scriptural learning, and the success and failure that a monk attains in each respective case, and how he attains it—all of this.

Ettha pana tīsu piṭakesu tividho pariyattibhedo daṭṭhabbo. Tisso hi pariyattiyo – alagaddūpamā nissaraṇatthā bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattīti.

Here, in the three Piṭakas, a threefold division of scriptural learning should be seen. For there are three kinds of learning: that which is like a water-snake, that which is for the purpose of escape, and the treasurer's learning.

Tattha yā duggahitā upārambhādihetu pariyāpuṭā ayaṃ alagaddūpamā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko alagaddagavesī alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno, so passeyya mahantaṃ alagaddaṃ, tamenaṃ bhoge vā naṅguṭṭhe vā gaṇheyya, tassa so alagaddo paṭiparivattitvā hatthe vā bāhāya vā aññatarasmiṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅge ḍaṃseyya, so tato nidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, alagaddassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacce moghapurisā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti suttaṃ…pe… vedallaṃ, te taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññāya atthaṃ na upaparikkhanti, tesaṃ te dhammā paññāya atthaṃ anupaparikkhataṃ na nijjhānaṃ khamanti, te upārambhānisaṃsā ceva dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā ca. Yassa catthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhonti. Tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitā dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.238).

Here, that learning which is poorly grasped and is undertaken for the sake of criticism and so on, is the learning that is like a water-snake. Regarding this, it was said: "Suppose, monks, a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, searching for a water-snake, should see a large water-snake. He might grasp it by its coils or by its tail. That water-snake, twisting back, might bite him on the hand, arm, or some other limb, and because of that he might meet death or deadly suffering. Why is that? Because of his poor grasp of the water-snake. In the same way, monks, some foolish men here learn the Dhamma—discourses… catechisms—but having learned that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. For them, not examining the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not lead to comprehension. They learn the Dhamma only for the sake of finding fault and for the sake of winning in debate. They do not experience the purpose for which they learn the Dhamma. Those teachings, poorly grasped by them, conduce to their harm and suffering for a long time. Why is that? Because of their poor grasp of the teachings, monks." (MN 22)

Yā pana suggahitā sīlakkhandhādipāripūriṃyeva ākaṅkhamānena pariyāpuṭā na upārambhādihetu, ayaṃ nissaraṇatthā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tesaṃ te dhammā suggahitā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Suggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.239).

But that which is well-grasped, acquired by one desiring only the complete fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so on, not for the sake of criticism and so on, this is for the purpose of release. Regarding this, it was said: "For them, these teachings, when well-grasped, conduce to their welfare and happiness for a long time. Why is that? Because, monks, the teachings are well-grasped." (MN 1.239)

Yaṃ pana pariññātakkhandho pahīnakileso bhāvitamaggo paṭividdhākuppo [P 0.0024] sacchikatanirodho khīṇāsavo kevalaṃ paveṇipālanatthāya vaṃsānurakkhaṇatthāya pariyāpuṇāti, ayaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattīti.

But that which is learned by one who has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, penetrated the unshakeable, realized cessation, and destroyed the taints, only for the sake of maintaining the tradition and preserving the lineage—this is the treasurer's learning.

Vinaye pana suppaṭipanno bhikkhu sīlasampadaṃ nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇāti, tāsaṃyeva [V 0.0026] ca tattha pabhedavacanato. Sutte suppaṭipanno samādhisampadaṃ nissāya chaḷabhiññā pāpuṇāti, tāsaṃyeva ca tattha pabhedavacanato. Abhidhamme suppaṭipanno paññāsampadaṃ nissāya catasso paṭisambhidā [M 0.0025] pāpuṇāti tāsañca tattheva pabhedavacanato. Evametesu suppaṭipanno yathākkamena imaṃ vijjāttayachaḷabhiññācatupaṭisambhidāppabhedaṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇāti.

In the Vinaya, a well-practiced monk, relying on the accomplishment of virtue, attains the three knowledges, and their distinctions are also stated therein. In the Suttas, a well-practiced monk, relying on the accomplishment of concentration, attains the six superknowledges, and their distinctions are also stated therein. In the Abhidhamma, a well-practiced monk, relying on the accomplishment of wisdom, attains the four analytical knowledges, and their distinctions are also stated therein. Thus, being well-practiced in these, one successively attains this accomplishment, distinguished by the three knowledges, six superknowledges, and four analytical knowledges.

Vinaye pana duppaṭipanno anuññātasukhasamphassaattharaṇapāvuraṇādiphassasāmaññato paṭikkhittesu upādinnakaphassādīsu anavajjasaññī hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā”ti (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.234). Tato dussīlabhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti. Sutte duppaṭipanno “cattārome, bhikkhave, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmi”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.5) adhippāyaṃ ajānanto duggahitaṃ gaṇhāti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “attanā duggahitena amhe ceva abbhācikkhati attānañca khanati bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavatī”ti (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.236). Tato micchādiṭṭhitaṃ pāpuṇāti. Abhidhamme duppaṭipanno dhammacintaṃ atidhāvanto acinteyyānipi cinteti, tato cittakkhepaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, acinteyyāni, na cintetabbāni, yāni cintento ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77). Evametesu duppaṭipanno yathākkamena imaṃ dussīlabhāvamicchādiṭṭhitācittakkhepappabhedaṃ vipattiṃ pāpuṇātīti. Ettāvatā ca –

In the Vinaya, one who practices wrongly, due to the commonality of contact with permitted things such as pleasant textures, bedding, and coverings, perceives no fault in prohibited things that are clung to, such as physical contact. For it is said: "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that those things declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive are not in fact obstructive for one who engages in them" (Pāc. 417; MN 1.234). From this, one falls into a state of immorality. In the Suttas, one who practices wrongly, not understanding the intention in passages such as, "Monks, these four kinds of persons are found existing in the world" (AN 4.5), grasps them incorrectly. Regarding this, it is said: "Having wrongly grasped it, one misrepresents us, digs oneself up by the roots, and produces much demerit" (Pāc. 417; MN 1.236). From this, one falls into a state of wrong view. In the Abhidhamma, one who practices wrongly, overextending the contemplation of phenomena, even ponders the unponderable, and from this, one attains mental derangement. For it is said: "Monks, there are these four unponderables that should not be pondered. Whoever ponders them would become a partaker of madness and vexation" (AN 4.77). Thus, one who practices wrongly in these ways successively attains this failure, distinguished by immorality, wrong view, and mental derangement. And to this extent—

Pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiñcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvayeti.

It also clarifies the division of scriptural learning, and the success and failure that a monk attains in each respective case, and how he attains it—all of this.

Ayampi gāthā vuttatthā hoti. Evaṃ nānappakārato piṭakāni ñatvā tesaṃ vasena sabbampetaṃ saṅgayhamānaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni honti.

This verse also has the meaning already stated. Thus, having understood the Piṭakas in these various ways, when all this is compiled according to them, there are three Piṭakas.

Kathaṃ [P 0.0025] nikāyato pañca nikāyāti? Sabbameva hetaṃ dīghanikāyo majjhimanikāyo saṃyuttanikāyo aṅguttaranikāyo khuddakanikāyoti pañcappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha katamo dīghanikāyo? Tivaggasaṅgahāni brahmajālādīni catuttiṃsa suttāni.

How, from the perspective of Nikāyas, are there five Nikāyas? All of this is of five kinds: the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among these, what is the Dīgha Nikāya? The thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla, collected into three sections (vaggas).

Catuttiṃseva [V 0.0027] suttantā, tivaggo yassa saṅgaho;

Esa dīghanikāyoti, paṭhamo anulomiko.

Thirty-four are the suttas, whose collection is in three sections; this is the Dīgha Nikāya, the first in sequence.

Kasmā [M 0.0026] panesa dīghanikāyoti vuccati? Dīghappamāṇānaṃ suttānaṃ samūhato nivāsato ca. Samūhanivāsā hi nikāyoti vuccanti. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi evaṃ cittaṃ yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā pāṇā (saṃ. ni. 3.100), poṇikanikāyo, cikkhallikanikāyo”ti. Evamādīni cettha sādhakāni sāsanato lokato ca. Evaṃ sesānampi nikāyabhāve vacanattho veditabbo.

But why is this called the Dīgha Nikāya? Because it is a collection (samūha) and an abode (nivāsa) for suttas of long measure. For collections and abodes are called 'nikāyas.' For example: "Monks, I do not perceive any other single group (nikāya) of beings so varied in mind as these animals" (SN 3.100); the Poṇika group; the Cikkhallika group. Such examples here are corroborative both from the Dispensation and from common usage. In this way, the meaning of the term 'nikāya' should be understood for the remaining ones as well.

Katamo majjhimanikāyo? Majjhimappamāṇāni pañcadasavaggasaṅgahāni mūlapariyāyasuttādīni diyaḍḍhasataṃ dve ca suttāni.

What is the Majjhima Nikāya? The one hundred and fifty-two suttas of medium length, beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, collected into fifteen sections.

Diyaḍḍhasatasuttantā, dve ca suttāni yattha so;

Nikāyo majjhimo pañca, dasavaggapariggaho.

Wherein there are one hundred and fifty-two suttas, that Majjhima Nikāya comprises fifteen sections.

Katamo saṃyuttanikāyo? Devatāsaṃyuttādivasena ṭhitāni oghataraṇādīni satta suttasahassāni satta suttasatāni ca dvāsaṭṭhi ca suttāni.

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? The seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas, beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta, arranged according to sections such as the Devatāsaṃyutta.

Satta suttasahassāni, satta suttasatāni ca;

Dvāsaṭṭhi ceva suttantā, eso saṃyuttasaṅgaho.

Seven thousand suttas, seven hundred suttas, and sixty-two suttas more: this is the Saṃyutta collection.

Katamo aṅguttaranikāyo? Ekekaaṅgātirekavasena ṭhitāni cittapariyādānādīni nava suttasahassāni pañca suttasatāni sattapaññāsañca suttāni.

What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? The nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas, beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta, arranged by way of successively increasing factors.

Nava suttasahassāni, pañca suttasatāni ca;

Sattapaññāsasuttāni, saṅkhyā aṅguttare ayaṃ.

Nine thousand suttas, five hundred suttas, and fifty-seven suttas: this is the count in the Aṅguttara.

Katamo [P 0.0026] khuddakanikāyo? Sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, khuddakapāṭha, dhammapadādayo [V 0.0028] ca pubbe dassitā pañcadasappabhedā; ṭhapetvā cattāro nikāye avasesaṃ buddhavacananti.

What is the Khuddaka Nikāya? The entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and the fifteen divisions previously shown—the Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, and so on. Excluding the four Nikāyas, it is the remaining word of the Buddha.

Ṭhapetvā caturopete, nikāye dīghaādike;

Tadaññaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, nikāyo khuddako matoti.

Excluding these four Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīgha, the remaining word of the Buddha is considered the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Evaṃ nikāyato pañca nikāyā honti.

Thus, by way of Nikāyas, there are five Nikāyas.

Kathaṃ [M 0.0027][V 0.0029] aṅgavasena navaṅgānīti? Sabbameva hidaṃ ‘suttaṃ geyyaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ gāthā udānaṃ itivuttakaṃ jātakaṃ abbhutadhammaṃ vedalla’nti navappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha ubhatovibhaṅganiddesakhandhakaparivārā suttanipāte maṅgalasuttaratanasuttanālakasuttatuvaṭṭakasuttāni aññampi ca suttanāmakaṃ tathāgatavacanaṃ suttanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbampi sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyanti veditabbaṃ. Visesena saṃyuttanikāye sakalopi sagāthāvaggo. Sakalampi abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ, yañca aññampi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi asaṅgahitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, taṃ veyyākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Dhammapadaṃ theragāthā therīgāthā suttanipāte nosuttanāmikā suddhikagāthā ca gāthāti veditabbā. Somanassañāṇamayikagāthāppaṭisaṃyuttā dvāsīti suttantā udānanti veditabbaṃ. ‘Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā’tiādinayappavattā (itivu. 1) dasuttarasatasuttantā itivuttakanti veditabbaṃ. Apaṇṇakajātakādīni paññāsādhikāni pañca jātakasatāni jātakanti veditabbaṃ. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, acchariyā abbhutā dhammā ānande”tiādinayapavattā (dī. ni. 2.209; a. ni. 4.129) sabbepi acchariyaabbhutadhammappaṭisaṃyuttā suttantā abbhutadhammanti veditabbaṃ.

How are there nine divisions by way of constituents? Indeed, all this is of nine kinds: 'sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, vedalla.' Herein, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, Parivāra, the Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, and Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta, and any other word of the Tathāgata named as a sutta, are to be understood as 'sutta.' All suttas with verses are to be understood as 'geyya'; especially, the entire verse section in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, suttas without verses, and any other word of the Buddha not included in the other eight divisions, are to be understood as 'veyyākaraṇa.' The Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and the purely metrical verses in the Suttanipāta not named as suttas, are to be understood as 'gāthā.' The eighty-two suttas connected with verses imbued with joyful knowledge are to be understood as 'udāna.' The one hundred and ten suttas that proceed in the manner of 'This was said by the Blessed One' are to be understood as 'itivuttaka.' The Apaṇṇaka Jātaka and others, totaling five hundred and fifty Jātakas, are to be understood as 'jātaka.' All suttas connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, which proceed in the manner of 'Monks, there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda,' are to be understood as 'abbhutadhamma'.

Cūḷavedallamahāvedallasammādiṭṭhisakkapañhasaṅkhārabhājanīyamahāpuṇṇamasuttādayo sabbepi vedañca tuṭṭhiñca laddhā laddhā pucchitasuttantā vedallanti veditabbaṃ. Evametaṃ aṅgato navaṅgāni.

The Cūḷavedalla, Mahāvedalla, Sammādiṭṭhi, Sakkapañha, Saṅkhārabhājanīya, Mahāpuṇṇama Suttas, and others—all suttas that were asked after knowledge and satisfaction had been repeatedly attained—are to be understood as 'vedalla'. Thus, by way of constituents, these are the nine divisions.

Kathaṃ dhammakkhandhato caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānīti? Sabbameva hidaṃ buddhavacanaṃ.

How are there eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates by way of Dhamma aggregates? All this is the word of the Buddha.

“Dvāsīti [P 0.0027] buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dve sahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti. (theragā. 1027);

“Eighty-two thousand I received from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks; eighty-four thousand in all, these are the Dhamma teachings that are current for me.”

Evaṃ paridīpitadhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ eko dhammakkhandho. Yaṃ anekānusandhikaṃ tattha anusandhivasena dhammakkhandhagaṇanā. Gāthābandhesu pañhāpucchanaṃ eko dhammakkhandho, vissajjanaṃ eko. Abhidhamme ekamekaṃ tikadukabhājanaṃ ekamekañca cittavārabhājanaṃ eko dhammakkhandho. Vinaye atthi vatthu, atthi mātikā, atthi padabhājanīyaṃ, atthi āpatti, atthi anāpatti, atthi [M 0.0028] antarāpatti, atthi tikacchedo. Tattha ekameko koṭṭhāso ekameko dhammakkhandhoti veditabbo. Evaṃ dhammakkhandhato caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassāni.

Thus, by way of the Dhamma aggregates that have been expounded, there are eighty-four thousand divisions. Herein, a sutta with a single connection is one Dhamma aggregate. Where there are multiple connections, the counting of Dhamma aggregates is according to the connections. In verse compositions, a question is one Dhamma aggregate, and an answer is one. In the Abhidhamma, each division into triads and dyads, and each division related to the series of consciousness, is one Dhamma aggregate. In the Vinaya, there is the case, there is the matrix, there is the analysis of words, there is the offense, there is the non-offense, there is the intermediate offense, and there is the threefold section. Therein, each portion should be understood as one Dhamma aggregate. Thus, by way of Dhamma aggregates, there are eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates.

Evametaṃ sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ pañcasatikasaṅgītikāle saṅgāyantena mahākassapappamukhena vasīgaṇena ayaṃ dhammo ayaṃ vinayo, idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ majjhimabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ pacchimabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ, idaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ, idaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, ayaṃ dīghanikāyo…pe… ayaṃ khuddakanikāyo, imāni suttādīni navaṅgāni, imāni caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānīti imaṃ pabhedaṃ vavatthapetvāva saṅgītaṃ. Na kevalañca imameva aññampi uddānasaṅgahavaggasaṅgahapeyyālasaṅgahaekanipātadukanipātādinipātasaṅgahasaṃyuttasaṅgaha paṇṇāsasaṅgahādianekavidhaṃ, tīsu piṭakesu sandissamānaṃ saṅgahappabhedaṃ vavatthapetvāva sattahi māsehi saṅgītaṃ.

Thus, all this word of the Buddha was recited at the time of the First Council by the assembly of masters headed by Mahākassapa, having established this classification: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first word of the Buddha, this is the middle word of the Buddha, this is the last word of the Buddha; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Suttanta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya... this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine divisions beginning with sutta; these are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.' And not only this, but also other various kinds of classifications appearing in the three Piṭakas, such as the summary collections, section collections, repetition collections, collections of ones, collections of twos and other numerical collections, connected collections, collections of fifties, etc., were established and recited in seven months.

Saṅgītipariyosāne cassa idaṃ mahākassapattherena dasabalassa sāsanaṃ pañcavassasahassaparimāṇakālaṃ pavattanasamatthaṃ katanti sañjātappamodā sādhukāraṃ viya dadamānā ayaṃ mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā anekappakāraṃ kampi saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi. Anekāni ca acchariyāni pāturahesuṃ.

And at the conclusion of the Council, because Elder Mahākassapa had made the Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One capable of enduring for a period of five thousand years, this great earth, having become joyful and as if giving its approval, shook, quaked, trembled, and vibrated in manifold ways down to its water boundaries. And many marvels appeared.

Evaṃ saṅgīte panettha ayaṃ abhidhammo piṭakato abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, nikāyato khuddakanikāyo, aṅgato [P 0.0028] veyyākaraṇaṃ, dhammakkhandhato katipayāni dhammakkhandhasahassāni honti.

Thus, in this recited collection, this Abhidhamma, by way of Piṭaka, is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; by way of Nikāya, is the Khuddaka Nikāya; by way of Aṅga, is the Exposition; and by way of aggregates of the Dhamma, it consists of several thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.

Taṃ [V 0.0030] dhārayantesu bhikkhūsu pubbe eko bhikkhu sabbasāmayikaparisāya nisīditvā abhidhammato suttaṃ āharitvā dhammaṃ kathento “rūpakkhandho abyākato, cattāro khandhā siyā kusalā siyā akusalā siyā abyākatā; dasāyatanā abyākatā, dve āyatanā siyā kusalā siyā akusalā siyā abyākatā; soḷasa dhātuyo abyākatā, dve dhātuyo siyā kusalā siyā akusalā siyā abyākatā; samudayasaccaṃ akusalaṃ, maggasaccaṃ kusalaṃ, nirodhasaccaṃ abyākataṃ, dukkhasaccaṃ siyā kusalaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākataṃ; dasindriyā abyākatā, domanassindriyaṃ akusalaṃ, anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ kusalaṃ, cattāri indriyāni siyā kusalā siyā abyākatā, cha [M 0.0029] indriyāni siyā kusalā siyā akusalā siyā abyākatā”ti dhammakathaṃ kathesi.

Among the monks who were upholding it, one monk, having previously sat down in an assembly of all persuasions and drawing a discourse from the Abhidhamma, expounded the Dhamma thus: “The aggregate of form is indeterminate; the four aggregates may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. The ten sense bases are indeterminate; the two sense bases may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. The sixteen elements are indeterminate; the two elements may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. The truth of the origin is unwholesome; the truth of the path is wholesome; the truth of cessation is indeterminate; the truth of suffering may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. The ten faculties are indeterminate; the faculty of displeasure is unwholesome; the faculty of ‘I shall know the unknown’ is wholesome; four faculties may be wholesome or indeterminate; six faculties may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.” Thus he gave the Dhamma talk.

Tasmiṃ ṭhāne eko bhikkhu nisinno ‘dhammakathika tvaṃ sineruṃ parikkhipanto viya dīghasuttaṃ āharasi, kiṃ suttaṃ nāmeta’nti āha. ‘Abhidhammasuttaṃ nāma, āvuso’ti. ‘Abhidhammasuttaṃ kasmā āharasi? Kiṃ aññaṃ buddhabhāsitaṃ suttaṃ āharituṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti? ‘Abhidhammo kena bhāsito’ti? ‘Na eso buddhabhāsito’ti. ‘Kiṃ pana te, āvuso, vinayapiṭakaṃ uggahita’nti? ‘Na uggahitaṃ, āvuso’ti. ‘Avinayadhāritāya maññe tvaṃ ajānanto evaṃ vadesī’ti. ‘Vinayamattameva, āvuso, uggahita’nti. ‘Tampi te duggahitaṃ, parisapariyante nisīditvā niddāyantena uggahitaṃ bhavissati; tumhādise hi pabbājento vā upasampādento vā sātisāro hoti’. ‘Kiṃ kāraṇā’? Vinayamattassapi duggahitattā; vuttañhetaṃ – “tattha anāpatti, na vivaṇṇetukāmo iṅgha tāva, āvuso, suttantaṃ vā gāthāyo vā abhidhammaṃ vā pariyāpuṇassu, pacchāpi vinayaṃ pariyāpuṇissasī”ti (pāci. 442) bhaṇati. “Suttante okāsaṃ kārāpetvā abhidhammaṃ vā vinayaṃ vā pucchati, abhidhamme okāsaṃ kārāpetvā suttantaṃ vā vinayaṃ vā pucchati, vinaye okāsaṃ kārāpetvā suttantaṃ vā abhidhammaṃ vā pucchatī”ti (pāci. 1221). ‘Tvaṃ pana ettakampi na jānāsī’ti ettakenapi paravādī niggahito hoti.

In that place, a monk sitting there said, "You, speaker of the Dhamma, are drawing out a long discourse as if encircling Mount Sineru. What is this discourse called?" "It is called the Abhidhamma discourse, friend." "Why do you bring forth the Abhidhamma discourse? Is it not proper to bring forth another discourse spoken by the Buddha?" "By whom was the Abhidhamma spoken?" "That was not spoken by the Buddha." "But have you, friend, mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka?" "I have not mastered it, friend." "I suppose you speak thus, not knowing, because you are not a holder of the Vinaya." "I have mastered only a little of the Vinaya, friend." "Even that you have poorly mastered; it must have been mastered while sitting drowsily at the edge of an assembly. For one who gives the going forth or the higher ordination to one such as you is at fault." "For what reason?" "Because even that little of the Vinaya was poorly mastered. For it is said: 'In that case, there is no offense for one who, not wishing to disparage, says: «Come now, friend, first learn the Suttanta, the verses, or the Abhidhamma; afterward you shall learn the Vinaya»' (Pāc. 442). And it is said: 'Having been given an opening concerning the Suttanta, one asks about the Abhidhamma or the Vinaya; having been given an opening concerning the Abhidhamma, one asks about the Suttanta or the Vinaya; having been given an opening concerning the Vinaya, one asks about the Suttanta or the Abhidhamma' (Pāc. 1221)." "But you do not even know this much." Thus, even with this much, the opponent is refuted.

Mahāgosiṅgasuttaṃ pana itopi balavataraṃ. Tatra hi dhammasenāpati sāriputtatthero aññamaññaṃ pucchitapañhañca vissajjanañca ārocetuṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā mahāmoggallānattherassa vissajjanaṃ ārocento “idhāvuso [P 0.0029] sāriputta, dve bhikkhū abhidhammakathaṃ kathenti[V 0.0031], te aññamaññaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanti, aññamaññassa pañhaṃ puṭṭhā vissajjenti, no ca saṃsādenti, dhammī ca nesaṃ kathāpavattinī hoti, evarūpena kho, āvuso, sāriputta, bhikkhunā gosiṅgasālavanaṃ sobheyyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.343) āha. Satthā ābhidhammikā nāma mama sāsane paribāhirāti avatvā suvaṇṇāliṅgasadisaṃ gīvaṃ unnāmetvā puṇṇacandasassirīkaṃ mahāmukhaṃ pūretvā brahmaghosaṃ nicchārento “sādhu sādhu [M 0.0030] sāriputtā”ti mahāmoggallānattherassa sādhukāraṃ datvā “yathā taṃ moggallāno ca sammā byākaramāno byākareyya, moggallāno hi sāriputta dhammakathiko”ti (ma. ni. 1.343) āha. Ābhidhammikabhikkhūyeva kira dhammakathikā nāma, avasesā dhammakathaṃ kathentāpi na dhammakathikā. Kasmā? Te hi dhammakathaṃ kathentā kammantaraṃ vipākantaraṃ rūpārūpaparicchedaṃ dhammantaraṃ āloḷetvā kathenti. Ābhidhammikā pana dhammantaraṃ na āloḷenti. Tasmā ābhidhammiko bhikkhu dhammaṃ kathetu vā mā vā, pucchitakāle pana pañhaṃ kathessatīti. Ayameva ekantadhammakathiko nāma hoti. Idaṃ sandhāya satthā sādhukāraṃ datvā ‘sukathitaṃ moggallānenā’ti āha.

However, the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta is even more powerful. There, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, went to the presence of the Teacher to report the questions and answers they had exchanged among themselves. While reporting the Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s answer, he said: "Here, friend Sāriputta, two monks are discussing the Abhidhamma. They ask each other questions, and when questioned, they answer each other without foundering. Their discussion proceeds according to the Dhamma. It is in this way, friend Sāriputta, that a monk would adorn the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove" (MN 1.343). The Teacher, without saying that those devoted to the Abhidhamma are outsiders in my dispensation, raised his neck, which resembled a golden pillar, filled his great face, which was like the full moon in its splendor, and uttering a Brahma-like voice declared, "Good, good, Sāriputta," giving approval to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, saying, "As Moggallāna would rightly explain, so he has explained. For Moggallāna, Sāriputta, is a speaker of the Dhamma" (MN 1.343). Indeed, it seems that only monks devoted to the Abhidhamma are called speakers of the Dhamma; others, even if they speak of the Dhamma, are not called speakers of the Dhamma. Why? Because when they speak of the Dhamma, they intermingle discussions on kamma, its results, the distinction between form and the formless, and other Dhamma topics. But those devoted to the Abhidhamma do not intermingle other Dhamma topics. Therefore, whether a monk devoted to the Abhidhamma speaks the Dhamma or not, when questioned, he will answer the question. This one is indeed called one who speaks solely of the Dhamma. Referring to this, the Teacher gave his approval, saying, "Well spoken by Moggallāna."

Abhidhammaṃ paṭibāhento imasmiṃ jinacakke pahāraṃ deti, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭibāhati, satthu vesārajjaññāṇaṃ paṭinivatteti, sotukāmaṃ parisaṃ visaṃvādeti, ariyamagge āvaraṇaṃ bandhati, aṭṭhārasasu bhedakaravatthūsu ekasmiṃ sandissati ukkhepanīyakammatajjanīyakammāraho hoti. Taṃ taṃ kammaṃ katvā uyyojetabbo ‘gaccha vighāsādo hutvā jīvissasī’ti.

One who rejects the Abhidhamma strikes a blow against this Wheel of the Conqueror, obstructs the knowledge of omniscience, turns back the Teacher’s knowledge of intrepidity, deceives the assembly eager to listen, creates a barrier to the Noble Path, and is seen in one of the eighteen grounds for division. He is worthy of an act of suspension and an act of censure. Having performed that action, he should be expelled with the words, ‘Go, live on gleanings.’

Athāpi evaṃ vadeyya – “sace abhidhammo buddhabhāsito, yathā anekesu suttasahassesu ‘ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharatī’tiādinā nayena nidānaṃ sajjitaṃ, evamassāpi nidānaṃ sajjitaṃ bhaveyyā”ti. So ‘jātakasuttanipātadhammapadādīnaṃ evarūpaṃ nidānaṃ natthi, na cetāni na buddhabhāsitānī’ti paṭikkhipitvā uttaripi evaṃ vattabbo – ‘paṇḍita, abhidhammo nāmesa sabbaññubuddhānaṃyeva visayo, na aññesaṃ visayo. Buddhānañhi okkanti pākaṭā, abhijāti pākaṭā, abhisambodhi pākaṭā, dhammacakkappavattanaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ [P 0.0030] pākaṭaṃ, tidivakkamo pākaṭo, devaloke desitabhāvo pākaṭo, devorohanaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Yathā nāma cakkavattirañño hatthiratanaṃ vā assaratanaṃ vā thenetvā yānake yojetvā vicaraṇaṃ nāma aṭṭhānaṃ akāraṇaṃ; cakkaratanaṃ vā pana thenetvā palālasakaṭe olambitvā vicaraṇaṃ nāma aṭṭhānaṃ akāraṇaṃ; yojanappamāṇaṃ obhāsanasamatthaṃ maṇiratanaṃ vā pana kappāsapacchiyaṃ pakkhipitvā vaḷañjanaṃ [M 0.0031][V 0.0032] nāma aṭṭhānaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Kasmā? Rājārahabhaṇḍatāya; evameva abhidhammo nāma na aññesaṃ visayo, sabbaññubuddhānaṃyeva visayo. Tesaṃ vasena desetabbadesanā. Buddhānañhi okkanti pākaṭā…pe… devorohanaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Abhidhammassa nidānakiccaṃ nāma natthi paṇḍitā’ti. Na hi sakkā evaṃ vutte paravādinā sahadhammikaṃ udāharaṇaṃ udāharituṃ.

Moreover, if someone were to say: ‘If the Abhidhamma were spoken by the Buddha, then just as in many thousands of suttas, the introduction is established with phrases like, “At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha,” so too should there be an established introduction for it.’ This should be refuted by saying, ‘The Jātaka, Sutta Nipāta, Dhammapada, and others lack such an introduction, yet it is not that they were not spoken by the Buddha.’ Further, it should be said: ‘Wise one, the Abhidhamma is the domain of only the Omniscient Buddhas, not of others. For the Buddhas, their conception is evident, their birth is evident, their supreme enlightenment is evident, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma is evident, the Twin Miracle is evident, the ascent to the threefold heaven is evident, their teaching in the deva realm is evident, and their descent from the deva realm is evident. Just as it would be improper and uncalled for for a wheel-turning king’s elephant treasure or horse treasure to be taken and yoked to a common cart for travel, or for the wheel treasure to be taken and hung on a straw cart for travel, or for a radiant jewel capable of illuminating a league to be placed in a cotton bag for use—why? Because they are possessions worthy of a king—so too, the Abhidhamma is not the domain of others but only of the Omniscient Buddhas. It is a teaching to be taught in a manner befitting them. For the Buddhas, their conception is evident… their descent from the deva realm is evident. The Abhidhamma has no need for an introductory section, O wise one.’ Indeed, when this is said, no opponent can offer a valid counterexample that accords with the Dhamma.

Maṇḍalārāmavāsī tissabhūtitthero pana mahābodhinidāno esa abhidhammo nāmāti dassetuṃ “yena svāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vihārena paṭhamābhisambuddho viharāmi tassa padesena vihāsi”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.11) imaṃ padesavihārasuttantaṃ āharitvā kathesi. Dasavidho hi padeso nāma – khandhapadeso, āyatanapadeso, dhātupadeso, saccapadeso, indriyapadeso, paccayākārapadeso, satipaṭṭhānapadeso, jhānapadeso, nāmapadeso, dhammapadesoti. Tesu satthā mahābodhimaṇḍe pañcakkhandhe nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ vedanākkhandhavaseneva vihāsi. Dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo nippadesena paṭivijjhi. Imaṃ temāsaṃ dhammāyatane vedanāvasena dhammadhātuyañca vedanāvaseneva vihāsi. Cattāri saccāni nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ dukkhasacce vedanāvaseneva vihāsi. Bāvīsatindriyāni nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ vedanāpañcakaindriyavasena vihāsi. Dvādasapadikaṃ paccayākāravaṭṭaṃ nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ phassapaccayā vedanāvaseneva vihāsi. Cattāro satipaṭṭhāne nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ vedanāsatipaṭṭhānavaseneva vihāsi. Cattāri [P 0.0031] jhānāni nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ jhānaṅgesu vedanāvaseneva vihāsi. Nāmaṃ nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ tattha vedanāvaseneva vihāsi. Dhamme nippadesena paṭivijjhi, imaṃ temāsaṃ vedanāttikavaseneva vihāsīti. Evaṃ thero padesavihārasuttantavasena abhidhammassa nidānaṃ kathesi.

The venerable Tissabhūti, a resident of Maṇḍalārāma, wishing to show that this Abhidhamma has its origin in the Great Enlightenment, cited the Padesavihāra Suttanta (Saṃ. Ni. 5.11): “Monks, of that state in which I dwelt when first I was fully enlightened, I dwelt in a portion thereof.” For there are ten kinds of portions, namely: the portion of aggregates, the portion of sense bases, the portion of elements, the portion of truths, the portion of faculties, the portion of the structure of dependent origination, the portion of the foundations of mindfulness, the portion of the jhānas, the portion of name, and the portion of dhammas. Among these, the Teacher fully comprehended the five aggregates without remainder at the great Bodhi seat, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of the aggregate of feeling. He fully comprehended the twelve sense bases and eighteen elements without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of feeling within the sense base of mind-objects and by way of feeling within the element of mind-objects. He fully comprehended the four truths without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of feeling within the truth of suffering. He fully comprehended the twenty-two faculties without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of the five faculties related to feeling. He fully comprehended the twelve-linked cycle of dependent origination without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of feeling conditioned by contact. He fully comprehended the four foundations of mindfulness without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings. He fully comprehended the four jhānas without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of feeling among the jhāna factors. He fully comprehended name without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of feeling therein. He fully comprehended dhammas without remainder, and for these three months, he dwelt by way of the triad of feeling. Thus, the elder explained the origin of the Abhidhamma by way of the Padesavihāra Suttanta.

Gāmavāsī sumanadevatthero pana heṭṭhālohapāsāde dhammaṃ parivattento ‘ayaṃ paravādī bāhā paggayha araññe kandanto viya, asakkhikaṃ aḍḍaṃ karonto viya ca, abhidhamme nidānassa atthibhāvampi na jānātī’ti vatvā nidānaṃ kathento evamāha – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā devesu viharati tāvatiṃsesu pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ. Tatra kho bhagavā devānaṃ [M 0.0032] tāvatiṃsānaṃ abhidhammakathaṃ kathesi – “kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammā”ti.

The Elder Sumanadeva, a village-dweller, however, while reciting the Dhamma in the lower Lohapāsāda, said, 'This opponent, raising his arms like one crying out in the wilderness, and like one making a claim without a witness, does not even know of the existence of an origin for the Abhidhamma.' And explaining the origin, he spoke thus: At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling among the devas in Tāvatiṃsa, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. There, the Blessed One delivered the Abhidhamma discourse to the Tāvatiṃsa devas: 'Wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states.'

Aññesu pana suttesu ekameva nidānaṃ. Abhidhamme dve nidānāni – adhigamanidānañca desanānidānañca[V 0.0033]. Tattha adhigamanidānaṃ dīpaṅkaradasabalato paṭṭhāya yāva mahābodhipallaṅkā veditabbaṃ. Desanānidānaṃ yāva dhammacakkappavattanā. Evaṃ ubhayanidānasampannassa panassa abhidhammassa nidānakosallatthaṃ idaṃ tāva pañhākammaṃ veditabbaṃ – ayaṃ abhidhammo nāma kena pabhāvito? Kattha paripācito? Kattha adhigato? Kadā adhigato? Kena adhigato? Kattha vicito? Kadā vicito? Kena vicito? Kattha desito? Kassatthāya desito? Kimatthaṃ desito? Kehi paṭiggahito? Ke sikkhanti? Ke sikkhitasikkhā? Ke dhārenti? Kassa vacanaṃ? Kenābhatoti?

In other suttas, there is only one origin. But in the Abhidhamma, there are two origins: the origin of attainment and the origin of teaching. Herein, the origin of attainment should be understood as extending from Dīpaṅkara the Ten-Powered One up to the great Bodhi-seat. The origin of teaching extends up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. Thus, for the Abhidhamma, which is endowed with both origins, the following preliminary inquiry should be understood for the sake of skill in understanding its origin: This Abhidhamma, by whom was it brought forth? Where was it matured? Where was it attained? When was it attained? By whom was it attained? Where was it investigated? When was it investigated? By whom was it investigated? Where was it taught? For whose sake was it taught? For what purpose was it taught? By whom was it received? Who learn it? Who are those with perfected training? Who preserve it? Whose word is it? By whom was it transmitted?

Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ – kena pabhāvitoti bodhiabhinīhārasaddhāya pabhāvito. Kattha paripācitoti aḍḍhachakkesu jātakasatesu. Kattha adhigatoti bodhimūle. Kadā adhigatoti visākhāpuṇṇamāsiyaṃ. Kenādhigatoti sabbaññubuddhena. Kattha vicitoti bodhimaṇḍe. Kadā [P 0.0032] vicitoti ratanagharasattāhe. Kena vicitoti sabbaññubuddhena. Kattha desitoti devesu tāvatiṃsesu. Kassatthāya desitoti devatānaṃ. Kimatthaṃ desitoti caturoghaniddharaṇatthaṃ. Kehi paṭiggahitoti devehi. Ke sikkhantīti sekkhā ca puthujjanakalyāṇā ca. Ke sikkhitasikkhāti arahanto khīṇāsavā. Ke dhārentīti yesaṃ vattati te dhārenti. Kassa vacananti bhagavato vacanaṃ, arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Kenābhatoti ācariyaparamparāya.

Here is the answer: By whom was it brought forth? It was brought forth by faith in the aspiration for enlightenment. Where was it matured? It was matured in many hundreds of Jātakas. Where was it attained? It was attained at the foot of the Bodhi tree. When was it attained? It was attained on the Visākha full-moon day. By whom was it attained? It was attained by the All-Knowing Buddha. Where was it investigated? It was investigated at the Bodhi-seat. When was it investigated? It was investigated during the week in the Jewel House. By whom was it investigated? It was investigated by the All-Knowing Buddha. Where was it taught? It was taught among the devas in Tāvatiṃsa. For whose sake was it taught? It was taught for the sake of the deities. For what purpose was it taught? It was taught for the purpose of overcoming the four floods. By whom was it received? It was received by the deities. Who learn it? Learners-on-the-path and virtuous worldlings learn it. Who are fully trained? The Arahants, whose cankers are destroyed, are fully trained. Who preserve it? Those who have it present within them preserve it. Whose word is it? It is the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. By whom was it transmitted? It was transmitted through the lineage of teachers.

Ayañhi sāriputtatthero bhaddaji sobhito piyajālī piyapālo piyadassī kosiyaputto siggavo sandeho moggaliputto sudatto dhammiyo dāsako soṇako revatoti evamādīhi yāva tatiyasaṅgītikālā ābhato. Tato uddhaṃ tesaṃyeva sissānusissehīti evaṃ tāva jambudīpatale ācariyaparamparāya ābhato. Imaṃ pana dīpaṃ –

For this was transmitted by the Elder Sāriputta, Bhaddaji, Sobhita, Piyajālī, Piyapāla, Piyadassī, Kosiyaputta, Siggava, Sandeha, Moggaliputta, Sudatta, Dhammiya, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, and Revata, and others like them, up to the time of the Third Council. From then onward, it was transmitted by the disciples of those very teachers and their disciples. Thus, indeed, it was transmitted in the land of Jambudīpa through the lineage of teachers. But as for this island—

Tato [M 0.0033] mahindo iṭṭiyo, uttiyo sambalo tathā;

Paṇḍito bhaddanāmo ca, ete nāgā mahāpaññā.

Then Mahinda, Iṭṭiya, Uttiya, Sambala, and also Paṇḍita; And Bhaddanāma, these were Nāgas of great wisdom.

Jambudīpā idhāgatāti (pari. 3, 8).

They have come here from Jambudīpa.

Imehi [V 0.0034] mahānāgehi ābhato. Tato uddhaṃ tesaṃyeva sissānusissasaṅkhātāya ācariyaparamparāya yāvajjatanakālā ābhato.

It was transmitted by these great Nāgas. From then onward, it has been transmitted up to the present day through the lineage of teachers, consisting of disciples and successive disciples.

Sumedhakathā

The Story of Sumedha

Evaṃ ābhatassa panassa yaṃ taṃ dīpaṅkaradasabalato paṭṭhāya yāva mahābodhipallaṅkā adhigamanidānaṃ, yāva dhammacakkappavattanā desanānidānañca vuttaṃ, tassa āvibhāvatthaṃ ayaṃ anupubbikathā veditabbā –

Now, concerning this teaching thus transmitted, to clarify what was stated as the origin of attainment—from Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, up to the great Bodhi-seat—and the origin of teaching—up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma—this sequential narrative should be understood.

Ito kira kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake amaravatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi. Tattha sumedho nāma brāhmaṇo paṭivasati ubhato sujāto, mātito ca pitito ca, saṃsuddhagahaṇiko, yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā akkhitto anupakuṭṭho jātivādena, abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato. So aññaṃ kammaṃ akatvā brāhmaṇasippameva uggaṇhi. Tassa daharakāleyeva mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Athassa rāsivaḍḍhako amacco āyapotthakaṃ āharitvā suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādipūrite gabbhe vivaritvā ‘ettakaṃ te kumāra mātu santakaṃ, ettakaṃ pitu santakaṃ, ettakā ayyakapayyakānaṃ santakāti yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā dhanaṃ ācikkhitvā etaṃ paṭipajjāhī’ti āha. Sumedhapaṇḍito cintesi – ‘imaṃ dhanaṃ saṃharitvā mayhaṃ pitupitāmahādayo paralokaṃ gacchantā ekakahāpaṇampi gahetvā na gatā, mayā pana gahetvā gamanakāraṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti so rañño ārocetvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā mahājanassa dānaṃ datvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne sumedhakathā kathetabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ buddhavaṃse (bu. vaṃ. 2.1-33) –

It is said that at the head of four incalculable aeons plus a hundred thousand aeons ago, there was a city named Amaravatī. There lived a brahmin named Sumedha, well-born on both sides, maternally and paternally, of pure lineage, unblemished and unreviled in regard to birth up to the seventh generation, handsome, pleasing to behold, gracious, and endowed with the highest beauty of complexion. Without engaging in any other work, he mastered only the brahminical arts. In his youth, his parents passed away. Then, his treasurer brought an account book and, opening vaults filled with gold, silver, jewels, pearls, and the like, declared, “Young master, this much is your mother’s wealth, this much your father’s, and this much belongs to your ancestors up to the seventh generation—take this and manage it.” The wise Sumedha reflected, “My forefathers, from my father and grandfather onwards, departed for the next world, but they did not take even a single kahāpaṇa with them. It is fitting, however, that I take it with me when I go.” He informed the king, had a drum proclaimed throughout the city, gave great alms to the people, and went forth into the life of an ascetic. At this point, the story of Sumedha should be told. As it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa (Bu. Va. 2.1-33):

Kappe ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye;

Amaraṃ nāma nagaraṃ, dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ.

A hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable aeons ago, there was a delightful and charming city named Amara.

Dasahi [M 0.0034] saddehi avivittaṃ, annapānasamāyutaṃ;

Hatthisaddaṃ assasaddaṃ, bherisaṅkharathāni ca;

Khādatha pivatha ceva, annapānena ghositaṃ.

It was not devoid of ten kinds of sounds, replete with food and drink: the sounds of elephants and horses, drums, conches, and chariots; and the calls “Eat and drink!” proclaimed amidst food and drink.

Nagaraṃ [V 0.0035] sabbaṅgasampannaṃ, sabbakammamupāgataṃ;

Sattaratanasampannaṃ, nānājanasamākulaṃ;

Samiddhaṃ devanagaraṃva, āvāsaṃ puññakamminaṃ.

The city was complete in every detail, well-equipped for all kinds of work, abounding in the seven treasures, crowded with people of all sorts, prosperous like a city of the gods, a dwelling place for those who had performed merit.

Nagare amaravatiyā, sumedho nāma brāhmaṇo;

Anekakoṭisannicayo, pahūtadhanadhaññavā.

In the city of Amarāvatī, there was a brahmin named Sumedha, possessing accumulated wealth of many crores, rich in wealth and grain.

Ajjhāyako mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Lakkhaṇe itihāse ca, sadhamme pāramiṃ gato.

A master of recitations, a knower of mantras, an expert in the three Vedas, skilled in signs and legends, he had reached the highest perfection in his own doctrine.

Rahogato nisīditvā, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā;

Dukkho punabbhavo nāma, sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ.

Retiring to solitude, I sat and reflected thus: “Painful is repeated existence, and the breaking apart of the body.”

Jātidhammo jarādhammo, byādhidhammo sahaṃ tadā;

Ajaraṃ amataṃ khemaṃ, pariyesissāmi nibbutiṃ.

I am subject to birth, subject to old age, subject to illness. I will seek the ageless, the deathless, the secure, Nibbāna.

Yaṃnūnimaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, nānākuṇapapūritaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gaccheyyaṃ, anapekkho anatthiko.

Why not discard this foul body, filled with various impurities, and go forth, without longing, without concern?

Atthi hehiti so maggo, na so sakkā na hetuye;

Pariyesissāmi taṃ maggaṃ, bhavato parimuttiyā.

There must be a path; it cannot be that there is not. I will seek that path for liberation from existence.

Yathāpi dukkhe vijjante, sukhaṃ nāmapi vijjati;

Evaṃ bhave vijjamāne, vibhavopi icchitabbako.

Just as where there is suffering, happiness is also found, so where there is existence, non-existence should be desired.

Yathāpi uṇhe vijjante, aparaṃ vijjati sītalaṃ;

Evaṃ tividhaggi vijjante, nibbānaṃ icchitabbakaṃ.

Just as where there is heat, coolness is found, so where there are the three fires, Nibbāna should be desired.

Yathāpi pāpe vijjante, kalyāṇamapi vijjati;

Evameva jāti vijjante, ajātipicchitabbakaṃ.

Just as where evil exists, good also exists; so where birth exists, the unborn should be desired.

Yathā [M 0.0035][V 0.0036] gūthagato puriso, taḷākaṃ disvāna pūritaṃ;

Na gavesati taṃ taḷākaṃ, na doso taḷākassa so.

Just as a man covered in excrement, seeing a pond filled with water, does not seek that pond—that is not the pond’s fault.

Evaṃ kilesamaladhove, vijjante amatantaḷe;

Na gavesati taṃ taḷākaṃ, na doso amatantaḷe.

So too, when the deathless pond exists to wash away the stain of defilements, if one does not seek it, the fault is not in the deathless pond.

Yathā arīhi pariruddho, vijjante gamanampathe;

Na palāyati so puriso, na doso añjasassa so.

Just as a man surrounded by enemies, though a path lies open, does not flee—the fault is not in the open path.

Evaṃ kilesapariruddho, vijjamāne sive pathe;

Na gavesati taṃ maggaṃ, na doso sivamañjase.

So too, though the peaceful path exists, one besieged by defilements does not seek it—the fault is not in the peaceful path itself.

Yathāpi byādhito puriso, vijjamāne tikicchake;

Na tikicchāpeti taṃ byādhiṃ, na doso so tikicchake.

Just as a sick man, though a physician exists, does not have his illness treated—the fault is not the physician's.

Evaṃ kilesabyādhīhi, dukkhito paripīḷito;

Na gavesati taṃ ācariyaṃ, na doso so vināyake.

So too, afflicted and tormented by the sickness of defilements, he does not seek a teacher—the fault is not in the guide.

Yathāpi kuṇapaṃ puriso, kaṇṭhe baddhaṃ jigucchiya;

Mocayitvāna gaccheyya, sukhī serī sayaṃvasī.

Just as a man disgusted by a corpse tied around his neck, casting it off, would go away free, happy, and self-possessed.

Tathevimaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, nānākuṇapasañcayaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gaccheyyaṃ, anapekkho anatthiko.

So too, this foul body, a heap of various corpses—I will discard it and go forth, without longing, without concern.

Yathā uccāraṭṭhānamhi, karīsaṃ naranāriyo;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gacchanti, anapekkhā anatthikā.

Just as men and women discard excrement in a latrine and go away without concern or desire,

Evamevāhaṃ [V 0.0037] imaṃ kāyaṃ, nānākuṇapapūritaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gacchissaṃ, vaccaṃ katvā yathā kuṭiṃ.

So too, I will discard this body, filled with various kinds of corpses, like leaving excrement in a hut.

Yathāpi jajjaraṃ nāvaṃ, paluggaṃ udagāhiniṃ;

Sāmī chaḍḍetvā gacchanti, anapekkhā anatthikā.

Just as owners abandon a rotten, leaking boat and go away without any concern or further use for it,

Evamevāhaṃ imaṃ kāyaṃ, navacchiddaṃ dhuvassavaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gacchissaṃ, jiṇṇanāvaṃva sāmikā.

So too will I discard this body, with its nine openings, constantly oozing, just as owners abandon a decrepit boat.

Yathāpi puriso corehi, gacchanto bhaṇḍamādiya;

Bhaṇḍacchedabhayaṃ disvā, chaḍḍayitvāna gacchati.

Just as a man carrying goods, waylaid by thieves, seeing the danger of plunder, discards them and goes on.

Evameva [M 0.0036] ayaṃ kāyo, mahācorasamo viya;

Pahāyimaṃ gamissāmi, kusalacchedanābhayā.

So too, this body is like a great thief. I will abandon it and go forth, for fear of the destruction of what is wholesome.

Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, nekakoṭisataṃ dhanaṃ;

Nāthānāthānaṃ datvāna, himavantamupāgamiṃ.

Having considered thus, and having given away countless crores in wealth to those with and without protectors, I went to the Himalayas.

Himavantassāvidūre, dhammiko nāma pabbato;

Assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā.

Not far from the Himālaya is a mountain named Dhammika; there my hermitage was well-made, my leaf-hut well-constructed.

Caṅkamaṃ tattha māpesiṃ, pañcadosavivajjitaṃ;

Aṭṭhaguṇasamupetaṃ, abhiññābalamāhariṃ.

There I had a walking path constructed, free from the five faults; endowed with eight qualities, I brought forth the power of higher knowledge.

Sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ tattha, navadosamupāgataṃ;

Vākacīraṃ nivāsesiṃ, dvādasaguṇamupāgataṃ.

There I abandoned the cloth, which had acquired nine faults; I wore bark garments, which had acquired twelve virtues.

Aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ[V 0.0038], pajahiṃ paṇṇasālakaṃ;

Upāgamiṃ rukkhamūlaṃ, guṇe dasahupāgataṃ.

I abandoned the leaf-hut, beset with eight faults; I approached the root of a tree, endowed with ten virtues.

Vāpitaṃ ropitaṃ dhaññaṃ, pajahiṃ niravasesato;

Anekaguṇasampannaṃ, pavattaphalamādiyiṃ.

I abandoned completely the grain that is sown and planted; I partook of fallen fruit, endowed with many virtues.

Tatthappadhānaṃ padahiṃ, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame;

Abbhantaramhi sattāhe, abhiññābala pāpuṇinti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.1-33);

There I applied effort in sitting, standing, and walking; within seven days, I attained the power of higher knowledge.

Tattha assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitāti imissā pāḷiyā sumedhapaṇḍitena assamapaṇṇasālācaṅkamā sahatthā māpitā viya vuttā. Ayaṃ panettha attho – mahāsattañhi “himavantaṃ ajjhogāhetvā ajja dhammikapabbataṃ pavisissāmī”ti nikkhantaṃ disvā sakko devānamindo vissakammadevaputtaṃ āmantesi – “gaccha, tāta, ayaṃ sumedhapaṇḍito ‘pabbajissāmī’ti nikkhanto etassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ māpehī”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā ramaṇīyaṃ assamaṃ suguttaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ, manoramaṃ caṅkamañca māpesi. Bhagavā pana tadā attano puññānubhāvena nipphannaṃ taṃ assamapadaṃ sandhāya “sāriputta tasmiṃ dhammikapabbate –

In this passage, “my hermitage was well-made, a leaf-hut well-constructed,” it is said as if the wise Sumedha had the hermitage, leaf-hut, and walking path built with his own hands. The meaning here is this: Seeing the Great Being setting out with the thought, “Having entered the Himālaya, today I will enter Dhammika Mountain,” Sakka, the king of the devas, addressed the devaputta Vissakamma: “Go, dear one, this wise Sumedha has set forth intending to go forth; prepare a dwelling place for him.” Accepting his command, he built a delightful hermitage, a well-protected leaf-hut, and a charming walking path. The Blessed One, however, referring to that hermitage site brought about by the power of his own merit, said to Sāriputta: “On that Dhammika Mountain—”

Assamo [M 0.0037] sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā;

Caṅkamaṃ tattha māpesiṃ, pañcadosavivajjita”nti. –

My hermitage was well-made, a leaf-hut well-constructed; there I had a walking path made, free from the five faults.

Āha. Tattha assamo sukato mayhanti sukato mayā. Paṇṇasālā sumāpitāti paṇṇacchannā sālāpi me sumāpitā ahosi.

He said. Therein, 'my hermitage was well-made' means it was well-made by me. 'A leaf-hut well-constructed' means a leaf-covered hall was also well-constructed for me.

Pañcadosavivajjitanti pañcime caṅkamadosā nāma thaddhavisamatā, antorukkhatā, gahanacchannatā, atisambādhatā, ativisālatāti. Thaddhavisamabhūmibhāgasmiñhi caṅkame caṅkamantassa pādā rujjanti, phoṭā uṭṭhahanti, cittaṃ ekaggataṃ na labhati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vipajjati. Mudusamatale pana phāsuvihāraṃ āgamma kammaṭṭhānaṃ sampajjati. Tasmā thaddhavisamabhūmibhāgatā eko dosoti veditabbo. Caṅkamanassa anto vā majjhe vā koṭiyaṃ vā [V 0.0039] rukkhe sati pamādamāgamma caṅkamantassa nalāṭaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā paṭihaññatīti antorukkhatā dutiyo doso. Tiṇalatādigahanacchanne caṅkame caṅkamanto andhakāravelāyaṃ uragādike pāṇe akkamitvā vā māreti, tehi vā daṭṭho dukkhaṃ āpajjatīti gahanacchannatā tatiyo doso. Atisambādhe caṅkame vitthārato ratanike vā aḍḍharatanike vā caṅkamantassa paricchede pakkhalitvā nakhāpi aṅguliyopi bhijjantīti atisambādhatā catuttho doso. Ativisāle caṅkame caṅkamantassa cittaṃ vidhāvati, ekaggataṃ na labhatīti ativisālatā pañcamo doso. Puthulato pana diyaḍḍharatanaṃ dvīsu passesu ratanamattaanucaṅkamaṃ dīghato saṭṭhihatthaṃ mudutalaṃ samavippakiṇṇavālukaṃ caṅkamaṃ vaṭṭati, cetiyagirimhi dīpappasādakamahāmahindattherassa caṅkamanaṃ viya, tādisaṃ taṃ ahosi. Tenāha “caṅkamaṃ tattha māpesiṃ, pañcadosavivajjita”nti.

'Free from the five faults' means these five faults of a walking path: hardness and unevenness, having trees within, being overgrown with thickets, excessive narrowness, and excessive width. For when walking on a hard and uneven surface, the feet ache, blisters arise, the mind cannot achieve one-pointedness, and the meditation subject is ruined. But on a soft and level ground, one dwells comfortably, and the meditation subject succeeds. Therefore, hardness and unevenness is understood to be the first fault. If there is a tree within, in the middle, or at the end of the walking path, the walker, being heedless, may strike their forehead or head against it. Thus, having trees within is the second fault. When walking on a path overgrown with grass, creepers, and thickets, the walker may step on and kill snakes or other creatures in the dark, or being bitten by them, they suffer pain. Hence, being overgrown with thickets is the third fault. In an excessively narrow path, when one walks within a space of a cubit or half a cubit in width, one may slip at the edge and break one's nails or toes. Thus, excessive narrowness is the fourth fault. In an excessively wide path, the walker’s mind wanders, and one-pointedness is not attained. Therefore, excessive width is the fifth fault. Generally, a suitable walking path is one and a half cubits wide, with a side-path of a cubit on either side, sixty cubits long, with a soft surface and evenly spread sand, like the walking path of the great elder Mahinda, the illuminator of the island, at Cetiyagiri. Such was that path. Therefore he said: 'There I had a walking path made, free from the five faults.'

Aṭṭhaguṇasamupetanti aṭṭhahi samaṇasukhehi upetaṃ. Aṭṭhimāni samaṇasukhāni nāma dhanadhaññapariggahābhāvo anavajjapiṇḍapariyesanabhāvo, nibbutapiṇḍabhuñjanabhāvo, raṭṭhaṃ pīḷetvā dhanasāraṃ vā sīsakahāpaṇādīni vā gaṇhantesu rājakulesu raṭṭhapīḷanakilesābhāvo, upakaraṇesu nicchandarāgabhāvo, coravilope nibbhayabhāvo, rājarājamahāmaccehi asaṃsaṭṭhabhāvo catūsu disāsu appaṭihatabhāvoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti [M 0.0038] “yathā tasmiṃ assame vasantena sakkā honti imāni aṭṭha samaṇasukhāni vindituṃ, evaṃ aṭṭhaguṇasamupetaṃ taṃ assamaṃ māpesi” nti.

'Endowed with eight qualities' means endowed with the eight pleasures of a recluse. These eight pleasures of a recluse are: absence of possessions such as wealth and grain; blameless seeking of alms; peaceful consumption of alms; freedom from the defilement of oppressing the country, as when royal families seize the essence of wealth or principal kahāpaṇas by oppressing the country; absence of desire and passion for requisites; freedom from fear of thieves and plunderers; non-association with kings and their great ministers; and being unobstructed in the four directions. This is what is meant: 'He had that hermitage made, endowed with eight qualities, so that one dwelling there would be able to experience these eight pleasures of a recluse.'

Abhiññābalamāharinti pacchā tasmiṃ assame vasanto kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā abhiññānañca samāpattīnañca uppādanatthāya aniccato dukkhato vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā thāmappattaṃ vipassanābalaṃ āhariṃ. Yathā tasmiṃ vasanto taṃ balaṃ āharituṃ sakkomi, evaṃ taṃ assamaṃ tassa abhiññatthāya vipassanābalassa anucchavikaṃ katvā māpesinti attho.

'I brought forth the power of higher knowledge' means: Later, while dwelling in that hermitage, having performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, I began insight meditation on impermanence and suffering in order to produce the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and I brought forth the power of insight that had reached full strength. The meaning is: I had that hermitage made suitable for that higher knowledge and power of insight, so that I would be able to bring forth that power while dwelling there.

Sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ tattha, navadosamupāgatanti etthāyaṃ anupubbikathā, tadā kira kuṭileṇacaṅkamādipaṭimaṇḍitaṃ pupphūpagaphalūpagarukkhasañchannaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ madhurasalilāsayaṃ apagatavāḷamigabhiṃsanakasakuṇaṃ pavivekakkhamaṃ assamaṃ māpetvā alaṅkatacaṅkamassa ubhosu antesu ālambanaphalakaṃ saṃvidhāya nisīdanatthāya caṅkamavemajjhe samatalaṃ muggavaṇṇasilaṃ māpetvā antopaṇṇasālāyaṃ jaṭāmaṇḍalavākacīratidaṇḍakuṇḍikādike tāpasaparikkhāre maṇḍape pānīyaghaṭapānīyasaṅkhapānīyasarāvāni aggisālāyaṃ aṅgārakapalladāruādīnīti evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ pabbajitānaṃ [V 0.0040] upakārāya saṃvattati, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ māpetvā paṇṇasālāya bhittiyaṃ “ye keci pabbajitukāmā ime parikkhāre gahetvā pabbajantū”ti akkharāni chinditvā devalokameva gate vissakammadevaputte sumedhapaṇḍito himavantapāde girikandarānusārena attano nivāsanānurūpaṃ phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ olokento nadīnivattane vissakammanimmitaṃ sakkadattiyaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ assamaṃ disvā caṅkamakoṭiṃ gantvā padavalañjaṃ apassanto “dhuvaṃ pabbajitā dhuragāme bhikkhaṃ pariyesitvā kilantarūpā āgantvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nisinnā bhavissantī”ti cintetvā thokaṃ āgametvā “ativiya cirāyanti, jānissāmī”ti paṇṇasālakuṭidvāraṃ vivaritvā anto pavisitvā ito cito ca olokento mahābhittiyaṃ akkharāni vācetvā “mayhaṃ kappiyaparikkhārā ete, ime gahetvā pabbajissāmī”ti attanā nivatthapārutaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ pajahi. Tenāha “sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ tatthā”ti. Evaṃ paviṭṭho ahaṃ sāriputta tassaṃ paṇṇasālāyaṃ sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ.

“There I discarded the garment, having come upon the nine faults”—herein is the sequential narrative. At that time, it is said, a hermitage was made, adorned with huts, caves, walking paths, and the like, covered with flowering and fruit-bearing trees, delightful, with reservoirs of sweet water, free from dangerous wild beasts and frightening birds, suitable for seclusion; and at both ends of the decorated walking path a support plank was prepared, and in the middle of the walking path a level, mung-bean-colored stone slab was made for sitting; and inside the leaf-hut, the ascetic’s requisites such as a coil of matted hair, bark-cloth garments, a three-pronged staff, a water pot, and so on; in the pavilion, water jars, water conches, and water bowls; in the fire-hall, a charcoal pan, firewood, and the like—thus, everything that is of use to those who have gone forth was made. On the wall of the leaf-hut, letters were carved: “Whoever wishes to go forth, let them take these requisites and go forth.” After Vissakamma, the son of a deva, had gone to the deva-world, the wise Sumedha, while searching in the foothills of the Himālaya along the mountain ravines for a comfortable place suitable for his dwelling, saw at a bend in the river the delightful hermitage created by Vissakamma, a gift from Sakka. Going to the end of the walking path and not seeing any footprints, he thought, “Surely, the renunciants, weary from seeking alms in a nearby village, have come, entered the leaf-hut, and are now sitting.” Having waited a little, he thought, “They are taking an exceedingly long time; I will find out.” Opening the door of the leaf-hut, he entered and looked around, and reading the letters on the great wall, he thought, “These requisites are suitable for me; taking these, I will go forth.” He then discarded the pair of garments he was wearing. Therefore, it is said, “There I discarded the garment.” Thus, Sāriputta, having entered that leaf-hut, I discarded the garment.

Navadosamupāgatanti [M 0.0039] sāṭakaṃ pajahanto nava dose disvā pajahinti dīpeti. Tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitānañhi sāṭakasmiṃ nava dosā upaṭṭhahanti. Tesu tassa mahagghabhāvo eko doso, parapaṭibaddhatāya uppajjanabhāvo eko, paribhogena lahuṃ kilissanabhāvo eko, kiliṭṭho hi dhovitabbo ca rajitabbo ca hoti, paribhogena lahukaṃ jīraṇabhāvo eko jiṇṇassa hi tunnaṃ vā aggaḷadānaṃ vā kātabbaṃ hoti. Punapariyesanāya durabhisambhavabhāvo eko, tāpasapabbajjāya asāruppabhāvo eko, paccatthikānaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvo eko, yathā hi naṃ paccatthikā na gaṇhanti, evaṃ gopetabbo hoti. Paribhuñjantassa vibhūsanaṭṭhānabhāvo eko, gahetvā carantassa khandhabhāramahicchabhāvo ekoti.

“Having come upon the nine faults” shows that in discarding the cloth garment, one discards it after seeing nine faults. Indeed, for those who have gone forth into the ascetic life, nine faults present themselves concerning a cloth garment. Among them: its high price is one fault; its arising being dependent on others is one; its quickly becoming soiled with use is one—for when soiled, it must be washed and dyed; its quickly wearing out with use is one—for when worn out, it must be mended or patched; the difficulty of obtaining another when seeking it again is one; its unsuitability for the ascetic life is one; its being common property for enemies is one—for it must be guarded so that enemies do not take it; its being a basis for adornment for the user is one; and for one who carries it about, its being a burden on the shoulder and a cause of great desire is one.

Vākacīraṃ nivāsesinti tadā ahaṃ sāriputta ime nava dose disvā sāṭakaṃ pahāya vākacīraṃ nivāsesiṃ muñjatiṇaṃ hīraṃ hīraṃ katvā ganthetvā kataṃ vākacīraṃ nivāsanapārupanatthāya ādiyinti attho.

“I put on a bark-cloth garment”: Then, Sāriputta, seeing these nine faults, I abandoned the cloth garment and put on a bark-cloth garment. The meaning is: I took up, for the purpose of wearing as a lower and upper garment, a bark-cloth garment made by taking muñja grass, making it into strips, and weaving them together.

Dvādasaguṇamupāgatanti dvādasahi ānisaṃsehi samannāgataṃ, vākacīrasmiñhi dvādasānisaṃsā – appagghaṃ sundaraṃ kappiyanti ayaṃ tāva eko ānisaṃso, sahatthā kātuṃ sakkāti ayaṃ dutiyo, paribhogena saṇikaṃ kilissati dhoviyamānepi papañco natthīti ayaṃ tatiyo, paribhogena jiṇṇepi sibbitabbābhāvo catuttho, puna pariyesantassa sukhena karaṇabhāvo [V 0.0041] pañcamo, tāpasapabbajjāya sāruppabhāvo chaṭṭho, paccatthikānaṃ nirupabhogabhāvo sattamo, paribhuñjantassa vibhūsanaṭṭhānābhāvo aṭṭhamo, dhāraṇe sallahukabhāvo navamo, cīvarapaccaye appicchabhāvo dasamo, vākuppattiyā dhammikaanavajjabhāvo ekādasamo vākacīre naṭṭhepi anapekkhabhāvo dvādasamoti.

“Endowed with twelve qualities” means possessed of twelve benefits. For in a bark-cloth garment there are twelve benefits: first, it is inexpensive, beautiful, and suitable; second, it can be made by one’s own hands; third, it becomes soiled slowly with use, and there is no complication when it is washed; fourth, when worn out with use, there is no need for sewing; fifth, when one seeks it again, it is easy to make; sixth, it is suitable for the ascetic life; seventh, it is of no use to enemies; eighth, for the user, it is not a basis for adornment; ninth, it is light to wear; tenth, it fosters fewness of wishes regarding the robe-requisite; eleventh, its acquisition from bark is righteous and blameless; twelfth, even if the bark-cloth garment is lost, there is no longing for it.

Aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ, pajahiṃ paṇṇasālakanti kathaṃ pajahiṃ?
