So kira varasāṭakayugaṃ omuñcanto cīvaravaṃse laggitaṃ anojapupphadāmasadisaṃ rattavākacīraṃ gahetvā nivāsetvā tassupari aparaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ vākacīraṃ paridahitvā punnāgapupphasantharasadisaṃ sakhuraṃ ajinacammaṃ ekaṃsaṃ katvā jaṭāmaṇḍalaṃ [M 0.0040] paṭimuñcitvā cūḷāya saddhiṃ niccalabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ sārasūciṃ pavesetvā muttājālasadisāya sikkāya pavāḷavaṇṇaṃ kuṇḍikaṃ odahitvā tīsu ṭhānesu vaṅkakājaṃ ādāya ekissā kājakoṭiyā kuṇḍikaṃ, ekissā aṅkusakapacchitidaṇḍakādīni olaggetvā khārikājaṃ aṃse katvā dakkhiṇena hatthena kattaradaṇḍaṃ gahetvā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā saṭṭhihatthe mahācaṅkame aparāparaṃ caṅkamanto attano vesaṃ oloketvā “mayhaṃ manoratho matthakaṃ patto, sobhati vata me pabbajjā, buddhapaccekabuddhādīhi sabbehipi dhīrapurisehi vaṇṇitā thomitā ayaṃ pabbajjā nāma, pahīnaṃ me gihibandhanaṃ, nikkhantosmi nekkhammaṃ, laddhā me uttamapabbajjā, karissāmi samaṇadhammaṃ, labhissāmi aggaphalasukha”nti ussāhajāto khārikājaṃ otāretvā caṅkamavemajjhe muggavaṇṇasilāpaṭṭe suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya nisinno divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā bidalamañcakapasse kaṭṭhattharikāya nipanno sarīraṃ utuṃ gāhāpetvā balavapaccūse pabujjhitvā attano āgamanaṃ āvajjesi “ahaṃ gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ disvā amitabhogaṃ anantayasaṃ pahāya araññaṃ pavisitvā nekkhamagavesako hutvā pabbajito, ito dāni paṭṭhāya pamādacāraṃ carituṃ na vaṭṭati, pavivekañhi pahāya vicarantaṃ micchāvitakkamakkhikā khādanti, idāni mayā pavivekamanubrūhetuṃ vaṭṭati, ahañhi gharāvāsaṃ palibodhato disvā nikkhanto, ayañca manāpā paṇṇasālā, beluvapakkavaṇṇā paribhaṇḍakatā bhūmi, rajatavaṇṇā setabhittiyo, kapotapādavaṇṇaṃ paṇṇacchadanaṃ, vicittattharaṇavaṇṇo bidalamañcako, nivāsaphāsukaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, na etto atirekatarā viya me gehasampadā paññāyatī”ti paṇṇasālāya dose vicinanto aṭṭha dose passi.

How did he abandon the leaf-hut, which was filled with eight faults? It is said that while removing his fine pair of garments, he took a reddish bark garment resembling a garland of Anojā flowers that was hanging from a robe-rack, and put it on. Over that, he draped another golden-hued bark garment. He placed an antelope skin with its hooves, resembling a spread of punnāga flowers, over one shoulder, arranged his matted hair, and inserted a pin of sāra wood into his topknot to keep it steady. From a carrying-net resembling a net of pearls, he hung a coral-colored water pot. Taking a crooked carrying-pole, from one end he suspended the water pot, and from the other, a goad, a small axe, and other implements. Placing the carrying-pole on his shoulder and holding a cutting staff in his right hand, he left the leaf-hut. Walking back and forth along a sixty-cubit-long promenade, he observed his own appearance and thought, “My aspiration has reached its peak. Truly, my ascetic life is splendid! This life of renunciation is praised and extolled by all wise persons—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others. I have abandoned the bondage of household life; I have gone forth into renunciation. I have obtained the supreme life of renunciation. I will practice the duties of a recluse; I shall attain the bliss of the supreme fruit.” Filled with enthusiasm, he lowered the carrying-pole and sat in the middle of the promenade on a mung-bean-colored stone slab, like a golden statue. After spending the day thus, he entered the leaf-hut in the evening. Lying on a wooden plank beside the split-bamboo bed, he allowed his body to adjust to the temperature and awoke at dawn. Reflecting on his arrival, he thought, “Having seen the drawbacks of household life, I abandoned immeasurable wealth and endless fame to enter the forest, seeking renunciation, and went forth. From now on, it is not fitting to be heedless. Indeed, those who abandon seclusion and wander about are devoured by the flies of wrong thoughts. Now, I must cultivate seclusion. I went forth, seeing the household life as an obstruction. And this leaf-hut is delightful—its prepared floor is the color of a ripe bel fruit, its white walls are the color of silver, its leaf roof is the color of a pigeon’s foot, the split-bamboo bed is like a colorful spread, and the dwelling is comfortable. The splendor of my home does not seem to be any greater than this.” Investigating the faults of the leaf-hut, he saw eight faults.

Paṇṇasālāparibhogasmiñhi aṭṭha ādīnavā – mahāsamārambhena? Dabbasambhāre samodhānetvā karaṇapariyesanabhāvo [V 0.0042] eko ādīnavo. Tiṇapaṇṇamattikāsu patitāsu tāsaṃ punappunaṃ ṭhapetabbatāya nibaddhajagganabhāvo [M 0.0041] dutiyo, senāsanaṃ nāma mahallakassa pāpuṇāti, avelāya vuṭṭhāpiyamānassa cittekaggatā na hotīti uṭṭhāpanīyabhāvo tatiyo, sītuṇhapaṭighātena kāyassa sukhumālakaraṇabhāvo catuttho, gehaṃ paviṭṭhena yaṃkiñci pāpaṃ sakkā kātunti garahapaṭicchādanabhāvo pañcamo, “mayha”nti pariggahakaraṇabhāvo chaṭṭho, gehassa atthibhāvo nāmesa dutiyakavāso viyāti sattamo ūkāmaṅgulagharagoḷikādīnaṃ sādhāraṇatāya bahusādhāraṇabhāvo aṭṭhamoti ime aṭṭha ādīnave disvā mahāsatto paṇṇasālaṃ pajahi. Tenāha “aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ, pajahiṃ paṇṇasālaka”nti.

Indeed, in the use of a leaf-hut, there are eight drawbacks. The first drawback is the great undertaking: the need to gather materials and to seek out the means of construction. The second is the need for constant upkeep: when grass, leaves, and clay fall away, they must be repeatedly replaced. The third is the liability of being displaced: for a lodging must be yielded to a senior, and if one is roused at an improper time, one’s concentration of mind is lost. The fourth is that it makes the body delicate through protection from cold and heat. The fifth is the concealment of what is blameworthy: for one who has entered a house can commit any kind of wrong. The sixth is the act of taking possession by thinking, “This is mine.” The seventh is that the very existence of a house is like having a companion. The eighth is that it is shared with many creatures: it is common property with lice, bugs, house lizards, and so forth. Seeing these eight drawbacks, the Great Being abandoned the leaf-hut. Therefore it is said: “I abandoned the leaf-hut, which was filled with eight faults.”

Upāgamiṃ rukkhamūlaṃ guṇe dasahupāgatanti channaṃ paṭikkhipitvā dasahi guṇehi upetaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upāgatosmīti vadati.

He says: “I approached the root of a tree, endowed with ten virtues,” meaning, “Having rejected the six faults, I approached the root of a tree endowed with ten virtues.”

Tatrime dasa guṇā – appasamārambhatā eko guṇo upagamanamattameva hi tattha hotīti. Appaṭijagganatā dutiyo tañhi sammaṭṭhampi asammaṭṭhampi paribhogaphāsukaṃ hotiyeva. Anuṭṭhāpanīyabhāvo tatiyo, garahaṃ nappaṭicchādeti, tattha hi pāpaṃ karonto lajjatīti garahāya appaṭicchādanabhāvo catuttho, abbhokāsāvāso viya kāyaṃ na santhambhetīti kāyassa asanthambhanabhāvo pañcamo. Pariggahakaraṇābhāvo chaṭṭho, gehālayapaṭikkhepo sattamo, bahusādhāraṇagehe viya “paṭijaggissāmi naṃ, nikkhamathā”ti nīharaṇābhāvo aṭṭhamo, vasantassa sappītikabhāvo navamo, rukkhamūlasenāsanassa gatagataṭṭhāne sulabhatāya anapekkhabhāvo dasamoti, ime dasa guṇe disvā rukkhamūlaṃ upāgatosmīti vadati.

Herein, these are the ten virtues. First, little undertaking, for one only has to go there. Second, no need for upkeep, for it is comfortable to use whether swept or unswept. Third, not being liable to be displaced. Fourth, not concealing what is blameworthy, for one who commits a wrong there feels shame. Fifth, not making the body soft, as it is like living in the open air. Sixth, the absence of taking possession. Seventh, the rejection of attachment to a dwelling. Eighth, the absence of having to evict others, unlike in a shared dwelling where one might say, “I will maintain this, so you must leave.” Ninth, a sense of joy for one who dwells there. Tenth, being without concern, as a lodging at the root of a tree is easy to find wherever one goes. Seeing these ten virtues, he says, “I approached the root of a tree.”

Imāni ettakāni kāraṇāni sallakkhetvā mahāsatto punadivase bhikkhāya gāmaṃ pāvisi. Athassa sampattagāme manussā mahantena ussāhena bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. So bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā assamaṃ āgamma nisīditvā cintesi “nāhaṃ ‘āhāraṃ na labhāmī’ti pabbajito siniddhāhāro nāmesa mānamadapurisamade vaḍḍheti. Āhāramūlakassa dukkhassa anto natthi yaṃnūnāhaṃ vāpitaṃ ropitaṃ dhaññanibbattakaṃ āhāraṃ pajahitvā pavattaphalabhojano bhaveyya”nti. So tato paṭṭhāya tathā [M 0.0042] katvā ghaṭento vāyamanto sattāhabbhantareyeva aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having considered these many reasons, the Great Being entered a village for alms-food on the following day. Then, in the village he had reached, the people offered him alms-food with great enthusiasm. Having finished his meal, he returned to the hermitage, sat down, and reflected: “I did not go forth thinking, ‘I will not obtain food.’ Indeed, rich food increases pride, intoxication, and manly vanity. There is no end to the suffering that is rooted in food. What if I were to abandon food produced from sown and planted grain and live on naturally fallen fruit?” From that time onward, he did so, and by striving and making an effort, within seven days he brought forth the eight attainments and the five supernormal knowledges. Therefore it was said:

“Vāpitaṃ [V 0.0043] ropitaṃ dhaññaṃ, pajahiṃ niravasesato;

Anekaguṇasampannaṃ, pavattaphalamādiyiṃ.

“The sown and planted grain I abandoned, leaving nothing behind; endowed with many virtues, I partook of the spontaneously fallen fruit.

“Tatthappadhānaṃ padahiṃ, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame;

Abbhantaramhi sattāhe, abhiññābala pāpuṇi”nti.

“There I applied myself to exertion, in sitting, standing, and walking; within seven days I attained the power of direct knowledge.”

Evaṃ me siddhippattassa, vasībhūtassa sāsane;

Dīpaṅkaro nāma jino, uppajji lokanāyako.

Thus, when I had attained success and mastery in the Dispensation, the Victor named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the world, arose.

Uppajjante ca jāyante, bujjhante dhammadesane;

Caturo nimitte nāddasaṃ, jhānaratisamappito.

During his arising, birth, awakening, and teaching of the Dhamma, I did not see the four omens, being devoted to the delight of jhāna.

Paccantadesavisaye, nimantetvā tathāgataṃ;

Tassa āgamanaṃ maggaṃ, sodhenti tuṭṭhamānasā.

In a border region, having invited the Tathāgata, they were clearing the path for his arrival with joyful hearts.

Ahaṃ tena samayena, nikkhamitvā sakassamā;

Dhunanto vākacīrāni, gacchāmi ambare tadā.

At that time, having left my own hermitage, shaking my bark garments, I was then travelling through the sky.

Vedajātaṃ janaṃ disvā, tuṭṭhahaṭṭhaṃ pamoditaṃ;

Orohitvāna gaganā, manusse pucchi tāvade.

Seeing the people filled with joy, delighted and happy, I descended from the sky and immediately asked them:

“Tuṭṭhahaṭṭho pamudito, vedajāto mahājano;

Kassa sodhīyati maggo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ”.

“The great crowd is joyful, delighted, and elated; for whom is this straight and even road being cleared?”

Te me puṭṭhā viyākaṃsu “buddho loke anuttaro;

Dīpaṅkaro nāma jino, uppajji lokanāyako;

Tassa sodhīyati maggo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ”.

They, being asked by me, answered: “The Buddha, unsurpassed in the world, the Victor named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the world, has arisen. For him this straight and even road is being cleared.”

“Buddho”ti vacanaṃ sutvāna, pīti uppajji tāvade;

“Buddho buddho”ti kathayanto, somanassaṃ pavedayiṃ.

Hearing the word ‘Buddha,’ rapture arose in me immediately; saying ‘Buddha, Buddha,’ I expressed my gladness.

Tattha [V 0.0044] ṭhatvā vicintesiṃ, tuṭṭho saṃviggamānaso;

“Idha bījāni ropissaṃ, khaṇo ve mā upaccagā”.

Standing there, I reflected, with a pleased and stirred mind: “Here I shall sow seeds; may the opportune moment not pass me by.”

Yadi buddhassa sodhetha, ekokāsaṃ dadātha me;

Ahampi sodhayissāmi, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ.

“If you are clearing the path for the Buddha, give me one section; I too shall clear the straight and even road.”

Adaṃsu [M 0.0043] te mamokāsaṃ, sodhetuṃ añjasaṃ tadā;

“Buddho buddho”ti cintento, maggaṃ sodhemahaṃ tadā.

They then gave me a section to clear the straight path; thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha,’ I then cleared the path.

Aniṭṭhite pamokāse, dīpaṅkaro mahāmuni;

Catūhi satasahassehi, chaḷabhiññehi tādihi;

Khīṇāsavehi vimalehi, paṭipajji añjasaṃ jino.

While my section was still unfinished, the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara, the Victor, proceeded along the straight path, together with four hundred thousand who possessed the six higher knowledges, were of such a nature, had destroyed the taints, and were stainless.

Paccuggamanā vattanti, vajjanti bheriyo bahū;

Āmoditā naramarū, sādhukāraṃ pavattayuṃ.

Processions to welcome him were taking place, many drums were sounding; humans and gods, delighted, raised a cry of approval.

Devā manusse passanti, manussāpi ca devatā;

Ubhopi te pañjalikā, anuyanti tathāgataṃ.

The gods saw the humans, and the humans also saw the gods; both, with hands folded in reverence, followed the Tathāgata.

Devā dibbehi turiyehi, manussā mānusehi ca;

Ubhopi te vajjayantā, anuyanti tathāgataṃ.

The gods with divine instruments, and humans with human ones, both playing music, followed the Tathāgata.

Dibbaṃ mandāravaṃ pupphaṃ, padumaṃ pārichattakaṃ;

Disodisaṃ okiranti, ākāsanabhagatā marū.

Celestial mandārava flowers, lotuses, and pārichattaka flowers, the gods in the sky scattered in all directions.

Dibbaṃ candanacuṇṇañca, varagandhañca kevalaṃ;

Disodisaṃ okiranti, ākāsanabhagatā marū.

Divine sandalwood powder and the choicest fragrances, the gods in the sky scattered in all directions.

Campakaṃ [V 0.0045] salalaṃ nīpaṃ, nāgapunnāgaketakaṃ;

Disodisaṃ ukkhipanti, bhūmitalagatā narā.

People on the ground tossed up campaka, salala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka flowers in all directions.

Kese muñcitvāhaṃ tattha, vākacīrañca cammakaṃ;

Kalale pattharitvāna, avakujjo nipajjahaṃ.

There I let loose my hair, and spread my bark garment and hide upon the mud; I then lay down face down.

Akkamitvāna maṃ buddho, saha sissehi gacchatu;

Mā naṃ kalale akkamittha, hitāya me bhavissati.

“May the Buddha, having stepped on me, go forth with his disciples. Let him not step on the mud; it will be for my welfare.”

Pathaviyaṃ nipannassa, evaṃ me āsi cetaso;

“Icchamāno ahaṃ ajja, kilese jhāpaye mama.

As I lay on the earth, this thought arose in me: “If I so wished, today I could burn up my defilements.

“Kiṃ me aññātavesena, dhammaṃ sacchikatenidha;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, buddho hessaṃ sadevake.

“What use is it for me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown guise? Having attained omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world with its gods.

“Kiṃ [M 0.0044] me ekena tiṇṇena, purisena thāmadassinā;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, santāressaṃ sadevakaṃ.

“What use is it for me, a man of strength, to cross over alone? Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world with its gods.

“Iminā me adhikārena, katena purisuttame;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, tāremi janataṃ bahuṃ.

“By this act of service of mine, performed for the foremost of men, having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across many people.

“Saṃsārasotaṃ chinditvā, viddhaṃsetvā tayo bhave;

Dhammanāvaṃ samāruyha, santāressaṃ sadevakaṃ”.

“Having cut the stream of saṃsāra, having shattered the three states of existence, and having boarded the boat of Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world with its gods.”

Dīpaṅkaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Ussīsake maṃ ṭhatvāna, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the Receiver of Offerings, stood at my head and spoke this word:

“Passatha [V 0.0046] imaṃ tāpasaṃ, jaṭilaṃ uggatāpanaṃ;

Aparimeyye ito kappe, buddho loke bhavissati.

“Behold this ascetic with matted hair, practicing intense austerity. In an incalculable aeon from now, he will become a Buddha in the world.

“Ahu kapilavhayā rammā, nikkhamitvā tathāgato;

Padhānaṃ padahitvāna, katvā dukkarakārikaṃ.

“Having gone forth from the lovely city named Kapila, as a Tathāgata he will undertake the exertion, performing the difficult practice.

“Ajapālarukkhamūle, nisīditvā tathāgato;

Tattha pāyāsaṃ paggayha, nerañjaramupehiti.

“At the foot of the goatherd's banyan tree, the Tathāgata will sit. There he will accept the milk-rice, and then approach the Nerañjarā River.

“Nerañjarāya tīramhi, pāyāsaṃ ada so jino;

Paṭiyattavaramaggena, bodhimūlamupehiti.

On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Victor will eat the milk-rice; by way of the excellent prepared path, he will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree.

“Tato padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, bodhimaṇḍaṃ anuttaro;

Assattharukkhamūlamhi, bujjhissati mahāyaso.

Then, having circumambulated the Bodhi-platform, the unsurpassed one, the greatly renowned one, will awaken at the foot of the Assattha tree.

“Imassa janikā mātā, māyā nāma bhavissati;

Pitā suddhodano nāma, ayaṃ hessati gotamo.

“This one's mother will be named Māyā, and his father Suddhodana. This one will be Gotama.

“Anāsavā vītarāgā, santacittā samāhitā;

Kolito upatisso ca, aggā hessanti sāvakā;

Ānando nāmupaṭṭhāko, upaṭṭhissatimaṃ jinaṃ.

“Kolita and Upatissa, free from taints, rid of lust, with tranquil minds, well-composed, will be the foremost disciples. Ānanda by name will be the attendant; he will attend upon this Victor.

“Khemā uppalavaṇṇā ca, aggā hessanti sāvikā;

Anāsavā vītarāgā, santacittā samāhitā.

“Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā will be the foremost female disciples, free from taints, rid of lust, with tranquil minds, well-composed.

“Bodhi [M 0.0045] tassa bhagavato, assatthoti pavuccati;

Citto ca hatthāḷavako, aggā hessantupaṭṭhakā;

Uttarā nandamātā ca, aggā hessantupaṭṭhikā”.

“The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Assattha. Citta and Hatthāḷavaka will be the foremost male lay-supporters; Uttarā and Nandamātā will be the foremost female lay-supporters.”

Idaṃ [V 0.0047] sutvāna vacanaṃ, asamassa mahesino;

Āmoditā naramarū, buddhabījaṃ kira ayaṃ.

Hearing this word of the unequalled great sage, gods and humans rejoiced: “This is indeed a Buddha-seed!”

Ukkuṭṭhisaddā vattanti, apphoṭenti hasanti ca;

Katañjalī namassanti, dasasahassī sadevakā.

Shouts of acclamation arose, they clapped their hands and laughed. With palms joined in reverence, the ten-thousandfold world-system with its gods paid homage.

Yadimassa lokanāthassa, virajjhissāma sāsanaṃ;

Anāgatamhi addhāne, hessāma sammukhā imaṃ.

“If we should miss the dispensation of this Lord of the World, in a future time, we will be face to face with this one.”

Yathā manussā nadiṃ tarantā, paṭititthaṃ virajjhiya;

Heṭṭhā titthe gahetvāna, uttaranti mahānadiṃ.

Just as people crossing a river, having missed the opposite ford, take a ford downstream and cross the great river,

Evameva mayaṃ sabbe, yadi muñcāmimaṃ jinaṃ;

Anāgatamhi addhāne, hessāma sammukhā imaṃ.

so too, all of us, if we miss this Victor, in a future time, we will be face to face with him.

Dīpaṅkaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mama kammaṃ pakittetvā, dakkhiṇaṃ pādamuddhari.

Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the Receiver of Offerings, having proclaimed my deed, raised his right foot.

Ye tatthāsuṃ jinaputtā, sabbe padakkhiṇamakaṃsu maṃ;

Narā nāgā ca gandhabbā, abhivādetvāna pakkamuṃ.

All the sons of the Victor who were there circumambulated me. Humans, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having paid homage, departed.

Dassanaṃ me atikkante, sasaṅghe lokanāyake;

Haṭṭhatuṭṭhena cittena, āsanā vuṭṭhahiṃ tadā.

When the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha, had passed from my sight, with a joyful and delighted heart, I then rose from my seat.

Sukhena sukhito homi, pāmojjena pamodito;

Pītiyā ca abhissanno, pallaṅkaṃ ābhujiṃ tadā.

With happiness I was happy, with joy I was joyful; suffused with rapture, I then folded my legs into the cross-legged posture.

Pallaṅkena [V 0.0048] nisīditvā, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā;

“Vasībhūto ahaṃ jhāne, abhiññāpāramiṃ gato.

Having sat in the cross-legged posture, I then reflected thus: "I have become a master of jhāna, I have attained the perfection of higher knowledge.

“Dasasahassilokamhi[M 0.0046], isayo natthi me samā;

Asamo iddhidhammesu, alabhiṃ īdisaṃ sukhaṃ”.

In the ten-thousandfold world-system, there are no seers equal to me. Unmatched in the qualities of psychic power, I have attained such happiness."

Pallaṅkābhujane mayhaṃ, dasasahassādhivāsino;

Mahānādaṃ pavattesuṃ, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Upon my sitting in the cross-legged posture, the inhabitants of the ten-thousandfold world-system uttered a great roar: "Surely, you will become a Buddha!

Yā pubbe bodhisattānaṃ, pallaṅkavaramābhuje;

Nimittāni padissanti, tāni ajja padissare.

The signs that appeared for past Bodhisattas upon sitting in the excellent cross-legged posture—those signs appear today.

Sītaṃ byapagataṃ hoti, uṇhañca upasammati;

Tāni ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

The cold departs, and the heat subsides; these signs appear today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Dasasahassī lokadhātū, nissaddā honti nirākulā;

Tāni ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

The ten-thousandfold world-system becomes silent and undisturbed; these signs appear today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Mahāvātā na vāyanti, na sandanti savantiyo;

Tāni ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

The great winds do not blow, the flowing rivers do not flow; these signs appear today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Thalajā dakajā pupphā, sabbe pupphanti tāvade;

Tepajja pupphitā sabbe, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

All flowers, both land-born and water-born, bloom at that moment; all these have bloomed today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Latā vā yadi vā rukkhā, phalabhārā honti tāvade;

Tepajja phalitā sabbe, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Vines and trees become heavy with fruit at that moment; all these have borne fruit today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Ākāsaṭṭhā [V 0.0049] ca bhūmaṭṭhā, ratanā jotanti tāvade;

Tepajja ratanā jotanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Jewels in the sky and on the earth shine at that moment; these jewels shine today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Mānussakā ca dibbā ca, turiyā vajjanti tāvade;

Tepajjubho abhiravanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Human and celestial musical instruments are played at that moment; both resound today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Vicittapupphā gaganā, abhivassanti tāvade;

Tepi ajja pavassanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Flowers of various kinds rain down from the sky at that moment; they rain down today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Mahāsamuddo ābhujati, dasasahassī pakampati;

Tepajjubho abhiravanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

The great ocean surges, the ten-thousandfold world-system quakes; both resound today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Nirayepi [M 0.0047] dasasahasse, aggī nibbanti tāvade;

Tepajja nibbutā aggī, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

In the ten-thousand hells, fires are extinguished at that moment; those fires are extinguished today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Vimalo hoti sūriyo, sabbā dissanti tārakā;

Tepi ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

The sun is spotless, and all the stars are seen; these too are visible today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Anovaṭṭhena udakaṃ, mahiyā ubbhijji tāvade;

Tampajjubbhijjate mahiyā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Without rain, water sprang forth from the earth at that moment; that too springs forth from the earth today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Tārāgaṇā virocanti, nakkhattā gaganamaṇḍale;

Visākhā candimāyuttā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Hosts of stars shine, constellations in the celestial sphere; Visākhā is conjoined with the moon—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Bilāsayā darīsayā, nikkhamanti sakāsayā;

Tepajja āsayā chuddhā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Creatures of holes and mountain clefts emerge from their own lairs; today those lairs are also abandoned—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Na [V 0.0050] hoti arati sattānaṃ, santuṭṭhā honti tāvade;

Tepajja sabbe santuṭṭhā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

There is no discontent among beings; they are satisfied at that very moment. Today also all are satisfied—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Rogā tadupasammanti, jighacchā ca vinassati;

Tānipajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Diseases then subside, and hunger is destroyed; these things too are seen today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Rogo tadā tanu hoti, doso moho vinassati;

Tepajja vigatā sabbe, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Illness then grows faint, aversion and delusion are destroyed; today all these have departed—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Bhayaṃ tadā na bhavati, ajjapetaṃ padissati;

Tena liṅgena jānāma, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Fear does not exist then; this too is seen today. By this sign we know—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Rajo nuddhaṃsati uddhaṃ, ajjapetaṃ padissati;

Tena liṅgena jānāma, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Dust is not blown upwards; this too is seen today. By this sign we know—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Aniṭṭhagandho pakkamati, dibbagandho pavāyati;

Sopajja vāyati gandho, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Unpleasant odors depart, a divine fragrance spreads; that fragrance too wafts today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Sabbe devā padissanti, ṭhapayitvā arūpino;

Tepajja sabbe dissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

All the gods are seen, except for the formless ones; all these are seen today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Yāvatā nirayā nāma, sabbe dissanti tāvade;

Tepajja sabbe dissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

As many hells as there are, all are seen at that very moment; all these are seen today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Kuṭṭā [M 0.0048] kavāṭā selā ca, na hontāvaraṇā tadā;

Akāsabhūtā tepajja, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Walls, gates, and rocks are then no obstruction; today they become like open space—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Cutī [V 0.0051] ca upapatti ca, khaṇe tasmiṃ na vijjati;

Tānipajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Passing away and rebirth are not found in that moment; these things too are seen today—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Daḷhaṃ paggaṇha vīriyaṃ, mā nivatta abhikkama;

Mayampetaṃ vijānāma, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

Firmly exert your energy, do not turn back, go forward; we too know this—surely, you will become a Buddha!

Buddhassa vacanaṃ sutvā, dasasahassīnacūbhayaṃ;

Tuṭṭhahaṭṭho pamodito, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā.

Having heard the word of the Buddha and of the inhabitants of the ten-thousandfold world-system, I was pleased, gladdened, and joyful; at that time, I thought thus:

Advejjhavacanā buddhā, amoghavacanā jinā;

Vitathaṃ natthi buddhānaṃ, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavāmahaṃ.

The Buddhas are of unambiguous speech, the Conquerors are of unfailing speech; there is no falsehood in the Buddhas—surely I will become a Buddha.

Yathā khittaṃ nabhe leḍḍu, dhuvaṃ patati bhūmiyaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

Just as a clod of earth thrown into the sky surely falls to the ground, so too is the word of the supreme Buddhas—certain and eternal.

Yathāpi sabbasattānaṃ, maraṇaṃ dhuvasassataṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

Just as for all beings death is certain and constant, so too is the word of the supreme Buddhas—certain and constant.

Yathā rattikkhaye patte, sūriyuggamanaṃ dhuvaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

Just as when the night has ended the rising of the sun is certain, so too is the word of the supreme Buddhas—certain and eternal.

Yathā nikkhantasayanassa, sīhassa nadanaṃ dhuvaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

Just as the roar of a lion that has come out of its lair is certain, so too is the word of the supreme Buddhas—certain and eternal.

Yathā āpannasattānaṃ, bhāramoropanaṃ dhuvaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

Just as for a pregnant woman the laying down of her burden is certain, so too is the word of the supreme Buddhas—certain and eternal.

Handa buddhakare dhamme, vicināmi ito cito;

Uddhaṃ adho dasa disā, yāvatā dhammadhātuyā.

Come now, let me investigate the qualities that make a Buddha, searching here and there, above, below, and in the ten directions, as far as the realm of the Dhamma extends.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, anuciṇṇaṃ mahāpathaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the first perfection of giving, a great path practiced by the great sages of the past.

Imaṃ [V 0.0052] tvaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Dānapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This first, then, you must firmly undertake; practice the perfection of giving, if you wish to attain awakening.

Yathāpi [M 0.0049] kumbho sampuṇṇo, yassa kassaci adhokato;

Vamate vudakaṃ nissesaṃ, na tattha parirakkhati.

Just as a full pot, when overturned by someone, pours out all its water completely, not holding any back,

Tatheva yācake disvā, hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime;

Dadāhi dānaṃ nissesaṃ, kumbho viya adhokato.

So too, seeing beggars—low, excellent, or middling—give your gift completely, like an overturned pot.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Indeed, the qualities for Buddhahood cannot be only this much; I will seek out other qualities as well that are conducive to awakening.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, dutiyaṃ sīlapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the second perfection of virtue, practiced and cultivated by the great sages of the past.

Imaṃ tvaṃ dutiyaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Sīlapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This second one, then, you must firmly undertake; practice the perfection of virtue, if you wish to attain awakening.

Yathāpi camarī vālaṃ, kismiñci paṭilaggitaṃ;

Upeti maraṇaṃ tattha, na vikopeti vāladhiṃ.

Just as a yak, when its tail is caught on something, meets death there but does not damage its tail,

Tatheva catūsu bhūmīsu, sīlāni paripūraya;

Parirakkha sadā sīlaṃ, camarī viya vāladhiṃ.

So too, in the four planes, fulfill your virtues; always protect your virtue, as a yak protects its tail.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Indeed, the qualities for Buddhahood cannot be only this much; I will seek out other qualities as well that are conducive to awakening.

Vicinanto [V 0.0053] tadādakkhiṃ, tatiyaṃ nekkhammapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the third perfection of renunciation, cultivated and practiced by the great sages of old.

Imaṃ tvaṃ tatiyaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Nekkhammapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This third one, then, you must firmly undertake; practice the perfection of renunciation, if you wish to attain awakening.

Yathā andughare puriso, ciravuttho dukhaṭṭito;

Na tattha rāgaṃ janeti, muttimeva gavesati.

Just as a man long dwelling in a prison, afflicted by suffering, generates no attachment there, but only seeks release,

Tatheva tvaṃ sabbabhave, passa andugharaṃ viya;

Nekkhammābhimukho hoti, bhavato parimuttiyā.

So too, you should see all existence as a prison; be intent on renunciation for the sake of release from existence.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Indeed, the qualities for Buddhahood cannot be only this much; I will seek out other qualities as well that are conducive to awakening.

Vicinanto [M 0.0050] tadādakkhiṃ, catutthaṃ paññāpāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the fourth perfection of wisdom, cultivated and practiced by the great sages of old.

Imaṃ tvaṃ catutthaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Paññāpāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This fourth one, then, you must firmly undertake; practice the perfection of wisdom, if you wish to attain awakening.

Yathāpi bhikkhu bhikkhanto, hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime;

Kulāni na vivajjento, evaṃ labhati yāpanaṃ.

Just as a monk on his alms round does not avoid families—low, high, or in between—and thus obtains his sustenance,

Tatheva tvaṃ sabbakālaṃ, paripucchaṃ budhaṃ janaṃ;

Paññāpāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

So too, you should at all times question the wise; having reached the perfection of wisdom, you will attain supreme awakening.

Na [V 0.0054] hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Indeed, the qualities for Buddhahood cannot be only this much; I will seek out other qualities as well that are conducive to awakening.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, pañcamaṃ vīriyapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the fifth perfection of energy, cultivated and practiced by the great sages of old.

Imaṃ tvaṃ pañcamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Vīriyapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This fifth one, then, you must firmly undertake; practice the perfection of energy, if you wish to attain awakening.

Yathāpi sīho migarājā, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame;

Alīnavīriyo hoti, paggahitamano sadā.

Just as the lion, the king of beasts, whether sitting, standing, or walking, is of unflagging energy, with mind always uplifted,

Tatheva tvaṃ sabbabhave, paggaṇha vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ;

Vīriyapāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

So too, in all states of existence, exert firm energy; having reached the perfection of energy, you will attain supreme awakening.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Indeed, the qualities for Buddhahood cannot be only this much; I will seek out other qualities as well that are conducive to awakening.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, chaṭṭhamaṃ khantipāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the sixth perfection of patience, cultivated and practiced by the great sages of old.

Imaṃ tvaṃ chaṭṭhamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tattha advejjhamānaso, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

This sixth one, then, having firmly undertaken it, with an unwavering mind therein, you will attain supreme awakening.

Yathāpi pathavī nāma, sucimpi asucimpi ca;

Sabbaṃ sahati nikkhepaṃ, na karoti paṭighaṃ tayā.

Just as the earth bears all that is cast upon it, both the pure and the impure, and shows no aversion,

Tatheva [M 0.0051][V 0.0055] tvampi sabbesaṃ, sammānāvamānakkhamo;

Khantipāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

So too, you should endure all honor and dishonor; having reached the perfection of patience, you will attain supreme awakening.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Indeed, the qualities for Buddhahood cannot be only this much; I will seek out other qualities as well that are conducive to awakening.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, sattamaṃ saccapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the seventh perfection of truth, cultivated and practiced by the great sages of old.

Imaṃ tvaṃ sattamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tattha advejjhavacano, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

This seventh one, then, having firmly undertaken it, with unwavering speech therein, you will attain supreme awakening.

Yathāpi osamī nāma, tulābhūtā sadevake;

Samaye utuvasse vā, na vokkamati, vīthito.

Just as the morning star, a standard for the world with its devas, does not deviate from its path in any season or weather,

Tatheva tvampi saccesu, mā vokkamasi vīthito;

Saccapāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

So too, you should not deviate from the path of the truths; having reached the perfection of truth, you will attain supreme awakening.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Indeed, the qualities for Buddhahood cannot be only this much; I will seek out other qualities as well that are conducive to awakening.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, aṭṭhamaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Investigating, I then saw the eighth perfection of resolve, cultivated and practiced by the great seers of old.

Imaṃ tvaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tattha tvaṃ acalo hutvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

This eighth one, then, having firmly undertaken it, being unshakeable therein, you will attain supreme awakening.

Yathāpi [V 0.0056] pabbato selo, acalo suppatiṭṭhito;

Na kampati bhusavātehi, sakaṭṭhāneva tiṭṭhati.

Just as a mountain of rock, unshakable and well-established, is not shaken by fierce winds, but remains in its very own place.

Tatheva tvampi adhiṭṭhāne, sabbadā acalo bhava;

Adhiṭṭhānapāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

So too, in your resolve, be always unshakable; having fulfilled the perfection of determination, you will attain supreme enlightenment.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

These alone are not all the qualities of a Buddha; I will seek out other qualities as well, those that lead to enlightenment.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, navamaṃ mettāpāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

While searching, I then saw the ninth perfection of loving-kindness, which was practiced and cultivated by the great seers of the past.

Imaṃ [M 0.0052] tvaṃ navamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Mettāya asamo hohi, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This ninth perfection you should firmly undertake; be without equal in loving-kindness, if you wish to attain enlightenment.

Yathāpi udakaṃ nāma, kalyāṇe pāpake jane;

Samaṃ pharati sītena, pavāheti rajomalaṃ.

Just as water bestows its coolness equally upon the virtuous and the wicked, and washes away dust and impurities.

Tatheva tvampi hitāhite, samaṃ mettāya bhāvaya;

Mettāpāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

So too, towards those who help and those who harm, develop loving-kindness equally; having fulfilled the perfection of loving-kindness, you will attain supreme enlightenment.

Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

These alone are not all the qualities of a Buddha; I will seek out other qualities as well, those that lead to enlightenment.

Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, dasamaṃ upekkhāpāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

While searching, I then saw the tenth perfection of equanimity, which was practiced and cultivated by the great seers of the past.

Imaṃ [V 0.0057] tvaṃ dasamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tulābhūto daḷho hutvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

This tenth perfection you should firmly undertake; becoming balanced and steadfast, you will attain supreme enlightenment.

Yathāpi pathavī nāma, nikkhittaṃ asuciṃ suciṃ;

Upekkhati ubhopete, kopānunayavajjitā.

Just as the earth regards with equanimity both the pure and the impure that are cast upon it, being free from aversion and approval.

Tatheva tvampi sukhadukkhe, tulābhūto sadā bhava;

Upekkhāpāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

So too, in happiness and suffering, always remain balanced; having fulfilled the perfection of equanimity, you will attain supreme enlightenment.

Ettakāyeva te loke, ye dhammā bodhipācanā;

Tatuddhaṃ natthi aññatra, daḷhaṃ tattha patiṭṭhaha.

These alone in the world are the qualities that lead to enlightenment; there are no others beyond them. Be firmly established therein.

Ime dhamme sammasato, sabhāvarasalakkhaṇe;

Dhammatejena vasudhā, dasasahassī pakampatha.

As I was contemplating these qualities—their intrinsic nature, essence, and characteristics—by the power of the Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold earth trembled.

Calatā ravati pathavī, ucchuyantaṃva pīḷitaṃ;

Telayante yathā cakkaṃ, evaṃ kampati medinī.

The shaking earth roared like a sugarcane press in operation; just as the wheel of an oil-press revolves, so did the earth tremble.

Yāvatā parisā āsi, buddhassa parivesane;

Pavedhamānā sā tattha, mucchitā sesi bhūmiyā.

The entire assembly that was in attendance on the Buddha, trembling violently there, fainted and fell upon the ground.

Ghaṭānekasahassāni[M 0.0053], kumbhīnañca satā bahū;

Sañcuṇṇamathitā tattha, aññamaññaṃ paghaṭṭitā.

Many thousands of pots and many hundreds of jars were crushed and smashed there, striking against one another.

Ubbiggā tasitā bhītā, bhantā byāthitamānasā;

Mahājanā samāgamma, dīpaṅkaramupāgamuṃ.

Agitated, terrified, and afraid, bewildered and with distressed minds, the great crowd of people gathered together and approached Dīpaṅkara.

Kiṃ [V 0.0058] bhavissati lokassa, kalyāṇamatha pāpakaṃ;

Sabbo upadduto loko, taṃ vinodehi cakkhuma.

“What will become of the world—good or evil? The whole world is in distress; dispel it, O One with Vision!”

Tesaṃ tadā saññāpesi, dīpaṅkaro mahāmuni;

Vissatthā hotha mā bhātha, imasmiṃ pathavikampane.

Then the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara reassured them: “Be at ease, do not be afraid of this earthquake.”

Yamahaṃ ajja byākāsiṃ, buddho loke bhavissati;

Eso sammasati dhammaṃ, pubbakaṃ jinasevitaṃ.

“The one of whom I prophesied today, ‘A Buddha will arise in the world,’ is now contemplating the Dhamma practiced by past Victors.”

Tassa sammasato dhammaṃ, buddhabhūmiṃ asesato;

Tenāyaṃ kampitā pathavī, dasasahassī sadevake.

“Because he is contemplating the Dhamma, the entire ground of Buddhahood, for this reason the earth has shaken, this ten-thousandfold world-system with its devas.”

Buddhassa vacanaṃ sutvā, mano nibbāyi tāvade;

Sabbe maṃ upasaṅkamma, punāpi abhivandisuṃ.

Hearing the Buddha's words, their minds were instantly calmed. All of them approached me and paid homage once again.

Samādayitvā buddhaguṇaṃ, daḷhaṃ katvāna mānasaṃ;

Dīpaṅkaraṃ namassitvā, āsanā vuṭṭhahiṃ tadā.

Having undertaken the qualities of a Buddha and made my mind firm, I paid homage to Dīpaṅkara and then rose from my seat.

Dibbaṃ mānusakaṃ pupphaṃ, devā mānusakā ubho;

Samokiranti pupphehi, vuṭṭhahantassa āsanā.

As I was rising from my seat, both devas and humans scattered divine and human flowers upon me.

Vedayanti ca te sotthiṃ, devā mānusakā ubho;

Mahantaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, taṃ labhassu yathicchitaṃ.

And both devas and humans proclaimed my well-being: “Great is your aspiration; may you obtain it just as you wish.”

Sabbītiyo vivajjantu, soko rogo vinassatu;

Mā te bhavantvantarāyā, phusa khippaṃ bodhimuttamaṃ.

“May all calamities be averted, may sorrow and disease perish; may there be no obstacles for you, and may you quickly attain supreme enlightenment.”

Yathāpi [V 0.0059] samaye patte, pupphanti pupphino dumā;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, buddhañāṇena pupphasu.

“Just as flowering trees blossom when their season arrives, so too, O Great Hero, may you blossom with the knowledge of a Buddha!”

Yathā [M 0.0054] ye keci sambuddhā, pūrayuṃ dasapāramī;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, pūrehi dasapāramī.

“Just as all the Buddhas whatsoever fulfilled the ten perfections, even so, O Great Hero, fulfill the ten perfections.”

Yathā ye keci sambuddhā, bodhimaṇḍamhi bujjhare;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, bujjhassu jinabodhiyaṃ.

“Just as all the Buddhas whatsoever have awakened at the seat of enlightenment, so too, O Great Hero, may you awaken to the enlightenment of a Victor.”

Yathā ye keci sambuddhā, dhammacakkaṃ pavattayuṃ;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, dhammacakkaṃ pavattaya.

“Just as all the Buddhas whatsoever set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, even so, O Great Hero, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.”

Puṇṇamāye yathā cando, parisuddho virocati;

Tatheva tvaṃ puṇṇamano, viroca dasasahassiyaṃ.

“As the full moon, perfectly pure, shines, so too, with a fulfilled mind, may you shine over the ten-thousandfold world-system.”

Rāhumutto yathā sūriyo, tāpena atirocati;

Tatheva lokā muñcitvā, viroca siriyā tuvaṃ.

“Just as the sun freed from Rāhu shines exceedingly with heat, even so you, released from the world, shine forth with glory!”

Yathā yā kāci nadiyo, osaranti mahodadhiṃ;

Evaṃ sadevakā lokā, osarantu tavantike.

“As whatever rivers flow into the great ocean, so may the worlds with their devas flow to your presence.”

Tehi thutappasattho so, dasa dhamme samādiya;

Te dhamme paripūrento, pavanaṃ pāvisī tadā.

Praised and extolled by them, he undertook the ten qualities; fulfilling those qualities, he then entered the forest.

Sumedhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The story of Sumedha is concluded.

Tadā te bhojayitvāna, sasaṅghaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Upagacchuṃ saraṇaṃ tassa, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno.

Having then fed the World-Leader together with his Sangha, they went for refuge to that Teacher, Dīpaṅkara.

Saraṇāgamane [V 0.0060] kañci, nivesesi tathāgato;

Kañci pañcasu sīlesu, sīle dasavidhe paraṃ.

The Tathāgata established some in the going for refuge, some in the five precepts, and others in the tenfold higher morality.

Kassaci deti sāmaññaṃ, caturo phalamuttame;

Kassaci asame dhamme, deti so paṭisambhidā.

To some he gave the ascetic life and the four supreme fruits; to others, he gave the analytical insights regarding the unsurpassed Dhamma.

Kassaci varasamāpattiyo, aṭṭha deti narāsabho;

Tisso kassaci vijjāyo, chaḷabhiññā pavecchati.

To some, the Bull among Men gave the eight excellent attainments; to some, the three knowledges; and to some he bestowed the six superknowledges.

Tena [M 0.0055] yogena janakāyaṃ, ovadati mahāmuni;

Tena vitthārikaṃ āsi, lokanāthassa sāsanaṃ.

By that method, the Great Sage instructed the populace. Thus the Dispensation of the Lord of the World was widely spread.

Mahāhanusabhakkhandho, dīpaṅkarasanāmako;

Bahū jane tārayati, parimoceti duggatiṃ.

The one named Dīpaṅkara, with mighty jaws and bull-like shoulders, leads many people across, releasing them from woeful states.

Bodhaneyyaṃ janaṃ disvā, satasahassepi yojane;

Khaṇena upagantvāna, bodheti taṃ mahāmuni.

Seeing people capable of being awakened, even a hundred thousand yojanas away, in an instant the Great Sage approaches and awakens them.

Paṭhamābhisamaye buddho, koṭisatamabodhayi;

Dutiyābhisamaye nātho, navutikoṭimabodhayi.

At the first comprehension, the Buddha awakened one hundred koṭis; at the second comprehension, the Protector awakened ninety koṭis.

Yadā ca devabhavanamhi, buddho dhammadesayi;

Navutikoṭisahassānaṃ, tatiyābhisamayo ahu.

And when the Buddha taught the Dhamma in the abode of the devas, the third comprehension for ninety thousand koṭis occurred.

Sannipātā tayo āsuṃ, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno;

Koṭisatasahassānaṃ, paṭhamo āsi samāgamo.

There were three assemblies of the Teacher, Dīpaṅkara; the first gathering was of one hundred thousand koṭis.

Puna [V 0.0061] nāradakūṭamhi, pavivekagate jine;

Khīṇāsavā vītamalā, samiṃsu satakoṭiyo.

Again at Nārada Peak, when the Victor had gone into seclusion, a hundred koṭis of those with taints destroyed, free from defilement, assembled.

Yamhi kāle mahāvīro, sudassanasiluccaye;

Navutikoṭisahassehi, pavāresi mahāmuni.

At the time when the Great Hero, the Great Sage, was on the Sudassana mountain peak, he concluded the rains-residence with ninety thousand koṭis.

Ahaṃ tena samayena, jaṭilo uggatāpano;

Antalikkhamhi caraṇo, pañcābhiññāsu pāragū.

At that time, I was a matted-hair ascetic of fierce austerity, a sky-farer, proficient in the five superknowledges.

Dasavīsasahassānaṃ, dhammābhisamayo ahu;

Ekadvinnaṃ abhisamayā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā.

For ten or twenty thousand, there was a comprehension of the Dhamma; for one or two, the comprehensions were incalculable by number.

Vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ, iddhaṃ phītaṃ ahu tadā;

Dīpaṅkarassa bhagavato, sāsanaṃ suvisodhitaṃ.

Widespread, populous, successful, and prosperous was it then; the Dispensation of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, thoroughly purified.

Cattāri satasahassāni, chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā;

Dīpaṅkaraṃ lokaviduṃ, parivārenti sabbadā.

Four hundred thousand with the six superknowledges and great psychic power always attended upon Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.

Ye [M 0.0056] keci tena samayena, jahanti mānusaṃ bhavaṃ;

Appattamānasā sekhā, garahitā bhavanti te.

Whoever at that time abandoned human existence while still a trainee who had not attained the goal, they were blameworthy.

Supupphitaṃ pāvacanaṃ, arahantehi tādihi;

Khīṇāsavehi vimalehi, upasobhati sadevake.

The well-blossomed teaching, adorned by the Arahants—the Such Ones, the stainless ones with taints destroyed—shines forth in the world with its devas.

Nagaraṃ rammavatī nāma, sudevo nāma khattiyo;

Sumedhā nāma janikā, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno.

The city was named Rammavatī, the khattiya was named Sudeva, and the mother of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sumedhā.

Sumaṅgalo [V 0.0062] ca tisso ca, ahesuṃ aggasāvakā;

Sāgato nāmupaṭṭhāko, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno.

Sumaṅgala and Tissa were the chief disciples; the attendant of the Teacher, Dīpaṅkara, was named Sāgata.

Nandā ceva sunandā ca, ahesuṃ aggasāvikā;

Bodhi tassa bhagavato, pipphalīti pavuccati.

Nandā and Sunandā were the chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Pipphalī.

Asītihatthamubbedho, dīpaṅkaro mahāmuni;

Sobhati dīparukkhova, sālarājāva pupphito;

Pabhā vidhāvati tassa, samantā dvādasayojane.

Eighty cubits in height, the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara shines like a lamp-tree, like a flowering Sāla king; his radiance spreads all around for twelve yojanas.

Satasahassavassāni, āyu tassa mahesino;

Tāvatā tiṭṭhamāno so, tāresi janataṃ bahuṃ.

A hundred thousand years was the lifespan of that great sage; remaining for that long, he ferried many people across.

Jotayitvāna saddhammaṃ, santāretvā mahājanaṃ;

Jalitvā aggikkhandhova, nibbuto so sasāvako.

Having illuminated the true Dhamma and ferried the great multitude across, he, like a blazing mass of fire, was extinguished along with his disciples.

Sā ca iddhi so ca yaso, tāni ca pādesu cakkaratanāni;

Sabbaṃ tamantarahitaṃ, nanu rittā sabbasaṅkhārāti.

That power and that glory, and those wheel-jewels on the feet—all that has disappeared. Are not all conditioned things truly empty?

Dīpaṅkarassa bhagavato aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā koṇḍañño nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassaṃ. Dutiye koṭisahassaṃ, tatiye navutikoṭiyo.

In the period following the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, after one incalculable aeon had passed, a teacher named Koṇḍañña arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand koṭis; in the second, one thousand koṭis; and in the third, ninety koṭis.

Tadā bodhisatto vijitāvī nāma cakkavattī hutvā koṭisatasahassasaṅkhassa buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Satthā bodhisattaṃ “buddho bhavissatī”ti byākaritvā dhammaṃ desesi. So satthu [M 0.0057] dhammakathaṃ sutvā rajjaṃ niyyātetvā pabbaji. So tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo, pañca ca abhiññāyo uppādetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke nibbatti. Koṇḍaññabuddhassa pana rammavatī nāma nagaraṃ, sunando nāma khattiyo pitā, sujātā [V 0.0063] nāma mātā, bhaddo ca subhaddo ca dve aggasāvakā, anuruddho nāma upaṭṭhāko, tissā ca upatissā ca dve aggasāvikā, sālakalyāṇī bodhi, aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ, vassasatasahassaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch named Vijitāvī, gave a great alms offering to the Sangha of monks numbering one hundred thousand koṭis, headed by the Buddha. The Teacher, making a prediction concerning the Bodhisatta, “He will become a Buddha,” then taught the Dhamma. Hearing the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he relinquished his kingdom and went forth. He mastered the three Piṭakas, produced the eight attainments and the five superknowledges, and, without declining from his jhāna, was reborn in the Brahma world. For Koṇḍañña Buddha, the city was named Rammavatī, his father was the khattiya Sunanda, and his mother was Sujātā. Bhadda and Subhadda were his two chief disciples, Anuruddha was his attendant, and Tissā and Upatissā were his two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the Sālakalyāṇī. His body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā ekasmiṃyeva kappe cattāro buddhā nibbattiṃsu maṅgalo sumano revato sobhitoti. Maṅgalassa pana bhagavato tīsu sāvakasannipātesu paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ. Dutiye koṭisahassaṃ. Tatiye navutikoṭiyo. Vemātikabhātā panassa ānandakumāro nāma navutikoṭisaṅkhyāya parisāya saddhiṃ dhammasavanatthāya satthu santikaṃ agamāsi, satthā tassa anupubbikathaṃ kathesi. So saddhiṃ parisāya saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Satthā tesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ pubbacariyakaṃ olokento iddhimayapattacīvarassa upanissayaṃ disvā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā “etha bhikkhavo”ti āha. Sabbe taṅkhaṇaññeva iddhimayapattacīvaradharā saṭṭhivassikattherā viya ākappasampannā hutvā satthāraṃ vanditvā parivārayiṃsu ayamassa tatiyo sāvakasannipāto ahosi.

In the period following him, after one incalculable aeon had passed, in one and the same aeon, four Buddhas arose: Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita. For the Blessed One Maṅgala, in his three assemblies of disciples, there were in the first assembly one hundred thousand koṭis of monks; in the second, one thousand koṭis; and in the third, ninety koṭis. His half-brother, Prince Ānanda by name, along with an assembly numbering ninety koṭis, approached the Teacher to hear the Dhamma. The Teacher gave him a gradual discourse. Together with his assembly, he attained arahantship along with the analytical insights. The Teacher, observing the past conduct of these noble sons and seeing their potential for the psychically created bowl and robe, extended his right hand and said, “Come, monks!” Instantly, they all became bearers of the psychically created bowl and robe, perfect in deportment like elders of sixty rains. They paid homage to the Teacher and surrounded him. This was his third assembly of disciples.

Yathā pana aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ samantā asītihatthappamāṇāyeva sarīrappabhā hoti, na, evaṃ tassa. Tassa pana bhagavato sarīrappabhā niccakālaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi. Rukkhapathavīpabbatasamuddādayo antamaso ukkhaliyādīni upādāya suvaṇṇapaṭa pariyonaddhā viya ahesuṃ. Āyuppamāṇaṃ panassa navutivassasahassāni ahosi. Ettakaṃ kālaṃ candimasūriyādayo attano pabhāya virocituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, rattindivaparicchedo na paññāyittha. Divā sūriyālokena viya sattā niccaṃ buddhālokeneva vicariṃsu. Sāyaṃ pupphitānaṃ kusumānaṃ, pāto ravanakasakuṇānañca vasena loko rattindivaparicchedaṃ sallakkhesi[M 0.0058]. Kiṃ pana aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ ayamānubhāvo natthīti? No natthi, tepi hi ākaṅkhamānā dasasahassiṃ vā lokadhātuṃ, tato vā bhiyyo ābhāya phareyyuṃ. Maṅgalassa pana bhagavato pubbapatthanāvasena aññesaṃ byāmappabhā viya sarīrappabhā niccameva dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi.

Now, it was not for him as it is for other Buddhas, whose bodily radiance extends only eighty cubits around. The bodily radiance of that Blessed One constantly pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system and remained. Trees, earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth, down to the very cooking pots, appeared as if covered with a golden cloth. His lifespan, however, was ninety thousand years. During that entire time, the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies could not shine with their own light, and the distinction between night and day was not discernible. Beings constantly moved about in the Buddha’s light, as if in daylight from the sun. The world marked the division of night and day only by the blooming of flowers in the evening and the singing of birds in the morning. Is it then that other Buddhas do not have this power? Not so. For they too, if they wished, could pervade the ten-thousandfold world-system or even more with their radiance. However, due to a previous aspiration of the Blessed One Maṅgala, his bodily radiance—unlike the fathom-long radiance of others—constantly pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system and remained.

So kira bodhisattacariyakāle vessantarasadise attabhāve ṭhito saputtadāro vaṅkapabbatasadise pabbate vasi. Atheko kharadāṭhiko nāma yakkho mahāpurisassa dānajjhāsayataṃ sutvā brāhmaṇavaṇṇena upasaṅkamitvā mahāsattaṃ dve dārake yāci. Mahāsatto “dadāmi [V 0.0064] brāhmaṇassa puttake”ti haṭṭhapahaṭṭho udakapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ kampento dvepi dārake adāsi. Yakkho caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ālambanaphalakaṃ nissāya ṭhatvā passantasseva mahāsattassa muḷālakalāpaṃ viya dve dārake khādi. Mahāpurisassa yakkhaṃ oloketvā vivaṭamatte aggijālaṃ viya lohitadhāraṃ uggiramānaṃ tassa mukhaṃ disvāpi kesaggamattampi domanassaṃ nuppajji, “sudinnaṃ vata me dāna”nti cintayato panassa sarīre mahantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ udapādi. So “imassa me nissandena anāgate imināva nīhārena sarīrato rasmiyo nikkhamantū”ti patthanaṃ akāsi. Tassa taṃ patthanaṃ nissāya buddhabhūtassa sarīrato rasmiyo nikkhamitvā ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ phariṃsu.

It is said that during his career as a Bodhisatta, in an existence similar to that of Vessantara, he lived on a mountain resembling Vaṅka Hill, together with his wife and children. Then a yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, hearing of the Great Being’s inclination for generosity, approached him in the guise of a brahmin and begged the Great Being for his two children. The Great Being, overjoyed and delighted, declared, “I give the children to the brahmin,” and as he gave away both children, the earth shook up to its watery limits. The yakkha, leaning against a railing post at the end of the walking path, devoured the two children right before the Great Being’s eyes, as if eating a bunch of lotus stalks. Even upon seeing the yakkha’s mouth, wide open like a blazing fire and spewing streams of blood, not even a hair’s breadth of sorrow arose in the Great Being. Instead, as he reflected, “Truly, my gift has been well given,” immense joy and happiness arose in his body. He then made this aspiration: “By the fruit of this deed of mine, in the future may rays of light emanate from my body in this very manner.” Based on that aspiration of his, when he became a Buddha, rays of light emanated from his body and pervaded such a great expanse.

Aparampissa pubbacaritaṃ atthi. So kira bodhisattakāle ekassa buddhassa cetiyaṃ disvā “imassa buddhassa mayā jīvitaṃ pariccajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti daṇḍakadīpikāveṭhananiyāmena sakalasarīraṃ veṭhāpetvā ratanamattamakulaṃ satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ sappissa pūrāpetvā tattha sahassavaṭṭiyo jālāpetvā taṃ sīsenādāya sakalasarīraṃ jālāpetvā cetiyaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto sakalarattiṃ vītināmesi. Evaṃ yāva aruṇuggamanā vāyamantassāpissa lomakūpamattampi usumaṃ na gaṇhi, padumagabbhaṃ paviṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Dhammo hi nāmesa attānaṃ rakkhantaṃ rakkhati. Tenāha bhagavā –

There is another past deed of his as well. It is said that during his time as a Bodhisatta, upon seeing a stupa of a Buddha, he thought, “It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for this Buddha.” Having his entire body wrapped with oil-soaked cloths in the manner of a torch-stick, he had a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, adorned with a jewel-bud, filled with ghee, lit a thousand wicks in it, and taking it on his head, he set his whole body ablaze. Circumambulating the stupa, he spent the entire night in this manner. Even as he strove thus until the rising of the dawn, not even the slightest heat touched him—it was as if he had entered the heart of a lotus. For truly, the Dhamma protects the one who protects himself. Thus said the Blessed One:

“Dhammo [M 0.0059] have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ,

Dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahāti;

Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe,

Na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī”ti. (theragā. 303; jā. 1.10.102; 1.15.385);

“The Dhamma, indeed, protects one who practices the Dhamma;

The Dhamma, well practiced, brings happiness.

This is the benefit of the well-practiced Dhamma:

One who practices the Dhamma does not go to a woeful state.”

Imassāpi kammassa nissandena tassa bhagavato sarīrobhāso dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi.

As a result of this deed also, the radiance of the Blessed One’s body pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system and remained.

Tadā amhākaṃ bodhisatto suruci nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā “satthāraṃ nimantessāmī”ti upasaṅkamitvā madhuradhammakathaṃ sutvā “sve mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhatha bhante”ti āha. Brāhmaṇa kittakehi [V 0.0065] te bhikkhūhi atthoti, kittakā pana vo bhante parivārā bhikkhūti. Tadā satthu paṭhamasannipātoyeva hoti. Tasmā “koṭisatasahassa”nti āha. “Bhante, sabbehipi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Satthā adhivāsesi. Brāhmaṇo svātanāya nimantetvā gehaṃ gacchanto cintesi “ahaṃ ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāgubhattavatthādīni dātuṃ no na sakkomi, nisīdanaṭṭhānaṃ pana kathaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Tassa sā cintā caturāsītiyojanasahassamatthake ṭhitassa devarañño paṇḍukambalasilāsanassa uṇhabhāvaṃ janesi. Sakko “ko nu kho maṃ imasmā ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti dibbacakkhunā olokento mahāpurisaṃ disvā “ayaṃ suruci brāhmaṇo buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā nisīdanaṭṭhānatthāya cintesi, mayāpi tattha gantvā puññakoṭṭhāsaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vaḍḍhakivaṇṇaṃ nimminitvā vāsipharasuhattho mahāpurisassa purato pāturahosi. “Atthi nu kho kassaci bhatiyā kattabbakicca”nti āha. Mahāpuriso taṃ disvā “kiṃ kammaṃ karissasī”ti āha. Mama ajānanasippaṃ nāma natthi, gehaṃ vā maṇḍapaṃ vā yo yaṃ kāreti, tassa taṃ kātuṃ jānāmīti. Tena hi mayhaṃ kammaṃ atthīti. Kiṃ, ayyāti? Svātanāya me koṭisatasahassabhikkhū nimantitā, tesaṃ nisīdanamaṇḍapaṃ karissasīti. Ahaṃ nāma kareyyaṃ, sace me bhatiṃ dātuṃ sakkhissathāti. Sakkhissāmi, tātāti. “Sādhu karissāmī”ti gantvā ekaṃ padesaṃ olokesi.

At that time, our Bodhisatta had become a brahmin named Suruci. Thinking, “I will invite the Teacher,” he approached him. After hearing the sweet Dhamma talk, he said, “Venerable sir, please accept my alms-food tomorrow.” The Teacher asked, “Brahmin, for how many monks do you require it?” The brahmin asked, “Venerable sir, how many monks are in your retinue?” At that time, it was the Teacher’s very first gathering. Therefore, he replied, “A hundred thousand koṭis.” The brahmin said, “Venerable sir, please accept my alms-food along with all of them.” The Teacher consented. As the brahmin went home after inviting them for the next day, he thought, “I am certainly able to provide rice gruel, food, robes, and so on for so many monks; but how will there be seating space for them?” His thought caused the Paṇḍukambala stone throne of Sakka, king of the devas, situated at a height of eighty-four thousand yojanas, to become hot. Sakka wondered, “Who now wishes to dislodge me from this place?” and surveying with his divine eye, he saw the great being. He thought, “This brahmin Suruci, having invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, is concerned about seating space. It is fitting for me to go there and receive a share of the merit.” Assuming the form of a carpenter, with an adze and axe in hand, he appeared before the great being. “Is there any work to be done for hire?” he asked. The great being, seeing him, asked, “What work can you do?” “There is no craft I do not know. Whatever house or pavilion someone has me build, I know how to build it for them.” “In that case, I have work for you.” “What is it, sir?” “For tomorrow, I have invited a hundred thousand koṭis of monks. Can you build a seating pavilion for them?” “I can indeed build it, if you are able to pay my wages.” “I am able, my good man.” “Very well, I will do it.” He then went and surveyed a suitable place.

Dvādasaterasayojanappamāṇo [M 0.0060] padeso kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ viya samatalo ahosi. So “ettake ṭhāne sattaratanamayo maṇḍapo uṭṭhahatū”ti cintetvā olokesi. Tāvadeva pathaviṃ bhinditvā maṇḍapo uṭṭhahi. Tassa suvaṇṇamayesu thambhesu rajatamayā ghaṭakā ahesuṃ, rajatamayesu thambhesu suvaṇṇamayā, maṇitthambhesu pavāḷamayā, pavāḷatthambhesu maṇimayā, sattaratanamayesu thambhesu sattaratanamayāva ghaṭakā ahesuṃ. Tato “maṇḍapassa antarantena kiṅkiṇikajālaṃ olambatū”ti olokesi. Saha olokaneneva kiṅkiṇikajālaṃ olambi, yassa mandavāteritassa pañcaṅgikasseva tūriyassa madhurasaddo niggacchati. Dibbasaṅgītivattanakālo viya ahosi. “Antarantarā gandhadāmamālādāmāni olambantū”ti cintesi. Tāvadeva dāmāni olambiṃsu. “Koṭisatasahassasaṅkhyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āsanāni ca ādhārakāni ca pathaviṃ bhinditvā uṭṭhahantū”ti cintesi. Tāvadeva uṭṭhahiṃsu. “Koṇe koṇe ekekā udakacāṭiyo uṭṭhahantū”ti cintesi, tāvadeva udakacāṭiyo uṭṭhahiṃsu ettakaṃ māpetvā brāhmaṇassa santikaṃ gantvā “ehi ayya tava maṇḍapaṃ oloketvā mayhaṃ bhatiṃ dehī”ti āha. Mahāpuriso gantvā maṇḍapaṃ olokesi[V 0.0066]. Olokentassevassa sakalasarīraṃ pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ ahosi. Athassa maṇḍapaṃ oloketvā etadahosi “nāyaṃ maṇḍapo manussabhūtena kato, mayhaṃ pana ajjhāsayaṃ mayhaṃ guṇaṃ āgamma addhā sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi. Tato sakkena devaraññā ayaṃ maṇḍapo kārito bhavissatī”ti. “Na kho pana me yuttaṃ evarūpe maṇḍape ekadivasaṃyeva dānaṃ dātuṃ, sattāhaṃ dassāmī”ti cintesi.

An area measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas became as level as a kasiṇa disc. He thought, “Let a pavilion made of the seven precious gems arise in this place,” and surveyed it. Instantly, splitting the earth, the pavilion arose. Its golden pillars had silver capitals, its silver pillars had golden capitals, its jeweled pillars had coral capitals, its coral pillars had jeweled capitals, and its pillars made of the seven precious gems had capitals also made of the seven precious gems. Then he thought, “Let a net of tinkling bells hang within the pavilion,” and surveyed it. As soon as he looked, the net of bells hung down, from which, stirred by a gentle breeze, a sweet sound like that of a five-piece orchestra emanated. It was as if the time for divine music had arrived. He thought, “Let garlands of fragrant flowers and wreaths hang at intervals,” and instantly the garlands hung down. He thought, “Let seats and supports for a hundred thousand koṭis of monks split the earth and arise,” and instantly they arose. He thought, “Let one water pot arise in each corner,” and instantly the water pots arose. Having created all this, he went to the brahmin and said, “Come, sir, inspect your pavilion and give me my wages.” The great being went and surveyed the pavilion. As he looked, his entire body was instantly and completely suffused with five-hued rapture. Then, having seen the pavilion, this thought occurred to him: “This pavilion was not made by a human being. Surely, on account of my resolve and my virtue, Sakka’s abode must have grown hot. Therefore, this pavilion must have been built by Sakka, the king of the devas.” He further thought, “It is not fitting for me to give alms in such a pavilion for only one day. I will give for seven days.”

Bāhirakadānañhi tattakampi samānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Alaṅkatasīsaṃ pana chinditvā añjitaakkhīni uppāṭetvā, hadayamaṃsaṃ vā uppāṭetvā dinnakāle bodhisattānaṃ cāgaṃ nissāya tuṭṭhi nāma hoti. Amhākampi hi bodhisattassa sivijātake devasikaṃ pañcasatasahassakahāpaṇāni vissajjetvā catūsu nagaradvāresu, majjhe nagare ca dānaṃ dadantassa taṃ dānaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ uppādetuṃ nāsakkhi. Yadā panassa brāhmaṇavaṇṇena āgantvā sakko devarājā akkhīni yāci, tadā tāni uppāṭetvā [M 0.0061] dadamānasseva hāso uppajji, kesaggamattampi cittassa aññathattaṃ nāhosi. Evaṃ dānaṃ nissāya bodhisattānaṃ titti nāma natthi. Tasmā sopi mahāpuriso “sattāhaṃ mayā koṭisatasahassasaṅkhyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā tasmiṃ maṇḍape buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā sattāhaṃ gavapānaṃ nāma adāsi. Gavapānanti mahante mahante kolambe khīrassa pūretvā uddhanesu āropetvā ghanapākapakke khīre thoke taṇḍule pakkhipitvā pakkamadhusakkaracuṇṇasappīhi abhisaṅkhataṃ bhojanaṃ vuccati. Manussāyeva pana parivisituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, devāpi ekantarikā hutvā parivisiṃsu. Dvādasaterasayojanappamāṇaṃ ṭhānampi bhikkhū gaṇhituṃ nappahotiyeva. Te pana bhikkhū attano ānubhāvena nisīdiṃsu. Pariyosānadivase sabbabhikkhūnaṃ pattāni dhovāpetvā bhesajjatthāya sappinavanītatelamadhuphāṇitānaṃ pūretvā ticīvarehi saddhiṃ adāsi. Saṅghanavakabhikkhunā laddhaticīvarasāṭakā satasahassagghanikā ahesuṃ. Satthā anumodanaṃ karonto “ayaṃ puriso evarūpaṃ mahādānaṃ adāsi, ko nu kho bhavissatī”ti upadhārento “anāgate kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ dvinnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake gotamo nāma buddho bhavissatī”ti disvā mahāpurisaṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ ettakaṃ nāma kālaṃ atikkamitvā gotamo nāma buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

Even an external gift, though of such a kind, cannot bring satisfaction to the Bodhisattvas. But when one offers a severed adorned head, plucks out one’s anointed eyes, or tears out one’s heart-flesh—only then does satisfaction arise in the Bodhisattvas, on account of such generosity. For even when our Bodhisattva, in the Sivi Jātaka, daily distributed five hundred thousand coins at the four city gates and in the city center, that gift could not bring him satisfaction. Yet when Sakka, the king of the devas, came disguised as a brahmin and asked for his eyes, the moment he plucked them out and gave them away, joy arose in him, and not even a hair's breadth of alteration arose in his mind. Thus, for Bodhisattvas, there is no satiation on account of giving. Therefore, that great being reflected, "It is fitting for me to give alms to monks numbering a hundred thousand koṭi for seven days." He seated the Sangha of monks, headed by the Buddha, in that pavilion and for seven days offered what is called "gavapāna." "Gavapāna" refers to a food prepared by filling very large pots with milk, placing them on hearths, boiling the milk until thick, adding a few grains of rice, and enriching it with cooked honey, sugar powder, and ghee. Humans alone were not able to serve it; the devas also served in alternation. The space, twelve or thirteen yojanas in extent, was not even sufficient to hold the monks. Yet by their own power, the monks seated themselves. On the final day, after having all the monks’ bowls washed, he filled them with ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses for medicinal purposes and gave them along with the three robes. The cloths for the three robes received by the most junior monk of the Sangha were worth a hundred thousand. The Teacher, expressing his appreciation, pondered, "This man has given such a great gift—who might he become?" Then, foreseeing that "In the future, at the end of two incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons more, he will become the Buddha named Gotama," he addressed the great being and prophesied, "After passing through such a period of time, you will become the Buddha named Gotama."

Mahāpuriso byākaraṇaṃ sutvā “ahaṃ kira buddho bhavissāmi, ko me gharāvāsena attho[V 0.0067], pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā tathārūpaṃ sampattiṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya pahāya satthu santike pabbaji. Pabbajitvā ca buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā abhiññā, samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā āyupariyosane brahmaloke nibbatti.

Having heard the prophecy, the Great Being thought, "Indeed, I shall become a Buddha. What use is the household life to me? I shall go forth." Thus, abandoning such prosperity like a lump of spittle, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher. After going forth, having learned the Buddha's word and developed the higher knowledges and attainments, at the end of his life-span, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

Maṅgalassa pana bhagavato uttaraṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi. Pitāpi uttaro nāma khattiyo, mātāpi uttarā nāma, sudevo ca dhammaseno ca dve aggasāvakā, pālito nāma upaṭṭhāko, sīvalī ca asokā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkho bodhi, aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi. Navutivassasahassāni ṭhatvā parinibbute pana tasmiṃ ekappahāreneva [M 0.0062] dasacakkavāḷasahassāni ekandhakārāni ahesuṃ. Sabbacakkavāḷesu manussānaṃ mahantaṃ ārodanaparidevanaṃ ahosi.

Now, the Blessed One Maṅgala had a city named Uttara. His father was a khattiya named Uttara, and his mother was named Uttarā. His two chief disciples were Sudeva and Dhammasena. His attendant was named Pālita. His two chief female disciples were Sīvalī and Asokā. His Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits in height. After living for ninety thousand years, upon his Parinibbāna, in a single instant, ten thousand world-systems became one darkness. Throughout all the world-systems, there was great weeping and lamentation among the people.

Evaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ andhakāraṃ katvā parinibbutassa tassa bhagavato aparabhāge sumano nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ. Dutiye kañcanapabbatamhi navutikoṭisahassāni, tatiye asītikoṭisahassāni. Tadā mahāsatto atulo nāma nāgarājā ahosi mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo, so “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā ñātisaṅghaparivuto nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā koṭisatasahassabhikkhuparivārassa tassa bhagavato dibbatūriyehi upahāraṃ kārāpetvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā paccekaṃ dussayugāni datvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāsi. Sopi naṃ satthā “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

Thus, after that Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, plunging the ten-thousandfold world-system into darkness, in a subsequent period a Teacher named Sumana arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were a hundred thousand koṭi of monks. In the second, on the Golden Mountain, there were ninety thousand koṭi, and in the third, eighty thousand koṭi. At that time, the Great Being was a nāga king named Atula, of great psychic power and great might. Hearing that "a Buddha has arisen," he left his nāga abode surrounded by his assembly of kinsfolk and, having arranged an offering with divine music for that Blessed One’s retinue of a hundred thousand koṭi of monks, he held a great almsgiving. He presented pairs of cloths to each one and was established in the refuges. That Teacher also prophesied to him, "In the future, you will become a Buddha."

Tassa bhagavato nagaraṃ mekhalaṃ nāma ahosi, sudatto nāma rājā pitā, sirimā nāma mātā, saraṇo ca bhāvitatto ca dve aggasāvakā, udeno nāma upaṭṭhāko, soṇā ca upasoṇā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkhova bodhi, navutihatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ, navutiyeva vassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosīti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Mekhala. His father was King Sudatta, and his mother was named Sirimā. Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta were his two chief disciples. His attendant was named Udena. Soṇā and Upasoṇā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a nāga tree. His body was ninety cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge revato nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ, paṭhamasannipāte gaṇanā nāma natthi, dutiye koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, tathā tatiye. Tadā bodhisatto atidevo nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ [V 0.0068] ṭhapetvā tassa satthuno kilesappahāne vaṇṇaṃ vatvā uttarāsaṅgena pūjamakāsi. Sopi naṃ “buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In the period after him, a Teacher named Revata arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there is no count; in the second, there were a hundred thousand koṭi of monks, and likewise in the third. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Atideva, heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, was established in the refuges, placed his joined hands on his head, spoke in praise of that Teacher's abandoning of defilements, and made an offering with his upper robe. That Teacher also prophesied to him, "You will become a Buddha."

Tassa pana bhagavato nagaraṃ sudhaññavatī nāma ahosi, pitā vipulo nāma khattiyo, mātāpi vipulā nāma, varuṇo ca brahmadevo ca dve aggasāvakā, sambhavo nāma upaṭṭhāko, bhaddā ca subhaddā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkhova bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, āyu saṭṭhivassasahassānīti.

Now, the city of that Blessed One was named Sudhaññavatī. His father was the khattiya Vipula, and his mother was also named Vipulā. His two chief disciples were Varuṇa and Brahmadeva. His attendant was named Sambhava. The two chief female disciples were Bhaddā and Subhaddā. His Bodhi tree was a nāga tree. His body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.

Tassa [M 0.0063] aparabhāge sobhito nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto ajito nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Sopi naṃ “buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In the period after him arose a Teacher named Sobhita. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one billion monks; in the second, nine hundred million; and in the third, eight hundred million. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a brahmin named Ajita, hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, established himself in the refuges and gave a great alms-offering to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. That Teacher also prophesied to him, "You will become a Buddha."

Tassa pana bhagavato nagaraṃ sudhammaṃ nāma ahosi, pitā sudhammo nāma rājā, mātāpi sudhammā nāma, asamo ca sunetto ca dve aggasāvakā, anomo nāma upaṭṭhāko, nakulā ca sujātā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkhova bodhi, aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi, navuti vassasahassāni āyuppamāṇanti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Sudhamma. His father was King Sudhamma, and his mother was also named Sudhammā. Asama and Sunetta were his two chief disciples. Anoma was his attendant. Nakulā and Sujātā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a nāga tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā ekasmiṃyeva kappe tayo buddhā nibbattiṃsu anomadassī, padumo, nāradoti. Anomadassissa bhagavato tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhame aṭṭha bhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye satta, tatiye cha tadā bodhisatto eko yakkhasenāpati ahosi mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo anekakoṭisatasahassānaṃ yakkhānaṃ adhipati. So “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā āgantvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Satthāpi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, after one incalculable aeon had passed, three Buddhas arose in a single aeon: Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada. During the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were eight hundred thousand monks; in the second, seven hundred thousand; and in the third, six hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a commander of the yakkhas, possessing great power and might, the lord of many trillions of yakkhas. Hearing that "a Buddha has arisen," he came and offered a great alms-offering to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. The Teacher also prophesied to him, "In the future you will become a Buddha."

Anomadassissa pana bhagavato candavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, yasavā nāma rājā pitā, yasodharā nāma mātā, nisabho ca anomo ca dve aggasāvakā, varuṇo nāma upaṭṭhāko[V 0.0069], sundarī ca sumanā ca dve aggasāvikā, ajjunarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

Now, the Blessed One Anomadassī had a city called Candavatī. His father was King Yasavā, and his mother was named Yasodharā. His two chief disciples were Nisabha and Anoma. His attendant was named Varuṇa. His two chief female disciples were Sundarī and Sumanā. His Bodhi tree was the Ajjuna tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge padumo nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye tīṇisatasahassāni, tatiye agāmake araññe mahāvanasaṇḍavāsīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dve satasahassāni. Tadā tathāgate tasmiṃyeva vanasaṇḍe vasante bodhisatto sīho hutvā satthāraṃ nirodhasamāpattisamāpannaṃ disvā pasannacitto vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā [M 0.0064] pītisomanassajāto tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā sattāhaṃ buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃavijahitvā pītisukheneva gocarāya apakkamitvā jīvitapariccāgaṃ katvā payirupāsamāno aṭṭhāsi. Satthā sattāhaccayena nirodhā vuṭṭhito sīhaṃ oloketvā “bhikkhusaṅghepi cittaṃ pasādetvā saṅghaṃ vandissatī”ti “bhikkhusaṅgho āgacchatū”ti cintesi. Bhikkhū tāvadeva āgamiṃsu. Sīho saṅghe cittaṃ pasādeti. Satthā tassa mānasaṃ oloketvā “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, a Teacher named Paduma arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
