In the first assembly, there were one trillion monks; in the second, three hundred thousand; and in the third, two hundred thousand monks dwelling in a great forest grove in the wilderness, without villages. At that time, while the Tathāgata was dwelling in that very forest grove, the Bodhisatta, having become a lion, saw the Teacher absorbed in the attainment of cessation. With a serene mind, he paid homage, circumambulated him, and, filled with rapture and gladness, roared a lion’s roar three times. For seven days, without abandoning the joy that had the Buddha as its object, sustained by that rapture and happiness alone, without going for prey, he made a sacrifice of his life and stood attending upon him. After seven days had passed, the Teacher emerged from cessation and, seeing the lion, thought, 'He will also feel confidence in the Sangha and will pay homage to the Sangha.' He then thought, 'May the Sangha of monks come.' Instantly, the monks arrived. The lion felt confidence in the Sangha. The Teacher, discerning his mind, prophesied to him, 'In the future, you will become a Buddha.'

Padumassa pana bhagavato campakaṃ nagaraṃ ahosi asamo nāma rājā pitā, mātā asamā nāma, sālo ca upasālo ca dve aggasāvakā, varuṇo nāma upaṭṭhāko, rāmā ca surāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, soṇarukkho nāma bodhi aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi, āyu vassasatasahassanti.

For the Blessed One Paduma, the city was Campaka. His father was King Asama, and his mother was named Asamā. His two chief disciples were Sāla and Upasāla. His attendant was named Varuṇa. His two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā. His Bodhi tree was the Soṇa tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge nārado nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭisahassāni, tatiye asītikoṭisahassāni. Tadā bodhisatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcasu abhiññāsu, aṭṭhasu ca samāpattīsu ciṇṇavasī hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā lohitacandanena pūjamakāsi, sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, a Teacher named Nārada arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one trillion monks; in the second, nine hundred billion; and in the third, eight hundred billion. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth into the ascetic life and having perfected mastery in the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments, after giving a great alms-offering to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, made an offering with red sandalwood. He too prophesied to him, 'In the future, you will become a Buddha.'

Tassa pana bhagavato dhaññavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, sudevo nāma khattiyo pitā, anomā nāma mātā, bhaddasālo ca jitamitto ca dve aggasāvakā, vāsiṭṭho nāma upaṭṭhāko, uttarā [V 0.0070] ca phaggunī ca dve aggasāvikā, mahāsoṇarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, navuti vassasahassāni āyūti.

For that Blessed One, the city was Dhaññavatī. His father was the khattiya named Sudeva, and his mother was named Anomā. His two chief disciples were Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta. His attendant was named Vāsiṭṭha. His two chief female disciples were Uttarā and Phaggunī. His Bodhi tree was the great Soṇa tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits in height. His lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Nāradabuddhassa pana aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā ito satasahassakappamatthake ekasmiṃ kappe ekova padumuttaro nāma buddho udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye vebhārapabbate navutikoṭisahassāni, tatiye asītikoṭisahassāni. Tadā bodhisatto jaṭilo nāma mahāraṭṭhiyo hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sacīvaraṃ dānaṃ [M 0.0065] adāsi. Sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Padumuttarassa pana bhagavato kāle titthiyā nāma nāhesuṃ sabbe devamanussā buddhameva saraṇamakaṃsu.

In the period after the Buddha Nārada, after one incalculable aeon had passed, one hundred thousand aeons ago, in a single aeon, only one Buddha, named Padumuttara, arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one trillion monks; in the second, on Mount Vebhāra, there were nine hundred billion; and in the third, eight hundred billion. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a great provincial governor named Jaṭila, who gave an offering with robes to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. He too prophesied to him, 'In the future, you will become a Buddha.' During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no sectarians; all gods and humans took refuge only in the Buddha.

Tassa nagaraṃ haṃsavatī nāma ahosi, pitā ānando nāma khattiyo, mātā sujātā nāma, devalo ca sujāto ca dve aggasāvakā sumano nāma upaṭṭhāko, amitā ca asamā ca dve aggasāvikā, salalarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā samantato dvādasa yojanāni gaṇhi vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

His city was named Haṃsavatī. His father was the khattiya named Ānanda, and his mother was named Sujātā. Devala and Sujāta were his two chief disciples. Sumana was his attendant. Amitā and Asamā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a Salala tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits high, and the radiance of his body extended twelve leagues in all directions. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge sattatikappasahassāni atikkamitvā ito tiṃsakappasahassamatthake sumedho ca sujāto cāti ekasmiṃ kappe dve buddhā nibbattiṃsu. Sumedhassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte sudassananagare koṭisatakhīṇāsavā ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto uttaro nāma brāhmaṇamāṇavo hutvā nidahitvā ṭhapitaṃyeva asītikoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā dhammaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya nikkhamitvā pabbaji. Sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

After his passing, seventy thousand aeons having passed, at the head of thirty thousand aeons from the present, two Buddhas named Sumedha and Sujāta arose in one aeon. Sumedha also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, in the city of Sudassana, there were a hundred koṭis of arahants; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Uttara, who, having given away wealth amounting to eighty koṭis that had been stored away, gave a great offering to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Having heard the Dhamma, he was established in the refuges and went forth into homelessness. He too made a prophecy concerning him, saying: 'In the future, you will become a Buddha.'

Sumedhassa bhagavato sudassanaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, sudatto nāma rājā pitā, mātāpi sudattā nāma, saraṇo ca sabbakāmo ca dve aggasāvakā, sāgaro nāma upaṭṭhāko, rāmā ca surāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, mahānīparukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, āyu navuti vassasahassānīti.

The Blessed One Sumedha's city was named Sudassana. His father was King Sudatta, and his mother was also named Sudattā. Saraṇa and Sabbakāma were his two chief disciples. Sāgara was his attendant. Rāmā and Surāmā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the great Nīpa tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits high. His lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Tassa [V 0.0071] aparabhāge sujāto nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte saṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ[M 0.0066], dutiye paññāsaṃ, tatiye cattālīsaṃ. Tadā bodhisatto cakkavattirājā hutvā “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa saddhiṃ sattahi ratanehi catumahādīparajjaṃ datvā satthu santike pabbaji. Sakalaraṭṭhavāsino raṭṭhuppādaṃ gahetvā ārāmikakiccaṃ sādhentā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa niccaṃ mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Sopi naṃ satthā byākāsi.

After his passing, a Teacher named Sujāta arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were sixty hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, fifty hundred thousand; and in the third, forty hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a wheel-turning monarch who, hearing that 'a Buddha has arisen,' approached him, listened to the Dhamma, and gave the kingdom of the four great continents along with the seven precious things to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Then he went forth into homelessness in the Teacher’s presence. The inhabitants of the entire kingdom, taking the produce of the kingdom, performed the duties of monastery attendants and continually gave great offerings to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. That Teacher also made a prophecy concerning him.

Tassa bhagavato nagaraṃ sumaṅgalaṃ nāma ahosi, uggato nāma rājā pitā, pabhāvatī nāma mātā, sudassano ca sudevo ca dve aggasāvakā, nārado nāma upaṭṭhāko, nāgā ca nāgasamālā ca dve aggasāvikā, mahāveḷurukkho bodhi, so kira mandacchiddo ghanakkhandho upariniggatāhi mahāsākhāhi morapiñchakalāpo viya virocittha. Tassa bhagavato sarīraṃ paṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, āyu navutivassasahassānīti.

That Blessed One's city was named Sumaṅgala. His father was King Uggata, and his mother was Pabhāvatī. His two chief disciples were Sudassana and Sudeva. His attendant was named Nārada. His two chief female disciples were Nāgā and Nāgasamālā. His Bodhi tree was the great bamboo tree, which, it is said, had few gaps, a solid trunk, and with its great branches emerging upwards, shone like a peacock's tail-plume. That Blessed One's body was fifty cubits high, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge ito aṭṭhārasakappasatamatthake ekasmiṃ kappe piyadassī, atthadassī, dhammadassīti tayo buddhā nibbattiṃsu. Piyadassissāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā. Paṭhame koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto kassapo nāma māṇavo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṅgato hutvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā koṭisatasahassadhanapariccāgena saṅghārāmaṃ kāretvā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthā “aṭṭhārasakappasataccayena buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

After him, at the head of eighteen hundred aeons from the present, in one aeon, three Buddhas arose: Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī. Piyadassī also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were a hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a brahmin youth named Kassapa who had mastered the three Vedas, after hearing the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, by the donation of a hundred thousand koṭis of wealth had a monastery built, and was established in the refuges and precepts. Then the Teacher prophesied to him, 'After the passing of eighteen hundred aeons, you will become a Buddha.'

Tassa bhagavato anomaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, pitā sudinno nāma rājā, mātā candā nāma, pālito ca sabbadassī ca dve aggasāvakā, sobhito nāma upaṭṭhāko, sujātā ca dhammadinnā ca dve aggasāvikā, piyaṅgurukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, navutivassasahassāni āyūti.

That Blessed One's city was named Anoma. His father was King Sudinna, and his mother was Candā. His two chief disciples were Pālita and Sabbadassī. His attendant was named Sobhita. His two chief female disciples were Sujātā and Dhammadinnā. His Bodhi tree was the Piyaṅgu tree. His body was eighty cubits high, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge atthadassī nāma bhagavā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā. Paṭhame aṭṭhanavutibhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye aṭṭhāsītisahassāni, tathā tatiye. Tadā bodhisatto [V 0.0072] susīmo [M 0.0067] nāma mahiddhiko tāpaso hutvā devalokato mandāravapupphacchattaṃ āharitvā satthāraṃ pūjesi. Sopi naṃ satthā byākāsi.

After his passing, the Blessed One named Atthadassī arose. He also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were ninety-eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, eighty-eight thousand; and likewise in the third. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a mighty ascetic named Susīma, brought a parasol of Mandārava flowers from the deva world and honored the Teacher. That Teacher also made a prophecy concerning him.

Tassa bhagavato sobhaṇaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, sāgaro nāma rājā pitā, sudassanā nāma mātā, santo ca upasanto ca dve aggasāvakā, abhayo nāma upaṭṭhāko, dhammā ca sudhammā ca dve aggasāvikā, campakarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā samantato sabbakālaṃ yojanamattaṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi, āyu vassasatasahassanti.

That Blessed One's city was named Sobhaṇa. His father was King Sāgara, and his mother was Sudassanā. Santo and Upasanto were his two chief disciples. Abhaya was his attendant. Dhammā and Sudhammā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Campaka tree. His body was eighty cubits in height, and the radiance of his body constantly pervaded the measure of a yojana in all directions. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge dhammadassī nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto sakko devarājā hutvā dibbagandhapupphehi ca dibbatūriyehi ca pūjamakāsi. Sopi naṃ satthā byākāsi.

After him, the Teacher named Dhammadassī arose. He also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were a hundred koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become Sakka, the king of devas, made offerings with divine fragrances, flowers, and celestial instruments. That Teacher also made a prophecy concerning him.

Tassa bhagavato saraṇaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, pitā saraṇo nāma rājā, mātā sunandā nāma, padumo ca phussadevo ca dve aggasāvakā, sunetto nāma upaṭṭhāko, khemā ca sabbanāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, rattaṅkurarukkho bodhi, “kakudharukkho”tipi “bimbijālo”tipi vuccati sarīraṃ panassa asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Saraṇa. His father was King Saraṇa, and his mother was Sunandā. Paduma and Phussadeva were his two chief disciples. His attendant was named Sunetta. Khemā and Sabbanāmā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Rattaṅkura tree, also called the Kakudha tree or the Bimbijāla tree. His body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge ito catunavutikappamatthake ekasmiṃ kappe ekova siddhattho nāma buddho udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto uggatejo abhiññābalasampanno maṅgalo nāma tāpaso hutvā mahājambuphalaṃ āharitvā tathāgatassa adāsi. Satthā taṃ phalaṃ paribhuñjitvā “catunavutikappamatthake buddho bhavissasī”ti bodhisattaṃ byākāsi.

In a later period, ninety-four aeons ago, in one aeon, a single Buddha named Siddhattha arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand koṭis of monks; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, endowed with great radiance and the power of supernormal knowledge, was an ascetic named Maṅgala. He brought a large rose-apple fruit and offered it to the Tathāgata. The Teacher consumed the fruit and prophesied to the Bodhisatta, saying, 'Ninety-four aeons hence, you will become a Buddha.'

Tassa [M 0.0068] bhagavato nagaraṃ vebhāraṃ nāma ahosi, pitā jayaseno nāma rājā, mātā suphassā nāma, sambalo ca sumitto ca dve aggasāvakā, revato nāma upaṭṭhāko, sīvalā ca [V 0.0073] surāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, kaṇikārarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ saṭṭhihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Vebhāra. His father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Suphassā. Sambala and Sumitta were his two chief disciples. Revata was his attendant. Sīvalā and Surāmā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Kaṇikāra tree. His body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge ito dvenavutikappamatthake tisso phussoti ekasmiṃ kappe dve buddhā nibbattiṃsu. Tissassa pana bhagavato tayo sāvakasannipātā. Paṭhamasannipāte bhikkhūnaṃ koṭisataṃ ahosi, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto mahābhogo mahāyaso sujāto nāma khattiyo hutvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā mahiddhikabhāvaṃ patvā “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā dibbamandāravapadumapāricchattakapupphāni ādāya catuparisamajjhe gacchantaṃ tathāgataṃ pūjesi, ākāse pupphavitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Sopi naṃ satthā “ito dvenavutikappamatthake buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, ninety-two aeons ago, in one aeon, two Buddhas arose: Tissa and Phussa. The Blessed One Tissa had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred koṭis of monks; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a khattiya named Sujāta, of great wealth and fame. Having gone forth into the ascetic life and attained great psychic power, upon hearing that a Buddha had arisen, he took divine mandārava, paduma, and pāricchattaka flowers and honored the Tathāgata as he was going into the midst of the four assemblies. A canopy of flowers then formed and remained in the sky. That Teacher also prophesied to him, saying, 'Ninety-two aeons from now, you will become a Buddha.'

Tassa bhagavato khemaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, pitā janasandho nāma khattiyo, mātā padumā nāma, brahmadevo ca udayo ca dve aggasāvakā samaṅgo nāma upaṭṭhāko, phussā ca sudattā ca dve aggasāvikā asanarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ saṭṭhihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Khema. His father was Janasandha, a khattiya, and his mother was Padumā. Brahmadeva and Udaya were his two chief disciples. His attendant was named Samaṅga. Phussā and Sudattā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Asana tree. His body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge phusso nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte saṭṭhi bhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye paṇṇāsa, tatiye dvattiṃsa. Tadā bodhisatto vijitāvī nāma khattiyo hutvā mahārajjaṃ pahāya satthu santike pabbajitvā tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā mahājanassa dhammakathaṃ kathesi. Sīlapāramiñca pūresi. Sopi naṃ “buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, a Teacher named Phussa arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were sixty hundred thousand monks; in the second, fifty hundred thousand; and in the third, thirty-two hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a khattiya named Vijitāvī, renounced his great kingdom, went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher, mastered the three Piṭakas, and preached the Dhamma to the masses. He also fulfilled the perfection of morality. That Teacher also prophesied to him, saying, 'You will become a Buddha.'

Tassa bhagavato kāsi nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, jayaseno nāma rājā pitā, sirimā nāma mātā, surakkhito ca dhammaseno ca dve aggasāvakā, sabhiyo nāma upaṭṭhāko, cālā ca upacālā ca dve aggasāvikā[M 0.0069], āmalakarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, navuti vassasahassāni āyūti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Kāsi. His father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Sirimā. Surakkhita and Dhammasena were his two chief disciples. Sabhiya was his attendant. Cālā and Upacālā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Āmalaka tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge ito ekanavutikappe vipassī nāma bhagavā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā[V 0.0074], paṭhamasannipāte aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye ekasatasahassaṃ, tatiye asītisahassāni. Tadā bodhisatto mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo atulo nāma nāgarājā hutvā sattaratanakhacitaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ mahāpīṭhaṃ bhagavato adāsi. Sopi naṃ satthā “ito ekanavutikappe buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, ninety-one aeons ago, the Blessed One named Vipassī arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were six million, eight hundred thousand monks; in the second, one hundred thousand; and in the third, eighty thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a nāga king named Atula, of great psychic power and might. He presented the Blessed One with a great golden throne adorned with the seven precious gems. That Teacher also prophesied to him, saying, 'Ninety-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha.'

Tassa bhagavato bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, bandhumā nāma rājā pitā. Bandhumatī nāma mātā, khaṇḍo ca tisso ca dve aggasāvakā, asoko nāma upaṭṭhāko, candā ca candamittā ca dve aggasāvikā pāṭalirukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā sadā satta yojanāni pharitvā aṭṭhāsi, asītivassasahassāni āyūti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Bandhumatī. His father was King Bandhumā, and his mother was Bandhumatī. Khaṇḍa and Tissa were his two chief disciples. His attendant was named Asoka. Candā and Candamittā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Pāṭali tree. His body was eighty cubits in height, and the radiance of his body always extended for seven leagues. His lifespan was eighty thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge ito ekatiṃsakappe sikhī, vessabhū cāti dve buddhā ahesuṃ. Sikhissāpi bhagavato tayo sāvakasannipātā, paṭhamasannipāte bhikkhusatasahassaṃ ahosi, dutiye asītisahassāni, tatiye sattati. Tadā bodhisatto arindamo nāma rājā hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sacīvaraṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā sattaratanapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ hatthiratanaṃ datvā hatthippamāṇaṃ katvā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ adāsi. Sopi naṃ “ito ekatiṃsakappe buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, thirty-one aeons ago, two Buddhas arose: Sikhī and Vessabhū. The Blessed One Sikhī also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand monks; in the second, eighty thousand; and in the third, seventy thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Arindama. He made a great offering, including robes, to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. He gave the elephant-treasure, adorned with the seven precious gems, along with other suitable goods of equal value. That Teacher also prophesied to him, saying, 'Thirty-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha.'

Tassa pana bhagavato aruṇavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, aruṇavā nāma khattiyo pitā, pabhāvatī nāma mātā, abhibhū ca sambhavo ca dve aggasāvakā khemaṅkaro nāma upaṭṭhāko, sakhilā ca padumā ca dve aggasāvikā, puṇḍarīkarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ sattatihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā yojanattayaṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi, sattahivassasahassāni āyūti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Aruṇavatī. His father was Aruṇavā, a khattiya, and his mother was Pabhāvatī. Abhibhū and Sambhava were his two chief disciples. His attendant was named Khemaṅkara. Sakhilā and Padumā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Puṇḍarīka tree. His body was seventy cubits in height, and the radiance of his body spread for three leagues. His lifespan was seven thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge vessabhū nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā paṭhamasannipāte asītibhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ dutiye [M 0.0070] sattati, tatiye saṭṭhi. Tadā bodhisatto sudassano nāma rājā hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sacīvaraṃ mahādānaṃ datvā satthu santike pabbajitvā ācāraguṇasampanno buddharatane cittīkārapītibahulo ahosi. Sopi naṃ “ito ekatiṃse kappe buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

In a later period, the Teacher named Vessabhū arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly there were eighty thousand monks, in the second seventy thousand, and in the third sixty thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a king named Sudassana, gave a great offering, including robes, to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, and then went forth in the Teacher’s presence. He was endowed with virtuous conduct and abounded in joy and reverence for the Buddha-jewel. That Teacher also prophesied to him, 'Thirty-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha.'

Tassa [V 0.0075] pana bhagavato anomaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, suppatīto nāma rājā pitā, yasavatī nāma mātā, soṇo ca uttaro ca dve aggasāvakā upasanto nāma upaṭṭhāko dāmā ca samālā ca dve aggasāvikā, sālarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ saṭṭhihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, saṭṭhivassasahassāni āyūti.

The city of that Blessed One, however, was named Anoma. His father was King Suppatīta, and his mother was Yasavatī. Soṇa and Uttara were his two chief disciples. Upasanta was his attendant. Dāmā and Samālā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Sāla tree. His body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge imasmiṃ kappe cattāro buddhā nibbattā kakusandho, koṇāgamano, kassapo, amhākaṃ bhagavāti. Kakusandhassa bhagavato eko sāvakasannipāto, tattha cattālīsabhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Tadā bodhisatto khemo nāma rājā hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sapattacīvaraṃ mahādānañca añjanādibhesajjāni ca datvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbaji. Sopi naṃ satthā byākāsi.

In a later period, during this very aeon, four Buddhas have arisen: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One. The Blessed One Kakusandha had one assembly of disciples, at which there were forty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a king named Khema, gave a great offering of bowls and robes, and medicines such as ointments, to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. After hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he went forth. That Teacher also prophesied to him.

Kakusandhassa pana bhagavato khemaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, aggidatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā, visākhā nāma brāhmaṇī mātā, vidhuro ca sañjīvo ca dve aggasāvakā, buddhijo nāma upaṭṭhāko sāmā ca campā ca dve aggasāvikā mahāsirīsarukkho bodhi sarīraṃ cattālīsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, cattālīsavassasahassāni āyūti.

For the Blessed One Kakusandha, the city was named Khema. His father was the brahmin Aggidatta, and his mother was the brahminī Visākhā. Vidhura and Sañjīva were the two chief disciples, Buddhija was the attendant, Sāmā and Campā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the great Sirīsa tree, his body was forty cubits in height, and his lifespan was forty thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge koṇāgamano nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi eko sāvakasannipāto, tattha tiṃsabhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Tadā bodhisatto pabbato nāma rājā hutvā amaccagaṇaparivuto satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā pattuṇṇacīnapaṭakoseyyakambaladukulāni ceva suvaṇṇapādukañca datvā satthu santike pabbaji. Sopi naṃ satthā byākāsi.

In a later period, the Teacher named Koṇāgamana arose. He too had one assembly of disciples, at which there were thirty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a king named Pabbata, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma discourse, invited the Sangha with the Buddha at its head, and, having provided a great donation, gave woolen cloths, Chinese cloth, silk, blankets, fine linen, and golden sandals, and then went forth in the Teacher’s presence. That Teacher also prophesied to him.

Tassa bhagavato sobhavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, yaññadatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā, uttarā nāma brāhmaṇī mātā, bhiyyoso ca uttaro [M 0.0071] ca dve aggasāvakā, sotthijo nāma upaṭṭhāko, samuddā ca uttarā ca dve aggasāvikā, udumbararukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ tiṃsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, tiṃsavassasahassāni āyūti.

For that Blessed One, the city was named Sobhavatī. His father was the brahmin Yaññadatta, and his mother was the brahminī Uttarā. Bhiyyosa and Uttara were the two chief disciples, Sotthija was the attendant, Samuddā and Uttarā were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Udumbara tree, his body was thirty cubits in height, and his lifespan was thirty thousand years.

Tassa aparabhāge kassapo nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi ekova sāvakasannipāto, tattha [V 0.0076] vīsatibhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Tadā bodhisatto jotipālo nāma māṇavo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū bhūmiyañceva antalikkhe ca pākaṭo ghaṭikārassa kumbhakārassa mitto ahosi, so tena saddhiṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammakathaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā āraddhavīriyo tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā vattasampattiyā buddhasāsanaṃ sobhesi. Sopi naṃ satthā byākāsi.

In a later period, the Teacher named Kassapa arose. He too had only one assembly of disciples, at which there were twenty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Jotipāla, a master of the three Vedas, renowned on earth and in the sky. He was a friend of the potter Ghaṭikāra. Together with him, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma discourse, and went forth. Having become energetic, he mastered the three Piṭakas and adorned the Buddha’s dispensation through his accomplishment in the observances. That Teacher also prophesied to him.

Tassa bhagavato jātanagaraṃ bārāṇasī nāma ahosi. Brahmadatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā, dhanavatī nāma brāhmaṇī mātā, tisso ca bhāradvājo ca dve aggasāvakā, sabbamitto nāma upaṭṭhāko anuḷā ca uruveḷā ca dve aggasāvikā, nigrodharukkho bodhi sarīraṃ vīsatihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vīsativassasahassāni āyūti.

For that Blessed One, the city of his birth was named Bārāṇasī. His father was the brahmin Brahmadatta, and his mother was the brahminī Dhanavatī. Tissa and Bhāradvāja were the two chief disciples, Sabbamitta was the attendant, Anuḷā and Uruvelā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was a Nigrodha tree, his body was twenty cubits in height, and his lifespan was twenty thousand years.

Tassa pana bhagavato orabhāge ṭhapetvā imaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ añño buddho nāma natthi. Iti dīpaṅkarādīnaṃ catuvīsatiyā buddhānaṃ santike laddhabyākaraṇo pana bodhisatto yenena –

In the period after that Blessed One, apart from this Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, there has been no other Buddha. Thus, the Bodhisatta, having received the predictions in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, then—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59);

“Human existence, completeness of gender, a cause, seeing a Teacher, going forth, accomplishment in qualities, a foundation of merit, and zealous desire—when these eight conditions converge, the aspiration succeeds.” (Bv. 2.59)

Ime aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā dīpaṅkarapādamūle katābhinīhārena “handa buddhakare dhamme vicināmi ito cito”ti ussāhaṃ katvā “vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapārami”nti dānapāramitādayo buddhakarā dhammā diṭṭhā, te pūrento yāva vessantarattabhāvā āgami. Āgacchanto ca ye te katābhinīhārānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ ānisaṃsā saṃvaṇṇitā –

Having brought together these eight qualities, and having made the aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, he made the effort, thinking, “Come now, I will seek the qualities that make a Buddha from here and there.” Seeking, he then saw, “First, the perfection of giving,” and thus the qualities that make a Buddha, beginning with the perfection of giving, were seen. Fulfilling them, he came up to the state of existence as Vessantara. And as he came, those benefits that are described for the bodhisattas who have made such an aspiration—

“Evaṃ [M 0.0072] sabbaṅgasampannā, bodhiyā niyatā narā;

Saṃsaraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ, kappakoṭisatehipi.

“Thus, endowed with all qualities, beings destined for enlightenment wander through the long course of saṃsāra, even for hundreds of koṭis of aeons.

“Avīcimhi nuppajjanti, tathā lokantaresu ca;

Nijjhāmataṇhā khuppipāsā, na honti kālakañjikā.

“They are not reborn in Avīci, nor in the Lokantara hells; burning craving, hunger, and thirst do not exist for them, nor do they become Kālakañjika asuras.

“Na [V 0.0077] honti khuddakā pāṇā, uppajjantāpi duggatiṃ;

Jāyamānā manussesu, jaccandhā na bhavanti te.

They are not born as insignificant beings, even when arising in a woeful state; when born among humans, they are not blind from birth.

“Sotavekallatā natthi, na bhavanti mūgapakkhikā;

Itthibhāvaṃ na gacchanti, ubhatobyañjanapaṇḍakā.

There is no deficiency of hearing, nor do they become mute or paralyzed; they do not attain the female state, nor are they hermaphrodites or eunuchs.

“Na bhavanti pariyāpannā, bodhiyā niyatā narā;

Muttā ānantarikehi, sabbattha suddhagocarā.

Beings destined for enlightenment are not subject to these; they are freed from the heinous crimes, and their sphere is pure everywhere.

“Micchādiṭṭhiṃ na sevanti, kammakiriyadassanā;

Vasamānāpi saggesu, asaññaṃ nupapajjare.

Holding the view of kamma and its results, they do not associate with wrong views; even while dwelling in the heavens, they are not reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings.

“Suddhāvāsesu devesu, hetu nāma na vijjati;

Nekkhammaninnā sappurisā, visaṃyuttā bhavābhave;

Caranti lokatthacariyāyo, pūrenti sabbapāramī”ti.

Among the deities in the Pure Abodes, no such cause is found. The noble ones, inclined to renunciation and detached from all states of being, practice for the welfare of the world, fulfilling all the perfections.

Te ānisaṃse adhigantvāva āgato. Pāramiyo pūrentassa ca tassa akittibrāhmaṇakāle saṅkhabrāhmaṇakāle dhanañcayarājakāle mahāsudassanarājakāle mahāgovindakāle nimimahārājakāle candakumārakāle visayhaseṭṭhikāle sivirājakāle vessantararājakāleti dānapāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa sasapaṇḍitajātakāle –

He came having attained those benefits. And for him, while fulfilling the perfections, during the time as Akitti the brahmin, Saṅkha the brahmin, King Dhanañcaya, King Mahāsudassana, Mahāgovinda, King Nimi, Prince Canda, the wealthy merchant Visayha, King Sivi, and King Vessantara—there is no measure to the existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of giving. But certainly, in his existence as the wise hare—

“Bhikkhāya upagataṃ disvā, sakattānaṃ pariccajiṃ;

Dānena me samo natthi, esā me dānapāramī”ti. (cariyā. 1.143 tassuddāna –

Seeing one who had come for alms, I sacrificed my own body; in giving, there is none equal to me—this is my perfection of giving.

Evaṃ attapariccāgaṃ karontassa dānapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him performing such self-sacrifice, the perfection of giving became the perfection of the highest order.

Tathā [M 0.0073] sīlavanāgarājakāle campeyyanāgarājakāle bhūridattanāgarājakāle chaddantanāgarājakāle [V 0.0078] jayaddisarājaputtakāle alīnasattukumārakāleti sīlapāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa saṅkhapālajātakāle –

Similarly, during the time as the Nāga king Sīlava, the Nāga king Campeyya, the Nāga king Bhūridatta, the Nāga king Chaddanta, Prince Jayaddisa, and Prince Alīnasattu—there is no measure to the existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of virtue. But certainly, in his existence as Saṅkhapāla—

“Sūlehipi vijjhiyanto, koṭṭiyantopi sattihi;

Bhojaputte na kuppāmi, esā me sīlapāramī”ti. (cariyā. 2.91) –

Though pierced with stakes and struck with spears, I felt no anger towards the sons of the Bhojas; this is my perfection of virtue.

Evaṃ attapariccāgaṃ karontassa sīlapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him performing such self-sacrifice, the perfection of virtue became the perfection of the highest order.

Tathā somanassakumārakāle hatthipālakumārakāle ayogharapaṇḍitakāleti mahārajjaṃ pahāya nekkhammapāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa cūḷasutasomajātakāle –

Similarly, during the time as Prince Somanassa, Prince Hatthipāla, and the wise Ayoghara, by relinquishing a great kingdom, there is no measure to the existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of renunciation. But certainly, in his existence as Cūḷasutasoma—

“Mahārajjaṃ hatthagataṃ, kheḷapiṇḍaṃva chaḍḍayiṃ;

Cajato na hoti laganaṃ, esā me nekkhammapāramī”ti. –

A great kingdom came into my hand, yet I cast it away like a lump of spittle; for one who renounces, there is no attachment—this is my perfection of renunciation.

Evaṃ nissaṅgatāya rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhamantassa nekkhammapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him who went forth, having renounced the kingdom without attachment, the perfection of renunciation became the perfection of the highest order.

Tathā vidhurapaṇḍitakāle mahāgovindapaṇḍitakāle kudālapaṇḍitakāle arakapaṇḍitakāle bodhiparibbājakakāle mahosadhapaṇḍitakāleti paññāpāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa sattubhastajātake senakapaṇḍitakāle –

Similarly, during the time as Vidhura the Wise, Mahāgovinda the Wise, Kudāla the Wise, Araka the Wise, the Bodhi-Paribbājaka, and Mahosadha the Wise—there is no measure to the existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of wisdom. But certainly, in the Sattubhasta Jātaka, during his time as Senaka the Wise—

“Paññāya vicinantohaṃ, brāhmaṇaṃ mocayiṃ dukhā;

Paññāya me samo natthi, esā me paññāpāramī”ti. –

Investigating with wisdom, I freed the brahmin from suffering; in wisdom, there is none equal to me—this is my perfection of wisdom.

Antobhastagataṃ sappaṃ dassentassa paññāpāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

For him who pointed out the snake inside the bag, the perfection of wisdom became the perfection of the highest order.

Tathā vīriyapāramitādīnampi pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa mahājanakajātake –

Similarly, there is no measure to the existences in which he fulfilled the perfections beginning with energy. But certainly, in the Mahājanaka Jātaka—

“Atīradassī jalamajjhe, hatā sabbeva mānusā;

Cittassa aññathā natthi, esā me vīriyapāramī”ti. –

In the middle of the ocean, not seeing the shore, all the other people perished; yet there was no wavering in my mind—this is my perfection of energy.

Evaṃ [M 0.0074][V 0.0079] mahāsamuddaṃ tarantassa vīriyapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him crossing the great ocean, the perfection of energy became the perfection of the highest order.

Khantivādījātake –

In the Khantivādī Jātaka—

“Acetanaṃva koṭṭente, tiṇhena pharasunā mamaṃ;

Kāsirāje na kuppāmi, esā me khantipāramī”ti. –

Though they hewed me with a sharp axe as if I were an insentient thing, I felt no anger towards the king of Kāsi—this is my perfection of patience.

Evaṃ acetanabhāvena viya mahādukkhaṃ adhivāsentassa khantipāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him enduring great suffering as if he were insentient, the perfection of patience became the perfection of the highest order.

Mahāsutasomajātake –

In the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka—

“Saccavācaṃ anurakkhanto, cajitvā mama jīvitaṃ;

Mocesiṃ ekasataṃ khattiye, esā me saccapāramī”ti. –

Protecting my truthful speech, I gave up my own life and released one hundred khattiyas; this is my perfection of truth.

Evaṃ jīvitaṃ cavitvā saccamanurakkhantassa saccapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him who protected the truth by relinquishing his life, the perfection of truth became the perfection of the highest order.

Mūgapakkhajātake –

In the Mūgapakkha Jātaka—

“Mātā pitā na me dessā, napi dessaṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā vatamadhiṭṭhahi”nti. –

My mother and father are not hateful to me, nor is great fame hateful; omniscience is dear to me, therefore I undertook this vow.

Evaṃ jīvitaṃ cajitvā vataṃ adhiṭṭhahantassa adhiṭṭhānapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him who undertook the vow by relinquishing his life, the perfection of resolve became the perfection of the highest order.

Ekarājajātake –

In the Ekarāja Jātaka—

“Na maṃ koci uttasati, napihaṃ bhāyāmi kassaci;

Mettābalenupatthaddho, ramāmi pavane tadā”ti. (cariyā. 3.113) –

No one intimidates me, nor do I fear anyone; supported by the power of loving-kindness, I then rejoice in the forest.

Evaṃ [V 0.0080] jīvitaṃ anapaloketvā mettāyantassa mettāpāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him who cultivated loving-kindness without regard for his life, the perfection of loving-kindness became the perfection of the highest order.

Lomahaṃsajātake [M 0.0075] –

In the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka—

“Susāne seyyaṃ kappemi, chavaṭṭhikaṃ upanidhāyahaṃ;

Gāmaṇḍalā upāgantvā, rūpaṃ dassenti nappaka”nti. –

I make my bed in the charnel ground, using a corpse's bone for a pillow; village boys approach and show me various forms.

Evaṃ gāmadārakesu niṭṭhubhanādīhi ceva mālāgandhūpahārādīhi ca sukhadukkhaṃ uppādentesupi upekkhanaṃ anativattentassa upekkhāpāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panesa attho cariyāpiṭakato gahetabbo.

Thus, for him who did not transgress equanimity even while village children were causing him pleasure and pain by such acts as spitting and offering garlands and scents, the perfection of equanimity became the perfection of the highest order. This is the summary here; this meaning, however, should be understood in detail from the Cariyāpiṭaka.

Evaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā vessantarattabhāve ṭhito –

Thus, having fulfilled the perfections, while in his existence as Vessantara—

“Acetanāyaṃ pathavī, aviññāya sukhaṃ dukhaṃ;

Sāpi dānabalā mayhaṃ, sattakkhattuṃ pakampathā”ti. (cariyā. 1.124);

This earth is insentient, unaware of pleasure and pain; yet even it, by the power of my giving, trembled seven times.

Evaṃ mahāpathavīkampanāni mahāpuññāni katvā āyupariyosāne tato cuto tusitabhavane nibbatti, tattha aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhitvā “yāvatāyukaṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavanto manussagaṇanāya [P 0.0033] idāni sattahi divasehi āyukkhayaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti vatthāni kilissanti, mālā milāyanti, kacchehi sedā muccanti, kāye vevaṇṇiyaṃ okkamati, devo devāsane na saṇṭhahatīti imesu pañcasu pubbanimittesu uppannesu tāni disvā “suññā vata bho saggā bhavissantī”ti saṃvegajātāhi devatāhi mahāsattassa pūritapāramibhāvaṃ ñatvā “imasmiṃ idāni aññaṃ devalokaṃ anupagantvā manussaloke uppajjitvā buddhabhāvaṃ patte puññāni katvā cutā cutā manussā devalokaṃ paripūressantī”ti cintetvā –

Having performed such great meritorious deeds that caused the great earth to tremble, at the end of his life, he passed away from there and was reborn in the Tusita realm. There, surpassing the other devas in ten respects, he experienced divine bliss for his entire lifespan. When the five premonitory signs appeared—his garments became soiled, his garlands withered, sweat was exuded from his armpits, a change of color came over his body, and the deva could no longer remain steady on his divine seat—indicating that ‘by human reckoning, in seven days he will reach the end of his life,’ the devas, seeing these signs and filled with a sense of urgency, thought, ‘Alas, the heavens will become empty!’ Knowing that the Great Being had fulfilled the perfections, they reflected, ‘Now, without going to another celestial world, he will be reborn in the human world and attain Buddhahood. Then, humans who have performed meritorious deeds will, upon passing away time and again, fill the celestial worlds.’

“Yatohaṃ tusite kāye, santusito nāmahaṃ tadā;

Dasasahassī samāgantvā, yācanti pañjalī mamaṃ.

“When I was in the Tusita host, I was then named Santusita; devas from ten thousand world-systems gathered and, with joined palms, entreated me:

“Kālo [V 0.0081] deva mahāvīra, uppajja mātukucchiyaṃ;

Sadevakaṃ tārayanto, bujjhassu amataṃ pada”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.66-67);

‘Now is the time, O Deva, Great Hero, arise in a mother’s womb; leading the world with its gods across, awaken to the Deathless State!’”

Evaṃ [M 0.0076] buddhabhāvatthāya āyācito kālaṃ, dīpaṃ, desaṃ, kulaṃ, janettiyā āyuppamāṇanti imāni pañca mahāvilokanāni viloketvā katasanniṭṭhāno tato cuto sakyarājakule paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā tattha mahāsampattiyā parihariyamāno anukkamena bhadrayobbanaṃ anupāpuṇi. Imasmiṃ antare “sato sampajāno ānanda bodhisatto tusitā kāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ okkamī”tiādīnaṃ (ma. ni. 3.200) suttapadānañceva tesaṃ aṭṭhakathāya ca vasena vitthāro veditabbo.

Thus, being requested for the sake of Buddhahood, he made the five great observations—the time, the continent, the country, the family, and the lifespan of his mother. Having made a firm decision, he passed away from there and took rebirth in the Sakyan royal family. There, being nurtured with great fortune, he gradually reached a blessed youth. The detailed account of this interval should be understood from the Sutta passages, such as, “Mindful and clearly aware, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita realm and entered his mother’s womb,” and from their commentaries.

So tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavikesu tīsu pāsādesu devalokasiriṃ viya rajjasiriṃ anubhavamāno uyyānakīḷāya gamanasamaye anukkamena jiṇṇabyādhimatasaṅkhāte tayo devadūte disvā sañjātasaṃvego nivattitvā catutthavāre pabbajitaṃ disvā ‘sādhu pabbajjā’ti pabbajjāya ruciṃ uppādetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā tattha divasabhāgaṃ khepetvā maṅgalapokkharaṇītīre nisinno kappakavesaṃ gahetvā āgatena vissakammena devaputtena alaṅkatapaṭiyatto rāhulabhaddassa [P 0.0034] jātasāsanaṃ sutvā puttasinehassa balavabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘yāva idaṃ bandhanaṃ na vaḍḍhati tāvadeva naṃ chindissāmī’ti cintetvā sāyaṃ nagaraṃ pavisanto –

Enjoying royal splendor like celestial glory in three palaces suitable for the three seasons, while going for pleasure-sport in the park, he saw in succession the three divine messengers known as an old man, a sick man, and a dead man. Filled with a sense of urgency, he turned back. On the fourth occasion, seeing a renunciant, he developed a liking for renunciation, thinking, ‘Good is renunciation.’ Having gone to the park and spent the day there, while sitting by the bank of the Mangala Lotus Pond, he was adorned and attired by the deva-son Vissakamma, who had come in the guise of a barber. Hearing the news of Rāhulabhadra’s birth and recognizing the strength of paternal affection, he thought, ‘I must sever this bond before it grows stronger.’ Entering the city in the evening—

“Nibbutā nūna sā mātā, nibbuto nūna so pitā;

Nibbutā nūna sā nārī, yassāyaṃ īdiso patī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 27 avidūrenidānakathā; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.10 sāriputtattheravatthu; apa. aṭṭha. 1.avidūrenidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.avidūrenidānakathā);

“Cooled indeed is that mother, cooled indeed is that father, cooled indeed is that woman, who has such a husband.”

Kisāgotamiyā nāma pitucchādhītāya bhāsitaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā, ‘ahaṃ imāya nibbutapadaṃ sāvito’ti gīvato satasahassagghanikaṃ muttāhāraṃ muñcitvā, tassā pesetvā, attano bhavanaṃ pavisitvā, sirisayane nisinno niddāvasena nāṭakānaṃ vippakāraṃ disvā, nibbinnahadayo channaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā, kaṇḍakaṃ āharāpetvā, kaṇḍakaṃ āruyha, channasahāyova dasasahassilokadhātudevatāhi kataparivāro mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā, teneva rattāvasesena tīṇi [V 0.0082] mahārajjāni atikkamma anomānadītīre pabbajitvā, anukkamena rājagahaṃ gantvā, tattha piṇḍāya caritvā, paṇḍavapabbatapabbhāre nisinno magadharājena rajjena nimantiyamāno taṃ paṭikkhipitvā, sabbaññutaṃ patvā tassa vijitaṃ āgamanatthāya tena gahitapaṭiñño[M 0.0077], āḷārañca udakañca upasaṅkamitvā, tesaṃ santike adhigatavisesena aparituṭṭho chabbassāni mahāpadhānaṃ padahitvā, visākhāpuṇṇamadivase pātova senānigame sujātāya dinnaṃ pāyāsaṃ paribhuñjitvā, nerañjarāya nadiyā suvaṇṇapātiṃ pavāhetvā, nerañjarāya tīre mahāvanasaṇḍe nānāsamāpattīhi divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā, sāyanhasamaye sotthiyena dinnaṃ aṭṭhatiṇamuṭṭhiṃ gahetvā, kāḷena nāgarājena abhitthutaguṇo bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha tiṇāni santharitvā, ‘na tāvimaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bhindissāmi yāva me na anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccissatī’ti paṭiññaṃ katvā, pācīnadisābhimukho nisīditvā, sūriye anatthaṅgamiteyeva mārabalaṃ vidhamitvā, paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ, majjhimayāme cutūpapātañāṇaṃ patvā, pacchimayāmāvasāne dasabalacatuvesārajjādisabbabuddhaguṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ [P 0.0035] sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhantoyeva imaṃ abhidhammanayasamuddaṃ adhigañchi. Evamassa adhigamanidānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Upon hearing this verse spoken by his paternal aunt’s daughter, named Kisāgotamī, thinking, “I have been made to hear of the state of Nibbāna by her,” he removed the pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand from his neck, sent it to her, and entered his own palace. Seated on the royal couch, he saw the disorder of the dancers while they were asleep. Disgusted at heart, he had Channa awakened and Kaṇṭhaka brought. Mounting Kaṇṭhaka, accompanied by Channa, surrounded by devas from ten thousand world-systems, he made the great renunciation and departed. In the remainder of that very night, he crossed three great kingdoms and took ordination on the banks of the Anomā River. Gradually, he went to Rājagaha, where he wandered for alms. Sitting on the slope of Paṇḍava Mountain, he declined the invitation of the king of Magadha to rule the kingdom, and having given a promise to him to come to his realm after attaining omniscience, he approached Āḷāra and Uddaka. But, unsatisfied with the special attainment he had gained in their presence, he practiced great striving for six years. On the full moon day of Visākha, early in the morning, he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā in Senānigama. He cast the golden bowl into the Nerañjarā River and spent the day in the great forest grove by the Nerañjarā, absorbed in various meditative attainments. In the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by Sotthiya. His virtues praised by the Nāga king Kāḷa, he ascended the seat of enlightenment, spread the grass, and made the resolve: “I will not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints without clinging.” Facing the eastern direction, he sat down. Even before the sun had set, he dispelled the forces of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of past lives; in the middle watch, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; and at the end of the last watch, he penetrated the omniscient knowledge, adorned with all the qualities of a Buddha, such as the ten powers and the four confidences, thus realizing this ocean of the Abhidhamma method. Thus should the origin of his attainment be understood.

Evaṃ adhigatābhidhammo ekapallaṅkena nisinnasattāhaṃ animisasattāhaṃ caṅkamanasattāhañca atikkamitvā, catutthe sattāhe sayambhūñāṇādhigamena adhigataṃ abhidhammaṃ vicinitvā aparānipi ajapālamucalindarājāyatanesu tīṇi sattāhāni vītināmetvā, aṭṭhame sattāhe ajapālanigrodharukkhamūle nisinno dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇena appossukkataṃ āpajjamāno dasasahassimahābrahmaparivārena sahampatibrahmunā āyācitadhammadesano buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ oloketvā, brahmuno ajjhesanaṃ ādāya “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya’nti olokento āḷārudakānaṃ kālaṅkatabhāvaṃ ñatvā, pañcavaggiyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakārataṃ anussaritvā, uṭṭhāyāsanā kāsipuraṃ gacchanto antarāmagge upakena saddhiṃ mantetvā, āsāḷhīpuṇṇamadivase isipatane migadāye pañcavaggiyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā,te ananucchavikena samudācārena samudācarante saññāpetvā, dhammacakkaṃ pavattento aññāsikoṇḍaññattherappamukhā aṭṭhārasa brahmakoṭiyo amatapānaṃ pāyesi. Evaṃ yāva dhammacakkappavattanā desanānidānaṃ [M 0.0078] veditabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana sāṭṭhakathānaṃ ariyapariyesana(ma. ni. 1.274) pabbajjasuttādīnaṃ (su. ni. 407 ādayo) vasena veditabbo.

Having thus mastered the Abhidhamma, he spent seven days seated in one posture, seven days without blinking, and seven days walking. In the fourth week, he reviewed the Abhidhamma he had attained through self-realized knowledge. Then, he spent another three weeks at the Ajapāla banyan tree, the Mucalinda tree, and the Rājāyatana tree. In the eighth week, seated at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma and inclined to inaction. Having been requested to teach the Dhamma by Sahampati Brahmā, who was accompanied by the great Brahmās of the ten-thousand-fold world system, the Buddha surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye. Accepting Brahmā’s plea, he pondered, "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?" Knowing that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, he recalled the great service of the group of five monks. Rising from his seat, he journeyed to Kāsipura. On the way, he conversed with Upaka and, on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, arrived at Isipatana in the Deer Park, the dwelling place of the group of five monks. As they were behaving disrespectfully, he convinced them and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, causing eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, led by the elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, to partake of the deathless drink. Thus, up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the origin of the teaching should be understood. This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be known from the Ariyapariyesana Sutta (MN 26), the Pabbajjā Sutta (Sn 407 and following), and others, together with their commentaries.

Evaṃ [V 0.0083] adhigamanidānadesanānidānasampannassa panassa abhidhammassa aparānipi dūrenidānaṃ, avidūrenidānaṃ, santikenidānanti tīṇi nidānāni. Tattha dīpaṅkarapādamūlato paṭṭhāya yāva tusitapurā dūrenidānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tusitapurato paṭṭhāya yāva bodhimaṇḍā avidūrenidānaṃ. ‘Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā devesu viharati tāvatiṃsesu pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ, tattha kho bhagavā devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ abhidhammakathaṃ kathesī’ti idamassa santikenidānaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva nidānakathā.

Thus, the Abhidhamma, endowed with the origin of attainment and the origin of exposition, has three other origins: a remote origin, a proximate origin, and an immediate origin. Herein, from the foot of Dīpaṅkara Buddha up to the Tusita heaven should be understood as the remote origin. From the Tusita heaven up to the Bodhi-maṇḍa is the proximate origin. "On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the devas in Tāvatiṃsa, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the Paṇḍukambala stone. There the Blessed One expounded the Abhidhamma to the devas of Tāvatiṃsa"—this is its immediate origin. This, then, is the account of the origins.

Nidānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Origins is complete.

1. Cittuppādakaṇḍo

1. The Section on the Arising of Consciousness

Tikamātikāpadavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Terms of the Triple Matrix

Idāni

Now

Iti [M 0.0079][P 0.0036][V 0.0084] me bhāsamānassa, abhidhammakathaṃ imaṃ;

Avikkhittā nisāmetha, dullabhā hi ayaṃ kathāti.

While I am speaking this discourse on the Abhidhamma, listen attentively without distraction, for rare indeed is this teaching.

Evaṃ paṭiññātāya abhidhammakathāya kathanokāso sampatto. Tattha yasmā abhidhammo nāma dhammasaṅgaṇīādīni sattappakaraṇāni; dhammasaṅgaṇīpi cittuppādakaṇḍādīnaṃ vasena cattāri kaṇḍāni; cittuppādakaṇḍampi mātikāpadabhājanīyavasena duvidhaṃ; tattha mātikā ādi; sāpi tikamātikā dukamātikāti duvidhā; tattha tikamātikā ādi; tikamātikāyapi kusalattikaṃ kusalattikepi kusalā dhammāti idaṃ padaṃ; tasmā –

The occasion for expounding the Abhidhamma discourse, as promised, has arrived. Herein, the Abhidhamma means the seven treatises beginning with the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī itself is divided into four sections, such as the section on the arising of consciousness. The section on the arising of consciousness is also twofold: the Matrix and the Exposition. Therein, the Matrix is primary. The Matrix is also twofold: the threefold matrix and the twofold matrix. Therein, the threefold matrix is primary. In the threefold matrix, the wholesome triad is primary; and within the wholesome triad, the term "wholesome states" is primary. Therefore—

Ito paṭṭhāya gambhīraṃ, abhidhammakathaṃ imaṃ;

Vuccamānaṃ nisāmetha, ekaggā sādhu sādhavoti.

From this point onward, O virtuous ones, listen well and with one-pointed mind to this profound Abhidhamma discourse as it is being spoken.

1. “Kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammā”ti ayaṃ tāva ādipadena laddhanāmo kusalattiko nāma. “Sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā, dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā”ti ayaṃ sabbapadehi laddhanāmo vedanāttiko nāma. Evaṃ ādipadavasena vā sabbapadavasena vā sabbesampi tikadukānaṃ nāmaṃ veditabbaṃ[V 0.0085]. Sabbeva cete pañcadasahi paricchedehi vavatthitā. Tikānañhi eko paricchedo, dukānaṃ catuddasa. “Hetū dhammā, nahetū dhammā”tiādayo hi cha dukā ganthato ca atthato ca aññamaññasambandhena kaṇṇikā viya ghaṭā viya hutvā ṭhitattā ‘hetugocchako’ti vuccati. Tato apare “sappaccayā dhammā appaccayā dhammā”tiādayo satta dukā, aññamaññaṃ asambandhā, kevalaṃ [P 0.0037] dukasāmaññato uccinitvā uccinitvā visuṃ visuṃ gocchakantare ṭhapitattā aññehi ca mahantaradukehi cūḷakattā ‘cūḷantaradukā’ti veditabbā. Tato paraṃ āsavadukādīnaṃ channaṃ vasena ‘āsavagocchako’[M 0.0080]; tathā saṃyojanadukādīnaṃ vasena ‘saṃyojanagocchako’; tathā ganthaoghayoganīvaraṇadukādīnaṃ vasena ‘ganthaoghayoganīvaraṇagocchakā’; parāmāsadukādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ vasena ‘parāmāsagocchako’ti. Sabbepi satta gocchakā veditabbā. Tato paraṃ “sārammaṇā dhammā”tiādayo catuddasa dukā ‘mahantaradukā’ nāma. Tato upādānadukādayo cha dukā ‘upādānagocchako’ nāma. Tato kilesadukādayo aṭṭha dukā ‘kilesagocchako’ nāma. Tato paraṃ dassanenapahātabbadukādayo aṭṭhārasa dukā abhidhammamātikāya pariyosāne ṭhapitattā ‘piṭṭhidukā’ nāma. “Vijjābhāgino dhammā avijjābhāgino dhammā”tiādayo pana dvācattālīsa dukā ‘suttantikadukā’ nāma. Evaṃ sabbepete pañcadasahi paricchedehi vavatthitāti veditabbā.

1. "Wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states"—this is called the 'wholesome triad', named by way of its initial term. "States associated with pleasant feeling, states associated with painful feeling, states associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"—this is called the 'feeling triad', named by way of all its terms. Thus, the names of all triads and dyads should be understood either by way of the initial term or by way of all terms. All these are classified into fifteen sections. For the triads, there is one section; for the dyads, there are fourteen. The six dyads beginning with "states that are roots, states that are not roots" are called the 'root collection' because they are interconnected by way of text and meaning, like a cluster or a bunch. After that, the seven dyads beginning with "states with conditions, states without conditions" are unrelated to each other; they are known as the 'minor intermediate dyads' because they are merely selected by the common characteristic of being dyads, placed separately in another collection, and are small compared to the other major dyads. Following these, the six dyads beginning with the taint dyad are the 'taint collection'; similarly, the dyads beginning with the fetter dyad are the 'fetter collection'; similarly, the dyads beginning with the bond, flood, yoke, and hindrance dyads are the 'bond, flood, yoke, and hindrance collections'; and the five dyads beginning with the misconception dyad are the 'misconception collection'. All seven collections should be understood. After that, the fourteen dyads beginning with "states with an object" are called the 'major dyads'. Then, the six dyads beginning with the clinging dyad are the 'clinging collection'. Following these, the eight dyads beginning with the defilement dyad are the 'defilement collection'. After that, the eighteen dyads beginning with the dyad of states to be abandoned by seeing are called the 'back dyads' because they are placed at the end of the Abhidhamma matrix. Furthermore, the forty-two dyads beginning with "states partaking of knowledge, states partaking of ignorance" are called the 'Suttanta dyads'. Thus, all these should be understood as classified into fifteen sections.

Evaṃ vavatthitā panete sappadesanippadesavasena dve koṭṭhāsā honti. Tesu hi nava tikā ekasattati ca dukā sappadesānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ pariggahitattā sappadesā nāma. Avasesā terasa tikā ekasattati ca dukā nippadesā nāma. Tattha tikesu tāva vedanāttiko vitakkattiko pītittiko uppannattiko atītattiko cattāro ārammaṇattikāti ime nava tikā sappadesā nāma. Dukesu hetugocchakādīnaṃ upādānagocchakapariyosānānaṃ navannaṃ gocchakānaṃ pariyosāne tayo tayo dukā, kilesagocchakapariyosāne [P 0.0038] cattāro dukā, “cittasampayuttā dhammā, cittavippayuttā dhammā”“cittasaṃsaṭṭhā dhammā, cittavisaṃsaṭṭhā dhammā”ti dve mahantaradukā, suttantikadukesu adhivacanadukaṃ niruttidukaṃ paññattidukaṃ nāmarūpadukanti ime cattāro duke ṭhapetvā avasesā aṭṭhatiṃsa dukā cāti ete sappadesā nāma. Vuttāvasesā tikadukā sabbepi nippadesāti veditabbā.

These, being thus established, are of two portions: the partial and the complete. Among them, nine triads and seventy-one dyads are called 'partial' because they encompass only a portion of the phenomena of form and the formless. The remaining thirteen triads and thirty-one dyads are called 'complete'. Here, among the triads, these nine are called 'partial': the feeling triad, the applied thought triad, the joy triad, the arisen triad, the past triad, and the four object triads. Among the dyads, the following are called 'partial': the three dyads at the end of each of the nine collections from the Root Collection to the Clinging Collection; the four dyads at the end of the Defilement Collection; the two major dyads—'states associated with mind and states dissociated from mind,' and 'states conjoined with mind and states disjoined from mind'; and, from the Suttanta dyads, the remaining thirty-eight dyads, excluding these four: the designation dyad, the language dyad, the concept dyad, and the name-and-form dyad. All the remaining triads and dyads that have not been mentioned should be understood as 'complete'.

Idāni kusalā dhammātiādīnaṃ mātikāpadānaṃ ayamanupubbapadavaṇṇanā – ‘kusala’-saddo tāva [V 0.0086] ārogyaanavajjachekasukhavipākesu dissati. Ayañhi “kacci nu bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmaya”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.15.146; 2.20.129) ārogye dissati. “Katamo pana, bhante, kāyasamācāro kusalo? Yo kho, mahārāja, kāyasamācāro anavajjo”ti (ma. ni. 2.361) ca, “aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ [M 0.0081] yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti kusalesu dhammesū”ti (dī. ni. 3.145) ca evamādīsu anavajje. “Kusalo tvaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ” (ma. ni. 2.87), “kusalā naccagītassa sikkhitā cāturitthiyo”tiādīsu (jā. 2.22.94) cheke. “Kusalānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ samādānahetu” (dī. ni. 3.80), “kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 431) sukhavipāke. Svāyamidha ārogyepi anavajjepi sukhavipākepi vattati.

Now, the following is a sequential explanation of the terms in the matrix beginning with 'wholesome states'. The word 'kusala', in the first place, is seen in the senses of health, blamelessness, skill, and pleasant result. For example, in instances such as, "I hope you are well, sir, I hope you are free from illness," it is seen in the sense of health. And in statements such as, "But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? Great king, bodily conduct that is blameless," and "Moreover, venerable sir, this is the unsurpassed teaching wherein the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding wholesome states," it is seen in the sense of blamelessness. In instances such as, "You are skilled in the parts and accessories of a chariot," and "Four women, skilled in dancing and singing, are trained," it is seen in the sense of skill. In passages such as, "Monks, for the sake of undertaking wholesome states," and "Because of having done and accumulated a wholesome deed," it is seen in the sense of pleasant result. This word, here, applies in the senses of health, blamelessness, and pleasant result.

Dhammasaddo panāyaṃ pariyattihetuguṇanissattanijjīvatādīsu dissati. Ayañhi “dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāti suttaṃ geyya”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.102) pariyattiyaṃ dissati. “Hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 720) hetumhi.

The word 'dhamma', however, is seen in such senses as scripture, cause, quality, soullessness, lifelessness, and so on. For it is seen in the sense of scripture in passages such as, 'one masters the Dhamma—Sutta, Geyya...' It is seen in the sense of cause in passages such as, 'knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of conditions...'

“Na hi dhammo adhammo ca, ubho samavipākino;

Adhammo nirayaṃ neti, dhammo pāpeti suggati”nti. (theragā. 304; jā. 1.15.386) –

"For Dhamma and Adhamma do not both have the same result; Adhamma leads to hell, while Dhamma brings one to a good destination."

Ādīsu guṇe. “Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā honti” (dha. sa. 121), “dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.373) nissattanijjīvatāyaṃ. Svāyamidhāpi nissattanijjīvatāyameva vaṭṭati.

and so on, in the sense of quality. In passages such as, 'Now, at that time, there are states (dhammā),' and 'one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena,' it is seen in the sense of soullessness and lifelessness. Here too, it applies precisely in this sense of soullessness and lifelessness.

Vacanattho [P 0.0039] panettha – kucchite pāpake dhamme salayanti calayanti kampenti viddhaṃsentīti kusalā. Kucchitena vā ākārena sayantīti kusā. Te akusalasaṅkhāte kuse lunanti chindantīti kusalā. Kucchitānaṃ vā sānato tanukaraṇato osānakaraṇato ñāṇaṃ kusaṃ nāma. Tena kusena lātabbāti kusalā; gahetabbā pavattetabbāti attho. Yathā vā kusā ubhayabhāgagataṃ hatthappadesaṃ lunanti, evamimepi uppannānuppannabhāvena ubhayabhāgagataṃ kilesapakkhaṃ lunanti. Tasmā kusā viya lunantītipi kusalā. Attano pana sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhammā. Dhāriyanti [V 0.0087] vā paccayehi, dhārīyanti vā yathāsabhāvatoti dhammā. Na kusalā akusalā. Mittapaṭipakkhā amittā viya, lobhādipaṭipakkhā alobhādayo viya ca, kusalapaṭipakkhāti attho. Na byākatāti abyākatā, kusalākusalabhāvena akathitāti attho. Tesu pana [M 0.0082] anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇā kusalā, sāvajjadukkhavipākalakkhaṇā akusalā, avipākalakkhaṇā abyākatā.

The meaning of the word here is as follows: Because they shake, agitate, disturb, and destroy vile, evil states, they are called 'wholesome' (kusalā). Or, because they lie down (sayanti) in a vile manner, they are kusā. They cut (lunanti) and sever those kusā which are designated as unwholesome; therefore, they are called 'wholesome' (kusalā). Or, knowledge is called kusa from its making keen (sānato), diminishing, and bringing to an end vile things. Because they are to be obtained (lātabbā) by that kusa (knowledge), they are kusalā; the meaning is that they are to be grasped and set in motion. Or, just as blades of kusa grass cut the hand that has grasped them on both sides, so too do these cut the faction of defilements, which is present on both sides in its arisen and unarisen states. Therefore, because they cut like kusa grass, they are also called 'wholesome' (kusalā). Furthermore, because they bear their own intrinsic nature, they are called 'dhammas'. Or, they are borne by conditions, or they are borne according to their intrinsic nature; thus they are 'dhammas'. Those that are not wholesome are unwholesome. Just as non-friends are the opposite of friends, and just as non-greed and so on are the opposite of greed and so on, the meaning is that they are the opposite of the wholesome. Because they are not declared, they are indeterminate; the meaning is that they are not spoken of as being wholesome or unwholesome. Among these, however, the wholesome have the characteristic of being blameless and having a pleasant result; the unwholesome have the characteristic of being blameworthy and having a painful result; and the indeterminate have the characteristic of having no result.

Kiṃ panetāni ‘kusalā’ti vā ‘dhammā’ti vātiādīni ekatthāni udāhu nānatthānīti? Kiñcettha? Yadi tāva ekatthāni ‘kusalā dhammā’ti idaṃ ‘kusalākusalā’tivuttasadisaṃ hoti. Atha nānatthāni tikadukānaṃ chakkacatukkabhāvo āpajjati padānañca asambandho.

Now, are these terms—such as 'wholesome' or 'dhammas'—of one meaning or of different meanings? What follows from this? If, in the first place, they are of one meaning, then this phrase 'wholesome dhammas' would be like the expression 'wholesome-wholesome'. But if they are of different meanings, the triads would become groups of six and the dyads groups of four, and there would be no connection between the words.

Yathā hi ‘kusalā’ ‘rūpaṃ’‘cakkhumā’ti vutte atthavasena aññamaññaṃ anolokentānaṃ padānaṃ na koci sambandho, evamidhāpi padānaṃ asambandho āpajjati. Pubbāparasambandharahitāni ca padāni nippayojanāni nāma honti. Yāpi cesā parato ‘katame dhammā kusalā’ti pucchā, tāyapi saddhiṃ virodho āpajjati. Neva hi dhammā kusalā; atha ca panidaṃ vuccati – katame dhammā ‘kusalā’ti. Aparo nayo – yadi etāni ekatthāni, tiṇṇaṃ ‘dhammānaṃ’ ekattā kusalādīnampi ekattaṃ āpajjati. Kusalādiparānañhi tiṇṇampi ‘dhammānaṃ’ dhammabhāvena ekattaṃ. Tasmā dhammattayena saddhiṃ atthato ninnānatthānaṃ kusalādīnampi ekattaṃ āpajjati. ‘Yadeva kusalaṃ, taṃ akusalaṃ, taṃ abyākata’nti. ‘Athāpi tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ ekattaṃ na sampaṭicchatha, aññova kusalaparo dhammo, añño [P 0.0040] akusalaparo dhammo, añño abyākataparo dhammoti vadatha, evaṃ sante dhammo nāma bhāvo, bhāvato ca añño abhāvoti kusalaparā bhāvasaṅkhātā dhammā añño akusalaparo dhammo abhāvo siyā, tathā abyākataparo. Tehi ca añño kusalaparopi. Evaṃ abhāvattaṃ āpannehi dhammehi anaññe kusalādayopi abhāvāyeva siyu’nti.

For just as when the words 'wholesome,' 'form,' and 'one with eyes' are spoken, there is no connection between the words, which do not regard each other in terms of meaning, so too here a disconnection of the words would result. And words that are devoid of connection between what precedes and what follows are indeed called useless. Furthermore, a contradiction would arise with the question that follows, 'Which dhammas are wholesome?'. For dhammas are not in themselves wholesome; and yet this is said: 'Which dhammas are wholesome?'. Another line of reasoning: if these terms are of one meaning, then from the oneness of the three 'dhammas', the oneness of the wholesome, etc., also follows. For the three 'dhammas'—qualified by wholesome, etc.—have a oneness through their nature as dhammas. Therefore, for the wholesome, etc., which are not different in meaning from the triad of dhammas, a oneness also follows, leading to the absurdity: 'Whatever is wholesome, that is unwholesome, that is indeterminate.' Now, if you do not accept the oneness of the three dhammas, and you say, 'The dhamma qualified by "wholesome" is one thing, the dhamma qualified by "unwholesome" is another, and the dhamma qualified by "indeterminate" is another,' this being so, 'dhamma' is existence, and what is other than existence is non-existence. Thus, the dhammas qualified by 'wholesome', designated as 'existence', would be one thing, while the dhamma qualified by 'unwholesome' would be another, a 'non-existence', and likewise the one qualified by 'indeterminate'. And the one qualified by 'wholesome' would also be other than them. In this way, with the dhammas having attained a state of non-existence, the wholesome, etc., not being different from them, would also be mere non-existence.

Sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Kasmā? Yathānumativohārasiddhitoti. Vohāro hi yathā yathā atthesu anumato sampaṭicchito tathā tatheva siddho. Na cāyaṃ “kusalā dhammā”tiādīsu kusalapubbo dhammābhilāpo dhammaparo ca kusalābhilāpo, yathā ‘kusalā kusalā’ti evaṃ, attano atthavisesābhāvena paṇḍitehi sampaṭicchito; na ca ‘kusalā’ ‘rūpaṃ’cakkhumāsaddā viya aññamaññaṃ anolokitatthabhāvena. ‘Kusala’-saddo panettha anavajjasukhavipākasaṅkhātassa atthassa [M 0.0083][V 0.0088] jotakabhāvena sampaṭicchito, ‘akusala’-saddo sāvajjadukkhavipākatthajotakattena, ‘abyākata’-saddo avipākatthajotakattena, ‘dhamma’-saddo sabhāvadhāraṇādiatthajotakattena. So etesaṃ aññatarānantare vuccamāno attano atthasāmaññaṃ dīpeti. Sabbeva hi ete sabhāvadhāraṇādinā lakkhaṇena dhammā. Kusalādisaddā cāpi dhammasaddassa purato vuccamānā attano attano atthavisesaṃ tassa dīpenti. Dhammo hi kusalo vā hoti akusalo vā abyākato vā. Evamete visuṃ visuṃ vuccamānā attano attano atthamattadīpakattena sampaṭicchitā. Dhammasaddena saha vuccamānā attano attano atthasāmaññaṃ atthavisesaṃ vā dīpakattena loke paṇḍitehi sampaṭicchitā. Tasmā yadetamettha ekatthanānātthataṃ vikappetvā dosāropanakāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva kusalattikassa anupubbapadavaṇṇanā. Imināva nayena sesatikadukānampi nayo veditabbo. Ito paraṃ pana visesamattameva vakkhāma.

All this is without reason. Why? Because of the establishment of conventional usage. For conventional usage is established in whatever way it is approved and accepted in various meanings. And this expression 'wholesome dhammas', etc., where the word 'dhamma' is preceded by 'wholesome', is not accepted by the wise as being without its own specific meaning, like the expression 'wholesome-wholesome'; nor is it accepted as having a meaning where the words do not regard each other, like the words 'wholesome', 'form', and 'one with eyes'. Here, the word 'wholesome' is accepted as illuminating the meaning designated as 'blameless and having a pleasant result'; the word 'unwholesome' as illuminating the meaning of 'blameworthy and having a painful result'; the word 'indeterminate' as illuminating the meaning of 'having no result'; and the word 'dhamma' as illuminating the meaning of 'bearing its own nature', etc. It, being spoken immediately after one of these, reveals its own general meaning. For all of these are indeed dhammas by the characteristic of bearing their own nature, etc. And the words 'wholesome', etc., being spoken before the word 'dhamma', reveal their own specific meaning to it. For a dhamma is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Thus, when spoken separately, they are accepted as revealing only their own respective meanings. When spoken together with the word 'dhamma', they are accepted by the wise in the world as revealing either their own general meaning or their specific meaning. Therefore, all this that has been said here—this reason for imputing a fault by speculating on whether the terms have one meaning or different meanings—is all without reason. This, in the first place, is the sequential explanation of the words of the wholesome triad. By this same method, the method for the remaining triads and dyads should also be understood. Hereafter, however, we will speak only of the specific points.

2. Sukhāya vedanāyātiādīsu ‘sukha’-saddo tāva sukhavedanāsukhamūlasukhārammaṇasukhahetusukhapaccayaṭṭhānaabyābajjhanibbānādīsu dissati. Ayañhi “sukhassa ca pahānā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.232) sukhavedanāyaṃ dissati. “Sukho buddhānaṃ uppādo” (dha. pa. 194), “sukhā virāgatā loke”tiādīsu (udā. 11; mahāva. 5) sukhamūle “yasmā [P 0.0041] ca kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkanta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.60) sukhārammaṇe. “Sukhassetaṃ, bhikkhave, adhivacanaṃ yadidaṃ puññānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.62) sukhahetumhi. “Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ yāva sukhā saggā” (ma. ni. 3.255), “na te sukhaṃ pajānanti ye na passanti nandana”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.11) sukhapaccayaṭṭhāne. “Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā ete dhammā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.82) abyābajjhe. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”ntiādisu (dha. pa. 203-204) nibbāne. Idha panāyaṃ sukhavedanāyameva daṭṭhabbo. ‘Vedanā’-saddo “viditā vedanā uppajjantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.208) vedayitasmiṃyeva vattati.

2. In passages beginning with 'pleasant feeling' (sukhāya vedanāya), etc., the term 'sukha' is seen in pleasant feeling, the root of pleasure, the object of pleasure, the cause of pleasure, the condition for pleasure, non-affliction, Nibbāna, etc. For instance, in passages like 'the abandoning of pleasure' (Dī. Ni. 1.232), it is seen in the sense of pleasant feeling. In 'The arising of the Buddhas is happiness' (Dhp. 194) and 'Dispassion is happiness in the world' (Ud. 11; Mahāva. 5), etc., it is seen in the sense of the root of happiness. In 'Mahāli, because form is pleasant, associated with pleasure, inclined to pleasure' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.60), etc., it is seen in the sense of the object of pleasure. In 'Monks, this is a designation for happiness, namely, merit' (A. Ni. 7.62), etc., it is seen in the sense of the cause of happiness. In 'Monks, it is not easy to convey by description how happy are the heavens' (Ma. Ni. 3.255) and 'Those who do not see Nandana do not understand happiness' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.11), etc., it is seen in the sense of the condition for happiness. In 'These states are the abiding in happiness in this very life' (Ma. Ni. 1.82), etc., it is seen in the sense of non-affliction. In 'Nibbāna is the highest happiness' (Dhp. 203-204), etc., it is seen in the sense of Nibbāna. Here, however, it should be understood specifically as pleasant feeling. The term 'vedanā' is used in contexts like 'feelings are known as they arise' (Ma. Ni. 3.208), etc., to refer to the felt (vedayita) itself.

‘Dukkha’-saddo [M 0.0084] dukkhavedanādukkhavatthudukkhārammaṇadukkhapaccayadukkhapaccayaṭṭhānādīsu dissati. Ayañhi “dukkhassa ca pahānā”tiādīsu dukkhavedanāyaṃ dissati. “Jātipi dukkhā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.387; vibha. 190) dukkhavatthusmiṃ. “Yasmā ca kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhānupatitaṃ dukkhāvakkanta”ntiādīsu dukkhārammaṇe. “Dukkho pāpassa [V 0.0089] uccayo”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 117) dukkhapaccaye. “Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ yāva dukkhā nirayā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.250) dukkhapaccayaṭṭhāne. Idha panāyaṃ dukkhavedanāyameva daṭṭhabbo.

The term 'dukkha' is seen in painful feeling, the basis of suffering, the object of suffering, the cause of suffering, the condition for suffering, etc. For instance, in passages like 'the abandoning of suffering,' etc., it is seen in the sense of painful feeling. In 'Birth is suffering' (Dī. Ni. 2.387; Vibh. 190), etc., it is seen in the sense of the basis of suffering. In 'Mahāli, because form is suffering, associated with suffering, inclined to suffering,' etc., it is seen in the sense of the object of suffering. In 'The accumulation of evil is suffering' (Dhp. 117), etc., it is seen in the sense of the cause of suffering. In 'Monks, it is not easy to convey through description how painful the hells are' (Ma. Ni. 3.250), etc., it is seen in the sense of the condition for suffering. Here, however, it should be understood specifically as painful feeling.

Vacanattho panettha – sukhayatīti sukhā. Dukkhayatīti dukkhā. Na dukkhā na sukhāti adukkhamasukhā. ‘Ma-kāro padasandhivasena vutto. Sabbāpi ārammaṇarasaṃ vedayanti anubhavantīti vedanā. Tāsu iṭṭhānubhavanalakkhaṇā sukhā, aniṭṭhānubhavanalakkhaṇā dukkhā, ubhayaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā adukkhamasukhā. Yopanāyaṃ tīsupi padesu ‘sampayutta’-saddo, tassattho – samaṃ pakārehi yuttāti sampayuttā. Katarehi pakārehīti? Ekuppādatādīhi. “Natthi [P 0.0042] keci dhammā kehici dhammehi sampayuttāti? Āmantā”ti hi imassa pañhassa paṭikkhepe “nanu atthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi sahagatā sahajātā saṃsaṭṭhā ekuppādā ekanirodhā ekavatthukā ekārammaṇā”ti (kathā. 473) evaṃ ekuppādatādīnaṃ vasena sampayogattho vutto. Iti imehi ekuppādatādīhi samaṃ pakārehi yuttāti sampayuttā.

Herein, the meaning of the words is: it is pleasant, thus it is 'pleasure' (sukhā); it is painful, thus it is 'pain' (dukkhā); it is neither painful nor pleasant, thus it is 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant' (adukkhamasukhā). The letter 'ma' is stated by way of euphonic conjunction. They are all called 'feeling' (vedanā) because they feel, that is, experience the taste of their objects. Among them, pleasant feeling is characterized by experiencing the desirable, painful feeling by experiencing the undesirable, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling by experiencing the opposite of both. As for the term 'associated' (sampayutta) in all three instances, its meaning is: 'associated' means 'conjoined by the same modes.' By what modes? By having the same arising, and so on. For in the rejection of the question, 'Are there no phenomena at all associated with any phenomena? – Yes,' it is stated, 'But are there not phenomena that are concurrent, co-arisen, conjoined, of single arising, of single cessation, of single base, of single object?'
