(Kathā. 473). Thus, the meaning of 'association' (sampayoga) is stated by way of having the same arising, and so on. Therefore, 'associated' means 'conjoined by the same modes,' such as having the same arising.

3. Vipākattike aññamaññavisiṭṭhānaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ pākāti vipākā. Vipakkabhāvamāpannānaṃ arūpadhammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vipākadhammadhammāti vipākasabhāvadhammā. Yathā jātijarāsabhāvā jātijarāpakatikā sattā jātidhammā jarādhammāti vuccanti evaṃ vipākajanakaṭṭhena vipākasabhāvā vipākapakatikā dhammāti attho. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayasabhāvapaṭikkhepavasena vuttaṃ.

3. In the triad of resultants, 'resultants' (vipākā) are the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome states that are distinct from one another. This is a designation for immaterial phenomena that have attained the state of fruition. 'Phenomena that have the nature of producing a result' (vipākadhammadhammā) means phenomena that have the nature of a resultant. Just as beings having the nature of birth and aging, whose intrinsic nature is birth and aging, are called 'subject to birth' and 'subject to aging,' so too, the meaning is that phenomena have the nature of a resultant, and an intrinsic nature of a resultant, because they generate a result. The third term is stated by way of rejecting both natures.

4. Upādinnupādāniyattike ārammaṇakaraṇavasena taṇhādiṭṭhīhi upetena kammunā ādinnā, phalabhāvena gahitāti upādinnā. Ārammaṇabhāvaṃ [M 0.0085] upagantvā upādānasambandhena upādānānaṃ hitāti upādāniyā. Upādānassa ārammaṇapaccayabhūtānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Upādiṇṇā ca te upādāniyā cāti upādiṇṇupādāniyā; sāsavakammanibbattānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iti iminā nayena sesapadadvayepi paṭisedhasahito attho veditabbo.

4. In the triad of the grasped and graspable, 'grasped' (upādinna) means that which is seized by action—accompanied by craving and views—by way of making it an object, and is taken as a fruit. 'Graspable' (upādāniya) means that which, having become an object, is conducive to the clingings through its connection with clinging. This is a designation for what serves as the object-condition for clinging. They are grasped and they are graspable, thus they are 'grasped and graspable' (upādiṇṇupādāniyā); this is a designation for material and immaterial phenomena produced by actions with taints. In this way, the meaning of the remaining two terms should be understood along with their negation.

5. Saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikattike saṃkilesetīti saṃkileso, vibādhati, upatāpeti cāti attho. Saṃkilesena samannāgatāti saṃkiliṭṭhā. Attānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanena saṃkilesaṃ arahanti[V 0.0090], saṃkilese vā niyuttā, tassa ārammaṇabhāvānatikkamanatoti saṃkilesikā. Saṃkilesassa ārammaṇapaccayabhūtānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saṃkiliṭṭhā ca te saṃkilesikā cāti saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā. Sesapadadvayampi purimattike vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

5. In the triad of the defiled and defiling, 'defilement' (saṃkilesa) means 'that which defiles'; that is, it oppresses and torments. 'Defiled' (saṃkiliṭṭhā) means 'endowed with defilement.' 'Defiling' (saṃkilesikā) means that, by occurring with themselves as object, they are worthy of defilement; or they are engaged in defilement, because of not transcending its state as an object. This is a designation for those things that serve as the object-condition for defilement. They are defiled and they are defiling, thus they are 'defiled and defiling' (saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā). The remaining two terms should also be understood in the same way as explained in the previous triad.

6. Vitakkattike [P 0.0043] sampayogavasena vattamānena saha vitakkena savitakkā. Saha vicārena savicārā. Savitakkā ca te savicārā cāti savitakkasavicārā. Ubhayarahitā avitakkaavicārā. Vitakkavicāresu vicārova mattā, pamāṇaṃ, etesanti vicāramattā. Vicārato uttari vitakkena saddhiṃ sampayogaṃ na gacchantīti attho. Avitakkā ca te vicāramattā cāti avitakkavicāramattā.

6. In the triad of initial application, 'with initial application' (savitakkā) means being together with initial application that is occurring by way of association. 'With sustained application' (savicārā) means being together with sustained application. They are with initial application and they are with sustained application, thus they are 'with initial and sustained application' (savitakkasavicārā). Those devoid of both are 'without initial and sustained application' (avitakkaavicārā). In 'with sustained application only' (vicāramattā), sustained application alone is their measure (mattā), their limit (pamāṇaṃ). The meaning is that, beyond sustained application, they do not enter into association with initial application. They are without initial application and with sustained application only, thus they are 'without initial application but with sustained application only' (avitakkavicāramattā).

7. Pītittike pītiyā saha ekuppādādibhāvaṃ gatāti pītisahagatā, pītisampayuttāti attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Upekkhāti cettha adukkhamasukhā vedanā vuttā. Sā hi sukhadukkhākārappavattiṃ upekkhati, majjhattākārasaṇṭhitattā tenākārena pavattatīti upekkhā. Iti vedanāttikato padadvayameva gahetvā nippītikassa sukhassa sappītikasukhato visesadassanavasena ayaṃ tiko vutto.

7. In the triad of joy, 'accompanied by joy' (pītisahagatā) means so because it has gone into a state of co-arising, etc., together with joy; the meaning is 'associated with joy.' The same principle applies to the remaining two terms. Here, 'equanimity' (upekkhā) refers to the feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For it is called 'equanimity' because it regards with equanimity the occurrence of pleasure and pain, and because it is established in a neutral state, it proceeds in that manner. Thus, taking just two terms from the triad of feeling, this triad is stated in order to show the distinction between happiness without joy and happiness with joy.

8. Dassanattike dassanenāti sotāpattimaggena. So hi paṭhamaṃ nibbānaṃ dassanato dassananti vutto. Gotrabhu pana kiñcāpi paṭhamataraṃ passati, yathā pana rañño santikaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena āgato puriso dūratova rathikāya carantaṃ hatthikkhandhagataṃ rājānaṃ disvāpi ‘diṭṭho te [M 0.0086] rājā’ti puṭṭho disvāpi kattabbakiccassa akatattā ‘na passāmī’ti āha. Evameva nibbānaṃ disvāpi kattabbassa kilesappahānassābhāvā na dassananti vuccati. Tañhi ñāṇaṃ maggassa āvajjanaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Bhāvanāyāti sesamaggattayena. Sesamaggattayañhi paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhasmiṃyeva dhamme bhāvanāvasena uppajjati, adiṭṭhapubbaṃ kiñci na passati, tasmā bhāvanāti vuccati. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepavasena vuttaṃ.

8. In the triad of seeing, 'by seeing' (dassanena) refers to the path of stream-entry. For it is called 'seeing' because it sees Nibbāna for the first time. However, although the change-of-lineage consciousness sees it even earlier, it is like a man who has come to the king on some business; even having seen the king from afar mounted on an elephant and travelling along the road, when asked, 'Have you seen the king?', he replies, 'I have not seen him,' because the task to be done has not been accomplished. In the same way, although Nibbāna has been seen, because the abandonment of defilements that is to be done has not occurred, it is not called 'seeing.' For that knowledge stands at the stage of adverting to the path. 'By development' (bhāvanāya) refers to the remaining three paths. For the remaining three paths arise by way of development with regard to the very Dhamma seen by the first path; they do not see anything not seen before, therefore they are called 'development.' The third term is stated by way of rejecting both.

9. Tadanantarattike dassanena pahātabbo hetu etesanti dassanena pahātabbahetukā. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Tatiyapade neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabbo hetu etesanti evamatthaṃ aggahetvā neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabbo hetu etesaṃ atthīti evamattho gahetabbo[P 0.0044][V 0.0091]. Itarathā hi ahetukānaṃ aggahaṇaṃ bhaveyya; hetuyeva hi tesaṃ natthi yo dassanabhāvanāhi pahātabbo siyā. Sahetukesupi hetuvajjānaṃ pahānaṃ āpajjati, na hetūnaṃ; hetuyeva hi etesaṃ ‘neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabbo’ti vutto, na te dhammā. Ubhayampi cetaṃ anadhippetaṃ. Tasmā neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabbo hetu etesaṃ atthīti nevadassanena nabhāvanāya pahātabbahetukāti ayamattho gahetabbo.

9. In the next triad, 'having a cause to be abandoned by seeing' (dassanena pahātabbahetukā) means that these have a cause that is to be abandoned by seeing. The same principle applies to the second term. In the third term, the meaning should not be taken as 'these have a cause that is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development,' but rather it should be taken as 'for these, there exists a cause that is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development.' Otherwise, the causeless states would not be included, for they have no cause at all that could be abandoned by seeing or by development. And even in the case of states with causes, it would imply the abandonment of things other than the causes, not of the causes themselves; for it is the cause itself of which it is said 'to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development,' not those other states. And both of these are unintended. Therefore, the meaning to be taken is: 'for these, there exists a cause that is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development,' hence they are called 'having a cause to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development' (nevadassanena nabhāvanāya pahātabbahetukā).

10. Ācayagāmittike kammakilesehi āciyatīti ācayo. Paṭisandhicutigatippavattānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Tassa kāraṇaṃ hutvā nipphādanakabhāvena taṃ ācayaṃ gacchanti, yassa vā pavattanti taṃ puggalaṃ yathāvuttameva ācayaṃ gamentītipi ācayagāmino; sāsavakusalākusalānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tato eva ācayasaṅkhātā cayā apetattā, nibbānaṃ apetaṃ cayāti apacayo. Taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanato apacayaṃ gacchantīti apacayagāmino; ariyamaggānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Apica pākāraṃ iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī viya pavattaṃ ācinantā gacchantīti ācayagāmino. Tena citaṃ citaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ viddhaṃsayamāno puriso viya tadeva pavattaṃ apacinantā gacchantīti apacayagāmino. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepena vuttaṃ.

10. In the triad of those leading to accumulation, 'accumulation' (ācayo) is so called because it is accumulated by kamma and defilements. This is a name for rebirth-linking, death, and the ongoing process of existence. Because they are a cause of that and bring it to completion, they 'lead to that accumulation'; or, because they cause the person in whom they occur to go to the accumulation as described, they are 'leading to accumulation' (ācayagāmino). This is a designation for wholesome and unwholesome states accompanied by taints. Because it is devoid of that which is called accumulation, Nibbāna, being without accumulation, is 'non-accumulation' (apacayo). Because they proceed having made that their object, they 'lead to non-accumulation' (apacayagāmino); this is a designation for the noble paths. Furthermore, like a brick-mason building a wall, they proceed by accumulating the process of existence, thus they are 'leading to accumulation.' Like a man demolishing that which has been built brick by brick, they proceed by dismantling that same process of existence, thus they are 'leading to non-accumulation.' The third term is stated by way of rejecting both.

11. Sekkhattike tīsu sikkhāsu jātāti sekkhā. Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ etetipi sekkhā. Apariyositasikkhattā sayameva sikkhantītipi sekkhā[M 0.0087]. Upari sikkhitabbābhāvato na sekkhāti asekkhā. Vuḍḍhippattā vā sekkhātipi asekkhā. Arahattaphaladhammānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepena vuttaṃ.

11. In the triad of the trainee, 'trainees' (sekkhā) are those engaged in the three trainings. This also refers to the seven kinds of trainees. Or, because their training is unfinished, they are still training, hence they are 'trainees.' Because there is nothing further to be trained in, one is a 'non-trainee' (asekkhā). Or, because they have attained the culmination, they are 'non-trainees.' This is a designation for the states associated with the fruit of Arahantship. The third term is stated by way of rejecting both.

12. Parittattike samantato khaṇḍitattā appamattakaṃ parittanti vuccati; ‘parittaṃ gomayapiṇḍa’ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.96) viya. Imepi appānubhāvatāya parittā viyāti parittā; kāmāvacaradhammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Kilesavikkhambhanasamatthatāya vipulaphalatāya dīghasantānatāya ca mahantabhāvaṃ gatā, mahantehi vā uḷāracchandavīriyacittapaññehi gatā paṭipannātipi mahaggatā. Pamāṇakarā [P 0.0045] dhammā rāgādayo pamāṇaṃ nāma. Ārammaṇato vā sampayogato vā natthi etesaṃ pamāṇaṃ, pamāṇassa ca paṭipakkhāti appamāṇā.

12. In the triad of the limited, a thing is called 'limited' (parittaṃ), meaning insignificant, because it is circumscribed on all sides; as in the phrase 'a small lump of cow-dung' and so on. These states, too, are 'limited' because they are of little power; this is a designation for sense-sphere states. States that have reached a great state (mahantabhāvaṃ gatā) on account of their capacity to suppress the defilements, their abundant fruit, and their long continuity are 'exalted' (mahaggatā); or, they are 'exalted' because they are attained or entered upon by means of great zeal, energy, mind, and wisdom. The states that create a measure, such as lust and so on, are called 'measure' (pamāṇa). Because there is no measure for these states, either by way of object or by way of association, and because they are the opposite of a measure, they are 'immeasurable' (appamāṇā).

13. Parittārammaṇattike [V 0.0092] parittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etesanti parittārammaṇā. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

13. In the triad of states with a limited object, 'with a limited object' (parittārammaṇā) are those states that have a limited object. The same principle applies to the remaining two terms.

14. Hīnattike hīnāti lāmakā akusalā dhammā. Hīnappaṇītānaṃ majjhe bhavāti majjhimā. Avasesā tebhūmakā dhammā uttamaṭṭhena atappakaṭṭhena ca paṇītā; lokuttarā dhammā.

14. In the triad of the inferior, the 'inferior' (hīnā) are the base, unwholesome states. Those that are in the middle of the inferior and the superior are the 'middling' (majjhimā). The remaining states of the three planes are 'superior' (paṇītā) in the sense of being supreme and because they are not distressing; the supramundane states are also superior.

15. Micchattattike ‘hitasukhāvahā me bhavissantī’ti evaṃ āsīsitāpi tathā abhāvato, ‘asubhādīsuyeva subha’ntiādi viparītappavattito ca micchāsabhāvāti micchattā; vipākadāne sati khandhabhedānantarameva vipākadānato niyatā; micchattā ca te niyatā cāti micchattaniyatā. Vuttaviparītena atthena sammāsabhāvāti sammattā; sammattā ca te niyatā ca anantarameva phaladānenāti sammattaniyatā. Ubhayathāpi na niyatāti aniyatā.

15. In the triad of wrongness, states are of a 'wrong nature' (micchattā) because, although they are wished for thus, 'They will bring me welfare and happiness,' they are not in fact so; and because they proceed in a contrary way, such as perceiving 'the beautiful in what is not beautiful,' and so on. They are 'fixed' (niyatā) because, when they give their result, they do so immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates. Because they are of a wrong nature and are fixed, they are 'fixed in wrongness' (micchattaniyatā). In the opposite sense to what has been said, states are of a 'right nature' (sammattā). Because they are of a right nature and are fixed in giving their fruit immediately, they are 'fixed in rightness' (sammattaniyatā). Those that are not fixed in either way are 'unfixed' (aniyatā).

16. Maggārammaṇattike nibbānaṃ maggati, gavesati, kilese vā mārento gacchatīti maggo. Maggo ārammaṇaṃ etesanti maggārammaṇā. Aṭṭhaṅgikopi maggo paccayaṭṭhena etesaṃ hetūti maggahetukā. Maggasampayuttā vā hetū magge vā hetūti maggahetū. Te etesaṃ hetūtipi [M 0.0088] maggahetukā. Sammādiṭṭhi sayaṃ maggo ceva hetu ca. Iti maggo hetu etesantipi maggahetukā. Abhibhavitvā pavattanaṭṭhena maggo adhipati etesanti maggādhipatino.

16. In the triad of path-object states, the path (maggo) is so called because one seeks (maggati) or searches for (gavesati) Nibbāna, or because one proceeds while destroying defilements. Those for which the path is the object are 'path-object' (maggārammaṇā). The Noble Eightfold Path is also a condition for them in the sense of a cause, hence they are 'path-caused' (maggahetukā). Alternatively, causes associated with the path or causes within the path are 'path-causes' (maggahetū); because these are their causes, they are also 'path-caused' (maggahetukā). Right view is itself both path and cause; thus, because the path is the cause for them, they are also 'path-caused' (maggahetukā). Because the path is the dominant factor for them in the sense of proceeding by overcoming, they are 'path-dominant' (maggādhipatino).

17. Uppannattike uppādato paṭṭhāya yāva bhaṅgā uddhaṃ pannā gatā pavattāti uppannā. Na uppannāti anuppannā. Pariniṭṭhitakāraṇekadesattā avassaṃ uppajjissantīti uppādino.

17. In the triad of the arisen, those that have proceeded from arising up to dissolution, having gone upwards, are called 'arisen'. Those not arisen are called 'unarisen'. Those that will certainly arise due to a partly completed cause are called 'about to arise'.

18. Atītattike attano sabhāvaṃ uppādādikkhaṇaṃ vā patvā atikkantāti atītā. Tadubhayampi na āgatāti anāgatā. Taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca uppannāti paccuppannā.

18. In the triad of the past, things that, having attained their own nature or the moment of arising, etc., have passed by, are called 'past'. That which has not come in either of these ways is called 'future'. That which has arisen dependent on this or that cause is called 'present'.

19. Anantarattike atītaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etesanti atītārammaṇā. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

19. In the triad of past-object states, those for which the past is the object are 'past-object'. This same method applies to the remaining two terms.

20. Ajjhattattike [P 0.0046] ‘evaṃ pavattamānā mayaṃ attā’ti gahaṇaṃ, ‘gamissāmā’ti iminā viya [V 0.0093] adhippāyena attānaṃ adhikāraṃ katvā pavattāti ajjhattā. ‘Ajjhatta’-saddo panāyaṃ gocarajjhatte niyakajjhatte ajjhattajjhatte visayajjhatteti catūsu atthesu dissati. “Tenānanda, bhikkhunā tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapetabbaṃ” (ma. ni. 3.188), “ajjhattarato samāhito”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 362) hi ayaṃ gocarajjhatte dissati. “Ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ” (dī. ni. 1.228; dha. sa. 161), “ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.373) niyakajjhatte. “Cha ajjhattikāni āyatanānī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.304) ajjhattajjhatte. “Ayaṃ kho panānanda, vihāro tathāgatena abhisambuddho yadidaṃ sabbanimittānaṃ amanasikārā ajjhattaṃ suññataṃ upasampajja viharatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.187) visayajjhatte; issariyaṭṭhāneti attho. Phalasamāpatti hi buddhānaṃ issariyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Idha pana niyakajjhatte adhippeto. Tasmā attano santāne pavattā pāṭipuggalikā dhammā ajjhattāti veditabbā. Tato bāhirabhūtā pana indriyabaddhā vā anindriyabaddhā vā bahiddhā nāma. Tatiyapadaṃ tadubhayavasena vuttaṃ.

20. In the triad of the internal, 'internal' refers to that which proceeds by taking oneself as the authority, with an intention like 'we will go,' a grasping such as 'we are the self that is thus proceeding.' The term 'internal' is seen in four senses: pertaining to the domain, pertaining to oneself, pertaining to the truly internal, and pertaining to the object. For example, in 'Therefore, Ānanda, a monk should establish the mind internally in that very preliminary sign of concentration' (MN 3.188) and 'internally delighting, composed' (Dhp 362), it refers to the domain. In 'internal serenity' (DN 1.228; Dhs 161) and 'dwells contemplating phenomena internally in phenomena' (DN 2.373), it refers to oneself. In 'the six internal sense bases' (MN 3.304), it refers to the truly internal. In 'This, Ānanda, is the dwelling fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely, entering and dwelling in internal emptiness by not attending to all signs' (MN 3.187), it refers to the object; the meaning is a state of mastery. For the fruition-attainment is called a state of mastery for the Buddhas. Here, however, it is intended in the sense of pertaining to oneself. Therefore, phenomena occurring in one’s own continuum, pertaining to the individual, should be understood as internal. Those that are external to that, whether bound to the faculties or not, are called external. The third term is stated by way of both.

21. Anantarattiko [M 0.0089] teyeva tippakārepi dhamme ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanavasena vutto.

21. The immediately following triad is stated in terms of its proceeding by taking those very same three kinds of phenomena as its object.

22. Sanidassanattike daṭṭhabbabhāvasaṅkhātena saha nidassanenāti sanidassanā. Paṭihananabhāvasaṅkhātena saha paṭighenāti sappaṭighā. Sanidassanā ca te sappaṭighā cāti sanidassanasappaṭighā. Natthi etesaṃ daṭṭhabbabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ nidassananti anidassanā. Anidassanā ca te vuttanayeneva sappaṭighā cāti anidassanasappaṭighā. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepena vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva tikamātikāya anupubbapadavaṇṇanā.

22. In the triad of the visible, 'visible' (sanidassanā) means with visibility, that is, with the characteristic of being seen. 'With resistance' (sappaṭighā) means with resistance, that is, with the characteristic of being struck. Those that are both visible and with resistance are called 'visible and with resistance' (sanidassanasappaṭighā). 'Invisible' (anidassanā) means that for these there is no visibility, which is the characteristic of being seen. Those that are invisible and, in the manner stated, with resistance are called 'invisible and with resistance' (anidassanasappaṭighā). The third term is stated by the negation of both. This, so far, is the sequential word explanation of the Triad Matrix.

Tikamātikāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the terms of the Triad Matrix is concluded.

Dukamātikāpadavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Terms of the Dyad Matrix

1-6. Dukamātikāyaṃ pana tikesu anāgatapadavaṇṇanaṃyeva karissāma. Hetugocchake tāva hetudhammāti [V 0.0094] mūlaṭṭhena hetusaṅkhātā dhammā. Hetū dhammātipi pāṭho. Na [P 0.0047] hetūti tesaṃyeva paṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Sampayogato pavattena saha hetunāti sahetukā. Tatheva pavatto natthi etesaṃ hetūti ahetukā. Ekuppādāditāya hetunā sampayuttāti hetusampayuttā. Hetunā vippayuttāti hetuvippayuttā. Imesaṃ dvinnampi dukānaṃ kiñcāpi atthato nānattaṃ natthi, desanāvilāsena pana tathā bujjhantānaṃ vā puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena vuttā. Tato paraṃ paṭhamadukaṃ dutiyatatiyehi saddhiṃ yojetvā tesaṃ ‘hetū na hetū’tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ vasena yathāsambhavato aparepi tayo dukā vuttā. Tattha yatheva ‘hetū ceva dhammā sahetukā cā’ti etaṃ sambhavati, tathā ‘hetū ceva dhammā ahetukā cā’ti idampi. Yathā ca ‘sahetukā ceva dhammā na ca hetū’ti etaṃ sambhavati, tathā ‘ahetukā ceva dhammā na ca hetū’ti idampi. Hetusampayuttadukena saddhiṃ yojanāyapi eseva nayo.

1-6. Now, in the Dyad Matrix, we will explain only the terms that were not covered in the Triads. First, in the Root-group: 'root-phenomena' are phenomena designated as roots in the sense of being a foundation. The reading 'roots which are phenomena' is also found. 'Not roots' is the negation of those very things. 'With roots' means with a root, occurring by way of association. Similarly, 'without roots' means that for these there is no root in their occurrence. 'Associated with roots' means associated with a root due to co-arising, etc. 'Dissociated from roots' means dissociated from a root. Although there is no difference in meaning between these two pairs of dyads, they are stated thus either for the elegance of the teaching or to suit the inclinations of individuals who understand it in this way. Thereafter, the first dyad is combined with the second and third, and accordingly, three more dyads are stated, as far as possible, based on terms such as 'roots, not roots'. Here, just as 'phenomena that are roots and are with roots' is possible, so too is 'phenomena that are roots and are without roots'. And just as 'phenomena that are with roots but are not roots' is possible, so too is 'phenomena that are without roots but are not roots'. The same method applies when combining with the 'associated with roots' dyad.

Tatra yadetaṃ ‘na hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpī’ti siddhe, ‘na hetū kho pana dhammā’ti atirittaṃ ‘kho panā’ti padaṃ vuttaṃ, tassa vasena [M 0.0090] ayaṃ atirekattho saṅgahitoti veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Na kevalaṃ ‘na hetu dhammā atha kho aññepi na ca sahetukāpi ahetukāpi icceva, atha kho aññathāpīti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yatheva hi ‘na hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi’, evaṃ ‘hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi’. Yathā ca ‘na hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi’, evaṃ ‘na hetū dhammā hetusampayuttāpi hetuvippayuttāpī’ti.

Here, since it is established that 'phenomena that are not roots are either with roots or without roots,' the additional words 'kho pana' are used in 'na hetū kho pana dhammā,' and by virtue of these, an additional meaning should be understood as included. How? It is not merely that 'phenomena that are not roots' are either with roots or without roots, but also otherwise. This is what is meant: just as 'phenomena that are not roots' are either with roots or without roots, so too 'phenomena that are roots' are either with roots or without roots. And just as 'phenomena that are not roots' are either with roots or without roots, so too 'phenomena that are not roots' are either associated with roots or dissociated from roots.

7-13. Cūḷantaradukesu attano nipphādakena saha paccayenāti sappaccayā. Natthi etesaṃ uppāde vā ṭhitiyaṃ vā paccayoti appaccayā. Paccayehi samāgantvā katāti saṅkhatā. Na saṅkhatāti asaṅkhatā. Avinibbhogavasena rūpaṃ etesaṃ atthīti rūpino. Tathāvidhaṃ natthi etesaṃ rūpanti arūpino. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ vā rūpaṃ; taṃ etesaṃ atthīti rūpino. Na rūpino arūpino. Lokiyā dhammāti loko vuccati lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena vaṭṭaṃ; tasmiṃ pariyāpannabhāvena loke niyuttāti lokiyā. Tato [P 0.0048] uttiṇṇāti uttarā; loke apariyāpannabhāvena lokato uttarāti lokuttarā. Kenaci viññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇādīsu kenaci ekena cakkhuviññāṇena vā sotaviññāṇena vā vijānitabbā. Kenaci na viññeyyāti teneva cakkhuviññāṇena vā sotaviññāṇena vā na vijānitabbā. Evaṃ sante dvinnampi padānaṃ atthanānattato duko hoti.

7-13. In the Minor Intermediate Dyads: 'With condition' means with a condition that produces them. 'Without condition' means that for these there is no condition for their arising or persistence. 'Conditioned' means made by coming together with conditions. 'Unconditioned' means not conditioned. 'With form' means having form by way of inseparability. 'Without form' means not having such form. Alternatively, 'form' has the characteristic of being afflicted; 'with form' means having that. Those that are not 'with form' are 'without form'. 'Worldly' refers to phenomena engaged in the world by being included therein; the round of existence is called 'world' in the sense of breaking up and dissolving. 'Supramundane' means transcending that; they are beyond the world by not being included in the world. 'Cognizable by something' means knowable by any one of the consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. 'Not cognizable by something' means not knowable by that same eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. Thus, due to the difference in meaning between these two terms, a dyad is formed.

14-19. Āsavagocchake [V 0.0095] āsavantīti āsavā. Cakkhutopi…pe… manatopi sandanti pavattantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammato yāva gotrabhuṃ, okāsato yāva bhavaggaṃ savantīti vā āsavā. Ete dhamme etañca okāsaṃ antokaritvā pavattantīti attho. Antokaraṇattho hi ayaṃ ‘ā’kāro. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madirādayo āsavā. Āsavā viyātipi āsavā. Lokasmiñhi cirapārivāsikā madirādayo āsavāti vuccanti. Yadi ca cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena āsavā, eteyeva bhavitumarahanti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya, ito pubbe avijjā nāhosī”tiādi (a. ni. 10.61). Āyataṃ vā saṃsāradukkhaṃ savanti pasavantītipi āsavā. Tato aññe no āsavā nāma. Attānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattehi [M 0.0091] saha āsavehīti sāsavā. Evaṃ pavattamānā natthi etesaṃ āsavāti anāsavā. Sesaṃ hetugocchake vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā tattha ‘na hetū kho pana dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpīti ayaṃ osānaduko paṭhamadukassa dutiyapadaṃ ādimhi ṭhapetvā vutto, evaṃ idha ‘no āsavā kho pana dhammā sāsavāpi anāsavāpī’ti na vutto. Kiñcāpi na vutto, atha kho ayañca añño ca bhedo tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

14-19. In the Taint-group: 'Taints' are so called because they flow out. This means it is said that they flow and proceed from the eye... and so on up to the mind. Alternatively, 'taints' are so called because they flow in terms of phenomena up to change-of-lineage and in terms of location up to the peak of existence. The meaning is that they proceed by encompassing these phenomena and this location, for this prefix 'ā' conveys the sense of encompassing. The taints are also like intoxicants, such as liquor, in the sense of long storage. They are 'taints' because they are like intoxicants. For in the world, intoxicants like liquor that have been long stored are called 'āsava'. And if they are taints in the sense of long storage, then these alone are fit to be so. For it has been said: 'Monks, the earliest point of ignorance is not discernible; before this, there was no ignorance,' and so on (AN 10.61). Alternatively, they are also called 'taints' because they cause the long suffering of saṃsāra to flow and stream forth. Other than these, there are no phenomena called taints. 'Tainted' means together with the taints that occur taking themselves as object. 'Untainted' means for these, occurring thus, there are no taints. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the Root-group. However, there is this distinction: whereas there it was said, 'But phenomena that are not roots are either with roots or without roots,' thus this final dyad was expressed by placing the second term of the first dyad at the beginning; here it is not said, 'But phenomena that are not taints are either tainted or untainted.' Although it is not said, this and other distinctions should be understood in the same way as explained there.

20-25. Saṃyojanagocchake yassa saṃvijjanti, taṃ puggalaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ saṃyojenti bandhantīti saṃyojanā. Tato aññe no saṃyojanā nāma. Ārammaṇabhāvaṃ upagantvā saṃyojanasambandhane saṃyojanānaṃ hitāti saṃyojaniyā. Saṃyojanassa ārammaṇapaccayabhūtānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Na saṃyojaniyā [P 0.0049] asaṃyojaniyā. Sesaṃ hetugocchake vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

20-25. In the Fetter-group: 'Fetters' are so called because they bind and fetter the person in whom they exist to the cycle of existence. Other than these, there are no other fetters. 'Liable to fetters' means those that, having become objects, are conducive to the connection of fetters. This is a designation for those things that serve as object-conditions for fetters. 'Not liable to fetters' means not liable to fetters. The rest should be connected in the same way as explained in the Root-group.

26-31. Ganthagocchake yassa saṃvijjanti taṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena vaṭṭasmiṃ ganthenti ghaṭentīti ganthā. Tato aññe no ganthā. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena ganthehi ganthitabbāti ganthaniyā. Sesaṃ hetugocchake vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ ito paresupi vuttāvasesaṃ tattha tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

26-31. In the Tie-group: 'Ties' are so called because they tie and connect the person in whom they exist to the cycle of existence by way of death and rebirth. Other than these, there are no other ties. 'Liable to ties' means those that are to be tied by ties by way of becoming an object. The rest should be connected in the same way as explained in the Root-group. And just as here, so too in the subsequent cases, what remains unsaid should be understood according to the method stated in each respective place.

32-37. Oghagocchake yassa saṃvijjanti taṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva ohananti osīdāpentīti oghā. Ārammaṇaṃ katvā atikkamanīyato oghehi atikkamitabbāti oghaniyā. Oghānaṃ ārammaṇadhammā eva veditabbā.

32-37. In the Flood-group: They are called 'floods' (oghā) because they cause the one in whom they exist to sink and be submerged in the very cycle of existence. They are called 'liable to floods' (oghaniyā) because, being things to be overcome, they are to be traversed by the floods by taking them as an object. They should be understood precisely as the phenomena that are the objects of the floods.

38-43. Yogagocchake [V 0.0096] vaṭṭasmiṃ yojentīti yogā. Yoganiyā oghaniyā viya veditabbā.

38-43. In the Yoke-group: They are called 'yokes' (yogā) because they yoke one to the cycle of existence. 'Liable to yokes' (yoganiyā) are to be understood in the same way as 'liable to floods' (oghaniyā).

44-49. Nīvaraṇagocchake cittaṃ nīvaranti pariyonandhantīti nīvaraṇā. Nīvaraṇiyā saṃyojaniyā viya veditabbā.

44-49. In the Hindrance-group: They are called 'hindrances' (nīvaraṇā) because they hinder and envelop the mind. 'Liable to hindrances' (nīvaraṇiyā) are to be understood in the same way as 'liable to fetters' (saṃyojaniyā).

50-54. Parāmāsagocchake [M 0.0092] dhammānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ aniccādiākāraṃ atikkamitvā ‘nicca’nti ādivasena pavattamānā parato āmasantīti parāmāsā. Parāmāsehi ārammaṇakaraṇavasena parāmaṭṭhattā parāmaṭṭhā.

50-54. In the Misapprehension-group: They are called 'misapprehensions' (parāmāsā) because, transgressing the true nature of phenomena as impermanence and so forth, they proceed by way of 'permanence' and so forth, and thus grasp perversely. Because things are grasped by these misapprehensions by way of being made an object, they are called 'the grasped' (parāmaṭṭhā).

55-68. Mahantaradukesu ārammaṇaṃ aggahetvā appavattito saha ārammaṇenāti sārammaṇā. Natthi etesaṃ ārammaṇanti anārammaṇā. Cintanaṭṭhena cittā, vicittaṭṭhena vā cittā. Avippayogavasena cetasi niyuttāti cetasikā. Nirantarabhāvūpagamanatāya, uppādato yāva bhaṅgā, cittena saṃsaṭṭhāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhā. Ekato vattamānāpi nirantarabhāvaṃ anupagamanatāya cittena visaṃsaṭṭhāti cittavisaṃsaṭṭhā. Samuṭṭhahanti etenāti samuṭṭhānaṃ. Cittaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ etesanti cittasamuṭṭhānā. Saha bhavantīti sahabhuno. Cittena sahabhuno cittasahabhuno. Anuparivattantīti anuparivattino. Kiṃ anuparivattanti? Cittaṃ. Cittassa anuparivattino cittānuparivattino. Cittasaṃsaṭṭhā ca te cittasamuṭṭhānā cāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānā. Cittasaṃsaṭṭhā [P 0.0050] ca te cittasamuṭṭhānā ca cittasahabhuno eva cāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānasahabhuno. Cittasaṃsaṭṭhā ca te cittasamuṭṭhānā ca cittānuparivattino eva cāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānānuparivattino. Sesāni sabbapadāni vuttapadānaṃ paṭikkhepavasena veditabbāni. Ajjhattajjhattaṃ sandhāya ajjhattattike vuttavasena ajjhattāva ajjhattikā. Tato bahibhūtāti bāhirā. Upādiyanteva bhūtāni, na bhūtāni viya upādiyantīti upādā. Na upādiyantevāti noupādā.

55-68. In the Great Dyads: Because they do not arise without taking an object, they are 'with an object' (sārammaṇā), that is, together with an object. For these there is no object, thus they are 'without an object' (anārammaṇā). They are 'consciousness' (cittā) in the sense of thinking, or in the sense of being variegated. Because they are yoked to consciousness (cetasi) by way of non-separation, they are 'mental factors' (cetasikā). By way of attaining an uninterrupted state from arising until dissolution, they are associated with consciousness, thus 'associated with consciousness' (cittasaṃsaṭṭhā). Though occurring simultaneously, because they do not attain an uninterrupted state, they are dissociated from consciousness, thus 'dissociated from consciousness' (cittavisaṃsaṭṭhā). One originates from this, thus it is 'origination' (samuṭṭhānaṃ). Consciousness is the origination of these, thus they are 'consciousness-originated' (cittasamuṭṭhānā). They exist together, thus they are 'co-existent' (sahabhuno). They are co-existent with consciousness, thus 'consciousness-co-existent' (cittasahabhuno). They follow in succession, thus they are 'following' (anuparivattino). What do they follow? Consciousness. Following consciousness, they are 'consciousness-following' (cittānuparivattino). They are both associated with consciousness and consciousness-originated, thus 'associated and consciousness-originated' (cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānā). They are associated with consciousness, consciousness-originated, and also co-existent, thus 'associated, consciousness-originated, and co-existent' (cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānasahabhuno). They are associated with consciousness, consciousness-originated, and also consciousness-following, thus 'associated, consciousness-originated, and consciousness-following' (cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānānuparivattino). The remaining terms are to be understood by way of negating the terms already explained. With reference to the internal, as stated in the triad on the internal, they are 'internal' (ajjhattikā). What is external to that is 'external' (bāhirā). They are clung to as real things, not as if they were real things, thus they are 'objects of clinging' (upādā). They are not clung to in this way, thus they are 'not objects of clinging' (noupādā).

69-74. Upādānagocchake bhusaṃ ādiyantīti upādānā; daḷhaggāhaṃ gaṇhantīti attho. Tato aññe noupādānā.

69-74. In the Clinging-group: They are called 'clingings' (upādānā) because they take up intensely; the meaning is that they grasp with a firm grip. Other than these, there are no clingings.

75-82. Kilesagocchake saṃkiliṭṭhattike vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

75-82. In the Defilement-group: The meaning should be understood in the very same way as explained in the triad on the defiled.

83-100. Piṭṭhidukesu [V 0.0097] kāme avacarantīti kāmāvacarā rūpe avacarantīti rūpāvacarā. Arūpe avacarantīti arūpāvacarā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana parato āvi bhavissati. Tebhūmakavaṭṭe pariyāpannā antogadhāti pariyāpannā. Tasmiṃ na pariyāpannāti apariyāpannā. Vaṭṭamūlaṃ chindantā nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vaṭṭato niyyantīti niyyānikā. Iminā [M 0.0093] lakkhaṇena na niyyantīti aniyyānikā. Cutiyā vā attano vā pavattiyā anantaraṃ phaladāne niyatattā niyatā. Tathā aniyatattā aniyatā. Aññe dhamme uttaranti pajahantīti uttarā. Attānaṃ uttarituṃ samatthehi saha uttarehīti sauttarā. Natthi etesaṃ uttarāti anuttarā. Raṇanti etehīti raṇā; yehi abhibhūtā sattā nānappakārena kandanti paridevanti, tesaṃ rāgādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sampayogavasena pahānekaṭṭhatāvasena ca saha raṇehīti saraṇā. Tenākārena natthi etesaṃ raṇāti araṇā.

83-100. In the Back-to-Back Dyads: They wander in the sensual realm, thus they are 'of the sensual sphere' (kāmāvacarā); they wander in the form realm, thus they are 'of the form sphere' (rūpāvacarā); they wander in the formless realm, thus they are 'of the formless sphere' (arūpāvacarā). This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, will become clear later. Because they are included and contained within the cycle of the three planes, they are 'included' (pariyāpannā). Not being included therein, they are 'unincluded' (apariyāpannā). Cutting off the root of the cycle, having made Nibbāna their object, they lead out from the cycle, thus they are 'leading to deliverance' (niyyānikā). Not leading out by this characteristic, they are 'not leading to deliverance' (aniyyānikā). Because they are fixed in giving their fruit immediately after their cessation or their own occurrence, they are 'fixed' (niyatā). Similarly, because they are not fixed, they are 'unfixed' (aniyatā). Because they surpass and abandon other states, they are 'superior' (uttarā). Because they exist together with superior states capable of surpassing them, they are 'with a superior' (sauttarā). There is nothing superior to these, thus they are 'unsurpassed' (anuttarā). One makes war with these, thus they are 'defilements' (raṇā); this is a designation for lust and so on, by which beings, being overwhelmed, cry out and lament in various ways. Because they are with defilements by way of association and by way of sharing what is to be abandoned, they are 'with defilements' (saraṇā). In a corresponding manner, they have no defilements, thus they are 'without defilements' (araṇā).

Suttantikadukamātikāpadavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Terms of the Suttanta Dyads

101-108. Suttantikadukesu sampayogavasena vijjaṃ bhajantīti vijjābhāgino; vijjābhāge vijjākoṭṭhāse vattantītipi vijjābhāgino. Tattha vipassanāñāṇaṃ, manomayiddhi, cha abhiññāti aṭṭha vijjā. Purimena atthena tāhi sampayuttadhammāpi vijjābhāgino. Pacchimena [P 0.0051] atthena tāsu yā kāci ekā vijjā vijjā. Sesā vijjābhāginoti. Evaṃ vijjāpi vijjāya sampayuttadhammāpi vijjābhāginotveva veditabbā. Idha pana sampayuttadhammāva adhippetā. Sampayogavaseneva avijjaṃ bhajantīti avijjābhāgino. Avijjābhāge avijjākoṭṭhāse vattantītipi avijjābhāgino. Tattha dukkhapaṭicchādakaṃ tamo samudayādipaṭicchādakanti catasso avijjā. Purimanayeneva tāhi sampayuttadhammāpi avijjābhāgino. Tāsu yā kāci ekā avijjā avijjā. Sesā avijjābhāginoti. Evaṃ avijjāpi avijjāya sampayuttadhammāpi avijjābhāginotveva veditabbā. Idha pana sampayuttadhammāva adhippetā.

101-108. In the Suttanta dyads, they are 'partakers of knowledge' (vijjābhāgino) because they partake of knowledge (vijjaṃ bhajanti) by way of association; they are also 'partakers of knowledge' because they exist in the sphere of knowledge (vijjābhāge), in the portion of knowledge (vijjākoṭṭhāse). Herein, the eight kinds of knowledge are: insight-knowledge, the mind-made power, and the six superknowledges. According to the former meaning, the states associated with these are also 'partakers of knowledge.' According to the latter meaning, any one of these is knowledge; the remaining ones are 'partakers of knowledge.' Thus, both knowledge itself and the states associated with knowledge should be understood as 'partakers of knowledge.' Here, however, only the associated states are intended. They are 'partakers of ignorance' (avijjābhāgino) because they partake of ignorance by way of association; they are also 'partakers of ignorance' because they exist in the sphere of ignorance, in the portion of ignorance. Herein, the four kinds of ignorance are: the darkness that conceals suffering, that which conceals the origin, and so on. According to the former method, the states associated with these are also 'partakers of ignorance.' Among these, any one is ignorance; the remaining ones are 'partakers of ignorance.' Thus, both ignorance itself and the states associated with ignorance should be understood as 'partakers of ignorance.' Here, however, only the associated states are intended.

Puna anajjhottharaṇabhāvena kilesandhakāraṃ viddhaṃsetuṃ asamatthatāya vijju upamā etesanti vijjūpamā. Nissesaṃ viddhaṃsanasamatthatāya vajiraṃ upamā etesanti vajirūpamā. Bālesu ṭhitattā yattha ṭhitā tadupacārena bālā. Paṇḍitesu ṭhitattā paṇḍitā. Bālakarattā vā bālā, paṇḍitakarattā [V 0.0098] paṇḍitā. Kaṇhāti kāḷakā, cittassa apabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Sukkāti odātā[M 0.0094], cittassa pabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Kaṇhābhijātihetuto vā kaṇhā; sukkābhijātihetuto sukkā. Idha ceva samparāye ca tapentīti tapanīyā. Na tapanīyā atapanīyā.

Again, because they are unable to dispel the darkness of defilements due to not overwhelming it, they are 'lightning-like' (vijjūpamā). Because they are capable of destroying it completely, they are 'thunderbolt-like' (vajirūpamā). Because they are established in fools, by transference of epithet they are called 'foolish'. Because they are established in the wise, they are called 'wise'. Or, because they make one a fool, they are 'foolish'; because they make one wise, they are 'wise'. 'Dark' (kaṇha) means black, because it causes the mind to be non-luminous. 'Bright' (sukka) means pure, because it causes the mind to be luminous. Or, they are 'dark' because they are a cause for a dark birth; they are 'bright' because they are a cause for a bright birth. Because they torment both here and in the hereafter, they are 'tormenting' (tapanīyā). Those that do not torment are 'non-tormenting' (atapanīyā).

Adhivacanadukādayo tayo atthato ninnānākaraṇā; byañjanamevettha nānaṃ. Sirivaḍḍhako dhanavaḍḍhakoti ādayo hi vacanamattameva adhikāraṃ katvā pavattā adhivacanā nāma. Adhivacanānaṃ pathā adhivacanapathā. “Abhisaṅkharontīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā saṅkhārā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79) evaṃ niddhāretvā sahetukaṃ katvā vuccamānā abhilāpā nirutti nāma. Niruttīnaṃ pathā niruttipathā. Takko vitakko saṅkappoti (dha. sa. 7) evaṃ tena tena pakārena ñāpanato paññatti nāma. Paññattīnaṃ pathā paññattipathā. Ettha [P 0.0052] ca ekaṃ dukaṃ vatvāpi itaresaṃ vacane payojanaṃ hetugocchake vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

The three dyads beginning with that on appellations are not different in meaning; only the letter is different. For example, names like 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' (Increaser of Fortune) and 'Dhanavaḍḍhaka' (Increaser of Wealth) are simply words that, having been made authoritative, are called 'appellations' (adhivacana). The paths of appellations are 'appellation-paths' (adhivacanapathā). 'They fashion, bhikkhus, therefore they are called "formations"' (SN 3.79)—when expressions are spoken in this way, having been defined with a reason, they are called 'expressions' (nirutti). The paths of expressions are 'expression-paths' (niruttipathā). 'Initial application, sustained application, conception' (Dhs §7)—because it makes something known in various ways, it is called a 'designation' (paññatti). The paths of designations are 'designation-paths' (paññattipathā). Here, although only one dyad is mentioned, the reason for mentioning the others should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the 'cluster of causes'.

109-118. Nāmarūpaduke nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena namanaṭṭhena nāmanaṭṭhena ca nāmaṃ. Ruppanaṭṭhena rūpaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana nikkhepakaṇḍe āvi bhavissati. Avijjāti dukkhādīsu aññāṇaṃ. Bhavataṇhāti bhavapatthanā. Bhavadiṭṭhīti bhavo vuccati sassataṃ; sassatavasena uppajjanadiṭṭhi. Vibhavadiṭṭhīti vibhavo vuccati ucchedaṃ; ucchedavasena uppajjanadiṭṭhi. Sassato attā ca loko cāti pavattā diṭṭhi sassatadiṭṭhi. Ucchijjissatīti pavattā diṭṭhi ucchedadiṭṭhi. Antavāti pavattā diṭṭhi antavādiṭṭhi. Anantavāti pavattā diṭṭhi anantavādiṭṭhi. Pubbantaṃ anugatā diṭṭhi pubbantānudiṭṭhi. Aparantaṃ anugatā diṭṭhi aparantānudiṭṭhi. Ahirikanti yaṃ na hiriyati hiriyitabbenāti (dha. sa. 387) evaṃ vitthāritā nillajjatā. Anottappanti yaṃ na ottappati ottappitabbenāti evaṃ vitthārito abhāyanakaākāro. Hiriyanā hirī, ottappanā ottappaṃ. Dovacassatādīsu dukkhaṃ vaco etasmiṃ vippaṭikūlagāhimhi vipaccanīkasāte anādare puggaleti dubbaco. Tassa kammaṃ dovacassaṃ. Tassa bhāvo dovacassatā. Pāpā assaddhādayo puggalā etassa mittāti pāpamitto; tassa bhāvo pāpamittatā. Sovacassatā ca kalyāṇamittatā ca vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbā.

109-118. In the dyad of Name-and-Form: It is 'name' (nāma) in the sense of bending (towards an object), in the sense of causing to bend, and in the sense of naming. It is 'form' (rūpa) in the sense of being afflicted. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation will become clear in the Chapter on Deposition. 'Ignorance' (avijjā) is not knowing the truths of suffering and so on. 'Craving for existence' (bhavataṇhā) is the desire for existence. 'View of existence' (bhavadiṭṭhi): here 'existence' (bhavo) is said to be eternal; it is the view that arises in the manner of eternalism. 'View of non-existence' (vibhavadiṭṭhi): here 'non-existence' (vibhavo) is said to be annihilation; it is the view that arises in the manner of annihilationism. The view that holds 'the self and the world are eternal' is the 'eternality view' (sassatadiṭṭhi). The view that holds 'it will be annihilated' is the 'annihilation view' (ucchedadiṭṭhi). The view that holds 'it is finite' is the 'finitude view' (antavādiṭṭhi). The view that holds 'it is infinite' is the 'infinitude view' (anantavādiṭṭhi). The view that follows after the past is the 'view following the past' (pubbantānudiṭṭhi). The view that follows after the future is the 'view following the future' (aparantānudiṭṭhi). 'Shamelessness' (ahirika) is 'that by which one is not ashamed of what one should be ashamed of' (Dhs §387); thus it is explained as impudence. 'Lack of moral dread' (anottappa) is 'that by which one does not dread what one should dread'; thus it is explained as the state of not fearing. 'Moral shame' (hirī) is being ashamed; 'moral dread' (ottappa) is dreading. Regarding 'difficulty of admonishment' (dovacassatā) and so on: one for whom speech is difficult, who is oppositional, contrary, and disrespectful, is a 'person difficult to admonish' (dubbaco). His action is 'difficulty of admonishment' (dovacassaṃ); the state of that is 'the quality of being difficult to admonish' (dovacassatā). One whose friends are evil persons, such as the faithless, is a 'person with evil friends' (pāpamitto); the state of that is 'evil friendship' (pāpamittatā). 'Easiness of admonishment' (sovacassatā) and 'good friendship' (kalyāṇamittatā) should be understood in the way opposite to what has been described.

119-123. ‘Pañcapi [M 0.0095] āpattikkhandhā āpattiyo, sattapi āpattikkhandhā āpattiyo’ti (dha. sa. 1336) evaṃ vuttāsu āpattīsu kusalabhāvo āpattikusalatā. Tāhi [V 0.0099] āpattīhi vuṭṭhāne kusalabhāvo āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā. Samāpattīsu kusalabhāvo samāpattikusalatā. Samāpattīnaṃ appanāparicchedapaññāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Samāpattīhi [P 0.0053] vuṭṭhāne kusalabhāvo samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā. Aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu kusalabhāvo dhātukusalatā. Tāsaṃyeva dhātūnaṃ manasikāre kusalabhāvo manasikārakusalatā. Cakkhāyatanādīsu kusalabhāvo āyatanakusalatā. Dvādasaṅge paṭiccasamuppāde kusalabhāvo paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne kusalabhāvo ṭhānakusalatā. Ṭhānanti kāraṇaṃ vuccati. Tasmiñhi tadāyattavuttitāya phalaṃ tiṭṭhati nāma, tasmā ṭhānanti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhāne kusalabhāvo aṭṭhānakusalatā.

119-123. 'The five aggregates of offenses are offenses; the seven aggregates of offenses are offenses' (Dhs §1336)—the state of being skilled in these offenses thus stated is 'skillfulness in offenses' (āpattikusalatā). The state of being skilled in emerging from those offenses is 'skillfulness in emerging from offenses' (āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā). The state of being skilled in the attainments is 'skillfulness in attainments' (samāpattikusalatā). This is a term for the wisdom that discerns the absorption of the attainments. The state of being skilled in emerging from the attainments is 'skillfulness in emerging from attainments' (samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā). The state of being skilled in the eighteen elements is 'skillfulness in elements' (dhātukusalatā). The state of being skilled in attending to those same elements is 'skillfulness in attention' (manasikārakusalatā). The state of being skilled in the sense bases, such as the eye base, is 'skillfulness in sense bases' (āyatanakusalatā). The state of being skilled in the twelve-factored dependent origination is 'skillfulness in dependent origination' (paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā). The state of being skilled in what is a possible case is 'skillfulness in possible cases' (ṭhānakusalatā). 'Possible case' (ṭhāna) refers to a cause. For in that, the result 'stands' (tiṭṭhati), its occurrence being dependent on that; therefore, it is called a 'standing place' or 'case' (ṭhāna). The state of being skilled in what is not a possible case is 'skillfulness in impossible cases' (aṭṭhānakusalatā).

124-134. Ujubhāvo ajjavo. Mudubhāvo maddavo. Adhivāsanasaṅkhāto khamanabhāvo khanti. Suratassa bhāvo soraccaṃ. Sammodakamudubhāvasaṅkhāto sakhilabhāvo sākhalyaṃ. Yathā parehi saddhiṃ attano chiddaṃ na hoti evaṃ dhammāmisehi paṭisantharaṇaṃ paṭisanthāro. Indriyasaṃvarabhedasaṅkhāto manacchaṭṭhesu indriyesu aguttadvārabhāvo indriyesu aguttadvāratā. Paṭiggahaṇaparibhogavasena bhojane mattaṃ ajānanabhāvo bhojane amattaññutā. Anantaraduko vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo. Sativippavāsasaṅkhāto muṭṭhassatibhāvo muṭṭhassaccaṃ. Asampajānabhāvo asampajaññaṃ. Saratīti sati. Sampajānātīti sampajaññaṃ. Appaṭisaṅkhāne akampanaṭṭhena paṭisaṅkhānasaṅkhātaṃ balaṃ paṭisaṅkhānabalaṃ. Vīriyasīsena satta bojjhaṅge bhāventassa uppannaṃ balaṃ bhāvanābalaṃ. Paccanīkadhamme sametīti samatho. Aniccādivasena vividhena ākārena passatīti vipassanā. Samathova taṃ ākāraṃ gahetvā puna pavattetabbassa samathassa nimittavasena samathanimittaṃ. Paggāhanimittepi eseva nayo. Sampayuttadhamme [P 0.0054] paggaṇhātīti paggāho. Na vikkhipatīti avikkhepo.

124-134. The state of being straight is rectitude. The state of being gentle is mildness. The state of forbearance, designated as endurance, is patience. The state of being well-disposed is amiability. The state of friendliness, designated as agreeableness and gentleness, is sociability. Friendly reception with the Dhamma and material things, in such a way that there is no fault of one's own with others, is hospitality. The state of having unguarded doors in the sense faculties with the mind as the sixth, designated as the breaking of sense-restraint, is unguardedness of the sense faculties. The state of not knowing moderation in food, by way of receiving and consuming, is immoderation in food. The immediately preceding pair should be understood by the method of the opposite of what has been stated. The state of lost mindfulness, designated as the absence of mindfulness, is forgetfulness. The state of not clearly comprehending is lack of clear comprehension. That which remembers is mindfulness. That which clearly comprehends is clear comprehension. The power of reflection is the strength designated as reflection, in the sense of being unshaken by non-reflection. The power of development is the strength that arises for one cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment with energy as the foremost. That which settles opposing states is calm. That which sees in various ways, by way of impermanence, etc., is insight. The sign of calm is so called by way of being a sign for the calm that is to be developed again, after calm itself has taken up that aspect. The same method applies to the sign of exertion. That which uplifts associated states is exertion. That which does not scatter is non-distraction.

135-142. Sīlavināsikā asaṃvarasaṅkhātā sīlassa vipatti sīlavipatti. Sammādiṭṭhivināsikā micchādiṭṭhisaṅkhātā diṭṭhiyā vipatti diṭṭhivipatti. Soraccameva [M 0.0096] sīlassa sampādanato sīlaparipūraṇato sīlassa sampadāti sīlasampadā. Diṭṭhipāripūribhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ diṭṭhiyā sampadāti diṭṭhisampadā. Visuddhibhāvaṃ sampattā sīlasaṅkhātā sīlassa visuddhi, sīlavisuddhi. Nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ visuddhiṃ pāpetuṃ samatthā, dassanasaṅkhātā, diṭṭhiyā visuddhi diṭṭhivisuddhi. Diṭṭhivisuddhi kho pana yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti kammassakataññāṇādisaṅkhātā diṭṭhivisuddhi ceva yathādiṭṭhissa ca anurūpadiṭṭhissa kalyāṇadiṭṭhissa taṃsampayuttameva padhānaṃ. Saṃvegoti jātiādīni [V 0.0100] paṭicca uppannabhayasaṅkhātaṃ saṃvijjanaṃ. Saṃvejaniyaṭṭhānanti saṃvegajanakaṃ jātiādikāraṇaṃ. Saṃviggassa ca yonisopadhānanti evaṃ saṃvegajātassa upāyapadhānaṃ. Asantuṭṭhitā ca kusalesu dhammesūti kusaladhammapūraṇe asantuṭṭhibhāvo. Appaṭivānitā ca padhānasminti arahattaṃ apatvā padhānasmiṃ anivattanatā anosakkanatā. Vijānanato vijjā. Vimuccanato vimutti. Khaye ñāṇanti kilesakkhayakare ariyamagge ñāṇaṃ. Anuppāde ñāṇanti paṭisandhivasena anuppādabhūte taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesānaṃ anuppādapariyosāne uppanne ariyaphale ñāṇaṃ. Ayaṃ mātikāya anupubbapadavaṇṇanā.

135-142. The failure of virtue, designated as non-restraint, which is destructive of virtue, is failure of virtue. The failure of view, designated as wrong view, which is destructive of right view, is failure of view. The accomplishment of virtue is so called from accomplishing and fulfilling virtue through amiability itself. The accomplishment of view is knowledge that has become the fulfillment of view. The purification of virtue is virtue, designated as having attained a state of purity. The purification of view is designated as seeing, which is able to lead to the purity designated as Nibbāna. Moreover, the purification of view is the exertion of one who sees rightly; that is, it is both the purification of view designated as knowledge of kamma's ownership, etc., and the very exertion associated with that of one who sees rightly, whose view is in accordance, whose view is wholesome. Spiritual urgency is agitation, designated as fear arisen dependent on birth, etc. A cause for spiritual urgency is a cause that generates spiritual urgency, such as birth, etc. And for one who is spiritually urgent, proper exertion is the exertion of means. And dissatisfaction with wholesome qualities is the state of not being content in the fulfillment of wholesome qualities. And not turning back in exertion is the state of not turning back, not retreating, in exertion until attaining arahantship. From knowing comes knowledge. From being liberated comes liberation. Knowledge of destruction is the knowledge in the Noble Path that causes the destruction of defilements. Knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge in the Noble Fruit that arises at the culmination of the non-arising of those defilements to be abandoned by the respective path, which has become non-arising by way of rebirth-linking. This is the sequential explanation of the terms in the matrix.

Dukamātikāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Terms of the Duka Matrix is concluded.

Kāmāvacarakusalapadabhājanīyaṃ

The Analysis of Terms for Wholesome Sense-Sphere States

1. Idāni [M 0.0097][V 0.0101] yathānikkhittāya mātikāya saṅgahite dhamme pabhedato dassetuṃ katame dhammā kusalāti idaṃ padabhājanīyaṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha yadetaṃ yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotīti paṭhamaṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ dassitaṃ, tassa tāva niddese dhammavavatthānavāro [P 0.0055] saṅgahavāro suññatavāroti tayo mahāvārā honti. Tesu dhammavavatthānavāro uddesaniddesavasena dvidhā ṭhito. Tesu uddesavārassa pucchā, samayaniddeso, dhammuddeso, appanāti cattāro paricchedā. Tesu ‘katame dhammā kusalā’ti ayaṃ pucchā nāma. ‘Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ…pe… tasmiṃ samaye’ti ayaṃ samayaniddeso nāma. ‘Phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hotī’ti ayaṃ dhammuddeso nāma. ‘Ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye aññepi atthi paṭiccasamuppannā arūpino dhammā ime dhammā kusalā’ti ayaṃ appanā nāma.

1. Now, to explain in detail the states included in the matrix as it was laid down, this analysis of terms, 'Which states are wholesome?', is commenced. Herein, that which is the wholesome sense-sphere state shown first with the phrase, 'On whatever occasion sense-sphere wholesome consciousness arises'—in its explanation, there are three major sections: the section on the determination of states, the section on grouping, and the section on emptiness. Among these, the section on the determination of states stands in two ways: by way of summary and detailed exposition. Of these, in the summary section, there are four divisions: the question, the explanation of the occasion, the enumeration of states, and the application. Herein: 'Which states are wholesome?'—this is called the question. 'On whatever occasion sense-sphere... at that time'—this is called the explanation of the occasion. 'Contact occurs... non-distraction occurs'—this is called the enumeration of states. 'Or whatever other dependently arisen, immaterial states exist on that occasion—these states are wholesome'—this is called the application.

Evaṃ catūhi paricchedehi ṭhitassa uddesavārassa yvāyaṃ paṭhamo pucchāparicchedo, tattha ‘katame dhammā kusalā’ti ayaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā. Pañcavidhāhi pucchā – adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā, diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā, vimaticchedanāpucchā, anumatipucchā, kathetukamyatāpucchāti. Tāsaṃ idaṃ nānattaṃ –

Thus, of the summary section, which is established by four divisions, this which is the first is the question-division. Therein, the question, 'Which phenomena are wholesome?' is a question from a desire to speak. For questions are of five kinds: the question for illuminating what is unseen, the question for comparing what is seen, the question for cutting off uncertainty, the question for seeking approval, and the question from a desire to speak. This is their distinction:

Katamā adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā? Pakatiyā lakkhaṇaṃ aññātaṃ hoti, adiṭṭhaṃ atulitaṃ atīritaṃ avibhūtaṃ avibhāvitaṃ. Tassa ñāṇāya dassanāya tulanāya tīraṇāya vibhūtatthāya vibhāvanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchati. Ayaṃ adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā (mahāni. 150; cūḷani. puṇṇakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 12).

What is the question for illuminating what is unseen? By nature, a characteristic is unknown, unseen, unweighed, unjudged, unclear, and unmanifested. One asks a question for the sake of knowing it, seeing it, weighing it, judging it, making it clear, and manifesting it. This is the question for illuminating what is unseen.

Katamā diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā? Pakatiyā lakkhaṇaṃ ñātaṃ hoti, diṭṭhaṃ tulitaṃ tīritaṃ vibhūtaṃ vibhāvitaṃ, so aññehi paṇḍitehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchati. Ayaṃ diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā (mahāni. 150; cūḷani. puṇṇakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 12).

What is the question for comparing what is seen? By nature, a characteristic is known, seen, weighed, judged, clear, and manifested. One asks a question for the sake of comparing it with other wise persons. This is the question for comparing what is seen.

Katamā [M 0.0098] vimaticchedanāpucchā? Pakatiyā saṃsayapakkhando hoti, vimatipakkhando dveḷhakajāto – ‘evaṃ nu kho, nanu kho, kiṃ nu kho, kathaṃ nu kho’ti. So vimaticchedanatthāya [V 0.0102] pañhaṃ pucchati. Ayaṃ vimaticchedanāpucchā (mahāni. 150; cūḷani. puṇṇakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 12).

What is the question for cutting off uncertainty? By nature, one is prone to doubt, prone to uncertainty, having become of two minds—‘Is it thus? Is it not thus? What could it be? How could it be?’ One asks a question for the purpose of cutting off uncertainty. This is the question for cutting off uncertainty.

Katamā anumatipucchā? Bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ anumatiyā pañhaṃ pucchati – ‘taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’ti? ‘Aniccaṃ, bhante’. ‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’ti? ‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’[P 0.0056]. ‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti? ‘Nohetaṃ, bhante’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79; mahāva. 21). Ayaṃ anumatipucchā.

What is the question for seeking approval? The Blessed One asks the bhikkhus a question for their approval: ‘What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?’ ‘Impermanent, venerable sir.’ ‘And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?’ ‘Suffering, venerable sir.’ ‘And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to be regarded thus: “This is mine, this I am, this is my self”?’ ‘It is not, venerable sir.’ This is the question for seeking approval.

Katamā kathetukamyatāpucchā? Bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ kathetukamyatāya pañhaṃ pucchati. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro”ti (dī. ni. 2.373)? Ayaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchāti.

What is the question from a desire to speak? The Blessed One asks the bhikkhus a question from a desire to speak: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?’ This is the question from a desire to speak.

Tattha buddhānaṃ purimā tisso pucchā natthi. Kasmā? Buddhānañhi tīsu addhāsu kiñci saṅkhataṃ, addhāvimuttaṃ vā asaṅkhataṃ, adiṭṭhaṃ anaññātaṃ ajotitaṃ atulitaṃ atīritaṃ avibhūtaṃ avibhāvitaṃ nāma natthi. Tena tesaṃ adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā natthi. Yaṃ pana bhagavatā attano ñāṇena paṭividdhaṃ, tassa aññena samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā saddhiṃ saṃsandanakiccaṃ natthi. Tenassa diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā natthi. Yasmā panesa akathaṃkathī tiṇṇavicikiccho sabbadhammesu vihatasaṃsayo, tenassa vimaticchedanāpucchā natthi. Itarā dve pana pucchā bhagavato atthi. Tāsu ayaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchāti veditabbā.

Herein, the first three questions do not exist for the Buddhas. Why? Because for the Buddhas, in the three periods of time, there is nothing conditioned, or unconditioned and liberated from time, that is by nature unseen, unknown, unillumined, unweighed, unjudged, unclear, or unmanifested. Therefore, for them the question for illuminating what is unseen does not exist. Furthermore, whatever has been penetrated by the Blessed One’s own knowledge, for that there is no need for comparison with any other ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā. Hence, for him the question for comparing what is seen does not exist. And because he is one without questioning, has crossed over doubt, and has dispelled uncertainty regarding all phenomena, for him the question for cutting off uncertainty does not exist. However, the other two questions do exist for the Blessed One. Among these, this one should be understood as the question from a desire to speak.

Tattha ‘katame’tipadena niddisitabbadhamme pucchati. ‘Dhammā kusalā’ti hi vacanamattena ‘kiṃ katā kiṃ vā karontī’ti na sakkā ñātuṃ. ‘Katame’ti vutte pana tesaṃ puṭṭhabhāvo paññāyati. Tena vuttaṃ ‘katametipadena niddisitabbadhamme pucchatī’ti. ‘Dhammā kusalā’tipadadvayena pucchāya puṭṭhadhamme dasseti. Tesaṃ attho heṭṭhā pakāsitova.

Herein, by the word ‘katame,’ one asks about the phenomena to be pointed out. For by the mere statement ‘dhammā kusalā,’ it is not possible to know ‘how they are constituted or what they do.’ But when ‘katame’ is said, the fact that they are being questioned becomes apparent. Therefore it is said, ‘by the word “katame” one asks about the phenomena to be pointed out.’ By the pair of words ‘dhammā kusalā,’ one shows the phenomena that are asked about in the question. Their meaning has already been explained below.

Kasmā panettha mātikāyaṃ viya ‘kusalā dhammā’ti avatvā ‘dhammā kusalā’ti padānukkamo katoti? Pabhedato dhammānaṃ desanaṃ dīpetvā pabhedavantadassanatthaṃ. Imasmiñhi abhidhamme [V 0.0103] dhammāva desetabbā. Te ca kusalādīhi pabhedehi anekappabhedā. Tasmā dhammāyeva idha desetabbā[M 0.0099]. Nāyaṃ vohāradesanā. Te ca anekappabhedato desetabbā, na dhammamattato. Pabhedato hi desanā ghanavinibbhogapaṭisambhidāñāṇāvahā hotīti ‘kusalā dhammā’ti evaṃ pabhedato dhammānaṃ desanaṃ dīpetvā, idāni ye tena pabhedena desetabbā dhammā te [P 0.0057] dassetuṃ, ayaṃ ‘katame dhammā kusalā’ti padānukkamo katoti veditabbo. Pabhedavantesu hi dassitesu pabhedo dassiyamāno yujjati suviññeyyo ca hotīti.

Why here, unlike in the Mātikā, was the word order ‘dhammā kusalā’ used, instead of saying ‘kusalā dhammā’? It was for the purpose of showing that which possesses distinctions, after having shown the teaching of phenomena according to their distinctions. For in this Abhidhamma, only phenomena are to be taught, and they are of many kinds according to distinctions such as ‘wholesome,’ etc. Therefore, only phenomena are to be taught here. This is not a conventional teaching. And they are to be taught according to their many distinctions, not merely as phenomena in general. For a teaching according to distinctions is conducive to the knowledge of breaking down compactness and the analytical knowledges. Therefore, having shown the teaching of phenomena according to their distinctions as ‘kusalā dhammā,’ now, in order to show those phenomena that are to be taught by means of that distinction, this word order—‘katame dhammā kusalā’—was used. This should be understood. For when those things that possess distinctions have been shown, the subsequent showing of the distinction is fitting and easily understood.

Idāni yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittanti. Ettha –

Now, regarding the passage ‘yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ.’ Herein—

Samaye niddisi cittaṃ, cittena samayaṃ muni;

Niyametvāna dīpetuṃ, dhamme tattha pabhedato.

The Sage pointed out consciousness in relation to time, and time by means of consciousness; having thus delimited, he did so in order to show the phenomena therein according to their distinctions.

‘Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ citta’nti hi niddisanto bhagavā samaye cittaṃ niddisi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tena samayaniyamitena cittena pariyosāne ‘tasmiṃ samaye’ti evaṃ samayaṃ niyametvāna, atha vijjamānepi samayanānatte yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ tasmiṃyeva samaye phasso hoti, vedanā hotīti evaṃ tasmiṃ cittaniyamite samaye ete santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanavasena duranubodhappabhede phassavedanādayo dhamme bodhetunti attho.

For in pointing out, ‘At which time a sense-sphere wholesome consciousness…,’ the Blessed One pointed out consciousness in relation to time. For what reason? By means of that consciousness which is delimited by time, and at the conclusion having delimited the time thus as ‘at that time,’ then—even though there is a diversity of times—at the very same time that consciousness is, contact is, and feeling is. Thus, the meaning is that within that time delimited by consciousness, he makes known these phenomena such as contact and feeling, whose distinctions are difficult to understand on account of the compactness of continuity, aggregation, function, and object.

Idāni ‘yasmiṃ samaye’tiādīsu ayamanupubbapadavaṇṇanā. Yasminti aniyamato bhummaniddeso. Samayeti aniyamaniddiṭṭhaparidīpanaṃ. Ettāvatā aniyamato samayo niddiṭṭho hoti. Tattha samayasaddo –

Now, in the phrases beginning with 'yasmiṃ samaye,' this is the sequential explanation of the words. 'Yasmiṃ' is an unspecified locative designation. 'Samaye' is an elucidation of what has been designated as unspecified. By this much, a time has been designated in an unspecified manner. Therein, the word 'samaya'—

Samavāye khaṇe kāle, samūhe hetu diṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati.

Is seen in the sense of concurrence, moment, time, group, cause, views, acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.

Tathā hissa “appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.447) evamādīsu samavāyo attho. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) khaṇo. “Uṇhasamayo pariḷāhasamayo”tiādīsu [V 0.0104] (pāci. 358) kālo. “Mahāsamayo pavanasmi”ntiādīsu samūho. “Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi [M 0.0100] – bhagavā kho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, bhagavāpi maṃ jānissati ‘bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.135) hetu. “Tena kho pana samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto [P 0.0058] samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.260) diṭṭhi.

Thus, in such instances as “Perhaps tomorrow we may approach, taking into account the time and the occasion” (Dī. Ni. 1.447), the meaning is concurrence. In passages like “Monks, there is only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life” (A. Ni. 8.29), it refers to a moment. In phrases like “The season of heat, the season of scorching” (Pāci. 358), it denotes a time. In expressions such as “A great assembly in the forest,” it signifies a group. In statements like “And this occasion, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you—the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One would know of me, ‘The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.’ This too, Bhaddāli, was an occasion not penetrated by you” (Ma. Ni. 2.135), it refers to a cause. In passages such as “Now at that time, the wandering ascetic Uggāhamāna, the son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was dwelling in the Mallikā grove, in a single hall at Tindukācīra, proclaiming his doctrine” (Ma. Ni. 2.260), it denotes a view.

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.129) –

“The welfare in this visible life, and the welfare pertaining to the future life; because of having penetrated this welfare, the steadfast one is called a sage.”

Ādīsu paṭilābho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.28) pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 2.8) paṭivedho. Evamanekesu samayesu –

In these and similar instances, it means acquisition. In passages like “Through the right penetration of conceit, he made an end of suffering” (Ma. Ni. 1.28), it means abandonment. In passages like “The characteristic of suffering is oppression, the characteristic of being conditioned, the characteristic of torment, the characteristic of change, the characteristic of penetration” (Paṭi. Ma. 2.8), it means penetration. Thus, in these many meanings of 'samaya'—

Samavāyo khaṇo kālo, samūho hetuyeva ca;

Ete pañcapi viññeyyā, samayā idha viññunā.

Concurrence, opportunity, time, group, and cause indeed; these five meanings of 'samaya' should be known here by the wise.

‘Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusala’nti imasmiñhi kusalādhikāre tesu navasu samayesu ete samavāyādayo pañca samayā paṇḍitena veditabbā.

In this section on the wholesome, concerning 'at which time sense-sphere wholesome [consciousness arises],' among those nine meanings of 'samaya,' these five meanings beginning with concurrence should be known by the wise.

Tesu paccayasāmaggī, samavāyo khaṇo pana;

Ekova navamo ñeyyo, cakkāni caturopi vā.

Among these, the concordance of conditions is `samavāya`. Furthermore, `khaṇa` should be known as the single ninth one, or also as all four wheels.

Yā hi esā sādhāraṇaphalanipphādakattena saṇṭhitā paccayānaṃ sāmaggī, sā idha samavāyoti ñātabbā. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”ti (a. ni. 8.29) evaṃ vutto pana navamova khaṇo eko khaṇoti veditabbo. Yāni vā [V 0.0105] panetāni “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”ti – ettha ‘patirūpadesavāso, sappurisūpanissayo, attasammāpaṇidhi, pubbe ca katapuññatā’ti (a. ni. 4.31) cattāri cakkāni vuttāni, etāni [M 0.0101] vā ekajjhaṃ katvā okāsaṭṭhena khaṇoti veditabbāni. Tāni hi kusaluppattiyā okāsabhūtāni.

Indeed, that concordance of conditions which is established as producing a common result should be known here as `samavāya`. Furthermore, that very ninth opportunity spoken of thus: “Monks, there is only one opportunity and one occasion for living the holy life” (A.N. 8.29), should be understood as the one opportunity. Or further, these four wheels spoken of in “Monks, there are these four wheels, for gods and humans endowed with which the four-wheeled vehicle rolls on”—namely, 'dwelling in a suitable region, reliance on a good person, proper direction of oneself, and having done meritorious deeds in the past' (A.N. 4.31)—these, when taken together, are to be understood as `khaṇa` in the sense of opportunity. For they are the opportunity for the arising of the wholesome.

Evaṃ samavāyañca khaṇañca ñatvā itaresu –

Having thus understood both concurrence and opportunity, among the remaining [meanings]—

Taṃ taṃ upādāya paññatto, kālo vohāramattako;

Puñjo phassādidhammānaṃ, samūhoti vibhāvito.

Time is designated in dependence on this or that, merely a conventional term; a heap of phenomena such as contact is explained as a group.

‘Cittakālo rūpakālo’tiādinā hi nayena dhamme vā, ‘atīto anāgato’tiādinā nayena dhammavuttiṃ vā, ‘bījakālo aṅkurakālo’ti ādinā nayena dhammapaṭipāṭiṃ vā, ‘uppādakālo [P 0.0059] jarākālo’tiādinā nayena dhammalakkhaṇaṃ vā, ‘vediyanakālo sañjānanakālo’tiādinā nayena dhammakiccaṃ vā, ‘nhānakālo pānakālo’tiādinā nayena sattakiccaṃ vā, ‘gamanakālo ṭhānakālo’tiādinā nayena iriyāpathaṃ vā, ‘pubbaṇho sāyanho divā rattī’tiādinā nayena candimasūriyādiparivattanaṃ vā, ‘aḍḍhamāso māso’tiādinā nayena ahorattādisaṅkhātaṃ kālasañcayaṃ vāti – evaṃ taṃ taṃ upādāya paññatto kālo nāma. So panesa sabhāvato avijjamānattā paññattimattako evāti veditabbo. Yo panesa phassavedanādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ puñjo, so idha samūhoti vibhāvito. Evaṃ kālasamūhepi ñatvā itaro pana –

Indeed, by the method beginning with 'time of mind, time of form,' in regard to phenomena; or by the method beginning with 'past, future,' in regard to the occurrence of phenomena; or by the method beginning with 'time of the seed, time of the sprout,' in regard to the sequence of phenomena; or by the method beginning with 'time of arising, time of aging,' in regard to the characteristics of phenomena; or by the method beginning with 'time of feeling, time of perceiving,' in regard to the function of phenomena; or by the method beginning with 'time of bathing, time of drinking,' in regard to the activities of beings; or by the method beginning with 'time of going, time of standing,' in regard to postures; or by the method beginning with 'morning, evening, day, night,' in regard to the revolution of the moon, sun, etc.; or by the method beginning with 'half-month, month,' in regard to the accumulation of time reckoned as days and nights, etc. Thus, what is designated by taking this and that as a basis is called time. But it should be understood that this, being non-existent in its intrinsic nature, is merely a designation. And this heap of phenomena such as contact, feeling, and so forth is explained here as a group. Thus, having also known `kāla` and `samūha`, as for the other—

Hetūti paccayovettha, tassa dvāravasena vā;

Anekabhāvo viññeyyo, paccayānaṃ vasena vā.

Here, `hetu` is simply `paccaya`. Its manifold nature should be known either by way of the doors or by way of the conditions.

Ettha hi paccayova hetu nāma, tassa dvārānaṃ vā paccayānaṃ vā vasena anekabhāvo veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Cakkhudvārādīsu hi uppajjamānānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ cakkhurūpaālokamanasikārādayo paccayā, mahāpakaraṇe ca “hetupaccayo ārammaṇapaccayo”tiādinā nayena catuvīsati paccayā vuttā. Tesu ṭhapetvā vipākapaccayañca pacchājātapaccayañca, sesā kusaladhammānaṃ paccayā hontiyeva. Te sabbepi idha hetūti adhippetā. Evamassa iminā dvāravasena [V 0.0106] vā paccayavasena vā anekabhāvo veditabbo[M 0.0102]. Evamete samavāyādayo pañca atthā idha samayasaddena pariggahitāti veditabbā.

Here, indeed, `paccaya` itself is called `hetu`. Its manifold nature should be known either by way of the doors or by way of the conditions. How? For the eye-consciousness and so forth arising at the eye-door and other doors, the eye, visible form, light, attention, and so on are the conditions. And in the Great Treatise, the twenty-four conditions are stated in the manner beginning with 'root condition, object condition.' Excluding the result-condition and the postnascence-condition, the remaining ones are indeed conditions for wholesome dhammas. All of them are intended here as `hetu`. Thus, its manifold nature should be understood in this way, either by way of the doors or by way of the conditions. In this way, it should be known that these five meanings—concurrence and so forth—are encompassed here by the word `samaya`.

‘Kasmā pana etesu yaṃkiñci ekaṃ apariggahetvā sabbesaṃ pariggaho kato’ti? ‘Tena tena tassa tassa atthavisesassa dīpanato. Etesu hi samavāyasaṅkhāto samayo anekahetuto vuttiṃ dīpeti. Tena ekakāraṇavādo paṭisedhito hoti. Samavāyo ca nāma sādhāraṇaphalanipphādane aññamaññāpekkho hoti. Tasmā ‘eko kattā nāma natthī’ti imampi atthaṃ dīpeti. Sabhāvena hi kāraṇe sati kāraṇantarāpekkhā ayuttāti. Evaṃ ekassa kassaci kāraṇassa abhāvadīpanena “sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”ntiādi paṭisedhitaṃ hoti.

‘But why, without taking up just any single one of these, is an encompassing of all of them made?’ ‘Because of the showing of this or that special meaning by means of this or that meaning.’ Indeed, among these, the samaya reckoned as concurrence reveals the occurrence from multiple causes. By this, the doctrine of a single cause is refuted. Moreover, what is called concurrence is mutually dependent in the production of a common result. Therefore, it also reveals this meaning: ‘there is no single creator.’ For when a cause exists by its own nature, dependence on another cause is improper. In this way, by demonstrating the absence of any single agent, doctrines such as ‘pleasure and pain are self-made’ are refuted.
