Tattha siyā – ‘yaṃ vuttaṃ anekahetuto vuttiṃ dīpetī’ti, taṃ na yuttaṃ. ‘Kiṃkāraṇā’[P 0.0060]?‘Asāmaggiyaṃ ahetūnaṃ sāmaggiyampi ahetubhāvāpattito’. ‘Na hi ekasmiṃ andhe daṭṭhuṃ asakkonte andhasataṃ passatī’ti. ‘No na yuttaṃ; sādhāraṇaphalanipphādakattena hi ṭhitabhāvo sāmaggī; na anekesaṃ samodhānamattaṃ. Na ca andhānaṃ dassanaṃ nāma sādhāraṇaphalaṃ’. ‘Kasmā’?‘Andhasate satipi tassa abhāvato. Cakkhādīnaṃ pana taṃ sādhāraṇaphalaṃ, tesaṃ bhāve bhāvato. Asāmaggiyaṃ ahetūnampi ca sāmaggiyaṃ hetubhāvo siddho. Svāyaṃ asāmaggiyaṃ phalābhāvena, sāmaggiyañcassa bhāvena, veditabbo. Cakkhādīnañhi vekalle cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ abhāvo, avekalle ca bhāvo, paccakkhasiddho lokassā’ti. Ayaṃ tāva samavāyasaṅkhātena samayena attho dīpito.

Herein, an objection might be raised: 'That which was stated, "it reveals the occurrence from multiple causes," is not appropriate.' 'For what reason?' 'Because for things that are not causes when there is no concurrence, there would be the consequence of their being non-causes even when there is concurrence.' 'Indeed, when one blind person is unable to see, a hundred blind persons do not see.' 'No, it is not that it is inappropriate. For concurrence is the state of being established by the production of a common result, not merely the combination of many. And seeing is not a common result for the blind.' 'Why?' 'Because of its absence even when a hundred blind persons are present. But for the eye and so on, that is a common result, because of its presence when they are present. And for things that are not causes when there is no concurrence, their state of being a cause is established when there is concurrence. This is to be understood through the absence of the result when there is no concurrence, and through its presence when there is concurrence. Indeed, for the world, the absence of eye-consciousness and so on when the eye and so on are deficient, and their presence when they are not deficient, is directly evident.' Thus far, this meaning has been explained by means of the samaya designated as 'concurrence'.

Yo panesa aṭṭhahi akkhaṇehi parivajjito navamo khaṇo, patirūpadesavāsādiko ca catucakkasaṅkhāto okāsaṭṭhena khaṇo vutto, so manussattabuddhuppādasaddhammaṭṭhitiādikaṃ khaṇasāmaggiṃ vinā natthi. Manussattādīnañca kāṇakacchapopamādīhi (ma. ni. 3.252) dullabhabhāvo. Iti khaṇassa dullabhattā suṭṭhutaraṃ khaṇāyattaṃ lokuttaradhammānaṃ upakārabhūtaṃ kusalaṃ dullabhameva[M 0.0103]. Evametesu khaṇasaṅkhāto samayo kusaluppattiyā dullabhabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Evaṃ dīpentena anena adhigatakhaṇānaṃ khaṇāyattasseva tassa kusalassa ananuṭṭhānena moghakhaṇaṃ kurumānānaṃ pamādavihāro paṭisedhito hoti. Ayaṃ khaṇasaṅkhātena samayena attho dīpito.

Furthermore, that ninth moment, which is devoid of the eight inopportune times, and that which is called a 'moment' in the sense of 'opportunity'—designated as the four wheels of accomplishment, such as residing in a suitable country—does not exist without the concurrence of moments such as human existence, the arising of a Buddha, the stability of the good Dhamma, and so on. And the state of being difficult to obtain of human existence and so on has been spoken of through similes such as that of the one-eyed turtle. Thus, because of the rarity of the moment, the wholesome state that is dependent on the moment and is beneficial to the supramundane states is even more difficult to obtain. In this way, among these, the samaya designated as 'moment' reveals the state of being difficult to obtain for the arising of wholesome states. By this, thus revealing, the negligent abiding of those who, having obtained the moment, make that moment fruitless by not undertaking that wholesome state which is dependent on the moment, is prohibited. This is the meaning explained by means of the samaya designated as 'moment'.

Yo [V 0.0107] panetassa kusalacittassa pavattikālo nāma hoti, so atiparitto. Sā cassa atiparittatā “yathā ca, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa javo, yathā ca candimasūriyānaṃ javo, yathā ca yā devatā candimasūriyānaṃ purato dhāvanti tāsaṃ devatānaṃ javo, tato sīghataraṃ āyusaṅkhārā khīyantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.228) – imassa suttassa aṭṭhakathāvasena veditabbā. Tatra hi so rūpajīvitindriyassa tāva parittako kālo vutto. Yāva paṭuppannaṃ rūpaṃ tiṭṭhati tāva soḷasa cittāni uppajjitvā bhijjanti. Iti tesaṃ kālaparittatāya upamāpi [P 0.0061] natthi. Tenevāha – “yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, upamāpi na sukarā yāva lahuparivattaṃ citta”nti (a. ni. 1.48). Evametesu kālasaṅkhāto samayo kusalacittappavattikālassa atiparittataṃ dīpeti. Evaṃ dīpentena cānena atiparittakālatāya, vijjulatobhāsena muttāvuṇanaṃ viya, duppaṭivijjhamidaṃ cittaṃ, tasmā etassa paṭivedhe mahāussāho ca ādaro ca kattabboti ovādo dinno hoti. Ayaṃ kālasaṅkhātena samayena attho dīpito.

Furthermore, that which is the time of occurrence of this wholesome consciousness is extremely short. And its extreme shortness is to be known by way of the commentary on this sutta: 'Just as, bhikkhus, the speed of that man, and the speed of the moon and sun, and the speed of those deities who run before the moon and sun—faster than that, the life-formations are exhausted.' Indeed, therein, the time of the material life-faculty is said to be just that short. For as long as a presently arisen material phenomenon stands, for that long sixteen consciousnesses arise and break up. Thus, for the shortness of their time, there is not even a simile. For that reason, he said: 'Indeed, bhikkhus, it is not easy to find even a simile for how swiftly the consciousness changes.' In this way, among these, the samaya designated as 'time' reveals the extreme shortness of the time of occurrence of a wholesome consciousness. And by this, thus revealing, because of the extreme shortness of the time, this consciousness is difficult to penetrate—like stringing pearls by a flash of lightning. Therefore, the exhortation is given that for its penetration, great exertion and respect should be made. This is the meaning explained by means of the samaya designated as 'time'.

Samūhasaṅkhāto pana samayo anekesaṃ sahuppattiṃ dīpeti. Phassādīnañhi dhammānaṃ puñjo samūhoti vutto. Tasmiñca uppajjamānaṃ cittaṃ saha tehi dhammehi uppajjatīti anekesaṃ sahuppatti dīpitā. Evaṃ dīpentena cānena ekasseva dhammassa uppatti paṭisedhitā hoti. Ayaṃ samūhasaṅkhātena samayena attho dīpito.

Furthermore, the samaya designated as 'group' reveals the co-arising of many states. Indeed, a heap of states such as contact and so on is called a 'group'. And a consciousness arising therein arises together with those states; thus, the co-arising of many is explained. And by this, thus revealing, the arising of just one single state is prohibited. This is the meaning explained by means of the samaya designated as 'group'.

Hetusaṅkhāto pana samayo parāyattavuttitaṃ dīpeti. ‘Yasmiṃ samaye’ti hi padassa yasmā ‘yasmiṃ hetumhi sati’ uppannaṃ hotīti ayamattho, tasmā ‘hetumhi sati’ pavattito parāyattavuttitā dīpitā. Evaṃ [M 0.0104] dīpentena cānena dhammānaṃ savasavattitābhimāno paṭisedhito hoti. Ayaṃ hetusaṅkhātena samayena attho dīpito.

Furthermore, the samaya designated as 'cause' reveals the state of having an occurrence dependent on another. Indeed, because the meaning of the phrase 'yasmiṃ samaye' is 'when which cause is present, it has arisen,' therefore, from its occurring 'when a cause is present,' the state of having an occurrence dependent on another is explained. And by this, thus revealing, the conceit that states have their own power is prohibited. This is the meaning explained by means of the samaya designated as 'cause'.

Tattha ‘yasmiṃ samaye’ti kālasaṅkhātassa samayassa vasena ‘yasmiṃ kāle’ti attho; samūhasaṅkhātassa ‘yasmiṃ samūhe’ti. Khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātānaṃ ‘yasmiṃ khaṇe sati, yāya sāmaggiyā sati, yamhi hetumhi sati’ kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva sati ‘phassādayopī’ti ayamattho veditabbo. Adhikaraṇañhi kālasaṅkhāto samūhasaṅkhāto ca samayo. Tattha vuttadhammānanti adhikaraṇavasenettha bhummaṃ. Khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa ca samayassa bhāvena tesaṃ bhāvo lakkhīyatīti bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇavasenettha bhummaṃ.

Therein, for the phrase 'yasmiṃ samaye', by way of the samaya designated as 'time', the meaning is 'at which time'; by way of that designated as 'group', 'in which group'. By way of those designated as 'moment', 'concurrence', and 'cause', this meaning is to be understood: When a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen 'when which moment is present, when which concurrence is present, when which cause is present,' then 'contact and so on are also' present when that very one is present. Indeed, the samaya designated as 'time' and the samaya designated as 'group' are a location for the states spoken of therein. Therefore, here the locative case is by way of location. And because the existence of those states is indicated by the existence of the samaya designated as 'moment', 'concurrence', and 'cause', here the locative case is by way of bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa.

Kāmāvacaranti [V 0.0108] “katame dhammā kāmāvacarā? Heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ uparito paranimmitavasavattiṃ pariyantaṃ katvā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1287) nayena vuttesu kāmāvacaradhammesu pariyāpannaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – uddānato [P 0.0062] dve kāmā, vatthukāmo ca kilesakāmo ca. Tattha kilesakāmo atthato chandarāgova vatthukāmo tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Kilesakāmo cettha kāmetīti kāmo; itaro pana kāmiyatīti kāmo. Yasmiṃ pana padese duvidhopeso kāmo pavattivasena avacarati, so catunnaṃ apāyānaṃ, manussānaṃ, channañca devalokānaṃ vasena ekādasavidho padeso. Kāmo ettha avacaratīti kāmāvacaro, sasatthāvacaro viya. Yathā hi yasmiṃ padese sasatthā purisā avacaranti, so vijjamānesupi aññesu dvipadacatuppadesu avacarantesu, tesaṃ abhilakkhitattā ‘sasatthāvacaro’tveva vuccati, evaṃ vijjamānesupi aññesu rūpāvacarādīsu tattha avacarantesu, tesaṃ abhilakkhitattā ayaṃ padeso ‘kāmāvacaro’tveva vuccati. Svāyaṃ yathā rūpabhavo rūpaṃ, evaṃ uttarapadalopaṃ katvā ‘kāmo’tveva vuccati. Evamidaṃ cittaṃ imasmiṃ ekādasapadesasaṅkhāte kāme avacaratīti kāmāvacaraṃ.

The term 'of the sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara) refers to what is included among the sense-sphere states, spoken of by the method beginning with, 'Which states are of the sense-sphere? Below, making the Avīci hell the lower limit, and above, the Paranimmitavasavatti devas the upper limit...' Herein, this is the word-analysis: in brief, there are two kinds of sensuality (kāma): objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and defilement sensuality (kilesakāma). Among these, defilement sensuality is, in essence, simply sensual passion, while objective sensuality is the round of existence in the three planes. Herein, defilement sensuality is called kāma because 'it desires' (kāmeti); the other, however, is called kāma because 'it is desired' (kāmiyati). Now, the region where this two-fold kāma ranges by way of occurrence is the eleven-fold region consisting of the four states of deprivation, human beings, and the six celestial worlds. It is kāmāvacara because kāma ranges (avacarati) here (ettha), like a region ranged by armed men (sasatthāvacara). For just as a region where armed men range is called 'a region ranged by armed men' because it is characterized by them, even though other bipeds and quadrupeds may be present and ranging there, so too this region is called 'of the sense-sphere' because it is characterized by these kāmas, even though other states such as those of the form-sphere may be present and ranging there. And this kāmāvacara, by eliding the latter word, is called simply kāma, just as form-existence (rūpabhava) is called rūpa. Thus, this consciousness is called 'of the sense-sphere' because it ranges in this kāma designated as the eleven-fold region.

Kiñcāpi hi etaṃ rūpārūpabhavesupi avacarati, yathā pana saṅgāme avacaraṇato saṅgāmāvacaroti laddhanāmako nāgo nagare carantopi ‘saṅgāmāvacaro’tveva vuccati, thalajalacarā ca pāṇā athale [M 0.0105] ajale ca ṭhitāpi ‘thalacarā jalacarā’tveva vuccanti, evamidaṃ aññattha avacarantampi kāmāvacaramevāti veditabbaṃ. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena vā ettha kāmo avacaratītipi kāmāvacaraṃ. Kāmañcesa rūpārūpāvacaresupi avacarati, yathā pana vadatīti ‘vaccho’, mahiyaṃ setīti ‘mahiṃso’ti vutte, na sattā yattakā vadanti, mahiyaṃ vā senti sabbesaṃ taṃ nāmaṃ hoti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Apica kāmabhavasaṅkhāte kāme paṭisandhiṃ avacāretītipi kāmāvacaraṃ.

Indeed, although this consciousness ranges even in the form and formless existences, it should be known as being only 'of the sense-sphere' even when it ranges elsewhere. Just as an elephant that has gained the name 'battle-ranger' from ranging in battle is still called 'battle-ranger' even when moving about in a city; and just as land-ranging and water-ranging beings are still called 'land-rangers' and 'water-rangers' even when they are in a place that is not land or not water; so too should this be understood. Alternatively, it is 'of the sense-sphere' also because sensuality (kāma) ranges in it by way of being taken as an object. And although this sensuality does range even in form-sphere and formless-sphere consciousnesses, this matter should be understood as follows: just as when it is said, 'because it speaks (vadati), it is a calf (vaccho)', or 'because it lies (seti) on the earth (mahiyaṃ), it is a buffalo (mahiṃso)', that name does not apply to all beings that speak or to all that lie on the earth. Furthermore, it is also 'of the sense-sphere' because it causes rebirth-linking to range in the kāma designated as sense-sphere existence.

Kusalanti kucchitānaṃ salanādīhi atthehi kusalaṃ. Apica ārogyaṭṭhena anavajjaṭṭhena kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena ca kusalaṃ. Yatheva hi ‘kacci nu bhoto kusala’nti (jā. 1.15.146; 2.20.129) rūpakāye anāturatāya agelaññena nibyādhitāya ārogyaṭṭhena kusalaṃ vuttaṃ, evaṃ arūpadhammepi kilesāturatāya kilesagelaññassa ca kilesabyādhino [P 0.0063] abhāvena ārogyaṭṭhena kusalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kilesavajjassa pana kilesadosassa kilesadarathassa ca abhāvā anavajjaṭṭhena [V 0.0109] kusalaṃ. Kosallaṃ vuccati paññā; kosallato sambhūtattā kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena kusalaṃ.

The term kusala is so called due to meanings such as the shaking (salana), etc., of contemptible (kucchita) states. Moreover, it is kusala in the sense of health, in the sense of blamelessness, and in the sense of being produced from skill. For just as in the passage, 'Is there health for you, sir?' (kacci nu bhoto kusalaṃ), the word kusala is used in the sense of health with regard to the physical body—meaning being without affliction, without illness, and without disease—so too, in the case of immaterial states, kusala should be understood in the sense of health due to the absence of the affliction of defilements, the illness of defilements, and the disease of defilements. Furthermore, it is kusala in the sense of blamelessness due to the absence of the fault of defilements, the blemish of defilements, and the vexation of defilements. Skill (kosalla) is a name for wisdom (paññā); because it is produced from skill, it is kusala in the sense of being produced from skill.

‘Ñāṇasampayuttaṃ’ tāva evaṃ hotu; ñāṇavippayuttaṃ kathanti. Tampi ruḷhīsaddena kusalameva. Yathā hi tālapaṇṇehi akatvā kilañjādīhi katampi taṃsarikkhattā ruḷhīsaddena tālavaṇṭantveva vuccati, evaṃ ‘ñāṇavippayutta’mpi kusalantveva veditabbaṃ. Nippariyāyena pana ‘ñāṇasampayuttaṃ’ ārogyaṭṭhena anavajjaṭṭhena kosallasambhūtaṭṭhenāti tividhenapi kusalanti nāmaṃ labhati, ñāṇavippayuttaṃ duvidheneva. Iti yañca jātakapariyāyena yañca bāhitikasuttapariyāyena yañca abhidhammapariyāyena kusalaṃ kathitaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ tīhipi atthehi imasmiṃ citte labbhati.

Let it be so for that which is 'associated with knowledge'; but how is it for that which is 'dissociated from knowledge'? That too is kusala simply by conventional usage (ruḷhīsadda). For just as a fan, even if made not with palm leaves but with reeds or other materials, is still called a 'palm-leaf fan' by conventional usage due to its resemblance, so too should that which is 'dissociated from knowledge' be understood as being simply kusala. However, in the direct sense (nippariyāyena), that which is 'associated with knowledge' obtains the name kusala in all three ways: in the sense of health, in the sense of blamelessness, and in the sense of being produced from skill. That which is 'dissociated from knowledge' obtains it in only two ways. Thus, whatever kusala has been spoken of—whether by the method of the Jātakas, by the method of the Bāhitika Sutta, or by the method of the Abhidhamma—all of it is obtained in this consciousness through these three meanings.

Tadetaṃ lakkhaṇādivasena anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ, akusalaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, vodānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Avajjapaṭipakkhattā vā anavajjalakkhaṇameva kusalaṃ, vodānabhāvarasaṃ, iṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yathāvuttapadaṭṭhānameva. Lakkhaṇādīsu hi tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvo vā sāmaññaṃ vā lakkhaṇaṃ nāma. Kiccaṃ vā sampatti vā raso nāma. Upaṭṭhānākāro vā phalaṃ vā paccupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Āsannakāraṇaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Iti yattha yattha lakkhaṇādīni vakkhāma tattha tattha imināva nayena tesaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This wholesome state, by way of its characteristic, etc., has the characteristic of blameless and pleasant results, the function of destroying the unwholesome, the manifestation of purity, and the proximate cause of wise attention. Alternatively, because it is the opposite of the blameworthy, the wholesome has the characteristic of being blameless, the function of being a state of purity, the manifestation of a desirable result, and the same proximate cause as stated before. For among characteristics, etc., the inherent nature (sabhāva) or commonality (sāmañña) of the various states is called the characteristic (lakkhaṇa). The function (kicca) or accomplishment (sampatti) is called the function (rasa). The mode of appearance (upaṭṭhānākāra) or the fruit (phala) is called the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna). The proximate cause (āsannakāraṇa) is called the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Thus, wherever we shall speak of characteristics, etc., there the diversity of these should be understood in this very way.

Cittanti [M 0.0106] ārammaṇaṃ cintetīti cittaṃ; vijānātīti attho. Yasmā vā ‘citta’nti sabbacittasādhāraṇo esa saddo, tasmā yadettha lokiyakusalākusalakiriyacittaṃ, taṃ javanavīthivasena attano santānaṃ cinotīti cittaṃ. Vipākaṃ kammakilesehi citanti cittaṃ. Apica sabbampi yathānurūpato cittatāya cittaṃ. Cittakaraṇatāya cittanti evampettha attho veditabbo. Tattha yasmā aññadeva sarāgaṃ cittaṃ, aññaṃ sadosaṃ[P 0.0064], aññaṃ samohaṃ; aññaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ, aññaṃ rūpāvacarādibhedaṃ; aññaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ saddādiārammaṇaṃ; rūpārammaṇesu cāpi aññaṃ nīlārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ pītādiārammaṇaṃ; saddādiārammaṇesupi eseva nayo; sabbesupi cetesu aññaṃ hīnaṃ aññaṃ majjhimaṃ aññaṃ paṇītaṃ; hīnādīsupi aññaṃ chandādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ vīriyādhipateyyaṃ aññaṃ cittādhipateyyaṃ, aññaṃ vīmaṃsādhipateyyaṃ, tasmā assa imesaṃ sampayuttabhūmiārammaṇahīnamajjhimapaṇītādhipatīnaṃ vasena cittatā veditabbā. Kāmañcettha [V 0.0110] ekameva evaṃ cittaṃ na hoti, cittānaṃ pana antogadhattā etesu yaṃkiñci ekampi cittatāya cittanti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ tāva cittatāya cittaṃ.

It is called 'citta' because it cognizes (cinteti) an object (ārammaṇa); the meaning is that it knows (vijānāti). Or, since this term 'citta' is common to all minds, therefore, whatever worldly wholesome, unwholesome, or functional mind there is, it arranges (cinoti) its own continuity by way of the javana process; thus it is called 'citta'. The resultant is called 'citta' because it is arranged (cita) by kamma and defilements. Furthermore, all mind is 'citta' due to being variegated (cittatā) in a corresponding way. The meaning here should also be understood thus: it is 'citta' due to performing a variegated act (cittakaraṇatā). Therein, since a mind with greed is one thing, a mind with hate another, and a mind with delusion another; a sense-sphere mind is one thing, and one of the fine-material sphere and so on is another; a mind with a form-object is one thing, and one with a sound-object and so on is another; and even among form-objects, a mind with a blue object is one thing, and one with a yellow object and so on is another—the same method applies to sound-objects and so on; and among all these, an inferior mind is one thing, a middling one another, and a sublime one another; and even among the inferior and so on, one with desire as dominant factor is one thing, one with energy as dominant factor another, one with consciousness as dominant factor another, and one with investigation as dominant factor another—therefore, its variegated nature (cittatā) should be known by way of these associated states, planes, objects, inferior, middling, and sublime grades, and dominant factors. And although it is not that just one mind is variegated in this way, yet because it is included within variegated minds, it is fitting to say of any one of these that it is 'citta' due to its variegated nature. Thus, firstly, it is 'citta' due to its variegated nature.

Kathaṃ cittakaraṇatāyāti? Lokasmiñhi cittakammato uttari aññaṃ cittaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmimpi caraṇaṃ nāma cittaṃ aticittameva hoti. Taṃ karontānaṃ cittakārānaṃ ‘evaṃvidhāni ettha rūpāni kātabbānī’ti cittasaññā uppajjati. Tāya cittasaññāya lekhāgahanarañjanaujjotanavattanādinipphādikā cittakiriyā uppajjanti, tato caraṇasaṅkhāte citte aññataraṃ vicittarūpaṃ nipphajjati. Tato ‘imassa rūpassa upari idaṃ hotu, heṭṭhā idaṃ, ubhayapasse ida’nti cintetvā yathācintitena kamena sesacittarūpanipphādanaṃ hoti, evaṃ yaṃkiñci loke vicittaṃ sippajātaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ citteneva kariyati, evaṃ imāya karaṇavicittatāya tassa tassa cittassa nipphādakaṃ cittampi tatheva cittaṃ hoti. Yathācintitassa vā anavasesassa anipphajjanato tatopi cittameva cittataraṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

How is it 'citta' due to performing a variegated act? Indeed, in the world, there is no other variegated thing called 'citta' superior to a work of art (cittakamma). Even in that, the variegated artwork called 'caraṇa' is exceedingly variegated. For the artists who create it, the artistic perception arises: 'Forms of this kind should be made here.' Through that artistic perception, mental activities that accomplish the outlining, grasping, coloring, illuminating, rounding, and so on, arise. Then, in the variegated artwork called 'caraṇa', a certain intricate form is produced. Thereafter, having conceived, 'Let this be above this form, this below, and this on both sides,' the production of the remaining variegated forms occurs in the conceived sequence. Thus, whatever intricate craft exists in the world, all of it is done by the mind alone. In this way, due to the variegatedness of this act of making, the mind that produces that variegated artwork is likewise variegated. Or, because not all of what is conceived is completely produced, the mind itself is even more variegated than that artwork. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Diṭṭhaṃ vo, bhikkhave, caraṇaṃ nāma cittanti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Tampi kho, bhikkhave, caraṇaṃ nāma cittaṃ citteneva cintitaṃ. Tenapi kho, bhikkhave, caraṇena cittena cittaṃyeva cittatara”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.100).

“Monks, have you seen the variegated artwork called ‘caraṇa’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Monks, that variegated artwork called ‘caraṇa’ is conceived by the mind itself. And, monks, the mind itself is even more variegated than that variegated artwork, caraṇa.”

Tathā [M 0.0107] yadetaṃ devamanussanirayatiracchānabhedāsu gatīsu kammaliṅgasaññāvohārādibhedaṃ ajjhattikaṃ cittaṃ tampi cittakatameva. Kāyakammādibhedañhi dānasīlavihiṃsāsāṭheyyādinayappavattaṃ kusalākusalakammaṃ cittanipphāditaṃ kammanānattaṃ. Kammanānatteneva ca tāsu tāsu gatīsu [P 0.0065] hatthapādakaṇṇaudaragīvāmukhādisaṇṭhānabhinnaṃ liṅganānattaṃ. Liṅganānattato yathāgahitasaṇṭhānavasena ‘ayaṃ itthī ayaṃ puriso’ti uppajjamānāya saññāya saññānānattaṃ. Saññānānattato saññānurūpena ‘itthī’ti vā ‘puriso’ti vā voharantānaṃ vohāranānattaṃ. Vohāranānattavasena pana yasmā ‘itthī bhavissāmi puriso bhavissāmi, khattiyo bhavissāmi brāhmaṇo bhavissāmī’ti evaṃ tassa tassa attabhāvassa janakaṃ kammaṃ karīyati, tasmā vohāranānattato kammanānattaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ kammanānattaṃ yathāpatthitaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattentaṃ yasmā gativasena nibbatteti tasmā kammanānattato gatinānattaṃ. Kammanānatteneva ca tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tassā tassā gatiyā apādakadvipādakāditā, tassā tassā upapattiyā uccanīcāditā, tasmiṃ [V 0.0111] tasmiṃ attabhāve suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāditā, lokadhammesu lābhālābhāditā ca paññāyati. Tasmā sabbametaṃ devamanussanirayatiracchānabhedāsu gatīsu kammaliṅgasaññāvohārādibhedaṃ ajjhattikaṃ cittaṃ citteneva katanti veditabbaṃ. Svāyamattho imassa saṅgītianāruḷhassa suttassa vasena veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Similarly, this internal variegated phenomenon, differentiated by kamma, physical form, perception, designation, and so on, in the various destinies of devas, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—that too is made by the mind alone. For the diversity of kamma—wholesome and unwholesome kamma proceeding by way of bodily action and so on, such as giving, virtue, harming, and deceit—is produced by the mind. And precisely through the diversity of kamma, in those various destinies, there is a diversity of physical form, distinguished by the configuration of hands, feet, ears, stomach, neck, face, and so on. From the diversity of physical form, there is a diversity of perception, arising according to the form apprehended, as ‘this is a woman,’ ‘this is a man.’ From the diversity of perception, there is a diversity of designation for those who designate according to the perception, as ‘woman’ or ‘man.’ Furthermore, by way of the diversity of designation, since one performs kamma that generates a particular existence, aspiring, ‘I shall be a woman,’ ‘I shall be a man,’ ‘I shall be a khattiya,’ ‘I shall be a brahmin,’ therefore, from the diversity of designation, there is a diversity of kamma. And since this diversity of kamma, in producing the aspired-for existence, produces it by way of destiny, therefore, from the diversity of kamma, there is a diversity of destiny. And precisely through the diversity of kamma, for these various beings in their respective destinies, their state of being footless, two-footed, and so on is apparent; in their respective modes of birth, their state of being high, low, and so on; in their respective individual existences, their state of being of good or bad complexion, and so on; and in worldly conditions, their state of gain, loss, and so on. Therefore, it should be known that all this internal variegated phenomenon in the destinies of devas, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, differentiated by kamma, physical form, perception, designation, and so on, is made by the mind alone. This meaning should be understood by way of this sutta, which is not included in the canonical recitations. For it has been said:

“Kammanānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānavasena liṅganānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānaṃ bhavati, liṅganānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānavasena saññānānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānaṃ bhavati, saññānānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānavasena vohāranānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānaṃ bhavati, vohāranānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānavasena kammanānattaputhuttappabhedavavatthānaṃ bhavati. Kammanānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ gatiyā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati – apadā dvipadā catuppadā bahuppadā, rūpino arūpino, saññino asaññino nevasaññīnāsaññino. Kammanānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ upapattiyā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati – uccanīcatā hīnapaṇītatā sugataduggatatā. Kammanānākaraṇaṃ [M 0.0108] paṭicca sattānaṃ attabhāve nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati – suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇatā sujātadujjātatā susaṇṭhitadussaṇṭhitatā. Kammanānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ lokadhamme nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati – lābhālābhe yasāyase nindāpasaṃsāyaṃ sukhadukkhe”ti.

By means of the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of kamma, there comes to be the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of characteristics; by means of the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of characteristics, there comes to be the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of perceptions; by means of the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of perceptions, there comes to be the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of designations; by means of the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of designations, there comes to be the determination of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of kamma. Dependent on the distinction made by kamma, the distinction in beings' destinies is apparent—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed; with form or formless; percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. Dependent on the distinction made by kamma, the distinction in beings' rebirth is apparent—high and low, inferior and superior, with good and bad destinations. Dependent on the distinction made by kamma, the distinction in beings' individual existences is apparent—good complexion and bad complexion, well-born and ill-born, well-proportioned and ill-proportioned. Dependent on the distinction made by kamma, the distinction in worldly conditions is apparent—gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.

Aparampi vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, it was said:

Kammato [P 0.0066] liṅgato ceva, liṅgasaññā pavattare;

Saññāto bhedaṃ gacchanti, itthāyaṃ purisoti vā.

From kamma and from characteristics, perceptions of characteristics proceed; from perception, they attain distinction, as 'this is a woman' or 'this is a man'.

“Kammunā vattate loko, kammunā vattate pajā;

Kammanibandhanā sattā, rathassāṇīva yāyato”. (ma. ni. 2.460; su. ni. 659);

The world is led by kamma, people are led by kamma; beings are bound by kamma, like the linchpin of a moving chariot.

Kammena kittiṃ labhate pasaṃsaṃ,

Kammena jāniñca vadhañca bandhaṃ;

Taṃ [V 0.0112] kammanānākaraṇaṃ viditvā,

Kasmā vade natthi kammanti loke. (kathā. 785);

By kamma one gains fame and praise, by kamma loss, death, and bondage; knowing this distinction made by kamma, why would one say, 'There is no kamma in the world'?

“Kammassakā māṇava sattā kammadāyādā kammayonī kammabandhū kammapaṭisaraṇā; kammaṃ satte vibhajati yadidaṃ hīnappaṇītatāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.289).

Beings are owners of their kamma, young man, heirs to their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, and have kamma as their refuge. Kamma is what distinguishes beings as inferior and superior.

Evaṃ imāya karaṇacittatāyapi cittassa cittatā veditabbā. Sabbānipi hi etāni vicitrāni citteneva katāni. Aladdhokāsassa pana cittassa yaṃ vā pana avasesapaccayavikalaṃ tassa ekaccacittakaraṇābhāvato yadetaṃ cittena kataṃ ajjhattikaṃ cittaṃ vuttaṃ, tatopi cittameva cittataraṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

Thus, by this variegated nature of what is created, the variegated nature of the mind should be understood. For all these variegated things are made by the mind alone. Furthermore, in the case of a mind that has not obtained an opportunity, or that is deficient in the remaining conditions, due to its not creating some variegated things, that which is called the internal variegated thing made by the mind—the mind itself is even more variegated than that. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi evaṃ cittaṃ yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā pāṇā… tehipi kho, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatehi pāṇehi cittaṃyeva cittatara”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.100).

Monks, I do not see any other single class of beings so variegated as these animals... And, monks, the mind is even more variegated than those animals.

Uppannaṃ hotīti ettha vattamānabhūtāpagatokāsakatabhūmiladdhavasena uppannaṃ nāma anekappabhedaṃ. Tattha sabbampi uppādajarābhaṅgasamaṅgīsaṅkhātaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ nāma. Ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddhaṃ, anubhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ kusalākusalaṃ[M 0.0109], uppādādittayaṃ anuppatvā niruddhaṃ, bhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ, sesasaṅkhatañca bhūtāpagatuppannaṃ nāma. “Yānissa tāni pubbe katāni kammānī”ti (ma. ni. 3.248) evamādinā nayena vuttaṃ kammaṃ atītampi samānaṃ, aññaṃ vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassokāsaṃ katvā ṭhitattā, tathā katokāsañca vipākaṃ anuppannampi samānaṃ evaṃ kate okāse ekantena uppajjanato okāsakatuppannaṃ nāma. Tāsu [P 0.0067] tāsu bhūmīsu asamūhataṃ akusalaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma. Ettha ca bhūmiyā bhūmiladdhassa ca nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Bhūmīti vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā. Bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma tesu khandhesu uppattārahaṃ kilesajātaṃ. Tena hesā bhūmi laddhā nāma hoti, tasmā bhūmiladdhanti vuccati. Evametesu catūsu uppannesu idha ‘vattamānuppannaṃ’ adhippetaṃ.

Herein, the term 'arisen' (uppanna) has many varieties, classified as: presently arisen (vattamānuppanna), arisen as that which has been and passed away (bhūtāpagatuppanna), arisen as having obtained an opportunity (okāsakatuppanna), and arisen as acquired in a plane (bhūmiladdhuppanna). Therein, all that is designated as possessing arising, aging, and dissolution is called 'presently arisen'. Wholesome and unwholesome states that have ceased after experiencing the taste of an object, reckoned as 'that which has been experienced and passed away' (anubhūtāpagata); and other conditioned things that have ceased after sequentially reaching the three moments beginning with arising, reckoned as 'that which has been and passed away' (bhūtāpagata), are called 'arisen as that which has been and passed away' (bhūtāpagatuppanna). As stated in the passage beginning, 'Whatever deeds he has done before,' kamma, though past, is called 'arisen as having obtained an opportunity' because it stands having created an opportunity for its own result by preventing another result; and its result, though not yet arisen, is also so called because it will certainly arise once such an opportunity has been created. Unwholesome states that have not been eradicated by the path in the various planes of existence are called 'arisen as acquired in a plane'. Herein, the difference between 'plane' (bhūmi) and 'acquired in a plane' (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. 'Plane' refers to the five aggregates in the three planes of existence that are the object of insight meditation. 'Acquired in a plane' refers to the host of defilements fit to arise in those aggregates. For it is by that host of defilements that this plane is said to be 'acquired'; therefore, it is called 'acquired in a plane'. Among these four kinds of 'arisen', what is intended here is the 'presently arisen'.

Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – pubbantato uddhaṃ uppādādiabhimukhaṃ pannanti uppannaṃ. ‘Uppanna’-saddo panesa [V 0.0113] atīte paṭiladdhe samuṭṭhite avikkhambhite asamucchinne khaṇattayagateti anekesu atthesu dissati. Ayañhi “tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena kakusandho bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.143) ettha atīte āgato. “Āyasmato ānandassa atirekacīvaraṃ uppannaṃ hotī”ti (pārā. 461) ettha paṭiladdhe. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, uppannaṃ mahāmeghaṃ tamenaṃ mahāvāto antarāyeva antaradhāpetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.157) ettha samuṭṭhite. “Uppannaṃ gamiyacittaṃ duppaṭivinodanīyaṃ (a. ni. 5.160; pari. 325); uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme ṭhānaso antaradhāpetī”ti (pārā. 165) ettha avikkhambhite. “Ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvento bahulīkaronto uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme ṭhānaso antarāyeva antaradhāpetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.156-157) ettha asamucchinne. “Uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā”ti (yama. 2.cittayamaka.81) ettha khaṇattayagate. Svāyamidhāpi khaṇattayagateva daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ‘uppannaṃ hotī’ti ettha khaṇattayagataṃ hoti, vattamānaṃ hoti, paccuppannaṃ hotīti. Ayaṃ saṅkhepattho.

Herein, this is the word analysis: it is 'arisen' (uppanna) because it has 'gone' (panna) towards the moments beginning with arising (uppāda), upwards from the end of the preceding state. This word 'uppanna' is seen in many senses: past, acquired, risen up, unsuppressed, un-eradicated, and gone to the three moments. For instance: 1. "At that time, monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had arisen (uppanno) in the world"—here it is used in the sense of 'past'. 2. "An extra robe had arisen (uppannaṃ) for the Venerable Ānanda"—here it is used in the sense of 'acquired'. 3. "Just as, monks, a great cloud that has risen up (uppannaṃ), a great wind might disperse it in mid-course"—here it is used in the sense of 'risen up'. 4. "A thought of going on a journey that has arisen (uppannaṃ) is hard to dispel"; "he instantly causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen again and again (uppannuppanne) to disappear"—here it is used in the sense of 'unsuppressed'. 5. "Developing and cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path, he instantly causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen again and again (uppannuppanne) to disappear in mid-course"—here it is used in the sense of 'un-eradicated'. 6. "Is that which is in the process of arising 'arisen' (uppannaṃ)? Yes"—here it is used in the sense of 'gone to the three moments'. This same term should be understood here also as 'gone to the three moments'. Therefore, in the phrase 'it has arisen' (uppannaṃ hoti), it means it has gone to the three moments, it is present, it is current. This is the meaning in brief.

Cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotīti cetaṃ desanāsīsameva. Na pana cittaṃ ekakameva uppajjati. Tasmā yathā rājā āgatoti vutte na parisaṃ pahāya ekakova āgato, rājaparisāya pana saddhiṃyeva āgatoti paññāyati[M 0.0110], evamidampi paropaṇṇāsakusaladhammehi saddhiṃyeva uppannanti veditabbaṃ. Pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena pana “cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti”cceva vuttaṃ.

In the phrase 'Consciousness has arisen,' this is merely the head of the discourse. Indeed, consciousness does not arise alone. Therefore, just as when it is said, 'The king has arrived,' it is understood that he has not come alone, having abandoned his retinue, but rather has arrived together with the royal retinue; in the same way, it should be understood that this consciousness also has arisen together with over fifty wholesome states. Furthermore, it is said only as 'Consciousness has arisen' because of its meaning as a forerunner.

Lokiyadhammañhi patvā cittaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ cittaṃ dhuraṃ cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ hoti. Lokuttaradhammaṃ [P 0.0068] patvā paññā jeṭṭhikā paññā dhurā paññā pubbaṅgamā. Teneva bhagavā vinayapariyāyaṃ patvā pañhaṃ pucchanto ‘kiṃphassosi, kiṃvedanosi, kiṃsaññosi, kiṃcetanosī’ti apucchitvā “kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhū”ti cittameva dhuraṃ katvā pucchati. “Atheyyacitto ahaṃ bhagavā”ti ca vutte ‘anāpatti atheyyaphassassā’tiādīni avatvā “anāpatti bhikkhu atheyyacittassā”ti vadati.

Indeed, when it comes to worldly phenomena, consciousness is chief, consciousness is principal, consciousness is the forerunner. When it comes to supramundane phenomena, wisdom is chief, wisdom is principal, wisdom is the forerunner. For that very reason, the Blessed One, when it comes to the discourse on the Vinaya, in asking a question, does not ask, 'What is your contact? What is your feeling? What is your perception? What is your volition?' Instead, making consciousness itself the principal thing, he asks, 'What consciousness are you, monk?' And when it is said, 'I am of a non-theft consciousness, Blessed One,' without saying things like 'There is no offense for one with non-theft contact,' he says, 'There is no offense, monk, for one with a non-theft consciousness.'

Na kevalañca vinayapariyāyaṃ, aññampi lokiyadesanaṃ desento cittameva dhuraṃ katvā deseti. Yathāha – “ye keci, bhikkhave, dhammā akusalā akusalabhāgiyā akusalapakkhikā sabbete manopubbaṅgamā. Mano tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppajjati” (a. ni. 1.56).

And not only when teaching the discourse on the Vinaya, but also when teaching other worldly discourses, he teaches making consciousness itself the principal thing. As it was said: 'Whatever states, monks, are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, on the side of the unwholesome—all of them have mind as their forerunner. Mind arises first among those states.'

“Manopubbaṅgamā [V 0.0114] dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā;

Manasā ce paduṭṭhena, bhāsati vā karoti vā;

Tato naṃ dukkhamanveti, cakkaṃva vahato padaṃ.

Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are mind-made. If with a corrupt mind one speaks or acts, then suffering follows one as the wheel follows the foot of the ox.

“Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā;

Manasā ce pasannena, bhāsati vā karoti vā;

Tato naṃ sukhamanveti, chāyāva anapāyinī”. (dha. pa. 1,2);

Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are mind-made. If with a pure mind one speaks or acts, then happiness follows one like a shadow that never departs.

“Cittena nīyati loko, cittena parikassati;

Cittassa ekadhammassa, sabbeva vasamanvagū”. (saṃ. ni. 1.62);

By consciousness the world is led, by consciousness it is dragged along. All have gone under the sway of the one thing that is consciousness.

“Cittasaṃkilesā, bhikkhave, sattā saṃkilissanti cittavodānā visujjhanti” (saṃ. ni. 3.100);

Monks, beings are defiled through the defilement of consciousness; they are purified through the purification of consciousness.

“Pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca kho āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhaṃ” (a. ni. 1.49);

Monks, this consciousness is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.

“Citte[M 0.0111], gahapati, arakkhite kāyakammampi arakkhitaṃ hoti, vacīkammampi arakkhitaṃ hoti, manokammampi arakkhitaṃ hoti; citte, gahapati, rakkhite…pe… citte, gahapati, byāpanne…pe… citte, gahapati, abyāpanne…pe… citte, gahapati, avassute…pe… citte, gahapati, anavassute kāyakammampi anavassutaṃ hoti, vacīkammampi anavassutaṃ hoti, manokammampi anavassutaṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 3.110).

Householder, when the mind is unguarded, bodily action is also unguarded, verbal action is also unguarded, and mental action is also unguarded. Householder, when the mind is guarded... and so on... Householder, when the mind is corrupted... and so on... Householder, when the mind is uncorrupted... and so on... Householder, when the mind is tainted... and so on... Householder, when the mind is untainted, bodily action is also untainted, verbal action is also untainted, and mental action is also untainted.

Evaṃ lokiyadhammaṃ patvā cittaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti, cittaṃ dhuraṃ hoti, cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Imesu [P 0.0069] pana suttesu ekaṃ vā dve vā aggahetvā suttānurakkhaṇatthāya sabbānipi gahitānīti veditabbāni.

Thus, it should be known that when it comes to worldly phenomena, consciousness is chief, consciousness is principal, and consciousness is the forerunner. Furthermore, it should be known that in these suttas, not just one or two have been taken, but all have been cited for the sake of protecting the suttas.

Lokuttaradhammaṃ pucchanto pana ‘kataraphassaṃ adhigatosi, kataravedanaṃ katarasaññaṃ kataracetanaṃ [V 0.0115] kataracitta’nti apucchitvā, ‘katarapaññaṃ tvaṃ bhikkhu adhigato’si, ‘kiṃ paṭhamaṃ maggapaññaṃ, udāhu dutiyaṃ…pe… tatiyaṃ…pe… catutthaṃ maggapaññaṃ adhigato’ti paññaṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ paññaṃ dhuraṃ katvā pucchati. Paññuttarā sabbe kusalā dhammā na parihāyanti. Paññā pana kimatthiyā (ma. ni. 1.451)? “Paññavato, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa tadanvayā saddhā saṇṭhāti, tadanvayaṃ vīriyaṃ saṇṭhāti, tadanvayā sati saṇṭhāti, tadanvayo samādhi saṇṭhātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.515) evamādīni panettha suttāni daṭṭhabbāni. Iti lokuttaradhammaṃ patvā paññā jeṭṭhikā hoti paññā dhurā paññā pubbaṅgamāti veditabbā. Ayaṃ pana lokiyadesanā. Tasmā cittaṃ dhuraṃ katvā desento “cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”ti āha.

On the other hand, when asking about the supramundane Dhamma, without asking, 'Which contact have you attained? Which feeling, which perception, which volition, which consciousness?', he asks by making wisdom chief and principal: 'Which wisdom have you attained, monk? Have you attained the wisdom of the first path, or the second... and so on... the third... and so on... the fourth path?' 'All wholesome states with wisdom as pre-eminent do not decline.' And, 'But for what purpose is wisdom?' Here, suttas such as the following should be noted: 'For a wise noble disciple, monks, faith, following in accordance with that wisdom, is well-established; energy, following that wisdom, is well-established; mindfulness, following in accordance with that wisdom, is well-established; concentration, following that wisdom, is well-established.' Thus, it should be known that when it comes to the supramundane Dhamma, wisdom is chief, wisdom is principal, and wisdom is the forerunner. This, however, is a worldly discourse. Therefore, teaching by making consciousness principal, he said, 'Consciousness has arisen.'

Somanassasahagatanti sātamadhuravedayitasaṅkhātena somanassena saha ekuppādādibhāvaṃ gataṃ. Ayaṃ pana ‘sahagata’-saddo tabbhāve vokiṇṇe nissaye ārammaṇe saṃsaṭṭheti imesu atthesu dissati. Tattha “yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobbhavikā nandirāgasahagatā”ti (vibha. 203) tabbhāve veditabbo; nandirāgabhūtāti attho. “Yā, bhikkhave, vīmaṃsā kosajjasahagatā kosajjasampayuttā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.832) vokiṇṇe veditabbo; antarantarā uppajjamānena kosajjena vokiṇṇāti ayamettha attho. “Aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ [M 0.0112] satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.238) nissaye veditabbo; aṭṭhikasaññaṃ nissāya aṭṭhikasaññaṃ bhāvetvā paṭiladdhanti attho. “Lābhī hoti rūpasahagatānaṃ vā samāpattīnaṃ arūpasahagatānaṃ vā”ti (pu. pa. 3-5) ārammaṇe; veditabbo rūpārūpārammaṇānanti attho. “Idaṃ sukhaṃ imāya pītiyā sahagataṃ hoti sahajātaṃ [P 0.0070] saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sampayutta”nti (vibha. 578) saṃsaṭṭhe. Imasmimpi pade ayamevattho adhippeto. Somanassasaṃsaṭṭhañhi idha somanassasahagatanti vuttaṃ.

'Accompanied by joy' means having attained the state of co-arising, etc., together with joy, which is designated as a pleasant and sweet feeling. Now, this word 'sahagata' is seen in these meanings: identity, intermixed, dependence, object, and association. Among these, in the phrase 'that craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust,' it should be understood in the sense of identity; the meaning is 'being delight and lust.' In 'Monks, that investigation which is accompanied by sloth, associated with sloth,' it should be understood in the sense of intermixed; the meaning here is 'intermixed with sloth arising intermittently.' In 'One develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of bones,' it should be understood in the sense of dependence; the meaning is 'attained by depending on the perception of bones, having developed the perception of bones.' In 'One is an obtainer of the attainments accompanied by form or accompanied by the formless,' it should be understood in the sense of object; the meaning is 'having form or formlessness as the object.' In 'This pleasure is accompanied by this joy, co-arisen, associated, conjoined,' it is in the sense of association. In this present term as well, this very meaning is intended. For here, 'associated with joy' is what is called 'accompanied by joy.'

‘Saṃsaṭṭha’-saddopi cesa sadise avassute mittasanthave sahajāteti bahūsu atthesu dissati. Ayañhi “kise thūle vivajjetvā saṃsaṭṭhā yojitā hayā”ti (jā. 2.22.70) ettha sadise āgato. “Saṃsaṭṭhāva tumhe ayye viharathā”ti (pāci. 727) avassute. “Gihi saṃsaṭṭho viharatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.3) mittasanthave. “Idaṃ sukhaṃ imāya pītiyā sahagataṃ hoti sahajātaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sampayutta”nti sahajāte. Idhāpi sahajāte adhippeto. Tattha ‘sahagataṃ’ asahajātaṃ asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ asampayuttaṃ nāma natthi. Sahajātaṃ pana saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sampayuttaṃ hotipi, na hotipi[V 0.0116]. Rūpārūpadhammesu hi ekato jātesu rūpaṃ arūpena sahajātaṃ hoti, na saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, na sampayuttaṃ; tathā arūpaṃ rūpena; rūpañca rūpena; arūpaṃ pana arūpena saddhiṃ niyamatova sahagataṃ sahajātaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sampayuttameva hotīti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ ‘somanassasahagata’nti.

The word 'saṃsaṭṭha' is also seen in many meanings, such as 'similar,' 'impure,' 'friendly association,' and 'co-arisen.' For indeed, in the passage, 'Having avoided the lean and the fat, the similar horses were yoked' (Jā 2.22.70), it appears in the sense of 'similar.' In, 'You, ladies, should dwell in an impure manner' (Pāci 727), it is in the sense of 'impure.' In, 'Dwells associated with householders' (SN 3.3), it is in the sense of 'friendly association.' In, 'This pleasure is accompanied by this joy, is co-arisen, intermixed, and associated,' it is in the sense of 'co-arisen.' Here too, it is intended in the sense of 'co-arisen.' Therein, there is no such thing as 'accompanied' that is not co-arisen, not intermixed, and not associated. But what is 'co-arisen' may or may not be intermixed and associated. For when material and immaterial phenomena arise together, a material phenomenon is co-arisen with an immaterial phenomenon, but it is not intermixed, not associated; similarly, an immaterial phenomenon with a material phenomenon, and a material phenomenon with a material phenomenon. An immaterial phenomenon, however, with another immaterial phenomenon, is invariably accompanied, co-arisen, intermixed, and associated. It is with reference to this that 'accompanied by joy' was said.

Ñāṇasampayuttanti ñāṇena sampayuttaṃ, samaṃ ekuppādādippakārehi yuttanti attho. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ siyā taṃ mātikāvaṇṇanāya vedanāttike vuttanayameva. Tasmā ekuppādā ekanirodhā ekavatthukā ekārammaṇāti iminā lakkhaṇenetaṃ sampayuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhaniddeso cesa. Arūpe pana vināpi ekavatthukabhāvaṃ sampayogo labbhati.

'Associated with knowledge' means associated with knowledge; that is, conjoined equally by modes such as single arising, etc. This is the meaning. Whatever should be said here follows the same method as was stated in the explanation of the Mātikā in the section on feeling. Therefore, it should be understood as 'associated' by this characteristic: having a single arising, a single ceasing, a single base, and a single object. And this is an exposition of the highest characteristics. But in the immaterial realm, association is obtained even without the state of having a single base.

Ettāvatā kiṃ kathitaṃ? Kāmāvacarakusalesu somanassasahagataṃ tihetukaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ mahācittaṃ kathitaṃ. “Katame dhammā kusalā”ti hi aniyamitapucchāya catubhūmakakusalaṃ gahitaṃ. ‘Kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī’ti vacanena pana tebhūmakaṃ kusalaṃ [M 0.0113] pariccajitvā, aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāmāvacarakusalameva gahitaṃ. ‘Somanassasahagata’nti vacanena tato catubbidhaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ pariccajitvā catubbidhaṃ somanassasahagatameva gahitaṃ. ‘Ñāṇasampayutta’nti vacanena tato duvidhaṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ pariccajitvā dve [P 0.0071] ñāṇasampayuttāneva gahitāni. Asaṅkhārikabhāvo pana anābhaṭṭhatāyeva na gahito. Kiñcāpi na gahito, parato pana ‘sasaṅkhārenā’ti vacanato idha ‘asaṅkhārenā’ti avuttepi asaṅkhārikabhāvo veditabbo. Sammāsambuddho hi āditova idaṃ mahācittaṃ bhājetvā dassetuṃ niyametvāva imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhīti evamettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

By this much, what has been explained? Among the sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, the great consciousness that is accompanied by joy, triple-rooted, associated with knowledge, and unprompted has been explained. For by the unrestricted question, 'Which states are wholesome?', the wholesome of the four planes was included. However, by the statement 'a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises,' abandoning the wholesome of the three planes, only the eightfold sense-sphere wholesome consciousness was included. By the statement 'accompanied by joy,' abandoning the fourfold accompanied by equanimity from that, only the fourfold accompanied by joy was included. By the statement 'associated with knowledge,' abandoning the twofold dissociated from knowledge from that, only the two associated with knowledge were included. The unprompted nature, however, was not included simply because it was not mentioned. Although it was not included, since later it is said 'with prompting,' here, even though 'unprompted' is not said, the unprompted nature should be understood. For the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, having from the very beginning analyzed this great consciousness in order to explain it, began this teaching only after having determined it. Thus, it should be understood that the conclusion here was made in this way.

Idāni tameva cittaṃ ārammaṇato dassetuṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vātiādimāha. Bhagavā hi arūpadhammaṃ dassento vatthunā vā dasseti, ārammaṇena vā, vatthārammaṇehi vā, sarasabhāvena vā. “Cakkhusamphasso…pe… manosamphasso; cakkhusamphassajā vedanā…pe… manosamphassajā vedanā; cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇa”ntiādīsu hi vatthunā arūpadhammā dassitā. “Rūpasaññā…pe… dhammasaññā, rūpasañcetanā…pe… dhammasañcetanā”tiādīsu ārammaṇena. “Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.60) vatthārammaṇehi. “Avijjāpaccayā[V 0.0117], bhikkhave, saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.1) sarasabhāvena arūpadhammā dassitā. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ārammaṇena dassento ‘rūpārammaṇaṃ’ vātiādimāha.

Now, to show that same consciousness by way of its object, he said, beginning with 'or a form-object.' For the Blessed One, when showing an immaterial phenomenon, shows it either by way of a base, or by way of an object, or by way of both base and object, or by way of its own characteristic. For in passages such as 'eye-contact... mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of mind-contact; eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness,' immaterial phenomena are shown by way of a base. In passages such as 'perception of form... perception of mental phenomena; volition regarding form... volition regarding mental phenomena,' they are shown by way of an object. In passages such as 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact... Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact' (SN 4.60), they are shown by way of both base and object. In passages such as 'With ignorance as condition, monks, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness' (SN 2.1), immaterial phenomena are shown by way of their own characteristic. But in this instance, showing it by way of the object, he said, beginning with 'or a form-object.'

Tattha catusamuṭṭhānaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ rūpameva rūpārammaṇaṃ. Dvisamuṭṭhāno atītānāgatapaccuppanno saddova saddārammaṇaṃ. Catusamuṭṭhāno atītānāgatapaccuppanno gandhova gandhārammaṇaṃ. Catusamuṭṭhāno atītānāgatapaccuppanno rasova rasārammaṇaṃ. Catusamuṭṭhānaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ phoṭṭhabbameva phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ. Ekasamuṭṭhānā dvisamuṭṭhānā tisamuṭṭhānā catusamuṭṭhānā nakutocisamuṭṭhānā atītānāgatapaccuppannā cittacetasikā, tathā navattabbā ca, vuttāvasesā cittagocarasaṅkhātā dhammāyeva dhammārammaṇaṃ. Ye [P 0.0072] pana anāpāthagatā rūpādayopi dhammārammaṇamicceva vadanti te iminā suttena paṭikkhipitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, form itself—which has four origins and is past, future, or present—is the form-object. Sound itself—which has two origins and is past, future, or present—is the sound-object. Odor itself—which has four origins and is past, future, or present—is the odor-object. Taste itself—which has four origins and is past, future, or present—is the taste-object. The tangible itself—which has four origins and is past, future, or present—is the tangible-object. Consciousness and mental factors—which have one, two, three, or four origins, or no origin, and are past, future, or present; and those that cannot be spoken of in that way; and the remaining phenomena designated as the sphere of consciousness—these dhammas themselves are the dhamma-object. But those who say that even forms, etc., that have not come into the range of the senses are a dhamma-object should be refuted by this sutta. For it was said:

“Imesaṃ [M 0.0114] kho, āvuso, pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ nānāvisayānaṃ nānāgocarānaṃ na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhontānaṃ mano paṭisaraṇaṃ mano nesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.455).

'Friends, for these five faculties—with different ranges, different domains, not experiencing each other’s range and domain—the mind is their resort; the mind experiences their range and domain' (MN 1.455).

Etesañhi rūpārammaṇādīni gocaravisayo nāma. Tāni manena paccanubhaviyamānānipi rūpārammaṇādīniyevāti ayamattho siddho hoti. Dibbacakkhuñāṇādīnañca rūpādiārammaṇattāpi ayamattho siddhoyeva hoti. Anāpāthagatāneva hi rūpārammaṇādīni dibbacakkhuādīnaṃ ārammaṇāni, na ca tāni dhammārammaṇāni bhavantīti vuttanayeneva ārammaṇavavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For indeed, for these faculties, the objects beginning with form are called their sphere of experience. Even when experienced by the mind, they are still just objects beginning with form—this meaning is established. And because the divine eye knowledge and so on also have form, etc., as their objects, this meaning is likewise established. Indeed, it is objects beginning with form that have not come into the range of the senses that are the objects of the divine eye and so on, and those objects do not become dhamma-objects. Thus, the determination of objects should be understood in the way already stated.

Tattha ekekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ dvīsu dvīsu dvāresu āpāthamāgacchati. Rūpārammaṇañhi cakkhupasādaṃ ghaṭṭetvā taṅkhaṇaññeva manodvāre āpāthamāgacchati; bhavaṅgacalanassa paccayo hotīti attho. Saddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbārammaṇesupi eseva nayo. Yathā hi sakuṇo ākāsenāgantvā rukkhagge nilīyamānova rukkhasākhañca ghaṭṭeti, chāyā cassa pathaviyaṃ paṭihaññati sākhāghaṭṭanachāyāpharaṇāni apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva bhavanti, evaṃ paccuppannarūpādīnaṃ cakkhupasādādighaṭṭanañca bhavaṅgacalanasamatthatāya manodvāre āpāthagamanañca apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva [V 0.0118] hoti. Tato bhavaṅgaṃ vicchinditvā cakkhudvārādīsu uppannānaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ voṭṭhabbanapariyosānānaṃ anantarā tesaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ idaṃ mahācittaṃ uppajjati.

Here, each object comes into the range of two doors. For instance, a form-object, having struck the eye-sensitivity, at that very moment also comes into the range of the mind-door; this means it becomes a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum. This same method applies also to sound, smell, taste, and tangible objects. For just as a bird, having come through the sky and alighting on a treetop, both strikes a branch and its shadow is cast upon the ground—the striking of the branch and the spreading of the shadow occur not before and not after, but in a single moment—so too, the striking of present form-objects and so on by the eye-sensitivity and so on, and their coming into the range of the mind-door by their capacity to cause the life-continuum to vibrate, occur not before and not after, but in a single moment. Then, having cut off the life-continuum, immediately after the adverting and so on, culminating in determining, which have arisen at the eye-door and so on, this great consciousness arises with respect to one of those objects.

Suddhamanodvāre pana pasādaghaṭṭanakiccaṃ natthi. Pakatiyā diṭṭhasutaghāyitasāyitaphuṭṭhavaseneva etāni ārammaṇāni āpāthamāgacchanti. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco katasudhākammaṃ haritālamanosilādivaṇṇavicittaṃ paggahitanānappakāradhajapaṭākaṃ mālādāmavinaddhaṃ dīpamālāparikkhittaṃ atimanoramāya siriyā virocamānaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mahācetiyaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā soḷasasu pādapiṭṭhikāsu pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha ullokento buddhārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0073] pītiṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati. Tassa evaṃ cetiyaṃ passitvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ nibbattetvā aparabhāge yattha katthaci gatassa rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu [M 0.0115] nisinnassa āvajjamānassa alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mahācetiyaṃ cakkhudvāre āpāthamāgatasadisameva hoti, padakkhiṇaṃ katvā cetiyavandanakālo viya hoti. Evaṃ tāva diṭṭhavasena rūpārammaṇaṃ āpāthamāgacchati.

At the pure mind-door, however, there is no function of striking the sensitivity. By nature, these objects come into range only by way of what has been seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched. How so? Here, a certain person circumambulates a great cetiya that has had plasterwork done, is variegated with colors such as orpiment and realgar, has various kinds of raised banners and flags, is entwined with garlands, is surrounded by rows of lamps, and is shining with an exceedingly delightful splendor, being adorned and prepared. Having circumambulated it and venerated it with the five-point prostration at the sixteen bases, he stands with joined palms raised, looking up, and takes up joy that has the Buddha as its object. For him, having seen the cetiya in this way and generated joy that has the Buddha as its object, later, having gone to some place or other, while sitting in a place for the night or a place for the day and reflecting, the adorned and prepared great cetiya is just like one that has come into the range of the eye-door, and it is as if it were the time of circumambulating and venerating the cetiya. Thus, firstly, by way of what has been seen, a form-object comes into range.

Madhurena pana sarena dhammakathikassa vā dhammaṃ kathentassa, sarabhāṇakassa vā sarena bhaṇantassa saddaṃ sutvā aparabhāge yattha katthaci nisīditvā āvajjamānassa dhammakathā vā sarabhaññaṃ vā sotadvāre āpāthamāgataṃ viya hoti, sādhukāraṃ datvā suṇanakālo viya hoti. Evaṃ sutavasena saddārammaṇaṃ āpāthamāgacchati.

Furthermore, having heard the sweet voice of a Dhamma-expounder speaking the Dhamma, or of a reciter reciting with a melodious voice, later, while sitting in some place or other and reflecting, the Dhamma talk or the recitation is as if it has come into the range of the ear-door, and it is as if it were the time of giving cries of approval and listening. Thus, by way of what has been heard, a sound-object comes into range.

Sugandhaṃ pana gandhaṃ vā mālaṃ vā labhitvā āsane vā cetiye vā gandhārammaṇena cittena pūjaṃ katvā aparabhāge yattha katthaci nisīditvā āvajjamānassa taṃ gandhārammaṇaṃ ghānadvāre āpāthamāgataṃ viya hoti, pūjākaraṇakālo viya hoti. Evaṃ ghāyitavasena gandhārammaṇaṃ āpāthamāgacchati.

Furthermore, having obtained a fragrant scent or flowers, and having made an offering at a seat or a cetiya with a mind that has the scent-object as its object, later, while sitting in some place or other and reflecting, that scent-object is as if it has come into the range of the nose-door, and it is as if it were the time of making the offering. Thus, by way of what has been smelled, a scent-object comes into range.

Paṇītaṃ pana khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā sabrahmacārīhi saddhiṃ saṃvibhajitvā paribhuñjitvā aparabhāge yattha katthaci kudrūsakādibhojanaṃ labhitvā ‘asukakāle paṇītaṃ bhojanaṃ sabrahmacārīhi saddhiṃ saṃvibhajitvā paribhutta’nti āvajjamānassa taṃ rasārammaṇaṃ jivhādvāre āpāthamāgataṃ viya hoti, paribhuñjanakālo viya hoti. Evaṃ sāyitavasena rasārammaṇaṃ āpāthamāgacchati.

Furthermore, having shared and partaken of excellent hard food or soft food together with fellow practitioners, and later, having obtained food such as millet in some place or other, when reflecting, 'At such-and-such a time, I shared and partook of excellent food together with fellow practitioners,' that taste-object is as if it has come into the range of the tongue-door, and it is as if it were the time of partaking. Thus, by way of what has been tasted, a taste-object comes into range.

Mudukaṃ [V 0.0119] pana sukhasamphassaṃ mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā attharaṇapāpuraṇaṃ vā paribhuñjitvā aparabhāge yattha katthaci dukkhaseyyaṃ kappetvā ‘asukakāle me mudukaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ attharaṇapāvuraṇaṃ paribhutta’nti āvajjamānassa taṃ phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ kāyadvāre āpāthamāgataṃ viya hoti. Sukhasamphassaṃ vedayitakālo viya hoti. Evaṃ phuṭṭhavasena phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ āpāthamāgacchati. Evaṃ suddhamanodvāre pasādaghaṭṭanakiccaṃ natthi. Pakatiyā diṭṭhasutaghāyitasāyitaphuṭṭhavaseneva etāni ārammaṇāni āpāthamāgacchantīti veditabbāni.

Furthermore, having used a soft, pleasantly-tangible bed, chair, or floor-covering and coverlet, and later, having prepared an uncomfortable lying-place somewhere, when reflecting, 'At such-and-such a time, I used a soft bed, chair, floor-covering, and coverlet,' that tangible object is as if it has come into the range of the body-door. It is as if it were the time of experiencing pleasant contact. Thus, by way of what has been touched, a tangible object comes into range. In this way, at the pure mind-door, there is no function of striking the sensitivity. It should be known that by nature, only by way of what has been seen, heard, smelled, tasted, and touched do these objects come into range.

Idāni [M 0.0116] pakatiyā diṭṭhādīnaṃ vasena āpāthagamane ayamaparopi [P 0.0074] aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo hoti. Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ ubhayasambandhanti ime tāva diṭṭhādayo veditabbā. Tattha ‘diṭṭhaṃ’ nāma pañcadvāravasena gahitapubbaṃ. ‘Suta’nti paccakkhato adisvā anussavavasena gahitā rūpādayova. Tehi dvīhipi sambandhaṃ ‘ubhayasambandhaṃ’ nāma. Iti imesampi diṭṭhādīnaṃ vasena etāni manodvāre āpāthamāgacchantīti veditabbāni. Tattha diṭṭhavasena tāva āpāthagamanaṃ heṭṭhā pañcahi nayehi vuttameva.

Now, regarding the natural coming into range by way of what has been seen and so on, there is this other method, which is independent of the commentaries. First, these terms—'seen,' 'heard,' and 'connected with both'—should be understood. Herein, 'seen' is that which has been previously grasped by way of the five doors. 'Heard' refers to form and so on, grasped not by direct experience but by way of hearsay. That which is connected with both of these is called 'connected with both.' Thus, it should be understood that by way of these—'seen' and so on—these objects come into the range of the mind-door. Therein, the coming into range by way of what has been seen has already been explained above in five ways.

Ekacco pana suṇāti – ‘bhagavato puññātisayanibbattaṃ evarūpaṃ nāma rūpaṃ, atimadhuro saddo, kismiñci padese kesañci pupphānaṃ atimanuñño gandho, kesañci phalānaṃ atimadhuro raso, kesañci pāvuraṇādīnaṃ atisukho samphasso’ti. Tassa, cakkhupasādādighaṭṭanaṃ vinā, sutamattāneva tāni manodvāre āpāthamāgacchanti. Athassa taṃ cittaṃ tasmiṃ rūpe vā sadde vā pasādavasena gandhādīsu ariyānaṃ dātukāmatāvasena aññehi dinnesu anumodanāvasena vā pavattati. Evaṃ sutavasena etāni manodvāre āpāthamāgacchanti.

Furthermore, a certain person hears: 'The form of the Blessed One, produced by the fruition of surpassing merit, is of such a nature; the voice is exceedingly sweet; in a certain place, the fragrance of certain flowers is most delightful; the taste of certain fruits is exceedingly sweet; the touch of certain coverings and so on is most pleasant.' For that person, without the striking of the eye-sensitivity and so on, merely by having been heard, those objects come into the range of the mind-door. Then that consciousness of his proceeds with respect to that form or sound by way of faith, or with respect to fragrances and so on by way of the desire to give to the noble ones, or by way of rejoicing when they are given by others. Thus, by way of what has been heard, these objects come into the range of the mind-door.

Aparena pana yathāvuttāni rūpādīni diṭṭhāni vā sutāni vā honti. Tassa ‘īdisaṃ rūpaṃ āyatiṃ uppajjanakabuddhassāpi bhavissatī’tiādinā nayena cakkhupasādādighaṭṭanaṃ vinā diṭṭhasutasambandheneva tāni manodvāre āpāthamāgacchanti. Athassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva tesu aññatarārammaṇaṃ idaṃ mahācittaṃ pavattati. Evaṃ ubhayasambandhavasena etāni manodvāre āpāthamāgacchanti.

Furthermore, for another person, the aforementioned forms and so on are either seen or heard. For that person, by the method beginning with, 'Such a form will exist even for a Buddha who is to arise in the future,' these objects, without the striking of the eye-sensitivity and so on, come into the range of the mind-door merely through the connection with what has been seen and heard. Then, for that person, by the method already stated below, this great consciousness proceeds with one or another of those objects as its object. Thus, by the power of connection with both, these objects come into the range of the mind-door.

Idampi ca mukhamattameva. Saddhāruciākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiādīnaṃ pana vasena [V 0.0120] vitthārato etesaṃ manodvāre āpāthagamanaṃ veditabbameva. Yasmā pana evaṃ āpāthaṃ āgacchantāni bhūtānipi honti abhūtānipi, tasmā ayaṃ nayo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na gahito. Evaṃ ekekārammaṇaṃ javanaṃ dvīsu dvīsu dvāresu uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Rūpārammaṇañhi javanaṃ cakkhudvārepi uppajjati manodvārepi. Saddādiārammaṇesupi eseva nayo.

And this is merely a preliminary statement. However, the coming into range of these objects at the mind-door should be understood in detail by the power of such things as faith, inclination, reflection on the characteristics, approval after scrutiny of a view, and so on. But since objects coming into range in this way are both real and unreal, this method is not accepted in the commentary. Thus, it should be understood that an impulsion with a single object arises in two doors each. For, the impulsion with a form-object arises at the eye-door and also at the mind-door. This same method applies also to objects such as sound and so on.

Tattha manodvāre uppajjamānaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ javanaṃ dānamayaṃ sīlamayaṃ bhāvanāmayanti tividhaṃ hoti[P 0.0075]. Tesu ekekaṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammanti [M 0.0117] tividhameva hoti. Saddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbadhammārammaṇesupi eseva nayo.

Therein, an impulsion with a form-object arising at the mind-door is threefold: consisting of giving, consisting of virtue, and consisting of mental development. Among them, each one is itself threefold: bodily action, verbal action, and mental action. This same method also applies in the case of objects of sound, smell, taste, touch, and mind-objects.

Tattha rūpaṃ tāva ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjamānaṃ etaṃ mahākusalacittaṃ nīlapītalohitodātavaṇṇesu pupphavatthadhātūsu aññataraṃ subhanimittasaṅkhātaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ rajanīyaṃ vaṇṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati. Nanu cetaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ lobhassa vatthu? Kathaṃ etaṃ cittaṃ kusalaṃ nāma jātanti? Niyamitavasena pariṇāmitavasena samudācāravasena ābhujitavasenāti. Yassa hi ‘kusalameva mayā kattabba’nti kusalakaraṇe cittaṃ niyamitaṃ hoti, akusalappavattito nivattetvā kusalakaraṇeyeva pariṇāmitaṃ, abhiṇhakaraṇena kusalasamudācāreneva samudācaritaṃ, patirūpadesavāsasappurisūpanissayasaddhammasavanapubbekatapuññatādīhi ca upanissayehi yoniso ca ābhogo pavattati, tassa iminā niyamitavasena pariṇāmitavasena samudācāravasena ābhujitavasena ca kusalaṃ nāma jātaṃ hoti.

Therein, this great wholesome consciousness, arising having first taken a form as its object, arises having taken as its object a color that is called a beautiful sign—one among flowers, cloths, or elements of blue, yellow, red, or white color—which is desirable, pleasing, agreeable, and attractive. Is not this desirable object a basis for greed? How has this consciousness come to be called wholesome? It is so by the power of being determined, by the power of being directed, by the power of being well-practiced, and by the power of attention. For one whose mind is determined in the performance of the wholesome, thinking, 'Only the wholesome should be done by me'; whose mind is turned away from the occurrence of the unwholesome and directed only to the performance of the wholesome; whose mind is well-practiced in the wholesome through repeated performance; and for whom wise attention occurs due to supportive conditions such as residing in a suitable place, associating with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, and having done meritorious deeds in the past—for such a person, what is called 'wholesome' has arisen by this power of being determined, by the power of being directed, by the power of being well-practiced, and by the power of attention.

Ārammaṇavasena panettha somanassasahagatabhāvo veditabbo. Iṭṭhārammaṇasmiñhi uppannattā etaṃ somanassasahagataṃ jātaṃ. Saddhābahulatādīnipettha kāraṇāniyeva. Assaddhānañhi micchādiṭṭhīnañca ekantaiṭṭhārammaṇabhūtaṃ tathāgatarūpampi disvā somanassaṃ nuppajjati. Ye ca kusalappavattiyaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ na passanti tesaṃ parehi ussāhitānaṃ kusalaṃ karontānampi somanassaṃ nuppajjati. Tasmā saddhābahulatā visuddhadiṭṭhitā ānisaṃsadassāvitāti. Evampettha somanassasahagatabhāvo veditabbo. Apica ekādasadhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – buddhānussati dhammānussati saṅghānussati sīlānussati cāgānussati devatānussati upasamānussati lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā siniddhapuggalasevanatā pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti[V 0.0121]. Imehipi [P 0.0076] kāraṇehettha somanassasahagatabhāvo veditabbo. Imesaṃ pana vitthāro bojjhaṅgavibhaṅge (vibha. aṭṭha. 367 bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā, 468-469) āvi bhavissati.

Herein, the state of being accompanied by joy should be understood by the power of the object. Because it has arisen in relation to a desirable object, it has become accompanied by joy. Abundance of faith and so on are also causes here. For the faithless and for those of wrong view, joy does not arise even after seeing the form of the Tathāgata, which is an exclusively desirable object. And for those who do not see the benefit in the occurrence of the wholesome, joy does not arise even while performing a wholesome deed when urged by others. Therefore, it is due to abundance of faith, purity of view, and seeing the benefits. Thus, the state of being accompanied by joy should be understood herein. Moreover, eleven factors conduce to the arising of the joy enlightenment-factor: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace, avoidance of coarse individuals, association with gentle individuals, reflection upon inspiring suttas, and being resolved on that. By these causes also, the state of being accompanied by joy should be understood herein. The detailed explanation of these, however, will become clear in the Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga.

Kammato, upapattito, indriyaparipākato, kilesadūrībhāvatoti imehi panettha kāraṇehi ñāṇasampayuttatā veditabbā. Yo hi paresaṃ [M 0.0118] dhammaṃ deseti anavajjāni sippāyatanakammāyatanavijjāṭṭhānāni sikkhāpeti dhammakathikaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā dhammaṃ kathāpeti, ‘āyatiṃ paññavā bhavissāmī’ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nānappakāraṃ dānaṃ deti, tassa evarūpaṃ kammaṃ upanissāya kusalaṃ uppajjamānaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ uppajjati. Abyāpajje loke uppannassa vāpi “tassa tattha sukhino dhammapadā pilavanti… dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādo, atha so satto khippaṃyeva visesagāmī hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.191) iminā nayena upapattiṃ nissāyapi uppajjamānaṃ kusalaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ uppajjati. Tathā indriyaparipākaṃ upagatānaṃ paññādasakappattānaṃ indriyaparipākaṃ nissāyapi kusalaṃ uppajjamānaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ uppajjati. Yehi pana kilesā vikkhambhitā tesaṃ kilesadūrībhāvaṃ nissāyapi uppajjamānaṃ kusalaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ uppajjati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Herein, the state of being associated with knowledge should be understood by these causes: from kamma, from rebirth, from the maturity of the faculties, and from the state of being far from defilements. For one who teaches the Dhamma to others, teaches blameless arts, crafts, and sciences, has a Dhamma-teacher teach the Dhamma after making an offering, or gives various kinds of donations after making the aspiration, 'In the future, may I be wise'—for such a person, the wholesome, when arising, arises associated with knowledge, being supported by such kamma. Or, for one who has been reborn in a world without affliction, in accordance with the method of the sutta, 'For that happy one, the principles of Dhamma appear... slow, O monks, is the arising of mindfulness, then that being quickly attains distinction,' the wholesome, when arising, arises associated with knowledge, being supported by that rebirth. Likewise, for those who have reached the maturity of the faculties, who have attained the decade of wisdom, the wholesome, when arising, arises associated with knowledge, being supported by the maturity of the faculties. And for those by whom the defilements have been suppressed, the wholesome, when arising, arises associated with knowledge, being supported by the state of being far from defilements. And this has been said:

“Yogā ve jāyatī bhūri, ayogā bhūrisaṅkhayo”ti (dha. pa. 282).

“Indeed, from practice wisdom arises; from non-practice, the destruction of wisdom.”

Evaṃ kammato upapattito indriyaparipākato kilesadūrībhāvatoti imehi kāraṇehi ñāṇasampayuttatā veditabbā.

Thus, by these causes—from kamma, from rebirth, from the maturity of the faculties, and from the state of being far from defilements—the state of being associated with knowledge should be understood.

Apica satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – paripucchakatā, vatthuvisadakiriyā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanā, duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā, paññavantapuggalasevanā, gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā, tadadhimuttatāti. Imehipi kāraṇehi ñāṇasampayuttatā veditabbā. Imesaṃ pana vitthāro bojjhaṅgavibhaṅge (vibha. aṭṭha. 367 bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā) āvi bhavissati.

Furthermore, seven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena: frequent questioning, the act of purifying the internal and external bases, bringing about the balance of the faculties, avoiding persons of little wisdom, associating with wise persons, reflecting on profound matters that are the domain of knowledge, and being firmly committed to that. For these reasons also, its association with knowledge should be understood. The detailed explanation of these, however, will become clear in the Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga.

Evaṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ hutvā uppannañcetaṃ asaṅkhārena [P 0.0077] appayogena anupāyacintanāya uppannattā [V 0.0122] asaṅkhāraṃ nāma jātaṃ. Tayidaṃ rajanīyavaṇṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā uppajjamānameva tividhena niyamena uppajjati – dānamayaṃ vā hoti, sīlamayaṃ vā, bhāvanāmayaṃ vā.

Thus, having become associated with knowledge, this consciousness, having arisen without prompting, without effort, and without contriving a means, is called 'unprompted'. And this, having a desirable color-object, arises, just as it is arising, by a threefold determination: it is either consisting of giving, or consisting of morality, or consisting of mental development.

Kathaṃ? Yadā hi nīlapītalohitodātesu pupphādīsu aññataraṃ labhitvā vaṇṇavasena ābhujitvā ‘vaṇṇadānaṃ mayha’nti buddharatanādīni pūjeti, tadā dānamayaṃ hoti. Tatridaṃ vatthu – bhaṇḍāgārikasaṅghamitto kira ekaṃ suvaṇṇakhacitaṃ vatthaṃ labhitvā idampi vatthaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ, sammāsambuddhopi suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ vatthaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇasseva anucchavikaṃ, amhākañca vaṇṇadānaṃ bhavissatīti mahācetiye āropesi. Evarūpe [M 0.0119] kāle dānamayaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Yadā pana tathārūpameva deyyadhammaṃ labhitvā ‘mayhaṃ kulavaṃso, kulatanti kulappaveṇī esā, kulavattaṃ eta’nti buddharatanādīni pūjeti tadā sīlamayaṃ hoti. Yadā pana tādiseneva vatthunā ratanattayassa pūjaṃ katvā ‘ayaṃ vaṇṇo khayaṃ gacchissati, vayaṃ gacchissatī’ti khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapeti, tadā bhāvanāmayaṃ hoti.

How? When, having obtained one among flowers and other such things that are blue, yellow, red, or white, and having adverted to it by way of its color, one venerates the Buddha-jewel and so forth, thinking, 'This is my offering of color,' then it is wholesomeness consisting of giving. Herein is a story: It is said that the minister Saṅghamitta, the treasurer, having obtained a cloth embroidered with gold, thought, 'This cloth is of a golden color, and the Perfectly Enlightened One is also of a golden color. A cloth of golden color is suitable only for one of a golden color. And this will be our offering of color.' Thus, he draped it over the Great Cetiya. It should be understood that at such a time, it is wholesomeness consisting of giving.
