When, however, having obtained just such an offerable object, one venerates the Buddha-jewel and so forth, thinking, 'This is my family lineage, my family continuity, my family tradition, this is the family practice,' then it is wholesomeness consisting of morality. When, however, having made a veneration to the Triple Gem with such an object, one establishes the contemplation of decay and passing away, thinking, 'This color will go to decay, it will go to destruction,' then it is wholesomeness consisting of mental development.

Dānamayaṃ pana hutvā vattamānampi yadā tīṇi ratanāni sahatthena pūjentassa pavattatti, tadā kāyakammaṃ hoti. Yadā tīṇi ratanāni pūjento puttadāradāsakammakaraporisādayopi āṇāpetvā pūjāpeti tadā vacīkammaṃ hoti. Yadā tadeva vuttappakāraṃ vijjamānakavatthuṃ ārabbha vaṇṇadānaṃ dassāmīti cinteti tadā manokammaṃ hoti. Vinayapariyāyaṃ patvā hi ‘dassāmi karissāmī’ti vācā bhinnā hotīti (pārā. 659) iminā lakkhaṇena dānaṃ nāma hoti. Abhidhammapariyāyaṃ patvā pana vijjamānakavatthuṃ ārabbha ‘dassāmī’ti manasā cintitakālato paṭṭhāya kusalaṃ hoti. Aparabhāge kāyena vā vācāya vā kattabbaṃ karissatīti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ dānamayaṃ kāyavacīmanokammavaseneva tividhaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, when it is wholesomeness consisting of giving and is occurring, if it proceeds from one who venerates the Three Jewels with their own hands, then it is bodily action. When, while venerating the Three Jewels, one commands one's children, spouse, servants, workers, men, and so forth, and has them venerate, then it is verbal action. When, taking that very existing object of the aforesaid kind as object, one thinks, 'I will give an offering of color,' then it is mental action. For, according to the Vinaya exposition, an act of giving is defined by this characteristic: the speech, 'I will give,' 'I will make,' is uttered. According to the Abhidhamma exposition, however, from the time one thinks with the mind, 'I will give,' taking an existing object as the basis, it is wholesome. It is said that in the future, what is to be done will be done by body or by speech. Thus, wholesomeness consisting of giving is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action.

Yadā pana taṃ vuttappakāraṃ vatthuṃ labhitvā kulavaṃsādivasena sahatthā ratanattayaṃ pūjeti tadā sīlamayaṃ kāyakammaṃ hoti. Yadā kulavaṃsādivaseneva puttadārādayo āṇāpetvā pūjāpeti tadā vacīkammaṃ hoti. Yadā [P 0.0078] ‘mayhaṃ kulavaṃso, kulatanti kulappaveṇī esā, kulavattameta’nti vijjamānakavatthuṃ ārabbha ‘vaṇṇadānaṃ dassāmī’ti cinteti tadā manokammaṃ hoti. Evaṃ sīlamayaṃ kāyavacīmanokammavasena tividhaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, when, having obtained an object of the aforesaid kind, one venerates the Triple Gem with one's own hands by way of family lineage and so forth, then it is bodily action consisting of morality. When, by way of family lineage and so forth, one commands one's children, spouse, and so forth, and has them venerate, then it is verbal action. When, taking an existing object as the basis, one thinks, 'This is my family lineage, my family continuity, my family tradition, this is the family practice,' and 'I will give an offering of color,' then it is mental action. Thus, wholesomeness consisting of morality is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action.

Yadā [V 0.0123] pana taṃ vuttappakāraṃ vatthuṃ labhitvā tīṇi ratanāni pūjetvā caṅkamanto khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapeti tadā bhāvanāmayaṃ kāyakammaṃ hoti. Vācāya sammasanaṃ paṭṭhapentassa vacīkammaṃ hoti, kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā manasāva sammasanaṃ paṭṭhapentassa manokammaṃ hoti. Evaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ kāyavacīmanokammavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Evametaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ kusalaṃ tividhapuññakiriyavatthuvasena navahi kammadvārehi bhājetvā dassesi dhammarājā. Saddārammaṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

Furthermore, when, having obtained an object of the aforesaid kind and having venerated the Three Jewels, one, while doing walking meditation, establishes the contemplation of decay and passing away, then it is bodily action consisting of mental development. For one who establishes comprehension by means of speech, it is verbal action. For one who establishes comprehension by mind alone, without moving the limbs of the body or speech, it is mental action. Thus, wholesomeness consisting of mental development is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action. In this way, the King of Dhamma has shown this wholesome consciousness which has a form-object, having divided it by the three bases of meritorious action and by the nine doors of action. This same method applies also to sound-objects and so forth.

Bherisaddādīsu [M 0.0120] hi rajanīyasaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva tīhi niyamehetaṃ kusalaṃ uppajjati. Tattha saddaṃ kandamūlaṃ viya uppāṭetvā nīluppalahatthakaṃ viya ca hatthe ṭhapetvā dātuṃ nāma na sakkā, savatthukaṃ pana katvā dento saddadānaṃ deti nāma. Tasmā yadā ‘saddadānaṃ dassāmī’ti bherimudiṅgādīsu aññataratūriyena tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ upahāraṃ karoti, ‘saddadānaṃ me’ti bheriādīni ṭhapāpeti, dhammakathikabhikkhūnaṃ sarabhesajjatelaphāṇitādīni deti, dhammasavanaṃ ghoseti, sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇati, dhammakathaṃ katheti, upanisinnakakathaṃ anumodanakathaṃ karoti, tadā dānamayaṃyeva hoti. Yadā etadeva vidhānaṃ kulavaṃsādivasena vattavasena karoti tadā sīlamayaṃ hoti. Yadā sabbampetaṃ katvā ayaṃ ettako saddo brahmalokappamāṇopi hutvā ‘khayaṃ gamissati, vayaṃ gamissatī’ti sammasanaṃ paṭṭhapeti tadā bhāvanāmayaṃ hoti.

For, among sounds of great drums and so forth, taking a desirable sound as object, this wholesome consciousness arises by the three determinations in the same way as described above. Therein, it is not possible to give sound by uprooting it like a lotus root or by placing it in the hand like a bunch of blue lotuses. But one who gives it by making it together with its physical basis is said to give the gift of sound. Therefore, when one makes an offering to the Three Jewels with one of the musical instruments among great drums, mudiṅga drums, and so forth, thinking, 'I will give the gift of sound'; or has great drums and so forth set up, thinking, 'This is my gift of sound'; or gives voice-clearing medicine, oil, molasses, and so forth to monks who are Dhamma-preachers; or announces the hearing of the Dhamma; or performs melodious recitation; or gives a Dhamma-talk, a talk to those sitting near, or a talk of appreciation, then it is solely wholesomeness consisting of giving. When one performs this very same procedure by way of family lineage, etc., or by way of family practice, then it is wholesomeness consisting of morality. When, having done all this, one establishes the comprehension, 'This sound, even if it were to reach the extent of the Brahma-world, will go to decay, will go to destruction,' then it is wholesomeness consisting of mental development.

Tattha dānamayaṃ tāva yadā bheriādīni gahetvā sahatthā upahāraṃ karoti, niccupahāratthāya ṭhapentopi sahatthā ṭhapeti, ‘saddadānaṃ me’ti dhammasavanaṃ ghosetuṃ gacchati, dhammakathaṃ sarabhaññaṃ kātuṃ vā gacchati, tadā kāyakammaṃ hoti. Yadā ‘gacchatha, tātā, amhākaṃ saddadānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ [P 0.0079] upahāraṃ karothā’ti āṇāpeti, ‘saddadānaṃ me’ti cetiyaṅgaṇesu ‘imaṃ bheriṃ, imaṃ mudiṅgaṃ ṭhapethā’ti āṇāpeti, sayameva dhammasavanaṃ ghoseti, dhammakathaṃ katheti, sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇati, tadā vacīkammaṃ hoti. Yadā kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā ‘saddadānaṃ dassāmī’ti vijjamānakavatthuṃ manasā pariccajati, tadā manokammaṃ hoti.

Among these, first, regarding merit based on giving: when one takes drums and other instruments and with one's own hand makes an offering, or even when placing them for the purpose of continuous offerings, one places them with one's own hand; when one goes to proclaim the hearing of the Dhamma, thinking, 'This will be my gift of sound,' or goes to give a Dhamma talk or to make a melodious recitation, then it is a meritorious bodily action. When one commands, 'Go, dear ones, make an offering of our gift of sound to the Three Jewels,' or commands, 'Place this great drum, place this mudiṅga drum in the stupa courtyards,' thinking, 'This will be my gift of sound,' or when one personally proclaims the hearing of the Dhamma, gives a Dhamma talk, or recites melodiously, then it is a meritorious verbal action. When, without moving the limbs of the body or speech, one mentally relinquishes an existing object with the thought, 'I will give the gift of sound,' then it is a meritorious mental action.

Sīlamayampi ‘saddadānaṃ nāma mayhaṃ kulavaṃso kulatanti kulappaveṇī’ti bheriādīhi sahatthā upahāraṃ karontassa, bheriādīni sahatthā cetiyaṅgaṇādīsu ṭhapentassa, dhammakathikānaṃ sarabhesajjaṃ sahatthā dadantassa, vattasīsena dhammasavanaghosanadhammakathākathanasarabhaññabhaṇanatthāya ca gacchantassa kāyakammaṃ hoti. ‘Saddadānaṃ nāma amhākaṃ kulavaṃso kulatanti kulappaveṇī, gacchatha[V 0.0124], tātā, buddharatanādīnaṃ upahāraṃ karothā’ti āṇāpentassa kulavaṃsavaseneva attanā dhammakathaṃ vā sarabhaññaṃ vā karontassa ca vacīkammaṃ hoti. ‘Saddadānaṃ nāma mayhaṃ kulavaṃso [M 0.0121] saddadānaṃ dassāmī’ti kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā manasāva vijjamānakavatthuṃ pariccajantassa manokammaṃ hoti.

Also, regarding merit based on virtue: for a person who, thinking, 'The gift of sound is my family lineage, my family continuity, my family tradition,' with one's own hand makes an offering with drums and the like; for one who with one's own hand places drums and the like in stupa courtyards and so on; for one who with one's own hand gives voice-clearing medicine to Dhamma speakers; and for one who goes, with observance as primary, for the purpose of proclaiming the hearing of the Dhamma, giving a Dhamma talk, or making a melodious recitation, it is a meritorious bodily action. For a person who commands, 'The gift of sound is our family lineage, our family continuity, our family tradition; go, dear ones, make an offering to the Buddha Jewel and the others'; and for one who, by the power of family lineage itself, personally gives a Dhamma talk or makes a melodious recitation, it is a meritorious verbal action. For a person who, thinking, 'The gift of sound is my family lineage; I will give the gift of sound,' relinquishes an existing object with the mind alone, without moving the limbs of the body or speech, it is a meritorious mental action.

Bhāvanāmayampi yadā caṅkamanto sadde khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapeti tadā kāyakammaṃ hoti. Kāyaṅgaṃ pana acopetvā vācāya sammasantassa vacīkammaṃ hoti. Kāyaṅgavācaṅgaṃ acopetvā manasāva saddāyatanaṃ sammasantassa manokammaṃ hoti. Evaṃ saddārammaṇampi kusalaṃ tividhapuññakiriyavatthuvasena navahi kammadvārehi bhājetvā dassesi dhammarājā.

Also, regarding merit based on mental development: when one, while walking meditation, establishes the perishing and passing away in sound, then it is a meritorious bodily action. Furthermore, for one who reflects with speech without moving a part of the body, it is a meritorious verbal action. For one who reflects on the sound-base with the mind alone, without moving the limbs of the body or speech, it is a meritorious mental action. Thus, the Dhamma King has shown, having divided the wholesome consciousness that has sound as its object through the nine doors of action by means of the threefold basis of meritorious action.

Mūlagandhādīsupi rajanīyagandhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva tīhi niyamehetaṃ kusalaṃ uppajjati. Tattha yadā mūlagandhādīsu yaṃkiñci gandhaṃ labhitvā gandhavasena ābhujitvā ‘gandhadānaṃ mayha’nti buddharatanādīni pūjeti, tadā dānamayaṃ hotīti sabbaṃ vaṇṇadāne vuttanayeneva vitthārato veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ gandhārammaṇampi kusalaṃ tividhapuññakiriyavatthuvasena navahi kammadvārehi bhājetvā dassesi dhammarājā.

Also, among root-scents and the like, taking a delightful scent as the object, this wholesome consciousness arises through the three principles in the same way as stated before. Therein, when, having obtained some scent or other among root-scents and the like, and having attended to it by way of the scent-object, one venerates the Buddha Jewel and the others, thinking, 'This will be my gift of scent,' then it is merit based on giving. All of this should be understood in detail in the same way as stated in the section on the gift of form. Thus, the Dhamma King has shown, having divided the wholesome consciousness that has a scent-object as its object through the nine doors of action by means of the threefold basis of meritorious action.

Mūlarasādīsu pana rajanīyarasaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva tīhi niyamehetaṃ kusalaṃ uppajjati. Tattha yadā mūlarasādīsu yaṃkiñci rajanīyaṃ rasavatthuṃ labhitvā [P 0.0080] rasavasena ābhujitvā ‘rasadānaṃ mayha’nti deti pariccajati, tadā dānamayaṃ hotīti sabbaṃ vaṇṇadāne vuttanayeneva vitthārato veditabbaṃ. Sīlamaye panettha ‘saṅghassa adatvā paribhuñjanaṃ nāma amhākaṃ na āciṇṇa’nti dvādasannaṃ bhikkhusahassānaṃ dāpetvā sādurasaṃ paribhuttassa duṭṭhagāmaṇiabhayarañño vatthuṃ ādiṃ katvā mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vatthūni āgatāni. Ayameva viseso. Evaṃ rasārammaṇampi kusalaṃ tividhapuññakiriyavatthuvasena navahi kammadvārehi bhājetvā dassesi dhammarājā.

Furthermore, among root-tastes and the like, taking a delightful taste as the object, this wholesome consciousness arises through the three principles in the same way as stated before. Therein, when, having obtained some delightful object that is a basis for taste among root-tastes and the like, and having attended to it by way of taste, one gives and relinquishes it, thinking, 'This will be my gift of taste,' then it is merit based on giving. All of this should be understood in detail in the same way as stated in the section on the gift of form. However, here in the section on virtue, stories have come down in the Great Commentary, beginning with the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya, who, thinking, 'Consuming without having given to the Sangha is not our practice,' caused a delicious taste to be given to twelve thousand monks and then partook of it. This itself is the distinction. Thus, the Dhamma King has shown, having divided the wholesome consciousness that has a taste-object as its object through the nine doors of action by means of the threefold basis of meritorious action.

Phoṭṭhabbārammaṇepi pathavīdhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātūti tīṇi mahābhūtāni phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ nāma. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne etesaṃ vasena yojanaṃ akatvā mañcapīṭhādivasena kātabbā. Yadā hi mañcapīṭhādīsu yaṃkiñci rajanīyaṃ phoṭṭhabbavatthuṃ labhitvā phoṭṭhabbavasena ābhujitvā ‘phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ [V 0.0125] mayha’nti deti pariccajati, tadā dānamayaṃ hotīti sabbaṃ vaṇṇadāne vuttanayeneva vitthārato veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ phoṭṭhabbārammaṇampi kusalaṃ tividhapuññakiriyavatthuvasena navahi kammadvārehi bhājetvā dassesi dhammarājā.

Regarding the tangible object as well: the three great elements—the earth element, the fire element, and the air element—are called the tangible object. In this place, the connection should be made not by means of these elements, but by means of beds, chairs, and the like. Indeed, when, having obtained some delightful object that is a basis for a tangible object among beds, chairs, and the like, and having attended to it by way of touch, one gives and relinquishes it, thinking, 'This will be my gift of touch,' then it is merit based on giving. All of this should be understood in detail in the same way as stated in the section on the gift of form. Thus, the Dhamma King has shown, having divided the wholesome consciousness that has a tangible object as its object through the nine doors of action by means of the threefold basis of meritorious action.

Dhammārammaṇe [M 0.0122] cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, tīṇi lakkhaṇāni, tayo arūpino khandhā, pannarasa sukhumarūpāni, nibbānapaññattīti ime dhammāyatane pariyāpannā ca, apariyāpannā ca, dhammā dhammārammaṇaṃ nāma. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne etesaṃ vasena yojanaṃ akatvā ojadānapānadānajīvitadānavasena kātabbā. Ojādīsu hi rajanīyaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva tīhi niyamehetaṃ kusalaṃ uppajjati.

Regarding the mental object: the six internal sense-bases, the three characteristics, the three immaterial aggregates, the fifteen subtle material forms, Nibbāna, and concepts—these dhammas, whether included or not included in the dhamma-base, are called the mental object. However, in this context, the connection should be made not by means of these dhammas, but by means of the gift of nutriment, the gift of drink, and the gift of life. Indeed, among nutriment and the like, taking a delightful mental object as the object, this wholesome consciousness arises through the three principles in the same way as stated before.

Tattha yadā ‘ojadānaṃ mayha’nti sappinavanītādīni deti, pānadānanti aṭṭha pānāni deti, jīvitadānanti salākabhattasaṅghabhattādīni deti, aphāsukānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhesajjaṃ deti, vejjaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti, jālaṃ phālāpeti, kumīnaṃ viddhaṃsāpeti, sakuṇapañjaraṃ viddhaṃsāpeti, bandhanamokkhaṃ kārāpeti, māghātabheriṃ carāpeti, aññānipi jīvitaparittāṇatthaṃ evarūpāni kammāni karoti tadā dānamayaṃ hoti. Yadā pana ‘ojadānapānadānajīvitadānāni mayhaṃ kulavaṃso kulatanti kulappaveṇī’ti vattasīsena ojadānādīni pavatteti tadā sīlamayaṃ hoti. Yadā dhammārammaṇasmiṃ khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapeti tadā [P 0.0081] bhāvanāmayaṃ hoti.

Therein, when one gives ghee, fresh butter, and so forth, thinking, ‘This will be my gift of sustenance’; gives the eight kinds of drinks, thinking, ‘This will be the gift of drink’; gives ticket-food, fortnightly food, Sangha-food, and so forth, thinking, ‘This will be the gift of life’; gives medicine to sick bhikkhus; makes a physician available; has a net destroyed; has a fish-trap destroyed; has a birdcage destroyed; arranges for release from bondage; has the drum of non-slaughter sounded; or performs other such deeds for the protection of life—then it is merit consisting of giving. But when, with family duty as the main principle, one undertakes the giving of sustenance and so on, thinking, ‘The giving of sustenance, drink, and life is my family lineage, my family line, my family tradition,’ then it is merit consisting of virtue. When one establishes the perception of perishing and passing away in a mind-object, then it is merit consisting of development.

Dānamayaṃ pana hutvā pavattamānampi yadā ojadānapānadānajīvitadānāni sahatthā deti, tadā kāyakammaṃ hoti. Yadā puttadārādayo āṇāpetvā dāpeti, tadā vacīkammaṃ hoti. Yadā kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā ojadānapānadānajīvitadānavasena vijjamānakavatthuṃ ‘dassāmī’ti manasā cinteti, tadā manokammaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, even when it is occurring as merit consisting of giving, when one gives the gifts of sustenance, drink, and life with one's own hand, then it is bodily action. When, having commanded one's children, wife, and so on, one causes them to give, then it is verbal action. When, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, one thinks with the mind, ‘I will give an existing object by way of the gift of sustenance, drink, or life,’ then it is mental action.

Yadā pana vuttappakāraṃ vijjamānakavatthuṃ kulavaṃsādivasena sahatthā deti, tadā sīlamayaṃ kāyakammaṃ hoti. Yadā kulavaṃsādivaseneva puttadārādayo āṇāpetvā dāpeti, tadā vacīkammaṃ hoti. Yadā kulavaṃsādivaseneva vuttappakāraṃ vijjamānakavatthuṃ ‘dassāmī’ti manasāva cinteti, tadā manokammaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, when one gives with one's own hand an existing object of the aforementioned kind by way of family lineage and so on, then it is bodily action that is merit consisting of virtue. When, by way of family lineage and so on, one, having commanded one's children, wife, and so on, causes them to give, then it is verbal action. When, by way of family lineage and so on, one thinks with the mind alone, ‘I will give an existing object of the aforementioned kind,’ then it is mental action.

Caṅkamitvā [V 0.0126] dhammārammaṇe khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapentassa pana bhāvanāmayaṃ kāyakammaṃ hoti. Kāyaṅgaṃ acopetvā vācāya khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapentassa vacīkammaṃ hoti. Kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā manasāva dhammārammaṇe khayavayaṃ [M 0.0123] paṭṭhapentassa manokammaṃ hoti. Evaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ kāyavacīmanokammavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Evametaṃ dhammārammaṇampi kusalaṃ tividhapuññakiriyavatthuvasena navahi kammadvārehi bhājetvā dassesi dhammarājā.

Furthermore, for one who, having done walking meditation, establishes the perception of perishing and passing away in a mind-object, it is bodily action that is merit consisting of development. For one who, without moving a bodily limb, establishes the perception of perishing and passing away by means of speech, it is verbal action. For one who, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, establishes the perception of perishing and passing away in a mind-object with the mind alone, it is mental action. Thus, merit consisting of development is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action. In this way, the King of Dhamma has shown this wholesome state, which has a mind-object, divided by the nine doors of action by way of the threefold basis of meritorious action.

Evamidaṃ cittaṃ nānāvatthūsu nānārammaṇavasena dīpitaṃ. Idaṃ pana ekavatthusmimpi nānārammaṇavasena labbhatiyeva. Kathaṃ? Catūsu hi paccayesu cīvare cha ārammaṇāni labbhanti – navarattassa hi cīvarassa vaṇṇo manāpo hoti dassanīyo, idaṃ vaṇṇārammaṇaṃ. Paribhogakāle paṭapaṭasaddaṃ karoti, idaṃ saddārammaṇaṃ. Yo tattha kāḷakacchakādigandho, idaṃ gandhārammaṇaṃ. Rasārammaṇaṃ pana paribhogarasavasena kathitaṃ. Yā tattha sukhasamphassatā, idaṃ phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ. Cīvaraṃ paṭicca uppannā sukhā vedanā, dhammārammaṇaṃ. Piṇḍapāte rasārammaṇaṃ nippariyāyeneva labbhati. Evaṃ catūsu paccayesu nānārammaṇavasena yojanaṃ katvā dānamayādibhedo veditabbo.

Thus this consciousness has been explained by way of various objects in various bases. Furthermore, this consciousness is indeed obtained by way of various objects even in a single base. How so? Indeed, among the four requisites, six objects are obtained in the robe. Indeed, the color of a newly dyed robe is pleasing and beautiful to see; this is a form-object. At the time of use, it makes a rustling sound; this is a sound-object. Whatever smell of black catechu dye and so on is in it, this is a smell-object. Furthermore, the taste-object is spoken of by way of the ‘taste of use,’ that is, the joy and gladness that arises. Whatever state of pleasant contact is in it, this is a tangible-object. The pleasant feeling that has arisen in dependence on the robe is a mind-object. In almsfood, a taste-object is obtained directly. Thus, having made the connection by way of various objects in the four requisites, the distinctions beginning with merit consisting of giving should be understood.

Imassa pana cittassa ārammaṇameva nibaddhaṃ, vinā ārammaṇena anuppajjanato. Dvāraṃ pana anibaddhaṃ. Kasmā? Kammassa anibaddhattā. Kammasmiñhi anibaddhe dvārampi anibaddhameva hoti.

For this consciousness, however, only the object is bound, because it does not arise without an object. The door, however, is not bound. Why? Because the kamma is not bound. Indeed, when the kamma is not bound, the door is also not bound.

Kāmāvacarakusalaṃ dvārakathā

Discourse on the Doors of Sense-Sphere Wholesome Kamma

Kāyakammadvārakathā

Discourse on the Door of Bodily Kamma

Imassa panatthassa [P 0.0082] pakāsanatthaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ dvārakathā kathitā. Tattha tīṇi kammāni, tīṇi kammadvārāni, pañca viññāṇāni, pañca viññāṇadvārāni, cha phassā, cha phassadvārāni, aṭṭha asaṃvarā, aṭṭha asaṃvaradvārāni, aṭṭha saṃvarā, aṭṭha saṃvaradvārāni, dasa kusalakammapathā, dasa akusalakammapathāti, idaṃ ettakaṃ dvārakathāya mātikāṭhapanaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, to clarify this meaning, in this context the discourse on the doors has been stated in the Great Commentary. Therein: three kammas, three doors of kamma; five consciousnesses, five doors of consciousness; six contacts, six doors of contact; eight non-restraints, eight doors of non-restraint; eight restraints, eight doors of restraint; ten wholesome courses of kamma, and ten unwholesome courses of kamma. This much is called the establishing of the mātikā for the discourse on the doors.

Tattha [V 0.0127] kiñcāpi tīṇi kammāni paṭhamaṃ vuttāni, tāni pana ṭhapetvā ādito tāva tīṇi kammadvārāni bhājetvā dassitāni. Katamāni tīṇi? Kāyakammadvāraṃ, vacīkammadvāraṃ, manokammadvāranti.

Therein, although the three kammas are stated first, setting those aside, to begin with the three doors of kamma are analyzed and shown. What are the three? The door of bodily kamma, the door of verbal kamma, and the door of mental kamma.

Tattha [M 0.0124] catubbidho kāyo – upādinnako, āhārasamuṭṭhāno, utusamuṭṭhāno, cittasamuṭṭhānoti. Tattha cakkhāyatanādīni jīvitindriyapariyantāni aṭṭha kammasamuṭṭhānarūpānipi, kammasamuṭṭhānāneva catasso dhātuyo vaṇṇo gandho raso ojāti aṭṭha upādinnakakāyo nāma. Tāneva aṭṭha āhārajāni āhārasamuṭṭhānikakāyo nāma. Aṭṭha utujāni utusamuṭṭhānikakāyo nāma. Aṭṭha cittajāni cittasamuṭṭhānikakāyo nāma.

Herein, the body is fourfold: appropriated, nutriment-originated, temperature-originated, and mind-originated. Therein, both the eight kamma-originated material phenomena beginning with the eye-base and ending with the life-faculty, and the eight phenomena that are indeed kamma-originated—the four great elements, color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence—are called the appropriated body. Those same eight, when nutriment-born, are called the nutriment-originated body. Those same eight, when temperature-born, are called the temperature-originated body. Those same eight, when mind-born, are called the mind-originated body.

Tesu kāyakammadvāranti neva upādinnakakāyassa nāmaṃ na itaresaṃ. Cittasamuṭṭhānesu pana aṭṭhasu rūpesu ekā viññatti atthi, idaṃ kāyakammadvāraṃ nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ kāyaviññatti? Yā kusalacittassa vā, akusalacittassa vā, abyākatacittassa vā, abhikkamantassa vā paṭikkamantassa vā, ālokentassa vā vilokentassa vā, samiñjentassa vā pasārentassa vā, kāyassa thambhanā santhambhanā santhambhitattaṃ, viññatti viññāpanā viññāpitattaṃ, idaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ kāyaviññattī”ti (dha. sa. 720). ‘Abhikkamissāmi paṭikkamissāmī’ti hi cittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tattha yā pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātu tannissito vaṇṇo gandho raso ojāti imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ rūpakalāpānaṃ abbhantare cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu, sā attanā sahajātaṃ rūpakāyaṃ santhambheti sandhāreti cāleti abhikkamāpeti paṭikkamāpeti.

Among these, the door of bodily kamma is a designation neither for the appropriated body nor for the others. But among the eight mind-originated material phenomena, there is one intimation; this is called the door of bodily kamma. With reference to this it was said: “What is that material phenomenon which is bodily intimation? That which, of a wholesome mind, or an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind, when going forward, or going backward, or looking ahead, or looking around, or bending, or stretching, is the stiffening, supporting, or sustained stiffening of the body; the intimation, making known, or state of being made known: this is the material phenomenon which is bodily intimation” (Dhs. 720). For when the thought arises, “I will go forward, I will go backward,” it produces material phenomena. Therein, within these eight material groups—the earth element, water element, fire element, air element, and the color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence dependent on them—the mind-originated air element stiffens, supports, moves, and causes the material body co-nascent with itself to go forward and go backward.

Tattha ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ sattasu javanesu paṭhamacittasamuṭṭhitā vāyodhātu [P 0.0083] attanā sahajātaṃ rūpakāyaṃ santhambhetuṃ sandhāretuṃ sakkoti, aparāparaṃ pana cāletuṃ na sakkoti. Dutiyādīsupi eseva nayo. Sattamacittena pana samuṭṭhitā vāyodhātu heṭṭhā chahi cittehi samuṭṭhitaṃ vāyodhātuṃ upatthambhanapaccayaṃ labhitvā attanā sahajātaṃ rūpakāyaṃ santhambhetuṃ sandhāretuṃ cāletuṃ abhikkamāpetuṃ paṭikkamāpetuṃ ālokāpetuṃ vilokāpetuṃ sammiñjāpetuṃ pasārāpetuṃ sakkoti. Tena gamanaṃ nāma jāyati, āgamanaṃ nāma jāyati, gamanāgamanaṃ nāma jāyati. ‘Yojanaṃ gato dasayojanaṃ gato’ti vattabbataṃ āpajjāpeti.

Therein, in a mind-door process with a single advertence, among the seven impulsions, the air element originated by the first impulsion is able to stiffen and maintain its co-nascent material body, but it is not able to move it to and fro. This same principle applies to the second and subsequent impulsions. But the air element originated by the seventh impulsion, having obtained the supporting condition of the air element originated by the six preceding consciousnesses, is able to stiffen, maintain, move, cause to go forward, cause to go backward, cause to look forward, cause to look around, cause to bend, and cause to stretch its co-nascent material body. By that, what is called going arises, what is called coming arises, and what is called going and coming arises. It brings about the state of being spoken of as: ‘He has gone a yojana, he has gone ten yojanas’.

Yathā [M 0.0125][V 0.0128] hi sattahi yugehi ākaḍḍhitabbe sakaṭe paṭhamayuge yuttagoṇā yugaṃ tāva santhambhetuṃ sandhāretuṃ sakkonti, cakkaṃ pana napavaṭṭenti; dutiyādīsupi eseva nayo; sattamayuge pana goṇe yojetvā yadā cheko sārathi dhure nisīditvā yottāni ādāya sabbapurimato paṭṭhāya patodalaṭṭhiyā goṇe ākoṭeti, tadā sabbeva ekabalā hutvā dhurañca sandhārenti cakkāni ca pavaṭṭenti. ‘Sakaṭaṃ gahetvā dasayojanaṃ vīsatiyojanaṃ gatā’ti vattabbataṃ āpādenti – evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For it is like a cart that is to be pulled by seven yokes: the oxen yoked to the first yoke are able to stiffen and maintain the yoke, but they do not make the wheels turn. This same principle applies to the second and subsequent yokes. But when a skilled charioteer, having yoked the oxen to the seventh yoke, sits on the shaft, takes the reins, and, starting from the very first ox, strikes the oxen with a goad, then all of them, having become of one strength, both maintain the shaft and make the wheels turn. They bring about the state of being spoken of as: ‘Having taken the cart, they have gone ten yojanas, twenty yojanas.’ This accomplishment should be understood in the same way.

Tattha yo cittasamuṭṭhānikakāyo na so viññatti, cittasamuṭṭhānāya pana vāyodhātuyā sahajātaṃ rūpakāyaṃ santhambhetuṃ sandhāretuṃ cāletuṃ paccayo bhavituṃ samattho eko ākāravikāro atthi, ayaṃ viññatti nāma. Sā aṭṭha rūpāni viya na cittasamuṭṭhānā. Yathā pana aniccādibhedānaṃ dhammānaṃ jarāmaraṇattā, “jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhata”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.20) vuttaṃ, evaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ viññattitāya sāpi cittasamuṭṭhānā nāma hoti.

Therein, whatever is the mind-originated body, that is not intimation. But there is a certain alteration of appearance that is a condition capable of causing the stiffening, maintaining, and moving of the material body co-nascent with the mind-originated air element—this is called intimation. It is not mind-originated like the eight material phenomena. But just as, because of the aging and death of phenomena classified as impermanent and so on, it is said, “Aging and death, bhikkhus, are impermanent, conditioned,” etc. (SN 12.20); so too, because it is the intimation of mind-originated material phenomena, it also comes to be called mind-originated.

Viññāpanattā panesā viññattīti vuccati. Kiṃ viññāpetīti? Ekaṃ kāyikakaraṇaṃ. Cakkhupathasmiñhi ṭhito hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā ukkhipati, sīsaṃ vā bhamukaṃ vā cāleti, ayaṃ hatthādīnaṃ ākāro cakkhuviññeyyo hoti. Viññatti pana na cakkhuviññeyyā manoviññeyyā eva. Cakkhunā hi hatthavikārādivasena vipphandamānaṃ vaṇṇārammaṇameva passati. Viññattiṃ pana manodvārikacittena cintetvā ‘idañcidañca esa kāreti maññe’ti jānāti.

Furthermore, it is called ‘intimation’ because it makes known. What does it make known? A certain bodily action. For when one standing in the range of vision raises a hand or a foot, or moves the head or an eyebrow, this gesture of the hand and so on is cognizable by eye-consciousness. But intimation is not cognizable by eye-consciousness; it is cognizable only by mind-consciousness. For with the eye one sees only the visible object, which is moving by way of the alteration of the hand and so on. But one knows the intimation by thinking with a mind-door consciousness, ‘I suppose this person wants to have such and such done.’

Yathā hi araññe nidāghasamaye udakaṭṭhāne manussā ‘imāya saññāya idha udakassa atthibhāvaṃ jānissantī’ti rukkhagge tālapaṇṇādīni bandhāpenti, surāpānadvāre dhajaṃ ussāpenti, uccaṃ vā [P 0.0084] pana rukkhaṃ vāto paharitvā cāleti, antoudake macche calante upari bubbuḷakāni uṭṭhahanti, mahoghassa gatamaggapariyante tiṇapaṇṇakasaṭaṃ ussāritaṃ hoti. Tattha tālapaṇṇadhajasākhācalanabubbuḷakatiṇapaṇṇakasaṭe disvā yathā cakkhunā adiṭṭhampi ‘ettha udakaṃ bhavissati, surā bhavissati, ayaṃ rukkho vātena pahato bhavissati, antoudake maccho bhavissati, ettakaṃ [M 0.0126] ṭhānaṃ ajjhottharitvā ogho gato bhavissatī’ti manoviññāṇena jānāti, evameva viññattipi na cakkhuviññeyyā manoviññeyyāva. Cakkhunā hi hatthavikārādivasena [V 0.0129] vipphandamānaṃ vaṇṇārammaṇameva passati. Viññattiṃ pana manodvārikacittena cintetvā ‘idañcidañca esa kāreti maññe’ti jānāti.

For example, in a forest during the hot season, at a place where there is water, people have signs such as palm leaves tied to the treetops, thinking, ‘By this sign, they will know of the presence of water here.’ They raise a flag at the door of a liquor shop. Furthermore, the wind, having struck a tall tree, moves it. When fish move in the water, bubbles rise to the surface. At the upper limit of the path taken by a great flood, grass, leaves, and debris are deposited. There, having seen the palm leaves, the flag, the movement of the branches, the bubbles, and the grass, leaves, and debris, just as one knows through mind-consciousness, although unseen by the eye, ‘There must be water here,’ ‘There must be liquor here,’ ‘This tree must have been struck by the wind,’ ‘There must be fish in the water,’ ‘The flood, having covered this much area, must have passed,’ so too, intimation is not cognizable by eye-consciousness; it is cognizable only by mind-consciousness. For with the eye, one sees only the visible object that is moving by way of the particular gesture of the hand and so on. But as for intimation, having considered with a mind-door consciousness, one knows thus: ‘It seems this person wants to have such and such an act done.’

Na kevalañcesā viññāpanatova viññatti nāma. Viññeyyatopi pana viññattiyeva nāma. Ayañhi paresaṃ antamaso tiracchānagatānampi pākaṭā hoti. Tattha tattha sannipatitā hi soṇasiṅgālakākagoṇādayo daṇḍaṃ vā leḍḍuṃ vā gahetvā paharaṇākāre dassite ‘ayaṃ no paharitukāmo’ti ñatvā yena vā tena vā palāyanti. Pākārakuṭṭādiantarikassa pana parassa apākaṭakālopi atthi. Kiñcāpi tasmiṃ khaṇe apākaṭā sammukhībhūtānaṃ pana pākaṭattā viññattiyeva nāma hoti.

This is not called 'intimation' merely because it makes known. But indeed, it is also called 'intimation' because it is knowable. For this is evident to others, even, at the very least, to animals. For creatures such as domestic dogs, wild dogs, crows, and oxen, gathered in various places, when shown the gesture of striking, having taken a stick or a clod, knowing, 'This person wants to strike us,' they flee by whatever way they can. But there is also a time when it is not evident to another who is concealed by a wall, partition, or the like. Although at that moment it may not be evident, nevertheless, because it is evident to those who are face-to-face, it is indeed called 'intimation'.

Cittasamuṭṭhānike pana kāye calante tisamuṭṭhāniko calati na calatīti? Sopi tatheva calati. Taṃgatiko tadanuvattakova hoti. Yathā hi udake gacchante udake patitāni sukkhadaṇḍakatiṇapaṇṇādīnipi udakagatikāneva bhavanti, tasmiṃ gacchante gacchanti, tiṭṭhante tiṭṭhanti – evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evamesā cittasamuṭṭhānesu rūpesu viññatti kāyakammadvāraṃ nāmāti veditabbā.

Furthermore, when the mind-originated body moves, does the body with three origins move or not move? That too moves in the very same way. It has a similar movement and follows it. For example, just as when water is flowing, dry sticks, dry grass, dry leaves, and other such things that have fallen into the water also come to have a movement similar to that of the water—they move when it moves, and they stop when it stops—this analogy should be understood as being thus complete. In this way, this intimation among mind-originated material phenomena should be understood as what is called the 'door of bodily kamma'.

Yā pana tasmiṃ dvāre siddhā cetanā yāya pāṇaṃ hanati, adinnaṃ ādiyati, micchācāraṃ carati, pāṇātipātādīhi viramati, idaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Evaṃ paravādimhi sati kāyo dvāraṃ, tamhi dvāre siddhā cetanā kāyakammaṃ ‘kusalaṃ vā akusalaṃ vā’ti ṭhapetabbaṃ. Paravādimhi pana asati ‘abyākataṃ vā’ti tikaṃ pūretvāva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Tattha yathā nagaradvāraṃ kataṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati, aṅgulamattampi aparāparaṃ na saṅkamati, tena tena pana dvārena mahājano sañcarati, evameva dvāre dvāraṃ na sañcarati, kammaṃ pana tasmiṃ tasmiṃ dvāre uppajjanato carati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Furthermore, the volition that is accomplished at that door, by which one kills a living being, takes what is not given, engages in wrong conduct, or abstains from misconduct such as killing, is called 'bodily kamma'. Thus, when there is an opponent in debate, the body is the door, and the volition accomplished at that door, being bodily kamma, should be established as either wholesome or unwholesome. But when there is no opponent in debate, it should be established only after completing the triad by adding 'or indeterminate'. Therein, just as a city gate stands only in the place where it is made and does not shift here and there even a finger's breadth, but a great multitude of people passes through that very gate, in this very way, a door does not move about at a door, but kamma moves about by arising at this or that door. Therefore, the ancient teachers have said:

Dvāre caranti kammāni, na dvārā dvāracārino;

Tasmā dvārehi kammāni, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitāti.

Kammas move about at the doors; the doors are not door-goers. Therefore, by the doors, kammas are distinguished from one another.

Tattha [M 0.0127][P 0.0085] kammenāpi dvāraṃ nāmaṃ labhati, dvārenāpi kammaṃ. Yathā hi viññāṇādīnaṃ uppajjanaṭṭhānāni [V 0.0130] viññāṇadvāraṃ phassadvāraṃ asaṃvaradvāraṃ saṃvaradvāranti nāmaṃ labhanti, evaṃ kāyakammassa uppajjanaṭṭhānaṃ kāyakammadvāranti nāmaṃ labhati. Vacīmanokammadvāresupi eseva nayo. Yathā pana tasmiṃ tasmiṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā simbalidevatā palāsadevatā pucimandadevatā phandanadevatāti tena tena rukkhena nāmaṃ labhati, evameva kāyadvārena kataṃ kammampi kāyakammanti dvārena nāmaṃ labhati. Vacīkammamanokammesupi eseva nayo. Tattha añño kāyo, aññaṃ kammaṃ, kāyena pana katattā taṃ kāyakammanti vuccati. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā –

Therein, a door also gets its name from the kamma, and the kamma also gets its name from the door. For example, just as the places of arising for consciousness, contact, non-restraint, and restraint get the names 'consciousness-door', 'contact-door', 'non-restraint-door', and 'restraint-door', so too, the place of arising for bodily kamma gets the name 'bodily-kamma-door'. This is also the method for the verbal-kamma-door and the mental-kamma-door. Furthermore, just as a deity dwelling in a particular tree gets its name from that tree—such as 'Simbali-deity', 'Palāsa-deity', 'Pucimanda-deity', or 'Phandana-deity'—in this very way, the kamma done through the body-door also gets its name 'bodily kamma' from the door. This is also the method for verbal kamma and mental kamma. Therein, the body is one thing, and the kamma is another; but because it is done by the body, that kamma is called 'bodily kamma'. Therefore, the commentary teachers have said:

Kāyena ce kataṃ kammaṃ, kāyakammanti vuccati;

Kāyo ca kāyakammañca, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitā.

If a kamma is done by the body, it is called 'bodily kamma'; the body and bodily kamma are distinguished from each other.

Sūciyā ce kataṃ kammaṃ, sūcikammanti vuccati;

Sūci ca sūcikammañca, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitā.

If a work is done with a needle, it is called 'needle-work'; the needle and the needle-work are distinguished from each other.

Vāsiyā ce kataṃ kammaṃ, vāsikammanti vuccati;

Vāsi ca vāsikammañca, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitā.

If a work is done with an adze, it is called 'adze-work'; the adze and the adze-work are distinguished from each other.

Purisena ce kataṃ kammaṃ, purisakammanti vuccati;

Puriso ca purisakammañca, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitā.

If a work is done by a man, it is called 'a man's work'; the man and the man's work are distinguished from each other.

Evamevaṃ.

In this very way.

Kāyena ce kataṃ kammaṃ, kāyakammanti vuccati;

Kāyo ca kāyakammañca, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitāti.

If a kamma is done by the body, it is called 'bodily kamma'; the body and bodily kamma are distinguished from each other.

Evaṃ sante neva dvāravavatthānaṃ yujjati, na kammavavatthānaṃ. Kathaṃ? Kāyaviññattiyañhi “dvāre caranti kammānī”ti vacanato vacīkammampi pavattati, tenassā kāyakammadvāranti vavatthānaṃ na yuttaṃ. Kāyakammañca vacīviññattiyampi pavattati, tenassa kāyakammanti vavatthānaṃ na yujjatī’ti. ‘No na yujjati. Kasmā? Yebhuyyavuttitāya ceva tabbahulavuttitāya ca. Kāyakammameva hi yebhuyyena kāyaviññattiyaṃ pavattati na itarāni, tasmā kāyakammassa yebhuyyena pavattito tassā kāyakammadvārabhāvo siddho. Brāhmaṇagāmaambavananāgavanādīnaṃ brāhmaṇagāmādibhāvo viyāti dvāravavatthānaṃ yujjati. Kāyakammaṃ pana kāyadvāramhiyeva bahulaṃ pavattati [V 0.0131] appaṃ vacīdvāre[M 0.0128]. Tasmā kāyadvāre bahulaṃ pavattito etassa [P 0.0086] kāyakammabhāvo siddho, vanacarakathullakumārikādigocarānaṃ vanacarakādibhāvo viyāti. Evaṃ kammavavatthānampi yujjatī’ti.

This being so, is not the designation of the door unfitting, and the designation of the kamma unfitting? How so? Because in bodily intimation, verbal kamma also occurs, according to the saying, 'Kammas proceed in the doors'; therefore, its designation as the 'body-kamma-door' is not suitable. And bodily kamma also occurs in verbal intimation; therefore, its designation as 'bodily kamma' is not fitting." "It is not that it is not fitting. Why so? Because of its general occurrence and its frequent occurrence therein. For it is bodily kamma that generally occurs in bodily intimation, not the others. Therefore, due to the general occurrence of bodily kamma, its status as the body-kamma-door is established, just as the status of being a Brahmin village, a mango grove, a Nāga forest, and so on, is established for them. Thus, the designation of the door is fitting. Bodily kamma, however, occurs frequently only in the body-door, and slightly in the speech-door. Therefore, because it occurs frequently in the body-door, its status as bodily kamma is established, just as the status of being a forest-dweller, and so on, is established for one whose sphere is that of forest-dwellers, coarse maidens, and the like. Thus, the designation of the kamma is also fitting.

Kāyakammadvārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the body-kamma-door is concluded.

Vacīkammadvārakathā

The Discourse on the Speech-Kamma-Door

Vacīkammadvārakathāyaṃ pana cetanāviratisaddavasena tividhā vācā nāma. Tattha “catūhi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgatā vācā subhāsitā hoti no dubbhāsitā, anavajjā ca ananuvajjā ca viññūna”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.213); ayaṃ cetanāvācā nāma. Yā “catūhi vacīduccaritehi ārati virati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati sammāvācā”ti (vibha. 206), ayaṃ virativācā nāma. “Vācā girā byappatho udīraṇaṃ ghoso ghosakammaṃ vācā vacībhedo”ti (dha. sa. 850), ayaṃ saddavācā nāma. Tāsu vacīkammadvāranti neva cetanāya nāmaṃ na viratiyā. Sahasaddā pana ekā viññatti atthi, idaṃ vacīkammadvāraṃ nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ vacīviññatti? Yā kusalacittassa vā akusalacittassa vā abyākatacittassa vā vācā girā byappatho udīraṇaṃ ghoso ghosakammaṃ vācā vacībhedo, ayaṃ vuccati vācā. Yā tāya vācāya viññatti viññāpanā viññāpitattaṃ, idaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ vacīviññattī”ti (dha. sa. 636).

Now, in the discourse on the speech-kamma-door, speech is of three kinds: by way of volition, abstinence, and sound. Therein, this which is stated, 'Bhikkhus, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken, not ill-spoken, blameless and not censured by the wise,' is called volition-speech. This which is stated, 'Whatever is abstaining from, refraining from... the four kinds of verbal misconduct... this is called right speech,' is called abstinence-speech. This which is stated, 'Speech, utterance, expression, declaration, sound, sound-production, speech, distinction of speech,' is called sound-speech. Among these, 'speech-kamma-door' is not the name for volition, nor for abstinence. However, there is a certain intimation that occurs together with sound; this is called the speech-kamma-door. With reference to this it was said: 'What is that form which is verbal intimation? Whatever speech—utterance, expression, declaration, sound, sound-production, speech, distinction of speech—of a wholesome mind, or of an unwholesome mind, or of an indeterminate mind, this is called speech. Whatever is the intimation, the making known, the state of having been made known by that speech, this is that form which is verbal intimation.'

‘Idaṃ vakkhāmi etaṃ vakkhāmī’ti hi vitakkayato vitakkavipphārasaddo nāma uppajjati. Ayaṃ na sotaviññeyyo manoviññeyyoti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgato. Āgamaṭṭhakathāsu pana ‘vitakkavipphārasadda’nti vitakkavipphāravasena uppannaṃ vippalapantānaṃ suttappamattādīnaṃ saddaṃ; ‘sutvā’ti taṃ sutvā, yaṃ vitakkayato tassa so saddo uppanno; tassa vasena ‘evampi te mano, itthampi te mano’ti ādisatīti vatvā vatthūnipi kathitāni. Paṭṭhānepi “cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ saddāyatanaṃ sotaviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti āgataṃ. Tasmā vinā viññattighaṭṭanāya [V 0.0132] uppajjamāno asotaviññeyyo vitakkavipphārasaddo nāma natthi. ‘Idaṃ vakkhāmi [M 0.0129] etaṃ vakkhāmī’ti uppajjamānaṃ pana cittaṃ pathavīdhātu āpodhātu [P 0.0087] tejodhātu vāyodhātu vaṇṇo gandho raso ojāti aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Tesaṃ abbhantare cittasamuṭṭhānā pathavīdhātu upādinnakaṃ ghaṭṭayamānāva uppajjati. Tena dhātusaṅghaṭṭanena saheva saddo uppajjatīti. Ayaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānasaddo nāma. Ayaṃ na viññatti. Tassā pana cittasamuṭṭhānāya pathavīdhātuyā upādinnakaghaṭṭanassa paccayabhūto eko ākāravikāro atthi, ayaṃ vacīviññatti nāma. Ito paraṃ sā aṭṭha rūpāni viya na cittasamuṭṭhānātiādi sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

For one who thinks, 'I will say this, I will say that,' a sound called 'thought-diffusion sound' arises. This is not cognizable by ear-consciousness but by mind-consciousness; so it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. In the Āgama-aṭṭhakathās, however, 'thought-diffusion sound' is the sound of those speaking incoherently, such as those who are sleeping or heedless, which arises by way of thought-diffusion. And 'having heard' means having heard that sound which arises for one who is thinking; and by means of that, one can declare, 'Thus is your mind, thus is your mind,' and instances are also related. In the Paṭṭhāna, too, it is stated: 'The sound-base arisen from mind is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of object-condition.' Therefore, there is no such thing as a 'thought-diffusion sound' that is not cognizable by ear-consciousness and arises without the impact of intimation. However, the mind that arises thinking, 'I will say this, I will say that,' originates eight forms: the earth element, water element, fire element, air element, color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence. Among these, the mind-originated earth element arises only while impinging on the appropriated earth element. Simultaneously with that impingement of the elements, sound arises. This is not intimation. But there is a certain alteration of mode which is a condition for the impingement of that mind-originated earth element on the appropriated element; this is called verbal intimation. What follows this—that it is not mind-originated like the eight forms, etc.—all this should be understood in the manner previously explained.

Idhāpi hi ‘tissa, datta, mittā’ti pakkosantassa saddaṃ sutvā viññattiṃ manodvārikacittena cintetvā ‘idañcidañca esa kāreti maññe’ti jānāti. Kāyaviññatti viya ca ayampi tiracchānagatānampi pākaṭā hoti. ‘Ehi, yāhī’ti hi saddaṃ sutvā tiracchānagatāpi ‘idaṃ nāmesa kāreti maññe’ti ñatvā āgacchanti ceva gacchanti ca. Tisamuṭṭhānikakāyaṃ cāleti na cāletīti, ayaṃ pana vāro idha na labbhati. Purimacittasamuṭṭhānāya upatthambhanakiccampi natthi. Yā pana tasmiṃ vacīdvāre siddhā cetanā, yāya musā katheti, pesuññaṃ katheti, pharusaṃ katheti, samphaṃ palapati, musāvādādīhi viramati, idaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Ito paraṃ sabbaṃ kammavavatthānañca dvāravavatthānañca heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Here also, having heard the sound of someone calling, 'Tissa, Datta, Mitta,' one considers the intimation with mind-door consciousness and knows, 'I suppose this person wants to have this and that done.' And like bodily intimation, this too is evident even to animals. For having heard sounds like, 'Come,' 'Go,' animals too, knowing, 'I suppose this person wants to have this particular thing done,' both come and go. However, this passage, 'it moves the body originated from three sources, or does not move it,' is not found here. There is also no function of supporting by what is originated from a preceding mind. But whatever volition is established in that speech-door—by which one tells lies, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, or chatters frivolously, or by which one abstains from false speech and so on—this is called verbal kamma. From this point on, all designation of kamma and designation of the door should be understood in the manner previously explained.

Vacīkammadvārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the speech-kamma-door is concluded.

Manokammadvārakathā

The Discourse on the Mind-Kamma-Door

Manokammadvārakathāyaṃ pana kāmāvacarādivasena catubbidho mano mano nāma. Tattha kāmāvacaro catupaññāsavidho hoti, rūpāvacaro pannarasavidho, arūpāvacaro dvādasavidho, lokuttaro aṭṭhavidhoti sabbopi ekūnanavutividho hoti. Tattha ayaṃ nāma mano manodvāraṃ na hotīti na vattabbo. Yathā hi ayaṃ nāma cetanā kammaṃ na hotīti na vattabbā, antamaso pañcaviññāṇasampayuttāpi [V 0.0133] hi cetanā mahāpakaraṇe kammantveva niddiṭṭhā, evameva ayaṃ nāma mano manodvāraṃ na hotīti na vattabbo.

Furthermore, in the discourse on the mind-kamma-door, mind is fourfold by way of the sense-sphere and so on, and is called 'mind'. Therein, sense-sphere mind is fifty-fourfold, form-sphere mind is fifteenfold, formless-sphere mind is twelvefold, and supramundane mind is eightfold—thus all mind is eighty-ninefold. Therein, it should not be said, “This so-called mind is not the mind-door.” For just as it should not be said, “This so-called volition is not kamma”—since at the very least, even volition associated with the five consciousnesses is designated as kamma in the Great Treatise—in just the same way, it should not be said, “This so-called mind is not the mind-door.”

Etthāha [M 0.0130] – kammaṃ nāmetaṃ kiṃ karotīti? Āyūhati, abhisaṅkharoti, piṇḍaṃ karoti, ceteti, kappeti, pakappetīti. Evaṃ sante pañcaviññāṇacetanā kiṃ āyūhati, abhisaṅkharoti, piṇḍaṃ [P 0.0088] karoti, ceteti, kappeti, pakappetīti?. Sahajātadhamme. Sāpi hi sahajāte sampayuttakkhandhe āyūhati abhisaṅkharoti piṇḍaṃ karoti ceteti kappeti pakappetīti. Kiṃ vā iminā vādena? Sabbasaṅgāhikavasena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – tebhūmakakusalākusalo ekūnatiṃsavidho mano manokammadvāraṃ nāma. Yā pana tasmiṃ manodvāre siddhā cetanā yāya abhijjhābyāpādamicchādassanāni ceva anabhijjhāabyāpādasammādassanāni ca gaṇhāti, idaṃ manokammaṃ nāma. Ito paraṃ sabbaṃ kammavavatthānañca dvāravavatthānañca heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti. Imāni tīṇi kammadvārāni nāma.

Herein it is said: What does this so-called kamma do? It accumulates, it prepares, it makes a mass, it intends, it arranges, and it plans. This being so, what does the volition of the five consciousnesses accumulate, prepare, make a mass, intend, arrange, or plan? Co-arisen phenomena. For it too accumulates, prepares, makes a mass, intends, arranges, and plans in regard to the co-arisen associated aggregates. Or what is the use of this argument? For this was stated by way of comprehensive inclusion. Herein, this is the conclusion: the twenty-ninefold mind that is wholesome and unwholesome pertaining to the three planes is called the mind-kamma-door. Furthermore, the volition that is established in that mind-door, by which one takes up covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, and non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—this is called mental kamma. Beyond this, all determination of kamma and determination of doors should be understood in the manner previously explained. These are the three kamma-doors.

Manokammadvārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the mind-kamma-door is concluded.

Kammakathā

Discourse on Kamma

Idāni yāni tīṇi kammāni ṭhapetvā imāni kammadvārāni dassitāni, tāni ādiṃ katvā avasesassa dvārakathāya mātikāṭhapanassa vitthārakathā hoti. Tīṇi hi kammāni – kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammanti. Kiṃ panetaṃ kammaṃ nāmāti? Cetanā ceva, ekacce ca cetanāsampayuttakā dhammā. Tattha cetanāya kammabhāve imāni suttāni –

Now, having set aside those three kammas, these doors of kamma were shown. Taking those as the beginning, there follows the detailed exposition of the establishment of the matrix for the remaining discourse on the doors. Indeed, there are three kammas: bodily kamma, verbal kamma, and mental kamma. Furthermore, what is this called 'kamma'? It is volition and also certain phenomena associated with volition. Therein, regarding the state of volition as kamma, these are the suttas:

“Cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi, cetayitvā kammaṃ karoti kāyena vācāya manasā” (a. ni. 6.63; kathā. 539). “Kāye vā hi, ānanda, sati kāyasañcetanāhetu uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ, vācāya vā, ānanda, sati vacīsañcetanāhetu uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ; mane vā, ānanda, sati manosañcetanāhetu [V 0.0134] uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ” (saṃ. ni. 2.25; a. ni. 4.171). “Tividhā, bhikkhave, kāyasañcetanā akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ dukkhudrayaṃ, dukkhavipākaṃ; catubbidhā, bhikkhave, vacīsañcetanā…pe… tividhā, bhikkhave, manosañcetanā akusalaṃ manokammaṃ dukkhudrayaṃ dukkhavipākaṃ tividhā[M 0.0131], bhikkhave, kāyasañcetanā kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ sukhudrayaṃ sukhavipākaṃ catubbidhā, bhikkhave, vacīsañcetanā…pe… tividhā, bhikkhave, manosañcetanā, kusalaṃ manokammaṃ sukhudrayaṃ sukhavipākaṃ” (kathā. 539; a. ni. 10.217 thokaṃ visadisaṃ). “Sacāyaṃ, ānanda, samiddhi moghapuriso pāṭaliputtassa paribbājakassa evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākareyya – sañcetaniyaṃ, āvuso pāṭaliputta, kammaṃ katvā kāyena vācāya manasā, sukhavedanīyaṃ sukhaṃ so vedayati…pe… adukkhamasukhavedanīyaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ so vedayatīti; evaṃ byākaramāno kho, ānanda, samiddhi moghapuriso pāṭaliputtassa paribbājakassa sammā byākaramāno byākareyyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.300; kathā. 539).

"Monks, I say that volition is kamma. Having willed, one performs kamma through body, speech, or mind." "Ānanda, when there is the body, internal pleasure or pain arises due to bodily volition. Ānanda, when there is speech, internal pleasure or pain arises due to verbal volition. Ānanda, when there is the mind, internal pleasure or pain arises due to mental volition." "Monks, threefold bodily volition is unwholesome bodily kamma, leading to suffering, resulting in suffering. Monks, fourfold verbal volition… threefold mental volition is unwholesome mental kamma, leading to suffering, resulting in suffering. Monks, threefold bodily volition is wholesome bodily kamma, leading to happiness, resulting in happiness. Monks, fourfold verbal volition… threefold mental volition is wholesome mental kamma, leading to happiness, resulting in happiness." "Ānanda, if this foolish Samiddhi, when questioned by the wanderer Pāṭaliputta, were to answer thus: 'Friend Pāṭaliputta, having performed kamma with volition through body, speech, or mind that is to be felt as pleasant, one feels pleasure… that is to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, one feels neither-painful-nor-pleasant'; answering in this way, Ānanda, Samiddhi the fool would be answering Pāṭaliputta the wanderer correctly."

Imāni tāva cetanāya kammabhāve suttāni. Cetanāsampayuttadhammānaṃ pana kammabhāvo kammacatukkena dīpito. Vuttañhetaṃ –

These, for now, are the suttas on the state of volition as kamma. Furthermore, the state as kamma of phenomena associated with volition is shown by means of the kamma-tetrad. For it has been said:

“Cattārimāni[P 0.0089], bhikkhave, kammāni mayā sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā paveditāni. Katamāni cattāri? Atthi, bhikkhave, kammaṃ kaṇhaṃ kaṇhavipākaṃ, atthi, bhikkhave, kammaṃ sukkaṃ sukkavipākaṃ, atthi, bhikkhave, kammaṃ kaṇhasukkaṃ kaṇhasukkavipākaṃ, atthi, bhikkhave, kammaṃ akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākaṃ kammakkhayāya saṃvattati (a. ni. 4.232-233).… Katamañca, bhikkhave, kammaṃ akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākaṃ kammakkhayāya saṃvattati? Yadidaṃ satta bojjhaṅgā – satisambojjhaṅgo…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kammaṃ akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākaṃ kammakkhayāya saṃvattati (a. ni. 4.238).… Katamañca, bhikkhave, kammaṃ akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākaṃ kammakkhayāya saṃvattati? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo – seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi [V 0.0135] …pe… sammāsamādhi. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kammaṃ akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākaṃ kammakkhayāya saṃvattatī”ti (a. ni. 4.237).

"Monks, there are these four kinds of kamma that I have declared after realizing them directly through my own higher knowledge. What are the four? There is, monks, dark kamma with dark result; there is, monks, bright kamma with bright result; there is, monks, dark and bright kamma with dark and bright result; and there is, monks, kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma. And what, monks, is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma? It is these seven factors of enlightenment—mindfulness as a factor of enlightenment…equanimity as a factor of enlightenment. This, monks, is called kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma. And what, monks, is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma? It is this Noble Eightfold Path—that is, right view…right concentration. This, monks, is called kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma."

Evaṃ ime bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgappabhedato pannarasa dhammā kammacatukkena dīpitā. Abhijjhā, byāpādo, micchādiṭṭhi, anabhijjhā, abyāpādo, sammādiṭṭhīti imehi pana chahi saddhiṃ ekavīsati cetanāsampayuttakā dhammā veditabbā.

Thus, these fifteen phenomena, classified by way of the factors of enlightenment and path factors, have been shown by the kamma-tetrad. Furthermore, together with these six—covetousness, ill will, wrong view, non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—twenty-one phenomena associated with volition should be understood.

Tattha [M 0.0132] lokuttaramaggo bhajāpiyamāno kāyakammādīni tīṇi kammāni bhajati. Yañhi kāyena dussīlyaṃ ajjhācarati, tamhā saṃvaro kāyikoti veditabbo. Yaṃ vācāya dussīlyaṃ ajjhācarati, tamhā saṃvaro vācasikoti veditabbo. Iti sammākammanto kāyakammaṃ, sammāvācā vacīkammaṃ. Etasmiṃ dvaye gahite sammāājīvo tappakkhikattā gahitova hoti. Yaṃ pana manena dussīlyaṃ ajjhācarati, tamhā saṃvaro mānasikoti veditabbo. So diṭṭhisaṅkappavāyāmasatisamādhivasena pañcavidho hoti. Ayaṃ pañcavidhopi manokammaṃ nāma. Evaṃ lokuttaramaggo bhajāpiyamāno tīṇi kammāni bhajati.

Therein, the supramundane path, when analyzed, enters into the three kammas beginning with bodily kamma. For whatever immorality one commits with the body, the restraint from that should be known as bodily. Whatever immorality one commits with speech, the restraint from that should be known as verbal. Thus, Right Action is bodily kamma, and Right Speech is verbal kamma. When this pair is taken, Right Livelihood is also taken, due to being in their faction. Furthermore, whatever immorality one commits with the mind, the restraint from that should be known as mental. That is fivefold by way of Right View, Right Resolve, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. This fivefold is called mental kamma. Thus, the supramundane path, when analyzed, enters into the three kammas.

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne dvārasaṃsandanaṃ nāma hoti. Kāyavacīdvāresu hi copanaṃ patvā kammapathaṃ appattampi atthi, manodvāre ca samudācāraṃ patvā kammapathaṃ appattampi [P 0.0090] atthi; taṃ gahetvā taṃtaṃdvārapakkhikameva akaṃsu.

In this instance, there is what is called the juncture of the doors. For at the body and speech doors, having reached a state of impulse, there is also kamma that has not reached the path of kamma; and at the mind door, having reached a state of manifestation, there is also kamma that has not reached the path of kamma. Taking this, they have made it pertain only to the faction of its respective door.

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – yo ‘migavaṃ gamissāmī’ti dhanuṃ sajjeti, jiyaṃ vaṭṭeti, sattiṃ niseti, bhattaṃ bhuñjati, vatthaṃ paridahati, ettāvatā kāyadvāre copanaṃ pattaṃ hoti. So araññe divasaṃ caritvā antamaso sasabiḷāramattampi na labhati, idaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma hoti na hotīti? Na hoti. Kasmā? Kammapathaṃ appattatāya. Kevalaṃ pana kāyaduccaritaṃ nāma hotīti veditabbaṃ. Macchaggahaṇādī supayogesupi eseva nayo.

Herein is the method: When someone, thinking, 'I will go hunting,' prepares the bow, twists the bowstring, sharpens the spear, eats a meal, and puts on an outer garment—by this much, the state of impulse at the body-door has been reached. If, after wandering in the forest for a day, they do not get even so much as a hare or a cat at the very least, is this unwholesome act called bodily kamma or not? It is not. Why? Because of not having reached the path of kamma. However, it should be known that it is merely called bodily misconduct. This is the very same method in undertakings such as fishing and so on.

Vacīdvārepi ‘migavaṃ gamissāmi’ ‘vegena dhanuādīni sajjethā’ti āṇāpetvā purimanayeneva araññe kiñci alabhantassa kiñcāpi vacīdvāre copanaṃ pattaṃ, kammapathaṃ appattatāya pana kāyakammaṃ na hoti. Kevalaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ nāma hotīti veditabbaṃ.

At the speech-door too, in the case of one who, having ordered, 'You shall go hunting! Quickly prepare the bows and so on!', gets nothing in the forest by the previous method—although an impulse is indeed reached at the speech-door, it is not bodily kamma, because of not having reached the path of kamma. It should be known that it is merely called verbal misconduct.

Manodvāre [V 0.0136] pana vadhakacetanāya uppannamattāya eva kammapathabhedova hoti. So ca kho byāpādavasena na pāṇātipātavasena. Akusalañhi kāyakammaṃ kāyavacīdvāresu samuṭṭhāti, na manodvāre; tathā akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ. Akusalaṃ manokammaṃ pana tīsupi dvāresu samuṭṭhāti; tathā kusalāni kāyavacīmanokammāni.

At the mind-door, however, the differentiation of the path of kamma occurs merely with the arising of the volition to kill. And that is by way of ill will, not by way of destroying life. For unwholesome bodily kamma arises at the body and speech doors, not at the mind-door; likewise, unwholesome verbal kamma. But unwholesome mental kamma arises at all three doors; likewise, wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental kammas.

Kathaṃ[M 0.0133]? Sahatthā hi pāṇaṃ hanantassa adinnaṃ ādiyantassa micchācāraṃ carantassa kammaṃ kāyakammameva hoti. Dvārampi kāyadvārameva hoti. Evaṃ tāva akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ kāyadvāre samuṭṭhāti. Tehi pana cittehi sahajātā abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhiyo cetanāpakkhikā vā bhavanti, abbohārikā vā. ‘Gaccha itthannāmaṃ jīvitā voropehi, itthannāmaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā’ti āṇāpentassa pana kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ hoti, dvāraṃ pana vacīdvāraṃ. Evaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīdvāre samuṭṭhāti. Tehi pana cittehi sahajātā abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhiyo cetanāpakkhikā vā bhavanti abbohārikā vā. Ettakā ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā nāma.

How so? For one who kills a living being with one's own hand, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct, the kamma is bodily kamma alone. The door is also the body-door alone. Thus, unwholesome bodily kamma arises at the body-door. But the covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that are co-arisen with those minds are either included in the faction of the volition or are non-designated. For one who orders, 'Go, deprive so-and-so of life,' or 'Go, steal such-and-such goods,' the kamma is bodily kamma, but the door is the speech-door. Thus, unwholesome bodily kamma arises at the speech-door. But the covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that are co-arisen with those minds are either included in the faction of the volition or are non-designated. This much is called the teachers' discourse of similar meaning.

Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – ‘akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ manodvārepi samuṭṭhātī’ti. So ‘tayo saṅgahe āruḷhaṃ suttaṃ āharāhī’ti vutto idaṃ kulumbasuttaṃ nāma āhari –

The sophist, however, says: 'Unwholesome bodily kamma also arises at the mind-door.' When told, 'Bring a sutta that has been included in the Three Councils,' he brought this so-called Kulumba Sutta:

“Puna caparaṃ[P 0.0091], bhikkhave, idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā iddhimā cetovasippatto aññissā kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ pāpakena manasā anupekkhako hoti – ‘aho vatāyaṃ kucchigato gabbho na sotthinā abhinikkhameyyā’ti. Evaṃ, bhikkhave, kulumbassa upaghāto hotī”ti.

“Furthermore, monks, here some ascetic or brahmin, possessing psychic power and mastery of mind, regards a fetus in another's womb with an evil mind, thinking: ‘Oh, may this fetus in the womb not come forth safely!’ Thus, monks, there is injury to the embryo.”

Idaṃ suttaṃ āharitvā āha – ‘evaṃ cintitamatteyeva manasā kucchigato gabbho pheṇapiṇḍo viya vilīyati. Ettha kuto kāyaṅgacopanaṃ vā vācaṅgacopanaṃ vā? Manodvārasmiṃyeva pana idaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ samuṭṭhātī’ti.

Having brought this sutta, he says: 'Merely upon thinking thus with the mind, the fetus in the womb dissolves like a lump of foam. Herein, where is there agitation of a bodily organ or agitation of a verbal organ? But it is only at the mind-door that this unwholesome bodily kamma arises.'

Tamenaṃ ‘tava suttassa atthaṃ tulayissāmā’ti vatvā evaṃ tulayiṃsu – ‘tvaṃ iddhiyā parūpaghātaṃ vadesi. Iddhi nāma cesā – adhiṭṭhāniddhi, vikubbaniddhi, manomayiddhi, ñāṇavipphāriddhi, samādhivipphāriddhi, ariyiddhi, kammavipākajiddhi, puññavato iddhi, vijjāmayiddhi[V 0.0137], tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena [M 0.0134] iddhīti dasavidhā (paṭi. ma. 3.10). Tattha kataraṃ iddhiṃ vadesī’ti? ‘Bhāvanāmaya’nti. ‘Kiṃ pana bhāvanāmayiddhiyā parūpaghātakammaṃ hotī’ti? ‘Āma, ekacce ācariyā ekavāraṃ hotī’ti; vadanti yathā hi paraṃ paharitukāmena udakabharite ghaṭe khitte ghaṭopi bhijjati, udakampi nassati, evameva bhāvanāmayiddhiyā ekavāraṃ parūpaghātakammaṃ hoti. Tato paṭṭhāya pana sā nassatīti. Atha naṃ ‘bhāvanāmayiddhiyā neva ekavāraṃ na dve vāre parūpaghātakammaṃ hotī’ti vatvā taṃ saññattiṃ āgacchantaṃ pucchiṃsu – ‘bhāvanāmayiddhi kiṃ kusalā, akusalā, abyākatā? Sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā? Savitakkasavicārā, avitakkavicāramattā, avitakkaavicārā? Kāmāvacarā, rūpāvacarā, arūpāvacarā’ti?

Then, having said to that sophist, 'We will examine the meaning of your discourse,' they examined it thus: 'You speak of harming others through psychic power. Now, this psychic power is of ten kinds: the psychic power of determination, the psychic power of transformation, the mind-made psychic power, the psychic power of the pervasion of knowledge, the psychic power of the pervasion of concentration, the noble psychic power, the psychic power born of kamma-result, the psychic power of the meritorious, the psychic power born of incantations, and psychic power in the sense of accomplishment in various matters due to the cause of right application. Among these, which psychic power do you mean?' 'That born of development.' 'But can an act of harming others occur through psychic power born of development?' 'Yes, some teachers say it can happen once. For example, just as when a pot filled with water is thrown by one who desires to strike another, the pot is broken and the water is also lost, even so, through psychic power born of development, an act of harming others occurs once. But from that time onwards, it is lost.' Then, having said to him, 'An act of harming others does not occur through psychic power born of development, not once, not twice,' they questioned him, who was not coming to that understanding: 'Is the psychic power born of development wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate? Is it associated with pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? Is it with initial and sustained thought, with only sustained thought, or without initial and sustained thought? Does it belong to the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, or the formless-sphere?'

Imaṃ pana pañhaṃ yo jānāti so evaṃ vakkhati – ‘bhāvanāmayiddhi kusalā vā hoti, abyākatā vā; adukkhamasukhavedanīyā eva, avitakkaavicārā eva, rūpāvacarā evā’ti. So vattabbo – ‘pāṇātipātacetanā kusalādīsu kataraṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ bhajatī’ti? Jānanto vakkhati – ‘pāṇātipātacetanā akusalā eva, dukkhavedanīyā eva, savitakkasavicārā eva kāmāvacarā evā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sante tava pañho neva kusalattikena sameti, na vedanāttikena[P 0.0092], na vitakkattikena, na bhūmantarenā’ti.

Now, whoever knows this question will say thus: 'Psychic power born of development is either wholesome or indeterminate; it is only accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is only without initial and sustained thought, and it pertains only to the form-sphere.' He should be told: 'To which category among the wholesome, and so on, does the volition for destroying life belong?' One who knows will say: 'The volition for destroying life is only unwholesome, it is only accompanied by painful feeling, it is only with initial and sustained thought, and it pertains only to the sense-sphere.' 'This being so, your proposition accords neither with the wholesome triad, nor with the feeling triad, nor with the thought triad, nor with the distinction of planes.'

‘Kiṃ pana evaṃ mahantaṃ suttaṃ niratthaka’nti? ‘No niratthakaṃ; tvaṃ panassa atthaṃ na jānāsi. “Iddhimā cetovasippatto”ti ettha hi neva bhāvanāmayiddhi adhippetā, āthabbaṇiddhi pana adhippetā. Sā hi ettha labbhamānā labbhati. Sā pana kāyavacīdvārāni muñcitvā kātuṃ na sakkā. Āthabbaṇiddhikā hi sattāhaṃ aloṇakaṃ bhuñjitvā dabbe attharitvā pathaviyaṃ sayamānā tapaṃ caritvā sattame divase susānabhūmiṃ sajjetvā sattame pade ṭhatvā hatthaṃ vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā mukhena vijjaṃ parijappanti. Atha nesaṃ kammaṃ samijjhati. Evaṃ ayampi iddhi kāyavacīdvārāni muñcitvā kātuṃ na sakkāti. ‘Na kāyakammaṃ manodvāre samuṭṭhātī’ti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

'But is such a great discourse meaningless?' 'It is not meaningless; you, however, do not know its meaning. For here, in the phrase "one with psychic power, who has attained mastery of mind," psychic power born of development is not intended; rather, psychic power from Atharva spells is intended. For that is the power that is applicable in this context. But that cannot be performed without employing the body-door and speech-door. For those with Atharva power, after eating saltless food for seven days, spreading kusa grass and lying on the ground, and having practiced austerities, on the seventh day, they prepare the charnel ground, stand at the seventh step, whirl their hand again and again, and mutter the spell with their mouth. Then their work succeeds. Thus, this psychic power also cannot be performed without employing the body-door and speech-door. Therefore, the conclusion should be reached here that "bodily kamma does not arise at the mind-door."

Hatthamuddāya [M 0.0135] pana musāvādādīni kathentassa kammaṃ vacīkammaṃ, dvāraṃ pana kāyadvāraṃ hoti[V 0.0138]. Evaṃ akusalaṃ vacīkammampi kāyadvāre samuṭṭhāti. Tehi pana cittehi sahajātā abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhiyo cetanāpakkhikā vā bhavanti, abbohārikā vā. Vacībhedaṃ pana katvā musāvādādīni kathentassa kammampi vacīkammaṃ dvārampi vacīdvārameva. Evaṃ akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ vacīdvāre samuṭṭhāti. Tehi pana cittehi sahajātā abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhiyo cetanāpakkhikā vā bhavanti abbohārikā vā. Ettakā ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā nāma.

Furthermore, for one who speaks falsehood, etc., by means of hand gestures, the kamma is verbal kamma, but the door is the body-door. Thus, unwholesome verbal kamma also arises in the body-door. But the covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that are co-nascent with those states of consciousness are either on the side of volition or are not designated as mental kamma. Furthermore, for one who speaks falsehood, etc., by making an utterance, the kamma is verbal kamma, and the door is the speech-door itself. Thus, unwholesome verbal kamma arises in the speech-door. And the covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that are co-nascent with those states of consciousness are either on the side of volition or are not designated as mental kamma. This much is what is called the teachers' explanation of the common meaning.

Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – ‘akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ manodvārepi samuṭṭhātī’ti. So ‘tayo saṅgahe āruḷhaṃ suttaṃ āharāhī’ti vutto idaṃ uposathakkhandhakato suttaṃ āhari –

But the sophist said: 'Unwholesome verbal kamma also arises in the mind-door.' When told, 'Bring a discourse that was included in the three Councils,' he brought this discourse from the Uposatha section:

“Yo pana bhikkhu yāvatatiyaṃ anussāviyamāne saramāno santiṃ āpattiṃ nāvikareyya sampajānamusāvādassa hotī”ti (mahāva. 134).

'Whatever bhikkhu, while the formal announcement is being made for the third time, remembering an existing offense, should not reveal it, for him it is a case of deliberate false speech.'

Idaṃ suttaṃ āharitvā āha – ‘evaṃ āpattiṃ anāvikaronto tuṇhībhūtova aññaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati, ettha kuto kāyaṅgacopanaṃ vā vācaṅgacopanaṃ vā? Manodvārasmiṃyeva pana idaṃ akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ samuṭṭhātī’ti.

Having brought this discourse, he said: 'Thus, by not revealing an offense, while remaining silent, one falls into another offense. Here, where is there any movement of a bodily limb or movement of a verbal limb? Indeed, this unwholesome verbal kamma arises only in the mind-door.'

So vattabbo – ‘kiṃ panetaṃ suttaṃ neyyatthaṃ udāhu nītattha’nti? ‘Nītatthameva mayhaṃ sutta’nti. So ‘mā evaṃ avaca, tulayissāmassa attha’nti vatvā evaṃ pucchitabbo – ‘sampajānamusāvāde kiṃ hotī’ti? Jānanto ‘sampajānamusāvāde dukkaṭaṃ hotī’ti vakkhati. Tato vattabbo ‘vinayassa dve [P 0.0093] mūlāni – kāyo ca vācā ca; sammāsambuddhena hi sabbāpattiyo imesuyeva dvīsu dvāresu paññattā, manodvāre āpattipaññapanaṃ nāma natthi. Tvaṃ ativiya vinaye pakataññū, yo satthārā apaññatte ṭhāne āpattiṃ paññapesi, sammāsambuddhaṃ abbhācikkhasi, jinacakkaṃ paharasī’tiādivacanehi niggaṇhitvā uttari pañhaṃ pucchitabbo – ‘sampajānamusāvādo kiriyato samuṭṭhāti udāhu akiriyato’ti? Jānanto ‘kiriyato’ti vakkhati. Tato vattabbo – ‘anāvikaronto kataraṃ kiriyaṃ karotī’ti? Addhā hi kiriyaṃ apassanto vighātaṃ āpajjissati. Tato imassa suttassa [M 0.0136] atthena saññāpetabbo. Ayañhettha attho – yvāyaṃ ‘sampajānamusāvādo hotī’ti vutto, so āpattito kiṃ hoti? ‘Katarāpatti hotī’ti [V 0.0139] attho. ‘Dukkaṭāpatti hoti’. Sā ca kho na musāvādalakkhaṇena, bhagavato pana vacanena vacīdvāre akiriyasamuṭṭhānā āpatti hotīti veditabbā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

He should be told, "Is this sutta of interpretable meaning or of definitive meaning?" "My sutta is of definitive meaning." He should be told, "Do not speak thus, we will weigh its meaning," and then asked, "What occurs in the case of intentional false speech?" Knowing, he will say, "In the case of intentional false speech, an offense of wrong-doing occurs." Then he should be told, "The Vinaya has two roots—body and speech; for by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One all offenses are laid down only in these two doors; there is no such thing as laying down an offense in the mind-door. You are exceedingly skilled in the Vinaya, you who lay down an offense in a case where the Teacher has not laid one down; you slander the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; you strike the wheel of the Conqueror." After rebuking him with such words, he should be further asked, "Does intentional false speech arise from an action or from an inaction?" Knowing, he will say, "From an action." Then he should be told, "When not making it manifest, what action does one perform?" Surely, not seeing the action, he will fall into distress. Then he should be made to understand by the meaning of this sutta. For this is the meaning here: as for what is said, 'There is intentional false speech,' what is it in terms of an offense? The meaning is, 'What kind of offense is it?' 'It is an offense of wrong-doing.' And that is not by the characteristic of false speech; rather, it should be understood as an offense arising from inaction at the speech-door, by the word of the Blessed One. And this has been said:

“Anālapanto manujena kenaci,

Vācāgiraṃ no ca pare bhaṇeyya;

Āpajjeyya vācasikaṃ na kāyikaṃ,

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (paṭi. 479);

“Not speaking with any person,

Nor uttering a word to another;

One would incur a verbal, not a bodily, offense—

This is a question considered by the wise.”

Evaṃ akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ na manodvāre samuṭṭhātīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be concluded here that unwholesome verbal kamma does not arise at the mind-door.

Yadā pana abhijjhāsahagatena cetasā kāyaṅgaṃ copento hatthaggāhādīni karoti, byāpādasahagatena cetasā daṇḍaparāmāsādīni, micchādiṭṭhisahagatena cetasā ‘khandasivādayo seṭṭhā’ti tesaṃ abhivādanaañjalikammabhūtapīṭhakaparibhaṇḍādīni karoti, tadā kammaṃ manokammaṃ hoti, dvāraṃ pana kāyadvāraṃ. Evaṃ akusalaṃ manokammaṃ kāyadvāre samuṭṭhāti. Cetanā panettha abbohārikā.

When, however, with a mind accompanied by covetousness, one performs actions such as grasping with the hand; with a mind accompanied by ill will, actions such as handling a stick; or with a mind accompanied by wrong view, thinking, 'Khanda, Siva, and others are supreme,' one performs for them acts such as paying homage, raising the joined palms, and preparing seats and requisites, then the kamma is mental kamma, but the door is the body-door. Thus, unwholesome mental kamma arises through the body-door. Herein, the volition is not designated as bodily kamma.

Yadā pana abhijjhāsahagatena cetasā vācaṅgaṃ copento ‘aho vata yaṃ parassa, taṃ mamassā’ti paravittūpakaraṇaṃ abhijjhāyati, byāpādasahagatena cetasā ‘ime sattā haññantu vā, bajjhantu vā, ucchijjantu vā, mā vā ahesu’nti vadati, micchādiṭṭhisahagatena cetasā ‘natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭha’ntiādīni vadati, tadā kammaṃ manokammaṃ hoti, dvāraṃ pana vacīdvāraṃ. Evaṃ akusalaṃ manokammaṃ vacīdvāre samuṭṭhāti. Cetanā panettha abbohārikā.

When, however, with a mind accompanied by covetousness, moving the organ of speech, one covets another's wealth and property, thinking, 'Oh, that what is another's might be mine!'; or with a mind accompanied by ill will, one says, 'May these beings be killed, or bound, or annihilated, or may they not exist!'; or with a mind accompanied by wrong view, one says such things as, 'There is nothing given, there is no offering,' then the kamma is mental kamma, but the door is the speech-door. Thus, unwholesome mental kamma arises through the speech-door. Herein, the volition is not designated as verbal kamma.

Yadā pana kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā raho nisinno abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhisahagatāni [P 0.0094] cittāni uppādeti, tadā kammaṃ manokammaṃ, dvārampi manodvārameva.
