Evaṃ akusalaṃ manokammaṃ manodvāre samuṭṭhāti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne cetanāpi cetanāsampayuttakā dhammāpi manodvāreyeva samuṭṭhahanti. Evaṃ akusalaṃ manokammaṃ tīsupi dvāresu samuṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ.

When, however, without moving the bodily or verbal organs, one sits in seclusion and generates thoughts accompanied by covetousness, ill will, or wrong view, then the kamma is mental kamma, and the door is the mind-door itself. Thus, unwholesome mental kamma arises at the mind-door. In this case, both the volition and the mental factors associated with volition arise at the mind-door alone. Thus, it should be understood that unwholesome mental kamma arises at all three doors.

Yaṃ [M 0.0137] pana vuttaṃ ‘tathā kusalāni kāyavacīmanokammānī’ti, tatrāyaṃ nayo – yadā hi kenaci [V 0.0140] kāraṇena vattuṃ asakkonto ‘pāṇātipātā adinnādānā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviramāmī’ti imāni sikkhāpadāni hatthamuddāya gaṇhāti, tadā kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ dvārampi kāyadvārameva. Evaṃ kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ kāyadvāre samuṭṭhāti. Tehi cittehi sahagatā anabhijjhādayo cetanāpakkhikā vā honti, abbohārikā vā.

As for what was said, “Similarly, wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental kammas,” here is the method: When, for some reason being unable to speak, one undertakes these precepts, 'I abstain from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct,' with a hand gesture, then the kamma is bodily kamma, and the door is the body-door itself. Thus, wholesome bodily kamma arises at the body-door. The non-covetousness and other such factors associated with those cittas either belong to the side of volition or are not designated as mental kamma.

Yadā pana tāneva sikkhāpadāni vacībhedaṃ katvā gaṇhāti, tadā kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ, dvāraṃ pana vacīdvāraṃ hoti. Evaṃ kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīdvāre samuṭṭhāti. Tehi cittehi sahagatā anabhijjhādayo cetanāpakkhikā vā honti, abbohārikā vā.

When, however, one undertakes those same precepts by making a verbal utterance, then the action is bodily action, but the door is the speech-door. Thus, wholesome bodily action arises through the speech-door. Non-covetousness and other such factors that arise together with those consciousnesses either belong to the side of volition or are not designated as mental action.

Yadā pana tesu sikkhāpadesu diyyamānesu kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā manasāva ‘pāṇātipātā adinnādānā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviramāmī’ti gaṇhāti, tadā kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ, dvāraṃ pana manodvāraṃ hoti. Evaṃ kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ manodvāre samuṭṭhāti. Tehi cittehi sahagatā anabhijjhādayo cetanāpakkhikā vā honti, abbohārikā vā.

When, however, while those precepts are being administered, one undertakes them with the mind alone, without moving the bodily or verbal organs, thinking, 'I abstain from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct,' then the action is bodily action, but the door is the mind-door. Thus, wholesome bodily action arises at the mind-door. Non-covetousness and other such factors that arise together with those consciousnesses either belong to the side of volition or are not designated as mental action.

‘Musāvādā veramaṇī’ādīni pana cattāri sikkhāpadāni vuttanayeneva kāyādīhi gaṇhantassa kusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ tīsu dvāresu samuṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ. Idhāpi anabhijjhādayo cetanāpakkhikā vā honti, abbohārikā vā.

Furthermore, it should be understood that for one who undertakes the four precepts beginning with 'abstinence from false speech' through the body-door and so on, in the same way as stated, wholesome verbal action arises at the three doors. Here too, non-covetousness and other such factors either belong to the side of volition or are not designated as mental action.

Anabhijjhādisahagatehi pana cittehi kāyaṅgaṃ copetvā cetiyaṅgaṇasammajjanagandhamālādipūjanacetiyavandanādīni karontassa kammaṃ manokammaṃ hoti, dvāraṃ pana kāyadvāraṃ. Evaṃ kusalaṃ manokammaṃ kāyadvāre samuṭṭhāti. Cetanā panettha abbohārikā. Anabhijjhāsahagatena cittena vācaṅgaṃ copetvā ‘aho vata yaṃ parassa vittūpakaraṇaṃ na taṃ mamassā’ti anabhijjhāyato abyāpādasahagatena cittena ‘sabbe sattā [P 0.0095] averā abyābajjhā anīghā sukhī attānaṃ pariharantū’ti vadantassa sammādiṭṭhisahagatena cittena ‘atthi dinna’ntiādīni udāharantassa kammaṃ manokammaṃ hoti, dvāraṃ pana vacīdvāraṃ. Evaṃ kusalaṃ manokammaṃ vacīdvāre samuṭṭhāti. Cetanā [M 0.0138] panettha abbohārikā. Kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni pana acopetvā raho nisinnassa manasāva anabhijjhādisahagatāni cittāni uppādentassa kammaṃ manokammaṃ, dvārampi manodvārameva. Evaṃ kusalaṃ [V 0.0141] manokammaṃ manodvāre samuṭṭhāti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne cetanāpi cetanāsampayuttakā dhammāpi manodvāreyeva samuṭṭhahanti.

Furthermore, for a person who, with minds accompanied by non-covetousness and so forth, having moved a bodily limb, performs actions such as sweeping the courtyard of a shrine, offering fragrances and garlands, and paying homage to a shrine, the kamma is mental kamma, but the door is the body-door. Thus, wholesome mental kamma arises at the body-door. Here, the volition is not designated as bodily kamma. For one who, with a mind accompanied by non-covetousness, having moved the organ of speech, does not covet, thinking, 'Oh, would that what belongs to another not be mine!'; or for one who, with a mind accompanied by non-ill-will, says, 'May all beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they look after themselves in happiness!'; or for one who, with a mind accompanied by right view, utters such things as, 'There is fruit of what is given,' the kamma is mental kamma, but the door is the speech-door. Thus, wholesome mental kamma arises at the speech-door. Here, the volition is not designated as verbal kamma. Furthermore, for a person who, sitting in a secluded place without moving the bodily and verbal organs, gives rise to minds accompanied by non-covetousness and so forth by mind alone, the kamma is mental kamma, and the door is the mind-door itself. Thus, wholesome mental kamma arises at the mind-door. In this case, both the volition and the mental states associated with volition arise in the mind-door itself.

Tattha āṇattisamuṭṭhitesu pāṇātipātaadinnādānesu kammampi kāyakammaṃ dvārampi kammavaseneva kāyadvāranti vadanto kammaṃ rakkhati, dvāraṃ bhindati nāma. Hatthamuddāya samuṭṭhitesu musāvādādīsu dvārampi kāyadvāraṃ, kammampi dvāravaseneva kāyakammanti vadanto dvāraṃ rakkhati kammaṃ bhindati nāma. Tasmā ‘kammaṃ rakkhāmī’ti dvāraṃ na bhinditabbaṃ, ‘dvāraṃ rakkhāmī’ti kammaṃ na bhinditabbaṃ. Yathāvutteneva pana nayena kammañca dvārañca veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ kathento hi neva kammaṃ na dvāraṃ bhindatīti.

Among these, in the case of killing and stealing that arise from giving a command, one who says, 'The kamma is bodily kamma, and the door, by virtue of the kamma, is the body-door,' is said to preserve the kamma but break the door. In the case of false speech and so forth that arise from a hand gesture, one who says, 'The door is the body-door, and the kamma, by virtue of the door, is bodily kamma,' is said to preserve the door but break the kamma. Therefore, thinking, 'I will preserve the kamma,' one should not break the door; and thinking, 'I will preserve the door,' one should not break the kamma. Rather, both the kamma and the door should be understood according to the method already stated. For one who explains it thus breaks neither the kamma nor the door.

Kammakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on Kamma is concluded.

Idāni ‘pañca viññāṇāni pañcaviññāṇadvārānī’tiādīsu cakkhuviññāṇaṃ sotaviññāṇaṃ ghānaviññāṇaṃ jivhāviññāṇaṃ kāyaviññāṇanti imāni pañca viññāṇāni nāma. Cakkhuviññāṇadvāraṃ sota… ghāna… jivhā… kāyaviññāṇadvāranti imāni pañca viññāṇadvārāni nāma. Imesaṃ pañcannaṃ dvārānaṃ vasena uppannā cetanā neva kāyakammaṃ hoti, na vacīkammaṃ, manokammameva hotīti veditabbā. Cakkhusamphasso sota… ghāna… jivhā… kāya… manosamphassoti ime pana cha samphassā nāma. Cakkhusamphassadvāraṃ sota… ghāna… jivhā… kāya… manosamphassadvāranti imāni cha samphassadvārāni nāma.

Now, in the mātikā phrases such as 'five consciousnesses' and 'five consciousness-doors': these are called the five consciousnesses: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness. These are called the five consciousness-doors: the eye-consciousness-door, the ear-consciousness-door, the nose-consciousness-door, the tongue-consciousness-door, and the body-consciousness-door. It should be known that the volition that has arisen by means of these five doors is neither bodily kamma nor verbal kamma, but is only mental kamma. Furthermore, these are called the six contacts: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. These are called the six contact-doors: the eye-contact-door, the ear-contact-door, the nose-contact-door, the tongue-contact-door, the body-contact-door, and the mind-contact-door.

Cakkhuasaṃvaro sota… ghāna… jivhā… pasādakāya… copanakāyaasaṃvaro vācāasaṃvaro manoasaṃvaroti – ime aṭṭha asaṃvarā nāma. Te atthato ‘dussīlyaṃ muṭṭhassaccaṃ aññāṇaṃ akkhanti kosajja’nti ime pañca dhammā honti. Tesu ekadhammopi pañcadvāre [P 0.0096] voṭṭhabbanapariyosānesu cittesu nuppajjati, javanakkhaṇeyeva uppajjati. Javane uppannopi pañcadvāre asaṃvaroti vuccati.

Non-restraint of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, sensitive body, motive body, speech, and mind—these are called the eight non-restraints. In terms of their meaning, they are these five states: immorality, lapsed mindfulness, ignorance, non-endurance, and laziness. Among these, not even one state arises in the minds at the five doors that culminate in determining; it arises only at the moment of impulsion. Even though it arises in the impulsion, it is called 'non-restraint at the five doors'.

Cakkhuviññāṇasahajāto hi phasso cakkhusamphasso nāma, cetanā manokammaṃ nāma, taṃ cittaṃ manokammadvāraṃ nāma. Ettha pañcavidho asaṃvaro natthi[M 0.0139]. Sampaṭicchanasahajāto phasso manosamphasso [V 0.0142] nāma, cetanā manokammaṃ nāma, taṃ cittaṃ manokammadvāraṃ nāma. Etthāpi asaṃvaro natthi. Santīraṇavoṭṭhabbanesupi eseva nayo. Javanasahajāto pana phasso manosamphasso nāma, cetanā manokammaṃ nāma, taṃ cittaṃ manokammadvāraṃ nāma. Ettha asaṃvaro cakkhuasaṃvaro nāma hoti. Sotaghānajivhāpasādakāyadvāresupi eseva nayo. Yadā pana rūpādīsu aññatarārammaṇaṃ manodvārikajavanaṃ vinā vacīdvārena suddhaṃ kāyadvārasaṅkhātaṃ copanaṃ pāpayamānaṃ uppajjati, tadā tena cittena sahajāto phasso manosamphasso nāma, cetanā kāyakammaṃ nāma, taṃ pana cittaṃ abbohārikaṃ, copanassa uppannattā manodvāranti saṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Ettha asaṃvaro copanakāyaasaṃvaro nāma. Yadā tādisaṃyeva javanaṃ vinā kāyadvārena suddhaṃ vacīdvārasaṅkhātaṃ copanaṃ pāpayamānaṃ uppajjati, tadā tena cittena sahajāto phasso manosamphasso nāma, cetanā vacīkammaṃ nāma, taṃ pana cittaṃ abbohārikaṃ, copanassa uppannattā manodvāranti saṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Ettha asaṃvaro vācāasaṃvaro nāma. Yadā pana tādisaṃ javanacittaṃ vinā kāyavacīdvārehi suddhaṃ manodvārameva hutvā uppajjati, tadā tena cittena sahajāto phasso manosamphasso nāma, cetanā manokammaṃ nāma, taṃ pana cittaṃ manokammadvāraṃ nāma. Ettha asaṃvaro manoasaṃvaro nāma. Iti imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ asaṃvarānaṃ vasena cakkhuasaṃvaradvāraṃ, sota… ghāna… jivhā… pasādakāya… copanakāya… vācā… manoasaṃvaradvāranti imāni aṭṭha asaṃvaradvārāni veditabbāni.

Indeed, contact co-arisen with eye-consciousness is called eye-contact; volition is called mental kamma; that consciousness is called the door of mental kamma. Herein, the fivefold non-restraint does not exist. Contact co-arisen with receiving-consciousness is called mind-contact; volition is called mental kamma; that consciousness is called the door of mental kamma. Herein too, non-restraint does not exist. In the cases of investigating and determining consciousnesses also, this is the method. Furthermore, contact co-arisen with impulsion is called mind-contact; volition is called mental kamma; that consciousness is called the door of mental kamma. Herein, the non-restraint is called non-restraint of the eye. In the cases of the ear, nose, tongue, and sensitive body doors also, this is the method. Furthermore, when a mind-door impulsion, having some object among forms and so forth, arises without the speech-door, causing a pure movement reckoned as the body-door, then the contact co-arisen with that consciousness is called mind-contact; the volition is called bodily kamma; but that consciousness is not conventional, and because of the arising of the movement, it is not counted as a mind-door. Herein, the non-restraint is called non-restraint of the impulsive body. When just such an impulsion arises without the body-door, causing a pure movement reckoned as the speech-door, then the contact co-arisen with that consciousness is called mind-contact; the volition is called verbal kamma; but that consciousness is not conventional, and because of the arising of the movement, it is not counted as a mind-door. Herein, the non-restraint is called non-restraint of speech. Furthermore, when such an impulsion-consciousness arises without the body and speech doors, being purely a mind-door, then the contact co-arisen with that consciousness is called mind-contact; the volition is called mental kamma; and that consciousness is called the door of mental kamma. Herein, the non-restraint is called non-restraint of the mind. Thus, by way of these eight non-restraints, these should be known as the eight non-restraint-doors: the eye-non-restraint-door, ear-non-restraint-door, nose-non-restraint-door, tongue-non-restraint-door, sensitive-body-non-restraint-door, impulsive-body-non-restraint-door, speech-non-restraint-door, and mind-non-restraint-door.

Cakkhusaṃvaro sota… ghāna… jivhā… pasādakāya… copanakāya… vācā… manosaṃvaroti ime pana aṭṭha saṃvarā nāma. Te atthato ‘sīlaṃ sati ñāṇaṃ khanti vīriya’nti ime pañca [P 0.0097] dhammā honti. Tesupi ekadhammopi pañcadvāre voṭṭhabbanapariyosānesu cittesu nuppajjati. Javanakkhaṇeyeva uppajjati. Javane uppannopi pañcadvāre saṃvaroti vuccati. Tassa sabbassāpi cakkhuviññāṇasahajāto hi phasso cakkhusamphassotiādinā asaṃvare vuttanayeneva uppatti veditabbā. Iti imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ saṃvarānaṃ vasena cakkhusaṃvaradvāraṃ…pe… manosaṃvaradvāranti imāni aṭṭha saṃvaradvārāni veditabbāni.

Furthermore, these are called the eight restraints: restraint of the eye, restraint of the ear, restraint of the nose, restraint of the tongue, restraint of the sensitive body, restraint of the impulsive body, restraint of speech, and restraint of the mind. In essence, they are these five states (dhammā): virtue, mindfulness, wisdom, patience, and energy. Among them, not even one state arises in the consciousnesses that end with determining at the five doors; it arises only at the moment of impulsion. Although it arises in the impulsion, it is called 'restraint at the five doors.' The arising of all of that restraint should be understood in the same way as was stated in the section on non-restraint, beginning with 'Indeed, contact co-arisen with eye-consciousness is called eye-contact.' Thus, by way of these eight restraints, these should be understood as the eight doors of restraint: the door of eye-restraint, the door of ear-restraint, the door of nose-restraint, the door of tongue-restraint, the door of sensitive-body-restraint, the door of impulsive-body-restraint, the door of speech-restraint, and the door of mind-restraint.

Akusalakammapathakathā

An Explanation of the Unwholesome Courses of Action

Pāṇātipāto[M 0.0140][V 0.0143], adinnādānaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro, musāvādo, pisuṇavācā, pharusavācā, samphappalāpo, abhijjhā, byāpādo, micchādiṭṭhīti ime pana dasa akusalakammapathā nāma.

Furthermore, the destruction of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—these are called the ten unwholesome courses of action.

Tattha pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto nāma; pāṇavadho, pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. So guṇavirahitesu tiracchānagatādīsu pāṇesu khuddake pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāsarīre mahāsāvajjo. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya. Payogasamattepi vatthumahantatāya. Guṇavantesu manussādīsu appaguṇe appasāvajjo, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjo. Sarīraguṇānaṃ pana samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjo, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjoti veditabbo.

Herein, the destruction of life is called 'pāṇātipāta'; it is also said to be 'pāṇavadha' or 'pāṇaghāta.' In this context, 'pāṇa' conventionally means a being, but in the ultimate sense, it refers to the life faculty. Regarding that being, the volition to kill, in one who perceives it as a being, which is produced by the effort to sever the life faculty and proceeds through either the body-door or the speech-door, is 'pāṇātipāta.' In the case of beings devoid of virtue, such as those in the animal realm, it is of little blame toward a small being, and of great blame toward a large-bodied one. Why? Due to the greatness of the effort. Even when the effort is the same, it is due to the greatness of the object. In the case of virtuous beings, such as humans, it is of little blame toward one of little virtue, and of great blame toward one of great virtue. Furthermore, when the qualities of the body and virtue are equal, it should be understood that it is of little blame due to the mildness of the defilements and the effort, and of great blame due to their intensity.

Tassa pañca sambhārā honti – pāṇo, pāṇasaññitā, vadhakacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena maraṇanti. Cha payogā – sāhatthiko, āṇattiko, nissaggiyo, thāvaro, vijjāmayo, iddhimayoti. Imasmiṃ panatthe vitthāriyamāne atipapañco hoti. Tasmā taṃ na vitthārayāma. Aññañca evarūpaṃ atthikehi pana samantapāsādikaṃ vinayaṭṭhakathaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.172) oloketvā gahetabbaṃ.

It has five components: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the thought of killing, the effort, and the resulting death. There are six means of application: by one's own hand, by command, by missile, by a fixed device, by magical knowledge, and by psychic power. But if this matter were to be explained in detail, it would become an excessive proliferation. Therefore, we do not elaborate upon it. Other such matters should be understood by those who are interested by consulting the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.172).

Adinnassa ādānaṃ ‘adinnādānaṃ’; parassaharaṇaṃ, theyyaṃ, corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ, yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo ca hoti. Tasmiṃ parapariggahite parapariggahitasaññino [P 0.0098] tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Taṃ hīne parasantake appasāvajjaṃ, paṇīte mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kasmā? Vatthupaṇītatāya. Vatthusamatte sati guṇādhikānaṃ santake vatthusmiṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ. Taṃtaṃguṇādhikaṃ upādāya tato tato hīnaguṇassa santake vatthusmiṃ appasāvajjaṃ.

The taking of what is not given is 'adinnādāna'; it is also said to be the carrying away of another's property, stealing, or theft. Herein, 'what is not given' means what is possessed by another, with regard to which the other person, acting as they please, is not liable to punishment and is blameless. Regarding that which is possessed by another, the volition to steal in one who perceives it as possessed by another, which is produced by the effort to take it, is 'adinnādāna.' This is of little blame in the case of an inferior possession belonging to another, and of great blame in the case of a superior one. Why? Due to the superiority of the object. When the objects are of equal value, it is of great blame in the case of an object belonging to one of superior qualities. In comparison with one of this or that superior quality, it is of little blame in the case of an object belonging to one of this or that inferior quality.

Tassa [M 0.0141] pañca sambhārā honti – parapariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitasaññitā, theyyacittaṃ, upakkamo[V 0.0144], tena haraṇanti. Cha payogā – sāhatthikādayova. Te ca kho yathānurūpaṃ theyyāvahāro, pasayhāvahāro, paṭicchannāvahāro, parikappāvahāro, kusāvahāroti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ avahārānaṃ vasena pavattanti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.138) vutto.

It has five components: another's property, the perception that it is another's property, the intention to steal, the attempt, and the removal by that attempt. There are six modes, beginning with acting by one's own hand. And these, according to suitability, occur by way of five kinds of theft: theft by stealth, theft by force, theft by disguise, theft by contrivance, and theft by deception. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, is stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.138).

‘Kāmesu micchācāro’ti ettha pana ‘kāmesū’ti methunasamācāresu; ‘micchācāro’ti ekantanindito lāmakācāro. Lakkhaṇato pana asaddhammādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā agamanīyaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā kāmesumicchācāro.

Now, in the phrase 'sexual misconduct,' 'in sexual matters' means in sexual practices; 'misconduct' means a practice that is absolutely blameworthy and base. Furthermore, by way of characteristic, sexual misconduct is the volition, occurring through the body-door with an unrighteous intention, of transgressing with regard to a forbidden partner.

Tattha agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma – purisānaṃ tāva māturakkhitā, piturakkhitā, mātāpiturakkhitā, bhāturakkhitā, bhaginirakkhitā, ñātirakkhitā, gottarakkhitā, dhammarakkhitā, sārakkhā, saparidaṇḍāti māturakkhitādayo dasa; dhanakkītā, chandavāsinī, bhogavāsinī, paṭavāsinī, odapattakinī, obhaṭacumbaṭā, dāsī ca bhariyā, kammakārī ca bhariyā, dhajāhaṭā, muhuttikāti etā dhanakkītādayo dasāti vīsati itthiyo. Itthīsu pana dvinnaṃ sārakkhasaparidaṇḍānaṃ, dasannañca dhanakkītādīnanti dvādasannaṃ itthīnaṃ aññe purisā idaṃ agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma.

Therein, what is called a forbidden partner is, first, for men, twenty types of women: the ten beginning with one protected by her mother—one protected by her mother, one protected by her father, one protected by her mother and father, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by her relatives, one protected by her clan, one protected by the Dhamma, one with a guardian, and one who is betrothed; and the ten beginning with one bought with wealth—one bought with wealth, one living by consent, one living for enjoyment, one living for clothing, a wife from a water ceremony, one freed from servitude, a slave who is a wife, a worker who is a wife, one captured in battle, and a temporary wife. Furthermore, for twelve of these women—the two who have a guardian and are betrothed, and the ten beginning with one bought with wealth—other men are what is called a forbidden partner.

So panesa micchācāro sīlādiguṇarahite agamanīyaṭṭhāne appasāvajjo, sīlādiguṇasampanne mahāsāvajjo. Tassa cattāro sambhārā – agamanīyavatthu, tasmiṃ sevanacittaṃ, sevanappayogo, maggenamaggappaṭipattiadhivāsananti. Eko payogo sāhatthiko eva.

This misconduct, however, is less blameworthy when committed with a forbidden partner who is lacking in virtues such as morality, and highly blameworthy when committed with one who is endowed with such virtues. It has four components: a forbidden partner, the intention to engage with that partner, the physical effort to engage, and consenting to the sexual act. The only mode of effort is that done by one's own hand.

‘Musā’ti visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjako vacīpayogo, kāyapayogo vā. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā [P 0.0099] musāvādo. Aparo nayo – ‘musā’ti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu. ‘Vādo’ti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. So yamatthaṃ bhañjati tassa appatāya appasāvajjo, mahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Apica gahaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0142] attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāya ‘natthī’tiādinayappavatto appasāvajjo. Sakkhinā hutvā atthabhañjanatthaṃ vutto mahāsāvajjo. Pabbajitānaṃ appakampi telaṃ vā sappiṃ vā [V 0.0145] labhitvā hasādhippāyena ‘ajja gāme telaṃ nadī maññe sandatī’ti pūraṇakathānayena pavatto appasāvajjo. Adiṭṭhaṃyeva pana diṭṭhantiādinā nayena vadantānaṃ mahāsāvajjo.

False speech is a verbal or bodily effort that destroys the benefit, having deception as its forerunner. The volition that originates the bodily or verbal effort to deceive another, with the intention of deceiving, is false speech. Another method: 'false' is an unreal, untrue thing. 'Speech' is the communicating of it as real and true. By way of characteristic, however, false speech is the volition that originates the communication, for one who desires to make another understand an untrue thing as true. It is slightly blameworthy due to the smallness of the matter it destroys, and greatly blameworthy due to its greatness. Moreover, for householders, that which proceeds in the manner of saying, 'There is none,' and so on, out of a desire not to give what is one's own is slightly blameworthy. When spoken for the purpose of destroying the benefit, having become a witness, it is greatly blameworthy. For monastics, having obtained even a little oil or ghee, that which proceeds in the manner of an exaggerated statement, with a joking intention, such as 'Today, I think a river of oil flows in the village,' is slightly blameworthy. But for those who speak in the manner of saying, 'What was not seen was seen,' and so on, it is greatly blameworthy.

Tassa cattāro sambhārā honti – atathaṃ vatthu, visaṃvādanacittaṃ, tajjo vāyāmo, parassa tadatthavijānananti. Eko payogo – sāhatthikova. So ca kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā vācāya vā paravisaṃvādakakiriyākaraṇe daṭṭhabbo. Tāya ce kiriyāya paro tamatthaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ kiriyasamuṭṭhāpikacetanākkhaṇeyeva musāvādakammunā bajjhati. Yasmā pana yathā kāyakāyappaṭibaddhavācāhi paraṃ visaṃvādeti, tathā imassa ‘imaṃ bhaṇāhī’ti āṇāpentopi, paṇṇaṃ likhitvā purato nissajjantopi, ‘ayamattho evaṃ daṭṭhabbo’ti kuṭṭādīsu likhitvā ṭhapentopi; tasmā ettha āṇattikanissaggiyathāvarāpi payogā yujjanti. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana anāgatattā vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbā.

Its components are four: an untrue matter, a mind set on deception, the effort produced from that, and another's understanding of that meaning. The application is one: by oneself. And that should be seen in the performance of an action that deceives another by means of the body, by what is connected to the body, or by speech. And if by that action another person understands that meaning, one is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that originated the action. But since, just as one deceives another by body, what is connected to the body, and speech, so too does one who commands, 'Say this,' or who, having written a leaf, throws it down in front of someone, or who, having written on a wall or the like, 'This matter should be understood thus,' places it there; therefore, here the applications by command, by emission, and by a fixed object are also suitable. But since they have not come down in the Commentaries, they should be accepted after investigation.

‘Pisuṇavācā’tiādīsu yāya vācāya yassa taṃ vācaṃ bhāsati tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā pisuṇavācā. Yāya pana attānampi parampi pharusaṃ karoti, yā vācā sayampi pharusā neva kaṇṇasukhā, na hadayaṅgamā, ayaṃ ‘pharusavācā’. Yena samphaṃ palapati, niratthakaṃ, so ‘samphappalāpo’. Tesaṃ mūlabhūtā cetanāpi pisuṇavācādināmameva labhati. Sā eva ca idha adhippetāti.

In the section beginning with 'divisive speech,' that speech by which one who speaks it creates in the heart of the one to whom one speaks it a state of affection for oneself and a state of alienation towards another, is divisive speech. But that speech by which one makes both oneself and another harsh, speech that is itself harsh, neither pleasant to the ear nor agreeable to the heart, this is 'harsh speech.' That by which one prattles what is rambling and meaningless is 'idle chatter.' The volition that is the root of these also obtains the name 'divisive speech,' and so on. And it is just that which is intended here.

Tattha saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa paresaṃ vā bhedāya attano piyakamyatāya vā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pisuṇavācā nāma. Sā yassa [P 0.0100] bhedaṃ karoti tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā.

Therein, the volition of one with a defiled mind, which originates bodily and verbal effort for the sake of dividing others or out of a desire for one's own likableness, is called divisive speech. It is slightly blameworthy due to the little virtue of the one whose division it causes, and greatly blameworthy due to their great virtue.

Tassā cattāro sambhārā – ‘bhinditabbo paro’ iti ‘ime nānā bhavissa’nti vinā bhavissantīti bhedapurekkhāratā vā, ‘iti ahaṃ piyo bhavissāmi vissāsiko’ti piyakamyatā vā, tajjo vāyāmo, tassa tadatthavijānananti[M 0.0143]. Pare pana abhinne kammapathabhedo natthi, bhinne eva hoti.

Its four components are: having division as a forerunner, thinking, 'That one is to be divided,' or 'These will become separate, they will be without each other'; or the desire to be liked, thinking, 'Thus I will be dear and trustworthy'; the effort produced from that; and the other's understanding of that meaning. However, when others are not divided, there is no breach of the course of action; it occurs only when they are divided.

Parassa mammacchedakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusacetanā ‘pharusavācā’. Tassā āvibhāvatthamidaṃ [V 0.0146] vatthu – eko kira dārako mātu vacanaṃ anādiyitvā araññaṃ gacchati. Taṃ mātā nivattetuṃ asakkontī ‘caṇḍā taṃ mahiṃsī anubandhatū’ti akkosi. Athassa tatheva araññe mahiṃsī uṭṭhāsi. Dārako ‘yaṃ mama mātā mukhena kathesi taṃ mā hotu, yaṃ cittena cintesi taṃ hotū’ti saccakiriyaṃ akāsi. Mahiṃsī tattheva baddhā viya aṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ mammacchedakopi payogo cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti. Mātāpitaro hi kadāci puttake evampi vadanti – ‘corā vo khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ karontū’ti, uppalapattampi ca nesaṃ upari patantaṃ na icchanti. Ācariyupajjhāyā ca kadāci nissitake evaṃ vadanti – ‘kiṃ ime ahirikā anottappino caranti, niddhamatha ne’ti; atha ca nesaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiṃ icchanti. Yathā ca cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti, evaṃ vacanasaṇhatāya apharusavācāpi na hoti. Na hi mārāpetukāmassa ‘imaṃ sukhaṃ sayāpethā’ti vacanaṃ apharusavācā hoti. Cittapharusatāya panesā pharusavācāva. Sā yaṃ sandhāya pavattitā tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā tayo sambhārā – akkositabbo paro, kupitacittaṃ, akkosananti.

The exclusively harsh volition that originates the bodily and verbal effort that cuts another's vital spots is 'harsh speech.' To illustrate this, here is a story: A certain boy, not heeding his mother's word, went into the forest. His mother, unable to make him return, cursed him, saying, 'May a fierce wild cow pursue you!' Then a wild cow rose up for him in the forest just so. The boy made an asseveration of truth, saying, 'May what my mother said with her mouth not be, may what she thought with her mind be!' The wild cow stood right there as if bound. Thus, even an application that cuts the vital spots, due to the gentleness of the mind, is not harsh speech. For parents sometimes say even this to their children: 'May thieves cut you into pieces!' yet they do not wish even a lotus petal to fall upon them. And teachers and preceptors sometimes say this to their dependents: 'Why do these shameless and reckless ones wander about? Drive them out!' yet they desire their accomplishment in study and realization. And just as it is not harsh speech due to the gentleness of the mind, so too it is not non-harsh speech due to the gentleness of the speech. For the speech 'Have this one lie down comfortably' of one who desires to have him killed is not non-harsh speech. But due to the harshness of the mind, this is indeed harsh speech. It is slightly blameworthy due to the little virtue of the one concerning whom it proceeds, and greatly blameworthy due to their great virtue. Its components are three: another who is to be reviled, an angry mind, and the reviling.

Anatthaviññāpikā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā akusalacetanā ‘samphappalāpo’. So āsevanamandatāya appasāvajjo. Āsevanamahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Tassa dve sambhārā – bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādiniratthakakathāpurekkhāratā, tathārūpīkathākathanañcāti. Pare pana taṃ [P 0.0101] kathaṃ agaṇhante kammapathabhedo natthi, parena samphappalāpe gahiteyeva hoti.

Frivolous speech is the unwholesome volition that originates the bodily and verbal effort which communicates what is unbeneficial. It is slightly blameworthy due to the slightness of its cultivation, and greatly blameworthy due to the greatness of its cultivation. Its components are two: having as a forerunner pointless talk such as about the Bharata war, the abduction of Sita, and so on; and the uttering of such talk. However, when another does not take that talk as true, there is no breach of the course of action; it occurs only when the frivolous speech is taken as true by another.

Abhijjhāyatīti ‘abhijjhā’. Parabhaṇḍābhimukhī hutvā tanninnatāya pavattatīti attho. Sā ‘aho tava idaṃ mamassā’ti evaṃ parabhaṇḍābhijjhāyanalakkhaṇā. Adinnādānaṃ viya appasāvajjā mahāsāvajjā ca. Tassā [M 0.0144] dve sambhārā – parabhaṇḍaṃ, attano pariṇāmanañcāti. Parabhaṇḍavatthuke hi lobhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo hoti yāva na ‘aho vata idaṃ mamassā’ti attano pariṇāmeti.

That which covets is called 'covetousness' (abhijjhā). The meaning is: it occurs by facing another's property and being inclined towards it. It has the characteristic of coveting another's property thus: 'Oh, may this be mine!' Like taking what is not given, it is of slight fault and of great fault. It has two components: another's property, and the inclining of it towards oneself. Indeed, even when greed has arisen with another's property as its object, the course of action is not yet broken so long as one does not incline it towards oneself thus: 'Oh, may this be mine!'

Hitasukhaṃ byāpādayatīti ‘byāpādo’. So paravināsāya manopadosalakkhaṇo. Pharusavācā viya appasāvajjo mahāsāvajjo ca. Tassa dve sambhārā – parasatto ca, tassa ca [V 0.0147] vināsacintāti. Parasattavatthuke hi kodhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo hoti yāva ‘aho vatāyaṃ ucchijjeyya vinasseyyā’ti tassa vināsanaṃ na cintesi.

That which corrupts welfare and happiness is called 'ill will' (byāpāda). It has the characteristic of corruption of mind for the destruction of another. Like harsh speech, it is of slight fault and of great fault. It has two components: another being, and the thought of that being's destruction. Indeed, even when anger has arisen with another being as its object, the course of action is not yet broken so long as one does not think of that being's destruction thus: 'Oh, may this one be cut off! May they perish!'

Yathābhuccagahaṇābhāvena micchā passatīti ‘micchādiṭṭhi’. Sā ‘natthi dinna’ntiādinā nayena viparītadassanalakkhaṇā. Samphappalāpo viya appasāvajjā mahāsāvajjā ca. Apica aniyatā appasāvajjā, niyatā mahāsāvajjā. Tassā dve sambhārā – vatthuno ca gahitākāraviparītatā, yathā ca taṃ gaṇhāti tathābhāvena tassupaṭṭhānanti. Tattha natthikāhetukaakiriyadiṭṭhīhi eva kammapathabhedo hoti, na aññadiṭṭhīhi.

Because it sees wrongly due to the absence of grasping things as they truly are, it is called 'wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhi). It has the characteristic of perverted seeing, in the manner of 'There is nothing given,' and so on. Like frivolous speech, it is of slight fault and of great fault. Moreover, the unfixed view is of slight fault; the fixed view is of great fault. It has two components: the perversion of the mode in which the object is grasped, and the presentation of that object in accordance with the mode in which it is grasped. Therein, the course of action is broken only by the nihilistic view, the view of non-causality, and the view of non-action; not by other views.

Imesaṃ pana dasannaṃ akusalakammapathānaṃ dhammato koṭṭhāsato ārammaṇato vedanāto mūlato cāti pañcahākārehi vinicchayo veditabbo –

Further, the determination of these ten unwholesome courses of action should be understood in five aspects: as to their nature, as to their division, as to their object, as to their feeling, and as to their root.

Tattha ‘dhammato’ti etesu hi paṭipāṭiyā satta cetanādhammāva honti, abhijjhādayo tayo cetanāsampayuttā.

Therein, as to 'nature': among these, seven in sequence are states of volition only; the three beginning with covetousness are associated with volition.

‘Koṭṭhāsato’ti paṭipāṭiyā satta, micchādiṭṭhi cāti ime aṭṭha kammapathā eva honti; no mūlāni. Abhijjhābyāpādā kammapathā ceva mūlāni ca. Abhijjhā hi mūlaṃ patvā ‘lobho akusalamūlaṃ’ hoti, byāpādo ‘doso akusalamūlaṃ’.

As to 'division': the seven in sequence and wrong view—these eight are only courses of action; they are not roots. Covetousness and ill will are both courses of action and roots. For covetousness, having reached the status of a root, becomes 'greed, an unwholesome root'; ill will becomes 'hatred, an unwholesome root'.

‘Ārammaṇato’ti pāṇātipāto jīvitindriyārammaṇato saṅkhārārammaṇo hoti. Adinnādānaṃ sattārammaṇaṃ vā hoti saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ vā. Micchācāro phoṭṭhabbavasena saṅkhārārammaṇo hoti; sattārammaṇotipi eke. Musāvādo sattārammaṇo vā, saṅkhārārammaṇo vā. Tathā pisuṇavācā. Pharusavācā [P 0.0102] sattārammaṇāva. Samphappalāpo diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena sattārammaṇo vā saṅkhārārammaṇo vā. Tathā abhijjhā. Byāpādo sattārammaṇova. Micchādiṭṭhi tebhūmakadhammavasena saṅkhārārammaṇāva.

As to 'object': Killing has formations as its object because its object is the life faculty. Taking what is not given has either a being or formations as its object. Sexual misconduct has formations as its object by way of the tangible; some say it also has a being as its object. False speech has either a being or formations as its object. So too, divisive speech. Harsh speech has only a being as its object. Frivolous speech has either a being or formations as its object by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. So too, covetousness. Ill will has only a being as its object. Wrong view has only formations as its object by way of the phenomena of the three planes.

‘Vedanāto’ti [M 0.0145] pāṇātipāto dukkhavedano hoti. Kiñcāpi hi rājāno coraṃ disvā hasamānāpi ‘gacchatha naṃ ghātethā’ti vadanti, sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā pana nesaṃ dukkhasampayuttāva hoti[V 0.0148]. Adinnādānaṃ tivedanaṃ. Tañhi parabhaṇḍaṃ disvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhassa gaṇhato sukhavedanaṃ hoti, bhītatasitassa gaṇhato dukkhavedanaṃ. Tathā vipākanissandaphalāni paccavekkhantassa. Gahaṇakāle majjhattabhāve ṭhitassa pana gaṇhato adukkhamasukhavedanaṃ hotīti. Micchācāro sukhamajjhattavasena dvivedano. Sanniṭṭhāpakacitte pana majjhattavedano na hoti. Musāvādo adinnādāne vuttanayeneva tivedano; tathā pisuṇavācā. Pharusavācā dukkhavedanā. Samphappalāpo tivedano. Paresu hi sādhukāraṃ dentesu celukkhepādīni khipantesu haṭṭhatuṭṭhassa sītāharaṇabhāratayuddhādīni kathanakāle so sukhavedano hoti. Paṭhamaṃ dinnavetanena ekena pacchā āgantvā ‘ādito paṭṭhāya kathehī’ti vutte ‘ananusandhikaṃ pakiṇṇakakathaṃ kathessāmi nu kho no’ti domanassitassa kathanakāle dukkhavedano hoti, majjhattassa kathayato adukkhamasukhavedano hoti. Abhijjhā sukhamajjhattavasena dvivedanā; tathā micchādiṭṭhi. Byāpādo dukkhavedano.

As to 'feeling': Killing is accompanied by painful feeling. For although kings, on seeing a thief, might say while laughing, 'Go and execute him,' their determining volition is in fact associated with pain. Taking what is not given is threefold as to feeling. For one who takes it, having seen another's property, with joy and delight, it is accompanied by pleasant feeling. For one who takes it with fear and terror, it is accompanied by painful feeling; likewise for one who reflects on the results and consequences. But for one who takes it while remaining in a state of neutrality at the time of taking, it is accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Sexual misconduct is twofold as to feeling, by way of pleasure and neutrality. But in the determining consciousness, it is not accompanied by neutral feeling. False speech is threefold as to feeling, in the way stated for taking what is not given; likewise divisive speech. Harsh speech is accompanied by painful feeling. Frivolous speech is threefold as to feeling. For when others are applauding, throwing up their cloths, and so on, for one who is joyful and delighted while recounting tales like the abduction of Sītā, the Bhārata war, and so on, it is accompanied by pleasant feeling. When someone who has already paid comes back later and says, 'Tell it from the beginning,' for one who is distressed, thinking, 'Should I tell this disconnected, miscellaneous story or not?', at the time of telling it is accompanied by painful feeling. For one who tells it with neutrality, it is accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Covetousness is twofold as to feeling, by way of pleasure and neutrality; likewise wrong view. Ill will is accompanied by painful feeling.

‘Mūlato’ti pāṇātipāto dosamohavasena dvimūlako hoti. Adinnādānaṃ dosamohavasena vā lobhamohavasena vā. Micchācāro lobhamohavasena. Musāvādo dosamohavasena vā lobhamohavasena vā; tathā pisuṇavācā samphappalāpo ca. Pharusavācā dosamohavasena. Abhijjhā mohavasena ekamūlā; tathā byāpādo. Micchādiṭṭhi lobhamohavasena dvimūlāti.

As to 'root': Killing has two roots, by way of hatred and delusion. Taking what is not given has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion. Sexual misconduct has two roots, by way of greed and delusion. False speech has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion; likewise divisive speech and frivolous speech. Harsh speech has two roots, by way of hatred and delusion. Covetousness has one root, by way of delusion; likewise ill will. Wrong view has two roots, by way of greed and delusion.

Akusalakammapathakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Unwholesome Courses of Action is concluded.

Kusalakammapathakathā

The Discourse on the Wholesome Courses of Action

Pāṇātipātādīhi pana viratiyo anabhijjhāabyāpādasammādiṭṭhiyo cāti ime dasa kusalakammapathā nāma. Tattha pāṇātipātādayo vuttatthā eva. Pāṇātipātādīhi etāya viramanti, sayaṃ vā viramati, viramaṇamattameva [M 0.0146] vā etanti virati. Yā pāṇātipātā viramantassa “yā tasmiṃ samaye pāṇātipātā ārati viratī”ti (dha. sa. 299-301) evaṃ vuttā kusalacittasampayuttā virati, sā pabhedato [P 0.0103] tividhā hoti – sampattavirati, samādānavirati, samucchedaviratīti.

Furthermore, the abstinences from the destruction of life and so forth, and non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—these are called the ten wholesome courses of action. Therein, the terms 'destruction of life' and so forth have meanings that have already been stated. Because by this state they abstain from the destruction of life and so forth, or it abstains by itself, or it is mere abstention—therefore, it is called 'abstinence'. That abstinence associated with a wholesome mind, spoken of for one who abstains from the destruction of life, as stated: 'Whatever at that time is abstention, refraining... from the destruction of life,' is threefold by classification: abstinence by occasion, abstinence by undertaking, and abstinence by eradication.

Tattha [V 0.0149] asamādinnasikkhāpadānaṃ attano jātivayabāhusaccādīni paccavekkhitvā ‘ayuttaṃ amhākaṃ evarūpaṃ pāpaṃ kātu’nti sampattaṃ vatthuṃ avītikkamantānaṃ uppajjamānā virati ‘sampattaviratī’ti veditabbā – sīhaḷadīpe cakkanaupāsakassa viya. Tassa kira daharakāleyeva mātuyā rogo uppajji. Vejjena ca ‘allasasamaṃsaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti vuttaṃ. Tato cakkanassa bhātā ‘gaccha, tāta, khettaṃ āhiṇḍāhī’ti cakkanaṃ pesesi. So tattha gato. Tasmiñca samaye eko saso taruṇasassaṃ khādituṃ āgato hoti. So taṃ disvāva vegena dhāvanto valliyā baddho ‘kiri kirī’ti saddamakāsi. Cakkano tena saddena gantvā taṃ gahetvā cintesi – ‘mātu bhesajjaṃ karomī’ti. Puna cintesi – ‘na metaṃ patirūpaṃ yvāhaṃ mātu jīvitakāraṇā paraṃ jīvitā voropeyya’nti. Atha naṃ ‘gaccha, araññe sasehi saddhiṃ tiṇodakaṃ paribhuñjā’ti muñci. Bhātarā ca ‘kiṃ tāta saso laddho’ti pucchito taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Tato naṃ bhātā paribhāsi. So mātusantikaṃ gantvā ‘yato ahaṃ jāto nābhijānāmi sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetā’ti saccaṃ vatvā aṭṭhāsi. Tāvadevassa mātā arogā ahosi.

Therein, for those who have not undertaken the training precepts, the abstinence that arises in those who, having reflected on their own birth, age, learning, and so forth, think, 'It is not suitable for us to do such an evil thing,' and do not transgress against an object that has presented itself, should be known as 'abstinence by occasion'—like that of the layman Cakkana on the island of Sīhaḷa. It is said that when he was still young, his mother fell ill. A physician said, 'It is necessary to get fresh rabbit meat.' Then Cakkana's brother sent him, saying, 'Go, my dear, and search the field.' He went there. At that time, a certain hare had come to eat the young grain. Seeing him, it ran with speed, but was caught in a vine and made a 'kiri-kiri' sound. Hearing that sound, Cakkana went and caught it, and thought, 'I will make medicine for my mother.' Again he thought, 'It is not suitable for me that I, for the sake of my mother's life, should deprive another of life.' Then, saying, 'Go, enjoy grass and water in the forest with the other hares,' he released it. When asked by his brother, 'My dear, did you get a hare?' he related what had happened. Then his brother scolded him. He went to his mother and, making an asseveration of truth, stood there and said: 'From the time I was born, I am not aware of ever having intentionally deprived a living being of life.' At that very moment, his mother became free from illness.

Samādinnasikkhāpadānaṃ pana sikkhāpadasamādāne ca tatuttariñca attano jīvitampi pariccajitvā vatthuṃ avītikkamantānaṃ uppajjamānā virati ‘samādānaviratī’ti veditabbā. Uttaravaḍḍhamānapabbatavāsīupāsakassa viya. So kira ambariyavihāravāsino piṅgalabuddharakkhitattherassa santike sikkhāpadāni gahetvā khettaṃ kasati. Athassa goṇo naṭṭho. So taṃ gavesanto uttaravaḍḍhamānapabbataṃ āruhi. Tatra naṃ mahāsappo aggahesi. So cintesi – ‘imāyassa tikhiṇavāsiyā sīsaṃ chindāmī’ti. Puna cintesi – ‘na metaṃ patirūpaṃ yvāhaṃ bhāvanīyassa garuno santike sikkhāpadāni gahetvā bhindeyya’nti evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ cintetvā [M 0.0147] ‘jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, na sikkhāpada’nti aṃse ṭhapitaṃ tikhiṇadaṇḍavāsiṃ araññe chaḍḍesi. Tāvadeva naṃ mahāvāḷo muñcitvā agamāsīti.

Furthermore, for those who have undertaken the training precepts, the abstinence that arises in those who—both at the time of undertaking the training precept and thereafter—do not transgress against the object even by giving up their own life, should be known as 'abstinence by undertaking.' Like that of the layman who dwelt on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna. It is said that he, having taken the training precepts from the Elder Piṅgalabuddharakkhita, who dwelt in the Ambariya monastery, was ploughing his field. Then his ox was lost. Searching for it, he climbed Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna. There a great serpent seized him. He thought, 'I will cut off its head with this sharp axe.' Again he thought, 'It is not suitable for me that I, having taken the training precepts in the presence of a venerable teacher, should break them.' Having thought thus up to the third time, he resolved, 'I shall give up my life, but not the training precept,' and threw the sharp-handled axe that was on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the great beast released him and went away.

Ariyamaggasampayuttā [P 0.0104] pana virati ‘samucchedaviratī’ti veditabbā, yassā uppattito pabhuti ‘pāṇaṃ ghātessāmī’ti ariyapuggalānaṃ cittampi nuppajjatīti.

Furthermore, the abstinence associated with the noble path should be known as 'abstinence by eradication,' because from the time of its arising, not even the thought 'I will destroy a living being' arises in noble persons.

Idāni [V 0.0150] yathā akusalānaṃ evaṃ imesampi kusalakammapathānaṃ dhammato koṭṭhāsato ārammaṇato vedanāto mūlatoti pañcahākārehi vinicchayo veditabbo –

Now, just as for the unwholesome courses of action, so also for these wholesome courses of action, the determination should be understood in five aspects: as to nature, as to components, as to object, as to feeling, and as to root.

Tattha ‘dhammato’ti etesu hi paṭipāṭiyā satta cetanāpi vaṭṭanti, viratiyopi; ante tayo cetanāsampayuttāva.

Therein, regarding ‘by nature’: among these, for the first seven in sequence, they are applicable as volitions and as abstinences; the last three are only associated with volition.

‘Koṭṭhāsato’ti paṭipāṭiyā satta kammapathā eva, no mūlāni. Ante tayo kammapathā ceva mūlāni ca. Anabhijjhā hi mūlaṃ patvā ‘alobho kusalamūlaṃ’ hoti. Abyāpādo ‘adoso kusalamūlaṃ’, sammādiṭṭhi ‘amoho kusalamūlaṃ’.

Regarding ‘by components’: in sequence, the first seven are only courses of action, not roots. The last three are both courses of action and roots. Indeed, non-covetousness, having reached the state of a root, becomes ‘non-greed, a wholesome root.’ Non-ill will becomes ‘non-hatred, a wholesome root,’ and right view becomes ‘non-delusion, a wholesome root.’

‘Ārammaṇato’ti pāṇātipātādīnaṃ ārammaṇāneva etesaṃ ārammaṇāni. Vītikkamitabbatoyeva hi veramaṇī nāma hoti. Yathā pana nibbānārammaṇo ariyamaggo kilese pajahati, evaṃ jīvitindriyādiārammaṇāpete kammapathā pāṇātipātādīni dussīlyāni pajahantīti veditabbā.

Regarding ‘by object’: the very objects of the destruction of life and so forth are the objects of these wholesome courses. For abstention is so-called precisely in relation to that which is to be transgressed. Furthermore, just as the noble path, which has Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so it should be known that these courses of action, which have the life-faculty and so forth as their objects, abandon immoralities such as the destruction of life.

‘Vedanāto’ti sabbe sukhavedanā vā honti majjhattavedanā vā. Kusalaṃ patvā hi dukkhavedanā nāma natthi.

Regarding ‘by feeling’: all are accompanied either by pleasant feeling or by neutral feeling. For, having reached the wholesome sphere, there is no such thing as painful feeling.

‘Mūlato’ti paṭipāṭiyā satta kammapathā ñāṇasampayuttacittena viramantassa alobhaadosaamohavasena timūlā honti; ñāṇavippayuttacittena viramantassa dvimūlā. Anabhijjhā ñāṇasampayuttacittena viramantassa dvimūlā hoti; ñāṇavippayuttacittena ekamūlā. Alobho pana attanāva attano mūlaṃ na hoti. Abyāpādepi eseva nayo. Sammādiṭṭhi alobhādosavasena dvimūlāva hoti. Ime dasa kusalakammapathā nāma.

Regarding ‘by root’: in sequence, for one who abstains with a mind associated with knowledge, the first seven courses of action are three-rooted by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; for one who abstains with a mind dissociated from knowledge, they are two-rooted. For one who abstains with a mind associated with knowledge, non-covetousness is two-rooted; for one who abstains with a mind dissociated from knowledge, it is one-rooted. Furthermore, non-greed is not its own root. This same principle applies to non-ill will. Right view is always two-rooted, by way of non-greed and non-hatred. These are called the ten wholesome courses of action.

Kammapathasaṃsandanakathā

The Discourse on the Coherence of the Courses of Action

Idāni [M 0.0148] imasmiṃ ṭhāne kammapathasaṃsandanaṃ nāma veditabbaṃ. Pañcaphassadvāravasena hi uppanno asaṃvaro akusalaṃ manokammameva hoti. Manophassadvāravasena uppanno tīṇipi kammāni [V 0.0151] honti – so hi kāyadvāre copanappatto akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ hoti, vacīdvāre akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, ubhayattha copanaṃ appatto akusalaṃ manokammaṃ. Pañcaasaṃvaradvāravasena uppannopi akusalaṃ manokammameva hoti. Copanakāyaasaṃvaradvāravasena uppanno akusalaṃ kāyakammameva hoti, vācāasaṃvaradvāravasena uppanno akusalaṃ vacīkammameva hoti, manoasaṃvaradvāravasena uppanno [P 0.0105] akusalaṃ manokammameva hoti. Tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammameva hoti, catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ akusalaṃ vacīkammameva hoti, tividhaṃ manoduccaritaṃ akusalaṃ manokammameva hoti.

Now, at this point, what is called the coherence of the courses of action should be understood. For unrestraint that has arisen by way of the five sense-impression doors is only unwholesome mental action. That which has arisen by way of the mind-impression door becomes all three kinds of action: for when it has reached a state of impulsion at the body-door, it becomes unwholesome bodily action; at the speech-door, it becomes unwholesome verbal action; and when it has not reached a state of impulsion at both, it is unwholesome mental action. Even that which has arisen by way of the five doors of non-restraint is only unwholesome mental action. That which has arisen by way of the door of non-restraint involving bodily impulsion is only unwholesome bodily action; that which has arisen by way of the door of non-restraint of speech is only unwholesome verbal action; and that which has arisen by way of the door of non-restraint of mind is only unwholesome mental action. The three kinds of bodily misconduct are only unwholesome bodily action, the four kinds of verbal misconduct are only unwholesome verbal action, and the three kinds of mental misconduct are only unwholesome mental action.

Pañcaphassadvāravasena uppanno saṃvaropi kusalaṃ manokammameva hoti. Manophassadvāravasena uppanno pana ayampi, asaṃvaro viya, tīṇipi kammāni honti. Pañcasaṃvaradvāravasena uppannopi kusalaṃ manokammameva hoti, copanakāyasaṃvaradvāravasena uppanno kusalaṃ kāyakammameva hoti, vācāsaṃvaradvāravasena uppanno kusalaṃ vacīkammameva hoti, manosaṃvaradvāravasena uppanno kusalaṃ manokammameva hoti. Tividhaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ kusalaṃ kāyakammameva hoti, catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritaṃ kusalaṃ vacīkammameva hoti, tividhaṃ manosucaritaṃ kusalaṃ manokammameva hoti.

Restraint that has arisen by way of the five sense-impression doors is also only wholesome mental action. Furthermore, this restraint that has arisen by way of the mind-impression door, like unrestraint, becomes all three kinds of action. Even restraint that has arisen by way of the five doors of restraint is only wholesome mental action. That which has arisen by way of the door of restraint involving bodily impulsion is only wholesome bodily action; that which has arisen by way of the door of restraint of speech is only wholesome verbal action; and that which has arisen by way of the door of restraint of mind is only wholesome mental action. The three kinds of bodily good conduct are only wholesome bodily action, the four kinds of verbal good conduct are only wholesome verbal action, and the three kinds of mental good conduct are only wholesome mental action.

Akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ pañcaphassadvāravasena nuppajjati; manophassadvāravaseneva uppajjati. Tathā akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ. Akusalaṃ manokammaṃ pana chaphassadvāravasena uppajjati; taṃ kāyavacīdvāresu copanaṃ pattaṃ akusalaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ hoti, copanaṃ appattaṃ akusalaṃ manokammameva. Yathā ca pañcaphassadvāravasena, evaṃ pañcaasaṃvaradvāravasenapi akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ nuppajjati, copanakāyaasaṃvaradvāravasena pana vācāasaṃvaradvāravasena ca uppajjati; manoasaṃvaradvāravasena nuppajjati. Akusalaṃ vacīkammampi pañcaasaṃvaradvāravasena nuppajjati, copanakāyavācāasaṃvaradvāravasena uppajjati; manoasaṃvaradvāravasena nuppajjati. Akusalaṃ manokammaṃ aṭṭhaasaṃvaradvāravasenapi uppajjateva. Kusalakāyakammādīsupi eseva nayo.

Unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five sense-impression doors; it arises only by way of the mind-impression door. The same applies to unwholesome verbal action. Unwholesome mental action, however, arises by way of the six sense-impression doors. When that has reached a state of impulsion at the body and speech doors, it becomes unwholesome bodily and verbal action; when it has not reached a state of impulsion, it is only unwholesome mental action. And just as unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five sense-impression doors, so too it does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint. However, it arises by way of the door of non-restraint involving bodily impulsion and by way of the door of non-restraint of speech; it does not arise by way of the door of non-restraint of mind. Unwholesome verbal action also does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint; it arises by way of the doors of non-restraint involving bodily impulsion and of speech; it does not arise by way of the door of non-restraint of mind. Unwholesome mental action certainly arises also by way of the eight doors of non-restraint. This is the same principle for wholesome bodily action and so on.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0149] pana viseso – yathā akusalakāyakammavacīkammāni manoasaṃvaradvāravasena nuppajjanti, na tathā etāni. Etāni pana kāyaṅgavācaṅgaṃ acopetvā sikkhāpadāni gaṇhantassa manosaṃvaradvārepi uppajjanti eva. Tattha kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ tividhakammadvāravasena uppajjati, pañcaviññāṇadvāravasena nuppajjati; ‘yamidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā [V 0.0152] uppajjati vedayitaṃ, sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā’ti iminā pana nayena chaphassadvāravasena uppajjati; aṭṭhaasaṃvaradvāravasena nuppajjati, aṭṭhasaṃvaradvāravasena uppajjati; dasaakusalakammapathavasena [P 0.0106] nuppajjati, dasakusalakammapathavasena uppajjati; tasmā idampi cittaṃ tividhakammadvāravasena vā uppannaṃ hotu, chaphassadvāravasena vā, aṭṭhasaṃvaradvāravasena vā dasakusalakammapathavasena vā. “Kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti…pe… rūpārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… dhammārammaṇaṃ vā”ti vutte sabbaṃ vuttameva hotīti.

This, however, is the distinction: it is not so with these wholesome actions as it is with the unwholesome bodily and verbal actions that do not arise by way of the door of non-restraint of mind. For these wholesome actions certainly arise also at the door of restraint of mind for one who undertakes the training rules without agitating the bodily and verbal faculties. Therein, wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises by way of the three kinds of action-doors; it does not arise by way of the five consciousness-doors. However, by this principle, ‘Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-impression—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant,’ it arises by way of the six sense-impression doors. It does not arise by way of the eight doors of non-restraint; it arises by way of the eight doors of restraint. It does not arise by way of the ten unwholesome courses of action; it arises by way of the ten wholesome courses of action. Therefore, whether this consciousness has arisen by way of the three kinds of action-doors, or by way of the six sense-impression doors, or by way of the eight doors of restraint, or by way of the ten wholesome courses of action, when it is said, ‘Wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen… with a visible object… or… with a mental object as its object,’ all of it is indeed said.

Dvārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Doors is concluded.

Yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbhāti ettha ayaṃ yojanā – heṭṭhā vuttesu rūpārammaṇādīsu rūpārammaṇaṃ vā ārabbha, ārammaṇaṃ katvāti attho. Saddārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… dhammārammaṇaṃ vā ārabbha uppannaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā etassa cittassa etesu ārammaṇesu yaṃkiñci ekameva ārammaṇaṃ anuññātasadisaṃ hoti. Idañca ekasmiṃ samaye ekassa vā puggalassa rūpārammaṇaṃ ārabbha uppannaṃ puna aññasmiṃ samaye aññassa vā puggalassa saddādīsupi aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārabbha uppajjati eva. Evaṃ uppajjamānassa cassa ekasmiṃ bhave paṭhamaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ ārabbha pavatti hoti, pacchā saddārammaṇanti ayampi kamo natthi. Rūpādīsu cāpi paṭhamaṃ nīlārammaṇaṃ pacchā pītārammaṇanti ayampi niyamo natthi. Iti imaṃ sabbārammaṇatañceva, kamābhāvañca, kamābhāvepi ca nīlapītādīsu niyamābhāvaṃ dassetuṃ ‘yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbhā’ti āha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – imesu rūpādīsu na yaṃkiñci ekameva, atha kho yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha uppannaṃ hoti. Evaṃ uppajjamānampi ca ‘paṭhamaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ pacchā saddārammaṇaṃ ārabbhā’ti evampi anuppajjitvā yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha uppannaṃ hoti; ‘paṭilomato vā anulomato vā, ekantarikadvantarikādinayena vā, rūpārammaṇādīsu yaṃ vā taṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaṃ hotī’ti attho. Rūpārammaṇesupi ca ‘paṭhamaṃ [M 0.0150] nīlārammaṇaṃ pacchā pītārammaṇa’nti imināpi niyamena anuppajjitvā, yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha ‘nīlapītakādīsu rūpārammaṇesu yaṃ vā taṃ vā rūpārammaṇaṃ ārabbha uppannaṃ hotī’ti attho. Saddārammaṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ tāva ekā yojanā.

Regarding 'yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha' (or whatever it may be that it arises in dependence upon), this is the explanation: Among the form-objects and so on mentioned below, it arises taking a form-object as its object; the meaning is 'having made it an object.' Or it arises taking a sound-object... or... a mind-object as its object. By this much, it is as if only some single object whatsoever among these objects is permitted for this consciousness. And this consciousness, having arisen at one time for one person taking a form-object as its object, can indeed arise again at another time for another person taking as its object any one of the sound-objects and so on. And for this consciousness arising thus, there is no such sequence in one existence that its occurrence is first by taking a form-object as object and afterwards a sound-object. And also among forms and so on, there is no such rule that it is first a blue object and afterwards a yellow object. Thus, to show this state of having all objects, the absence of sequence, and also, even in the absence of sequence, the absence of a rule among blue, yellow, and so on, He said, 'yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha.' This is what is meant: among these forms and so on, it is not that it arises taking as object just any single one, but rather it arises taking as object whatsoever it may be. And even when arising thus, it does not arise in a way such as 'first taking a form-object, afterwards a sound-object'; rather, it arises taking as object whatsoever it may be. The meaning is: 'it arises having made as its object whatever it may be among form-objects and so on, whether in reverse order or in forward order, or by the method of skipping one, skipping two, and so on.' And also among form-objects, it does not arise by this rule, 'first a blue object, afterwards a yellow object'; rather, it arises taking as object whatsoever it may be. The meaning is: 'it arises taking as its object whatever form-object it may be among the blue, yellow, and other form-objects.' For sound-objects and so on, this is the same method. This, for now, is one explanation.

Ayaṃ pana aparā – rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etassāti rūpārammaṇaṃ…pe… dhammo ārammaṇaṃ etassāti [V 0.0153] dhammārammaṇaṃ[P 0.0107]. Iti rūpārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… dhammārammaṇaṃ vā cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotīti vatvā puna ‘yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbhā’ti āha. Tassattho – etesu rūpādīsu heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yaṃ vā taṃ vā pana ārabbha uppannaṃ hotīti. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana yevāpanake abhinavaṃ natthi, heṭṭhā gahitameva gahita’nti vatvā ‘rūpaṃ vā ārabbha…pe… dhammaṃ vā ārabbha, idaṃ vā idaṃ vā ārabbhāti kathetuṃ idaṃ vutta’nti ettakameva āgataṃ.

But this is another explanation: 'Form is its object,' hence it is 'rūpārammaṇa' (having form as object)... 'Dhamma is its object,' hence it is 'dhammārammaṇa' (having Dhamma as object). Thus, having said, 'The consciousness that has form as its object... or that has Dhamma as its object arises,' He again said, 'yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha.' The meaning of this is: among these forms and so on, it arises taking as its object whatever it may be, by the very method spoken of above. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, regarding the 'yevāpanaka' section, only this much has come down: having said, 'There is nothing new; what was taken up above is simply taken up again,' it states, 'This was said in order to declare: "taking form as object... or taking Dhamma as object, or taking this or that as object".'

Dhammuddesavāro

The Section on the Exposition of Dhammas

Phassapañcamakarāsivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Group of Five beginning with Contact

Tasmiṃ samayeti idaṃ aniyamaniddiṭṭhassa samayassa niyamato paṭiniddesavacanaṃ. Tasmā ‘yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva samaye phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hotī’ti ayamattho veditabbo. Tattha yatheva cittaṃ evaṃ phassādīsupi phasso hoti. Kiṃ hoti? ‘Kāmāvacaro hoti, kusalo hoti, uppanno hoti, somanassasahagato hotī’tiādinā nayena labbhamānapadavasena yojanā kātabbā. Vedanāyañhi ‘somanassasahagatā’ti paññindriye ca ‘ñāṇasampayutta’nti na labbhati, tasmā ‘labbhamānapadavasenā’ti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ aṭṭhakathāmuttakaṃ ācariyānaṃ mataṃ; na panetaṃ sārato daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The phrase 'tasmiṃ samaye' (at that time) is a statement that specifically re-indicates the time that was indicated without specification [by 'yasmiṃ samaye']. Therefore, this meaning should be understood: 'At whatever time a sense-sphere wholesome consciousness has arisen, at that very time there is contact... and so on... there is non-distraction.' Therein, just as the consciousness is, so also among contact and the other factors, contact is. What is it? The connection should be made according to the obtainable terms by the method of 'it is of the sense-sphere, it is wholesome, it has arisen, it is accompanied by joy,' and so on. For in the case of feeling, the term 'accompanied by joy' is not obtained, and in the case of the wisdom faculty, the term 'associated with knowledge' is not obtained. Therefore, it was said 'according to the obtainable terms.' This is the view of the teachers, independent of the ancient commentaries; but this should not be regarded as the essential meaning.

Kasmā panettha phassova paṭhamaṃ vuttoti? Cittassa paṭhamābhinipātattā. Ārammaṇasmiñhi cittassa paṭhamābhinipāto hutvā phasso ārammaṇaṃ phusamāno uppajjati, tasmā paṭhamaṃ vutto. Phassena pana phusitvā vedanāya vedayati, saññāya sañjānāti, cetanāya ceteti. Tena vuttaṃ – “phuṭṭho, bhikkhave, vedeti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti phuṭṭho cetetī”ti.

Why here is only contact mentioned first? Because it is the first impact of consciousness. For contact arises touching the object, being the first impact of consciousness on the object; therefore, it is mentioned first. But having touched with contact, one feels with feeling, one perceives with perception, and one wills with volition. For that reason it was said: 'Being touched, O monks, one feels; being touched, one perceives; being touched, one wills.'

Apica[M 0.0151], ayaṃ phasso nāma yathā pāsādaṃ patvā thambho nāma sesadabbasambhārānaṃ balavapaccayo, tulāsaṅghāṭabhittipādakūṭagopānasīpakkhapāsakamukhavaṭṭiyo thambhābaddhā thambhe patiṭṭhitā, evameva sahajātasampayuttadhammānaṃ balavapaccayo hoti. Thambhasadiso hi esa. Avasesā dabbasambhārasadisāti. Tasmāpi paṭhamaṃ vutto. Idaṃ pana akāraṇaṃ. Ekacittasmiñhi uppannadhammānaṃ ‘ayaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppanno ayaṃ pacchā’ti idaṃ vattuṃ na labbhā. Balavapaccayabhāvepi phassassa kāraṇaṃ na [V 0.0154] dissati. Desanāvāreneva pana [P 0.0108] phasso paṭhamaṃ vutto. Vedanā hoti phasso hoti, saññā hoti phasso hoti, cetanā hoti phasso hoti, cittaṃ hoti phasso hoti, vedanā hoti saññā hoti, cetanā hoti vitakko hotīti āharitumpi hi vaṭṭeyya. Desanāvārena pana phassova paṭhamaṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Yathā cettha evaṃ sesadhammesupi pubbāparakkamo nāma na pariyesitabbo. Vacanatthalakkhaṇarasādīhi pana dhammā eva pariyesitabbā.

Furthermore, this so-called contact is a strong condition for its co-arisen and associated states, just as in a palace a pillar is a strong condition for the other building materials—the beams, tie-beams, wall-bases, pinnacles, rafters, side-planks, and architraves are bound to the pillar and established on the pillar. For this contact is like the pillar, and the remaining states are like the building materials. For this reason, too, it is mentioned first. But this is not a valid reason. For, regarding states that have arisen in a single consciousness-moment, it is not possible to say, 'This one arose first, this one later.' Even with regard to contact's being a strong condition, a reason for its primacy is not seen. Rather, contact is mentioned first simply by the turn of the discourse. For it would also be proper to present it as: 'There is feeling, there is contact'; 'There is perception, there is contact'; 'There is volition, there is contact'; 'There is consciousness, there is contact'; 'There is feeling, there is perception'; 'There is volition, there is applied thought.' But it should be understood that contact is mentioned first simply by the turn of the discourse. And just as here, so also in the remaining states, a sequence of prior and posterior should not be sought. Rather, the dhammas should be investigated only by way of their verbal meaning, characteristic, function, and so on.

Seyyathidaṃ – phusatīti phasso. Svāyaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo, saṅghaṭṭanaraso, sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno, āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno.

As follows: 'It touches' (phusati), hence it is 'contact' (phasso). This contact has touching as its characteristic, impact as its function, conjunction as its manifestation, and an object that has come into range as its proximate cause.

Ayañhi arūpadhammopi samāno ārammaṇe phusanākāreneva pavattatīti phusanalakkhaṇo. Ekadesena ca anallīyamānopi rūpaṃ viya cakkhuṃ, saddo viya ca sotaṃ, cittaṃ ārammaṇañca saṅghaṭṭetīti saṅghaṭṭanaraso. Vatthārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanato vā uppannattā sampattiatthenapi rasena saṅghaṭṭanarasoti veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ – “catubhūmakaphasso hi nophusanalakkhaṇo nāma natthi. Saṅghaṭṭanaraso pana pañcadvārikova hoti. Pañcadvārikassa hi phusanalakkhaṇotipi saṅghaṭṭanarasotipi nāmaṃ; manodvārikassa phusanalakkhaṇotveva nāmaṃ, na saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti.

Indeed, even though this is an immaterial phenomenon, it occurs only in the mode of touching the object; thus, it has the characteristic of touching. And though not completely adhering, it strikes consciousness and the object, like form striking the eye or sound striking the ear; thus, its function is impact. Or, because it arises from the impact of the base and object, it should be understood that by its function, which also has the meaning of accomplishment, it has the function of impact. For this was stated in the commentary: “Indeed, there is no contact in the four planes that is not named as having the characteristic of touching. However, the function of impact is only the five-door contact. For the five-door contact, its name is both ‘characteristic of touching’ and ‘function of impact’; for the mind-door contact, its name is only ‘characteristic of touching,’ not ‘function of impact.’”

Idañca vatvā idaṃ suttaṃ ābhataṃ – “yathā, mahārāja, dve meṇḍā yujjheyyuṃ, tesu yathā eko meṇḍo evaṃ cakkhu daṭṭhabbaṃ, yathā dutiyo meṇḍo evaṃ rūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ; yathā tesaṃ sannipāto evaṃ phasso daṭṭhabbo”. Evaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo ca phasso, saṅghaṭṭanaraso ca. “Yathā, mahārāja, dve [M 0.0152] sammā vajjeyyuṃ…pe… dve pāṇī vajjeyyuṃ, yathā eko pāṇi evaṃ cakkhu daṭṭhabbaṃ, yathā dutiyo pāṇi evaṃ rūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, yathā tesaṃ sannipāto evaṃ phasso daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo ca phasso saṅghaṭṭanaraso cā”ti (mi. pa. 2.3.8) vitthāro.

And having said this, this Sutta was brought forth: “Just as, great king, two rams might fight; among them, as one ram is, so the eye should be regarded; as the second ram is, so form should be regarded; as their coming together is, so contact should be regarded.” Thus, contact has both the characteristic of touching and the function of impact. “Just as, great king, two cymbals might be sounded… and so on… two hands might be clapped; as one hand is, so the eye should be regarded; as the second hand is, so form should be regarded; as their coming together is, so contact should be regarded. Thus, contact has both the characteristic of touching and the function of impact.” (Milindapañha 2.3.8) This is the detailed account.

Yathā vā “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1352, 1354) cakkhuviññāṇādīni cakkhuādināmena vuttāni, evamidhāpi tāni cakkhuādināmena vuttānīti veditabbāni. Tasmā ‘evaṃ cakkhu daṭṭhabba’ntiādīsu evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbanti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Evaṃ sante cittārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanato [P 0.0109] imasmimpi sutte kiccaṭṭheneva rasena saṅghaṭṭanarasoti siddho hoti.

Or, just as in passages such as “having seen a form with the eye” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1352, 1354), eye-consciousness and so on are spoken of by the name ‘eye’ and so on, so also here it should be understood that they are spoken of by the name ‘eye’ and so on. Therefore, in passages such as ‘thus the eye should be regarded,’ the meaning should be understood according to this method: ‘thus eye-consciousness should be regarded.’ This being so, because of the impact of consciousness and object, in this Sutta also, it is established that by its function, which has the meaning of function, it has the function of impact.

Tikasannipātasaṅkhātassa [V 0.0155] pana attano kāraṇassa vasena paveditattā sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno. Ayañhi tattha tattha “tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”ti evaṃ kāraṇassa vasena paveditoti. Imassa ca suttapadassa tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā phassoti ayamattho; na saṅgatimattameva phassoti.

Furthermore, because it is made known by the power of its own cause, which is called the conjunction of the triad, it has conjunction as its manifestation. For this contact is made known here and there by the power of its cause as “the coming together of the three is contact.” And of this Sutta passage, this is the meaning: contact is because of the coming together of the three; the meaning is not that mere coming together is contact.

Evaṃ paveditattā pana tenevākārena paccupaṭṭhātīti sannipātapaccupaṭṭhānoti vutto. Phalaṭṭhena pana paccupaṭṭhānenesa vedanāpaccupaṭṭhāno nāma hoti. Vedanañhesa paccupaṭṭhāpeti uppādetīti attho. Uppādayamāno ca yathā bahiddhā uṇhapaccayāpi lākhāsaṅkhātadhātunissitā usmā attano nissaye mudubhāvakārī hoti, na attano paccayabhūtepi bahiddhā vītaccitaṅgārasaṅkhāte uṇhabhāve, evaṃ vatthārammaṇasaṅkhātaaññapaccayopi samāno, cittanissitattā attano nissayabhūte citte eva esa vedanuppādako hoti, na attano paccayabhūtepi vatthumhi ārammaṇe vāti veditabbo. Tajjāsamannāhārena pana indriyena ca parikkhate visaye anantarāyena uppajjanato esa āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhānoti vuccati.

Furthermore, because it is made known in this way, it manifests in that very mode, and so it is said to have conjunction as its manifestation. By its manifestation which has the meaning of result, however, this contact is named ‘having feeling as its manifestation.’ For it causes feeling to manifest—that is, it produces it. And in producing it, just as heat, which is dependent on the substance called lac and has an external cause, produces softness in its own support, but not in its own cause, the external heat in the form of flameless embers; so too, this contact, though having other causes, namely the base and object, because it is dependent on consciousness, produces feeling only in consciousness, its own support, and not in its own causes, the base or the object—this should be understood. Furthermore, because it arises without obstruction in an object that is prepared by the faculty and by the appropriate attention born of that, it is said to have an object that has come into range as its proximate cause.

Vedayatīti vedanā. Sā vedayitalakkhaṇā, anubhavanarasā iṭṭhākārasambhogarasā vā, cetasikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānā, passaddhipadaṭṭhānā.

It feels, thus it is feeling. It has the characteristic of being experienced, the function of experiencing or the function of enjoying the agreeable aspect of an object, the manifestation as mental delight, and tranquility as its proximate cause.

‘Catubhūmikavedanā [M 0.0153] hi novedayitalakkhaṇā nāma natthi. Anubhavanarasatā pana sukhavedanāyameva labbhatī’ti vatvā puna taṃ vādaṃ paṭikkhipitvā ‘sukhavedanā vā hotu, dukkhavedanā vā, adukkhamasukhavedanā vā, sabbā anubhavanarasā’ti vatvā ayamattho dīpito – ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā sesasampayuttadhammā ekadesamattakameva anubhavanti. Phassassa hi phusanamattakameva hoti, saññāya sañjānanamattakameva, cetanāya cetanāmattakameva, viññāṇassa vijānanamattakameva. Ekaṃsato pana issaravatāya vissavitāya sāmibhāvena vedanāva ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavati.

“Indeed, there is no feeling of the four planes that is not named as having the characteristic of being experienced. The state of having the function of experiencing, however, is obtained only in pleasant feeling.” Having stated this, and then having refuted that view, this meaning was clarified by saying, “Be it pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, all have the function of experiencing”: Having come to the position of experiencing the savor of the object, the remaining associated states experience only a mere portion. For contact, there is only mere touching; for perception, there is only mere perceiving; for volition, there is only mere willing; for consciousness, there is only mere cognizing. However, certainly, by way of its sovereignty, competence, and mastery, feeling alone experiences the savor of the object.

Rājā viya hi vedanā, sūdo viya sesadhammā. Yathā sūdo nānārasabhojanaṃ sampādetvā peḷāya pakkhipitvā lañchanaṃ datvā rañño santike otāretvā lañchanaṃ bhinditvā peḷaṃ vivaritvā sabbasūpabyañjanehi aggaggaṃ [P 0.0110] ādāya bhājane pakkhipitvā sadosaniddosabhāvavīmaṃsanatthaṃ ajjhoharati, tato rañño nānaggarasabhojanaṃ upanāmeti. Rājā issaravatāya vissavitāya [V 0.0156] sāmī hutvā icchiticchitaṃ bhuñjati. Tattha hi sūdassa bhattavīmaṃsanamattamiva avasesadhammānaṃ ārammaṇarasassa ekadesānubhavanaṃ. Yathā hi sūdo bhattekadesamattameva vīmaṃsati evaṃ sesadhammāpi ārammaṇarasekadesameva anubhavanti. Yathā pana rājā issaravatāya vissavitāya sāmī hutvā yadicchakaṃ bhuñjati, evaṃ vedanāpi issaravatāya vissavitāya sāmibhāvena ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavati. Tasmā anubhavanarasāti vuccati.

For feeling is like a king, and the remaining states are like a cook. Just as a cook, having prepared a meal of various savors, placed it in a container, applied a seal, and set it down in the king’s presence, breaks the seal, opens the container, takes the choicest portions from all the curries and sauces, places them in a vessel, and consumes them for the purpose of investigating their quality, whether faulty or faultless, and then presents the meal of various excellent savors to the king. The king, being the master, eats what he desires by way of his sovereignty and competence. In this simile, the experiencing of a portion of the object’s savor by the remaining states is like the cook’s mere tasting of the food. For just as the cook investigates only a mere portion of the food, so too the remaining states experience only a mere portion of the object’s savor. But just as the king, being the master, eats as he wishes by way of his sovereignty and competence, so too feeling, by way of its sovereignty, competence, and mastery, experiences the savor of the object. Therefore, it is said to have the function of experiencing.

Dutiye atthavikappe ayaṃ idha adhippetā vedanā yathā vā tathā vā ārammaṇassa iṭṭhākārameva sambhuñjatīti iṭṭhākārasambhogarasāti vuttā. Cetasikaassādato panesā attano sabhāveneva upaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya cetasikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānāti vuttā. Yasmā pana “passaddhikāyo sukhaṃ vedeti” tasmā passaddhipadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

In the second interpretation, the feeling intended here, in whatever way it occurs, enjoys only the agreeable aspect of the object. Thus, it is said to have the function of enjoying the agreeable aspect. Furthermore, it is said to have mental delight as its manifestation, with reference to its manifestation by its own nature as a mental delight.
