And since it is said, “One whose body is tranquil feels pleasure,” it should be understood as having tranquility as its proximate cause.

Nīlādibhedaṃ ārammaṇaṃ sañjānātīti saññā. Sā sañjānanalakkhaṇā paccābhiññāṇarasā. Catubhūmikasaññā hi nosañjānanalakkhaṇā nāma natthi[M 0.0154]. Sabbā sañjānanalakkhaṇāva. Yā panettha abhiññāṇena sañjānāti sā paccābhiññāṇarasā nāma hoti.

Perception (saññā) is so called because it perceives an object differentiated as blue, and so on. It has the characteristic of perceiving and the function of recognition. Indeed, there is no perception in the four planes that is without the characteristic of perceiving. All perception has the characteristic of perceiving. Among these, that perception which perceives by means of a sign is called 'having the function of recognition'.

Tassā, vaḍḍhakissa dārumhi abhiññāṇaṃ katvā puna tena abhiññāṇena taṃ paccābhijānanakāle, purisassa kāḷatilakādiabhiññāṇaṃ sallakkhetvā puna tena abhiññāṇena asuko nāma esoti tassa paccābhijānanakāle, rañño piḷandhanagopakabhaṇḍāgārikassa tasmiṃ tasmiṃ piḷandhane nāmapaṇṇakaṃ bandhitvā ‘asukaṃ piḷandhanaṃ nāma āharā’ti vutte dīpaṃ jāletvā ratanagabbhaṃ pavisitvā paṇṇaṃ vācetvā tassa tasseva piḷandhanassa āharaṇakāle ca pavatti veditabbā.

Its function should be understood as occurring, for example, just as a carpenter makes a mark on a piece of wood and later recognizes it again by that same mark; or as a person observes a black mole or other such mark and later recognizes that person again by that same mark, thinking, 'This is so-and-so'; or as the king’s treasurer of ornaments, having tied name tags to each ornament, when told, 'Bring such-and-such an ornament,' lights a lamp, enters the jewel chamber, reads the tag, and fetches that very ornament.

Aparo nayo – sabbasaṅgāhikavasena hi sañjānanalakkhaṇā saññā. Punasañjānanapaccayanimittakaraṇarasā, dāruādīsu tacchakādayo viya. Yathāgahitanimittavasena abhinivesakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā, hatthidassakaandhā viya. Ārammaṇe anogāḷhavuttitāya [P 0.0111] aciraṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, vijju viya. Yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā, tiṇapurisakesu migapotakānaṃ ‘purisā’ti uppannasaññā viya. Yā panettha ñāṇasampayuttā hoti sā saññā ñāṇameva anuvattati. Sasambhārapathavīādīsu sesadhammā pathavīādīni viyāti veditabbā.

Another method: Indeed, by way of a comprehensive statement, perception has the characteristic of perceiving. Its function is making a sign as a condition for perceiving again, like carpenters and so on with wood. Its manifestation is causing adherence according to the sign as it was apprehended, like the blind men describing the elephant. Or, its manifestation is being short-lived due to not deeply engaging with the object, like lightning. Its proximate cause is the object as it appears, like the perception 'men' that arises in young deer towards scarecrows. Among these, that perception which is associated with knowledge follows knowledge, just as in the earth element with its components, the remaining phenomena follow the earth element and so on; thus it should be understood.

Cetayatīti [V 0.0157] cetanā saddhiṃ attanā sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇe abhisandahatīti attho. Sā cetayitalakkhaṇā, cetanābhāvalakkhaṇāti attho. Āyūhanarasā. Catubhūmikacetanā hi nocetayitalakkhaṇā nāma natthi. Sabbā cetayitalakkhaṇāva. Āyūhanarasatā pana kusalākusalesu eva hoti. Kusalākusalakammāyūhanaṭṭhānañhi patvā sesasampayuttadhammānaṃ ekadesamattakameva kiccaṃ hoti. Cetanā pana atirekaussāhā atirekavāyāmā, diguṇussāhā diguṇavāyāmā. Tenāhu porāṇā – “thāvariyasabhāvasaṇṭhitā ca panesā cetanā”ti. Thāvariyoti khettasāmī vuccati. Yathā khettasāmī puriso pañcapaṇṇāsa balipurise gahetvā ‘lāyissāmī’ti ekato khettaṃ otarati. Tassa atireko ussāho atireko vāyāmo, diguṇo ussāho diguṇo vāyāmo hoti, ‘nirantaraṃ gaṇhathā’tiādīni vadati, sīmaṃ ācikkhati, tesaṃ surābhattagandhamālādīni jānāti, maggaṃ samakaṃ harati. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ[M 0.0155]. Khettasāmipuriso viya hi cetanā. Pañcapaṇṇāsa balipurisā viya cittaṅgavasena uppannā pañcapaṇṇāsa kusalā dhammā. Khettasāmipurisassa diguṇussāhadiguṇavāyāmakaraṇakālo viya kusalākusalakammāyūhanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā cetanāya diguṇussāho diguṇavāyāmo hoti. Evamassā āyūhanarasatā veditabbā.

Volition (cetanā) is so called because it wills; it binds associated states, together with itself, to an object—this is the meaning. It has the characteristic of willing, meaning it has the characteristic of the state of volition. Its function is accumulating. Indeed, there is no volition in the four planes that is without the characteristic of willing. All have the characteristic of willing. However, the function of accumulating occurs only in wholesome and unwholesome states. For when the point of accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma is reached, the remaining associated states have only a partial task. But volition has superior effort and superior exertion, double effort and double exertion. Therefore, the ancients said: 'This volition is established in its nature like a landowner (thāvariya).' A 'thāvariya' is said to be a landowner. Just as a landowner, taking fifty-five laborers, enters the field together with them, thinking, 'I will reap,' his effort is superior, his exertion is superior—double effort and double exertion. He says, 'Take it up continuously,' points out the boundary, knows their drink, food, perfumes, and garlands, and makes the path even. This should be understood in its completeness. For volition is like the landowner. The fifty-five wholesome states that arise as mental factors are like the fifty-five laborers. Just as the time of double effort and double exertion for the landowner is like the time when volition, having reached the point of accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma, has double effort and double exertion. Thus, its function of accumulating should be understood.

Sā panesā saṃvidahanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Saṃvidahamānā hi ayaṃ upaṭṭhāti, sakiccaparakiccasādhakā, jeṭṭhasissamahāvaḍḍhakīādayo viya. Yathā hi jeṭṭhasisso upajjhāyaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā sayaṃ adhīyamāno itarepi dārake attano attano ajjhayanakamme pavattayati, tasmiñhi adhīyituṃ āraddhe tepi adhīyanti, tadanuvattitāya. Yathā ca mahāvaḍḍhakī sayaṃ tacchanto itarepi tacchake attano attano [P 0.0112] tacchanakamme pavattayati, tasmiñhi tacchituṃ āraddhe tepi tacchanti, tadanuvattitāya. Yathā ca yodhanāyako sayaṃ yujjhamāno itarepi yodhe sampahāravuttiyaṃ pavattayati, tasmiñhi yujjhituṃ āraddhe tepi anivattamānā yujjhanti, tadanuvattitāya. Evamesāpi attano kiccena ārammaṇe pavattamānā aññepi sampayuttadhamme attano attano kiriyāya pavatteti. Tassā hi attano kiccaṃ āraddhāya, taṃsampayuttāpi ārabhanti. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘sakiccaparakiccasādhakā, jeṭṭhasissamahāvaḍḍhakīādayo viyā’ti. Accāyikakammānussaraṇādīsu ca panāyaṃ sampayuttānaṃ ussāhanabhāvena pavattamānā pākaṭā hotīti veditabbā.

Furthermore, this volition has manifestation as coordinating. For it manifests as coordinating, accomplishing its own and others' tasks, like a senior student, a master carpenter, and so on. Just as when a senior student sees his preceptor approaching from afar, he himself begins to recite and also sets the other children to their own recitation tasks; for when he starts to recite, they too recite, following his lead. And just as a master carpenter, while carving himself, also sets the other carpenters to their own carving tasks; for when he starts to carve, they too carve, following his lead. And just as an army commander, while fighting himself, also sets the other soldiers to their battle duties; for when he starts to fight, they too fight without retreating, following his lead. In the same way, this volition, while engaged in its own task regarding the object, also sets the other associated states to their respective actions. For when it has begun its own task, the states associated with it also begin theirs. Hence it is said: 'accomplishing its own and others' tasks, like a senior student, a master carpenter, and so on.' Moreover, it should be understood that this volition becomes evident as it proceeds by way of urging on the associated states in instances of recalling urgent tasks and the like.

‘Ārammaṇaṃ [V 0.0158] cintetī’ti cittanti nayena cittassa vacanattho vutto eva. Lakkhaṇādito pana vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ cittaṃ, pubbaṅgamarasaṃ, sandahanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Catubhūmakacittañhi novijānanalakkhaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Sabbaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇameva. Dvāraṃ pana patvā ārammaṇavibhāvanaṭṭhāne cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ hoti. Cakkhunā hi diṭṭhaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ citteneva vijānāti…pe… manena viññātaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ citteneva vijānāti. Yathā hi nagaraguttiko nāma nagaramajjhe siṅghāṭake nisīditvā ‘ayaṃ nevāsiko ayaṃ āgantuko’ti āgatāgataṃ janaṃ upadhāreti vavatthapeti – evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ mahātherena – “yathā, mahārāja[M 0.0156], nagaraguttiko nāma majjhe nagarassa siṅghāṭake nisinno puratthimato disato purisaṃ āgacchantaṃ passeyya… pacchimato… dakkhiṇato… uttarato disato purisaṃ āgacchantaṃ passeyya, evameva kho, mahārāja, yaṃ cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati taṃ viññāṇena vijānāti, yaṃ sotena saddaṃ suṇāti, ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyati, jivhāya rasaṃ sāyati, kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusati, manasā dhammaṃ vijānāti, taṃ viññāṇena vijānātī”ti (mi. pa. 2.3.12). Evaṃ dvāraṃ patvā ārammaṇavibhāvanaṭṭhāne cittameva pubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ. Tasmā pubbaṅgamarasanti [P 0.0113] vuccati.

The verbal meaning of 'citta' has already been stated by the method of 'It thinks of an object, thus it is citta.' However, with regard to its characteristic and so on, citta has the characteristic of cognizing, the function of being a forerunner, the manifestation of continuity, and mentality-materiality as its proximate cause. Indeed, there is no citta in the four planes that is called 'lacking the characteristic of cognizing.' All citta has only the characteristic of cognizing. However, having reached a door, in the place where the object is made clear, citta is a forerunner, a leader. For it is only by citta that one cognizes a visible object seen by the eye... and it is only by citta that one cognizes a mental object known by the mind. Just as a city guard, seated at a crossroads in the middle of the city, notes and determines the people who come and go, thinking, 'This is a resident; this is a visitor'—this analogy should be understood as such. And this was also stated by the Great Elder: 'Just as, great king, a city guard seated at a crossroads in the middle of the city might see a person coming from the eastern direction... from the western... from the southern... from the northern direction, so too, great king, whatever form one sees with the eye, one cognizes that with consciousness; whatever sound one hears with the ear, whatever odor one smells with the nose, whatever taste one savors with the tongue, whatever tangible object one touches with the body, whatever mental object one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes that with consciousness.' Thus, having reached a door, in the place where the object is made clear, citta itself is the forerunner, the leader. Therefore, it is said to have the function of being a forerunner.

Tadetaṃ pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ uppajjamānaṃ purimaṃ purimaṃ nirantaraṃ katvā sandahanameva upaṭṭhātīti sandahanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Pañcavokārabhave panassa niyamato nāmarūpaṃ, catuvokārabhave nāmameva padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tasmā nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ.

That citta, arising successively later, makes the successively earlier citta without interval, and manifests only as a connection; therefore, its manifestation is continuity. Furthermore, in the five-aggregate existence, its proximate cause is invariably mentality-materiality; in the four-aggregate existence, only mentality is the proximate cause. Therefore, it is said to have mentality-materiality as its proximate cause.

Kiṃ panetaṃ cittaṃ purimaniddiṭṭhacittena saddhiṃ ekameva udāhu aññanti? Ekameva. Atha kasmā purimaniddiṭṭhaṃ puna vuttanti? Avicāritaṃ etaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha yutti – yathā hi rūpādīni upādāya paññattā sūriyādayo na atthato rūpādīhi aññe honti, teneva yasmiṃ samaye sūriyo udeti tasmiṃ samaye tassa tejasaṅkhātaṃ rūpampīti. Evaṃ vuccamānepi na rūpādīhi añño sūriyo nāma atthi. Na tathā cittaṃ; phassādayo dhamme upādāya paññāpiyati; atthato panetaṃ tehi aññameva. Tena ‘yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti ekaṃseneva tasmiṃ samaye phassādīhi atthato aññameva taṃ hotī’ti imassatthassa dīpanatthāya etaṃ puna vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Now, is this citta one and the same with the citta previously indicated, or is it another? It is one and the same. Then why is the previously indicated citta stated again? This was not investigated in the commentary. Herein, this is the rationale: Just as the sun and so on, which are designated in dependence on materiality, etc., are not in reality different from materiality, etc.—and for that very reason, when the sun rises, at that time its materiality, called 'radiance,' also arises; even when spoken of thus, there is no so-called sun that is different from materiality, etc. Citta is not like that; it is not designated in dependence on states such as contact. In reality, however, it is different from them. Therefore, it should be understood that this is stated again to clarify this meaning: 'At the time when citta has arisen, at that time it is, with certainty, different in reality from contact and so on.'

Yathā ca “yasmiṃ samaye rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti…pe… pathavīkasiṇaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye [V 0.0159] phasso hoti vedanā hotī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 160) pana bhāventena vavatthāpite samaye yo bhāveti na so atthato uppajjati nāma, teneva tattha yathā “phasso hoti vedanā hotī”ti vuttaṃ, na evaṃ “yo bhāveti so hotī”ti vuttaṃ. “Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”tiādīsu pana cittena vavatthāpite samaye samayavavatthāpitaṃ cittaṃ na tathā atthato nuppajjati[M 0.0157]. Yatheva pana tadā ‘phasso hoti vedanā hoti’, tathā ‘cittampi hotī’ti imassapi atthassa dīpanatthamidaṃ puna vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – uddesavāre saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ niddesavāre ca vibhajanatthaṃ purimena hi ‘citta’-saddena kevalaṃ samayo vavatthāpito. Tasmiṃ pana cittena vavatthāpitasamaye ye dhammā honti tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ “phasso hotī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Cittañcāpi tasmiṃ samaye hotiyeva. Tasmā tassāpi saṅgaṇhanatthametaṃ [P 0.0114] puna vuttaṃ. Imasmiñca ṭhāne etasmiṃ avuccamāne “katamaṃ tasmiṃ samaye citta”nti na sakkā bhaveyya niddesavāre vibhajituṃ. Evamassa vibhajanaṃyeva parihāyetha. Tasmā tassa niddesavāre vibhajanatthampi etañca vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

And just as in passages such as, 'At the time when one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm… the earth kasiṇa, at that time there is contact, there is feeling,' the one who develops does not, in reality, arise at the time established by the developer. For that reason, it is stated there, 'there is contact, there is feeling,' but it is not stated, 'the one who develops exists.' However, in passages such as, 'At the time when a wholesome sense-sphere citta has arisen,' the citta that establishes the time does not fail to arise in reality in that way. Just as at that time 'there is contact, there is feeling,' so too 'there is also citta'—it should be understood that this is stated again to clarify this meaning as well. Herein, this is the conclusion: it is stated again for the purpose of inclusion in the enumeration section and for the purpose of analysis in the exposition section. For by the preceding word 'citta,' only the time was established. But to show the states that exist at that time established by citta, the passage 'there is contact,' etc., was begun. And citta, too, indeed exists at that time. Therefore, this is stated again to include it as well. And if it were not stated in this place, it would not be possible to analyze in the exposition section, 'What, at that time, is citta?' Thus, its very analysis would be omitted. Therefore, it should be understood that this is also stated for the purpose of its analysis in the exposition section.

Yasmā vā “uppannaṃ hotī”ti ettha cittaṃ uppannanti etaṃ desanāsīsameva, ‘na pana cittaṃ ekameva uppajjatī’ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vicāritaṃ, tasmā cittaṃ “uppanna”nti etthāpi cittamattameva aggahetvā paropaṇṇāsakusaladhammehi saddhiṃyeva cittaṃ gahitaṃ. Evaṃ tattha saṅkhepato sabbepi cittacetasikadhamme gahetvā idha sarūpena pabhedato dassetuṃ “phasso hotī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Iti phassādayo viya cittampi vuttamevāti veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, because in the phrase 'has arisen,' the statement 'citta has arisen' is merely the heading of the teaching, and it is investigated in the commentary that 'citta does not arise alone.' Therefore, in the phrase 'citta has arisen,' not just citta alone is taken, but citta is taken together with the more than fifty wholesome states. Thus, having taken all mind and mental-factor states in brief there, here the passage 'there is contact,' etc., was begun in order to show them by their individual nature and in detail. Thus, it should be understood that just as states such as contact were stated, so too citta was also stated.

Dhammuddesavāro

The Section on the Enumeration of States

Jhānaṅgarāsivaṇṇanā

Description of the Collection of Jhāna Factors

Vitakketīti vitakko; vitakkanaṃ vā vitakko; ūhananti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇo. So hi ārammaṇe cittaṃ āropeti. Yathā hi koci rājavallabhaṃ ñātiṃ vā mittaṃ vā nissāya rājagehaṃ ārohati, evaṃ vitakkaṃ nissāya cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārohati. Tasmā so ārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇoti vutto. Nāgasenatthero panāha – ākoṭanalakkhaṇo vitakko. “Yathā, mahārāja, bherī ākoṭitā atha pacchā [V 0.0160] anuravati anusaddāyati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yathā ākoṭanā evaṃ vitakko daṭṭhabbo. Yathā pacchā anuravanā anusaddāyanā evaṃ vicāro daṭṭhabbo”ti (mi. pa. 2.3.14 thokaṃ visadisaṃ). Svāyaṃ āhananapariyāhananaraso. Tathā hi tena yogāvacaro ārammaṇaṃ vitakkāhataṃ vitakkapariyāhataṃ karotīti vuccati. Ārammaṇe cittassa ānayanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Because it applies the mind, it is called 'initial application' (vitakka); or, the act of applying is 'initial application'; it is said to be 'pondering'. This has the characteristic of directing the mind onto an object, for it directs the mind onto an object. Just as someone, relying on a royal favorite—a relative or a friend—ascends to the royal palace, so the mind, relying on initial application, ascends to the object. Therefore, it is said to have the characteristic of directing the mind onto an object. The Elder Nāgasena, however, said: 'Initial application has the characteristic of striking. Just as, Your Majesty, when a drum is struck, it subsequently resounds and reverberates, so too, Your Majesty, initial application should be seen as the striking, and sustained application as the subsequent resounding and reverberating.' This has the function of striking and striking all around. For by this, the meditator is said to make the object struck and struck all around by initial application. Its manifestation is the bringing of the mind to the object.

Ārammaṇe [M 0.0158] tena cittaṃ vicaratīti vicāro; vicaraṇaṃ vā vicāro. Anusañcaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo. Tattha sahajātānuyojanaraso. Cittassa anuppabandhapaccupaṭṭhāno. Santepi ca nesaṃ katthaci aviyoge oḷārikaṭṭhena pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena ca ghaṇṭābhighāto viya abhiniropanaṭṭhena ca cetaso paṭhamābhinipāto vitakko[P 0.0115]. Sukhumaṭṭhena anumajjanasabhāvaṭṭhena ca ghaṇṭānuravo viya anuppabandho vicāro. Vipphāravā cettha vitakko, paṭhamuppattikāle paripphandabhūto cittassa. Ākāse uppatitukāmassa pakkhino pakkhavikkhepo viya. Padumābhimukhapāto viya ca gandhānubaddhacetaso bhamarassa. Santavutti vicāro nātiparipphandanabhāvo cittassa, ākāse uppatitassa pakkhino pakkhappasāraṇaṃ viya, paribbhamanaṃ viya ca padumābhimukhapatitassa bhamarassa padumassa uparibhāge.

Because the mind roams on an object by means of it, it is called 'sustained application' (vicāra); or, roaming is 'sustained application'. It is said to be 'continued traversing'. This has the characteristic of scrutinizing the object. Its function is to yoke co-nascent states to it. It manifests as the continuous binding of the mind. And although they are in some cases inseparable, because of its grossness, its nature as a forerunner, and its nature of directing, initial application (vitakka) is the mind's first impact, like the initial striking of a bell. And because of its subtlety and its nature of scrutinizing, sustained application (vicāra) is the continuous binding, like the reverberation of a bell. Herein, initial application is expansive, being the agitation of the mind at the moment of first arising, like the flapping of a bird's wings when it desires to fly into the sky, and like the flight of a bee, whose mind is drawn by the fragrance, towards a lotus. Sustained application is of calm occurrence, the state of the mind not being excessively agitated, like the spreading of a bird's wings once it has flown up into the sky, and like the hovering of a bee, which has flown towards a lotus, above that lotus.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ākāse gacchato mahāsakuṇassa ubhohi pakkhehi vātaṃ gahetvā pakkhe sannisīdāpetvā gamanaṃ viya ārammaṇe cetaso abhiniropanabhāvena pavatto vitakko. So hi ekaggo hutvā appeti vātaggahaṇatthaṃ pakkhe phandāpayamānassa gamanaṃ viya. Anumajjabhāvena pavatto vicāro. So hi ārammaṇaṃ anumajjatīti vuttaṃ, taṃ anuppabandhanena pavattiyaṃ ativiya yujjati. So pana nesaṃ viseso paṭhamadutiyajjhānesu pākaṭo hoti. Apica malaggahitaṃ kaṃsabhājanaṃ ekena hatthena daḷhaṃ gahetvā itarena hatthena cuṇṇatelavālaṇḍupakena parimajjantassa daḷhaggahaṇahattho viya vitakko, parimajjanahattho viya vicāro. Tathā kumbhakārassa daṇḍappahārena cakkaṃ bhamayitvā bhājanaṃ karontassa uppīḷanahattho viya vitakko, ito cito ca sañcaraṇahattho viya vicāro. Tathā maṇḍalaṃ karontassa majjhe sannirumbhitvā ṭhitakaṇṭako viya abhiniropano vitakko, bahiparibbhamanakaṇṭako viya anumajjamāno vicāro.

However, in the commentary it is said: 'Initial application (vitakka) occurs with the nature of directing the mind onto the object, like the flight of a great bird going in the sky, which, having gathered the wind with both wings, steadies its wings and proceeds. For it, becoming one-pointed, attains absorption. Sustained application (vicāra) occurs with the nature of scrutinizing, like the flight of one flapping its wings to catch the wind. For it is said that it scrutinizes the object.' That fits very well with its occurrence as a continuous binding. But that distinction between them becomes clear in the first and second jhānas. Furthermore, initial application is like the hand that firmly grasps a tarnished bronze vessel, while sustained application is like the other hand that rubs it with powder, oil, or a scrubber. Likewise, for a potter who makes a pot by spinning the wheel with a strike of a stick, initial application is like the hand that presses down, and sustained application is like the hand that moves here and there. Likewise, for one drawing a circle, initial application, which directs, is like the pin fixed and pressed down in the center; sustained application, which scrutinizes, is like the pin revolving around the outside.

Piṇayatīti [V 0.0161] pīti. Sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā. Kāyacittapīṇanarasā, pharaṇarasā vā. Odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā. Sā panesā khuddikāpīti, khaṇikāpīti, okkantikāpīti, ubbegāpīti, pharaṇāpītīti pañcavidhā hoti.

Because it delights, it is called 'joy' (pīti). It has the characteristic of gladdening. Its function is to nourish the body and mind, or its function is to suffuse. It manifests as elation. This joy, however, is of five kinds: minor joy, momentary joy, flooding joy, transporting joy, and suffusing joy.

Tattha [M 0.0159] khuddikāpīti sarīre lomahaṃsamattameva kātuṃ sakkoti. Khaṇikāpīti khaṇe khaṇe vijjuppādasadisā hoti. Okkantikāpīti[P 0.0116], samuddatīraṃ vīci viya, kāyaṃ okkamitvā okkamitvā bhijjati. Ubbegāpīti balavatī hoti, kāyaṃ uddhaggaṃ katvā ākāse laṅghāpanappamāṇappattā. Tathā hi puṇṇavallikavāsī mahātissatthero puṇṇamadivase sāyaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā candālokaṃ disvā mahācetiyābhimukho hutvā ‘imāya vata velāya catasso parisā mahācetiyaṃ vandantī’ti pakatiyā diṭṭhārammaṇavasena buddhārammaṇaṃ ubbegaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā sudhātale pahaṭacitrageṇḍuko viya ākāse uppatitvā mahācetiyaṅgaṇeyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Herein, minor joy is only able to cause the hairs of the body to stand on end. Momentary joy is like flashes of lightning occurring from moment to moment. Flooding joy, like a wave on the seashore, descends upon the body again and again and breaks. Transporting joy is powerful; having made the body rise up, it reaches the state of being able to leap into the air. Indeed, the Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Puṇṇavallika, on a full-moon day, went to the cetiya-courtyard in the evening. Seeing the moonlight and facing the Great Cetiya, he thought, 'Ah, at this time, the four assemblies must be worshipping the Great Cetiya!' By means of an object habitually seen, with the Buddha as his object, he aroused transporting joy and, like a colorful ball struck on a plastered surface, leapt up into the air and stood right in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya.

Tathā girikaṇḍakavihārassa upanissaye vattakālakagāme ekā kuladhītāpi balavabuddhārammaṇāya ubbegāya pītiyā ākāse laṅghesi. Tassā kira mātāpitaro sāyaṃ dhammasavanatthāya vihāraṃ gacchantā ‘amma, tvaṃ garubhārā, akāle vicarituṃ na sakkosi, mayaṃ tuyhaṃ pattiṃ katvā dhammaṃ sossāmā’ti agamaṃsu. Sā gantukāmāpi tesaṃ vacanaṃ paṭibāhituṃ asakkontī ghare ohīyitvā gharadvāre ṭhatvā candālokena girikaṇḍake ākāsacetiyaṅgaṇaṃ olokentī cetiyassa dīpapūjaṃ addasa. Catasso ca parisā mālāgandhādīhi cetiyapūjaṃ katvā padakkhiṇaṃ karontiyo bhikkhusaṅghassa ca gaṇasajjhāyasaddaṃ assosi. Athassā ‘dhaññā vatime manussā ye vihāraṃ gantvā evarūpe cetiyaṅgaṇe anusañcarituṃ evarūpañca madhuraṃ dhammakathaṃ sotuṃ labhantī’ti muttarāsisadisaṃ cetiyaṃ passantiyā eva ubbegāpīti udapādi. Sā ākāse laṅghitvā mātāpitūnaṃ purimataraṃyeva ākāsato cetiyaṅgaṇe oruyha cetiyaṃ vanditvā dhammaṃ suṇamānā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro āgantvā ‘amma, tvaṃ katarena maggena āgatāsī’ti pucchiṃsu. Sā ‘ākāsena āgatāmhi, na maggenā’ti vatvā ‘amma, ākāsena nāma khīṇāsavā sañcaranti, tvaṃ kathaṃ āgatā’ti puṭṭhā āha – ‘mayhaṃ candālokena cetiyaṃ olokentiyā ṭhitāya buddhārammaṇā balavapīti uppajjati, athāhaṃ neva attano ṭhitabhāvaṃ na nisinnabhāvaṃ aññāsiṃ, gahitanimitteneva pana ākāsaṃ [M 0.0160] laṅghitvā cetiyaṅgaṇe patiṭṭhitāmhī’ti. Evaṃ ubbegāpīti ākāse laṅghāpanappamāṇā hoti.

Furthermore, in the village of Vattagālaka in the dependency of Girikaṇḍaka Monastery, a certain daughter of a good family, due to powerful transporting joy with the Buddha as its object, leapt into the sky. It is said that her parents, going to the monastery in the evening to hear the Dhamma, told her, 'Dear, you are heavily pregnant and cannot travel at an unsuitable time. We will make a share of merit on your behalf and listen to the Dhamma.' Though she wished to go, unable to refuse their words, she remained at home. Standing at the door, she looked at the stupa courtyard at Girikaṇḍaka in the open air by the moonlight and saw the lamp offerings to the stupa. She also saw the four assemblies making offerings of flowers and incense to the stupa and circumambulating it, and heard the sound of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus reciting in unison. Then she thought, 'How fortunate are these people who are able to go to the monastery, wander in such a stupa courtyard, and hear such a sweet Dhamma talk!' While looking at the stupa, which was like a heap of pearls, transporting joy arose in her. She leapt into the air and, descending from the sky, landed in the stupa courtyard even before her parents, paid homage to the stupa, and stood listening to the Dhamma. When her parents arrived, they asked, 'Dear, by which path did you come?' She replied, 'I came through the sky, not by the path.' When she was asked, 'Dear, it is those whose taints are destroyed who travel through the sky; how did you come?' she answered, 'While I stood looking at the stupa by the moonlight, powerful joy with the Buddha as its object arose in me. Then I was not aware of my standing or sitting posture, but with the object that had been grasped, I leapt into the sky and landed in the stupa courtyard.' Thus, transporting joy has the measure of causing one to leap into the air.

Pharaṇapītiyā [P 0.0117][V 0.0162] pana uppannāya sakalasarīraṃ dhamitvā pūritavatthi viya, mahatā udakoghena pakkhandapabbatakucchi viya ca anuparipphuṭaṃ hoti. Sā panesā pañcavidhā pīti gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī duvidhaṃ passaddhiṃ paripūreti – kāyapassaddhiñca cittapassaddhiñca. Passaddhi gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī duvidhaṃ sukhaṃ paripūreti – kāyikaṃ cetasikañca. Sukhaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhantaṃ paripākaṃ gacchantaṃ tividhaṃ samādhiṃ paripūreti – khaṇikasamādhiṃ upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhinti. Tāsu ṭhapetvā appanāsamādhipūrikaṃ itarā dvepi idha yujjanti.

Furthermore, when pervasive joy arises, it successively pervades the entire body, like a bladder being inflated with air, or like a mountain cavern being flooded by a great torrent of water. This fivefold joy, as it is conceived and matures, fulfills the two kinds of tranquility: bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Tranquility, as it is conceived and matures, fulfills the two kinds of happiness: physical and mental. Happiness, as it is conceived and matures, fulfills the three kinds of concentration: momentary concentration, access concentration, and absorption concentration. Among these, setting aside the joy that fulfills absorption concentration, the joys that fulfill the other two are applicable here.

Sukhayatīti sukhaṃ; yassa uppajjati taṃ sukhitaṃ karotīti attho. Suṭṭhu vā khādati, khanati ca kāyacittābādhanti sukhaṃ. Somanassavedanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tassa lakkhaṇādīni vedanāpade vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

It makes one happy, thus it is happiness; the meaning is that for whomever it arises, it makes that one happy. Or, it thoroughly consumes and digs up physical and mental affliction, thus it is happiness. This is a name for pleasant mental feeling. Its characteristics and so on should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on feeling.

Aparo nayo – sātalakkhaṇaṃ sukhaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ upabrūhanarasaṃ, anuggahaṇapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Satipi ca nesaṃ pītisukhānaṃ katthaci avippayoge, iṭṭhārammaṇapaṭilābhatuṭṭhi pīti; paṭiladdharasānubhavanaṃ sukhaṃ. Yattha pīti tattha sukhaṃ. Yattha sukhaṃ tattha na niyamato pīti. Saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahitā pīti, vedanākkhandhasaṅgahitaṃ sukhaṃ. Kantārakhinnassa vanantodakadassanasavanesu viya pīti. Vanacchāyāpavesanaudakaparibhogesu viya sukhaṃ.

Another method: Happiness has the characteristic of agreeableness, the function of enhancing associated states, and the manifestation of support. And although there is sometimes inseparability of this joy and happiness, joy is the satisfaction at obtaining a desirable object; happiness is the experiencing of the taste of what has been obtained. Where there is joy, there is happiness. Where there is happiness, there is not necessarily joy. Joy is included in the aggregate of formations; happiness is included in the aggregate of feeling. For one exhausted in a wasteland, joy is like the seeing and hearing of water in a forest. Happiness is like entering the forest's shade and using the water.

Yathā hi puriso mahākantāramaggaṃ paṭipanno ghammapareto tasito pipāsito paṭipathe purisaṃ disvā ‘kattha pānīyaṃ atthī’ti puccheyya. So ‘aṭaviṃ uttaritvā jātassaravanasaṇḍo atthi, tattha gantvā labhissasī’ti vadeyya. So tassa kathaṃ sutvā haṭṭhapahaṭṭho bhaveyya. Tato gacchanto bhūmiyaṃ patitāni uppaladalanālapattādīni disvā suṭṭhutaraṃ haṭṭhapahaṭṭho hutvā gacchanto allavatthe allakese purise passeyya, vanakukkuṭamorādīnaṃ saddaṃ suṇeyya, jātassarapariyante jātaṃ maṇijālasadisaṃ nīlavanasaṇḍaṃ passeyya, sare jātāni uppalapadumakumudādīni passeyya, acchaṃ vippasannaṃ udakaṃ passeyya. So bhiyyo [M 0.0161] bhiyyo haṭṭhapahaṭṭho hutvā jātassaraṃ [P 0.0118] otaritvā yathāruci nhatvā ca pivitvā ca paṭippassaddhadaratho bhisamuḷālapokkharādīni khāditvā nīluppalādīni piḷandhitvā mandālakamūlāni khandhe karitvā uttaritvā sāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā, udakasāṭakaṃ ātape katvā, sītacchāyāya mandamande vāte paharante nipanno ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’nti vadeyya. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For it is as if a man, having entered upon a great wasteland path, overcome by heat, weary, and thirsty, might see a man on the path ahead and ask, 'Where is there drinking water?' That man might say, 'Having crossed the wilderness, there is a dense forest with a natural lake; going there, you will get it.' Hearing his words, he would become joyful and elated. Then, as he goes along, seeing lotus petals, stalks, and leaves fallen on the ground, he would become even more joyful and elated. Continuing on, he might see men with wet clothes and wet hair; he might hear the sound of jungle fowl, peacocks, and so on; he might see, at the edge of the natural lake, a dark green forest grove like a net of jewels; he might see blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses growing in the lake; he might see the clear, exceptionally limpid water. Becoming more and more joyful and elated, he would descend into the natural lake and, having bathed and drunk as he wished, his fatigue allayed, he would eat lotus roots, bulbs, and seeds, adorn himself with blue lotuses, place bundles of mandālaka roots on his shoulder, and, having come out of the water, put on his garment, place his bathing cloth in the sun, and, lying down in the cool shade while a gentle breeze blows, he would say, 'Ah, what happiness! Ah, what happiness!' This successful outcome should be understood in this way.

Tassa [V 0.0163] hi purisassa jātassaravanasaṇḍasavanato paṭṭhāya yāva udakadassanā haṭṭhapahaṭṭhakālo viya pubbabhāgārammaṇe haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākārā pīti. Nhatvā ca pivitvā ca sītacchāyāya mandamande vāte paharante ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’nti vadato nipannakālo viya balavappattaṃ ārammaṇarasānubhavanākārasaṇṭhitaṃ sukhaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye pākaṭabhāvato cetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yattha pana pīti sukhampi tattha atthīti vuttamevetaṃ.

For that man, like the period of being joyful and elated from the time of hearing of the dense forest with the natural lake up until the seeing of the water, so should joy be understood as the state of being joyful and elated regarding the preliminary object. And like the time of lying down for the one who, after bathing and drinking, says 'Ah, what happiness! Ah, what happiness!' while a gentle breeze blows in the cool shade, so should happiness be understood, which has reached a powerful state and is established in the mode of experiencing the taste of the object. And it should be understood that this was said because of its manifestation at each of those respective times. But 'Where there is joy, there is also happiness'—this has already been stated.

Cittassekaggatāti cittassa ekaggabhāvo; samādhissetaṃ nāmaṃ. Lakkhaṇādīsu panassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāva vuttaṃ – “pāmokkhalakkhaṇo ca samādhi avikkhepalakkhaṇo ca”. Yathā hi kūṭāgārakaṇṇikā sesadabbasambhārānaṃ ābandhanato pamukhā hoti evameva sabbakusaladhammānaṃ samādhicittena ijjhanato sabbesampi tesaṃ dhammānaṃ samādhi pāmokkho hoti. Tena vuttaṃ –

One-pointedness of mind is the state of the mind having a single object; this is a name for concentration. Moreover, regarding its characteristics and so on, it is first stated in the commentary: 'Concentration has the characteristic of being pre-eminent and the characteristic of non-distraction.' For just as the pinnacle of a gabled house is pre-eminent because it binds the remaining building materials, so too, because all wholesome states are accomplished through a concentrated mind, concentration is pre-eminent among all those wholesome states. Therefore, it is said:

“Yathā, mahārāja, kūṭāgārassa yā kāci gopānasiyo sabbā tā kūṭaṅgamā honti, kūṭaninnā kūṭasamosaraṇā, kūṭaṃ tāsaṃ aggamakkhāyati, evameva kho, mahārāja, ye keci kusalā dhammā sabbe te samādhininnā honti, samādhipoṇā, samādhipabbhārā, samādhi tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.14).

"Just as, great king, whatever rafters there are of a peaked house, all go to the peak, incline towards the peak, converge at the peak, and the peak is declared to be their chief; just so, great king, whatever wholesome states there are, all incline towards concentration, slope towards concentration, converge on concentration, and concentration is declared to be their chief."

Yathā ca senaṅgaṃ patvā rājā nāma yattha yattha senā osīdati taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati, tassa gatagataṭṭhāne senā paripūrati, parasenā bhijjitvā rājānameva anuvattati, evameva sahajātadhammānaṃ vikkhipituṃ vippakirituṃ appadānato samādhi avikkhepalakkhaṇo nāma hotīti.

And just as a king, having gone to the battlefield, wherever the army falters, goes to that very place, and in every place he goes, the army is replenished, and the enemy army, having been broken, follows that very king; so too, because it does not allow co-arisen states to be scattered or dispersed, concentration is called that which has the characteristic of non-distraction.

Aparo [M 0.0162] pana nayo – ayaṃ cittassekaggatāsaṅkhāto samādhi nāma avisāralakkhaṇo vā avikkhepalakkhaṇo vā, sahajātadhammānaṃ, sampiṇḍanaraso nhāniyacuṇṇānaṃ udakaṃ viya, upasamapaccupaṭṭhāno ñāṇapaccupaṭṭhāno [P 0.0119] vā. “Samāhito yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Visesato sukhapadaṭṭhāno, nivāte dīpaccīnaṃ ṭhiti viya cetaso ṭhitīti daṭṭhabbo.

Furthermore, there is another method: This concentration, known as one-pointedness of mind, has the characteristic of non-diffusion or non-distraction. Its function is to unify co-arisen states, like water for bath powder. Its manifestation is tranquility, or its manifestation is knowledge. For it is said: 'One who is concentrated knows and sees things as they truly are.' Specifically, it has happiness as its proximate cause. It should be seen as the stability of the mind, like the stability of a lamp's flame in a windless place.

Indriyarāsivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Aggregate of Faculties

Saddahanti etāya, sayaṃ vā saddahati, saddahanamattameva vā esāti saddhā. Sāva assaddhiyassa [V 0.0164] abhibhavanato adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ. Adhimokkhalakkhaṇe vā indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Saddhāva indriyaṃ saddhindriyaṃ. Sā panesā sampasādanalakkhaṇā ca saddhā sampakkhandanalakkhaṇā ca.

They believe by means of it, or it itself believes, or it is mere believing; thus, it is faith (saddhā). It is a faculty (indriya) in the sense of exercising sovereignty by overpowering faithlessness. Or, it is a faculty because it causes the exercise of sovereignty in the characteristic of resolution. Faith itself as a faculty is the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). Moreover, this faith has both the characteristic of clarifying and the characteristic of leaping forward.

Yathā hi rañño cakkavattissa udakappasādako maṇi udake pakkhitto paṅkasevālapaṇakakaddamaṃ sannisīdāpeti, udakaṃ acchaṃ karoti vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ, evameva saddhā uppajjamānā nīvaraṇe vikkhambheti, kilese sannisīdāpeti, cittaṃ pasādeti, anāvilaṃ karoti. Pasannena cittena yogāvacaro kulaputto dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ samādiyati, uposathakammaṃ karoti, bhāvanaṃ ārabhati. Evaṃ tāva saddhā sampasādanalakkhaṇāti veditabbā. Tenāha āyasmā nāgaseno –

For just as the water-clarifying gem of a wheel-turning king, when placed in water, causes the mud, algae, and mire to settle down, and makes the water clear, exceptionally clear, and unclouded; so too, faith, when it arises, suppresses the hindrances, causes the defilements to settle down, clarifies the mind, and makes it unclouded. With a clarified mind, the clansman who is a practitioner gives gifts, undertakes the precepts, performs the Uposatha observance, and begins development. Thus, faith should first be understood as having the characteristic of clarifying. Therefore, the Venerable Nāgasena said:

“Yathā, mahārāja, rājā cakkavatti caturaṅginiyā senāya saddhiṃ addhānamaggappaṭipanno parittaṃ udakaṃ tareyya, taṃ udakaṃ hatthīhi ca assehi ca rathehi ca pattīhi ca saṅkhubhitaṃ bhaveyya āvilaṃ lulitaṃ kalalībhūtaṃ, uttiṇṇo ca rājā cakkavatti manusse āṇāpeyya ‘pānīyaṃ bhaṇe āharatha, taṃ pivissāmī’ti. Rañño ca udakappasādako maṇi bhaveyya. ‘Evaṃ devā’ti kho te manussā rañño cakkavattissa paṭissutvā taṃ udakappasādakaṃ maṇiṃ udake pakkhipeyyuṃ. Tasmiṃ udake pakkhittamatte paṅkasevālapaṇakaṃ vigaccheyya, kaddamo ca sannisīdeyya, acchaṃ bhaveyya udakaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ, tato rañño cakkavattissa pānīyaṃ upanāmeyyuṃ – ‘pivatu devo pānīya’nti.

"Just as, great king, a wheel-turning monarch traveling along a road with his fourfold army might cross a small body of water, and that water would be stirred up by the elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, becoming turbid, agitated, and miry; and having crossed, the wheel-turning monarch might command his men, 'Friends, bring water, I wish to drink.' And the king would have a water-clarifying gem. 'So be it, Your Majesty,' those men would reply to the wheel-turning monarch, and they would place that water-clarifying gem in the water. The moment it was placed in the water, the slime, algae, and water-plants would vanish, the mud would settle, and the water would become clear, exceptionally clear, and unclouded. Then they would bring the drinking water to the wheel-turning monarch, saying: 'May Your Majesty drink the water.'"

“Yathā[M 0.0163], mahārāja, udakaṃ evaṃ cittaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā te manussā evaṃ yogāvacaro daṭṭhabbo. Yathā paṅkasevālapaṇakaṃ kaddamo ca evaṃ kilesā daṭṭhabbā. Yathā udakappasādako maṇi evaṃ saddhā daṭṭhabbā. Yathā udakappasādake maṇimhi pakkhittamatte paṅkasevālapaṇakaṃ vigacchati kaddamo ca sannisīdati, acchaṃ bhavati udakaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ, evameva kho, mahārāja, saddhā uppajjamānā nīvaraṇe vikkhambheti, vinīvaraṇaṃ [P 0.0120] cittaṃ hoti acchaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvila”nti (mi. pa. 2.1.10).

"In this way, great king, the mind should be seen as the water. Those men should be seen as the practitioner. The slime, algae, water-plants, and mud should be seen as the defilements. The water-clarifying gem should be seen as faith. Just as when the water-clarifying gem is placed in the water, the slime, algae, and water-plants vanish, the mud settles, and the water becomes clear, exceptionally clear, and unclouded; even so, great king, when faith arises, it suppresses the hindrances, and the mind, free from hindrances, becomes clear, exceptionally clear, and unclouded."

Yathā pana kumbhilamakaragāharakkhasādikiṇṇaṃ pūraṃ mahānadiṃ āgamma bhīrukajano ubhosu tīresu [V 0.0165] tiṭṭhati. Saṅgāmasūro pana mahāyodho āgantvā ‘kasmā ṭhitatthā’ti pucchitvā ‘sappaṭibhayabhāvena otarituṃ na visahāmā’ti vutte sunisitaṃ asiṃ gahetvā ‘mama pacchato etha, mā bhāyitthā’ti vatvā nadiṃ otaritvā āgatāgate kumbhilādayo paṭibāhitvā orimatīrato manussānaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ karonto pārimatīraṃ neti. Pārimatīratopi sotthinā orimatīraṃ āneti. Evameva dānaṃ dadato sīlaṃ rakkhato uposathakammaṃ karoto bhāvanaṃ ārabhato saddhā pubbaṅgamā purecārikā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘sampakkhandanalakkhaṇā ca saddhā’ti.

Furthermore, it is as when fearful people, having come to a great, full river teeming with crocodiles, sea-monsters, seizing demons, and so on, stand on the banks. A great warrior, brave on the battlefield, might then arrive and, after asking, 'Why are you all standing there?', is told, 'We do not dare to enter because it is dangerous.' Taking up a well-sharpened sword and saying, 'Come behind me, do not be afraid,' he enters the river. Warding off the crocodiles and other creatures as they approach, he brings the people safely from this shore to the far shore. And from the far shore, he brings them safely to this shore. In the same way, for one who is giving gifts, guarding virtue, performing the Uposatha observance, or beginning development, faith is the forerunner and leader. Therefore it was said, 'Faith also has the characteristic of leaping forward.'

Aparo nayo – saddahanalakkhaṇā saddhā, okappanalakkhaṇā vā. Pasādanarasā udakappasādakamaṇi viya, pakkhandanarasā vā oghuttaraṇo viya. Akālusiyapaccupaṭṭhānā, adhimuttipaccupaṭṭhānā vā. Saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā sotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānā vā, sā hatthavittabījāni viya daṭṭhabbā.

Another method: Faith has the characteristic of believing, or the characteristic of conviction. Its function is clarifying, like the water-clarifying gem; or its function is leaping forward, like one crossing a flood. Its manifestation is non-turbidity, or its manifestation is resolution. Its proximate cause is an object of faith, or its proximate cause is the factors of stream-entry. It should be seen as being like a hand, wealth, and seeds.

Vīrassa bhāvo vīriyaṃ, vīrānaṃ vā kammaṃ vīriyaṃ. Vidhinā vā nayena upāyena īrayitabbaṃ pavattayitabbanti vīriyaṃ. Tadeva kosajjassa abhibhavanato adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ. Paggahaṇalakkhaṇe vā indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Vīriyameva indriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ upatthambhanalakkhaṇañca vīriyaṃ paggahaṇalakkhaṇañca. Yathā hi jiṇṇagharaṃ āgantukena thūṇupatthambhena tiṭṭhati, evameva yogāvacaro vīriyupatthambhena upatthambhito hutvā sabbakusaladhammehi na hāyati, na parihāyati. Evaṃ tāvassa upatthambhanalakkhaṇatā veditabbā. Tenāha thero nāgaseno –

Energy (vīriya) is the state of a heroic person, or the work of heroic persons. Alternatively, it is energy because it is a state that should be brought into being by arrangement, by method, or by suitable means. That very energy, because it overcomes laziness, is a faculty in the sense of exercising supremacy. Alternatively, it is a faculty because in the characteristic of uplifting, it causes its own state of sovereignty to be exercised. Energy itself is the faculty, the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya). Furthermore, this energy has the characteristic of supporting and the characteristic of uplifting. For instance, just as an old house stands by means of a supporting pillar brought from elsewhere, in the same way, a yogāvacara, being supported by the pillar of energy, does not decline or fall away from all wholesome states. Thus, its characteristic of supporting should be understood first. Therefore, the Elder Nāgasena said:

“Yathā[M 0.0164], mahārāja, puriso gehe patante tamaññena dārunā upatthambheyya, upatthambhitaṃ santaṃ evaṃ taṃ gehaṃ na pateyya, evameva kho mahārāja upatthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ [P 0.0121] vīriyaṃ, vīriyupatthambhitā sabbe kusalā dhammā na hāyanti na parihāyantī”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.12).

"Just as, great king, a man might prop up a falling house with another piece of wood, and the house, thus propped up, would not fall, in the same way, great king, energy has the characteristic of supporting. All wholesome states, supported by energy, do not decline or fall away."

Yathā vā pana khuddikāya ca mahatikāya ca senāya saṅgāme pavatte khuddikā senā olīyeyya, tato rañño āroceyya, rājā balavāhanaṃ peseyya, tena paggahitā sakasenā parasenaṃ parājeyya, evameva vīriyaṃ sahajātasampayuttadhammānaṃ olīyituṃ osakkituṃ na deti, ukkhipati, paggaṇhāti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘paggahaṇalakkhaṇañca vīriya’nti.

Furthermore, just as when a battle occurs between a small army and a large one, the small army might falter. Then, they would inform the king. The king would send a strong military force. Just as their own army, being uplifted by that force, would defeat the other enemy army, in the same way, energy does not allow the co-arisen associated states to shrink back or to falter. It raises them up; it uplifts them. Therefore, it was said, 'Energy also has the characteristic of uplifting.'

Aparo [V 0.0166] nayo – ussāhalakkhaṇaṃ vīriyaṃ, sahajātānaṃ upatthambhanarasaṃ, asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, “saṃviggo yoniso padahatī”ti (a. ni. 4.113) vacanato saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ, vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Sammā āraddhaṃ sabbāsaṃ sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Another method: energy has the characteristic of striving. Its function is to support co-arisen states. Its manifestation is a state of not sinking. Its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency, in accordance with the saying, 'Being stirred, one strives wisely,' or its proximate cause is the grounds for arousing energy. It should be seen that energy, when rightly initiated, is the root of all attainments.

Saranti etāya, sayaṃ vā sarati, saraṇamattameva vā esāti sati. Sāva muṭṭhassaccassa abhibhavanato adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ, upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇe vā indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Sati eva indriyaṃ satindriyaṃ. Sā panesā apilāpanalakkhaṇā ca sati upaggaṇhanalakkhaṇā ca. Yathā hi rañño bhaṇḍāgāriko dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ gopayanto sāyaṃpātaṃ rājānaṃ issariyasampattiṃ sallakkhāpeti sāreti, evameva sati kusalaṃ dhammaṃ sallakkhāpeti sarāpeti. Tenāha thero –

Because they remember by means of it, or because it remembers by itself, or because it is mere remembering, it is called mindfulness (sati). That very mindfulness, because it overcomes forgetfulness, is a faculty in the sense of exercising supremacy. Alternatively, it is a faculty because in the characteristic of attending, it causes its own state of sovereignty to be exercised. Mindfulness itself is the faculty, the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya). Furthermore, this mindfulness has the characteristic of not floating away and the characteristic of grasping. For instance, just as a king's treasurer, while guarding the ten kinds of jewels, makes the king mark and remember his sovereign prosperity evening and morning, in the same way, mindfulness makes one mark and remember wholesome states. Therefore, the Elder said:

“Yathā, mahārāja, rañño cakkavattissa bhaṇḍāgāriko rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ sāyaṃpātaṃ yasaṃ sarāpeti – ‘ettakā, deva, hatthī, ettakā assā, ettakā rathā, ettakā pattī, ettakaṃ hiraññaṃ, ettakaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ, ettakaṃ sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ, taṃ devo saratū’ti, evameva kho, mahārāja, sati kusale dhamme apilāpeti – ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, ime cattāro sammappadhānā, ime cattāro iddhipādā, imāni pañcindriyāni, imāni pañca balāni, ime satta bojjhaṅgā, ayaṃ ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, ayaṃ samatho, ayaṃ vipassanā, ayaṃ vijjā, ayaṃ vimutti, ime lokuttarā dhammāti. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, apilāpanalakkhaṇā satī”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.13).

"Just as, great king, the treasurer of a wheel-turning monarch makes the wheel-turning king remember his glory evening and morning: 'So many elephants, lord, so many horses, so many chariots, so many foot soldiers, so much silver, so much gold, so much is all the wealth; may the lord remember that,' in the same way, great king, mindfulness makes one not forget wholesome states: 'These are the four foundations of mindfulness, these are the four right exertions, these are the four bases of spiritual power, these are the five faculties, these are the five powers, these are the seven factors of enlightenment, this is the noble eightfold path, this is serenity, this is insight, this is knowledge, this is liberation, these are the supramundane qualities.' Thus, great king, mindfulness has the characteristic of not floating away."

Yathā [M 0.0165] pana rañño cakkavattissa pariṇāyakaratanaṃ rañño ahite ca hite ca ñatvā ahite apayāpeti, hite upayāpeti, evameva sati hitāhitānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesitvā ‘ime kāyaduccaritādayo dhammā ahitā’ti ahite dhamme apanudeti[P 0.0122], ‘ime kāyasucaritādayo dhammā hitā’ti hite dhamme upaggaṇhāti. Tenāha thero –

Furthermore, just as the adviser-gem of a wheel-turning king, knowing those who are unbeneficial and beneficial to the king, makes the unbeneficial depart and makes the beneficial approach, in the same way, mindfulness, having thoroughly investigated the courses of beneficial and unbeneficial states, and knowing, 'These states such as bodily misconduct are unbeneficial,' dispels the unbeneficial states. And knowing, 'These states such as bodily good conduct are beneficial,' it grasps the beneficial states. Therefore, the Elder said:

“Yathā, mahārāja, rañño cakkavattissa pariṇāyakaratanaṃ rañño hitāhite jānāti ‘ime rañño hitā ime ahitā, ime upakārā ime anupakārā’ti, tato ahite apanudeti hite upaggaṇhāti, evameva kho, mahārāja, sati uppajjamānā hitāhitānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesati ‘ime dhammā hitā ime dhammā ahitā, ime dhammā upakārā ime dhammā anupakārā’ti[V 0.0167], tato ahite dhamme apanudeti hite dhamme upaggaṇhāti. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, upaggaṇhanalakkhaṇā satī”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.13).

"Great king, just as the adviser-gem of a wheel-turning king knows what is beneficial and what is unbeneficial to the king—'These are beneficial to the king, these are unbeneficial; these are helpful, these are unhelpful'—and then dispels the unbeneficial and grasps the beneficial, so too, great king, when mindfulness arises, it investigates the courses of beneficial and unbeneficial states: 'These states are beneficial, these states are unbeneficial; these states are helpful, these are unhelpful.' Then it dispels unbeneficial states and grasps beneficial states. Thus, great king, mindfulness has the characteristic of grasping."

Aparo nayo – apilāpanalakkhaṇā sati, asammosanarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā visayābhimukhībhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā, kāyādisatipaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānā vā, ārammaṇe daḷhaṃ patiṭṭhitattā pana esikā viya, cakkhudvārādirakkhaṇato dovāriko viya ca daṭṭhabbā.

Another method: Mindfulness has the characteristic of not floating away. Its function is non-bewilderment. Its manifestation is guarding, or alternatively, the state of facing the object. Its proximate cause is firm perception, or alternatively, the foundations of mindfulness concerning the body and so on. Furthermore, because it is firmly established in the object, it should be seen as being like a city gate-post; and because it guards the sense doors, such as the eye door, it should be seen as being like a gatekeeper.

Ārammaṇe cittaṃ sammā adhiyati ṭhapetīti samādhi. Sova vikkhepassa abhibhavanato adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ. Avikkhepalakkhaṇe vā indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Samādhiyeva indriyaṃ samādhindriyaṃ. Lakkhaṇādīni panassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

Because it places the mind well on an object, it is called concentration (samādhi). That very concentration, because it overcomes distraction, is a faculty in the sense of exercising supremacy. Alternatively, because in the characteristic of non-distraction it causes its own state of sovereignty to be exercised, it is a faculty. Concentration itself is the faculty, the faculty of concentration. Its characteristics and so on should be known in the manner already stated below.

Pajānātīti paññā. Kiṃ pajānāti? ‘Idaṃ dukkha’ntiādinā nayena ariyasaccāni. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ‘paññāpetīti paññā’ti vuttaṃ. Kinti paññāpetīti? Aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti paññāpeti. Sāva avijjāya abhibhavanato adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ. Dassanalakkhaṇe vā indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Paññāva indriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ. Sā panesā obhāsanalakkhaṇā ca paññā pajānanalakkhaṇā ca. Yathā hi catubhittike gehe rattibhāge dīpe jalite andhakāro nirujjhati āloko pātubhavati, evameva obhāsanalakkhaṇā [M 0.0166] paññā. Paññobhāsasamo obhāso nāma natthi. Paññavato hi ekapallaṅkena nisinnassa dasasahassilokadhātu ekālokā hoti. Tenāha thero –

It discerns, thus it is wisdom. What does it discern? It discerns the Noble Truths in the manner of 'This is suffering,' and so forth. In the commentaries, however, it is said: 'It makes known, thus it is wisdom.' How does it make known? It makes known: 'impermanent, suffering, and non-self.' That very wisdom is a faculty in the sense of its mastery in overcoming ignorance. Or, because it exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of seeing, it is a faculty. Wisdom itself is the faculty, the wisdom-faculty. Furthermore, this wisdom has the characteristic of illumination and the characteristic of discerning. For just as in a four-walled house, when a lamp is lit at night, darkness is dispelled and light appears, even so wisdom has the characteristic of illumination. There is no illumination equal to the illumination of wisdom. For when a person of wisdom is seated in a single cross-legged posture, the ten-thousandfold world-system becomes a single light. Therefore, the Elder said:

“Yathā, mahārāja, puriso andhakāre gehe padīpaṃ paveseyya, paviṭṭho padīpo andhakāraṃ viddhaṃseti, obhāsaṃ janeti, ālokaṃ [P 0.0123] vidaṃseti, pākaṭāni ca rūpāni karoti, evameva kho, mahārāja, paññā uppajjamānā avijjandhakāraṃ viddhaṃseti, vijjobhāsaṃ janeti, ñāṇālokaṃ vidaṃseti, pākaṭāni ca ariyasaccāni karoti. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, obhāsanalakkhaṇā paññā”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.15).

Great king, just as a person might bring a lamp into a dark house—the lamp, being brought in, dispels the darkness, produces illumination, reveals the light, and makes forms apparent—even so, great king, when wisdom arises, it dispels the darkness of ignorance, produces the illumination of true knowledge, reveals the light of insight, and makes the Noble Truths apparent. Thus, great king, wisdom has the characteristic of illumination.

Yathā pana cheko bhisakko āturānaṃ sappāyāsappāyāni bhojanāni jānāti, evaṃ paññā uppajjamānā kusalākusale sevitabbāsevitabbe hīnappaṇītakaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaappaṭibhāge [V 0.0168] dhamme pajānāti. Vuttampi cetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā – “pajānāti pajānātīti kho, āvuso, tasmā paññavāti vuccati. Kiñca pajānāti? Idaṃ dukkhanti pajānātī”ti (ma. ni. 1.449) vitthāretabbaṃ. Evamassā pajānanalakkhaṇatā veditabbā.

Furthermore, just as a skilled physician knows for the sick which foods are suitable and unsuitable, so too, when wisdom arises, it discerns states that are wholesome and unwholesome, to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, inferior and superior, dark and bright, with their counterparts and without their counterparts. And this was said by the General of the Dhamma: 'One discerns, one discerns, friend; therefore it is called wisdom. And what does one discern? One discerns: "This is suffering."' This should be elaborated. Thus, its characteristic of discerning is to be known.

Aparo nayo – yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā paññā; akkhalitapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā vā kusalissāsakhittausupaṭivedho viya. Visayobhāsarasā padīpo viya. Asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā araññagatasudesako viya.

Another method: Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their intrinsic nature; or, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer, the characteristic of unerring penetration. Its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp. Its manifestation is non-bewilderment, like a good guide in a forest.

Manatīti mano; vijānātīti attho. Aṭṭhakathācariyā panāhu – nāḷiyā minamāno viya, mahātulāya dhārayamāno viya ca, ārammaṇaṃ minati pajānātīti manoti. Tadeva mananalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Manova indriyaṃ manindriyaṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttacittassevetaṃ vevacanaṃ.

It knows, thus it is mind; the meaning is, it cognizes. The commentary teachers, however, say: 'Like one measuring with a nāḷi, or like one weighing with a great balance, it measures the object, it does not discern it; thus it is called mind.' That very mind, in its characteristic of knowing, exercises sovereignty; thus it is a faculty. Mind itself is the faculty, the mind-faculty. This is a synonym for the consciousness mentioned previously.

Pītisomanassasampayogato sobhanaṃ mano assāti sumano. Sumanassa bhāvo somanassaṃ. Sātalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Somanassameva indriyaṃ somanassindriyaṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttavedanāyevetaṃ vevacanaṃ.

Because of its association with joy and gladness, it has an excellent mind, thus it is 'sumano'. The state of having an excellent mind is gladness. In the characteristic of satisfaction, it exercises sovereignty; thus it is a faculty. Gladness itself is the faculty, the faculty of gladness. This is a synonym for the feeling mentioned previously.

Jīvanti [M 0.0167] tena taṃsampayuttakā dhammāti jīvitaṃ. Anupālanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Jīvitameva indriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ. Taṃ pavattasantatādhipateyyaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇādīhi pana attanā avinibhuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesaṃyeva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbadhammapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Santepi ca anupālanalakkhaṇādimhi vidhāne atthikkhaṇeyeva [P 0.0124] taṃ te dhamme anupāleti udakaṃ viya uppalādīni, yathāsakaṃpaccayuppannepi ca dhamme pāleti dhātī viya kumāraṃ, sayaṃpavattitadhammasambandheneva ca pavattati niyāmako viya, na bhaṅgato uddhaṃ pavattayati attano ca pavattayitabbānañca abhāvā, na bhaṅgakkhaṇe ṭhapeti sayaṃ bhijjamānattā khīyamāno viya vaṭṭisineho dīpasikhaṃ. Na ca anupālanapavattanaṭṭhapanānubhāvavirahitaṃ yathāvuttakkhaṇe tassa tassa sādhanatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The states associated with it live by means of it, thus it is 'life'. In the characteristic of maintaining, it exercises sovereignty; thus it is a faculty. Life itself is the faculty, the life-faculty. It has lordship over the continuity of occurrence. Furthermore, by way of its characteristics, etc., the life-faculty has the characteristic of maintaining states inseparable from itself; its function is to cause them to occur; its manifestation is the establishing of those very states; its proximate cause is the states that are to be maintained. And although this is its arrangement with the characteristic of maintaining, etc., it maintains those states only at the moment of their existence, like water does lotuses; and it protects states that have arisen from their own respective conditions, like a nurse does a child; and it proceeds only in connection with the states it causes to proceed, like a pilot with the ship he steers. It does not cause them to proceed beyond their dissolution, due to the absence of both itself and of those that are to be made to proceed. It does not establish them at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself dissolving, like the consuming oil of a wick does not sustain the lamp's flame. And it should be seen that it is not devoid of the power of maintaining, causing to occur, and establishing, because at the respective aforesaid moments, it accomplishes each of these.

Maggaṅgarāsivaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Group of Path Factors

Sammādiṭṭhiādīsu [V 0.0169] dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi. Abhiniropanaṭṭhena sammāsaṅkappo, paggahanaṭṭhena sammāvāyāmo, upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena sammāsati, avikkhepanaṭṭhena sammāsamādhīti veditabbo. Vacanatthato pana sammā passati, sammā vā tāya passantīti sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā saṅkappeti, sammā vā tena saṅkappentīti sammāsaṅkappo. Sammā vāyāmeti, sammā vā tena vāyamantīti sammāvāyāmo. Sammā sarati, sammā vā tāya sarantīti sammāsati. Sammā samādhiyati, sammā vā tena samādhiyantīti sammāsamādhi. Apica, pasatthā sundarā vā diṭṭhi sammādiṭṭhīti. Imināpi nayena tesaṃ vacanattho veditabbo. Lakkhaṇādīni pana heṭṭhā vuttāneva.

Regarding the terms beginning with Right View: Right View is so called in the sense of seeing. Right Thought is so called in the sense of applying the mind. Right Effort is so called in the sense of exertion. Right Mindfulness is so called in the sense of establishing. Right Concentration is so called in the sense of non-distraction. As for the verbal meaning: it is 'Right View' because it sees rightly, or because by it associated states see rightly. It is 'Right Thought' because it thinks rightly, or because by it associated states think rightly. It is 'Right Effort' because it strives rightly, or because by it associated states strive rightly. It is 'Right Mindfulness' because it is mindful rightly, or because by it associated states are mindful rightly. It is 'Right Concentration' because it concentrates rightly, or because by it associated states concentrate rightly. Furthermore, Right View is a view that is praised or beautiful. In this way too, the verbal meaning of these terms should be understood. As for their characteristics and so forth, they have already been stated previously.

Balarāsivaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Group of Powers

Saddhābalādīsupi saddhādīni vuttatthāneva. Akampiyaṭṭhena pana balanti veditabbaṃ. Evametesu assaddhiye na kampatīti saddhābalaṃ. Kosajje na kampatīti vīriyabalaṃ. Muṭṭhassacce na kampatīti satibalaṃ. Uddhacce na kampatīti samādhibalaṃ. Avijjāya na kampatīti paññābalaṃ. Ahirike na kampatīti hiribalaṃ[M 0.0168]. Anottappe na kampatīti ottappabalanti. Ayaṃ ubhayapadavasena atthavaṇṇanā hoti.

In the terms beginning with the faith-power, 'faith' and the other terms have the same meaning as already stated. However, 'power' should be understood in the sense of being unshakable. Thus, among these: it is the 'faith-power' because it is not shaken by faithlessness; it is the 'energy-power' because it is not shaken by laziness; it is the 'mindfulness-power' because it is not shaken by forgetfulness; it is the 'concentration-power' because it is not shaken by restlessness; it is the 'wisdom-power' because it is not shaken by ignorance; it is the 'moral shame-power' because it is not shaken by shamelessness; it is the 'moral dread-power' because it is not shaken by lack of moral dread. This is the explanation of the meaning by way of both terms.

Tattha purimāni pañca heṭṭhā lakkhaṇādīhi pakāsitāneva. Pacchimadvaye kāyaduccaritādīhi hiriyatīti hirī; lajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tehi eva ottappatīti ottappaṃ; pāpato ubbegassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tesaṃ nānākaraṇadīpanatthaṃ ‘samuṭṭhānaṃ adhipati lajjā bhayalakkhaṇena cā’ti imaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā ayaṃ [P 0.0125] vitthārakathā vuttā.

Among these, the first five have already been explained below by their characteristics and so forth. In the latter pair: it is 'moral shame' (hirī) because one is ashamed of bodily misconduct and so forth; this is a designation for shame. It is 'moral dread' (ottappa) because one is apprehensive of those very same things; this is a designation for dread of evil. To explain their distinction, this detailed explanation was given after laying down this matrix: 'Origin, sovereign, shame, and by the characteristic of fear.'

Ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī nāma; bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ nāma. Attādhipati hirī nāma; lokādhipati ottappaṃ nāma. Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī nāma; bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ nāma. Sappatissavalakkhaṇā hirī nāma; vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ nāma.

Moral shame (hirī) is internally arisen; moral dread (ottappa) is externally arisen. Moral shame has the self as its sovereign; moral dread has the world as its sovereign. Moral shame is established in the nature of shame; moral dread is established in the nature of fear. Moral shame has the characteristic of reverence; moral dread has the characteristic of fearing wrongdoing and seeing it as a danger.

Tattha ajjhattasamuṭṭhānaṃ hiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti – jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā, vayaṃ paccavekkhitvā, sūrabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā, bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā. Kathaṃ? ‘Pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ na [V 0.0170] jātisampannānaṃ kammaṃ, hīnajaccānaṃ kevaṭṭādīnaṃ idaṃ kammaṃ. Mādisassa jātisampannassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta’nti, evaṃ tāva jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā ‘pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ daharehi kattabbaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa vaye ṭhitassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta’nti, evaṃ vayaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā ‘pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ dubbalajātikānaṃ kammaṃ, na sūrabhāvānaṃ. Mādisassa sūrabhāvasampannassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta’nti, evaṃ sūrabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā ‘pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ andhabālānaṃ kammaṃ, na paṇḍitānaṃ. Mādisassa paṇḍitassa bahussutassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta’nti, evaṃ bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ ajjhattasamuṭṭhānahiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti. Samuṭṭhāpetvā ca pana attano citte hiriṃ pavesetvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī nāma hoti.

Herein, one arouses internally-arisen moral shame for four reasons: by reflecting on one's lineage, by reflecting on one's age, by reflecting on one's courage, and by reflecting on one's great learning. How? 'This act of wrongdoing is not the work of the well-born; this is the work of those of low birth, such as fishermen. It is not fitting for one like me, who is well-born, to do this work.' Thus, first, by reflecting on one's lineage, one who does not commit evil deeds such as killing living beings arouses moral shame. Similarly: 'This act of wrongdoing is work to be done by the young. It is not fitting for one like me, who is advanced in age, to do this work.' Thus, by reflecting on one's age, one who does not commit evil deeds such as killing living beings arouses moral shame. Similarly: 'This evil work is the work of the weak, not of the courageous. It is not fitting for one like me, endowed with courage, to do this work.' Thus, by reflecting on one's courage, one who does not commit evil deeds such as killing living beings arouses moral shame. Similarly: 'This evil work is the work of the blind and foolish, not of the wise. It is not fitting for one like me, who is wise and of great learning, to do this work.' Thus, by reflecting on one's great learning, one who does not commit evil deeds such as killing living beings arouses moral shame. In this way, one arouses internally-arisen moral shame for these four reasons. And having aroused it, one lets moral shame enter one's mind and does not commit evil deeds. Thus, moral shame is internally arisen.

Kathaṃ [M 0.0169] bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ nāma? Sace tvaṃ pāpakammaṃ karissasi catūsu parisāsu garahappatto bhavissasi.

How is moral dread (ottappa) externally arisen? 'If you commit an evil deed, you will incur blame in the four assemblies.'

Garahissanti taṃ viññū, asuciṃ nāgariko yathā;

Vajjito sīlavantehi, kathaṃ bhikkhu karissasīti.

The wise will censure you, as a city-dweller does an impure thing; shunned by the virtuous, O monk, what will you do?

Evaṃ paccavekkhanto hi bahiddhāsamuṭṭhitena ottappena pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ nāma hoti.

Indeed, reflecting thus, one does not commit an evil deed on account of externally-arisen moral dread. In this way, moral dread is externally arisen.

Kathaṃ attādhipati hirī nāma? Idhekacco kulaputto attānaṃ [P 0.0126] adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā ‘mādisassa saddhāpabbajitassa bahussutassa dhutaṅgadharassa na yuttaṃ pāpakammaṃ kātu’nti pāpaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ attādhipati hirī nāma hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “so attānaṃyeva adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ karitvā akusalaṃ pajahati kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhamattānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 3.40).

How does moral shame (hirī) have the self as its sovereign? Here, a certain clansman, having made himself the sovereign and chief, does not commit evil, thinking, 'It is not fitting for one like me—who has gone forth in faith, is of great learning, and observes the ascetic practices—to commit an evil deed.' Thus, moral shame has the self as its sovereign. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'He, having made himself his own sovereign and chief, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity.' (AN 3.40)

Kathaṃ lokādhipati ottappaṃ nāma? Idhekacco kulaputto lokaṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pāpakammaṃ [V 0.0171] na karoti. Yathāha – “mahā kho panāyaṃ lokasannivāso. Mahantasmiṃ kho pana lokasannivāse santi samaṇabrāhmaṇā iddhimanto dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduno, te dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ pajānanti, tepimaṃ evaṃ jānissanti ‘passatha bho imaṃ kulaputtaṃ, saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti. Santi devatā iddhimantiniyo dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduniyo. Tā dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ pajānanti, tāpi maṃ jānissanti ‘passatha bho imaṃ kulaputtaṃ, saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti… so lokaṃyeva adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā akusalaṃ pajahati kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhamattānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 3.146). Evaṃ lokādhipati ottappaṃ nāma hoti.

How does moral dread (ottappa) have the world as its sovereign? Here, a certain clansman, having made the world his sovereign and chief, does not commit evil deeds. As it is said: 'This world-abode is vast. In this vast world-abode, there are ascetics and brahmins who possess psychic powers, the divine eye, and knowledge of others' minds. They see even from afar; though near, they are not seen by others. With their own minds, they know the minds of others. They too will know me thus: “Sirs, look at this clansman. Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he dwells intermingled with evil, unwholesome states.” There are deities who possess psychic powers, the divine eye, and knowledge of others' minds. They see even from afar; though near, they are not seen by others. With their own minds, they know the minds of others. They too will know me thus: “Sirs, look at this clansman. Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he dwells intermingled with evil, unwholesome states.” … So, having made the world itself his sovereign and chief, he abandons the unwholesome and cultivates the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy and cultivates the blameless, and maintains himself in purity.' Thus, moral dread has the world as its sovereign.

Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā [M 0.0170] hirī, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappanti. Ettha pana lajjāti lajjanākāro; tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitā hirī. Bhayanti apāyabhayaṃ; tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ. Tadubhayampi pāpaparivajjane pākaṭaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi, yathā nāma eko kulaputto uccārapassāvādīni karonto lajjitabbayuttakaṃ ekaṃ disvā lajjanākārappatto bhaveyya hīḷito, evameva ajjhattaṃ lajjidhammaṃ okkamitvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Ekacco apāyabhayabhīto hutvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti.

Moral shame is established in the nature of shame; moral dread is established in the nature of fear. Herein, lajjā is the state of being ashamed; hirī is well-established in that nature. Bhaya is fear of the lower realms; ottappa is well-established in that nature. Both of them become manifest in the avoidance of evil. For instance, just as a certain clansman, while defecating, urinating, and so on, upon seeing someone before whom it is proper to feel shame, would attain the state of being ashamed and feel censured, in the very same way, one who has internally arrived at the state of shame does not commit evil deeds. Another, being afraid of the lower realms, does not commit evil deeds.

Tatridaṃ opammaṃ – yathā hi dvīsu ayoguḷesu eko sītalo bhaveyya gūthamakkhito, eko uṇho āditto. Tattha paṇḍito sītalaṃ gūthamakkhitattā jigucchanto na gaṇhāti, itaraṃ ḍāhabhayena. Tattha sītalassa gūthamakkhanajigucchāya agaṇhanaṃ viya ajjhattaṃ lajjidhammaṃ okkamitvā [P 0.0127] pāpassa akaraṇaṃ. Uṇhassa ḍāhabhayena agaṇhanaṃ viya apāyabhayena pāpassa akaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein is the simile: Just as, of two iron balls, one might be cold and smeared with excrement, and the other hot and blazing. Therein, a wise person, being disgusted, would not take the cold one because it is smeared with excrement, nor the other out of fear of being burned. In this simile, like not taking the cold one out of disgust for its being smeared with excrement, so should the non-doing of evil be understood, having internally entered into the state of shame. Like not taking the hot one out of fear of being burned, so should the non-doing of evil be understood out of fear of the lower realms.

Sappatissavalakkhaṇā hirī, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappanti. Idampi dvayaṃ pāpaparivajjane eva pākaṭaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇā satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇā dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇā sabrahmacārīmahattapaccavekkhaṇāti catūhi kāraṇehi [V 0.0172] sappatissavalakkhaṇaṃ hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā pāpaṃ na karoti. Ekacco attānuvādabhayaṃ parānuvādabhayaṃ daṇḍabhayaṃ duggatibhayanti catūhi kāraṇehi vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā pāpaṃ na karoti. Tattha jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇādīni ceva attānuvādabhayādīni ca vitthāretvā kathetabbāni.

Hirī has the characteristic of respectfulness; ottappa has the characteristic of fearing what is blameworthy and seeing it as a danger. This pair, too, becomes manifest only in the avoidance of evil. For, a certain person—by reflecting on the greatness of their birth, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of their inheritance, and reflecting on the greatness of their companions in the holy life—by these four reasons, having aroused hirī which has the characteristic of respectfulness, does not commit evil. Another person—due to fear of self-reproach, fear of others' reproach, fear of punishment, and fear of a woeful destination—by these four reasons, having aroused ottappa which has the characteristic of fearing what is blameworthy and seeing it as a danger, does not commit evil. Herein, the reflections on the greatness of birth and so on, and the fears of self-reproach and so on, should be explained in detail.

Mūlarāsivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Root Aggregate

Na lubbhanti etena, sayaṃ vā na lubbhati, alubbhanamattameva vā tanti alobho. Adosāmohesupi eseva nayo. Tesu alobho ārammaṇe cittassa agedhalakkhaṇo, alaggabhāvalakkhaṇo vā kamaladale jalabindu viya. Apariggahaṇaraso muttabhikkhu viya[M 0.0171]. Anallīnabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno asucimhi patitapuriso viya. Adoso acaṇḍikkalakkhaṇo, avirodhalakkhaṇo vā anukūlamitto viya. Āghātavinayaraso pariḷāhavinayaraso vā candanaṃ viya. Sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno puṇṇacando viya. Amoho lakkhaṇādīhi heṭṭhā paññindriyapade vibhāvito eva.

Associated states are not greedy by means of it; or it is not greedy itself; or it is merely a state of non-greediness—thus it is alobha (non-greed). The same method applies to adosa (non-hatred) and amoha (non-delusion). Among these, non-greed has the characteristic of the mind's non-craving for an object, or the characteristic of non-adherence, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Its function is non-grasping, like a liberated monk. It is manifested as non-clinging, like a man fallen into filth. Non-hatred has the characteristic of non-fierceness, or the characteristic of non-opposition, like a congenial friend. Its function is the removal of resentment, or the dispelling of the heat of hatred, like sandalwood. It is manifested as gentleness, like the full moon. Non-delusion, with its characteristics and so on, has already been explained below in the section on the faculty of wisdom.

Imesu pana tīsu alobho maccheramalassa paṭipakkho, adoso dussīlyamalassa, amoho kusalesu dhammesu abhāvanāya paṭipakkho. Alobho cettha dānahetu, adoso sīlahetu, amoho bhāvanāhetu. Tesu ca alobhena anadhikaṃ gaṇhāti, luddhassa adhikaggahaṇato. Adosena anūnaṃ, duṭṭhassa ūnaggahaṇato. Amohena aviparītaṃ, mūḷhassa viparītaggahaṇato.

Now, among these three, non-greed is the opposite of the stain of stinginess, non-hatred is the opposite of the stain of immorality, and non-delusion is the opposite of the non-development of wholesome states. Furthermore, herein, non-greed is the cause of giving, non-hatred is the cause of virtue, and non-delusion is the cause of mental development. And among them, through non-greed one does not take what is excessive, because a greedy person takes what is excessive. Through non-hatred one does not take what is deficient, because a hateful person takes what is deficient. Through non-delusion one does not take what is perverted, because a deluded person takes what is perverted.

Alobhena cettha vijjamānaṃ dosaṃ dosato dhārento dose pavattati; luddho hi dosaṃ paṭicchādeti. Adosena vijjamānaṃ guṇaṃ guṇato dhārento guṇe pavattati; duṭṭho hi guṇaṃ [P 0.0128] makkheti. Amohena yāthāvasabhāvaṃ yāthāvasabhāvato dhārento yāthāvasabhāve pavattati. Mūḷho hi ‘tacchaṃ atacchanti atacchaṃ ca taccha’nti gaṇhāti.
