Alobhena ca piyavippayogadukkhaṃ na hoti, luddhassa piyasabhāvato piyavippayogāsahanato ca. Adosena appiyasampayogadukkhaṃ na hoti, duṭṭhassa hi appiyasabhāvato appiyasampayogāsahanato ca. Amohena icchitālābhadukkhaṃ na hoti, amūḷhassa hi ‘taṃ kutettha labbhā’tievamādipaccavekkhaṇasambhavato (dī. ni. 3.34; a. ni. 9.30).

Herein, through non-greed, holding an existing fault as a fault, one acts with regard to the fault; for a greedy person conceals a fault. Through non-hatred, holding an existing virtue as a virtue, one acts with regard to the virtue; for a hateful person denigrates a virtue. Through non-delusion, holding the true nature as its true nature, one acts with regard to the true nature; for a deluded person takes what is true as untrue and what is untrue as true. And through non-greed, the suffering of separation from the beloved does not arise, because of the greedy person's nature of attachment and inability to bear separation from the beloved. Through non-hatred, the suffering of association with the unloved does not arise, because of the hateful person's nature of aversion and inability to bear association with the unloved. Through non-delusion, the suffering of not obtaining what is desired does not arise, for in the undeluded person there is the possibility of reflecting, 'How could that be obtained here?'

Alobhena [V 0.0173] cettha jātidukkhaṃ na hoti, alobhassa taṇhāpaṭipakkhato taṇhāmūlakattā ca jātidukkhassa. Adosena jarādukkhaṃ na hoti, tikkhadosassa khippaṃ jarāsambhavato. Amohena maraṇadukkhaṃ na hoti, sammohamaraṇañhi dukkhaṃ, na cetaṃ amūḷhassa hoti. Alobhena ca gahaṭṭhānaṃ, amohena pabbajitānaṃ, adosena pana sabbesampi sukhasaṃvāsatā hoti.

Herein, through non-greed, the suffering of birth does not arise, because non-greed is the opposite of craving, and the suffering of birth has craving as its root. Through non-hatred, the suffering of aging does not arise, because for one with sharp hatred, aging occurs quickly. Through non-delusion, the suffering of death does not arise, for death with delusion is suffering, and this does not happen for one who is undeluded. And through non-greed, there is pleasant cohabitation for householders; through non-delusion, for renunciants; and moreover, through non-hatred, there is pleasant cohabitation for all.

Visesato [M 0.0172] cettha alobhena pettivisaye upapatti na hoti. Yebhuyyena hi sattā taṇhāya pettivisayaṃ upapajjanti, taṇhāya ca paṭipakkho alobho. Adosena niraye upapatti na hoti. Dosena hi caṇḍajātitāya dosasadisaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Dosassa ca paṭipakkho adoso. Amohena tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbatti na hoti. Mohena hi niccasammūḷhaṃ tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjanti. Mohassa paṭipakkho ca amoho. Etesu ca alobho rāgavasena upagamanassa abhāvakaro, adoso dosavasena apagamanassa, amoho mohavasena amajjhattabhāvassa.

Specifically herein, through non-greed, rebirth in the sphere of petas does not occur. For, for the most part, beings are reborn in the sphere of petas through craving, and non-greed is the opposite of craving. Through non-hatred, rebirth in hell does not occur. For through hatred, due to their fierce nature, they are reborn in a hell similar to hatred. And non-hatred is the opposite of hatred. Through non-delusion, birth in the animal womb does not occur. For through delusion, beings are reborn in the animal womb, which is perpetually and intensely deluded. And non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. And among these, non-greed causes the non-occurrence of approaching by way of lust, non-hatred causes the non-occurrence of departing by way of hatred, and non-delusion causes the non-occurrence of non-equanimity by way of delusion.

Tīhipi cetehi yathāpaṭipāṭiyā nekkhammasaññā abyāpādasaññā avihiṃsāsaññāti imā tisso. Asubhasaññā appamāṇasaññā dhātusaññāti imā ca tisso saññāyo honti. Alobhena pana kāmasukhallikānuyogaantassa, adosena attakilamathānuyogaantassa parivajjanaṃ hoti; amohena majjhimāya paṭipattiyā paṭipajjanaṃ. Tathā alobhena abhijjhākāyaganthassa pabhedanaṃ hoti, adosena byāpādakāyaganthassa, amohena sesaganthadvayassa. Purimāni ca dve satipaṭṭhānāni purimānaṃ dvinnaṃ ānubhāvena, pacchimāni pacchimasseva ānubhāvena ijjhanti.

And by these three, in respective order, these three perceptions arise: the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, and the perception of non-harming. And these three perceptions also arise: the perception of foulness, the perception of the immeasurables, and the perception of elements. Moreover, through non-greed, there is the avoidance of the extreme of indulgence in sensual pleasures; through non-hatred, there is the avoidance of the extreme of self-mortification; and through non-delusion, there is the practice of the middle path. Likewise, through non-greed, there is the breaking of the bodily knot of covetousness; through non-hatred, the bodily knot of ill will; and through non-delusion, the remaining two knots. And the first two establishments of mindfulness are accomplished through the power of the first two, while the latter two are accomplished through the power of the last one alone.

Alobho cettha ārogyassa paccayo hoti; aluddho hi lobhanīyampi asappāyaṃ na sevati, tena kho arogo hoti. Adoso [P 0.0129] yobbanassa; aduṭṭho hi valipalitāvahena dosagginā aḍayhamāno dīgharattaṃ yuvā hoti. Amoho dīghāyukatāya; amūḷho hi hitāhitaṃ ñatvā ahitaṃ parivajjanto hitañca paṭisevamāno dīghāyuko hoti.

Herein, non-greed is a condition for health; for one who is not greedy does not indulge in what is unsuitable, even if it is desirable, and because of that, one is healthy. Non-hatred is a condition for youthfulness; for one who is not hateful, not being burned by the fire of hatred which brings wrinkles and grey hair, remains young for a long time. Non-delusion is a condition for longevity; for one who is not deluded, knowing what is beneficial and harmful, avoiding the harmful and cultivating the beneficial, has a long life.

Alobho cettha bhogasampattiyā paccayo hoti, aluddhassa hi cāgena bhogapaṭilābho. Adoso mittasampattiyā, mettāya mittānaṃ paṭilābhato ceva aparihānato ca. Amoho attasampattiyā[V 0.0174], amūḷho hi attano hitameva karonto attānaṃ sampādeti[M 0.0173]. Alobho ca dibbavihārassa paccayo hoti, adoso brahmavihārassa, amoho ariyavihārassa.

Herein, non-greed is a condition for the accomplishment of wealth; for the ungreedy, there is the acquisition of wealth through generosity. Non-hatred is a condition for the accomplishment of friends, because through loving-kindness, there is both the acquisition and non-decline of friends. Non-delusion is a condition for the accomplishment of self; for the undeluded one, doing only what is beneficial for oneself, brings oneself to accomplishment. And non-greed is a condition for divine abiding, non-hatred for Brahma-abiding, and non-delusion for noble abiding.

Alobhena cettha sakapakkhesu sattasaṅkhāresu nibbuto hoti, tesaṃ vināsena abhisaṅgahetukassa dukkhassa abhāvā; adosena parapakkhesu, aduṭṭhassa hi verīsupi verisaññāya abhāvato; amohena udāsīnapakkhesu, amūḷhassa sabbābhisaṅgatāya abhāvato.

Herein, through non-greed, one is at peace with regard to beings and formations of one's own side, due to the absence of suffering—which is caused by strong attachment—upon their destruction. Through non-hatred, one is at peace with regard to beings and formations of the other side, because for one without hatred, there is an absence of the perception of 'enemy' even towards enemies. Through non-delusion, one is at peace with regard to beings and formations of the neutral side, because for the undeluded one, there is an absence of all attachment.

Alobhena ca aniccadassanaṃ hoti; luddho hi upabhogāsāya aniccepi saṅkhāre aniccato na passati. Adosena dukkhadassanaṃ; adosajjhāsayo hi pariccattaāghātavatthupariggaho saṅkhāreyeva dukkhato passati. Amohena anattadassanaṃ; amūḷho hi yāthāvagahaṇakusalo apariṇāyakaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ apariṇāyakato bujjhati. Yathā ca etehi aniccadassanādīni evametepi aniccadassanādīhi honti. Aniccadassanena hi alobho hoti, dukkhadassanena adoso, anattadassanena amoho hoti. Ko hi nāma ‘aniccamida’nti sammā ñatvā tassatthāya pihaṃ uppādeyya, saṅkhāre vā ‘dukkha’nti jānanto aparampi accantatikhiṇaṃ kodhadukkhaṃ uppādeyya, attasuññatañca bujjhitvā puna sammohamāpajjeyyāti?

Furthermore, through non-greed there is the discernment of impermanence; for one who is greedy, due to attachment to enjoyment, does not see even impermanent formations as impermanent. Through non-hatred, there is the discernment of suffering; for one with a disposition of non-hatred, having relinquished the grasping of the basis for resentment, sees formations themselves as suffering. Through non-delusion, there is the discernment of non-self; for one who is not deluded, being skilled in correct apprehension, understands the five aggregates, which are without a leader, as being without a leader. And just as through these there arise the discernment of impermanence and so on, so too do these arise through the discernment of impermanence and so on. Indeed, through the discernment of impermanence, non-greed arises; through the discernment of suffering, non-hatred arises; through the discernment of non-self, non-delusion arises. For who, having rightly known, ‘This is impermanent,’ would generate a longing for its sake? Or, knowing formations to be suffering, would produce the further, extremely sharp suffering of anger? Or, having understood the voidness of self, would again fall into delusion?

Kammapatharāsivaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Collection of Courses of Action

Nābhijjhāyatīti anabhijjhā. Kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ idhalokaparalokahitaṃ guṇānubhāvapaṭiladdhaṃ kittisaddañca na byāpādetīti abyāpādo. Sammā passati, sobhanā vā diṭṭhīti sammādiṭṭhi. Alobhādīnaṃyeva tāni nāmāni. Heṭṭhā panete dhammā mūlavasena gahitā, idha kammapathavasenāti veditabbā.

'It does not covet,' thus it is non-covetousness. 'It does not destroy bodily and mental happiness, welfare in this world and the next, and the sound of fame attained through the power of virtues,' thus it is non-ill-will. 'It sees rightly,' or 'it is an excellent view,' thus it is right view. Those are indeed names for non-greed and so on. However, previously these states were taken in the sense of roots; here they are to be understood in the sense of courses of action.

Lokapāladukavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Pair of World-Protectors

Hirottappānipi heṭṭhā balavasena gahitāni, idha lokapālavasena. Lokañhi ime dve dhammā pālayanti. Yathāha –

Conscience and prudence were also taken previously in the sense of powers, but here in the sense of world-protectors. For these two qualities protect the world. As it is said:

“Dveme, bhikkhave, sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālenti. Katame dve? Hirī ca ottappañca[V 0.0175]. Ime kho, bhikkhave, dve [P 0.0130] sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālenti[M 0.0174]. Sace, bhikkhave, dve sukkā dhammā lokaṃ na pāleyyuṃ, nayidha paññāyetha mātāti vā, mātucchāti vā, mātulānīti vā, ācariyabhariyāti vā, garūnaṃ dārāti vā. Sambhedaṃ loko agamissa yathā ajeḷakā kukkuṭasūkarā soṇasiṅgālā. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, ime dve sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālenti, tasmā paññāyati mātāti vā mātucchāti vā mātulānīti vā ācariyabhariyāti vā garūnaṃ dārāti vā”ti (a. ni. 2.9).

“Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world. What two? Conscience and prudence. These, monks, are the two bright qualities that protect the world. If, monks, these two bright qualities did not protect the world, there would not be recognized here ‘mother,’ or ‘maternal aunt,’ or ‘maternal uncle’s wife,’ or ‘teacher’s wife,’ or ‘wives of respected persons.’ The world would fall into promiscuity, like goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, dogs and jackals. But because, monks, these two bright qualities protect the world, there is recognition of ‘mother,’ or ‘maternal aunt,’ or ‘maternal uncle’s wife,’ or ‘teacher’s wife,’ or ‘wives of respected persons.’”

Passaddhādiyugalavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Pairs Beginning with Tranquility

Kāyassa passambhanaṃ kāyapassaddhi. Cittassa passambhanaṃ cittapassaddhi. Kāyoti cettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā. Ubhopi panetā ekato katvā kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā kāyacittapassaddhiyo, kāyacittadarathanimmaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ aparipphandasītibhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ avūpasamakarauddhaccādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The calming of the mental body is tranquility of the mental body. The calming of the mind is tranquility of the mind. Herein, 'mental body' refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Furthermore, these two, taken together, have the characteristic of calming the torment of the mental body and mind; they have the function of suppressing the torment of the mental body and mind; they manifest as the state of non-trembling and coolness of the mental body and mind; and they have the mental body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opponent of the defilements, principally restlessness, that cause the non-tranquility of the mental body and mind.

Kāyassa lahubhāvo kāyalahutā. Cittassa lahubhāvo cittalahutā. Tā kāyacittagarubhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittagarubhāvanimmaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ adandhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ garubhāvakarathinamiddhādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The lightness of the mental body is lightness of the mental body. The lightness of the mind is lightness of the mind. They have the characteristic of calming the heaviness of the mental body and mind; they have the function of suppressing the heaviness of the mental body and mind; they manifest as the state of non-sluggishness of the mental body and mind; and they have the mental body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opponent of the defilements, principally sloth and torpor, that cause heaviness in the mental body and mind.

Kāyassa mudubhāvo kāyamudutā. Cittassa mudubhāvo cittamudutā. Tā kāyacittathaddhabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittathaddhabhāvanimmaddanarasā, appaṭighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ thaddhabhāvakaradiṭṭhimānādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The softness of the mental body is softness of the mental body. The softness of the mind is softness of the mind. They have the characteristic of calming the rigidity of the mental body and mind; they have the function of suppressing the rigidity of the mental body and mind; they manifest as non-opposition; and they have the mental body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opponent of the defilements, principally wrong view and conceit, that cause rigidity in the mental body and mind.

Kāyassa kammaññabhāvo kāyakammaññatā. Cittassa kammaññabhāvo cittakammaññatā. Tā kāyacittaakammaññabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittānaṃ akammaññabhāvanimmaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇasampattipaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ akammaññabhāvakarāvasesanīvaraṇapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā. Tā pasādanīyavatthūsu pasādāvahā, hitakiriyāsu [P 0.0131] viniyogakkhemabhāvāvahā suvaṇṇavisuddhi viyāti daṭṭhabbā.

The serviceability of the mental body is serviceability of the mental body. The serviceability of the mind is serviceability of the mind. They have the characteristic of calming the unserviceability of the mental body and mind; they have the function of suppressing the unserviceability of the mental body and mind; they manifest as the basis for accomplishment in taking an object; and they have the mental body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opponent of the remaining hindrances that cause unserviceability in the mental body and mind. They bring about confidence in objects that inspire confidence; in beneficial actions, they bring about a state of fitness for application, like highly purified gold. Thus they should be understood.

Kāyassa [M 0.0175][V 0.0176] pāguññabhāvo kāyapāguññatā. Cittassa pāguññabhāvo cittapāguññatā. Tā kāyacittānaṃ agelaññabhāvalakkhaṇā, kāyacittagelaññanimmaddanarasā, nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittagelaññakaraassaddhiyādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The state of proficiency of the mental body is proficiency of the mental body. The state of proficiency of the mind is proficiency of the mind. They have the characteristic of being without affliction in the mental body and mind; they have the function of suppressing the affliction of the mental body and mind; they manifest as being without fault; and they have the mental body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opponent of the defilements, such as lack of faith, that cause affliction in the mental body and mind.

Kāyassa ujukabhāvo kāyujukatā. Cittassa ujukabhāvo cittujukatā. Tā kāyacittānaṃ ajjavalakkhaṇā, kāyacittakuṭilabhāvanimmaddanarasā, ajimhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ kuṭilabhāvakaramāyāsāṭheyyādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The state of uprightness of the mental body is uprightness of the mental body. The state of uprightness of the mind is uprightness of the mind. They have uprightness of the mental body and mind as their characteristic; they have the function of suppressing the crookedness of the mental body and mind; they manifest as non-crookedness; and they have the mental body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opponent of the defilements, principally deceit and craftiness, that cause crookedness in the mental body and mind.

Saratīti sati. Sampajānātīti sampajaññaṃ; samantato pakārehi jānātīti attho. Sātthakasampajaññaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññanti imesaṃ catunnaṃ panassa vasena bhedo veditabbo. Lakkhaṇādīni ca tesaṃ satindriyapaññindriyesu vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Iti heṭṭhā vuttamevetaṃ dhammadvayaṃ puna imasmiṃ ṭhāne upakāravasena gahitaṃ.

It remembers; hence, it is mindfulness (sati). It clearly comprehends; hence, it is clear comprehension (sampajañña); the meaning is that it knows all-round and in detail. Furthermore, its distinction should be understood by way of these four: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of the domain, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. And their characteristics and so on should be understood in the very way stated previously under the faculties of mindfulness and wisdom. Thus, this pair of states, which has already been mentioned previously, is taken up again in this place by way of its assistance.

Kāmacchandādayo paccanīkadhamme sametīti samatho. Aniccādivasena vividhehi ākārehi dhamme passatīti vipassanā. Paññāvesā atthato. Imesampi dvinnaṃ lakkhaṇādīni heṭṭhā vuttāneva. Idha panete yuganaddhavasena gahitā.

It pacifies opposing states such as sensual desire; hence, it is tranquility (samatha). It sees phenomena in various ways by way of impermanence and so on; hence, it is insight (vipassanā). In essence, this is wisdom itself. The characteristics and so on of these two have also been stated previously. Here, however, they are taken by way of being yoked as a pair.

Sahajātadhamme paggaṇhātīti paggāho. Uddhaccasaṅkhātassa vikkhepassa paṭipakkhabhāvato na vikkhepoti avikkhepo. Etesampi lakkhaṇādīni heṭṭhā vuttāneva. Idha panetaṃ dvayaṃ vīriyasamādhiyojanatthāya gahitanti veditabbaṃ.

It uplifts co-nascent states; hence, it is exertion (paggāha). Because it is the opponent of distraction, which is known as restlessness, it is not distraction; hence, it is non-distraction (avikkhepa). The characteristics and so on of these have also been stated previously. Here, however, it should be understood that this pair is taken for the purpose of yoking energy and concentration.

Yevāpanakavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Supplementary Factors

Ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye aññepi atthi paṭiccasamuppannā arūpino dhammā, ime dhammā kusalāti ‘phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hotī’ti na kevalaṃ padapaṭipāṭiyā uddiṭṭhā ime paropaṇṇāsadhammā eva, atha kho yasmiṃ [P 0.0132] samaye kāmāvacaraṃ tihetukaṃ somanassasahagataṃ paṭhamaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ mahācittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye ye vā pana aññepi tehiyeva phassādīhi sampayuttā [V 0.0177] hutvā pavattamānā atthi, attano [M 0.0176] attano anurūpaṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca samuppannā rūpābhāvena arūpino, sabhāvato upalabbhamānā dhammā sabbepi ime dhammā kusalā.

“And whatever other dependently arisen, non-material states exist at that time—these states are wholesome.” It is not merely these fifty-odd states that are listed in sequence as “contact occurs… non-distraction occurs.” Rather, at the time when a first, unprompted, great wholesome consciousness, accompanied by joy and with three roots, has arisen in the sense-sphere, whatever other states exist at that time, arising in association with those same states beginning with contact, etc., dependently arisen in accordance with their respective, suitable conditions, being non-material due to the absence of materiality, states discernible by way of their own nature—all these states are wholesome.

Ettāvatā cittaṅgavasena pāḷiyaṃ āruḷhe paropaṇṇāsadhamme dīpetvā yevāpanakavasena aparepi nava dhamme dhammarājā dīpeti. Tesu tesu hi suttapadesu ‘chando adhimokkho manasikāro tatramajjhattatā karuṇā muditā kāyaduccaritavirati vacīduccaritavirati micchājīvaviratī’ti ime nava dhammā paññāyanti. Imasmiñcāpi mahācitte kattukamyatākusaladhammacchando atthi, cittaṅgavasena pana pāḷiyaṃ na āruḷho. So idha yevāpanakavasena gahito.

Having thus explained the fifty-odd states that are included in the Pāḷi by way of constituents of consciousness, the King of Dhamma further explains nine other states by way of the supplementary factors. For in various passages of the suttas, these nine states are recognized: 'desire, determination, attention, neutrality of mind, compassion, sympathetic joy, abstinence from bodily misconduct, abstinence from verbal misconduct, and abstinence from wrong livelihood.' And in this great consciousness, there is also the wholesome desire which is the wish to act, but it is not included in the Pāḷi by way of constituents of consciousness. Here, it is included by way of the supplementary factors.

Adhimokkho atthi, manasikāro atthi, tatramajjhattatā atthi. Mettāpubbabhāgo atthi; so adose gahite gahito eva hoti. Karuṇāpubbabhāgo atthi, muditāpubbabhāgo atthi. Upekkhāpubbabhāgo atthi; so pana tatramajjhattatāya gahitāya gahitova hoti. Sammāvācā atthi, sammākammanto atthi. Sammāājīvo atthi; cittaṅgavasena pana pāḷiyaṃ na āruḷho. Sopi idha yevāpanakavasena gahito.

Determination is present, attention is present, neutrality of mind is present. The preliminary stage of loving-kindness is present; it is included when non-aversion is included. The preliminary stage of compassion is present, the preliminary stage of sympathetic joy is present. The preliminary stage of equanimity is present; but it is included when neutrality of mind is included. Right speech is present, right action is present. Right livelihood is present; but it is not included in the Pāḷi by way of constituents of consciousness. It too is included here by way of the supplementary factors.

Imesu pana navasu chando adhimokkho manasikāro tatramajjhattatāti ime cattārova ekakkhaṇe labbhanti, sesā nānākkhaṇe. Yadā hi iminā cittena micchāvācaṃ pajahati, virativasena sammāvācaṃ pūreti, tadā chandādayo cattāro, sammāvācā cāti ime pañca ekakkhaṇe labbhanti. Yadā micchākammantaṃ pajahati, virativasena sammākammantaṃ pūreti…pe… micchāājīvaṃ pajahati, virativasena sammāājīvaṃ pūreti…pe… yadā karuṇāya parikammaṃ karoti…pe… yadā muditāya parikammaṃ karoti, tadā chandādayo cattāro, muditāpubbabhāgo cāti ime pañca ekakkhaṇe labbhanti. Ito pana muñcitvā, dānaṃ dentassa sīlaṃ pūrentassa yoge kammaṃ karontassa cattāri apaṇṇakaṅgāneva labbhanti.

Among these nine, however, desire, determination, attention, and neutrality of mind—only these four are obtained in a single moment; the rest, in different moments. For when with this mind one abandons wrong speech and fulfills right speech by way of abstinence, then these five—the four beginning with desire, and right speech—are obtained in a single moment. When one abandons wrong action and fulfills right action by way of abstinence… when one abandons wrong livelihood and fulfills right livelihood by way of abstinence… when one performs the preliminary practice with compassion… when one performs the preliminary practice with sympathetic joy, then these five—the four beginning with desire, and the preliminary stage of sympathetic joy—are obtained in a single moment. But apart from this, for one giving a gift, fulfilling virtue, or doing the work in the practice of meditation, only the four certain factors are obtained.

Evametesu navasu yevāpanakadhammesu ‘chando’ti kattukamyatāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā so kattukamyatālakkhaṇo chando, ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, ārammaṇena atthikatāpaccupaṭṭhāno[P 0.0133]. Tadevassa padaṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0177]. Ārammaṇassa gahaṇe cāyaṃ cetaso hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo.

Thus, among these nine supplementary states, 'desire' is a designation for the wish to act. Therefore, that desire has the characteristic of the wish to act, the function of searching for an object, and manifests as being in need of an object. That very object is its proximate cause. And in the grasping of an object, this should be seen as the mind's stretching forth of its hand.

Adhimuccanaṃ [V 0.0178] ‘adhimokkho’. So sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo, asaṃsappanaraso, nicchayapaccupaṭṭhāno sanniṭṭhātabbadhammapadaṭṭhāno. Ārammaṇe niccalabhāvena indakhīlo viya daṭṭhabbo.

Deciding is 'determination' (adhimokkha). It has the characteristic of concluding, the function of not wavering, manifests as certainty, and has the state to be decided upon as its proximate cause. It should be seen as being like a city-pillar due to its unmoving nature in the object.

Kiriyā kāro, manasmiṃ kāro ‘manasikāro’. Purimamanato visadisaṃ manaṃ karotītipi manasikāro. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇapaṭipādako vīthipaṭipādako javanapaṭipādakoti tippakāro. Tattha ārammaṇapaṭipādako manasmiṃ kāroti manasikāro. So sāraṇalakkhaṇo, sampayuttānaṃ ārammaṇe sampayojanaraso, ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno. Ārammaṇapaṭipādakattena sampayuttānaṃ sārathi viya daṭṭhabbo. Vīthipaṭipādakoti pana pañcadvārāvajjanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Javanapaṭipādakoti manodvārāvajjanassa. Na te idha adhippetā.

Doing is 'kāra'; making in the mind is 'attention' (manasikāra). It is also 'manasikāra' because it makes the mind dissimilar to the preceding mind. This is of three kinds: object-producing, process-producing, and impulsion-producing. Among these, the object-producing is 'manasikāra' because it is a 'making in the mind'. It has the characteristic of directing, the function of yoking associated states to the object, and manifests as facing the object. It is included in the aggregate of formations. It should be seen as like a charioteer for the associated states by virtue of its producing the object for them. 'Process-producing,' however, is a designation for the five-door adverting consciousness. 'Impulsion-producing' is for the mind-door adverting consciousness. These are not intended here.

Tesu dhammesu majjhattatā ‘tatramajjhattatā’. Sā cittacetasikānaṃ samavāhitalakkhaṇā, ūnādhikanivāraṇarasā, pakkhapātupacchedanarasā vā; majjhattabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Cittacetasikānaṃ ajjhupekkhanavasena samappavattānaṃ ājāneyyānaṃ ajjhupekkhanasārathi viya daṭṭhabbā.

Neutrality regarding those states is 'neutrality-therein' (tatramajjhattatā). It has the characteristic of conveying the mind and mental factors evenly, the function of preventing deficiency and excess, or the function of cutting off partisanship; it manifests as a state of impartiality. It should be seen as like a charioteer who looks on with equanimity at evenly-proceeding thoroughbreds, by way of looking on with equanimity at the mind and mental factors.

‘Karuṇāmuditā’ brahmavihāraniddese āvi bhavissanti. Kevalañhi tā appanappattā rūpāvacarā, idha kāmāvacarāti ayameva viseso.

Compassion and sympathetic joy will become evident in the exposition of the Divine Abodes. For those, when they have reached absorption, are of the form-sphere, whereas here they are of the sense-sphere—this is the only difference.

Kāyaduccaritato virati ‘kāyaduccaritavirati’. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Lakkhaṇādito panetā tissopi kāyaduccaritādivatthūnaṃ avītikkamalakkhaṇā; amaddanalakkhaṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyaduccaritādivatthuto saṅkocanarasā, akiriyapaccupaṭṭhānā, saddhāhirottappaappicchatādiguṇapadaṭṭhānā. Pāpakiriyato cittassa vimukhībhāvabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

Abstinence from bodily misconduct is 'abstinence from bodily misconduct' (kāyaduccaritavirati). The same method applies to the remaining two terms as well. But as to their characteristics and so on, all three have the characteristic of non-transgression of the bases of bodily misconduct, etc.; that is to say, they have the characteristic of non-violation. Their function is shrinking back from the bases of bodily misconduct, etc.; they manifest as non-action, and have qualities such as faith, moral shame, moral dread, and desiring little as their proximate cause. They should be regarded as being the mind's state of turning away from evil action.

Iti phassādīni chappaññāsa yevāpanakavasena vuttāni navāti sabbānipi imasmiṃ dhammuddesavāre pañcasaṭṭhi dhammapadāni bhavanti. Tesu ekakkhaṇe kadāci ekasaṭṭhi bhavanti, kadāci samasaṭṭhi. Tāni hi sammāvācāpūraṇādivasena. Uppattiyaṃ [M 0.0178] pañcasu ṭhānesu ekasaṭṭhi bhavanti. Tehi mutte ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samasaṭṭhi bhavanti. Ṭhapetvā [P 0.0134] pana yevāpanake pāḷiyaṃ yathārutavasena gayhamānāni chappaññāsāva honti. Aggahitaggahaṇena panettha phassapañcakaṃ, vitakko vicāro pīti cittekaggatā, pañcindriyāni, hiribalaṃ ottappabalanti dve balāni, alobho [V 0.0179] adosoti dve mūlāni, kāyapassaddhicittapassaddhiādayo dvādasa dhammāti samatiṃsa dhammā honti.

Thus, the fifty-six states beginning with contact, and the nine spoken of by way of the supplementary section—all together become sixty-five groups of states in this section of the enumeration of states. Among them, at a single moment, there are sometimes sixty-one, and sometimes exactly sixty. Indeed, this is by way of factors such as the completion of Right Speech. At the time of their arising, there are sixty-one in five instances. In the one instance apart from those, there are exactly sixty. However, setting aside the supplementary states, when taken according to what is directly stated in the Pāli, there are only fifty-six. But by the inclusion of what was not previously included, herein there are: the pentad with contact as its fifth member; initial application, sustained application, zest, and one-pointedness of mind; the five faculties; the two powers, namely the power of moral shame and the power of moral dread; the two roots, namely non-greed and non-hatred; and the twelve states beginning with tranquility of the mental body and tranquility of consciousness—thus, there are exactly thirty states.

Tesu samatiṃsāya dhammesu aṭṭhārasa dhammā avibhattikā honti, dvādasa savibhattikā. Katame aṭṭhārasa? Phasso saññā cetanā vicāro pīti jīvitindriyaṃ, kāyapassaddhiādayo dvādasa dhammāti ime aṭṭhārasa avibhattikā. Vedanā cittaṃ vitakko cittekaggatā, saddhindriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ satindriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ, hiribalaṃ ottappabalaṃ, alobho adosoti ime dvādasa dhammā savibhattikā. Tesu satta dhammā dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattā, eko tīsu, dve catūsu, eko chasu, eko sattasu ṭhānesu vibhatto.

Among those thirty states, eighteen states are indivisible, and twelve are divisible. Which are the eighteen? Contact, perception, volition, sustained application, zest, the life faculty, and the twelve states beginning with tranquility of the mental body—these eighteen are indivisible. Feeling, consciousness, initial application, one-pointedness of mind, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, non-greed, and non-hatred—these twelve states are divisible. Among them, seven states are divided into two instances, one into three, two into four, one into six, and one state is divided into seven instances.

Kathaṃ? Cittaṃ vitakko saddhā hirī ottappaṃ alobho adosoti ime satta dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattā.

How so? Consciousness, initial application, faith, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, and non-hatred—these seven states are divided into two instances.

Etesu hi cittaṃ tāva phassapañcakaṃ patvā cittaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ, indriyāni patvā manindriyanti. Vitakko jhānaṅgāni patvā vitakko hotīti vutto, maggaṅgāni patvā sammāsaṅkappoti. Saddhā indriyāni patvā saddhindriyaṃ hotīti vuttā, balāni patvā saddhābalanti. Hirī balāni patvā hiribalaṃ hotīti vuttā, lokapāladukaṃ patvā hirīti. Ottappepi eseva nayo. Alobho mūlaṃ patvā alobho hotīti vutto, kammapathaṃ patvā anabhijjhāti. Adoso mūlaṃ patvā adoso hotīti vutto, kammapathaṃ patvā abyāpādoti. Ime satta dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattā.

Indeed, among these, firstly, consciousness, having reached the pentad with contact as its fifth member, is spoken of as 'consciousness'; having reached the faculties, it is spoken of as the 'mind faculty'. Initial application, having reached the absorption factors, is spoken of as 'initial application'; having reached the path factors, it is spoken of as 'Right Intention'. Faith, having reached the faculties, is spoken of as the 'faculty of faith'; having reached the powers, it is spoken of as the 'power of faith'. Moral shame, having reached the powers, is spoken of as the 'power of moral shame'. The same method applies to moral dread. Non-greed, having reached the roots, is spoken of as 'non-greed'; having reached the courses of action, it is spoken of as 'non-covetousness'. Non-hatred, having reached the roots, is spoken of as 'non-hatred'; having reached the courses of action, it is spoken of as 'non-ill will'. Thus, these seven states are divided into two instances.

Vedanā pana phassapañcakaṃ patvā vedanā hotīti vuttā, jhānaṅgāni patvā sukhanti, indriyāni patvā somanassindriyanti. Evaṃ eko dhammo tīsu ṭhānesu vibhatto.

Furthermore, feeling, having reached the pentad with contact as its fifth member, is spoken of as 'feeling'; having reached the absorption factors, it is spoken of as 'happiness'; having reached the faculties, it is spoken of as the 'faculty of mental pleasure'. Thus, this one state is divided into three instances.

Vīriyaṃ pana indriyāni patvā vīriyindriyaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ, maggaṅgāni patvā sammāvāyāmoti, balāni patvā vīriyabalanti, piṭṭhidukaṃ patvā paggāhoti. Satipi [M 0.0179] indriyāni patvā satindriyaṃ hotīti vuttā, maggaṅgāni patvā sammāsatīti, balāni patvā satibalanti, piṭṭhidukaṃ [P 0.0135] patvā sati hotīti vuttā. Evaṃ ime dve dhammā catūsu ṭhānesu vibhattā.

Furthermore, energy, having reached the faculties, is spoken of as the 'faculty of energy'; having reached the path factors, as 'Right Effort'; having reached the powers, as the 'power of energy'; and having reached the pair of backing states, as 'exertion'. Mindfulness also, having reached the faculties, is spoken of as the 'faculty of mindfulness'; having reached the path factors, as 'Right Mindfulness'; having reached the powers, as the 'power of mindfulness'; and having reached the pair of backing states, it is spoken of as 'mindfulness'. Thus, these two states are divided into four instances.

Samādhi [V 0.0180] pana jhānaṅgāni patvā cittassekaggatā hotīti vutto, indriyāni patvā samādhindriyanti, maggaṅgāni patvā sammāsamādhīti. Balāni patvā samādhibalanti, piṭṭhidukaṃ patvā samatho avikkhepoti. Evamayaṃ eko dhammo chasu ṭhānesu vibhatto.

Furthermore, concentration, having reached the absorption factors, is spoken of as 'one-pointedness of mind'; having reached the faculties, as the 'faculty of concentration'; having reached the path factors, as 'Right Concentration'; having reached the powers, as the 'power of concentration'; and having reached the pair of backing states, as 'calm' and 'non-distraction'. Thus, this one state is divided into six instances.

Paññā pana indriyāni patvā paññindriyaṃ hotīti vuttā, maggaṅgāni patvā sammādiṭṭhīti, balāni patvā paññābalanti, mūlāni patvā amohoti, kammapathaṃ patvā sammādiṭṭhīti, piṭṭhidukaṃ patvā sampajaññaṃ vipassanāti. Evaṃ eko dhammo sattasu ṭhānesu vibhatto.

Furthermore, wisdom, having reached the faculties, is spoken of as the 'faculty of wisdom'; having reached the path factors, as 'Right View'; having reached the powers, as the 'power of wisdom'; having reached the roots, as 'non-delusion'; having reached the courses of action, as 'Right View'; and having reached the pair of backing states, as 'clear comprehension' and 'insight'. Thus, this one state is divided into seven instances.

Sace pana koci vadeyya – ‘ettha apubbaṃ nāma natthi, heṭṭhā gahitameva gaṇhitvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne padaṃ pūritaṃ, ananusandhikā kathā uppaṭipāṭiyā corehi ābhatabhaṇḍasadisā, goyūthena gatamagge ālulitatiṇasadisā ajānitvā kathitā’ti, so ‘māheva’nti paṭisedhetvā vattabbo – ‘buddhānaṃ desanā ananusandhikā nāma natthi, sānusandhikā va hoti. Ajānitvā kathitāpi natthi, sabbā jānitvā kathitāyeva. Sammāsambuddho hi tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ kiccaṃ jānāti, taṃ ñatvā kiccavasena vibhattiṃ āropento aṭṭhārasa dhammā ekekakiccāti ñatvā ekekasmiṃ ṭhāne vibhattiṃ āropesi. Satta dhammā dvedvekiccāti ñatvā dvīsu dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattiṃ āropesi. Vedanā tikiccāti ñatvā tīsu ṭhānesu vibhattiṃ āropesi. Vīriyasatīnaṃ cattāri cattāri kiccānīti ñatvā catūsu catūsu ṭhānesu vibhattiṃ āropesi. Samādhi chakiccoti ñatvā chasu ṭhānesu vibhattiṃ āropesi. Paññā sattakiccāti ñatvā sattasu ṭhānesu vibhattiṃ āropesi’.

Furthermore, if someone were to say: ‘Herein, there is nothing new; what was already included below is simply taken again to fill out the term in each respective instance. The discourse is disconnected, out of order, like goods brought haphazardly by thieves, like grass trampled on a path trodden by a herd of cattle—it is spoken without understanding,’ he should be refuted with the words, ‘Do not say so!’ and one should reply: ‘There is no such thing as a disconnected teaching of the Buddhas; it is always connected. Nor is anything spoken without understanding; everything is spoken only after having fully understood it. Indeed, the Perfectly Enlightened One knows the function of each of these states. Knowing that, and establishing the division according to function—knowing that the eighteen states each have a single function, he established the division in a single instance for each. Knowing that the seven states each have two functions, he established the division in two instances for each. Knowing that feeling has three functions, he established the division in three instances. Knowing that energy and mindfulness each have four functions, he established the division in four instances for each. Knowing that concentration has six functions, he established the division in six instances. Knowing that wisdom has seven functions, he established the division in seven instances.’

Tatridaṃ opammaṃ – eko kira paṇḍito rājā rahogato cintesi – ‘imaṃ rājakulasantakaṃ na yathā vā tathā vā khāditabbaṃ, sippānucchavikaṃ vetanaṃ [M 0.0180] vaḍḍhessāmī’ti. So sabbe sippike sannipātāpetvā ‘ekekasippajānanake pakkosathā’ti āha. Evaṃ pakkosiyamānā aṭṭhārasa janā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Tesaṃ ekekaṃ paṭivīsaṃ dāpetvā vissajjesi. ‘Dve dve sippāni jānantā āgacchantū’ti vutte pana satta janā āgamaṃsu. Tesaṃ dve dve paṭivīse dāpesi. ‘Tīṇi sippāni jānantā āgacchantū’ti vutte ekova āgacchi. Tassa tayo paṭivīse dāpesi. ‘Cattāri sippāni jānantā āgacchantū’ti vutte dve janā āgamaṃsu. Tesaṃ cattāri cattāri paṭivīse dāpesi. ‘Pañca sippāni jānantā āgacchantū’ti vutte ekopi nāgacchi[V 0.0181]. ‘Cha sippāni jānantā āgacchantū’ti vutte ekova āgacchi. Tassa cha paṭivīse dāpesi. ‘Satta sippāni jānantā [P 0.0136] āgacchantū’ti vutte ekova āgacchi. Tassa satta paṭivīse dāpesi.

Here is a simile: Indeed, a certain wise king, having gone to a secluded place, thought: ‘This wealth belonging to the royal lineage should not be consumed in any old way. I shall increase the wages appropriate to the skills.’ Having caused all the artisans to assemble, he commanded: ‘Call those who know one skill each.’ When summoned in this way, eighteen people arose. Having caused one portion of provisions to be given to each of them, he dismissed them. But when it was said, ‘Let those who know two skills each come,’ seven people came. He caused two portions of provisions to be given to each of them. When it was said, ‘Let those who know three skills come,’ only one came. He caused three portions of provisions to be given to him. When it was said, ‘Let those who know four skills come,’ two people came. He caused four portions of provisions to be given to each of them. When it was said, ‘Let those who know five skills come,’ not even one came. When it was said, ‘Let those who know six skills come,’ only one came. He caused six portions of provisions to be given to him. When it was said, ‘Let those who know seven skills come,’ only one came. He caused seven portions of provisions to be given to him.

Tattha paṇḍito rājā viya anuttaro dhammarājā. Sippajānanakā viya cittacittaṅgavasena uppannā dhammā. Sippānucchavikavetanavaḍḍhanaṃ viya kiccavasena tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ vibhattiāropanaṃ.

Therein, the unsurpassed King of Dhamma should be regarded as being like the wise king. The dhammas that have arisen by way of consciousness and its components should be regarded as being like those who know a skill. The assignment of classification to those respective dhammas by way of their function should be regarded as being like the increase of provisions appropriate to the skill.

Sabbepi panete dhammā phassapañcakavasena jhānaṅgavasena indriyavasena maggavasena balavasena mūlavasena kammapathavasena lokapālavasena passaddhivasena lahutāvasena mudutāvasena kammaññatāvasena pāguññatāvasena ujukatāvasena satisampajaññavasena samathavipassanāvasena paggāhāvikkhepavasenāti sattarasa rāsayo hontīti.

Furthermore, all these dhammas become seventeen groups: by way of the pentad with contact, by way of the jhāna factors, by way of the faculties, by way of the path factors, by way of the powers, by way of the roots, by way of the courses of action, by way of the guardians of the world, by way of tranquility, by way of lightness, by way of pliancy, by way of wieldiness, by way of proficiency, by way of straightness, by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension, by way of tranquility and insight, and by way of exertion and non-distraction.

Dhammuddesavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the section of the summary of dhammas is concluded.

Kāmāvacarakusalaṃ niddesavārakathā

The Discourse on the Exposition Section of Wholesome States Pertaining to the Sense-Sphere.

2. Idāni tāneva dhammuddesavāre pāḷiāruḷhāni chappaññāsa padāni vibhajitvā dassetuṃ ‘katamo tasmiṃ samaye phasso hotī’tiādinā nayena niddesavāro āraddho.

2. Now, in order to show in detail by analyzing those very fifty-six terms that are included in the Pāli text in the Dhammuddesavāra, the Exposition Section has been commenced with the method beginning, ‘What, at that time, is contact?’

Tattha pucchāya tāva ayamattho – yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ somanassasahagataṃ tihetukaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ mahācittaṃ uppajjati, tasmiṃ [M 0.0181] samaye phasso hotīti vutto, katamo so phassoti iminā nayena sabbapucchāsu attho veditabbo.

Therein, first, this is the meaning of the question: At the time when a wholesome great consciousness of the sense-sphere, accompanied by joy, having three roots, and unprompted, arises, at that time it is said, ‘there is contact.’ What is that contact? By this method, the meaning in all questions should be understood.

Yo tasmiṃ samaye phassoti tasmiṃ samaye yo phusanakavasena uppanno phasso, so phassoti. Idaṃ phassassa sabhāvadīpanato sabhāvapadaṃ nāma. Phusanāti phusanākāro. Samphusanāti phusanākārova upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vutto. Samphusitattanti samphusitabhāvo. Ayaṃ panettha yojanā [V 0.0182] – yo tasmiṃ samaye phusanakavasena phasso, yā tasmiṃ samaye phusanā, yā tasmiṃ samaye samphusanā, yaṃ tasmiṃ samaye samphusitattaṃ; atha vā, yo tasmiṃ samaye phusanavasena phasso, aññenāpi pariyāyena phusanā samphusanā samphusitattanti vuccati, ayaṃ tasmiṃ samaye phasso hotīti. Vedanādīnampi niddesesu imināva nayena padayojanā veditabbā.

As for ‘Whatever contact there is at that time’: at that time, whatever contact has arisen by way of touching, that is contact. This term is called an ‘intrinsic-nature term’ because it reveals the intrinsic nature of contact. ‘Phusanā’ is the mode of touching. ‘Samphusanā’ is the very mode of touching, spoken of by augmenting the term with a prefix. ‘Samphusitattaṃ’ is the state of having thoroughly touched. This is the syntactical connection here: Whatever contact there is at that time by way of touching, whatever touching (phusanā) there is at that time, whatever thorough touching (samphusanā) there is at that time, whatever state of having thoroughly touched (samphusitattaṃ) there is at that time. Or alternatively: whatever contact there is at that time by way of touching is also called by other terms, namely ‘phusanā,’ ‘samphusanā,’ and ‘samphusitattaṃ.’ This is the contact that occurs at that time. In the expositions of feeling and the other terms as well, the syntactical connection of the terms should be understood by this very method.

Ayaṃ panettha sabbasādhāraṇo vibhattivinicchayo. Yānimāni bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ [P 0.0137] mahācittaṃ bhājetvā dassentena atirekapaṇṇāsapadāni mātikāvasena ṭhapetvā puna ekekapadaṃ gahetvā vibhattiṃ āropitāni, tāni vibhattiṃ gacchantāni tīhi kāraṇehi vibhattiṃ gacchanti; nānā hontāni catūhi kāraṇehi nānā bhavanti. Aparadīpanā panettha dve ṭhānāni gacchati. Kathaṃ? Etānihi byañjanavasena upasaggavasena atthavasenāti imehi tīhi kāraṇehi vibhattiṃ gacchanti. Tattha kodho kujjhanā kujjhitattaṃ, doso dussanā dussitattanti evaṃ byañjanavasena vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha hi ekova kodho byañjanavasena evaṃ vibhattiṃ gato. Cāro vicāro anuvicāro upavicāroti evaṃ pana upasaggavasena vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paṇḍiccaṃ kosallaṃ nepuññaṃ vebhabyā cintā upaparikkhāti evaṃ atthavasena vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tesu phassapadaniddese tāva imā tissopi vibhattiyo labbhanti. ‘Phasso phusanā’ti hi byañjanavasena vibhattigamanaṃ hoti. ‘Samphusanā’ti upasaggavasena. ‘Samphusitatta’nti atthavasena. Iminā nayena sabbapadaniddesesu vibhattigamanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This, herein, is the general determination of classification. Those more than fifty terms which the Blessed One, when demonstrating by first analyzing the wholesome great consciousness of the sense-sphere, set down by way of a matrix and then, taking each term one by one, subjected to classification—those terms, in undergoing classification, do so for three reasons; in becoming various, they become various for four reasons. Herein, the explanation by way of alternative terms extends to two points. How so? For these terms undergo classification for these three reasons: by way of expression, by way of prefix, and by way of meaning. Therein, as in 'anger (kodho), being angry (kujjhanā), the state of being angry (kujjhitattaṃ)' and 'hatred (doso), being hostile (dussanā), the state of being hostile (dussitattaṃ)', thus the process of classification by way of expression should be understood. For here, the single concept of anger has undergone classification in this way by way of expression. Furthermore, as in 'initial application (cāro), sustained application (vicāro), repeated application (anuvicāro), close application (upavicāro)', thus the process of classification by way of prefix should be understood. As in 'wisdom (paṇḍiccaṃ), skillfulness (kosallaṃ), cleverness (nepuññaṃ), ingenuity (vebhabyā), thought (cintā), examination (upaparikkhā)', thus the process of classification by way of meaning should be understood. Among these, in the exposition of the term 'contact', these three classifications are also found. For 'contact (phasso), touching (phusanā)' is the process of classification by way of expression. 'Thorough touching (samphusanā)' is by way of prefix. 'The state of having thoroughly touched (samphusitattaṃ)' is by way of meaning. By this method, the process of classification in the expositions of all terms should be understood.

Nānā hontānipi pana nāmanānattena lakkhaṇanānattena kiccanānattena paṭikkhepanānattenāti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi nānā honti. Tattha katamo tasmiṃ samaye byāpādo hoti? Yo tasmiṃ [M 0.0182] samaye doso dussanāti (dha. sa. 419) ettha byāpādoti vā, dosoti vā, dvepi ete kodho eva, nāmena nānattaṃ gatāti. Evaṃ ‘nāmanānattena’ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, although they become various, they become various for these four reasons: by diversity of name, by diversity of characteristic, by diversity of function, and by diversity of that which is rejected. Therein, in the passage 'What, at that time, is ill will? Whatever at that time is hatred, hostility...' (Dhs. § 419), whether it is 'ill will' (byāpāda) or 'hatred' (dosa), both of these are just anger; they have attained diversity by name. Thus, diversity 'by diversity of name' should be understood.

Rāsaṭṭhena ca pañcapi khandhā ekova khandho hoti. Ettha pana rūpaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ, vedanā vedayitalakkhaṇā, saññā sañjānanalakkhaṇā, cetanā cetayitalakkhaṇā, viññāṇaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇanti iminā lakkhaṇanānattena pañcakkhandhā honti. Evaṃ ‘lakkhaṇanānattena’ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

And by the meaning of 'heap', the five aggregates are indeed a single aggregate. Herein, however, form has the characteristic of being afflicted, feeling has the characteristic of being felt, perception has the characteristic of perceiving, volition has the characteristic of intending, and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing—thus, due to this diversity of characteristic, there are five aggregates. In this way, diversity 'by diversity of characteristic' should be understood.

Cattāro [V 0.0183] sammappadhānā – “idha bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya…pe… [P 0.0138] cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahatī”ti (vibha. 390; dī. ni. 2.402) ekameva vīriyaṃ kiccanānattena catūsu ṭhānesu āgataṃ. Evaṃ ‘kiccanānattena’ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The four right strivings: 'Here, a bhikkhu... arouses his mind and exerts himself for the non-arising of unarisen, evil, unwholesome states...' (Vibh. 390). Here, one and the same energy is presented in four instances due to a diversity of function. Thus, diversity 'by diversity of function' should be understood.

Cattāro asaddhammā – kodhagarutā na saddhammagarutā, makkhagarutā na saddhammagarutā, lābhagarutā na saddhammagarutā, sakkāragarutā na saddhammagarutāti, evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.44) pana ‘paṭikkhepanānattena’ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The four ignoble qualities: reverence for anger, not reverence for the good Dhamma; reverence for denigration, not reverence for the good Dhamma; reverence for gain, not reverence for the good Dhamma; reverence for honor, not reverence for the good Dhamma. In such cases (AN 4.44), however, diversity 'by diversity of what is rejected' should be understood.

Imāni pana cattāri nānattāni na phasseyeva labbhanti, sabbesupi phassapañcakādīsu labbhanti. Phassassa hi phassoti nāmaṃ…pe… cittassa cittanti. Phasso ca phusanalakkhaṇo, vedanā vedayitalakkhaṇā, saññā sañjānanalakkhaṇā, cetanā cetayitalakkhaṇā, viññāṇaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Tathā phasso phusanakicco, vedanā anubhavanakiccā, saññā sañjānanakiccā, cetanā cetayitakiccā, viññāṇaṃ vijānanakiccanti. Evaṃ kiccanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, these four diversities are not found only in contact; they are found in all such groups as the contact-pentad. For contact is named 'contact'... and consciousness is named 'consciousness.' And contact has the characteristic of touching, feeling has the characteristic of being felt, perception has the characteristic of perceiving, volition has the characteristic of intending, and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing. Similarly, contact has the function of touching, feeling has the function of experiencing, perception has the function of perceiving, volition has the function of intending, and consciousness has the function of cognizing. Thus, diversity 'by diversity of function' should be understood.

Paṭikkhepanānattaṃ phassapañcamake natthi. Alobhādiniddese pana alobho alubbhanā alubbhitattantiādinā nayena labbhatīti evaṃ paṭikkhepanānattena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ sabbapadaniddesesu labbhamānavasena catubbidhampi nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Diversity by way of what is rejected is not found in the contact-pentad. However, in the exposition of non-greed and so on, it is found by the method beginning with 'non-greed, non-coveting, the state of non-coveting.' Thus, diversity 'by diversity of what is rejected' should be understood. In this way, in all expositions of terms, the fourfold diversity should be understood according to what is obtainable.

Aparadīpanā pana padatthuti vā hoti daḷhīkammaṃ vāti evaṃ dve ṭhānāni gacchati. Yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷentena viya hi sakimeva phassoti vutte etaṃ padaṃ phullitamaṇḍitavibhūsitaṃ nāma na hoti. Punappunaṃ byañjanavasena upasaggavasena [M 0.0183] atthavasena ‘phasso phusanā samphusanā samphusitatta’nti vutte phullitamaṇḍitavibhūsitaṃ nāma hoti. Yathā hi daharakumāraṃ nhāpetvā, manoramaṃ vatthaṃ paridahāpetvā pupphāni piḷandhāpetvā akkhīni añjetvā athassa nalāṭe ekameva manosilābinduṃ kareyyuṃ, tassa na ettāvatā cittatilako nāma hoti. Nānāvaṇṇehi pana parivāretvā bindūsu katesu cittatilako nāma hoti. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ ‘padatthuti’ nāma.

An alternative explanation, however, extends to two points: it is either the elucidation of a term or its reinforcement. For, like one pressing down with the tip of a staff, if 'contact' is said only once, that term is not called 'blossomed, adorned, and embellished.' But when it is repeatedly said by way of expression, by way of prefix, and by way of meaning—'contact, touching, thorough touching, the state of having thoroughly touched'—then it is called 'blossomed, adorned, and embellished.' For example, if after bathing a young boy, dressing him in beautiful clothes, adorning him with flowers, and applying collyrium to his eyes, one were to place just a single spot of red arsenic on his forehead, by that much he is not called one with a variegated forehead mark (`cittatilaka`). But when spots are made surrounding it with various colors, then he is called one with a variegated forehead mark (`cittatilaka`). This successful analogy should be understood thus. This is called 'elucidation of a term'.

Byañjanavasena [V 0.0184] upasaggavasena atthavasena ca punappunaṃ bhaṇanameva daḷhīkammaṃ nāma. Yathā hi ‘āvuso’ti vā ‘bhante’ti vā ‘yakkho’ti vā ‘sappo’ti [P 0.0139] vā vutte daḷhīkammaṃ nāma na hoti. ‘Āvuso āvuso’‘bhante bhante’‘yakkho yakkho’‘sappo sappo’ti vutte pana daḷhīkammaṃ nāma hoti. Evameva sakideva yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷentena viya ‘phasso’ti vutte padaṃ daḷhīkammaṃ nāma na hoti. Punappunaṃ byañjanavasena upasaggavasena atthavasena ‘phasso phusanā samphusanā samphusitatta’nti vutteyeva ‘daḷhīkammaṃ’ nāma hotīti. Evaṃ aparadīpanā dve ṭhānāni gacchati. Etassāpi vasena labbhamānakapadaniddesesu sabbattha attho veditabbo.

The very act of repeating by way of literal expression, by way of prefix, and by way of meaning is called reinforcement. For example, when 'friend' or 'venerable sir' or 'yakkha' or 'snake' is said, it is not called reinforcement. But when 'friend, friend,' 'venerable sir, venerable sir,' 'yakkha, yakkha,' 'snake, snake' is said, then it is called reinforcement. Just so, when 'contact' is said only once, as if pressing down with the tip of a staff, the term is not called reinforcement. But only when it is repeatedly said by way of literal expression, by way of prefix, and by way of meaning—'contact, touching, thorough touching, the state of having thoroughly touched'—is it called 'reinforcement.' In this way, further explanation extends to two points. And by way of this, the meaning should be understood everywhere in the expositions of obtainable terms.

Ayaṃ tasmiṃ samaye phasso hotīti yasmiṃ samaye paṭhamaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ mahākusalacittaṃ uppajjati, tasmiṃ samaye ayaṃ phasso nāma hotīti attho. Ayaṃ tāva phassapadaniddesassa vaṇṇanā. Ito paresu pana vedanādīnaṃ padānaṃ niddesesu visesamattameva vaṇṇayissāma. Sesaṃ idha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

This is 'contact at that time': the meaning is that at the time when the first great wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises, at that time this which is called contact occurs. This, for now, is the explanation of the exposition of the term 'contact'. Henceforth, in the expositions of the terms such as feeling, we shall explain only the specific points. The remainder should be understood by the method stated here.

3. Yaṃ tasmiṃ samayeti ettha kiñcāpi katamā tasmiṃ samaye vedanā hotīti āraddhaṃ, ‘sātapadavasena pana ‘ya’nti vuttaṃ. Tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātusamphassajanti ettha ‘tajjā’ vuccati tassa sātasukhassa anucchavikā sāruppā. Anucchavikatthopi hi ayaṃ ‘tajjā’-saddo hoti. Yathāha – “tajjaṃ tassāruppaṃ kathaṃ mantetī”ti (ma. ni. 3.246). Tehi vā rūpādīhi ārammaṇehi imassa ca sukhassa paccayehi jātātipi tajjā. Manoviññāṇameva nissattaṭṭhena dhātūti manoviññāṇadhātu. Samphassato jātaṃ, samphasse vā jātanti samphassajaṃ. Cittanissitattā cetasikaṃ. Madhuraṭṭhena [M 0.0184] sātaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ tasmiṃ samaye yathāvuttena atthena tajjāya manoviññāṇadhātuyā samphassajaṃ cetasikaṃ sātaṃ, ayaṃ tasmiṃ samaye vedanā hotīti. Evaṃ sabbapadehi saddhiṃ yojanā veditabbā.

3. Regarding 'whatever at that time' (`yaṃ tasmiṃ samaye`): although the passage begins with 'what feeling is there at that time?' (`katamā tasmiṃ samaye vedanā hoti`), the word `yaṃ` (neuter) is used on account of the word `sāta` (neuter). Regarding 'born of contact with the corresponding mind-consciousness element' (`tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātusamphassajaṃ`): here, `tajjā` ('corresponding') is said to be that which is suitable and appropriate to that pleasant happiness. For this word `tajjā` also has the meaning of 'suitable,' as it is said: 'How does one deliberate on what is suitable, what is appropriate to it?' Alternatively, it is also `tajjā` because it is born from those objects such as forms, which are the conditions for this happiness. Mind-consciousness itself is an 'element' (`dhātu`) in the sense of being devoid of a being. 'Born of contact' (`samphassajaṃ`) means born from contact or born in contact. It is a mental concomitant (`cetasikaṃ`) because it is dependent on the mind. It is pleasant (`sātaṃ`) in the sense of sweetness. This is what is said: 'Whatever pleasant mental concomitant there is at that time, born of contact with the corresponding mind-consciousness element in the sense explained above—this is the feeling at that time.' Thus, the application of meaning should be understood in connection with all the terms.

Idāni cetasikaṃ sukhantiādīsu cetasikapadena kāyikasukhaṃ paṭikkhipati, sukhapadena cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ. Cetosamphassajanti cittasamphasse jātaṃ. Sātaṃ sukhaṃ vedayitanti [P 0.0140] sātaṃ vedayitaṃ, na asātaṃ vedayitaṃ; sukhaṃ vedayitaṃ, na dukkhaṃ vedayitaṃ. Parato tīṇi padāni itthiliṅgavasena vuttāni. Sātā vedanā, na asātā; sukhā vedanā, na dukkhāti. Ayameva panettha attho.

Now, in such phrases as 'mental pleasure,' by the word 'mental,' physical pleasure is excluded; by the word 'pleasure,' mental pain is excluded. 'Born of mind-contact' means born from contact with the mind. 'An agreeable, pleasant feeling' means an agreeable feeling, not a disagreeable feeling; a pleasant feeling, not a painful feeling. Further on, three terms are stated in the feminine gender: 'agreeable feeling, not disagreeable; pleasant feeling, not painful.' This is the very meaning here.

4. Saññāniddese [V 0.0185] tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātusamphassajāti tassākusalasaññāya anucchavikāya manoviññāṇadhātuyā samphassamhi jātā. Saññāti sabhāvanāmaṃ. Sañjānanāti sañjānanākāro. Sañjānitattanti sañjānitabhāvo.

4. In the exposition of perception, 'born of contact with the corresponding mind-consciousness-element' means born from contact with the mind-consciousness-element that is suitable for that wholesome perception. 'Perception' is a name for its intrinsic nature. 'Perceiving' is the mode of perceiving. 'The state of having perceived' is the state of having perceived.

5. Cetanāniddesepi imināva nayena veditabbo.

5. In the exposition of volition also, the meaning should be understood in this very same way.

Cittaniddese cittavicittatāya cittaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ minamānaṃ jānātīti mano. Mānasanti mano eva. “Antalikkhacaro pāso yvāyaṃ carati mānaso”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.151; mahāva. 33) hi ettha pana sampayuttakadhammo ‘mānaso’ti vutto.

In the exposition of mind (citta), it is called 'citta' because of its variegated nature. Because it knows the object by measuring it, it is called 'mano.' 'Mānasa' is just 'mano.' For in the passage, 'The snare that roams the sky, that which is of the mind (mānasa),' it is an associated state that is called 'mānasa.'

“Kathañhi bhagavā tuyhaṃ, sāvako sāsane rato;

Appattamānaso sekkho, kālaṃ kayirā jane sutā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.159);

How indeed, O Blessed One, could a disciple of yours, delighting in the teaching, a learner well-known among the people who has not yet attained the goal (mānasa), pass away?

Ettha arahattaṃ ‘mānasa’nti vuttaṃ. Idha pana ‘manova’ mānasaṃ. Byañjanavasena hetaṃ padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

Here, Arahantship is called 'mānasa.' In this context, however, 'mānasa' is just 'mano.' This word has been augmented by way of a syllable.

Hadayanti cittaṃ. “Cittaṃ vā te khipissāmi, hadayaṃ vā te phālessāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.237; su. ni. āḷavakasutta) ettha uro hadayanti vuttaṃ. “Hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.63) ettha cittaṃ. “Vakkaṃ hadaya”nti (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110) ettha hadayavatthu. Idha [M 0.0185] pana cittameva abbhantaraṭṭhena ‘hadaya’nti vuttaṃ. Tameva parisuddhaṭṭhena paṇḍaraṃ. Bhavaṅgaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathāha – “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca kho āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭha”nti (a. ni. 1.49). Tato nikkhantattā pana akusalampi, gaṅgāya nikkhantā nadī gaṅgā viya, godhāvarito nikkhantā godhāvarī viya ca, paṇḍarantveva vuttaṃ.

'Heart' (hadaya) means the mind (citta). In the passage, "I will throw out your mind (citta), or I will split your heart (hadaya)," 'heart' is used to mean the chest (uro). In, "From heart to heart, I deem, he carves by knowing," it means the mind (citta). In, "The kidneys, the heart," it means the physical heart-base (hadayavatthu). Here, however, the mind itself is called 'heart' in the sense of being internal. That very mind, in the sense of being pure, is called 'luminous' (paṇḍara). This is said with reference to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). As it is said: "This mind, monks, is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements." Furthermore, because it issues from that (bhavaṅga), even an unwholesome state is called 'luminous,' just as a river that issues from the Ganges is called 'Ganges,' and one that issues from the Godhāvarī is called 'Godhāvarī.'

Mano manāyatananti idha pana manoggahaṇaṃ manasseva āyatanabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Tenetaṃ dīpeti – ‘nayidaṃ devāyatanaṃ viya manassa āyatanattā manāyatanaṃ, atha kho mano eva āyatanaṃ [V 0.0186] manāyatana’nti. Tattha nivāsaṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭhānaṭṭhena [P 0.0141] sañjātidesaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhena ca āyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi loke ‘issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatana’ntiādīsu nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ āyatananti vuccati. ‘Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ rajatāyatana’ntiādīsu ākaro. Sāsane pana “manorame āyatane sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.38) samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana”ntiādīsu sañjātideso. “Tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.158) kāraṇaṃ. Idha pana sañjātidesaṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭhānaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhenāti tidhāpi vaṭṭati.

Furthermore, in the phrase 'mind, the mind-base' (mano manāyatanaṃ), the inclusion of the word 'mano' is for the purpose of showing that the mind itself is the base. By this, it is shown: 'This is not called the mind-base because it is a base for the mind, like a celestial abode (devāyatana) is an abode for the devas; rather, the mind (mano) itself is the base (āyatana), hence 'mind-base' (manāyatana).' In that context, 'base' (āyatana) is to be understood in the sense of a dwelling place, a source, a meeting place, a place of origin, and a cause. For in the world, in expressions such as 'the abode of the Lord' and 'the abode of Vāsudeva,' 'āyatana' is used to mean a dwelling place. In expressions such as 'a source of gold' and 'a source of silver,' it means a mine. In the Teaching, however, in passages such as, 'Birds resort to that delightful meeting place (āyatana),' it means a meeting place. In passages such as, 'The Southern region is the birthplace (āyatana) of cattle,' it means a place of origin. In passages such as, 'When the base of mindfulness is present, one attains the state of being able to witness it then and there,' it means a cause. Here, however, it is applicable in three ways: in the sense of a place of origin, a meeting place, and a cause.

Phassādayo hi dhammā ettha sañjāyantīti sañjātidesaṭṭhenapi etaṃ āyatanaṃ. Bahiddhā rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbā ārammaṇabhāvenettha osarantīti samosaraṇaṭhānaṭṭhenapi āyatanaṃ. Phassādīnaṃ pana sahajātādipaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇattā kāraṇaṭṭhenapi āyatananti veditabbaṃ. Manindriyaṃ vuttatthameva.

Indeed, since states such as contact arise here, it is a base (āyatana) in the sense of a place of origin. Since external forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects converge here as objects, it is a base in the sense of a meeting place. Furthermore, because it is a cause for states such as contact by way of co-nascence condition and so on, it is to be understood as a base in the sense of a cause. 'Mind-faculty' (manindriya) has the meaning already explained.

Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ viññāṇameva khandho viññāṇakkhandho. Tassa rāsiādivasena attho veditabbo. Mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti (a. ni. 4.51). Ettha hi rāsaṭṭhena khandho vutto. “Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.355) guṇaṭṭhena. “Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.241) ettha paṇṇattimattaṭṭhena. Idha pana ruḷhito khandho vutto. Rāsaṭṭhena hi viññāṇakkhandhassa [M 0.0186] ekadeso ekaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Tasmā yathā rukkhassa ekadesaṃ chindanto rukkhaṃ chindatīti vuccati, evameva viññāṇakkhandhassa ekadesabhūtaṃ ekampi viññāṇaṃ ruḷhito viññāṇakkhandhoti vuttaṃ.

It cognizes distinctly, therefore it is 'consciousness' (viññāṇa). Consciousness itself is an aggregate (khandha), hence the 'consciousness aggregate' (viññāṇakkhandha). Its meaning is to be understood in the sense of a mass, and so on. In the passage, 'It is counted as a great mass of water,' the word 'khandha' is used in the sense of a mass. In expressions such as 'the aggregate of virtue' and 'the aggregate of concentration,' it is used in the sense of a quality. In, 'The Blessed One saw a great log (dārukkhandha),' it is used in the sense of a mere concept. Here, however, 'khandha' is used by convention (ruḷhi). For, in the sense of a mass, a single consciousness is one part of the consciousness aggregate. Therefore, just as one who cuts a part of a tree is said to be 'cutting the tree,' in the same way a single consciousness, which is a part of the consciousness aggregate, is conventionally called the 'consciousness aggregate.'

Tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātūti tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ anucchavikā manoviññāṇadhātu. Imasmiñhi pade ekameva cittaṃ minanaṭṭhena mano, vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇaṃ, sabhāvaṭṭhena nissattaṭṭhena vā dhātūti tīhi nāmehi vuttaṃ. Iti imasmiṃ phassapañcamake phasso tāva yasmā phasso eva, na tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātusamphassajo, cittañca yasmā tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātu eva, tasmā imasmiṃ padadvaye [P 0.0142] ‘tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātusamphassajā’ti paññatti na āropitā. Vitakkapadādīsu pana labbhamānāpi idha pacchinnattā na uddhaṭā.

'The mind-consciousness-element corresponding to that' (tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātu): this is the mind-consciousness-element that is suitable for those states such as contact. For in this term, one and the same consciousness (citta) is spoken of by three names: 'mano' in the sense of measuring; 'viññāṇa' in the sense of distinctly cognizing; and 'dhātu' (element) in the sense of its intrinsic nature or in the sense of being non-sentient. Thus, in this pentad beginning with contact, since contact is just contact—not born of contact with the corresponding mind-consciousness-element—and since consciousness is the corresponding mind-consciousness-element itself, the designation 'born of contact with the corresponding mind-consciousness-element' is not applied to these two terms. And although this designation is applicable to terms such as 'initial application' (vitakka), it is not cited here because it has been demarcated.

Imesañca [V 0.0187] pana phassapañcamakānaṃ dhammānaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vinibbhogaṃ katvā paññattiṃ uddharamānena bhagavatā dukkaraṃ kataṃ. Nānāudakānañhi nānātelānaṃ vā ekabhājane pakkhipitvā divasaṃ nimmathitānaṃ vaṇṇa gandharasānaṃ nānatāya disvā vā ghāyitvā vā sāyitvā vā nānākaraṇaṃ sakkā bhaveyya ñātuṃ. Evaṃ santepi taṃ dukkaranti vuttaṃ. Sammāsambuddhena pana imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vinibbhogaṃ katvā paññattiṃ uddharamānena atidukkaraṃ kataṃ. Tenāha āyasmā nāgasenatthero –

Moreover, a difficult thing was done by the Blessed One, who, having individually distinguished these states of the contact-pentad, set forth their designation. For, of various waters or various oils that have been put into a single vessel and churned for a day, it might be possible to know the distinction of their color, scent, and taste by seeing, smelling, or tasting them, due to their difference. Even so, that is said to be difficult. But by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who, having individually distinguished each of these formless states—mind and mental factors—that occur on a single object, set forth their designation, a most difficult thing was done. Therefore, the Venerable Elder Nāgasena said:

“Dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā katanti. ‘Kiṃ, bhante nāgasena, bhagavatā dukkaraṃ kata’nti. ‘Dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā kataṃ, yaṃ imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ vavatthānaṃ akkhātaṃ – ayaṃ phasso, ayaṃ vedanā, ayaṃ saññā, ayaṃ cetanā, idaṃ citta’nti. ‘Opammaṃ, bhante, karohī’ti. ‘Yathā, mahārāja, kocideva puriso nāvāya samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā hatthapuṭena udakaṃ gahetvā jivhāya sāyitvā jāneyya nu kho, mahārāja, so puriso – idaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ, idaṃ yamunāya udakaṃ, idaṃ aciravatiyā udakaṃ, idaṃ sarabhuyā udakaṃ, idaṃ mahiyā udaka’nti? ‘Dukkaraṃ, bhante, jānitu’nti. ‘Tato dukkarataraṃ [M 0.0187] kho, mahārāja, bhagavatā kataṃ yaṃ imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ…pe… idaṃ citta’”nti (mi. pa. 2.7.16).

"A difficult thing, great king, was done by the Blessed One." "What difficult thing was done by the Blessed One, Venerable Nāgasena?" "A difficult thing, great king, was done by the Blessed One, in that he declared the analysis of these formless mental states—mind and mental factors—occurring with a single object: 'This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is mind.'" "Give me an analogy, Venerable." "Suppose, great king, a man were to embark on the ocean in a boat, take up water in his cupped hand, taste it with his tongue, and know: 'This is the water of the Ganges, this is the water of the Yamunā, this is the water of the Aciravatī, this is the water of the Sarabhū, this is the water of the Mahī.' Would that man, great king, indeed know this?" "It would be difficult, Venerable, to know." "Even more difficult than that, great king, was the task accomplished by the Blessed One when he declared the analysis of these formless mental states—mind and mental factors—occurring with a single object: 'This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is mind.'"

7. Vitakkaniddese takkanavasena takko. Tassa tittakaṃ takkesi kumbhaṃ takkesi sakaṭaṃ takkesi yojanaṃ takkesi addhayojanaṃ takkesīti evaṃ takkanavasena pavatti veditabbā. Idaṃ takkassa sabhāvapadaṃ. Vitakkanavasena vitakko. Balavataratakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Suṭṭhu kappanavasena saṅkappo. Ekaggaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇe appetīti appanā. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ[P 0.0143]. Balavatarā vā appanā byappanā. Ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropeti patiṭṭhāpetīti cetaso abhiniropanā. Yāthāvatāya niyyānikatāya ca kusalabhāvappatto pasattho saṅkappoti sammāsaṅkappo.

7. In the exposition of initial application (vitakka), 'takka' is so called by way of directing. Its process should be understood by way of directing thus: 'He directed a little, he directed a pot-full, he directed a cart-load, he directed a yojana, he directed half a yojana.' This is the term for the intrinsic nature of takka. Vitakka is so called by way of applying variously; this is the name for a stronger takka. Saṅkappa is so called by way of thinking well. Appanā is so called because it applies the one-pointed mind to an object. The second term, byappanā, is augmented by way of a prefix, or byappanā is a stronger appanā. Cetaso abhiniropanā is so called because it places the mind upon an object and establishes it there. Sammāsaṅkappa (Right Intention) is a praised intention that has attained a wholesome state due to its accordance with reality and its quality of leading out [of saṃsāra].

8. Vicāraniddese ārammaṇe caraṇakavasena cāro. Idamassa sabhāvapadaṃ. Vicaraṇavasena vicāro[V 0.0188]. Anugantvā vicaraṇavasena anuvicāro. Upagantvā vicaraṇavasena upavicāroti. Upasaggavasena vā padāni vaḍḍhitāni. Ārammaṇe cittaṃ, saraṃ viya jiyāya, anusandahitvā ṭhapanato cittassa anusandhānatā. Ārammaṇaṃ anupekkhamāno viya tiṭṭhatīti anupekkhanatā. Vicaraṇavasena vā upekkhanatā anupekkhanatā.

8. In the exposition of sustained application (vicāra), 'cāra' is by way of moving about on an object. This is its term of intrinsic nature. Vicāra is by way of moving around. Anuvicāra is by way of moving around, having followed after. Upavicāra is by way of moving around, having approached. Or, the terms are augmented by way of prefixes. The mind's connecting (cittassa anusandhānatā) is from placing the mind on the object by connecting it, like an arrow to a bowstring. Anupekkhanatā is so called because it abides as if repeatedly observing the object. Or, anupekkhanatā is the state of observing (upekkhanatā) by way of moving around (vicaraṇa).

9. Pītiniddese pītīti sabhāvapadaṃ. Pamuditassa bhāvo pāmojjaṃ. Āmodanākāro āmodanā. Pamodanākāro pamodanā. Yathā vā bhesajjānaṃ vā telānaṃ vā uṇhodakasītodakānaṃ vā ekatokaraṇaṃ modanāti vuccati, evamayampi pīti dhammānaṃ ekatokaraṇena modanā. Upasaggavasena pana maṇḍetvā āmodanā pamodanāti vuttā. Hāsetīti hāso. Pahāsetīti pahāso. Haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākārānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vittīti vittaṃ; dhanassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ayaṃ pana somanassapaccayattā vittisarikkhatāya vitti. Yathā hi dhanino dhanaṃ paṭicca somanassaṃ uppajjati, evaṃ pītimatopi pītiṃ paṭicca somanassaṃ uppajjati, tasmā vittīti vuttā. Tuṭṭhisabhāvasaṇṭhitāya pītiyā etaṃ nāmaṃ. Pītimā pana puggalo kāyacittānaṃ uggatattā abbhuggatattā udaggoti vuccati[M 0.0188]. Udaggassa bhāvo odagyaṃ. Attano manatā attamanatā. Anabhiraddhassa hi mano dukkhapadaṭṭhānattā attano mano nāma na hoti, abhiraddhassa pana sukhapadaṭṭhānattā attano mano nāma hoti. Iti attano manatā attamanatā, sakamanatā. Sakamanassa bhāvoti attho. Sā pana yasmā na aññassa kassaci attano manatā, cittasseva paneso bhāvo, cetasiko dhammo, tasmā attamanatā cittassāti vuttā.

9. In the exposition of rapture (pīti), 'pīti' is the term for its intrinsic nature. Pāmojja is the state of one who is delighted. Āmodanā is the mode of rejoicing. Or, just as the combining of medicines, oils, or hot and cold water is called 'modanā' (mixing/delighting), so too this pīti is called modanā because it combines the associated states. However, having been embellished by way of prefixes, they are called āmodanā and pamodanā. Hāsa is so called because it causes joy. Pahāsa is so called because it causes great joy. This is a designation for the modes of gladness and great gladness. Vitti means wealth; this is a name for riches. This pīti, however, is called vitti because it is a condition for mental pleasure and because of its similarity to wealth. For just as mental pleasure arises for a wealthy person in dependence on wealth, so too for a person with rapture, mental pleasure arises in dependence on rapture; therefore, it is called vitti. This is a name for rapture that is well-established in the nature of contentment. Furthermore, a person with rapture is called udagga (uplifted) because their body and mind are uplifted and greatly uplifted. The state of being uplifted is odagya. Attamanatā is the state of one's own mind. For one who is displeased, the mind is not called 'one's own mind' because it is a proximate cause of suffering; but for one who is pleased, it is called 'one's own mind' because it is a proximate cause of happiness. Thus, attamanatā is the state of one's own mind, that is, sakamanatā. The meaning is the state of one's own mind. And since that state of one's own mind does not belong to anyone else, but is a state of the mind itself, a mental factor, it is therefore called attamanatā cittassa (the mind's gladness).

11. Ekaggatāniddese acalabhāvena ārammaṇe tiṭṭhatīti ṭhiti. Parato padadvayaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Apica sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇamhi sampiṇḍetvā tiṭṭhatīti [P 0.0144] saṇṭhiti. Ārammaṇaṃ ogāhetvā anupavisitvā tiṭṭhatīti avaṭṭhiti. Kusalapakkhasmiñhi cattāro dhammā ārammaṇaṃ ogāhanti – saddhā sati samādhi paññāti. Teneva saddhā okappanāti vuttā, sati apilāpanatāti, samādhi avaṭṭhitīti, paññā pariyogāhanāti. Akusalapakkhe pana tayo dhammā ārammaṇaṃ ogāhanti – taṇhā diṭṭhi avijjāti. Teneva te oghāti vuttā. Cittekaggatā panettha na balavatī hoti. Yathā hi rajuṭṭhānaṭṭhāne udakena siñcitvā sammaṭṭhe thokameva kālaṃ rajo sannisīdati, sukkhante sukkhante puna pakatibhāvena vuṭṭhāti, evameva akusalapakkhe cittekaggatā na balavatī hoti. Yathā pana tasmiṃ ṭhāne ghaṭehi udakaṃ āsiñcitvā [V 0.0189] kudālena khanitvā ākoṭanamaddanaghaṭṭanāni katvā upalitte ādāse viya chāyā paññāyati, vassasatātikkamepi taṃmuhuttakataṃ viya hoti, evameva kusalapakkhe cittekaggatā balavatī hoti.

11. In the exposition of one-pointedness, ṭhiti is standing on the object with an unshaken nature. The two subsequent terms are augmented by means of prefixes. Furthermore, saṇṭhiti is standing by gathering together the associated states on the object. Avaṭṭhiti is standing by entering and penetrating the object. Indeed, in the wholesome faction, four states enter into the object: faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, faith is called placing trust (okappanā), mindfulness is called non-superficiality (apilāpanatā), concentration is called firm standing (avaṭṭhiti), and wisdom is called thorough investigation (pariyogāhanā). In the unwholesome faction, however, three states enter into the object: craving, wrong view, and ignorance. Therefore, they are called floods (oghā). Herein, one-pointedness of mind is not strong. For just as in a place where dust rises, when it is sprinkled with water and swept, the dust settles for only a short time, and as it dries, it rises again to its natural state; even so, in the unwholesome faction, one-pointedness of mind is not strong.
