But just as when that place is poured with water from pots, dug with a spade, and after the actions of pounding, kneading, and tamping have been done, it is plastered so that a reflection appears, and even after the passing of a hundred years it is as if it were made in that moment; even so, in the wholesome faction, one-pointedness of mind is strong.

Uddhaccavicikicchāvasena pavattassa visāhārassa paṭipakkhato avisāhāro. Uddhaccavicikicchāvaseneva gacchantaṃ cittaṃ vikkhipati nāma. Ayaṃ pana tathāvidho vikkhepo na hotīti avikkhepo. Uddhaccavicikicchāvaseneva ca cittaṃ visāhaṭaṃ nāma hoti, ito cito ca harīyati. Ayaṃ pana evaṃ avisāhaṭassa mānasassa bhāvoti avisāhaṭamānasatā.

Avisāhāra is so called because it is the opposite of the dispersal (visāhāra) that occurs by means of restlessness and doubt. A mind proceeding by means of restlessness and doubt is said to scatter. But this one-pointedness is not that kind of scattering; therefore, it is avikkhepa (non-scattering). And by means of restlessness and doubt, the mind is said to be carried away (visāhaṭaṃ); it is carried to this and that. But this is the state of a mind that is thus not carried away; therefore, it is avisāhaṭamānasatā (the state of a mind not carried away).

Samathoti tividho samatho – cittasamatho, adhikaraṇasamatho, sabbasaṅkhārasamathoti. Tattha aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu cittekaggatā cittasamatho [M 0.0189] nāma. Tañhi āgamma cittacalanaṃ cittavipphanditaṃ sammati vūpasammati, tasmā so cittasamathoti vuccati. Sammukhāvinayādisattavidho samatho adhikaraṇasamatho nāma. Tañhi āgamma tāni tāni adhikaraṇāni sammanti vūpasammanti, tasmā so adhikaraṇasamathoti vuccati. Yasmā pana sabbe saṅkhārā nibbānaṃ āgamma sammanti vūpasammanti, tasmā taṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamathoti vuccati. Imasmiṃ atthe cittasamatho adhippeto. Samādhilakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti samādhindriyaṃ. Uddhacce na kampatīti samādhibalaṃ. Sammāsamādhīti yāthāvasamādhi niyyānikasamādhi kusalasamādhi.

Samatha (tranquility) is of three kinds: tranquility of mind, settlement of disputes, and calming of all formations. Herein, the one-pointedness of mind in the eight attainments is called tranquility of mind. For by resorting to it, the agitation and oscillation of the mind are calmed and especially calmed; therefore, it is called tranquility of mind. The sevenfold samatha beginning with settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) is called settlement of disputes. For by resorting to it, those various disputes are settled and especially settled; therefore, it is called settlement of disputes. Furthermore, because all formations are calmed and especially calmed upon reaching Nibbāna, that Nibbāna is called the calming of all formations. In this context, tranquility of mind is intended. It is the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) because it exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of concentration. It is the power of concentration (samādhibalaṃ) because it is not shaken by restlessness. Right concentration is concentration as it actually is, concentration leading to deliverance, and wholesome concentration.

12. Saddhindriyaniddese [P 0.0145] buddhādiguṇānaṃ saddahanavasena saddhā. Buddhādīni vā ratanāni saddahati pattiyāyatīti saddhā. Saddahanāti saddahanākāro. Buddhādīnaṃ guṇe ogāhati, bhinditvā viya anupavisatīti okappanā. Buddhādīnaṃ guṇesu etāya sattā ativiya pasīdanti, sayaṃ vā abhippasīdatīti abhippasādo. Idāni yasmā saddhindriyādīnaṃ samāsapadānaṃ vasena aññasmiṃ pariyāye āraddhe ādipadaṃ gahetvāva padabhājanaṃ karīyati – ayaṃ abhidhamme dhammatā – tasmā puna saddhāti vuttaṃ. Yathā vā itthiyā indriyaṃ itthindriyaṃ, na tathā idaṃ. Idaṃ pana saddhāva indriyaṃ saddhindriyanti. Evaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvañāpanatthampi puna saddhāti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbapadaniddesesu ādipadassa puna vacane payojanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Adhimokkhalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti saddhindriyaṃ. Asaddhiye na kampatīti saddhābalaṃ.

12. In the exposition of the faculty of faith, saddhā (faith) is so called by means of believing in the qualities of the Buddha and so on. Or, it is saddhā because one believes in and relies upon the jewels such as the Buddha. Believing (saddahanā) is the mode of believing. It is okappanā (placing trust) because it enters the qualities of the Buddha and so on, penetrating as if breaking through. By means of it, beings become exceedingly serene towards the qualities of the Buddha and so on; or, it itself becomes exceedingly serene, thus it is abhippasāda (profound serenity). Now, because when another method is undertaken for compound words such as saddhindriya, the word analysis is done by taking the first word—this is the nature (dhammatā) in the Abhidhamma—therefore, 'faith' is stated again. Or, this is not like the case of itthindriya (the female faculty), which is 'a woman's faculty'. Rather, here, faith itself is the faculty, thus saddhindriya. Thus, 'faith' is stated again also to make known the state of having the same referent. In this way, the purpose for the repetition of the initial word in all expositions of terms should be understood. It is the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) because it exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of determination. It is the power of faith (saddhābala) because it is not shaken by faithlessness.

13. Vīriyindriyaniddese [V 0.0190] cetasikoti idaṃ vīriyassa niyamato cetasikabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Idañhi vīriyaṃ “yadapi, bhikkhave, kāyikaṃ vīriyaṃ tadapi vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, yadapi cetasikaṃ vīriyaṃ tadapi vīriyasambojjhaṅgoti. Itihidaṃ uddesaṃ gacchatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.233) evamādīsu suttesu caṅkamādīni karontassa uppannattā ‘kāyika’nti vuccamānampi kāyaviññāṇaṃ viya kāyikaṃ nāma natthi, cetasikameva panetanti dassetuṃ ‘cetasiko’ti vuttaṃ. Vīriyārambhoti vīriyasaṅkhāto ārambho. Iminā sesārambhe paṭikkhipati. Ayañhi ‘ārambha’-saddo kamme āpattiyaṃ kiriyāyaṃ vīriye hiṃsāya vikopaneti anekesu atthesu āgato.

13. In the exposition of the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), the word 'mental' (cetasika) is stated to show that energy is invariably a mental factor. For although this energy is called 'physical' because it arises in one who is doing walking meditation and so on, in reference to such suttas as: “Bhikkhus, whatever physical energy there is, that is the enlightenment factor of energy; whatever mental energy there is, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy. Thus this is included in the summary,” there is nothing called 'physical' in the way that body-consciousness is physical. Rather, to show that it is purely mental, 'mental' is stated. 'Undertaking of energy' (vīriyārambha) is the undertaking designated as energy. By this, other undertakings are rejected. For this word ārambha occurs in many meanings: in action, transgression, activity, energy, injury, and destruction.

“Yaṃkiñci [M 0.0190] dukkhaṃ sambhoti, sabbaṃ ārambhapaccayā;

Ārambhānaṃ nirodhena, natthi dukkhassa sambhavo”ti. (su. ni. 749);

“Whatever suffering arises, all of it is conditioned by undertaking; with the cessation of undertakings, there is no arising of suffering.”

Ettha hi kammaṃ ‘ārambho’ti āgataṃ. “Ārambhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hotī”ti (a. ni. 5.142; pu. pa. 191) ettha āpatti. “Mahāyaññā mahārambhā na te honti mahapphalā”ti (a. ni. 4.39; saṃ. ni. 1.120) ettha yūpussāpanādikiriyā. “Ārambhatha [P 0.0146] nikkamatha yuñjatha buddhasāsane”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.185) ettha vīriyaṃ. “Samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhantī”ti (ma. ni. 2.51-52) ettha hiṃsā. “Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.10; ma. ni. 1.293) ettha chedanabhañjanādikaṃ vikopanaṃ. Idha pana vīriyameva adhippetaṃ. Tenāha – ‘vīriyārambhoti vīriyasaṅkhāto ārambho’ti. Vīriyañhi ārambhanakavasena ārambhoti vuccati. Idamassa sabhāvapadaṃ. Kosajjato nikkhamanavasena nikkamo. Paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanavasena parakkamo. Uggantvā yamanavasena uyyāmo. Byāyamanavasena vāyāmo. Ussāhanavasena ussāho. Adhimattussāhanavasena ussoḷhī. Thirabhāvaṭṭhena thāmo. Cittacetasikānaṃ dhāraṇavasena avicchedato vā pavattanavasena kusalasantānaṃ dhāretīti dhiti.

Here, 'action' (kamma) is given as 'ārambha'. In the passage, “One undertakes and then has remorse,” it refers to an offense. In, “Great sacrifices, great undertakings, they are not of great fruit,” it refers to the act of erecting sacrificial posts and so on. In, “Undertake, go forth, strive in the Buddha’s dispensation,” it refers to energy. In, “For the sake of the ascetic Gotama, they undertake [the killing of] a living being,” it refers to harm. In, “He is one who abstains from the destruction of seed-life and plant-life,” it refers to destroying, such as cutting and breaking. Here, however, only energy is intended. Therefore, it is said: 'the undertaking of energy means the undertaking designated as energy.' For energy, by way of undertaking, is called 'undertaking.' This is its term of intrinsic nature. By way of emerging from laziness, it is 'going forth' (nikkama). By way of advancing to a progressively higher state, it is 'striving' (parakkama). By way of striving having risen up, it is 'endeavor' (uyyāma). By way of distinctive exertion, it is 'effort' (vāyāma). By way of exertion, it is 'exertion' (ussāha). By way of excessive exertion, it is 'great effort' (ussoḷhī). In the sense of being steadfast, it is 'strength' (thāma). By way of upholding mind and mental factors, or because it upholds the continuity of wholesome states by way of proceeding without interruption, it is 'resolve' (dhiti).

Aparo nayo – nikkamo ceso kāmānaṃ panudanāya, parakkamo ceso bandhanacchedāya, uyyāmo ceso oghanittharaṇāya, vāyāmo ceso pāraṅgamanaṭṭhena, ussāho ceso pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena, ussoḷhī [V 0.0191] ceso adhimattaṭṭhena, thāmo ceso palighugghāṭanatāya, dhiti ceso avaṭṭhitikāritāyāti.

Another method: This [energy] is 'going forth' (nikkama) for the dispelling of sensual pleasures. This is 'striving' (parakkama) for the cutting of bonds. This is 'endeavor' (uyyāma) for crossing over the floods. This is 'effort' (vāyāma) in the sense of going to the far shore. This is 'exertion' (ussāha) in the sense of being a forerunner. This is 'great effort' (ussoḷhī) in the sense of being excessive. This is 'strength' (thāma) for unbarring the bolt. This is 'resolve' (dhiti) for causing steadfastness.

“Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca aṭṭhi ca avasissatū”ti (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.22, 237; a. ni. 2.5; mahāni. 196; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 154) evaṃ pavattikāle asithilaparakkamavasena asithilaparakkamatā; thiraparakkamo, daḷhaparakkamoti attho. Yasmā panetaṃ vīriyaṃ kusalakammakaraṇaṭṭhāne chandaṃ na nikkhipati, dhuraṃ na nikkhipati, na otāreti, na vissajjeti, anosakkitamānasataṃ āvahati, tasmā anikkhittachandatā anikkhittadhuratāti vuttaṃ. Yathā pana tajjātike udakasambhinnaṭṭhāne dhuravāhagoṇaṃ gaṇhathāti vadanti[M 0.0191], so jaṇṇunā bhūmiṃ uppīḷetvāpi dhuraṃ vahati, bhūmiyaṃ patituṃ na deti, evameva vīriyaṃ kusalakammakaraṇaṭṭhāne dhuraṃ ukkhipati paggaṇhāti, tasmā dhurasampaggāhoti vuttaṃ. Paggahalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti vīriyindriyaṃ. Kosajje [P 0.0147] na kampatīti vīriyabalaṃ. Yāthāvaniyyānikakusalavāyāmatāya sammāvāyāmo.

“Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain…”—thus, at such a time of practice, by way of unslackened striving, it is 'unslackened striving' (asithilaparakkamatā); the meaning is firm striving, strong striving. Furthermore, because this energy, in the place of performing wholesome deeds, does not lay down intention, does not lay down the burden, does not lower it, does not cast it away, and brings about a state of mind that does not shrink back, it is therefore called 'unrelinquished intention' and 'unrelinquished burden' (anikkhittachandatā, anikkhittadhuratā). Just as, in a muddy place mixed with water of that kind, they say, “Take the draft-ox,” and it, even while pressing the ground with its knees, carries the burden and does not let it fall to the ground; even so, energy lifts up and takes up the burden in the place of performing wholesome deeds. Therefore, it is called 'taking up the burden' (dhurasampaggāho). Because it exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of uplifting, it is the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya). Because it does not tremble on account of laziness, it is the power of energy (vīriyabala). Because it is effort that is actual, that leads out, and that is wholesome, it is right effort (sammāvāyāmo).

14. Satindriyaniddese saraṇakavasena sati. Idaṃ satiyā sabhāvapadaṃ. Punappunaṃ saraṇato anussaraṇavasena anussati. Abhimukhaṃ gantvā viya saraṇato paṭisaraṇavasena paṭissati. Upasaggavasena vā vaḍḍhitamattametaṃ. Saraṇākāro saraṇatā. Yasmā pana saraṇatāti tiṇṇaṃ saraṇānampi nāmaṃ, tasmā taṃ paṭisedhetuṃ puna satiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Satisaṅkhātā saraṇatāti ayañhettha attho. Sutapariyattassa dhāraṇabhāvato dhāraṇatā. Anupavisanasaṅkhātena ogāhanaṭṭhena apilāpanabhāvo apilāpanatā. Yathā hi lābukaṭāhādīni udake plavanti, na anupavisanti, na tathā ārammaṇe sati. Ārammaṇañhesā anupavisati, tasmā apilāpanatāti vuttā. Cirakatacirabhāsitānaṃ asammussanabhāvato asammussanatā. Upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇe jotanalakkhaṇe ca indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Satisaṅkhātaṃ indriyaṃ satindriyaṃ. Pamāde na kampatīti satibalaṃ. Yāthāvasati niyyānikasati kusalasatīti sammāsati.

14. In the exposition of the faculty of mindfulness, 'mindfulness' (sati) is so called by way of remembering. This is a term for the intrinsic nature of mindfulness. By way of remembering again and again, it is 'recollection' (anussati). As if going towards an object, by way of remembering, it is 'recollection towards' (paṭissati). Or, this is merely a term augmented by way of the prefix. The mode of remembering is 'the state of remembering' (saraṇatā). Furthermore, since 'the state of remembering' is also a name for the three refuges, the term 'mindfulness' is taken up again to exclude that meaning. The meaning here is: the mode of remembering designated as mindfulness. Because it is a state of retaining what has been heard and learned, it is 'retention' (dhāraṇatā). Because it is a state of not floating about, in the sense of immersion which is designated as penetrating, it is called 'the state of not floating about' (apilāpanatā). For just as gourds and so on float on the water and do not penetrate it, mindfulness is not like that with regard to its object. For it penetrates the object; therefore, it is called 'the state of not floating about.' Because it is a state of not forgetting things done and said long ago, it is 'unforgetfulness' (asammussanatā). Because it exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of presence and in the characteristic of illuminating, it is a 'faculty' (indriya). The faculty designated as mindfulness is the 'faculty of mindfulness' (satindriya). Because it does not tremble on account of heedlessness, it is the 'power of mindfulness' (satibala). Because it is mindfulness that is actual, mindfulness that leads out, and wholesome mindfulness, it is 'right mindfulness' (sammāsati).

16. Paññindriyaniddese tassa tassa atthassa pākaṭakaraṇasaṅkhātena paññāpanaṭṭhena paññā. Tena tena vā aniccādinā pakārena dhamme jānātītipi paññā. Idamassā sabhāvapadaṃ. Pajānanākāro pajānanā. Aniccādīni vicinātīti vicayo. Pavicayoti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ[V 0.0192]. Catusaccadhamme vicinātīti dhammavicayo. Aniccādīnaṃ sallakkhaṇavasena sallakkhaṇā. Sāyeva puna upasagganānattena upalakkhaṇā paccupalakkhaṇāti vuttā. Paṇḍitassa bhāvo paṇḍiccaṃ. Kusalassa bhāvo kosallaṃ. Nipuṇassa bhāvo nepuññaṃ. Aniccādīnaṃ vibhāvanavasena vebhabyā. Aniccādīnaṃ cintanakavasena cintā. Yassa vā uppajjati taṃ aniccādīni cintāpetītipi cintā. Aniccādīni upaparikkhatīti upaparikkhā. Bhūrīti pathaviyā [M 0.0192] nāmaṃ. Ayampi saṇhaṭṭhena vitthaṭaṭṭhena ca bhūrī viyāti bhūrī. Tena vuttaṃ – “bhūrī vuccati pathavī[P 0.0148]. Tāya pathavīsamāya vitthaṭāya vipulāya paññāya samannāgatoti bhūripaññoti (mahāni. 27). Apica paññāya etaṃ adhivacanaṃ bhūrī”ti. Bhūte atthe ramatītipi bhūrī. Asani viya siluccaye kilese medhati hiṃsatīti medhā. Khippaṃ gahaṇadhāraṇaṭṭhena vā medhā. Yassa uppajjati taṃ attahitapaṭipattiyaṃ sampayuttadhamme ca yāthāvalakkhaṇapaṭivedhe parinetīti pariṇāyikā. Aniccādivasena dhamme vipassatīti vipassanā. Sammā pakārehi aniccādīni jānātīti sampajaññaṃ. Uppathapaṭipanne sindhave vīthiāropanatthaṃ patodo viya uppathe dhāvanakaṃ kūṭacittaṃ vīthiāropanatthaṃ vijjhatīti patodo viya patodo. Dassanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Paññāsaṅkhātaṃ indriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ. Avijjāya na kampatīti paññābalaṃ. Kilesacchedanaṭṭhena paññāva satthaṃ paññāsatthaṃ. Accuggataṭṭhena paññāva pāsādo paññāpāsādo.

16. In the exposition of the faculty of wisdom, 'wisdom' (paññā) is so called because of the meaning of making clear, designated as the state of making manifest the meaning of this or that. Or, it is also 'wisdom' (paññā) because it knows phenomena in this or that way, such as impermanence. This is the term for its intrinsic nature. The mode of discerning is 'discernment' (pajānanā). It investigates things such as impermanence, hence it is called 'investigation' (vicayo). As ‘pavicayo,’ the term is augmented with a prefix. It investigates the four noble truths, hence it is called 'investigation of phenomena' (dhammavicayo). By means of correctly marking things such as impermanence, it is 'correct marking' (sallakkhaṇā). The same, due to the variation of prefixes, is taught as 'marking' (upalakkhaṇā) and 'remarking' (paccupalakkhaṇā). The state of a wise person is 'sagacity' (paṇḍiccaṃ). The state of a skillful person is 'skillfulness' (kosallaṃ). The state of a refined person is 'refinement' (nepuññaṃ). By means of analyzing things such as impermanence, it is 'analysis' (vebhabyā). By means of thinking about things such as impermanence, it is 'thought' (cintā). Or, when it arises in a person, it causes that person to think about things such as impermanence, hence it is also 'thought' (cintā). It closely examines things such as impermanence, hence it is 'close examination' (upaparikkhā). ‘Bhūrī’ is a name for the earth. This wisdom is also ‘bhūrī’ because, like the earth, it is subtle and extensive. Therefore it is said: ‘“Bhūrī” is said of the earth. One who is endowed with wisdom that is extensive and vast like that earth is called “one of vast wisdom” (bhūripañño). Moreover, “bhūrī” is a designation for wisdom.’ It is also ‘bhūrī’ because it delights in the true meaning. Like a thunderbolt on a heap of rock, it strikes and destroys defilements, hence it is ‘intelligence’ (medhā). Or, because of its meaning of quick grasping and retention, it is ‘medhā.’ When it arises in a person, it guides that person in the practice for their own welfare and in the penetration of the true characteristics of associated states, hence it is the 'guide' (pariṇāyikā). It sees phenomena by way of impermanence, etc., hence it is 'insight' (vipassanā). It knows things such as impermanence correctly and in various ways, hence it is 'clear comprehension' (sampajaññaṃ). Like a goad for piercing a thoroughbred horse that has gone astray from the path to put it back on the road, it is a 'goad' (patodo) for piercing the deceitful mind that runs astray on the wrong path to put it on the road. It exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of seeing, hence it is a 'faculty' (indriya). The faculty designated as wisdom is the 'faculty of wisdom' (paññindriya). It is not shaken by ignorance, hence it is the 'power of wisdom' (paññābala). Because of its meaning of cutting off defilements, wisdom itself is a sword, the 'sword of wisdom' (paññāsatthaṃ). Because of its meaning of being exceedingly lofty, wisdom itself is a palace, the 'palace of wisdom' (paññāpāsādo).

Ālokanaṭṭhena paññāva āloko paññāāloko. Obhāsanaṭṭhena paññāva obhāso paññāobhāso. Pajjotanaṭṭhena paññāva pajjoto paññāpajjoto. Paññavato hi ekapallaṅkena nisinnassa dasasahassilokadhātu ekālokā ekobhāsā ekapajjotā hoti, tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Imesu pana tīsu padesu ekapadenapi etasmiṃ atthe siddhe, yāni panetāni “cattārome, bhikkhave, ālokā. Katame cattāro? Candāloko sūriyāloko agyāloko paññāloko. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro ālokā. Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, imesaṃ catunnaṃ ālokānaṃ yadidaṃ paññāloko”. Tathā “cattārome, bhikkhave, obhāsā…pe… cattārome, bhikkhave, pajjotā”ti (a. ni. 4.144) sattānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena suttāni desitāni, tadanurūpeneva idhāpi desanā katā. Attho hi anekehi ākārehi vibhajjamāno suvibhatto hoti. Aññathā ca añño bujjhati, aññathā ca aññoti.

Because it illuminates, wisdom itself is light—the light of wisdom. Because it shines, wisdom itself is radiance—the radiance of wisdom. Because it brightens, wisdom itself is brilliance—the brilliance of wisdom. For one endowed with wisdom, seated in a single cross-legged posture, the ten-thousandfold world-system becomes of one light, one radiance, one brilliance—therefore, this was said. Moreover, although in these three terms this meaning is accomplished even by a single term, the suttas—such as: “Monks, there are these four lights. What four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. These, monks, are the four lights. Of these four lights, monks, this is the foremost, that is, the light of wisdom.”—and similarly, “Monks, there are these four radiances…” and “Monks, there are these four brilliances…” (AN 4.144), were taught according to the dispositions of beings, and in accordance with that, the teaching here has also been given. For the meaning, when analyzed in many ways, becomes well-analyzed. One person understands it one way, and another understands it another way.

Ratikaraṇaṭṭhena pana ratidāyakaṭṭhena ratijanakaṭṭhena cittīkataṭṭhena dullabhapātubhāvaṭṭhena atulaṭṭhena [V 0.0193] anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhena ca paññāva ratanaṃ paññāratanaṃ. Na tena sattā muyhanti, sayaṃ vā ārammaṇe na muyhatīti [M 0.0193] amoho. Dhammavicayapadaṃ vuttatthameva. Kasmā panetaṃ puna vuttanti? Amohassa mohapaṭipakkhabhāvadīpanatthaṃ[P 0.0149]. Tenetaṃ dīpeti – yvāyaṃ amoho so na kevalaṃ mohato añño dhammo, mohassa pana paṭipakkho, dhammavicayasaṅkhāto amoho nāma idha adhippetoti. Sammādiṭṭhīti yāthāvaniyyānikakusaladiṭṭhi.

Because it creates delight, gives delight, generates delight, is esteemed, is of rare appearance, is incomparable, and is used as a requisite by superior beings, wisdom itself is a jewel, the jewel of wisdom. Beings are not deluded by it, or it itself is not deluded in regard to an object—this is non-delusion (amoho). The term ‘investigation of phenomena’ has a meaning that has already been stated. But why is it stated again? To show that non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. By this it is shown that this non-delusion is not merely a state different from delusion, but it is the opposite of delusion; here, the state called non-delusion, designated as investigation of phenomena, is intended. Right view is the correct, emancipating, wholesome view.

19. Jīvitindriyaniddese yo tesaṃ arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ āyūti tesaṃ sampayuttakānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ yo āyāpanaṭṭhena āyu, tasmiñhi sati arūpadhammā ayanti gacchanti pavattanti, tasmā āyūti vuccati. Idamassa sabhāvapadaṃ. Yasmā panete dhammā āyusmiṃyeva sati tiṭṭhanti yapenti yāpenti iriyanti vattanti pālayanti, tasmā ṭhitītiādīni vuttāni. Vacanattho panettha – etāya tiṭṭhantīti ṭhiti. Yapentīti yapanā. Tathā yāpanā. Evaṃ bujjhantānaṃ pana vasena purimapade rassattaṃ kataṃ. Etāya iriyantīti iriyanā. Vattantīti vattanā. Pālayantīti pālanā. Jīvanti etenāti jīvitaṃ. Anupālanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti jīvitindriyaṃ.

19. In the exposition of the life faculty, ‘the life of those immaterial states’ refers to the life which, by reason of causing those associated immaterial states to arise, is called ‘life’ (āyu). For when it is present, the immaterial states arise, proceed, and continue. Therefore, it is called ‘life.’ This is the term for its intrinsic nature. And because it is only when life is present that these states stand, subsist, are sustained, occur, continue, and are maintained, the terms ‘stability’ (ṭhiti), and so on, are stated. Herein, the etymological meaning is: by this they stand (tiṭṭhanti), thus it is stability (ṭhiti). By this they subsist (yapenti), thus it is subsistence (yapanā). Similarly, sustenance (yāpanā). However, for the sake of those who understand it thus, the vowel in the preceding term was shortened. By this they are sustained (iriyanti), thus it is sustenance (iriyanā). By this they continue (vattanti), thus it is continuance (vattanā). By this they are maintained (pālayanti), thus it is maintenance (pālanā). By this they live (jīvanti), thus it is life (jīvita). It exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of maintaining, thus it is the life faculty (jīvitindriya).

30. Hiribalaniddese yaṃ tasmiṃ samayeti yena dhammena tasmiṃ samaye. Liṅgavipallāsaṃ vā katvā yo dhammo tasmiṃ samayetipi attho veditabbo. Hiriyitabbenāti upayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Hiriyitabbayuttakaṃ kāyaduccaritādidhammaṃ hiriyati jigucchatīti attho. Pāpakānanti lāmakānaṃ. Akusalānaṃ dhammānanti akosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Samāpattiyāti idampi upayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Tesaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiṃ paṭilābhaṃ samaṅgībhāvaṃ hiriyati jigucchatīti attho.

30. In the exposition of the power of moral shame, ‘what is at that time’ (yaṃ tasmiṃ samaye) means ‘by which state at that time.’ Or, having made a change of gender, the meaning should also be understood as ‘which state is at that time.’ The word ‘hiriyitabbena’ (by what ought to be an object of shame) is an instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative. The meaning is: one is ashamed of, is disgusted by, a state such as bodily misconduct that ought to be an object of shame. ‘Pāpakānaṃ’ (of evil things) means ‘of base things.’ ‘Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ’ (of unwholesome states) means ‘of states that have arisen from unskillfulness.’ The word ‘samāpattiyā’ (by attainment) is also an instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative. The meaning is: one is ashamed of, is disgusted by, the attainment, acquisition, or state of being endowed with those states.

31. Ottappabalaniddese ottappitabbenāti hetvatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Ottappitabbayuttakena ottappassa hetubhūtena kāyaduccaritādinā vuttappakārāya ca samāpattiyā ottappassa hetubhūtāya ottappati, bhāyatīti attho.

31. In the exposition of the power of moral dread, the word `ottappitabbena` is an instrumental term in the sense of cause. The meaning is: one dreads, one fears, on account of bodily misconduct and so forth—which is associated with what ought to be dreaded and has become a cause for moral dread—and on account of the attainment of the aforesaid kind, which has become a cause for moral dread.

32. Alobhaniddese alubbhanakavasena alobho. Na lubbhatītipi alobho. Idamassa sabhāvapadaṃ. Alubbhanāti alubbhanākāro. Lobhasamaṅgī puggalo lubbhito nāma. Na lubbhito alubbhito[M 0.0194][V 0.0194]. Alubbhitassa [P 0.0150] bhāvo alubbhitattaṃ. Sārāgapaṭipakkhato na sārāgoti asārāgo. Asārajjanāti asārajjanākāro. Asārajjitassa bhāvo asārajjitattaṃ. Na abhijjhāyatīti anabhijjhā. Alobho kusalamūlanti alobhasaṅkhātaṃ kusalamūlaṃ. Alobho hi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ mūlaṃ paccayaṭṭhenāti kusalamūlaṃ. Kusalañca taṃ paccayaṭṭhena mūlañcātipi kusalamūlaṃ.

32. In the exposition of non-greed: `alobha` (non-greed) is so called by way of not being greedy. It is also `alobha` because ‘one is not greedy.’ This is the term expressing its intrinsic nature. `Alubbhanā` is the mode of not being greedy. A person endowed with greed is called `lubbhita` (greedy). Not greedy is `alubbhita`. The state of one who is not greedy is `alubbhitattaṃ`. Due to being the opposite of intense passion (`sārāga`), it is `asārāga` (non-passion), meaning ‘not intense passion.’ `Asārajjanā` is the mode of not being intensely passionate. The state of one who is not intensely passionate is `asārajjitattaṃ`. It is `anabhijjhā` (non-covetousness) because ‘one does not covet.’ As for `alobho kusalamūlaṃ` (non-greed is a wholesome root): it is the wholesome root designated as non-greed. Indeed, `alobha` is the root of wholesome states in the sense of being a condition; therefore, it is a wholesome root. It is also a wholesome root because it is both wholesome and, in the sense of being a condition, a root.

33. Adosaniddese adussanakavasena adoso. Na dussatītipi adoso. Idamassa sabhāvapadaṃ. Adussanāti adussanākāro. Adussitassa bhāvo adussitattaṃ. Byāpādapaṭipakkhato na byāpādoti abyāpādo. Kodhadukkhapaṭipakkhato na byāpajjoti abyāpajjo. Adosasaṅkhātaṃ kusalamūlaṃ adoso kusalamūlaṃ. Taṃ vuttatthameva.

33. In the exposition of non-hatred: `adosa` (non-hatred) is so called by way of non-corruption. It is also `adosa` because ‘one is not corrupted.’ This is the term expressing its intrinsic nature. `Adussanā` is the mode of the mind's non-corruption. The state of a non-corrupted mind is `adussitattaṃ`. Due to being the opposite of ill will (`byāpāda`), it is `abyāpāda` (non-ill will), meaning ‘not ill will.’ Due to being the opposite of the suffering that is anger, it is `abyāpajjo` (non-affliction), meaning ‘not the suffering that oppresses.’ The wholesome root designated as non-hatred is a wholesome root. That has the same meaning as was already stated.

40-41. Kāyapassaddhiniddesādīsu yasmā kāyoti tayo khandhā adhippetā, tasmā vedanākkhandhassātiādi vuttaṃ. Passambhanti etāya te dhammā, vigatadarathā bhavanti, samassāsappattāti passaddhi. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Passambhanāti passambhanākāro. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Passaddhisamaṅgitāya paṭippassambhitassa khandhattayassa bhāvo paṭippassambhitattaṃ. Sabbapadehipi tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ kilesadarathapaṭippassaddhi eva kathitā. Dutiyanayena viññāṇakkhandhassa darathapaṭippassaddhi kathitā.

In the expositions of tranquility of the mental body, and so forth: because by `kāya` (body) the three mental aggregates are intended, it is therefore said, ‘of the aggregate of feeling,’ and so forth. `Passaddhi` (tranquility) is so called because by it those states are calmed, they become free from the heat of defilements, and they reach a state of great relief. The second term (`paṭipassaddhi`) is an augmentation by way of a prefix. `Passambhanā` is the mode of calming. The second term (`paṭipassambhanā`) is an augmentation by way of a prefix. `Paṭippassambhitattaṃ` is the state of the triad of aggregates being thoroughly calmed due to being endowed with tranquility. By all the terms, only the calming of the heat of the defilements of the three aggregates is spoken of. By the second method, the calming of the heat of the consciousness aggregate is spoken of.

42-43. Lahutāti lahutākāro. Lahupariṇāmatāti lahupariṇāmo etesaṃ dhammānanti lahupariṇāmā; tesaṃ bhāvo lahupariṇāmatā; sīghaṃ sīghaṃ parivattanasamatthatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Adandhanatāti garubhāvapaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ; abhāriyatāti attho. Avitthanatāti mānādikilesabhārassa abhāvena athaddhatā. Evaṃ paṭhamena tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ lahutākāro kathito. Dutiyena viññāṇakkhandhassa lahutākāro kathito.

In the expositions of lightness of the mental body, and so forth: `Lahutā` (lightness) is the mode of lightness. As for `lahupariṇāmatā` (swiftness of transformation): these states have a swift transformation, thus they are `lahupariṇāmā`; their state is `lahupariṇāmatā`. This is said to be the capacity to change very quickly. `Adandhatā` (non-sluggishness) is a term that rejects the state of heaviness; the meaning is being unburdensome. `Avitthambhanā` (non-rigidity) is non-stiffness due to the absence of the burden of defilements such as conceit. Thus, by the first method, the mode of lightness of the three aggregates is spoken of. By the second method, the mode of lightness of the consciousness aggregate is spoken of.

44-45. Mudutāti [P 0.0151] mudubhāvo. Maddavatāti maddavaṃ vuccati siniddhaṃ, maṭṭhaṃ; maddavassa bhāvo maddavatā. Akakkhaḷatāti akakkhaḷabhāvo. Akathinatāti akathinabhāvo. Idhāpi purimanayena tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ, pacchimanayena viññāṇakkhandhassa mudutākārova kathito.

In the expositions of softness of the mental body, and so forth: `Mudutā` (softness) is the state of being soft. As for `maddavatā` (malleability): a smooth and refined mind is called `maddava`; the state of `maddava` is `maddavatā`. `Akakkhaḷatā` (non-harshness) is the state of a non-harsh mind. Here too, by the former method, the mode of softness of the three aggregates is spoken of, and by the latter method, only the mode of softness of the consciousness aggregate is spoken of.

46-47. Kammaññatāti [M 0.0195][V 0.0195] kammani sādhutā; kusalakiriyāya viniyogakkhamatāti attho. Sesapadadvayaṃ byañjanavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Padadvayenāpi hi purimanayena tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ, pacchimanayena viññāṇakkhandhassa kammaniyākārova kathito.

In the expositions of workableness of the mental body, and so forth: `Kammaññatā` (workableness) is goodness in action; the meaning is the fitness for being applied to the performance of wholesome action. The remaining two terms (`kammaññattaṃ`, `kammaññabhāvo`) are augmentations by way of expression. Indeed, by this pair of terms, in accordance with the former method, the mode of workableness of the three aggregates is spoken of, and in accordance with the latter method, only the mode of workableness of the consciousness aggregate is spoken of.

48-49. Paguṇatāti paguṇabhāvo, anāturatā niggilānatāti attho. Sesapadadvayaṃ byañjanavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Idhāpi purimanayena tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ, pacchimanayena viññāṇakkhandhassa niggilānākārova kathito.

In the expositions of proficiency of the mental body, and so forth: `Paguṇatā` (proficiency) is the state of being proficient; the meaning is unafflictedness, the state of being without sickness. The remaining two terms (`paguṇattaṃ`, `paguṇabhāvo`) are augmentations by way of expression. Here too, by the former method, the mode of being without sickness of the three aggregates is spoken of, and by the latter method, only the mode of being without sickness of the consciousness aggregate is spoken of.

50-51. Ujukatāti ujukabhāvo, ujukenākārena pavattanatāti attho. Ujukassa khandhattayassa viññāṇakkhandhassa ca bhāvo ujukatā. Ajimhatāti gomuttavaṅkabhāvapaṭikkhepo. Avaṅkatāti candalekhāvaṅkabhāvapaṭikkhepo. Akuṭilatāti naṅgalakoṭivaṅkabhāvapaṭikkhepo.

In the expositions of straightness of the mental body, and so forth: `Ujukatā` (straightness) is the state of being straight; the meaning is the state of proceeding in a straight manner. `Ujukatā` is the state of the triad of aggregates and of the consciousness aggregate being straight. `Ajimhatā` (non-crookedness) is the rejection of the state of crookedness like cow's urine. `Avaṅkatā` (non-bentness) is the rejection of the state of crookedness like the crescent moon. `Akuṭilatā` (non-dishonesty) is the rejection of the state of crookedness like the tip of a plough.

Yo hi pāpaṃ katvāva ‘na karomī’ti bhāsati, so gantvā paccosakkanatāya ‘gomuttavaṅko’ nāma hoti. Yo pāpaṃ karontova ‘bhāyāmahaṃ pāpassā’ti bhāsati, so yebhuyyena kuṭilatāya ‘candalekhāvaṅko’ nāma hoti. Yo pāpaṃ karontova ‘ko pāpassa na bhāyeyyā’ti bhāsati, so nātikuṭilatāya ‘naṅgalakoṭivaṅko’ nāma hoti. Yassa vā tīṇipi kammadvārāni asuddhāni, so ‘gomuttavaṅko’ nāma hoti. Yassa yāni kānici dve, so ‘candalekhāvaṅko’ nāma. Yassa yaṃkiñci ekaṃ, so ‘naṅgalakoṭivaṅko nāma.

Indeed, one who, after having done an evil deed, says, ‘I did not do it,’ is called gomuttavaṅko (crooked like cow's urine) because of going forward and then drawing back. One who, while doing an evil deed, says, ‘I fear evil,’ is called candalekhāvaṅko (crooked like the crescent moon) because of being crooked for the most part. One who, while doing an evil deed, says, ‘Who would not fear evil?’ is called naṅgalakoṭivaṅko (crooked like the tip of a plough) because of not being excessively crooked. Alternatively, one whose three doors of action are impure is called gomuttavaṅko. One who has any two impure is called candalekhāvaṅko. One who has any one impure is called naṅgalakoṭivaṅko.

Dīghabhāṇakā panāhu – ekacco bhikkhu sabbavaye ekavīsatiyā anesanāsu, chasu ca agocaresu carati, ayaṃ ‘gomuttavaṅko’ nāma. Eko paṭhamavaye catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paripūreti, lajjī kukkuccako sikkhākāmo hoti, majjhimavayapacchimavayesu purimasadiso, ayaṃ [P 0.0152] ‘candalekhāvaṅko’ nāma. Eko paṭhamavaye majjhimavayepi catupārisuddhisīlaṃ pūreti, lajjī kukkuccako sikkhākāmo hoti, pacchimavaye purimasadiso. Ayaṃ ‘naṅgalakoṭivaṅko’ nāma.

The reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya, however, say: A certain monk, in all stages of life, conducts himself in the twenty-one kinds of improper livelihood and in the six improper resorts; this one is called gomuttavaṅko. Another monk, in the first stage of life, fulfills the fourfold purification of morality, is modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, but in the middle and last stages of life, he is similar to the former person; this one is called candalekhāvaṅko. Another monk, in the first and middle stages of life, fulfills the fourfold purification of morality, is modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, but in the last stage of life, he is similar to the former person; this one is called naṅgalakoṭivaṅko.

Tassa kilesavasena evaṃ vaṅkassa puggalassa bhāvo jimhatā vaṅkatā kuṭilatāti vuccati. Tāsaṃ paṭikkhepavasena ajimhatādikā vuttā. Khandhādhiṭṭhānāva [M 0.0196] desanā katā. Khandhānañhi etā ajimhatādikā, no puggalassāti. Evaṃ sabbehipi imehi padehi purimanayena [V 0.0196] tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ, pacchimanayena viññāṇakkhandhassāti arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ nikkilesatāya ujutākārova kathitoti veditabbo.

By the power of the defilements, the state of such a crooked person is called deceitfulness (jimhatā), crookedness (vaṅkatā), and crookedness (kuṭilatā). By way of their opposite, non-deceitfulness and so on are spoken of. The teaching is given with the aggregates as its very basis. For these qualities, such as non-deceitfulness, belong to the aggregates, not to the person. Thus, it should be understood that by all these terms, according to the former method for the three aggregates and the latter method for the consciousness aggregate, only the mode of straightness of immaterial phenomena, due to their being without defilements, is described.

Idāni yvāyaṃ yevāpanāti appanāvāro vutto, tena dhammuddesavāre dassitānaṃ ‘yevāpanakānaṃ’yeva saṅkhepato niddeso kathito hotīti.

Now, this section on application (appanāvāra), the yevāpanā, has been spoken of. By it, a brief exposition of the very yevāpanaka dhammas shown in the section on the enumeration of the Dhamma is said to be given.

Niddesavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the section of exposition is concluded.

Ettāvatā pucchā samayaniddeso dhammuddeso appanāti uddesavāre catūhi paricchedehi, pucchā samayaniddeso dhammuddeso appanāti niddesavāre catūhi paricchedehīti aṭṭhaparicchedapaṭimaṇḍito dhammavavatthānavāro niṭṭhitova hoti.

By this much—with the four divisions in the summary section, namely: question, explanation of the occasion, enumeration of the Dhamma, and application; and with the four divisions in the exposition section, namely: question, explanation of the occasion, exposition of the Dhamma, and application—the section on the determination of phenomena, adorned with eight divisions, is indeed concluded.

Koṭṭhāsavāro

The Section on Divisions

58-120. Idāni tasmiṃ kho pana samaye cattāro khandhā hontīti saṅgahavāro āraddho. So uddesaniddesapaṭiniddesānaṃ vasena tividho hoti. Tattha ‘tasmiṃ kho pana samaye cattāro khandhā’ti evamādiko uddeso. Katame tasmiṃ samaye cattāro khandhā’tiādiko niddeso. Katamo tasmiṃ samaye vedanākkhandhotiādiko paṭiniddesoti veditabbo.

Now, the section on inclusion, beginning with 'At that time, there are four aggregates,' is commenced. It is threefold by way of summary, exposition, and counter-exposition. Therein, that which begins with 'At that time, there are four aggregates' is the summary. That which begins with 'Which four aggregates are there at that time?' is the exposition. That which begins with 'Which is the aggregate of feeling at that time?' should be understood as the counter-exposition.

Tattha uddesavāre cattāro khandhātiādayo tevīsati koṭṭhāsā honti. Tesaṃ evamattho veditabbo – yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ paṭhamaṃ mahākusalacittaṃ uppajjati, ye tasmiṃ samaye cittaṅgavasena uppannā, ṭhapetvā yevāpanake, pāḷiāruḷhā atirekapaṇṇāsadhammā, te sabbepi saṅgayhamānā rāsaṭṭhena cattārova khandhā honti[P 0.0153]. Heṭṭhā vuttena āyatanaṭṭhena dve āyatanāni honti. Sabhāvaṭṭhena suññataṭṭhena nissattaṭṭhena dveva dhātuyo honti. Paccayasaṅkhātena āhāraṭṭhena tayovettha dhammā āhārā honti. Avasesā no āhārā.

Therein, in the summary section, there are twenty-three divisions, beginning with 'the four aggregates.' Their meaning should be understood thus: At the time when the first great wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense sphere arises, there are over fifty phenomena included in the Pāḷi that have arisen at that time as constituents of consciousness, setting aside the yevāpanaka dhammas. All of them, when being grouped together, become just four aggregates in the sense of a heap. By the meaning of 'base' spoken of below, there are two bases. In the sense of intrinsic nature, in the sense of emptiness, and in the sense of being non-sentient, there are just two elements. In the sense of nutriment, which is reckoned as a condition, just three phenomena here are nutriments. The remaining are not nutriments.

‘Kiṃ [M 0.0197] panete aññamaññaṃ vā taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpassa vā paccayā na hontī’ti? ‘No na honti. Ime pana tathā ca honti, aññathā cāti samānepi paccayatte atirekapaccayā honti, tasmā [V 0.0197] āhārāti vuttā. Kathaṃ? Etesu hi phassāhāro, yesaṃ dhammānaṃ avasesā cittacetasikā paccayā honti, tesañca paccayo hoti, tisso ca vedanā āharati. Manosañcetanāhāro tesañca paccayo hoti tayo ca bhave āharati. Viññāṇāhāro tesañca paccayo hoti paṭisandhināmarūpañca āharatī’ti. ‘Nanu ca so vipākova idaṃ pana kusalaviññāṇa’nti? ‘Kiñcāpi kusalaviññāṇaṃ, taṃsarikkhatāya pana viññāṇāhāro’tveva vuttaṃ. Upatthambhakaṭṭhena vā ime tayo āhārāti vuttā. Ime hi sampayuttadhammānaṃ, kabaḷīkārāhāro viya rūpakāyassa, upatthambhakapaccayā honti. Teneva vuttaṃ – “arūpino āhārā sampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ āhārapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.15).

'But are these not conditions for one another or for the materiality produced by them?' 'It is not that they are not. But these are so in one way, and also in another way. Thus, even though their state as a condition is the same, they are extraordinary conditions; therefore, they are called nutriments. How? Indeed, among these, the nutriment of contact is a condition for those remaining phenomena, and it also brings forth the three feelings. The nutriment of mental volition is a condition for them, and it also brings forth the three kinds of existence. The nutriment of consciousness is a condition for them, and it also brings forth rebirth-linking name-and-form.' 'Is it not so that that is resultant, whereas this is wholesome consciousness?' 'Although it is wholesome consciousness, it is called consciousness-nutriment because of its similarity to that.' Or, these three are called nutriments in the sense of being a support. For these are supporting conditions for associated phenomena, just as physical nutriment is for the physical body. For that very reason it is said: “The immaterial nutriments are a condition for associated phenomena and for the materiality co-arisen with them by way of nutriment-condition.”

Aparo nayo – ajjhattikasantatiyā visesapaccayattā kabaḷīkārāhāro ca ime ca tayo dhammā āhārāti vuttā. Visesapaccayo hi kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhānaṃ sattānaṃ rūpakāyassa kabaḷīkāro āhāro; nāmakāye vedanāya phasso, viññāṇassa manosañcetanā, nāmarūpassa viññāṇaṃ. Yathāha –

Another method: Because of being a special condition for the internal continuity, both physical nutriment and these three phenomena are called nutriments. Indeed, physical nutriment is a special condition for the physical body of beings who consume physical nutriment; in the mental body, contact is for feeling, mental volition is for consciousness, and consciousness is for name-and-form. As it was said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayaṃ kāyo āhāraṭṭhitiko, āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati, anāhāro no tiṭṭhati” (saṃ. ni. 5.183). Tathā phassapaccayā vedanā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti (saṃ. ni. 2.1).

“Just as, monks, this body is sustained by nutriment, it stands depending on nutriment; without nutriment, it does not stand.” Similarly: from contact as condition, feeling; from formations as condition, consciousness; from consciousness as condition, name-and-form.

Adhipatiyaṭṭhena pana aṭṭheva dhammā indriyāni honti, na avasesā. Tena vuttaṃ – aṭṭhindriyāni hontīti. Upanijjhāyanaṭṭhena pañceva dhammā jhānaṅgāni honti. Tena vuttaṃ – pañcaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hotīti.

But in the sense of dominance, just eight phenomena are faculties, not the remaining ones. Therefore it is said: 'There are eight faculties.' In the sense of closely contemplating, just five phenomena are absorption factors. Therefore it is said: 'The absorption is five-factored.'

Niyyānaṭṭhena [P 0.0154] ca hetvaṭṭhena ca pañceva dhammā maggaṅgāni honti. Tena vuttaṃ – pañcaṅgiko maggo hotīti. Kiñcāpi hi aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyamaggo, lokiyacitte [M 0.0198] pana ekakkhaṇe tisso viratiyo na labbhanti, tasmā pañcaṅgikoti vutto. ‘Nanu ca “yathāgatamaggoti kho, bhikkhu, ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.245) imasmiṃ sutte ‘yatheva lokuttaramaggo aṭṭhaṅgiko, pubbabhāgavipassanāmaggopi tatheva aṭṭhaṅgiko’ti yathāgatavacanena imassatthassa dīpitattā, lokiyamaggenāpi aṭṭhaṅgikena bhavitabbanti? Na bhavitabbaṃ[V 0.0198]. Ayañhi suttantikadesanā nāma pariyāyadesanā. Tenāha – “pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.431). Ayaṃ pana nippariyāyadesanā. Lokiyacittasmiñhi tisso viratiyo ekakkhaṇe na labbhanti, tasmā ‘pañcaṅgiko’va vuttoti.

Both in the sense of leading out and in the sense of being a cause, just five phenomena are path factors. Therefore it is said: 'The path is five-factored.' For although the Noble Path is eight-factored, in a mundane consciousness the three abstinences are not obtained in a single moment; therefore, it is called 'five-factored.' 'Is it not so that in this sutta, “Indeed, monk, ‘the path as it has come’ is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path,” since it is shown by the word ‘yathāgata’ that just as the supramundane path is eight-factored, so too the preliminary insight path is eight-factored, should not the mundane path also be eight-factored?' It should not be. For this Suttanta teaching is a teaching with an indirect meaning. Therefore, He said: “But previously, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are already well-purified.” This, however, is a teaching with a direct meaning. For in a mundane consciousness, the three abstinences are not obtained in a single moment; therefore, it is said to be 'five-factored' only.

Akampiyaṭṭhena pana satteva dhammā balāni honti. Mūlaṭṭhena tayova dhammā hetū. Phusanaṭṭhena ekova dhammo phasso. Vedayitaṭṭhena ekova dhammo vedanā. Sañjānanaṭṭhena ekova dhammo saññā. Cetayanaṭṭhena ekova dhammo cetanā. Cittavicittaṭṭhena ekova dhammo cittaṃ. Rāsaṭṭhena ceva vedayitaṭṭhena ca ekova dhammo vedanākkhandho. Rāsaṭṭhena ca sañjānanaṭṭhena ca ekova dhammo saññākkhandho. Rāsaṭṭhena ca abhisaṅkharaṇaṭṭhena ca ekova dhammo saṅkhārakkhandho. Rāsaṭṭhena ca cittavicittaṭṭhena ca ekova dhammo viññāṇakkhandho. Vijānanaṭṭhena ceva heṭṭhā vuttaāyatanaṭṭhena ca ekameva manāyatanaṃ. Vijānanaṭṭhena ca adhipatiyaṭṭhena ca ekameva manindriyaṃ. Vijānanaṭṭhena ca sabhāvasuññatanissattaṭṭhena ca ekova dhammo manoviññāṇadhātu nāma hoti, na avasesā. Ṭhapetvā pana cittaṃ, yathāvuttena atthena avasesā sabbepi dhammā ekaṃ dhammāyatanameva, ekā ca dhammadhātuyeva hotīti.

Furthermore, in the sense of being unshakable, only seven phenomena are powers. In the sense of being a root, only three phenomena are roots. In the sense of touching, only one phenomenon is contact. In the sense of experiencing, only one phenomenon is feeling. In the sense of perceiving, only one phenomenon is perception. In the sense of intending, only one phenomenon is volition. In the sense of being variegated, only one phenomenon is mind. Both in the sense of being an aggregate and in the sense of experiencing, only one phenomenon is the feeling-aggregate. Both in the sense of being an aggregate and in the sense of perceiving, only one phenomenon is the perception-aggregate. Both in the sense of being an aggregate and in the sense of constructing, only one phenomenon is the formations-aggregate. Both in the sense of being an aggregate and in the sense of being variegated, only one phenomenon is the consciousness-aggregate. Both in the sense of cognizing and in the sense of the base as stated previously, there is only one mind-base. Both in the sense of cognizing and in the sense of dominance, there is only one mind-faculty. Both in the sense of cognizing, and in the sense of its own nature, of being void, and of being without a living being, only one phenomenon is called the mind-consciousness-element, not the remaining ones. However, excluding the mind, by the meaning as stated, all the remaining phenomena are only one mind-object-base and only one mind-object-element.

Ye vā pana tasmiṃ samayeti iminā pana appanāvārena idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttā yevāpanakāva saṅgahitā. Yathā ca idha evaṃ sabbattha[P 0.0155]. Ito parañhi ettakampi na vicārayissāma. Niddesapaṭiniddesavāresu heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabboti.

Furthermore, by this section on application, `Ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye`, here also in this section on inclusion, only the `yevāpanaka` factors stated previously are included. And as it is here, so it is everywhere. Indeed, from now on, we will not investigate even this much. In the sections on exposition and counter-exposition, the meaning should be understood only by the method stated previously.

Saṅgahavāro niṭṭhito.

The Section on Inclusion is concluded.

Koṭṭhāsavārotipi etasseva nāmaṃ.

The Section on Divisions is also a name for this very section.

Suññatavāro

The Section on Voidness

121-145. Idāni [M 0.0199] tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā hontīti suññatavāro āraddho. So [V 0.0199] uddesaniddesavasena dvidhā vavatthito. Tattha uddesavāre ‘dhammā hontī’ti iminā saddhiṃ catuvīsati koṭṭhāsā honti. Sabbakoṭṭhāsesu ca ‘cattāro dve tayo’ti gaṇanaparicchedo na vutto. Kasmā? Saṅgahavāre paricchinnattā. Tattha paricchinnadhammāyeva hi idhāpi vuttā. Na hettha satto vā bhāvo vā attā vā upalabbhati. Dhammāva ete dhammamattā asārā apariṇāyakāti imissā suññatāya dīpanatthaṃ vuttā. Tasmā evamettha attho veditabbo – yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ paṭhamaṃ mahākusalacittaṃ uppajjati, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṅgavasena uppannā atirekapaṇṇāsadhammā sabhāvaṭṭhena dhammā eva honti. Na añño koci satto vā bhāvo vā poso vā puggalo vā hotīti. Tathā rāsaṭṭhena khandhāva hontīti. Evaṃ purimanayeneva sabbapadesu atthayojanā veditabbā. Yasmā pana jhānato aññaṃ jhānaṅgaṃ, maggato vā aññaṃ maggaṅgaṃ natthi, tasmā idha ‘jhānaṃ hoti, maggo hoti’ icceva vuttaṃ. Upanijjhāyanaṭṭhena hi jhānameva hetvaṭṭhena maggova hoti. Na añño koci satto vā bhāvo vāti. Evaṃ sabbapadesu atthayojanā kātabbā. Niddesavāro uttānatthoyevāti.

Now, the Section on Voidness, beginning with 'At that time, phenomena exist,' is commenced. It is established in two ways: by way of outline and by way of exposition. Therein, in the outline section, along with 'phenomena exist,' there are twenty-four divisions. And in all divisions, the numerical determination as 'four, two, three' is not stated. Why? Because they have been determined in the Section on Inclusion. Indeed, only the phenomena determined there are stated here also. Herein, no being, or entity, or self is found. These are only phenomena, mere phenomena, without essence, without a leader; they are stated in order to explain this voidness. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: At the time when the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere arises, at that time, the more than fifty phenomena that arise as constituents of consciousness are, in the sense of their own nature, only phenomena. There is no other being, or entity, or man, or person. Similarly, in the sense of being an aggregate, they are only aggregates. Thus, the application of the meaning should be understood in all sections according to the previous method. Furthermore, because there is no jhāna-factor other than jhāna, or no path-factor other than the path, therefore, here it is stated only as 'jhāna exists, the path exists.' Indeed, in the sense of contemplating, it is only jhāna; in the sense of being a cause, it is only the path. There is no other being or entity. Thus, the application of the meaning should be made in all sections. The exposition section has an obvious meaning.

Suññatavāro niṭṭhito.

The Section on Voidness is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca tīhi mahāvārehi maṇḍetvā niddiṭṭhassa

And thus is concluded the exposition of that which was expounded, having been adorned with the three great sections:

Paṭhamacittassa atthavaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Meaning of the First Consciousness.

Dutiyacittaṃ

The Second Consciousness

146. Idāni dutiyacittādīni dassetuṃ puna “katame dhammā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tesu sabbesupi paṭhamacitte vuttanayeneva [P 0.0156] tayo tayo mahāvārā veditabbā. Na kevalañca mahāvārā eva, paṭhamacitte vuttasadisānaṃ sabbapadānaṃ atthopi vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ito parampi apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃyeva karissāma. Imasmiṃ tāva dutiyacittaniddese sasaṅkhārenāti idameva apubbaṃ. Tassattho – saha saṅkhārenāti sasaṅkhāro. Tena sasaṅkhārena [M 0.0200] sappayogena saupāyena paccayagaṇenāti attho. Yena hi ārammaṇādinā paccayagaṇena paṭhamaṃ mahācittaṃ uppajjati, teneva sappayogena saupāyena idaṃ uppajjati.

Now, to show the second consciousness and so on, the passage beginning 'Which are the states?' is again undertaken. In all of these, by the very same method as stated in the first consciousness, three great sections each should be understood. And not only the great sections, but the meaning of all terms similar to those stated in the first consciousness should also be understood by the same stated method. Hereafter, we will provide only the explanation of new terms. In this exposition of the second consciousness, this very term 'sasaṅkhārena' is new. Its meaning is: 'sasaṅkhāra' means 'with prompting.' The meaning is: by that group of conditions which is with prompting, with effort, with means. For, by whichever group of conditions—such as the object, etc.—the first great consciousness arises, by that very same group of conditions which is with effort and with means, this consciousness arises.

Tassevaṃ [V 0.0200] uppatti veditabbā – idhekacco bhikkhu vihārapaccante vasamāno cetiyaṅgaṇasammajjanavelāya vā therupaṭṭhānavelāya vā sampattāya, dhammasavanadivase vā sampatte ‘mayhaṃ gantvā paccāgacchato atidūraṃ bhavissati, na gamissāmī’ti cintetvā puna cinteti – ‘bhikkhussa nāma cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ vā therupaṭṭhānaṃ vā dhammasavanaṃ vā agantuṃ asāruppaṃ, gamissāmī’ti gacchati. Tassevaṃ attano payogena vā, parena vā vattādīnaṃ akaraṇe ca ādīnavaṃ karaṇe ca ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā ovadiyamānassa, niggahavaseneva vā ‘ehi, idaṃ karohī’ti kāriyamānassa uppannaṃ kusalacittaṃ sasaṅkhārena paccayagaṇena uppannaṃ nāma hotīti.

Its arising should be understood thus: Here, a certain monk, dwelling on the outskirts of a monastery, when the time for sweeping the cetiya courtyard or for attending upon an elder arrives, or when the day for hearing the Dhamma arrives, thinks, 'For me, going and returning will be very far; I will not go.' Having thought thus, he thinks again: 'For one called a monk, it is unseemly not to go to the cetiya courtyard, or to attend upon an elder, or to hear the Dhamma. I shall go,' and so he goes. Thus, the wholesome consciousness that has arisen in him through his own effort; or in one who is being admonished by another showing the danger in not performing duties and the benefit in performing them; or in one who is being made to do it by way of coercion with, 'Come, do this!'—such a consciousness is called 'arisen with prompting through a collection of conditions.'

Dutiyacittaṃ.

End of the Second Consciousness.

Tatiyacittaṃ

The Third Consciousness

147-148. Tatiye ñāṇena vippayuttanti ñāṇavippayuttaṃ. Idampi hi ārammaṇe haṭṭhapahaṭṭhaṃ hoti paricchindakañāṇaṃ panettha na hoti. Tasmā idaṃ daharakumārakānaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā ‘ayaṃ thero mayha’nti vandanakāle, teneva nayena cetiyavandanadhammasavanakālādīsu ca uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ panettha sattasu ṭhānesu paññā parihāyati. Sesaṃ pākatikamevāti.

In the third consciousness, 'disassociated from knowledge' means it is not associated with knowledge. For this consciousness is also joyful and elated regarding the object, yet discerning knowledge is not present in it. Therefore, it should be understood that this consciousness arises in young boys who, upon seeing a monk, pay homage thinking, 'This elder is mine,' and by that same method, it also arises at times of paying homage to a cetiya, hearing the Dhamma, and so on. In the Pāḷi, wisdom is deficient herein in seven instances. The remainder is as in the natural order.

Tatiyacittaṃ.

End of the Third Consciousness.

Catutthacittaṃ

The Fourth Consciousness

149. Catutthacittepi eseva nayo. Idaṃ pana sasaṅkhārenāti vacanato yadā mātāpitaro daharakumārake sīse gahetvā cetiyādīni vandāpenti te ca anatthikā samānāpi haṭṭhapahaṭṭhāva vandanti. Evarūpe kāle labbhatīti veditabbaṃ.

149. For the fourth consciousness as well, this is the method. This, however, is 'with prompting.' It should be understood that it is obtained at such a time when parents, taking young children by the head, have them pay homage to cetiyas and so on; and though they are unwilling, they pay homage joyfully and elatedly.

Catutthacittaṃ.

End of the Fourth Consciousness.

Pañcamacittaṃ

The Fifth Consciousness

150. Pañcame [M 0.0201][V 0.0201] upekkhāsahagatanti upekkhāvedanāya sampayuttaṃ[P 0.0157]. Idañhi ārammaṇe majjhattaṃ hoti. Paricchindakañāṇaṃ panettha hotiyeva. Pāḷiyaṃ panettha jhānacatukke upekkhā hotīti indriyaṭṭhake upekkhindriyaṃ hotīti vatvā sabbesampi vedanādipadānaṃ niddese sātāsātasukhadukkhapaṭikkhepavasena desanaṃ katvā adukkhamasukhavedanā kathitā. Tassā majjhattalakkhaṇe indattakaraṇavasena upekkhindriyabhāvo veditabbo. Padapaṭipāṭiyā ca ekasmiṃ ṭhāne pīti parihīnā. Tasmā cittaṅgavasena pāḷiāruḷhā pañcapaṇṇāseva dhammā honti. Tesaṃ vasena sabbakoṭṭhāsesu sabbavāresu ca vinicchayo veditabbo.

150. In the fifth consciousness, 'accompanied by equanimity' means it is associated with the feeling of equanimity. Indeed, this consciousness is neutral towards its object, and discerning knowledge is certainly present in it. In the Pāḷi, having stated in the tetrad of jhānas, 'there is equanimity,' and in the octad of faculties, 'there is the faculty of equanimity,' and having delivered the teaching in the explanation of all terms beginning with 'feeling' by way of rejecting the pleasant and unpleasant, pleasure and pain, the neither-painful-nor-pleasurable feeling is taught. Its state as the faculty of equanimity should be understood by way of its exercising sovereignty in its characteristic of neutrality. And, in the sequence of terms, in one place joy is absent. Therefore, by way of the mental factors mentioned in the Pāḷi, there are only fifty-five states. Based on these, the determination should be understood in all sections and in all recitations.

Pañcamacittaṃ.

End of the Fifth Consciousness.

Chaṭṭhacittādi

The Sixth Consciousness and so forth

156-9. Chaṭṭhasattamaaṭṭhamāni dutiyatatiyacatutthesu vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Kevalañhi imesu vedanāparivattanañceva pītiparihānañca hoti. Sesaṃ saddhiṃ uppattinayena tādisameva. Karuṇāmuditā parikammakālepi hi imesaṃ uppatti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuññātā eva. Imāni aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacittāni nāma.

The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses should be understood by the very method explained for the second, third, and fourth. In these, there is merely a change of feeling and a diminution of joy. The rest, together with the mode of arising, is just the same. Indeed, the arising of these even at the time of the preliminary work for compassion and sympathetic joy is permitted in the Great Commentary. These eight are called wholesome consciousnesses of the sense-sphere.

Puññakiriyavatthādikathā

Discourse on the Bases of Meritorious Action and so forth

Tāni sabbānipi dasahi puññakiriyavatthūhi dīpetabbāni. Kathaṃ? Dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu, sīlamayaṃ… bhāvanāmayaṃ… apacitisahagataṃ… veyyāvaccasahagataṃ… pattānuppadānaṃ… abbhanumodanaṃ… desanāmayaṃ… savanamayaṃ… diṭṭhijukammaṃ puññakiriyavatthūti imāni dasa puññakiriyavatthūni nāma. Tattha dānameva dānamayaṃ. Puññakiriyā ca sā tesaṃ tesaṃ ānisaṃsānaṃ vatthu cāti puññakiriyavatthu. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

All of those consciousnesses should be explained by way of the ten bases of meritorious action. How so? The basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, that consisting of virtue, that consisting of mental development, that accompanied by reverence, that accompanied by service, the sharing of merit, rejoicing in merit, teaching the Dhamma, listening to the Dhamma, and the straightening of one's view—these are called the ten bases of meritorious action. Therein, giving itself is that 'consisting of giving.' And because it is a meritorious action and also a basis for various benefits, it is called a 'basis of meritorious action.' For the remaining ones also, this is the very same method.

Tattha [V 0.0202] cīvarādīsu catūsu paccayesu, rūpādīsu vā chasu ārammaṇesu, annādīsu vā dasasu dānavatthūsu, taṃ taṃ dentassa tesaṃ tesaṃ uppādanato paṭṭhāya [M 0.0202] pubbabhāge, pariccāgakāle, pacchā somanassacittena anussaraṇakāle cāti tīsu kālesu pavattā cetanā ‘dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma.

Therein, the volition that occurs at three times—in the prior phase, beginning from the production of the various items to be given, whether among the four requisites such as robes, or the six sense-objects such as forms, or the ten gift-objects such as food; at the time of relinquishing; and afterwards, at the time of recollecting with a mind accompanied by gladness—this volition is called the 'basis of meritorious action consisting of giving'.

Pañcasīlaṃ aṭṭhasīlaṃ dasasīlaṃ samādiyantassa, ‘pabbajissāmī’ti vihāraṃ gacchantassa, pabbajantassa, ‘manorathaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā pabbajito vata’mhi, ‘sādhu sādhū’ti āvajjentassa, pātimokkhaṃ saṃvarantassa, cīvarādayo paccaye paccavekkhantassa, āpāthagatesu rūpādīsu cakkhudvārādīni saṃvarantassa[P 0.0158], ājīvaṃ sodhentassa ca pavattā cetanā ‘sīlamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma.

The volition that occurs in one who is undertaking the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts; in one who is going to the monastery thinking, 'I will go forth'; in one who is going forth; in one who reflects, 'Having brought my aspiration to its culmination, I have indeed gone forth! Excellent, excellent!'; in one who is restraining oneself according to the Pātimokkha; in one who is reflecting on the requisites such as robes; in one who is restraining the sense-doors, beginning with the eye-door, in regard to sense-objects, beginning with forms, that have come into range; and in one who is purifying one's livelihood—this is called the 'basis of meritorious action consisting of virtue'.

Paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttena vipassanāmaggena cakkhuṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato bhāventassa…pe… manaṃ… rūpe…pe… dhamme… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ,… cakkhusamphassaṃ…pe… manosamphassaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ, …pe… rūpasaññaṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato bhāventassa pavattā cetanā, aṭṭhatiṃsāya vā ārammaṇesu appanaṃ appattā sabbāpi cetanā ‘bhāvanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma.

The volition that occurs in one who, by means of the path of insight taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, develops the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self... (and so on for) ...the mind... forms... phenomena... eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness... feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of mind-contact... perception of form... up to... aging-and-death as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; or, any volition whatsoever concerning the thirty-eight objects that has not yet reached absorption—this is called the 'basis of meritorious action consisting of development'.

Mahallakaṃ pana disvā paccuggamanapattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇaabhivādanamaggasampadānādivasena ‘apacitisahagataṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, upon seeing a senior person, actions such as going out to meet them, taking their bowl and robe, paying homage, and making way for them, should be understood as 'that accompanied by reverence'.

Vuḍḍhatarānaṃ vattappaṭipattikaraṇavasena gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā pattaṃ gahetvā gāme bhikkhaṃ samādapetvā upasaṃharaṇavasena, ‘gaccha bhikkhūnaṃ pattaṃ āharā’ti sutvā vegena gantvā pattāharaṇādivasena ca kāyaveyyāvaṭikakāle ‘veyyāvaccasahagataṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

By way of performing duties and observances for one's seniors; or upon seeing a monk who has entered a village for alms-food, by way of taking his bowl, having him receive alms in the village, and then bringing it to him; or, having heard the instruction, 'Go, bring the monks' bowls,' by way of going quickly and bringing the bowls, and so on—at the time of such bodily service, it should be known as 'that accompanied by service'.

Dānaṃ datvā gandhādīhi pūjaṃ katvā ‘asukassa nāma patti hotū’ti vā, ‘sabbasattānaṃ hotū’ti vā pattiṃ dadato ‘pattānuppadānaṃ’ veditabbaṃ. Kiṃ panevaṃ pattiṃ dadato puññakkhayo hotīti? Na hoti. Yathā pana ekaṃ dīpaṃ jāletvā tato dīpasahassaṃ jālentassa paṭhamadīpo khīṇoti [V 0.0203] na vattabbo; purimālokena pana saddhiṃ pacchimāloko ekato hutvā atimahā hoti. Evameva pattiṃ dadato parihāni nāma natthi. Vuḍḍhiyeva pana hotīti veditabbo.

Having given a gift or having made an offering with fragrances and so on, for one who gives a share of the merit, thinking, 'May the merit be for so-and-so,' or, 'May it be for all beings,' this should be known as 'the sharing of merit.' But for one who shares merit in this way, is there a depletion of merit? There is not. Just as when one lights a lamp and from it lights a thousand lamps, it cannot be said that the first lamp is exhausted; rather, the later light, together with the former light, becomes one and is exceedingly great. In the very same way, for one who shares merit, there is no such thing as diminution. It should be known that there is, in fact, only increase.

Parehi [M 0.0203] dinnāya pattiyā vā aññāya vā puññakiriyāya ‘sādhu sādhū’ti anumodanavasena ‘abbhanumodanaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

By way of rejoicing with 'Good, good!' in the share of merit given by others, or in any other meritorious action performed by them, this should be known as 'rejoicing in merit'.

Eko ‘evaṃ maṃ dhammakathikoti maṃ jānissantī’ti icchāya ṭhatvā lābhagaruko hutvā deseti, taṃ na mahapphalaṃ. Eko attano paguṇaṃ dhammaṃ apaccāsīsamāno vimuttāyatanasīsena paresaṃ deseti, idaṃ ‘desanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma.

One person, established in the desire, 'Thus they will know me as a preacher of the Dhamma,' teaches while being reverential towards gain; that is not of great fruit. Another person, not expecting gain, teaches to others the Dhamma that they have well-mastered, with the sphere of liberation as the primary aim. This is called the 'basis of meritorious action consisting of teaching'.

Eko suṇanto ‘iti maṃ saddhoti jānissantī’ti suṇāti, taṃ na mahapphalaṃ. Eko ‘evaṃ me mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī’ti hitapharaṇena muducittena dhammaṃ suṇāti, idaṃ ‘savanamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma.

A certain person, while listening, listens thinking, 'Thus they will know me as one with faith'; that is not of great fruit. A certain person listens to the Dhamma with a beneficial disposition and a gentle mind, thinking, 'Thus it will be of great fruit for me'; this is called 'the basis of meritorious action consisting of listening'.

Diṭṭhiṃ [P 0.0159] ujuṃ karontassa ‘diṭṭhijukammaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma. Dīghabhāṇakā panāhu – ‘diṭṭhijukammaṃ sabbesaṃ niyamalakkhaṇaṃ, yaṃkiñci puññaṃ karontassa hi diṭṭhiyā ujukabhāveneva mahapphalaṃ hotī’ti.

For one who makes their view straight, it is called 'the basis of meritorious action of straightening the view.' But the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya say: 'The straightening of the view is the determining characteristic of all bases of meritorious action; for, whatever merit one performs, it is of great fruit precisely because of the straightness of one's view.'

Etesu pana puññakiriyavatthūsu dānamayaṃ tāva ‘dānaṃ dassāmī’ti cintentassa uppajjati, dānaṃ dadato uppajjati, ‘dinnaṃ me’ti paccavekkhantassa uppajjati. Evaṃ pubbacetanaṃ muñcanacetanaṃ aparacetananti tissopi cetanā ekato katvā ‘dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma hoti. Sīlamayampi ‘sīlaṃ pūressāmī’ti cintentassa uppajjati, sīlapūraṇakāle uppajjati, ‘pūritaṃ me’ti paccavekkhantassa uppajjati. Tā sabbāpi ekato katvā ‘sīlamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma hoti…pe… diṭṭhijukammampi ‘diṭṭhiṃ ujukaṃ karissāmī’ti cintentassa uppajjati, diṭṭhiṃ ujuṃ karontassa uppajjati, ‘diṭṭhi me ujukā katā’ti paccavekkhantassa uppajjati. Tā sabbāpi ekato katvā ‘diṭṭhijukammaṃ puññakiriyavatthu’ nāma hoti.

Now, among these bases of meritorious action, that consisting of giving arises, first, for one who thinks, 'I will give a gift'; it arises for one who is giving a gift; and it arises for one who reflects, 'A gift has been given by me.' Thus, the prior volition, the volition of relinquishing, and the subsequent volition—these three volitions, having been taken together, are called 'the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving.' That consisting of virtue also arises for one who thinks, 'I will fulfill virtue'; it arises at the time of fulfilling virtue; and it arises for one who reflects, 'Virtue has been fulfilled by me.' All those volitions, having been taken together, are called 'the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtue.' … The straightening of the view also arises for one who thinks, 'I will make my view straight'; it arises for one who is making their view straight; and it arises for one who reflects, 'My view has been made straight by me.' All those volitions, having been taken together, are called 'the basis of meritorious action of straightening the view.'

Sutte [V 0.0204] pana tīṇiyeva puññakiriyavatthūni āgatāni. Tesu itaresampi saṅgaho veditabbo. Apacitiveyyāvaccāni hi sīlamaye saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Pattānuppadānaabbhanumodanāni dānamaye. Desanāsavanadiṭṭhijukammāni bhāvanāmaye. Ye pana ‘diṭṭhijukammaṃ sabbesaṃ niyamalakkhaṇa’nti vadanti tesaṃ taṃ tīsupi saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Evametāni saṅkhepato tīṇi hutvā vitthārato dasa honti.

In the Suttas, however, only three bases of meritorious action have come down. The inclusion of the others in these should be understood. For reverence and service are included in that consisting of virtue. The giving of a share of merit and rejoicing in merit are included in that consisting of giving. Teaching, listening, and straightening the view are included in that consisting of mental development. But for those who say, 'The straightening of the view is the determining characteristic of all,' for them it is included in all three. Thus, these are three in brief, and become ten in detail.

Tesu [M 0.0204] ‘dānaṃ dassāmī’ti cintento aṭṭhannaṃ kāmāvacarakusalacittānaṃ aññatareneva cinteti; dadamānopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena deti; ‘dānaṃ me dinna’nti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati. ‘Sīlaṃ pūressāmī’ti cintentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena cinteti; sīlaṃ pūrentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena pūreti, ‘sīlaṃ me pūrita’nti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati. ‘Bhāvanaṃ bhāvessāmī’ti cintentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena cinteti; bhāventopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena bhāveti; ‘bhāvanā me bhāvitā’ti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati.

Among these, when one thinks, 'I will give a gift,' one thinks with one of the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses; when giving, one also gives with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, 'A gift has been given by me,' one also reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, 'I will fulfill virtue,' one also thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when fulfilling virtue, one also fulfills it with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, 'Virtue has been fulfilled by me,' one also reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, 'I will develop mental cultivation,' one also thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when developing it, one also develops it with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, 'Mental cultivation has been developed by me,' one also reflects with one of those same consciousnesses.

‘Jeṭṭhāpacitikammaṃ [P 0.0160] karissāmī’ti cintentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena cinteti, karontopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena karoti, ‘kataṃ me’ti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati. ‘Kāyaveyyāvaṭikakammaṃ karissāmī’ti cintentopi, karontopi, ‘kataṃ me’ti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati. ‘Pattiṃ dassāmī’ti cintentopi, dadantopi, ‘dinnaṃ me’ti paccavekkhantopi, ‘pattiṃ vā sesakusalaṃ vā anumodissāmī’ti cintentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena cinteti; anumodantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena anumodati, ‘anumoditaṃ me’ti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati. ‘Dhammaṃ desessāmī’ti cintentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena cinteti, desentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena deseti, ‘desito me’ti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati. ‘Dhammaṃ sossāmī’ti cintentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena cinteti, suṇantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena suṇāti, ‘suto me’ti paccavekkhantopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena paccavekkhati. ‘Diṭṭhiṃ ujukaṃ karissāmī’ti cintentopi tesaṃyeva aññatarena cinteti, ujuṃ karonto pana catunnaṃ ñāṇasampayuttānaṃ aññatarena karoti, ‘diṭṭhi me ujukā katā’ti paccavekkhanto aṭṭhannaṃ aññatarena paccavekkhati.

When one thinks, ‘I will perform acts of reverence towards elders,’ one thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when performing them, one does so with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, ‘It has been done by me,’ one reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, ‘I will perform acts of service,’ one thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when performing them, one does so with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, ‘It has been done by me,’ one reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, ‘I will give a share of merit,’ one thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when giving, one gives with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, ‘It has been given by me,’ one reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, ‘I will rejoice in the share of merit or other wholesome deeds,’ one thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when rejoicing, one rejoices with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, ‘I have rejoiced,’ one reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, ‘I will teach the Dhamma,’ one thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when teaching, one teaches with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, ‘It has been taught by me,’ one reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, ‘I will listen to the Dhamma,’ one thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; when listening, one listens with one of those same consciousnesses; when reflecting, ‘It has been heard by me,’ one reflects with one of those same consciousnesses. When one thinks, ‘I will make my view straight,’ one thinks with one of those same consciousnesses; but when making it straight, one does so with one of the four great wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge; when reflecting, ‘My view has been made straight by me,’ one reflects with one of the eight great wholesome consciousnesses.

Imasmiṃ [V 0.0205] ṭhāne cattāri anantāni nāma gahitāni. Cattāri hi anantāni – ākāso ananto, cakkavāḷāni anantāni, sattanikāyo ananto, buddhaññāṇaṃ [M 0.0205] anantaṃ. Ākāsassa hi puratthimāya disāya vā pacchimuttaradakkhiṇāsu vā ettakāni vā yojanasatāni ettakāni vā yojanasahassānīti paricchedo natthi. Sinerumattampi ayokūṭaṃ pathaviṃ dvidhā katvā heṭṭhā khittaṃ bhassetheva, no patiṭṭhaṃ labhetha, evaṃ ākāsaṃ anantaṃ nāma.

In this place, four things called ‘the infinites’ are taken. Indeed, there are four infinites: space is infinite, the world-systems are infinite, the host of beings is infinite, and the Buddha’s knowledge is infinite. For, regarding space, whether in the eastern direction or in the western, northern, and southern directions, there is no limit, such as ‘so many hundreds of yojanas’ or ‘so many thousands of yojanas.’ Even if an iron ball the size of Sineru, having split the earth in two, were thrown downwards, it would just keep falling and would not find a resting place. Thus, space is called infinite.

Cakkavāḷānampi satehi vā sahassehi vā paricchedo natthi. Sacepi hi akaniṭṭhabhavane nibbattā, daḷhathāmadhanuggahassa lahukena sarena tiriyaṃ tālacchāyaṃ atikkamanamattena kālena cakkavāḷasatasahassaṃ atikkamanasamatthena javena samannāgatā cattāro mahābrahmāno [P 0.0161] ‘cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ passissāmā’ti tena javena dhāveyyuṃ, cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ adisvāva parinibbāyeyyuṃ, evaṃ cakkavāḷāni anantāni nāma.

For the world-systems, too, there is no limit by hundreds or thousands. For if four great Brahmās, born in the Akaniṭṭha realm and endowed with a speed capable of traversing a hundred thousand world-systems in the time it takes for a light arrow from a strong and powerful archer to cross the shadow of a palm tree sideways—if they were to run with that speed, thinking, ‘We will see the end of the world-systems,’ they would attain Parinibbāna without ever having seen the end of the world-systems. Thus, the world-systems are called infinite.

Ettakesu pana cakkavāḷesu udakaṭṭhakathalaṭṭhakasattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi. Evaṃ sattanikāyo ananto nāma. Tatopi buddhañāṇaṃ anantameva.

Furthermore, in these many world-systems, there is no measure of the beings dwelling in water and on land. Thus, the multitude of beings is called infinite. Even beyond that, the Buddha’s knowledge is truly infinite.

Evaṃ aparimāṇesu cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ kāmāvacarasomanassasahagatañāṇasampayuttaasaṅkhārikakusalacittāni ekassa bahūni uppajjanti. Bahūnampi bahūni uppajjanti. Tāni sabbānipi kāmāvacaraṭṭhena somanassasahagataṭṭhena ñāṇasampayuttaṭṭhena asaṅkhārikaṭṭhena ekattaṃ gacchanti. Ekameva somanassasahagataṃ tihetukaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ mahācittaṃ hoti. Tathā sasaṅkhārikaṃ mahācittaṃ…pe… tathā upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ dvihetukaṃ sasaṅkhārikacittanti. Evaṃ sabbānipi aparimāṇesu cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uppajjamānāni kāmāvacarakusalacittāni sammāsambuddho mahātulāya tulayamāno viya, tumbe pakkhipitvā minamāno viya, sabbaññutaññāṇena paricchinditvā ‘aṭṭhevetānī’ti sarikkhaṭṭhena aṭṭheva koṭṭhāse katvā dassesi.

Thus, in immeasurable world-systems, for immeasurable beings, many sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted, arise for a single being. For many beings, too, many such consciousnesses arise. All these, by way of being of the sense-sphere, by way of being accompanied by joy, by way of being associated with knowledge, and by way of being unprompted, become one. There is just one great consciousness accompanied by joy, triple-rooted, and unprompted. Similarly, the prompted great consciousness... and so forth... and so too the consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, double-rooted, and prompted.
