Thus, all the sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses arising for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems—the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, weighing them as if with a great scale, measuring them as if placing them in a bushel, having delimited them with His omniscient knowledge, showed them as eight by way of their similarity, saying, ‘These are just eight.’

Puna imasmiṃ ṭhāne chabbidhena puññāyūhanaṃ nāma gahitaṃ. Puññañhi atthi sayaṃkāraṃ atthi paraṃkāraṃ, atthi sāhatthikaṃ atthi āṇattikaṃ, atthi sampajānakataṃ atthi asampajānakatanti.

Furthermore, in this context, the accumulation of merit is taken as sixfold. For merit is self-done and other-prompted; it is done with one’s own hand and by command; it is done with full understanding and without full understanding.

Tattha [V 0.0206] attano dhammatāya kataṃ ‘sayaṃkāraṃ’ nāma. Paraṃ karontaṃ disvā kataṃ ‘paraṃkāraṃ’ nāma. Sahatthena kataṃ ‘sāhatthikaṃ’ nāma. Āṇāpetvā kāritaṃ [M 0.0206] ‘āṇattikaṃ’ nāma. Kammañca phalañca saddahitvā kataṃ ‘sampajānakataṃ’ nāma. Kammampi phalampi ajānitvā kataṃ ‘asampajānakataṃ’ nāma. Tesu sayaṃkāraṃ karontopi imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ kusalacittānaṃ aññatareneva karoti. Paraṃkāraṃ karontopi, sahatthena karontopi, āṇāpetvā karontopi imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ kusalacittānaṃ aññatareneva karoti. Sampajānakaraṇaṃ pana catūhi ñāṇasampayuttehi hoti. Asampajānakaraṇaṃ catūhi ñāṇavippayuttehi.

Herein, what is done by one’s own nature is called ‘self-done.’ What is done upon seeing another doing it is called ‘other-prompted.’ What is done with one’s own hand is called ‘done by one’s own hand.’ What is caused to be done by giving an order is called ‘done by command.’ What is done with faith in kamma and its result is called ‘done with full understanding.’ What is done without knowing kamma and its result is called ‘done without full understanding.’ Among these, one who performs a ‘self-done’ act does so with one of these eight wholesome consciousnesses. Likewise, one who performs an ‘other-prompted’ act, one who acts with one’s own hand, or one who causes an act to be done by giving an order, also does so with one of these eight wholesome consciousnesses. However, the performance with full understanding occurs with the four consciousnesses associated with knowledge, while the performance without full understanding occurs with the four consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge.

Aparāpi imasmiṃ ṭhāne catasso dakkhiṇāvisuddhiyo gahitā – paccayānaṃ dhammikatā, cetanāmahattaṃ, vatthusampatti, guṇātirekatāti. Tattha dhammena samena uppannā paccayā ‘dhammikā’ nāma. Saddahitvā [P 0.0162] okappetvā dadato pana ‘cetanāmahattaṃ’ nāma hoti. Khīṇāsavabhāvo ‘vatthusampatti’ nāma. Khīṇāsavasseva nirodhā vuṭṭhitabhāvo ‘guṇātirekatā’ nāma. Imāni cattāri samodhānetvā dātuṃ sakkontassa kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Puṇṇakaseṭṭhikākavaliyasumanamālākārādīnaṃ (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.225 puṇṇadāsīvatthu) (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.67 sumanamālākāravatthu) viya.

Furthermore, in this context, four purities of an offering are taken up: the lawfulness of the requisites, the greatness of volition, the perfection of the recipient, and the pre-eminence of the recipient's virtue. Herein, requisites that have arisen through lawful and just means are called 'lawful.' Moreover, for one who gives with faith and conviction, there is what is called 'greatness of volition.' The state of being one whose taints are destroyed is called 'perfection of the recipient.' The state of that very one whose taints are destroyed having just arisen from the attainment of cessation is called 'pre-eminence of virtue.' For one who is able to combine these four and give, the sense-sphere wholesome kamma gives its result in this very existence, as in the cases of the wealthy merchant Puṇṇa, the lay devotee Kāḷavaliya, the garland-maker Sumana, and others.

Saṅkhepato panetaṃ sabbampi kāmāvacarakusalacittaṃ ‘citta’nti karitvā cittavicittaṭṭhena ekameva hoti. Vedanāvasena somanassasahagataṃ upekkhāsahagatanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Ñāṇavibhattidesanāvasena catubbidhaṃ hoti. Somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ mahācittañhi upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ mahācittañca ñāṇasampayuttaṭṭhena asaṅkhārikaṭṭhena ca ekameva hoti. Tathā ñāṇasampayuttaṃ sasaṅkhārikaṃ, ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ, ñāṇavippayuttaṃ sasaṅkhārikañcāti. Evaṃ ñāṇavibhattidesanāvasena catubbidhe panetasmiṃ asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravibhattito cattāri asaṅkhārikāni cattāri sasaṅkhārikānīti aṭṭheva kusalacittāni honti. Tāni yāthāvato ñatvā bhagavā sabbaññū gaṇīvaro muniseṭṭho ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkarotīti.

In brief, however, all this wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, being regarded as 'consciousness,' is one in the sense of being consciousness. By way of feeling, it is twofold: accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity. By way of the teaching that classifies by knowledge, it is fourfold. For the great consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted, and the great consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and unprompted, are one in the sense of being associated with knowledge and in the sense of being unprompted. Similarly for that which is associated with knowledge and prompted; dissociated from knowledge and unprompted; and dissociated from knowledge and prompted. Thus, in this fourfold classification according to the teaching that classifies by knowledge, from the division into unprompted and prompted, there come to be four unprompted and four prompted, making eight wholesome consciousnesses in total. Knowing them as they truly are, the Blessed One—the All-Knowing, the Leader of the Multitude, the Chief of Sages—declares, teaches, formulates, establishes, reveals, analyzes, and makes them clear.

Aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāya

In the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī.

Kāmāvacarakusalaniddeso samatto.

The Exposition of Sense-Sphere Wholesome Consciousness is completed.

Rūpāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā

An Exposition of Wholesome States Pertaining to the Fine-Material Sphere

Catukkanayo paṭhamajjhānaṃ

The Fourfold Method: The First Jhāna

160. Idāni [M 0.0207][V 0.0207] rūpāvacarakusalaṃ dassetuṃ katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāvetīti rūpaṃ vuccati rūpabhavo. Upapattīti nibbatti jāti sañjāti. Maggoti upāyo. Vacanattho panettha – taṃ upapattiṃ maggati gavesati janeti nipphādetīti maggo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yena maggena rūpabhave upapatti hoti nibbatti jāti sañjāti, taṃ maggaṃ bhāvetīti. Kiṃ panetena niyamato rūpabhave upapatti hotīti? Na hoti. “Samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha, samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071; netti. 40; mi. pa. 2.1.15) evaṃ vuttena hi nibbedhabhāgiyena rūpabhavātikkamopi hoti. Rūpūpapattiyā pana ito añño maggo nāma [P 0.0163] natthi, tena vuttaṃ ‘rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāvetī’ti. Atthato cāyaṃ maggo nāma cetanāpi hoti, cetanāya sampayuttadhammāpi, tadubhayampi. “Nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi nirayagāmiñca magga”nti (ma. ni. 1.153) hi ettha cetanā maggo nāma.

160. Now, to explain the wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material sphere, the passage beginning 'Which states are wholesome?' is commenced. Therein, regarding the passage 'develops the path for rebirth in the form realm,' it is 'form existence' (rūpabhava) that is called 'form' (rūpa). 'Rebirth' means arising, birth, conception. 'Path' means the means. The etymological meaning here is: it seeks, searches for, generates, and accomplishes that rebirth; thus, it is called the path. This is what is said: 'One develops that path by which there is rebirth—arising, birth, conception—in the form existence.' But does rebirth in the form existence occur necessarily because of this? It does not. For by what was said—'Monks, develop concentration; one who is concentrated understands and sees things as they really are'—even the transcending of form existence occurs through this path that partakes of penetration. However, for rebirth in the form realm, there is no other path apart from this; therefore, it is said, 'one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm.' And in terms of its intrinsic nature, this path is volition, or the states associated with volition, or both. For in the passage, 'I, Sāriputta, understand hell and the path leading to hell,' it is volition that is called the path.

“Saddhā hiriyaṃ kusalañca dānaṃ, dhammā ete sappurisānuyātā;

Etañhi maggaṃ diviyaṃ vadanti, etena hi gacchati devaloka”nti. (a. ni. 8.32);

“Faith, moral shame, the wholesome, and giving—these are the qualities followed by good people. This, they say, is the divine path; by this one goes to the celestial world.”

Ettha cetanāsampayuttadhammā maggo nāma. “Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo, ayaṃ paṭipadā”ti saṅkhārupapattisuttādīsu (ma. ni. 3.161 ādayo) cetanāpi cetanāsampayuttadhammāpi maggo nāma. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ‘jhāna’nti vacanato cetanāsampayuttā adhippetā. Yasmā pana jhānacetanā paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati, tasmā cetanāpi cetanāsampayuttadhammāpi vaṭṭantiyeva.

Here, the states associated with volition are called the path. In the Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta and others, where it is said, 'This, monks, is the path, this is the practice,' both volition and the states associated with volition are called the path. In this context, however, because of the word 'jhāna,' the states associated with volition are intended. Furthermore, since jhāna-volition draws forth rebirth-linking, it is indeed suitable to call both volition and the states associated with volition 'the path'.

Bhāvetīti janeti uppādeti vaḍḍheti. Ayaṃ tāva idha bhāvanāya attho. Aññattha pana upasaggavasena sambhāvanā paribhāvanā vibhāvanāti evaṃ aññathāpi attho hoti. Tattha “idhudāyi mama sāvakā adhisīle sambhāventi – sīlavā samaṇo gotamo, paramena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato”ti [M 0.0208][V 0.0208] (ma. ni. 2.243) ayaṃ sambhāvanā nāma; okappanāti attho. “Sīlaparibhāvito samādhi mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso, samādhiparibhāvitā paññā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā, paññāparibhāvitaṃ cittaṃ sammadeva āsavehi vimuccatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.186) ayaṃ paribhāvanā nāma; vāsanāti attho. “Iṅgha rūpaṃ vibhāvehi, vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ vibhāvehī”ti ayaṃ vibhāvanā nāma; antaradhāpanāti attho. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāventī”ti (ma. ni. 2.247), ayaṃ pana uppādanavaḍḍhanaṭṭhena bhāvanā nāma. Imasmimpi ṭhāne ayameva adhippetā. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘bhāvetīti janeti uppādeti vaḍḍhetī’ti.

'To develop' means to generate, to produce, to increase. This, for now, is the meaning of 'development' here. Elsewhere, however, by the power of prefixes, the meaning is also otherwise, such as sambhāvanā, paribhāvanā, and vibhāvanā. Therein, 'Here, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me in regard to higher virtue: “The ascetic Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the highest aggregate of virtue”'—this is called sambhāvanā; the meaning is trust. 'Concentration perfumed by virtue bears great fruit and great benefit; wisdom perfumed by concentration bears great fruit and great benefit; the mind perfumed by wisdom is rightly liberated from the taints'—this is called paribhāvanā; the meaning is perfuming. 'Come, dispel form, dispel feeling… perception… formations… consciousness'—this is called vibhāvanā; the meaning is causing to disappear. 'Furthermore, Udāyi, the path has been declared by me to my disciples, and following that path, my disciples develop the four establishments of mindfulness'—this, however, is called 'development' in the sense of producing and increasing. In this context as well, this very meaning is intended. Therefore, it was said: '“to develop” means to generate, to produce, to increase.'

Kasmā panettha, yathā kāmāvacarakusalaniddese dhammapubbaṅgamā desanā katā tathā akatvā, puggalapubbaṅgamā [P 0.0164] katāti? Paṭipadāya sādhetabbato. Idañhi catūsu paṭipadāsu aññatarāya sādhetabbaṃ; na kāmāvacaraṃ viya vinā paṭipadāya uppajjati. Paṭipadā ca nāmesā paṭipannake sati hotīti etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ puggalapubbaṅgamaṃ desanaṃ karonto ‘rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāvetī’ti āha.

Why here, unlike in the exposition of wholesome sense-sphere states where the teaching was presented with the Dhamma at the forefront, is it not done so, but is instead presented with the person at the forefront? Because it must be accomplished by practice. For this must be accomplished through one of the four practices; it does not arise without practice, as wholesome sense-sphere states do. And this practice exists only when there is a practitioner. To show this meaning, presenting the teaching with the person at the forefront, the Blessed One said, 'He develops the path for rebirth in the form realm.'

Vivicceva kāmehīti kāmehi viviccitvā, vinā hutvā, apakkamitvā. Yo panāyamettha ‘eva’-kāro so niyamatthoti veditabbo. Yasmā ca niyamattho, tasmā tasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇasamaye avijjamānānampi kāmānaṃ tassa paṭhamajjhānassa paṭipakkhabhāvaṃ, kāmapariccāgeneva cassa adhigamaṃ dīpeti. Kathaṃ? ‘Vivicceva kāmehī’ti evañhi niyame kariyamāne idaṃ paññāyati – nūnimassa kāmā paṭipakkhabhūtā yesu sati idaṃ na pavattati, andhakāre sati padīpobhāso viya? Tesaṃ pariccāgeneva cassa adhigamo hoti orimatīrapariccāgena pārimatīrasseva. Tasmā niyamaṃ karotīti.

“Secluded indeed from sensual pleasures” means having secluded oneself from sensual pleasures, having become separated, having withdrawn. The particle ‘eva’ here should be understood as having the meaning of restriction. And because it has the meaning of restriction, it shows that the first jhāna is opposed to sensual pleasures and that its attainment is achieved precisely by abandoning sensual pleasures, even though those sensual pleasures are non-existent at the time of attaining and dwelling in the first jhāna. How? When restriction is established by saying, “Secluded indeed from sensual pleasures,” this becomes apparent: ‘Surely, sensual pleasures are an obstacle to this jhāna, for when they are present, it does not occur, just as the light of a lamp does not appear in darkness.’ And its attainment is achieved precisely by abandoning them, just as the far shore is reached by abandoning the near shore. Therefore, the particle establishes restriction.

Tattha siyā – ‘kasmā panesa pubbapadeyeva vutto, na uttarapade? Kiṃ akusalehi dhammehi aviviccāpi jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyyā’ti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃnissaraṇato hi pubbapade esa vutto. Kāmadhātusamatikkamanato [M 0.0209] hi kāmarāgapaṭipakkhato ca idaṃ jhānaṃ kāmānameva nissaraṇaṃ. Yathāha – “kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhamma”nti (itivu. 72; dī. ni. 3.353). Uttarapadepi pana, yathā “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti [V 0.0209] (ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241) ettha ‘eva’-kāro ānetvā vuccati, evaṃ vattabbo. Na hi sakkā ito aññehipi nīvaraṇasaṅkhātehi akusalehi dhammehi avivicca jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ, tasmā ‘vivicceva kāmehi vivicceva akusalehi dhammehī’ti evaṃ padadvayepi esa daṭṭhabbo. Padadvayepi ca kiñcāpi viviccāti iminā sādhāraṇavacanena tadaṅgavivekādayo kāyavivekādayo ca sabbepi vivekā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, tathāpi kāyaviveko cittaviveko vikkhambhanavivekoti tayo eva idha daṭṭhabbā.

Here, it might be said: 'Why is this stated only in the earlier phrase, and not in the later one? Could one attain and dwell in jhāna even without being secluded from unwholesome states?' This, however, should not be seen in that way. It is stated in the earlier phrase because it is the liberation from them. For this jhāna, by transcending the sense-sphere and being the antidote to sensual lust, is indeed the liberation from sensual pleasures. As it is said: 'This is the liberation from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation.' As for the later phrase, just as the particle ‘eva’ (indeed) is brought in and spoken in the passage, 'Here, bhikkhus, is the ascetic; here is the second ascetic,' so it should be supplied here. For it is impossible to attain and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from other unwholesome states known as the hindrances. Therefore, it should be understood in both phrases as: 'secluded indeed from sensual pleasures, secluded indeed from unwholesome states.' And although in both phrases the general term 'secluded' (vivicca) encompasses all types of seclusion—such as seclusion by substitution of opposites, physical seclusion, and so on—nevertheless, here only three types of seclusion should be understood: physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression.

Kāmehīti iminā pana padena ye ca niddese “katame vatthukāmā? Manāpiyā rūpā”tiādinā (mahāni. 1) nayena vatthukāmā vuttā, ye ca tattheva vibhaṅge ca “chando kāmo, rāgo [P 0.0165] kāmo, chandarāgo kāmo; saṅkappo kāmo, rāgo kāmo, saṅkapparāgo kāmo; ime vuccanti kāmā”ti (mahāni. 1; vibha. 564) evaṃ kilesakāmā vuttā, te sabbepi saṅgahitāicceva daṭṭhabbā. Evañhi sati vivicceva kāmehīti vatthukāmehipi viviccevāti attho yujjati. Tena kāyaviveko vutto hoti.

By this phrase 'from sensual pleasures' (kāmehi), it should be understood that all are indeed included: both the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāmā) mentioned in the Niddesa in the passage beginning, 'What are the objects of sensual pleasure? Agreeable forms...,' and the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesakāmā) stated there and in the Vibhaṅga thus: 'Desire is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, desire-and-lust is sensual pleasure; intention is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, intention-and-lust is sensual pleasure; these are called sensual pleasures.' For this being so, the meaning 'secluded from sensual pleasures' is fittingly applied to being secluded from the objects of sensual pleasure. Thereby, physical seclusion is stated.

Vivicca akusalehi dhammehīti kilesakāmehi sabbākusalehi vā viviccāti attho yujjati. Tena cittaviveko vutto hoti. Purimena cettha vatthukāmehi vivekavacanato eva kāmasukhapariccāgo, dutiyena kilesakāmehi vivekavacanato nekkhammasukhapariggaho vibhāvito hoti. Evaṃ vatthukāmakilesakāmavivekavacanatoyeva ca etesaṃ paṭhamena saṃkilesavatthuppahānaṃ, dutiyena saṃkilesappahānaṃ; paṭhamena lolabhāvassa hetupariccāgo, dutiyena bālabhāvassa; paṭhamena ca payogasuddhi, dutiyena āsayaposanaṃ vibhāvitaṃ hotīti ñātabbaṃ. Esa tāva nayo ‘kāmehī’ti ettha vuttakāmesu vatthukāmapakkhe.

'Secluded from unwholesome states' means secluded from the defilements of sensual pleasure or from all unwholesome states. Thereby, mental seclusion is stated. Here, by the first phrase, through the mention of seclusion from the objects of sensual pleasure, the abandonment of sensual happiness is shown; by the second, through the mention of seclusion from the defilements of sensual pleasure, the acceptance of the happiness of renunciation is shown. Thus, by the very mention of seclusion from the objects and defilements of sensual pleasure, it should be known that by the first is shown the abandoning of the basis of defilement, and by the second, the abandoning of defilement; by the first, the abandonment of the cause of greed, and by the second, of foolishness; and by the first, the purity of endeavor, and by the second, the fostering of disposition. This, so far, is the method concerning the interpretation of 'from sensual pleasures' on the side of the objects of sensual pleasure.

Kilesakāmapakkhe pana ‘chandoti ca rāgo’ti ca evamādīhi anekabhedo kāmacchandoyeva kāmoti adhippeto. So ca akusalapariyāpannopi [M 0.0210] samāno “tattha katamo kāmacchando kāmo”tiādinā nayena vibhaṅge (vibha. 564) jhānapaṭipakkhato visuṃ vutto. Kilesakāmattā vā purimapade vutto, akusalapariyāpannattā dutiyapade. Anekabhedato cassa ‘kāmato’ti avatvā ‘kāmehī’ti vuttaṃ. Aññesampi ca dhammānaṃ akusalabhāve vijjamāne “tattha katame akusalā dhammā? Kāmacchando”tiādinā nayena vibhaṅge uparijhānaṅgapaccanīkapaṭipakkhabhāvadassanato [V 0.0210] nīvaraṇāneva vuttāni. Nīvaraṇāni hi jhānaṅgapaccanīkāni. Tesaṃ jhānaṅgāneva paṭipakkhāni, viddhaṃsakāni, vighātakānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi “samādhi kāmacchandassa paṭipakkho, pīti byāpādassa, vitakko thinamiddhassa, sukhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccassa, vicāro vicikicchāyā”ti peṭake vuttaṃ.

However, on the side of the defilements of sensual pleasure, it is sensual desire (kāmacchanda) itself, with its many varieties such as 'desire' and 'lust', that is intended by 'sensual pleasures' (kāma). And although it is included under the unwholesome, it is stated separately in the Vibhaṅga as an opponent to jhāna, in the manner of 'Therein, which sensual desire is sensual pleasure?'. Alternatively, it is stated in the first phrase because it is a defilement of sensual pleasure, and in the second phrase because it is included under the unwholesome. And because of its many varieties, it is said as 'from sensual pleasures' (kāmehi) instead of 'from sensual pleasure' (kāmato). And although other states also exist that are unwholesome, in the Vibhaṅga, only the hindrances are mentioned, because they are shown to be the hostile opponents of the higher jhāna factors, in the manner of 'Therein, what are the unwholesome states? Sensual desire...'. For the hindrances are the hostile opponents of the jhāna factors. It is said that the jhāna factors themselves are their counterparts, their destroyers, and their eliminators. Thus it is said in the Peṭaka: 'Concentration is the counterpart to sensual desire, zest to ill will, applied thought to sloth and torpor, happiness to restlessness and remorse, and sustained thought to doubt.'

Evamettha ‘vivicceva kāmehī’ti iminā kāmacchandassa vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hoti. ‘Vivicca akusalehi dhammehī’ti iminā pañcannampi nīvaraṇānaṃ. Aggahitaggahaṇena pana paṭhamena kāmacchandassa, dutiyena sesanīvaraṇānaṃ; tathā paṭhamena tīsu akusalamūlesu pañcakāmaguṇabhedavisayassa lobhassa, dutiyena āghātavatthubhedādivisayānaṃ [P 0.0166] dosamohānaṃ. Oghādīsu vā dhammesu paṭhamena kāmoghakāmayogakāmāsavakāmupādānaabhijjhākāyaganthakāmarāgasaṃyojanānaṃ, dutiyena avasesaoghayogāsavaupādānaganthasaṃyojanānaṃ. Paṭhamena ca taṇhāya taṃsampayuttakānañca, dutiyena avijjāya taṃsampayuttakānañca. Apica paṭhamena lobhasampayuttaaṭṭhacittuppādānaṃ, dutiyena sesānaṃ catunnaṃ akusalacittuppādānaṃ vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hotīti veditabbo. Ayaṃ tāva ‘vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehī’ti ettha atthappakāsanā.

Thus, here, by 'secluded from sensual pleasures,' the seclusion by suppression of sensual desire is stated. By 'secluded from unwholesome states,' that of all five hindrances is stated. However, by way of including what was not included, the first refers to sensual desire, the second to the remaining hindrances. Similarly, among the three unwholesome roots, the first refers to greed, which has as its object the various five strands of sensual pleasure; the second, to hatred and delusion, which have as their objects the various grounds for vexation and so on. Or, among states such as the floods, the first refers to the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the effluent of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of sensual lust; the second, to the remaining floods, yokes, effluents, clingings, ties, and fetters. And by the first, to craving and its associated states; by the second, to ignorance and its associated states. Furthermore, it should be understood that by the first, the seclusion by suppression of the eight consciousnesses rooted in greed is stated; by the second, that of the remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses. This, so far, is the explanation of the meaning of 'secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states.'

Ettāvatā ca paṭhamassa jhānassa pahānaṅgaṃ dassetvā idāni sampayogaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ savitakkaṃ savicārantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha heṭṭhā vuttalakkhaṇādivibhāgena appanāsampayogato rūpāvacarabhāvappattena vitakkena ceva vicārena ca saha vattati. Rukkho viya pupphena ca phalena cāti idaṃ jhānaṃ savitakkaṃ savicāranti vuccati. Vibhaṅge pana “iminā ca vitakkena iminā ca vicārena [M 0.0211] upeto hoti samupeto”tiādinā (vibha. 565) nayena puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā katā. Attho pana tatrapi evameva daṭṭhabbo.

And having thus far shown the factor of abandoning of the first jhāna, now, to show the factor of association, 'with initial application, with sustained application,' etc., was said. Therein, it occurs together with initial application and sustained application, which have attained the state of the fine-material sphere by way of the distinction of characteristics, etc., stated below and due to association with absorption. Just as a tree exists with both flower and fruit, so this jhāna is called 'with initial application and sustained application.' In the Vibhaṅga, however, the teaching was given with the individual as its basis, by the method beginning with 'he is endowed, fully endowed with this initial application and this sustained application,' and so on. But the meaning there too should be understood in just this way.

Vivekajanti – ettha vivitti viveko. Nīvaraṇavigamoti attho. Vivittoti vā viveko, nīvaraṇavivitto jhānasampayuttadhammarāsīti attho. Tasmā vivekā, tasmiṃ vā viveke, jātanti vivekajaṃ. Pītisukhanti – ettha pītisukhāni heṭṭhā pakāsitāneva. Tesu pana vuttappakārāya pañcavidhāya pītiyā yā appanāsamādhissa mūlaṃ hutvā vaḍḍhamānā samādhisampayogaṃ gatā pharaṇāpīti – ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā pītīti. Ayañca pīti idañca sukhaṃ assa [V 0.0211] jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne atthīti idaṃ jhānaṃ pītisukhanti vuccati. Atha vā pīti ca sukhañca pītisukhaṃ, dhammavinayādayo viya. Vivekajaṃ pītisukhamassa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne, atthīti evampi vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ. Yatheva hi jhānaṃ evaṃ pītisukhampettha vivekajameva hoti. Tañcassa atthi. Tasmā ekapadeneva ‘vivekajaṃ pītisukha’nti vattuṃ yujjati. Vibhaṅge pana “idaṃ sukhaṃ imāya pītiyā sahagata”ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ. Attho pana tatthāpi evameva daṭṭhabbo.

Regarding 'born of seclusion' (vivekajaṃ): here, seclusion (viveka) is the state of being secluded. The meaning is the removal of the hindrances. Or, 'seclusion' is that which is secluded; the meaning is the collection of states associated with jhāna that is secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, it is 'born of seclusion' because it is born from that seclusion, or in that seclusion. Regarding 'rapture-and-happiness' (pītisukhaṃ): here, rapture and happiness have already been explained below. However, among them, of the five kinds of rapture with their explained distinctions, that all-pervading rapture (pharaṇāpīti) which, having become the basis of absorption concentration and having grown, has reached association with concentration—this is intended as 'rapture' in this context. And this rapture and this happiness exist for this jhāna, or in this jhāna; therefore, this jhāna is called 'with rapture and happiness.' Alternatively, 'rapture' and 'happiness' form the compound pītisukhaṃ, like dhammavinaya, etc. The rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion belongs to this jhāna, or exists in this jhāna; thus also it is 'rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion.' For just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too the rapture-and-happiness herein is born of seclusion. And that exists for it. Therefore, it is fitting to say 'rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion' as a single compound. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated by the method beginning with 'this happiness is accompanied by this rapture,' and so on. But the meaning there too should be understood in just this way.

Paṭhamaṃ [P 0.0167] jhānanti – ettha gaṇanānupubbatā paṭhamaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ uppannanti paṭhamaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ samāpajjitabbantipi paṭhamaṃ. Idaṃ pana na ekantalakkhaṇaṃ. Ciṇṇavasībhāvo hi aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī ādito paṭṭhāya matthakaṃ pāpentopi samāpajjituṃ sakkoti. Matthakato paṭṭhāya ādiṃ pāpentopi samāpajjituṃ sakkoti. Antarantarā okkamantopi sakkoti. Evaṃ pubbuppattiyaṭṭhena pana paṭhamaṃ nāma hoti.

In the term paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ (the first jhāna): here, it is 'first' by way of numerical sequence. It is 'first' because it arises first. It is also 'first' because it is to be entered upon first. However, this last is not an invariable characteristic. For a person who has mastery through practice and has obtained the eight attainments is able to enter upon them starting from the beginning and reaching the summit; is able to enter upon them starting from the summit and reaching the beginning; and is able to enter upon them by descending in between. Thus, however, it is called 'first' in the sense of arising first.

Jhānanti duvidhaṃ jhānaṃ – ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṃ lakkhaṇūpanijjhānanti. Tattha aṭṭha samāpattiyo pathavikasiṇādiārammaṇaṃ upanijjhāyantīti ārammaṇūpanijjhānanti saṅkhyaṃ gatā. Vipassanāmaggaphalāni pana lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ nāma. Tattha vipassanā aniccādilakkhaṇassa upanijjhānato lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. Vipassanāya katakiccassa maggena ijjhanato maggo lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. Phalaṃ pana nirodhasaccaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ upanijjhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ nāma. Tesu imasmiṃ atthe ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tasmā ārammaṇūpanijjhānato paccanīkajjhāpanato vā jhānanti veditabbaṃ.

Jhāna is of two kinds: contemplation of an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and contemplation of characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Therein, the eight attainments contemplate an object such as the earth kasiṇa, and are therefore designated as 'contemplation of an object.' Insight, the path, and fruition, however, are called 'contemplation of characteristics.' Therein, insight is 'contemplation of characteristics' because it contemplates characteristics such as impermanence. The path is 'contemplation of characteristics' because what is to be done by insight is accomplished by the path. Fruition, however, is called 'contemplation of characteristics' because it contemplates the truth of cessation, which has the characteristic of being true. Among these two, in this context, 'contemplation of an object' is intended. Therefore, jhāna should be understood as 'contemplation of an object' or as 'the burning up of opposing factors'.

Upasampajjāti [M 0.0212] upagantvā, pāpuṇitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasampādayitvā vā nipphādetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vibhaṅge pana “upasampajjāti paṭhamassa jhānassa lābho paṭilābho patti sampatti phusanā sacchikiriyā upasampadā”ti (vibha. 570) vuttaṃ. Tassāpi evamevattho daṭṭhabbo. Viharatīti tadanurūpena iriyāpathavihārena itivuttappakārajjhānasamaṅgī hutvā attabhāvassa iriyanaṃ vuttiṃ pālanaṃ yapanaṃ yāpanaṃ cāraṃ vihāraṃ abhinipphādeti. Vuttañhetaṃ vibhaṅge – “viharatīti iriyati vattati pāleti yapeti yāpeti carati viharati, tena vuccati viharatī”ti (vibha. 512, 571).

Regarding 'having entered upon' (upasampajja): this means 'having approached, having attained.' Or it means 'having brought about, having accomplished.' But in the Vibhaṅga it is said: '“Having entered upon” means the gain, acquisition, attainment, accomplishment, contact, realization, and entry upon the first jhāna.' The meaning of that too should be understood in just this way. Regarding 'he dwells' (viharati): this means that, by dwelling in a posture suitable to it, and having become endowed with the jhāna of the kind thus stated, he brings to completion the moving, occurring, maintaining, sustaining, carrying on, proceeding, and dwelling of his individual existence. For this is stated in the Vibhaṅga: '“He dwells” means: he moves, he occurs, he maintains, he sustains, he carries on, he proceeds, he dwells; therefore, he is said to “dwell.”'

Pathavikasiṇanti [V 0.0212] ettha pathavimaṇḍalampi sakalaṭṭhena pathavikasiṇanti vuccati. Taṃ nissāya paṭiladdhaṃ nimittampi. Pathavikasiṇanimitte paṭiladdhajjhānampi. Tattha imasmiṃ atthe jhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇanti veditabbaṃ. Pathavikasiṇasaṅkhātaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti ayañhettha saṅkhepattho. Imasmiṃ pana [P 0.0168] pathavikasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catukkapañcakajjhānāni nibbattetvā jhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattukāmena kulaputtena kiṃ kattabbanti? Ādito tāva pātimokkhasaṃvaraindriyasaṃvaraājīvapārisuddhipaccayasannissitasaṅkhātāni cattāri sīlāni visodhetvā suparisuddhe sīle patiṭṭhitena, yvāssa āvāsādīsu dasasu palibodhesu palibodho atthi, taṃ upacchinditvā kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pāḷiyā āgatesu aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu attano cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ upaparikkhantena sacassa idaṃ pathavikasiṇaṃ anukūlaṃ hoti, idameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā jhānabhāvanāya ananurūpaṃ vihāraṃ pahāya anurūpe vihāre viharantena khuddakapalibodhupacchedaṃ katvā kasiṇaparikammanimittānurakkhaṇasattaasappāyaparivajjanasattasappāyasevanadasavidhaappanākosallappabhedaṃ sabbaṃ bhāvanāvidhānaṃ aparihāpentena jhānādhigamatthāya paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.51 ādayo) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yathā cettha evaṃ ito paresupi. Sabbakammaṭṭhānānañhi bhāvanāvidhānaṃ sabbaṃ aṭṭhakathānayena gahetvā visuddhimagge [M 0.0213] vitthāritaṃ. Kiṃ tena tattha tattha puna vuttenāti na naṃ puna vitthārayāma. Pāḷiyā pana heṭṭhā anāgataṃ atthaṃ aparihāpentā nirantaraṃ anupadavaṇṇanameva karissāma.

Herein, regarding 'earth kasiṇa': the earth-disk, in the sense of 'the whole,' is called 'earth kasiṇa.' The sign obtained by relying on it is also called 'earth kasiṇa,' as is the jhāna attained with the earth kasiṇa sign as its object. Among these, in this context, the jhāna should be understood as 'earth kasiṇa.' 'He dwells having attained the jhāna called the earth kasiṇa'—this is the concise meaning here. Now, what should be done by a clansman who, having performed the preliminary work on this earth kasiṇa, having produced the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, having developed insight which has jhāna as its proximate cause, desires to attain arahantship? First of all, having purified the four kinds of virtue called the Pātimokkha restraint, the sense-faculty restraint, the purity of livelihood, and the virtue concerning requisites, and having become established in perfectly pure virtue, he should cut off whatever impediment exists for him among the ten impediments beginning with the dwelling. Having approached a good friend who is a giver of a meditation subject, and while examining among the thirty-eight meditation subjects that have come down in the Pāḷi for one that is suitable to his own temperament, if this earth kasiṇa is suitable for him, he should take up this very meditation subject. Having abandoned a monastery unsuitable for the development of jhāna, while dwelling in a suitable monastery, having cut off the minor impediments, without neglecting the entire method of development—differentiated as the preliminary work on the kasiṇa, the guarding of the sign, the avoidance of the seven unsuitable things, the cultivation of the seven suitable things, and the ten kinds of absorption skill—he should practice for the sake of attaining jhāna. This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be understood according to the method explained in the Visuddhimagga. As it is here, so too in the meditation subjects that follow this one. For the entire method of development for all meditation subjects has been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga, having been taken according to the method of the ancient commentaries. 'What is the use of that which has been said again and again in those various places?'—thus, we do not elaborate on it again. However, without omitting the meaning that has not yet been discussed under the Pāḷi text, we will provide just the continuous word-by-word explanation.

Tasmiṃ samayeti tasmiṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇasamaye. Phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hotīti ime kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusalacitte vuttappakārāya padapaṭipāṭiyā chapaṇṇāsa dhammā honti. Kevalañhi te kāmāvacarā, ime bhūmantaravasena mahaggatā rūpāvacarāti ayamettha viseso. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Yevāpanakā panettha chandādayo cattārova labbhanti. Koṭṭhāsavārasuññatavārā pākatikā evāti.

'At that time' means: at that time of dwelling, having attained the first jhāna. 'Contact occurs… up to… non-distraction occurs'—thus, these fifty-six states occur according to the sequence of terms of the type spoken of in the first wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. Indeed, those are merely of the sense-sphere, whereas these, by way of a different plane, are sublime, of the form-sphere—this is the distinction here. The remainder is just the same. Here, however, only the four optional factors beginning with desire are obtained. The sections on parts and the sections on emptiness are just as they are naturally.

Paṭhamaṃ.

The first (jhāna is concluded).

Dutiyajjhānaṃ

The Second Jhāna

161-162. Dutiyajjhānaniddese [V 0.0213] vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti [P 0.0169] vitakkassa ca vicārassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ vūpasamā, samatikkamā; dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe apātubhāvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha kiñcāpi dutiyajjhāne sabbepi paṭhamajjhānadhammā na santi, aññeyeva hi paṭhamajjhāne phassādayo aññe idha, oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamo hotīti dīpanatthaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ajjhattanti idha – niyakajjhattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Vibhaṅge pana “ajjhattaṃ paccatta”nti (vibha. 573) ettakameva vuttaṃ. Yasmā niyakajjhattaṃ adhippetaṃ, tasmā attani jātaṃ, attano santāne nibbattanti ayamettha attho.

In the exposition of the second jhāna, 'from the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought' means: from the stilling, the transcending, of these two, namely applied thought and sustained thought; it means their non-appearance at the moment of the second jhāna. Therein, although in the second jhāna not all the states of the first jhāna are present—for the contact and so on in the first jhāna are indeed different, and those here are different—however, the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, which are beyond the first jhāna, occurs from the transcending of the grosser factor. Thus, it should be known that it was said, 'from the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought,' for the purpose of showing this. Here, 'internal' is intended to mean one's own internality. In the Vibhaṅga, however, only 'internal, personal' is stated. Because one's own internality is intended, the meaning here is: 'born in oneself, produced in one's own continuity.'

Sampasādananti sampasādanaṃ vuccati saddhā. Sampasādanayogato jhānampi sampasādanaṃ, nīlavaṇṇayogato nīlavatthaṃ viya. Yasmā vā taṃ jhānaṃ sampasādanasamannāgatattā vitakkavicārakkhobhavūpasamanena ca ceto sampasādayati, tasmāpi sampasādananti vuttaṃ. Imasmiñca atthavikappe ‘sampasādanaṃ cetaso’ti evaṃ padasambandho veditabbo. Purimasmiṃ pana atthavikappe ‘cetaso’ti etaṃ ekodibhāvena saddhiṃ yojetabbaṃ.

As for 'serene confidence' (sampasādana): faith (saddhā) is called sampasādana. Due to its connection with serene confidence, the jhāna is also called 'serene confidence,' like a blue cloth is called 'blue' due to its connection with the color blue. Or, because that jhāna, being endowed with serene confidence and by the calming of the disturbance of applied thought and sustained thought, clarifies the mind, it is therefore also called 'serene confidence.' And in this alternative explanation of the meaning, the connection of the words should be understood as 'serene confidence of the mind.' In the previous alternative explanation of the meaning, however, this word 'of the mind' should be connected with 'unification'.

Tatrāyaṃ atthayojanā – eko udetīti ekodi, vitakkavicārehi anajjhāruḷhattā aggo seṭṭho hutvā udetīti attho. Seṭṭhopi [M 0.0214] hi loke ekoti vuccati. Vitakkavicāravirahato vā eko asahāyo hutvātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Atha vā sampayuttadhamme udāyatīti udi. Uṭṭhāpetīti attho. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena eko ca so udi cāti ekodi. Samādhissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iti imaṃ ekodiṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti idaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ ekodibhāvaṃ. So panāyaṃ ekodi yasmā cetaso, na sattassa, na jīvassa, tasmā etaṃ ‘cetaso ekodibhāva’nti vuttaṃ.

Herein, this is the application of the meaning: Ekodi means 'one arises.' The meaning is: because it is not overcome by applied thought and sustained thought, it arises having become foremost, best. For in the world, even the best is called 'one.' Or, it is possible to say that because it is devoid of applied thought and sustained thought, it is 'one' in the sense of being alone, without a companion. Or alternatively, udi means 'it causes associated states to arise.' The meaning is 'it makes them arise.' Because it is 'one' (eko) in the sense of being the best, and it is that which causes to arise (udi), it is ekodi. This is a designation for concentration. Thus, 'one develops, one cultivates this ekodi'—this second jhāna is the state of unification (ekodibhāva). Moreover, since this ekodi is of the mind—not of a being, not of a life-principle—it is therefore called 'the unification of mind'.

‘Nanu cāyaṃ saddhā paṭhamajjhānepi atthi, ayañca ekodināmako samādhi, atha kasmā idameva sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvañcāti vuttanti? Vuccate – ‘aduñhi paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicārakkhobhena vīcitaraṅgasamākulamiva jalaṃ na suppasannaṃ hoti, tasmā satiyāpi saddhāya [V 0.0214] sampasādana’nti [P 0.0170] na vuttaṃ. Na suppasannattā eva cettha samādhipi na suṭṭhu pākaṭo. Tasmā ekodibhāvantipi na vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana jhāne vitakkavicārapalibodhābhāvena laddhokāsā balavatī saddhā, balavasaddhāsahāyapaṭilābheneva samādhipi pākaṭo. Tasmā idameva evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Vibhaṅge pana “sampasādananti yā saddhā saddahanā okappanā abhippasādo; cetaso ekodibhāvanti yā cittassa ṭhiti…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti (vibha. 574-575) ettakameva vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttena panetena saddhiṃ ayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā yathā na virujjhati aññadatthu saṃsandati ceva sameti ca, evaṃ veditabbā.

‘But is not this faith also present in the first jhāna, and this concentration called unification as well? So why are only serene confidence and unification of mind mentioned here?’ It is said: ‘Because the first jhāna is disturbed by applied thought and sustained thought, like water agitated by waves, it is not perfectly serene. Therefore, even though faith is present, “serene confidence” is not mentioned. Due to this lack of perfect serenity, the concentration here is not fully manifest. Hence, “unification of mind” is also not mentioned. In this jhāna, however, because there is no impediment from applied thought and sustained thought, faith gains an opportunity and becomes powerful. With the acquisition of strong faith as an ally, concentration also becomes manifest. Therefore, it should be understood that only this is stated in this way. In the Vibhaṅga, however, only this much is stated: “Serene confidence is the faith, conviction, trust, and clarity of confidence; unification of mind is the stability of the mind... right concentration.” This explanation should be understood in such a way that it does not conflict with what has been stated, but on the contrary, corresponds and concurs with it.’

Avitakkaṃ avicāranti bhāvanāya pahīnattā etasmiṃ etassa vā vitakko natthīti avitakkaṃ. Imināva nayena avicāraṃ. Vibhaṅgepi vuttaṃ – “iti ayañca vitakko ayañca vicāro santā honti samitā vūpasantā atthaṅgatā abbhatthaṅgatā appitā byappitā sositā visositā byantīkatā, tena vuccati avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti.

Without applied thought, without sustained thought: because they are abandoned through cultivation, there is no applied thought in this jhāna, thus it is ‘without applied thought.’ By this same method, it is ‘without sustained thought.’ In the Vibhaṅga it is also said: ‘Thus, this applied thought and this sustained thought are calmed, stilled, subsided, set, completely set, given up, relinquished, dried up, utterly dried up, and brought to an end. Therefore, it is called “without applied thought, without sustained thought.”’

Etthāha – nanu ca vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti imināpi ayamattho siddho? Atha kasmā puna ‘vuttaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāra’nti? Vuccate – evametaṃ, siddhovāyamattho, na panetaṃ tadatthadīpakaṃ. Nanu avocumha – ‘oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ [M 0.0215] samadhigamo hotīti dīpanatthaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti evaṃ vutta’nti.

Here it is said: ‘But is not this meaning already established by “with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought”? Then why is it said again, “without applied thought, without sustained thought”?’ It is said: ‘Yes, it is so; this meaning is established, but that phrase is not indicative of this meaning. Have we not said that the phrase “with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought” is stated for the purpose of showing that the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, which are beyond the first jhāna, occurs by transcending the grosser factor?’

Apica vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ sampasādanaṃ, na kilesakālusiyassa; vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā ekodibhāvaṃ, na upacārajjhānamiva nīvaraṇappahānā; na paṭhamajjhānamiva ca aṅgapātubhāvāti evaṃ sampasādanaekodibhāvānaṃ hetuparidīpakamidaṃ vacanaṃ. Tathā vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ, na tatiyacatutthajjhānāni viya, cakkhuviññāṇādīni viya ca, abhāvāti evaṃ avitakkaavicārabhāvassa hetuparidīpakañca, na vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakaṃ. Vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakameva pana avitakkaṃ avicāranti idaṃ vacanaṃ, tasmā purimaṃ vatvāpi puna vattabbamevāti.

Furthermore, this serene confidence arises from the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, not from the stilling of the impurity of the defilements; and unification arises from the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, not as in access concentration from the abandoning of the hindrances, nor as in the first jhāna from the manifestation of its factors. Thus, this statement demonstrates the cause of serene confidence and unification. Similarly, this state is without applied thought and without sustained thought due to the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, not like the third and fourth jhānas, nor like eye-consciousness and so on, due to their mere absence. Thus, this demonstrates the cause of the state of being without applied thought and without sustained thought, not merely indicating the absence of applied thought and sustained thought. The statement ‘without applied thought, without sustained thought,’ however, merely indicates the absence of applied thought and sustained thought. Therefore, even though the former has been stated, the latter must be stated again.

Samādhijanti paṭhamajjhānasamādhito sampayuttasamādhito vā jātanti attho. Tattha kiñcāpi [P 0.0171][V 0.0215] paṭhamampi sampayuttasamādhito jātaṃ, atha kho ayameva samādhi ‘samādhī’ti vattabbataṃ arahati, vitakkavicārakkhobhavirahena ativiya acalattā suppasannattā ca. Tasmā imassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ idameva samādhijanti vuttaṃ. Pītisukhanti idaṃ vuttanayameva.

Born of concentration: this means it is born from the concentration of the first jhāna or from its associated concentration. In this regard, although the first jhāna is also born from associated concentration, it is only this concentration that deserves to be called ‘concentration’ par excellence, being exceedingly unshaken and perfectly serene due to the absence of the agitation of applied thought and sustained thought. Therefore, to praise its quality, it is said, ‘born of concentration.’ As for ‘joy and happiness,’ this is in the way already stated.

Dutiyanti gaṇanānupubbatā dutiyaṃ. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ samāpajjatītipi dutiyaṃ. Tasmiṃ samaye phasso hotītiādīsu jhānapañcake vitakkavicārapadāni maggapañcake ca sammāsaṅkappapadaṃ parihīnaṃ. Tesaṃ vasena savibhattikāvibhattikapadavinicchayo veditabbo. Koṭṭhāsavārepi tivaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti, caturaṅgiko maggo hotīti āgataṃ. Sesaṃ paṭhamajjhānasadisamevāti.

Second: it is second in numerical sequence. It is also second because one attains this second jhāna. In the passages beginning ‘At that time, there is contact,’ in the fivefold jhāna analysis, the terms for applied thought and sustained thought are absent; and in the fivefold path analysis, the term for right thought is absent. By means of these, the determination of terms with and without case endings should be understood. Also in the section on constituents, it is stated: ‘the jhāna is threefold’ and ‘the path is fourfold.’ The rest is just like the first jhāna.

Dutiyaṃ.

The Second is concluded.

Tatiyajjhānaṃ

The Third Jhāna

163. Tatiyajjhānaniddese pītiyā ca virāgāti virāgo nāma vuttappakārāya pītiyā jigucchanaṃ vā samatikkamo vā. Ubhinnaṃ pana antarā ‘ca’-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. So vūpasamaṃ vā sampiṇḍeti vitakkavicāravūpasamaṃ vā. Tattha yadā vūpasamameva sampiṇḍeti tadā pītiyā virāgā ca, kiñca bhiyyo ‘vūpasamā’ cāti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Imissā ca yojanāya virāgo jigucchanattho hoti. Tasmā pītiyā jigucchanā ca vūpasamā [M 0.0216] cāti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo. Yadā pana vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamaṃ sampiṇḍeti tadā pītiyā ca virāgā kiñca bhiyyo ‘vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā’ti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Imissā ca yojanāya virāgo samatikkamanattho hoti, tasmā pītiyā ca samatikkamā vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamāti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo.

163. In the exposition of the third jhāna, regarding “from the fading away of rapture,” fading away means either disgust with rapture as described above or the transcending of it. The word “ca” (“and”) between the two serves to connect them. It connects either “cessation” or “the cessation of applied and sustained thought.” Here, when it connects only “cessation,” the construction should be understood as: “from the fading away of rapture and, moreover, from ‘cessation.’” In this construction, “fading away” has the meaning of disgust. Therefore, the meaning should be seen as: “from disgust with rapture and from cessation.” But when it connects “the cessation of applied and sustained thought,” the construction should be understood as: “from the fading away of rapture and, moreover, from ‘the cessation of applied and sustained thought.’” In this construction, “fading away” has the meaning of transcending. Therefore, the meaning should be seen as: “from the transcending of rapture and from the cessation of applied and sustained thought.”

Kāmañcete vitakkavicārā dutiyajjhāneyeva vūpasantā, imassa pana jhānassa maggaparidīpanatthaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthañcetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamāti hi vutte idaṃ paññāyati – nūna vitakkavicāravūpasamo maggo imassa jhānassāti? Yathā ca tatiye ariyamagge [V 0.0216] appahīnānampi sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ “pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ [P 0.0172] saṃyojanānaṃ pahānā”ti (ma. ni. 2.132) evaṃ pahānaṃ vuccamānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti, tadadhigamāya ussukkānaṃ ussāhajanakaṃ, evameva idha avūpasantānampi vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamo vuccamāno vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti. Tenāyamattho vutto – ‘pītiyā ca samatikkamā vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā’ti.

Although these applied and sustained thoughts have already subsided in the second jhāna, this is stated here to clarify the path to this jhāna and for the purpose of commendation. For when it is said, 'from the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,' this is understood: 'Surely the path to this jhāna is the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.' Just as in the third noble path, though identity view and other defilements have not yet been abandoned, their abandonment is spoken of as 'from the abandoning of the five lower fetters' (MN 2.132), and this being spoken of serves as a commendation—generating effort in those striving to attain it—so too here, speaking of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, even though they have already subsided, serves as a commendation. Therefore, this meaning is stated: 'from the transcendence of rapture and from the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.'

Upekkhako ca viharatīti – ettha upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā. Samaṃ passati, apakkhapatitā hutvā passatīti attho. Tāya visadāya vipulāya thāmagatāya samannāgatattā tatiyajjhānasamaṅgī upekkhakoti vuccati.

"And he dwells equanimous"—here, equanimity (upekkhā) is so called because it oversees impartially (upapattito ikkhati). The meaning is that one sees evenly, seeing without partiality. Because one is endowed with this clear, expansive, and powerful equanimity, one possessing the third jhāna is called "equanimous."

Upekkhā pana dasavidhā hoti – chaḷaṅgupekkhā brahmavihārupekkhā bojjhaṅgupekkhā vīriyupekkhā saṅkhārupekkhā vedanupekkhā vipassanupekkhā tatramajjhattupekkhā jhānupekkhā pārisuddhupekkhāti.

Now, equanimity is of ten kinds: six-factored equanimity, divine-abiding equanimity, enlightenment-factor equanimity, effort equanimity, equanimity regarding formations, feeling equanimity, insight equanimity, equanimity of balance, jhāna equanimity, and purification equanimity.

Tattha yā “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti, na dummano, upekkhako ca viharati sato sampajāno”ti (a. ni. 5.1; mahāni. 90; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 18; paṭi. ma. 3.17) evamāgatā khīṇāsavassa chasu dvāresu iṭṭhāniṭṭhachaḷārammaṇāpāthe parisuddhapakatibhāvāvijahanākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘chaḷaṅgupekkhā’ nāma.

Herein, the equanimity described thus: "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and fully aware" (AN 5.1; Mahāni 90; etc.)—this equanimity, which occurs in the six sense doors of one whose taints are destroyed, and which has the characteristic of not abandoning the state of natural purity in the face of agreeable and disagreeable sense objects—is called "six-factored equanimity."

Yā [M 0.0217] pana “upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.556; ma. ni. 1.77) evamāgatā sattesu majjhattākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘brahmavihārupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "With a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction" (DN 1.556; MN 1.77)—this equanimity, which has the characteristic of neutrality towards beings, is called 'divine-abiding equanimity'.

Yā “upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissita”nti (ma. ni. 1.27; 3.247) evamāgatā sahajātadhammānaṃ majjhattākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘bojjhaṅgupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "He develops the equanimity enlightenment factor, dependent on seclusion" (MN 1.27; 3.247)—this equanimity, which has the characteristic of neutrality towards co-arisen states, is called "enlightenment-factor equanimity."

Yā [V 0.0217] pana “kālena kālaṃ upekkhānimittaṃ manasi karotī”ti (a. ni. 3.103) evamāgatā anaccāraddhanātisithilavīriyasaṅkhātā upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘vīriyupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "From time to time one attends to the sign of equanimity" (AN 3.103)—this equanimity, known as effort that is neither too exerted nor too lax, is called 'effort-equanimity'.

Yā “kati saṅkhārupekkhā samathavasena uppajjanti, kati saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanāvasena uppajjanti? Aṭṭha saṅkhārupekkhā samathavasena uppajjanti, dasa saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanāvasena uppajjantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.57) evamāgatā nīvaraṇādipaṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanāgahaṇe majjhattabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘saṅkhārupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity? How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight? Eight kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity, and ten kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.57)—this equanimity, which is neutral in taking up the contemplation and firm stability concerning hindrances and so forth, is called 'equanimity regarding formations.'

Yā pana “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti upekkhāsahagata”nti (dha. sa. 150) evamāgatā adukkhamasukhasaṅkhātā upekkhā ayaṃ ‘vedanupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "At the time when a wholesome sense-sphere mind arises, accompanied by equanimity" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 150)—this equanimity, reckoned as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, is called 'feeling-equanimity'.

Yā “yadatthi, yaṃ bhūtaṃ, taṃ pajahati, upekkhaṃ paṭilabhatī”ti [P 0.0173] (ma. ni. 3.71; a. ni. 7.55) evamāgatā vicinane majjhattabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘vipassanupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "One abandons what there is, what has come to be, and attains equanimity" (Majjhima Nikāya 3.71; Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.55)—this equanimity, which is neutral in investigation, is called 'insight-equanimity'.

Yā pana chandādīsu yevāpanakesu āgatā sahajātānaṃ samavāhitabhūtā upekkhā ayaṃ, ‘tatramajjhattupekkhā’ nāma.

And that equanimity which arises in relation to factors such as desire and other miscellaneous factors, and which has the nature of applying effort evenly among co-arisen states—this is called 'equanimity of balance'.

Yā “upekkhako ca viharatī”ti (dha. sa. 163; dī. ni. 1.230) evamāgatā aggasukhepi tasmiṃ apakkhapātajananī upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘jhānupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "And one dwells equanimous" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 163; Dīgha Nikāya 1.230)—this equanimity, which does not generate partiality even toward that highest bliss, is called 'jhāna-equanimity'.

Yā “upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhāna”nti evamāgatā sabbapaccanīkaparisuddhā paccanīkavūpasamanepi abyāpārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ ‘pārisuddhupekkhā’ nāma.

The equanimity described thus: "the fourth jhāna, with purity of mindfulness due to equanimity"—this equanimity, which is purified of all opposing factors and is of a nature where there is no activity even in the subsiding of opposing factors, is called 'purification-equanimity'.

Tattha chaḷaṅgupekkhā ca brahmavihārupekkhā ca bojjhaṅgupekkhā ca tatramajjhattupekkhā ca jhānupekkhā ca pārisuddhupekkhā ca atthato ekā tatramajjhattupekkhāva hoti. Tena tena avatthābhedena panassā ayaṃ bhedo[M 0.0218]. Ekassāpi sato sattassa kumārayuvathera senāpatirājādivasena bhedo viya. Tasmā tāsu yattha chaḷaṅgupekkhā na tattha bojjhaṅgupekkhādayo, yattha vā pana bojjhaṅgupekkhā na tattha chaḷaṅgupekkhādayo hontīti veditabbā.

Herein, the six-factored equanimity, the divine-abiding equanimity, the enlightenment-factor equanimity, the equanimity of balance, the jhāna-equanimity, and the purification equanimity are, in essential meaning, one: the equanimity of balance itself. However, this distinction arises for it due to different states, just as a single being may be distinguished as a child, a youth, an elder, a general, or a king. Therefore, it should be known that among them, where the six-factored equanimity occurs, the enlightenment-factor equanimity and others do not; and where the enlightenment-factor equanimity occurs, the six-factored equanimity and others do not.

Yathā [V 0.0218] cetāsaṃ atthato ekībhāvo, evaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāvipassanupekkhānampi. Paññā eva hi esā kiccavasena dvidhā bhinnā. Yathā hi purisassa sāyaṃ gehaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ sappaṃ ajapadadaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pariyesamānassa taṃ thusakoṭṭhake nipannaṃ disvā ‘sappo nu kho no’ti avalokentassa sovatthikattayaṃ disvā nibbematikassa ‘sappo, na sappo’ti vicinane majjhattatā hoti; evameva yā āraddhavipassakassa vipassanāñāṇena lakkhaṇattaye diṭṭhe saṅkhārānaṃ aniccabhāvādivicinane majjhattatā uppajjati, ayaṃ ‘vipassanupekkhā’. Yathā pana tassa purisassa ajapadadaṇḍakena gāḷhaṃ sappaṃ gahetvā ‘kintāhaṃ imaṃ sappaṃ aviheṭhento attānañca iminā aḍaṃsāpento muñceyya’nti muñcanākārameva pariyesato gahaṇe majjhattatā hoti; evameva yā lakkhaṇattayassa diṭṭhattā, āditte viya tayo bhave passato, saṅkhāraggahaṇe majjhattatā, ayaṃ ‘saṅkhārupekkhā’. Iti vipassanupekkhāya siddhāya saṅkhārupekkhāpi siddhāva hoti. Iminā panesā vicinanaggahaṇesu majjhattasaṅkhātena kiccena dvidhā bhinnāti. Viriyupekkhā pana vedanupekkhā ca aññamaññañca avasesāhi [P 0.0174] ca atthato bhinnāyevāti.

Just as these are one in essential meaning, so too are equanimity towards formations and insight-equanimity. Indeed, this is simply wisdom, divided into two by way of function. For instance, it is like a man who, having entered his house in the evening and taken up a goat's-foot-shaped stick, is searching for a snake. Seeing it lying in a pile of husks, he looks at it thinking, 'Is it a snake or not?' Upon seeing the three beautiful folds on its neck, he becomes free from doubt, and there is neutrality in his investigation of 'Is it a snake, or is it not a snake?'. In the very same way, for a practitioner who has undertaken insight, when the three characteristics have been seen with insight-knowledge, the neutrality that arises in investigating the nature of formations as impermanent and so on, this is 'insight-equanimity'. Furthermore, it is like that man who, having firmly grasped the snake with the goat's-foot-shaped stick, seeks only a way to release it, thinking, 'How might I release this snake without harming it and without being bitten by it?' and there is neutrality in the act of grasping. In the very same way, because the three characteristics have been seen, for one who sees the three states of existence as if ablaze, the neutrality that arises in the grasping of formations, this is 'equanimity towards formations'. Thus, when insight-equanimity is accomplished, equanimity towards formations is also accomplished. However, by this function, designated as neutrality in investigating and in grasping, it is divided into two. But equanimity of energy and equanimity of feeling are, in essence, indeed distinct from each other and from the remaining types.

Imāsu dasasu upekkhāsu ‘jhānupekkhā’ idha adhippetā. Sā majjhattalakkhaṇā anābhogarasā abyāpārapaccupaṭṭhānā pītivirāgapadaṭṭhānāti. Etthāha – nanu cāyaṃ atthato tatramajjhattupekkhāva hoti? Sā ca paṭhamadutiyajjhānesupi atthi, tasmā tatrāpi ‘upekkhako ca viharatī’ti evamayaṃ vattabbā siyā. Sā kasmā na vuttāti? Aparibyattakiccato. Aparibyattañhi tassā tattha kiccaṃ, vitakkādīhi abhibhūtattā. Idha panāyaṃ vitakkavicārapītīhi anabhibhūtattā ukkhittasirā viya hutvā paribyattakiccā jātā, tasmā vuttāti.

Among these ten kinds of equanimity, 'jhāna-equanimity' is intended here. It has the characteristic of neutrality, its function is non-application, its manifestation is non-exertion, and it has dispassion for rapture as its proximate cause. Here it is said: Is this not, in essence, just the equanimity of neutrality? And that also exists in the first and second jhānas; therefore, there too it should be stated, 'and he dwells equanimous.' Why is it not stated? Because its function is not manifest. Indeed, its function there is not manifest because it is overwhelmed by initial thought and so on. Here, however, not being overwhelmed by initial thought, sustained thought, and rapture, it becomes like one with head held high, and its function becomes manifest. Therefore, it is stated.

Niṭṭhitā upekkhako ca viharatīti etassa

The explanation of 'and he dwells equanimous' is concluded.

Sabbaso atthavaṇṇanā.

The complete explanation of the meaning.

Idāni [M 0.0219] sato ca sampajānoti ettha saratīti sato. Sampajānātīti sampajāno. Iti puggalena sati ca sampajaññañca vuttaṃ. Tattha saraṇalakkhaṇā sati, asammussanarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā. Asammohalakkhaṇaṃ sampajaññaṃ, tīraṇarasaṃ, pavicayapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Now, concerning 'mindful and clearly comprehending': here, 'one who remembers' is mindful. 'One who clearly comprehends' is clearly comprehending. Thus, mindfulness and clear comprehension are spoken of in reference to a person. Here, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, its function is not forgetting, and its manifestation is protection. Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion, its function is discernment, and its manifestation is investigation.

Tattha kiñcāpi idaṃ satisampajaññaṃ purimajjhānesupi atthi – muṭṭhassatissa hi asampajānassa [V 0.0219] upacāramattampi na sampajjati, pageva appanā – oḷārikattā pana tesaṃ jhānānaṃ, bhūmiyaṃ viya purisassa, cittassa gati sukhā hoti, abyattaṃ tattha satisampajaññakiccaṃ. Oḷārikaṅgappahānena pana sukhumattā imassa jhānassa, purisassa khuradhārāyaṃ viya, satisampajaññakiccapariggahitā eva cittassa gati icchitabbāti idheva vuttaṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo? Yathā dhenupago vaccho dhenuto apanīto arakkhiyamāno punadeva dhenuṃ upagacchati, evamidaṃ tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ pītito apanītampi satisampajaññārakkhena arakkhiyamānaṃ punadeva pītiṃ upagaccheyya, pītisampayuttameva siyā. Sukhe vāpi sattā sārajjanti, idañca atimadhuraṃ sukhaṃ, tato paraṃ sukhābhāvā. Satisampajaññānubhāvena panettha sukhe asārajjanā hoti, no aññathāti imampi atthavisesaṃ dassetuṃ idamidheva vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the earlier jhānas—for one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension cannot even achieve access concentration, let alone absorption—due to the coarseness of those jhānas, the mind's movement is easy, like a man on the ground. There, the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not manifest. However, by abandoning the coarser factors, due to the subtlety of this jhāna, the mind's movement must be guided by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a man on a razor's edge. It is for this reason that it has been stated here. Furthermore, just as a calf that follows the cow, when separated from the cow and left unguarded, returns again to the cow, so too this happiness of the third jhāna, though separated from rapture, if unguarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension, might return again to rapture and become associated with rapture. Moreover, beings are attached to happiness, and this happiness is extremely sweet, as there is no happiness beyond it. Yet here, through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, there is no attachment to this happiness; it is not otherwise. To show this special meaning, this has been stated here, it should be understood.

Idāni sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti ettha [P 0.0175] kiñcāpi tatiyajjhānasamaṅgino sukhapaṭisaṃvedanābhogo natthi, evaṃ santepi yasmā tassa nāmakāyena sampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, yaṃ vā taṃ nāmakāyasampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānenassa yasmā atipaṇītena rūpena rūpakāyo phuṭo, yassa phuṭattā jhānā vuṭṭhitopi sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeyya, tasmā etamatthaṃ dassento ‘sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetī’ti āha.

Now, concerning 'and he experiences happiness with the body': here, although one who has attained the third jhāna has no deliberate enjoyment of experiencing happiness, still, because there is happiness associated with his mental body, and because, originating from that happiness associated with the mental body, his physical body is pervaded by a very sublime material form—due to which pervasion he might experience happiness even after emerging from the jhāna—therefore, to show this meaning, it is said, 'and he experiences happiness with the body.'

Idāni yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti ettha yaṃjhānahetu yaṃjhānakāraṇā taṃ tatiyajjhānasamaṅgīpuggalaṃ buddhādayo ariyā “ācikkhanti desenti paññāpenti paṭṭhapenti vivaranti vibhajanti uttānīkaronti pakāse”nti pasaṃsantīti adhippāyo – kinti? ‘Upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti – taṃ tatiyajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti evamettha yojanā veditabbā.

Now, concerning 'that which the noble ones describe: "equanimous, mindful, a happy dweller"': here, the intended meaning is that the noble ones, such as the Buddhas, praise that person endowed with the third jhāna—on account of which jhāna, for which reason—by 'describing, teaching, making known, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, clarifying, and revealing' him. How? As: 'equanimous, mindful, a happy dweller'. The connection here should be understood thus: he abides having attained that third jhāna.

Kasmā [M 0.0220] pana taṃ te evaṃ pasaṃsantīti? Pasaṃsārahato. Ayañhi yasmā atimadhurasukhe sukhapāramippattepi tatiyajjhāne upekkhako, na tattha sukhābhisaṅgena ākaḍḍhīyati, ‘yathā ca pīti na uppajjati’ evaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitāya satimā, yasmā ca ariyakantaṃ ariyajanasevitameva asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ nāmakāyena paṭisaṃvedeti tasmā pasaṃsāraho; iti pasaṃsārahato naṃ ariyā te evaṃ pasaṃsāhetubhūte guṇe pakāsentā ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti evaṃ pasaṃsantīti veditabbaṃ.

But why do they praise him thus? Because he is worthy of praise. For since he is equanimous in the third jhāna, which is supremely sweet happiness and has attained the highest happiness, he is not drawn in by attachment to that happiness; and he is mindful, with mindfulness well established, so that rapture does not arise. And since he experiences with the mental body that untainted happiness which is beloved by the noble ones and resorted to by noble people, he is worthy of praise. Thus, because he is worthy of praise, the noble ones, revealing these qualities which are the cause for praise, praise him thus: 'equanimous, mindful, a happy dweller.' It should be understood thus.

Tatiyanti [V 0.0220] gaṇanānupubbatā tatiyaṃ. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ samāpajjatītipi tatiyaṃ. Tasmiṃ samaye phasso hotītiādīsu jhānapañcake pītipadampi parihīnaṃ. Tassāpi vasena savibhattikāvibhattikapadavinicchayo veditabbo. Koṭṭhāsavārepi duvaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hotīti āgataṃ. Sesaṃ dutiyajjhānasadisamevāti.

It is the third according to the numerical sequence. It is also the third because one attains this third jhāna. In the passages beginning with 'At that time, there is contact,' in the fivefold jhāna classification, the term for rapture is also omitted. With reference to that omission as well, the determination of terms with and without inflection should be understood. In the section on constituents, it is also stated, 'the jhāna has two factors.' The remainder is just like that of the second jhāna.

Tatiyaṃ.

The Third Jhāna.

Catutthajjhānaṃ

The Fourth Jhāna.

165. Catutthajjhānaniddese sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānāti kāyikasukhassa ca kāyikadukkhassa ca pahānā. Pubbevāti tañca kho pubbeva na catutthajjhānakkhaṇe. Somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cetasikasukhassa ca cetasikadukkhassa cāti imesampi [P 0.0176] dvinnaṃ pubbeva atthaṅgamā; pahānā icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Kadā pana nesaṃ pahānaṃ hoti? Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇe. Somanassañhi catutthajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyati. Dukkhadomanassasukhāni paṭhamadutiyatatiyajjhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇesu. Evametesaṃ pahānakkamena avuttānaṃ indriyavibhaṅge pana indriyānaṃ uddesakkameneva idhāpi vuttānaṃ sukhadukkhasomanassadomanassānaṃ pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

165. In the exposition of the fourth jhāna, 'the abandoning of pleasure and pain' refers to the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain. 'Previously' means even before, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna. 'The disappearance of joy and grief' refers to the abandoning of mental pleasure and mental pain—thus, the disappearance of these two also occurs previously; 'abandoning' is simply what is stated. But when does their abandoning take place? At the access concentration of the four jhānas. For joy is abandoned precisely at the access concentration of the fourth jhāna. Pain, grief, and pleasure are abandoned at the access concentrations for the first, second, and third jhānas, respectively. Thus, regarding these feelings whose order of abandoning is not stated here, the abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief, which are also mentioned here, should be understood to be in accordance with the order of exposition of the faculties in the Indriyavibhaṅga.

Yadi panetāni tassa tassa jhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyanti, atha kasmā “kattha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva [M 0.0221] kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati. Kattha cuppannaṃ domanassindriyaṃ… sukhindriyaṃ… somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Etthuppannaṃ somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.510) evaṃ jhānesveva nirodho vuttoti? Atisayanirodhattā. Atisayanirodho hi tesaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu, na nirodhoyeva. Nirodhoyeva pana upacārakkhaṇe, nātisayanirodho. Tathā hi nānāvajjane paṭhamajjhānupacāre [V 0.0221] niruddhassāpi dukkhindriyassa ḍaṃsamakasādisamphassena vā, visamāsanupatāpena vā siyā uppatti, natveva antoappanāyaṃ. Upacāre vā niruddhampetaṃ na suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti, paṭipakkhena avihatattā. Antoappanāyaṃ pana pītipharaṇena sabbo kāyo sukhokkanto hoti. Sukhokkantakāyassa ca suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti dukkhindriyaṃ, paṭipakkhena vihatattā. Nānāvajjaneyeva ca dutiyajjhānupacāre pahīnassa domanassindriyassa yasmā etaṃ vitakkavicārapaccayepi kāyakilamathe cittupaghāte ca sati uppajjati, vitakkavicārābhāve neva uppajjati; yattha pana uppajjati tattha vitakkavicārabhāve; appahīnā eva ca dutiyajjhānupacāre vitakkavicārāti tatthassa siyā uppatti, natveva dutiyajjhāne, pahīnapaccayattā. Tathā tatiyajjhānupacāre pahīnassāpi sukhindriyassa pītisamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭakāyassa siyā uppatti, natveva tatiyajjhāne. Tatiyajjhāne hi sukhassa paccayabhūtā pīti sabbaso niruddhāti. Tathā [P 0.0177] catutthajjhānupacāre pahīnassāpi somanassindriyassa āsannattā, appanāppattāya upekkhāya abhāvena sammā anatikkantattā ca, siyā uppatti, natveva catutthajjhāne. Tasmā eva ca ‘etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī’ti tattha tattha aparisesaggahaṇaṃ katanti.

But if these faculties are abandoned only during the access moment of each jhāna, then why is it said: 'Where does the arisen pain faculty cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. There, the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder. Where does the arisen grief faculty... pleasure faculty... joy faculty cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. There, the arisen joy faculty ceases without remainder' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.510)? Why is their cessation thus stated to be in the jhānas themselves? Because of their surpassing cessation. For in the first jhāna and so on, there is a surpassing cessation of these faculties, not merely cessation. In the access moment, however, there is only cessation, not surpassing cessation. For instance, even when the pain faculty has ceased in the access to the first jhāna, it might arise from contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or from the affliction of an unsuitable posture, but it certainly would not arise within full absorption. Or, even though it has ceased in the access, it is not well ceased, because it has not been overcome by its opposite. But within full absorption, the entire body is suffused with bliss by the pervasion of rapture. For one whose body is suffused with bliss, the pain faculty is well ceased, because it has been overcome by its opposite. Similarly, since the grief faculty arises when there is bodily fatigue and mental affliction, which are conditioned by thought and examination, and it never arises in the absence of thought and examination; and since thought and examination are not yet abandoned in the access to the second jhāna, it might arise there. But it certainly does not arise in the second jhāna, because its conditions have been abandoned. Likewise, though the pleasure faculty has been abandoned in the access to the third jhāna, it might arise for one whose body is touched by refined matter produced by rapture, but it certainly does not arise in the third jhāna. For in the third jhāna, rapture, which is the condition for pleasure, has completely ceased. Similarly, though the joy faculty has been abandoned in the access to the fourth jhāna, it might arise due to its proximity to the third jhāna, and because it has not been properly transcended due to the absence of the equanimity that has reached full absorption. But it certainly does not arise in the fourth jhāna. Therefore, in each respective case, the term 'without remainder' is included in the phrase 'there, the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder'.

Etthāha – ‘athevaṃ tassa tassa jhānassupacāre pahīnāpi etā vedanā idha kasmā samāhaṭā’ti? ‘Sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ’. Yā hi ayaṃ ‘adukkhamasukha’nti ettha adukkhamasukhā vedanā vuttā, sā sukhumā, dubbiññeyyā, na sakkā sukhena gahetuṃ. Tasmā yathā nāma duṭṭhassa yathā tathā vā upasaṅkamitvā gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa goṇassa gahaṇatthaṃ gopo ekasmiṃ vaje sabbā gāvo samāharati, athekekaṃ nīharanto paṭipāṭiyā āgataṃ ‘ayaṃ [M 0.0222] so, gaṇhatha na’nti tampi gāhāpayati; evameva bhagavā sukhagahaṇatthaṃ sabbāpi etā samāharīti. Evañhi samāhaṭā etā dassetvā yaṃ neva sukhaṃ na dukkhaṃ, na somanassaṃ na domanassaṃ, ayaṃ adukkhamasukhāvedanāti sakkā hoti esā gāhayituṃ.

Here it is said: ‘But if these feelings have been abandoned in the access to each respective jhāna, why are they assembled here?’ ‘For the purpose of easy grasping.’ For this feeling called ‘neither-painful-nor-pleasant,’ mentioned here, is subtle, hard to discern, and cannot be grasped easily. Therefore, just as a cowherd, in order to catch a vicious bull that cannot be approached and caught in just any way, gathers all the cows into one enclosure, and then, bringing them out one by one in order, has that one caught by saying, ‘This is it, catch it!’; in the same way, the Blessed One assembles all these feelings here for the purpose of easy grasping. For when they have been assembled and shown in this way, it becomes possible to have this feeling grasped by explaining: ‘That which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither joy nor grief—this is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

Apica adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā paccayadassanatthañcāpi etā vuttāti veditabbā. Sukhadukkhappahānādayo hi tassā paccayā. Yathāha – “cattāro kho, āvuso, paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā. Idhāvuso bhikkhu, sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ime kho, āvuso, cattāro paccayā adukkhamasukhāya [V 0.0222] cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.458). Yathā vā aññattha pahīnāpi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo tatiyamaggassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ tattha pahīnāti vuttā, evaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthampetassa jhānassetā idha vuttāti veditabbā. Paccayaghātena vā ettha rāgadosānaṃ atidūrabhāvaṃ dassetumpetā vuttāti veditabbā. Etāsu hi sukhaṃ somanassassa paccayo, somanassaṃ rāgassa; dukkhaṃ domanassassa, domanassaṃ dosassa. Sukhādighātena ca sappaccayā rāgadosā hatāti atidūre hontīti.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these are also mentioned for the purpose of showing the conditions for the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and so on, are its conditions. As it is said: ‘There are, friend, four conditions for the attainment of the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Here, friend, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. These, friend, are the four conditions for the attainment of the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant’ (MN 1.458). Or, just as elsewhere, although identity-view and so on have been abandoned, they are said to be abandoned there for the purpose of speaking in praise of the third path, so too, it should be understood that these are mentioned here for the purpose of speaking in praise of this jhāna. Alternatively, it should be understood that they are mentioned here to show the state of being extremely far from lust and hatred through the striking down of their conditions. For among these, pleasure is a condition for mental pleasure, and mental pleasure for lust; pain is a condition for mental pain, and mental pain for hatred. And by the striking down of pleasure and so on, lust and hatred together with their conditions are struck down, thus they become extremely far away.

Adukkhamasukhanti dukkhābhāvena adukkhaṃ, sukhābhāvena asukhaṃ. Etenettha dukkhasukhappaṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tatiyavedanaṃ dīpeti, na dukkhasukhābhāvamattaṃ. Tatiyavedanā nāma adukkhamasukhā. Upekkhātipi vuccati. Sā [P 0.0178] iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā, majjhattarasā, avibhūtapaccupaṭṭhānā, sukhanirodhapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

‘Neither-painful-nor-pleasant’ means: not painful due to the absence of pain, not pleasant due to the absence of pleasure. By this, it indicates the third feeling, which is the counterpart to pain and pleasure, not the mere absence of pain and pleasure.
