The third feeling is named ‘neither-painful-nor-pleasant.’ It is also called ‘equanimity.’ It should be understood as having the characteristic of neutral experience, the function of impartiality, the manifestation of being subtle, and the proximate cause of the cessation of pleasure.

Upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti upekkhāya janitasatipārisuddhiṃ. Imasmiñhi jhāne suparisuddhā sati. Yā ca tassā satiyā pārisuddhi sā upekkhāya katā, na aññena. Tasmā etaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhīti vuccati. Vibhaṅgepi vuttaṃ – “ayaṃ sati imāya upekkhāya visadā hoti parisuddhā pariyodātā, tena vuccati upekkhāsatipārisuddhī”ti (vibha. 597). Yāya ca upekkhāya ettha sati pārisuddhi hoti sā atthato tatramajjhattatāti veditabbā. Na kevalañcettha tāya satiyeva parisuddhā apica kho sabbepi sampayuttadhammā. Satisīsena pana desanā vuttā.

‘The purity of mindfulness due to equanimity’ means the purity of mindfulness generated by equanimity. For in this jhāna, mindfulness is exceedingly pure. And the purity of that mindfulness is brought about by equanimity, not by anything else. Therefore, this is called ‘the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’ In the Vibhaṅga it is also said: ‘This mindfulness becomes clear, purified, and cleansed through this equanimity, hence it is called “the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity”’ (Vibh 597). And the equanimity by which mindfulness becomes pure here should be understood as, in essence, specific neutrality. And not only is mindfulness purified by it here, but so too are all associated states. The teaching, however, is given with mindfulness as the chief factor.

Tattha [M 0.0223] kiñcāpi ayaṃ upekkhā heṭṭhāpi tīsu jhānesu vijjati – yathā pana divā sūriyappabhābhibhavā sommabhāvena ca attano upakārakattena vā sabhāgāya rattiyā alābhā divā vijjamānāpi candalekhā aparisuddhā hoti apariyodātā – evamayampi tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā vitakkādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavā sabhāgāya ca upekkhāvedanārattiyā appaṭilābhā vijjamānāpi paṭhamādijjhānabhedesu aparisuddhā hoti. Tassā ca aparisuddhāya divā aparisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo aparisuddhāva honti. Tasmā tesu ekampi ‘upekkhāsatipārisuddhī’ti na vuttaṃ. Idha pana vitakkādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavābhāvā sabhāgāya ca upekkhā vedanārattiyā paṭilābhā ayaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā [V 0.0223] ativiya parisuddhā. Tassā parisuddhattā parisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo parisuddhā honti pariyodātā. Tasmā idameva upekkhāsatipārisuddhīti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, although this equanimity exists in the three lower jhānas, it is like this: just as the crescent moon, though present by day, is impure and not cleansed because it is overpowered by the sun’s radiance and because it does not obtain its kindred night, so too this crescent moon of specific neutrality, though existing in the divisions of the first jhāna and so on, is impure because it is overpowered by the radiance of opposing states beginning with initial thought, and because it does not obtain its kindred night of equanimous feeling. And just as the light of that impure crescent moon by day is impure, so too are the co-arisen mindfulness and other states impure. Therefore, not one of those jhānas is called ‘the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’ Here, however, because there is no overpowering by the radiance of opposing states beginning with initial thought, and because it has obtained its kindred night of equanimous feeling, this crescent moon of specific neutrality is exceedingly pure. Due to its purity, the co-arisen mindfulness and other states are pure and cleansed, just like the light of a pure crescent moon. Therefore, it should be understood that this alone is called ‘the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’

Catutthanti gaṇanānupubbatā catutthaṃ. Idaṃ catutthaṃ samāpajjatītipi catutthaṃ. Phasso hotītiādīsu phassapañcake tāva vedanāti upekkhāvedanā veditabbā. Jhānapañcakaindriyaaṭṭhakesu pana upekkhā hoti upekkhindriyaṃ [P 0.0179] hotīti (dha. sa. 165) vuttameva. Sesāni tatiye parihīnapadāni idhāpi parihīnāneva. Koṭṭhāsavārepi duvaṅgikaṃ jhānanti upekkhācittekaggatāvaseneva veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ tatiyasadisamevāti.

‘Fourth’ means fourth by way of numerical sequence. It is also ‘fourth’ because one attains this fourth jhāna. In the pentad of contact beginning with ‘contact occurs,’ ‘feeling’ should be understood as equanimous feeling. But in the pentad of jhāna factors and the octad of faculties, it has already been stated: ‘there is equanimity, there is the faculty of equanimity’ (Dhs 165). The remaining terms that were abandoned in the third jhāna are also abandoned here. Also in the section on divisions, the two-factored jhāna should be understood by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind. All the rest is just the same as the third.

Catukkanayo niṭṭhito.

The fourfold method is concluded.

Pañcakanayo

The Fivefold Method

167. Idāni katame dhammā kusalāti pañcakanayo āraddho. Kasmāti ce, puggalajjhāsayavasena ceva desanāvilāsena ca. Sannisinnadevaparisāya kira ekaccānaṃ devānaṃ vitakko eva oḷārikato upaṭṭhāsi, vicārapītisukhacittekaggatā santato. Tesaṃ sappāyavasena satthā caturaṅgikaṃ avitakkaṃ vicāramattaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ nāma bhājesi. Ekaccānaṃ [M 0.0224] vicāro oḷārikato upaṭṭhāsi, pītisukhacittekaggatā santato. Tesaṃ sappāyavasena tivaṅgikaṃ tatiyajjhānaṃ nāma bhājesi. Ekaccānaṃ pīti oḷārikato upaṭṭhāsi, sukhacittekaggatā santato. Tesaṃ sappāyavasena duvaṅgikaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ nāma bhājesi. Ekaccānaṃ sukhaṃ oḷārikato upaṭṭhāsi, upekkhācittekaggatā santato. Tesaṃ sappāyavasena duvaṅgikaṃ pañcamajjhānaṃ nāma bhājesi. Ayaṃ tāva ‘puggalajjhāsayo’.

167. Now, with the words “Which states are wholesome?” the fivefold method is introduced. If it is asked why, it is because of the individual’s inclination and the elegance of the teaching. It is said that in the assembly of seated devas, for some devas, initial thought arose as coarse, while sustained thought, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind were serene. For their benefit, the Teacher expounded the second jhāna, which has four factors and is without initial thought but with sustained thought only. For some, sustained thought arose as coarse, while joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind were serene. For their benefit, he expounded the third jhāna, which has three factors. For some, joy arose as coarse, while happiness and one-pointedness of mind were serene. For their benefit, he expounded the fourth jhāna, which has two factors. For some, happiness arose as coarse, while equanimity and one-pointedness of mind were serene. For their benefit, he expounded the fifth jhāna, which has two factors. This, for a start, is ‘the individual’s inclination.’

Yassā pana dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā desanāvilāsappatto nāma hoti – sā tathāgatassa suṭṭhu paṭividdhā – tasmā ñāṇamahattatāya desanāvidhānesu kusalo desanāvilāsappatto satthā yaṃ yaṃ [V 0.0224] aṅgaṃ labbhati tassa tassa vasena yathā yathā icchati tathā tathā desanaṃ niyāmetīti so idha pañcaṅgikaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ bhājesi, caturaṅgikaṃ avitakkaṃ vicāramattaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ, bhājesi tivaṅgikaṃ tatiyajjhānaṃ, bhājesi duvaṅgikaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ, duvaṅgikameva pañcamajjhānaṃ bhājesi. Ayaṃ ‘desanāvilāso’ nāma.

Furthermore, he is called ‘one who has attained elegance in exposition’ because the Dhamma element has been thoroughly penetrated by him—that element is indeed well penetrated by the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Teacher, being skilled in the methods of exposition due to the greatness of his knowledge and having attained elegance in exposition, directs the teaching in whatever way he wishes according to whichever factor is obtained. Thus, here he expounded the first jhāna with five factors; he expounded the second jhāna with four factors, which is without initial thought but with sustained thought only; he expounded the third jhāna with three factors; he expounded the fourth jhāna with two factors; and he expounded the fifth jhāna, also with two factors. This is called ‘elegance in exposition.’

Apica ye bhagavatā “tayome, bhikkhave, samādhī – savitakkasavicāro samādhi, avitakkavicāramatto samādhi, avitakkaavicāro samādhī”ti (dī. ni. 3.305) suttante tayo samādhī desitā, tesu heṭṭhā savitakkasavicāro samādhi avitakkaavicāro [P 0.0180] samādhi ca bhājetvā dassito, avitakkavicāramatto na dassito. Taṃ dassetumpi ayaṃ pañcakanayo āraddhoti veditabbo.

Moreover, in the Suttanta where the Blessed One taught, “Monks, there are these three kinds of concentration: concentration with initial and sustained thought, concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, and concentration without initial and sustained thought” (DN 33), of these, concentration with initial and sustained thought and concentration without initial and sustained thought were shown by way of division below, but concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only was not shown. It should be understood that this fivefold method was introduced in order to show that as well.

Tattha dutiyajjhānaniddese phassādīsu vitakkamattaṃ parihāyati, koṭṭhāsavāre “caturaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti caturaṅgiko maggo hotī”ti ayameva viseso. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ paṭhamajjhānasadisameva. Yāni ca catukkanaye dutiyatatiyacatutthāni tāneva idha tatiyacatutthapañcamāni. Tesaṃ adhigamapaṭipāṭidīpanatthaṃ ayaṃ nayo veditabbo –

Therein, in the exposition of the second jhāna, among the states beginning with contact, only initial thought is abandoned. In the section on the constituents, the only difference is this: “the jhāna has four factors; the path has four factors.” All the rest is just like the first jhāna. And those which are the second, third, and fourth jhānas in the fourfold method are here the third, fourth, and fifth. This method should be understood for the purpose of showing the sequence of their attainment.

Eko kira amaccaputto rājānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ janapadato nagaraṃ āgato. So ekadivasameva rājānaṃ disvā pānabyasanena sabbaṃ vibhavajātaṃ nāsesi. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ surāmadamattaṃ niccoḷaṃ katvā jiṇṇakaṭasārakamattena [M 0.0225] paṭicchādetvā pānāgārato nīhariṃsu. Tamenaṃ saṅkārakūṭe nipajjitvā niddāyantaṃ eko aṅgavijjāpāṭhako disvā ‘ayaṃ puriso mahājanassa avassayo bhavissati, paṭijaggitabbo eso’ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā mattikāya nhāpetvā thūlasāṭakayugaṃ nivāsāpetvā puna gandhodakena nhāpetvā sukhumena dukūlayugaḷena acchādetvā pāsādaṃ āropetvā subhojanaṃ bhojetvā ‘evaṃ naṃ paricāreyyāthā’ti paricārake paṭipādetvā pakkāmi. Atha naṃ te sayanaṃ āropesuṃ. Pānāgāragamanapaṭibāhanatthañca naṃ cattāro tāva janā catūsu hatthapādesu uppīḷetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Eko pāde parimajji. Eko tālavaṇṭaṃ gahetvā bīji. Eko vīṇaṃ vādayamāno gāyanto nisīdi.

It is said that a certain minister's son came from the countryside to the city to attend upon the king. Having seen the king on just one day, he destroyed his entire fortune through the vice of drinking. One day, when he was intoxicated with liquor, they stripped him naked, covered him with just a worn-out rush mat, and carried him out of the tavern. As he was lying asleep on a rubbish heap, a reader of the science of bodily marks saw him and, having made the conclusion, “This man will become a refuge for the great populace; he ought to be cared for,” he had him bathed with clay, had him wear a pair of thick cloths, had him bathed again with scented water, covered him with a pair of fine linen cloths, brought him up to a palace, had him eat fine food, and entrusting him to attendants with the words, “Thus should you care for him,” he departed. Then they laid him on a bed. And to prevent him from going to the tavern, four men stood pressing on his four hands and feet. One massaged his feet. One took a palm-leaf fan and fanned him. One sat singing while playing the lute.

So sayanupagamanena vigatakilamatho thokaṃ niddāyitvā vuṭṭhito hatthapādanippīḷanaṃ asahamāno [V 0.0225] ‘ko me hatthapāde uppīḷeti? Apagacchathā’ti tajjesi. Te ekavacaneneva apagacchiṃsu. Tato puna thokaṃ niddāyitvā vuṭṭhito pādaparimajjanaṃ asahamāno ‘ko me pāde parimajjati? Apagacchā’ti āha. Sopi ekavacaneneva apagacchi. Puna thokaṃ niddāyitvā vuṭṭhito vātavuṭṭhi viya tālavaṇṭavātaṃ asahanto ‘ko esa? Apagacchatū’ti āha. Sopi ekavacaneneva apagacchi. Puna thokaṃ niddāyitvā vuṭṭhito kaṇṇasūlaṃ viya gītavāditasaddaṃ asahamāno vīṇāvādakaṃ tajjesi. Sopi ekavacaneneva apagacchi. Athevaṃ [P 0.0181] anukkamena pahīnakilamathuppīḷanaparimajjanavātappahāragītavāditasaddupaddavo sukhaṃ sayitvā vuṭṭhāya rañño santikaṃ agamāsi. Rājāpissa mahantaṃ issariyamadāsi. So mahājanassa avassayo jāto.

His fatigue gone from having gone to bed, he slept a little and then rose. Unable to bear the pressing of his hands and feet, he rebuked them, “Who is pressing my hands and feet? Go away!” They left at his mere word. Then, after sleeping a little more and rising, he could not bear the massaging of his feet and said, “Who is massaging my feet? Go away!” That one also left at his mere word. Again, after sleeping a little and rising, unable to bear the wind from the palm-leaf fan, which was like a squall, he said, “Who is this? Let him go away!” That one too left at his mere word. Once more, after sleeping a little and rising, unable to bear the sound of singing and musical instruments, which was like a thorn in his ear, he rebuked the lute player. That one also left at his mere word. Thus, in sequence, freed from the disturbances of fatigue, pressing, massaging, the blast of wind, and the sound of singing and musical instruments, he slept comfortably, and upon rising, went to the king. The king granted him great lordship, and he became a refuge for the great populace.

Tattha pānabyasanena pārijuññappatto so amaccaputto viya anekabyasanapārijuññappatto gharāvāsagato kulaputto daṭṭhabbo. Aṅgavijjāpāṭhako puriso viya tathāgato. Tassa purisassa ‘ayaṃ mahājanassa avassayo bhavissati, paṭijagganaṃ arahatī’ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ viya tathāgatassa ‘ayaṃ mahājanassa avassayo bhavissati, pabbajjaṃ arahati kulaputto’ti sanniṭṭhānakaraṇaṃ.

Therein, a son of good family living the household life who has come to ruin through many vices should be seen as like that minister's son who came to ruin through the vice of drinking. The Tathāgata should be seen as like the man who was a reader of the science of bodily marks. Just as that man made the conclusion, “This one will become a refuge for the great populace; he is worthy of being cared for,” so too should be understood the Tathāgata’s making of the conclusion, “This one will become a refuge for the great populace; the son of good family is worthy of going forth.”

Athassa [M 0.0226] amaccaputtassa mattikāmattena nhāpanaṃ viya kulaputtassāpi pabbajjāpaṭilābho. Athassa thūlasāṭakanivāsanaṃ viya imassāpi dasasikkhāpadasaṅkhātasīlavatthanivāsanaṃ. Puna tassa gandhodakanhāpanaṃ viya imassāpi pātimokkhasaṃvarādisīlagandhodakanhāpanaṃ. Puna tassa sukhumadukūlayugaḷacchādanaṃ viya imassāpi yathāvuttasīlavisuddhisampadāsaṅkhātadukūlacchādanaṃ.

Then, just as that minister's son was bathed with fine clay, so too is the attainment of the going forth for this son of good family. Just as he was clothed in a coarse garment, so too is the clothing of this one in the garment of virtue called the ten training rules. Again, just as he was bathed with perfumed water, so too is the bathing of this one with the perfumed water of virtue, such as the Pātimokkha restraint. Again, just as he was covered with a pair of fine linen cloths, so too is the covering of this one with the fine garment called the accomplishment of purity of virtue as described.

Dukūlacchāditassa panassa pāsādāropanaṃ viya imassāpi sīlavisuddhidukūlacchāditassa samādhibhāvanāpāsādārohanaṃ. Tato tassa subhojanabhuñjanaṃ viya imassāpi samādhiupakārakasatisampajaññādidhammāmataparibhuñjanaṃ.

Furthermore, just as for that one, covered with a fine garment, there was the being led up to the palace, so too for this one, covered with the fine garment of purity of virtue, there is the ascending of the palace of the development of concentration. Then, just as for that one there was the partaking of excellent food, so too for this one there is the partaking of the ambrosia of qualities beneficial to concentration, such as mindfulness and clear comprehension.

Bhuttabhojanassa pana tassa paricārakehi sayanāropanaṃ viya imassāpi vitakkādīhi upacārajjhānāropanaṃ. Puna tassa pānāgāragamanapaṭibāhanatthaṃ hatthapāduppīḷanakapurisacatukkaṃ viya imassāpi kāmasaññābhimukhagamanapaṭibāhanatthaṃ ārammaṇe cittuppīḷanako nekkhammavitakko. Tassa [V 0.0226] pādaparimajjakapuriso viya imassāpi ārammaṇe cittānumajjanako vicāro. Tassa tālavaṇṭavātadāyako viya imassāpi cetaso sītalabhāvadāyikā pīti.

Furthermore, after having eaten, just as he was placed upon a bed by his attendants, so too is this one raised to access concentration by applied thought and so forth. Again, just as he had a group of four men pressing his hands and feet to prevent him from going to the drinking hall, so too is there the thought of renunciation, which presses the mind onto its object to prevent it from moving towards sensual perceptions. Just as there was a man who massaged his feet, so too is there sustained thought, which repeatedly strokes the mind on its object. Just as there was one who provided a breeze with a palm-leaf fan, so too is there rapture, which gives a state of coolness to the mind.

Tassa sotānuggahakaro gandhabbapuriso viya imassāpi cittānuggāhakaṃ somanassaṃ. Tassa sayanupagamanena vigatakilamathassa thokaṃ niddupagamanaṃ viya imassāpi upacārajjhānasannissayena vigatanīvaraṇakilamathassa paṭhamajjhānupagamanaṃ.

Just as for that one there was a musician who gratified the ear, so too for this one there is gladness, which gratifies the mind. And just as that one, being without fatigue from having approached his bed, fell into a light slumber, so too this one, being without the fatigue of the hindrances through reliance on access concentration, attains the first jhāna.

Athassa niddāyitvā vuṭṭhitassa hatthapāduppīḷanāsahanena hatthapāduppīḷakānaṃ santajjanaṃ tesañca apagamanena puna thokaṃ niddupagamanaṃ viya imassāpi paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhitassa [P 0.0182] cittuppīḷakavitakkāsahanena vitakkadosadassanaṃ, vitakkappahānā ca puna avitakkavicāramattadutiyajjhānupagamanaṃ.

Then, just as for that one, having awakened from slumber, there was the rebuking of those who pressed his hands and feet due to his inability to bear their pressing, and upon their departure, the falling into a light slumber again; so too for this one, having arisen from the first jhāna, there is the seeing of the fault in applied thought due to his inability to bear applied thought which presses the mind, and with the abandoning of applied thought, the attainment again of the second jhāna, which is with only sustained thought and without applied thought.

Tato tassa punappunaṃ niddāyitvā vuṭṭhitassa yathāvuttena kamena pādaparimajjanādīnaṃ asahanena paṭipāṭiyā pādaparimajjakādīnaṃ santajjanaṃ, tesaṃ tesañca apagamanena punappunaṃ thokaṃ niddupagamanaṃ viya imassāpi punappunaṃ dutiyādīhi jhānehi vuṭṭhitassa yathāvuttadosānaṃ vicārādīnaṃ asahanena [M 0.0227] paṭipāṭiyā vicārādidosadassanaṃ. Tesaṃ tesañca pahānā punappunaṃ avitakkaavicāranippītika pahīnasomanassajjhānupagamanaṃ.

Then, just as for that one, repeatedly awakening from slumber, there was the sequential rebuking of the foot-massagers and so on due to his inability to bear them as described, and upon their respective departures, the repeated falling into a light slumber; so too for this one, repeatedly arising from the second jhāna and so forth, there is the sequential seeing of the faults in sustained thought and so on due to his inability to bear them as described. And by abandoning each of these in turn, there is the repeated attainment of the jhānas: the second without applied thought, the third without sustained thought, the fourth without rapture, and the fifth with abandoned gladness.

Tassa pana sayanā vuṭṭhāya rañño santikaṃ gatassa issariyappatti viya imassāpi pañcamajjhānato vuṭṭhitassa vipassanā maggaṃ upagatassa arahattappatti.

Furthermore, just as that one, having arisen from his bed and gone to the king's presence, attained sovereignty, so too this one, having arisen from the fifth jhāna and entered upon the path of insight, attains Arahantship.

Tassa pattissariyassa bahūnaṃ janānaṃ avassayabhāvo viya imassāpi arahattappattassa bahūnaṃ avassayabhāvo veditabbo. Ettāvatā hi esa anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ nāma hotīti.

Just as that one, having attained sovereignty, became a refuge for many people, so too this one, having attained Arahantship, should be understood as a refuge for many. For to this extent, he is indeed called the unsurpassed field of merit.

Pañcakanayo niṭṭhito.

The fivefold method is concluded.

Ettāvatā catukkapañcakanayadvayabhedo suddhikanavako nāma pakāsito hoti. Atthato panesa pañcakanaye catukkanayassa paviṭṭhattā jhānapañcako evāti veditabbo.

To this extent, the pure ninefold method, which is the division into the pair of fourfold and fivefold methods, has been explained. In terms of meaning, however, because the fourfold method is included within the fivefold method, it should be understood as simply the fivefold jhāna.

Paṭipadācatukkaṃ

The Tetrad of Practice

176-180. Idāni [V 0.0227] yasmā etaṃ jhānaṃ nāma paṭipadākamena sijjhati, tasmā tassa paṭipadābhedaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha dukkhā paṭipadā assāti dukkhapaṭipadaṃ. Dandhā abhiññā assāti dandhābhiññaṃ. Iti dukkhapaṭipadanti vā dandhābhiññanti vā pathavīkasiṇanti vā tīṇipi jhānasseva nāmāni. Dukkhapaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññantiādīsupi eseva nayo.

176-180. Now, because this so-called jhāna is accomplished by the sequence of practice, therefore, to show the distinction of its practice, the passage beginning with 'Which states are wholesome?' is begun again. Herein, because its practice is difficult, it is called 'difficult practice.' Because its direct knowledge is slow, it is called 'slow direct knowledge.' Thus, 'difficult practice,' or 'slow direct knowledge,' or 'earth kasiṇa'—these three are all names for the jhāna itself. This same method applies also to the cases beginning with 'difficult practice, swift direct knowledge,' and so on.

Tattha paṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya yāva tassa tassa jhānassa upacāraṃ uppajjati tāva pavattā jhānabhāvanā ‘paṭipadā’ti vuccati. Upacārato pana paṭṭhāya yāva appanā tāva pavattā paññā ‘abhiññā’ti vuccati. Sā panesā paṭipadā ekaccassa dukkhā hoti. Nīvaraṇādipaccanīkadhammasamudācāragahanatāya [P 0.0183] kicchā asukhasevanāti attho. Ekaccassa tadabhāvena sukhā. Abhiññāpi ekaccassa dandhā hoti, mandā, asīghappavatti. Ekaccassa khippā amandā sīghappavatti. Tasmā yo ādito kilese vikkhambhento dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilamanto vikkhambheti[M 0.0228], tassa dukkhā paṭipadā nāma hoti. Yo pana vikkhambhitakileso appanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena aṅgapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa dandhābhiññā nāma hoti. Yo khippaṃ aṅgapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti tassa khippābhiññā nāma hoti. Yo kilese vikkhambhento sukhena akilamanto vikkhambheti, tassa sukhā paṭipadā nāma hoti.

Herein, starting from the first application of mind, the development of jhāna that proceeds until access concentration for that respective jhāna arises is called 'practice.' But starting from access concentration, the wisdom that proceeds until absorption is called 'direct knowledge.' Now, for a certain person, this practice is difficult. The meaning is: it is troublesome and not easily cultivated, due to the denseness of the frequent occurrence of opposing states such as the hindrances. For a certain person, due to the absence of that, it is easy. Direct knowledge, too, is slow for a certain person; it is dull, not arising swiftly. For a certain person, it is swift, not dull, arising swiftly. Therefore, for one who, from the beginning, suppresses the defilements with difficulty, with exertion, with effort, becoming weary, for him the practice is called 'difficult practice.' But for one who, having suppressed the defilements, dwells cultivating for absorption and attains the manifestation of the factors after a long time, for him the direct knowledge is called 'slow direct knowledge.' For one who attains the manifestation of the factors quickly, for him the direct knowledge is called 'swift direct knowledge.' For one who suppresses the defilements with ease, without becoming weary, for him the practice is called 'easy practice'.

Tattha yāni sappāyāsappāyāni ca palibodhupacchedādīni pubbakiccāni ca appanākosallāni ca visuddhimagge cittabhāvanāniddese niddiṭṭhāni, tesu yo asappāyasevī hoti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā dandhā ca abhiññā hoti. Sappāyasevino sukhā paṭipadā khippā ca abhiññā. Yo pana pubbabhāge asappāyaṃ sevitvā aparabhāge sappāyasevī hoti, pubbabhāge vā sappāyaṃ sevitvā aparabhāge asappāyasevī, tassa vomissakatā veditabbā. Tathā palibodhupacchedādikaṃ pubbakiccaṃ asampādetvā bhāvanaṃ anuyuttassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti, vipariyāyena sukhā. Appanākosallāni pana asampādentassa dandhā abhiññā hoti, sampādentassa khippā.

Herein, regarding those suitable and unsuitable things, the preliminary duties such as the cutting off of impediments, and the skills in absorption that were pointed out in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition on the development of consciousness—among these, for one who resorts to the unsuitable, the practice is difficult and the direct knowledge is slow. For one who resorts to the suitable, the practice is easy and the direct knowledge is swift. But for one who, having resorted to the unsuitable in the earlier part, resorts to the suitable in the later part, or having resorted to the suitable in the earlier part, resorts to the unsuitable in the later part, for him the condition should be understood as mixed. Likewise, for one who engages in the development without having accomplished the preliminary duties such as the cutting off of impediments, the practice is difficult; in the opposite case, it is easy. But for one who does not accomplish the skills in absorption, the direct knowledge is slow; for one who does accomplish them, it is swift.

Apica [V 0.0228] taṇhāavijjāvasena samathavipassanākatādhikāravasena cāpi etāsaṃ pabhedo veditabbo. Taṇhābhibhūtassa hi dukkhā paṭipadā hoti, anabhibhūtassa sukhā. Avijjābhibhūtassa ca dandhā abhiññā hoti, anabhibhūtassa khippā. Yo ca samathe akatādhikāro tassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti, katādhikārassa sukhā. Yo pana vipassanāya akatādhikāro hoti, tassa dandhā abhiññā hoti, katādhikārassa khippā.

Furthermore, the distinction of these should also be understood by way of craving and ignorance, and by way of having made a special effort in serenity and insight. For one who is overcome by craving, the practice is difficult; for one not overcome, it is easy. And for one who is overcome by ignorance, the direct knowledge is slow; for one not overcome, it is swift. And for one who has not made a special effort in serenity, the practice is difficult; for one who has made a special effort, it is easy. But for one who has not made a special effort in insight, the direct knowledge is slow; for one who has made a special effort, it is swift.

Kilesindriyavasena cāpi etāsaṃ pabhedo veditabbo. Tibbakilesassa hi mudindriyassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti dandhā ca abhiññā, tikkhindriyassa pana khippā abhiññā. Mandakilesassa ca mudindriyassa sukhā paṭipadā hoti dandhā ca abhiññā, tikkhindriyassa pana khippā abhiññāti.

The distinction of these should also be understood by way of defilements and faculties. For one with strong defilements and dull faculties, the practice is difficult and the direct knowledge is slow; but for one with sharp faculties, the direct knowledge is swift. And for one with weak defilements and dull faculties, the practice is easy and the direct knowledge is slow; but for one with sharp faculties, the direct knowledge is swift.

Iti imāsu paṭipadāabhiññāsu yo puggalo dukkhāya paṭipadāya [P 0.0184] dandhāya abhiññāya jhānaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa taṃ jhānaṃ dukkhapaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññanti vuccati. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

Thus, among these practices and direct knowledges, whichever person attains jhāna by means of a difficult practice and a slow direct knowledge, for that person that jhāna is called 'difficult practice, slow direct knowledge.' In the remaining cases, too, this is the method.

Tattha [M 0.0229] ‘tadanudhammatā sati santiṭṭhati ṭhitibhāginī paññā’ti (vibha. 799) evaṃ vuttasatiyā vā taṃtaṃjhānanikantiyā vā vikkhambhane paṭipadā, taṃtaṃjhānupacārappattassa appanāya parivāse abhiññā ca veditabbā. Āgamanavasenāpi ca paṭipadā abhiññā hontiyeva. Dukkhapaṭipadañhi dandhābhiññaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ patvā pavattaṃ dutiyampi tādisameva hoti. Tatiyacatutthesupi eseva nayo. Yathā ca catukkanaye evaṃ pañcakanayepi paṭipadāvasena catudhā bhedo veditabbo. Iti paṭipadāvasenapi cattāro navakā vuttā honti. Tesu pāṭhato chattiṃsa cittāni, atthato pana pañcakanaye catukkanayassa paviṭṭhattā vīsatimeva bhavantīti.

Herein, 'practice' should be understood as being in the suppression either of a lack of mindfulness thus stated: 'Mindfulness is established in conformity with that state; wisdom partakes of stability,' or of craving for this or that jhāna. And 'direct knowledge' should be understood as being in the cultivation for absorption on the part of one who has reached the access to this or that jhāna. And practice and direct knowledge also come to be by way of progression. For having reached the first jhāna that is of difficult practice and slow direct knowledge, the second jhāna that proceeds from it is also of the same kind. In the third and fourth jhānas, too, this is the method. And just as in the fourfold method, so too in the fivefold method, the fourfold distinction by way of practice should be understood. Thus, by way of practice, four groups of nine have been stated. Among them, according to the text, there are thirty-six consciousnesses; but in terms of meaning, because the fourfold method is included in the fivefold method, there are only twenty.

Paṭipadācatukkaṃ.

The Tetrad of Practice is concluded.

Ārammaṇacatukkaṃ

The Tetrad of the Object

181. Idāni [V 0.0229] yasmā etaṃ jhānaṃ nāma yathā paṭipadābhedena evaṃ ārammaṇabhedenāpi catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tasmāssa taṃ pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha parittaṃ parittārammaṇantiādīsu yaṃ appaguṇaṃ hoti, uparijjhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, idaṃ parittaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana avaḍḍhite suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā ārammaṇe pavattaṃ, taṃ parittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ assāti parittārammaṇaṃ. Yaṃ paguṇaṃ subhāvitaṃ uparijjhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ sakkoti, idaṃ appamāṇaṃ nāma. Yaṃ vipule ārammaṇe pavattaṃ taṃ vuḍḍhippamāṇattā appamāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ assāti appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Vuttalakkhaṇavomissakatāya pana vomissakanayo veditabbo. Iti ārammaṇavasenapi cattāro navakā vuttā honti. Cittagaṇanāpettha purimasadisā evāti.

181. Now, because this which is called jhāna is fourfold by way of the division of practice, just so it is also fourfold by way of the division of object. Therefore, to show that division of it, the passage beginning 'Which states are wholesome?' is again commenced. Therein, in passages such as 'limited' and 'with a limited object,' that which is unmastered and cannot become a condition for a higher jhāna, this is called 'limited.' Furthermore, that which occurs in an undeveloped object, or one the size of a winnowing basket or a small bowl, is called 'with a limited object' because its object is limited. That which is well-practiced, well-developed, and can become a condition for a higher jhāna, this is called 'immeasurable.' That which occurs in a vast object is called 'with an immeasurable object' because its object is of an expanded measure. The mixed method, however, should be understood by way of the mixture of the aforementioned characteristics. Thus, by way of the object also, four sets of nine have been stated. Herein, the counting of consciousnesses is just the same as the preceding.

Ārammaṇacatukkaṃ.

The Tetrad of the Object is concluded.

Ārammaṇapaṭipadāmissakaṃ

The Mixture of Object and Practice

186. Idāni ārammaṇapaṭipadāmissakaṃ soḷasakkhattukanayaṃ [P 0.0185] dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭhamanaye vuttajjhānaṃ [M 0.0230] dukkhapaṭipadattā dandhābhiññattā parittattā parittārammaṇattāti catūhi kāraṇehi hīnaṃ, soḷasamanaye vuttajjhānaṃ sukhapaṭipadattā khippābhiññattā appamāṇattā appamāṇārammaṇattāti catūhi kāraṇehi paṇītaṃ. Sesesu cuddasasu ekena dvīhi tīhi ca kāraṇehi hīnappaṇītatā veditabbā.

186. Now, to show the sixteenfold method, which is a mixture of object and practice, the passage beginning 'Which states are wholesome?' is again commenced. Therein, in the first method, the stated jhāna is inferior for four reasons: due to its difficult practice, slow direct knowledge, being limited, and having a limited object. In the sixteenth method, the stated jhāna is superior for four reasons: due to its easy practice, swift direct knowledge, being immeasurable, and having an immeasurable object. In the remaining fourteen methods, the state of being inferior or superior should be understood by one, two, or three reasons.

Kasmā panāyaṃ nayo desitoti? Jhānuppattikāraṇattā. Sammāsambuddhena hi pathavīkasiṇe suddhikajjhānaṃ catukkanayavasena pañcakanayavasena ca dassitaṃ; tathā suddhikapaṭipadā, tathā suddhikārammaṇaṃ. Tattha yā devatā pathavīkasiṇe suddhikajjhānaṃ catukkanayavasena desiyamānaṃ bujjhituṃ sakkonti, tāsaṃ sappāyavasena suddhikajjhāne catukkanayo desito. Yā pañcakanayavasena desiyamānaṃ bujjhituṃ sakkonti, tāsaṃ sappāyavasena pañcakanayo. Yā suddhikapaṭipadāya[V 0.0230], suddhikārammaṇe catukkanayavasena desiyamānaṃ bujjhituṃ sakkonti, tāsaṃ sappāyavasena suddhikapaṭipadāya suddhikārammaṇe catukkanayo desito. Yā pañcakanayavasena desiyamānaṃ bujjhituṃ sakkonti tāsaṃ sappāyavasena pañcakanayo. Iti heṭṭhā puggalajjhāsayavasena desanā katā.

But why was this method taught? Because it is a cause for the arising of jhāna. Indeed, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has shown the pure jhāna in relation to the earth kasiṇa by way of the fourfold method and the fivefold method; likewise, the pure practice, and likewise, the pure object. Therein, for those deities who are able to understand the pure jhāna in relation to the earth kasiṇa when it is taught by way of the fourfold method, the fourfold method was taught regarding the pure jhāna in a way suitable for them. For those who are able to understand it when taught by way of the fivefold method, the fivefold method was taught in a way suitable for them. For those who are able to understand the pure practice and the pure object when taught by way of the fourfold method, the fourfold method was taught regarding the pure practice and the pure object in a way suitable for them. For those who are able to understand it when taught by way of the fivefold method, the fivefold method was taught in a way suitable for them. Thus, previously, the teaching was given according to the disposition of individuals.

Desanāvilāsappatto cesa pabhinnapaṭisambhido dasabalacatuvesārajjavisadañāṇo dhammānaṃ yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇassa suppaṭividdhattā dhammapaññattikusalatāya yo yo nayo labbhati tassa tassa vasena desanaṃ niyametuṃ sakkoti, tasmā imāya desanāvilāsappattiyāpi tena esā pathavīkasiṇe suddhikacatukkanayādivasena desanā katā.

And this one, having attained the grace of exposition, possessing the analytical knowledges, and the clear knowledge of the ten powers and four grounds of self-confidence, is able, due to having thoroughly penetrated the individual characteristics of phenomena as they are in their own nature and due to skill in the designation of phenomena, to determine the teaching according to whatever method is available. Therefore, also because of this attainment of the grace of exposition, this teaching was given by him in relation to the earth kasiṇa by way of the pure fourfold method and so on.

Yasmā pana ye keci jhānaṃ uppādenti nāma na te ārammaṇapaṭipadāhi vinā uppādetuṃ sakkonti, tasmā niyamato jhānuppattikāraṇattā ayaṃ soḷasakkhattukanayo kathito.

Furthermore, because whoever produces jhāna is unable to produce it without an object and practice, this sixteenfold method has been taught as it is definitively a cause for the arising of jhāna.

Ettāvatā suddhikanavako, cattāro paṭipadānavakā, cattāro ārammaṇanavakā, ime ca soḷasa navakāti pañcavīsati navakā kathitā honti. Tattha ekekasmiṃ navake catukkapañcakavasena dve dve nayāti paññāsa nayā. Tattha “pañcavīsatiyā catukkanayesu [P 0.0186] sataṃ, pañcakanayesu pañcavīsasata”nti pāṭhato pañcavīsādhikāni dve jhānacittasatāni honti. Pañcakanaye pana catukkanayassa paviṭṭhattā atthato pañcavīsādhikameva cittasataṃ [M 0.0231] hoti. Yāni cetāni pāṭhe pañcavīsādhikāni dve cittasatāni tesu ekekassa niddese dhammavavatthānādayo tayo tayo mahāvārā honti. Te pana tattha tattha nayamattameva dassetvā saṃkhittāti.

With this much, the pure set of nine, the four sets of nine on practice, the four sets of nine on objects, and these sixteen sets of nine—thus twenty-five sets of nine have been taught. Therein, in each set of nine, by way of the fourfold and fivefold methods, there are two methods each, thus fifty methods. Therein, according to the text, 'in the twenty-five fourfold methods, one hundred; in the fivefold methods, one hundred and twenty-five,' thus there are two hundred and twenty-five jhāna-consciousnesses. But in the fivefold method, because the fourfold method is included, in terms of meaning, there are only one hundred and twenty-five consciousnesses. And in these two hundred and twenty-five consciousnesses in the text, in the exposition of each one, there are three great sections each, beginning with the determination of states. But these have been abbreviated, showing only the method in each respective case.

Pathavīkasiṇaṃ.

The Earth Kasiṇa.

203. Idāni yasmā āpokasiṇādīsupi etāni jhānāni uppajjanti, tasmā tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tesu sabbo pāḷinayo ca atthavibhāvanā ca cittagaṇanā ca vārasaṅkhepo ca pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Bhāvanānayo pana kasiṇaparikammaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbo visuddhimagge (visuddhi 1.91 ādayo) pakāsitoyeva. Mahāsakuludāyisutte pana dasakasiṇāni (ma. ni. 2.250) vuttāni. Tesu viññāṇakasiṇaṃ ākāse [V 0.0231] pavattitamahaggataviññāṇampi tattha parikammaṃ katvā nibbattā viññāṇañcāyatanasamāpattipi hotīti sabbappakārena āruppadesanameva bhajati, tasmā imasmiṃ ṭhāne na kathitaṃ.

203. Now, because these jhānas also arise in relation to the water kasiṇa and so on, therefore, to show them, the passage beginning 'Which states are wholesome?' is again commenced. In these, the entire textual method, the explanation of the meaning, the counting of consciousnesses, and the summary of sections should be understood by the very method stated for the earth kasiṇa. The method of development, however, beginning with the preliminary work on the kasiṇa, has all been explained in the Visuddhimagga. In the Mahāsakuludāyisutta, however, ten kasiṇas are stated. Among them, the consciousness kasiṇa—since the sublime consciousness arisen in space, after preliminary work is done on it, also becomes the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness—in every way pertains to the teaching on the formless realm. Therefore, it is not taught in this place.

Ākāsakasiṇanti pana kasiṇugghāṭimamākāsampi, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattakkhandhāpi, bhitticchiddādīsu aññatarasmiṃ gahetabbanimittaparicchedākāsampi, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaṃ catukkapañcakajjhānampi vuccati. Tattha purimanayo āruppadesanaṃ bhajati, pacchimanayo rūpāvacaradesanaṃ. Iti missakattā imaṃ rūpāvacaradesanaṃ na āruḷhaṃ. Paricchedākāse nibbattajjhānaṃ pana rūpūpapattiyā maggo hoti tasmā taṃ gahetabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana catukkapañcakajjhānameva uppajjati, arūpajjhānaṃ nuppajjati. Kasmā? Kasiṇugghāṭanassa alābhato. Tañhi punappunaṃ ugghāṭiyamānampi ākāsameva hotīti na tattha kasiṇugghāṭanaṃ labbhati, tasmā tatthuppannaṃ jhānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati, abhiññāpādakaṃ hoti, vipassanāpādakaṃ hoti, nirodhapādakaṃ na hoti. Anupubbanirodho panettha yāva [P 0.0187] pañcamajjhānā labbhati vaṭṭapādakaṃ hotiyeva. Yathā cetaṃ evaṃ purimakasiṇesu uppannaṃ jhānampi. Nirodhapādakabhāvo panettha viseso. Sesamettha ākāsakasiṇe yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.98-99) vuttameva.

The space kasiṇa, however, is said to be: the space obtained by the removal of a kasiṇa, and the aggregates that arise taking that as an object; and also the limited space apprehended as a sign in a wall-opening or the like, and the fourth and fifth jhānas that arise taking that as an object. Therein, the former method pertains to the teaching on the formless realm, while the latter method pertains to the teaching on the fine-material sphere. Because of this mixed nature, this is not included in the teaching on the fine-material sphere. However, the jhāna that arises in the limited space is a path to rebirth in the fine-material realm; therefore, that should be taken. In that, however, only the fourth and fifth jhānas arise; the formless jhāna does not arise. Why? Because of the non-obtaining of the removal of the kasiṇa. Indeed, that, even when repeatedly removed, remains just space; thus, the removal of the kasiṇa is not obtained there. Therefore, the jhāna that arises there conduces to a pleasant abiding in the present life, is a basis for direct knowledge, and is a basis for insight; it is not a basis for the attainment of cessation. Here, the successive cessation is obtained up to the fifth jhāna, and it is indeed a basis for the round of existence. Just as this is so, so too is the jhāna that arises in the previous kasiṇas. The state of being a basis for the attainment of cessation is the distinction here. Whatever else should be said here regarding the space kasiṇa, all that has already been said in the Visuddhimagga.

‘Ekopi [M 0.0232] hutvā bahudhā hotī’tiādinayaṃ (dī. ni. 1.239; paṭi. ma. 1.102) pana vikubbanaṃ icchantena purimesu aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā kasiṇānulomato kasiṇapaṭilomato, kasiṇānulomapaṭilomato; jhānānulomato, jhānapaṭilomato, jhānānulomapaṭilomato; jhānukkantikato, kasiṇukkantikato, jhānakasiṇukkantikato; aṅgasaṅkantikato, ārammaṇasaṅkantikato, aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantikato; aṅgavavatthānato, ārammaṇavavatthānatoti imehi cuddasahākārehi cittaṃ paridametabbaṃ. Tesaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.365-366) vuttāyeva.

Furthermore, one who desires the transformations of psychic power according to the method beginning, ‘Being one, he becomes many,’ having produced the eight attainments in the eight preceding kasiṇas, should thoroughly train the mind by these fourteen modes: by means of the forward order of the kasiṇas, the reverse order of the kasiṇas, and the forward and reverse order of the kasiṇas; by means of the forward order of the jhānas, the reverse order of the jhānas, and the forward and reverse order of the jhānas; by means of skipping jhānas, by means of skipping kasiṇas, and by means of skipping jhānas and kasiṇas; by means of transferring the factors, by means of transferring the object, and by means of transferring the factors and object; by means of defining the factors, and by means of defining the object. The detailed explanation of these has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Evaṃ pana cuddasahākārehi cittaṃ aparidametvā, pubbe abhāvitabhāvano ādikammiko yogāvacaro iddhivikubbanaṃ sampādessatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ādikammikassa hi kasiṇaparikammampi bhāro; satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Katakasiṇaparikammassa nimittuppādanaṃ bhāro; satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Uppanne nimitte taṃ vaḍḍhetvā appanādhigamo [V 0.0232] bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Adhigatappanassa cuddasahākārehi cittaparidamanaṃ bhāro; satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Cuddasahākārehi paridamitacittassāpi iddhivikubbanaṃ nāma bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Vikubbanappattassāpi khippanisantibhāvo nāma bhāro; satesu sahassesu vā ekova khippanisanti hoti. Therambatthale mahārohanaguttattherassa gilānupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatesu tiṃsamattesu iddhimantasahassesu upasampadāya aṭṭhavassiko rakkhitatthero viya. Sabbaṃ vatthu visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.367) vitthāritamevāti.

However, without having thoroughly trained the mind by these fourteen modes, that a yogī who is a beginner, who has not developed the meditation in previous lives, will accomplish the transformations of psychic power—this is not possible. Indeed, for a beginner, even the preliminary work on the kasiṇa is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand is able. For one who has done the preliminary work on the kasiṇa, producing the sign is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand is able. When the sign has arisen, developing it and attaining absorption is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand is able. For one who has attained absorption, thoroughly training the mind by the fourteen modes is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand is able. Even for one whose mind has been thoroughly trained by the fourteen modes, what is called the transformations of psychic power is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand is able. Even for one who has attained the transformations, what is called the state of quick intuition is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand has quick intuition, like the Elder Rakkhita, who was of eight years’ standing in the higher ordination, among the thirty thousand with psychic power who had come to attend to the ailing Elder Mahārohanagutta at Therambatthala. The entire story has been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga.

Kasiṇakathā.

The Discourse on the Kasiṇas.

Abhibhāyatanakathā

The Discourse on the Spheres of Mastery.

204. Evaṃ aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu rūpāvacarakusalaṃ niddisitvā, idāni yasmā samānepi ārammaṇe bhāvanāya asamānaṃ imesu aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu aññampi abhibhāyatanasaṅkhātaṃ rūpāvacarakusalaṃ [P 0.0188] pavattati, tasmā [M 0.0233] taṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti alābhitāya vā anatthikatāya vā ajjhattarūpe parikammasaññāvirahito. Bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti bahiddhā aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu kataparikammatāya parikammavasena ceva appanāvasena ca tāni bahiddhā aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu rūpāni passati. Parittānīti avaḍḍhitāni. Tāni abhibhuyyāti yathā nāma sampannagahaṇiko kaṭacchumattaṃ bhattaṃ labhitvā ‘kiṃ ettha bhuñjitabbaṃ atthī’ti saṅkaḍḍhitvā ekakabaḷameva karoti, evameva ñāṇuttariko puggalo visadañāṇo ‘kimettha parittake ārammaṇe samāpajjitabbaṃ atthi, nāyaṃ mama bhāro’ti tāni rūpāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati. Saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ nibbattetīti attho. Jānāmi passāmīti iminā panassa pubbabhāgo kathito. Āgamaṭṭhakathāsu pana vuttaṃ – imināssa pana ābhogo kathito. So ca kho samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa, na antosamāpattiyanti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.65).

204. Having thus explained the form-sphere wholesome consciousness in the eight kasiṇas, now, because although the object is the same, through a dissimilar development another form-sphere wholesome consciousness, known as a sphere of mastery, also occurs in these eight kasiṇas, therefore, to show that, the passage beginning, “Which states are wholesome?” is again taken up. Herein, “internally, perceiving formlessness” means one who, due to not having attained or due to disinterest, lacks the preliminary perception regarding internal forms. “Sees forms externally” means one who has performed the preliminary work on the eight external kasiṇas sees those forms externally, both by way of preliminary practice and by way of absorption. “Limited” means not expanded. “Mastering them” is like a person with good digestion who, upon receiving only a spoonful of food, thinks, “What is there to eat here?” and rolls it into a single mouthful. Similarly, a person of superior knowledge, with clear understanding, thinks, “What is there to attain in this limited object? This is not my burden,” masters those forms, and attains absorption. The meaning is that one produces absorption here simultaneously with the appearance of the sign. By “I know, I see,” his preliminary attention is stated. However, in the Sutta commentaries, it is said: “By this, his directing of the mind is described.” And that is for one who has arisen from absorption, not for one during absorption itself.

Appamāṇānīti [V 0.0233] vaḍḍhitappamāṇāni. Abhibhuyyāti ettha pana yathā mahagghaso puriso ekaṃ bhattavaḍḍhitakaṃ labhitvā ‘aññāpi hotu ‘kimesā mayhaṃ karissatī’ti taṃ na mahantato passati, evameva ñāṇuttaro puggalo visadaññāṇo ‘kimettha samāpajjitabbaṃ, na idaṃ appamāṇaṃ, na mayhaṃ cittekaggatākaraṇe bhāro atthī’ti tāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati. Saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ nibbattetīti attho.

“Immeasurable” means having an increased measure. Regarding “mastering them,” it is as if a gluttonous person, receiving a large helping of food, thinks, “Let there be other food as well! What will this do for me?” and does not regard it as substantial. Similarly, a person with superior wisdom and clear understanding thinks, “What is there to be attained here? This is not immeasurable; there is no burden for me in making the mind one-pointed,” and mastering them, attains absorption. The meaning is that one produces absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign.

Parittaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ appamāṇaṃ parittārammaṇanti idha parittānīti āgatattā appamāṇārammaṇatā na gahitā, parato appamāṇānīti āgatattā parittārammaṇatā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – ‘imasmiṃ ṭhāne cattāri cattāri ārammaṇāni aggahetvā dve dveva gahitāni[P 0.0189]. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Catūsu hi gahitesu desanā soḷasakkhattukā hoti, satthārā ca heṭṭhā soḷasakkhattukā desanā kilañjamhi tile pattharantena viya vitthārato kathitā. Tassa imasmiṃ ṭhāne aṭṭhakkhattukaṃ desanaṃ kātuṃ ajjhāsayo. Tasmā dve dveyeva gahitānīti veditabbānīti.

Regarding the limited object and the immeasurable object: here, because 'limited' (parittāni) is stated, the state of having an immeasurable object is not taken; and later, because 'immeasurable' (appamāṇāni) is stated, the state of having a limited object is not taken. But in the commentary it is said: 'In this place, four objects each are not taken, but only two each are taken. For what reason? Because if four were taken, the teaching would be sixteenfold. And the Teacher has previously taught the sixteenfold teaching in detail, like one spreading sesame seeds on a mat. In this place, his intention is to give an eightfold teaching. Therefore, it should be understood that only two each are taken.'

Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānīti [M 0.0234] parisuddhāparisuddhavaṇṇāni. Parisuddhāni hi nīlādīni suvaṇṇāni, aparisuddhāni ca dubbaṇṇānīti idha adhippetāni. Āgamaṭṭhakathāsu pana ‘suvaṇṇāni vā hontu dubbaṇṇāni vā, parittaappamāṇavaseneva imāni abhibhāyatanāni desitānī’ti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.65) vuttaṃ. Imesu pana catūsu parittaṃ vitakkacaritavasena āgataṃ, appamāṇaṃ mohacaritavasena, suvaṇṇaṃ dosacaritavasena, dubbaṇṇaṃ rāgacaritavasena. Etesañhi etāni sappāyāni. Sā ca tesaṃ sappāyatā vitthārato visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.43) cariyaniddese vuttā.

“Beautiful and ugly” refers to pure and impure colors. For pure colors like blue, etc., are called beautiful, while impure ones are termed ugly—this is the intended meaning here. However, in the Sutta commentaries, it is said: “Whether they are beautiful or ugly, these spheres of mastery are taught solely in terms of limited and immeasurable.” Among these four, the limited is for one with a discursive temperament, the immeasurable for one with a deluded temperament, the beautiful for one with a hateful temperament, and the ugly for one with a lustful temperament. For these objects are suitable for them. And their suitability is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga in the section on temperaments.

Kasmā pana, yathā suttante “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittānī”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.173; ma. ni. 2.249; a. ni. 8.65) vuttaṃ, evaṃ avatvā idha catūsupi abhibhāyatanesu ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitāva vuttāti? Ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato. Tattha vā hi idha vā bahiddhārūpāneva abhibhavitabbāni, tasmā tāni niyamato vattabbānīti tatrapi idhapi vuttāni. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti idaṃ pana satthu desanāvilāsamattameva. Ayaṃ tāva catūsu abhibhāyatanesu apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Suddhikanayapaṭipadābhedo panettha pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva ekekasmiṃ abhibhāyatane veditabbo. Kevalañcettha [V 0.0234] ārammaṇacatukkaṃ ārammaṇadukaṃ hoti, soḷasakkhattukañca aṭṭhakkhattukaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Evamettha ekekasmiṃ abhibhāyatane eko suddhikanavako, cattāro paṭipadānavakā, dve ārammaṇanavakā, ārammaṇapaṭipadāmissake aṭṭha navakāti pannarasa navakāti catūsupi abhibhāyatanesu samasaṭṭhi navakā veditabbā.

But why, whereas in the Suttas it is said, “Being one who perceives form internally, one sees limited forms externally,” etc., is it not stated so here, but instead, in all four spheres of mastery, only the internal perception of formlessness is stated? Because internal forms are not to be mastered. Whether there or here, only external forms are to be mastered; therefore, they must be stated definitively both there and here. The phrase “internally perceiving formlessness” is merely a stylistic flourish of the Teacher’s instruction. So much for the explanation of the unprecedented terms in the four spheres of mastery. The distinction in the method of pure practice here is to be understood in the same way as explained for the earth kasiṇa in each sphere of mastery. The only difference here is that the fourfold object becomes a twofold object, and the sixteenfold occasion becomes an eightfold one. The rest is similar. Thus, in each sphere of mastery, there is one pure ninefold, four path-ninefolds, two object-ninefolds, and in the mixed object-and-path section, eight ninefolds—making fifteen ninefolds. Therefore, across all four spheres of mastery, sixty ninefolds are to be understood.

246. Pañcamaabhibhāyatanādīsu [P 0.0190] nīlānīti sabbasaṅgāhikavasena vuttaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇānīti vaṇṇavasena, nīlanidassanānīti nidassanavasena, apaññāyamānavivarāni, asambhinnavaṇṇāni, ekanīlāneva hutvā dissantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Nīlanibhāsānīti idaṃ pana obhāsanavasena vuttaṃ; nīlobhāsāni nīlappabhāyuttānīti attho. Etena nesaṃ suvisuddhataṃ dasseti. Suvisuddhavaṇṇavasena hi imāni cattāri abhibhāyatanāni vuttāni. Pītānītiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Nīlakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto nīlasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti. Pupphasmiṃ vā vatthasmiṃ vā vaṇṇadhātuyā vātiādikaṃ [M 0.0235] panettha kasiṇakaraṇañca parikammañca appanāvidhānañca sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.93 ādayo) vitthārato vuttameva. Yathā ca pathavīkasiṇe evamettha ekekasmiṃ abhibhāyatane pañcavīsati pañcavīsati navakā veditabbā.

246. In the fifth sphere of mastery and so on, 'blue' is stated comprehensively. 'Blue-colored' is stated by way of color, 'blue-appearing' by way of appearance, meaning they have no perceptible gaps, their colors are unmixed, and they appear as uniformly blue. 'Blue-radiant,' however, is stated by way of luminosity—they are endowed with blue radiance or blue effulgence. This shows their utter purity. For these four spheres of mastery are described in terms of utterly pure colors. The meaning of 'yellow,' and so on, should also be understood in this same way. The method of preparing the kasiṇa, the preliminary work, and the method of attainment are all explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. And as with the earth kasiṇa, here too, in each sphere of mastery, twenty-five sets of nine should be understood.

Abhibhāyatanakathā.

The Discourse on the Spheres of Mastery is concluded.

Vimokkhakathā

The Discourse on Liberations

248. Idāni yasmā idaṃ rūpāvacarakusalaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ ārammaṇasaṅkhātānaṃ āyatanānaṃ abhibhavanato abhibhāyatanavaseneva uppajjati, atha kho vimokkhavasenapi uppajjati, tasmā tampi nayaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ.

248. Now, because this wholesome state of the form-sphere arises not only by way of being a sphere of mastery due to mastering the bases which are called objects, but indeed also arises by way of being a liberation, therefore, to show that method also, the exposition is undertaken again beginning with, “Which states are wholesome?”

Kenaṭṭhena pana vimokkho veditabboti? Adhimuccanaṭṭhena. Ko ayaṃ adhimuccanaṭṭho nāma? Paccanīkadhammehi ca suṭṭhu vimuccanaṭṭho, ārammaṇe ca abhirativasena suṭṭhu vimuccanaṭṭho[V 0.0235]. Pituaṅke vissaṭṭhaaṅgapaccaṅgassa dārakassa sayanaṃ viya aniggahitabhāvena nirāsaṅkatāya ārammaṇe pavattīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃlakkhaṇañhi vimokkhabhāvappattaṃ rūpāvacarakusalaṃ dassetuṃ ayaṃ nayo āraddho.

By what meaning, however, should liberation be understood? By the meaning of being resolved. What is this meaning of being resolved? It is the meaning of being well freed from opposing states, and the meaning of being well released by way of delighting in the object. It is said to mean its proceeding upon the object without being restrained and without anxiety, like the sleeping of a child with its limbs relaxed on its father's lap. Indeed, this method is undertaken to show the wholesome state of the form-sphere that has attained the state of liberation having such a characteristic.

Tattha rūpīti ajjhattaṃ kesādīsu uppāditaṃ rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ, tadassatthīti rūpī. Ajjhattañhi nīlaparikammaṃ karonto kese vā pitte vā akkhitārakāya vā karoti. Pītaparikammaṃ karonto mede vā chaviyā vā akkhīnaṃ [P 0.0191] pītaṭṭhāne vā karoti. Lohitaparikammaṃ karonto maṃse vā lohite vā jivhāya vā hatthatalapādatalesu vā akkhīnaṃ rattaṭṭhāne vā karoti. Odātaparikammaṃ karonto aṭṭhimhi vā dante vā nakhe vā akkhīnaṃ setaṭṭhāne vā karoti. Evaṃ parikammaṃ katvā uppannajjhānasamaṅginaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Rūpāni passatīti bahiddhāpi nīlakasiṇādirūpāni jhānacakkhunā passati. Iminā ajjhattabahiddhāvatthukesu kasiṇesu jhānapaṭilābho dassito.

Therein, 'one with form' (rūpī) means: the form-sphere jhāna produced internally in the hair, etc., is ‘form’ (rūpa); one has that, therefore one is 'one with form.' For one undertaking the blue preliminary work internally does so with respect to the hair, bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One undertaking the yellow preliminary work does so with respect to the fat, skin, or the yellow areas of the eyes. One undertaking the red preliminary work does so with respect to the flesh, blood, tongue, the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or the red areas of the eyes. One undertaking the white preliminary work does so with respect to the bones, teeth, nails, or the white areas of the eyes. This is said with reference to one who, having done the preliminary work thus, is endowed with the arisen jhāna. 'Sees forms' (rūpāni passati) means one sees external forms such as the blue kasiṇa with the jhāna-eye. By this, the attainment of jhāna in kasiṇas based on internal and external objects is shown.

Ajjhattaṃ [M 0.0236] arūpasaññīti ajjhattaṃ na rūpasaññī. Attano kesādīsu anuppāditarūpāvacarajjhānoti attho. Iminā bahiddhā parikammaṃ katvā bahiddhāva paṭiladdhajjhānatā dassitā.

‘Internally perceiving no form’ means not perceiving form internally. The meaning is that one has not produced the form-sphere jhāna focused on one’s own hair, etc. By this, it is shown that one has undertaken the preliminary work externally and attained the jhāna externally.

Subhanti iminā suvisuddhesu nīlādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇesu jhānāni dassitāni. Tattha kiñcāpi antoappanāya ‘subha’nti ābhogo natthi, yo pana suvisuddhaṃ subhakasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā viharati, so yasmā ‘subha’nti…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, tathā dutiyādīni, tasmā evaṃ desanā katā. Paṭisambhidāmagge pana “kathaṃ subhantveva adhimutto hotīti vimokkho? Idha bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ…pe… viharati, mettāya bhāvitattā sattā appaṭikūlā honti; karuṇā… muditā… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ…pe… viharati, upekkhāya bhāvitattā sattā appaṭikūlā honti, evaṃ subhantveva adhimutto hotī”ti vimokkhoti (paṭi. ma. 1.212) vuttaṃ. Idha pana upari pāḷiyaṃyeva brahmavihārānaṃ āgatattā taṃ nayaṃ paṭikkhipitvā sunīlakasupītakasulohitakasuodātakaparisuddhanīlakaparisuddhapītakaparisuddhalohitakaparisuddhaodātakavaseneva subhavimokkho anuññāto. Iti kasiṇanti vā abhibhāyatananti vā vimokkhoti vā rūpāvacarajjhānameva[V 0.0236]. Tañhi ārammaṇassa sakalaṭṭhena kasiṇaṃ nāma, ārammaṇaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena abhibhāyatanaṃ nāma, ārammaṇe adhimuccanaṭṭhena paccanīkadhammehi ca vimuccanaṭṭhena [P 0.0192] vimokkho nāmāti vuttaṃ. Tattha kasiṇadesanā abhidhammavasena, itarā pana suttantadesanāvasena vuttāti veditabbā. Ayamettha apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Ekekasmiṃ pana vimokkhe pathavīkasiṇe viya pañcavīsati pañcavīsatīti katvā pañcasattati navakā veditabbā.

By 'beautiful' (subha), the jhānas in the utterly pure color kasiṇas, such as blue, are shown. Therein, although there is no advertence 'it is beautiful' before absorption, one who dwells making the utterly pure, beautiful kasiṇa the object, since 'it is beautiful'… he attains and dwells in the first jhāna, and similarly the second and so on; therefore the teaching is given in this way. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, it is said: “How is it a liberation in that one is resolved upon ‘the beautiful’? Here, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness… because loving-kindness is developed, beings are not repulsive… with compassion… with appreciative joy… with a mind accompanied by equanimity… because equanimity is developed, beings are not repulsive; thus it is a liberation in that one is resolved upon ‘the beautiful’.” Here, however, since the divine abodes have already come up in the Pāḷi text above, rejecting that method, the liberation through the beautiful is permitted only by way of the very blue, very yellow, very red, very white, the perfectly pure blue, perfectly pure yellow, perfectly pure red, and the perfectly pure white. Thus, whether it is called kasiṇa, or sphere of mastery, or liberation, it is just the form-sphere jhāna. For it is called kasiṇa because of the meaning of 'entirety' of the object; it is called sphere of mastery (abhibhāyatana) because of the meaning of 'mastering' the object; and it is called liberation (vimokkha) because of the meaning of 'being resolved' upon the object and 'being freed' from opposing states. Therein, the teaching on kasiṇa is said to be by way of the Abhidhamma method, while the others are by way of the Suttanta method. This is the explanation of the unprecedented terms here. Furthermore, in each liberation, as in the earth kasiṇa, twenty-five sets of nine are to be understood; thus, seventy-five sets of nine should be understood.

Vimokkhakathā.

The Discourse on Liberations is concluded.

Brahmavihārakathā

The Discourse on the Divine Abodes

251. Idāni mettādibrahmavihāravasena pavattamānaṃ rūpāvacarakusalaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha mettāsahagatanti [M 0.0237] mettāya samannāgataṃ. Parato karuṇāsahagatādīsupi eseva nayo. Yena panesa vidhānena paṭipanno mettādisahagatāni jhānāni upasampajja viharati, taṃ mettādīnaṃ bhāvanāvidhānaṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.240) vitthāritameva. Avasesāya pāḷiyā attho pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

251. Now, in order to show the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere that occur by way of the divine abodes beginning with loving-kindness, the passage beginning, 'Which states are wholesome?' is again taken up. Herein, 'accompanied by loving-kindness' means endowed with loving-kindness. Hereafter, this same method applies also to the terms beginning with 'accompanied by compassion.' Furthermore, the entire method of development for loving-kindness and so forth, by which this practitioner, having practiced, abides having attained the jhānas accompanied by loving-kindness and so forth, has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. The meaning of the remaining Pāḷi should be understood according to the method stated in the earth-kasiṇa section.

Kevalañhi pathavīkasiṇe pañcavīsati navakā, idha purimāsu tīsu tikacatukkajjhānikavasena pañcavīsati sattakā, upekkhāya catutthajjhānavasena pañcavīsati ekakā, karuṇāmuditāsu ca chandādīhi catūhi saddhiṃ karuṇāmuditāti imepi yevāpanakā labbhanti. Dukkhapaṭipadādibhāvo cettha mettāya tāva byāpādavikkhambhanavasena, karuṇāya vihiṃsāvikkhambhanavasena, muditāya arativikkhambhanavasena, upekkhāya rāgapaṭighavikkhambhanavasena veditabbo. Parittārammaṇatā pana nabahusattārammaṇavasena; appamāṇārammaṇatā bahusattārammaṇavasena hotīti ayaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

Indeed, in the earth-kasiṇa there are only twenty-five nonads. Here, in the first three divine abodes, by way of the three-fold and four-fold jhānic systems, there are twenty-five heptads. In equanimity, by way of the fourth jhāna, there are twenty-five monads. And in compassion and sympathetic joy, these yevāpanaka factors are also obtained, that is, compassion and sympathetic joy together with the four beginning with desire. And here, the state of painful progress and so forth should be understood thus: for loving-kindness, by way of suppressing ill will; for compassion, by way of suppressing cruelty; for sympathetic joy, by way of suppressing discontent; and for equanimity, by way of suppressing lust and aversion. The state of having a limited object, however, is by way of having not many beings as its object; the state of having an immeasurable object is by way of having many beings as its object. This is the difference. The rest is just the same.

Evaṃ tāva pāḷivaseneva –

Thus far by way of the Pāḷi—

Brahmuttamena [V 0.0237] kathite, brahmavihāre ime iti viditvā;

Bhiyyo etesu ayaṃ, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

Having thus known these divine abodes taught by the Supreme among Brahmas, this miscellaneous discourse concerning them should be further understood.

Etāsu hi mettākaruṇāmuditāupekkhāsu atthato tāva mejjatīti mettā, siniyhatīti attho. Mitte vā bhavā, mittassa vā esā pavattatīpi mettā. Paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ hadayakampanaṃ karotīti karuṇā. Kiṇāti vā paradukkhaṃ hiṃsati vināsetīti karuṇā[P 0.0193]. Kirīyati vā dukkhitesu pharaṇavasena pasāriyatīti karuṇā. Modanti tāya taṃsamaṅgino, sayaṃ vā modati, modanamattameva vā tanti muditā. ‘Averā hontū’tiādibyāpārappahānena majjhattabhāvūpagamanena ca upekkhatīti upekkhā.

Indeed, among these—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—firstly, as to their meaning: It is 'mettā' because it 'mejjati' (is affectionate); the meaning is that it is fond. Or, it is 'mettā' because it exists in a friend, or because this is the conduct of a friend. It is 'karuṇā' because, when there is the suffering of others, it causes the hearts of the good to tremble. Or, it is 'karuṇā' because it 'kiṇāti' (assails), harms, and destroys the suffering of others. Or, it is 'karuṇā' because it is 'kirīyati' (strewn) or spread out among the suffering by way of pervading. It is 'muditā' because those endowed with it rejoice by means of it, or one rejoices oneself, or it is merely the act of rejoicing. It is 'upekkhā' because one 'upekkhati' (looks on) by abandoning such activities as, 'May they be free from enmity,' and by approaching a state of neutrality.

Lakkhaṇādito panettha hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā ‘mettā’, hitūpasaṃhārarasā, āghātavinayapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Byāpādūpasamo etissā sampatti, sinehasambhavo vipatti. Dukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā ‘karuṇā’, paradukkhāsahanarasā, avihiṃsāpaccupaṭṭhānā[M 0.0238], dukkhābhibhūtānaṃ anāthabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Vihiṃsūpasamo tassā sampatti, sokasambhavo vipatti. Sattesu pamodanalakkhaṇā ‘muditā’, anissāyanarasā, arativighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ sampattidassanapadaṭṭhānā. Arativūpasamo tassā sampatti, pahāsasambhavo vipatti. Sattesu majjhattākārappavattilakkhaṇā ‘upekkhā’, sattesu samabhāvadassanarasā, paṭighānunayavūpasamapaccupaṭṭhānā, “kammassakā sattā, te kassa ruciyā sukhitā vā bhavissanti, dukkhato vā muccissanti, pattasampattito vā na parihāyissantī”ti? Evaṃ pavattakammassakatādassanapadaṭṭhānā. Paṭighānunayavūpasamo tassā sampatti, gehassitāya aññāṇupekkhāya sambhavo vipatti.

Herein, as to their characteristics and so forth: Loving-kindness has the characteristic of promoting the aspect of welfare, the function of bringing about benefit, the manifestation of removing animosity, and the proximate cause of seeing beings as agreeable. The subsiding of ill will is its success; the arising of worldly affection is its failure. Compassion has the characteristic of promoting the aspect of removing suffering, the function of being unable to bear the suffering of others, the manifestation of non-cruelty, and the proximate cause of seeing the helplessness of those overwhelmed by suffering. The subsiding of cruelty is its success; the arising of sorrow is its failure. Sympathetic joy has the characteristic of rejoicing in beings, the function of non-envy, the manifestation of dispelling discontent, and the proximate cause of seeing the success of beings. The subsiding of discontent is its success; the arising of merriment is its failure. Equanimity has the characteristic of promoting the aspect of neutrality towards beings, the function of seeing equality in beings, the manifestation of the subsiding of aversion and approval, and the proximate cause of seeing the ownership of kamma thus: 'Beings are owners of their kamma. By whose wish will they become happy, or be freed from suffering, or not decline from the success they have attained?' The subsiding of aversion and approval is its success; the arising of the household-based equanimity of ignorance is its failure.

Catunnampi panetesaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ vipassanāsukhañceva bhavasampatti ca sādhāraṇappayojanaṃ, byāpādādipaṭighāto āveṇikaṃ. Byāpādapaṭighātappayojanā hettha mettā, vihiṃsāaratirāgapaṭighātappayojanā itarā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Furthermore, for all four of these divine abodes, the happiness of insight and accomplishment in existence are the common benefit, while the removal of ill will and so forth is their particular benefit. Herein, loving-kindness has the benefit of removing ill will; the others have the benefit of removing cruelty, discontent, and lust. And this has been said:

“Nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, byāpādassa yadidaṃ mettācetovimutti, nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, vihesāya yadidaṃ karuṇācetovimutti; nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, aratiyā yadidaṃ [V 0.0238] muditācetovimutti, nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, rāgassa yadidaṃ upekkhācetovimuttī”ti (dī. ni. 3.326; a. ni. 6.13).

This, friends, is the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. This, friends, is the escape from cruelty, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion. This, friends, is the escape from discontent, namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy. This, friends, is the escape from lust, namely, the liberation of mind through equanimity.

Ekamekassa cettha āsannadūravasena dve dve paccatthikā. Mettābrahmavihārassa hi, samīpacāro viya purisassa sapatto, guṇadassanasabhāgatāya rāgo āsannapaccatthiko. So lahuṃ otāraṃ labhati. Tasmā tato suṭṭhu mettā rakkhitabbā. Pabbatādigahananissito viya purisassa sapatto sabhāvavisabhāgatāya byāpādo dūrapaccatthiko. Tasmā tato [P 0.0194] nibbhayena mettāyitabbaṃ. Mettāyissati ca nāma kopañca karissatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

And herein, for each one, there are two enemies, a near and a far. For the divine abode of loving-kindness, lust is the near enemy—like a rival who is a man's close associate—due to its similarity in seeing good qualities. It quickly finds an opening. Therefore, loving-kindness must be well guarded from it. Ill will is the far enemy—like a rival of a man who is based in a mountain thicket—due to its dissimilarity in nature. Therefore, one should develop loving-kindness fearlessly of it. For it is impossible that one would develop loving-kindness and at the same time produce anger.

Karuṇābrahmavihārassa “cakkhuviññeyyānaṃ rūpānaṃ iṭṭhānaṃ kantānaṃ manāpānaṃ manoramānaṃ lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ appaṭilābhaṃ vā appaṭilābhato samanupassato pubbe vā paṭiladdhapubbaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ vipariṇataṃ samanussarato [M 0.0239] uppajjati domanassaṃ. Yaṃ evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ idaṃ vuccati gehassitaṃ domanassa”ntiādinā nayena āgataṃ gehassitaṃ domanassaṃ vipattidassanasabhāgatāya āsannapaccatthikaṃ. Sabhāvavisabhāgatāya vihesā dūrapaccatthikā. Tasmā tato nibbhayena karuṇāyitabbaṃ. Karuṇañca nāma karissati pāṇiādīhi ca vihesissatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

For the divine abode of compassion, the household-based grief that is spoken of in the way beginning, 'Grief arises for one who perceives the non-acquisition of forms cognizable by the eye... or who recollects what was formerly acquired but is now past, ceased, and changed... such grief is called household-based grief,' is the near enemy, due to its similarity in seeing misfortune. Cruelty is the far enemy, due to its dissimilarity in nature. Therefore, one should develop compassion fearlessly of it. For it is impossible that one would develop compassion and at the same time harm with one's hands and so forth.

Muditābrahmavihārassa “cakkhuviññeyyānaṃ rūpānaṃ iṭṭhānaṃ kantānaṃ manāpānaṃ manoramānaṃ lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ paṭilābhaṃ vā paṭilābhato samanupassato pubbe vā paṭiladdhapubbaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ vipariṇataṃ samanussarato uppajjati somanassaṃ. Yaṃ evarūpaṃ somanassaṃ idaṃ vuccati gehassitaṃ somanassa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.306) nayena āgataṃ gehassitaṃ somanassaṃ sampattidassanasabhāgatāya āsannapaccatthikaṃ. Sabhāvavisabhāgatāya arati dūrapaccatthikā. Tasmā tato nibbhayena muditā bhāvetabbā. Pamudito ca nāma bhavissati pantasenāsanesu ca adhikusaladhammesu ca ukkaṇṭhissatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

For the divine abiding of sympathetic joy, the household joy that comes according to the method beginning, 'Joy arises in one who sees or recollects the acquisition of forms cognizable by the eye... this is called household joy,' is the near enemy because of its similarity in nature through seeing attainment. Discontent is the far enemy because of its dissimilarity in nature. Therefore, being fearless of that discontent, sympathetic joy should be developed. And it is an impossible condition that one who is joyful would become weary of secluded lodgings and of higher wholesome states.

Upekkhābrahmavihārassa pana “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjati upekkhā bālassa mūḷhassa puthujjanassa anodhijinassa avipākajinassa anādīnavadassāvino assutavato puthujjanassa. Yā evarūpā upekkhā rūpaṃ sā nātivattati. Tasmā sā upekkhā gehassitāti vuccatī”tiādinā [V 0.0239] (ma. ni. 3.308) nayena āgatā gehassitā aññāṇupekkhā dosaguṇānaṃ avicāraṇavasena sabhāgattā āsannapaccatthikā. Sabhāvavisabhāgatāya rāgapaṭighā dūrapaccatthikā. Tasmā tato nibbhayena upekkhitabbaṃ. Upekkhissati ca nāma rajjissati ca paṭihaññissati cāti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

Furthermore, for the divine abiding of equanimity, the household equanimity based on ignorance that comes according to the method beginning, 'Having seen a form with the eye, equanimity arises in a foolish, deluded ordinary person... this is called household equanimity,' is the near enemy because of its similarity in nature by way of not investigating faults and virtues. Lust and aversion are the far enemies because of their dissimilarity in nature. Therefore, being fearless of them, one should be equanimous. And it is an impossible condition that one who is equanimous would also be lustful or hostile.

Sabbesampi ca etesaṃ kattukāmatāchando ādi, nīvaraṇādivikkhambhanaṃ majjhaṃ, appanā pariyosānaṃ, paññattidhammavasena [P 0.0195] eko vā satto anekā vā sattā ārammaṇaṃ, upacāre vā appanāya vā pattāya ārammaṇavaḍḍhanaṃ.

And for all of these divine abidings, the desire of wishing to do is the beginning, the suppression of the hindrances and so forth is the middle, and absorption is the end. By way of concept-phenomena, one being or many beings are the object. The expansion of the object is possible upon reaching either access concentration or absorption.

Tatrāyaṃ vaḍḍhanakkamo – yathā hi kusalo kassako kasitabbaṭṭhānaṃ paricchinditvā kasati, evaṃ paṭhamameva ekaṃ āvāsaṃ paricchinditvā tattha sattesu ‘imasmiṃ āvāse sattā averā hontū’tiādinā nayena mettā bhāvetabbā. Tattha cittaṃ muduṃ kammaniyaṃ katvā dve āvāsā paricchinditabbā[M 0.0240]. Tato anukkamena tayo cattāro pañca cha satta aṭṭha nava dasa, ekā racchā, upaḍḍhagāmo, gāmo, janapado, rajjaṃ, ekā disāti evaṃ yāva ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ, tato vā pana bhiyyo tattha tattha sattesu mettā bhāvetabbā. Tathā karuṇādayoti. Ayamettha ārammaṇavaḍḍhanakkamo.

Herein, this is the sequence of expansion: Just as a skilled farmer, having demarcated the area to be cultivated, cultivates it, so too, one should first demarcate a single dwelling and develop loving-kindness towards the beings there according to the method, 'May the beings in this dwelling be without enmity,' and so forth. Having made the mind pliant and workable towards the beings in that place, two dwellings should be demarcated. Then, in sequence, three dwellings, and so on, up to ten; one street; half a village; a whole village; a province; a kingdom; one direction. In this way, up to one world-system should be demarcated. Or even beyond that, loving-kindness should be developed towards the beings in each respective place. Likewise for compassion and the others. This, herein, is the sequence of expanding the object.

Yathā pana kasiṇānaṃ nissando āruppā, samādhīnaṃ nissando nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, vipassanānaṃ nissando phalasamāpatti, samathavipassanānaṃ nissando nirodhasamāpatti, evaṃ purimabrahmavihārattayassa nissando ettha upekkhābrahmavihāro. Yathā hi thambhe anussāpetvā tulāsaṅghāṭaṃ anāropetvā na sakkā ākāse kūṭagopānasiyo ṭhapetuṃ, evaṃ purimesu tatiyajjhānaṃ vinā na sakkā catutthaṃ bhāvetuṃ. Kasiṇesu pana uppannatatiyajjhānassapesā nuppajjati visabhāgārammaṇattāti.

Furthermore, just as the result of the kasiṇas is the formless attainments, the result of concentrations is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the result of insights is fruition attainment, and the result of serenity and insight is cessation attainment, so too, herein, the result of the triad of the former divine abidings is the divine abiding of equanimity. For just as it is not possible to place rafters in the sky without erecting pillars and placing the main timbers, so too, it is not possible to develop the fourth divine abiding without the third jhāna in the former ones. But for one who has attained the third jhāna on the kasiṇas, this equanimity does not arise, because of having a dissimilar object.

Ettha siyā – ‘kasmā panetā mettā karuṇā muditā upekkhā brahmavihārāti vuccanti? Kasmā ca, catassova? Ko ca etāsaṃ kamo? Vibhaṅge ca kasmā appamaññāti vuttā’ti? Vuccate – seṭṭhaṭṭhena tāva niddosabhāvena cettha brahmavihāratā veditabbā. Sattesu sammāpaṭipattibhāvena hi seṭṭhā ete vihārā. Yathā ca brahmāno niddosacittā viharanti, evaṃ etehi [V 0.0240] sampayuttā yogino brahmasamāva hutvā viharantīti seṭṭhaṭṭhena niddosabhāvena ca brahmavihārāti vuccanti.

Herein, there might be this question: 'Why are these—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—called divine abidings? And why are only four taught? And what is their sequence? And in the Vibhaṅga, why are they called immeasurables?' The answer is stated: First, their being divine abidings should be understood herein in the sense of being supreme and because of their faultless nature. For these abidings are supreme because of their nature of right conduct towards beings. And just as Brahmās dwell with faultless minds, so too, yogis associated with these dwell having become like Brahmā. Thus, they are called divine abidings in the sense of being supreme and because of their faultless nature.

Kasmā ca catassotiādipañhassa pana idaṃ vissajjanaṃ –

Furthermore, for the question beginning, 'And why four?' this is the answer:

Visuddhimaggādivasā catasso,

Hitādiākāravasā panāsaṃ;
