Kamo pavattanti ca appamāṇe,

Tā gocare yena tadappamaññā.

They are four by way of being the path of purification and so forth. Furthermore, their sequence is by way of the mode of welfare and so forth. And because they proceed in an immeasurable domain, for that reason they are called the immeasurables.

Etāsu hi yasmā mettā byāpādabahulassa, karuṇā vihiṃsābahulassa, muditā aratibahulassa, upekkhā rāgabahulassa visuddhimaggo; yasmā ca hitūpasaṃhāraahitāpanayanasampattimodanaanābhogavasena [P 0.0196] catubbidhoyeva sattesu manasikāro; yasmā ca yathā mātā daharagilānayobbanappattasakiccapasutesu [M 0.0241] catūsu puttesu daharassa abhivuḍḍhikāmā hoti, gilānassa gelaññāpanayanakāmā, yobbanappattassa yobbanasampattiyā ciraṭṭhitikāmā, sakiccapasutassa kismiñcipi pariyāye abyāvaṭā hoti, tathā appamaññāvihārikenāpi sabbasattesu mettādivasena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā ito visuddhimaggādivasā catassova appamaññā.

For among these, because loving-kindness is the path of purification for one with much ill will, compassion for one with much cruelty, sympathetic joy for one with much discontent, and equanimity for one with much lust; and because attention towards beings is of only four kinds, by way of wishing to bring welfare, wishing to remove what is not welfare, rejoicing in prosperity, and not attending to them; and because, just as a mother towards her four sons—a young one, a sick one, one who has reached youth, and one engaged in his own affairs—desires growth for the young one, desires the removal of illness for the sick one, desires the long-lastingness of the attainment of youth for the one who has reached youth, and is not involved in any way with the one engaged in his own affairs; so too should one dwelling in the immeasurables be towards all beings by way of loving-kindness and so on. Therefore, from this, by way of being the path of purification and so forth, the immeasurables are only four.

Yasmā pana catassopetā bhāvetukāmena paṭhamaṃ hitākārappavattivasena sattesu paṭipajjitabbaṃ, hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā ca mettā; tato evaṃ patthitahitānaṃ sattānaṃ dukkhābhibhavaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā sambhāvetvā vā dukkhāpanayanākārappavattivasena, dukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā ca karuṇā; athevaṃ patthitahitānaṃ patthitadukkhāpagamānañca nesaṃ sampattiṃ disvā sampattippamodanavasena, pamodanalakkhaṇā ca muditā; tato paraṃ pana kattabbābhāvato ajjhupekkhakatāsaṅkhātena majjhattākārena paṭipajjitabbaṃ, majjhattākārappavattilakkhaṇā ca upekkhā; tasmā ito hitādiākāravasā panāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ mettā vuttā. Atha karuṇā muditā upekkhāti ayaṃ kamo veditabbo.

Furthermore, because one who wishes to develop these four should first practice towards beings by way of the occurrence of the mode of wishing for their welfare, and loving-kindness has the characteristic of the occurrence of the mode of wishing for welfare; then, after that, having seen, heard, or considered the overwhelming by suffering of beings for whom welfare has thus been wished, one should practice by way of the occurrence of the mode of wishing to remove suffering, and compassion has the characteristic of the occurrence of the mode of wishing to remove suffering; then, having seen the success of those beings for whom welfare has been wished and the removal of suffering has been wished, one should practice by way of rejoicing in their success, and sympathetic joy has the characteristic of rejoicing; after that, again, due to the absence of anything further to be done, one should practice by the mode of neutrality, which is called the state of one who looks on indifferently, and equanimity has the characteristic of the occurrence of the mode of neutrality; therefore, by way of these modes beginning with welfare, among these, loving-kindness is taught first. Then compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—thus this sequence should be understood.

Yasmā pana sabbāpetā appamāṇe gocare pavattanti, tasmā appamaññāti vuccanti. Appamāṇā [V 0.0241] hi sattā etāsaṃ gocarabhūtā, ‘ekasattassāpi ca ettake padese mettādayo bhāvetabbā’ti evaṃ pamāṇaṃ aggahetvā sakalapharaṇavaseneva pavattāti, tena vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, because all of these proceed in an immeasurable range, they are called 'immeasurables.' Indeed, the beings who are their object are immeasurable. And, without taking a measure such as, 'loving-kindness and so forth should be developed towards even a single being in such a limited area,' they proceed only by way of pervading the whole. Therefore, it is said:

Visuddhimaggādivasā catasso,

Hitādiākāravasā panāsaṃ;

Kamo pavattanti ca appamāṇe,

Tā gocare yena tadappamaññāti.

By way of the Visuddhimagga and so forth, they are four; furthermore, their sequence is by way of the modes beginning with welfare. And they proceed in an immeasurable range, by which they are called 'the immeasurables.'

Evaṃ appamāṇagocaratāya ekalakkhaṇāsu cāpi etāsu purimā tisso tikacatukkajjhānikāva honti. Kasmā? Somanassāvippayogato. Kasmā panāsaṃ somanassena avippayogoti? Domanassasamuṭṭhitānaṃ [M 0.0242] byāpādādīnaṃ nissaraṇattā. Pacchimā pana avasesekajjhānikāva. Kasmā? Upekkhāvedanāsampayogato. Na hi sattesu majjhattākārappavattā [P 0.0197] brahmavihārupekkhā upekkhāvedanaṃ vinā vattatīti.

Thus, although these have a single characteristic on account of having an immeasurable range, the first three are only associated with the three-fold and four-fold jhānas. Why? Because of their non-separation from joy. But why is there non-separation from joy for them? Because they are an escape from ill will and so forth, which arise from displeasure. The last one, however, is only associated with the one remaining jhāna. Why? Because of its association with the feeling of equanimity. Indeed, the divine abiding of equanimity, which proceeds towards beings with a mode of neutrality, does not occur without the feeling of equanimity.

Brahmavihārakathā.

The Discourse on the Divine Abidings is finished.

Asubhakathā

The Discourse on the Foul

263. Idāni rāgacaritasattānaṃ ekantahitaṃ nānārammaṇesu ekekajjhānavaseneva pavattamānaṃ rūpāvacarakusalaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ.

263. Now, in order to show the form-sphere wholesome consciousness—which is exclusively beneficial for beings of lustful temperament and which proceeds on various objects only by way of each single jhāna—the passage beginning, 'What things are wholesome?' is again commenced.

Tattha uddhumātakasaññāsahagatantiādīsu, bhastā viya vāyunā, uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena dhumātattā uddhumātaṃ. Uddhumātameva uddhumātakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ uddhumātanti uddhumātakaṃ. Tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vinīlaṃ vuccati viparibhinnanīlavaṇṇaṃ. Vinīlameva vinīlakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ. Maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa, pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa, yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa[V 0.0242], nīlaṭṭhāne nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paribhinnaṭṭhānesu vissandamānaṃ pubbaṃ vipubbaṃ. Vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ. Tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vicchiddaṃ vuccati dvidhā chindanena apadhāritaṃ, vicchiddameva vicchiddakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vicchiddanti vicchiddakaṃ. Vemajjhe chinnassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ito ca etto ca vividhākārena soṇasiṅgālādīhi khāyitaṃ vikkhāyitaṃ. Vikkhāyitameva vikkhāyitakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vikkhāyitanti vikkhāyitakaṃ. Tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vividhā khittaṃ vikkhittaṃ. Vikkhittameva vikkhittakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vikkhittanti vikkhittakaṃ. ‘Aññena hatthaṃ aññena pādaṃ aññena sīsa’nti evaṃ tato tato khittassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Hatañca taṃ purimanayeneva vikkhittakañcāti hatavikkhittakaṃ. Kākapadākārena aṅgapaccaṅgesu satthena hanitvā [P 0.0198] vuttanayena vikkhittakassa chavasarīrassetaṃ [M 0.0243] adhivacanaṃ. Lohitaṃ kirati, vikkhipati, ito cito ca paggharatīti lohitakaṃ. Paggharitalohitamakkhitassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Puḷavā vuccanti kimayo. Puḷave vikiratīti puḷavakaṃ. Kimiparipuṇṇassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aṭṭhiyeva aṭṭhikaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ aṭṭhīti aṭṭhikaṃ. Aṭṭhisaṅkhalikāyapi ekaṭṭhikassapi etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Imāni ca pana uddhumātakādīni nissāya uppannanimittānampi nimittesu paṭiladdhajjhānānampi etāneva nāmāni.

Herein, in the phrases beginning with 'associated with the perception of a bloated corpse,' the following should be understood. Like a bellows inflated by wind, or because it is swollen with a bloatedness that has gradually arisen after the cessation of life, it is called a 'bloated corpse' (uddhumāta). A bloated corpse itself is a uddhumātaka. Or, because it is repulsive, a contemptible bloated corpse is a uddhumātaka. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature. A 'discolored corpse' (vinīla) is said to be one of a discolored blue hue. A discolored corpse itself is a vinīlaka. Or, because it is repulsive, a contemptible discolored corpse is a vinīlaka. This is a designation for a corpse that is red in fleshy areas, white where pus has accumulated, and predominantly of a blue hue, as if wrapped in a blue cloth in the blue areas. A 'festering corpse' (vipubba) has pus oozing from its broken parts. A festering corpse itself is a vipubbaka. Or, because it is repulsive, a contemptible festering corpse is a vipubbaka. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature. A 'cut-up corpse' (vicchidda) is said to be one severed by being cut in two. A cut-up corpse itself is a vicchiddaka. Or, because it is repulsive, a contemptible cut-up corpse is a vicchiddaka. This is a designation for a corpse cut in the middle. A 'gnawed corpse' (vikkhāyita) is one eaten in various ways, here and there, by dogs, jackals, and so forth. A gnawed corpse itself is a vikkhāyitaka. Or, because it is repulsive, a contemptible gnawed corpse is a vikkhāyitaka. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature. A 'scattered corpse' (vikkhitta) is one scattered in various ways. A scattered corpse itself is a vikkhittaka. Or, because it is repulsive, a contemptible scattered corpse is a vikkhittaka. This is a designation for a corpse scattered here and there, such that 'a hand is in one place, a foot in another, the head in another.' A 'hacked and scattered corpse' (hatavikkhittaka) is one that is both hacked and, in the aforementioned manner, scattered. This is a designation for a corpse that, after being hacked with a weapon on its limbs and members in the shape of a crow's foot, is scattered in the manner described. A 'bleeding corpse' (lohitaka) is so called because it scatters, disperses, and oozes blood from here and there. This is a designation for a corpse smeared with oozing blood. Worms are called puḷavā. A 'worm-infested corpse' (puḷavaka) is one that is teeming with worms. This is a designation for a corpse full of worms. A bone itself is an aṭṭhika. Or, because it is repulsive, a contemptible bone is an aṭṭhika. This is a designation for both a chain of bones (a skeleton) and a single bone. Furthermore, these same names—bloated corpse and so on—also apply to the signs that have arisen depending on them, and to the jhānas that have been attained on those signs.

Tattha uddhumātakanimitte appanāvasena uppannā saññā uddhumātakasaññā. Tāya uddhumātakasaññāya sampayogaṭṭhena sahagataṃ uddhumātakasaññāsahagataṃ. Vinīlakasaññāsahagatādīsupi eseva nayo. Yaṃ panettha bhāvanāvidhānaṃ vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, taṃ sabbākārena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.103 ādayo) vuttameva. Avasesā pāḷivaṇṇanā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Kevalañhi idha, catutthajjhānavasena upekkhābrahmavihāre viya, paṭhamajjhānavasena ekekasmiṃ pañcavīsati ekakā honti. Asubhārammaṇassa ca avaḍḍhanīyattā, paritte uddhumātakaṭṭhāne uppannanimittārammaṇaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ, mahante appamāṇārammaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayoti.

Therein, the perception that arises by way of absorption in the counterpart sign of a bloated corpse is the 'perception of a bloated corpse.' The jhāna that is associated with that perception of a bloated corpse, in the sense of association, is 'associated with the perception of a bloated corpse.' This same method applies also to the jhānas associated with the perception of a livid corpse and so on. Whatever method of development should be spoken of here, that has already been stated in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga. The remaining commentary on the Pāḷi should be understood according to the method stated previously. For here, merely, just as in the divine abiding of equanimity by way of the fourth jhāna, there are twenty-five single factors in each case by way of the first jhāna. And because the foul object cannot be expanded, the jhāna with the counterpart sign that has arisen in a small place of a bloated corpse as its object should be understood as having a limited object; in a large place, it should be understood as having an immeasurable object. This is the method for the remaining cases as well.

Iti [V 0.0243] asubhāni subhaguṇo,

Dasasatalocanena thutakitti;

Yāni avoca dasabalo,

Ekekajjhānahetūni.

Thus, the Ten-Powered One—He of excellent qualities, whose fame is praised by the Thousand-Eyed One—declared which foul objects are causes for each single jhāna.

Evaṃ pāḷinayeneva, tāva sabbāni tāni jānitvā;

Tesveva ayaṃ bhiyyo, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā. (visuddhi. 1.120);

Thus, having first understood all those foul objects according to the method of the Pāḷi itself, this miscellaneous discourse concerning them should also be further understood.

Etesu hi yattha katthaci adhigatajjhāno suvikkhambhitarāgattā vītarāgo viya nilloluppacāro hoti. Evaṃ santepi yvāyaṃ asubhabhedo vutto, so sarīrasabhāvappattivasena ca rāgacaritabhedavasena cāti veditabbo.

For, in any one of these foul objects, one who has attained jhāna, because lust has been well suppressed, becomes steady in conduct, like one who is free from lust. Even so, this division of foulness that has been taught should be understood as being by way of the physical state attained by the corpse and by way of the differences in lustful temperament.

Chavasarīrañhi paṭikūlabhāvaṃ āpajjamānaṃ uddhumātakasabhāvappattaṃ vā siyā, vinīlakādīnaṃ vā aññatarasabhāvappattaṃ. Iti yādisaṃ yādisaṃ sakkā [M 0.0244] hoti laddhuṃ tādise [P 0.0199] tādise uddhumātakapaṭikūlaṃ vinīlakapaṭikūlanti evaṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbamevāti sarīrasabhāvappattivasena dasadhā asubhappabhedo vuttoti veditabbo.

For a corpse, in the process of becoming repulsive, may have reached the state of a bloated corpse, or it may have reached one of the other states, such as a livid corpse. Therefore, whatever state it is possible to find, in that very state the sign should be grasped thus: 'the bloated is repulsive,' 'the livid is repulsive.' It should be understood that the tenfold division of foulness is taught by way of the physical state attained by the corpse.

Visesato cettha uddhumātakaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānavipattippakāsanato sarīrasaṇṭhānarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vinīlakaṃ chavirāgavipattippakāsanato sarīravaṇṇarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vipubbakaṃ kāyavaṇapaṭibaddhassa duggandhabhāvassa pakāsanato mālāgandhādivasena samuṭṭhāpitasarīragandharāgino sappāyaṃ. Vicchiddakaṃ antosusirabhāvappakāsanato sarīre ghanabhāvarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vikkhāyitakaṃ maṃsūpacayasampattivināsappakāsanato thanādīsu sarīrappadesesu maṃsūpacayarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vikkhittakaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ vikkhepappakāsanato aṅgapaccaṅgalīlārāgino sappāyaṃ. Hatavikkhittakaṃ sarīrasaṅghāṭabhedavikārappakāsanato sarīrasaṅghāṭasampattirāgino sappāyaṃ. Lohitakaṃ lohitamakkhitapaṭikūlabhāvappakāsanato alaṅkārajanitasobharāgino sappāyaṃ. Puḷavakaṃ kāyassa anekakimikulasādhāraṇabhāvappakāsanato kāye mamattarāgino sappāyaṃ. Aṭṭhikaṃ sarīraṭṭhīnaṃ paṭikūlabhāvappakāsanato dantasampattirāgino sappāyanti. Evaṃ rāgacaritavasenāpi dasadhā asubhappabhedo vuttoti veditabbo.

And here, specifically: The bloated corpse, as it reveals the destruction of the body’s form, is suitable for one with lust for the body’s form. The livid corpse, as it reveals the destruction of the skin’s attractive quality, is suitable for one with lust for the body’s complexion. The festering corpse, as it reveals the state of foul smell connected to the body-as-a-wound, is suitable for one with lust for the body’s scent produced by things like garlands and perfumes. The cut-up corpse, as it reveals the hollow nature of the interior, is suitable for one with lust for the body’s solidity. The gnawed-to-pieces corpse, as it reveals the destruction of the perfection of fleshy abundance, is suitable for one with lust for the fleshy abundance in parts of the body such as the breasts. The scattered-in-pieces corpse, as it reveals the scattering of the limbs major and minor, is suitable for one with lust for the graceful deportment of the limbs. The hacked-and-scattered corpse, as it reveals the breaking and distortion of the body’s composition, is suitable for one with lust for the perfection of the body’s composition. The bloody corpse, as it reveals the repulsive state of being smeared with blood, is suitable for one with lust for the beauty produced by adornments. The worm-infested corpse, as it reveals the state of being shared with many families of worms, is suitable for one with lust for 'mineness' regarding the body. The skeleton, as it reveals the repulsive nature of the body’s bones, is suitable for one with lust for the perfection of the teeth. In this way, it should be understood that the tenfold division of foulness is also taught by way of the differences in lustful temperament.

Yasmā [V 0.0244] pana dasavidhepi etasmiṃ asubhe seyyathāpi nāma aparisaṇṭhitajalāya sīghasotāya nadiyā arittabaleneva nāvā tiṭṭhati, vinā arittena na sakkā ṭhapetuṃ, evameva dubbalattā ārammaṇassa vitakkabaleneva cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, vinā vitakkena na sakkā ṭhapetuṃ, tasmā paṭhamajjhānamevettha hoti, na dutiyādīni. Paṭikūlepi cetasmiṃ ārammaṇe ‘addhā imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇamhā parimuccissāmī’ti evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvitāya ceva nīvaraṇasantāpappahānena ca pītisomanassaṃ [P 0.0200] uppajjati, ‘bahuṃ dāni vetanaṃ labhissāmī’ti ānisaṃsadassāvino pupphachaḍḍakassa gūtharāsimhi viya, ussannabyādhidukkhassa rogino vamanavirecanappavattiyaṃ viya ca.

Furthermore, since in these ten kinds of foul objects—just as in a swift-flowing river with turbulent water, a boat is held steady only by the power of a punt-pole and cannot be kept in place without the pole—so too, because of the weakness of the object, the mind becomes one-pointed and is held steady only by the power of applied thought; it cannot be kept in place without applied thought. Therefore, only the first jhāna arises here, not the second and so on. And even with this repulsive object, rapture and gladness arise both from seeing the benefit—'Surely, by this practice, I will be freed from aging and death'—and from the abandoning of the torment of the hindrances. This is like the rapture and gladness of a scavenger who, seeing the benefit, thinks, 'Now I will get a large payment!' while in the midst of a heap of excrement; and like that of a patient suffering from a severe illness during an episode of vomiting and purging.

Dasavidhampi cetaṃ asubhaṃ lakkhaṇato ekameva hoti. Dasavidhassapi hi etassa asuciduggandhajegucchapaṭikūlabhāvo eva lakkhaṇaṃ. Tadetaṃ iminā [M 0.0245] lakkhaṇena na kevalaṃ matasarīreyeva dantaṭṭhikadassāvino pana cetiyapabbatavāsino mahātissattherassa viya, hatthikkhandhagataṃ rājānaṃ ullokentassa saṅgharakkhitattherupaṭṭhākasāmaṇerassa viya ca, jīvamānakasarīrepi upaṭṭhāti. Yatheva hi matasarīraṃ evaṃ jīvamānakampi asubhameva. Asubhalakkhaṇaṃ panettha āgantukena alaṅkārena paṭicchannattā na paññāyatīti.

And this tenfold foulness is one in characteristic. For the characteristic of all ten kinds is simply the state of being impure, foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive. And this, by means of this characteristic, appears not only in a dead body but also in a living body, as it did for the Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Cetiyapabbata, who saw the tooth-bone, and for the novice attendant of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, who looked up at the king seated on an elephant's shoulder. For just as a dead body is foul, so too is a living one. But in this case, the characteristic of foulness is not discerned because it is concealed by adventitious adornment.

Asubhakathā.

The Section on Foulness.

Kiṃ pana pathavīkasiṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā aṭṭhikasaññāpariyosānāvesā rūpāvacarappanā, udāhu aññāpi atthīti? Atthi; ānāpānajjhānañhi kāyagatāsatibhāvanā ca idha na kathitā. Kiñcāpi na kathitā vāyokasiṇe pana gahite ānāpānajjhānaṃ gahitameva; vaṇṇakasiṇesu ca gahitesu kesādīsu catukkapañcakajjhānavasena uppannā kāyagatāsati, dasasu asubhesu gahitesu dvattiṃsākāre paṭikūlamanasikārajjhānavasena ceva navasivathikāvaṇṇajjhānavasena ca pavattā kāyagatāsati gahitāvāti. Sabbāpi rūpāvacarappanā idha kathitāva hotīti.

Now, is form-sphere absorption only that which begins with the earth kasiṇa and ends with the perception of bones, or is there other absorption as well? There is. For the jhāna on mindfulness of breathing and the development of mindfulness of the body are not taught here. Although they are not taught, when the air kasiṇa is taken, the jhāna on mindfulness of breathing is indeed included. And when the color kasiṇas are taken, mindfulness of the body that arises in relation to hair, etc., by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas is included. When the ten foul objects are taken, mindfulness of the body that proceeds by way of the jhāna of attention to repulsiveness regarding the thirty-two parts, and by way of the jhāna on the nine kinds of charnel-ground signs, is included. Thus, all form-sphere absorption is indeed taught here.

Rūpāvacarakusalakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Section on Form-Sphere Wholesome States is concluded.

Arūpāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Wholesome Immaterial Sphere.

Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ

The Base of Infinite Space.

265. Idāni [V 0.0245] arūpāvacarakusalaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha arūpūpapattiyāti arūpabhavo arūpaṃ, arūpe upapatti arūpūpapatti, tassā arūpūpapattiyā. Maggaṃ bhāvetīti upāyaṃ hetuṃ kāraṇaṃ uppādeti vaḍḍheti. Sabbasoti sabbākārena. Sabbāsaṃ vā anavasesānanti attho. Rūpasaññānanti saññāsīsena vuttarūpāvacarajjhānānañceva [P 0.0201] tadārammaṇānañca. Rūpāvacarajjhānampi hi rūpanti vuccati ‘rūpī rūpāni passatī’tiādīsu (dha. sa. 248; dī. ni. 2.129). Tassa ārammaṇampi “bahiddhā rūpāni passati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 244-246; dī. ni. 2.173); tasmā idha rūpe saññā rūpasaññāti evaṃ saññāsīsena [M 0.0246] vuttarūpāvacarajjhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Rūpaṃ saññā assāti rūpasaññaṃ, rūpamassa nāmanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ pathavīkasiṇādibhedassa tadārammaṇassa cetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ.

265. Now, in order to set forth the wholesome immaterial-sphere states, the text begins again with 'Which states are wholesome?' and so on. Here, 'for rebirth in the immaterial sphere' (arūpūpapattiyā) means: immaterial existence (arūpabhava) is the immaterial [realm]; rebirth in the immaterial [realm] (arūpe upapatti) is rebirth in the immaterial sphere (arūpūpapatti); for that rebirth in the immaterial sphere. 'Develops the path' means: one produces and increases the means, cause, and reason. 'Completely' (sabbaso) means: in every way. Or, the meaning is 'of all without remainder.' 'Perceptions of form' (rūpasaññānaṃ) means: this refers to the form-sphere jhānas and their objects, mentioned under the heading of perception. For the form-sphere jhāna is also called 'form,' as in 'one with form sees forms.' Its object is also [called 'form'], as in 'externally, one sees forms, beautiful and ugly'; therefore, here, 'perception in form is perception-of-form' (rūpe saññā rūpasaññā); thus, this is a designation for the form-sphere jhāna mentioned under the heading of perception. That which has the designation 'form' is 'rūpasaññaṃ' (having the designation of form); it is said that 'form' is its name. Thus, this should be understood as a designation for its object, which is differentiated as the earth kasiṇa and so forth.

Samatikkamāti virāgā nirodhā ca. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Etāsaṃ kusalavipākakiriyavasena pañcadasannaṃ jhānasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpasaññānaṃ, etesañca pathavīkasiṇādivasena aṭṭhannaṃ ārammaṇasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpasaññānaṃ, sabbākārena anavasesānaṃ vā virāgā ca nirodhā ca virāgahetu ceva nirodhahetu ca ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Na hi sakkā sabbaso anatikkantarūpasaññena etaṃ upasampajja viharitunti.

'Transcends' means through dispassion and cessation. What is meant by this? Through dispassion for and cessation of these fifteen perceptions of form known as jhānas—by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional—and these eight perceptions of form known as objects—by way of the earth kasiṇa, etc.—which are in every way and without remainder; and through the cause of dispassion and the cause of cessation, one attains and dwells in the base of infinite space. For it is not possible for one who has not completely transcended the perceptions of form to attain and dwell in this.

Tattha yasmā ārammaṇe avirattassa saññāsamatikkamo na hoti, samatikkantāsu ca saññāsu ārammaṇaṃ samatikkantameva hoti, tasmā ārammaṇasamatikkamaṃ avatvā “tattha katamā rūpasaññā? Rūpāvacarasamāpattiṃ samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa vā saññā sañjānanā sañjānitattaṃ, imā vuccanti rūpasaññāyo. Imā rūpasaññāyo atikkanto hoti, vītikkanto, samatikkanto, tena vuccati sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā”ti (vibha. 602) evaṃ vibhaṅge saññānaṃyeva samatikkamo vutto. Yasmā pana ārammaṇasamatikkamena [V 0.0246] pattabbā etā samāpattiyo, na ekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe paṭhamajjhānādīni viya, tasmā ayaṃ ārammaṇasamatikkamavasenāpi atthavaṇṇanā katāti veditabbā.

Herein, since for one who is not dispassionate towards the object there is no transcending of perception, and when perceptions are transcended, the object is also transcended, therefore, without mentioning the transcendence of the object, in the Vibhaṅga only the transcendence of perceptions is spoken of: 'Herein, what is perception of form? The perception, perceiving, or state of having perceived of one who has attained the form-sphere meditative attainment, or of one who has been reborn [in the form realm], or of one who dwells happily in the present life—these are called perceptions of form. One has gone beyond, overcome, and completely transcended these perceptions of form; therefore it is said: "the complete transcendence of all perceptions of form."' However, since these attainments are to be reached by the transcendence of the object, not on a single object like the first jhāna and so on, therefore it should be known that this explanation is made also in terms of the transcendence of the object.

Paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānañca paṭighātena samuppannā saññā paṭighasaññā. Rūpasaññādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamā paṭighasaññā? Rūpasaññā saddasaññā gandhasaññā rasasaññā phoṭṭhabbasaññā, imā vuccanti paṭighasaññāyo”ti (vibha. 603). Tāsaṃ kusalavipākānaṃ pañcannaṃ akusalavipākānaṃ pañcannanti sabbaso [P 0.0202] dasannampi paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā pahānā asamuppādā appavattiṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

The cessation of perceptions of resistance: Perceptions that arise due to the impact of the bases, such as the eye, and the objects, such as forms, are perceptions of resistance. This is a designation for perceptions of form and so forth. As it is said: 'Herein, what are perceptions of resistance? Perception of form, perception of sound, perception of smell, perception of taste, perception of tactile object—these are called perceptions of resistance.' Regarding these ten perceptions of resistance in their entirety—five wholesome-resultant and five unwholesome-resultant—it is said that one brings about their non-occurrence through their cessation, abandonment, and non-arising.

Kāmañcetā paṭhamajjhānādīni samāpannassāpi na santi – na hi tasmiṃ samaye pañcadvāravasena cittaṃ pavattati – evaṃ santepi, aññattha pahīnānaṃ sukhadukkhānaṃ [M 0.0247] catutthajjhāne viya, sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ tatiyamagge viya ca, imasmiṃ jhāne ussāhajananatthaṃ imassa jhānassa pasaṃsāvasena etāsaṃ ettha vacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Atha vā kiñcāpi tā rūpāvacaraṃ samāpannassa na santi, atha kho na pahīnattā na santi. Na hi rūpavirāgāya rūpāvacarabhāvanā saṃvattati, rūpāyattā ca etāsaṃ pavatti. Ayaṃ pana bhāvanā rūpavirāgāya saṃvattati. Tasmā tā ettha pahīnāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Na kevalañca vattuṃ, ekaṃseneva evaṃ dhāretumpi vaṭṭati. Tāsañhi ito pubbe appahīnattāyeva paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpannassa “saddo kaṇṭako”ti (a. ni. 10.72) vutto bhagavatā. Idha ca pahīnattāyeva arūpasamāpattīnaṃ āneñjatā santavimokkhatā ca vuttā. Āḷāro ca kāḷāmo āruppasamāpanno pañcamattāni sakaṭasatāni nissāya nissāya atikkantāni neva addasa, na pana saddaṃ assosīti (dī. ni. 2.192).

Although it is true that these do not exist for one who has attained the first jhāna and so forth—for at that time the mind does not proceed by way of the five doors—even so, just as with the mention in the fourth jhāna of pleasure and pain which were abandoned elsewhere, or of identity-view and so forth in the third path, the mention of these here in this jhāna should be understood as being by way of praise for this jhāna in order to generate enthusiasm. Alternatively, although they do not exist for one who has attained the form-sphere absorption, yet they do not exist not because they have been abandoned. For the development of the form-sphere does not lead to dispassion toward form, and the occurrence of these is dependent on form. But this development leads to dispassion toward form. Therefore, it is fitting to say that they are abandoned here. And not only is it fitting to say so, it is also proper to hold it so definitively. For it is precisely because they were not abandoned before this that the Blessed One said of one who has attained the first jhāna, 'Sound is a thorn.' And here, precisely because they are abandoned, the immaterial attainments are described as imperturbability and peaceful liberation. Moreover, Āḷāra Kālāma, while having attained the formless attainment, did not see five hundred carts passing by very close, nor did he hear the sound.

Nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārāti nānatte gocare pavattānaṃ saññānaṃ nānattānaṃ vā saññānaṃ. Yasmā hi etā “tattha katamā nānattasaññā? Asamāpannassa manodhātusamaṅgissa vā manoviññāṇadhātusamaṅgissa vā saññā sañjānanā sañjānitattaṃ, imā vuccanti nānattasaññāyo”ti (vibha. 604) evaṃ vibhaṅge vibhajitvā vuttā idha adhippetā; asamāpannassa manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātusaṅgahitā saññā rūpasaddādibhede nānatte nānāsabhāve gocare pavattanti; yasmā cetā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, dvādasa akusalasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakusalavipākasaññā[V 0.0247], dve akusalavipākasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakiriyasaññāti evaṃ catucattālīsampi saññā nānattā nānāsabhāvā aññamaññaṃ asadisā, tasmā nānattasaññāti vuttā. Tāsaṃ sabbaso nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā anāvajjanā asamannāhārā apaccavekkhaṇā. Yasmā tā nāvajjati, na manasikaroti, na paccavekkhati, tasmāti [P 0.0203] vuttaṃ hoti.

“By not attending to perceptions of diversity” means not attending to the perceptions that arise in diverse objects, or to the perceptions that are themselves diverse. For these are the perceptions intended here, which are explained in the Vibhaṅga as follows: “Herein, what are perceptions of diversity? For one who has not attained absorption, whether endowed with the mind-element or the mind-consciousness-element, there is perception, perceiving, the state of having perceived—these are called perceptions of diversity” (Vibh. 604). The perceptions of one who has not attained absorption, included in the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, arise in diverse objects of diverse natures, such as forms, sounds, and so on. And because these forty-four perceptions—eight sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven sense-sphere wholesome resultant perceptions, two unwholesome resultant perceptions, and eleven sense-sphere functional perceptions—are diverse, of diverse natures, and dissimilar to one another, they are called “perceptions of diversity.” The complete non-attention to these perceptions of diversity is non-adverting, not bringing to mind, and not reviewing. Because one does not advert to them, does not attend to them, and does not review them, it is thus stated.

Yasmā cettha purimā rūpasaññā paṭighasaññā ca iminā jhānena nibbatte bhavepi na vijjanti, pageva tasmiṃ bhave imaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇakāle, tasmā tāsaṃ ‘samatikkamā atthaṅgamā’ti dvedhāpi abhāvoyeva vutto. Nānattasaññāsu pana yasmā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, nava [M 0.0248] kiriyāsaññā, dasa akusalasaññāti imā sattavīsati saññā iminā jhānena nibbatte bhave vijjanti, tasmā tāsaṃ amanasikārāti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāpi hi imaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharanto tāsaṃ amanasikārāyeva upasampajja viharati. Tā pana manasikaronto asamāpanno hotīti. Saṅkhepato cettha ‘rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā’ti iminā sabbarūpāvacaradhammānaṃ pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā’ti iminā sabbesaṃ kāmāvacaracittacetasikānañca pahānaṃ amanasikāro ca vuttoti veditabbo.

Since, in this case, the former perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance do not exist even in the existence produced by this jhāna—let alone at the time of dwelling having attained this jhāna in that existence—therefore their absence is stated in two ways as “overcoming” and “disappearance.” As for perceptions of diversity, however, since these twenty-seven perceptions—eight sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, nine functional perceptions, and ten unwholesome perceptions—do exist in the existence produced by this jhāna, it should be understood that for them “non-attention” is stated. For even there, one who dwells having attained this jhāna does so only by not attending to them. But one who attends to them is not one who has attained absorption. In brief, it should be understood that herein, by “the overcoming of perceptions of form,” the abandonment of all form-sphere phenomena is stated. By “the disappearance of perceptions of resistance and the non-attention to perceptions of diversity,” both the abandonment and the non-attention to all sense-sphere consciousness and mental factors are stated.

Iti bhagavā ‘pannarasannaṃ rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamena, dasannaṃ paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamena, catucattālīsāya nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārenā’ti tīhi padehi ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyā vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Kiṃ kāraṇāti ce sotūnaṃ ussāhajananatthañceva palobhanatthañca. Sace hi keci apaṇḍitā vadeyyuṃ ‘satthā ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiṃ nibbattethāti vadati, ko nu kho etāya nibbattitāya attho? Ko ānisaṃso’ti te evaṃ vattuṃ mā labhantūti imehi ākārehi samāpattiyā vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Tañhi nesaṃ sutvā evaṃ bhavissati – ‘evaṃsantā kira ayaṃ samāpatti, evaṃpaṇītā, nibbattessāma na’nti. Athassa nibbattanatthāya ussāhaṃ karissantīti.

Thus the Blessed One, with three phrases—“by the overcoming of the fifteen perceptions of form, by the disappearance of the ten perceptions of resistance, and by the non-attention to the forty-four perceptions of diversity”—extolled the attainment of the base of infinite space. If it is asked, “For what reason?” It was for the purpose of generating enthusiasm and enticing the listeners. For he extolled the attainment in these ways so that any unwise persons might not get the chance to say, “The Teacher says to produce the attainment of the base of infinite space, but what is the purpose of producing it? What is the benefit?” For having heard this praise, it will occur to them: “It seems this attainment is so peaceful, so sublime; we shall produce it!” Then they will make an effort for the purpose of producing it.

Palobhanatthañcāpi nesaṃ etissā vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, visakaṇṭakavāṇijo viya. Visakaṇṭakavāṇijo nāma guḷavāṇijo vuccati. So kira guḷaphāṇitakhaṇḍasakkarādīni sakaṭenādāya [V 0.0248] paccantagāmaṃ gantvā ‘visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhatha visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhathā’ti ugghosesi. Taṃ sutvā gāmikā ‘visaṃ nāma kakkhaḷaṃ, yo naṃ khādati so marati, kaṇṭakopi vijjhitvā māreti. Ubhopete kakkhaḷā, ko ettha ānisaṃso’ti gehadvārāni thakesuṃ, dārake ca palāpesuṃ. Taṃ disvā vāṇijo ‘avohārakusalā ime [P 0.0204] gāmikā, handa ne upāyena gaṇhāpemī’ti ‘atimadhuraṃ gaṇhatha atisāduṃ gaṇhatha, guḷaṃ phāṇitaṃ sakkaraṃ samagghaṃ labbhati, kūṭamāsakakūṭakahāpaṇādīhipi labbhatī’ti ugghosesi. Taṃ sutvā gāmikā haṭṭhapahaṭṭhā niggantvā bahumpi mūlaṃ datvā gahesuṃ.

He also extolled its virtues to entice them, like the “poison-thorn” merchant. A “poison-thorn” merchant is what a jaggery merchant is called. It is said that he, having loaded a cart with jaggery, molasses, raw sugar, powdered sugar, and so on, went to a border village and called out, “Get your poison-thorn! Get your poison-thorn!” Hearing this, the villagers thought, “Poison is harsh; whoever eats it dies. A thorn also pierces and kills. Both of these are harsh. What benefit is there in this?” and they shut their house doors and made their children flee. Seeing this, the merchant thought, “These villagers are unskilled in trade terms. Come, I will make them buy it by a stratagem.” He then called out, “Get the very sweet! Get the very delicious! Jaggery, molasses, sugar! It can be gotten cheaply; it can even be obtained with counterfeit māsakas and counterfeit kahāpaṇas!” Hearing this, the villagers, greatly delighted, came out and, giving a high price, bought it.

Tattha vāṇijassa ‘visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhathā’ti ugghosanaṃ viya bhagavato ‘ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiṃ nibbattethā’ti vacanaṃ. ‘Ubhopete kakkhaḷā[M 0.0249], ko ettha ānisaṃso’ti? Gāmikānaṃ cintanaṃ viya ‘bhagavā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ nibbattethāti āha, ko ettha ānisaṃso? Nāssa guṇaṃ jānāmā’ti sotūnaṃ cintanaṃ. Athassa vāṇijassa ‘atimadhuraṃ gaṇhathā’tiādivacanaṃ viya bhagavato rūpasaññāsamatikkamanādikaṃ ānisaṃsappakāsanaṃ. Idañhi sutvā te bahumpi mūlaṃ datvā, gāmikā viya guḷaṃ, iminā ānisaṃsena palobhitacittā mahantampi ussāhaṃ katvā imaṃ samāpattiṃ nibbattessantīti ussāhajananatthaṃ palobhanatthañca kathesi.

Herein, the Blessed One’s statement, “Produce the attainment of the base of infinite space,” is like the merchant’s call, “Get your poison-thorn!” The listeners’ thought, “The Blessed One said to produce the base of infinite space, but what is the benefit in this? We do not know its virtue,” is like the villagers’ thought, “Both are harsh, what benefit is there in this?” Then, the Blessed One’s explanation of the benefits, beginning with the overcoming of perceptions of form, is like that merchant’s words, “Get the very sweet!” and so on. For having heard this, they, their minds enticed by this benefit, will make a great effort and produce this attainment—just as the villagers, giving a high price, bought the jaggery. Thus, he spoke for the purpose of generating enthusiasm and for the purpose of enticing.

Ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagatanti ettha nāssa antoti anantaṃ. Ākāsaṃ anantaṃ ākāsānantaṃ. Ākāsānantameva ākāsānañcaṃ. Taṃ ākāsānañcaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanamassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa, devānaṃ devāyatanamivāti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Iti ākāsānañcaṃ ca taṃ āyatanañcātipi ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmiṃ ākāsānañcāyatane appanāppattāya saññāya sahagataṃ ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ.

Regarding “endowed with the perception of the base of infinite space”: Herein, that which has no end (na assa anto) is endless (anantaṃ). Space is endless, thus “endless space” (ākāsānantaṃ). “Endless space” itself is ākāsānañca. That ākāsānañca is a base (āyatana) for this jhāna with its associated states in the sense of being a foundation, just as the abode of the gods (devāyatana) is for the gods; thus it is the “base of the infinity of space” (ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ). Or, it is the “base of the infinity of space” because it is both the infinity of space (ākāsānañca) and it is that base (āyatana). This is a designation for the space obtained by the removal of the kasiṇa. “Endowed with the perception of the base of infinite space” means endowed with the perception that has reached absorption in that base of the infinity of space.

Yathā pana aññattha ‘ananto ākāso’ti (vibha. 508; dī. ni. 2.129) vuttaṃ, evamidha anantanti vā parittanti vā na gahitaṃ. Kasmā? Anante hi gahite parittaṃ na gayhati, paritte gahite anantaṃ na gayhati. Evaṃ sante ārammaṇacatukkaṃ na pūrati, desanā soḷasakkhattukā na hoti. Sammāsambuddhassa ca imasmiṃ ṭhāne desanaṃ soḷasakkhattukaṃ kātuṃ [V 0.0249] ajjhāsayo, tasmā anantanti vā parittanti vā avatvā ‘ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagata’nti āha. Evañhi sati ubhayampi gahitameva hoti. Ārammaṇacatukkaṃ pūrati, desanā soḷasakkhattukā sampajjati. Avaseso pāḷiattho heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānanikantipariyādānadukkhatāya [P 0.0205] cettha dukkhā paṭipadā, pariyādinnanikantikassa appanāparivāsadandhatāya dandhābhiññā hoti. Vipariyāyena sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā ca veditabbā. Parittakasiṇugghāṭimākāse pana pavattaṃ jhānaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ vipulakasiṇugghāṭimākāse pavattaṃ appamāṇārammaṇanti veditabbaṃ. Upekkhābrahmavihāre viya ca idhāpi catutthajjhānavasena pañcavīsati ekakā honti[M 0.0250]. Yathā cettha evaṃ ito paresupi. Visesamattameva pana tesu vaṇṇayissāma.

Furthermore, just as elsewhere it is said, ‘Space is infinite’ (Vibh. 406; Dī. Ni. 2.129), so here it is not taken as ‘infinite’ or ‘limited.’ Why? For if the infinite is taken, the limited is not taken; if the limited is taken, the infinite is not taken. This being so, the fourfold object is not fulfilled, and the teaching does not become sixteen-fold. And the Perfectly Enlightened One’s intention in this instance is to make the teaching sixteen-fold; therefore, without saying ‘infinite’ or ‘limited,’ he said, ‘accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space.’ For when this is so, both are indeed taken. The fourfold object is fulfilled, and the sixteen-fold teaching is accomplished. The remaining meaning of the Pāḷi should be understood in the same way as stated below. And here, the practice is difficult due to the difficulty of completely removing the craving for the fourth form-sphere jhāna, and for one whose craving has been completely removed, direct knowledge is slow due to the sluggishness of the practice leading to absorption. Conversely, the pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge are to be understood. Furthermore, it should be understood that the jhāna occurring in the conceptual space from the removal of a limited kasiṇa has a limited object, while that occurring in the conceptual space from the removal of an extensive kasiṇa has a boundless object. And just as in the case of the divine abiding of equanimity, here too, by way of the fourth jhāna, there are twenty-five single factors. As it is here, so it is in the subsequent jhānas. However, we will explain only the differences among them.

Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ

Exposition of the Jhāna of the Base of Infinite Consciousness

266. Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammāti, ettha tāva pubbe vuttanayena ākāsānañcaṃ āyatanamassa adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti jhānampi ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Vuttanayeneva ārammaṇampi. Evametaṃ jhānañca ārammaṇañcāti ubhayampi appavattikaraṇena ca amanasikaraṇena ca samatikkamitvāva yasmā idaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihātabbaṃ, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā ‘ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammā’ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

266. Having transcended the base of infinite space: Here, first, as explained previously, because for this jhāna the infinite space is its base in the sense of being its foundation, the jhāna too is called ‘the base of infinite space.’ In the same way as stated, so too is the object. Thus, since this base of infinite consciousness is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after having transcended both the jhāna and the object by causing their non-occurrence and by not attending to them, it should be understood that, having combined both of these, this was said: ‘having transcended the base of infinite space.’

Viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāsahagatanti, ettha pana anantanti manasikātabbavasena nāssa antoti anantaṃ. Anantameva ānañcaṃ. Viññāṇaṃ ānañcaṃ viññāṇānañcanti avatvā viññāṇañcanti vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha rūḷhīsaddo. Tadeva viññāṇañcaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena imāya saññāya āyatananti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ. Tasmiṃ viññāṇañcāyatane pavattāya saññāya sahagatanti viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ. Ākāse pavattaviññāṇārammaṇassa jhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyā nikantipariyādānadukkhatāya dukkhā paṭipadā, pariyādinnanikantikassa appanāparivāsadandhatāya dandhābhiññā. Vipariyāyena sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā ca. Parittakasiṇugghāṭimākāsārammaṇaṃ samāpattiṃ ārabbha pavattiyā parittārammaṇatā, vipariyāyena appamāṇārammaṇatā veditabbā. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

Accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness: Here, ‘infinite’ (ananta) means that, because it is to be attended to as ‘infinite,’ it has no end; hence it is infinite. The infinite itself is ānañca. Instead of saying ‘consciousness is ānañca’ (viññāṇaṃ ānañcaṃ) or ‘the ānañca of consciousness’ (viññāṇānañcaṃ), it is said ‘consciousness-infinity’ (viññāṇañcaṃ). This is a conventional term here. That very ‘consciousness-infinity,’ in the sense of being the foundation for this perception, is its base; therefore, it is the ‘base of infinite consciousness’ (viññāṇañcāyatana). The jhāna is ‘accompanied by the perception’ that occurs in that base of infinite consciousness; therefore, it is called ‘accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.’ This is a designation for the jhāna that has as its object the consciousness that occurred in relation to space. Here, the practice is difficult due to the difficulty of completely removing the craving for the attainment of the base of infinite space; for one whose craving has been completely removed, direct knowledge is slow due to the sluggishness of the practice leading to absorption. Conversely, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is swift. The state of having a limited object should be understood from its arising in dependence on the attainment that has as its object the space from the removal of a limited kasiṇa; conversely, the state of having a boundless object should be understood. The rest is just as previously stated.

Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ

Exposition of the Jhāna of the Base of Nothingness

267. Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ [V 0.0250] samatikkammāti etthāpi pubbe vuttanayeneva viññāṇañca āyatanamassa adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti jhānampi viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ. Vuttanayeneva ca ārammaṇampi. Evametaṃ jhānañca ārammaṇañcāti [P 0.0206] ubhayampi appavattikaraṇena ca amanasikaraṇena ca samatikkamitvāva yasmā idaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihātabbaṃ, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā ‘viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammā’ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

267. Having transcended the base of infinite consciousness: Here too, by the method already stated previously, because for that jhāna the infinite consciousness is its base in the sense of being its foundation, the jhāna is also called ‘the base of infinite consciousness.’ And by the method already stated, the object is also so called. Thus, since this base of nothingness is to be entered upon and abided in only after having transcended both these—the jhāna and the object—by causing their non-occurrence and by not attending to them, it should be understood that, having combined both of these, this was said: ‘having transcended the base of infinite consciousness.’

Ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāsahagatanti [M 0.0251] ettha pana nāssa kiñcananti akiñcanaṃ; antamaso bhaṅgamattampi assa avasiṭṭhaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Akiñcanassa bhāvo ākiñcaññaṃ. Ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇāpagamassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ ākiñcaññaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena imissā saññāya āyatananti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Tasmiṃ ākiñcaññāyatane pavattāya saññāya sahagatanti ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ. Ākāse pavattitaviññāṇāpagamārammaṇassa jhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha viññāṇañcāyatanasamāpattiyā nikantipariyādānadukkhatāya dukkhā paṭipadā, pariyādinnanikantikassa appanā parivāsadandhatāya dandhābhiññā. Vipariyāyena sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā ca. Parittakasiṇugghāṭimākāse pavattitaviññāṇāpagamārammaṇatāya parittārammaṇatā, vipariyāyena appamāṇārammaṇatā veditabbā. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

As for ‘accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness’: Here, ‘nothing’ (akiñcana) means ‘there is nothing of it’; it is meant that not even a remnant to the extent of a moment of dissolution remains for it. The state of that which has nothing is ‘nothingness’ (ākiñcañña). This is a designation for the cessation of the consciousness of the base of infinite space. That ‘nothingness’ is the base (āyatana) for this perception in the sense of being its foundation; therefore, it is called ‘the base of nothingness’ (ākiñcaññāyatana). The jhāna is ‘accompanied by the perception that occurs in that base of nothingness’; therefore, it is called ‘accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness.’ This is a designation for the jhāna that has as its object the cessation of the consciousness that had been made to occur in relation to space. Here, the practice is difficult due to the difficulty of completely removing the craving for the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness. For one whose craving has been completely removed, direct knowledge is slow due to the sluggishness of the practice leading to absorption. Conversely, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is swift. Because its object is the cessation of the consciousness that had been made to occur in relation to the space produced by the removal of a limited kasiṇa, its object is limited; conversely, its object is to be understood as boundless. The rest is just as before.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ

Exposition of the Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception

Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkammāti etthāpi pubbe vuttanayeneva ākiñcaññaṃ āyatanamassa adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti jhānampi ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Vuttanayeneva ārammaṇampi. Evametaṃ jhānañca ārammaṇañcāti ubhayampi appavattikaraṇena ca amanasikaraṇe ca samatikkamitvāva yasmā idaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihātabbaṃ, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā ‘ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkammā’ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Having transcended the base of nothingness: Here too, by the method already stated previously, because for that jhāna ‘nothingness’ is its base in the sense of being its foundation, the jhāna is also called ‘the base of nothingness.’ By the method already stated, the object is also so called. Thus, since this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is to be entered upon and abided in only after having transcended both these—the jhāna and the object—by causing their non-occurrence and by not attending to them, it should be understood that, having combined both of these, this was said: ‘having transcended the base of nothingness.’

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagatanti ettha pana yāya saññāya bhāvato taṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti vuccati, yathā paṭipannassa sā saññā hoti, taṃ tāva dassetuṃ vibhaṅge “nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti uddharitvā “taññeva ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasikaroti [P 0.0207][V 0.0251] saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāveti, tena vuccati nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti (vibha. 619) vuttaṃ. Tattha ‘santato manasikarotī’ti ‘santā vatāyaṃ samāpatti, yatra hi nāma natthibhāvampi ārammaṇaṃ karitvā ṭhassatī’ti evaṃ santārammaṇatāya naṃ ‘santā’ti manasikaroti. Santato ce manasikaroti, kathaṃ samatikkamo hotīti? Anāvajjitukāmatāya. So hi kiñcāpi naṃ santato [M 0.0252] manasikaroti, atha khvassa ‘ahametaṃ āvajjissāmi samāpajjissāmi adhiṭṭhahissāmi vuṭṭhahissāmi paccavekkhissāmī’ti esa ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro na hoti. Kasmā? Ākiñcaññāyatanato nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassa santatarapaṇītataratāya.

As for 'accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception': Here, it is called 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' because of the existence of a certain perception. In order to show how that perception arises for one who is practicing, it is first stated in the Vibhaṅga by quoting, 'neither percipient nor non-percipient,' and then it is said: 'He attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful and cultivates the attainment with residual formations; therefore, he is called "neither percipient nor non-percipient."' Therein, 'attends to it as peaceful' means: he attends to it as 'peaceful,' thinking, 'Peaceful indeed is this attainment, since it can stand having made even the state of non-existence its object!' Thus, he attends to it as 'peaceful' because its object is peaceful. If he attends to it as peaceful, how does transcendence occur? Through the desire not to advert to it. For although he attends to it as peaceful, for him this advertence, this application of mind, this attention—'I will advert to it, I will attain it, I will resolve upon it, I will emerge from it, I will review it'—does not occur. Why? Because the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is more peaceful and more sublime than the base of nothingness.

Yathā hi rājā mahaccarājānubhāvena hatthikkhandhagato nagaravīthiyaṃ vicaranto dantakārādayo sippike ekaṃ vatthaṃ daḷhaṃ nivāsetvā ekena sīsaṃ veṭhetvā dantacuṇṇādīhi samokiṇṇagatte anekāni dantavikatiādīni karonte disvā ‘aho vata re chekā ācariyā, īdisānipi nāma sippāni karissantī’ti, evaṃ tesaṃ chekatāya tussati, na cassa evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vatāhaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya evarūpo sippiko bhaveyya’nti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Rajjasiriyā mahānisaṃsatāya. So sippike samatikkamitvāva gacchati. Evamevesa kiñcāpi taṃ samāpattiṃ santato manasikaroti, atha khvassa ‘ahametaṃ samāpattiṃ āvajjissāmi samāpajjissāmi adhiṭṭhahissāmi vuṭṭhahissāmi paccavekkhissāmī’ti neva esa ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro hoti. So taṃ santato manasi karonto taṃ paramasukhumaṃ appanāppattaṃ saññaṃ pāpuṇāti, yāya ‘nevasaññīnāsaññī nāma hoti, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāvetī’ti vuccati. ‘Saṅkhārāvasesasamāpatti’nti accantasukhumabhāvappattasaṅkhāraṃ catutthāruppasamāpattiṃ.

For it is like a king who, with great royal majesty, mounted on the back of an elephant and traveling through the city streets, sees ivory carvers and other craftsmen—wearing one garment tightly, with their heads wrapped in another, their bodies covered with ivory dust and the like, making various ivory ornaments—and thinks, 'Oh, how skilled these masters are! They can indeed create such crafts!' Thus he is pleased with their skill, but it does not occur to him, 'Oh, that I might abandon the kingdom and become such a craftsman!' For what reason? Because of the great benefit of the glory of kingship. He goes on, having simply passed by the craftsmen. In just the same way, although this person attends to that attainment as peaceful, for him this advertence, this application of mind, this attention—'I will advert to this attainment, I will attain it, I will resolve upon it, I will emerge from it, I will review it'—never occurs. He, while attending to it as peaceful, reaches that extremely subtle perception that has attained absorption, by which he is called 'neither percipient nor non-percipient,' and it is said that 'he develops the attainment with residual formations.' 'The attainment with residual formations' means the fourth formless attainment, which consists of formations that have reached a state of extreme subtlety.

Idāni yaṃ taṃ evaṃ adhigatāya saññāya vasena nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti vuccati, taṃ atthato dassetuṃ “nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa vā, upapannassa vā, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa vā cittacetasikā dhammā”ti (vibha. 620) vuttaṃ. Tesu idha samāpannassa cittacetasikā dhammā adhippetā.

Now, in order to show in substance that which is called 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' by the power of the perception thus attained, it is said: 'The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception means the mental and mental concomitant states of one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or of one who has been reborn there, or of one who is dwelling happily in the present life.' Among these, here the mental and mental concomitant states of one who has attained the attainment are intended.

Vacanattho panettha – oḷārikāya saññāya abhāvato, sukhumāya ca bhāvato, nevassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa saññā, nāsaññāti nevasaññānāsaññaṃ. Nevasaññānāsaññañca taṃ manāyatanadhammāyatanapariyāpannattā [V 0.0252] āyatanañcāti [P 0.0208] nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ. Atha vā yāyamettha saññā, sā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya nevasaññā[M 0.0253], saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā nāsaññāti nevasaññānāsaññā. Nevasaññānāsaññā ca sā sesadhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanañcāti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ.

Here, the meaning of the term is to be understood thus: Because of the absence of coarse perception and the presence of subtle perception, for that jhāna together with its associated states, there is neither perception, nor is it without perception; thus it is called 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' And because this 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' is included within the mind-base and the dhamma-base, it is also a base; thus it is the 'base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Alternatively, the perception here, due to its inability to perform the function of keen perception, is 'neither-perception'; yet because it exists in a subtle state as a remainder of formations, it is 'not non-perception'; hence 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' And this 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' because it serves as a foundation for the remaining states, is also a base; thus it is the 'base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.'

Na kevalañcettha saññāva edisī, atha kho vedanāpi nevavedanā nāvedanā, cittampi nevacittaṃ nācittaṃ, phassopi nevaphasso nāphassoti. Esa nayo sesasampayuttadhammesu. Saññāsīsena panāyaṃ desanā katāti veditabbā. Pattamakkhanatelappabhutīhi ca upamāhi esamattho vibhāvetabbo – sāmaṇero kira telena pattaṃ makkhetvā ṭhapesi. Taṃ yāgupānakāle thero ‘pattamāharā’ti āha. So ‘patte telamatthi, bhante’ti āha. Tato ‘āhara, sāmaṇera, telaṃ nāḷiṃ pūressāmī’ti vutte ‘natthi, bhante, tela’nti āha. Tattha yathā antovutthattā yāguyā saddhiṃ akappiyaṭṭhena telaṃ atthīti hoti, nāḷipūraṇādīnaṃ abhāvavasena natthīti hoti, evaṃ sāpi saññā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya nevasaññā, saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā nāsaññā hoti.

And not only is perception of such a kind here, but indeed, feeling is also neither-feeling-nor-not-feeling, consciousness is also neither-consciousness-nor-not-consciousness, and contact is also neither-contact-nor-not-contact. This is the method for the remaining associated states. It should be understood, however, that this teaching is given with perception as the heading. And this meaning should be clarified by similes, such as that of the oil for smearing a bowl. It seems a novice smeared a bowl with oil and set it aside. At the time for drinking gruel, the elder said, 'Bring the bowl.' He replied, 'Venerable sir, there is oil in the bowl.' Then, when told, 'Bring the oil, novice, I will fill a measure,' he replied, 'Venerable sir, there is no oil.' Here, just as there is oil in the sense that, being inside, it would be unsuitable to use with gruel, yet there is no oil in the sense of there being an absence of enough to fill a measure and so on, so too that perception, due to its inability to perform the function of keen perception, is 'neither-perception'; and due to its existence in a subtle state as a remainder of formations, it is 'not non-perception'.

Kimpanettha saññākiccanti? Ārammaṇasañjānanañceva vipassanāya ca visayabhāvaṃ upagantvā nibbidājananaṃ. Dahanakiccamiva hi sukhodake tejodhātu, sañjānanakiccampesā paṭuṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Sesasamāpattīsu saññā viya vipassanāya visayabhāvaṃ upagantvā nibbidājananampi kātuṃ na sakkoti. Aññesu hi khandhesu akatābhiniveso bhikkhu nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakkhandhe sammasitvā nibbidaṃ pattuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Apica āyasmā sāriputto, pakativipassako pana mahāpañño sāriputtasadisova sakkuṇeyya. Sopi “evaṃ kirime dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventī”ti (ma. ni. 3.95) evaṃ kalāpasammasanavaseneva, no anupadadhammavipassanāvasena. Evaṃ sukhumattaṃ gatā esā samāpatti.

But what here is the function of perception? It is recognizing the object and, by becoming a domain for insight, generating disenchantment. For just as the fire element in cool water cannot perform the function of burning, so this perception cannot perform the function of recognizing clearly. Like perception in the other attainments, it cannot generate disenchantment by becoming a domain for insight. For a monk who has not directed his mind to insight regarding the other aggregates, there is indeed no one capable of attaining disenchantment by contemplating the aggregates of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. However, a natural insight meditator of great wisdom, such as the Venerable Sāriputta, would be able to. He too could do so only by means of contemplating in groups, thinking: 'Indeed, these phenomena, not having been, come to be; having been, they pass away,' not by means of insight into phenomena one by one. So subtle has this attainment become.

Yathā ca pattamakkhanatelūpamāya evaṃ maggudakūpamāyapi ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Maggapaṭipannassa [P 0.0209] kira therassa purato gacchanto sāmaṇero thokamudakaṃ disvā ‘udakaṃ, bhante, upāhanā omuñcathā’ti āha. Tato therena ‘sace udakamatthi, āhara nhānasāṭakaṃ, nhāyissāmī’ti [M 0.0254] vutte ‘natthi, bhante’ti āha. Tattha yathā upāhanatemanamattaṭṭhena udakaṃ atthīti hoti[V 0.0253], nhānaṭṭhena natthīti hoti, evampi sā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya neva saññā, saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā nāsaññā hoti. Na kevalañca etāheva, aññāhipi anurūpāhi upamāhi esa attho vibhāvetabbo. Iti imāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatane pavattāya saññāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanabhūtāya vā saññāya sahagatanti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ. Ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiārammaṇassa jhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

And just as with the simile of the oil for anointing a bowl, so too should this meaning be clarified by the simile of the water on the path. It seems a novice, walking ahead of an elder on a path, saw a little water and said, 'Venerable sir, there is water; please remove your sandals.' Then, when the elder said, 'If there is water, bring a bathing cloth, I will bathe,' he replied, 'Venerable sir, there is none.' Here, just as there is water in the sense that it is enough to wet the sandals, but no water in the sense of being enough for bathing, so too that perception, due to its inability to perform the function of distinct perception, is 'neither perception'; and due to its existence in a subtle state as a remainder of formations, it is 'not non-perception.' And not only by these, this meaning should be clarified by other suitable similes as well. Thus, 'accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' means accompanied by this perception that occurs in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or by the perception that has become the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is a designation for the jhāna that has the attainment of the base of nothingness as its object.

Idha ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiyā nikantipariyādānadukkhatāya dukkhā paṭipadā, pariyādinnanikantikassa appanāparivāsadandhatāya dandhābhiññā. Vipariyāyena sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā ca. Parittakasiṇugghāṭimākāse pavattitaviññāṇāpagamārammaṇaṃ samāpattiṃ ārabbha pavattitāya parittārammaṇatā, vipariyāyena appamāṇārammaṇatā veditabbā. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

Here, due to the difficulty of exhausting delight in the attainment of the base of nothingness, the practice is difficult; for one whose delight is exhausted, due to the sluggishness of practicing to reach absorption, direct knowledge is slow. Conversely, the practice is easy and direct knowledge is swift. Because it arises in relation to an attainment whose object is the disappearance of the consciousness that arose in the space of the removed limited kasiṇa, the state of having a limited object should be known; conversely, the state of having a measureless object should be known. The rest is just like the previous.

Asadisarūpo nātho, āruppaṃ yaṃ catubbidhaṃ āha;

Taṃ iti ñatvā tasmiṃ, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

The Lord of incomparable nature spoke of the fourfold formless attainment; having known it in this way, miscellaneous points concerning it should also be understood.

Arūpasamāpattiyo hi –

For the formless attainments—

Ārammaṇātikkamato, catassopi bhavantimā;

Aṅgātikkamametāsaṃ, na icchanti vibhāvino.

By transcending the object, these four come to be; the transcending of their factors, the discerning do not accept.

Etāsu hi rūpanimittātikkamato paṭhamā, ākāsātikkamato dutiyā, ākāse pavattitaviññāṇātikkamato tatiyā, ākāse pavattitaviññāṇassa apagamātikkamato catutthāti sabbathā ‘ārammaṇātikkamato catassopi bhavantimā’ arūpasamāpattiyoti veditabbā. Aṅgātikkamaṃ pana etāsaṃ na icchanti paṇḍitā. Na hi rūpāvacarasamāpattīsu viya etāsu aṅgātikkamo atthi. Sabbāsupi hi etāsu upekkhā cittekaggatāti dve eva jhānaṅgāni honti. Evaṃ santepi –

For among these, the first is by transcending the form-sign; the second, by transcending space; the third, by transcending the consciousness that arose in space; the fourth, by transcending the disappearance of the consciousness that arose in space. Thus, it should be known that in every way 'these four formless attainments come to be by transcending the object.' However, the wise do not accept the transcending of factors for these. For there is no transcending of factors in these as there is in the form-sphere attainments. Indeed, in all of these, there are only two jhāna factors: equanimity and one-pointedness of mind. Even so—

Supaṇītatarā honti, pacchimā pacchimā idha;

Upamā tattha viññeyyā, pāsādatalasāṭikā.

Here, each succeeding attainment is exceedingly sublime; the similes of the palace floor and the cloth should be understood therein.

Yathā [M 0.0255][P 0.0210][V 0.0254] hi catubhūmakapāsādassa heṭṭhimatale dibbanaccagītavāditasurabhigandhamālāsādurasapānabhojanasayanacchādanādivasena paṇītā pañca kāmaguṇā paccupaṭṭhitā assu, dutiye tato paṇītatarā, tatiye tato paṇītatamā, catutthe sabbapaṇītā; tattha kiñcāpi tāni cattāripi pāsādatalāneva, natthi nesaṃ pāsādatalabhāvena viseso, pañcakāmaguṇasamiddhivisesena pana heṭṭhimato heṭṭhimato uparimaṃ uparimaṃ paṇītataraṃ hoti.

For instance, just as in a four-storied palace, on the lowest floor five excellent sense-pleasures may be present by way of divine dancing, singing, music, fragrant flowers, delicious drinks and food, bedding, clothing, and so on; on the second, they may be more excellent than that; on the third, even more excellent than that; and on the fourth, the most excellent of all. Therein, although all four are indeed palace floors and there is no difference among them in being palace floors, yet by the distinction in the abundance of the five sense-pleasures, each higher floor is more excellent than each lower one.

Yathā ca ekāya itthiyā kantitathūlasaṇhasaṇhatarasaṇhatamasuttānaṃ catupalatipaladvipalaekapalasāṭikā assu, āyāmena vitthārena ca samappamāṇā; tattha kiñcāpi tā sāṭikā catassopi āyāmato ca vitthārato ca samappamāṇā, natthi tāsaṃ pamāṇato viseso, sukhasamphassasukhumabhāvamahagghabhāvehi pana purimāya purimāya pacchimā pacchimā paṇītatarā honti, evameva kiñcāpi catūsupi etāsu upekkhā cittekaggatāti etāni dveyeva aṅgāni honti, atha kho bhāvanāvisesena tesaṃ aṅgānaṃ paṇītapaṇītatarabhāvena supaṇītatarā honti pacchimā pacchimā idhāti veditabbā. Evaṃ anupubbena paṇītapaṇītā cetā –

And just as a woman might have cloths of four palas, three palas, two palas, and one pala, made from spun coarse, fine, finer, and finest threads, all of equal measure in length and width; and therein, although all four of those cloths are of equal measure in length and width, and there is no difference among them in terms of measure, yet by way of pleasantness of touch, fineness, and high value, each succeeding one is more excellent than each preceding one; even so, although in all four of these attainments there are only these two factors, namely equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, yet through the distinction in development, by the state of those factors being excellent and more excellent, it should be known that here each succeeding attainment is exceedingly more excellent. Thus, these are successively excellent and more excellent:

Asucimhi maṇḍape laggo, eko taṃ nissito paro;

Añño bahi anissāya, taṃ taṃ nissāya cāparo.

One is attached to a pavilion in a filthy place; another relies on him. Another is outside, not relying on him; and still another relies on that one.

Ṭhito catūhi etehi, purisehi yathākkamaṃ;

Samānatāya ñātabbā, catassopi vibhāvinā. (visuddhi. 1.291);

All four attainments should be known by the discerning one, in due order, by way of similarity with these four men.

Tatrāyamatthayojanā – asucimhi kira dese eko maṇḍapo. Atheko puriso āgantvā taṃ asuciṃ jigucchamāno taṃ maṇḍapaṃ hatthehi ālambitvā tattha laggo, laggito viya aṭṭhāsi. Athāparo āgantvā taṃ maṇḍapalaggaṃ purisaṃ nissito. Athañño āgantvā cintesi – ‘yo esa maṇḍape laggo, yo ca taṃ nissito, ubhopete duṭṭhitā; dhuvo ca nesaṃ maṇḍapapapāte pāto, handāhaṃ bahiyeva tiṭṭhāmī’ti so tannissitaṃ anissāya bahiyeva aṭṭhāsi. Athāparo āgantvā maṇḍapalaggassa [M 0.0256] tannissitassa ca akhemabhāvaṃ cintetvā bahiṭhitañca suṭṭhitoti mantvā taṃ nissāya aṭṭhāsi.

Herein, this is the application of the meaning: Indeed, in a filthy place, there is a pavilion. Then a man came, and being disgusted with that filth, he held onto the pavilion with his hands and stood there attached, as if stuck. Then another came and relied on the man attached to the pavilion. Then another came and thought: ‘This one who is attached to the pavilion, and the one who relies on him—both of them are badly situated. Their fall is certain if the pavilion collapses. Well then, I shall stand right outside.’ So, not relying on the one relied upon by the second man, he stood right outside. Then another came, and having considered the unsafe state of the one attached to the pavilion and the one relying on him, and having thought, ‘The one standing outside is well-situated,’ he stood relying on him.

Tattha [V 0.0255] asucimhi dese maṇḍapo viya kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asucijigucchāya maṇḍapalaggo puriso viya rūpanimittajigucchāya ākāsārammaṇaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ[P 0.0211]. Maṇḍapalaggaṃ purisaṃ nissito viya ākāsārammaṇaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ. Tesaṃ dvinnampi akhemabhāvaṃ cintetvā anissāya taṃ maṇḍapalaggaṃ, bahiṭhito viya, ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ akatvā tadabhāvārammaṇaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Maṇḍapalaggassa tannissitassa ca akhemataṃ cintetvā bahiṭhitañca ‘suṭṭhito’ti mantvā taṃ nissāya ṭhito viya viññāṇābhāvasaṅkhāte bahipadese ṭhitaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ pavattamānañca –

Therein, the space which is the removal of the kasiṇa should be seen as a pavilion in a filthy place. The base of infinite space, which has space as its object due to disgust with the form-sign, should be seen as a man attached to the pavilion due to disgust with filth. The base of infinite consciousness, which arises by taking as its object the base of infinite space, should be seen as one relying on the man attached to the pavilion. The base of nothingness, which has the absence of that first attainment as its object and does not make the base of infinite space its object, should be seen as one standing outside, not relying on that man attached to the pavilion, having considered the unsafe state of both of them. The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which arises by taking as its object the base of nothingness that is situated in the external region designated as the absence of consciousness, should be seen as one who stands in reliance on that third man, having considered the unsafe state of the one attached to the pavilion and the one relying on him, and having thought, ‘The one standing outside is well-situated.’ And as it thus arises—

Ārammaṇaṃ karoteva, aññābhāvena taṃ idaṃ;

Diṭṭhadosampi rājānaṃ, vuttihetu yathā jano. (visuddhi. 1.292);

This attainment certainly makes that its object due to the absence of another, just as a person for the sake of livelihood relies on a king even though his fault is seen.

Idañhi nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ ‘āsannaviññāṇañcāyatanapaccatthikā ayaṃ samāpattī’ti evaṃ diṭṭhadosampi taṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ aññassa ārammaṇassa abhāvā ārammaṇaṃ karoteva. Yathā kiṃ? ‘Diṭṭhadosampi rājānaṃ vuttihetu yathā jano’. Yathā hi asaṃyataṃ pharusakāyavacīmanosamācāraṃ kañci sabbadisampatiṃ rājānaṃ ‘pharusasamācāro aya’nti evaṃ diṭṭhadosampi aññattha vuttiṃ alabhamāno jano vuttihetu nissāya vattati, evaṃ diṭṭhadosampi taṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ aññaṃ ārammaṇaṃ alabhamānamidaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoteva. Evaṃ kurumānañca –

For this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, even though its fault is seen thus, ‘This attainment has the base of infinite consciousness as a near enemy,’ certainly makes that base of nothingness its object, due to the absence of another object. How so? ‘Just as a person for the sake of livelihood relies on a king even though his fault is seen.’ For just as a person, unable to find a livelihood elsewhere, relies for the sake of livelihood on some king who is a lord of all directions, unrestrained, and of harsh conduct in body, speech, and mind, even though his fault is seen thus, ‘This one is of harsh conduct’; even so, this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, unable to find another object, certainly makes that base of nothingness its object, even though its fault is seen. And in so doing—

Āruḷho dīghanisseṇiṃ, yathā nisseṇibāhukaṃ;

Pabbataggañca āruḷho, yathā pabbatamatthakaṃ.

Just as one who has climbed a long ladder leans on the ladder's side-rail; and just as one who has climbed to a mountain peak leans on the mountain's summit.

Yathā vā girimāruḷho, attanoyeva jaṇṇukaṃ;

Olubbhati tathevetaṃ, jhānamolubbha vattatīti. (visuddhi. 1.293);

Or just as one who has climbed a mountain leans on one's own knee, even so does this attainment proceed by leaning on that jhāna.

Arūpāvacarakusalakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion on wholesome states of the immaterial sphere is concluded.

Tebhūmakakusalavaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of Wholesome States Pertaining to the Three Planes

269. Idāni [M 0.0257][V 0.0256] yasmā sabbānipetāni tebhūmakakusalāni hīnādinā pabhedena vattanti, tasmā tesaṃ taṃ pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha hīnanti lāmakaṃ. Taṃ āyūhanavasena veditabbaṃ. Hīnuttamānaṃ [P 0.0212] majjhe bhavaṃ majjhimaṃ. Padhānabhāvaṃ nītaṃ paṇītaṃ, uttamanti attho. Tānipi āyūhanavaseneva veditabbāni. Yassa hi āyūhanakkhaṇe chando vā hīno hoti, vīriyaṃ vā, cittaṃ vā, vīmaṃsā vā, taṃ hīnaṃ nāma. Yassa te dhammā majjhimā ceva paṇītā, ca taṃ majjhimañceva paṇītañca. Yaṃ pana kattukāmatāsaṅkhātaṃ chandaṃ dhuraṃ chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ chandaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā āyūhitaṃ, taṃ chandādhipatito āgatattā chandādhipateyyaṃ nāma. Vīriyādhipateyyādīsupi eseva nayo.

269. Now, because all these wholesome states of the three planes exist with the classification of inferior, etc., therefore, to show that classification of them, the passage beginning with "Which states are wholesome?" is commenced again. Therein, 'inferior' means base. That should be understood by way of exertion. That which is in the middle of the inferior and the superior is 'middling'. What is brought to a state of prominence is 'refined' (paṇīta); the meaning is 'superior' (uttama). These too should be understood by way of exertion alone. For at the moment of exertion of which wholesome state the desire is inferior, or the energy, or the consciousness, or the investigation, that is called 'inferior'. That wholesome state for which those factors are middling is 'middling,' and that for which they are refined is 'refined.' But that which is applied having made desire—which is designated as the wish-to-do—the foremost, having made desire the chief, having made desire the forerunner, that, because of coming from the dominance of desire, is called 'desire-dominant'. In energy-dominance, etc., this is the same method.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā nayā gaṇetabbā. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ vibhatto hi eko nayo, hīnanti eko, majjhimanti eko, paṇītanti eko, chandādhipateyyanti eko. Ime tāva chandādhipateyye pañca nayā. Evaṃ vīriyādhipateyyādīsupīti cattāro pañcakā vīsati honti. Purimo vā eko suddhikanayo, hīnantiādayo tayo, chandādhipateyyantiādayo cattāro, chandādhipateyyaṃ hīnantiādayo dvādasāti evampi vīsati nayā honti.

However, standing in this place, the methods should be counted. Indeed, first of all, there is one analyzed method; 'inferior' is one, 'middling' is one, 'refined' is one, and 'desire-dominant' is one. To begin with, these are the five methods under desire-dominance. Similarly, in energy-dominance and so on, four pentads make twenty. Alternatively, the first is one pure method; 'inferior' and so on are three; 'desire-dominant' and so on are four; and 'desire-dominant inferior' and so on are twelve—thus, in this way also, there are twenty methods.

Ime vīsati mahānayā kattha vibhattāti? Mahāpakaraṇe (paṭṭhā. 2.14.1) hīnattike vibhattā. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne hīnattikato majjhimarāsiṃ gahetvā hīnamajjhimapaṇītavasena tayo koṭṭhāsā kātabbā. Tatopi majjhimarāsiṃ ṭhapetvā hīnapaṇīte gahetvā nava nava koṭṭhāsā kātabbā. Hīnasmiṃyeva hi hīnaṃ atthi majjhimaṃ atthi paṇītaṃ atthi. Paṇītasmimpi hīnaṃ atthi majjhimaṃ atthi paṇītaṃ atthi. Tathā hīnahīnasmiṃ hīnaṃ, hīnahīnasmiṃ majjhimaṃ, hīnahīnasmiṃ paṇītaṃ. Hīnamajjhimasmiṃ hīnaṃ, hīnamajjhimasmiṃ majjhimaṃ, hīnamajjhimasmiṃ paṇītaṃ. Hīnapaṇītasmiṃ hīnaṃ, hīnapaṇītasmiṃ majjhimaṃ, hīnapaṇītasmiṃ paṇītanti ayameko navako. Paṇītahīnasmimpi hīnaṃ nāma atthi, paṇītahīnasmiṃ majjhimaṃ, paṇītahīnasmiṃ paṇītaṃ. Tathā paṇītamajjhimasmiṃ hīnaṃ, paṇītamajjhimasmiṃ majjhimaṃ, paṇītamajjhimasmiṃ paṇītaṃ. Paṇītapaṇītasmiṃ hīnaṃ, paṇītapaṇītasmiṃ majjhimaṃ, paṇītapaṇītasmiṃ paṇītanti. Ayaṃ dutiyo navakoti dve navakā aṭṭhārasa. Imāni aṭṭhārasa kammadvārāni [P 0.0213] nāma[M 0.0258]. Imehi pabhāvitattā[V 0.0257], imesaṃ vasena, aṭṭhārasa khattiyā, aṭṭhārasa brāhmaṇā, aṭṭhārasa vessā, aṭṭhārasa suddā, aṭṭhacattālīsa gottacaraṇāni veditabbāni.

Where are these twenty great methods analyzed? They are analyzed in the Mahāpakaraṇa (Paṭṭhāna 2.14.1) within the Inferior Triad. Here, however, taking the middling group from the Inferior Triad, three portions should be made: inferior, middling, and refined. Then, setting aside the middling group and taking the inferior and the refined, nine portions should be made for each. For within the inferior itself, there is the inferior, there is the middling, and there is the refined. And within the refined, there is the inferior, there is the middling, and there is the refined. Thus: within the inferior-inferior is the inferior, within the inferior-inferior is the middling, and within the inferior-inferior is the refined. Within the inferior-middling is the inferior, within the inferior-middling is the middling, and within the inferior-middling is the refined. Within the inferior-refined is the inferior, within the inferior-refined is the middling, and within the inferior-refined is the refined—this is one nonad. Also, within the refined-inferior is what is called the inferior, within the refined-inferior is the middling, and within the refined-inferior is the refined. Similarly, within the refined-middling is the inferior, within the refined-middling is the middling, and within the refined-middling is the refined.
