Within the refined-refined is the inferior, within the refined-refined is the middling, and within the refined-refined is the refined—this is the second nonad. Thus, the two nonads make eighteen. These eighteen are called the doors of kamma. Because the following are generated in their diversity by these, by means of these, eighteen khattiyas, eighteen brāhmaṇas, eighteen vessas, eighteen suddas, and forty-eight gottacaraṇas are to be understood.

Imesu ca pana tebhūmakesu kusalesu kāmāvacarakusalaṃ tihetukampi duhetukampi hoti ñāṇasampayuttavippayuttavasena. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaraṃ pana tihetukameva ñāṇasampayuttameva. Kāmāvacarampettha adhipatinā sahāpi uppajjati vināpi. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaraṃ adhipatisampannameva hoti. Kāmāvacarakusale cettha ārammaṇādhipati sahajātādhipatīti dvepi adhipatayo labbhanti. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaresu ārammaṇādhipati na labbhati, sahajātādhipatiyeva labbhati. Tattha cittassa cittādhipateyyabhāvo sampayuttadhammānaṃ vasena vutto. Dvinnaṃ pana cittānaṃ ekato abhāvena sampayuttacittassa cittādhipati nāma natthi. Tathā chandādīnaṃ chandādhipatiādayo. Keci pana ‘sace cittavato kusalaṃ hoti, mayhaṃ bhavissatīti evaṃ yaṃ cittaṃ dhuraṃ katvā jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā aparaṃ kusalacittaṃ āyūhitaṃ, tassa taṃ purimacittaṃ cittādhipati nāma hoti, tato āgatattā idaṃ cittādhipateyyaṃ nāmā’ti evaṃ āgamanavasenāpi adhipatiṃ nāma icchanti. Ayaṃ pana nayo neva pāḷiyaṃ na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dissati. Tasmā vuttanayeneva adhipatibhāvo veditabbo. Imesu ca ekūnavīsatiyā mahānayesu purime suddhikanaye vuttaparimāṇāneva cittāni ca navakā ca pāṭhavārā ca honti. Tasmā ñāṇasampayuttesu vuttaparimāṇato vīsatiguṇo cittanavakavārabhedo veditabbo, catūsu ñāṇavippayuttesu soḷasaguṇoti, ayaṃ tebhūmakakusale pakiṇṇakakathā nāmāti.

Moreover, among these wholesome states of the three planes, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness can be both triple-rooted and double-rooted, by way of being associated with or dissociated from knowledge. Form-sphere and formless-sphere wholesome consciousness, however, are only triple-rooted and only associated with knowledge. Herein, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness arises both with and without a dominant condition. Form-sphere and formless-sphere wholesome consciousness are always endowed with a dominant condition. And herein, in sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, both dominant conditions—object-dominance and conascence-dominance—are obtained. In form-sphere and formless-sphere wholesome states, object-dominance is not obtained; only conascence-dominance is obtained. Therein, the mind's state of mind-predominance is spoken of in relation to its associated states. However, since two minds do not occur simultaneously, there is no such thing as a mind-dominant condition for an associated mind. Similarly, there is no such thing as desire-dominance for desire itself, and so on for the other factors. Some, however, accept a dominant condition even by way of succession, saying: 'If a wholesome state belongs to one who has a mind, and if a subsequent wholesome mind is applied, having made that former mind the primary factor, having made it the chief, thinking, "It will be mine," then that former mind is called the mind-dominant condition, and because this subsequent mind comes from that, it is called mind-predominance.' But this method is not seen in the Pāḷi texts or the commentaries. Therefore, the nature of a dominant condition should be understood only in the way stated. And among these nineteen great methods, in the first, the pure method, there are only the cittas, nonads, and textual recitations of the stated amount. Therefore, in the knowledge-associated states, the classification of cittas, nonads, and recitations should be understood as twenty-fold of the stated amount; and in the four knowledge-dissociated states, as sixteen-fold. This is called the Miscellaneous Discourse on the Wholesome States of the Three Planes.

Tebhūmakakusalaṃ.

The [section on] Wholesome States of the Three Planes is concluded.

Lokuttarakusalavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Supramundane Wholesome

277. Evaṃ bhavattayasampattinibbattakaṃ kusalaṃ dassetvā idāni sabbabhavasamatikkamanāya lokuttarakusalaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha lokuttaranti kenaṭṭhena lokuttaraṃ? Lokaṃ [M 0.0259][P 0.0214] taratīti, lokuttaraṃ lokaṃ uttaratīti lokuttaraṃ; lokaṃ [V 0.0258] samatikkamma abhibhuyya tiṭṭhatīti lokuttaraṃ (paṭi. ma. 2.43). Jhānaṃ bhāvetīti ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ appanājhānaṃ bhāveti janeti vaḍḍheti.

277. Having thus shown the wholesome that brings about attainment in the three existences, now, in order to show the supramundane wholesome for the purpose of transcending all existence, the passage beginning 'What things are wholesome?' is taken up again. Therein, as for 'supramundane' (lokuttaraṃ), by what meaning is it 'supramundane'? Because it crosses over (tarati) the world (lokaṃ), it is 'supramundane' (lokuttaraṃ); because it transcends (uttarati) the world, it is 'supramundane'; because it stands having transcended (samatikkamma) and overcome (abhibhuyya) the world, it is 'supramundane'. As for 'develops the jhāna' (jhānaṃ bhāveti), it means: one develops, generates, and increases the absorption jhāna that is of a single mind-moment.

Lokato niyyāti vaṭṭato niyyātīti niyyānikaṃ. Niyyāti vā etenāti niyyānikaṃ. Taṃsamaṅgī hi puggalo dukkhaṃ parijānanto niyyāti, samudayaṃ pajahanto niyyāti, nirodhaṃ sacchikaronto niyyāti, maggaṃ bhāvento niyyāti. Yathā ca pana tebhūmakakusalaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ cutipaṭisandhiyo ācināti vaḍḍhetīti ācayagāmī nāma hoti, na tathā idaṃ. Idaṃ pana yathā ekasmiṃ purise aṭṭhārasahatthaṃ pākāraṃ cinante aparo mahāmuggaraṃ gahetvā tena citacitaṭṭhānaṃ apacinanto viddhaṃsento eva gaccheyya, evameva tebhūmakakusalena citā cutipaṭisandhiyo paccayavekallakaraṇena apacinantaṃ viddhaṃsentaṃ gacchatīti apacayagāmi.

It leads forth (niyyāti) from the world, it leads forth from the round of suffering; thus it is 'leading forth' (niyyānikaṃ). Or, one leads forth by means of this, thus it is 'leading forth'. Indeed, a person endowed with it leads forth while fully understanding suffering; leads forth while abandoning the origin; leads forth while realizing cessation; leads forth while developing the path. Furthermore, just as the wholesome of the three planes accumulates and increases deaths and rebirth-linkings in the round, and is thus called 'leading to accumulation' (ācayagāmī), this is not so. Rather, just as when one man is building an eighteen-cubit wall, another might take a great hammer and go along dismantling and destroying the very place that has been built, in the same way, this goes along dismantling and destroying the deaths and rebirth-linkings accumulated by the wholesome of the three planes by causing a deficiency of their conditions; thus it is called 'leading to de-accumulation' (apacayagāmi).

Diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyāti, ettha diṭṭhiyo eva diṭṭhigatāni, gūthagataṃ muttagatantiādīni (a. ni. 9.11) viya. Dvāsaṭṭhiyā vā diṭṭhīnaṃ antogadhattā diṭṭhīsu gatānītipi diṭṭhigatāni. Diṭṭhiyā vā gataṃ etesantipi diṭṭhigatāni. Diṭṭhisadisagamanāni diṭṭhisadisappavattānīti attho. Kāni pana tānīti? Sasampayuttāni sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsaapāyagamanīyarāgadosamohākusalāni. Tāni hi yāva paṭhamamaggabhāvanā tāva pavattisabbhāvato diṭṭhisadisagamanānīti vuccanti. Iti diṭṭhiyo ca diṭṭhigatāni ca diṭṭhigatāni. Tesaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ. Pahānāyāti samucchedavaseneva pajahanatthāya. Paṭhamāyāti gaṇanavasenapi paṭhamuppattivasenapi paṭhamāya. Bhūmiyāti “anantarahitāya bhūmiyā”tiādīsu (pārā. 27; ma. ni. 2.296) tāva ayaṃ mahāpathavī bhūmīti vuccati. “Sukhabhūmiyaṃ kāmāvacare”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 988) cittuppādo. Idha pana sāmaññaphalaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tañhi sampayuttānaṃ nissayabhāvato te dhammā bhavanti etthāti bhūmi. Yasmā vā samānepi lokuttarabhāve sayampi bhavati uppajjati, na nibbānaṃ viya apātubhāvaṃ, tasmāpi bhūmīti vuccati; tassā paṭhamāya bhūmiyā. Pattiyāti sotāpattiphalasaṅkhātassa [P 0.0215] paṭhamassa sāmaññaphalassa [M 0.0260] pattatthāya paṭilābhatthāyāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Viviccāti samucchedavivekavasena viviccitvā, vinā hutvā.

As for 'for the abandoning of things related to views' (diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya): herein, views (diṭṭhiyo) themselves are 'things related to views' (diṭṭhigatāni), like 'gone to excrement' (gūthagataṃ), 'gone to urine' (muttagataṃ), and so on. Or, because of being included within the sixty-two views, they are 'gone into the views' (diṭṭhīsu gatāni), and thus 'things related to views' (diṭṭhigatāni). Or, because their proceeding is like that of view, they are 'things related to views'. The meaning is that their proceeding is similar to view, their occurrence is similar to view. But what are they? They are identity-view, doubt, clinging to rites and rituals, and the unwholesome states of greed, hatred, and delusion that lead to the plane of misery, along with their associated states. Indeed, because they are manifestly present up until the development of the first path, they are said to have a proceeding similar to view. Thus, both views and things gone into views are 'things related to views'. 'For the abandoning' (pahānāya) of these things related to views means for the purpose of abandoning them by way of eradication. 'Of the first' (paṭhamāya) means first by way of counting and by way of first arising. As for 'ground' (bhūmiyā): in passages such as 'on a ground without interval' (anantarahitāya bhūmiyā), this great earth is called 'ground'. In passages such as 'in the sense-sphere ground of happiness' (sukhabhūmiyaṃ kāmāvacare), a mind-moment is called 'ground'. Here, however, a fruit of recluseship is intended. For, because it is a basis for its associated states, those states exist in it (bhavanti etthā), thus it is a 'ground' (bhūmi). Or, because, although its nature is supramundane, it itself arises and comes to be—it is not non-manifest like Nibbāna—it is therefore also called 'ground'. 'For the attainment' (pattiyā) of that first ground means for the purpose of attaining, for the purpose of acquiring the first fruit of recluseship, described as the fruit of stream-entry. Thus should the meaning here be understood. 'Secluded' (vivicca) means having been secluded by way of the seclusion of eradication, having become without.

Idāni kiñcāpi lokiyajjhānampi na vinā paṭipadāya ijjhati, evaṃ santepi idha suddhikanayaṃ [V 0.0259] pahāya lokuttarajjhānaṃ paṭipadāya saddhiṃyeva garuṃ katvā desetukāmatāya dukkhapaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññantiādimāha.

Now, although even mundane jhāna is not accomplished without a practice, this being so, here, because of the desire to teach by setting aside the pure method and giving weight to the supramundane jhāna only together with its practice, He said, 'The painful practice with slow direct knowledge,' and so on.

Tattha yo āditova kilese vikkhambhento dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilamanto vikkhambheti tassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti; yo pana vikkhambhita kileso vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti tassa dandhābhiññā hoti. Iti yo koci vāro dukkhapaṭipadadandhābhiñño nāma kato.

Therein, for the yogi who, from the very beginning, suppresses the defilements with difficulty, with exertion, and with effort, becoming weary while suppressing them—for him, the practice is painful. Furthermore, for the yogi who, having suppressed the defilements, dwells cultivating insight and attains the manifestation of the path only after a long time—for him, the direct knowledge is slow. Thus, any such case is designated as 'painful practice with slow direct knowledge'.

Katamaṃ pana vāraṃ rocesunti? Yattha sakiṃ vikkhambhitā kilesā samudācaritvā dutiyampi vikkhambhitā puna samudācaranti, tatiyaṃ vikkhambhite pana tathāvikkhambhiteva katvā maggena samugghātaṃ pāpeti, imaṃ vāraṃ rocesuṃ. Imassa vārassa dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññāti nāmaṃ kataṃ. Ettakena pana na pākaṭaṃ hoti. Tasmā evamettha ādito paṭṭhāya vibhāvanā veditabbā – yo hi cattāri mahābhūtāni pariggahetvā upādārūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti, arūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti, ‘rūpārūpaṃ’ pana pariggaṇhanto dukkhena kasirena kilamanto pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā nāma hoti. Pariggahitarūpārūpassa pana vipassanāparivāse maggapātubhāvadandhatāya dandhābhiññā nāma hoti.

But which case do they prefer? The case where defilements, having been suppressed once, arise again, and having been suppressed a second time, arise yet again; but on the third suppression, having kept them suppressed just so, one brings them to eradication by the path—this is the case they prefer. This case has been given the name 'painful practice with slow direct knowledge'. However, by this much it is not yet clear. Therefore, the clarification should be understood from the beginning thus: Indeed, for one who, having comprehended the four great elements, comprehends derived matter and comprehends non-matter, but in comprehending matter-and-non-matter is able to comprehend them only with difficulty, with trouble, becoming weary—for him, it is called 'painful practice'. Furthermore, for one who has comprehended matter-and-non-matter, due to the slowness of the path's manifestation during the cultivation of insight, it is called 'slow direct knowledge'.

Yopi rūpārūpaṃ pariggahetvā ‘nāmarūpaṃ’ vavatthapento dukkhena kasirena kilamanto vavatthapeti, vavatthāpite ca nāmarūpe vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkoti, tassāpi dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti.

Also, for one who, having comprehended matter-and-non-matter, determines 'name-and-form' with difficulty, with trouble, becoming weary; and who, when name-and-form has been determined, dwells cultivating insight and is able to generate the path only after a long time—for him, too, it is called 'painful practice with slow direct knowledge'.

Aparo nāmarūpampi vavatthapetvā ‘paccaye’ pariggaṇhanto dukkhena kasirena kilamanto pariggaṇhāti, paccaye ca pariggahetvā vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ [P 0.0216] uppādeti, evampi dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti.

Another, having determined name-and-form, comprehends the 'conditions' with difficulty, with trouble, becoming weary; and having comprehended the conditions, while dwelling cultivating insight, he generates the path only after a long time. In this way, too, it is called 'painful practice with slow direct knowledge'.

Aparo [M 0.0261] paccayepi pariggahetvā ‘lakkhaṇāni’ paṭivijjhanto dukkhena kasirena kilamanto paṭivijjhati, paṭividdhalakkhaṇo ca vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ uppādeti, evampi dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti.

Another, having comprehended even the conditions, penetrates the 'characteristics' with difficulty, with trouble, becoming weary; and having penetrated the characteristics, while dwelling in the practice of insight, he gives rise to the path only after a long time. Thus, this too is called 'painful practice with slow direct knowledge'.

Aparo [V 0.0260] lakkhaṇānipi paṭivijjhitvā vipassanāñāṇe tikkhe sūre pasanne vahante uppannaṃ ‘vipassanānikantiṃ’ pariyādiyamāno dukkhena kasirena kilamanto pariyādiyati, nikantiñca pariyādiyitvā vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ uppādeti, evampi dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti. Imaṃ vāraṃ rocesuṃ. Imassa vārassa etaṃ nāmaṃ kataṃ. Imināva upāyena parato tisso paṭipadā veditabbā.

Another, having penetrated even the characteristics, while the insight knowledge is sharp, heroic, clear, and proceeding, overcomes the arisen 'delight in insight' with difficulty, with trouble, and with weariness. And having overcome that delight, while dwelling in the practice of insight, he gives rise to the path only after a long time. Thus, this too is called 'painful practice with slow direct knowledge'. The commentary teachers preferred this instance. This name was given to this instance. By this very method, the three subsequent practices should be understood.

Phasso hotītiādīsu anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvoti cattāri padāni adhikāni. Niddesavāre ca vitakkādiniddesesu ‘maggaṅga’ntiādīni padāni adhikāni. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttasadisameva. Bhūmantaravasena pana lokuttaratāva idha viseso.

In the enumeration of dhammas beginning with 'There is contact,' the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these four terms are additional. And in the exposition section, in the expositions of thought and so on, the terms beginning with 'path factor' are additional. All the rest is just the same as what was stated below. However, by way of the difference in plane, the supramundane nature itself is the distinction here.

Tattha anaññātaññassāmītindriyanti ‘anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe anaññātaṃ amataṃ padaṃ catusaccadhammameva vā jānissāmī’ti paṭipannassa iminā pubbābhogena uppannaṃ indriyaṃ. Lakkhaṇādīni panassa heṭṭhā paññindriye vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

Therein, the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' is the faculty that has arisen in one who has undertaken the practice with this prior inclination: 'In the beginningless round of rebirth, I shall know the hitherto unknown deathless state, or the doctrine of the Four Truths itself.' Furthermore, its characteristics and so on should be understood in the very way stated below in the section on the faculty of wisdom.

Sundarā pasatthā vā vācā sammāvācā. Vacīduccaritasamugghāṭikāya micchāvācāviratiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sā pariggahalakkhaṇā viramaṇarasā micchāvācappahānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Sundaro pasattho vā kammanto sammākammanto. Micchākammantasamucchedikāya pāṇātipātādiviratiyā etaṃ nāmaṃ. So samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇo viramaṇaraso micchākammantappahānapaccupaṭṭhāno. Sundaro pasattho vā ājīvo sammāājīvo. Micchājīvaviratiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. So vodānalakkhaṇo ñāyājīvappavattiraso [P 0.0217] micchājīvappahānapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Good or praised speech is right speech. This is a designation for the abstinence from wrong speech, which eradicates verbal misconduct. It has the characteristic of embracing (associated states), the function of abstaining, and manifests as the abandoning of wrong speech. Good or praised action is right action. This is a name for the abstinence from killing living beings and so on, which severs wrong action. It has the characteristic of initiating (bodily action), the function of abstaining, and manifests as the abandoning of wrong action. Good or praised livelihood is right livelihood. This is a designation for the abstinence from wrong livelihood. It has the characteristic of purification, the function of proceeding with a proper livelihood, and manifests as the abandoning of wrong livelihood.

Apica heṭṭhā viratittaye vuttavasenapettha lakkhaṇādīni veditabbāni. Iti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ vasena heṭṭhā vuttaṃ maggapañcakaṃ idha maggaṭṭhakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yevāpanakesu ca imesaṃ abhāvo. Tathā karuṇāmuditānaṃ. Ime [M 0.0262] hi tayo dhammā idha pāḷiyaṃ āgatattāva yevāpanakesu na gahitā. Karuṇāmuditā pana sattārammaṇā, ime dhammā nibbānārammaṇāti tāpettha na gahitā. Ayaṃ tāva uddesavāre visesattho.

Furthermore, the characteristics and so on should be understood here also by way of what was stated below concerning the triad of abstinences. Thus, by way of these three dhammas, the fivefold path stated below should be understood here as the eightfold path. And in the yevāpanaka dhammas, these are absent. Likewise, compassion and appreciative joy are absent. Indeed, because these three dhammas are included directly in the Pāḷi here, they are not included among the yevāpanaka dhammas. Compassion and appreciative joy, however, have beings as their object, whereas these dhammas have Nibbāna as their object; therefore, they too are not included here. This, for now, is the special meaning in the summary section.

283. Niddesavāre [V 0.0261] pana maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpannanti ettha tāva maggassa aṅganti maggaṅgaṃ; maggakoṭṭhāsoti attho. Yathā pana araññe pariyāpannaṃ araññapariyāpannaṃ nāma hoti, evaṃ magge pariyāpannanti maggapariyāpannaṃ. Maggasannissitanti attho.

283. However, in the exposition section, regarding the text 'a path factor, included in the path': first, 'a component of the path' (maggassa aṅgaṃ), therefore it is a 'path factor' (maggaṅgaṃ); the meaning is 'a constituent of the path.' And just as what is included in the forest is called 'forest-included,' so too 'what is included in the path' (magge pariyāpannaṃ) is 'path-included' (maggapariyāpannaṃ); the meaning is 'dependent on the path.'

285. Pītisambojjhaṅgoti ettha pīti eva sambojjhaṅgoti pītisambojjhaṅgo. Tattha bodhiyā bodhissa vā aṅgoti bojjhaṅgo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā ayaṃ dhammasāmaggī yāya lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhattakilamathānuyogaucchedasassatābhinivesādīnaṃ anekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayavīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsaṅkhātāya dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhatīti katvā bodhīti vuccati. Bujjhatīti kilesasantānaniddāya uṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikaroti. Tassā dhammasāmaggīsaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgotipi bojjhaṅgo, jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādīni viya. Yopesa yathāvuttappakārāya etāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvako bodhīti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgotipi bojjhaṅgo; senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā – “bujjhanakassa puggalassa aṅgāti vā bojjhaṅgā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 466; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.182).

285. In the text 'pītisambojjhaṅgo' (joy-enlightenment-factor), it is 'joy itself is the enlightenment factor' (pīti eva sambojjhaṅgo), hence 'joy-enlightenment-factor'.

Apica “bojjhaṅgāti kenaṭṭhena bojjhaṅgā? Bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgā, bujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, anubujjhantīti [P 0.0218] bojjhaṅgā, paṭibujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, sambujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.17) iminā paṭisambhidānayenāpi bojjhaṅgattho veditabbo. Pasattho sundaro vā bojjhaṅgoti sambojjhaṅgo. Evaṃ pīti eva sambojjhaṅgo pītisambojjhaṅgoti. Cittekaggatāniddesādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

A praised enlightenment factor, or a good enlightenment factor, is therefore a 'true enlightenment factor' (sambojjhaṅga). Thus, 'joy itself is the true enlightenment factor,' hence 'joy-enlightenment-factor.' Also in the expositions of one-pointedness of mind and so on, the meaning should be understood by this very method.

296. Tesaṃ dhammānanti ye tasmiṃ samaye paṭivedhaṃ gacchanti catusaccadhammā, tesaṃ dhammānaṃ. Anaññātānanti kiñcāpi paṭhamamaggena te dhammā ñātā [M 0.0263] nāma honti, yathā pana pakatiyā anāgatapubbaṃ vihāraṃ āgantvā vihāramajjhe ṭhitopi puggalo pakatiyā anāgatabhāvaṃ upādāya ‘anāgatapubbaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgatomhī’ti vadati, yathā ca pakatiyā apiḷandhapubbaṃ mālaṃ piḷandhitvā, anivatthapubbaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsetvā, abhuttapubbaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā, pakatiyā abhuttabhāvaṃ upādāya abhuttapubbaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuttomhīti vadati, evamidhāpi [V 0.0262] yasmā pakatiyā iminā puggalena ime dhammā na ñātapubbā tasmā anaññātānanti vuttaṃ. Adiṭṭhādīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha adiṭṭhānanti ito pubbe paññācakkhunā adiṭṭhānaṃ. Appattānanti adhigamanavasena appattānaṃ. Aviditānanti ñāṇena apākaṭakatānaṃ. Asacchikatānanti apaccakkhakatānaṃ. Sacchikiriyāyāti paccakkhakaraṇatthaṃ. Yathā ca iminā padena, evaṃ sesehipi saddhiṃ anaññātānaṃ ñāṇāya, adiṭṭhānaṃ dassanāya, appattānaṃ pattiyā, aviditānaṃ vedāyāti yojanā kātabbā.

296. Regarding 'those truths' (tesaṃ dhammānaṃ): these are the four noble truths that are penetrated at that moment; 'those truths' refers to these truths. Regarding 'not known before' (anaññātānaṃ): although with the first path those truths are indeed known, it is like a person who has never before come to a monastery; having come and stood in the middle of the monastery, based on the fact of its having been unvisited before, they say, 'I have come to a place never visited before.' And just as one who has never before worn a garland, having worn it; or never before put on a garment, having put it on; or never before eaten a meal, having eaten it, based on the fact of its having been uneaten before, says, 'I have eaten a meal never eaten before'—in the same way here, because these truths were not previously known by this person in the ordinary sense, they are therefore called 'not known before.' The same principle applies to 'not seen' (adiṭṭha) and so forth. Therein, 'not seen' means not seen before this moment by the eye of wisdom. 'Not attained' (appatta) means not attained by way of realization. 'Not understood' (avidita) means not made manifest by knowledge. 'Not realized' (asacchikata) means not directly experienced. 'For realization' (sacchikiriyāya) means for the purpose of direct experience. And just as the connection is made with this term, so too should it be made with the others: 'for the knowledge of things not known before,' 'for the seeing of things not seen before,' 'for the attainment of things not attained before,' 'for the understanding of things not understood before.'

299. Catūhi vacīduccaritehītiādīsu vacīti vacīviññatti veditabbā. Tiṇṇaṃ dosānaṃ yena kenaci duṭṭhāni caritānīti duccaritāni. Vacīto pavattāni duccaritāni vacīduccaritāni, vaciyā vā nipphāditāni duccaritāni vacīduccaritāni. Tehi vacīduccaritehi. Ārakā ramatīti ārati. Vinā tehi ramatīti virati. Tato tato paṭinivattāva hutvā tehi vinā ramatīti paṭivirati. Upasaggavasena vā padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Sabbamidaṃ oramaṇabhāvassevādhivacanaṃ. Veraṃ maṇati, vināsetīti veramaṇī. Idampi oramaṇasseva vevacanaṃ. Yāya [P 0.0219] pana cetanāya musāvādādīni bhāsamāno karoti nāma, ayaṃ lokuttaramaggavirati. Uppajjitvā taṃ kiriyaṃ kātuṃ na deti, kiriyāpathaṃ pacchindatīti akiriyā. Tathā taṃ karaṇaṃ kātuṃ na deti, karaṇapathaṃ pacchindatīti akaraṇaṃ. Yāya ca cetanāya catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ bhāsamāno ajjhāpajjati nāma, ayaṃ uppajjitvā tathā ajjhāpajjituṃ na detīti anajjhāpatti.

299. In the phrase 'by four kinds of verbal misconduct' (catūhi vacīduccaritehi) and so forth, 'verbal' (vacī) should be understood as verbal intimation (vacīviññatti). 'Misconduct' (duccaritāni) are actions corrupted by any of the three defilements. Misconduct that arises from speech is verbal misconduct (vacīduccaritāni), or misconduct produced by speech is verbal misconduct. From that verbal misconduct: 'Ārati' is so called because one delights (ramati) far away (ārakā) from it. 'Virati' is so called because one delights (ramati) without (vinā) it. 'Paṭivirati' is so called because, having turned back from this and that, one delights without it. Alternatively, the word is expanded by means of prefixes. All of these are designations for the state of abstention. 'Veramaṇī' is so called because it destroys (maṇati, vināseti) hostility (veraṃ). This too is a synonym for abstention. Furthermore, regarding the volition by which one, in speaking falsely and so forth, performs an action, this supramundane path-abstinence, having arisen, does not allow that action to be done; it cuts off the path of action, thus it is 'non-action' (akiriyā). Similarly, it does not allow that deed to be done; it cuts off the path of doing, thus it is 'non-doing' (akaraṇa). And regarding the volition by which one, in speaking, incurs the fourfold verbal misconduct, this abstinence, having arisen, does not allow one to incur it in that way, thus it is 'non-incurrence' (anajjhāpatti).

Velāanatikkamoti ettha “tāya velāyā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.154; mahāva. 1-3; udā. 1 ādayo) tāva kālo velāti āgato. “Uruvelāyaṃ viharatī”ti (mahāva. 1; saṃ. ni. 1.137) ettha rāsi. “Ṭhitadhammo velaṃ nātivattatī”ti (cūḷava. 384; a. ni. 8.19; udā. 45) ettha sīmā. Idhāpi sīmāva. Anatikkamanīyaṭṭhena [M 0.0264] hi cattāri vacīsucaritāni velāti adhippetāni. Iti yāya cetanāya cattāri vacīduccaritāni bhāsamāno velaṃ atikkamati nāma, ayaṃ uppajjitvā taṃ velaṃ atikkamituṃ na detīti velāanatikkamoti vuttā. Velāyatīti vā velā, calayati viddhaṃsetīti attho. Kiṃ velāyati? Catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ. Iti velāyanato ‘velā’. Purisassa [V 0.0263] pana hitasukhaṃ anatikkamitvā vattatīti ‘anatikkamo’. Evamettha padadvayavasenāpi attho veditabbo.

Regarding 'non-transgression of the boundary' (velāanatikkamo): in passages such as 'at that time' (tāya velāya), the word 'velā' appears with the meaning of 'time.' In 'he dwells at Uruvelā,' it appears with the meaning of 'a heap.' In 'one of steadfast nature does not transgress the boundary,' it appears with the meaning of 'a limit.' Here too, it is a limit. For, by way of the meaning 'not to be transgressed,' the four kinds of good verbal conduct are intended as the 'boundary' (velā). Thus, regarding the volition by which one, in speaking the four kinds of verbal misconduct, is said to 'transgress the boundary,' this abstinence, having arisen, does not allow one to transgress that boundary. Therefore, it is called 'non-transgression of the boundary.' Alternatively, it is 'velā' because it shakes (velayati); the meaning is that it agitates, it destroys. What does it shake? The fourfold verbal misconduct. Thus, from shaking, it is 'velā.' Furthermore, it is 'non-transgression' (anatikkamo) because it proceeds without transgressing a person's welfare and happiness. In this way, the meaning here should also be understood by way of the two terms.

Setuṃ hanatīti setughāto; catunnaṃ vacīduccaritānaṃ padaghāto paccayaghātoti attho. Paccayo hi idha setūti adhippeto. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – rāgādiko catunnaṃ vacīduccaritānaṃ paccayo vaṭṭasmiṃ puggalaṃ sinoti bandhatīti setu. Setussa ghāto setughāto. Vacīduccaritapaccayasamugghāṭikāya viratiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayaṃ pana sammāvācāsaṅkhātā virati pubbabhāge nānācittesu labbhati. Aññeneva hi cittena musāvādā viramati, aññena pesuññādīhi. Lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana ekacittasmiṃyeva labbhati. Catubbidhāya hi vacīduccaritacetanāya padapacchedaṃ kurumānā maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva virati uppajjati.

It destroys the cause (setu), thus it is the 'cause-destroyer' (setughāta); the meaning is the destruction of the basis of the four kinds of verbal misconduct, that is, the destruction of their condition. For here, 'condition' is intended by the word 'cause' (setu). Herein, this is the etymological meaning: the condition for the four kinds of verbal misconduct, such as greed, binds (sinoti) a person in the cycle of existence, thus it is a 'cause' (setu). The destruction of the cause is 'cause-destroyer' (setughāta). This is a designation for the abstinence that uproots the condition for verbal misconduct. This abstinence, known as Right Speech, is obtained in the preliminary stage in various minds. For one abstains from false speech with one mind, and from divisive speech and so forth with another. At the moment of the supramundane path, however, it is obtained in a single mind only. For, while cutting off the basis of the fourfold volition of verbal misconduct and fulfilling the path factor, a single abstinence arises.

300. Kāyaduccaritehīti kāyato pavattehi kāyena vā nipphāditehi pāṇātipātādīhi duccaritehi. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayampi sammākammantasaṅkhātā virati pubbabhāge nānācittesu labbhati. Aññeneva hi cittena pāṇātipātā [P 0.0220] viramati, aññena adinnādānamicchācārehi. Lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana ekacittasmiṃyeva labbhati. Tividhāya hi kāyaduccaritacetanāya padapacchedaṃ kurumānā maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva virati uppajjati.

300. 'By bodily misconduct' (kāyaduccaritehi) means by misconduct such as the taking of life, which arises from the body or is produced by the body. The rest should be understood in the same way as before. This abstinence, known as Right Action, is also obtained in the preliminary stage in various minds. For one abstains from taking life with one mind, and from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct with another. At the moment of the supramundane path, however, it is obtained in a single mind only. For, while cutting off the basis of the threefold volition of bodily misconduct and fulfilling the path factor, a single abstinence arises.

301. Sammāājīvaniddese akiriyātiādīsu yāya cetanāya micchājīvaṃ ājīvamāno kiriyaṃ karoti nāma, ayaṃ uppajjitvā taṃ kiriyaṃ kātuṃ na detīti akiriyāti. Iminā nayena yojanā veditabbā. Ājīvo ca nāmesa pāṭiyekko natthi, vācākammantesu gahitesu gahitova hoti, tappakkhikattā. Dhuvapaṭisevanavasena panāyaṃ tato nīharitvā dassitoti. Evaṃ sante sammāājīvo sakiccako na hoti[M 0.0265], aṭṭha maggaṅgāni na paripūrenti, tasmā sammāājīvo sakiccako kātabbo, aṭṭha maggaṅgāni paripūretabbānīti. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – ājīvo nāma bhijjamāno kāyavacīdvāresuyeva bhijjati. Manodvāre ājīvabhedo nāma natthi. Pūrayamānopi tasmiṃyeva dvāradvaye pūrati. Manodvāre ājīvapūraṇaṃ nāma natthi. Kāyadvāre pana vītikkamo ājīvahetukopi atthi naājīvahetukopi. Tathā vacīdvāre.

301. In the exposition of Right Livelihood, regarding 'non-action' and so forth: by whichever volition one, living by wrong livelihood, performs an action, this [abstinence], having arisen, does not allow that action to be performed; therefore, it is called 'non-action.' The application of the meaning should be understood in this way. Furthermore, this so-called livelihood is not something separate; when verbal and bodily actions are taken, it is indeed taken, because of being included on their side. However, by the power of constant practice, this [livelihood] is extracted from them and shown. If this were so, Right Livelihood would not have its own function, and the eight path factors would not be fulfilled. Therefore, Right Livelihood must be made to have its own function, and the eight path factors must be fulfilled. In this regard, this is the method: Livelihood, when it is broken, is broken only at the body-door and speech-door. At the mind-door, there is no such thing as the breaking of livelihood. Even when being fulfilled, it is fulfilled only in that pair of doors. At the mind-door, there is no such thing as the fulfillment of livelihood. However, at the body-door, there is transgression that has livelihood as its cause and also that which does not have livelihood as its cause. Likewise at the speech-door.

Tattha [V 0.0264] yaṃ rājarājamahāmattā khiḍḍāpasutā sūrabhāvaṃ dassentā migavadhaṃ vā panthaduhanaṃ vā paradāravītikkamaṃ vā karonti, idaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Tato viratipi ‘sammākammanto’ nāma. Yaṃ pana naājīvahetukaṃ catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ bhāsanti, idaṃ akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Tato viratipi ‘sammāvācā’ nāma.

Therein, when kings and great ministers of kings, being devoted to sport and displaying their prowess, commit the killing of beasts, or highway robbery, or transgression against another's wife—this is called unwholesome bodily action. Abstinence from that is called 'Right Action.' Furthermore, whatever fourfold verbal misconduct, which does not have livelihood as its cause, they speak—this is called unwholesome verbal action. Abstinence from that is called 'Right Speech.'

Yaṃ pana ājīvahetu nesādamacchabandhādayo pāṇaṃ hananti, adinnaṃ ādiyanti, micchācāraṃ caranti, ayaṃ micchājīvo nāma. Tato virati ‘sammāājīvo’ nāma. Yampi lañjaṃ gahetvā musā bhaṇanti, pesuññapharusasamphappalāpe pavattenti, ayampi micchājīvo nāma. Tato virati sammāājīvo nāma.

Furthermore, when on account of livelihood, hunters, fishermen, and so forth kill a living being, take what is not given, or practice sexual misconduct—this is called wrong livelihood. Abstinence from that is called 'Right Livelihood.' And also when, having taken a bribe, they speak a lie, or engage in slanderous speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—this too is called wrong livelihood. Abstinence from that is called 'Right Livelihood.'

Mahāsīvatthero panāha – ‘kāyavacīdvāresupi vītikkamo ājīvahetuko [P 0.0221] vā hotu no vā ājīvahetuko, akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīkammantveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tato viratipi sammākammanto sammāvācātveva vuccatī’ti. ‘Ājīvo kuhi’nti vutte pana ‘tīṇi kuhanavatthūni nissāya cattāro paccaye uppādetvā tesaṃ paribhogo’ti āha. Ayaṃ pana koṭippatto micchājīvo. Tato virati sammāājīvo nāma.

However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: 'At the body-door and speech-door, whether a transgression has livelihood as its cause or does not have livelihood as its cause, it is reckoned only as unwholesome bodily action and verbal action. Abstinence from that is also called only "Right Action" and "Right Speech."' But when it was said, 'Where, then, is livelihood?' he replied: 'It is the use of the four requisites, having produced them by relying on the three grounds of deceit.' This, however, is wrong livelihood that has reached the extreme. Abstinence from that is called 'Right Livelihood.'

Ayampi sammāājīvo pubbabhāge nānācittesu labbhati, aññeneva hi cittena kāyadvāravītikkamā viramati, aññena vacīdvāravītikkamā. Lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana ekacittasmiṃyeva labbhati. Kāyavacīdvāresu hi sattakammapathavasena uppannāya micchājīvasaṅkhātāya dussīlyacetanāya padapacchedaṃ kurumānā maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva virati uppajjatīti. Ayaṃ niddesavāre viseso.

This Right Livelihood is also obtained in the preliminary stage in various minds; for one abstains from transgression at the body-door with one mind, and from transgression at the speech-door with another. However, at the moment of the supramundane path, it is obtained in a single mind only. Indeed, at the body-door and speech-door, while cutting off the cause of the immoral volition—called wrong livelihood—which has arisen by way of the seven courses of action, and while fulfilling the path factor, a single abstinence arises. This is the distinction in the Exposition Section.

Yaṃ [M 0.0266] panetaṃ indriyesu anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ, maggaṅgesu ca sammāvācādīni, tesaṃ vasena saṅgahavāre “navindriyāni, aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti vuttaṃ. Suññatavāro pākatikoyevāti. Ayaṃ tāva suddhikapaṭipadāya viseso.

Furthermore, that faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' which has been developed among the faculties, and Right Speech and so forth which have been developed among the path factors—by way of these, in the Inclusion Section, it was said: 'Nine faculties, the eightfold path.' The Emptiness Section is just of its natural state. This, first of all, is the distinction in the Pure Path.

343. Ito paraṃ suddhikasuññatā suññatapaṭipadā suddhikaappaṇihitā appaṇihitapaṭipadāti ayaṃ desanābhedo hoti. Tattha suññatanti lokuttaramaggassa nāmaṃ. So hi [V 0.0265] āgamanato saguṇato ārammaṇatoti tīhi kāraṇehi nāmaṃ labhati. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhu anattato abhinivisitvā anattato saṅkhāre passati. Yasmā pana anattato diṭṭhamatteneva maggavuṭṭhānaṃ nāma na hoti, aniccatopi dukkhatopi daṭṭhumeva vaṭṭati, tasmā ‘aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā’ti tividhaṃ anupassanaṃ āropetvā sammasanto carati. Vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā panassa tebhūmakepi saṅkhāre suññatova passati. Ayaṃ vipassanā suññatā nāma hoti. Sā āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano maggassa ‘suññata’nti nāmaṃ deti. Evaṃ maggo ‘āgamanato’ suññatanāmaṃ labhati. Yasmā pana so rāgādīhi suñño tasmā ‘saguṇeneva’ suññatanāmaṃ labhati. Nibbānampi rāgādīhi suññattā suññatanti vuccati. Taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannattā maggo ‘ārammaṇato’ suññatanāmaṃ labhati.

343. After this, there is this division of the teaching: pure emptiness, the path of emptiness; pure undirectedness, the path of undirectedness. Therein, 'emptiness' is a name for the supramundane path. Indeed, it obtains this name for three reasons: from its approach, from its own quality, and from its object. How so? Here, a monk, having firmly inclined towards non-self, sees formations as non-self. Furthermore, because the emergence of the path does not happen merely by seeing as non-self, it is proper to see also as impermanent and as suffering. Therefore, having applied the mind to the threefold contemplation—'impermanent, suffering, non-self'—he fares, comprehending. Moreover, his insight leading to emergence sees the formations, even those in the three planes, only as empty. This insight is called 'emptiness.' That insight, standing in the position of being the approach, gives the name 'emptiness' to its own path. Thus the path obtains the name 'emptiness' from its approach. Furthermore, because that path is empty of lust and so on, it obtains the name 'emptiness' from its own quality. Nibbāna, too, because of its emptiness of lust and so on, is called 'emptiness.' Because the path arises having made that its object, it obtains the name 'emptiness' from its object.

Tattha suttantikapariyāyena [P 0.0222] saguṇatopi ārammaṇatopi nāmaṃ labhati. Pariyāyadesanā hesā. Abhidhammakathā pana nippariyāyadesanā. Tasmā idha saguṇato vā ārammaṇato vā nāmaṃ na labhati, āgamanatova labhati. Āgamanameva hi dhuraṃ. Taṃ duvidhaṃ hoti – vipassanāgamanaṃ maggāgamananti. Tattha maggassa āgataṭṭhāne vipassanāgamanaṃ dhuraṃ, phalassa āgataṭṭhāne maggāgamanaṃ dhuraṃ. Idha maggassa āgatattā vipassanāgamanameva dhuraṃ jātaṃ.

Therein, according to the Suttanta method, it obtains the name from its own quality and from its object. For this is a teaching with an indirect meaning. But the Abhidhamma discourse is a teaching with a direct meaning. Therefore, here it does not obtain the name from its own quality or from its object; it obtains it only from the approach. Indeed, the approach alone is the principal factor. That is twofold: the approach of insight and the approach of the path. Therein, in the place where the path has arisen, the approach of insight is the principal factor; in the place where the fruit has arisen, the approach of the path is the principal factor. Here, because the path has arisen, the approach of insight alone has become the principal factor.

350. Appaṇihitanti, etthāpi appaṇihitanti maggasseva nāmaṃ. Idampi nāmaṃ maggo tīheva kāraṇehi labhati. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhu āditova dukkhato abhinivisitvā dukkhatova saṅkhāre passati. Yasmā pana dukkhato diṭṭhamatteneva maggavuṭṭhānaṃ nāma na hoti, aniccatopi anattatopi daṭṭhumeva vaṭṭati, tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā’ti tividhaṃ anupassanaṃ āropetvā [M 0.0267] sammasanto carati. Vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā panassa tebhūmakasaṅkhāresu paṇidhiṃ sosetvā pariyādiyitvā vissajjeti. Ayaṃ vipassanā appaṇihitā nāma hoti. Sā āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano maggassa ‘appaṇihita’nti nāmaṃ deti. Evaṃ maggo ‘āgamanato’ appaṇihitanāmaṃ labhati. Yasmā pana tattha rāgadosamohapaṇidhayo natthi, tasmā ‘saguṇeneva’ appaṇihitanāmaṃ labhati. Nibbānampi tesaṃ paṇidhīnaṃ abhāvā appaṇihitanti vuccati. Taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannattā maggo appaṇihitanāmaṃ labhati.

350. 'Undirected'—here too, 'undirected' is a name for the path itself. This name, too, the path obtains for three reasons. How so? Here, a monk, having firmly inclined towards suffering from the very beginning, sees formations only as suffering. However, since the emergence of the path does not happen merely by seeing them as suffering, it is proper to see them also as impermanent and as non-self. Therefore, having applied the mind to the threefold contemplation of 'impermanent, suffering, non-self,' he proceeds comprehending. Furthermore, his insight leading to emergence dries up, exhausts, and relinquishes the craving for formations in the three planes. This insight is called 'undirected.' It, standing in the position of being the approach, gives the name 'undirected' to its own path. Thus, the path obtains the name 'undirected' from its approach. And because there are no aspirations of lust, hatred, or delusion in it, it obtains the name 'undirected' from its own quality. Nibbāna, too, is called 'undirected' due to the absence of those aspirations. Because it arises having taken that as its object, the path obtains the name 'undirected' from its object.

Tattha suttantikapariyāyena saguṇatopi ārammaṇatopi nāmaṃ labhati. Pariyāyadesanā hesā[V 0.0266]. Abhidhammakathā pana nippariyāyadesanā. Tasmā idha saguṇato vā ārammaṇato vā nāmaṃ na labhati, āgamanatova labhati. Āgamanameva hi dhuraṃ. Taṃ duvidhaṃ hoti – vipassanāgamanaṃ maggāgamananti. Tattha maggassa āgataṭṭhāne vipassanāgamanaṃ dhuraṃ, phalassa āgataṭṭhāne [P 0.0223] maggāgamanaṃ dhuraṃ. Idha maggassa āgatattā vipassanāgamanameva dhuraṃ jātaṃ.

Therein, by the Suttanta method, it obtains a name from its own quality and from its object. For this is a teaching by way of interpretation. The Abhidhamma discourse, however, is a teaching without interpretation. Therefore, here it does not obtain a name from its own quality or from its object; it obtains it only from its approach. For the approach itself is the principal factor. It is twofold: the approach of insight and the approach of the path. Therein, in the place where the path has arisen, the approach of insight is the principal factor; in the place where the fruit has arisen, the approach of the path is the principal factor. Here, because the path has arisen, the approach of insight alone has become the principal factor.

Nanu ca suññato animitto appaṇihitoti tīṇi maggassa nāmāni? Yathāha – “tayome, bhikkhave, vimokkhā – suññato vimokkho, animitto vimokkho, appaṇihito vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.209). Tesu idha dve magge gahetvā animitto kasmā na gahitoti? Āgamanābhāvato. Animittavipassanā hi sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano maggassa nāmaṃ dātuṃ na sakkoti. Sammāsambuddho pana attano puttassa rāhulattherassa.

Is it not so that 'empty,' 'signless,' and 'undirected' are the three names of the path? As it was said: 'These three, O monks, are liberations—the empty liberation, the signless liberation, and the undirected liberation.' Among these, why, having taken two paths here, is the signless not taken? Because of the absence of an approach. For signless insight, standing itself in the position of being the approach, is not able to give a name to its own path. The Perfectly Enlightened One, however, taught it to his son, the Elder Rāhula.

“Animittañca bhāvehi, mānānusayamujjaha;

Tato mānābhisamayā, upasanto carissasī”ti. (su. ni. 344);

“Develop the signless, abandon the underlying tendency to conceit; Then, through the full understanding of conceit, you will fare in peace.”

Animittavipassanaṃ kathesi. Vipassanā hi niccanimittaṃ dhuvanimittaṃ sukhanimittaṃ attanimittañca ugghāṭeti. Tasmā animittāti kathitā. Sā ca kiñcāpi taṃ nimittaṃ ugghāṭeti, sayaṃ pana nimittadhammesu caratīti sanimittāva hoti. Tasmā sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano maggassa nāmaṃ dātuṃ na sakkoti.

He taught signless insight. For insight uproots the sign of permanence, the sign of stability, the sign of pleasure, and the sign of self. Therefore, it is called 'signless.' And although it uproots that sign, it itself proceeds among phenomena that are signs, thus it is indeed 'with a sign.' Therefore, standing itself in the position of being the approach, it is not able to give a name to its own path.

Aparo [M 0.0268] nayo – abhidhammo nāma paramatthadesanā. Animittamaggassa ca paramatthato hetuvekallameva hoti. Kathaṃ? Aniccānupassanāya hi vasena animittavimokkho kathito. Tena ca vimokkhena saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti. Taṃ ariyamagge ekaṅgampi na hoti, amaggaṅgattā attano maggassa paramatthato nāmaṃ dātuṃ na sakkoti. Itaresu pana dvīsu anattānupassanāya tāva vasena suññatavimokkho, dukkhānupassanāya vasena appaṇihitavimokkho kathito. Tesu suññatavimokkhena paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti, appaṇihitavimokkhena samādhindriyaṃ. Tāni ariyamaggassa aṅgattā attano maggassa paramatthato nāmaṃ dātuṃ sakkonti. Maggārammaṇattikepi hi maggādhipatidhammavibhajane chandacittānaṃ adhipatikāle [V 0.0267] tesaṃ dhammānaṃ amaggaṅgattāva maggādhipatibhāvo na vutto. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbanti. Ayamettha aṭṭhakathāmuttako ekassa ācariyassa mativinicchayo.

Another method: Abhidhamma is the teaching of ultimate reality. And for the signless path, in an ultimate sense, there is only a deficiency of cause. How so? For the signless liberation is taught by way of the contemplation of impermanence. And through that liberation, the faculty of faith becomes predominant. That is not even a single factor in the noble path; because it is not a path-factor, it is not able to give a name in an ultimate sense to its own path. But among the other two, the liberation of emptiness is taught by way of the contemplation of non-self, and the desireless liberation by way of the contemplation of suffering. Among these, through the liberation of emptiness the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant, and through the desireless liberation, the faculty of concentration. They, being factors of the noble path, are able to give a name in an ultimate sense to their own path. For even in the Triad on Path-Objects, in the analysis of path-dominant states, at the time when desire and consciousness are dominant, their status as path-dominant is not stated precisely because those states are not path-factors. This should be understood as being thus accomplished. This, herein, is the reasoned decision of a certain teacher, independent of the commentary.

Evaṃ [P 0.0224] sabbathāpi animittavipassanā sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano maggassa nāmaṃ dātuṃ na sakkotīti animittamaggo na gahito. Keci pana ‘animittamaggo āgamanato nāmaṃ alabhantopi suttantapariyāyena saguṇato ca ārammaṇato ca nāmaṃ labhatī’ti āhaṃsu. Te idaṃ vatvā paṭikkhittā – animittamagge saguṇato ca ārammaṇato ca nāmaṃ labhante suññataappaṇihitamaggāpi saguṇatoyeva ārammaṇatoyeva ca idha nāmaṃ labheyyuṃ. Na pana labhanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Ayañhi maggo nāma dvīhi kāraṇehi nāmaṃ labhati – sarasato ca paccanīkato ca; sabhāvato ca paṭipakkhato cāti attho. Tattha suññataappaṇihitamaggā sarasatopi paccanīkatopi nāmaṃ labhanti. Suññataappaṇihitamaggā hi rāgādīhi suññā, rāgapaṇidhiādīhi ca appaṇihitāti evaṃ ‘sarasato’ nāmaṃ labhanti. Suññato ca attābhinivesassa paṭipakkho, appaṇihito paṇidhissāti evaṃ ‘paccanīkato’ nāmaṃ labhanti. Animittamaggo pana rāgādinimittānaṃ niccanimittādīnañca abhāvena sarasatova nāmaṃ labhati, no paccanīkato. Na hi so saṅkhāranimittārammaṇāya aniccānupassanāya paṭipakkho. Aniccānupassanā panassa anulomabhāve ṭhitāti. Sabbathāpi abhidhammapariyāyena animittamaggo nāma natthīti.

Thus, in every way, since signless insight, standing itself in the position of being the approach, is not able to give a name to its own path, the signless path is not taken. Some, however, have said: 'Although the signless path does not obtain a name from its approach, by the Suttanta method it obtains a name from its own quality and from its object.' They were refuted by saying this: If the signless path were to obtain a name from its own quality and from its object, then the paths of emptiness and desirelessness, too, would obtain a name here only from their own quality and only from their object. But they do not. For what reason? For this path obtains a name for two reasons: from its own essence and from its opposition; the meaning is: from its intrinsic nature and from its counteraction. Therein, the paths of emptiness and desirelessness obtain a name from their own essence and from their opposition. For the paths of emptiness and desirelessness are empty of lust and so on, and are without desire for aspirations of lust and so on; thus they obtain a name 'from their own essence.' And emptiness is the counteraction to the adherence to self, and desirelessness is the counteraction to aspiration; thus they obtain a name 'from their opposition.' The signless path, however, obtains a name only 'from its own essence'—due to the absence of the signs of lust and so on, and of the signs of permanence and so on—but not 'from its opposition.' For it is not the counteraction to the contemplation of impermanence, which has the sign of formations as its object. Rather, the contemplation of impermanence stands in conformity with it. Thus, in every way, according to the Abhidhamma method, there is no such thing as a signless path.

Suttantikapariyāyena [M 0.0269] panesa evaṃ āharitvā dīpito – yasmiñhi vāre maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tīṇi lakkhaṇāni ekāvajjanena viya āpāthamāgacchanti, tiṇṇañca ekato āpāthagamanaṃ nāma natthi. Kammaṭṭhānassa pana vibhūtabhāvadīpanatthaṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ādito hi yattha katthaci abhiniveso hotu, vuṭṭhānagāminī pana vipassanā yaṃ yaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti tassa tasseva vasena āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano maggassa nāmaṃ deti. Kathaṃ? Aniccādīsu hi yattha katthaci abhinivisitvā itarampi lakkhaṇadvayaṃ daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭati eva. Ekalakkhaṇadassanamatteneva hi maggavuṭṭhānaṃ nāma na hoti, tasmā aniccato abhiniviṭṭho bhikkhu [P 0.0225] na kevalaṃ aniccatova vuṭṭhāti, dukkhatopi anattatopi vuṭṭhātiyeva. Dukkhato anattato abhiniviṭṭhepi eseva nayo. Iti ādito yattha katthaci abhiniveso hotu, vuṭṭhānagāminī pana vipassanā yaṃ yaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti tassa tasseva vasena āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā [V 0.0268] attano maggassa nāmaṃ deti. Tattha aniccato vuṭṭhahantassa maggo animitto nāma hoti, dukkhato vuṭṭhahantassa appaṇihito, anattato vuṭṭhahantassa suññatoti. Evaṃ suttantapariyāyena āharitvā dīpito.

However, by way of the Suttanta method, this is brought forth and explained thus: Indeed, at the time when the emergence of the path occurs, the three characteristics come into range as if with a single advertence, yet there is no such thing as the three coming into range all at once. This, however, was stated to clarify the distinct nature of the meditation subject. For, let there be an intent focus on any one characteristic at the outset; the insight leading to emergence, having comprehended whichever characteristic it emerges from, stands in the position of the practice that is the cause for the path's arising and, by the power of that very characteristic, gives a name to its own path. How so? For, having intently focused on any one characteristic among impermanence and so on, it is indeed proper to see the other two characteristics as well. For the emergence of the path does not occur merely by seeing a single characteristic. Therefore, a bhikkhu who is intently focused on impermanence does not emerge only from that which is impermanent; he emerges also from that which is suffering and that which is not-self. This same method applies also to one who is intently focused on suffering and not-self. Thus, let there be an intent focus on any one characteristic at the outset; the insight leading to emergence, having comprehended whichever characteristic it emerges from, stands in the position of the practice that is the cause for the path's arising and, by the power of that very characteristic, gives a name to its own path. Therein, for one emerging from impermanence, the path is called 'signless'; for one emerging from suffering, it is called 'desireless'; and for one emerging from not-self, it is called 'empty.' In this way, it is brought forth and explained according to the Suttanta method.

Vuṭṭhānagāminī pana vipassanā kimārammaṇāti? Lakkhaṇārammaṇāti. Lakkhaṇaṃ nāma paññattigatikaṃ na vattabbadhammabhūtaṃ. Yo pana aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti tīṇi lakkhaṇāni sallakkheti, tassa pañcakkhandhā kaṇṭhe baddhakuṇapaṃ viya honti. Saṅkhārārammaṇameva ñāṇaṃ saṅkhārato vuṭṭhāti. Yathā hi eko bhikkhu pattaṃ kiṇitukāmo pattavāṇijena pattaṃ ābhataṃ disvā haṭṭhapahaṭṭho gaṇhissāmīti cintetvā vīmaṃsamāno tīṇi chiddāni passeyya, so na chiddesu nirālayo hoti, patte pana nirālayo hoti; evameva tīṇi lakkhaṇāni sallakkhetvā saṅkhāresu nirālayo hoti. Saṅkhārārammaṇeneva ñāṇena saṅkhārato vuṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ. Dussopamāyapi eseva nayo.

But what is the object of the insight leading to emergence? It has the characteristics as its object. A characteristic is of the nature of a concept; it is a state that cannot be spoken of. For one who marks the three characteristics—impermanence, suffering, and not-self—the five aggregates become like a rotten corpse tied to the neck. The knowledge that has only formations as its object emerges from formations. For instance, just as a bhikkhu wishing to buy a bowl, upon seeing a bowl brought by a bowl merchant, becomes delighted and thinks, 'I will take it,' but upon inspecting it, should see three cracks; he does not become detached from the cracks, but rather becomes detached from the bowl. In the very same way, having marked the three characteristics, one becomes detached from formations. It should be understood that one emerges from formations by means of the knowledge that has only formations as its object. In the simile of the cloth as well, this is the same method.

Iti bhagavā lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhājento suddhikapaṭipadāya catukkanayaṃ pañcakanayanti dvepi naye āhari. Tathā suddhikasuññatāya suññatapaṭipadāya suddhikaappaṇihitāya appaṇihitapaṭipadāyāti. Kasmā evaṃ āharīti? Puggalajjhāsayena ceva desanāvilāsena ca. Tadubhayampi heṭṭhā [M 0.0270] vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāvetīti ettha suddhikapaṭipadāya catukkapañcakavasena dve nayā, tathā sesesūti sabbesupi pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu dasa nayā bhājitā.

Thus the Blessed One, when analyzing the supramundane jhāna, brought forth both methods in the pure practice—the fourfold method and the fivefold method. Likewise for the pure voidness, the path of voidness, the pure undirectedness, and the path of undirectedness. Why did he bring them forth in this way? Due to the disposition of individuals and the elegance of the teaching. Both of these should be understood by the same method spoken of below. Thus, herein, regarding 'develops the supramundane jhāna,' two methods are analyzed in the pure practice by way of the fourfold and fivefold methods, and likewise in the remaining sections. Thus, in all five sections, ten methods have been analyzed.

Lokuttarakusalaṃ pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse on Supramundane Wholesome States

Tatridaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ –

Therein, this is the miscellaneous section:

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, rūpārūpesu pañcasu;

Sattaṭṭhaṅgapariṇāmaṃ, nimittaṃ paṭipadāpatīti.

Internal and external; in the five material and immaterial aggregates; the transformation of the seven and eight factors; the sign, the path, and the dominant factor.

Lokuttaramaggo hi ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā ajjhattaṃ vuṭṭhāti[P 0.0226], ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā bahiddhā vuṭṭhāti, bahiddhā abhinivisitvā [V 0.0269] bahiddhā vuṭṭhāti, bahiddhā abhinivisitvā ajjhattaṃ vuṭṭhāti. Rūpe abhinivisitvā rūpā vuṭṭhāti, rūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā vuṭṭhāti. Arūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā vuṭṭhāti, arūpe abhinivisitvā rūpā vuṭṭhāti, ekappahāreneva pañcahi khandhehi vuṭṭhāti.

For the supramundane path, having intently focused internally, one emerges internally; having intently focused internally, one emerges externally; having intently focused externally, one emerges externally; having intently focused externally, one emerges internally. Having intently focused on form, one emerges from form; having intently focused on form, one emerges from non-form. Having intently focused on non-form, one emerges from non-form; having intently focused on non-form, one emerges from form. One emerges from the five aggregates all at once.

‘Sattaṭṭhaṅgapariṇāma’nti so panesa maggo aṭṭhaṅgikopi hoti sattaṅgikopi. Bojjhaṅgāpi satta vā honti cha vā. Jhānaṃ pana pañcaṅgikaṃ vā hoti caturaṅgikaṃ vā; tivaṅgikaṃ vā duvaṅgikaṃ vā. Evaṃ sattaaṭṭhādīnaṃ aṅgānaṃ pariṇāmo veditabboti attho.

Regarding 'the transformation of seven and eight factors': this path can be eight-factored or seven-factored. The enlightenment factors can be seven or six. And jhāna can be five-factored or four-factored, three-factored or two-factored. The meaning is that the transformation of the factors—seven, eight, and so on—should be understood in this way.

‘Nimittaṃ paṭipadāpatī’ti nimittanti yato vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti; ‘paṭipadāpatī’ti paṭipadāya ca adhipatino ca calanācalanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'the sign, the path, and the dominant factor': 'sign' is that from which emergence occurs. Regarding 'the path and the dominant factor,' the movement and non-movement of both the path and the dominant factor should be understood.

Tattha ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā ajjhattaṃ vuṭṭhātītiādīsu tāva idhekacco āditova ajjhattaṃ pañcasu khandhesu abhinivisati, abhinivisitvā te aniccādito passati, yasmā pana na suddhaajjhattadassanamatteneva maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, bahiddhāpi daṭṭhabbameva, tasmā parassa khandhepi anupādinnasaṅkhārepi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti passati. So kālena ajjhattaṃ sammasati kālena bahiddhāti. Tassevaṃ sammasato ajjhattaṃ sammasanakāle vipassanā maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati. Evaṃ ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā ajjhattaṃ vuṭṭhāti nāma. Sace panassa bahiddhā sammasanakāle vipassanā maggena [M 0.0271] saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati, evaṃ ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā bahiddhā vuṭṭhāti nāma. Eseva nayo bahiddhā abhinivisitvā bahiddhā ca ajjhattañca vuṭṭhānepi.

Therein, regarding the phrases beginning with 'having intently focused internally, one emerges internally,' it should be understood thus: Here, a certain individual from the outset focuses intently on the five internal aggregates. Having focused intently, one sees them as impermanent, and so on. But since the emergence of the path does not occur merely by seeing the purely internal, the external must also be seen. Therefore, one sees the aggregates of another and also external formations not clung to as impermanent, suffering, and not-self. At times one comprehends the internal, at other times the external. For one comprehending in this way, if insight connects with the path during the time of comprehending the internal, it is called 'having intently focused internally, one emerges internally.' But if, for that person, insight connects with the path during the time of comprehending the external, it is called 'having intently focused internally, one emerges externally.' This is the same method also for emerging externally and internally after having intently focused externally.

Aparo āditova rūpe abhinivisati abhinivisitvā bhūtarūpañca upādārūpañca paricchinditvā aniccādito passati, yasmā pana na suddharūpadassanamatteneva vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti arūpampi daṭṭhabbameva, tasmā taṃ rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā [P 0.0227] uppannaṃ vedanaṃ saññaṃ saṅkhāre viññāṇañca idaṃ arūpanti paricchinditvā aniccādito passati. So kālena rūpaṃ sammasati kālena arūpaṃ. Tassevaṃ sammasato rūpasammasanakāle vipassanā maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati. Evaṃ rūpe abhinivisitvā rūpā vuṭṭhāti nāma. Sace panassa arūpasammasanakāle vipassanā [V 0.0270] maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati, evaṃ rūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā vuṭṭhāti nāma. Esa nayo arūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā ca rūpā ca vuṭṭhānepi.

Another person from the outset resolutely attends to form. Having resolutely attended, and having defined primary matter and derived matter, one contemplates them as impermanent, and so on. But since emergence does not occur merely by contemplating form alone, the formless must also be contemplated. Therefore, taking that form as an object, one defines the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that have arisen as ‘this is formless,’ and contemplates them as impermanent, and so on. At a suitable time, one comprehends form; at a suitable time, the formless. For one comprehending thus, if insight is conjoined with the path during the comprehension of form, this is called ‘emerging from form after having resolutely attended to form.’ If, however, for that person, insight is conjoined with the path during the comprehension of the formless, this is called ‘emerging from the formless after having resolutely attended to form.’ This is the same method for emerging from the formless and from form after having resolutely attended to the formless.

“Yaṃkiñci samudayadhammaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti (mahāva. 16; dī. ni. 1.298) evaṃ abhinivisitvā evameva vuṭṭhānakāle pana ekappahārena pañcahi khandhehi vuṭṭhāti nāmāti. Ayaṃ tikkhavipassakassa mahāpaññassa bhikkhuno vipassanā.

‘Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease’—having resolutely attended thus, at the time of emergence, one emerges from the five aggregates with a single stroke. This is the insight of a bhikkhu with keen insight and great wisdom.

Yathā hi chātajjhattassa purisassa majjhe gūthapiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā nānaggarasabhojanapuṇṇaṃ pātiṃ upaneyyuṃ, so byañjanaṃ hatthena viyūhanto taṃ gūthapiṇḍaṃ disvā ‘kimida’nti pucchitvā gūthapiṇḍoti vutte ‘dhi dhi, apanethā’ti bhattepi pātiyampi nirālayo hoti. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For instance, it is as if for a man afflicted by hunger they were to bring a bowl filled with food of various excellent flavors, having placed a lump of excrement in the middle of the rice. While pushing aside the curry with his hand, that man, upon seeing the lump of excrement and asking, ‘What is this?’, and being told, ‘It is a lump of excrement,’ would say, ‘Fie, fie! Take it away!’ and become unattached to both the rice and the bowl. This matter should be understood as being thus accomplished.

Bhojanapātidassanasmiñhi tassa attamanakālo viya imassa bhikkhuno bālaputhujjanakāle pañcakkhandhe ‘ahaṃ mamā’ti gahitakālo. Gūthapiṇḍassa diṭṭhakālo viya tiṇṇaṃ lakkhaṇānaṃ sallakkhitakālo. Bhattepi pātiyampi nirālayakālo viya tikkhavipassakassa mahāpaññassa bhikkhuno “yaṃkiñci samudayadhammaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti pañcahi khandhehi ekappahārena vuṭṭhitakālo veditabbo.

For, the time of grasping the five aggregates as ‘I’ and ‘mine’ when this bhikkhu was a foolish worldling should be understood as being like the time of that man's delight at the sight of the food bowl. The time of discerning the three characteristics should be understood as being like the time of seeing the lump of excrement. The time of emerging from the five aggregates with a single stroke, with the understanding, ‘Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease,’ for the bhikkhu with keen insight and great wisdom, should be understood as being like the time of being unattached to both the rice and the bowl.

‘Sattaṭṭhaṅgapariṇāma’nti ettha ayaṃ vuttappabhedo aṅgapariṇāmo yathā hoti tathā veditabbo. Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇameva hi ariyamaggassa bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgavisesaṃ [M 0.0272] niyameti. Keci pana therā ‘bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgavisesaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ niyametī’ti vadanti. Keci ‘vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentī’ti vadanti. Keci ‘puggalajjhāsayo niyametī’ti vadanti. Tesampi vādesu ayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāsaṅkhātā pubbabhāgā vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāva niyametīti veditabbā.

Regarding ‘the transformation of seven or eight factors,’ this transformation of factors with its aforementioned distinctions should be understood as it occurs. For it is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations alone that determines the distinction of the noble path into enlightenment factors, path factors, and jhāna factors. However, some elders say, ‘The foundational jhāna determines the distinction into enlightenment factors, path factors, and jhāna factors.’ Others say, ‘The aggregates that are the object of insight determine it.’ Still others say, ‘The individual’s disposition determines it.’ Even in their views, it should be known that it is this very insight leading to emergence in the preliminary stage, known as equanimity towards formations, that determines it.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbīkathā – vipassanāniyamena hi sukkhavipassakassa [P 0.0228] uppannamaggopi samāpattilābhino jhānaṃ pādakaṃ akatvā uppannamaggopi paṭhamajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā pakiṇṇakasaṅkhāre sammasitvā uppāditamaggopi paṭhamajjhānikova hoti. Sabbesu satta bojjhaṅgāni aṭṭha maggaṅgāni pañca jhānaṅgāni honti. Tesañhi pubbabhāgavipassanā somanassasahagatāpi [V 0.0271] upekkhāsahagatāpi hutvā vuṭṭhānakāle saṅkhārupekkhābhāvaṃ pattā somanassasahagatāva hoti.

Herein is the sequential discourse: By the determination of insight, the path arisen for a dry-insight practitioner, the path arisen for one who has attained absorption without making jhāna its basis, and the path produced by making the first jhāna its basis and comprehending miscellaneous formations, are all like the first jhāna. In all of them, there are seven enlightenment factors, eight path factors, and five jhāna factors. For their preliminary insight, although it may be accompanied by joy or by equanimity, having reached the state of equanimity towards formations at the time of emergence, is accompanied only by joy.

Pañcakanaye dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānāni pādakāni katvā uppāditamaggesu yathākkameneva jhānaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ tivaṅgikaṃ duvaṅgikañca hoti. Sabbesu pana satta maggaṅgāni honti, catutthe cha bojjhaṅgāni. Ayaṃ viseso pādakajjhānaniyamena ceva vipassanāniyamena ca hoti. Tesampi hi pubbabhāgavipassanā somanassasahagatāpi upekkhāsahagatāpi hoti. Vuṭṭhānagāminī somanassasahagatāva.

In the fivefold system, in the paths produced by making the second, third, and fourth jhānas their bases, the jhāna is, respectively, four-factored, three-factored, and two-factored. In all of them, however, there are seven path factors, and in the fourth, there are six enlightenment factors. This distinction occurs due to the determination of the foundational jhāna and the determination of insight. For their preliminary insight can be accompanied by joy or by equanimity, but the insight leading to emergence is only accompanied by joy.

Pañcamajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā nibbattitamagge pana upekkhācittekaggatāvasena dve jhānaṅgāni bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgāni cha satta ceva. Ayampi viseso ubhayaniyamavasena hoti. Imasmiñhi naye pubbabhāgavipassanā somanassasahagatā vā upekkhāsahagatā vā hoti, vuṭṭhānagāminī upekkhāsahagatāva. Arūpajjhānāni pādakāni katvā uppāditamaggepi eseva nayo. Evaṃ pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya ye keci saṅkhāre sammasitvā nibbattitamaggassa āsannapadese vuṭṭhitā samāpatti attanā sadisabhāvaṃ karoti, bhūmivaṇṇo viya godhāvaṇṇassa.

However, in the path produced by making the fifth jhāna its basis, there are two jhāna factors, by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, and there are six enlightenment factors and seven path factors. This distinction also occurs by means of the twofold determination. For in this method, the preliminary insight is accompanied by joy or by equanimity, while the insight leading to emergence is only accompanied by equanimity. This same method applies also to the path produced by making the formless jhānas its bases. Thus, having emerged from the foundational jhāna and having comprehended whatever formations, the attainment that has arisen in the vicinity of the produced path makes that path similar to itself, just as the color of the earth makes the color of a monitor lizard similar to itself.

Dutiyattheravāde pana yato yato samāpattito vuṭṭhāya ye ye samāpattidhamme sammasitvā maggo nibbattito hoti taṃtaṃsamāpattisadisova hoti, sammasitasamāpattisadisoti attho. Sace [M 0.0273] pana kāmāvacaradhamme sammasati paṭhamajjhānikova hoti. Tatrāpi vipassanāniyamo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Furthermore, in the view of the second group of elders, from whichever attainment one has emerged and whichever factors of that attainment one has comprehended, the path that is produced is just like that very attainment. The meaning is that it is similar to the comprehended attainment. If, however, one comprehends sense-sphere phenomena, the path is just like the first jhāna. Therein also, the determination of insight should be understood in the very manner already stated.

Tatiyattheravāde [P 0.0229] ‘aho vatāhaṃ sattaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ pāpuṇeyyaṃ, aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ pāpuṇeyya’nti attano ajjhāsayānurūpena yaṃ yaṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ye vā ye vā jhānadhamme sammasitvā maggo nibbattito taṃtaṃjhānasadisova hoti. Pādakajjhānaṃ pana sammasitajjhānaṃ vā vinā, ajjhāsayamatteneva taṃ na ijjhati. Svāyamattho nandakovādasuttena dīpetabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

In the view of the third group of elders, in accordance with one's own disposition, aspiring, ‘Oh, how wonderful it would be if I could attain the seven-factored path! Oh, how wonderful it would be if I could attain the eight-factored path!’, the path that is produced by making whichever jhāna the basis, or by comprehending whichever jhāna factors, is just like that very jhāna. However, without either a foundational jhāna or a comprehended jhāna, this is not accomplished by mere disposition alone. This meaning should be clarified by the Nandakovāda Sutta. For this was said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe pannarase na hoti bahuno janassa kaṅkhā vā vimati [V 0.0272] vā ‘ūno nu kho cando puṇṇo nu kho cando’ti, atha kho puṇṇo candotveva hoti, evameva kho, bhikkhave, tā bhikkhuniyo nandakassa dhammadesanāya attamanā ceva paripuṇṇasaṅkappā ca. Tāsaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ bhikkhunisatānaṃ yā pacchimikā bhikkhunī sā sotāpannā avinipātadhammā niyatā sambodhiparāyaṇā”ti (ma. ni. 3.415).

“Just as, bhikkhus, on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, there is no doubt or perplexity among the people as to whether the moon is deficient or full, but it is just full; in the same way, bhikkhus, those bhikkhunīs were delighted and fully resolved by Nandaka’s Dhamma teaching. Among those five hundred bhikkhunīs, bhikkhus, the last bhikkhunī was a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, assured, bound for full enlightenment.”

Tāsu hi yassā bhikkhuniyā sotāpattiphalassa upanissayo, sā sotāpattiphaleneva paripuṇṇasaṅkappā ahosi…pe… yassā arahattassa upanissayo sā arahatteneva. Evameva attano ajjhāsayānurūpena yaṃ yaṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ye vā ye vā jhānadhamme sammasitvā maggo nibbattito taṃtaṃjhānasadisova so hoti. Pādakajjhānaṃ pana sammasitajjhānaṃ vā vinā, ajjhāsayamatteneva taṃ na ijjhatīti. Etthāpi ca vipassanāniyamo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Among them, whichever bhikkhunī had the predisposition for the fruit of stream-entry, her resolution was fulfilled by the fruit of stream-entry; …and so on… whichever had the predisposition for arahantship, hers was fulfilled by arahantship. Just so, according to one's own inclination, whichever jhāna is made the basis, and whichever jhāna factors are contemplated, the path that arises resembles that particular jhāna. But without either a foundational jhāna or a comprehended jhāna, it does not succeed merely through inclination. Here too, the determination of insight should be understood in the way already stated.

Tattha ‘pādakajjhānameva niyametī’ti evaṃvādiṃ tipiṭakacūḷanāgattheraṃ antevāsikā āhaṃsu – ‘bhante, yattha tāva pādakajjhānaṃ atthi tattha taṃ niyametu; yasmiṃ pana pādakajjhānaṃ natthi, tasmiṃ arūpabhave kiṃ niyametī’ti? ‘Āvuso, tatthapi pādakajjhānameva niyameti. Yo hi bhikkhu aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī paṭhamajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā sotāpattimaggaphalāni nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā arūpabhave nibbatto, paṭhamajjhānikāya sotāpattiphalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā upari [M 0.0274] tīṇi maggaphalāni nibbatteti, tassa tāni paṭhamajjhānikāneva honti. Dutiyajjhānikādīsupi eseva nayo. Arūpe [P 0.0230] tikacatukkajjhānaṃ uppajjati, tañca kho lokuttaraṃ na lokiyaṃ. Evaṃ tatthāpi pādakajjhānameva niyameti āvuso’ti. ‘Sukathito, bhante, pañho’ti.

Therein, the disciples of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, who was of the view, 'The foundational jhāna alone determines,' asked him: 'Venerable sir, where a foundational jhāna exists, let it determine; but in that formless existence where there is no foundational jhāna, what determines?' 'Friends, even there the foundational jhāna alone determines. For a bhikkhu who, having attained the eight attainments, makes the first jhāna his foundation, produces the path and fruit of stream-entry, and, with his jhāna undiminished, passes away and is reborn in the formless existence, then emerges from the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry associated with the first jhāna, establishes insight, and produces the three higher paths and fruits—for him, those attainments are associated only with the first jhāna. This same method applies also to the second jhāna and so on. In the formless realm, the jhānas of the triad and tetrad arise, and they are supramundane, not mundane. Thus, friends, even there the foundational jhāna alone determines.' 'Venerable sir, the question has been well answered.'

‘Vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamenti; yaṃ yaṃ hi pañcakkhandhaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti taṃtaṃsadisova maggo hotī’ti vādiṃ moravāpivāsimahādattattherampi antevāsikā āhaṃsu ‘bhante, tumhākaṃ vāde doso paññāyati – rūpaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhitabhikkhuno hi rūpasadisena abyākatena maggena bhavitabbaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ nayato pariggahetvā vuṭṭhitassa taṃsadiseneva nevasaññānāsaññābhāvappattena maggena bhavitabba’nti. ‘Na, āvuso, evaṃ hoti. Lokuttaramaggo hi appanaṃ appatto nāma natthi, tasmā rūpaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhitassa aṭṭhaṅgiko somanassasahagatamaggo [V 0.0273] hoti, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhitassapi na sabbākārena tādiso hoti, sattaṅgiko pana upekkhāsahagatamaggo hotī’ti.

The disciples also said to the Elder Mahādatta of Moravāpi, who was of the view, 'The aggregates that have become the object of insight determine; for whatever five aggregates one comprehends and emerges from, the path is just like that': 'Venerable sir, a flaw appears in your doctrine. For a bhikkhu who has emerged after comprehending form, the path ought to be similar to form, and thus indeterminate; and for one who has emerged after grasping the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception according to the method, the path ought to be just like that, having reached the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' 'No, friends, it is not so. For there is no such thing as a supramundane path that has not reached absorption. Therefore, for one who has emerged after comprehending form, there is an eight-factored path accompanied by gladness. But for one who has emerged after comprehending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is not like that in all aspects; rather, there is a seven-factored path accompanied by equanimity.'

‘Puggalajjhāsayo niyametī’tivādino cūḷābhayattherassāpi vādaṃ āharitvā tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherassa kathayiṃsu. So āha – ‘yassa tāva pādakajjhānaṃ atthi tassa puggalajjhāsayo niyametu, yassa taṃ natthi tassa katarajjhāsayo niyamessati niddhanassa vuḍḍhigavesanakālo viya hotī’ti.

Having brought the doctrine of the Elder Cūḷābhaya, who was of the view, 'Personal inclination determines,' they also reported it to the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga. He said: 'For one who, in the first place, has a foundational jhāna, let personal inclination determine. But for one who does not have that, what inclination will determine it? It is like the time for a destitute person to seek interest.'

Taṃ kathaṃ āharitvā tipiṭakacūḷābhayattherassa puna kathayiṃsu. So ‘pādakajjhānavato idaṃ kathitaṃ āvuso’ti āha. Yathā pana pādakajjhānavato, sammasitajjhānavatopi tatheva veditabbaṃ. Pañcamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya hi paṭhamādīni sammasato uppannamaggo paṭhamattheravādena pañcamajjhāniko. Dutiyavādena paṭhamādijjhāniko āpajjatīti dvepi vādā virujjhanti. Tatiyavādena panettha ‘yaṃ icchati tajjhāniko hotī’ti te ca vādā na virujjhanti, ajjhāsayo ca sātthako hotīti. Evaṃ tayopi therā paṇḍitā byattā buddhisampannāva[P 0.0231]. Tena tesaṃ vādaṃ tantiṃ katvā ṭhapayiṃsu. Idha pana atthameva uddharitvā tayopete vāde vipassanāva niyametīti dassitaṃ.

Having brought that statement, they spoke again to the Elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya. He said, 'Friends, this was spoken with reference to one who possesses a foundational jhāna.' Furthermore, just as it is for one who possesses a foundational jhāna, so too it should be understood for one who possesses a comprehended jhāna. For when one emerges from the fifth jhāna and comprehends the first jhāna and so forth, the path that arises, according to the first elder's doctrine, is associated with the fifth jhāna. According to the second doctrine, it becomes associated with the first jhāna and so on. Thus, both doctrines conflict. But according to the third doctrine, herein, 'one becomes associated with whichever jhāna one desires'; thus those doctrines do not conflict, and the inclination becomes meaningful. In this way, all three elders were wise, astute, and endowed with intelligence. Therefore, the ancient commentators established their doctrines as a textual tradition. Here, however, having extracted only the meaning, it is shown that in these three doctrines, it is insight alone that determines.

Idāni [M 0.0275] ‘nimittaṃ paṭipadāpatī’ti ettha evaṃ aṅgapariṇāmavato maggassa uppādakāle gotrabhu kuto vuṭṭhāti? Maggo kutoti?
