Gotrabhu tāva nimittato vuṭṭhāti, pavattaṃ chettuṃ na sakkoti, ekatovuṭṭhāno hesa. Maggo nimittato vuṭṭhāti, pavattampi chindati ubhatovuṭṭhāno hesa. Tesaṃ ayaṃ uppattinayo – yasmiñhi vāre maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ anulomaṃ neva ekaṃ hoti, na pañcamaṃ. Ekañhi āsevanaṃ na labhati, pañcamaṃ bhavaṅgassa āsannattā pavedhati. Tadā hi javanaṃ patitaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmā neva ekaṃ hoti na pañcamaṃ. Mahāpaññassa pana dve anulomāni honti, tatiyaṃ gotrabhu, catutthaṃ maggacittaṃ, tīṇi phalāni, tato bhavaṅgotaraṇaṃ. Majjhimapaññassa tīṇi anulomāni honti, catutthaṃ gotrabhu, pañcamaṃ maggacittaṃ, dve phalāni, tato bhavaṅgotaraṇaṃ. Mandapaññassa cattāri anulomāni, honti pañcamaṃ gotrabhu, chaṭṭhaṃ maggacittaṃ, sattamaṃ phalaṃ, tato bhavaṅgotaraṇaṃ. Tatra mahāpaññamandapaññānaṃ vasena akathetvā majjhimapaññassa vasena kathetabbaṃ.

Now, herein, regarding the phrase ‘nimittaṃ paṭipadāpati,’ it is thus: At the time of the arising of the path, which possesses the transformation of factors, from where does gotrabhū (change-of-lineage) arise? And from where does the path arise? In the first place, gotrabhū arises from the sign. It cannot cut off the continuity of existence, for it is an emergence from one side. The path arises from the sign and also cuts off the continuity of existence, for it is an emergence from both sides. This is the method of their arising: For in whichever turn the path-emergence occurs, in that turn, conformity occurs neither once nor a fifth time. For a single occurrence does not obtain the repetition condition, and a fifth occurrence trembles due to its proximity to bhavaṅga. For at that time, the impulsion is said to have fallen. Therefore, it occurs neither once nor a fifth time. For a person of great wisdom, however, there are two conformity moments, the third is gotrabhū, the fourth is the path-consciousness, and then there are three fruition moments, followed by the descent into bhavaṅga. For a person of medium wisdom, there are three conformity moments, the fourth is gotrabhū, the fifth is the path-consciousness, and then there are two fruition moments, followed by the descent into bhavaṅga. For a person of dull wisdom, there are four conformity moments, the fifth is gotrabhū, the sixth is the path-consciousness, the seventh is a fruition moment, followed by the descent into bhavaṅga. Therein, this should be explained not in terms of the persons of great and dull wisdom, but in terms of the person of medium wisdom.

Yasmiñhi [V 0.0274] vāre maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu upekkhāsahagatā manodvārāvajjanaṃ hutvā vipassanāgocare khandhe ārammaṇaṃ katvā bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭeti. Tadanantaraṃ teneva āvajjanena gahitakkhandhe gahetvā uppajjati paṭhamaṃ javanaṃ anulomañāṇaṃ. Taṃ tesu khandhesu aniccāti vā dukkhāti vā anattāti [P 0.0232] vā pavattitvā oḷārikaṃ oḷārikaṃ saccapaṭicchādakatamaṃ vinodetvā tīṇi lakkhaṇāni bhiyyo bhiyyo pākaṭāni katvā nirujjhati. Tadanantaraṃ uppajjati dutiyānulomaṃ. Tesu purimaṃ anāsevanaṃ. Dutiyassa purimaṃ āsevanaṃ hoti. Tampi laddhāsevanattā tikkhaṃ sūraṃ pasannaṃ hutvā tasmiṃyevārammaṇe tenevākārena pavattitvā majjhimappamāṇaṃ saccapaṭicchādakatamaṃ vinodetvā tīṇi lakkhaṇāni bhiyyo bhiyyo pākaṭāni katvā nirujjhati. Tadanantaraṃ uppajjati tatiyānulomaṃ. Tassa dutiyaṃ āsevanaṃ hoti. Tampi laddhāsevanattā tikkhaṃ sūraṃ pasannaṃ hutvā tasmiṃyevārammaṇe tenevākārena pavattitvā tadavasesaṃ aṇusahagataṃ saccapaṭicchādakatamaṃ vinodetvā niravasesaṃ katvā tīṇi lakkhaṇāni bhiyyo bhiyyo pākaṭāni [M 0.0276] katvā nirujjhati. Evaṃ tīhi anulomehi saccapaṭicchādakatame vinodite tadanantaraṃ uppajjati gotrabhuññāṇaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kurumānaṃ.

For in whichever turn the emergence of the path occurs, in that turn, the functional, rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, having become the mind-door adverting, and having made the aggregates which are the object of insight its object, causes the bhavaṅga to turn back. Immediately after that, the first impulsion, the conformity knowledge, arises, taking the aggregates that were taken by that same adverting. It, having occurred in regard to those aggregates as 'impermanent,' or 'suffering,' or 'non-self,' and having dispelled the gross darkness of delusion which conceals the truths, and having made the three characteristics more and more evident, ceases. Immediately after that, the second conformity arises. Among these, the preceding one is without the repetition condition. For the second, the preceding one becomes the repetition condition. It too, due to having obtained the repetition condition, having become sharp, courageous, and clear, and having occurred in regard to that very object in that very manner, and having dispelled the medium-grade darkness of delusion which conceals the truths, and having made the three characteristics more and more evident, ceases. Immediately after that, the third conformity arises. For it, the second becomes the repetition condition. It too, due to having obtained the repetition condition, having become sharp, courageous, and clear, and having occurred in regard to that very object in that very manner, and having dispelled the remaining, subtle darkness of delusion which conceals the truths, making it so there is no remainder, and having made the three characteristics more and more evident, ceases. Thus, when the darkness of delusion which conceals the truths has been dispelled by the three conformities, immediately after that, the change-of-lineage knowledge arises, making Nibbāna its object.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – eko kira cakkhumā puriso nakkhattayogaṃ jānissāmīti rattibhāge nikkhamitvā candaṃ passituṃ uddhaṃ ullokesi. Tassa valāhakehi paṭicchannattā cando na paññāyittha. Atheko vāto uṭṭhahitvā thūlathūle valāhake viddhaṃsesi. Aparo majjhime. Aparo sukhume. Tato so puriso vigatavalāhake nabhe candaṃ disvā nakkhattayogaṃ aññāsi.

Therein, this is the simile: It is said that a certain man with good eyesight, thinking, 'I will know the moon's conjunction with the stars,' went out in the night and looked up to see the moon. For him, because it was covered by clouds, the moon did not appear. Then one wind arose and destroyed the very thick clouds. Another destroyed the medium ones. Another destroyed the subtle ones. Thereafter, that man, having seen the moon in the sky devoid of clouds, knew the moon's conjunction with the stars.

Tattha tayo valāhakā viya saccapaṭicchādakathūlamajjhimasukhumakilesandhakārā. Tayo vātā viya tīṇi anulomacittāni. Cakkhumā puriso viya gotrabhuññāṇaṃ. Cando viya nibbānaṃ. Ekekassa vātassa yathākkamena valāhakattayaviddhaṃsanaṃ viya ekekassa anulomacittassa saccapaṭicchādakatamavinodanaṃ. Vigatavalāhake nabhe tassa purisassa visuddhacandadassanaṃ viya vigate saccapaṭicchādake [P 0.0233] tame gotrabhuññāṇassa suvisuddhanibbānārammaṇakaraṇaṃ.

Therein, like the three clouds, so should be regarded the thick, medium, and subtle darkness of defilements which conceals the truths. Like the three winds, so should be regarded the three conformity consciousnesses. Like the man with eyes, so should be regarded the change-of-lineage knowledge. Like the moon, so should be regarded Nibbāna. Like the destruction of the triad of clouds in sequence by each wind, so should be regarded the dispelling of the darkness of delusion which conceals the truths by each conformity consciousness. Like the seeing of the very pure moon by that man in the sky devoid of clouds, so should be regarded the making of the very pure Nibbāna its object by the change-of-lineage knowledge when the darkness which conceals the truths is gone.

Yatheva hi tayo vātā candapaṭicchādake valāhakeyeva viddhaṃsetuṃ sakkonti, na candaṃ daṭṭhuṃ, evaṃ anulomāni saccapaṭicchādakatameyeva vinodetuṃ sakkonti, na nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kātuṃ[V 0.0275]. Yathā so puriso candameva daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti na valāhake viddhaṃsetuṃ, evaṃ gotrabhuññāṇaṃ nibbānameva ārammaṇaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti na kilesatamaṃ vinodetuṃ. Evaṃ anulomaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ hoti, gotrabhu nibbānārammaṇaṃ.

For just as the three winds are able to destroy only the clouds that conceal the moon, and are not able to see the moon, so too, the conformities are able to dispel only the darkness of delusion which conceals the truths, and are not able to make Nibbāna their object. Just as that man is able to see only the moon, and is not able to destroy the clouds, so too, the change-of-lineage knowledge is able to make only Nibbāna its object, and is not able to dispel the darkness of defilements. Thus, conformity has formations as its object, and change-of-lineage has Nibbāna as its object.

Yadi hi gotrabhu anulomena gahitārammaṇaṃ gaṇheyya puna anulomaṃ taṃ anubandheyyāti maggavuṭṭhānameva na bhaveyya. Gotrabhuññāṇaṃ pana anulomassa ārammaṇaṃ aggahetvā taṃ apacchatopavattikaṃ katvā sayaṃ anāvajjanampi samānaṃ āvajjanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā evaṃ nibbattāhīti maggassa saññaṃ datvā viya nirujjhati. Maggopi tena dinnasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva avīcisantativasena taṃ ñāṇaṃ anubandhamāno anibbiddhapubbaṃ apadālitapubbaṃ lobhakkhandhaṃ dosakkhandhaṃ mohakkhandhaṃ nibbijjhamānova padālayamānova nibbattati.

For if change-of-lineage were to take the object taken by conformity, conformity would follow it again, and thus the emergence of the path would not occur at all. The change-of-lineage knowledge, however, without taking the object of conformity, having made it non-occurring afterwards, and although being itself not an adverting, having stood in the place of an adverting, ceases as if giving a sign to the path, saying, 'Arise thus!' The path too, without releasing the sign given by it, following that knowledge by way of an uninterrupted continuity, arises while piercing and splitting the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion, which were never before pierced, never before split.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 0.0277] upamā – eko kira issāso dhanusatamatthake phalakasataṃ ṭhapāpetvā vatthena mukhaṃ veṭhetvā saraṃ sannayhitvā cakkayante aṭṭhāsi. Añño puriso cakkayantaṃ āvañchitvā yadā issāsassa phalakasataṃ abhimukhaṃ hoti tadā tattha daṇḍakena saññaṃ deti, issāso daṇḍakasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva saraṃ khipitvā phalakasataṃ nibbijjhati. Tattha daṇḍakasaññā viya gotrabhuññāṇaṃ. Issāso viya maggañāṇaṃ. Issāsassa daṇḍakasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva phalakasatanibbijjhanaṃ viya maggañāṇassa gotrabhuññāṇena dinnasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā anibbiddhapubbaapadālitapubbānaṃ lobhakkhandhādīnaṃ nibbijjhanapadālanaṃ. Bhūmiladdhavaṭṭasetusamugghātakaraṇantipi [P 0.0234] etadeva. Maggassa hi ekameva kiccaṃ anusayappajahanaṃ. Iti so anusaye pajahanto nimittā vuṭṭhāti nāma, pavattaṃ chindati nāma. ‘Nimitta’nti rūpavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇanimittaṃ. ‘Pavatta’mpi rūpavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇapavattameva. Taṃ duvidhaṃ hoti – upādinnakaṃ anupādinnakanti. Tesu maggassa anupādinnakato vuṭṭhānacchāyā dissatīti vatvā anupādinnakato vuṭṭhātīti vadiṃsu.

In this regard, this is the simile: It is said that a certain archer, having had a hundred planks placed at a distance of a hundred bow-lengths, having wrapped his face with a cloth, and having fitted an arrow, stood on a wheeled mechanism. Another man, having pulled the wheeled mechanism, when the hundred planks were directly in front of the archer, then gave a signal with a stick on the plank. The archer, without letting go of the stick-signal, shot the arrow and pierced the hundred planks. Therein, the change-of-lineage knowledge is like the stick-signal. The path-knowledge is like the archer. Just as the archer, without letting go of the stick-signal, pierces the hundred planks, so too the path-knowledge, without letting go of the signal given by the change-of-lineage knowledge, having made Nibbāna its object, pierces and splits the masses of greed and so forth, which were previously unpierced and unsplit. This very act is also called the effecting of the utter destruction of the causeway of the round of existence that has found a plane. For the path has only one function: the abandoning of latent tendencies. Thus, while abandoning the latent tendencies, it is said to 'emerge from the sign' and to 'cut off the continuity.' 'Sign' means the sign of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. 'Continuity' also means the very continuity of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. That is twofold: appropriated and unappropriated. Among these, saying, 'The semblance of the path's emergence from the unappropriated is seen,' they said, 'It emerges from the unappropriated.'

Sotāpattimaggena hi cattāri diṭṭhigatasampayuttāni vicikicchāsahagatanti pañca cittāni pahīyanti. Tāni rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti. Taṃ anupādinnakarūpakkhandho. Tāni cittāni viññāṇakkhandho. Taṃsampayuttā vedanā saññā saṅkhārā tayo arūpakkhandhā. Tattha sace sotāpannassa sotāpattimaggo abhāvito abhavissa tāni pañca cittāni chasu ārammaṇesu pariyuṭṭhānaṃ [V 0.0276] pāpuṇeyyuṃ. Sotāpattimaggo pana tesaṃ pariyuṭṭhānenappattiṃ vārayamāno setusamugghātaṃ abhabbuppattikabhāvaṃ kurumāno anupādinnakato vuṭṭhāti nāma.

Indeed, by the path of stream-entry, five consciousnesses are abandoned: four associated with wrong view and one accompanied by doubt. They give rise to form. That is the unappropriated aggregate of form. Those consciousnesses are the aggregate of consciousness. The feeling, perception, and formations associated with them are the three formless aggregates. Therein, if for the stream-enterer the path of stream-entry had not been developed, those five consciousnesses would attain to obsession in the six sense-objects. But the path of stream-entry, preventing their attainment of obsession, effecting the utter destruction of the causeway and the state of being incapable of arising, is said to emerge from the unappropriated.

Sakadāgāmimaggena cattāri diṭṭhigatavippayuttāni dve domanassasahagatānīti oḷārikakāmarāgabyāpādavasena cha cittāni pahīyanti. Anāgāmimaggena aṇusahagatakāmarāgabyāpādavasena tāni eva cha cittāni pahīyanti. Arahattamaggena cattāri diṭṭhigatavippayuttāni uddhaccasahagatañcāti pañca akusalacittāni pahīyanti. Tattha sace tesaṃ ariyānaṃ te maggā abhāvitā assu, tāni cittāni chasu ārammaṇesu pariyuṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇeyyuṃ. Te pana tesaṃ maggā pariyuṭṭhānappattiṃ vārayamānā setusamugghātaṃ [M 0.0278] abhabbuppattikabhāvaṃ kurumānā anupādinnakato vuṭṭhahanti nāma.

By the path of once-returning, six consciousnesses—four dissociated from wrong view and two accompanied by displeasure—are abandoned by way of coarse sensual desire and ill will. By the path of non-returning, by way of subtle sensual desire and ill will, those same six consciousnesses are abandoned. By the path of Arahantship, five unwholesome consciousnesses—four dissociated from wrong view and one accompanied by restlessness—are abandoned. Therein, if for those noble ones those paths had not been developed, those consciousnesses would attain to obsession in the six sense-objects. But those paths, preventing their attainment of obsession, effecting the utter destruction of the causeway and the state of being incapable of arising, are said to emerge from the unappropriated.

Upādinnakato vuṭṭhānacchāyā dissatīti vatvā upādinnakato [P 0.0235] vuṭṭhātītipi vadiṃsu. Sace hi sotāpannassa sotāpattimaggo abhāvito abhavissa, ṭhapetvā satta bhave anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe upādinnakappavattaṃ pavatteyya. Kasmā? Tassa pavattiyā hetūnaṃ atthitāya. Tīṇi saṃyojanāni diṭṭhānusayo vicikicchānusayoti ime pana pañca kilese sotāpattimaggo uppajjamānova samugghāteti. Idāni kuto sotāpannassa satta bhave ṭhapetvā anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe upādinnakappavattaṃ pavattissati? Evaṃ sotāpattimaggo upādinnakappavattaṃ appavattaṃ kurumāno upādinnakato vuṭṭhāti nāma.

Saying, 'The semblance of emergence from the appropriated is seen,' they also said, 'It emerges from the appropriated.' For if the stream-enterer's path of stream-entry had been undeveloped, then, setting aside seven existences, the appropriated continuity would proceed in the round of saṃsāra with its unknowable beginning. Why? Because of the existence of the causes for its proceeding. But the path of stream-entry, just as it arises, utterly eradicates these five defilements: the three fetters, the latent tendency of wrong view, and the latent tendency of doubt. Now, whence will the appropriated continuity proceed for the stream-enterer in the round of saṃsāra with its unknowable beginning, setting aside seven existences? Thus the path of stream-entry, by making the appropriated continuity a non-continuity, is said to emerge from the appropriated.

Sace sakadāgāmissa sakadāgāmimaggo abhāvito abhavissa, ṭhapetvā dve bhave pañcasu bhavesu upādinnakapavattaṃ pavatteyya. Kasmā? Tassa pavattiyā hetūnaṃ atthitāya. Oḷārikāni kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojanāni oḷāriko kāmarāgānusayo paṭighānusayoti ime pana cattāro kilese so maggo uppajjamānova samugghāteti. Idāni kuto sakadāgāmissa dve bhave ṭhapetvā pañcasu bhavesu upādinnakappavattaṃ pavattissati? Evaṃ sakadāgāmimaggo upādinnakappavattaṃ appavattaṃ kurumāno upādinnakato vuṭṭhāti nāma.

If for the once-returner the path of once-returning had been undeveloped, then, setting aside two existences, the appropriated continuity would proceed in five existences. Why? Because of the existence of the causes for its proceeding. But that path, just as it arises, utterly eradicates these four defilements: the coarse fetters of sensual desire and aversion, the coarse latent tendency of sensual desire, and the latent tendency of aversion. Now, whence for the once-returner, setting aside two existences, will the appropriated continuity proceed in five existences? Thus the path of once-returning, by making the appropriated continuity a non-continuity, is said to emerge from the appropriated.

Sace anāgāmissa anāgāmimaggo abhāvito abhavissa, ṭhapetvā ekaṃ bhavaṃ dutiyabhave upādinnakappavattaṃ pavatteyya. Kasmā? Tassa pavattiyā hetūnaṃ atthitāya. Aṇusahagatāni [V 0.0277] kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojanāni aṇusahagato kāmarāgānusayo paṭighānusayoti ime pana cattāro kilese so maggo uppajjamānova samugghāteti. Idāni kuto anāgāmissa ekaṃ bhavaṃ ṭhapetvā dutiyabhave upādinnakappavattaṃ pavattissati? Evaṃ anāgāmimaggo upādinnakappavattaṃ appavattaṃ kurumāno upādinnakato vuṭṭhāti nāma.

If for the non-returner the path of non-returning had been undeveloped, then, setting aside one existence, the appropriated continuity would proceed in a second existence. Why? Because of the existence of the causes for its proceeding. But that path, just as it arises, utterly eradicates these four defilements: the subtle fetters of sensual desire and aversion, and the subtle latent tendencies of sensual desire and aversion. Now, whence for the non-returner, setting aside one existence, will the appropriated continuity proceed in a second existence? Thus the path of non-returning, by making the appropriated continuity a non-continuity, is said to emerge from the appropriated.

Sace arahato arahattamaggo abhāvito abhavissa, rūpārūpabhavesu upādinnakappavattaṃ pavatteyya. Kasmā? Tassa pavattiyā hetūnaṃ atthitāya[M 0.0279]. Rūparāgo arūparāgo māno uddhaccaṃ avijjā mānānusayo bhavarāgānusayo avijjānusayoti ime pana aṭṭha kilese so maggo uppajjamānova samugghāteti. Idāni kuto khīṇāsavassa punabbhave upādinnakappavattaṃ pavattissati? Evaṃ arahattamaggo [P 0.0236] upādinnakappavattaṃ appavattaṃ kurumāno upādinnakato vuṭṭhāti nāma.

If, for an Arahant, the path to Arahantship had not been developed, the appropriated continuity would proceed in the form and formless existences. Why? Because of the existence of the causes for its proceeding. Furthermore, that path, in the very moment of arising, eradicates these eight defilements: passion for form, passion for the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to passion for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. Now, from where would the appropriated continuity proceed in a future existence for one whose taints are destroyed? Thus, the path to Arahantship, by causing the appropriated continuity not to proceed, is said to emerge from the appropriated.

Sotāpattimaggo cettha apāyabhavato vuṭṭhāti, sakadāgāmimaggo sugatikāmabhavekadesato, anāgāmimaggo kāmabhavato, arahattamaggo rūpārūpabhavato sabbabhavehipi vuṭṭhāti evāti vadanti.

Furthermore, herein, the path of stream-entry rises up from the plane of misery; the path of once-returning, from a portion of the sensuous happy-destination existence; the path of non-returning, from the sensuous existence; and the path of Arahantship rises up from the form and formless existences, indeed from all existences—so they say.

Imassa panatthassa vibhāvanatthaṃ ayaṃ pāḷi – “sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena satta bhave ṭhapetvā anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe ye uppajjeyyuṃ, nāmañca rūpañca etthete nirujjhanti vūpasamanti atthaṃ gacchanti paṭippassambhanti.

To clarify this meaning, the following passage is cited: 'Through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, with the cessation of consciousness conditioned by formations, whatever name and form would arise in the beginningless round of saṃsāra, apart from seven existences, these cease here, subside, come to an end, and are stilled.'

‘Sakadāgāmimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena dve bhave ṭhapetvā pañcasu bhavesu ye uppajjeyyuṃ, nāmañca rūpañca etthete nirujjhanti vūpasamanti atthaṃ gacchanti paṭippassambhanti.

Through the knowledge of the path of once-returning, with the cessation of consciousness conditioned by formations, whatever name and form would arise in the five existences, apart from two existences, these cease here, subside, come to an end, and are stilled.

‘Anāgāmimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena ekaṃ bhavaṃ ṭhapetvā kāmadhātuyā dvīsu bhavesu ye uppajjeyyuṃ, nāmañca rūpañca etthete nirujjhanti vūpasamanti atthaṃ gacchanti paṭippassambhanti.

Through the knowledge of the path of non-returning, with the cessation of consciousness conditioned by formations, whatever name and form would arise in the two existences of the sensuous realm, apart from one existence, these cease here, subside, come to an end, and are stilled.

‘Arahattamaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena rūpadhātuyā vā arūpadhātuyā vā ye uppajjeyyuṃ[V 0.0278], nāmañca rūpañca etthete nirujjhanti vūpasamanti atthaṃ gacchanti paṭippassambhanti. Arahato anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyantassa carimaviññāṇassa nirodhena paññā ca sati ca nāmañca rūpañca etthete nirujjhanti vūpasamanti atthaṃ gacchanti paṭippassambhantī”ti (cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 6). Ayaṃ tāva nimitte vinicchayo.

This, then, is the determination concerning the characteristic.

‘Paṭipadāpatī’ti – ettha pana paṭipadā calati na calatīti? Calati. Tathāgatassa hi sāriputtattherassa ca cattāropi maggā sukhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā ahesuṃ. Mahāmoggallānattherassa paṭhamamaggo sukhapaṭipado khippābhiñño, upari tayo maggā dukkhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā. Kasmā? Niddābhibhūtattā. Sammāsambuddho [M 0.0280] kira sattāhaṃ daharakumārakaṃ viya theraṃ parihari. Theropi ekadivasaṃ niddāyamāno nisīdi. Atha naṃ satthā āha – “pacalāyasi no tvaṃ, moggallāna, pacalāyasi no tvaṃ moggallānā”ti (a. ni. 7.61). Evarūpassapi mahābhiññappattassa sāvakassa paṭipadā [P 0.0237] calati, sesānaṃ kiṃ na calissati? Ekaccassa hi bhikkhuno cattāropi maggā dukkhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā honti, ekaccassa dukkhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā, ekaccassa sukhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā, ekaccassa sukhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā. Ekaccassa paṭhamamaggo dukkhapaṭipado dandhābhiñño hoti, dutiyamaggo dukkhapaṭipado khippābhiñño, tatiyamaggo sukhapaṭipado dandhābhiñño, catutthamaggo sukhapaṭipado khippābhiññoti.

Furthermore, concerning 'Paṭipadāpatī' herein: does the practice waver or not? It wavers. Indeed, for the Tathāgata and for the Elder Sāriputta, all four paths were of easy practice and quick direct knowledge. For the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the first path was of easy practice and quick direct knowledge; the upper three paths were of difficult practice and quick direct knowledge. Why? Because of being overcome by drowsiness. It is said that the Perfectly Enlightened One looked after the Elder for seven days as if he were a young boy. The Elder also sat one day, drowsing. Then the Teacher said to him, 'Are you nodding, Moggallāna? Are you nodding, Moggallāna?' Even for such a disciple who had attained great direct knowledge, the practice wavers; for the remaining ones, why would it not waver? Indeed, for a certain monk, all four paths are of difficult practice and slow direct knowledge; for a certain one, of difficult practice and quick direct knowledge; for a certain one, of easy practice and slow direct knowledge; for a certain one, of easy practice and quick direct knowledge. For a certain one, the first path is of difficult practice and slow direct knowledge, the second path is of difficult practice and quick direct knowledge, the third path is of easy practice and slow direct knowledge, and the fourth path is of easy practice and quick direct knowledge.

Yathā ca paṭipadā evaṃ adhipatipi calati eva. Ekaccassa hi bhikkhuno cattāropi maggā chandādhipateyyā honti, ekaccassa vīriyādhipateyyā, ekaccassa cittādhipateyyā, ekaccassa vīmaṃsādhipateyyā. Ekaccassa pana paṭhamamaggo chandādhipateyyo hoti, dutiyo vīriyādhipateyyo, tatiyo cittādhipateyyo, catuttho vīmaṃsādhipateyyoti.

And just as the practice wavers, so too the dominant factor indeed wavers. For a certain monk, all four paths have desire as the dominant factor; for a certain one, energy as the dominant factor; for a certain one, consciousness as the dominant factor; and for a certain one, investigation as the dominant factor. Furthermore, for a certain one, the first path has desire as the dominant factor, the second has energy as the dominant factor, the third has consciousness as the dominant factor, and the fourth has investigation as the dominant factor.

Pakiṇṇakakathā niṭṭhitā.

The miscellaneous discourse is concluded.

Paṭhamamaggavīsatimahānayo

The Twenty Great Methods of the First Path

357. Idāni [V 0.0279] yasmā lokuttarakusalaṃ bhāvento na kevalaṃ upanijjhāyanaṭṭhena jhānaṃyeva bhāveti, niyyānaṭṭhena pana maggampi bhāveti, upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena satipaṭṭhānampi, padahanaṭṭhena sammappadhānampi, ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhipādampi, adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyampi, akampiyaṭṭhena balampi, bujjhanaṭṭhena bojjhaṅgampi, tathaṭṭhena saccampi, avikkhepaṭṭhena samathampi, suññataṭṭhena dhammampi, rāsaṭṭhena khandhampi, āyatanaṭṭhena āyatanampi, suññasabhāvanissattaṭṭhena dhātumpi, paccayaṭṭhena āhārampi, phusanaṭṭhena phassampi, vedayitaṭṭhena vedanampi, sañjānanaṭṭhena saññampi, cetayitaṭṭhena cetanampi, vijānanaṭṭhena cittampi bhāveti, tasmā etesaṃ ekūnavīsatiyā padānaṃ dassanatthaṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ ‘idampi bhāveti, idampi bhāvetī’ti puggalajjhāsayena ceva desanāvilāsena ca vīsati nayā desitā honti[M 0.0281]. Dhammaṃ sotuṃ nisinnadevaparisāya hi ye upanijjhāyanaṭṭhena lokuttaraṃ [P 0.0238] ‘jhāna’nti kathite bujjhanti, tesaṃ sappāyavasena jhānanti kathitaṃ…pe… ye vijānanaṭṭhena ‘citta’nti vutte bujjhanti, tesaṃ sappāyavasena cittanti kathitaṃ. Ayamettha ‘puggalajjhāsayo’.

357. Now, because one who develops the supramundane wholesome does not merely develop jhāna in the sense of close contemplation, but also develops the path in the sense of leading out, the foundations of mindfulness in the sense of establishing, the right efforts in the sense of exertion, the bases of psychic power in the sense of accomplishment, the faculties in the sense of dominance, the powers in the sense of unshakability, the enlightenment factors in the sense of awakening, the truths in the sense of truthfulness, calm in the sense of non-distraction, the Dhamma in the sense of voidness, the aggregates in the sense of a mass, the sense bases in the sense of a sphere, the elements in the sense of being void by nature and non-sentient, nutriment in the sense of being a condition, contact in the sense of touching, feeling in the sense of experiencing, perception in the sense of perceiving, volition in the sense of willing, and consciousness in the sense of cognizing—therefore, to show these nineteen terms, it is said again, “Which states are wholesome?” and so on. Thus, “This too one develops, this too one develops”—in this way, twenty methods are taught according to both the inclination of the individual and the elegance of the teaching. For, in the assembly of devas seated to hear the Dhamma, for those who understand when the supramundane is taught as ‘jhāna’ in the sense of close contemplation, it is taught as ‘jhāna’ according to what is suitable for them… for those who understand when it is said ‘consciousness’ in the sense of cognizing, it is taught as ‘consciousness’ according to what is suitable for them. This here is the ‘inclination of the individual’.

Sammāsambuddho pana attano buddhasubodhitāya dasabalacatuvesārajjacatupaṭisambhidatāya chaasādhāraṇañāṇayogena ca desanaṃ yadicchakaṃ niyametvā dasseti. Icchanto upanijjhāyanaṭṭhena lokuttaraṃ jhānanti dasseti, icchanto niyyānaṭṭhena…pe… vijānanaṭṭhena lokuttaraṃ cittanti. Ayaṃ ‘desanāvilāso’ nāma. Tattha yatheva lokuttaraṃ jhānanti vuttaṭṭhāne dasa nayā vibhattā, evaṃ maggādīsupi teyeva veditabbā. Iti vīsatiyā ṭhānesu dasa dasa katvā dve nayasatāni vibhattāni honti.

However, the Perfectly Enlightened One, by virtue of his own excellent understanding as a Buddha, his ten powers, four grounds of confidence, four analytical knowledges, and his endowment with the six unique knowledges, presents the teaching as he desires, having determined it. If he desires, he shows the supramundane as jhāna in the sense of close contemplation; if he desires… as consciousness in the sense of cognizing. This is called the ‘elegance of the teaching.’ Herein, just as ten methods are distinguished in the passage where ‘supramundane jhāna’ is spoken of, so too should those same methods be understood in relation to the path and so forth. Thus, in twenty instances, by making ten each, two hundred methods are distinguished.

358. Idāni adhipatibhedaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha chandaṃ dhuraṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā nibbattitaṃ lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ chandādhipateyyaṃ nāma. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Iti purimasmiṃ suddhike dvenayasatāni chandādhipateyyādīsupi dve dveti nayasahassena bhājetvā paṭhamamaggaṃ dassesi dhammarājā.

358. Now, to show the classification by predominance, the passage begins again with “Which states are wholesome?” and so on. Therein, the supramundane jhāna produced by making desire the burden, the chief, and the forerunner is called ‘desire-predominated.’ This same method applies to the remaining cases. Thus, in the previous pure section there are two hundred methods, and for desire-predominance and so forth there are two hundred each. In this way, the King of Dhamma showed the first path by analyzing it into a thousand methods.

Paṭhamamaggo niṭṭhito.

The First Path is concluded.

Dutiyamaggo

The Second Path

361. Idāni [V 0.0280] dutiyamaggādīnaṃ dassanatthaṃ puna katame dhammā kusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ tanubhāvāyāti etesaṃ kilesānaṃ tanubhāvatthāya. Tattha dvīhi kāraṇehi tanubhāvo veditabbo – adhiccuppattiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya ca. Sakadāgāmissa hi, vaṭṭānusārimahājanasseva, kilesā abhiṇhaṃ nuppajjanti, kadāci kadāci uppajjanti; uppajjantāpi viraḷākārā hutvā uppajjanti, viraḷavāpitakhette aṅkurā viya. Uppajjamānāpi, ca vaṭṭānusārimahājanasseva, maddantā pharantā chādentā andhakāraṃ [P 0.0239] karontā nuppajjanti. Dvīhi pana maggehi pahīnattā mandā mandā [M 0.0282] uppajjanti. Tanukākārā hutvā uppajjanti, abbhapaṭalaṃ viya makkhikāpattaṃ viya ca.

361. Now, to explain the second path and so on, the passage is taken up again, beginning with 'Which states are wholesome?' etc. Herein, 'for the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will' means for the purpose of the attenuation of these defilements. Herein, attenuation is to be understood through two causes: by way of occasional arising and by way of the sluggishness of manifestation. For a once-returner, indeed, unlike for the great mass of people who follow the round of existence, defilements do not arise constantly; they arise only occasionally. When they do arise, they arise having a sparse nature, like sprouts in a sparsely sown field. And when they do arise, they do not arise crushing, pervading, enveloping, and creating darkness, as do the defilements of the great mass of people who follow the round of existence. Rather, because they have been abandoned by two paths, they arise sluggishly. They arise having a subtle form, like a film of cloud or a fly's wing.

Tattha keci therā vadanti – ‘sakadāgāmissa kilesā kiñcāpi cirena uppajjanti, bahalāva pana hutvā uppajjanti, tathā hissa puttā ca dhītaro ca dissantī’ti. Etaṃ pana appamāṇaṃ. Puttadhītaro hi aṅgapaccaṅgaparāmasanamattenapi honti. Dvīhi pana maggehi pahīnattā natthi kilesānaṃ bahalatāti. Dvīhi eva kāraṇehissa kilesānaṃ tanubhāvo veditabbo – adhiccuppattiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya cāti.

Herein, some elders say: 'Although the defilements of a once-returner arise after a long time, they nevertheless arise coarsely; indeed, for him, sons and daughters are seen.' But this is not authoritative. For sons and daughters can come to be even by the mere touching of major and minor limbs. In truth, because they have been abandoned by two paths, there is no coarseness of the defilements. Thus, the attenuation of his defilements is to be understood through just two causes: by way of occasional arising and by way of the sluggishness of manifestation.

Dutiyāyāti gaṇanavasenāpi dutiyuppattivasenāpi dutiyāya. Bhūmiyā pattiyāti sāmaññaphalassa paṭilābhatthāya. Tatiyacatutthesupi eseva nayo. Visesamattaṃyeva pana vakkhāma.

'Second' means second both by way of enumeration and by way of the second arising. 'For the attainment of a stage' means for the sake of attaining the fruit of recluseship. This same method applies to the third and fourth paths as well. However, we will speak only of the distinction.

Aññindriyanti ājānanakaṃ indriyaṃ. Paṭhamamaggena ñātamariyādaṃ anatikkamitvā tesaṃyeva tena maggena ñātānaṃ catusaccadhammānaṃ jānanakaṃ indriyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Niddesavārepissa imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Koṭṭhāsavārepi imināva saddhiṃ navindriyāni honti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

'The faculty of final knowledge' is the faculty of knowing. Not transgressing the limit known through the first path, it is said to be the faculty of knowing those very four noble truths known by that path. The meaning in the section of exposition should also be understood in this same way. In the section on divisions, there are nine faculties together with this one. The rest is to be understood in the same way as before.

Dutiyamaggo niṭṭhito.

The Second Path is completed.

Tatiyacatutthamaggā

The Third and Fourth Paths

362. Tatiye [V 0.0281] anavasesappahānāyāti tesaṃyeva sakadāgāmimaggena tanubhūtānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ nissesapajahanatthāya.

362. In the third path, 'for abandonment without remainder' means for the purpose of abandoning without remainder those very fetters that have been attenuated by the path of the once-returner.

Catutthe rūparāgaarūparāgamānauddhaccaavijjāya anavasesappahānāyāti etesaṃ pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ nissesapajahanatthāya. Tattha rūparāgoti rūpabhave chandarāgo. Arūparāgoti arūpabhave chandarāgo. Mānoti arahattamaggavajjhako māno eva. Tathā [P 0.0240] uddhaccāvijjā. Imesupi dvīsu maggesu navamaṃ aññindriyameva hoti.

In the fourth path, 'for the abandonment without remainder of lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance' means for the purpose of abandoning without remainder these five higher fetters. Therein, 'lust for form' is craving and lust for the form realm. 'Lust for the formless' is craving and lust for the formless realm. 'Conceit' is the very conceit that is to be destroyed by the path of Arahantship. Likewise for restlessness and ignorance. In these two paths as well, the ninth faculty is indeed the faculty of final knowledge.

Catumagganayasahassaṃ

The Thousand Methods of the Four Paths

Sabbamaggesu [M 0.0283] padapaṭipāṭiyā samasaṭṭhipadāni, catūhi apaṇṇakaṅgehi saddhiṃ catusaṭṭhi honti. Asambhinnato pana tettiṃsa. Koṭṭhāsavārasuññatavārā pākatikā eva. Yathā ca pana paṭhamamagge evaṃ dutiyādīsupi nayasahassamevāti cattāro magge catūhi nayasahassehi bhājetvā dassesi dhammarājā.

In all the paths, by way of the sequence of terms, there are exactly sixty terms; together with the four infallible factors, there are sixty-four. However, taken separately, there are thirty-three. The Section on Parts and the Section on Emptiness are as in the original text. And just as there are a thousand methods in the first path, so too in the second and subsequent paths there are a thousand methods each. Thus, the King of Dhamma taught by analyzing the four paths with four thousand methods.

Saccavibhaṅge pana saṭṭhi nayasahassāni lokuttarāni imesaṃ eva vasena nikkhittāni. Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅge vīsati nayasahassāni lokuttarāni, sammappadhānavibhaṅge vīsati, iddhipādavibhaṅge dvattiṃsa, bojjhaṅgavibhaṅge dvattiṃsa, maggaṅgavibhaṅge aṭṭhavīsati nayasahassāni lokuttarāni imesaṃ eva vasena nikkhittāni.

Furthermore, in the Analysis of the Truths, sixty thousand supramundane methods are laid down by means of these very paths. In the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness, twenty thousand supramundane methods; in the Analysis of the Right Exertions, twenty thousand; in the Analysis of the Bases of Power, thirty-two thousand; in the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment, thirty-two thousand; and in the Analysis of the Path Factors, twenty-eight thousand supramundane methods are laid down by means of these very paths.

Idha pana catūsu maggesu cattāriyeva nayasahassāni. Tesu paṭhamajjhānike paṭhamamagge aṭṭhaṅgāni bhājitāni; tathā dutiyādīsu. Tattha paṭhamamagge sammādiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajahatīti sammādiṭṭhi. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi micchāsaṅkappādīnaṃ pajahanaṭṭheneva veditabbā. Evaṃ sante ‘paṭhamamaggeneva dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahīnattā uparimaggattayena pahātabbā diṭṭhi nāma natthi. Tattha sammādiṭṭhīti nāmaṃ kathaṃ hotī’ti? ‘Yathā visaṃ atthi vā, hotu mā vā, agado agado tveva vuccati, evaṃ micchādiṭṭhi atthi vā, hotu mā vā, ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhi eva nāma’.

Here, however, in the four paths, only four thousand methods are laid down. Among them, in the first path associated with the first jhāna, the eight factors are analyzed; similarly in the second and subsequent paths. Therein, in the first path, 'right view' is so called because it abandons wrong view. Right intention and the others, too, should be understood in the sense of abandoning wrong intention and the others. This being so, it is asked: 'Since the sixty-two kinds of wrong views are abandoned by the first path alone, there is no view to be abandoned by the three higher paths. In that case, how can there be the name "right view"?' The reply is: 'Just as, whether poison is present or not, an antidote is still called an antidote, so too, whether wrong view is present or not, this is still called "right view".'

‘Yadi [V 0.0282] evaṃ nāmamattamevetaṃ hoti, uparimaggattaye pana sammādiṭṭhiyā kiccābhāvo āpajjati, maggaṅgāni na paripūrenti, tasmā sammādiṭṭhi sakiccakā kātabbā maggaṅgāni pūretabbānī’ti. Sakiccakā cettha sammādiṭṭhi yathālābhaniyamena dīpetabbā. Uparimaggattayavajjho hi eko māno atthi, so diṭṭhiṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Sā taṃ mānaṃ pajahatīti sammādiṭṭhi. Sotāpattimaggasmiñhi sammādiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Sotāpannassa pana sakadāgāmimaggavajjho māno atthi, so diṭṭhiṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati sā taṃ mānaṃ pajahatīti sammādiṭṭhi. Tasseva sattaakusalacittasahajāto saṅkappo atthi. Teheva cittehi vācaṅgacopanaṃ atthi, kāyaṅgacopanaṃ atthi[P 0.0241], paccayaparibhogo atthi, sahajātavāyāmo [M 0.0284] atthi, asatibhāvo atthi, sahajātacittekaggatā atthi. Ete micchāsaṅkappādayo nāma sakadāgāmimagge sammāsaṅkappādayo. Tesaṃ pahānena sammāsaṅkappādayoti veditabbā. Evaṃ sakadāgāmimagge aṭṭhaṅgāni sakiccakāni katvā āgatāni. Sakadāgāmissa anāgāmimaggavajjho māno atthi. So diṭṭhiṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Tasseva sattahi cittehi sahajātā saṅkappādayo. Tesaṃ pahānena anāgāmimagge aṭṭhannaṃ aṅgānaṃ sakiccakatā veditabbā. Anāgāmissa arahattamaggavajjho māno atthi. So diṭṭhiṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Yāni panassa pañca akusalacittāni, tehi sahajātā saṅkappādayo. Tesaṃ pahānena arahattamagge aṭṭhannaṃ aṅgānaṃ sakiccakatā veditabbā.

‘If this is so, this is merely a name, and it would follow that right view has no function in the three higher paths, and the path factors would not be fulfilled. Therefore, right view must be made to have its own function, and the path factors must be fulfilled.’ In this matter, that right view has its own function should be explained according to the principle of what is obtainable. For there is a certain conceit to be destroyed by the three higher paths, and it stands in the place of view. That right view abandons that conceit, and thus it is ‘right view’. Indeed, in the path of stream-entry, right view abandons wrong view. For a stream-enterer, however, there is a conceit to be destroyed by the path of the once-returner; it stands in the place of view, and that right view abandons that conceit, thus it is ‘right view’. For that same person, there is wrong intention co-arisen with seven unwholesome states of consciousness. With those same states of consciousness, there is movement of the verbal faculty, movement of the bodily faculty, enjoyment of requisites, co-arisen effort, lack of mindfulness, and co-arisen one-pointedness of mind. These are called wrong intention and so on. In the path of the once-returner, right intention and so on should be understood as ‘right intention and so on’ through the abandonment of those wrong factors. Thus, in the path of the once-returner, the eight factors come having performed their own function. For a once-returner, there is a conceit to be destroyed by the path of the non-returner; it stands in the place of view. For that same person, there are intention and so on co-arisen with seven states of consciousness. Through the abandonment of these, the fact that the eight factors in the path of the non-returner have their own function should be understood. For a non-returner, there is a conceit to be destroyed by the path of Arahantship; it stands in the place of view. And for that person, there are five unwholesome states of consciousness; with them are co-arisen intention and so on. Through the abandonment of these, the fact that the eight factors in the path of Arahantship have their own function should be understood.

Imesu catūsu maggesu paṭhamamaggena cattāri saccāni diṭṭhāni. ‘Uparimaggattayaṃ diṭṭhakameva passati, adiṭṭhakaṃ passatī’ti diṭṭhakameva passatīti ayaṃ ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā. Vitaṇḍavādī panāha ‘adiṭṭhaṃ passatī’ti. So vattabbo – ‘paṭhamamagge katamaṃ indriyaṃ bhājesī’ti? Jānamāno ‘anaññātaññassāmītindriya’nti vakkhati. ‘Uparimaggesu katara’nti? Vuttepi ‘aññindriya’nti vakkhati. So vattabbo – ‘adiṭṭhasaccadassane sati uparimaggesupi anaññātaññassāmītindriyameva bhājehi. Evaṃ te pañho samessatī’ti. ‘Kilese pana aññe añño pajahati; pahīne eva pajahatī’ti? ‘Aññe añño pajahatī’ti. ‘Yadi aññe añño, appahīne kilese pajahati. Saccānipi adiṭṭhāneva passatī’ti evaṃvādī puggalo pucchitabbo – ‘saccāni nāma katī’ti? Jānanto ‘cattārī’ti vakkhati. So vattabbo – ‘tava vāde soḷasa saccāni āpajjanti. Tvaṃ buddhehipi adiṭṭhaṃ passasi. Bahusaccako nāma tvaṃ. Evaṃ mā gaṇha. Saccadassanaṃ nāma apubbaṃ natthi, kilese pana appahīne pajahatī’ti.

Among these four paths, the four truths are seen by the first path. As to the question, ‘Do the three higher paths see what has already been seen, or do they see what has not been seen?’, the common teaching of the masters is that they see what has already been seen. A sophist, however, says, ‘It sees what has not been seen.’ He should be told: ‘In the first path, which faculty do you analyze?’ Knowing, he will say, ‘The faculty of “I shall know the unknown.”’ When asked, ‘And which in the higher paths?’, he will say, ‘The faculty of final knowledge.’ He should then be told: ‘If there is the seeing of a truth not yet seen, then in the higher paths too you should analyze the faculty of “I shall know the unknown.” In that way, your problem will be resolved.’ Furthermore, a question is posed: ‘Does a different path abandon different defilements, or does it abandon those already abandoned?’ The reply is: ‘A different path abandons different defilements.’ The sophist says: ‘If a different path abandons different, unabandoned defilements, then it must also see truths not yet seen.’ A person who speaks thus should be asked: ‘How many truths are there?’ Knowing, he will say, ‘Four.’ He should then be told: ‘According to your doctrine, it follows that there are sixteen truths. You see what was not seen even by the Buddhas. You are indeed one of many truths! Do not understand it in this way. There is no new seeing of the truths, but one does abandon defilements that were previously unabandoned.’

Tattha [P 0.0242][V 0.0283] saccadassanassa apubbābhāve peḷopamaṃ nāma gahitaṃ – ekassa kira cattāro ratanapeḷā sāragabbhe ṭhapitā. So rattibhāge peḷāsu uppannakicco dvāraṃ vivaritvā, dīpaṃ jāletvā, dīpena vihate andhakāre, peḷāsu pākaṭabhāvaṃ gatāsu, tāsu kiccaṃ katvā dvāraṃ pidahitvā gato. Puna andhakāraṃ avatthari. Dutiyavārepi tatiyavārepi tatheva akāsi. Catutthavāre dvāre vivaṭe andhakāre peḷā na paññāyantīti vīmaṃsantasseva [M 0.0285] sūriyo uggañchi, sūriyobhāsena vihate andhakāre peḷāsu kiccaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

Here, concerning the fact that the seeing of the truths is not something new, the simile of the chests is taken. It is said that a certain man had four jewel-chests placed in a storeroom. At night, having business that arose concerning the chests, he opened the door, lit a lamp, and when the darkness was dispelled by the lamp and the chests became manifest, he did what was to be done with them, closed the door, and went away. Again, darkness spread. He did likewise on the second and third occasions. On the fourth occasion, just as he was investigating, ‘When the door is opened, the chests are not visible in the darkness,’ the sun rose. When the darkness was dispelled by the sunlight, he did what was to be done with the chests and departed.

Tattha cattāro peḷā viya cattāri saccāni. Tāsu kicce uppanne dvāravivaraṇakālo viya sotāpattimaggassa vipassanābhinīharaṇakālo. Andhakāraṃ viya saccapaṭicchādakatamaṃ. Dīpo bhāso viya sotāpattimaggobhāso. Vihate andhakāre tassa purisassa peḷānaṃ pākaṭabhāvo viya maggañāṇassa saccānaṃ pākaṭabhāvo. Maggañāṇassa pākaṭāni pana maggasamaṅgissa puggalassa pākaṭāneva honti. Peḷāsu kiccaṃ katvā gatakālo viya sotāpattimaggassa attanā pahātabbakilese pajahitvā niruddhakālo. Puna andhakārāvattharaṇaṃ viya uparimaggattayavajjhasaccapaṭicchādakatamaṃ.

In this, the four chests are like the four truths. The time of opening the door when business has arisen concerning them is like the time of directing insight for the path of stream-entry. The darkness is like the darkness that conceals the truths. The light of the lamp is like the light of the path of stream-entry. When the darkness is dispelled, the manifestation of the chests to that man is like the manifestation of the truths to the path-knowledge. Furthermore, what is manifest to the path-knowledge is indeed manifest to the person endowed with the path. The time of having done the task with the chests and departed is like the time of the cessation of the path of stream-entry, after it has abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by itself. The spreading over of darkness again is like the darkness that conceals the truths, which is to be destroyed by the three higher paths.

Dutiyavāre dvāravivaraṇakālo viya sakadāgāmimaggassa vipassanābhinīharaṇakālo. Dīpobhāso viya sakadāgāmimaggobhāso. Peḷāsu kiccaṃ katvā gatakālo viya sakadāgāmimaggassa attanā pahātabbakilese pajahitvā niruddhakālo. Puna andhakārāvattharaṇaṃ viya uparimaggadvayavajjhasaccapaṭicchādakatamaṃ.

The time of opening the door on the second occasion is like the time of directing insight for the path of the once-returner. The light of the lamp is like the light of the path of the once-returner. The time of having done the task with the chests and departed is like the time of the cessation of the path of the once-returner, after it has abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by itself. The spreading over of darkness again is like the darkness that conceals the truths, which is to be destroyed by the two higher paths.

Tatiyavāre dvāravivaraṇakālo viya anāgāmimaggassa vipassanābhinīharaṇakālo. Dīpobhāso viya anāgāmimaggobhāso. Peḷāsu kiccaṃ katvā gatakālo viya anāgāmimaggassa attanā pahātabbakilese pajahitvā niruddhakālo. Puna andhakārāvattharaṇaṃ viya upariarahattamaggavajjhasaccapaṭicchādakatamaṃ.

The time of opening the door on the third occasion is like the time of directing insight for the path of the non-returner. The light of the lamp is like the light of the path of the non-returner. The time of having done the task with the chests and departed is like the time of the cessation of the path of the non-returner, after it has abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by itself. The spreading over of darkness again is like the darkness that conceals the truths, which is to be destroyed by the higher path of Arahantship.

Catutthavāre dvāravivaraṇakālo viya arahattamaggassa vipassanābhinīharaṇakālo. Sūriyuggamanaṃ viya arahattamagguppādo. Andhakāravidhamanaṃ viya arahattamaggassa saccapaṭicchādakatamavinodanaṃ[P 0.0243]. Vihate andhakāre tassa peḷānaṃ pākaṭabhāvo viya arahattamaggañāṇassa catunnaṃ [V 0.0284] saccānaṃ pākaṭabhāvo. Ñāṇassa pākaṭāni pana puggalassa pākaṭāneva honti. Peḷāsu kiccaṃ katvā gatakālo viya arahattamaggassa sabbakilesakhepanaṃ. Sūriyuggamanato paṭṭhāya ālokasseva pavattikālo viya arahattamaggassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya puna saccapaṭicchādakatamābhāvo[M 0.0286]. Idaṃ tāva saccadassanassa apubbābhāve opammaṃ.

In the fourth instance, the time of directing insight toward the path of Arahantship is like the time of opening the door. The arising of the path of Arahantship is like the rising of the sun. The removal by the path of Arahantship of the darkness that conceals the truths is like the dispelling of darkness. When the darkness is dispelled, the manifestation of the four truths to the knowledge of the path of Arahantship is like the manifestation of the chests to that man. Furthermore, what is manifest to the knowledge is indeed manifest to the person. The exhaustion of all defilements by the path of Arahantship is like the time of having done the task with the chests and departed. Just as from the rising of the sun onwards is the time for the continuation of light alone, so from the time of the arising of the path of Arahantship onwards, there is again no darkness that conceals the truths. This, for now, is the simile concerning the fact that the seeing of the truths is not something new.

Diṭṭhakameva hi passati. ‘Kilese pana aññe añño pajahatī’ti ettha khāropamaṃ nāma gahitaṃ. Eko puriso kiliṭṭhaṃ vatthaṃ rajakassa adāsi. Rajako ūsakhāraṃ chārikakhāraṃ gomayakhāranti tayo khāre datvā khārehi khāditabhāvaṃ ñatvā udake vikkhāletvā oḷārikoḷārikaṃ malaṃ pavāhesi. Tato na tāva parisuddhanti dutiyampi tatheva khāre datvā, udake vikkhāletvā, tato nātisaṇhataraṃ malaṃ pavāhesi. Tato na tāva parisuddhanti tatiyampi te khāre datvā udake vikkhāletvā tato saṇhataraṃ malaṃ pavāhesi. Tato na tāva parisuddhanti catutthampi te khāre datvā, udake vikkhāletvā aṃsuabbhantaragatampi nissesaṃ malaṃ pavāhetvā sāmikassa adāsi. So gandhakaraṇḍake pakkhipitvā icchiticchitakāle paridahati.

Indeed, one sees only what has already been seen. Here, in the passage ‘But as for defilements, one path abandons some, another path abandons others,’ the simile of the lye is taken. A certain man gave a soiled cloth to a washerman. The washerman applied three kinds of lye—natural soda, ash lye, and cow-dung lye—and knowing it had been treated by the lyes, he washed it in water and removed the very coarse dirt. Then, as it was not yet clean, a second time he likewise applied the lyes, washed it in water, and then removed the dirt that was not yet fine. Then, as it was not yet clean, a third time he applied those lyes, washed it in water, and then removed the finer dirt. Then, as it was not yet clean, a fourth time he applied those lyes, washed it in water, and having washed away without remainder all the dirt, even that which had gone inside the threads, he gave it to the owner. That owner, having placed it in a perfumed casket, wears it whenever he desires.

Tattha kiliṭṭhavatthaṃ viya kilesānugataṃ cittaṃ. Tividhakhāradānakālo viya tīsu anupassanāsu kammassa pavattanakālo. Udake vikkhāletvā oḷārikoḷārikamalappavāhanaṃ viya sotāpattimaggena pañcakilesakhepanaṃ. Dutiyampi tesaṃ khārānaṃ anuppadānaṃ viya ‘na tāva parisuddhaṃ idaṃ citta’nti tāsuyeva tīsu anupassanāsu kammappavattanaṃ. Tato nātisaṇhataramalappavāhanaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggena oḷārikasaṃyojanadvayakhepanaṃ. Tato ‘na tāva parisuddhaṃ vattha’nti puna khārattayadānaṃ viya ‘na tāva parisuddhaṃ [P 0.0244] idaṃ citta’nti tāsuyeva tīsu anupassanāsu kammappavattanaṃ. Tato saṇhataramalappavāhanaṃ viya anāgāmimaggena aṇusahagatasaṃyojanadvayakhepanaṃ. ‘Na tāva parisuddhaṃ vattha’nti puna khārattayadānaṃ viya ‘na tāva parisuddhaṃ idaṃ citta’nti tāsuyeva tīsu anupassanāsu kammappavattanaṃ. Tato vikkhālanena aṃsuabbhantaragate male pavāhetvā parisuddhassa rajatapaṭṭasadisassa gandhakaraṇḍake nikkhittassa vatthassa icchiticchitakkhaṇe paridahanaṃ viya arahattamaggena aṭṭhannaṃ kilesānaṃ khepitattā parisuddhassa khīṇāsavacittassa icchiticchitakkhaṇe phalasamāpattivihārena vītināmanaṃ. Idaṃ ‘aññe añño kilese pajahatī’ti ettha opammaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

There, a mind imbued with defilements is like a soiled cloth. The time of applying the three kinds of lye is like the time of engaging in the meditative practice concerning the three contemplations. Washing it in water and removing the very coarse dirt is like the destruction of five defilements by the path of stream-entry. Applying those lyes a second time is like continuing the meditative practice concerning the three contemplations, thinking, “This mind is not yet pure.” Then, removing the dirt that was not yet fine is like the destruction of the two coarse fetters by the path of once-returning. Again, thinking, “This cloth is not yet clean,” and applying the three lyes once more is like continuing the meditative practice concerning the three contemplations, thinking, “This mind is not yet pure.” Then, removing the finer dirt is like the destruction of the two fetters accompanied by subtle tendencies by the path of non-returning. Again, thinking, “This cloth is not yet clean,” and applying the three lyes once more is like continuing the meditative practice concerning the three contemplations, thinking, “This mind is not yet pure.” Then, the wearing at any desired moment of the cloth—which, after the dirt that had penetrated the inner threads has been washed away, has become perfectly pure like a silver plate and placed in a scented casket—is like the passing of time by the perfectly pure mind of one whose taints are destroyed, which, because the eight defilements have been destroyed by the path of Arahantship, passes the time at any desired moment by dwelling in the attainment of fruition. This is the simile here for ‘one path abandons some defilements, another path abandons others.’ And this has also been said:

“Seyyathāpi[V 0.0285], āvuso, vatthaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ malaggahitaṃ, tamenaṃ sāmikā rajakassa anupadajjeyyuṃ. Tamenaṃ rajako ūse vā [M 0.0287] khāre vā gomaye vā sammadditvā acche udake vikkhāleti. Kiñcāpi taṃ hoti vatthaṃ parisuddhaṃ pariyodātaṃ, atha khvassa hotiyeva ‘aṇusahagato ūsagandho vā khāragandho vā gomayagandho vā asamūhato’. Tamenaṃ rajako sāmikānaṃ deti. Tamenaṃ sāmikā gandhaparibhāvite karaṇḍake nikkhipanti. Yopissa hoti aṇusahagato ūsagandho vā khāragandho vā gomayagandho vā asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṃ gacchati. Evameva kho, āvuso, kiñcāpi ariyasāvakassa pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni pahīnāni bhavanti, atha khvassa hotiyeva pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu aṇusahagato ‘asmī’ti māno, ‘asmī’ti chando, ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato, so aparena samayena pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassī viharati – ‘iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā iti saññā iti saṅkhārā iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti. Tassimesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassino viharato yopissa hoti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu aṇusahagato ‘asmī’ti māno, ‘asmī’ti chando, ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṃ gacchatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.89).

“Just as, friend, a cloth that is soiled and stained would be given by its owners to a washerman. The washerman would scrub it with saline earth, lye, or cow dung, and rinse it in clear water. Although the cloth becomes clean and pure, still there remains a subtle, accompanying smell of saline earth, lye, or cow dung that has not been uprooted. The washerman then returns it to the owners. The owners place it in a scented chest, and whatever subtle, accompanying smell of saline earth, lye, or cow dung has not been uprooted, that too is completely uprooted. In the same way, friend, although a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, there still remains a subtle, accompanying ‘I am’ conceit, ‘I am’ desire, and ‘I am’ underlying tendency regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging that has not been uprooted. Then, after some time, they dwell contemplating the rise and fall of the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling… such is perception… such are volitional formations… such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.’ As they dwell contemplating the rise and fall of these five aggregates subject to clinging, whatever subtle, accompanying ‘I am’ conceit, ‘I am’ desire, and ‘I am’ underlying tendency regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging has not been uprooted, that too is completely uprooted.”

Tattha [P 0.0245] sotāpattimaggena pañca akusalacittāni pahīyanti saddhiṃ cittaṅgavasena uppajjanakapāpadhammehi. Sakadāgāmimaggena dve domanassasahagatacittāni tanukāni bhavanti saddhiṃ cittaṅgavasena uppajjanakapāpadhammehi. Anāgāmimaggena tāniyeva pahīyanti saddhiṃ sampayuttadhammehi. Arahattamaggena pañca akusalacittāni pahīyanti saddhiṃ cittaṅgavasena uppajjanakapāpadhammehi. Imesaṃ dvādasannaṃ akusalacittānaṃ pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya khīṇāsavassa cittaṅgavasena puna pacchatopavattanakakileso nāma na hoti.

Therein, by the path of stream-entry, five unwholesome consciousnesses are abandoned together with the evil qualities that arise as their mental components. By the path of once-returning, two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure become attenuated, together with the evil qualities that arise as their mental components. By the path of non-returning, those very same are abandoned together with their associated qualities. By the path of arahantship, five unwholesome consciousnesses are abandoned together with the evil qualities that arise as their mental components. From the time of the abandonment of these twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, for one whose taints are destroyed, there is no defilement called 'that which recurs afterwards as a mental component'.

Tatridaṃ opammaṃ – eko kira mahārājā paccante ārakkhaṃ datvā mahānagare issariyaṃ anubhavanto vasati. Athassa paccanto kuppi. Tasmiṃ samaye dvādasa corajeṭṭhakā anekehi purisasahassehi saddhiṃ [M 0.0288] raṭṭhaṃ vilumpanti. Paccantavāsino mahāmattā ‘paccanto kupito’ti rañño pahiṇiṃsu. Rājā ‘vissaṭṭhā gaṇhatha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ kattabbaṃ karissāmī’ti sāsanaṃ pahiṇi[V 0.0286]. Te paṭhamasampahāreneva anekehi purisasahassehi saddhiṃ pañca corajeṭṭhake ghātayiṃsu. Sesā satta janā attano attano parivāre gahetvā pabbataṃ pavisiṃsu. Amaccā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño pesayiṃsu.

Herein is this simile: It is said that a certain great king, having established a guard in the border region, was enjoying his sovereignty in the capital city. Then, his border region became agitated. At that time, twelve bandit chiefs, along with many thousands of men, were plundering the kingdom. The great ministers living at the border sent a message to the king: “The border is agitated.” The king sent an order: “Seize them boldly. I will do for you what should be done.” With the very first assault, they killed five bandit chiefs along with many thousands of men. The remaining seven men, each taking their own followers, entered the mountains. The ministers reported this event to the king.

Rājā ‘tumhākaṃ kattabbayuttaṃ ahaṃ jānissāmi, tepi gaṇhathā’ti dhanaṃ pahiṇi. Te dutiyasampahārena dve corajeṭṭhake pahariṃsu, parivārepi tesaṃ dubbale akaṃsu. Te sabbepi palāyitvā pabbataṃ pavisiṃsu. Tampi pavattiṃ amaccā rañño pesayiṃsu.

The king sent wealth, saying, “I will know what is proper to be done for you; seize them too.” With a second assault, they struck the two bandit chiefs and weakened their followers. All of them fled and entered the mountains. The ministers also reported this event to the king.

Puna rājā ‘vissaṭṭhā gaṇhantū’ti dhanaṃ pahiṇi. Te tatiyasampahārena saddhiṃ sahāyapurisehi dve corajeṭṭhake ghātayitvā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño pesayiṃsu.

Again, the king sent wealth, saying, “Let them seize them boldly.” With the third assault, they killed the two bandit chiefs along with their companion men and sent the report to the king.

Puna rājā ‘avasese vissaṭṭhā gaṇhantū’ti dhanaṃ pahiṇi. Te catutthasampahārena saparivāre pañca corajeṭṭhake ghātayiṃsu. Dvādasannaṃ corajeṭṭhakānaṃ ghātitakālato paṭṭhāya koci coro nāma natthi. Khemā janapadā ure putte naccentā maññe viharanti. Rājā vijitasaṅgāmehi yodhehi parivuto [P 0.0246] varapāsādagato mahāsampattiṃ anubhavi.

Again, the king sent wealth, saying, 'Let them boldly seize the remaining ones.' With the fourth assault, they killed the five chief bandits along with their retinue. From the time the twelve chief bandits were killed, there was no one called a bandit. The countrysides were secure, and it was as if people lived making their children dance on their chests. The king, surrounded by warriors victorious in battle, went to his excellent palace and enjoyed great prosperity.

Tattha mahanto rājā viya dhammarājā. Paccantavāsino amaccā viya yogāvacarā kulaputtā. Dvādasa corajeṭṭhakā viya dvādasa akusalacittāni. Tesaṃ sahāyā anekasahassapurisā viya cittaṅgavasena uppajjanakapāpadhammā. Rañño paccanto kupitoti pahitakālo viya ārammaṇe kilesesu uppannesu ‘bhante, kileso me uppanno’ti satthu ārocanakālo. ‘Vissaṭṭhā gaṇhantū’ti dhanadānaṃ viya ‘kilese niggaṇha bhikkhū’ti dhammarañño kammaṭṭhānācikkhanaṃ. Saparivārānaṃ pañcannaṃ corajeṭṭhakānaṃ ghātitakālo viya sotāpattimaggena sampayuttānaṃ pañcannaṃ akusalacittānaṃ pahānaṃ.

Therein, the great king is to be understood as the Dhamma King. The ministers dwelling in the border regions are to be understood as the sons of good family who are meditators. The twelve chief bandits are to be understood as the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. Their companions, the many thousands of men, are to be understood as the evil states that arise as components of consciousness. The time of sending a message, 'The king's border region is in revolt,' is to be understood as the time of reporting to the Teacher, 'Venerable sir, a defilement has arisen in me,' when defilements have arisen in an object. The giving of wealth with the command, 'Let them seize them boldly,' is to be understood as the Dhamma King's instruction on a meditation subject, 'O monk, restrain the defilements.' The time of killing the five chief bandits with their retinue is to be understood as the abandonment, by the path of stream-entry, of the five unwholesome types of consciousness together with their associated states.

Puna [M 0.0289] rañño pavattipesanaṃ viya sammāsambuddhassa paṭiladdhaguṇārocanaṃ. ‘Sesake ca gaṇhantū’ti puna dhanadānaṃ viya bhagavato sakadāgāmimaggassa vipassanācikkhanaṃ. Dutiyasampahārena saparivārānaṃ dvinnaṃ corajeṭṭhakānaṃ dubbalīkaraṇaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggena sasampayuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ domanassacittānaṃ tanubhāvakaraṇaṃ.

Again, the sending of a report to the king is to be understood as the reporting of the attained qualities to the Perfectly Enlightened One. The giving of wealth again with the command, 'Let them seize the remaining ones too,' is to be understood as the Blessed One's instruction in insight for the path of the once-returner. The weakening of the two chief bandits with their retinue by the second assault is to be understood as the attenuation, by the path of the once-returner, of the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure, along with their associated states.

Puna [V 0.0287] rañño pavattipesanaṃ viya satthu paṭiladdhaguṇārocanaṃ. ‘Vissaṭṭhā gaṇhantū’ti puna dhanadānaṃ viya bhagavato anāgāmimaggassa vipassanācikkhanaṃ. Tatiyasampahārena saparivārānaṃ dvinnaṃ corajeṭṭhakānaṃ ghātanaṃ viya anāgāmimaggena sasampayuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ domanassacittānaṃ pahānaṃ.

Again, the sending of a report to the king is to be understood as the reporting of the attained qualities to the Teacher. The giving of wealth again with the command, 'Let them seize them boldly,' is to be understood as the Blessed One's instruction in insight for the path of the non-returner. The killing of the two chief bandits with their retinue by the third assault is to be understood as the abandonment, by the path of the non-returner, of the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure, together with their associated states.

Puna rañño pavattipesanaṃ viya tathāgatassa paṭiladdhaguṇārocanaṃ. ‘Vissaṭṭhā gaṇhantū’ti puna dhanadānaṃ viya bhagavato arahattamaggassa vipassanācikkhanaṃ. Catutthasampahārena saparivārānaṃ pañcannaṃ corajeṭṭhakānaṃ ghātitakālato paṭṭhāya janapadassa khemakālo viya arahattamaggena sasampayuttesu pañcasu akusalacittesu pahīnesu dvādasannaṃ akusalacittānaṃ pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya puna cittaṅgavasena uppajjanakassa akusaladhammassa abhāvo. Rañño vijitasaṅgāmassa amaccagaṇaparivutassa varapāsāde mahāsampattianubhavanaṃ viya khīṇāsavaparivutassa dhammarañño suññataanimittaappaṇihitabhedesu samāpattisukhesu [P 0.0247] icchiticchitaphalasamāpattisukhānubhavanaṃ veditabbanti.

Again, the sending of a report to the king is to be understood as the reporting of the attained qualities to the Tathāgata. The giving of wealth again with the command, 'Let them seize them boldly,' is to be understood as the Blessed One's instruction in insight for the path of Arahantship. Just as the time of security for the countryside from the time the five chief bandits with their retinue were killed by the fourth assault is to be understood, so too, when the five unwholesome types of consciousness with their associated states have been abandoned by the path of Arahantship, the non-existence of any unwholesome state that would arise again as a component of consciousness from the time the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness were abandoned is to be understood. Just as the king, victorious in battle and surrounded by his host of ministers, experiencing great prosperity in his excellent palace is to be understood, so too, the Dhamma King, surrounded by those whose taints are destroyed, experiencing the bliss of the fruition attainment as and when he wishes among the blissful attainments of the kinds of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, is to be understood.

Kusalā dhammātipadassa vaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the term 'Kusalā Dhammā' is concluded.

Akusalapadaṃ

The Section on the Unwholesome

Dhammuddesavārakathā

Discourse on the Section of the Exposition of Dhammas

Paṭhamacittaṃ

The First Consciousness

365. Idāni akusaladhammapadaṃ bhājetvā dassetuṃ katame dhammā akusalātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha dhammavavatthānādivārappabhedo ca heṭṭhā āgatānaṃ padānaṃ atthavinicchayo ca heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tattha tattha pana visesamattameva vaṇṇayissāma. Tattha samayavavatthāne tāva yasmā, kusalassa viya, akusalassa bhūmibhedo natthi, tasmā ekantaṃ kāmāvacarampi samānaṃ etaṃ ‘kāmāvacara’nti na vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhigatasampayuttanti ettha diṭṭhi [M 0.0290] eva diṭṭhigataṃ ‘gūthagataṃ [V 0.0288] muttagata’ntiādīni (a. ni. 9.11) viya. Gantabbābhāvato vā diṭṭhiyā gatamattamevetantipi diṭṭhigataṃ. Tena sampayuttaṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ.

365. Now, having analyzed the section on unwholesome states in order to expound upon it, the passage beginning with 'What states are unwholesome?' has been commenced. Therein, the division into sections, such as the demarcation of states, and the determination of the meaning of the terms that have come below, should be understood by the same method as explained previously. However, in various places, we shall explain only the special points. Therein, firstly, in the demarcation of the occasion, because, unlike for the wholesome, there is no distinction of planes for the unwholesome, therefore, although it is exclusively of the sense-sphere, it is not stated as 'of the sense-sphere.' In the phrase 'associated with what has become a view' (diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ), 'view' (diṭṭhi) itself is 'what has become a view' (diṭṭhigataṃ), just as in 'what has become excrement' (gūthagataṃ), 'what has become urine' (muttagataṃ), and so on. Or, because there is nothing to be gone to, it is merely what has become a view; thus it is also diṭṭhigataṃ. Associated with that is diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ.

Tattha asaddhammasavanaṃ, akalyāṇamittatā, ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādīni ayoniso manasikāroti evamādīhi kāraṇehi imassa diṭṭhigatasaṅkhātassa micchādassanassa uppatti veditabbā. Ye hi ete diṭṭhivādapaṭisaṃyuttā asaddhammā tesaṃ bahumānapubbaṅgamena atikkantamajjhattena upaparikkhārahitena savanena, ye ca diṭṭhivipannā akalyāṇamittā taṃsampavaṅkatāsaṅkhātāya akalyāṇamittatāya, buddhādīnaṃ ariyānañceva sappurisānañca adassanakāmatāya catusatipaṭṭhānādibhede ariyadhamme akovidattena pātimokkhasaṃvaraindriyasaṃvarasatisaṃvarañāṇasaṃvarapahānasaṃvarappabhede ariyadhamme ceva sappurisadhamme ca saṃvarabhedasaṅkhātena avinayena teheva kāraṇehi paribhāvitena ayoniso manasikārena kotūhalamaṅgalādipasutatāya ca etaṃ uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Asaṅkhārabhāvo panassa cittassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Therein, the arising of this wrong view, designated as diṭṭhigata, should be known to be from such causes as: hearing the non-true Dhamma, having bad friends, not wishing to see the noble ones, and so on, and improper attention. For it should be known that this arises: by hearing those non-true Dhammas connected with dogmatic views, preceded by great respect, with impartiality overcome, and devoid of investigation; by bad friendship, known as being inclined towards those bad friends whose views are corrupt; by not wishing to see the noble ones such as the Buddha and virtuous persons; by being unskilled in the noble Dhamma with its divisions such as the four foundations of mindfulness; by lack of discipline, known as the breach of restraint, regarding the noble Dhamma and the Dhamma of virtuous persons with its divisions such as the Pātimokkha restraint, restraint of the senses, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, and restraint of abandoning; by improper attention cultivated by those very causes; and by being devoted to curiosities, ceremonies, and the like. However, the unprompted nature of this consciousness should be understood by the same method as explained previously.

Dhammuddesavāre [P 0.0248] phassoti akusalacittasahajāto phasso. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Iti akusalamattameva etesaṃ purimehi viseso.

In the Section on the Exposition of Dhammas, 'contact' means contact co-arisen with unwholesome consciousness. This same method applies to feeling and so on. Thus, merely being unwholesome is the distinction of these from the previous ones.

Cittassekaggatā hotīti pāṇātipātādīsupi avikkhittabhāvena cittassa ekaggatā hoti. Manussā hi cittaṃ samādahitvā avikkhittā hutvā avirajjhamānāni satthāni pāṇasarīresu nipātenti, susamāhitā paresaṃ santakaṃ haranti, ekarasena cittena micchācāraṃ āpajjanti. Evaṃ akusalappavattiyampi cittassa ekaggatā hoti.

As for 'the mind becomes one-pointed': even in acts such as taking life, one-pointedness of mind occurs due to the state of non-distraction. For people, having concentrated their minds and being undistracted, they unerringly strike weapons into the bodies of living beings. Being well-concentrated, they steal the property of others. With a mind of a single purpose, they engage in sexual misconduct. Thus, even in the occurrence of the unwholesome, there is one-pointedness of mind.

Micchādiṭṭhīti ayāthāvadiṭṭhi, virajjhitvā gahaṇato vā vitathā diṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhi. Anatthāvahattā paṇḍitehi jigucchitā diṭṭhītipi micchādiṭṭhi. Micchāsaṅkappādīsupi eseva nayo. Apica micchā passanti tāya, sayaṃ vā micchā passati, micchādassanamattameva vā esāti micchādiṭṭhi. Sā ayoniso abhinivesalakkhaṇā, parāmāsarasā, micchābhinivesapaccupaṭṭhānā, ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādipadaṭṭhānā; paramaṃ vajjanti daṭṭhabbā. Micchāsaṅkappādīsu [M 0.0291] ‘micchā’ti padamattameva viseso. Sesaṃ kusalādhikāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

'Wrong view' means a view not in accordance with reality, or a distorted view because it is grasped erroneously. Because it brings what is not beneficial and is despised by the wise, it is also wrong view. This same method applies to wrong intention and so on. Furthermore, it is wrong view because associated states see wrongly by means of it, or it itself sees wrongly, or it is merely wrong seeing. It has the characteristic of improper adherence, the function of tenacious grasping, the manifestation of wrong insistence, and the proximate cause of not wishing to see the noble ones, and so on. It should be seen as the supreme fault. In the case of wrong intention and the rest, the only difference is the word 'wrong.' The rest should be understood by the same method as explained in the section on the wholesome.

Ahirikabalaṃ [V 0.0289] anottappabalanti ettha balattho niddesavāre āvi bhavissati. Itaresu pana – na hiriyatīti ahiriko. Ahirikassa bhāvo ahirikaṃ. Na ottappaṃ anottappaṃ. Tesu ahirikaṃ kāyaduccaritādīhi ajigucchanalakkhaṇaṃ, alajjālakkhaṇaṃ vā. Anottappaṃ teheva asārajjanalakkhaṇaṃ anuttāsanalakkhaṇaṃ vā. Ahirikameva balaṃ ahirikabalaṃ. Anottappameva balaṃ anottappabalaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepattho. Vitthāro pana heṭṭhā vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbo.

Herein, in 'the power of shamelessness' and 'the power of lack of moral dread,' the meaning of 'power' will become clear in the Exposition Section. As for the other terms: one who is not ashamed is ahiriko (shameless). The state of being shameless is ahirikaṃ (shamelessness). What is not moral dread (ottappa) is anottappaṃ (lack of moral dread). Among these, shamelessness has the characteristic of not being disgusted by bodily misconduct and so on, or the characteristic of being without shame. Lack of moral dread has the characteristic of not shrinking back from those same things, or the characteristic of being without dread. Shamelessness itself is the power of shamelessness. Lack of moral dread itself is the power of lack of moral dread. This is the brief meaning here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood by way of the opposite of what was explained previously.

Lubbhanti tena, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva [P 0.0249] vā tanti lobho. Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, muyhanamattameva vā tanti moho. Tesu lobho ārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇo makkaṭālepo viya, abhisaṅgaraso tattakapāle khittamaṃsapesi viya, apariccāgapaccupaṭṭhāno telañjanarāgo viya, saṃyojaniyadhammesu assādadassanapadaṭṭhāno. So taṇhānadībhāvena vaḍḍhamāno, sīghasotā nadī viya mahāsamuddaṃ, apāyameva gahetvā gacchatīti daṭṭhabbo.

Associated states are greedy by means of it, or it itself is greedy, or it is merely greediness; thus it is lobha (greed). Associated states are deluded by means of it, or it itself is deluded, or it is merely delusion; thus it is moho (delusion). Among these, greed has the characteristic of grasping an object, like monkey-lime; the function of clinging, like a piece of meat thrown on a hot pan; the manifestation of non-relinquishment, like an oil stain; and the proximate cause of seeing gratification in things that are objects of the fetters. It should be seen that, growing as the river of craving, it takes one only to the lower realms, just as a swift-flowing river goes to the great ocean.

Moho cittassa andhabhāvalakkhaṇo aññāṇalakkhaṇo vā, asampaṭivedharaso ārammaṇasabhāvacchādanaraso vā, asammāpaṭipattipaccupaṭṭhāno andhakārapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhāno. Sabbākusalānaṃ mūlanti daṭṭhabbo.

Delusion has the characteristic of the mind's state of blindness, or the characteristic of non-knowledge; the function of non-penetration, or the function of concealing the intrinsic nature of the object; the manifestation of wrong practice, or the manifestation of darkness; and the proximate cause of improper attention. It should be seen as the root of all unwholesome states.

Abhijjhāyanti tāya, sayaṃ vā abhijjhāyati, abhijjhāyanamattameva vā esāti abhijjhā. Sā parasampattīnaṃ sakakaraṇaicchālakkhaṇā, tenākārena esanabhāvarasā, parasampatti-abhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, parasampattīsu abhiratipadaṭṭhānā. Parasampattiabhimukhā eva hi sā upaṭṭhahati. Tāsu ca abhiratiyā sati pavattati, parasampattīsu cetaso hatthappasāroviyāti daṭṭhabbā.

Associated states covet by means of it, or it itself covets, or it is merely coveting; thus it is abhijjhā (covetousness). It has the characteristic of desiring to make others' property one's own; the function of searching in that manner; the manifestation of facing towards others' property; and the proximate cause of delighting in others' property. For it arises only when facing others' property. And when there is delight in those things, it proceeds. It should be seen as like the stretching out of the mind's hand towards others' property.

Samatho hotītiādīsu aññesu kiccesu vikkhepasamanato samatho. Akusalappavattiyaṃ cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti paggāho. Na vikkhipatīti avikkhepo.

In such texts as 'tranquility arises,' samatha (tranquility) is so called because it is the calming of distraction in regard to other matters. Paggāha (exertion) is so called because it uplifts the mind in the occurrence of the unwholesome. Avikkhepa (non-distraction) is so called because it does not scatter.

Imasmiṃ [M 0.0292] citte saddhā, sati, paññā, cha yugaḷakānīti ime dhammā na gahitā. Kasmā? Assaddhiyacitte pasādo nāma natthi. Tasmā tāva saddhā na gahitā. Kiṃ pana diṭṭhigatikā [V 0.0290] attano attano satthārānaṃ na saddahantīti? Saddahanti. Sā pana saddhā nāma na hoti, vacanasampaṭicchanamattamevetaṃ. Atthato anupaparikkhā vā [P 0.0250] hoti, diṭṭhi vā. Asatiyacitte pana sati natthīti na gahitā. Kiṃ diṭṭhigatikā attanā katakammaṃ na sarantīti? Saranti. Sā pana sati nāma na hoti. Kevalaṃ tenākārena akusalacittappavatti. Tasmā sati na gahitā. Atha kasmā “micchāsatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.333; saṃ. ni. 5.1) suttante vuttā? Sā pana akusalakkhandhānaṃ sativirahitattā satipaṭipakkhattā ca micchāmaggamicchattānaṃ pūraṇatthaṃ tattha pariyāyena desanā katā. Nippariyāyena panesā natthi. Tasmā na gahitā. Andhabālacitte pana paññā natthīti na gahitā. Kiṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ vañcanāpaññā natthīti? Atthi. Na panesā paññā, māyā nāmesā hoti. Sā atthato taṇhāva. Idaṃ pana cittaṃ sadarathaṃ garukaṃ bhāriyaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ thaddhaṃ akammaññaṃ gilānaṃ vaṅkaṃ kuṭilaṃ. Tasmā passaddhādīni cha yugaḷakāni na gahitāni.
