In this mind, faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and the six pairs—these states are not included. Why? Because in a mind lacking faith, there is nothing called serene confidence. Therefore, faith is not included. But do those with wrong views not have faith in their own teachers? They do have faith. However, that is not what is called true faith; it is merely the acceptance of their word. In reality, it is either non-investigation or wrong view. Furthermore, in a mind lacking mindfulness, there is no mindfulness; therefore, it is not included. Do those with wrong views not remember the deeds they have done? They do remember. But that is not what is called true mindfulness. It is merely the occurrence of an unwholesome mind in that manner. Therefore, mindfulness is not included. Then why is 'wrong mindfulness' spoken of in the Suttas? Because the unwholesome aggregates are devoid of mindfulness and because it is the opposite of mindfulness, it is taught there figuratively for the purpose of fulfilling the wrong path and wrongness. But in a direct sense, it does not exist. Therefore, it is not included. Furthermore, in the mind of a blind fool, there is no wisdom; therefore, it is not included. Do those with wrong views not have a cunning wisdom? They do. But this is not true wisdom; this is called deceit. In reality, it is craving. Furthermore, this mind is agitated, heavy, burdensome, rough, stiff, unworkable, crooked, and warped. Therefore, the six pairs, beginning with tranquility, are not included.

Ettāvatā padapaṭipāṭiyā cittaṅgavasena pāḷiāruḷhāni dvattiṃsa padāni dassetvā idāni yevāpanakadhamme dassetuṃ ye vā pana tasmiṃ samayetiādimāha. Tattha sabbesupi akusalacittesu chando adhimokkho manasikāro māno issā macchariyaṃ thinaṃ middhaṃ uddhaccaṃ kukkuccanti ime daseva yevāpanakā honti dhammā, suttāgatā, suttapadesu dissareti vuttā. Imasmiṃ pana citte chando adhimokkho manasikāro uddhaccanti ime apaṇṇakaṅgasaṅkhātā cattārova yevāpanakā honti.

Having thus far shown, in sequence of terms and by way of the mind's components, the thirty-two sets of states that are found in the Pāḷi, now, to show the yevāpanaka states, it is said, 'Or whatever other... at that time,' and so on. Therein, in all unwholesome minds, it is said that only these ten states are the yevāpanaka: desire, decision, attention, conceit, envy, avarice, sloth, torpor, restlessness, and worry; they are found in the Suttas and seen in the Sutta passages. But in this mind, only these four yevāpanaka states, known as the invariable components, occur: desire, decision, attention, and restlessness.

Tattha chandādayo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Kevalañhi te kusalā, ime akusalā. Itaraṃ pana uddhatassa bhāvo ‘uddhaccaṃ’. Taṃ cetaso avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ vātābhighātacalajalaṃ viya, anavaṭṭhānarasaṃ vātābhighātacaladhajapaṭākā viya, bhantattapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ pāsāṇābhighātasamuddhatabhasmā viya, cetaso avūpasame ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Cittavikkhepoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Therein, the states beginning with desire should be understood in the same way as stated before. The only difference is that those are wholesome, while these are unwholesome. As for the other, restlessness (uddhacca) is the state of being agitated. It has the characteristic of the mind's non-tranquility, like water agitated by the striking of the wind; its function is instability, like a flag or banner agitated by the striking of the wind; it manifests as bewilderment, like ashes thrown up by the striking of a stone; its proximate cause is unwise attention to the mind's non-tranquility. It should be understood as mental distraction.

Iti phassādīni dvattiṃsa, yevāpanakavasena vuttāni cattārīti sabbānipi [P 0.0251] imasmiṃ dhammuddesavāre chattiṃsa dhammapadāni bhavanti. Cattāri apaṇṇakaṅgāni hāpetvā [M 0.0293] pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni dvattiṃsameva. Aggahitaggahaṇena panettha phassapañcakaṃ, vitakko vicāro pīti cittassekaggatā [V 0.0291] vīriyindriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ micchādiṭṭhi ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ lobho mohoti soḷasa dhammā honti.

Thus, the thirty-two states beginning with contact and the four spoken of by way of yevāpanaka—altogether in this section on the enumeration of states, there are thirty-six terms for states. Excluding the four invariable components, those that come in the Pāḷi are only thirty-two. Herein, by the principle of not taking what has already been taken, there are sixteen states: the contact-pentad, applied thought, sustained thought, joy, one-pointedness of mind, the faculty of energy, the life faculty, wrong view, lack of shame, lack of compunction, greed, and delusion.

Tesu soḷasasu satta dhammā avibhattikā nava savibhattikā honti. Katame satta? Phasso saññā cetanā vicāro pīti jīvitindriyaṃ mohoti ime satta avibhattikā. Vedanā cittaṃ vitakko cittassekaggatā vīriyindriyaṃ micchādiṭṭhi ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ lobhoti ime nava savibhattikā.

Among these sixteen states, seven states are unanalyzed and nine are analyzed. Which seven? Contact, perception, volition, sustained thought, joy, the life faculty, and delusion—these seven are unanalyzed. Feeling, consciousness, applied thought, one-pointedness of mind, the faculty of energy, wrong view, lack of shame, lack of compunction, and greed—these nine are analyzed.

Tesu cha dhammā dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattā, eko tīsu, eko catūsu, eko chasu. Kathaṃ? Cittaṃ vitakko micchādiṭṭhi ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ lobhoti ime cha dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattā. Tesu hi cittaṃ tāva phassapañcakaṃ patvā cittaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ, indriyāni patvā manindriyanti. Vitakko jhānaṅgāni patvā vitakko hotīti vutto, maggaṅgāni patvā micchāsaṅkappoti. Micchādiṭṭhi maggaṅgesupi kammapathesupi micchādiṭṭhiyeva. Ahirikaṃ balāni patvā ahirikabalaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ, lokanāsakadukaṃ patvā ahirikanti. Anottappepi eseva nayo. Lobho mūlaṃ patvā lobho hotīti vutto. Kammapathaṃ patvā abhijjhāti. Ime cha dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattā.

Among them, six states are analyzed in two places, one in three, one in four, and one in six. How? Consciousness, applied thought, wrong view, lack of shame, lack of compunction, and greed—these six are analyzed in two places. Among them, consciousness, on reaching the contact-pentad, is called 'consciousness'; on reaching the faculties, it is called 'the mind faculty.' Applied thought, on reaching the jhāna factors, is called 'applied thought'; on reaching the path factors, it is called 'wrong thought.' Wrong view is 'wrong view' among both the path factors and the courses of action. Lack of shame, on reaching the powers, is called 'the power of shamelessness'; on reaching the world-destroying couplet, it is called 'lack of shame.' The same method applies to lack of compunction. Greed, on reaching the roots, is called 'greed'; on reaching the course of action, it is called 'covetousness.' These six are analyzed in two places.

Vedanā pana phassapañcakaṃ patvā vedanā hotīti vuttā, jhānaṅgāni patvā sukhanti, indriyāni patvā somanassindriyanti. Evaṃ ekova dhammo tīsu ṭhānesu vibhatto.

Feeling, on the other hand, on reaching the contact-pentad, is called 'feeling'; on reaching the jhāna factors, it is called 'happiness'; on reaching the faculties, it is called 'the faculty of gladness.' Thus, this one state is analyzed in three places.

Vīriyaṃ pana indriyāni patvā vīriyindriyaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ, maggaṅgāni patvā micchāvāyāmo hotīti, balāni patvā vīriyabalanti, piṭṭhidukaṃ patvā paggāho hotīti. Evaṃ ayaṃ eko dhammo catūsu ṭhānesu vibhatto.

Energy, furthermore, on reaching the faculties, is called 'the faculty of energy'; on reaching the path factors, it is called 'wrong effort'; on reaching the powers, it is called 'the power of energy'; on reaching the support-couplet, it is called 'exertion.' Thus, this one state is analyzed in four places.

Samādhi pana jhānaṅgāni patvā cittassekaggatā hotīti vutto, indriyāni patvā samādhindriyanti, maggaṅgāni patvā micchāsamādhīti, balāni patvā samādhibalanti, piṭṭhidukaṃ patvā dutiyaduke [P 0.0252] ekakavaseneva samathoti[M 0.0294], tatiye avikkhepoti. Evamayaṃ eko dhammo chasu ṭhānesu vibhatto.

Concentration, on the other hand, on reaching the jhāna factors, is called 'one-pointedness of mind'; on reaching the faculties, it is called 'the faculty of concentration'; on reaching the path factors, it is called 'wrong concentration'; on reaching the powers, it is called 'the power of concentration'; on reaching the support-couplet, in the second couplet, by way of the single factor, it is called 'tranquility'; in the third, it is called 'non-distraction.' Thus, this one state is analyzed in six places.

Sabbepi [V 0.0292] panete dhammā phassapañcakavasena jhānaṅgavasena indriyavasena maggaṅgavasena balavasena mūlavasena kammapathavasena lokanāsakavasena piṭṭhidukavasenāti nava rāsayo honti. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ paṭhamakusalacittaniddese vuttamevāti.

Furthermore, all these phenomena—by way of the contact-pentad, the jhāna-factors, the faculties, the path-factors, the powers, the roots, the courses of action, the world-destroying pair, and the supporting pair—become nine groups. Therein, what should be said has already been said in the exposition of the first wholesome consciousness.

Dhammuddesavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discussion on the Summary of Dhammas is concluded.

Niddesavārakathā

The Discourse on the Exposition Section

375. Niddesavāre cittassekaggatāniddese tāva saṇṭhiti avaṭṭhitīti. Idaṃ dvayaṃ ṭhitivevacanameva. Yaṃ pana kusalaniddese ‘ārammaṇaṃ ogāhetvā anupavisitvā tiṭṭhatīti avaṭṭhitī’ti vuttaṃ, taṃ idha na labbhati. Akusalasmiñhi dubbalā cittassekaggatāti heṭṭhā dīpitameva.

375. In the Exposition Section, in the exposition of one-pointedness of mind, firstly, there are ‘stability’ (saṇṭhiti) and ‘steadiness’ (avaṭṭhiti). This pair are merely synonyms for ‘standing firm’ (ṭhiti). However, what was said in the exposition of the wholesome—‘it stands having plunged into and entered upon the object, thus it is steadiness’—is not obtained here. For in the unwholesome, one-pointedness of mind is weak, as was already explained below.

384. Uddhaccavicikicchāvasena pavattassa visāhārassa paṭipakkhato avisāhāroti evarūpopi attho idha na labbhati. Sahajātadhamme pana na visāharatīti avisāhāro. Na vikkhipatīti avikkhepo. Akusalacittekaggatāvasena avisāhaṭassa mānasassa bhāvo avisāhaṭamānasatā. Sahajātadhammesu na kampatīti samādhibalaṃ. Ayāthāvasamādhānato micchāsamādhīti evamidha attho daṭṭhabbo.

384. Even such a meaning as ‘non-scattering’ (avisāhāra) being the opposite of the scattering (visāhāra) that occurs by way of restlessness and doubt is not obtained here. Rather, it does not scatter co-nascent phenomena, thus it is ‘non-scattering’ (avisāhāra). It does not distract, thus it is ‘non-distraction’ (avikkhepa). By the power of unwholesome one-pointedness, the state of a mind that is not scattered is ‘unscattered-mindedness’ (avisāhaṭamānasatā). It does not tremble among co-nascent phenomena, thus it is the ‘power of concentration’ (samādhibala). Due to incorrect placement of the mind, it is ‘wrong concentration’ (micchāsamādhi). Thus the meaning should be understood here.

385. Vīriyindriyaniddese yo heṭṭhā ‘nikkamo ceso kāmānaṃ panudanāyā’tiādi nayo vutto, so idha na labbhati. Sahajātadhammesu akampanaṭṭheneva vīriyabalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

385. In the exposition of the faculty of energy, the method spoken of below, beginning with ‘this is the exertion for the dispelling of sensual pleasures,’ is not obtained here. The power of energy should be known precisely by the meaning of non-trembling among co-nascent phenomena.

386. Micchādiṭṭhiniddese ayāthāvadassanaṭṭhena micchādiṭṭhi. Diṭṭhīsu gataṃ idaṃ dassanaṃ, dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiantogatattāti diṭṭhigataṃ. Heṭṭhāpissa attho vuttoyeva. Diṭṭhiyeva duratikkamanaṭṭhena diṭṭhigahanaṃ, tiṇagahanavanagahanapabbatagahanāni viya. Diṭṭhiyeva sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayaṭṭhena diṭṭhikantāro[M 0.0295], corakantāravāḷakantāramarukantāranirudakakantāradubbhikkhakantārā [P 0.0253] viya. Sammādiṭṭhiyā [V 0.0293] vinivijjhanaṭṭhena vilomanaṭṭhena ca diṭṭhivisūkāyikaṃ. Micchādassanañhi uppajjamānaṃ sammādassanaṃ vinivijjhati ceva vilometi ca. Kadāci sassatassa kadāci ucchedassa gahaṇato diṭṭhiyā virūpaṃ phanditanti diṭṭhivipphanditaṃ. Diṭṭhigatiko hi ekasmiṃ patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, kadāci sassataṃ anupatati kadāci ucchedaṃ. Diṭṭhiyeva bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojananti diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ.

386. In the exposition of wrong view: by the meaning of incorrect seeing, it is ‘wrong view’ (micchādiṭṭhi). This seeing is ‘gone’ among the views, because it is included within the sixty-two views, thus it is ‘gone to a view’ (diṭṭhigata). The meaning of this has already been stated below. View itself, by the meaning of being difficult to overcome, is a ‘thicket of views’ (diṭṭhigahana), like thickets of grass, forest thickets, and mountain thickets. View itself, by the meaning of being with apprehension and with fear, is a ‘wilderness of views’ (diṭṭhikantāra), like a wilderness of thieves, a wilderness of wild beasts, a desert wilderness, a waterless wilderness, and a famine wilderness. By the meaning of piercing and by the meaning of being contrary to right view, it is a ‘spasm of views’ (diṭṭhivisūkāyika). For wrong view, when arising, both pierces and is contrary to right view. Due to grasping sometimes at eternalism and sometimes at annihilationism, it is a distorted trembling of view, thus it is ‘trembling of view’ (diṭṭhivipphandita). For one who has gone to a view is not able to become established in one position; sometimes one falls into eternalism, sometimes into annihilationism. View itself, by the meaning of binding, is a fetter, thus it is the ‘fetter of views’ (diṭṭhisaṃyojana).

Susumārādayo viya purisaṃ, ārammaṇaṃ daḷhaṃ gaṇhātīti gāho. Patiṭṭhahanato patiṭṭhāho. Ayañhi balavappavattibhāvena patiṭṭhahitvā gaṇhāti. Niccādivasena abhinivisatīti abhiniveso. Dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā niccādivasena parato āmasatīti parāmāso. Anatthāvahattā kucchito maggo, kucchitānaṃ vā apāyānaṃ maggoti kummaggo. Ayāthāvapathato micchāpatho. Yathā hi disāmūḷhena ayaṃ asukagāmassa nāma pathoti gahitopi taṃ gāmaṃ na sampāpeti, evaṃ diṭṭhigatikena sugatipathoti gahitāpi diṭṭhi sugatiṃ na pāpetīti ayāthāvapathato, micchāpatho. Micchāsabhāvato micchattaṃ. Tattheva paribbhamanato taranti ettha bālāti titthaṃ. Titthañca taṃ anatthānañca āyatananti titthāyatanaṃ. Titthiyānaṃ vā sañjātidesaṭṭhena nivāsaṭhānaṭṭhena ca āyatanantipi titthāyatanaṃ. Vipariyesabhūto gāho, vipariyesato vā gāhoti vipariyesaggāho; vipallattha gāhoti attho.

Like crocodiles and other creatures seizing a person firmly, it seizes the object firmly, thus it is ‘grasping’ (gāho). From establishing, it is ‘establishment’ (patiṭṭhāho). For this view grasps after having become established with a powerful occurrence. It adheres by way of permanence, etc., thus it is ‘adherence’ (abhiniveso). Having transgressed the true nature of phenomena, it misapprehends by way of permanence, etc., as something other than what it is, thus it is ‘misapprehension’ (parāmāso). Because it brings harm, it is a ‘bad path’ (kummaggo); or it is the path of the contemptible states of loss, thus it is a ‘bad path’. From being an incorrect path, it is a ‘wrong path’ (micchāpatho). For just as a path taken by one who is lost, thinking, ‘This is the path to such-and-such a village,’ does not lead to that village; so too, a view taken by one who has gone to a view, thinking, ‘This is the path to a good destination,’ does not lead to a good destination. Thus, from being an incorrect path, it is a ‘wrong path’. From its wrong nature, it is ‘wrongness’ (micchattaṃ). Because fools cross over or flounder about right there, it is a ‘ford’ (titthaṃ). It is a ford and it is a basis for what is not beneficial, thus it is a ‘basis for sectarianism’ (titthāyatana). Or, by the meaning of being the birthplace and dwelling place for sectarians, it is a basis, thus it is a ‘basis for sectarianism’. A grasp that is a perversion, or a grasp by way of perversion, is a ‘perverse grasp’ (vipariyesaggāho); the meaning is a distorted grasp.

387-388. Ahirikānottappaniddesesu hirottappaniddesavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Sahajātadhammesu pana akampanaṭṭheneva ahirikabalaṃ anottappabalañca veditabbaṃ.

In the expositions of shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing, the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of the expositions of shame and fear of wrongdoing. Furthermore, the power of shamelessness and the power of fearlessness of wrongdoing should be known precisely by the meaning of non-trembling among co-nascent phenomena.

389. Lobhamohaniddesesu lubbhatīti lobho. Lubbhanāti lubbhanākāro. Lobhasampayuttacittaṃ, puggalo vā lubbhito; lubbhitassa bhāvo lubbhitattaṃ. Sārajjatīti sārāgo. Sārajjanākāro sārajjanā. Sārajjitassa bhāvo sārajjitattaṃ. Abhijjhāyanaṭṭhena abhijjhā[M 0.0296]. Puna ‘lobha’-vacane kāraṇaṃ [P 0.0254] vuttameva. Akusalañca taṃ mūlañca akusalānaṃ vā mūlanti akusalamūlaṃ.

389. In the expositions of greed and delusion: It is greedy, thus it is ‘greed’ (lobha). Greediness is the mode of being greedy. A mind associated with greed, or a person, is ‘greedy’ (lubbhita); the state of one who is greedy is ‘greediness’ (lubbhitattaṃ). It is intensely attached, thus it is ‘passion’ (sārāga). The mode of intense attachment is ‘being intensely attached’ (sārajjanā). The state of one who is intensely attached is ‘intense attachment’ (sārajjitattaṃ). By the meaning of coveting, it is ‘covetousness’ (abhijjhā). Again, the reason for the word ‘greed’ has already been stated. It is unwholesome and it is a root, or it is the root of unwholesome states, thus it is an ‘unwholesome root’ (akusalamūla).

390. Ñāṇadassanapaṭipakkhato aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ. Abhimukho hutvā dhammena na sameti, na samāgacchatīti anabhisamayo. Anurūpato dhamme bujjhatīti anubodho. Tappaṭipakkhatāya [V 0.0294] ananubodho. Aniccādīhi saddhiṃ yojetvā na bujjhatīti asambodho. Asantaṃ asamañca bujjhatītipi asambodho. Catusaccadhammaṃ nappaṭivijjhatīti appaṭivedho. Rūpādīsu ekadhammampi aniccādisāmaññato na saṅgaṇhātīti asaṃgāhanā. Tameva dhammaṃ na pariyogāhatīti apariyogāhanā. Na samaṃ pekkhatīti asamapekkhaṇā. Dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ pati na apekkhatīti apaccavekkhaṇā.

390. From being the opposite of knowledge and vision, it is ‘unknowing’ (aññāṇa) and ‘unseeing’ (adassana). Not properly knowing the dhammas face-to-face, not comprehending them, is ‘non-comprehension’ (anabhisamaya). One understands the dhammas accordingly, thus it is ‘understanding’ (anubodha); from being the opposite of that, it is ‘non-understanding’ (ananubodha). One does not awaken by connecting phenomena with impermanence, etc., thus it is ‘non-awakening’ (asambodha). It is also ‘non-awakening’ because one awakens to what is non-existent and unequal. One does not penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Truths, thus it is ‘non-penetration’ (appaṭivedha). One does not properly grasp even a single phenomenon among form, etc., by way of the general characteristic of impermanence, etc., thus it is ‘non-grasping’ (asaṅgāhanā). One does not fathom that very Dhamma, thus it is ‘non-fathoming’ (apariyogāhanā). One does not look evenly, thus it is ‘uneven-looking’ (asamapekkhaṇā). One does not reflect back upon the true nature of phenomena, thus it is ‘non-reflection’ (apaccavekkhaṇā).

Kusalākusalakammesu viparītavuttiyā sabhāvaggahaṇābhāvena vā ekampi kammaṃ etassa paccakkhaṃ natthi, sayaṃ vā kassaci kammassa paccakkhakaraṇaṃ nāma na hotīti appaccakkhakammaṃ. Yaṃ etasmiṃ anuppajjamāne cittasantānaṃ mejjhaṃ bhaveyya, suci, vodānaṃ, taṃ duṭṭhaṃ mejjhaṃ imināti dummejjhaṃ. Bālānaṃ bhāvoti bālyaṃ. Muyhatīti moho. Balavataro moho pamoho. Samantato muyhatīti sammoho. Vijjāya paṭipakkhabhāvato na vijjāti avijjā. Oghayogattho vuttoyeva. Thāmagataṭṭhena anusetīti anusayo. Cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti, abhibhavatīti pariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Hitaggahaṇābhāvena hitābhimukhaṃ gantuṃ na sakkoti, aññadatthu laṅgatiyevāti laṅgī; khañjatīti attho. Durugghāṭanaṭṭhena vā laṅgī. Yathā hi mahāpalighasaṅkhātā laṅgī durugghāṭā hoti, evamayampi laṅgī viyāti laṅgī. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Saṅgahavārasuññatavārāpi [P 0.0255] heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva atthato veditabbāti.

In wholesome and unwholesome actions, due to its perverse occurrence or due to the absence of grasping their true nature, not even a single action is directly evident to this delusion. Alternatively, delusion itself is not able to make any action directly evident; therefore, it is called 'that which has no directly evident action' (apaccakkhakamma). When this delusion does not arise, the stream of consciousness would be pure, clean, and bright; that pure mind-stream is corrupted by this delusion, and therefore it is called 'corrupted purity' (dummejjhaṃ). The state of fools is foolishness (bālyaṃ). One is deluded by it; therefore, it is delusion (moho). A stronger delusion is great delusion (pamoho). One is deluded all around by it; therefore, it is complete delusion (sammoho). Because it is the opposite of knowledge, it is not knowledge; therefore, it is ignorance (avijjā). The meaning of 'flood' and 'yoke' has already been stated. In the sense of having attained strength, it lies dormant (anuseti); therefore, it is a latent tendency (anusayo). It assails and overpowers the mind; therefore, it is an obsession (pariyuṭṭhānaṃ). Due to the absence of grasping what is beneficial, one is unable to go towards what is beneficial; on the contrary, one just limps (laṅgatiyeva); therefore, it is called 'that which limps' (laṅgī); the meaning is, one is lame (khañcati). Alternatively, it is a bolt (laṅgī) in the sense of being difficult to unfasten. For just as a bolt known as a great crossbar is difficult to unfasten, so too this delusion is like a bolt; therefore, it is called a bolt (laṅgī). The rest has a plain meaning. The sections on inclusion and emptiness should also be understood in terms of their meaning according to the method stated previously in the exposition on the wholesome.

Dutiyacittaṃ

The Second Consciousness

399. Dutiyacitte sasaṅkhārenāti padaṃ visesaṃ. Tampi heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Idaṃ pana cittaṃ kiñcāpi chasu ārammaṇesu somanassitassa lobhaṃ uppādetvā ‘satto satto’tiādinā nayena parāmasantassa uppajjati, tathāpi sasaṅkhārikattā sappayogena saupāyena uppajjanato – yadā [M 0.0297] kulaputto micchādiṭṭhikassa kulassa kumārikaṃ pattheti. Te ca ‘aññadiṭṭhikā tumhe’ti kumārikaṃ na denti. Athaññe ñātakā ‘yaṃ tumhe karotha tamevāyaṃ karissatī’ti dāpenti. So tehi saddhiṃ titthiye upasaṅkamati. Āditova vematiko hoti. Gacchante gacchante kāle etesaṃ kiriyā manāpāti laddhiṃ roceti, diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti – evarūpe kāle idaṃ labbhatīti veditabbaṃ.

399. In the second consciousness, the word `sasaṅkhārena` is the distinguishing feature. Its meaning is also as has been explained previously. However, although this consciousness arises in one who misapprehends with notions such as 'a being, a being,' having generated greed accompanied by joy in the six objects, nevertheless, because it is prompted, it arises with effort and with means. For instance, when a clansman desires the daughter of a family holding wrong views, and they do not give her, saying, 'You are of another view.' Then other relatives have them give her, saying, 'Whatever you do, he will do the same.' He approaches the sectarians with them. At first, he is doubtful. As time goes on, thinking, 'Their conduct is pleasing,' he approves of their doctrine and adopts their view. It should be understood that at such a time, this consciousness is obtained.

Yevāpanakesu [V 0.0295] panettha thinamiddhaṃ adhikaṃ. Tattha thinanatā ‘thinaṃ’. Middhanatā ‘middhaṃ’; anussāhasaṃhananatā asattivighāto cāti attho. Thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ. Tattha thinaṃ anussāhalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyavinodanarasaṃ, saṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Middhaṃ akammaññatālakkhaṇaṃ, onahanarasaṃ, līnabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ pacalāyikāniddāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Ubhayampi aratitandīvijambhitādīsu ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānanti.

Here, among the `yevāpanaka` factors, sloth and torpor are additional. Therein, the state of being slothful (thinanatā) is 'sloth' (thinaṃ); the state of being torpid (middhanatā) is 'torpor' (middhaṃ). The meaning of the former is lack of exertion and shrinking back, and of the latter, the fatigue from lack of power. Sloth and torpor together are 'sloth-and-torpor'. Therein, sloth has the characteristic of lack of exertion, the function of dispelling energy, and manifests as sinking. Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness, the function of enveloping, and manifests as shrinking, or alternatively, as nodding and sleepiness. Both have unwise attention to discontent, laziness, stretching, and so on, as their proximate cause.

Tatiyacittaṃ

The Third Consciousness

400. Tatiyaṃ chasu ārammaṇesu somanassitassa lobhaṃ uppādetvā ‘satto satto’tiādinā nayena aparāmasantassa nārāyaṇavirājanamallayuddhanaṭasamajjādīni passato manāpiyasaddasavanādipasutassa [P 0.0256] vā uppajjati. Idha mānena saddhiṃ pañca apaṇṇakaṅgāni honti. Tattha maññatīti ‘māno’. So unnatilakkhaṇo, sampaggaharaso, ketukamyatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, diṭṭhivippayuttalobhapadaṭṭhāno, ummādo viya daṭṭhabboti.

400. The third consciousness arises in one who, having generated greed with joy towards the six objects, while not wrongly grasping in the manner of 'a being, a being,' etc., is watching performances such as the splendid display of the deity Nārāyaṇa, wrestling matches, and gatherings of dancers, or is devoted to hearing pleasant sounds and so forth. Herein, there are five unfailing mental factors together with conceit. Therein, 'conceit' (māno) is so called because it conceives (maññati). It has the characteristic of loftiness, the function of uplifting associated states, it manifests as the desire to be like a banner, its proximate cause is greed dissociated from wrong view, and it should be regarded as being like madness.

Catutthacittaṃ

The Fourth Consciousness

402. Catutthaṃ vuttappakāresu eva ṭhānesu yadā sīse kheḷaṃ khipanti, pādapaṃsuṃ okiranti, tadā tassa pariharaṇatthaṃ saussāhena antarantarā olokentānaṃ rājanāṭakesu nikkhantesu ussāraṇāya vattamānāya tena tena chiddena olokentānañcāti evamādīsu ṭhānesu uppajjati. Idha [M 0.0298] pana thinamiddhehi saddhiṃ satta yevāpanakā honti. Ubhayatthāpi micchādiṭṭhi parihāyati. Taṃ ṭhapetvā sesānaṃ vasena dhammagaṇanā veditabbāti.

402. The fourth consciousness arises in the very situations of the kinds already mentioned. For instance, when they spit saliva on one's head or scatter dust from their feet, it arises in those who, for the purpose of avoiding it, look around from time to time with effort. And it arises in those who, when the king's dancers have come out and a clearing of the way is occurring, are peeking through this or that opening, and in other such situations. But here, there are seven `yevāpanaka` factors together with sloth and torpor. In both cases [the third and fourth consciousnesses], wrong view is absent. Setting that aside, the enumeration of states should be understood by way of the remaining ones.

Pañcamacittaṃ

The Fifth Consciousness

403. Pañcamaṃ chasu ārammaṇesu vedanāvasena majjhattassa lobhaṃ uppādetvā ‘satto satto’tiādinā nayena parāmasantassa uppajjati. Somanassaṭṭhāne panettha upekkhāvedanā hoti, pītipadaṃ parihāyati. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ paṭhamacittasadisameva.

403. The fifth consciousness arises in one who, being neutral by way of feeling towards the six objects, generates greed while grasping in the manner of 'a being, a being,' and so forth. Here, in the place of joy, there is equanimous feeling; the factor of zest is absent. All the rest of the explanation is just the same as that of the first consciousness.

Chaṭṭhacittādi

The Sixth Consciousness and so forth

409-412. Chaṭṭhasattamaṭṭhamānipi [V 0.0296] vedanaṃ parivattetvā pītipadañca hāpetvā dutiyatatiyacatutthesu vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Imesu aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatacittesu sahajātādhipati ārammaṇādhipatīti dvepi adhipatayo labbhanti.

The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses should also be understood in the very same way as explained for the second, third, and fourth, by changing the feeling and by removing the factor of zest. In these eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed, both predominances, that is, conascence predominance and object predominance, are obtained.

Navamacittaṃ

The Ninth Consciousness

413. Navamaṃ chasu ārammaṇesu domanassitassa paṭighaṃ uppādayato uppajjati. Tassa samayavavatthānavāre tāva duṭṭhu mano, hīnavedanattā vā kucchitaṃ manoti dummano; dummanassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Tena sahagatanti domanassasahagataṃ. Asampiyāyanabhāvena ārammaṇasmiṃ paṭihaññatīti paṭighaṃ. Tena sampayuttanti paṭighasampayuttaṃ.

413. The ninth consciousness arises in one who, having displeasure towards the six objects, generates aversion. First, in the section on the determination of its occasion: The mind is corrupted (duṭṭhu mano), therefore it is `dummana` ('afflicted mind'). Or, because of having an inferior feeling, the mind is contemptible (kucchitaṃ mano), therefore it is `dummana`. The state of `dummana` is `domanassa` (displeasure). 'Accompanied by that' (tena sahagataṃ) is therefore `domanassasahagataṃ` ('accompanied by displeasure'). It strikes against the object (ārammaṇasmiṃ paṭihaññati) with a state of not being dear (asampiyāyanabhāvena), therefore it is `paṭigha` (aversion). 'Associated with that' (tena sampayuttaṃ) is therefore `paṭighasampayuttaṃ` ('associated with aversion').

Dhammuddese [P 0.0257] tīsupi ṭhānesu domanassavedanāva āgatā. Tattha vedanāpadaṃ vuttameva. Tathā dukkhadomanassapadāni lakkhaṇādito pana aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ domanassaṃ, yathātathā vā aniṭṭhākārasambhogarasaṃ, cetasikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ekanteneva hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ.

In the exposition of states, only the feeling of displeasure is mentioned in all three places. Therein, the term 'feeling' has already been explained. Likewise the terms 'pain' and 'displeasure'. But as to the characteristics and so on: displeasure has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object; its function is the partaking of the undesirable aspect, whether it is actually so or not; its manifestation is a mental affliction; and its proximate cause is exclusively the heart-base.

Mūlakammapathesu yathā purimacittesu lobho hoti, abhijjhā hotīti āgataṃ, evaṃ doso hoti, byāpādo hotīti vuttaṃ. Tattha dussanti tena, sayaṃ vā dussati, dussanamattameva vā tanti doso [M 0.0299] so caṇḍikkalakkhaṇo pahaṭāsiviso viya, visappanaraso visanipāto viya, attano nissayadahanaraso vā dāvaggi viya, dussanapaccupaṭṭhāno laddhokāso viya sapatto, āghātavatthupadaṭṭhāno visasaṃsaṭṭhapūtimuttaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo.

In the sections on the roots and the courses of action, just as for the preceding consciousnesses it is stated, 'There is greed, there is covetousness,' so too it is said, 'There is hatred, there is ill will.' Therein, because associated states are corrupted by it, or because it itself is corrupted, or because it is merely corruption, it is therefore called dosa (hatred). It has the characteristic of ferocity, like a venomous snake that has been struck; it has the function of spreading, like a thunderbolt, or the function of burning its own support, like a forest fire; it manifests as corruption, like an enemy who has found an opportunity; and it has the grounds for resentment as its proximate cause, to be regarded as being like foul urine mixed with poison.

Byāpajjati tena cittaṃ, pūtibhāvaṃ upagacchati, byāpādayati vā vinayācārarūpasampattihitasukhādīnīti byāpādo. Atthato panesa dosoyeva. Idha padapaṭipāṭiyā ekūnatiṃsa padāni honti. Aggahitaggahaṇena cuddasa. Tesaṃ vasena savibhattikāvibhattikarāsibhedo veditabbo.

The mind is corrupted by it and reaches a state of putrefaction, or it destroys such good things as discipline, conduct, physical perfection, welfare, and happiness; therefore, it is byāpāda (ill will). In terms of its intrinsic nature, however, this is simply dosa. Here, in the sequence of terms, there are twenty-nine groups of states. By not taking what has already been taken, there are fourteen. By means of these, the distinction between the inflected and uninflected, and the classification into aggregates, should be understood.

Yevāpanakesu chandādhimokkhamanasikārauddhaccāni niyatāni. Issāmacchariyakukkuccesu pana [V 0.0297] aññatarena saddhiṃ pañca pañca hutvāpi uppajjanti. Evamepi tayo dhammā aniyatayevāpanakā nāma. Tesu issatīti ‘issā’. Sā parasampattīnaṃ usūyanalakkhaṇā, tattheva anabhiratirasā, tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, parasampattipadaṭṭhānā. Saṃyojananti daṭṭhabbā. Maccherabhāvo ‘macchariyaṃ’. Taṃ laddhānaṃ vā labhitabbānaṃ vā attano sampattīnaṃ nigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ, tāsaṃyeva parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaakkhamanarasaṃ, saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ [P 0.0258] kaṭukañcukatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, attasampattipadaṭṭhānaṃ. Cetaso virūpabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukataṃ. Tassa bhāvo ‘kukkuccaṃ’. Taṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ, katākatānusocanarasaṃ, vippaṭisārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, katākatapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Dāsabyaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva uddesavāre viseso.

Among the yevāpanaka factors, desire, decision, attention, and restlessness are fixed. Envy, stinginess, and worry, however, can also arise along with one or another of these, forming groups of five. Thus, these three states are called unfixed yevāpanaka. Among them, issā (envy) has the characteristic of jealousy towards the prosperity of others, its function is not delighting in it, its manifestation is turning away from it, and its proximate cause is the prosperity of others. It should be regarded as a fetter. Macchariya (stinginess) is the state of being miserly. It has the characteristic of concealing one's own prosperity, whether obtained or obtainable; its function is intolerance of it being shared with others; its manifestation is miserliness or being like a bitter taste; and its proximate cause is one's own prosperity. It should be regarded as a distortion of the mind. A contemptible deed is kukata; the state of that is kukkucca (worry). It has the characteristic of subsequent regret, its function is sorrowing over what was done and not done, its manifestation is remorse, and its proximate cause is what was done and not done. It should be regarded as being like slavery. This, for now, is the specific explanation in the summary section.

415. Niddesavāre vedanāniddese asātaṃ sātapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbaṃ.

415. In the exposition section, in the exposition of feeling, 'unpleasant' should be understood as the opposite of 'pleasant'.

418. Dosaniddese dussatīti doso. Dussanāti dussanākāro. Dussitattanti dussitabhāvo. Pakatibhāvavijahanaṭṭhena byāpajjanaṃ byāpatti. Byāpajjanāti byāpajjanākāro. Virujjhatīti virodho. Punappunaṃ virujjhatīti paṭivirodho. Viruddhākārapaṭiviruddhākāravasena vā idaṃ vuttaṃ. Caṇḍiko vuccati caṇḍo, thaddhapuggalo; tassa bhāvo caṇḍikkaṃ. Na etena suropitaṃ vacanaṃ hoti, duruttaṃ aparipuṇṇameva hotīti asuropo. Kuddhakāle hi paripuṇṇavacanaṃ nāma natthi. Sacepi kassaci hoti taṃ appamāṇaṃ. Apare [M 0.0300] pana assujananaṭṭhena assuropanato assuropoti vadanti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ, somanassassāpi assujananato. Heṭṭhā vuttaattamanatāpaṭipakkhato na attamanatāti anattamanatā. Sā pana yasmā cittasseva, na sattassa, tasmā cittassāti vuttaṃ. Sesamettha saṅgahasuññatavāresu ca heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

418. In the exposition of hatred: because 'it corrupts' (dussati), it is dosa. 'Corrupting' (dussanā) is the manner of corrupting. 'The state of being corrupted' (dussitatta) is the state of a corrupted mind. 'Degradation' (byāpatti) is the falling into corruption, in the sense of abandoning the natural state. 'Degrading' (byāpajjanā) is the manner of falling into corruption. Because 'it opposes' (virujjhati), it is 'opposition' (virodho). Because 'it opposes again and again' (punappunaṃ virujjhati), it is 'repeated opposition' (paṭivirodho). Or, this is stated by way of the manner of opposing and the manner of repeatedly opposing. A harsh, stubborn person is called a caṇḍika; his state is caṇḍikka (fierceness). Because of this, speech is not well-formed; it is only ill-spoken and incomplete, hence it is called asuropa. For, at a time of anger, there is no such thing as complete speech. Even if it occurs for someone, that is not the standard. Others, however, say it is assuropa because it generates tears, in the sense of generating tears. That is not the reason, because pleasant mental feeling also generates tears. Because it is the opposite of the satisfaction (attamanatā) mentioned before, it is 'not satisfaction' (na attamanatā), thus it is 'displeasure' (anattamanatā). And since that displeasure is of the mind only, not of a being, it is therefore said 'of the mind'. The rest here, and in the sections on inclusion and emptiness, should be understood in the same way as stated before.

Dasamacittaṃ

The Tenth Consciousness

421. Dasamaṃ sasaṅkhārattā parehi ussāhitassa vā, paresaṃ vā aparādhaṃ sāritassa, sayameva vā paresaṃ aparādhaṃ anussaritvā kujjhamānassa uppajjati.

The tenth consciousness, being prompted, arises in one who is becoming angry: either having been encouraged by others, or having been reminded of the faults of others, or having recollected the faults of others by oneself.

Idhāpi padapaṭipāṭiyā ekūnatiṃsa, aggahitaggahaṇena ca cuddaseva padāni honti. Yevāpanakesu [V 0.0298] pana thinamiddhampi labbhati. Tasmā ettha vinā issāmacchariyakukkuccehi cattāri apaṇṇakaṅgāni thinamiddhanti ime cha issādīnaṃ uppattikāle tesu aññatarena saddhiṃ satta yevāpanakā ekakkhaṇe uppajjanti. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ sabbavāresu navamasadisameva. Imesu pana dvīsu domanassacittesu sahajātādhipatiyeva [P 0.0259] labbhati, na ārammaṇādhipati. Na hi kuddho kiñci garuṃ karotīti.

421. Here too, in the sequence of terms, there are twenty-nine terms; and by not taking what has already been taken, there are only fourteen. Among the yevāpanaka factors, however, sloth and torpor are also obtained. Therefore, herein, the four invariable factors and sloth-and-torpor—these six—can arise in a single moment together with any one of envy, stinginess, or worry, making seven yevāpanaka factors. The rest, in all sections, is just like the ninth consciousness. In these two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure, however, only co-nascent dominance is obtained, not object-dominance. For an angry person does not hold anything as important.

Ekādasamacittaṃ

The Eleventh Consciousness

422. Ekādasamaṃ chasu ārammaṇesu vedanāvasena majjhattassa kaṅkhāpavattikāle uppajjati. Tassa samayavavatthāne vicikicchāsampayuttanti padaṃ apubbaṃ. Tassattho – vicikicchāya sampayuttanti vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ. Dhammuddese ‘vicikicchā hotī’ti padameva viseso. Tattha vigatā cikicchāti vicikicchā. Sabhāvaṃ vā vicinanto etāya kicchati kilamatīti vicikicchā. Sā saṃsayalakkhaṇā, kampanarasā, anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā anekaṃsagāhapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānā. Paṭipattiantarāyakarāti daṭṭhabbā.

The eleventh consciousness arises in relation to the six sense-objects, being neutral by way of feeling, at the time of the occurrence of doubt. In its section on the determination of the occasion, the term 'associated with doubt' (vicikicchāsampayutta) is a new one. Its meaning is: 'associated with doubt' (vicikicchāya sampayutta). In the enumeration of states, the term 'there is doubt' (vicikicchā hoti) is the specific point. Therein, vicikicchā is so called because 'remedy is departed' (vigatā cikicchā). Or, it is vicikicchā because while investigating the true nature of things, one is troubled and wearied by it. It has the characteristic of doubt, the function of wavering, the manifestation of indecisiveness or of grasping multiple sides, and has unwise attention as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as an obstacle to practice.

Idha padapaṭipāṭiyā tevīsati padāni honti. Aggahitaggahaṇena cuddasa. Tesaṃ vasena savibhattikāvibhattikarāsivinicchayo veditabbo. Manasikāro uddhaccanti dveyeva yevāpanakā.

Here, in the sequence of terms, there are twenty-three terms. By not taking what has already been taken, there are fourteen. Based on these, the determination of the groups of inflected and uninflected terms should be understood. Attention and restlessness are the only two yevāpanaka factors.

424. Niddesavārassa [M 0.0301] cittassekaggatāniddese yasmā idaṃ dubbalaṃ cittaṃ pavattiṭṭhitimattakamevettha hoti, tasmā ‘saṇṭhitī’tiādīni avatvā cittassa ‘ṭhitī’ti ekameva padaṃ vuttaṃ. Teneva ca kāraṇena uddesavārepi ‘samādhindriya’ntiādi na vuttaṃ.

422. In the exposition of one-pointedness of mind in the Exposition Section, because this consciousness is weak, there is here only a mere occurrence and duration. Therefore, without saying 'stability' (saṇṭhiti) and so forth, only the single term 'duration of the mind' (cittassa ṭhiti) is stated. And for that very reason, in the Enumeration Section as well, 'faculty of concentration' (samādhindriya) and so forth are not stated.

425. Vicikicchāniddese kaṅkhanavasena kaṅkhā. Kaṅkhāya āyanāti kaṅkhāyanā. Purimakaṅkhā hi uttarakaṅkhaṃ āneti nāma. Ākāravasena vā etaṃ vuttaṃ. Kaṅkhāsamaṅgicittaṃ kaṅkhāya āyitattā kaṅkhāyitaṃ nāma. Tassa bhāvo kaṅkhāyitattaṃ. Vimatīti namati. Vicikicchā vuttatthā eva. Kampanaṭṭhena dvidhā eḷayatīti dveḷhakaṃ. Paṭipattinivāraṇena dvidhāpatho viyāti dvedhāpatho. ‘Niccaṃ nu kho idaṃ, aniccaṃ nu kho’tiādipavattiyā ekasmiṃ ākāre saṇṭhātuṃ asamatthatāya samantato [P 0.0260] setīti saṃsayo. Ekaṃsaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthatāya na ekaṃsaggāhoti anekaṃsaggāho[V 0.0299]. Nicchetuṃ asakkontī ārammaṇato osakkatīti āsappanā. Ogāhituṃ asakkontī parisamantato sappatīti parisappanā. Pariyogāhituṃ asamatthatāya apariyogāhanā. Nicchayavasena ārammaṇe pavattituṃ asamatthatāya thambhitattaṃ; cittassa thaddhabhāvoti attho. Vicikicchā hi uppajjitvā cittaṃ thaddhaṃ karoti. Yasmā panesā uppajjamānā ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā manaṃ vilikhantī viya, tasmā manovilekhoti vuttā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva.

425. In the explanation of doubt (vicikicchā): by way of wavering (kaṅkhanavasena), it is kaṅkhā. It is a cause of doubt (kaṅkhāya āyanā), thus kaṅkhāyanā. For a preceding doubt indeed brings about a subsequent doubt. Or, this is stated by way of its manner. A mind endowed with doubt is called kaṅkhāyitaṃ because it is caused by doubt. Its state is kaṅkhāyitattaṃ. Vimati means 'not knowing' (na mati). Vicikicchā has the meaning already stated. Because it makes the mind waver in two ways (dvidhā eḷayati) with the meaning of trembling, it is dveḷhakaṃ. Because it obstructs practice, it is like a forked path (dvidhāpatho viya), thus dvedhāpatho. Because of occurring in such ways as 'Is this permanent or is it impermanent?', and due to the inability to stand firm on one aspect, it lies all around (samantato seti), thus it is saṃsayo. Due to the inability to grasp one side, it is 'not a one-sided grasp' (na ekaṃsaggāho), thus anekaṃsaggāho. Being unable to decide, it withdraws from the object, thus it is āsappanā. Being unable to penetrate, it creeps all around, thus it is parisappanā. Due to the inability to fully penetrate, it is apariyogāhanā. Due to the inability to proceed with decisiveness in the object, there is stiffness (thambhitattaṃ); the meaning is the stiff state of the mind. For doubt, having arisen, makes the mind stiff. Furthermore, since this doubt, while arising, having grasped the object, is as if scratching the mind, it is called manovilekha (mental scratching). The rest everywhere has a plain meaning.

Dvādasamacittaṃ

The Twelfth Consciousness

427. Dvādasamassa samayavavatthāne uddhaccena sampayuttanti uddhaccasampayuttaṃ. Idañhi cittaṃ chasu ārammaṇesu vedanāvasena majjhattaṃ hutvā uddhataṃ hoti. Idha dhammuddese ‘vicikicchā’-ṭhāne ‘uddhaccaṃ hotī’ti āgataṃ. Padapaṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhavīsati padāni honti. Aggahitaggahaṇena cuddasa. Tesaṃ vasena savibhattikāvibhattikarāsividhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Adhimokkho manasikāroti dveyeva yevāpanakā.

427. In the section on the determination of the occasion of the twelfth [unwholesome consciousness]: it is called 'associated with restlessness' because it is associated with restlessness (uddhaccena sampayuttaṃ). Indeed, this consciousness, being neutral by way of feeling with regard to the six sense-objects, becomes agitated. Here, in the section on the enumeration of phenomena, in the place of 'doubt,' it is stated, 'there is restlessness.' In the sequence of terms, there are twenty-eight terms. By taking what has not yet been taken, there are fourteen. By means of them, the method concerning inflected terms, uninflected terms, and grouped terms should be understood. Determination and attention—these two alone are the particular concomitants (yevāpanakā).

429. Niddesavārassa uddhaccaniddese cittassāti na sattassa, na posassa. Uddhaccanti uddhatākāro. Na vūpasamoti avūpasamo. Ceto vikkhipatīti [M 0.0302] cetasovikkhepo. Bhantattaṃ cittassāti cittassa bhantabhāvo, bhantayānabhantagoṇādīni viya. Iminā ekārammaṇasmiṃyeva vipphandanaṃ kathitaṃ. Uddhaccañhi ekārammaṇe vipphandati, vicikicchā nānārammaṇe. Sesaṃ sabbavāresu heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

429. In the exposition of restlessness in the section of exposition: 'of the consciousness' means not of a being, not of a person. 'Restlessness' means the characteristic of agitation. 'It is not calmed'; therefore, it is 'uncalmed'. 'It scatters the mind'; therefore, it is 'mental distraction'. 'Agitation of the consciousness' means the agitated state of the consciousness, like agitated vehicles, agitated oxen, and so on. By this, agitation on a single object alone is spoken of. Indeed, restlessness is agitated on a single object, while doubt is agitated on various objects. The remainder in all sections should be understood in the very manner stated previously.

Idāni imasmiṃ cittadvaye pakiṇṇakavinicchayo hoti. ‘Ārammaṇe pavaṭṭanakacittāni nāma katī’ti? Hi vutte ‘imāneva dve’ti vattabbaṃ. Tattha vicikicchāsahagataṃ [P 0.0261] ekantena pavaṭṭati, uddhaccasahagataṃ pana laddhādhimokkhattā laddhapatiṭṭhaṃ pavaṭṭati. Yathā hi vaṭṭacaturassesu dvīsu maṇīsu pabbhāraṭṭhāne pavaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhesu vaṭṭamaṇi ekanteneva pavaṭṭati, caturasso patiṭṭhāya patiṭṭhāya pavaṭṭati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sabbesupi hīnādibhedo na uddhaṭo, sabbesaṃ ekantahīnattā. Sahajātādhipati labbhamānopi na uddhaṭo, heṭṭhā dassitanayattā. Ñāṇābhāvato panettha vīmaṃsādhipati nāma natthi. Pacchimadvaye sesopi natthi eva. Kasmā? Kañci dhammaṃ dhuraṃ katvā anuppajjanato, paṭṭhāne ca paṭisiddhato.

Now, in this pair of consciousnesses, there is a miscellaneous determination. When it is asked, 'How many consciousnesses are there that proceed on an object?' it should be said, 'Just these two.' Therein, the consciousness accompanied by doubt proceeds exclusively, but the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, because it has obtained determination, proceeds having obtained a footing. Just as when two gems, one round and one square, are set rolling on a slope and released, the round gem rolls exclusively, while the square one rolls, establishing a footing again and again; this analogy should be understood as being thus accomplished. For all [unwholesome consciousnesses], the distinction of inferior, etc., is not pointed out, because all are exclusively inferior. Although the conascence-predominance condition is obtainable, it is not pointed out, because of the method shown previously. Here, due to the absence of knowledge, there is no predominance by investigation. In the final pair, the remaining [predominance condition] also does not exist at all. Why? Because it does not arise having made some phenomenon a leader, and because it is prohibited in the Paṭṭhāna.

Imehi [V 0.0300] pana dvādasahipi akusalacittehi kamme āyūhite, ṭhapetvā uddhaccasahagataṃ, sesāni ekādaseva paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhanti. Vicikicchāsahagate aladdhādhimokkhe dubbalepi paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhamāne uddhaccasahagataṃ laddhādhimokkhaṃ balavaṃ kasmā nākaḍḍhatīti? Dassanena pahātabbābhāvato. Yadi hi ākaḍḍheyya ‘dassanenapahātabba’-padavibhaṅge āgaccheyya, tasmā, ṭhapetvā taṃ, sesāni ekādasa ākaḍḍhanti. Tesu hi yena kenaci kamme āyūhite tāya cetanāya catūsu apāyesu paṭisandhi hoti. Akusalavipākesu ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātuupekkhāsahagatāya paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhāti. Itarassāpi ettheva paṭisandhidānaṃ bhaveyya. Yasmā panetaṃ natthi, tasmā ‘dassanenapahātabba’-padavibhaṅge nāgatanti.

Furthermore, when kamma has been generated by these twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, setting aside the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, only the remaining eleven can draw forth rebirth-linking. When the consciousness accompanied by doubt, not having obtained determination and being weak, can draw forth rebirth-linking, why can the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, which has obtained determination and is strong, not draw it forth? Because it is not something to be abandoned by vision. Indeed, if it were to draw forth rebirth-linking, it would appear in the Vibhaṅga's analysis of the term 'to be abandoned by vision'. Therefore, setting that aside, the remaining eleven draw forth rebirth-linking. Indeed, among them, when kamma has been generated by any one of those consciousnesses, through that volition, rebirth-linking occurs in the four planes of misery. Among the unwholesome results, one takes rebirth-linking with the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity. For the other one too, the giving of rebirth-linking would occur right here. But since this does not exist, therefore it does not appear in the Vibhaṅga's analysis of the term 'to be abandoned by vision'.

Akusalā dhammātipadassa vaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the term 'unwholesome phenomena' is concluded.

Abyākatapadaṃ

The Term 'Indeterminate'

Ahetukakusalavipāko

Rootless Wholesome Resultant

431. Idāni [M 0.0303] abyākatapadaṃ bhājetvā dassetuṃ katame dhammā abyākatātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha catubbidhaṃ abyākataṃ – vipākaṃ kiriyaṃ rūpaṃ nibbānanti. Tesu vipākābyākataṃ. Vipākābyākatepi kusalavipākaṃ. Tasmimpi parittavipākaṃ. Tasmimpi ahetukaṃ. Tasmimpi pañcaviññāṇaṃ. Tasmimpi dvārapaṭipāṭiyā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ[P 0.0262]. Tassāpi, ṭhapetvā dvārārammaṇādisādhāraṇapaccayaṃ, asādhāraṇakammapaccayavaseneva uppattiṃ dīpetuṃ kāmāvacarassa kusalassa kammassa katattātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha katattāti katakāraṇā. Upacitattāti ācitattā, vaḍḍhitakāraṇā. Cakkhuviññāṇanti kāraṇabhūtassa cakkhussa viññāṇaṃ, cakkhuto vā pavattaṃ, cakkhusmiṃ vā nissitaṃ viññāṇanti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Parato sotaviññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

431. Now, in order to analyze and explain the indeterminate term, the passage beginning with 'Which states are indeterminate?' was introduced. Therein, the indeterminate is fourfold: resultant, functional, material form, and Nibbāna. Among these is the resultant indeterminate. Within the resultant indeterminate is the wholesome resultant. Within that is the sense-sphere resultant. Within that is the rootless. Within that are the five sense-consciousnesses. Within those, following the order of the doors, is eye-consciousness. To explain its arising solely by the power of the uncommon condition of kamma—setting aside common conditions such as door and object—the passage beginning 'due to a wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere having been done...' was stated. Therein, 'due to having been done' means for the reason that it was done. 'Due to having been accumulated' means because it was amassed, or for the reason that it was increased. 'Eye-consciousness' means the consciousness of the eye-sensitivity which is its cause; or, the consciousness that proceeds from the eye; or, the consciousness that is dependent on the eye—thus it is eye-consciousness. For ear-consciousness and so on hereafter, the method is the same.

Tattha cakkhusannissitarūpavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, rūpamattārammaṇarasaṃ, rūpābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ[V 0.0301], rūpārammaṇāya kiriyamanodhātuyā apagamapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Parato āgatāni sotādisannissitasaddādivijānanalakkhaṇāni sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni saddādimattārammaṇarasāni, saddādiabhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāni, saddādiārammaṇānaṃ kiriyamanodhātūnaṃ apagamapadaṭṭhānāni.

Therein, eye-consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing a form-object while being dependent on the eye-sensitivity; its function is to take merely a form-object as its object; its manifestation is the state of facing a form-object; its proximate cause is the cessation of the functional mind-element that has a form-object as its object. The ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses that come after have the characteristic of cognizing sound-objects, etc., while being dependent on the ear-sensitivity, etc.; their function is to take merely a sound-object, etc., as their object; their manifestation is the state of facing a sound-object, etc.; their proximate cause is the cessation of the functional mind-elements that have a sound-object, etc., as their object.

Idha padapaṭipāṭiyā dasa padāni honti. Aggahitaggahaṇena satta. Tesu pañca avibhattikāni, dve savibhattikāni. Tesu cittaṃ phassapañcakavasena ceva indriyavasena ca dvīsu ṭhānesu vibhattiṃ gacchati, vedanā phassapañcakajhānaṅgaindriyavasena tīsuyeva. Rāsayopi imeva tayo honti. Yevāpanako eko manasikāro eva.

Here, by the order of the terms, there are ten terms. By way of including what has not been included, there are seven. Among these, five are unanalyzed, and two are analyzed. Among those, consciousness is analyzed in two places: by way of the contact-pentad and by way of the faculties. Feeling is analyzed in three places: by way of the contact-pentad, the jhāna factors, and the faculties. The groups are also just these three. The 'yevāpanaka' factor is only the one, attention.

436. Niddesavāre cakkhuviññāṇaṃ paṇḍaranti vatthuto vuttaṃ. Kusalañhi attano parisuddhatāya paṇḍaraṃ nāma, akusalaṃ bhavaṅganissandena, vipākaṃ vatthupaṇḍarattā.

436. In the exposition section, eye-consciousness is called 'white' with reference to its basis. For the wholesome is called 'white' due to its own purity, the unwholesome due to the outflow of the life-continuum, and the resultant due to the purity of its basis.

439. Cittassekaggatāniddese cittassa ṭhitīti ekameva padaṃ vuttaṃ. Idampi hi dubbalaṃ cittaṃ pavattiṭṭhitimattamevettha labbhati, ‘saṇṭhitiavaṭṭhiti’-bhāvaṃ [M 0.0304] pāpuṇituṃ na sakkoti. Saṅgahavāre jhānaṅgamaggaṅgāni na uddhaṭāni. Kasmā? Vitakkapacchimakañhi jhānaṃ nāma, hetupacchimako maggo nāma. Pakatiyā avitakkacitte jhānaṅgaṃ na labbhati, ahetukacitte ca maggaṅgāni. Tasmā idha ubhayampi [P 0.0263] na uddhaṭaṃ. Saṅkhārakkhandhopettha caturaṅgikoyeva bhājito. Suññatavāro pākatikoyeva. Sotaviññāṇādiniddesāpi imināva nayena veditabbā.

439. In the exposition of one-pointedness of mind, only the single term 'stability of mind' is stated. For this is a weak consciousness; herein, only the mere stability of its occurrence is obtained; it is unable to reach the state of firm stability and steadfastness. In the summary section, the jhāna factors and path factors are not extracted. Why? Because jhāna is that which has initial application as its final constituent, and the path is that which has a root as its final constituent. By nature, a jhāna factor is not obtained in a consciousness without initial application, and path factors are not obtained in a rootless consciousness. Therefore, neither is extracted here. Herein, the aggregate of formations is also analyzed as having only four factors. The section on emptiness is as in the original. The expositions of ear-consciousness and so on should be understood by this same method.

Kevalañhi cakkhuviññāṇādīsu ‘upekkhā’ bhājitā, kāyaviññāṇe ‘sukha’nti, ayamettha viseso. Sopi ca ghaṭṭanavasena hotīti veditabbo. Cakkhudvārādīsu hi catūsu upādārūpameva upādārūpaṃ ghaṭṭeti, upādārūpeyeva upādārūpaṃ ghaṭṭente paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃso balavā na hoti. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇīnaṃ upari cattāro kappāsapicupiṇḍe ṭhapetvā picupiṇḍeheva pahatakālo viya phuṭṭhamattameva hoti. Vedanā majjhattaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Kāyadvāre pana bahiddhā mahābhūtārammaṇaṃ ajjhattikakāyapasādaṃ ghaṭṭetvā pasādapaccayesu mahābhūtesu paṭihaññati. Yathā adhikaraṇīmatthake kappāsapicupiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā kūṭena paharantassa kappāsapicupiṇḍaṃ chinditvā kūṭaṃ [V 0.0302] adhikaraṇiṃ gaṇhatīti, nighaṃso balavā hoti, evameva paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃso balavā hoti. Iṭṭhe ārammaṇe sukhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, aniṭṭhe dukkhasahagataṃ.

However, in eye-consciousness and so on, 'equanimity' is analyzed, while in body-consciousness, 'pleasure' is analyzed—this is the distinction herein. And it should be known that this occurs by way of impact. For in the four doors beginning with the eye-door, derived material form itself strikes derived material form; when derived material form strikes derived material form, the friction of the counter-impact is not strong. It is like the time when four cotton balls are placed upon four anvils and struck with cotton balls themselves; there is only mere contact. The feeling remains in a neutral state. At the body-door, however, an external great-element-object strikes the internal body-sensitivity and is struck back upon the great elements which are the conditions for that sensitivity. Just as when one places a cotton ball on top of an anvil and strikes it with a hammer, the hammer, having penetrated the cotton ball, makes contact with the anvil, so the friction is strong. In the same way, the friction of the counter-impact is strong. When the object is desirable, body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure arises; when it is undesirable, body-consciousness accompanied by pain arises.

Imesaṃ pana pañcannaṃ cittānaṃ vatthudvārārammaṇāni nibaddhāneva honti, vatthādisaṅkamanaṃ nāmettha natthi. Kusalavipākacakkhuviññāṇañhi cakkhupasādaṃ vatthuṃ katvā iṭṭhe ca iṭṭhamajjhatte ca catusamuṭṭhānikarūpārammaṇe dassanakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ cakkhudvāre ṭhatvā vipaccati. Sotaviññāṇādīni sotapasādādīni vatthuṃ katvā iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattesu saddādīsu savanaghāyanasāyanaphusanakiccāni sādhayamānāni sotadvārādīsu ṭhatvā vipaccanti. Saddo panettha dvisamuṭṭhānikoyeva hoti.

Furthermore, for these five consciousnesses, the basis, door, and object are indeed fixed; there is no such thing as a transference of basis and so on. For wholesome resultant eye-consciousness, having made the eye-sensitivity its basis, ripens while standing at the eye-door, accomplishing the function of seeing in relation to a form-object—originated from four causes—that is desirable or moderately desirable. Ear-consciousness and the others, having made ear-sensitivity and so on their basis, ripen while standing at the ear-door and so on, accomplishing the functions of hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching in relation to sound-objects and so on that are desirable or moderately desirable. Herein, however, the sound-object is of only twofold origin.

455. Manodhātuniddese sabhāvasuññatanissattaṭṭhena manoyeva dhātu manodhātu. Sā cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ anantaraṃ rūpādivijānanalakkhaṇā, rūpādīnaṃ sampaṭicchanarasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cakkhuviññāṇādiapagamapadaṭṭhānā[P 0.0264]. Idha dhammuddese dvādasa padāni honti. Aggahitaggahaṇena [M 0.0305] nava. Tesu satta avibhattikāni dve savibhattikāni. Adhimokkho manasikāroti dve yevāpanakā. Vitakkaniddeso abhiniropanaṃ pāpetvā ṭhapito. Yasmā panetaṃ cittaṃ neva kusalaṃ nākusalaṃ, tasmā sammāsaṅkappoti vā micchāsaṅkappoti vā na vuttaṃ. Saṅgahavāre labbhamānampi jhānaṅgaṃ pañcaviññāṇasote patitvā gatanti. Maggaṅgaṃ pana na labbhatiyevāti na uddhaṭaṃ. Suññatavāro pākatikoyeva. Imassa cittassa vatthu nibaddhaṃ hadayavatthumeva hoti. Dvārārammaṇāni anibaddhāni. Tattha kiñcāpi dvārārammaṇāni saṅkamanti, ṭhānaṃ pana ekaṃ. Sampaṭicchanakiccameva hetaṃ hoti. Idañhi pañcadvāre pañcasu ārammaṇesu sampaṭicchanaṃ hutvā vipaccati. Kusalavipākesu cakkhuviññāṇādīsu niruddhesu taṃsamanantarā tāneva ṭhānappattāni rūpārammaṇādīni sampaṭicchati.

455. In the exposition of the mind-element, because it is in the sense of being empty of own-nature, devoid of a self, and not a living being, the mind-element is the element that is mere knowing. It has the characteristic of cognizing forms, etc., immediately after eye-consciousness, etc. It has the function of receiving forms, etc. It is manifested as that state. It has the cessation of eye-consciousness, etc., as its proximate cause. Here in the exposition of states, there are twelve terms. By way of comprehensive inclusion, there are nine terms. Among these, seven are undivided and two are divided. Decision and attention—these two are yevāpanaka factors. The exposition of thought is established having brought it to the point of application. Since this consciousness is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is not called either right thought or wrong thought. In the section on inclusion, although the jhāna factor is obtainable, it is not extracted because it has fallen into and passed along with the stream of the five consciousnesses. But the path factor is not obtainable at all, hence it is not extracted. The section on emptiness is just as it is by nature. The base of this consciousness is fixed; it is only the heart-base. The doors and objects are unfixed. Therein, although the doors and objects shift, the location is one. For this has only the function of receiving. Indeed, this ripens by becoming the receiving of the five objects at the five doors. When wholesome resultant eye-consciousness, etc., have ceased, immediately after them, it receives those very same forms, etc., which have arrived at their position.

469. Manoviññāṇadhātuniddesesu paṭhamamanoviññāṇadhātuyaṃ ‘pīti’padaṃ adhikaṃ. Vedanāpi ‘somanassa’-vedanā hoti. Ayañhi iṭṭhārammaṇasmiṃyeva pavattati. Dutiyamanoviññāṇadhātu iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇe. Tasmā tattha ‘upekkhā’ vedanā hotīti. Padāni manodhātuniddesasadisāneva. Ubhayatthāpi pañcaviññāṇasote patitvā gatattāyeva jhānaṅgāni na uddhaṭāni. Maggaṅgāni alābhatoyeva. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Lakkhaṇādito panesā duvidhāpi manoviññāṇadhātu [V 0.0303] ahetukavipākā, chaḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā, santīraṇādirasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

469. In the expositions of the mind-consciousness element, in the first mind-consciousness element, the term 'pīti' is additional. The feeling is also pleasant mental feeling. For this arises only in relation to a desirable object. The second mind-consciousness element arises in relation to a desirable or neutral object. Therefore, there the feeling is equanimity. The terms are just like those in the exposition of the mind-element. In both cases as well, the jhāna factors are not extracted precisely because they have fallen into and passed along with the stream of the five consciousnesses. The path factors are not extracted precisely because they are not obtained. The remainder in all sections should be understood in the very way that has been stated. Furthermore, from the perspective of characteristic and so on, these two types of mind-consciousness element, which are rootless resultants, should be understood as having the characteristic of cognizing the six objects, having the function of investigating and so on, manifesting as that state, and having the heart-base as their proximate cause.

Tattha paṭhamā dvīsu ṭhānesu vipaccati. Sā hi pañcadvāre kusalavipākacakkhuviññāṇādianantaraṃ, vipākamanodhātuyā taṃ ārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchitvā niruddhāya, tasmiṃ yevārammaṇe santīraṇakiccaṃ sādhayamānā pañcasu dvāresu ṭhatvā vipaccati. Chasu dvāresu pana balavārammaṇe [P 0.0265] tadārammaṇā hutvā vipaccati. Kathaṃ? Yathā hi caṇḍasote, tiriyaṃ nāvāya gacchantiyā, udakaṃ chijjitvā thokaṃ ṭhānaṃ nāvaṃ anubandhitvā yathāsotameva gacchati, evameva chasu dvāresu balavārammaṇe palobhayamāne āpāthagate javanaṃ javati. Tasmiṃ javite bhavaṅgassa vāro. Idaṃ pana cittaṃ bhavaṅgassa vāraṃ adatvā javanena gahitārammaṇaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ dve cittavāre pavattitvā bhavaṅgameva [M 0.0306] otarati. Gavakkhandhe nadiṃ tarantepi evameva upamā vitthāretabbā. Evamesā yaṃ javanena gahitārammaṇaṃ tasseva gahitattā tadārammaṇaṃ nāma hutvā vipaccati.

Therein, the first mind-consciousness element ripens in two instances. For, at the five doors, immediately after wholesome resultant eye-consciousness and so on, when the resultant mind-element, having received that object, has ceased, this consciousness ripens by standing at the five doors while accomplishing the function of investigating that very object. Moreover, at the six doors, in the case of a strong object, it ripens by becoming registering-consciousness. How? Just as in a strong current, when a boat is going across, the water, having been cut, follows the boat for a short distance and then goes along with the current itself; even so, at the six doors, when a strong object, having come into range, is enticing, the impulsion runs. When that impulsion has run, it is the turn of the life-continuum. But this consciousness, not giving the turn to the life-continuum, takes the object taken by the impulsion and, after arising for one or two thought-moments, sinks back into the life-continuum itself. The simile should be expanded in the same way also in the case of a herd of cattle crossing a river. Thus, because this consciousness takes that very object which was taken by the impulsion, it becomes what is called 'registering-consciousness' and ripens.

Dutiyā pana pañcasu ṭhānesu vipaccati. Kathaṃ? Manussaloke tāva jaccandhajaccabadhirajaccaeḷajaccummattakaubhatobyañjanakanapuṃsakānaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle paṭisandhi hutvā vipaccati. Paṭisandhiyā vītivattāya yāvatāyukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā vipaccati. Iṭṭhamajjhatte pañcārammaṇavīthiyā santīraṇaṃ hutvā, balavārammaṇe chasu dvāresu tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā, maraṇakāle cuti hutvāti imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu vipaccatīti.

The second, however, ripens in five instances. How? First, in the human world, at the time of taking rebirth-linking for those born blind, born deaf, born mute, born insane, those with both sexual characteristics, and eunuchs, it ripens by becoming the rebirth-linking. When rebirth-linking has passed, for as long as life lasts, it ripens by becoming the life-continuum. It ripens by becoming investigating-consciousness in a five-object process with a desirable or neutral object; by becoming registering-consciousness at the six doors with a strong object; and by becoming death-consciousness at the time of death. Thus, it ripens in these five instances.

Manoviññāṇadhātudvayaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The two mind-consciousness elements are concluded.

Aṭṭhamahāvipākacittavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Eight Great Resultant Consciousnesses

498. Idāni aṭṭhamahāvipākacittāni dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā abyākatātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha pāḷiyaṃ nayamattaṃ dassetvā sabbavārā saṃkhittā. Tesaṃ attho heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yo panettha viseso taṃ dassetuṃ alobho abyākatamūlantiādi vuttaṃ. Yampi na vuttaṃ [V 0.0304] taṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – yo hi kāmāvacarakusalesu kammadvārakammapathapuññakiriyavatthubhedo vutto so idha natthi. Kasmā? Aviññattijanakato avipākadhammato tathā appavattito ca. Yāpi tā yevāpanakesu [P 0.0266] karuṇāmuditā vuttā, tā sattārammaṇattā vipākesu na santi. Ekantaparittārammaṇāni hi kāmāvacaravipākāni. Na kevalañca karuṇāmuditā, viratiyopettha na santi. ‘Pañca sikkhāpadāni kusalānevā’ti (vibha. 715) hi vuttaṃ.

498. Now, in order to present the eight great resultant consciousnesses, the passage beginning with 'Which states are indeterminate?' and so forth was commenced again. Therein, in the Pāḷi, only the method is shown, and all sections are condensed. Their meaning should be understood according to the method stated previously. Whatever distinction there is here, to show that, it is said, 'Non-greed is an indeterminate root,' and so forth. What was not stated should be understood thus: indeed, the distinctions of action-doors, courses of action, and bases of meritorious action, which are stated in connection with the sense-sphere wholesome states, are not present here. Why? Because of not generating intimation, because of not being a state that produces a result, and because of not occurring as such. Moreover, the compassion and appreciative joy that are mentioned among the yevāpanaka factors are not found in the resultants because they have the concept of a being as their object. For the sense-sphere resultants have exclusively sense-sphere objects. And not only compassion and appreciative joy, but the abstinences are also not found here. For it is said, 'The five training rules are only wholesome' (Vibh. 715).

Asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravidhānañcettha kusalato ceva paccayabhedato ca veditabbaṃ. Asaṅkhārikassa hi kusalassa asaṅkhārikameva vipākaṃ, sasaṅkhārikassa sasaṅkhārikaṃ. Balavapaccayehi ca uppannaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ, itarehi itaraṃ. Hīnādibhedepi imāni hīnamajjhimapaṇītehi chandādīhi anipphāditattā hīnamajjhimapaṇītāni nāma na honti. Hīnassa pana kusalassa vipākaṃ hīnaṃ, majjhimassa [M 0.0307] majjhimaṃ, paṇītassa paṇītaṃ. Adhipatino pettha na santi. Kasmā? Chandādīni dhuraṃ katvā anuppādetabbato. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ aṭṭhasu kusalesu vuttasadisameva.

And here, the arrangement of unprompted and prompted should be understood from the wholesome state and from the distinction of conditions. For of an unprompted wholesome state, the resultant is unprompted; of a prompted one, it is prompted. And that which has arisen from strong conditions is unprompted; from other conditions, the other. Also, in the distinction of inferior and so forth, these are not called inferior, medium, or superior, because they are not produced by inferior, medium, and superior zeal and so forth. However, the resultant of an inferior wholesome state is inferior; of a medium one, medium; of a superior one, superior. Dominances are also not present here. Why? Because they are not to be produced by making zeal and so forth the primary factor. All the rest is just the same as what was said regarding the eight wholesome states.

Idāni imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ mahāvipākacittānaṃ vipaccanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Etāni hi catūsu ṭhānesu vipaccanti – paṭisandhiyaṃ, bhavaṅge, cutiyaṃ, tadārammaṇeti. Kathaṃ? Manussesu tāva kāmāvacaradevesu ca puññavantānaṃ duhetukatihetukānaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle paṭisandhi hutvā vipaccanti. Paṭisandhiyā vītivattāya pavatte saṭṭhipi asītipi vassāni asaṅkhyeyyampi āyukālaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā, balavārammaṇe chasu dvāresu tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā, maraṇakāle cuti hutvāti. Evaṃ catūsu ṭhānesu vipaccanti.

Now, the occasions of ripening for these eight great resultant consciousnesses should be understood. For they ripen on four occasions: as rebirth-linking, as life-continuum, as death, and as registering. How? Firstly, among humans and sense-sphere devas, for meritorious beings with two or three roots, at the time of grasping rebirth-linking, they ripen by becoming rebirth-linking. When rebirth-linking has passed, during the course of existence, they ripen by becoming the life-continuum for a lifespan of sixty years, eighty years, or even an incalculable period; in the case of a strong object at the six doors, by becoming registering consciousness; and at the time of death, by becoming death consciousness. Thus, they ripen on these four occasions.

Tattha sabbepi sabbaññubodhisattā pacchimapaṭisandhiggahaṇe paṭhamena somanassasahagatatihetukaasaṅkhārikamahāvipākacittena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Taṃ pana mettāpubbabhāgacittassa vipākaṃ hoti. Tena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā asaṅkhyeyyaṃ āyu. Kālavasena pana pariṇamati. Mahāsīvatthero panāha – ‘somanassasahagatato upekkhāsahagataṃ balavataraṃ. Tena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Tena gahitapaṭisandhikā hi mahajjhāsayā honti. Dibbesupi ārammaṇesu uppilāvino na honti, tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherādayo viyā’ti[P 0.0267]. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – ‘ayaṃ therassa manoratho,’‘natthi eta’nti paṭikkhipitvā ‘sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ hitūpacāro balavā hoti[V 0.0305], tasmā mettāpubbabhāgakāmāvacarakusalavipākasomanassasahagatatihetukaasaṅkhārikacittena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantī’ti vuttaṃ.

Therein, all Bodhisattas seeking omniscience, at the time of grasping their final rebirth-linking, grasp rebirth-linking with the first great resultant consciousness, which is accompanied by joy, has three roots, and is unprompted. That, however, is the resultant of a wholesome consciousness preceded by loving-kindness. Through the rebirth-linking given by that, the lifespan is incalculable. It changes, however, according to the age. But the Elder Mahāsīva said: 'The equanimity-accompanied consciousness is stronger than the joy-accompanied. They grasp rebirth-linking with that. For those who have grasped rebirth-linking with that have great aspirations. They are not frivolous even with respect to divine objects, like the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga and others.' But in the Commentary, having rejected this by saying, 'This is the Elder's mere wish,' and 'This is not so,' it is stated: 'The practice for the welfare of others by Bodhisattas seeking omniscience is strong; therefore, they grasp rebirth-linking with the unprompted, three-rooted, joy-accompanied resultant consciousness of a sense-sphere wholesome state preceded by loving-kindness.'

Vipākuddhārakathā

Discourse on the Extraction of Results

Idāni vipākuddhārakathāya mātikā ṭhapetabbā – tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero tāva āha – ekāya kusalacetanāya soḷasa vipākacittāni uppajjanti. Ettheva dvādasakamaggopi ahetukaṭṭhakampīti. Moravāpivāsī mahādattatthero panāha – ekāya kusalacetanāya dvādasa vipākacittāni uppajjanti. Ettheva dasakamaggopi ahetukaṭṭhakampīti. Tipiṭakamahādhammarakkhitatthero āha – ekāya kusalacetanāya dasa vipākacittāni uppajjanti, ettheva ahetukaṭṭhakanti.

Now, in the discourse on the extraction of results, the mātikā should be established. First, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said: 'From one wholesome volition, sixteen resultant consciousnesses arise. Right here, the group of twelve results and the group of eight rootless results also arise.' But the Elder Mahādatta of Moravāpi said: 'From one wholesome volition, twelve resultant consciousnesses arise. Right here, the group of ten results and the group of eight rootless results also arise.' The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahādhammarakkhita said: 'From one wholesome volition, ten resultant consciousnesses arise; right here, the group of eight rootless results arises.'

Imasmiṃ [M 0.0308] ṭhāne sāketapañhaṃ nāma gaṇhiṃsu. Sākete kira upāsakā sālāyaṃ nisīditvā ‘kiṃ nu kho ekāya cetanāya kamme āyūhite ekā paṭisandhi hoti udāhu nānā’ti? Pañhaṃ nāma samuṭṭhāpetvā nicchetuṃ asakkontā ābhidhammikatthere upasaṅkamitvā pucchiṃsu. Therā ‘yathā ekasmā ambabījā ekova aṅkuro nikkhamati, evaṃ ekāva paṭisandhi hotī’ti saññāpesuṃ. Athekadivasaṃ ‘kiṃ nu kho nānācetanāhi kamme āyūhite paṭisandhiyo nānā honti udāhu ekā’ti? Pañhaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā nicchetuṃ asakkontā there pucchiṃsu. Therā ‘yathā bahūsu ambabījesu ropitesu bahū aṅkurā nikkhamanti, evaṃ bahukāva paṭisandhiyo hontī’ti saññāpesuṃ.

In this context, they took up a question called the Sāketa problem. It is said that in Sāketa, lay devotees sitting in a hall wondered, "When kamma is accumulated by a single volition, does one rebirth-linking occur, or many?" Unable to resolve the question they had formulated, they approached the Abhidhamma scholar elders and asked. The elders explained, "Just as from one mango seed, only one sprout emerges, so too only one rebirth-linking occurs." Then one day, they wondered, "When kamma is accumulated by many volitions, do many rebirth-linkings occur, or just one?" Unable to resolve the question they had formulated, they asked the elders. The elders explained, "Just as when many mango seeds are planted, many sprouts emerge, so too many rebirth-linkings occur."

Aparampi imasmiṃ ṭhāne ussadakittanaṃ nāma gahitaṃ. Imesañhi sattānaṃ lobhopi ussanno hoti, dosopi mohopi; alobhopi adosopi amohopi. Taṃ nesaṃ ussannabhāvaṃ ko niyāmetīti? Pubbahetu niyāmeti. Kammāyūhanakkhaṇeyeva nānattaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? “Yassa hi kammāyūhanakkhaṇe lobho balavā hoti alobho mando, adosāmohā balavanto dosamohā mandā, tassa mando alobho lobhaṃ pariyādātuṃ na sakkoti, adosāmohā pana balavanto dosamohe [P 0.0268] pariyādātuṃ sakkonti. Tasmā so tena kammena dinnapaṭisandhivasena nibbatto luddho hoti, sukhasīlo akkodhano, paññavā pana hoti vajirūpamañāṇo”ti.

Furthermore, in this context, a discourse called the 'Enumeration of Prominence' is taken up. For these beings, greed is prominent, as are hatred and delusion; non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are also prominent. What determines this state of prominence for them? A prior cause determines it. Diversity arises at the very moment of accumulating kamma. How? 'For one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, greed is strong and non-greed is weak, while non-hatred and non-delusion are strong and hatred and delusion are weak, their weak non-greed is not able to overcome greed, but their strong non-hatred and non-delusion are able to overcome hatred and delusion. Therefore, having been reborn by the power of the rebirth-linking given by that kamma, one is greedy, yet of pleasant disposition and not wrathful; but one is wise, possessing wisdom like a diamond.'

‘Yassa [V 0.0306] pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe lobhadosā balavanto honti alobhādosā mandā, amoho balavā moho mando, so purimanayeneva luddho ceva hoti duṭṭho ca, paññavā pana hoti vajirūpamañāṇo dattābhayatthero viya.

But for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, greed and hatred are strong and non-greed and non-hatred are weak, while non-delusion is strong and delusion is weak, by the previous method, one is both greedy and hateful, but is wise, possessing wisdom like a diamond, like the Elder Dattābhaya.

‘Yassa pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe lobhādosamohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva luddho ceva hoti dandho ca, sukhasīlako pana hoti akkodhano.

But for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, by the previous method, one is both greedy and dull, but is of pleasant disposition and not wrathful.

‘Tathā yassa kammāyūhanakkhaṇe tayopi lobhadosamohā balavanto honti alobhādayo mandā, so purimanayeneva luddho ceva hoti duṭṭho ca mūḷho ca.

Similarly, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, all three—greed, hatred, and delusion—are strong and non-greed and so on are weak, by the previous method, one is greedy, hateful, and deluded.

‘Yassa [M 0.0309] pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe alobhadosamohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva appakileso hoti, dibbārammaṇampi disvā niccalo, duṭṭho pana hoti dandhapañño cāti.

But for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, by the previous method, one has few defilements and is unshaken even upon seeing a divine object; but one is hateful and dull in wisdom.

‘Yassa pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe alobhādosamohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva aluddho ceva hoti, sukhasīlako ca, dandho pana hoti.

But for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, by the previous method, one is not greedy and is of a pleasant disposition, but one is dull.

‘Tathā yassa kammāyūhanakkhaṇe alobhadosāmohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva aluddho ceva hoti paññavā ca, duṭṭho ca pana hoti kodhano.

Similarly, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, hatred, and non-delusion are strong while the others are weak, by the previous method, one is not greedy and is wise, but one is hateful and wrathful.

‘Yassa pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe tayopi alobhādayo balavanto honti lobhādayo mandā, so mahāsaṅgharakkhitatthero viya aluddho aduṭṭho paññavā ca hotī’ti.

But for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, all three—non-greed and so on—are strong while greed and so on are weak, like the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, one is not greedy, not hateful, and wise.
