Even when kamma is accumulated by the second, third, and fourth wholesome consciousnesses, only this many resultant consciousnesses arise. This same method applies even when kamma is accumulated by the four consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity. Here, however, first a moderately agreeable object should be shown. Afterwards, the feeling should be changed by means of an agreeable object. The discussion of the mango simile and the fixed-course simile is as it is naturally. The machine simile is not obtained. Starting from the passage, 'However, from the wholesome, when kamma is accumulated by one or another of the four consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge,' everything should be elaborated and the group of eight rootless consciousnesses should be explained. With this much, in the view of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, the tenfold path is concluded, together with the group of eight rootless consciousnesses.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ therānaṃ katarassa vādo gahetabboti? Na kassaci ekaṃsena. Sabbesaṃ pana vādesu yuttaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Paṭhamavādasmiñhi sasaṅkhārāsaṅkhāravidhānaṃ paccayabhedato adhippetaṃ. Tenettha[V 0.0323], asaṅkhārikakusalassa dubbalapaccayehi uppannaṃ sasaṅkhārikavipākaṃ, sasaṅkhārikakusalassa balavapaccayehi uppannaṃ asaṅkhārikavipākañca gahetvā, labbhamānānipi kiriyajavanāni pahāya, kusalajavanena tadārammaṇaṃ ārammaṇena ca vedanaṃ [P 0.0288] niyāmetvā, sekkhaputhujjanavasena soḷasakamaggo kathito. Yaṃ panettha akusalajavanāvasāne ahetukavipākameva tadārammaṇaṃ dassitaṃ, taṃ itaresu na dassitameva. Tasmā taṃ tattha tesu vuttaṃ sahetukavipākañca, etthāpi sabbamidaṃ labbhateva. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – yadā hi kusalajavanānaṃ antarantarā akusalaṃ javati, tadā kusalāvasāne āciṇṇasadisameva, akusalāvasāne [M 0.0327] sahetukaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ yuttaṃ. Yadā nirantaraṃ akusalameva tadā ahetukaṃ. Evaṃ tāva paṭhamavāde yuttaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

But among these three elders, whose view should be taken? Not that of any one exclusively. Rather, from all the views, what is suitable should be taken. For in the first view, the arrangement of prompted and unprompted is intended based on the difference of conditions. Therefore, here, having taken the prompted resultant that arose from weak conditions for an unprompted wholesome kamma, and the unprompted resultant that arose from strong conditions for a prompted wholesome kamma, and having set aside the functional impulsions that are obtainable, the sixteenfold path is explained according to trainees and ordinary people by determining the tadārammaṇa by the wholesome impulsion and the feeling by the object. That tadārammaṇa which was shown here at the end of unwholesome impulsion as being only a rootless resultant, that was not shown at all in the other views. Therefore, that rootless tadārammaṇa there, and the rooted resultant spoken of in those other views—all this is indeed obtainable here as well. In that regard, this is the method: for when unwholesome impels intermittently among wholesome impulsions, then at the end of the wholesome impulsion, the tadārammaṇa is just like what is habitual; at the end of the unwholesome impulsion, a rooted tadārammaṇa is suitable. When it is uninterruptedly unwholesome only, then a rootless tadārammaṇa is suitable. Thus, for now, what is suitable in the first view should be taken.

Dutiyavāde pana kusalato sasaṅkhārāsaṅkhāravidhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tenettha asaṅkhārikakusalassa asaṅkhārikameva vipākaṃ, sasaṅkhārikakusalassa ca sasaṅkhārikameva gahetvā, javanena tadārammaṇaniyāmaṃ akatvā, sabbesampi sekkhāsekkhaputhujjanānaṃ uppattiraho piṇḍajavanavaseneva dvādasakamaggo kathito. Tihetukajavanāvasāne panettha tihetukaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ yuttaṃ. Duhetukajavanāvasāne duhetukaṃ, ahetukajavanāvasāne ahetukaṃ bhājetvā pana na vuttaṃ. Evaṃ dutiyavāde yuttaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

But in the second view, the arrangement of prompted and unprompted is intended based on the wholesome. Therefore, here, having taken that for an unprompted wholesome kamma the resultant is only unprompted, and for a prompted wholesome kamma it is only prompted, and without making a determination of the tadārammaṇa by the impulsion, the twelvefold path is explained for all trainees, non-trainees, and ordinary people who are fit for it to arise, solely by way of the collective impulsion. Here, at the end of a three-rooted impulsion, a three-rooted tadārammaṇa is suitable. At the end of a two-rooted impulsion, a two-rooted tadārammaṇa is suitable; at the end of a rootless impulsion, a rootless tadārammaṇa is suitable. But it was not stated having been divided up in this way. Thus, in the second view, what is suitable should be taken.

Tatiyavādepi kusalatova asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāravidhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. ‘Tihetukakammaṃ tihetukavipākampi duhetukavipākampi ahetukavipākampi detī’ti pana vacanato asaṅkhārikatihetukapaṭisandhikassa asaṅkhārikaduhetukenapi tadārammaṇena bhavitabbaṃ. Taṃ adassetvā hetusadisameva tadārammaṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Taṃ purimāya hetukittanaladdhiyā na yujjati. Kevalaṃ dasakamaggavibhāvanatthameva vuttaṃ. Itarampi pana labbhateva. Evaṃ tatiyavādepi yuttaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Ayañca sabbāpi paṭisandhijanakasseva kammassa vipākaṃ sandhāya tadārammaṇakathā. ‘Sahetukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ ahetukassa bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayena paccayo’ti (paṭṭhā. 3.1.102) vacanato pana nānākammena ahetukapaṭisandhikassāpi sahetukavipākaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ uppajjati. Tassa uppattividhānaṃ mahāpakaraṇe āvi bhavissatīti.

In the third view also, the arrangement of unprompted and prompted is intended based on the wholesome. However, according to the statement, 'Three-rooted kamma gives three-rooted resultant, two-rooted resultant, and rootless resultant,' for one who has an unprompted, three-rooted rebirth-linking, there should also be a tadārammaṇa that is unprompted and two-rooted. Without showing that, a tadārammaṇa that is only similar in roots was shown. That does not accord with the previous doctrine of stating the roots. It was stated merely for the purpose of explaining the tenfold path. But the other is indeed obtainable. Thus, in the third view also, what is suitable should be taken. And all this discussion of tadārammaṇa is with reference to the resultant of the very kamma that generates rebirth-linking. However, according to the statement, 'A rooted life-continuum is a condition for a rootless life-continuum by way of proximity condition' (Paṭṭhāna 3.1.102), a rooted resultant tadārammaṇa arises even for one with a rootless rebirth-linking through a different kamma. The method of its arising will become clear in the Great Book.

Kāmāvacarakusalavipākakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the resultant of sense-sphere wholesome kamma is concluded.

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaravipākakathā

Discussion of the Resultants of the Form Sphere and Formless Sphere

499. Idāni [P 0.0289][V 0.0324] rūpāvacarādivipākaṃ dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā abyākatātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yasmā kāmāvacaravipākaṃ attano kusalena sadisampi hoti, asadisampi, tasmā na taṃ kusalānugatikaṃ katvā bhājitaṃ. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaravipākaṃ pana yathā hatthiassapabbatādīnaṃ chāyā hatthiādisadisāva honti, tathā attano kusalasadisameva hotīti kusalānugatikaṃ katvā bhājitaṃ. Kāmāvacarakammañca yadā kadāci [M 0.0328] vipākaṃ deti, rūpāvacarārūpāvacaraṃ pana anantarāyena, dutiyasmiṃyeva attabhāve, vipākaṃ detītipi kusalānugatikameva katvā bhājitaṃ. Sesaṃ kusale vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – paṭipadādibhedo ca hīnapaṇītamajjhimabhāvo ca etesu jhānāgamanato veditabbo. Chandādīnaṃ pana aññataraṃ dhuraṃ katvā anuppādanīyattā niradhipatikāneva etānīti.

499. Now, in order to show the resultants of the form sphere and so forth, the section beginning 'Which states are indeterminate?' is again commenced. Herein, since the resultants of the sense sphere may be similar or dissimilar to their wholesome states, they are not classified by following their wholesome states. But the resultants of the form sphere and formless sphere, just as the shadows of elephants, horses, mountains, and so forth, are similar to the elephants and so forth, so too are they similar only to their wholesome states; hence they are classified by following their wholesome states. And while sense-sphere kamma yields its resultant at any time, form-sphere and formless-sphere kamma, without obstruction, yields its resultant in the very next existence; for this reason also, they are classified by making them follow only their wholesome states. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on wholesome states. This, however, is the distinction: the difference in practice, etc., and the inferior, sublime, and middling nature, should be understood in these from the jhāna that is their source. As for desire and the rest, since they are not produced by making any one of them a chief factor, they are without a predominant factor.

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaravipākakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discussion of the Resultants of the Form Sphere and Formless Sphere is concluded.

Lokuttaravipākakathā

Discussion of the Supramundane Resultant

505. Lokuttaravipākampi kusalasadisattā kusalānugatikameva katvā bhājitaṃ. Yasmā pana tebhūmakakusalaṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena vaṭṭaṃ ācināti vaḍḍheti, tasmā tattha katattā upacitattāti vuttaṃ. Lokuttaraṃ pana tena ācitampi apacināti, sayampi cutipaṭisandhivasena na ācināti, tenettha ‘katattā upacitattā’ti avatvā katattā bhāvitattāti vuttaṃ.

505. The supramundane resultant, too, is classified by making it follow only the wholesome, because it is similar to the wholesome. However, since the wholesome kamma of the three planes accumulates and increases the round of existence by way of death and rebirth-linking, it is therefore said there 'because it is done and accumulated'. But the supramundane wholesome dismantles even that which was accumulated by that mundane wholesome, and it itself does not accumulate by way of death and rebirth-linking; therefore, here, instead of saying 'because it is done and accumulated', it is said 'because it is done and developed'.

Suññatantiādīsu ‘maggo’ tāva ‘āgamanato saguṇato ārammaṇatoti tīhi kāraṇehi nāmaṃ labhatī’ti, idaṃ heṭṭhā kusalādhikāre vitthāritaṃ. Tattha suttantikapariyāyena saguṇatopi ārammaṇatopi nāmaṃ labhati. Pariyāyadesanā hesā. Abhidhammakathā pana nippariyāyadesanā. Tasmā idha saguṇato vā ārammaṇato vā nāmaṃ na labhati, āgamanatova labhati. Āgamanameva hi dhuraṃ. Taṃ duvidhaṃ hoti – vipassanāgamanaṃ maggāgamananti.

In the passages beginning with 'emptiness', it is said that the path, in the first place, obtains its name for three reasons: from its approach, from its own quality, and from its object. This was elaborated previously in the section on wholesome states.

Tattha [V 0.0325] maggassa āgataṭṭhāne vipassanāgamanaṃ dhuraṃ, phalassa [P 0.0290] āgataṭṭhāne maggāgamanaṃ dhuranti, idampi heṭṭhā vuttameva. Tesu idaṃ phalassa āgataṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā idha maggāgamanaṃ dhuranti veditabbaṃ. So panesa maggo āgamanato ‘suññata’nti nāmaṃ labhitvā saguṇato ca ārammaṇato ca ‘animitto’‘appaṇihito’tipi vuccati. Tasmā sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano phalassa tīṇi nāmāni deti. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi suddhāgamanavaseneva laddhanāmo ‘suññatamaggo’ sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano phalassa nāmaṃ dadamāno ‘suññata’nti nāmaṃ akāsi. ‘Suññataanimittamaggo’ sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano phalassa nāmaṃ dadamāno ‘animitta’nti nāmaṃ akāsi. ‘Suññataappaṇihitamaggo’ sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne [M 0.0329] ṭhatvā attano phalassa nāmaṃ dadamāno ‘appaṇihita’nti nāmaṃ akāsi. Imāni pana tīṇi nāmāni maggānantare phalacittasmiṃyeva iminā nayena labbhanti, no aparabhāge vaḷañjanakaphalasamāpattiyā. Aparabhāge pana aniccatādīhi tīhi vipassanāhi vipassituṃ sakkoti. Athassa vuṭṭhitavuṭṭhitavipassanāvasena animittaappaṇihitasuññatasaṅkhātāni tīṇi phalāni uppajjanti. Tesaṃ tāneva saṅkhārārammaṇāni. Aniccānupassanādīni ñāṇāni anulomañāṇāni nāma honti.

Herein, it has also been stated previously that at the place of the path's arrival, the approach of insight is the principal factor, and at the place of the fruit's arrival, the approach of the path is the principal factor. Among these, this is the place of the fruit's arrival; therefore, here the approach of the path should be understood as the principal factor. And this path, having obtained the name 'emptiness' from its approach, is also called 'signless' and 'undirected' from its own quality and from its object. Therefore, it itself, standing in the position of being the approach for the fruit, gives three names to its own fruit. How? For this 'emptiness-path', which has obtained its name solely by way of the pure approach, itself standing in the position of being the approach for the fruit, in giving a name to its own fruit, made the name 'emptiness'. The 'emptiness-signless path', itself standing in the position of being the approach for the fruit, in giving a name to its own fruit, made the name 'signless'. The 'emptiness-undirected path', itself standing in the position of being the approach for the fruit, in giving a name to its own fruit, made the name 'undirected'. These three names, however, are obtained in this way only in the fruition-consciousness immediately following the path, not afterwards in the utilized fruition-attainment. Afterwards, however, one is able to contemplate with the three insights, beginning with impermanence. Then, for that person, by the power of the insight that has emerged from the sign of formations, the three fruits—called signless, undirected, and emptiness—arise. Their objects are those same formations. The knowledges, beginning with the contemplation of impermanence, are called adaptation knowledges.

Yo cāyaṃ suññatamagge vutto. Appaṇihitamaggepi eseva nayo. Ayampi hi suddhāgamanavasena laddhanāmo ‘appaṇihitamaggo’ sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano phalassa nāmaṃ dadamāno ‘appaṇihita’nti nāmaṃ akāsi. ‘Appaṇihitaanimittamaggo’ sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano phalassa nāmaṃ dadamāno ‘animitta’nti nāmaṃ akāsi. ‘Appaṇihitasuññatamaggo’ sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano phalassa nāmaṃ dadamāno ‘suññata’nti nāmaṃ [P 0.0291] akāsi. Imānipi tīṇi nāmāni maggānantare phalacittasmiṃyeva iminā nayena labbhanti, na aparabhāge vaḷañjanakaphalasamāpattiyāti. Evaṃ imasmiṃ vipākaniddese kusalacittehi tiguṇāni vipākacittāni veditabbāni.

And the method that was stated for the emptiness-path, that same method applies also to the undirected path. For this 'undirected path', too, which has obtained its name solely by way of the pure approach, itself standing in the position of being the approach for the fruit, in giving a name to its own fruit, made the name 'undirected'. The 'undirected-signless path', itself standing in the position of being the approach for the fruit, in giving a name to its own fruit, made the name 'signless'. The 'undirected-emptiness path', itself standing in the position of being the approach for the fruit, in giving a name to its own fruit, made the name 'emptiness'. These three names, too, are obtained in this way only in the fruition-consciousness immediately following the path, not afterwards in the utilized fruition-attainment. Thus, in this exposition of resultants, the resultant consciousnesses should be understood as threefold the wholesome consciousnesses.

Yathā pana tebhūmakakusalāni attano vipākaṃ adhipatiṃ labhāpetuṃ na sakkonti, na evaṃ lokuttarakusalāni. Kasmā? Tebhūmakakusalānañhi añño āyūhanakālo añño vipaccanakālo. Tena tāni attano vipākaṃ adhipatiṃ labhāpetuṃ na sakkonti. Lokuttarāni pana tāya saddhāya, tasmiṃ vīriye, tāya satiyā, tasmiṃ samādhimhi, tāya paññāya avūpasantāya[V 0.0326], apaṇṇakaṃ aviraddhaṃ maggānantarameva vipākaṃ paṭilabhanti, tena attano vipākaṃ adhipatiṃ labhāpetuṃ sakkonti.

However, the supramundane wholesome states are not like the wholesome states of the three planes, which cannot cause their own resultant to obtain a predominant factor. Why? For the wholesome states of the three planes, the time of accumulation is one, and the time of ripening is another. Therefore, they cannot cause their own resultant to obtain a predominant factor. But the supramundane states—with that faith, that energy, that mindfulness, that concentration, and that wisdom not yet subsided—unfailingly and without error obtain their resultant immediately after the path; therefore, they are able to cause their own resultant to obtain a predominant factor.

Yathā hi parittakassa aggino gataṭṭhāne aggismiṃ nibbutamatteyeva uṇhākāro nibbāyitvā kiñci na hoti, mahantaṃ pana ādittaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetvā [M 0.0330] gomayaparibhaṇḍe katepi uṇhākāro avūpasantova hoti, evameva tebhūmakakusale añño kammakkhaṇo añño vipākakkhaṇo parittaaggiṭṭhāne uṇhabhāvanibbutakālo viya hoti. Tasmā taṃ attano vipākaṃ adhipatiṃ labhāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Lokuttare pana tāya saddhāya…pe… tāya paññāya avūpasantāya, maggānantarameva phalaṃ uppajjati, tasmā taṃ attano vipākaṃ adhipatiṃ labhāpetīti veditabbaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā – ‘vipāke adhipati natthi ṭhapetvā lokuttara’nti.

For just as, when a small fire is extinguished in the place where it was, the state of heat disappears as soon as the fire is extinguished, becoming nothing; but when a great, blazing mass of fire is extinguished, even when a plastering with cow-dung is made, the state of heat is not allayed; even so, in the case of wholesome kamma of the three planes, the moment of kamma is one thing and the moment of result is another, like the time when the state of heat in the place of a small fire is extinguished. Therefore, that wholesome kamma is not able to cause its own result to obtain dominance. But in the supramundane, with that faith... with that wisdom unallayed, the fruit arises immediately after the path; therefore, it should be understood that it causes its own result to obtain dominance. Therefore, the ancients have said: 'In the result, there is no dominant condition, except for the supramundane'.

555. Catutthaphalaniddese aññātāvindriyanti aññātāvino catūsu saccesu niṭṭhitañāṇakiccassa indriyaṃ, aññātāvīnaṃ vā catūsu saccesu niṭṭhitakiccānaṃ cattāri saccāni ñatvā paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitānaṃ dhammānaṃ abbhantare [P 0.0292] indaṭṭhasādhanena indriyaṃ. Niddesavārepissa aññātāvīnanti ājānitvā ṭhitānaṃ. Dhammānanti sampayuttadhammānaṃ abbhantare. Aññāti ājānanā, paññā pajānanātiādīni vuttatthāneva. Maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpannanti phalamaggassa aṅgaṃ, phalamagge ca pariyāpannanti attho.

555. In the exposition of the fourth fruit, 'the faculty of one who has known' (aññātāvindriya) means the faculty of one who has known, whose task of knowledge regarding the four truths is completed; or, it is a faculty because it accomplishes the meaning of 'mastery' among the associated states of those who have known, whose task regarding the four truths is completed, who stand having known and penetrated the four truths. And in its section of explanation, 'of those who have known' means of those who stand, having known distinctly. 'Of states' means among the associated states. 'Knowing' is distinct knowing; the terms 'wisdom', 'discerning', and so forth have the meaning already stated. 'A factor of the path, included in the path' means it is a factor of the path called 'fruit' and is included in the path called 'fruit'—this is the meaning.

Apicettha idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ – ekaṃ indriyaṃ ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati, ekaṃ cha ṭhānāni gacchati, ekaṃ ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati. Ekañhi ‘anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ’ ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati sotāpattimaggaṃ. Ekaṃ ‘aññindriyaṃ’ heṭṭhā tīṇi phalāni, upari tayo maggeti cha ṭhānāni gacchati. Ekaṃ ‘aññātāvindriyaṃ’ ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati arahattaphalaṃ. Sabbesupi maggaphalesu atthato aṭṭha aṭṭha indriyānīti catusaṭṭhi lokuttarindriyāni kathitāni. Pāḷito pana nava nava katvā dvāsattati honti. Magge maggaṅganti vuttaṃ. Phalepi maggaṅgaṃ. Magge bojjhaṅgoti vutto phalepi bojjhaṅgo. Maggakkhaṇe ārati viratīti vuttā phalakkhaṇepi ārati viratīti. Tattha maggo maggabhāveneva maggo, phalaṃ pana maggaṃ upādāya maggo nāma; phalaṅgaṃ phalapariyāpannanti vattumpi vaṭṭati. Magge bujjhanakassa aṅgoti sambojjhaṅgo, phale buddhassa [V 0.0327] aṅgoti sambojjhaṅgo. Magge āramaṇaviramaṇavaseneva ārati virati. Phale pana ārativirativasenāti.

Furthermore, herein this is a miscellaneous decision. One faculty goes to one place, one goes to six places, and one goes to one place. For one, the 'faculty of I shall know the unknown' goes to one place: the path of stream-entry. One, the 'faculty of knowing', goes to six places: the three fruits below and the three paths above. One, the 'faculty of one who has known', goes to one place: the fruit of Arahantship. In all paths and fruits, in terms of substance, there are eight faculties each; thus sixty-four supramundane faculties are taught. But according to the Pāḷi text, taking nine each, there are seventy-two. In the path, 'path factor' is said. In the fruit also, 'path factor'. In the path, 'enlightenment factor' is said; in the fruit also, 'enlightenment factor'. In the moment of the path, 'abstinence' and 'refraining' are said; in the moment of the fruit also, 'abstinence' and 'refraining' are said. Therein, the path is 'path' simply by virtue of being the path, but the fruit is called 'path' by depending on the path; it is also suitable to say 'fruit factor, included in the fruit'. In the path, it is a factor of one who is awakening, thus it is an 'enlightenment factor'; in the fruit, it is a factor of one who has awakened, thus it is an 'enlightenment factor'. In the path, 'abstinence' and 'refraining' are so called solely by way of delighting in being far from and delighting in being without. But in the fruit, they are so called by way of having delighted in being far from and having delighted in being without.

Lokuttaravipākakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion of supramundane results is concluded.

Akusalavipākakathā

The Discussion of Unwholesome Resultants

556. Ito [M 0.0331] parāni akusalavipākāni – pañca cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni, ekā manodhātu, ekā manoviññāṇadhātūti imāni satta cittāni – pāḷito ca atthato ca heṭṭhā vuttehi tādiseheva kusalavipākacittehi sadisāni.

Subsequent to this, the unwholesome resultants—the five consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; one mind-element; and one mind-consciousness-element, thus these seven consciousnesses—are similar, both in terms of the Pāḷi and in terms of meaning, to those very same wholesome resultant consciousnesses spoken of before.

Kevalañhi tāni kusalakammapaccayāni imāni akusalakammapaccayāni. Tāni ca iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattesu ārammaṇesu vattanti, imāni aniṭṭhaaniṭṭhamajjhattesu. Tattha ca sukhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, idha dukkhasahagataṃ[P 0.0293]. Tattha ca upekkhāsahagatā manoviññāṇadhātu manussesu jaccandhādīnaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ādiṃ katvā pañcasu ṭhānesu vipaccati. Idha pana ekādasavidhenāpi akusalacittena kamme āyūhite kammakammanimittagatinimittesu aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā catūsu apāyesu paṭisandhi hutvā vipaccati; dutiyavārato paṭṭhāya yāvatāyukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā, aniṭṭhaaniṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇāya pañcaviññāṇavīthiyā santīraṇaṃ hutvā, balavārammaṇe chasu dvāresu tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā, maraṇakāle cuti hutvāti, evaṃ pañcasu eva ṭhānesu vipaccatīti.

556. For there is only this difference: those are conditioned by wholesome kamma, while these are conditioned by unwholesome kamma. And those arise in relation to desirable and desirable-neutral objects, while these arise in relation to undesirable and undesirable-neutral objects. And there, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure; here, it is accompanied by pain. And there, the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity ripens in five instances, beginning with the rebirth-linking of those born blind, etc., among humans. Here, however, when kamma has been generated by any of the eleven kinds of unwholesome consciousness, taking as object one of kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign, it ripens by becoming rebirth-linking in the four woeful states. From the second moment onwards, for as long as life lasts, it ripens by becoming the life-continuum; by becoming investigating consciousness in the five-sense-door process with an undesirable or undesirable-neutral object; when the object is strong, by becoming registering consciousness at the six doors; and at the time of death, by becoming the death consciousness. Thus, it ripens in just these five instances.

Akusalavipākakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion of unwholesome resultants is concluded.

Kiriyābyākatavaṇṇanā

Manodhātucittaṃ

The Mind-Element Consciousness

566. Idāni [V 0.0328] kiriyābyākataṃ bhājetvā dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā abyākatātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kiriyāti karaṇamattaṃ. Sabbesuyeva hi kiriyacittesu yaṃ javanabhāvaṃ appattaṃ taṃ vātapupphaṃ viya. Yaṃ javanabhāvappattaṃ taṃ chinnamūlakarukkhapupphaṃ viya aphalaṃ hoti, taṃtaṃ kiccasādhanavasena pavattattā pana karaṇamattameva hoti. Tasmā kiriyāti vuttaṃ. Nevakusalānākusalātiādīsu kusalamūlasaṅkhātassa kusalahetuno abhāvā ‘nevakusalā’; akusalamūlasaṅkhātassa akusalahetuno abhāvā ‘nevaakusalā’; yonisomanasikāraayonisomanasikārasaṅkhātānampi [M 0.0332] kusalākusalapaccayānaṃ abhāvā ‘nevakusalānākusalā’. Kusalākusalasaṅkhātassa janakahetuno abhāvā nevakammavipākā.

566. Now, in order to divide and show the functional-indeterminate, the passage beginning, “Which states are indeterminate?” and so on, is taken up again. Therein, ‘functional’ (kiriyā) means mere doing. Indeed, in all functional consciousnesses, that which has not reached the state of impulsion is like a wind-flower. That which has reached the state of impulsion is fruitless, like the flower of a tree with its root cut; however, since it occurs by way of accomplishing such and such a function, it is mere doing. Therefore, it is called ‘functional.’ In the phrases “neither wholesome nor unwholesome,” etc.: due to the absence of wholesome causes, designated as wholesome roots, they are ‘not wholesome’; due to the absence of unwholesome causes, designated as unwholesome roots, they are ‘not unwholesome’; and also due to the absence of wholesome and unwholesome conditions, designated as wise and unwise attention, they are ‘neither wholesome nor unwholesome.’ Due to the absence of a generative cause, designated as wholesome and unwholesome, they are not the result of kamma.

Idhāpi cittassekaggatāniddese pavattiṭṭhitimattameva labbhati. Dve pañcaviññāṇāni, tisso manodhātuyo, tisso manoviññāṇadhātuyo, vicikicchāsahagatanti imesu sattarasasu cittesu dubbalattā saṇṭhiti avaṭṭhitiādīni na labbhanti. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ vipākamanodhātuniddese vuttanayeneva [P 0.0294] veditabbaṃ, aññatra uppattiṭṭhānā. Tañhi cittaṃ pañcaviññāṇānantaraṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ pana pañcadvāre vaḷañjanakappavattikāle sabbesaṃ pure uppajjati. Kathaṃ? Cakkhudvāre tāva iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattaaniṭṭhaaniṭṭhamajjhattesu rūpārammaṇesu yena kenaci pasāde ghaṭṭite taṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā āvajjanavasena purecārikaṃ hutvā bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭayamānaṃ uppajjati. Sotadvārādīsupi eseva nayoti.

In these seventeen consciousnesses—the two sets of five-sense-consciousnesses, the three mind-elements, the three mind-consciousness-elements, and that accompanied by doubt—due to their weakness, terms such as stability, persistence, and so on, are not obtained. All the rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the exposition of the resultant mind-element, except for the place of arising. For that consciousness arises immediately after the five-sense-consciousnesses. This one, however, arises at the five doors at the time of the process of experiencing an object, before all others. How? At the eye-door, for instance, when any kind of visual object—desirable, desirable-neutral, undesirable, or undesirable-neutral—impinges on the sensitivity, it arises, taking that object, becoming a forerunner by way of adverting, and causing the life-continuum to turn. This is the same method for the ear-door and so on.

Kiriyamanodhātucittaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The functional mind-element consciousness is concluded.

Kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātucittāni

Functional Mind-Consciousness-Element Consciousnesses.

568. Manoviññāṇadhātu [V 0.0329] uppannā hoti…pe… somanassasahagatāti, idaṃ cittaṃ aññesaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ. Khīṇāsavasseva pāṭipuggalikaṃ. Chasu dvāresu labbhati. Cakkhudvāre hi padhānasāruppaṃ ṭhānaṃ disvā khīṇāsavo iminā cittena somanassito hoti. Sotadvāre bhaṇḍabhājanīyaṭṭhānaṃ patvā mahāsaddaṃ katvā luddhaluddhesu gaṇhantesu ‘evarūpā nāma me loluppataṇhā pahīnā’ti iminā cittena somanassito hoti. Ghānadvāre gandhehi vā pupphehi vā cetiyaṃ pūjento iminā cittena somanassito hoti. Jivhādvāre rasasampannaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ laddhā bhājetvā paribhuñjanto ‘sāraṇīyadhammo vata me pūrito’ti iminā cittena somanassito hoti. Kāyadvāre abhisamācārikavattaṃ karonto ‘kāyadvāre me vattaṃ pūrita’nti iminā cittena somanassito hoti. Evaṃ tāva pañcadvāre labbhati.

568. The mind-consciousness element... accompanied by joy. This consciousness is not common to others; it is personal to an Arahant alone. It is obtained in the six doors. Indeed, at the eye-door, having seen a place suitable for striving, the Arahant becomes joyful with this consciousness. At the ear-door, having reached a place where goods are distributed, while others, making a loud noise, are taking things with extreme greed, the Arahant thinks, 'Such fickle craving has been abandoned by me,' and becomes joyful with this consciousness. At the nose-door, while honoring a cetiya with perfumes or flowers, the Arahant becomes joyful with this consciousness. At the tongue-door, having received almsfood endowed with flavor, while consuming it after sharing, the Arahant thinks, 'Indeed, the practice worthy of remembrance has been fulfilled by me,' and becomes joyful with this consciousness. At the body-door, while performing the duties of proper conduct, the Arahant thinks, 'My duty at the body-door has been fulfilled,' and becomes joyful with this consciousness. Thus, for now, it is obtained in the five doors.

Manodvāre [M 0.0333] pana atītānāgatamārabbha uppajjati. Jotipālamāṇava(ma. ni. 2.282 ādayo) magghadevarāja(ma. ni. 2.308 ādayo) kaṇhatāpasādikālasmiñhi (jā. 1.10.11 ādayo) kataṃ kāraṇaṃ āvajjetvā tathāgato sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Taṃ pana pubbenivāsañāṇasabbaññutaññāṇānaṃ kiccaṃ. Tesaṃ pana dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante idaṃ cittaṃ hāsayamānaṃ uppajjati. Anāgate ‘tantissaro mudiṅgassaro [P 0.0295] paccekabuddho bhavissatī’ti sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Tampi anāgataṃsañāṇasabbaññutaññāṇānaṃ kiccaṃ. Tesaṃ pana dvinna ñāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante idaṃ cittaṃ hāsayamānaṃ uppajjati.

At the mind-door, however, it arises taking a past or future object. Indeed, having reflected on a cause established in the past—in the time of the youth Jotipāla, King Magghadeva, the ascetic Kaṇha, and so on—the Tathāgata made a smile manifest. That, however, is the function of the knowledge of past abodes and the knowledge of omniscience. But at the culmination of the practice of those two knowledges, this consciousness arises, causing delight. Regarding the future, seeing, 'Tantissara and Mudiṅgassara will become Paccekabuddhas,' he made a smile manifest. That too is the function of the knowledge of the future and the knowledge of omniscience. But at the culmination of the practice of those two knowledges, this consciousness arises, causing delight.

Niddesavāre panassa sesaahetukacittehi balavataratāya cittekaggatā samādhibalaṃ pāpetvā ṭhapitā. Vīriyampi vīriyabalaṃ pāpetvā. Uddesavāre pana ‘samādhibalaṃ hoti vīriyabalaṃ hotī’ti anāgatattā paripuṇṇena balaṭṭhenetaṃ dvayaṃ balaṃ nāma na hoti. Yasmā pana ‘neva kusalaṃ nākusalaṃ’ tasmā balanti vatvāna ṭhapitaṃ. Yasmā ca na nippariyāyena balaṃ, tasmā saṅgahavārepi ‘dve balāni hontī’ti na vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ somanassasahagatāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātuniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In its exposition section, however, because of its being stronger than the other rootless consciousnesses, one-pointedness of mind is established, having been brought to the level of the power of concentration. Energy, too, is brought to the level of the power of energy. But in the summary section, because the statement 'there is the power of concentration, there is the power of energy' is not made, this pair is not called 'power' in the complete sense of the term. Furthermore, because it is 'neither wholesome nor unwholesome,' it is therefore not designated as a 'power.' And because it is not a power in the direct sense, it is not stated in the inclusion section either that 'there are two powers.' All the rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the exposition of the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy.

574. Upekkhāsahagatāti idaṃ cittaṃ tīsu bhavesu sabbesaṃ sacittakasattānaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ, na [V 0.0330] kassaci sacittakassa nuppajjati nāma. Uppajjamānaṃ pana pañcadvāre voṭṭhabbanaṃ hoti, manodvāre āvajjanaṃ. Cha asādhāraṇañāṇānipi iminā gahitārammaṇameva gaṇhanti. Mahāgajaṃ nāmetaṃ cittaṃ; imassa anārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi. ‘Asabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇagatikaṃ nāma katama’nti vutte ‘ida’nti vattabbaṃ. Sesamettha purimacitte vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kevalañhi tattha sappītikattā navaṅgiko saṅkhārakkhandho vibhatto. Idha nippītikattā aṭṭhaṅgiko.

574. Accompanied by equanimity: This consciousness is common to all beings with mind in the three realms of existence; there is no being with mind for whom it does not arise. When arising, however, it is determining at the five doors and adverting at the mind-door. Even the six uncommon knowledges take only an object that has been apprehended by this consciousness. This consciousness is called the great elephant; for it, there is nothing that is not an object. When asked, 'What is that which, while not being the knowledge of omniscience, has the nature of the knowledge of omniscience?' the answer should be, 'This.' The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated for the previous consciousness. For, only there, because it is accompanied by zest, the aggregate of formations was analyzed as ninefold. Here, because it is without zest, it is eightfold.

Idāni [M 0.0334] yāni kusalato aṭṭha mahācittāneva khīṇāsavassa uppajjanatāya kiriyāni jātāni, tasmā tāni kusalaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

Now, the eight great wholesome consciousnesses, by virtue of arising in one whose cankers are destroyed, have become functional. Therefore, they should be understood in the same way as stated in the exposition of the wholesome.

Idha ṭhatvā hasanakacittāni samodhānetabbāni. Kati panetāni hontīti? Vuccate terasa. Puthujjanā hi kusalato catūhi somanassasahagatehi, akusalato catūhīti, aṭṭhahi cittehi hasanti. Sekkhā kusalato catūhi somanassasahagatehi, akusalato dvīhi diṭṭhigatavippayuttehi somanassasahagatehīti, chahi cittehi hasanti. Khīṇāsavā kiriyato pañcahi somanassasahagatehi hasantīti.

At this point, the consciousnesses that cause smiling should be summarized. 'But how many are there?' It is said, thirteen. Indeed, worldlings laugh with eight consciousnesses: with four wholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy, and with four unwholesome consciousnesses. Learners laugh with six consciousnesses: with four wholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy, and with two unwholesome consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view and accompanied by joy. Arahants laugh with five functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy.

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakiriyaṃ

Functional Fine-Material and Immaterial-Sphere Consciousness

577. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakiriyaniddesesu [P 0.0296] diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti diṭṭhadhamme, imasmiṃyeva attabhāve, sukhavihāramattaṃ. Tattha khīṇāsavassa puthujjanakāle nibbattitā samāpatti yāva na naṃ samāpajjati tāva kusalāva samāpannakāle kiriyā hoti. Khīṇāsavakāle panassa nibbattitā samāpatti kiriyāva hoti. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ taṃsadisattā kusalaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

577. In the expositions of the fine-material and immaterial-sphere functional consciousness, 'a pleasant abiding in the present life' means merely a cause for dwelling happily in the present life, in this very existence. Therein, for one whose cankers are destroyed, the attainment produced during the time of being a worldling is only wholesome for as long as one does not enter it; at the time of having entered it, it is functional. Furthermore, for that one, the attainment produced at the time of becoming one whose cankers are destroyed is only functional. All the rest should be understood by the method stated in the exposition of the wholesome, because of its similarity to that.

Aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaaṭṭhakathāya

In the Aṭṭhasālinī, the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī,

Cittuppādakaṇḍakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Chapter of the Arising of Consciousness is finished.

Abyākatapadaṃ pana neva tāva niṭṭhitanti.

However, the term 'indeterminate' is not yet finished.

Cittuppādakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on the Arising of Consciousness is completed.

2. Rūpakaṇḍo

2. The Section on Material Form

Uddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Summary

Idāni [M 0.0335][V 0.0331] rūpakaṇḍaṃ bhājetvā dassetuṃ puna katame dhammā abyākatātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi heṭṭhā cittuppādakaṇḍe vipākābyākatañceva kiriyābyākatañca nissesaṃ katvā bhājitaṃ, rūpābyākatanibbānābyākatāni pana akathitāni, tāni kathetuṃ catubbidhampi abyākataṃ samodhānetvā dassento kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipākātiādimāha. Tattha kusalākusalānanti catubhūmakakusalānañceva akusalānañca. Evaṃ tāva vipākābyākataṃ kusalavipākākusalavipākavasena dvīhi padehi pariyādiyitvā dassitaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ sabbampi kāmāvacaraṃ vā hoti, rūpāvacarādīsu vā aññataraṃ, tasmā ‘kāmāvacarā’tiādinā nayena tadeva vipākābyākataṃ bhūmantaravasena pariyādiyitvā dassitaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ vedanākkhandhopi hoti…pe… viññāṇakkhandhopi, tasmā puna sampayuttacatukkhandhavasena pariyādiyitvā dassitaṃ.

Now, in order to analyze and show the Section on Material Form, the passage beginning 'What states are indeterminate?' was again undertaken. Therein, although in the preceding Section on the Arising of Consciousness both the resultant-indeterminate and the functional-indeterminate were analyzed without remainder, the material-indeterminate and Nibbāna-indeterminate were not yet taught. In order to teach them, wishing to show all four kinds of indeterminate states by combining them, he spoke the passage beginning, 'The resultants of wholesome and unwholesome states.' Therein, 'of wholesome and unwholesome' refers to the wholesome states of the four planes and to the unwholesome states. Thus, first, the resultant-indeterminate was shown, having been completely encompassed by two terms: by way of wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. Furthermore, since all of that is either of the sense-sphere or one of the others, such as the fine-material sphere, therefore, by the method beginning 'of the sense-sphere,' that same resultant-indeterminate was shown, having been completely encompassed by way of the different planes. Furthermore, since it is also the aggregate of feeling... and the aggregate of consciousness, therefore it was again shown, having been completely encompassed by way of the four associated mental aggregates.

Evaṃ vipākābyākataṃ kusalākusalavasena bhūmantaravasena sampayuttakkhandhavasenāti tīhi nayehi pariyādāya dassetvā, puna kiriyābyākataṃ [P 0.0297] dassento ye ca dhammā kiriyātiādimāha. Tattha ‘kāmāvacarā rūpāvacarā arūpāvacarā vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho’ti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya. Heṭṭhā pana gahitamevāti nayaṃ dassetvā nissajjitaṃ. Idāni avibhattaṃ dassento sabbañca rūpaṃ asaṅkhatā ca dhātūti āha. Tattha ‘sabbañca rūpa’nti padena pañcavīsati rūpāni channavutirūpakoṭṭhāsā nippadesato gahitāti veditabbā. ‘Asaṅkhatā ca [V 0.0332] dhātū’ti padena nibbānaṃ nippadesato gahitanti. Ettāvatā ‘abyākatā dhammā’ti padaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ hoti.

Thus, having shown the resultant-indeterminate, having completely encompassed it by three methods—by way of wholesome and unwholesome, by way of the different planes, and by way of the associated aggregates—again, wishing to show the functional-indeterminate, he spoke the passage beginning, 'And those states that are functional…' Therein, it should have been said: 'of the sense-sphere, of the fine-material sphere, of the immaterial sphere, the aggregate of feeling… and the aggregate of consciousness.' However, since it was already taken up in the preceding section, having shown the method, it was omitted. Now, wishing to show what was not yet analyzed, he said: 'and all material form, and the unconditioned element.' Therein, it should be known that by the term 'and all material form,' the twenty-five material forms and the ninety-six divisions of material form are taken without remainder. By the term 'and the unconditioned element,' Nibbāna is taken without remainder. With this, the term 'indeterminate states' is finished.

584. Tattha katamaṃ sabbaṃ rūpanti idaṃ kasmā gahitaṃ? Heṭṭhā rūpābyākataṃ saṅkhepena kathitaṃ. Idāni taṃ ekakadukatikacatukka…pe… ekādasakavasena vitthārato bhājetvā dassetuṃ idaṃ gahitaṃ. Tassattho – yaṃ vuttaṃ ‘sabbañca rūpaṃ, asaṅkhatā ca dhātū’ti, tasmiṃ padadvaye ‘katamaṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ nāma’? Idāni taṃ dassento cattāro ca mahābhūtātiādimāha[M 0.0336]. Tattha cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Tena tesaṃ ūnādhikabhāvaṃ nivāreti. ‘Ca’-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena na kevalaṃ ‘cattāro mahābhūtāva’ rūpaṃ, aññampi atthīti ‘upādārūpaṃ’ sampiṇḍeti.

584. Herein, why is the question, 'What is all material form?' taken up? Previously, the material-indeterminate was stated concisely. Now, this is taken up to show it in detail by analyzing it by way of ones, twos, threes, fours… up to elevens. Its meaning is: of the two terms that were stated, 'and all material form, and the unconditioned element,' what is 'all material form'? Now, to show that, he says, 'the four great primary elements…' Here, 'four' is a numerical specification. Thereby he prevents them from being deficient or excessive. The word 'and' has the meaning of inclusion. Thereby, it is not only 'the four great primary elements' that are material form; it also includes 'derived material form,' showing that there is more.

Mahābhūtāti ettha mahantapātubhāvādīhi kāraṇehi mahābhūtatā veditabbā. Etāni hi mahantapātubhāvato, mahābhūtasāmaññato, mahāparihārato, mahāvikārato, mahantabhūtattā cāti imehi kāraṇehi mahābhūtānīti vuccanti. Tattha ‘mahantapātubhāvato’ti, etāni hi anupādinnakasantānepi upādinnakasantānepi mahantāni pātubhūtāni. Tesaṃ anupādinnakasantāne evaṃ mahantapātubhāvatā veditabbā – ekañhi cakkavāḷaṃ āyāmato ca vitthārato ca yojanānaṃ dvādasa satasahassāni tīṇi sahassāni cattāri satāni paññāsañca yojanāni. Parikkhepato –

As to 'great primary elements': here, their quality of being great primary elements should be known for reasons such as their great manifestation. For these are called 'great primary elements' for these reasons: because of their great manifestation, their resemblance to great beings, their great sustenance, their great transformation, and their being great existing things. Herein, 'because of their great manifestation': these are manifested as great in both the unappropriated continuity and in the appropriated continuity. Their great manifestation in the unappropriated continuity should be understood thus: a single world-system is one million, two hundred and three thousand, four hundred and fifty yojanas in length and in breadth. In circumference—

Sabbaṃ [P 0.0298] satasahassāni, chattiṃsa parimaṇḍalaṃ;

Dasa ceva sahassāni, aḍḍhuḍḍhāni satāni ca. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.1; visuddhi. 1.137);

Thirty-six hundred-thousands in all,

And ten thousand, make the circumference;

And three hundred and fifty more.

Tattha –

Therein—

Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharā. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.1; visuddhi. 1.137);

Two hundred thousand and four myriads more;

Such is reckoned the thickness of this earth.

Tassāyeva sandhārakaṃ –

That which supports it—

Cattāri [V 0.0333] satasahassāni, aṭṭheva nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, jalaṃ vāte patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Four hundred thousand and eighty thousand more;

Such is the thickness of the water established on the wind.

Tassāpi sandhārako –

Its supporter too—

Navasatasahassāni, māluto nabhamuggato;

Saṭṭhi ceva sahassāni, esā lokassa saṇṭhiti.

Nine hundred thousand and sixty thousand more;

The wind has risen up into the sky.

This is the foundation of the world.

Evaṃ saṇṭhite cettha yojanānaṃ –

Thus it being established, herein of the yojanas—

Caturāsītisahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave;

Accuggato tāvadeva, sineru pabbatuttamo.

Eighty-four thousand yojanas plunged in the great ocean,

And risen up just as high, is Sineru, best of mountains.

Tato [M 0.0337] upaḍḍhupaḍḍhena, pamāṇena yathākkamaṃ;

Ajjhogāḷhuggatā dibbā, nānāratanacittitā.

Thence, by a measure of half and half in succession,

Are divine mountains, plunged and risen,

Adorned with various jewels.

Yugandharo īsadharo, karavīko sudassano;

Nemindharo vinatako, assakaṇṇo giri brahā.

Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana,

Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa—great mountains.

Ete satta mahāselā, sinerussa samantato;

Mahārājānamāvāsā devayakkhanisevitā.

These seven great mountains are all around Sineru,

Abodes of the Great Kings, frequented by devas and yakkhas.

Yojanānaṃ satānucco, himavā pañca pabbato;

Yojanānaṃ sahassāni, tīṇi āyatavitthato;

Caturāsītisahassehi, kūṭehi paṭimaṇḍito.

The Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas high,

Three thousand yojanas in length and breadth,

Adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks.

Tipañcayojanakkhandhaparikkhepā nagavhayā;

Paññāsayojanakkhandhasākhāyāmā samantato.

The tree has a trunk fifteen yojanas in circumference; its main branches are fifty yojanas long all around.

Satayojanavitthiṇṇā[V 0.0334], tāvadeva ca uggatā;

Jambū yassānubhāvena, jambudīpo pakāsito. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.1; visuddhi. 1.137);

A hundred yojanas is the spread of its branches, and it is just as high; the Jambu tree, by whose power Jambudīpa is made known.

Yañcetaṃ jambuyā pamāṇaṃ tadeva asurānaṃ cittapāṭaliyā, garuḷānaṃ simbalirukkhassa, aparagoyāne kadambarukkhassa, uttarakurumhi kapparukkhassa, pubbavidehe sirīsassa, tāvatiṃsesu pāricchattakassāti. Tenāhu [P 0.0299] porāṇā –

And this dimension of the Jambu tree is the same for the Cittapāṭali tree of the asuras, the Simbali tree of the garuḷas, the Kadamba tree in Aparagoyāna, the Kappa tree in Uttarakuru, the Sirīsa tree in Pubbavideha, and the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Therefore the ancients have said:

Pāṭalī simbalī jambū, devānaṃ pāricchattako;

Kadambo kapparukkho ca, sirīsena bhavati sattamanti.

The Pāṭalī, the Simbalī, the Jambū, the Pāricchattaka of the devas, the Kadamba, and the Kappa tree; the Sirīsa is the seventh.

Dveasītisahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave;

Accuggato tāvadeva, cakkavāḷasiluccayo;

Parikkhipitvā taṃ sabbaṃ, lokadhātumayaṃ ṭhitoti.

Eighty-two thousand yojanas plunged in the great ocean, and risen up just as high, stands the Cakkavāḷa mountain range; enclosing all that, the world-system stands.

Upādinnakasantānepi macchakacchapadevadānavādisarīravasena mahantāneva pātubhūtāni. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “santi, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde yojanasatikāpi attabhāvāti”ādi.

Also in the appropriated continuity, they have appeared as very large by way of the bodies of fish, turtles, devas, dānavas, and so on. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, in the great ocean there are individual existences a hundred yojanas long,' and so on.

‘Mahābhūtasāmaññato’ti [M 0.0338] etāni hi yathā māyākāro amaṇiṃyeva udakaṃ maṇiṃ katvā dasseti, asuvaṇṇaṃyeva leḍḍuṃ suvaṇṇaṃ katvā dasseti, yathā ca sayaṃ neva yakkho na pakkhī samāno yakkhabhāvampi pakkhibhāvampi dasseti, evameva sayaṃ anīlāneva hutvā nīlaṃ upādārūpaṃ dassenti, apītāni… alohitāni… anodātāneva hutvā odātaṃ upādārūpaṃ dassentīti māyākāramahābhūtasāmaññato mahābhūtāni. Yathā ca yakkhādīni mahābhūtāni yaṃ gaṇhanti neva tesaṃ tassa anto na bahiṭhānaṃ upalabbhati, na ca taṃ nissāya na tiṭṭhanti, evameva etānipi neva aññamaññassa anto na bahi ṭhitāni hutvā upalabbhanti, na ca aññamaññaṃ nissāya na tiṭṭhantīti. Acinteyyaṭṭhānatāya yakkhādimahābhūtasāmaññatopi mahābhūtāni.

‘Because of their resemblance to great beings’: For just as a magician shows water that is not a gem as a gem, and shows a clod that is not gold as gold, and just as, though he is himself neither a yakkha nor a bird, he shows the state of a yakkha and the state of a bird; so too, though they are themselves not blue, they show derived material form as blue; though not yellow… not red… not white, they show derived material form as white. Thus they are great elements because of their resemblance to the great beings that are magicians. And just as, in the case of the great beings such as yakkhas, when they seize someone, they are found neither inside nor outside of that person, yet they do not fail to stand in dependence on that person; so too these elements are found neither inside nor outside one another, yet they do not fail to stand in dependence on one another. Thus they are also great elements because of their resemblance to the great beings such as yakkhas in having an inconceivable basis.

Yathā ca yakkhinīsaṅkhātāni mahābhūtāni manāpehi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavikkhepehi attano bhayānakabhāvaṃ [V 0.0335] paṭicchādetvā satte vañcenti, evameva etānipi itthipurisasarīrādīsu manāpena chavivaṇṇena, manāpena aṅgapaccaṅgasaṇṭhānena, manāpena ca hatthapādaṅgulibhamukavikkhepena attano kakkhaḷatādibhedaṃ sarasalakkhaṇaṃ paṭicchādetvā bālajanaṃ vañcenti, attano sabhāvaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na denti. Iti vañcakaṭṭhena yakkhinīmahābhūtasāmaññatopi mahābhūtāni.

And just as the great beings called yakkhinīs conceal their own terrifying nature with pleasing displays of color, shape, and gestures, and deceive beings, so too do these elements, in the bodies of women and men, conceal their own intrinsic characteristics, such as hardness, etc., with a pleasing skin color, a pleasing shape of the major and minor limbs, and a pleasing display of hands, feet, fingers, and eyebrows, and thereby deceive foolish people, not allowing their real nature to be seen. Thus, in the sense of being deceptive, they are great elements also because of their resemblance to the great beings that are yakkhinīs.

‘Mahāparihārato’ti [P 0.0300] mahantehi paccayehi pariharitabbato. Etāni hi divase divase upanetabbattā mahantehi ghāsacchādanādīhi bhūtāni pavattānīti mahābhūtāni. Mahāparihārāni vā bhūtānīti mahābhūtāni.

‘Because of great sustenance’: This means because they have to be sustained by great supports. For these elements, having to be supplied day after day, are sustained by great provisions such as food and clothing; hence they are ‘greatly sustained’ (mahābhūtāni). Or, they are great elements because they are elements that require great sustenance.

‘Mahāvikārato’ti bhūtānaṃ mahāvikārato. Etāni hi upādiṇṇānipi anupādiṇṇānipi mahāvikārāni honti. Tattha anupādiṇṇānaṃ kappavuṭṭhāne vikāramahattaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, upādiṇṇānaṃ dhātukkhobhakāle. Tathā hi –

‘Because of great transformation’: This means because of the great transformation of the elements. For these elements, whether appropriated or unappropriated, undergo great transformation. In the case of the unappropriated, the magnitude of the transformation becomes evident at the end of the aeon; in the case of the appropriated, at a time of elemental disturbance. Thus:

Bhūmito vuṭṭhitā yāva, brahmalokā vidhāvati;

Acci accimato loke, dayhamānamhi tejasā.

Risen from the earth, it rushes up as far as the Brahmā-world; the flame of the flaming one, in a world being consumed by fire.

Koṭisatasahassekaṃ, cakkavāḷaṃ vilīyati;

Kupitena yadā loko, salilena vinassati.

One hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems dissolve when the world is destroyed by the destructive water.

Koṭisatasahassekaṃ[M 0.0339], cakkavāḷaṃ vikīrati;

Vāyodhātuppakopena, yadā loko vinassati.

One hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems are scattered when the world perishes by the agitation of the wind element.

Patthaddho bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho kaṭṭhamukhena vā;

Pathavīdhātuppakopena, hoti kaṭṭhamukheva so.

The body becomes rigid, as if bitten by a kaṭṭhamukha snake; through disturbance of the earth element, that body becomes like wood itself.

Pūtiyo bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho pūtimukhena vā;

Āpodhātuppakopena, hoti pūtimukheva so.

The body becomes putrid, as if bitten by a pūtimukha snake; through disturbance of the water element, that body becomes putrid itself.

Santatto [V 0.0336] bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho aggimukhena vā;

Tejodhātuppakopena, hoti aggimukheva so.

The body becomes intensely hot, as if bitten by an aggimukha snake; through disturbance of the fire element, that body becomes fiery itself.

Sañchinno bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho satthamukhena vā;

Vāyodhātuppakopena, hoti satthamukheva so. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.238);

The body is cut all around, as if bitten by a satthamukha snake; through disturbance of the wind element, that body is itself cut all around.

Iti mahāvikārāni bhūtānīti mahābhūtāni.

Thus, they are elements with great transformations, hence they are called ‘great elements’.

‘Mahantabhūtattā cā’ti etāni hi mahantāni mahatā vāyāmena pariggahetabbattā, bhūtāni vijjamānattāti, mahantabhūtattā ca mahābhūtāni. Evaṃ mahantapātubhāvādīhi kāraṇehi mahābhūtāni.

‘And because of being great and real’: For these are ‘great’ because they must be comprehended with great effort, and they are ‘elements’ because they are truly existent. Thus, because of being great and real, they are also ‘great elements’. In this way, for reasons such as their great manifestation, they are called the great elements.

Catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya rūpanti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Cattāri mahābhūtāni upādāya, nissāya, amuñcitvā pavattarūpanti attho. Idaṃ vuccati sabbaṃ rūpanti idaṃ cattāri mahābhūtāni, padapaṭipāṭiyā niddiṭṭhāni tevīsati upādārūpānīti, sattavīsatippabhedaṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ nāma.

As to ‘form derived from the four great elements,’ the genitive case is used here in the sense of connection. The meaning is form that proceeds by taking up, relying on, and not departing from the four great elements. ‘This is called all form.’ This means the four great elements and the twenty-three kinds of derived form enumerated in the sequence of terms; thus, ‘all form’ by name comprises these twenty-seven divisions.

Ekavidharūpasaṅgaho

The Onefold Classification of Form

Idāni [P 0.0301] taṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ ekavidhādīhi ekādasahi saṅgahehi mātikaṃ ṭhapento sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetūtiādimāha.

Now, to explain this in detail, setting forth the matrix with the eleven classifications beginning with the onefold, he states the passage beginning: 'All form is not a root condition....'

Tattha ‘sabbaṃ rūpa’nti idaṃ padaṃ ‘sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetu’ ‘sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ahetuka’nti evaṃ sabbapadehi saddhiṃ yojetabbaṃ. Sabbāneva cetāni ‘na hetū’tiādīni tecattālīsapadāni uddiṭṭhāni. Tesu paṭipāṭiyā cattālīsapadāni mātikato gahetvā ṭhapitāni, avasāne tīṇi mātikāmuttakānīti. Evaṃ tāva paṭhame saṅgahe pāḷivavatthānameva veditabbaṃ. Tathā dutiyasaṅgahādīsu.

Herein, the term 'all form' should be connected with all the terms, such as 'all form is not a root condition,' 'all form is rootless,' and so on. In total, forty-three terms beginning with 'not a root condition' are listed. Among them, forty terms are taken from the matrix in sequence and set down, while the final three are external to the matrix. Thus, in the first classification, this is how the arrangement of the Pāli text is to be understood. The same applies to the second classification and so on.

Duvidharūpasaṅgaho

The Twofold Classification of Form

Tatrāyaṃ [M 0.0340][V 0.0337] nayo – dutiyasaṅgahe tāva sataṃ cattāro ca dukā. Tattha atthi rūpaṃ upādā, atthi rūpaṃ noupādātiādayo ādimhi cuddasa dukā aññamaññasambandhābhāvato pakiṇṇakadukā nāma. Tato atthi rūpaṃ cakkhusamphassassa vatthūtiādayo pañcavīsati dukā vatthuavatthuupaparikkhaṇavasena pavattattā vatthudukā nāma. Tato atthi rūpaṃ cakkhusamphassassa ārammaṇantiādayo pañcavīsati ārammaṇānārammaṇaupaparikkhaṇavasena pavattattā ārammaṇadukā nāma. Tato atthi rūpaṃ cakkhāyatananti ādayo dasa āyatanānāyatanaupaparikkhaṇavasena pavattattā āyatanadukā nāma. Tato atthi rūpaṃ cakkhudhātūtiādayo dasa dhātuadhātuupaparikkhaṇavasena pavattattā dhātudukā nāma. Tato atthi rūpaṃ cakkhundriyantiādayo aṭṭha indriyānindriyaupaparikkhaṇavasena pavattattā indriyadukā nāma. Tato atthi rūpaṃ kāyaviññattītiādayo dvādasa sukhumāsukhumarūpaupaparikkhaṇavasena pavattattā sukhumarūpadukā nāmāti. Idaṃ dutiyasaṅgahe pāḷivavatthānaṃ.

Herein, this is the method. In the second classification, there are one hundred and four dyads. Among them, the first fourteen dyads—such as 'There is form that is derived, there is form that is not derived'—are called 'miscellaneous dyads' because they lack mutual connection. Then, the twenty-five dyads—such as 'There is form that is a basis for eye-contact'—are called 'basis dyads' because they proceed by way of examining basis and non-basis. Then, the twenty-five dyads—such as 'There is form that is an object of eye-contact'—are called 'object dyads' because they proceed by way of examining object and non-object. Then, the ten dyads—such as 'There is form that is the eye-base'—are called 'base dyads' because they proceed by way of examining base and non-base. Then, the ten dyads—such as 'There is form that is the eye-element'—are called 'element dyads' because they proceed by way of examining element and non-element. Then, the eight dyads—such as 'There is form that is the eye-faculty'—are called 'faculty dyads' because they proceed by way of examining faculty and non-faculty. Then, the twelve dyads—such as 'There is form that is bodily intimation'—are called 'subtle form dyads' because they proceed by way of examining subtle and gross form. This is the arrangement of the Pāli text in the second classification.

Tividharūpasaṅgaho

The Threefold Classification of Form

585. Tatiyasaṅgahe sataṃ tīṇi ca tikāni. Tattha dutiyasaṅgahe vuttesu cuddasasu pakiṇṇakadukesu ekaṃ ajjhattikadukaṃ sesehi terasahi yojetvā yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ ajjhattikaṃ taṃ upādā; yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ bāhiraṃ taṃ atthi upādā[P 0.0302], atthi noupādātiādinā nayena ṭhapitā terasa pakiṇṇakatikā nāma. Tato tameva dukaṃ sesadukehi saddhiṃ yojetvā yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ bāhiraṃ taṃ cakkhusamphassassa na vatthu, yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ ajjhattikaṃ taṃ atthi cakkhusamphassassa vatthu, atthi cakkhusamphassassa na vatthūtiādinā nayena sesatikā ṭhapitā. Tesaṃ nāmañca gaṇanā ca tesaṃyeva vatthudukādīnaṃ vasena veditabbāti. Idaṃ tatiyasaṅgahe pāḷivavatthānaṃ.

585. In the third classification, there are one hundred and three triads. Therein, from the fourteen miscellaneous dyads mentioned in the second classification, the 'internal' dyad is combined with the remaining thirteen. Thus, thirteen miscellaneous triads are established by the method: 'Whatever form is internal, that is derived; whatever form is external, some is derived, some is not derived.' Then, that same dyad is combined with the other dyads. The remaining triads are established by the method: 'Whatever form is external is not a basis for eye-contact; whatever form is internal, some is a basis for eye-contact, some is not a basis for eye-contact.' Their names and enumeration are to be understood in accordance with those same basis dyads, etc. This is the arrangement of the Pāli text in the third classification.

Catubbidhādirūpasaṅgahā

Exposition of the Fourfold and Other Classifications of Form

586. Catutthasaṅgahe dvāvīsati catukkā. Tattha sabbapacchimo atthi rūpaṃ upādā atthi rūpaṃ noupādāti evaṃ idha vuttaṃ mātikaṃ anāmasitvā ṭhapito[M 0.0341]. Itare pana āmasitvā ṭhapitā. Kathaṃ? Ye tāva idha duvidhasaṅgahe pakiṇṇakesu ādito tayo dukā, tesu ekekaṃ gahetvā [V 0.0338] yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ upādā taṃ atthi upādiṇṇaṃ, atthi anupādiṇṇantiādinā nayena pañcahi pañcahi dukehi saddhiṃ yojetvā dukattayamūlakā ādimhi pañcadasa catukkā ṭhapitā.

586. In the fourth classification, there are twenty-two tetrads. Among them, the very last tetrad is established without reference to the matrix spoken here thus: 'There is form that is derived, there is form that is not derived.' The others, however, are established with reference to it. How? First, in this twofold classification, taking each of the three dyads from the beginning of the miscellaneous section, and combining each with five dyads according to the method beginning with 'Whatever form is derived, some is appropriated, some is unappropriated,' fifteen tetrads based on the three dyads are established at the beginning.

Idāni yo yaṃ catukko sanidassanaduko so yasmā yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ sanidassanaṃ taṃ atthi sappaṭighaṃ, atthi appaṭighantiādinā nayena parehi vā, atthi upādā atthi noupādātiādinā nayena purimehi vā, dukehi saddhiṃ atthābhāvato kamābhāvato visesābhāvato ca yogaṃ na gacchati. Sanidassanañhi ‘appaṭighaṃ’ nāma, ‘no upādā’ vā natthīti atthābhāvato yogaṃ na gacchati. ‘Upādiṇṇaṃ pana anupādiṇṇañca atthi taṃ kamābhāvā yogaṃ na gacchati. Sabbadukā hi pacchimapacchimeheva saddhiṃ yojitā. Ayamettha kamo. Purimehi pana saddhiṃ kamābhāvoti. ‘Sati atthe kamābhāvo akāraṇaṃ. Tasmā upādiṇṇapadādīhi saddhiṃ yojetabbo’ti ce – na, visesābhāvā; upādiṇṇapadādīni hi iminā saddhiṃ yojitāni. Tattha ‘upādiṇṇaṃ vā sanidassanaṃ, sanidassanaṃ vā upādiṇṇa’nti vutte viseso natthīti visesābhāvāpi yogaṃ na gacchati. Tasmā taṃ catutthadukaṃ anāmasitvā, tato parehi atthi rūpaṃ sappaṭighantiādīhi tīhi dukehi saddhiṃ ‘yaṃ [P 0.0303] taṃ rūpaṃ sappaṭighaṃ taṃ atthi indriyaṃ, atthi na indriyaṃ, yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ appaṭighaṃ taṃ atthi indriyaṃ, atthi na indriya’ntiādinā nayena yujjamāne dve dve duke yojetvā cha catukkā ṭhapitā.

Now, as for this fourth dyad, the 'visible' dyad, it does not combine with other dyads—either with subsequent ones such as the 'impingent' dyad, or with preceding ones such as the 'derived' dyad—due to an absence of meaning, an absence of sequence, and an absence of distinction. For the visible is never called 'non-impingent' nor 'not derived'; therefore, it does not combine due to an absence of meaning. And although there is visible form that is appropriated and unappropriated, it does not combine due to an absence of sequence. For all dyads are combined only with subsequent ones; this is the sequence here. But with preceding ones, there is an absence of sequence. If it is argued: 'When the meaning exists, absence of sequence is not a valid reason; therefore, it should be combined with terms like 'appropriated,'' the reply is: No, due to an absence of distinction. For terms like 'appropriated' have already been combined with this one, and if one says, 'What is appropriated is visible' or 'What is visible is appropriated,' there is no distinction. Thus it does not combine, also due to an absence of distinction. Therefore, not referring to that fourth dyad, six tetrads are established by combining the three subsequent dyads—beginning with 'There is form that is impingent'—with two dyads each, according to the method: 'Whatever form is impingent, some is a faculty, some is not a faculty; whatever form is non-impingent, some is a faculty, some is not a faculty,' and so on.

Yathā cāyaṃ catutthaduko yogaṃ na gacchati, tathā tena saddhiṃ ādidukopi. Kasmā? Anupādārūpassa ekantena anidassanattā. So hi yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ noupādā taṃ atthi sanidassanaṃ, atthi anidassananti – evaṃ catutthena dukena saddhiṃ yojiyamāno yogaṃ na gacchati. Tasmā taṃ atikkamitvā pañcamena saha yojito. Evaṃ yo yena saddhiṃ yogaṃ gacchati, yo ca na gacchati so veditabboti. Idaṃ catutthasaṅgahe pāḷivavatthānaṃ. Ito pare pana pañcavidhasaṅgahādayo satta saṅgahā asammissā eva. Evaṃ sakalāyapi mātikāya pāḷivavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

And just as this fourth dyad does not combine, so too the first dyad does not combine with it. Why? Because form that is not derived is exclusively invisible. For that first dyad, being combined with the fourth dyad thus: 'Whatever form is not derived, some is visible, some is invisible,' does not combine. Therefore, passing over that one, it is combined with the fifth. In this way, it should be understood which combines with which, and which does not. This is the arrangement of the Pāli in the fourth classification. From here on, the seven classifications from the fivefold onwards are unmixed. Thus the arrangement of the Pāli for the entire matrix should be understood.

Rūpavibhattiekakaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Single-Item Exposition of the Division of Form

594. Idāni [M 0.0342][V 0.0339] tassā atthaṃ bhājetvā dassetuṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetumevātiādi āraddhaṃ. Kasmā panettha ‘katamaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetū’ti pucchā na katāti? Bhedābhāvato. Yathā hi dukādīsu ‘upādārūpa’mpi atthi ‘noupādārūpa’mpi, evamidha hetu na hetūtipi sahetukamahetukantipi bhedo natthi, tasmā pucchaṃ akatvāva vibhattaṃ. Tattha ‘sabba’nti sakalaṃ, niravasesaṃ. ‘Rūpa’nti ayamassa sītādīhi ruppanabhāvadīpano sāmaññalakkhaṇaniddeso. Na hetumevāti sādhāraṇahetupaṭikkhepaniddeso.

594. Now, in order to show its meaning by analyzing it, the passage beginning, “All form is by no means a cause,” has been introduced. Why was the question, “Which is all that form that is not a cause?” not posed here? Because of the absence of a division. For just as in the dyads and so on there is both “derived form” and “non-derived form,” so here there is no division such as “a cause” and “not a cause,” or “with a cause” and “without a cause.” Therefore, it has been analyzed without a question being posed. Therein, “all” means the whole, without remainder. “Form” is the exposition of its general characteristic, indicating its nature of being afflicted by cold and so on. “By no means a cause” is the exposition of the emphatic negation of a cause.

Tattha hetuhetu paccayahetu uttamahetu sādhāraṇahetūti catubbidho hetu. Tesu ‘tayo kusalahetū, tayo akusalahetū, tayo abyākatahetū’ti (dha. sa. 1059) ayaṃ ‘hetuhetu’ nāma. “Cattāro kho, bhikkhu, mahābhūtā hetu, cattāro mahābhūtā paccayo rūpakkhandhassa paññāpanāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.85; saṃ. ni. 3.82) ayaṃ ‘paccayahetu’ nāma. “Kusalākusalaṃ attano vipākaṭṭhāne, uttamaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ kusalavipākaṭṭhāne, uttamaṃ aniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ akusalavipākaṭṭhāne”ti ayaṃ ‘uttamahetu’ nāma. Yathāha – ‘atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ [P 0.0304] kammasamādānānaṃ ṭhānaso hetuso vipākaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī’ti (ma. ni. 1.148; vibha. 810; pāṭi. ma. 2.44), “eseva hetu esa paccayo saṅkhārānaṃ yadidaṃ avijjā”ti avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ sādhāraṇahetu hutvā paccayaṭṭhaṃ pharatīti ayaṃ ‘sādhāraṇahetu’ nāma. Yathā hi pathavīraso āporaso ca madhurassāpi amadhurassāpi paccayo, evaṃ avijjā kusalasaṅkhārānampi akusalasaṅkhārānampi sādhāraṇapaccayo hoti. Imasmiṃ panatthe ‘hetuhetu’ adhippeto. Iti ‘hetū dhammā na hetū dhammā’ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 1) mātikāya āgataṃ hetubhāvaṃ rūpassa niyametvā paṭikkhipanto ‘na hetumevā’ti āha. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu paṭikkhepaniddeso ca appaṭikkhepaniddeso ca veditabbo. Vacanattho pana sabbapadānaṃ mātikāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttoyeva.

Therein, cause is fourfold: cause as root (hetuhetu), cause as condition (paccayahetu), supreme cause (uttamahetu), and common cause (sādhāraṇahetu). Among these, “Three wholesome causes, three unwholesome causes, three indeterminate causes” (Dhs §1059) is called “cause as root.” “The four great elements, O monk, are a cause; the four great elements are a condition for the designation of the form aggregate” (MN 28; SN 22.82) is called “cause as condition.” “Wholesome and unwholesome are the supreme cause in the place of their own result; a desirable object is the supreme cause in the place of a wholesome result; an undesirable object is the supreme cause in the place of an unwholesome result” is called “supreme cause.” As it is said: “He understands as it really is the result of actions undertaken in the past, future, and present, according to reason and cause” (MN 12; Vibh §810; Paṭis II 44), and “This is the cause, this is the condition for volitional formations, that is, ignorance”—ignorance, being the common cause of volitional formations, fulfills the function of a condition; this is called “common cause.” For just as the essence of earth and the essence of water are a condition for both what is sweet and what is not sweet, so ignorance is a common condition for both wholesome and unwholesome volitional formations. In this context, however, “cause as root” is intended. Thus, intending to negate the nature of form as a cause, which comes from the mātikā, “dhammas that are causes, dhammas that are not causes” (Dhs, Dukamātikā §1), by delimiting it, he said, “it is by no means a cause.” In this way, the exposition of negation and the exposition of non-negation should be understood in all sections. The meaning of the words of all the terms, however, has already been stated in the Commentary on the Mātikā.

Sappaccayamevāti ettha pana kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ kammapaccayameva hoti, āhārasamuṭṭhānādīni āhārādipaccayānevāti evaṃ rūpasseva vuttacatupaccayavasena [M 0.0343] attho veditabbo. Rūpamevāti ‘rūpino dhammā arūpino dhammā’ti mātikāya vuttaṃ arūpībhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Uppannaṃ chahi viññāṇehīti [V 0.0340] paccuppannarūpameva cakkhuviññāṇādīhi chahi veditabbaṃ. Niyāmo pana cakkhuviññāṇādīni sandhāya gahito. Na hi tāni atītānāgataṃ vijānanti. Manoviññāṇaṃ pana atītampi anāgatampi vijānāti. Taṃ imasmiṃ pañcaviññāṇasote patitattā sotapatitameva hutvā gataṃ. Hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena pana aniccameva. Jarāya abhibhavitabbadhammakattā jarābhibhūtameva. Yasmā vā rūpakāye jarā pākaṭā hoti, tasmāpi ‘jarābhibhūtamevā’ti vuttaṃ.

As to ‘It is exclusively conditioned’: here, what has kamma as its origin is conditioned only by kamma, and what has nutriment, etc., as its origin is conditioned only by nutriment, etc. Thus the meaning should be understood in terms of the four conditions stated for form alone. As to ‘It is exclusively form’: this negates the state of being immaterial, which is mentioned in the mātikā, “dhammas that are material, dhammas that are immaterial.” As to ‘Arisen and knowable by the six consciousnesses’: it is only present form that is to be known by the six consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and so on. The restriction, however, is adopted with reference to the five sense consciousnesses, for they do not know the past or the future. Mind-consciousness, however, knows both the past and the future. Since it has fallen into this stream of the five consciousnesses, it is treated as having been swept along in the current. But in the sense of ‘having come to be and then ceasing to be,’ it is exclusively impermanent. Because it has the nature of being overcome by aging, it is exclusively overcome by aging. Or, because aging is manifest in the material body, it is therefore said, ‘it is exclusively overcome by aging.’

Evaṃ ekavidhena rūpasaṅgahoti ettha ‘vidhā’-saddo mānasaṇṭhānakoṭṭhāsesu dissati. “Seyyohamasmīti vidhā, sadisohamasmīti vidhā”tiādīsu (vibha. 962) hi māno vidhā nāma. “Kathaṃvidhaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti, kathaṃvidhaṃ paññavantaṃ vadantī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.95) saṇṭhānaṃ. ‘Kathaṃvidha’nti [P 0.0305] hi padassa kathaṃsaṇṭhānanti attho. “Ekavidhena ñāṇavatthuṃ duvidhena ñāṇavatthū”tiādīsu (vibha. 751-752) koṭṭhāso vidhā nāma. Idhāpi koṭṭhāsova adhippeto.

In the phrase, 'Thus the inclusion of form is onefold,' the word 'vidhā' is seen in the senses of conceit, configuration, and division. For in passages such as, “The conceit ‘I am better’ is a vidhā; the conceit ‘I am equal’ is a vidhā” (Vibh §962), conceit is called vidhā. In passages such as, “Of what kind do they say is a virtuous one? Of what kind do they say is a wise one?” (SN 3.24), it means configuration. For the word 'kathaṃvidha' means 'of what configuration?' In passages such as, “The ground for knowledge is onefold; the grounds for knowledge are twofold” (Vibh §§751–52), vidhā is called division. Here too, division is intended.

Saṅgahasaddopi sajātisañjātikiriyāgaṇanavasena catubbidho. Tattha “sabbe khattiyā āgacchantu, sabbe brāhmaṇā sabbe vessā sabbe suddā āgacchantu”, “yā cāvuso visākha, sammāvācā, yo ca sammākammanto, yo ca sammāājīvo – ime dhammā sīlakkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462) ayaṃ ‘sajātisaṅgaho’ nāma. ‘Ekajātikā āgacchantū’ti vuttaṭṭhāne viya hi idha sabbe jātiyā ekasaṅgahaṃ gatā. “Sabbe kosalakā āgacchantu, sabbe māgadhakā, sabbe bhārukacchakā āgacchantu”, “yo cāvuso visākha, sammāvāyāmo, yā ca sammāsati, yo ca sammāsamādhi – ime dhammā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti ayaṃ ‘sañjātisaṅgaho’ nāma. Ekaṭṭhāne jātā saṃvuddhā āgacchantūti vuttaṭṭhāne viya hi idha sabbe sañjātiṭṭhānena nivutthokāsena ekasaṅgahaṃ gatā. “Sabbe hatthārohā āgacchantu, sabbe assārohā, sabbe rathikā āgacchantu”, “yā cāvuso visākha, sammādiṭṭhi, yo ca sammāsaṅkappo – ime dhammā paññākkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462) ayaṃ ‘kiriyāsaṅgaho’ nāma. Sabbeva [M 0.0344] hete attano kiriyākaraṇena ekasaṅgahaṃ gatā. “Cakkhāyatanaṃ katamakkhandhagaṇanaṃ gacchati? Cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpakkhandhagaṇanaṃ gacchati. Hañci cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpakkhandhagaṇanaṃ gacchati, tena vata re vattabbe – cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpakkhandhena [V 0.0341] saṅgahita”nti (kathā. 471), ayaṃ ‘gaṇanasaṅgaho’ nāma. Ayamidha adhippeto. Ekakoṭṭhāsena rūpagaṇanāti ayañhettha attho. Esa nayo sabbattha.

The word 'saṅgaha' (inclusion) is also fourfold, by way of similar birth, common origin, action, and enumeration. Therein, the examples, “Let all khattiyas come, all brahmins, all vessas, all suddas come,” and “Friend Visākha, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these states are included in the aggregate of virtue” (MN 44) are called ‘inclusion by similar birth’ (sajātisaṅgaho). For here, just as when it is said, “Let those of one birth come,” all are included together by birth. The examples, “Let all Kosalans come, all Magadhans, all Bhārukacchans come,” and “Friend Visākha, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration” are called ‘inclusion by common origin’ (sañjātisaṅgaho). For here, just as when it is said, “Let those born and raised in one place come,” all are included together by their place of origin, the place where they have dwelt. The examples, “Let all elephant-riders come, all horse-riders, all charioteers come,” and “Friend Visākha, right view and right thought—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom” (MN 44) are called ‘inclusion by action’ (kiriyāsaṅgaho). For all these are included together by the performance of their respective actions. The statement, “Into which aggregate-count does the eye-base go? The eye-base goes into the form-aggregate-count. If the eye-base goes into the form-aggregate-count, then, sir, it should be said: ‘The eye-base is included in the form aggregate’” (Kv 5.1) is called ‘inclusion by enumeration’ (gaṇanasaṅgaho). This is what is intended here. The meaning here is ‘the counting of form as one division.’ This is the method everywhere.

Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Dyads

Upādābhājanīyakathā

Discourse on the Analysis of What is Grasped

595. Idāni duvidhasaṅgahādīsu ‘atthi rūpaṃ upādā, atthi rūpaṃ noupādā’ti evaṃ bhedasabbhāvato pucchāpubbaṅgamaṃ padabhājanaṃ dassento katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ upādātiādimāha. Tattha upādiyatīti ‘upādā’; mahābhūtāni gahetvā, amuñcitvā, tāni nissāya pavattatīti attho. Idāni [P 0.0306] taṃ pabhedato dassento cakkhāyatanantiādimāha.

595. Now, in the summaries of the dyads and so on, since there is a clear division such as, 'There is material form that is grasped, there is material form that is not grasped,' in order to set forth the analysis of terms preceded by a question, the author says, beginning with: 'What is that material form that is grasped?' Herein, 'upādā' is so called because 'it is grasped'; the meaning is that it proceeds depending on the great elements, having taken hold of them and not released them. Now, to show this in its various kinds, he says, beginning with 'the eye-base.'

596. Evaṃ tevīsatividhaṃ upādārūpaṃ saṅkhepato uddisitvā puna tadeva vitthārato niddisanto katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ cakkhāyatanantiādimāha. Tattha duvidhaṃ cakkhu – maṃsacakkhu paññācakkhu ca. Etesu ‘buddhacakkhu samantacakkhu ñāṇacakkhu dibbacakkhu dhammacakkhū’ti pañcavidhaṃ paññācakkhu. Tattha “addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento satte apparajakkhe…pe… duviññāpaye”ti (ma. ni. 1.283) idaṃ buddhacakkhu nāma. “Samantacakkhu vuccati sabbaññutaññāṇa”nti idaṃ samantacakkhu nāma. “Cakkhuṃ udapādi ñāṇaṃ udapādī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 15) idaṃ ñāṇacakkhu nāma. “Addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhenā”ti (ma. ni. 1.284) idaṃ dibbacakkhu nāma. “Tasmiṃ yevāsane virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādī”ti (ma. ni. 2.395) idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggattayasaṅkhātaṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammacakkhu nāma.

596. Having thus briefly pointed out the twenty-three kinds of grasped material form, and again expounding the same in detail, he says, beginning with: 'What is that material form, the eye-base?' Herein, the eye is of two kinds: the fleshly eye and the wisdom-eye. Among these, the wisdom-eye is fivefold: the Buddha-eye, the all-seeing eye, the knowledge-eye, the divine eye, and the Dhamma-eye. Herein, 'I saw, bhikkhus, with the Buddha-eye, surveying the world, beings with little dust... and those who are difficult to teach' (MN 26) — this is called the Buddha-eye. 'The all-seeing eye is called the knowledge of omniscience' — this is called the all-seeing eye. 'The eye arose, knowledge arose' (SN 56.11) — this is called the knowledge-eye. 'I saw, bhikkhus, with the divine eye, purified...' (MN 26) — this is called the divine eye. 'On that very seat the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose' (Vin. Mahā. 1) — this knowledge, which is designated as the three lower paths, is called the Dhamma-eye.

Maṃsacakkhupi pasādacakkhu sasambhāracakkhūti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha yoyaṃ akkhikūpake patiṭṭhito heṭṭhā akkhikūpakaṭṭhikena, upari bhamukaṭṭhikena, ubhato akkhikūṭehi, anto matthaluṅgena, bahiddhā akkhilomehi paricchinno [M 0.0345] maṃsapiṇḍo. Saṅkhepato ‘catasso dhātuyo, vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā, sambhavo saṇṭhānaṃ, jīvitaṃ bhāvo kāyapasādo cakkhupasādo’ti cuddasasambhāro. Vitthārato ‘catasso dhātuyo, taṃsannissitavaṇṇagandharasaojāsaṇṭhānasambhavā cā’ti [V 0.0342] imāni dasa catusamuṭṭhānikattā cattālīsaṃ honti. Jīvitaṃ bhāvo kāyapasādo cakkhupasādoti cattāri ekantakammasamuṭṭhānānevāti imesaṃ catucattālīsāya [P 0.0307] rūpānaṃ vasena catucattālīsasambhāro. Yaṃ loko setaṃ cakkhuṃ puthulaṃ visaṭaṃ vitthiṇṇaṃ ‘cakkhu’nti sañjānanto na cakkhuṃ sañjānāti, vatthuṃ cakkhuto sañjānāti, so maṃsapiṇḍo akkhikūpe patiṭṭhito, nhārusuttakena matthaluṅge ābaddho, yattha setampi atthi, kaṇhampi lohitakampi, pathavīpi āpopi tejopi vāyopi, yaṃ semhūssadattā setaṃ, pittussadattā kaṇhaṃ, ruhirussadattā lohitakaṃ, pathavussadattā patthiṇṇaṃ hoti, āpussadattā paggharati, tejussadattā paridayhati, vāyussadattā sambhamati, idaṃ sasambhāracakkhu nāma.

The fleshly eye is also of two kinds: the sensitive eye and the composite eye. Herein, that lump of flesh established in the eye socket—bounded below by the bone of the eye socket, above by the eyebrow bone, on both sides by the corners of the eye, inside by the brain, and outside by the eyelashes—is, in brief, composed of fourteen components: the four great elements, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, origin, configuration, life, sex, body sensitivity, and eye sensitivity. In detail, the four great elements and the six forms dependent on them, namely color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, configuration, and origin—these ten, being of fourfold origination, amount to forty. The life faculty, sex, body sensitivity, and eye sensitivity are four forms that are exclusively originated by kamma. Thus, in terms of these forty-four kinds of material form, it is composed of forty-four components. That which the world perceives as the white, broad, diffuse, and extensive 'eye'—it does not perceive the true eye, but perceives the physical basis as the eye.
