That lump of flesh is established in the eye socket, bound to the brain by sinew-threads, wherein there is white, black, and red, and earth, water, fire, and air. It is white due to a predominance of phlegm, black due to a predominance of bile, red due to a predominance of blood, firm due to a predominance of earth, oozing due to a predominance of water, burning due to a predominance of fire, and moving due to a predominance of air—this is called the composite eye.

Yo panettha sito ettha paṭibaddho catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo, idaṃ pasādacakkhu nāma. Tadetaṃ tassa sasambhāracakkhuno setamaṇḍalaparikkhittassa kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe, abhimukhe ṭhitānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattidesabhūte diṭṭhimaṇḍale, sattasu picupaṭalesu āsittatelaṃ picupaṭalāni viya, sattakkhipaṭalāni byāpetvā, dhāraṇanhāpanamaṇḍanabījanakiccāhi catūhi dhātīhi khattiyakumāro viya, sandhāraṇaābandhanaparipācanasamudīraṇakiccāhi catūhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ, utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ, āyunā anupāliyamānaṃ, vaṇṇagandharasādīhi parivutaṃ, pamāṇato ūkāsiramattaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Vuttampi cetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā –

The sensitivity that is located and bound there, derived from the four great elements, is called the sensitive eye. This is situated in the middle of the black circle, which is surrounded by the white circle of the composite eye, in the pupil, the place where the reflection of the body-form of those standing in front appears. Pervading the seven layers of the eye, just as oil poured on cotton wicks would pervade seven layers of cotton, it is assisted by the four great elements with their functions of supporting, binding, maturing, and moving, just as a royal prince is attended by four nurses with their duties of holding, bathing, adorning, and fanning. It is supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, maintained by life, and surrounded by color, odor, taste, and so on. In size, it is about the measure of a louse's head, and it stands accomplishing its function as the physical basis and door, as appropriate, for eye-consciousness and so on. And this was stated by the General of the Dhamma:

“Yena cakkhuppasādena, rūpāni manupassati;

Parittaṃ sukhumaṃ etaṃ, ūkāsirasamūpama”nti.

By which eye-sensitivity one sees forms; it is minute and subtle, like the head of a louse.

Cakkhu ca taṃ āyatanañcāti cakkhāyatanaṃ. Yaṃ cakkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādoti idhāpi upayogattheyeva sāmivacanaṃ; cattāri mahābhūtāni [M 0.0346] upādiyitvā pavattappasādoti attho. Iminā pasādacakkhumeva gaṇhāti, sesacakkhuṃ paṭikkhipati. Yaṃ pana indriyagocarasutte “ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ upādāya [P 0.0308] pasādo pathavīdhātuyā tīhi mahābhūtehi saṅgahito āpodhātuyā ca tejodhātuyā ca vāyodhātuyā ca,” catuparivattasutte “dvinnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo pathavīdhātuyā ca āpodhātuyā ca dvīhi mahābhūtehi saṅgahito tejodhātuyā ca vāyodhātuyā cā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pariyāyena vuttaṃ. Ayañhi suttantikakathā nāma pariyāyadesanā[V 0.0343]. Yo ca catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo so tesu ekekassāpi dinnaṃ dvinnampi pasādoyevāti iminā pariyāyena tattha desanā āgatā. Abhidhammo pana nippariyāyadesanā nāma. Tasmā idha ‘catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo’ti vuttaṃ.

The eye and that base—thus, the eye-base. In the phrase 'sensitivity derived from the four great elements,' the genitive case ('of the four great elements') has the sense of relation; the meaning is 'the sensitivity that proceeds by grasping the four great elements.' By this, only the sensitive eye is included, while the other kinds of eye are rejected. However, in the Indriyagocara Sutta it is said: 'Sensitivity derived from one great element, the earth element, is comprised of three great elements—the water element, the fire element, and the air element.' And in the Catuparivatta Sutta it is said: 'Sensitivity derived from two great elements, the earth element and the water element, is comprised of two great elements—the fire element and the air element.' That was stated figuratively. For the Suttanta method of discourse is figurative teaching. And since the sensitivity derived from the four great elements is also the sensitivity of each one of them, or of any two of them, the teaching is given there in this figurative way. But the Abhidhamma is non-figurative teaching. Therefore, here it is said: 'sensitivity derived from the four great elements.'

‘Ayaṃ me attā’ti bālajanena pariggahitattā attabhāvo vuccati sarīrampi khandhapañcakampi. Tasmiṃ pariyāpanno tannissitoti attabhāvapariyāpanno cakkhuviññāṇena passituṃ na sakkāti anidassano. Paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃso ettha jāyatīti sappaṭigho.

Because it is grasped by foolish people with the thought, 'This is my self,' both the body and the five aggregates are called 'individual existence.' Being included in that and dependent on it, it is 'included in individual existence.' Because it cannot be seen with eye-consciousness, it is non-manifest. Because impact and collision arise in it, it is 'with impact.'

Yenātiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yena karaṇabhūtena cakkhunā ayaṃ satto idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ rūpaṃ atīte passi vā, vattamāne passati vā, anāgate passissati vā, sacassa aparibhinnaṃ cakkhu bhaveyya, athānena āpāthagataṃ rūpaṃ passe vā, atītaṃ vā rūpaṃ atītena cakkhunā passi, paccuppannaṃ paccuppannena passati, anāgataṃ anāgatena passissati, sace taṃ rūpaṃ cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgaccheyya cakkhunā taṃ rūpaṃ passeyyāti idamettha parikappavacanaṃ. Dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhena cakkhuṃpetaṃ, sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhena cakkhāyatanaṃpetaṃ, suññatabhāvanissattaṭṭhena cakkhudhātupesā. Dassanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti cakkhundriyaṃpetaṃ. Lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokopeso. Vaḷañjanaṭṭhena dvārāpesā. Apūraṇīyaṭṭhena samuddopeso. Parisuddhaṭṭhena paṇḍaraṃpetaṃ. Phassādīnaṃ abhijāyanaṭṭhena khettaṃpetaṃ. Tesaṃyeva patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena vatthuṃpetaṃ. Samavisamaṃ dassentaṃ attabhāvaṃ netīti nettaṃpetaṃ. Tenevaṭṭhena nayanaṃpetaṃ[M 0.0347]. Sakkāyapariyāpannaṭṭhena [P 0.0309] orimaṃ tīraṃpetaṃ. Bahusādhāraṇaṭṭhena assāmikaṭṭhena ca suñño gāmopesoti.

In the passage beginning with 'yena,' this is the concise meaning: with the eye as the instrument, this being saw a form of the kind described in the past, or sees it in the present, or will see it in the future. If their eye were intact, they would see a form that comes into range. Or, they saw a past form with a past eye, see a present form with a present eye, and will see a future form with a future eye. 'If that form were to come into the range of the eye, they would see that form with the eye'—this is a hypothetical statement here. Because it leads in the matter of seeing, it is the eye. Because it is a place of arising and meeting for states such as contact, it is the eye-base. Because it is void and without a being, it is the eye-element. Because it exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of seeing, it is the eye-faculty. Because it wears away and breaks up, it is the world. Because it is a means of resort, it is a door. Because it cannot be filled, it is the ocean. Because it is pure, it is 'white.' Because it is the birthplace of states such as contact, it is a field. Because it is their foundation, it is a basis. Because it leads the individual existence by showing the even and uneven, it is the 'leader.' For the same reason, it is the 'guide.' Because it is included in the personal identity, it is the 'near shore.' Because it is common to many forms and is ownerless, it is an 'empty village.'

Ettāvatā ‘passi vā’tiādīhi catūhi padehi cakkhuṃpetantiādīni cuddasa nāmāni yojetvā cakkhāyatanassa cattāro vavatthāpananayā vuttāti veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Ettha hi yena cakkhunā anidassanena sappaṭighena rūpaṃ sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ passi vā cakkhuṃpetaṃ…pe… suñño gāmopeso, idaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ cakkhāyatananti ayameko nayo. Evaṃ sesāpi veditabbā.

Thus it should be understood that by connecting the fourteen names beginning with 'the eye' with the four phrases beginning with 'one saw,' four methods of defining the eye-base have been stated. How? Here, the first method is as follows: 'With which eye, which is non-manifest and with impact, one saw a form that is manifest and with impact—that eye, which is the eye ... (and so on, up to) ... the empty village, this is that material phenomenon, the eye-base.' The remaining methods should be understood in the same way.

597. Idāni yasmā vijjuniccharaṇādikālesu anoloketukāmassāpi rūpaṃ cakkhupasādaṃ ghaṭṭeti, tasmā taṃ ākāraṃ dassetuṃ dutiyo niddesavāro āraddho. Tattha yamhi cakkhumhīti yamhi adhikaraṇabhūte cakkhumhi. Rūpanti paccattavacanametaṃ. Tattha paṭihaññi vāti atītattho. Paṭihaññati [V 0.0344] vāti paccuppannattho. Paṭihaññissati vāti anāgatattho. Paṭihaññe vāti vikappanattho. Atītañhi rūpaṃ atīte cakkhusmiṃ paṭihaññi nāma. Paccuppannaṃ paccuppanne paṭihaññati nāma. Anāgataṃ anāgate paṭihaññissati nāma. Sace taṃ rūpaṃ cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgaccheyya, cakkhumhi paṭihaññeyya taṃ rūpanti ayamettha parikappo. Atthato pana pasādaṃ ghaṭṭayamānameva rūpaṃ paṭihaññati nāma. Idhāpi purimanayeneva cattāro vavatthāpananayā veditabbā.

597. Now, because even when one does not intend to look, a visible form strikes the eye-sensitivity during such times as a lightning flash, the second section of the exposition is begun to show that mode. Herein, 'in which eye' means in the eye that is the basis. 'Visible form' is a term in the nominative case. Herein, 'it struck' has a past-tense meaning. 'It strikes' has a present-tense meaning. 'It will strike' has a future-tense meaning. 'It might strike' has an optative meaning. Indeed, a past visible form is said to have struck a past eye. A present visible form is said to strike a present eye. A future visible form is said to be going to strike a future eye. 'If that visible form were to come into the range of the eye, that visible form might strike the eye'—this is the supposition here. In terms of meaning, however, a visible form is said to 'strike' only when it is impinging upon the sensitivity. Here too, the four modes of determination should be understood in the same way as before.

598. Idāni yasmā attano icchāya oloketukāmassa rūpe cakkhuṃ upasaṃharato cakkhu rūpasmiṃ paṭihaññati, tasmā taṃ ākāraṃ dassetuṃ tatiyo niddesavāro āraddho. So atthato pākaṭoyeva. Ettha pana cakkhu ārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchamānameva rūpamhi paṭihaññati nāma. Idhāpi purimanayeneva cattāro vavatthāpananayā veditabbā.

598. Now, because when one who wishes to look directs the eye towards a visible form out of one's own desire, the eye strikes the visible form, the third section of the exposition is begun to show that mode. Its meaning is quite clear. Here, however, the eye is said to strike the visible form precisely when it is receiving the object. Here too, the four methods of determination should be understood in the same way as before.

599. Ito [P 0.0310] paraṃ phassapañcamakānaṃ uppattidassanavasena pañca, tesaṃyeva ārammaṇapaṭibaddhauppattidassanavasena pañcāti, dasa vārā dassitā. Tattha cakkhuṃ nissāyāti cakkhuṃ nissāya, paccayaṃ katvā. Rūpaṃ ārabbhāti rūpārammaṇaṃ āgamma, sandhāya, paṭicca. Iminā cakkhupasādavatthukānaṃ phassādīnaṃ purejātapaccayena [M 0.0348] cakkhudvārajavanavīthipariyāpannānaṃ ārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayapaccayehi rūpassa paccayabhāvo dassito. Itaresu pañcasu vāresu rūpaṃ ārammaṇamassāti rūpārammaṇoti evaṃ ārammaṇapaccayamatteneva paccayabhāvo dassito. Yathā pana purimesu tīsu, evaṃ imesupi dasasu vāresu cattāro cattāro vavatthāpananayā veditabbā. Evaṃ katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ cakkhāyatananti pucchāya uddhaṭaṃ cakkhuṃ ‘idaṃ ta’nti nānappakārato dassetuṃ, purimā tayo, ime dasāti, terasa niddesavārā dassitā. Ekekasmiñcettha catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vavatthāpananayānaṃ āgatattā dvipaññāsāya nayehi paṭimaṇḍetvāva dassitāti veditabbā.

599. After this, five sections are shown by way of demonstrating the arising of the pentads headed by contact, and another five by way of demonstrating the arising of those same states as connected with an object—thus, ten sections are presented. Herein, 'dependent on the eye' means relying on the eye, making it a condition. 'With reference to form' means approaching form as the object, referring to it, being conditioned by it. By this is shown the role of form as a condition for contact, etc., which have the eye-sensitivity as their physical base and are included in the cognitive process of impulsion at the eye-door: as a pre-nascence condition, and as object, object-predominance, and object-decisive-support conditions. In the other five sections, its role as a condition is shown merely by way of the object condition, as in 'having form as its object.' Just as in the preceding three sections, so too in these ten sections, four methods of determination should be understood for each. Thus, to show in various ways 'this is that' eye which was raised by the question, 'What is that form which is the eye-base?', thirteen sections of exposition are presented: the preceding three and these ten. And it should be understood that since four methods of determination are given for each one, they are presented only after being adorned with fifty-two methods.

600. Ito paresu sotāyatanādiniddesesupi eseva nayo. Visesamattaṃ panettha evaṃ veditabbaṃ – suṇātīti sotaṃ. Taṃ sasambhārasotabilassa anto tanutambalomācite aṅgulivedhakasaṇṭhāne padese vuttappakārāhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ, utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ, āyunā anupāliyamānaṃ, vaṇṇādīhi parivutaṃ sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

600. The same method applies to the expositions of the ear-base and so forth. Here, however, only the distinctions should be understood as follows: 'It hears,' hence 'ear.' That ear-sensitivity, inside the ear cavity with its components, in a place shaped like a finger-ring and covered with fine, reddish hairs, is rendered serviceable by the elements of the kind already described, is sustained by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, is maintained by life, is surrounded by color, etc., and stands accomplishing, as is fitting, its function as the physical base and door for ear-consciousness and so on.

Ghāyatīti [V 0.0345] ghānaṃ. Taṃ sasambhāraghānabilassa anto ajappadasaṇṭhāne padese yathāvuttappakāraupakārupatthambhanānupālanaparivāraṃ hutvā ghānaviññāṇādīnaṃ [P 0.0311] yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

'It smells,' hence 'nose.' That nose-sensitivity, located inside the nasal passage with its components, in a place shaped like a goat's hoof, stands, being rendered serviceable, sustained, maintained, and surrounded in the manner described, accomplishing as is fitting its function as the physical base and door for nose-consciousness and so on.

Sāyanaṭṭhena jivhā. Sā sasambhārajivhāmajjhassa upari uppaladalaggasaṇṭhāne padese yathāvuttappakāraupakārupatthambhanānupālanaparivārā hutvā jivhāviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānā tiṭṭhati.

'Tongue' in the sense of tasting. That tongue-sensitivity, located on the upper part of the middle of the tongue with its components, in a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal, stands, being rendered serviceable, sustained, maintained, and surrounded in the manner described, accomplishing as is fitting its function as the physical base and door for tongue-consciousness and so on.

Yāvatā pana imasmiṃ kāye upādiṇṇakarūpaṃ nāma atthi, sabbattha kāyāyatanaṃ, kappāsapaṭale sneho viya, yathāvuttappakāraupakārupatthambhanānupālanaparivārameva hutvā kāyaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Ayamettha viseso. Seso pāḷippabhedo ca attho ca cakkhuniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kevalañhi idha cakkhupadassa ṭhāne sotapadādīni, rūpapadassa ṭhāne saddapadādīni, passīti ādīnaṃ ṭhāne suṇītiādipadāni ca āgatāni. ‘Nettaṃpetaṃ[M 0.0349], nayanaṃpeta’nti imassa ca padadvayassa abhāvā dvādasa dvādasa nāmāni honti. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttasadisameva.

Now, wherever in this body there is what is called appropriated material form, the body-base is found everywhere there, like oil in a layer of cotton. It stands, being rendered serviceable, sustained, maintained, and surrounded in the manner described, accomplishing as is fitting its function as the physical base and door for body-consciousness and so on. This is the distinction here. The remaining textual divisions and meaning should be understood in the same way as explained in the exposition of the eye-base. For only here, the terms 'ear' and so on replace the term 'eye'; the terms 'sound' and so on replace the term 'form'; and the terms 'he hears' and so on replace 'he sees' and so on. And because of the absence of the pair of terms, 'the leader' and 'the guide,' there are twelve names in each case. The rest is similar to what has been said everywhere.

Tattha siyā – yadi yāvatā imasmiṃ kāye upādiṇṇakarūpaṃ nāma atthi, sabbattha kāyāyatanaṃ, kappāsapaṭale sneho viya. ‘Evaṃ sante lakkhaṇasammissatā āpajjatī’ti. ‘Nāpajjatī’ti. ‘Kasmā’? ‘Aññassa aññattha abhāvato’. ‘Yadi evaṃ, na sabbattha kāyāyatana’nti? ‘Neva paramatthato sabbattha. Vinibbhujitvā panassa nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetuṃ na sakkā, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hi rūparasādayo, vālikācuṇṇāni viya, vivecetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya aññamaññabyāpinoti vuccanti, na ca paramatthato rūpe raso atthi. Yadi siyā rūpaggahaṇeneva rasaggahaṇaṃ gaccheyya. Evaṃ kāyāyatanampi paramatthato neva sabbattha atthi, na ca sabbattha natthi, vivecetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāyāti. Evamettha na lakkhaṇasammissatā āpajjatīti veditabbā’.

Here it might be said: If wherever in this body there is what is called appropriated material form, the body-base is found everywhere there, like oil in a layer of cotton, 'in that case, would a confusion of characteristics result?' 'It would not.' 'Why?' 'Because one does not exist in another.' 'If so, is the body-base not everywhere?' 'In the ultimate sense, it is not everywhere. But it is impossible to analyze it out and make known its distinctness, so it is spoken of thus. For just as visible form, taste, etc., are said to be mutually pervasive, like sand and powder, because of the impossibility of distinguishing them, yet in the ultimate sense there is no taste in visible form. If there were, the grasping of taste would occur with the very grasping of visible form. So too, in the ultimate sense, the body-base is not present everywhere; yet it is not absent everywhere, because of the impossibility of distinguishing it. Thus it should be understood that in this case no confusion of characteristics results.'

Apica [P 0.0312] lakkhaṇādivavatthāpanatopetesaṃ asammissatā veditabbā – etesu hi rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā cakkhu, rūpesu [V 0.0346] āviñchanarasaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Moreover, their non-confusion should be understood from the determination of their characteristics, etc. For among these: the eye has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that is fit for the impact of forms, or as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that originates from kamma which has as its cause the desire to see; its function is to draw towards forms; its manifestation is its state as a support for eye-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma which has as its cause the desire to see.

Saddābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ sotukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā sotaṃ, saddesu āviñchanarasaṃ, sotaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, sotukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The ear has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that is fit for the impact of sounds, or as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that originates from kamma which has as its cause the desire to hear; its function is to draw towards sounds; its manifestation is its state as a support for ear-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma which has as its cause the desire to hear.

Gandhābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ ghāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā ghānaṃ, gandhesu āviñchanarasaṃ, ghānaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ ghāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The nose has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that is fit for the impact of odors, or as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that originates from kamma which has as its cause the desire to smell; its function is to draw towards odors; its manifestation is its state as a support for nose-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma which has as its cause the desire to smell.

Rasābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā sāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā vā jivhā, rasesu āviñchanarasā, jivhāviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānā.

The tongue has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that is fit for the impact of flavors, or as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that originates from kamma caused by the desire to taste; its function is to draw towards flavors; its manifestation is its state as a support for tongue-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma caused by the desire to taste.

Phoṭṭhabbābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇo [M 0.0350] phusitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇo vā kāyo, phoṭṭhabbesu āviñchanaraso, kāyaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, phusitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhāno.

The body has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that is fit for the impact of tangibles, or as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements that originates from kamma caused by the desire to touch; its function is to draw towards tangibles; its manifestation is its state as a support for body-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma caused by the desire to touch.

Keci pana ‘tejādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo cakkhu, vāyupathavīāpādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādā sotaghānajivhā, kāyo sabbesa’nti vadanti. Apare ‘tejādhikānaṃ pasādo cakkhu, vivaravāyuāpapathavādhikānaṃ pasādā sotaghānajivhākāyā’ti vadanti. Te vattabbā – ‘suttaṃ āharathā’ti. Addhā suttameva na dakkhissanti. Keci panettha ‘tejādīnaṃ guṇehi rūpādīhi anuggayhabhāvato’ti kāraṇaṃ vadanti. Te ca vattabbā – ‘ko panevamāha [P 0.0313] – rūpādayo tejādīnaṃ guṇā’ti? Avinibbhogesu hi rūpesu ‘ayaṃ imassa guṇo, ayaṃ imassa guṇo’ti na labbhā vattuṃ. Athāpi vadeyyuṃ – ‘yathā tesu tesu sambhāresu tassa tassa bhūtassa adhikatāya pathavīādīnaṃ sandhāraṇādīni kiccāni icchatha, evaṃ tejādiadhikesu sambhāresu rūpādīnaṃ adhikabhāvadassanato icchitabbametaṃ rūpādayo tesaṃ guṇā’ti. Te vattabbā – iccheyyāma[V 0.0347], yadi āpādhikassa āsavassa gandhato pathavīadhike kappāse gandho adhikataro siyā, tejādhikassa ca uṇhodakassa vaṇṇatopi sītūdakassa vaṇṇo parihāyetha. Yasmā panetaṃ ubhayampi natthi, tasmā pahāyethetaṃ etesaṃ nissayabhūtānaṃ visesakappanaṃ, yathā avisesepi ekakalāpe bhūtānaṃ rūparasādayo aññamaññaṃ visadisā honti, evaṃ cakkhupasādādayo, avijjamānepi aññasmiṃ visesakāraṇeti gahetabbametaṃ.

Some, however, say: 'The eye is the sensitivity of the primary elements in which the fire element is predominant; the ear, nose, and tongue are the sensitivities of the primary elements in which the wind, earth, and water elements are respectively predominant; the body is the sensitivity of all primary elements.' Others say: 'The eye is the sensitivity of the primary elements in which the fire element is predominant; the ear, nose, tongue, and body are the sensitivities of the primary elements in which aperture, wind, water, and earth are respectively predominant.' They should be told: 'Bring forth a sutta.' Surely, they will not find a sutta. Some among them state the reason: 'Because of being supported by the qualities of the fire element, etc., which are form, etc.' They too should be told: 'Who, then, has said thus: "Form, etc., are the qualities of the fire element, etc."? For in inseparable material phenomena, it is not possible to say, "This is a quality of this; this is a quality of this." And if they should say: "Just as you accept the functions of supporting, etc., of earth, etc., due to the predominance of this or that primary element in these or those composites, so too, because of seeing the predominance of form, etc., in composites where the fire element, etc., are predominant, it should be accepted that form, etc., are their qualities," they should be told: "We would accept this, if the smell in cotton, where the earth element is predominant, were stronger than the smell of liquor, where the water element is predominant, and if the color of cold water were to diminish compared to the color of hot water, where the fire element is predominant. But since neither of these is the case, this speculation about the distinction of their supporting primary elements should be abandoned. Just as in a single material aggregate, although there is no distinction among the primary elements, form, taste, etc., are dissimilar to one another, so too, the eye-sensitivity, etc., are dissimilar to one another, even when no other distinguishing cause exists. Thus it should be understood."

Kiṃ pana taṃ yaṃ aññamaññassa asādhāraṇaṃ? Kammameva nesaṃ visesakāraṇaṃ. Tasmā kammavisesato etesaṃ viseso, na bhūtavisesato. Bhūtavisese hi sati pasādova nuppajjati. Samānānañhi pasādo, na visamānānanti porāṇā. Evaṃ kammevisasato visesavantesu ca etesu cakkhusotāni asampattavisayaggāhakāni attano nissayaṃ anallīnanissaye eva visaye viññāṇahetuttā. Ghānajivhākāyā [M 0.0351] sampattavisayaggāhakā, nissayavasena ceva sayañca attano nissayaṃ allīneyeva visaye viññāṇahetuttā.

What, then, is that which is not common to one another? Kamma alone is their distinguishing cause. Therefore, their distinction is due to the distinction of kamma, not due to the distinction of the primary elements. For if there were a distinction in the primary elements, the sensitivity itself would not arise. For, the ancients say, sensitivity arises from similar primary elements, not from dissimilar ones. Thus, among these sensitivities which possess distinctions due to the distinction of kamma, the eye and ear are apprehenders of unreached objects, because they are a cause for consciousness with respect to an object whose support does not adhere to their own support. The nose, tongue, and body are apprehenders of reached objects, because they are a cause for consciousness with respect to an object that adheres to their own support, both by means of its support and by itself.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “āpāthagatattāva ārammaṇaṃ sampattaṃ nāma. Candamaṇḍalasūriyamaṇḍalānañhi dvācattālīsayojanasahassamatthake ṭhitānaṃ vaṇṇo cakkhupasādaṃ ghaṭṭeti. So dūre ṭhatvā paññāyamānopi sampattoyeva nāma. Taṃgocarattā cakkhu sampattagocarameva nāma. Dūre rukkhaṃ chindantānampi, rajakānañca vatthaṃ dhovantānaṃ dūratova kāyavikāro paññāyati. Saddo pana dhātuparamparāya āgantvā sotaṃ ghaṭṭetvā saṇikaṃ vavatthānaṃ gacchatī”ti vuttaṃ.

In the Commentary, however, it is said: 'An object is called 'reached' simply because of having come into range. For the color of the moon and sun disks, stationed forty-two thousand yojanas above, strikes the eye-sensitivity. Though perceived while being far away, it is indeed called 'reached.' Because that is its range, the eye is indeed said to have a 'reached range.' The bodily movements of those cutting a tree at a distance, and of washermen washing clothes, are perceived from afar. But sound, having come through a succession of elements and striking the ear, is gradually determined.'

Tattha [P 0.0314] kiñcāpi āpāthagatattā ārammaṇaṃ sampattanti vuttaṃ, candamaṇḍalādivaṇṇo pana cakkhuṃ asampatto dūre ṭhitova paññāyati. Saddopi sace saṇikaṃ āgaccheyya, dūre uppanno cirena suyyeyya, paramparaghaṭṭanāya ca āgantvā sotaṃ ghaṭṭento asukadisāya nāmāti na paññāyeyya. Tasmā asampattagocarāneva tāni.

Although it is said therein that an object is reached by having come into range, the color of the moon's disk and so forth is perceived while remaining at a distance, without having reached the eye. And if a sound were to come slowly, one that arose at a distance would be heard after a long time; and, arriving by way of successive impacts and striking the ear, it would not be perceived as 'This is a sound from such-and-such a direction.' Therefore, they, the eye and ear, indeed have an unreached range.

Ahiādisamānāni cetāni. Yathā hi ahi nāma bahi sittasammaṭṭhaṭṭhāne nābhiramati, saṅkāraṭṭhānatiṇapaṇṇagahanavammikāniyeva pana pavisitvā nipannakāle abhiramati, ekaggataṃ āpajjati, evameva cakkhupetaṃ visamajjhāsayaṃ maṭṭhesu suvaṇṇabhittiādīsu nābhiramati, oloketumpi [V 0.0348] na icchati, rūpacittapupphalatādicittesuyeva pana abhiramati. Tādisesu hi ṭhānesu cakkhumhi appahonte mukhampi vivaritvā oloketukāmā honti.

And these sensitivities are similar to a snake, etc. For just as a snake does not delight in a sprinkled and swept place outside, but rather, having entered a rubbish heap, a thicket of grass and leaves, or an anthill, it delights and attains one-pointedness when it is lying down; in the very same way, this eye, having an uneven disposition, does not delight in smooth things like a golden wall, nor does it even wish to look. But it delights only in varied things like painted figures, flowers, and creepers. For in such places, when the eye is insufficient, people desire to look even by opening their mouths.

Susumāropi bahi nikkhanto gahetabbaṃ na passati, akkhīni nimmīletvāva carati. Yadā pana byāmasatamattaṃ udakaṃ ogāhitvā bilaṃ pavisitvā nipanno hoti, tadā tassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti sukhaṃ supati, evameva sotaṃ tampe bilajjhāsayaṃ ākāsasannissitaṃ kaṇṇacchiddakūpakeyeva ajjhāsayaṃ karoti. Kaṇṇacchiddākāsoyeva tassa saddasavane paccayo hoti. Ajaṭākāsopi vaṭṭatiyeva. Antoleṇasmiñhi sajjhāye kariyamāne na leṇacchadanaṃ bhinditvā saddo bahi nikkhamati, dvāravātapānacchiddehi pana nikkhamitvā dhātuparamparāyeva ghaṭṭento gantvā sotapasādaṃ ghaṭṭeti. Atha [M 0.0352] tasmiṃ kāle ‘asuko nāma sajjhāyatī’ti leṇapiṭṭhe nisinnā jānanti.

The crocodile, too, when it comes out, does not see what is to be caught; it moves about with its eyes closed. But when, having dived into water about a hundred fathoms deep and entered a hole, it is lying down, then its mind becomes one-pointed and it sleeps happily. In the very same way, this ear, also having a hole-dwelling disposition and being dependent on space, makes its abode only in the well that is the ear-hole. The space of the ear-hole itself is the condition for its hearing of sound. Even un-delimited space is suitable. For when recitation is being done inside a cave, the sound does not break through the cave's roof and go outside. But, having exited through the openings of doors and windows, and going along striking through a succession of elements, it strikes the ear-sensitivity. Then, at that time, those sitting on top of the cave know, 'So-and-so is reciting.'

Evaṃ sante sampattagocaratā hoti. ‘Kiṃ panetaṃ sampattagocara’nti? ‘Āma, sampattagocaraṃ’. ‘Yadi evaṃ, dūre bherīādīsu vajjamānesu dūre saddoti jānanaṃ na bhaveyyā’ti? ‘No na bhavati. Sotapasādasmiñhi ghaṭṭite dūre saddo āsanne saddo, paratīre orimatīreti tathā tathā jānanākāro hoti. Dhammatā esā’ti. ‘Kiṃ etāya dhammatāya? Yato yato chiddaṃ tato tato [P 0.0315] savanaṃ hoti, candimasūriyādīnaṃ dassanaṃ viyāti asampattagocaramevetaṃ’.

This being so, there is the state of having a reached object-domain. 'But is this a reached object-domain?' 'Yes, it is a reached object-domain.' 'If it is so, when great drums and so forth are being sounded at a distance, would there not be the knowing, "the sound is distant"?' 'No, it is not that it does not happen. For when the ear-sensitivity is struck, the mode of knowing occurs in such and such a way as "the sound is distant," "the sound is near," "on the far shore," "on this shore." This is its nature.' 'What is the use of this nature? Wherever there is an opening, there is hearing, like the seeing of the moon, sun, and so forth. Therefore, this is indeed one with an unreached object-domain.'

Pakkhīpi rukkhe vā bhūmiyaṃ vā na ramati. Yadā pana ekaṃ vā dve vā leḍḍupāte atikkamma ajaṭākāsaṃ pakkhando hoti, tadā ekaggacittataṃ āpajjati, evameva ghānampi ākāsajjhāsayaṃ vātūpanissayagandhagocaraṃ. Tathā hi gāvo navavuṭṭhe deve bhūmiyaṃ ghāyitvā ghāyitvā ākāsābhimukhā hutvā vātaṃ ākaḍḍhanti. Aṅgulīhi gandhapiṇḍaṃ gahetvāpi ca upasiṅghanakāle vātaṃ anākaḍḍhanto neva tassa gandhaṃ jānāti.

Just as a bird does not delight in a tree or on the ground, but when, having passed one or two stone-throws, it flies into the open sky, it then reaches a state of one-pointedness of mind; in the very same way, the nose, too, has an inclination for space and has scent, which has wind as its support-condition, as its object-domain. For so it is: when the rain has newly fallen, cows, having sniffed the ground repeatedly, turn their faces towards the sky and draw in the wind. And furthermore, even having taken a lump of scent with the fingers, at the time of sniffing, one who is not drawing in the wind does not know its scent at all.

Kukkuropi bahi vicaranto khemaṭṭhānaṃ na passati leḍḍupahārādīhi upadduto hoti. Antogāmaṃ pavisitvā uddhanaṭṭhāne chārikaṃ byūhitvā nipannassa pana phāsukaṃ hoti, evameva jivhāpi gāmajjhāsayā āposannissitarasārammaṇā. Tathā hi tiyāmarattiṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvāpi pātova [V 0.0349] pattacīvaramādāya gāmo pavisitabbo hoti. Sukkhakhādanīyassa ca na sakkā kheḷena atemitassa rasaṃ jānituṃ.

Just as a domestic dog, wandering outside, does not see a safe place and is afflicted by being struck with stones and so forth, but for one that has entered a village, scattered the ashes in the place of the hearth, and lies down, it is comfortable; in the very same way, the tongue, too, has an inclination for water and has taste-object, which is dependent on the water element, as its object-domain. For so it is: even after having practiced the ascetic's duties for the three watches of the night, early in the morning, having taken bowl and robe, the village is to be entered. And it is not possible to know the taste of dry food that has not been moistened by saliva.

Siṅgālopi bahi caranto ratiṃ na vindati, āmakasusāne manussamaṃsaṃ khāditvā nipannasseva panassa phāsukaṃ hoti, evameva kāyopi upādiṇṇakajjhāsayo pathavīnissitaphoṭṭhabbārammaṇo. Tathā hi aññaṃ upādiṇṇakaṃ alabhamānā sattā attanova hatthatale sīsaṃ katvā nipajjanti. Ajjhattikabāhirā cassa pathavī ārammaṇaggahaṇe paccayo hoti. Susanthatassapi hi sayanassa, hatthe ṭhapitānampi vā phalānaṃ, na sakkā anisīdantena vā anippīḷentena vā thaddhamudubhāvo jānitunti. Ajjhattikabāhirāpathavī [M 0.0353] etassa kāyapasādassa phoṭṭhabbajānane paccayo hoti. Evaṃ lakkhaṇādivavatthānatopetesaṃ asammissatā veditabbā. Aññeyeva hi cakkhupasādassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānagocarajjhāsayanissayā aññe sotapasādādīnanti [P 0.0316] asammissāneva cakkhāyatanādīni.

Just as a jackal, wandering outside, does not find delight, but for one that has eaten human flesh in a charnel ground with fresh corpses and lies down, it is comfortable; in the very same way, the body, too, has an inclination for what is appropriated and has tangible-object, which is dependent on the earth element, as its object-domain. For so it is: beings, not getting another appropriated thing, place their heads on their own palms and lie down. And for it, the internal and external earth element is a condition for the grasping of the object. Indeed, of a well-laid-out bed, or of fruits placed in the hand, it is not possible for one who is not sitting on it or not pressing them to know their state of hardness and softness. The internal and external earth element is a condition for this body-sensitivity in knowing the tangible object. Thus, their unmixed nature should be known also from the determination of their characteristics and so forth. Indeed, the characteristic, function, manifestation, proximate cause, object-domain, inclination, and support of the eye-sensitivity are quite different, and those of the ear-sensitivity and so forth are different. Therefore, the eye-base and so forth are indeed unmixed.

Apica nesaṃ asammissatāya ayaṃ upamāpi veditabbā – yathā hi pañcavaṇṇānaṃ dhajānaṃ ussāpitānaṃ kiñcāpi chāyā ekābaddhā viya hoti, tassa tassa pana aññamaññaṃ asammissāva yathā ca pañcavaṇṇena kappāsena vaṭṭiṃ katvā dīpe jālite kiñcāpi jālā ekābaddhā viya hoti, tassa tassa pana aṃsuno pāṭiyekkā pāṭiyekkā jālā asammissā eva, evameva kiñcāpi imāni pañcāyatanāni ekasmiṃ attabhāve samosaṭāni aññamaññaṃ pana asammissāneva. Na kevalañca imāneva pañca, sesarūpānipi asammissāneva. Imasmiñhi sarīre heṭṭhimakāyo majjhimakāyo uparimakāyoti tayo koṭṭhāsā. Tattha nābhito paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā heṭṭhimakāyo nāma. Tasmiṃ kāyadasakaṃ, bhāvadasakaṃ, āhārasamuṭṭhānāni aṭṭha, utusamuṭṭhānāni aṭṭha, cittasamuṭṭhānāni aṭṭhāti catucattālīsa rūpāni. Nābhito uddhaṃ yāva galavāṭakā majjhimakāyo nāma. Tattha ca kāyadasakaṃ, bhāvadasakaṃ, vatthudasakaṃ, āhārasamuṭṭhānādīni tīṇi aṭṭhakānīti catupaññāsa rūpāni. Galavāṭakato uddhaṃ uparimakāyo nāma. Tattha cakkhudasakaṃ, sotadasakaṃ, ghānadasakaṃ, jivhādasakaṃ, kāyadasakaṃ, bhāvadasakaṃ, āhārasamuṭṭhānādīni tīṇi aṭṭhakānīti caturāsīti rūpāni.

Furthermore, for their unmixed state, this simile also should be known: just as, although the shadow of five-colored banners that have been raised is as if connected together, the shadow of each one is indeed unmixed with one another; and just as when a lamp is lit with a wick made of five-colored cotton, although the flame is as if connected together, the flame from each individual strand is separate and indeed unmixed; in the very same way, although these five sense-bases are assembled in a single existence, they are indeed unmixed with one another. And not only these five, but the remaining material phenomena are also unmixed. For in this body, there are three sections: the lower body, the middle body, and the upper body. Therein, from the navel downwards is called the lower body. In it there are the body-decad, the sex-decad, eight material phenomena originated by nutriment, eight originated by temperature, and eight originated by consciousness, totaling forty-four material phenomena. From the navel upwards to the throat-pit is called the middle body. Therein, there are the body-decad, the sex-decad, the heart-base-decad, and three octads originated by nutriment and so forth, totaling fifty-four material phenomena. From the throat-pit upwards is called the upper body. Therein, there are the eye-decad, the ear-decad, the nose-decad, the tongue-decad, the body-decad, the sex-decad, and three octads originated by nutriment and so forth, totaling eighty-four material phenomena.

Tattha cakkhupasādassa paccayāni cattāri mahābhūtāni, vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā, jīvitindriyaṃ [V 0.0350] cakkhupasādoti idaṃ ekantato avinibhuttānaṃ dasannaṃ nipphannarūpānaṃ vasena cakkhudasakaṃ nāma. Iminā nayena sesānipi veditabbāni. Tesu heṭṭhimakāye rūpaṃ majjhimakāyauparimakāyarūpehi saddhiṃ asammissaṃ. Sesakāyadvayepi rūpaṃ itarehi saddhiṃ asammissameva. Yathā hi sāyanhasamaye pabbatacchāyā ca rukkhacchāyā ca kiñcāpi ekābaddhā viya honti aññamaññaṃ pana asammissāva evaṃ imesupi kāyesu catucattālīsa catupaññāsa caturāsīti rūpāni ca kiñcāpi ekābaddhāni viya honti, aññamaññaṃ pana asammissānevāti.

Therein, the four great elements which are the support of the eye-sensitivity, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, the life faculty, and the eye-sensitivity—this is called the eye-decad by way of the ten produced material phenomena that are absolutely inseparable. By this method, the remaining ones should also be known. Among them, the material phenomena in the lower body are unmixed with the material phenomena of the middle and upper bodies. In the remaining two bodies also, the material phenomena are indeed unmixed with those of the others. Just as in the evening time, although the mountain's shadow and the tree's shadow are as if connected together, they are indeed unmixed with one another; in the same way, in these bodies too, the forty-four, fifty-four, and eighty-four material phenomena, although they are as if connected together, are indeed unmixed with one another.

616. Rūpāyatananiddese [M 0.0354] vaṇṇova vaṇṇanibhā; nibhātīti vā nibhā. Cakkhuviññāṇassa pākaṭā hotīti attho. Vaṇṇova [P 0.0317] nibhā vaṇṇanibhā. Saddhiṃ nidassanena sanidassanaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇena passitabbanti attho. Saddhiṃ paṭighena sappaṭighaṃ, paṭighaṭṭananighaṃsajanakanti attho. Nīlādīsu umāpupphasamānaṃ nīlaṃ, kaṇikārapupphasamānaṃ pītakaṃ, bandhujīvakapupphasamānaṃ lohitakaṃ, osadhitārakasamānaṃ odātaṃ. Jhāmaṅgārasamānaṃ kāḷakaṃ, mandarattaṃ sinduvārakaravīramakuḷasamānaṃ mañjiṭṭhakaṃ. “Harittacahemavaṇṇakāmaṃsumukhapakkamā”ti (jā. 1.15.133) ettha pana kiñcāpi ‘harī’ti suvaṇṇaṃ vuttaṃ, parato panassa jātarūpaggahaṇena gahitattā idha sāmaṃ hari nāma. Imāni satta vatthuṃ anāmasitvā sabhāveneva dassitāni.

616. In the exposition of the form-base: 'color' itself is 'appearance of color' (vaṇṇanibhā); or, because 'it shines' (nibhāti), it is 'appearance' (nibhā). The meaning is that it becomes manifest to eye-consciousness. 'Color' itself is 'appearance,' thus 'appearance of color.' 'Visible' (sanidassanaṃ) is that which occurs together with visibility; the meaning is that it is a form to be seen by eye-consciousness. 'Resistant' (sappaṭighaṃ) is that which occurs together with resistance; the meaning is that it is a form that produces impact, which is friction. Among the colors such as blue: blue is like the flax flower; yellow is like the kaṇikāra flower; red is like the bandhujīvaka flower; white is like the morning star. Black is like a burnt ember; slightly red, like the bud of the sinduvāra or karavīra, is the mañjiṭṭhaka color. In the quote 'harittacahemavaṇṇakāmaṃsumukhapakkamā,' although 'hari' is said to be gold, since this is taken up later by the term 'jātarūpa,' here 'hari' is the name for a yellowish color. These seven are shown by their intrinsic nature alone, without referring to a physical basis.

Harivaṇṇanti haritasaddalavaṇṇaṃ. Ambaṅkuravaṇṇanti ambaṅkurena samānavaṇṇaṃ. Imāni dve vatthuṃ āmasitvā dassitāni. Dīghādīni dvādasa vohārato dassitāni. So ca nesaṃ vohāro upanidhāyasiddho ceva sannivesasiddho ca. Dīghādīni hi aññamaññaṃ upanidhāyasiddhāni, vaṭṭādīni sannivesavisesena. Tattha rassaṃ upanidhāya tato uccataraṃ dīghaṃ, taṃ upanidhāya tato nīcataraṃ rassaṃ. Thūlaṃ upanidhāya tato khuddakataraṃ aṇuṃ, taṃ upanidhāya tato mahantataraṃ thūlaṃ. Cakkasaṇṭhānaṃ vaṭṭaṃ, kukkuṭaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ. Catūhi aṃsehi yuttaṃ caturaṃsaṃ. Chaḷaṃsādīsupi eseva nayo. Ninnanti onataṃ, thalanti unnataṃ.

'Green color' means the color of a lush green meadow. 'The color of a mango sprout' means a color similar to a mango sprout. These two are shown by referring to the physical basis of the color. The twelve terms beginning with 'long' are shown by way of convention. And their convention is established both by comparison and by configuration. Indeed, 'long,' etc., are established by mutual comparison; 'round,' etc., by specific configuration. Therein, in comparison with 'short,' that which is taller is 'long'; in comparison with that, that which is lower is 'short.' In comparison with 'gross,' that which is smaller is 'subtle'; in comparison with that, that which is larger is 'gross.' That which has the shape of a wheel is 'round'; that which has the shape of a hen's egg is 'oval.' That which is endowed with four sides is 'square.' The same method applies to 'hexagonal,' etc. 'Low' means a depressed place; 'high' means a raised place.

Tattha yasmā dīghādīni phusitvā sakkā jānituṃ, nīlādīni panevaṃ na sakkā, tasmā na nippariyāyena dīghaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ; tathā rassādīni. Taṃ taṃ nissāya pana tathā tathā ṭhitaṃ dīghaṃ rassanti [V 0.0351] tena tena vohārena rūpāyatanamevettha bhāsitanti veditabbaṃ. Chāyā ātapoti idaṃ aññamaññaparicchinnaṃ; tathā āloko andhakāro ca. Abbhā mahikātiādīni cattāri vatthunāva dassitāni. Tattha ‘abbhā’ti valāhako. ‘Mahikā’ti himaṃ. Imehi catūhi abbhādīnaṃ vaṇṇā dassitā. Candamaṇḍalassa vaṇṇanibhātiādīhi tesaṃ tesaṃ pabhāvaṇṇā [P 0.0318] dassitā.

Therein, because things such as 'long' can be known by touching, while colors such as 'blue' cannot be known in this way, a long object is not the form-base in the primary sense; similarly for 'short,' etc. However, it should be understood that when a composite of primary elements, established in a particular way in dependence on this or that, is called 'long' or 'short,' it is the form-base itself that is spoken of here by that particular convention. 'Shade' and 'sunlight' are mutually delimited; similarly 'light' and 'darkness.' The four beginning with 'cloud' and 'mist' are shown by the physical basis itself. Herein, 'abbhā' is a cloud. 'Mahikā' is mist. By these four terms, the colors of clouds, etc., are shown. By such phrases as 'the appearance of the color of the moon's disk,' the radiant colors of those respective things are shown.

Tattha candamaṇḍalādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ evaṃ viseso veditabbo – maṇimayaṃ rajatapaṭicchannaṃ ekūnapaññāsayojanāyāmavitthāraṃ candassa devaputtassa vimānaṃ [M 0.0355] candamaṇḍalaṃ nāma. Sovaṇṇamayaṃ phalikapaṭicchannaṃ samapaṇṇāsayojanāyāmavitthāraṃ sūriyassa devaputtassa vimānaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ nāma. Sattaratanamayāni sattaṭṭhadasadvādasayojanāyāmavitthārāni tesaṃ tesaṃ devaputtānaṃ vimānāni tārakarūpāni nāma.

Herein, the distinction among the objects such as the moon's disk should be understood as follows: The mansion of the deva Canda, which is made of jewels, covered with silver, and is forty-nine yojanas in length and breadth, is called the moon's disk. The mansion of the deva Sūriya, which is made of gold, covered with crystal, and is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, is called the sun's disk. The mansions of various devas, which are made of the seven kinds of gems and are seven, eight, ten, or twelve yojanas in length and breadth, are called the star-forms.

Tattha heṭṭhā cando, sūriyo upari, ubhinnamantaraṃ yojanaṃ hoti. Candassa heṭṭhimantato sūriyassa uparimanto yojanasataṃ hoti. Dvīsu passesu nakkhattatārakā gacchanti. Etesu pana tīsu cando dandhagamano, sūriyo sīghagamano, nakkhattatārakā sabbasīghagamanā. Kālena candimasūriyānaṃ purato honti kālena pacchā.

Therein, the moon is below and the sun is above; the distance between them is one yojana. From the lower edge of the moon to the upper edge of the sun is one hundred yojanas. On the two sides, the constellations and stars travel. Among these three, the moon is slow-moving, the sun is fast-moving, and the constellations and stars are the fastest-moving of all. At times they are in front of the moon and sun, at times they are behind.

Ādāsamaṇḍalanti kaṃsamayaṃ. Maṇīti ṭhapetvā veḷuriyaṃ seso jotirasādianekappabhedo. Saṅkhoti sāmuddiko; muttā sāmuddikāpi, sesāpi. Veḷuriyoti veḷuvaṇṇamaṇi. Jātarūpaṃ vuccati satthuvaṇṇo. Satthā hi suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, suvaṇṇampi satthuvaṇṇaṃ. Rajataṃ vuccati kahāpaṇo – lohamāsako dārumāsako jatumāsako, ye ‘vohāraṃ gacchantī’ti (pārā. 584) vuttaṃ taṃ sabbampi idha gahitaṃ.

'Mirror-disk' means something made of bronze. 'Gem,' apart from beryl, means the remaining many kinds such as the jotirasa gem. 'Conch' is from the sea; pearls are from the sea and also from other sources. 'Beryl' is a gem the color of bamboo. 'Jātarūpa' is said to be the color of the Teacher; for the Teacher was of golden color, and gold is the color of the Teacher. 'Silver' is said to be a kahāpaṇa coin—a metal māsaka, a wooden māsaka, a lac māsaka, whatever is said to 'be used in transactions'—all this is included here.

Yaṃ vā panaññampīti iminā pāḷiāgataṃ ṭhapetvā sesaṃ taṭṭikapilotikakaṇṇikavaṇṇādibhedaṃ rūpaṃ gahitaṃ. Tañhi sabbaṃ yevāpanakesu paviṭṭhaṃ.

By the phrase 'Or whatever else,' setting aside what has come in the Pāḷi text, the remaining form is included, which has distinctions such as the color of rush-mats, pieces of cloth, and mushrooms. For all of that is included in the miscellaneous category.

Evametaṃ nīlādinā bhedena bhinnampi rūpaṃ sabbaṃ lakkhaṇādīhi abhinnameva. Sabbañhetaṃ cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa visayabhāvarasaṃ, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, catumahābhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā cetaṃ tathā sabbānipi upādārūpāni. Yattha pana viseso atthi tattha [V 0.0352] vakkhāma. Sesamettha cakkhāyatananiddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kevalañhi [P 0.0319] tattha cakkhupubbaṅgamo niddeso idha rūpapubbaṅgamo. Tattha ‘cakkhuṃ peta’ntiādīni cuddasa nāmāni, idha ‘rūpaṃpeta’ntiādīni tīṇi. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Yathā hi catūhi catūhi nayehi paṭimaṇḍetvā cakkhuṃ vavatthāpetuṃ terasa vārā vuttā, idhāpi te tatheva vuttāti.

Thus, although this visible object is divided by such distinctions as blue, etc., it is all undivided as to its characteristics, etc. All this visible object has the characteristic of impinging on the eye, the function of being the objective field for eye-consciousness, manifestation as its resort, and the four great primary elements as its proximate cause. As this is, so too are all derived material phenomena. However, where there is a difference, we shall state it. The rest here should be understood in the way stated in the exposition of the eye-base. It is just that there the exposition is preceded by the eye, while here it is preceded by visible object. There there are fourteen terms such as 'the eye is that which...'; here there are three such as 'visible object is that which...'. The rest is similar. For just as thirteen sections were stated to define the eye, embellishing it with four methods each, so too they are stated here in the same way.

620. Saddāyatananiddese bherisaddoti mahābherīpahaṭabherīnaṃ saddo. Mudiṅgasaṅkhapaṇavasaddāpi mudiṅgādipaccayā saddā. Gītasaṅkhāto saddo gītasaddo[M 0.0356]. Vuttāvasesānaṃ vīṇādīnaṃ tantibaddhānaṃ saddo vāditasaddo. Sammasaddoti kaṃsatālakaṭṭhatālasaddo. Pāṇisaddoti pāṇippahārasaddo. Sattānaṃ nigghosasaddoti bahūnaṃ sannipatitānaṃ apaññāyamānapadabyañjananigghosasaddo. Dhātūnaṃ sannighātasaddoti rukkhānaṃ aññamaññanighaṃsanaghaṇṭikākoṭanādisaddo. Vātassa vāyato saddo vātasaddo. Udakassa sandamānassa vā paṭihatassa vā saddo udakasaddo. Manussānaṃ sallāpādisaddo manussasaddo. Taṃ ṭhapetvā seso sabbopi amanussasaddo. Iminā padadvayena sabbopi saddo pariyādinno. Evaṃ santepi vaṃsaphālanapilotikaphālanādīsu pavatto pāḷiyaṃ anāgatasaddo yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhoti veditabbo.

620. In the exposition of the sound-base, the sound of a drum is the sound of great drums and kettle-drums. The sounds of small drums (mudiṅga), conches, and tabors are sounds caused by small drums and so on. The sound classified as song is the song-sound. The sound of the remaining stringed instruments, such as the lute, is the instrumental sound. The sound of cymbals is the sound of bronze cymbals and wooden clappers. The sound of hands is the sound of clapping hands. The sound of the clamor of beings is the indistinct clamorous sound of many gathered together, where words and syllables are not discernible. The sound of the striking together of elements is the sound of trees rubbing against each other, the striking of bells, and so on. The sound of wind blowing is the wind-sound. The sound of water flowing or being struck is the water-sound. The sound of human conversation and so on is the human-sound. Setting that aside, all remaining sound is non-human-sound. By these two terms, all sound is encompassed. Even so, sounds not mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as the sound of splitting bamboo or tearing cloth, should be understood as included in the general category.

Evamayaṃ bherīsaddādinā bhedena bhinnopi saddo lakkhaṇādīhi abhinnoyeva. Sabbopi hesa sotapaṭihananalakkhaṇo saddo sotaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhāno. Sesaṃ cakkhāyatananiddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idhāpi hi catūhi catūhi nayehi paṭimaṇḍitā terasa vārā vuttā. Tesaṃ attho sakkā vuttanayeneva jānitunti na vitthārito.

Thus, although this sound is divided by distinctions such as the sound of a drum, it is undivided in terms of characteristics and so on. For all this sound has the characteristic of impinging on the ear, the function of being the objective field of ear-consciousness, and the manifestation of being its resort. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the exposition of the eye-base. Here too, thirteen sections are stated, adorned with four methods each. Their meaning can be known in the same way as previously explained, so it is not elaborated.

624. Gandhāyatananiddese mūlagandhoti yaṃ kiñci mūlaṃ paṭicca nibbatto gandho. Sāragandhādīsupi eseva nayo. Asiddhadusiddhānaṃ ḍākādīnaṃ gandho āmakagandho. Macchasakalikāpūtimaṃsasaṃkiliṭṭhasappiādīnaṃ gandho vissagandho. Sugandhoti [P 0.0320] iṭṭhagandho. Duggandhoti aniṭṭhagandho. Iminā padadvayena sabbopi gandho pariyādinno. Evaṃ santepi kaṇṇakagandhapilotikagandhādayo pāḷiyaṃ anāgatā sabbepi gandhā yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhāti veditabbā.

624. In the exposition of the odor-base, 'root odor' means any odor that arises dependent on a root. The same method applies to heartwood odor and the like. The odor of uncooked or badly cooked things like pot-herbs and so on is raw odor. The odor of fish scales, putrid meat, defiled ghee, and so on is a foul, fleshy odor. 'Pleasant odor' means a desirable odor. 'Unpleasant odor' means an undesirable odor. By these two terms, all odor is encompassed. Even so, odors not mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as the odor of mushrooms or the odor of cloth, should be understood as included in the general category.

Evamayaṃ mūlagandhādinā bhedena bhinnopi gandho lakkhaṇādīhi abhinnoyeva. Sabbopi hesa ghānapaṭihananalakkhaṇo [V 0.0353] gandho, ghānaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhāno. Sesaṃ cakkhāyatananiddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idhāpi hi tatheva dvipaññāsanayapaṭimaṇḍitā terasa vārā vuttā. Te atthato pākaṭāyeva.

Thus, although this odor is divided by distinctions such as root-odor, it is undivided in terms of characteristics and so on. All this odor has the characteristic of impinging on the nose, the function of being the objective field of nose-consciousness, and the manifestation of being its resort. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the exposition of the eye-base. Here too, thirteen sections are stated, adorned with fifty-two methods. Their meanings are indeed evident.

628. Rasāyatananiddese [M 0.0357] mūlarasoti yaṃkiñci mūlaṃ paṭicca nibbattaraso. Khandharasādīsupi eseva nayo. Ambilanti takkambilādi. Madhuranti ekantato gosappiādi. Madhu pana kasāvayuttaṃ ciranikkhittaṃ kasāvaṃ hoti. Phāṇitaṃ khāriyuttaṃ ciranikkhittaṃ khāriyaṃ hoti. Sappi pana ciranikkhittaṃ vaṇṇagandhe jahantampi rasaṃ na jahatīti tadeva ekantamadhuraṃ. Tittakanti nimbapaṇṇādi. Kaṭukanti siṅgiveramaricādi. Loṇikanti sāmuddikaloṇādi. Khārikanti vātiṅgaṇakaḷīrādi. Lambilanti badarāmalakakapiṭṭhasālavādi. Kasāvanti haritakādi. Ime sabbepi rasā vatthuvasena vuttā. Taṃtaṃvatthuto panettha rasova ambilādīhi nāmehi vuttoti veditabbo. Sādūti iṭṭharaso, asādūti aniṭṭharaso. Iminā padadvayena sabbopi raso pariyādinno. Evaṃ santepi leḍḍurasabhittirasapilotikarasādayo pāḷiyaṃ anāgatā sabbepi rasā yevāpanakaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhāti veditabbā.

628. In the exposition of the taste-base, 'root taste' refers to any taste produced dependent on a root. The same principle applies to tastes originating from trunks and so on. 'Sour' refers to sour gruel with buttermilk and the like. 'Sweet' refers exclusively to things like cow’s ghee. Honey, however, being conjoined with astringency, becomes astringent when kept for a long time. Molasses, being conjoined with alkalinity, becomes alkaline when kept for a long time. Ghee, however, even when kept for a long time and losing its color and odor, does not lose its taste, and thus it alone is purely sweet. 'Bitter' refers to neem leaves and the like. 'Pungent' refers to ginger, pepper, and the like. 'Salty' refers to sea salt and the like. 'Alkaline' refers to young eggplants, bamboo shoots, and the like. 'Slightly sour' refers to jujube, myrobalan, wood-apple preserves, and the like. 'Astringent' refers to chebulic myrobalan and the like. All these tastes are stated in terms of their material basis. It should be understood that here the taste itself, arising from this or that basis, is referred to by names like 'sour,' and so on. 'Agreeable taste' means a desirable taste, and 'disagreeable taste' means an undesirable taste. By these two terms, all taste is encompassed. Even so, tastes not mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as the taste of a clod of earth, the taste of a wall, or the taste of a piece of cloth, should be understood as included in the general category.

Evamayaṃ mūlarasādinābhedena bhinnopi raso lakkhaṇādīhi abhinnoyeva. Sabbopi hesa jivhāpaṭihananalakkhaṇo raso, jivhāviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhāno. Sesaṃ cakkhāyatananiddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idhāpi [P 0.0321] hi tatheva dvipaññāsanayapaṭimaṇḍitā terasa vārā vuttā.

Thus, even though this taste is divided by distinctions such as root taste, it is undivided in terms of characteristics and so on. All this taste has the characteristic of impinging on the tongue, the function of being the objective field of tongue-consciousness, and the manifestation of being its resort. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the exposition of the eye-base. Here too, in the same way, thirteen sections are stated, adorned with fifty-two methods.

632. Itthindriyaniddese yanti karaṇavacanaṃ. Yena kāraṇena itthiyā itthiliṅgādīni hontīti ayamettha attho. Tattha ‘liṅga’nti saṇṭhānaṃ. Itthiyā hi hatthapādagīvāurādīnaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ na purisassa viya hoti. Itthīnañhi heṭṭhimakāyo visado hoti, uparimakāyo avisado. Hatthapādā khuddakā, mukhaṃ khuddakaṃ. Nimittanti sañjānanaṃ. Itthīnañhi uramaṃsaṃ avisadaṃ hoti, mukhaṃ nimmassudāṭhikaṃ. Kesabandhavatthaggahaṇampi na purisānaṃ viya hoti. Kuttanti kiriyā. Itthiyo hi daharakāle suppakamusalakehi kīḷanti, cittadhītalikāya kīḷanti, mattikavākena suttakaṃ nāma kantanti. Ākappoti gamanādiākāro. Itthiyo hi gacchamānā avisadā gacchanti, tiṭṭhamānā nipajjamānā nisīdamānā khādamānā bhuñjamānā avisadā [V 0.0354] bhuñjanti. Purisampi hi avisadaṃ disvā mātugāmo [M 0.0358] viya gacchati tiṭṭhati nipajjati nisīdati khādati bhuñjatīti vadanti.

632. In the explanation of the female faculty, `yaṃ` is a term expressing cause. The meaning here is: the cause by which the female sign and so on come to be in a woman. Here, ‘sign’ (liṅga) means form (saṇṭhāna). For a woman, the form of her hands, feet, neck, breasts, and so on is not like that of a man. For women, the lower body is distinct, while the upper body is not distinct. Their hands and feet are small, and their faces are small. ‘Mark’ (nimitta) is for recognition. For women, the flesh of the breast is not distinct, and their faces are without beard and mustache. Their manner of tying hair and wearing clothes is also not like that of men. ‘Demeanor’ (kutta) means activity. In their youth, girls play with small winnowing baskets and small pestles, they play with painted dolls, and they spin what is called a small thread with a clay spindle. ‘Manner’ (ākappa) refers to the mode of walking and so on. When women walk, they walk in an indistinct manner; when standing, lying down, sitting, chewing, and eating, they do so in an indistinct manner. For indeed, upon seeing a man who is indistinct, they say, 'He walks, stands, lies down, sits, chews, and eats like a woman.'

Itthattaṃ itthibhāvoti ubhayampi ekatthaṃ; itthisabhāvoti attho. Ayaṃ kammajo paṭisandhisamuṭṭhito. Itthiliṅgādīni pana itthindriyaṃ paṭicca pavatte samuṭṭhitāni. Yathā hi bīje sati, bījaṃ paṭicca, bījapaccayā rukkho vaḍḍhitvā sākhāviṭapasampanno hutvā ākāsaṃ pūretvā tiṭṭhati, evameva itthibhāvasaṅkhāte itthindriye sati itthiliṅgādīni honti. Bījaṃ viya hi itthindriyaṃ, bījaṃ paṭicca vaḍḍhitvā ākāsaṃ pūretvā ṭhitarukkho viya itthindriyaṃ paṭicca itthiliṅgādīni pavatte samuṭṭhahanti. Tattha itthindriyaṃ na cakkhuviññeyyaṃ, manoviññeyyameva. Itthiliṅgādīni cakkhuviññeyyānipi manoviññeyyānipi.

‘Femaleness’ and ‘the state of being a woman’ both have the same meaning: the nature of a woman. This is born of kamma and arises with rebirth-linking. The female sign and so on, however, arise during the course of life dependent on the female faculty. For just as when a seed exists, a tree grows dependent on the seed, conditioned by the seed, and becomes endowed with branches and foliage, filling the sky and standing firm, so too, when the female faculty, designated as ‘the state of being a woman,’ exists, the female sign and so on come to be. For the female faculty is like the seed; the female sign and so on, which arise during the course of life dependent on the female faculty, are like the tree that has grown dependent on the seed and stands filling the sky. Therein, the female faculty is not cognizable by eye-consciousness, only by mind-consciousness. The female sign and so on, however, are cognizable by both eye-consciousness and mind-consciousness.

Idaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ itthindriyanti idaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ, yathā cakkhundriyādīni purisassāpi honti, na evaṃ; niyamato pana itthiyā eva indriyaṃ ‘itthindriyaṃ’.

This is that form, the female faculty. This form is not like the eye faculty and so on, which exist in a man as well; rather, as a rule, the faculty belonging only to a woman is the ‘female faculty.’

633. Purisindriyepi eseva [P 0.0322] nayo. Purisaliṅgādīni pana itthiliṅgādīnaṃ paṭipakkhato veditabbāni. Purisassa hi hatthapādagīvāurādīnaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ na itthiyā viya hoti. Purisānañhi uparimakāyo visado hoti heṭṭhimakāyo avisado, hatthapādā mahantā, mukhaṃ mahantaṃ, uramaṃsaṃ visadaṃ, massudāṭhikā uppajjanti. Kesabandhanavatthaggahaṇaṃ na itthīnaṃ viya hoti. Daharakāle rathanaṅgalādīhi kīḷanti, vālikapāḷiṃ katvā vāpiṃ nāma khananti, gamanādīni visadāni honti. Itthimpi gamanādīni visadāni kurumānaṃ disvā ‘puriso viya gacchatī’tiādīni vadanti. Sesaṃ itthindriye vuttasadisameva.

633. The same method applies to the male faculty. Male characteristics, however, should be understood as the opposite of female characteristics. For a man, the form of his hands, feet, neck, chest, and so on is not like that of a woman. For men, the upper body is prominent and the lower body is not prominent; their hands and feet are large, their faces are large, the flesh of the chest is prominent, and beards and mustaches grow. Their manner of tying hair and wearing clothes is not like that of women. In their youth, boys play with toy chariots and plows; making a ridge of sand, they dig what they call a reservoir. Their walking and so on is prominent. On seeing a woman performing prominent movements like walking, they say, “She walks like a man,” and so on. The rest is similar to what was said regarding the female faculty.

Tattha itthibhāvalakkhaṇaṃ itthindriyaṃ, itthīti pakāsanarasaṃ, itthiliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Purisabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ purisindriyaṃ, purisoti pakāsanarasaṃ, purisaliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Ubhayampetaṃ paṭhamakappikānaṃ pavatte samuṭṭhāti. Aparabhāge paṭisandhiyaṃ. Paṭisandhisamuṭṭhitampi pavatte calati parivattati.

Therein, the female faculty has the state of being a woman as its characteristic; its function is to indicate ‘woman’; its manifestation is being the cause for a woman’s sign, mark, demeanor, and manner. The male faculty has the state of being a man as its characteristic; its function is to indicate ‘man’; its manifestation is being the cause for a man’s sign, mark, demeanor, and manner. Both of these arise during the course of life in the case of beings of the first aeon. In a later period, they arise at rebirth-linking. Even what has arisen with rebirth-linking moves and changes during the course of life.

Yathāha [M 0.0359] –

As it was said:

“Tena [V 0.0355] kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhūtaṃ hoti. Tena kho pana samayena aññatarissā bhikkhuniyā purisaliṅgaṃ pātubhūtaṃ hotī”ti (pārā. 69).

“Now at that time, the female organ had appeared in a certain bhikkhu. Now at that time, the male organ had appeared in a certain bhikkhunī.”

Imesu pana dvīsu purisaliṅgaṃ uttamaṃ, itthiliṅgaṃ hīnaṃ. Tasmā purisaliṅgaṃ balavaakusalena antaradhāyati, itthiliṅgaṃ dubbalakusalena patiṭṭhāti. Itthiliṅgaṃ pana antaradhāyantaṃ dubbalaakusalena antaradhāyati, purisaliṅgaṃ balavakusalena patiṭṭhāti. Evaṃ ubhayampi akusalena antaradhāyati, kusalena patiṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ.

Among these two, the male sex is superior and the female sex is inferior. Therefore, the male sex disappears through strong unwholesome kamma, while the female sex becomes established through weak wholesome kamma. The female sex, in turn, disappears through weak unwholesome kamma, while the male sex becomes established through strong wholesome kamma. Thus it should be understood that in both cases a sex disappears through unwholesome kamma and a sex is established through wholesome kamma.

Ubhatobyañjanakassa pana kiṃ ekaṃ indriyaṃ udāhu dveti? Ekaṃ. Tañca kho itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthindriyaṃ, purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisindriyaṃ. ‘Evaṃ sante dutiyabyañjanakassa abhāvo āpajjati. Indriyañhi byañjanakāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tañcassa natthī’ti? ‘Na tassa indriyaṃ byañjanakāraṇaṃ’. ‘Kasmā’? ‘Sadā [P 0.0323] abhāvato. Itthiubhatobyañjanakassa hi yadā itthiyā rāgacittaṃ uppajjati, tadāva purisabyañjanaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, itthibyañjanaṃ paṭicchannaṃ guḷhaṃ hoti. Tathā itarassa itaraṃ.

Now, for a hermaphrodite, is there one faculty or two? There is one. It is the female faculty for a female hermaphrodite, and the male faculty for a male hermaphrodite. 'If that is so, does it not follow that the second characteristic is absent? For the faculty is said to be the cause of the characteristic, and that [second faculty] is absent for this one.' 'For this one, the faculty is not the cause of that characteristic.' 'Why?' 'Because of its constant absence. For in the case of a female hermaphrodite, it is only when lustful consciousness towards a woman arises that the male characteristic becomes manifest and the female characteristic becomes hidden and concealed. So too for the other in the other case.'

Yadi ca tesaṃ indriyaṃ dutiyabyañjanakāraṇaṃ bhaveyya, sadāpi byañjanadvayaṃ tiṭṭheyya. Na pana tiṭṭhati. Tasmā veditabbametaṃ na tassa taṃ byañjanakāraṇaṃ. Kammasahāyaṃ pana rāgacittamevettha kāraṇaṃ. Yasmā cassa ekameva indriyaṃ hoti, tasmā itthiubhatobyañjanako sayampi gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, parampi gaṇhāpeti. Purisaubhatobyañjanako paraṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpeti, sayaṃ pana na gaṇhātīti.

For if their faculty were the cause of the second characteristic, a pair of characteristics would always be present. But they are not. Therefore it should be understood that for this one, that [faculty] is not the cause of the [second] characteristic. Rather, it is lustful consciousness, assisted by kamma, that is the cause here. And since this one has only one faculty, a female hermaphrodite can both conceive herself and cause another to conceive. A male hermaphrodite can cause another to conceive but cannot conceive himself.

634. Jīvitindriyaniddese yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ heṭṭhā arūpajīvitindriye vuttameva. Kevalañhi tattha yo tesaṃ arūpīnaṃ dhammānanti vuttaṃ, idha rūpajīvitindriyattā yo tesaṃ rūpīnaṃ dhammānanti ayameva viseso. Lakkhaṇādīni panassa evaṃ veditabbāni – sahajātarūpānupālanalakkhaṇaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesaṃ yeva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbabhūtapadaṭṭhānanti.

634. In the exposition of the life faculty, what should be said has already been stated above in connection with the immaterial life faculty. The only difference is this: there it was said, 'of those immaterial phenomena,' whereas here, since this is the material life faculty, it is said, 'of those material phenomena.' Its characteristics, etc., should be understood as follows: the life faculty has the characteristic of guarding co-nascent material phenomena; its function is to cause them to occur; its manifestation is their establishment; its proximate cause is the primary material phenomena that are to be maintained.

635. Kāyaviññattiniddese [M 0.0360][V 0.0356] kāyaviññattīti ettha tāva kāyena attano bhāvaṃ viññāpentānaṃ tiracchānehipi purisānaṃ, purisehi vā tiracchānānampi kāyagahaṇānusārena gahitāya etāya bhāvo viññāyatīti ‘viññatti’. Sayaṃ kāyagahaṇānusārena viññāyatītipi ‘viññatti’. “Kāyena saṃvaro sādhū”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 361) āgato copanasaṅkhāto kāyova viññatti ‘kāyaviññatti’. Kāyavipphandanena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttā, sayañca tathā viññeyyattā kāyena viññattītipi ‘kāyaviññatti’.

635. In the exposition of bodily intimation, regarding the term 'bodily intimation': firstly, it is 'intimation' (viññatti) because by means of this [movement], when grasped in accordance with the perception of the body, the intention of those making their intention known—whether of humans to animals, or of animals to humans—is made known. Or it is 'intimation' because it is itself made known in accordance with the perception of the body. The body itself, designated as 'movement,' which is mentioned in such passages as, 'Good is restraint in body' (Dhp 361), is 'bodily intimation.' Because it is a cause for intimating one's intention through bodily movement, and because it is itself to be known in such a way, it is 'intimation by means of the body,' thus 'bodily intimation.'

Kusalacittassa vātiādīsu aṭṭhahi kāmāvacarehi abhiññācittena cāti navahi kusalacittehi kusalacittassa vā, dvādasahipi akusalacittehi akusalacittassa vā, aṭṭhahi mahākiriyehi dvīhi ahetukakiriyehi abhiññāppattena ekena rūpāvacarakiriyenāti ekādasahi kiriyacittehi abyākatacittassa vā. Ito aññāni hi cittāni viññattiṃ na janenti. Sekkhāsekkhaputhujjanānaṃ [P 0.0324] pana ettakeheva cittehi viññatti hotīti etesaṃ kusalādīnaṃ vasena tīhi padehi ‘hetuto’ dassitā.

In the passage beginning with 'of one with a wholesome consciousness, etc.': by means of nine wholesome consciousnesses—that is, the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses and the superknowledge consciousness—[intimation arises] for one with a wholesome consciousness; or by means of all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses for one with an unwholesome consciousness; or by means of eleven functional consciousnesses—that is, the eight great functional, the two rootless functional, and the one form-sphere functional that has attained superknowledge—for one with an indeterminate consciousness. Indeed, consciousnesses other than these do not generate intimation. Now, since intimation occurs for trainees, those beyond training, and worldlings by just these consciousnesses, it is shown 'from the cause' by means of these three phrases based on the wholesome, etc.

Idāni chahi padehi ‘phalato’ dassetuṃ abhikkamantassa vātiādi vuttaṃ. Abhikkamādayo hi viññattivasena pavattattā viññattiphalaṃ nāma. Tattha ‘abhikkamantassā’ti purato kāyaṃ abhiharantassa. Paṭikkamantassāti pacchato paccāharantassa. Ālokentassāti ujukaṃ pekkhantassa. Vilokentassāti ito cito ca pekkhantassa. Samiñjentassāti sandhayo saṅkocentassa. Pasārentassāti sandhayo paṭipaṇāmentassa.

Now, to show this 'from the result' with six phrases, the passage beginning 'of one who advances' is stated. Since advancing and so on occur by way of intimation, they are called 'the result of intimation.' Therein, 'of one who advances' means of one who moves the body forward. 'Of one who retreats' means of one who moves it backward. 'Of one who looks ahead' means of one who looks straight. 'Of one who looks around' means of one who looks here and there. 'Of one who contracts' means of one who bends the joints. 'Of one who extends' means of one who stretches the joints.

Idāni chahi padehi ‘sabhāvato’ dassetuṃ kāyassa thambhanāti ādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ‘kāyassā’ti sarīrassa. Kāyaṃ thambhetvā thaddhaṃ karotīti thambhanā. Tameva upasaggena vaḍḍhetvā santhambhanāti āha. Balavatarā vā thambhanā ‘santhambhanā’. Santhambhitattanti santhambhitabhāvo. Viññāpanavasena viññatti. Viññāpanāti viññāpanākāro. Viññāpitabhāvo viññāpitattaṃ. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ heṭṭhā dvārakathāyaṃ vuttameva. Tathā vacīviññattiyaṃ.

Now, to show this 'from its own-being' with six phrases, the passage beginning 'stiffening of the body' is stated. Therein, 'of the body' means of the physical frame. 'Stiffening' (thambhanā) is what makes the body stiff, having supported it. Having augmented this very term with a prefix, it is called 'thorough stiffening' (santhambhanā). Or, 'thorough stiffening' is a more powerful stiffening. 'The state of being thoroughly stiffened' (santhambhitattaṃ) is the state of having been thoroughly stiffened. 'Intimation' (viññatti) is by way of making known. 'Making known' (viññāpanā) is the mode of making known. 'The state of having been made known' (viññāpitattaṃ) is the state of having been made known. Whatever else should be said here has already been stated above in the discourse on the doors. The same applies to verbal intimation.

636. Vacīviññattītipadassa [M 0.0361] pana niddesapadānañca attho tattha na vutto, so evaṃ veditabbo – vācāya attano bhāvaṃ viññāpentānaṃ tiracchānehipi purisānaṃ, purisehi vā tiracchānānampi[V 0.0357], vacīgahaṇānusārena gahitāya etāya bhāvo viññāyatīti viññatti. Sayañca vacīgahaṇānusārena viññāyatītipi viññatti. “Sādhu vācāya saṃvaro”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 361) āgatā copanasaṅkhātā vacī eva viññatti ‘vacīviññatti’. Vacīghosena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttā sayañca tathāviññeyyattā vācāya viññattītipi ‘vacīviññatti’. Vācā girātiādīsu vuccatīti ‘vācā’. Giriyatīti ‘girā’. Byappathoti vākyabhedo. Vākyañca taṃ patho ca atthaṃ ñātukāmānaṃ ñāpetukāmānañcātipi ‘byappatho’. Udīriyatīti udīraṇaṃ. Ghussatīti ghoso. Kariyatīti kammaṃ. Ghosova kammaṃ ghosakammaṃ. Nānappakārehi kato [P 0.0325] ghosoti attho. Vaciyā bhedo vacībhedo. So pana ‘na bhaṅgo, pabhedagatā vācā evā’ti ñāpanatthaṃ vācā vacībhedoti vuttaṃ. Imehi sabbehipi padehi ‘saddavācāva’ dassitā. Idāni tāya vācāya saddhiṃ yojetvā heṭṭhā vuttatthānaṃ viññattiādīnaṃ padānaṃ vasena tīhākārehi sabhāvato taṃ dassetuṃ yā tāya vācāya viññattītiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva.

636. Now, the meaning of the term 'verbal intimation' and of its expositional terms was not stated there; it should be understood thus: it is 'intimation' (viññatti) because by means of this, when it is grasped in accordance with the grasp of speech, the intention of those making their intention known—whether of humans by animals, or of animals by humans—is made known. And it is also 'intimation' because it is itself made known in accordance with the grasp of speech. In passages such as, 'Good is restraint in speech' (Dhp 361), the speech that is mentioned, designated as 'copana' (instigation), is itself the intimation, 'verbal intimation.' Because it is a cause for intimating one's intention through the sound of speech, and because it is itself to be known in such a way, it is also 'intimation by way of speech' (vācāya viññatti), thus 'verbal intimation.' In the passage beginning 'vācā, girā,' etc.: because it is spoken (vuccati), it is 'speech' (vācā). Because it is uttered (girīyati), it is 'utterance' (girā). 'Discourse' (byappatho) is a division of speech (vākyabhedo). And because it is both speech (vākya) and a path (patha) for those who wish to know and to make known the meaning, it is also 'discourse' (byappatho). Because it is pronounced (udīriyati), it is 'pronouncement' (udīraṇaṃ). Because it is sounded (ghussati), it is 'sound' (ghoso). Because it is done (karīyati), it is 'action' (kammaṃ). The sound itself is the action; 'sound-action' (ghosakammaṃ). The meaning is: sound made in various ways. 'Division of speech' (vacībhedo) is a division of speech (vaciyā bhedo). Now, to make known that this is 'not a breaking (bhaṅgo), but is speech that has attained diversity (pabheda),' it is stated as 'speech, division of speech' (vācā vacībhedo). By all these terms, 'audible speech' is shown. Now, in order to show that speech 'from its own-being' in three ways—by means of the terms 'intimation,' etc., whose meanings were stated above, connecting them with that speech—the passage beginning 'that which is the intimation by that speech' is stated. Since this follows the method stated above, its meaning is plain.

Idāni viññattisamuṭṭhāpakacittesu asammohatthaṃ dvattiṃsa chabbīsa ekūnavīsati soḷasa pacchimānīti idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ – dvattiṃsa cittāni hi rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, iriyāpathampi upatthambhenti, duvidhampi viññattiṃ janenti. Chabbīsati viññattimeva na janenti, itaradvayaṃ karonti. Ekūnavīsati rūpameva samuṭṭhāpenti, itaradvayaṃ na karonti. Soḷasa imesu tīsu ekampi na karonti.

Now, for the sake of non-confusion regarding the consciousnesses that originate intimation, this miscellany should be understood: thirty-two, twenty-six, nineteen, and the final sixteen. For thirty-two consciousnesses originate material form, support the postures, and generate both kinds of intimation. Twenty-six do not generate intimation but perform the other two functions. Nineteen originate only material form and do not perform the other two. Sixteen do not perform any of these three.

Tattha dvattiṃsāti heṭṭhā vuttāneva kāmāvacarato aṭṭha kusalāni, dvādasa akusalāni, kiriyato dasa cittāni, sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ abhiññācittaṃ, khīṇāsavānaṃ abhiññācittanti. Chabbīsāti rūpāvacarato pañca kusalāni, pañca kiriyāni, arūpāvacarato cattāri kusalāni, cattāri kiriyāni, cattāri maggacittāni, cattāri phalacittānīti. Ekūnavīsatīti kāmāvacarakusalavipākato ekādasa, akusalavipākato dve[M 0.0362], kiriyato kiriyamanodhātu, rūpāvacarato pañca vipākacittānīti. Soḷasāti dve pañcaviññāṇāni, sabbasattānaṃ paṭisandhicittaṃ, khīṇāsavānaṃ cuticittaṃ, arūpe cattāri vipākacittānīti. Imāni soḷasa rūpiriyāpathaviññattīsu ekampi na karonti. Aññānipi bahūni arūpe uppannāni anokāsagatattā rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpenti. Na tāneva, kāyavacīviññattiyopi.

Therein, the thirty-two are just as stated above: from the sense-sphere, eight wholesome consciousnesses, twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, and ten functional consciousnesses; the superknowledge consciousness of trainees and worldlings, and the superknowledge consciousness of the taint-freed ones. The twenty-six are: from the form-sphere, five wholesome and five functional; from the formless-sphere, four wholesome and four functional; the four path consciousnesses, and the four fruition consciousnesses. The nineteen are: from the sense-sphere wholesome resultants, eleven; from the unwholesome resultants, two; from the functional, the functional mind-element; and from the form-sphere, five resultant consciousnesses. The sixteen are: the two sets of fivefold sense consciousness, the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings, the decease consciousness of the taint-freed ones, and the four resultant consciousnesses in the formless realm. These sixteen do not perform even one of the functions concerning material form, postures, and intimations. Many other consciousnesses that have arisen in the formless realm also do not originate material form because they have reached a locationless state. Not only that, they also do not generate bodily and verbal intimations.

637. Ākāsadhātuniddese [V 0.0358] na kassati, na nikassati, kasituṃ vā chindituṃ vā bhindituṃ vā na sakkāti ākāso. Ākāsova ākāsagataṃ[P 0.0326], kheḷagatādi viya. Ākāsoti vā gatanti ‘ākāsagataṃ’. Na haññatīti aghaṃ, aghaṭṭanīyanti attho. Aghameva aghagataṃ. Chiddaṭṭhena vivaro. Vivarova vivaragataṃ. Asamphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehīti etehi asamphuṭṭhaṃ nijjaṭākāsaṃva kathitaṃ.
