Lakkhaṇādito pana rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇā ākāsadhātu, rūpapariyantappakāsanarasā, rūpamariyādapaccupaṭṭhānā asamphuṭṭhabhāvachiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, paricchinnarūpapadaṭṭhānā, yāya paricchinnesu rūpesu ‘idamito uddhaṃ adho tiriya’nti ca hoti.

637. In the exposition of the space element: 'space' (ākāsa) is so called because it is not scratched (na kassati), not etched (na nikassati), and cannot be scratched, cut, or broken. 'Gone to space' (ākāsagataṃ) is simply space, like 'gone to phlegm,' etc. Or it is 'gone to space' because it is a place known as space. 'Unobstructed' (aghaṃ) is so called because it is not struck (na haññati); the meaning is 'unimpingeable.' 'Gone to the unobstructed' (aghagataṃ) is simply the unobstructed. 'Opening' (vivaro) is in the sense of an aperture. 'Gone to the opening' (vivaragataṃ) is simply the opening. 'Untouched by the four great elements': by this it is described as untouched, like unentangled space. But as to its characteristics and so on, the space element has the characteristic of delimiting material form; its function is to display the boundary of material form; its manifestation is the limit of material form, or its manifestation is the state of being untouched, an aperture, an opening; its proximate cause is the material form that is delimited, by which, in regard to delimited material forms, there comes to be [the cognition]: 'This is above that, below it, and across from it.'

638. Ito pare rūpassalahutādīnaṃ niddesā cittassalahutādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Lakkhaṇādito panettha adandhatālakkhaṇā rūpassa lahutā, rūpānaṃ garubhāvavinodanarasā, lahuparivattitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, lahurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Athaddhatālakkhaṇā rūpassa mudutā, rūpānaṃ thaddhabhāvavinodanarasā, sabbakiriyāsu avirodhitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, mudurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Sarīrakiriyānukūlakammaññabhāvalakkhaṇā rūpassa kammaññatā, akammaññatāvinodanarasā, adubbalabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammaññarūpapadaṭṭhānā.

638. From here onward, the expositions of lightness of form and so on should be understood in the same way as was explained for lightness of consciousness and so on. Here, as to characteristics and so on, lightness of form has non-sluggishness as its characteristic, dispelling the heaviness of forms as its function, quick changing as its manifestation, and light form as its proximate cause. Softness of form has non-rigidity as its characteristic, dispelling the rigidity of forms as its function, non-opposition to all actions as its manifestation, and soft form as its proximate cause. Wieldiness of form has the state of being wieldy and suitable for bodily actions as its characteristic, dispelling unwieldiness as its function, a state of non-feebleness as its manifestation, and wieldy form as its proximate cause.

Etā pana tisso na aññamaññaṃ vijahanti. Evaṃ santepi yo arogino viya rūpānaṃ lahubhāvo, adandhatālahuparivattippakāro, rūpadandhattakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhāno, so rūpavikāro ‘rūpassalahutā’. Yo suparimadditacammasseva rūpānaṃ mudubhāvo sabbakiriyāvisesesu sarasavattanabhāvo vasavattanabhāvamaddavappakāro rūpathaddhattakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhāno[M 0.0363], so rūpavikāro ‘rūpassa mudutā’. Yo pana sudhantasuvaṇṇasseva rūpānaṃ kammaññabhāvo sarīrakiriyānukūlabhāvappakāro sarīrakiriyānaṃ [P 0.0327] ananukūlakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhāno, so rūpavikāro ‘rūpassa kammaññatā’ti. Evametāsaṃ viseso veditabbo.

These three, however, do not abandon one another. Even so, the alteration of form that is like the lightness of a healthy person, a mode of non-sluggishness and quick changing, arising from conditions that are the opposite of the elemental disturbance that produces sluggishness in form—this alteration of form is called ‘lightness of form.’ The alteration of form that is like the softness of well-tanned leather, a state of being able to perform its own function in all special actions, a mode of being controllable and soft, arising from conditions that are the opposite of the elemental disturbance that produces rigidity in form—this alteration of form is called ‘softness of form.’ And the alteration of form that is like the wieldiness of well-refined gold, a mode of suitability for bodily actions, arising from conditions that are the opposite of the elemental disturbance that produces unsuitability for bodily actions—this alteration of form is called ‘wieldiness of form.’ Thus, the distinction among these should be understood.

Etā pana tissopi kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, āhārādayova karonti. Tathā hi yogino ‘ajja amhehi bhojanasappāyaṃ laddhaṃ, kāyo no lahu mudu kammañño’ti vadanti. ‘Ajja utusappāyaṃ laddhaṃ, ajja amhākaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ, kāyo no lahu mudu kammañño’ti vadantīti.

Furthermore, kamma cannot produce these three; only nutriment and so on do so. For meditators say, ‘Today we have obtained suitable food; our body is light, soft, and wieldy.’ They also say, ‘Today we have obtained suitable weather; today our mind is concentrated; our body is light, soft, and wieldy.’

641. Upacayasantatiniddesesu [V 0.0359] āyatanānanti aḍḍhekādasannaṃ rūpāyatanānaṃ. Ācayoti nibbatti. So rūpassa upacayoti yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo punappunaṃ nibbattamānānaṃ, sova rūpassa upacayo nāma hoti; vaḍḍhīti attho. Yo rūpassa upacayo sā rūpassa santatīti yā evaṃ upacitānaṃ rūpānaṃ vaḍḍhi, tato uttaritaraṃ pavattikāle sā rūpassa santati nāma hoti; pavattīti attho. Naditīre khatakūpasmiñhi udakuggamanakālo viya ācayo, nibbatti; paripuṇṇakālo viya upacayo, vaḍḍhi; ajjhottharitvā gamanakālo viya santati, pavattīti veditabbā.

641. In the exposition of build-up and continuity: ‘of the bases’ refers to the eleven and a half material bases. ‘Accumulation’ means production. ‘That is the build-up of form’: the accumulation of the bases that are being repeatedly produced—this itself is called the build-up of form; the meaning is growth. ‘That build-up of form is the continuity of form’: the growth of forms thus built up, their further occurrence in the course of proceeding, is called the continuity of form; the meaning is proceeding. For it should be understood thus: the time of the water’s rising in a well dug on a riverbank is like accumulation, that is, production; the time of its being full is like build-up, that is, growth; and the time of its overflowing and flowing on is like continuity, that is, proceeding.

Evaṃ kiṃ kathitaṃ hotīti? Āyatanena hi ācayo kathito, ācayena āyatanaṃ kathitaṃ. Ācayova kathito āyatanameva kathitaṃ. Evampi kiṃ kathitaṃ hotīti? Catusantatirūpānaṃ ācayo upacayo nibbatti vaḍḍhi kathitā. Atthato hi ubhayampetaṃ jātirūpasseva adhivacanaṃ. Ākāranānattena pana veneyyavasena ca upacayo santatīti uddesadesanaṃ katvā yasmā ettha atthato nānattaṃ natthi, tasmā niddese “yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo so rūpassa upacayo, yo rūpassa upacayo sā rūpassa santatī”ti vuttaṃ.

What is meant by this? Accumulation is spoken of by means of the bases, and the bases are spoken of by means of accumulation. Accumulation itself is spoken of; the bases themselves are spoken of. What is also meant by this? The accumulation, build-up, production, and growth of the forms of the four continuities are spoken of. For in meaning, both of these are designations for arisen form itself. However, due to the variety of expression and for the sake of those to be trained, the summary exposition was made using the terms ‘build-up’ and ‘continuity.’ Since there is no difference here in meaning, therefore in the detailed explanation it is said: ‘The accumulation of the bases is the build-up of form, and the build-up of form is the continuity of form.’

Yasmā ca ubhayampetaṃ jātirūpasseva adhivacanaṃ tasmā ettha ācayalakkhaṇo rūpassa upacayo, pubbantato rūpānaṃ ummujjāpanaraso, niyyātanapaccupaṭṭhāno [M 0.0364] paripuṇṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāno. Pavattilakkhaṇā rūpassa santati, anuppabandharasā, anupacchedapaccupaṭṭhānā, anuppabandharūpapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

And since both of these are a designation for arisen form itself, therefore, it should be understood that here the build-up of form has accumulation as its characteristic, causing forms to emerge from a prior state as its function, and handing them over or a state of completion as its manifestation, with built-up form as its proximate cause. Continuity of form has proceeding as its characteristic, uninterrupted connection as its function, non-severance as its manifestation, and uninterruptedly connected form as its proximate cause.

643. Jaratāniddese jīraṇakavasena jarā; ayamettha sabhāvaniddeso[P 0.0328]. Jīraṇākāro jīraṇatā. Khaṇḍiccanti ādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Pacchimā dve pakatiniddesā. Ayañhi ‘jarā’ti iminā padena sabhāvato dīpitā; tenassāyaṃ sabhāvaniddeso. ‘Jīraṇatā’ti iminā ākārato; tenassāyaṃ ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccanti iminā kālātikkame dantanakhānaṃ khaṇḍitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Pāliccanti iminā kesalomānaṃ palitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Valittacatāti iminā maṃsaṃ milāpetvā tace valibhāvakaraṇakiccato dīpitā. Tenassā ime ‘khaṇḍicca’ntiādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Tehi imesaṃ vikārānaṃ dassanavasena pākaṭībhūtā pākaṭajarā dassitā. Yatheva hi [V 0.0360] udakassa vā aggino vā tiṇarukkhādīnaṃ saṃbhaggapalibhaggatāya vā jhāmatāya vā gatamaggo pākaṭo hoti, na ca so gatamaggo tāneva udakādīni, evameva jarāya dantādīsu khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, cakkhuṃ ummīletvāpi gayhati, na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarā. Na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā hoti.

643. In the exposition of aging, jarā is so called by way of decaying; this here is an exposition of its intrinsic nature. The mode of decaying is agedness (jīraṇatā). ‘Broken-toothedness’ (khaṇḍicca) and the next two terms are expositions of its function over the passage of time. The last two are expositions of its natural state. For this aging is revealed by the term ‘jarā’ in terms of its intrinsic nature; hence this is an exposition of its intrinsic nature. It is revealed by ‘agedness’ in terms of its mode; hence this is an exposition of its mode. It is revealed by ‘broken-toothedness’ through its function of causing the breaking of teeth and nails over the passage of time; by ‘greyness’ (pālicca) through its function of causing the greying of head hair and body hair; by ‘wrinkled skin’ (valittacatā) through its function of causing the skin to wrinkle after the flesh has withered. Therefore, these three terms—‘broken-toothedness’ and so on—are expositions of its function over the passage of time. Through them, by way of observing these alterations, manifest aging which has become apparent is shown. Just as the path taken by water or fire becomes evident in grass, trees, and the like through their being broken, shattered, or burnt, yet that path taken is not the water or fire itself, so too the path taken by aging becomes evident in teeth and so on by way of broken-toothedness and the like, and is grasped even with eyes open. Yet broken-toothedness and the like are not aging itself, for aging is not cognizable by eye-consciousness.

Āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripākoti imehi pana padehi kālātikkameyeva abhibyattāya āyukkhayacakkhādiindriyaparipākasaññitāya pakatiyā dīpitā. Tenassime pacchimā dve pakatiniddesāti veditabbā. Tattha yasmā jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati, tasmā jarā ‘āyuno saṃhānī’ti phalūpacārena vuttā. Yasmā ca daharakāle suppasannāni, sukhumampi attano visayaṃ sukheneva gaṇhanasamatthāni cakkhādīni indriyāni jaraṃ pattassa paripakkāni āluḷitāni avisadāni, oḷārikampi attano visayaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthāni honti, tasmā ‘indriyānaṃ paripāko’tipi phalūpacāreneva vuttā.

By the terms ‘the decline of life’ and ‘the maturation of the faculties,’ however, aging is revealed by its natural state, which is designated as the decay of life and the maturation of the faculties such as the eye, becoming fully manifest only with the passage of time. Therefore, these last two are to be understood as expositions of its natural state. Herein, because the life of one who has reached old age diminishes, aging is called ‘the decline of life’ by way of a figurative expression based on the result. And because the faculties such as the eye, which in youth are very clear and capable of easily grasping even their own subtle objects, become, in one who has reached old age, overripe, confused, and unclear, incapable of grasping even their own coarse objects, it is also called ‘the maturation of the faculties’ by way of a figurative expression based on the result.

Sā panāyaṃ evaṃ niddiṭṭhā sabbāpi jarā pākaṭā paṭicchannāti duvidhā hoti. Tattha dantādīsu khaṇḍabhāvādidassanato rūpadhammesu jarā pākaṭajarā nāma[M 0.0365]. Arūpadhammesu pana jarā tādisassa vikārassa adassanato paṭicchannajarā nāma. Puna avīci savīcīti evampi duvidhā hoti. Tattha maṇikanakarajatapavāḷacandimasūriyādīnaṃ viya, mandadasakādīsu pāṇīnaṃ viya ca, pupphaphalapallavādīsu [P 0.0329] ca apāṇīnaṃ viya, antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ duviññeyyattā jarā avīcijarā nāma; nirantarajarāti attho. Tato aññesu pana yathāvuttesu antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā jarā savīcijarā nāmāti veditabbā.

Further, all this aging, thus described, is of two kinds: manifest and concealed. Herein, aging in material phenomena, where alterations such as the state of being broken are visible in teeth and so on, is called manifest aging. But aging in immaterial phenomena, where such an alteration is not visible, is called concealed aging. Again, it is also of two kinds: uninterrupted (avīci) and interrupted (savīci). Herein, as with gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and so on, and as with living beings in the first decade of life and so on, and as with non-living things like flowers, fruits, and shoots, and so on, because the specific changes in color and so on are difficult to discern from time to time, aging is called uninterrupted aging; the meaning is continuous aging. But in others than those, as stated, because the specific changes in color and so on are easily discernible from time to time, aging is to be understood as interrupted aging.

Lakkhaṇāditopi rūpaparipākalakkhaṇā rūpassa jaratā, upanayanarasā, sabhāvānapagamepi navabhāvāpagamapaccupaṭṭhānā, vīhipurāṇabhāvo viya paripaccamānarūpapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

Also from the perspective of characteristics and so on, it should be understood that the aging of form has the ripening of form as its characteristic, the function of leading on to death, the manifestation of the departure of newness even while its intrinsic nature has not departed—like the state of rice becoming old—and has ripening form as its proximate cause.

644. Aniccatāniddese khayagamanavasena khayo, vayagamanavasena vayo, bhijjanavasena bhedo. Atha vā, yasmā taṃ patvā rūpaṃ khīyati, veti, bhijjati ca, tasmā khīyati etasminti ‘khayo’, veti etasminti ‘vayo’, bhijjati etasminti ‘bhedo’. Upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā bhedova paribhedo. Hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena, na niccanti aniccaṃ. Tassa bhāvo aniccatā[V 0.0361]. Antaradhāyati etthāti antaradhānaṃ. Maraṇañhi patvā rūpaṃ antaradhāyati, adassanaṃ gacchati. Na kevalañca rūpameva, sabbepi pañcakkhandhā. Tasmā pañcannampi khandhānaṃ aniccatāya idameva lakkhaṇanti veditabbaṃ. Lakkhaṇādito pana paribhedalakkhaṇā rūpassa aniccatā, saṃsīdanarasā, khayavayapaccupaṭṭhānā, paribhijjamānarūpapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

644. In the exposition of impermanence, it is called khaya (destruction) by way of its going to destruction, vaya (vanishing) by way of its going to vanish, and bheda (breaking up) by way of its breaking up. Alternatively, because form, having reached it, is destroyed, vanishes, and breaks up, therefore ‘that in which it is destroyed’ is khaya; ‘that in which it vanishes’ is vaya; and ‘that in which it breaks up’ is bheda. By way of a prefix, the word is expanded, and bheda itself is called paribheda (complete breaking). In the sense of ‘having been and then ceasing to be,’ ‘not permanent’ (na niccaṃ) is impermanent (aniccaṃ). The state of that is impermanence (aniccatā). ‘It disappears herein,’ thus it is disappearance (antaradhāna). For form, having reached death, disappears, becomes unseen. And not only form, but all five aggregates. Therefore, this should be understood as the very characteristic of impermanence for all five aggregates. But from the perspective of characteristics and so on, it should be understood that the impermanence of form has complete breaking as its characteristic, crumbling as its function, destruction and vanishing as its manifestation, and form that is breaking up as its proximate cause.

Heṭṭhā jāti gahitā jarā gahitā, imasmiṃ ṭhāne maraṇaṃ gahitaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā imesaṃ sattānaṃ ukkhittāsikapaccāmittasadisā. Yathā hi purisassa tayo paccāmittā otāraṃ gavesamānā vicareyyuṃ. Tesu eko evaṃ vadeyya – ‘etaṃ nīharitvā aṭavipavesanaṃ mayhaṃ bhāro hotū’ti. Dutiyo ‘aṭavigatakāle pothetvā pathaviyaṃ pātanaṃ mayhaṃ bhāro’ti. Tatiyo ‘pathavigatakālato paṭṭhāya asinā sīsacchedanaṃ mayhaṃ bhāro’ti. Evarūpā ime jāti ādayo. Nīharitvā aṭavipavesanapaccāmittasadisā hettha jāti, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne nibbattāpanato. Aṭavigataṃ pothetvā pathaviyaṃ pātanapaccāmittasadisā jarā[M 0.0366], nibbattakkhandhānaṃ dubbalaparādhīnamañcaparāyaṇabhāvakaraṇato. Pathavigatassa [P 0.0330] asinā sīsacchedakapaccāmittasadisaṃ maraṇaṃ, jarāppattānaṃ khandhānaṃ jīvitakkhayapāpanatoti.

Previously, birth was taken up and aging was taken up; in this place, death is taken up. These three states are like enemies with raised swords for these beings. For it is as if three enemies of a man might wander about seeking an opportunity. Among them, one might say: ‘Let it be my task to drag this one out and make him enter the forest.’ The second might say: ‘Let it be my task to strike him and make him fall to the ground when he has reached the forest.’ The third might say: ‘Let it be my task to cut off his head with a sword from the time he is on the ground.’ Such are these states—birth and so on. Herein, birth is like the enemy who drags one out and makes one enter the forest, because it causes generation in this or that place. Aging is like the enemy who strikes one who has reached the forest and makes him fall to the ground, because it makes the generated aggregates weak, dependent, and destined for the sickbed. Death is like the enemy who cuts off with a sword the head of one who has reached the ground, because it brings the aggregates that have reached old age to the exhaustion of life.

645. Kabaḷīkārāhāraniddese kabaḷaṃ karīyatīti kabaḷīkāro. Āharīyatīti āhāro. Kabaḷaṃ katvā ajjhoharīyatīti attho. Rūpaṃ vā āharatītipi ‘āhāro’. Evaṃ vatthuvasena nāmaṃ uddharitvā puna vatthuvasenevetaṃ pabhedato dassetuṃ odano kummāsotiādi vuttaṃ. Odanādīni hi phāṇitapariyantāni dvādasa idhādhippetassa āhārassa vatthūni. Pāḷiyaṃ anāgatāni mūlaphalādīni yevāpanakaṃ paviṭṭhāni.

645. In the explanation of nutriment as morsels of food: Because it is made into a morsel (kabaḷaṃ karīyati), it is called a morsel (kabaḷīkāro). Because it is consumed (āharīyati), it is called nutriment (āhāro). The meaning is that it is ingested after being made into a morsel. Or, because it brings forth material form (rūpa), it is also called ‘nutriment.’ Thus, having derived the name in connection with the physical basis, to show its divisions again in connection with the physical basis itself, it is said: ‘rice, gruel,’ and so on. For the twelve items beginning with rice and ending with molasses are the physical bases of the nutriment intended here. Roots, fruits, and so on, which are not mentioned in the Pāli text, are included under the general category of nutriment (yevāpanaka).

Idāni tāni mūlaphalādīni kattabbato dassetuṃ yamhi yamhi janapadetiādimāha. Tattha mukhena asitabbaṃ bhuñjitabbanti mukhāsiyaṃ. Dantehi vikhāditabbanti dantavikhādanaṃ. Galena ajjhoharitabbanti galajjhoharaṇīyaṃ. Idāni taṃ kiccavasena dassetuṃ kucchivitthambhananti āha. Tañhi mūlaphalādi odanakummāsādi vā ajjhohaṭaṃ kucchiṃ vitthambheti. Idamassa kiccaṃ. Yāya ojāya sattā yāpentīti heṭṭhā sabbapadehi savatthukaṃ āhāraṃ dassetvā idāni nibbaṭṭitaojameva dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ.

Now, to show those roots, fruits, and so on, by way of what is to be done with them, he says, beginning with ‘In whatever region...’ Therein, ‘that which is to be eaten with the mouth’ is mukhāsiyaṃ; ‘that which is to be chewed with the teeth’ is dantavikhādanaṃ; ‘that which is to be swallowed with the throat’ is galajjhoharaṇīyaṃ. Now, to show its function, he says, ‘distending the stomach.’ For that nutriment—be it roots, fruits, etc., or rice, gruel, etc.—when swallowed, distends the stomach. This is its function. Having previously shown nutriment together with its physical basis by means of all the terms, now, to show only the nutritive essence produced from it, this is said: ‘by which nutritive essence beings maintain themselves.’

Kiṃ [V 0.0362] panettha vatthussa kiccaṃ? Kiṃ ojāya? Parissayaharaṇapālanāni. Vatthuhi parissayaṃ harati pāletuṃ na sakkoti, ojā pāleti parissayaṃ harituṃ na sakkoti. Dvepi ekato hutvā pāletumpi sakkonti parissayampi harituṃ. Ko panesa parissayo nāma? Kammajatejo. Antokucchiyañhi odanādivatthusmiṃ asati, kammajatejo uṭṭhahitvā udarapaṭalaṃ gaṇhāti, ‘chātomhi, āhāraṃ me dethā’ti vadāpeti. Bhuttakāle udarapaṭalaṃ muñcitvā vatthuṃ gaṇhāti. Atha satto ekaggo hoti.

Herein, what is the function of the physical basis? What of the nutritive essence? The removal of danger and maintaining. The physical basis removes danger but cannot maintain; the nutritive essence maintains but cannot remove danger. When they are together, they can both maintain and remove danger. Now what is this danger? The heat born of kamma. For when there is no physical basis like rice inside the stomach, the heat born of kamma arises, seizes the lining of the stomach, and makes one say, ‘I am hungry, give me food.’ When one has eaten, it releases the stomach lining and seizes the physical basis. Then the being becomes one-pointed.

Yathā hi chāyārakkhaso chāyaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ gahetvā devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā attano bhavane modanto chātakāle āgantvā sīse ḍaṃsati. So ḍaṭṭhattā viravati. Taṃ viravaṃ sutvā ‘dukkhappatto ettha atthī’ti tato tato manussā āgacchanti. So āgatāgate [P 0.0331] gahetvā khāditvā [M 0.0367] bhavane modati. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Chāyārakkhaso viya hi kammajatejo, devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā ṭhapitasatto viya udarapaṭalaṃ, puna āgatamanussā viya odanādivatthu, otaritvā sīse ḍaṃsanaṃ viya kammajatejassa vatthuto muttassa udarapaṭalaggahaṇaṃ, ḍaṭṭhassa viravanakālo viya ‘āhāraṃ dethā’ti vacanakālo, tāya saññāya āgatāgate gahetvā khāditvā bhavane modanakālo viya kammajatejena udarapaṭalaṃ muñcitvā vatthusmiṃ gahite ekaggacittatā.

For it is as if a shadow-ogre, having seized someone who has entered its shadow, binds them with a divine chain and, delighting in its own dwelling, returns when hungry to bite their head. Being bitten, the person cries out. Hearing that cry, people come from all around, thinking, ‘Someone is in distress here.’ The ogre seizes and devours those who arrive, then delights in its dwelling. The application of this simile should be understood as follows. The heat born of kamma is like the shadow-ogre. The stomach lining is like the person bound with a divine chain and set aside. The physical basis of food, such as rice, is like the people who arrive again. The seizing of the stomach lining by the heat born of kamma when it is released from the physical basis is like its descending and biting the head. The time of saying, ‘Give me food,’ is like the time the bitten person cries out. The one-pointedness of mind that occurs when the heat born of kamma releases the stomach lining and seizes the physical basis is like the time the ogre seizes and devours those who have arrived on that sign and delights in its dwelling.

Tattha oḷārike vatthusmiṃ ojā mandā hoti. Sukhume balavatī. Kudrūsakabhattādīni hi bhuñjitvā muhutteneva chāto hoti. Sappiādīni pivitvā ṭhitassa divasampi bhattaṃ na ruccati. Ettha ca upādāyupādāya oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā. Kumbhīlānañhi āhāraṃ upādāya morānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Kumbhīlā kira pāsāṇe gilanti. Te ca nesaṃ kucchippattā vilīyanti. Morā sappavicchikādipāṇe khādanti. Morānaṃ pana āhāraṃ upādāya taracchānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te kira tivassachaḍḍitāni visāṇāni ceva aṭṭhīni ca khādanti. Tāni ca nesaṃ kheḷena temitamattāneva kandamūlaṃ viya mudukāni honti. Taracchānampi āhāramupādāya hatthīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te hi nānārukkhasākhādayo khādanti. Hatthīnaṃ āhārato gavayagokaṇṇamigādīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te kira nissārāni nānārukkhapaṇṇādīni khādanti. Tesampi āhārato gunnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te allasukkhatiṇāni khādanti. Tesampi āhārato sasānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Sasānaṃ āhārato sakuṇānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Sakuṇānaṃ āhārato paccantavāsīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Paccantavāsīnaṃ [V 0.0363] āhārato gāmabhojakānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Gāmabhojakānaṃ āhārato rājarājamahāmattānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Tesampi āhārato cakkavattino āhāro sukhumo. Cakkavattino āhārato bhummadevānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Bhummadevānaṃ āhārato cātumahārājikānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Evaṃ yāva paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ [M 0.0368][P 0.0332] āhāro vitthāretabbo. Tesaṃ panāhāro sukhumotveva niṭṭhaṃ patto.

Herein, in a coarse physical basis, the nutritive essence is weak; in a subtle one, it is strong. For after eating coarse food like millet, one quickly becomes hungry. But for one who has drunk ghee and so on, food is not appealing even for a whole day. And here, coarseness and subtlety should be understood by way of successive comparison. For example, compared to the food of crocodiles, the food of peacocks is subtle. Crocodiles, it is said, swallow stones, and these dissolve upon reaching their stomachs. Peacocks eat creatures like snakes and scorpions. But compared to the food of peacocks, the food of hyenas is subtle. They, it is said, eat horns and bones discarded for three years, and these, merely moistened by their saliva, become as soft as a tuberous root. Compared to the food of hyenas, the food of elephants is subtle. They eat the branches of various trees. Compared to the food of elephants, the food of such animals as gayals and gokaṇṇa deer is subtle. They, it is said, eat the pithless leaves of various trees. Compared to their food, the food of cattle is subtle. They eat fresh and dry grass. Compared to their food, the food of hares is subtle. Compared to the food of hares, the food of birds is subtle. Compared to the food of birds, the food of border-dwellers is subtle. Compared to the food of border-dwellers, the food of village headmen is subtle. Compared to the food of village headmen, the food of kings and their great ministers is subtle. Compared to their food, the food of a wheel-turning monarch is subtle. Compared to the food of a wheel-turning monarch, the food of earth-deities is subtle. Compared to the food of earth-deities, the food of the devas of the Four Great Kings is subtle. In this way, it should be elaborated up to the food of the devas Who Wield Power over the Creations of Others. But their food reaches the conclusion of being simply subtle.

Lakkhaṇāditopi ojālakkhaṇo kabaḷīkāro āhāro, rūpāharaṇaraso, upatthambhanapaccupaṭṭhāno, kabaḷaṃ katvā āharitabbavatthupadaṭṭhānoti veditabbo.

From the perspective of its characteristic, etc., nutriment as morsels of food should be understood as having nutritive essence as its characteristic, the production of material form as its function, support as its manifestation, and the physical basis that is to be made into a morsel and consumed as its proximate cause.

646. Noupādāniddese yathā upādārūpaṃ upādiyateva, na aññena upādiyati, evametaṃ na upādiyatevāti noupādā.

646. In the explanation of ‘not derived’: Just as derived matter is only derived and is not that from which another is derived, so this is not only derived; thus it is ‘not derived.’

647. Phusitabbanti phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Phusitvā jānitabbanti attho. Phoṭṭhabbañca taṃ āyatanañcāti phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ. Āpo ca taṃ nissattasuññatasabhāvaṭṭhena dhātu cāti āpodhātu. Idāni yasmā tīṇi rūpāni phusitvā jānitabbāni tasmā tāni bhājetvā dassetuṃ katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ? Pathavīdhātūtiādimāha. Tattha kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu, patiṭṭhānarasā, sampaṭicchanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Tejodhātu uṇhattalakkhaṇā, paripācanarasā, maddavānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Vāyodhātu vitthambhanalakkhaṇā, samudīraṇarasā, abhinīhārapaccupaṭṭhānā. Purimā pana ‘āpodhātu’ paggharaṇalakkhaṇā, brūhanarasā, saṅgahapaccupaṭṭhānā. Ekekā cettha sesattayapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

647. ‘That which is to be touched’ is the tangible. The meaning is ‘that which is to be known by touching.’ ‘The tangible and that base’ is the tangible-base. ‘Water and that element’—in the sense of its nature of being non-sentient and void—is the water-element. Now, since three kinds of matter are to be known by touching, in order to show them dividedly, it is said: ‘What kind of matter is the tangible-base? The earth-element,’ etc. Herein, the earth-element has the characteristic of hardness, the function of acting as a foundation, and the manifestation of receiving. The fire-element has the characteristic of heat, the function of maturing, and the manifestation of producing softness. The air-element has the characteristic of supporting, the function of causing motion, and the manifestation of conveying. The aforementioned water-element, however, has the characteristic of flowing, the function of increasing, and the manifestation of cohesion. And it should be understood that each of these has the other three as its proximate cause.

Kakkhaḷanti thaddhaṃ. Mudukanti athaddhaṃ. Saṇhanti maṭṭhaṃ. Pharusanti kharaṃ. Sukhasamphassanti sukhavedanāpaccayaṃ iṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbaṃ. Dukkhasamphassanti dukkhavedanāpaccayaṃ aniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbaṃ. Garukanti bhāriyaṃ. Lahukanti abhāriyaṃ, sallahukanti attho. Ettha ca ‘kakkhaḷaṃ mudukaṃ saṇhaṃ pharusaṃ garukaṃ lahuka’nti padehi pathavīdhātu eva bhājitā. “Yadāyaṃ kāyo āyusahagato ca hoti usmāsahagato ca viññāṇasahagato ca tadā lahutaro ca hoti mudutaro ca kammaññataro [P 0.0333] cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.424) suttepi lahumudubhūtaṃ pathavīdhātumeva sandhāya vuttaṃ.

‘Hard’ means stiff. ‘Soft’ means not stiff. ‘Smooth’ means polished. ‘Rough’ means coarse. ‘Pleasant to touch’ means a desirable tangible object that is a condition for pleasant feeling. ‘Painful to touch’ means an undesirable tangible object that is a condition for painful feeling. ‘Heavy’ means weighty. ‘Light’ means not weighty; the meaning is ‘very light.’ And here, by the terms ‘hard, soft, smooth, rough, heavy, light,’ only the earth element is analyzed. In the sutta passage, “When this body is accompanied by life, heat, and consciousness, it is then lighter, softer, and more workable” (DN 29), it is also with reference to the earth element having become light and soft that this was said.

‘Sukhasamphassaṃ [V 0.0364] dukkhasamphassa’nti padadvayena pana tīṇipi mahābhūtāni bhājitāni. Pathavīdhātu hi sukhasamphassāpi atthi dukkhasamphassāpi. Tathā tejodhātuvāyodhātuyo. Tattha sukhasamphassā pathavīdhātu mudutaluṇahatthe [M 0.0369] dahare pāde sambāhante assādetvā assādetvā ‘sambāha tāta, sambāha tātā’ti vadāpanākāraṃ karoti. Sukhasamphassā tejodhātu sītasamaye aṅgārakapallaṃ āharitvā gattaṃ sedente assādetvā assādetvā ‘sedehi tāta, sedehi tātā’ti vadāpanākāraṃ karoti. Sukhasamphassā vāyodhātu uṇhasamaye vattasampanne dahare bījanena bījante assādetvā assādetvā ‘bīja tāta, bīja tātā’ti vadāpanākāraṃ karoti. Thaddhahatthe pana dahare pāde sambāhante aṭṭhīnaṃ bhijjanakālo viya hoti. Sopi ‘apehī’ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Uṇhasamaye aṅgārakapalle ābhate ‘apanehi na’nti vattabbaṃ hoti. Sītasamaye bījanena bījante ‘apehi, mā bījā’ti vattabbaṃ hoti. Evametāsaṃ sukhasamphassatā dukkhasamphassatā ca veditabbā.

By the pair of terms ‘pleasant to touch’ and ‘painful to touch,’ however, all three great elements are classified. For the earth element can be pleasant to touch or painful to touch; likewise for the fire element and the air element. Herein, the pleasant-to-touch earth element is when a young monk with soft, tender hands massages one's feet; savoring it again and again, one is made to say, “Massage, dear, massage!” The pleasant-to-touch fire element is when, in the cold season, one brings a pan of coals to warm the body; savoring it again and again, one is made to say, “Warm me, dear, warm me!” The pleasant-to-touch air element is when, in the hot season, a young monk, complete in his duties, fans one with a fan; savoring it again and again, one is made to say, “Fan, dear, fan!” But when a young monk with a rough hand massages one's feet, it is as if the bones are breaking, and he becomes fit to be told, “Go away!” When a pan of coals is brought in the hot season, it becomes necessary to say, “Take it away!” When one is fanned in the cold season, it becomes necessary to say, “Go away, do not fan!” Thus their quality of being pleasant to touch and painful to touch should be understood.

Yaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ anidassanaṃ sappaṭighantiādinā nayena vuttā pana catūhi catūhi nayehi paṭimaṇḍitā terasa vārā heṭṭhā rūpāyatanādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

The tangible object, described by the method ‘non-manifest with impact,’ etc.—the thirteen turns, each adorned with four methods, should be understood in the same way as explained above under the visible-form base and so on.

Kiṃ panetāni tīṇi mahābhūtāni ekappahāreneva āpāthaṃ āgacchanti udāhu noti? Āgacchanti. Evaṃ āgatāni kāyapasādaṃ ghaṭṭenti na ghaṭṭentīti? Ghaṭṭenti. Ekappahāreneva tāni ārammaṇaṃ katvā kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati nuppajjatīti? Nuppajjati. Ābhujitavasena vā hi ussadavasena vā ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ hoti.

Now, do these three great elements come into range all at once, or not? They do. Having come thus, do they strike the body sensitivity, or not? They strike. Does body-consciousness arise all at once by taking them as an object, or not? It does not arise. For the taking of an object occurs either by way of inclination or by way of prominence.

Tattha ābhujitavasena tāva, pattasmiñhi odanena pūretvā ābhate ekaṃ sitthaṃ gahetvā thaddhaṃ vā mudukaṃ vāti vīmaṃsanto kiñcāpi tattha tejopi atthi vāyopi atthi, pathavīdhātumeva pana ābhujati. Uṇhodake hatthaṃ otāretvā vīmaṃsanto kiñcāpi tattha pathavīpi atthi vāyopi atthi, tejodhātumeva pana ābhujati. Uṇhasamaye vātapānaṃ vivaritvā vātena sarīraṃ paharāpento ṭhito mandamande vāte paharante [P 0.0334] kiñcāpi tattha pathavīpi atthi tejopi atthi, vāyodhātumeva pana ābhujati. Evaṃ ābhujitavasena ārammaṇaṃ karoti nāma.

Here, first, by way of inclination: When a bowl filled with rice is brought, one takes a lump of it and examines whether it is hard or soft. Although the fire element and the air element are also present there, one inclines only towards the earth element. When one dips a hand into hot water and examines it, although the earth element and the air element are also present there, one inclines only towards the fire element. When one stands opening a window in the hot season and lets the wind strike the body, as a gentle breeze blows, although the earth element and the fire element are also present there, one inclines only towards the air element. Thus it is called making an object by way of inclination.

Yo [M 0.0370] pana upakkhalati vā sīsena vā rukkhaṃ paharati bhuñjanto vā sakkharaṃ ḍaṃsati, so [V 0.0365] kiñcāpi tattha tejopi atthi vāyopi atthi, ussadavasena pana pathavīdhātumeva ārammaṇaṃ karoti. Aggiṃ akkamantopi kiñcāpi tattha pathavīpi atthi vāyopi atthi, ussadavasena pana tejodhātumeva ārammaṇaṃ karoti. Balavavāte kaṇṇasakkhaliṃ paharitvā badhirabhāvaṃ karonte. Kiñcāpi tattha pathavīpi atthi tejopi atthi, ussadavasena pana vāyodhātumeva ārammaṇaṃ karoti.

But when one stumbles, or strikes a tree with one’s head, or bites a pebble while eating, although the fire element and the air element are also present there, by way of prominence one makes only the earth element the object. Even when stepping on fire, although the earth element and the air element are also present there, by way of prominence one makes only the fire element the object. When a strong wind strikes the ear and causes deafness, although the earth element and the fire element are also present there, by way of prominence one makes only the air element the object.

Yaṃkiñci dhātuṃ ārammaṇaṃ karontassa kāyaviññāṇampi ekappahārena nuppajjati. Sūcikalāpena viddhassa ekappahārena kāyo ghaṭṭiyati. Yasmiṃ yasmiṃ pana ṭhāne kāyapasādo ussanno hoti, tattha tattha kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Yattha yatthāpi paṭighaṭṭananighaṃso balavā hoti tattha tattha paṭhamaṃ uppajjati. Kukkuṭapattena vaṇe dhoviyamāne aṃsuaṃsu kāyapasādaṃ ghaṭṭeti. Yattha yattha pana pasādo ussanno hoti, tattha tattheva kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Evaṃ ussadavasena ārammaṇaṃ karoti. Ussadavaseneva ca kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati nāma.

When one makes any element whatsoever the object, body-consciousness also does not arise all at once. When one is pierced by a bundle of needles, the body is struck all at once. But in whatever place the body-sensitivity is abundant, there body-consciousness arises. And wherever the friction of the impact is strong, there it arises first. When a wound is being washed with a chicken feather, each fiber strikes the body-sensitivity. But wherever the sensitivity is abundant, only there does body-consciousness arise. Thus, one makes it an object by way of abundance. And it is by way of abundance that body-consciousness is said to arise.

Kathaṃ pana cittassa ārammaṇato saṅkanti hotīti? Dvīhākārehi hoti – ajjhāsayato vā visayādhimattato vā. Vihārapūjādīsu hi ‘tāni tāni cetiyāni ceva paṭimāyo ca vandissāmi, potthakammacittakammāni ca olokessāmī’ti ajjhāsayena gato ekaṃ vanditvā vā passitvā vā itarassa vandanatthāya vā dassanatthāya vā manaṃ katvā vanditumpi passitumpi gacchatiyeva, evaṃ ajjhāsayato saṅkamati nāma.

But how does the mind’s transition from one object to another occur? It occurs in two ways: either by inclination or by the preponderance of the object. For, in monastery worship and the like, when one goes with the inclination, 'I will venerate those various stupas and images, and I will look at the manuscript work and paintings,' having venerated or seen one, one makes up one's mind to venerate or see another and indeed goes to venerate and to see. Thus, it is called 'transitioning by inclination.'

Kelāsakūṭapaṭibhāgaṃ pana mahācetiyaṃ olokento ṭhitopi aparabhāge sabbatūriyesu paggahitesu rūpārammaṇaṃ vissajjetvā saddārammaṇaṃ saṅkamati. Manuññagandhesu pupphesu vā gandhesu vā ābhatesu saddārammaṇaṃ vissajjetvā gandhārammaṇaṃ saṅkamati. Evaṃ visayādhimattato saṅkamati nāma.

But even while one is standing looking at a great stupa that resembles the peak of Mount Kelāsa, when all the musical instruments are played in another area, one abandons the form-object and transitions to the sound-object. When flowers with pleasing scents or perfumes are brought, one abandons the sound-object and transitions to the scent-object. Thus, it is called 'transitioning due to the preponderance of the object.'

651. Āpodhātuniddese [P 0.0335] āpoti sabhāvaniddeso. Āpova āpogataṃ. Sinehavasena sineho, sinehova sinehagataṃ. Bandhanattaṃ [M 0.0371] rūpassāti pathavīdhātuādikassa bhūtarūpassa bandhanabhāvo. Ayopiṇḍiādīni hi āpodhātu ābandhitvā baddhāni karoti. Tāya ābaddhattā tāni baddhāni nāma honti. Pāsāṇapabbatatālaṭṭhihatthidantagosiṅgādīsupi eseva nayo[V 0.0366]. Sabbāni hetāni āpodhātu eva ābandhitvā baddhāni karoti. Āpodhātuyā ābaddhattāva baddhāni honti.

651. In the exposition of the water element, 'water' is an exposition of its intrinsic nature. Water itself is the watery state. By way of cohesion, it is 'cohesion'; cohesion itself is the cohesive state. 'The binding nature of matter' is the binding state of primary matter beginning with the earth element. For the water element binds lumps of iron and the like, making them bound. Because they are bound by it, they are called 'bound.' The same principle applies to rocks, mountains, palm-seeds, elephant tusks, cow horns, and so on. For the water element itself binds all these, making them bound. It is precisely because they are bound by the water element that they are bound.

Kiṃ pana pathavīdhātu sesadhātūnaṃ patiṭṭhā hoti na hotīti hoti phusitvā hoti udāhu aphusitvā? Āpodhātu vā sesā ābandhamānā phusitvā ābandhati udāhu aphusitvāti? Pathavīdhātu tāva āpodhātuyā aphusitvāva patiṭṭhā hoti, tejodhātuyā ca vāyodhātuyā ca phusitvā. Āpodhātu pana pathavīdhātumpi tejovāyodhātuyopi aphusitvāva ābandhati. Yadi phusitvā ābandheyya phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ nāma bhaveyya.

Now, is the earth element a support for the other elements or not? Is it a support by contact, or without contact? And does the water element, when binding the others, bind by contact, or without contact? First, the earth element is a support for the water element without contact, but for the fire element and the air element, it is a support by contact. The water element, however, binds the earth element and also the fire and air elements without contact. If it were to bind by contact, it would be called the tangible base.

Tejodhātuvāyodhātūnampi sesadhātūsu sakasakakiccakaraṇe eseva nayo. Tejodhātu hi pathavīdhātuṃ phusitvā jhāpeti. Sā pana na uṇhā hutvā jhāyati. Yadi uṇhā hutvā jhāyeyya uṇhattalakkhaṇā nāma bhaveyya. Āpodhātuṃ pana aphusitvāva tāpeti. Sāpi tapamānā na uṇhā hutvā tapati. Yadi uṇhā hutvā tapeyya uṇhattalakkhaṇā nāma bhaveyya. Vāyodhātuṃ pana phusitvāva tāpeti. Sāpi tapamānā na uṇhā hutvā tapati. Yadi uṇhā hutvā tapeyya uṇhattalakkhaṇā nāma bhaveyya. Vāyodhātu pathavīdhātuṃ phusitvā vitthambheti, tathā tejodhātuṃ āpodhātuṃ [P 0.0336] pana aphusitvāva vitthambheti.

For the fire and air elements too, in performing their respective functions among the other elements, the same principle applies. For the fire element burns the earth element by contact. But the latter does not burn by becoming hot. If it were to burn by becoming hot, it would be called 'that which has the characteristic of heat.' But it heats the water element without contact. That too, while being heated, is not heated by becoming hot. If it were to be heated by becoming hot, it would be called 'that which has the characteristic of heat.' But it heats the air element by contact. That too, while being heated, is not heated by becoming hot. If it were to be heated by becoming hot, it would be called 'that which has the characteristic of heat.' The air element supports the earth element by contact, and likewise the fire element; but it supports the water element without contact.

Ucchurasaṃ pacitvā phāṇitapiṇḍe kariyamāne āpodhātu thaddhā hoti na hotīti? Na hoti. Sā hi paggharaṇalakkhaṇā. Pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā. Omattaṃ pana āpo adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jātaṃ. Sā hi rasākārena ṭhitabhāvaṃ vijahati, lakkhaṇaṃ na vijahati. Phāṇitapiṇḍe vilīyamānepi pathavīdhātu na vilīyati. Kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā hi pathavīdhātu paggharaṇalakkhaṇā āpodhātu. Omattā pana pathavī adhimattaāpagatikā hoti. Sā piṇḍākārena ṭhitabhāvaṃ vijahati, lakkhaṇaṃ na vijahati. Catunnañhi [M 0.0372] mahābhūtānaṃ bhāvaññathattameva hoti, lakkhaṇaññathattaṃ nāma natthi. Tassa abhāvo aṭṭhānaparikappasuttena dīpito. Vuttañhetaṃ –

When sugarcane juice has been boiled and lumps of molasses are being made, does the water element become hard or not? It does not. For it has the characteristic of flowing. The earth element has the characteristic of hardness. However, a small amount of water has come to be in a state like that of an excessive amount of earth. For it abandons its state of existing in the form of a liquid, but it does not abandon its characteristic. Even when a lump of molasses is dissolving, the earth element does not dissolve. For the earth element has the characteristic of hardness, and the water element has the characteristic of flowing. However, a small amount of earth has come to be in a state like that of an excessive amount of water. It abandons its state of existing in the form of a solid, but it does not abandon its characteristic. For of the four great elements, there is only otherness of state; there is no such thing as otherness of characteristic. The absence of this is shown by the Sutta on Impossible Suppositions. For this has been said:

“Siyā, ānanda, catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ aññathattaṃ, pathavīdhātuyā…pe… vāyodhātuyā[V 0.0367]; na tveva buddhe aveccappasādena samannāgatassa ariyasāvakassa siyā aññathatta”nti (a. ni. 3.76).

“Ānanda, there might be an alteration of the four great elements—of the earth element… of the air element; but there could never be an alteration for a noble disciple who is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Buddha.”

Ayañhettha attho – ānanda, kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu parivattitvā paggharaṇalakkhaṇā āpodhātu nāma bhaveyya, ariyasāvakassa pana aññathattaṃ nāma natthīti. Evamettha aṭṭhānaparikappo āgato.

This is the meaning here: Ānanda, the earth element, which has the characteristic of hardness, might change and become what is called the water element, which has the characteristic of flowing; but for a noble disciple, there is no such thing as an alteration of their confidence. Thus, the impossible supposition is presented here.

652. Ito paresu upādiṇṇarūpādiniddesesu upādiṇṇapadādīnaṃ attho mātikākathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Cakkhāyatanādīni heṭṭhā vitthāritāneva. Tattha tattha pana visesamattameva vakkhāma.

652. In the subsequent expositions of clung-to form and so on, the meaning of the term 'clung-to' and other such terms should be understood in the same way as stated in the commentary on the mātikā. The eye-base and so on have already been explained in detail below. In each respective place, however, we will state only the specific points.

Upādiṇṇaniddese tāva cakkhāyatanādīni ekantaupādiṇṇattā vuttāni. Yasmā pana rūpāyatanādīni upādiṇṇānipi atthi anupādiṇṇānipi, tasmā tāni yaṃ vā panāti saṅkhepato dassetvā puna kammassa katattā rūpāyatanantiādinā nayena vitthāritāni. Iminā upāyena sabbayevāpanakesu attho veditabbo.

First, in the exposition of 'clung-to,' the eye-base and so on are mentioned because they are exclusively clung-to. But since the form-base and so on exist as both clung-to and unclung-to, they are first indicated concisely with the phrase 'or whatever,' and then explained in detail by the method beginning, 'the form-base, because of being produced by kamma.' By this method, the meaning should be understood in all cases of assignment.

Kasmā pana ‘kammassa katattā’ti ca ‘na kammassa katattā’ti ca ubhinnampi niddese ‘jaratā ca aniccatā ca’ na gahitā, anupādiṇṇādīnaṃyeva niddesesu gahitāti? Na kammassa [P 0.0337] katattāti ettha tāva kammato aññapaccayasamuṭṭhānaṃ saṅgahitaṃ. ‘Kammassa katattā’ti ettha kammasamuṭṭhānameva. Imāni ca dve rūpāni neva kammato na aññasmā rūpajanakapaccayā uppajjanti, tasmā na gahitāni. Sā ca nesaṃ anuppatti parato āvi bhavissati. Anupādiṇṇantiādīsu pana kevalaṃ anupādiṇṇādiggahaṇena kammādisamuṭṭhānatā paṭikkhittā, naaññapaccayasamuṭṭhānatā anuññātā. Tasmā tattha gahitānīti veditabbāni.

But why are 'aging' and 'impermanence' not taken in the exposition of both 'because of kamma having been done' and 'not because of kamma having been done,' but are taken only in the expositions of 'unappropriated' and so on? Herein, in 'not because of kamma having been done,' matter originated from a cause other than kamma is included. In 'because of kamma having been done,' only matter originated from kamma is included. And these two forms of matter arise neither from kamma nor from another form-producing condition; therefore, they are not taken. And their non-arising will become clear later. But in 'unappropriated' and so on, by the mere taking of 'unappropriated' and so on, origination from kamma and so on is rejected, but origination from another cause is not permitted. Therefore, it should be understood that they are taken therein.

666. Cittasamuṭṭhānaniddese kāyaviññatti vacīviññattīti idaṃ dvayaṃ yasmā ekantacittasamuṭṭhānāni bhūtāni upādāya paññāyati, tasmā vuttaṃ. Paramatthato [M 0.0373] pana tassa nissayabhūtāni bhūtāneva cittasamuṭṭhānāni, taṃnissitattā. Yathā aniccassa rūpassa jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccaṃ nāma hoti, evamidampi cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

666. In the exposition of the mind-originated, this pair—bodily intimation and verbal intimation—is mentioned because it is discerned by relying on the primary elements which are exclusively mind-originated. Ultimately, however, it is only the primary elements that are their support which are mind-originated. Because the intimations are dependent on them, just as the aging and death of impermanent form are called 'impermanent,' so this pair has come to be called 'mind-originated.'

668. Cittasahabhuniddesepi [V 0.0368] eseva nayo. Yāva cittaṃ tāva paññāyanato idameva dvayaṃ vuttaṃ. Na panetaṃ cittena saha bhūtāni viya, cetanādayo viya ca uppajjati.

668. In the exposition of what is co-nascent with consciousness, too, this same method applies. This same pair is mentioned because it is discerned for as long as consciousness lasts. But this pair does not arise together with consciousness in the way the primary elements do, or in the way volition and other mental factors do.

670. Cittānuparivattitāyapi eseva nayo. Yāva cittaṃ tāva paññāyanato eva hetaṃ dvayaṃ cittānuparivattīti vuttaṃ.

670. In the case of what revolves in accordance with consciousness, too, this same method applies. This pair is said to 'revolve in accordance with consciousness' precisely because it is discerned for as long as consciousness lasts.

674. Oḷārikanti vatthārammaṇabhūtattā saṃṅghaṭṭanavasena gahetabbato thūlaṃ. Vuttavipallāsato sukhumaṃ veditabbaṃ.

674. 'Coarse' means gross because it serves as a physical basis and an object, and because it is apprehended by way of impact. 'Subtle' should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.

676. Dūreti ghaṭṭanavasena aggahetabbattā dubbiññeyyabhāvena samīpe ṭhitampi dūre. Itaraṃ pana ghaṭṭanavasena gahetabbattā suviññeyyabhāvena dūre ṭhitampi santike. Cakkhāyatanādiniddesā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva vitthārato veditabbā. Idaṃ [P 0.0338] tāva duvidhena rūpasaṅgahe visesamattaṃ. Tividhasaṅgaho uttānatthova.

676. 'Far' means that even what is situated nearby is 'far' because it is not apprehendable by way of impact and is thus difficult to cognize. The other, 'near,' however, means that even what is situated far away is 'near' because it is apprehendable by way of impact and is thus easy to cognize. The expositions of the eye-base and so on should be understood in detail in the same way as stated above. This, for now, is what is specific in the twofold summary of form. The threefold summary is obvious in meaning.

Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition of the Tetrad

966. Catubbidhasaṅgahāvasāne diṭṭhādīnaṃ pacchimapadassa bhedābhāvena ādito paṭṭhāya pucchaṃ akatvāva rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ saddāyatanaṃ sutantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhunā oloketvā dakkhituṃ sakkāti ‘diṭṭhaṃ’ nāma jātaṃ. Saddāyatanaṃ sotena sutvā jānituṃ sakkāti ‘sutaṃ’ nāma jātaṃ. Gandhāyatanādittayaṃ ghānajivhākāyehi patvā gahetabbato munitvā jānitabbaṭṭhena mutaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Phusitvā viññāṇuppattikāraṇato ‘mutaṃ’ nāmātipi vuttaṃ. Sabbameva pana rūpaṃ manoviññāṇena jānitabbanti manasā viññātaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

966. At the conclusion of the fourfold summary, since there is no division in the last term of 'seen,' etc., it is stated without asking a question from the start: 'The form-base is seen, the sound-base is heard,' and so on. Therein, the form-base has come to be called 'seen' (diṭṭha) because it can be seen by looking with the eye. The sound-base has come to be called 'heard' (suta) because it can be known by hearing with the ear. The triad beginning with the odor-base has come to be called 'sensed' (muta) because it is to be grasped by reaching it with the nose, tongue, and body, and in the sense that it is to be known by being cognized. It is also said to be called 'sensed' because it is a cause for the arising of consciousness upon being touched. However, all form whatsoever is to be known by mind-consciousness; thus it has come to be called 'cognized by the mind' (manasā viññāta).

Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition of the Pentad

967. Pañcavidhasaṅgahaniddese [M 0.0374] kakkhaḷanti thaddhaṃ. Kharameva kharagataṃ, pharusanti attho. Itare dvepi sabhāvaniddesā eva. Ajjhattanti niyakajjhattaṃ. Bahiddhāti bāhiraṃ. Upādiṇṇanti na kammasamuṭṭhānameva. Avisesena pana sarīraṭṭhakassetaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sarīraṭṭhakañhi upādiṇṇaṃ vā hotu anupādiṇṇaṃ vā, ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhavasena sabbaṃ upādiṇṇameva nāma.

967. In the exposition of the fivefold summary: 'Hard' (kakkhaḷa) means stiff. It is hardness itself that is 'possessed of hardness' (kharagata); the meaning is 'harsh' (pharusa). The other two terms are also simply designations of a state. 'Internal' (ajjhatta) means one's own internal. 'External' (bahiddhā) means external. 'Appropriated' (upādiṇṇa) does not mean only what is kamma-originated. But rather, this is a general term for all matter located in the body. For whether the matter located in the body is appropriated (upādiṇṇa) or unappropriated (anupādiṇṇa), it is all called 'appropriated' (upādiṇṇa) in the sense of having been taken up, grasped, and misapprehended.

969. Tejogatanti [V 0.0369] sabbatejesu gataṃ uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ, tejo eva vā tejobhāvaṃ gatanti ‘tejogataṃ’. Usmāti usmākāro. Usmāgatanti usmābhāvaṃ gataṃ. Usmākārassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Usumanti balavausmā. Usumameva usumabhāvaṃ gatanti usumagataṃ.

969. 'Pertaining to the heat element' (tejoga­ta) means the characteristic of heat found in all heat, or it is the heat element itself that has reached the state of heat; thus 'pertaining to the heat element.' 'Heat' (usmā) is the state of heat. 'Pertaining to heat' (usmāgata) means having reached the state of heat; this is a name for the state of heat itself. 'Hot' (usuma) means strong heat. It is strong heat itself that has reached the state of being hot; thus 'pertaining to what is hot' (usumagata).

970. Vāyanakavasena vāyo. Vāyova vāyobhāvaṃ gatattā vāyogataṃ. Thambhitattanti uppalanāḷatacādīnaṃ viya vātapuṇṇānaṃ thambhitabhāvo rūpassa.

970. 'Air element' (vāyo) is so called because of its nature of moving. It is the air element itself that has reached the state of air; thus 'pertaining to the air element' (vāyogata). 'Stiffness' (thambhitatta) is the stiff state of matter, like that of things such as the skin of a lotus stalk when filled with air.

Chakkādiniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition Beginning with the Sixes

972-4. Chabbidhādisaṅgahānaṃ [P 0.0339] tiṇṇaṃ osānapadassa bhedābhāvato ādito paṭṭhāya apucchitvāva niddeso kato. Tattha cakkhuviññāṇena jānituṃ sakkāti cakkhuviññeyyaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇena jānituṃ sakkāti manoviññeyyaṃ. Tividhāya manodhātuyā jānituṃ sakkāti manodhātuviññeyyaṃ sabbaṃ rūpanti ettha yasmā ekaṃ rūpampi manoviññāṇadhātuyā ajānitabbaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā ‘sabbaṃ rūpa’nti vuttaṃ. Sammāsambuddhena hi abhidhammaṃ patvā nayaṃ kātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne nayo akato nāma natthi. Idañca ekarūpassāpi manoviññāṇadhātuyā ajānitabbassa abhāvena nayaṃ kātuṃ yuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, tasmā nayaṃ karonto ‘sabbaṃ rūpa’nti āha.

For the three classifications beginning with the sixfold one, since there is no difference in the final term, the exposition is given from the beginning without asking a question. Therein, 'cognizable by eye-consciousness' is so called because it can be known by eye-consciousness... and so on... 'cognizable by mind-consciousness' is so called because it can be known by mind-consciousness. 'Cognizable by the mind-element' is so called because it can be known by the threefold mind-element. Here, regarding 'all form,' since there is not even a single form that is not to be known by the mind-consciousness-element, it is therefore said, 'all form.' Indeed, for the Perfectly Enlightened One, having arrived at the Abhidhamma, there is no such thing as a method not applied in a place suitable for applying a method. And this is a place suitable for applying a method due to the absence of even a single form that is not to be known by the mind-consciousness-element. Therefore, applying the method, he said, 'all form.'

974. Sukhasamphassoti sukhavedanāpaṭilābhapaccayo. Dukkhasamphassoti dukkhavedanāpaṭilābhapaccayo. Idhāpi phoṭṭhabbārammaṇassa sukhadukkhassa sabbhāvato ayaṃ nayo dinno.

'Pleasurable contact' is the cause for the attainment of pleasant feeling. 'Painful contact' is the cause for the attainment of painful feeling. Here also, this method is given because of the actual existence of the tangible object as agreeable and disagreeable.

Navakādiniddesavaṇṇanā

974. Explanation of the Exposition Beginning with the Ninefold

975. Navake [M 0.0375] pana indriyarūpassa nāma atthitāya nayo dinno. Tasseva sappaṭighaappaṭighatāya dasake nayo dinno. Ekādasake aḍḍhekādasa āyatanāni vibhattāni. Tesaṃ niddesavārā heṭṭhā vuttanayena vitthārato veditabbā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva.

In the ninefold classification, however, the method is given based on the existence of what is called faculty-form. In the tenfold, the method is given based on its being resistant and non-resistant. In the elevenfold classification, ten and a half bases are distinguished. Their sections of exposition should be understood in detail according to the method stated above. The rest is everywhere of clear meaning.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

975. Miscellaneous Discussion

Imesu [V 0.0370] pana rūpesu asammohatthaṃ samodhānaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ parinipphannañca saṅkhatanti idaṃ ‘pakiṇṇakaṃ’ veditabbaṃ.

Now, among these forms, for the sake of non-bewilderment, this should be understood as the 'miscellaneous' section: combination, origination, the completely produced, and the conditioned.

Tattha ‘samodhāna’nti sabbameva hidaṃ rūpaṃ samodhānato cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… kabaḷīkāro āhāro, phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ āpodhātūti pañcavīsatisaṅkhyaṃ hoti. Taṃ vatthurūpena saddhiṃ chabbīsatisaṅkhyaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ito [P 0.0340] aññaṃ rūpaṃ nāma natthi. Keci pana ‘middharūpaṃ nāma atthī’ti vadanti. Te “addhā munīsi sambuddho, natthi nīvaraṇā tavā”tiādīni (su. ni. 546) vatvā middharūpaṃ nāma natthīti paṭisedhetabbā. Apare balarūpena saddhiṃ sattavīsati, sambhavarūpena saddhiṃ aṭṭhavīsati, jātirūpena saddhiṃ ekūnatiṃsati, rogarūpena saddhiṃ samatiṃsati rūpānīti vadanti. Tepi tesaṃ visuṃ abhāvaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Vāyodhātuyā hi gahitāya balarūpaṃ gahitameva, aññaṃ balarūpaṃ nāma natthi. Āpodhātuyā sambhavarūpaṃ, upacayasantatīhi jātirūpaṃ, jaratāaniccatāhi gahitāhi rogarūpaṃ gahitameva. Aññaṃ rogarūpaṃ nāma natthi. Yopi kaṇṇarogādi ābādho so visamapaccayasamuṭṭhitadhātumattameva. Na añño tattha rogo nāma atthīti samodhānato chabbīsatimeva rūpāni.

Therein, regarding 'combination': by way of combination, all this materiality—the eye-base... the tangible base, the water element—amounts to twenty-five. Together with the base-materiality, it should be understood as twenty-six. Apart from this, there is no other so-called materiality. Some, however, say, 'There is such a thing as materiality of torpor.' They should be refuted by quoting, 'Surely you are a sage, a fully enlightened one; you have no hindrances,' etc., and stating that there is no such thing as materiality of torpor. Others say that with materiality of strength it is twenty-seven, with materiality of semen it is twenty-eight, with materiality of birth it is twenty-nine, and with materiality of disease it is thirty material phenomena. They too should be rejected by showing that these do not exist separately. For when the air element is included, materiality of strength is also included; there is no other so-called materiality of strength. By the water element, materiality of semen is included; by accumulation and continuity, materiality of birth is included; when aging and impermanence are included, materiality of disease is also included. There is no other so-called materiality of disease. Even an affliction such as an ear disease is merely the elements originated from unsuitable conditions. There is no other so-called disease there. Thus, by way of combination, there are just twenty-six material phenomena.

‘Samuṭṭhāna’nti kati rūpāni katisamuṭṭhānāni? Dasa ekasamuṭṭhānāni, ekaṃ dvisamuṭṭhānaṃ, tīṇi tisamuṭṭhānāni, nava catusamuṭṭhānāni, dve na kenaci samuṭṭhahanti.

Regarding 'origination': How many material phenomena have how many origins? Ten have a single origin; one has two origins; three have three origins; nine have four origins; and two do not arise from any cause.

Tattha cakkhupasādo…pe… jīvitindriyanti imāni aṭṭha ekantaṃ kammatova samuṭṭhahanti. Kāyaviññattivacīviññattidvayaṃ ekantena cittato samuṭṭhātīti dasa [M 0.0376] ‘ekasamuṭṭhānāni’ nāma. Saddo ututo ca cittato ca samuṭṭhātīti eko ‘dvisamuṭṭhāno’ nāma. Tattha aviññāṇakasaddo ututo samuṭṭhāti, saviññāṇakasaddo cittato. Lahutādittayaṃ pana utucittāhārehi samuṭṭhātīti tīṇi ‘tisamuṭṭhānāni’ nāma. Avasesāni nava rūpāni tehi kammena cāti catūhi samuṭṭhahantīti nava ‘catusamuṭṭhānāni’ nāma. Jaratā aniccatā pana etesu ekatopi na samuṭṭhahantīti dve ‘na kenaci samuṭṭhahanti’ nāma. Kasmā? Ajāyanato. Na hi etāni jāyanti. Kasmā? Jātassa pākabhedattā. Uppannañhi rūpaṃ jīrati bhijjatīti [V 0.0371] avassaṃ [P 0.0341] panetaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Na hi uppannaṃ rūpaṃ arūpaṃ vā akkhayaṃ nāma dissati. Yāva pana na bhijjati tāvassa paripākoti siddhametaṃ. ‘Jātassa pākabhedattā’ti yadi ca tāni jāyeyyuṃ tesampi pākabhedā bhaveyyuṃ. Na ca pāko paccati, bhedo vā bhijjatīti jātassa pākabhedattā netaṃ dvayaṃ jāyati.

Therein, eye-sensitivity... up to the life-faculty—these eight arise exclusively from kamma. The pair, bodily intimation and verbal intimation, arises exclusively from consciousness. Thus ten are called 'of single origin.' Sound arises from temperature and from consciousness, so it is called 'of double origin.' Therein, inanimate sound arises from temperature; animate sound arises from consciousness. The triad beginning with lightness, however, arises from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, so these three are called 'of triple origin.' The remaining nine material phenomena arise from those and from kamma, thus from four causes, so they are called 'of quadruple origin.' Aging and impermanence, however, do not arise from even one of these, so these two are called 'not arising from any cause.' Why? Because of not being born. For these are not born. Why? Because they are the maturation and dissolution of what has been born. For arisen materiality ages and dissolves—this must certainly be accepted. For no arisen phenomenon, material or immaterial, is seen to be indestructible. But as long as it has not dissolved, its maturation occurs; thus this is established: 'because they are the maturation and dissolution of what has been born.' And if they were to be born, they too would have maturation and dissolution. But maturation does not mature again, nor does dissolution dissolve again. Therefore, because they are the maturation and dissolution of what has been born, this pair is not born.

Tattha siyā – yathā ‘kammassa katattā’ti ādiniddesesu ‘rūpassa upacayo rūpassa santatī’ti vacanena ‘jāti’ jāyatīti sampaṭicchitaṃ hoti, evaṃ ‘pāko’pi paccatu ‘bhedo’pi bhijjatūti. “Na tattha ‘jāti jāyatī’ti sampaṭicchitaṃ. Ye pana dhammā kammādīhi nibbattanti tesaṃ abhinibbattibhāvato jātiyā tappaccayabhāvavohāro anumato. Na pana paramatthato jāti jāyati. Jāyamānassa hi abhinibbattimattaṃ jātī”ti.

Herein, an objection might be raised: Just as in the expositions beginning 'because kamma has been done,' etc., by the statement 'the accumulation of materiality, the continuity of materiality,' it is accepted that 'birth' is born, so too let 'maturation' mature and 'dissolution' dissolve. — It is not accepted there that 'birth is born.' But for those phenomena that are produced by kamma, etc., because of their state of being newly produced, the designation for birth of having them as its cause is approved. But in an ultimate sense, birth is not born. For birth is merely the new production of what is being born.

Tattha siyā – ‘yatheva jāti yesaṃ dhammānaṃ abhinibbatti tappaccayabhāvavohāraṃ abhinibbattivohārañca labhati, tathā pākabhedāpi yesaṃ dhammānaṃ pākabhedā tappaccayabhāvavohāraṃ abhinibbattivohārañca labhantu. Evaṃ idampi dvayaṃ kammādisamuṭṭhānamevāti vattabbaṃ bhavissatī’ti. ‘Na pākabhedā taṃ vohāraṃ labhanti. Kasmā? Janakapaccayānubhāvakkhaṇe abhāvato. Janakapaccayānañhi uppādetabbadhammassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva ānubhāvo, na tato uttari. Tehi abhinibbattitadhammakkhaṇasmiñca jāti paññāyamānā tappaccayabhāvavohāraṃ abhinibbattivohārañca labhati, tasmiṃ khaṇe sabbhāvato; na itaradvayaṃ, tasmiṃ khaṇe abhāvatoti nevetaṃ jāyatī’ti vattabbaṃ. “Jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) āgatattā [M 0.0377] idampi dvayaṃ jāyatīti ce – ‘na, pariyāyadesitattā. Tattha hi paṭiccasamuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ jarāmaraṇattā pariyāyena taṃ paṭiccasamuppanna’nti vuttaṃ.

Herein, an objection might be raised: 'Just as birth, which is the new production of certain phenomena, obtains the designation of having them as its cause and the designation of new production, so too let maturation and dissolution, which are the maturation and dissolution of certain phenomena, obtain the designation of having them as their cause and the designation of new production. Thus it will be fit to say that this pair, too, is originated from kamma and so forth.' — Maturation and dissolution do not obtain that designation. Why? Because of their absence at the moment of the generative condition's power. For the power of generative conditions exists only at the production-moment of the phenomenon to be produced, not beyond that. And at the moment of the phenomenon newly produced by them, birth, being manifest, obtains the designation of having them as its cause and the designation of new production, because of its presence at that moment; the other two do not, because of their absence at that moment. Therefore, it should be said that this pair is not born. If it is said that this pair is also born because it is stated, 'Aging-and-death, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen,' the reply is: No, because this was taught figuratively. For there, because dependently arisen phenomena are subject to aging-and-death, it is said figuratively that aging-and-death is dependently arisen.

‘Yadi evaṃ, tayampetaṃ ajātattā sasavisāṇaṃ [P 0.0342] viya natthi; nibbānaṃ viya vā nicca’nti ce – na, nissayapaṭibaddhavuttito; pathavīādīnañhi nissayānaṃ bhāve jātiādittayaṃ paññāyati, tasmā na natthi. Tesañca abhāve na paññāyati, tasmā na niccaṃ. Etampi ca abhinivesaṃ paṭisedhetuṃ eva idaṃ vuttaṃ – “jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ [V 0.0372] paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20). Evamādīhi nayehi tāni dve rūpāni na kehici samuṭṭhahantīti veditabbaṃ.

If so, then this triad, being unborn, either does not exist, like a rabbit's horn, or is permanent, like Nibbāna.' — No, because its occurrence is bound to a support. For when the supports such as the earth element exist, the triad beginning with birth is manifest; therefore it is not non-existent. And when they are absent, it is not manifest; therefore it is not permanent. And it was to refute this very adherence that this was said: 'Aging-and-death, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen.' By such methods it should be understood that those two material phenomena do not arise from any cause.

Apica ‘samuṭṭhāna’nti ettha ayamaññopi attho. Tassāyaṃ mātikā – ‘kammajaṃ kammapaccayaṃ kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ, āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ āhārapaccayaṃ āhārapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ, utusamuṭṭhānaṃ utupaccayaṃ utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ cittapaccayaṃ cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna’nti.

Furthermore, 'origination' here has still another meaning. This is its matrix: 'kamma-produced, kamma-conditioned, kamma-conditioned-and-temperature-produced; nutriment-produced, nutriment-conditioned, nutriment-conditioned-and-temperature-produced; temperature-produced, temperature-conditioned, temperature-conditioned-and-temperature-produced; consciousness-produced, consciousness-conditioned, consciousness-conditioned-and-temperature-produced.'

Tattha cakkhupasādādi aṭṭhavidhaṃ rūpaṃ saddhiṃ hadayavatthunā ‘kammajaṃ’ nāma. Kesamassu hatthidantā assavālā camaravālāti evamādi ‘kammapaccayaṃ’ nāma. Cakkaratanaṃ devatānaṃ uyyānavimānādīnīti evamādi ‘kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ’ nāma.

Therein, the eightfold materiality beginning with eye-sensitivity, together with the heart-base, is called 'kamma-produced.' Hair of the head, beard, elephant tusks, horse's tail-hairs, yak's tail-hairs, and so forth are called 'kamma-conditioned.' The wheel-treasure, the parks and mansions of the deities, and so forth are called 'kamma-conditioned-and-temperature-produced.'

Āhārato samuṭṭhitaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ ‘āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ’ nāma. Kabaḷīkāro āhāro dvinnampi rūpasantatīnaṃ paccayo hoti āhārasamuṭṭhānassa ca upādinnassa ca. Āhārasamuṭṭhānassa janako hutvā paccayo hoti, kammajassa anupālako hutvāti idaṃ āhārānupālitaṃ kammajarūpaṃ ‘āhārapaccayaṃ’ nāma. Visabhāgāhāraṃ sevitvā ātape gacchantassa tilakakāḷakuṭṭhādīni uppajjanti, idaṃ ‘āhārapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ’ nāma.

The pure octad arisen from nutriment is called 'nutriment-produced.' Edible food is a condition for two continuities of materiality: the nutriment-produced and the appropriated. It is a condition for the nutriment-produced by being its generator, and for the kamma-produced by being its sustainer. This kamma-produced materiality sustained by nutriment is called 'nutriment-conditioned.' When one consumes unsuitable food and goes out in the heat of the sun, moles, black spots, leprosy, etc., arise. This is called 'nutriment-conditioned-and-temperature-produced.'

Ututo samuṭṭhitaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ ‘utusamuṭṭhānaṃ’ nāma. Tasmiṃ utu aññaṃ aṭṭhakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, idaṃ ‘utupaccayaṃ’ [P 0.0343] nāma. Tasmimpi utu aññaṃ aṭṭhakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, idaṃ ‘utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ’ nāma. Evaṃ tissoyeva santatiyo ghaṭṭetuṃ sakkoti. Na tato paraṃ. Imamatthaṃ anupādinnakenāpi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Utusamuṭṭhāno nāma valāhako. Utupaccayā nāma [M 0.0378] vuṭṭhidhārā. Deve pana vuṭṭhe bījāni virūhanti, pathavī gandhaṃ muñcati, pabbatā nīlā khāyanti, samuddo vaḍḍhati, etaṃ utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma.

The pure octad arisen from temperature is called 'temperature-produced.' In that, temperature originates another octad; this is called 'temperature-conditioned.' In that too, temperature originates another octad; this is called 'temperature-conditioned-and-temperature-produced.' Thus it can link only three continuities, not beyond that. This meaning can be illustrated even by what is non-appropriated. The temperature-produced is a rain cloud. The temperature-conditioned are showers of rain. And when it rains, seeds sprout, the earth releases its fragrance, mountains appear blue, and the ocean swells; this is called 'temperature-conditioned-and-temperature-produced.'

Cittato samuṭṭhitaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ ‘cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ’ nāma. “Pacchājātā cittacetasikā dhammā purejātassa imassa kāyassa pacchājātapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.11) idaṃ ‘cittapaccayaṃ’ nāma. Ākāse antalikkhe hatthimpi dasseti, assampi dasseti, rathampi dasseti[V 0.0373], vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassetitī (paṭi. ma. 3.18) idaṃ ‘cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ’ nāma.

The pure octad arisen from consciousness is called 'consciousness-produced.' 'Subsequently arisen consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-arisen body by way of postnascence condition'; this is called 'consciousness-conditioned.' 'In the sky, in the atmosphere, one displays an elephant, one displays a horse, one displays a chariot, one displays various military formations'; this is called 'consciousness-conditioned-and-temperature-produced.'

‘Parinipphanna’nti pannarasa rūpāni parinipphannāni nāma, dasa aparinipphannāni nāma. ‘Yadi aparinipphannā, asaṅkhatā nāma bhaveyyuṃ’. “Tesaṃyeva pana rūpānaṃ kāyavikāro ‘kāyaviññatti’ nāma, vacīvikāro ‘vacīviññatti’ nāma, chiddaṃ vivaraṃ ‘ākāsadhātu’ nāma, lahubhāvo ‘lahutā’ nāma, mudubhāvo ‘mudutā’ nāma, kammaññabhāvo ‘kammaññatā’ nāma, nibbatti ‘upacayo’ nāma, pavatti ‘santati’ nāma, jīraṇākāro ‘jaratā’ nāma, hutvā abhāvākāro ‘aniccatā’ nāmāti. Sabbaṃ parinipphannaṃ saṅkhatameva hotī”ti.

‘Produced’: fifteen material phenomena are called ‘produced,’ and ten are called ‘unproduced.’ ‘If they were unproduced, they would be unconditioned.’ But of those same material phenomena, bodily alteration is called ‘bodily intimation,’ verbal alteration is called ‘verbal intimation,’ an aperture or opening is called the ‘space element,’ the state of lightness is called ‘lightness,’ the state of softness is called ‘softness,’ the state of wieldiness is called ‘wieldiness,’ production is called ‘growth,’ occurrence is called ‘continuity,’ the mode of aging is called ‘decay,’ and the mode of non-existence after having been is called ‘impermanence.’ Everything produced is indeed conditioned.

Aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Aṭṭhasālinī, the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī.

Rūpakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Matter is concluded.

3. Nikkhepakaṇḍo

3. The Chapter of Synopsis

Tikanikkhepakathā

Discourse on the Synopsis of the Triads

985. Ettāvatā [M 0.0379][V 0.0374] kusalattiko sabbesaṃ kusalādidhammānaṃ padabhājananayena vitthārito hoti. Yasmā pana yvāyaṃ kusalattikassa vibhajananayo vutto, sesatikadukānampi eseva vibhajananayo hoti – yathā hi ettha, evaṃ ‘katame dhammā sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… [P 0.0344] ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye aññepi atthi paṭiccasamuppannā arūpino dhammā ṭhapetvā vedanākhandhaṃ, ime dhammā sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā’tiādinā anukkamena sabbatikadukesu sakkā paṇḍitehi vibhājananayaṃ sallakkhetuṃ – tasmā taṃ vitthāradesanaṃ nikkhipitvā, aññena nātisaṅkhepanātivitthāranayena sabbatikadukadhammavibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ katame dhammā kusalāti nikkhepakaṇḍaṃ āraddhaṃ. Cittuppādakaṇḍañhi vitthāradesanā, aṭṭhakathākaṇḍaṃ saṅkhepadesanā. Idaṃ pana nikkhepakaṇḍaṃ cittuppādakaṇḍaṃ upādāya saṅkhepo, aṭṭhakathākaṇḍaṃ upādāya vitthāroti saṅkhittavitthāradhātukaṃ hoti. Tayidaṃ, vitthāradesanaṃ nikkhipitvā desitattāpi, heṭṭhā vuttakāraṇavasenāpi, nikkhepakaṇḍaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

985. Thus far, the wholesome triad has been explained in detail by the method of verbal analysis of all wholesome and other states. However, since the method of analysis stated for the wholesome triad is the very same method of analysis for the remaining triads and dyads—for just as here, so in all triads and dyads the wise can discern the method of analysis in sequence, as for example: ‘What states are associated with pleasant feeling? At a time when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, having a form as object… or whatever other dependently arisen formless states there are on that occasion, apart from the feeling aggregate, these states are associated with pleasant feeling,’ and so on—therefore, having set aside that detailed exposition, the Chapter of Synopsis, beginning with ‘What states are wholesome?,’ has been undertaken to show the division of all states of the triads and dyads by another method that is neither too condensed nor too diffuse. For the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness is a detailed exposition, while the Commentary Chapter is a condensed exposition. This Chapter of Synopsis, however, is a condensation in relation to the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness and an elaboration in relation to the Commentary Chapter; thus it has the nature of being not too condensed and not too elaborate. This should be understood as the ‘Chapter of Synopsis’ both because it is taught having set aside the detailed exposition and for the reason stated below. For it has been said:

Mūlato khandhato cāpi, dvārato cāpi bhūmito;

Atthato dhammato cāpi, nāmato cāpi liṅgato;

Nikkhipitvā desitattā, nikkhepoti pavuccatīti.

Because it is taught by way of synopsis

From the viewpoint of root, aggregates, and doors,

And from the viewpoint of plane;

From meaning, phenomena, and name,

And from characteristic,

It is therefore called a ‘synopsis.’

Idañhi tīṇi kusalamūlānītiādinā nayena mūlato nikkhipitvā desitaṃ. Taṃsampayutto vedanākkhandhoti [V 0.0375] khandhato. Taṃsamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyakammanti dvārato. Kāyadvārappavattañhi kammaṃ kāyakammanti vuccati. Sukhabhūmiyaṃ, kāmāvacareti bhūmito nikkhipitvā desitaṃ. Tattha tattha atthadhammanāmaliṅgānaṃ vasena desitattā atthādīhi nikkhipitvā desitaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

For this is taught by way of synopsis from the viewpoint of root with the method beginning, ‘The three wholesome roots.’ By ‘the feeling aggregate associated therewith,’ it is taught from the viewpoint of aggregates. By ‘the bodily kamma originated therefrom,’ it is taught from the viewpoint of doors; for kamma that occurs through the body door is called bodily kamma. By ‘in the plane of bliss, in the sense sphere,’ it is taught by way of synopsis from the viewpoint of plane. It should be understood that because it is taught in the various sections according to meaning, phenomena, name, and characteristic, it is said to be taught by way of synopsis from the viewpoint of meaning and so on.

Tattha [M 0.0380] kusalapadaniddese tāva tīṇīti gaṇanaparicchedo. Kusalāni ca tāni mūlāni ca, kusalānaṃ vā dhammānaṃ hetupaccayapabhavajanakasamuṭṭhānanibbattakaṭṭhena mūlānīti kusalamūlāni. Evaṃ atthavasena dassetvā idāni nāmavasena dassetuṃ alobho adoso amohoti āha. Ettāvatā yasmā mūlena muttaṃ kusalaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā catubhūmakakusalaṃ tīhi mūlehi pariyādiyitvā dassesi dhammarājā. Taṃsampayuttoti [P 0.0345] tehi alobhādīhi sampayutto. Tattha alobhena sampayutte saṅkhārakkhandhe, adosāmohāpi alobhena sampayuttasaṅkhārakkhandhagaṇanaṃyeva gacchanti. Sesadvayavasena sampayogepi eseva nayo. Iti catubhūmakakusalaṃ puna taṃsampayuttakacatukkhandhavasena pariyādiyitvā dassesi dhammarājā. Taṃsamuṭṭhānanti tehi alobhādīhi samuṭṭhitaṃ. Imināpi nayena tadeva catubhūmikakusalaṃ tiṇṇaṃ kammadvārānaṃ vasena pariyādiyitvā dassesi dhammarājā. Evaṃ tāva kusalaṃ tīsu ṭhānesu pariyādiyitvā dassitaṃ.

Here, in the exposition of the term ‘wholesome,’ first, ‘three’ is a numerical determination. They are wholesome and they are roots; or they are roots of wholesome states in the sense of being their cause, condition, source, generator, origin, and producer—thus they are ‘wholesome roots.’ Having shown this by way of meaning, now to show it by way of name, he says, ‘non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion.’ By this much, since there is no wholesome state apart from a root, the King of the Dhamma has shown the wholesome of the four planes by comprehending it through the three roots. ‘Associated therewith’ means associated with those, non-greed, etc. Here, in the formations aggregate associated with non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion are also included in the count of the formations aggregate associated with non-greed. The same method applies to the association with the other two. Thus the King of the Dhamma has again shown the wholesome of the four planes by comprehending it through the four mental aggregates associated therewith. ‘Originated therefrom’ means originated from those, non-greed, etc. By this method, too, the King of the Dhamma has shown that same wholesome of the four planes by comprehending it through the three doors of kamma. In this way, first, the wholesome has been shown by comprehending it in three respects.

986. Akusalepi eseva nayo. Dvādasannañhi akusalacittānaṃ ekampi mūlena muttaṃ nāma natthīti mūlena pariyādiyitvā dassesi dhammarājā. Taṃsampayuttacatukkhandhato ca uddhaṃ akusalaṃ nāma natthīti tāneva dvādasa akusalacittāni catukkhandhavasena pariyādiyitvā dassesi. Dhammarājā kāyakammādivasena pana nesaṃ pavattisabbhāvato kammadvāravasena pariyādiyitvā dassesi dhammarājā.
