Yaṃ panettha tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesātiādi vuttaṃ, tattha ekasmiṃ citte puggale vā ṭhitanti ‘ekaṭṭhaṃ’. Tattha ekasmiṃ citte ṭhitaṃ sahajekaṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti. Ekasmiṃ puggale ṭhitaṃ pahānekaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Tena lobhādinā aññena vā tattha tattha niddiṭṭhena saha ekasmiṃ ṭhitanti tadekaṭṭhaṃ. Tattha ‘katame dhammā saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho doso moho, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā’ti saṃkiliṭṭhattike; ‘katame dhammā hīnā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho doso moho, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā’ti hīnattike ‘katame dhammā akusalā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho doso moho, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā’ti imasmiṃ [P 0.0346] kusalattike; ‘katame [M 0.0381] dhammā saṃkiliṭṭhā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho doso moho, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā’ti kilesagocchake ‘katame dhammā saraṇā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni [V 0.0376] – lobho doso moho, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesāti saraṇaduke’ti – imesu ettakesu ṭhānesu ‘sahajekaṭṭhaṃ’ āgataṃ.

986. In the unwholesome, too, this is the method. For among the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness, not even one is apart from a root; thus the King of the Dhamma has shown them by comprehending them through their roots. And since there is nothing unwholesome beyond the four mental aggregates associated with them, he has shown those very twelve unwholesome types of consciousness by comprehending them through the four mental aggregates. Further, since their occurrence exists by way of bodily kamma, etc., the King of the Dhamma has shown them by comprehending them through the doors of kamma. As to what is said here, ‘and the defilements co-existent with them,’ etc., here ‘co-existent’ (ekaṭṭha) means existing in a single consciousness or person. What exists in a single consciousness is called ‘conascence-coexistence’ (sahajekaṭṭha). What exists in a single person is called ‘coexistence for abandonment’ (pahānekaṭṭha). ‘Co-existent with them’ (tadekaṭṭha) means existing in a single place together with that greed, etc., or with another factor specified in the various contexts. Here, ‘conascence-coexistence’ is found in these many instances: in the triad on the defiled: ‘What states are defiled and corrupting? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements co-existent with them’; in the triad on the inferior: ‘What states are inferior? The three unwholesome roots… and the defilements co-existent with them’; in this wholesome triad: ‘What states are unwholesome? The three unwholesome roots… and the defilements co-existent with them’; in the Defilement Group: ‘What states are defiled? The three unwholesome roots… and the defilements co-existent with them’; and in the dyad on states with outflows: ‘What states have outflows? The three unwholesome roots… and the defilements co-existent with them’.

Dassanenapahātabbattike pana ‘imāni tīṇi saṃyojanāni, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā’ti, dassanenapahātabbahetukattikepi ‘imāni tīṇi saṃyojanāni, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā’ti, puna tattheva tīṇi saṃyojanāni – sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāso, ime dhammā dassanenapahātabbā; tadekaṭṭho lobho doso moho, ime dhammā dassanenapahātabbahetū; tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā taṃsampayutto vedanākhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammaṃ, ime dhammā dassanenapahātabbahetukāti; sammappadhānavibhaṅge “tattha katame pāpakā akusalā dhammā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho doso moho, tadekaṭṭhā ca kilesā”ti (vibha. 391) – imesu pana ettakesu ṭhānesu ‘pahānekaṭṭhaṃ’ āgatanti veditabbaṃ.

But in the triad on states to be abandoned by vision, it is said: ‘These three fetters and the defilements co-existent with them.’ And in the triad on states that are roots of what is to be abandoned by vision, it is said: ‘These three fetters and the defilements co-existent with them.’ Again, in the same place: ‘The three fetters—identity view, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances—these states are to be abandoned by vision. Greed, hatred, and delusion co-existent with them—these states are roots of what is to be abandoned by vision. And the defilements co-existent with them, the feeling aggregate associated therewith…pe… the consciousness aggregate, the bodily kamma, verbal kamma, and mental kamma originated therefrom—these states are roots of what is to be abandoned by vision.’ In the Analysis of the Right Exertions it is said: ‘Therein, what are the evil unwholesome states? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements co-existent with them’ (Vibh 219). It should be understood that in these many instances, ‘coexistence for abandonment’ is found.

987. Abyākatapadaniddeso uttānatthoyevāti. Imasmiṃ tike tīṇi lakkhaṇāni tisso paññattiyo kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ ajaṭākāsaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanassa ārammaṇaṃ nirodhasamāpatti ca na labbhatīti vuttaṃ.

987. The exposition of the term ‘indeterminate’ is of clear meaning. It is said that in this triad, the three characteristics, the three concepts, space revealed by the removal of a kasiṇa, unobstructed space, the object of the base of nothingness, and the attainment of cessation are not obtained.

988. Vedanāttikaniddese sukhabhūmiyanti ettha yathā tambabhūmi kaṇhabhūmīti tambakaṇhabhūmiyova vuccanti, evaṃ sukhampi sukhabhūmi nāma. Yathā ucchubhūmi sālibhūmīti ucchusālīnaṃ uppajjanaṭṭhānāni vuccanti, evaṃ sukhassa uppajjanaṭṭhānaṃ cittampi sukhabhūmi nāma. Taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Yasmā pana sā kāmāvacare vā hoti, rūpāvacarādīsu vā, tasmāssā [P 0.0347] taṃ pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ kāmāvacaretiādi vuttaṃ. Sukhavedanaṃ ṭhapetvāti yā sā sukhabhūmiyaṃ sukhavedanā, taṃ ṭhapetvā. Taṃsampayuttoti tāya ṭhapitāya sukhavedanāya sampayutto. Sesapadadvayepi imināva nayena attho veditabboti.

988. In the exposition of the triad on feeling, regarding 'the basis of pleasure' (sukhabhūmi), just as reddish and blackish grounds are called 'copper ground' (tambabhūmi) and 'black ground' (kaṇhabhūmi), so too pleasure (sukha) itself is called the basis of pleasure. Just as 'sugarcane ground' (ucchubhūmi) and 'rice ground' (sālibhūmi) refer to the places where sugarcane and rice arise, so too the mind, the place where pleasure arises, is called the basis of pleasure. This latter is what is intended here. And since that basis exists in the sense sphere or in the form sphere and so on, in order to show its classification, 'of the sense sphere,' etc., is said. 'Excluding pleasant feeling' means: excluding that pleasant feeling which is in the basis of pleasure. 'Associated therewith' means: associated with that pleasant feeling which has been set aside. The meaning of the remaining two phrases should also be understood in this same way.

Imasmiṃ [M 0.0382] tike tisso vedanā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ, nibbānanti idampi na labbhati. Ayañhi tiko kusalattike ca alabbhamānehi imehi ca tīhi koṭṭhāsehi muttako nāma. Ito paresu pana tikadukesu pāḷito ca atthato ca yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā taṃ sabbaṃ padānukkamena mātikākathāyañceva kusalādīnaṃ niddese ca vuttameva. Yaṃ pana yattha visesamattaṃ tadeva vakkhāma.

In this triad, the three feelings, all form, and Nibbāna—this too is not obtained. For this triad is called 'the isolated one' (muttaka) because it is free both from those things unobtainable in the wholesome triad and from these three portions. As for the subsequent triads and dyads, whatever should be said both from the Pāli and from the meaning has all been stated already in the order of the terms, both in the discussion of the matrix and in the exposition of the wholesome and so on. But whatever mere distinction there is in any case, that alone we will explain.

991. Tattha [V 0.0377] vipākattike tāva kiñcāpi arūpadhammā viya rūpadhammāpi kammasamuṭṭhānā atthi, anārammaṇattā pana te kammasarikkhakā na hontīti sārammaṇā arūpadhammāva kammasarikkhakattā vipākāti vuttā, bījasarikkhakaṃ phalaṃ viya. Sālibījasmiñhi vapite aṅkurapattādīsu nikkhantesupi sāliphalanti na vuccati. Yadā pana sālisīsaṃ pakkaṃ hoti pariṇataṃ, tadā bījasarikkhako sāli eva sāliphalanti vuccati. Aṅkurapattādīni pana bījajātāni bījato nibbattānīti vuccanti, evameva rūpampi kammajanti vā upādiṇṇanti vā vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

991. Therein, in the triad on resultants, first, although there are form-phenomena that are kamma-born just like formless phenomena, because they are without an object they are not similar to kamma. Therefore only formless phenomena, which have an object, are called 'resultants' because of their similarity to kamma, like a fruit similar to a seed. For when a rice seed is sown, even when sprouts, leaves, and so on have come forth, they are not called 'rice fruit.' But when the ear of rice is ripe and mature, then the rice itself, being similar to the seed, is called 'rice fruit.' The sprouts, leaves, and so on, however, are said to be 'seed-born,' 'produced from the seed.' Similarly, it is appropriate to say of form that it is 'kamma-born' or 'kammically acquired.'

994. Upādiṇṇattike kiñcāpi khīṇāsavassa khandhā ‘amhākaṃ mātulatthero amhākaṃ cūḷapitutthero’ti vadantānaṃ paresaṃ upādānassa paccayā honti, maggaphalanibbānāni pana aggahitāni aparāmaṭṭhāni anupādiṇṇāneva. Tāni hi, yathā divasaṃ santatto ayoguḷo makkhikānaṃ abhinisīdanassa paccayo na hoti, evameva tejussadattā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena gahaṇassa paccayā na honti. Tena vuttaṃ – ime dhammā anupādiṇṇaanupādāniyāti.

994. In the triad on the kammically acquired, although the aggregates of one whose cankers are destroyed can be a condition for the clinging of others who say, 'This is our maternal uncle, the elder,' 'This is our paternal uncle, the elder,' the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, however, are ungrasped, unmisapprehended, and indeed not kammically acquired. For just as a red-hot iron ball is not a condition for flies to alight on it during the day, so too, because of their brilliance, they are not a condition for grasping by way of craving, conceit, and views.

998. Asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesikesupi eseva nayo.

998. This same principle applies also to the undefiled and non-defiling states.

1000. Vitakkattike vitakkasahajātena vicārena saddhiṃ kusalattike alabbhamānāva na labbhanti.

1000. In the triad on thought-conception, sustained application that is co-nascent with thought-conception, along with those very states that are unobtainable in the wholesome triad, are not obtained.

1003. Pītisahagatattike [P 0.0348] pītiādayo attanā sahajātadhammānaṃ pītisahagatādibhāvaṃ datvā sayaṃ piṭṭhivaṭṭakā jātā. Imasmiñhi tike dve domanassasahagatacittuppādā [M 0.0383] dukkhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ upekkhāvedanā rūpaṃ nibbānanti – idampi na labbhati. Ayañhi tiko kusalattike ca alabbhamānehi imehi ca pañcahi koṭṭhāsehi muttako nāma.

1003. In the triad on states accompanied by rapture, rapture and so on, having conferred the state of being 'accompanied by rapture,' etc., upon their co-nascent dhammas, have themselves been set aside. In this triad, the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure, the bodily consciousness accompanied by pain, equanimous feeling, form, and Nibbāna—this too is not obtained. For this triad is called 'the isolated one' because it is free from the states unobtainable in the wholesome triad and from these five portions.

1006. Dassanenapahātabbattike saññojanānīti bandhanāni. Sakkāyadiṭṭhīti vijjamānaṭṭhena sati khandhapañcakasaṅkhāte kāye; sayaṃ vā satī tasmiṃ kāye diṭṭhīti ‘sakkāyadiṭṭhi’. Sīlena sujjhituṃ sakkā, vatena sujjhituṃ sakkā, sīlavatehi sujjhituṃ sakkāti gahitasamādānaṃ pana sīlabbataparāmāso nāma.

1006. In the triad on states to be abandoned by vision, 'fetters' (saññojanāni) means bonds. 'Identity view' (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is the view regarding the body—designated as the five aggregates—which is existing (sat), in the sense of being actually present (vijjamāna); or, it is a view that is itself an existing thing (satī) in that body. The grasping and undertaking that 'one can be purified by rules,' 'one can be purified by vows,' or 'one can be purified by rules and vows' is called 'the misapprehension of rules and vows' (sīlabbataparāmāso).

1007. Idhāti [V 0.0378] desāpadese nipāto. Svāyaṃ katthaci lokaṃ upādāya vuccati. Yathāha – “idha tathāgato loke uppajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.189). Katthaci sāsanaṃ. Yathāha – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241). Katthaci okāsaṃ. Yathāha –

1007. 'Here' (idha) is a particle indicating a place or region. It is sometimes used with reference to the world, as when it is said: 'Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world.' Sometimes it refers to the Dispensation, as when it is said: 'Here, bhikkhus, is a recluse, here a second recluse.' Sometimes it refers to a location, as when it is said:

“Idheva tiṭṭhamānassa, devabhūtassa me sato;

Punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisā”ti. (dī. ni. 2.369);

'While I was standing right here, having become a deva and being mindful, a further life-span was gained by me; thus you should know, sirs.'

Katthaci padapūraṇamattameva. Yathāha – “idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhuttāvī assaṃ pavārito”ti (ma. ni. 1.30). Idha pana lokaṃ upādāya vuttoti veditabbo.

Sometimes it is a mere expletive, as when it is said: 'Here, bhikkhus, having eaten, I would be satisfied.' But here it should be understood as spoken with reference to the world.

Assutavā puthujjanoti ettha pana ‘āgamādhigamābhāvā ñeyyo assutavā iti’. Yassa hi khandhadhātuāyatanapaccayākārasatipaṭṭhānādīsu uggahaparipucchāvinicchayarahitattā diṭṭhipaṭisedhako neva ‘āgamo’, paṭipattiyā adhigantabbassa anadhigatattā neva ‘adhigamo’ atthi, so ‘āgamādhigamābhāvā ñeyyo assutavā iti’. Svāyaṃ –

Now, in this text 'an uninstructed worldling,' it should be known that one is 'uninstructed' due to the absence of learning and realization. Indeed, for one who, being devoid of study, repeated inquiry, and the wisdom of decision concerning the aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, the establishments of mindfulness, etc., has neither the 'learning' (āgama)—that is, the Pāḷi canon which refutes wrong views—nor the 'realization' (adhigama)—the supramundane Dhamma to be attained through practice—since it has not been attained; such a one, due to the absence of learning and realization, is to be known as 'uninstructed.' This one is:

Puthūnaṃ jananādīhi, kāraṇehi puthujjano;

Puthujjanantogadhattā, puthuvāyaṃ jano iti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.2; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.51; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.130; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 88; netti. aṭṭha. 56);

'From generating many varied things, and other such reasons, a 'puthujjana'; From being included among the many folk, this person is 'of the many.'

So [P 0.0349] hi puthūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ kilesādīnaṃ jananādīhi kāraṇehi puthujjano. Yathāha – “puthu kilese janentīti puthujjanā. Puthu avihatasakkāyadiṭṭhikāti puthujjanā. Puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikāti puthujjanā. Puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitāti puthujjanā. Puthu nānābhisaṅkhāre abhisaṅkharontīti [M 0.0384] puthujjanā. Puthu nānāoghehi vuyhantīti puthujjanā. Puthu nānāsantāpehi santappantīti puthujjanā. Puthu nānāpariḷāhehi pariḍayhantīti puthujjanā. Puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rattā giddhā gadhitā mucchitā ajjhosannā laggā laggitā palibuddhāti puthujjanā. Puthu [V 0.0379] pañcahi nīvaraṇehi āvutā nivutā ovutā pihitā paṭicchannā paṭikujjitāti puthujjanā”ti (mahāni. 94). Puthūnaṃ vā gaṇanapathamatītānaṃ ariyadhammaparammukhānaṃ nīcadhammasamācārānaṃ janānaṃ antogadhattāpi puthujjanā. Puthu vā ayaṃ – visuṃyeva saṅkhyaṃ gato, visaṃsaṭṭho sīlasutādiguṇayuttehi ariyehi – janotipi puthujjano. Evametehi ‘assutavā puthujjano’ti dvīhi padehi ye te –

For they are 'worldlings' (puthujjana) for reasons such as generating (janana) many (puthu) varied kinds of defilements, etc. As it is said: 'They are worldlings because they generate many defilements. They are worldlings because they have various kinds of uneradicated identity-views. They are worldlings because they look to the faces of various teachers. They are worldlings because they have not risen out of all destinies. They are worldlings because they fashion various formations. They are worldlings because they are swept away by various floods. They are worldlings because they are tormented by various torments. They are worldlings because they are burned by various fevers. They are worldlings because they are impassioned, greedy, besotted, infatuated, engrossed in, attached to, cleaving to, and bound by the five cords of sensual pleasure. They are worldlings because they are obstructed, hindered, enveloped, covered, concealed, and shut in by the five hindrances' (Mahāni. 94). Or, they are worldlings because they are included among the many folk—a multitude beyond calculation who have turned their backs on the noble Dhamma and practice low dhammas. Or, this person (jana) is 'many' (puthu)—that is, counted apart, dissociated from the noble ones endowed with such qualities as virtue and learning—hence a 'worldling' (puthujjana). Thus, by these two terms—'uninstructed worldling'—those who...

“Duve puthujjanā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Andho puthujjano eko, kalyāṇeko puthujjano”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.51; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.130; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 88);

'Two worldlings have been declared by the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun: one is the blind worldling, the other, the virtuous worldling.'

Dve puthujjanā vuttā, tesu andhaputhujjano vutto hotīti veditabbo.

Two worldlings are spoken of; of these, it should be understood that the blind worldling is meant.

Ariyānaṃ adassāvītiādīsu ariyāti ārakattā kilesehi, anaye na iriyanato, aye iriyanato, sadevakena lokena ca araṇīyato buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca vuccanti. Buddhā eva vā idha ariyā. Yathāha – “sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… tathāgato ariyoti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1098).

In such phrases as 'one who does not see the noble ones,' 'noble ones' (ariyā) refers to the Buddhas, paccekabuddhas, and the Buddha's disciples, who are so called because they are far (ārakā) from the defilements, because they do not proceed on a wrong course (anaya), because they proceed on a right course (aya), and because they are to be approached (araṇīya) by the world with its gods. Or, in this context, 'noble ones' refers only to the Buddhas. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, in this world with its gods... the Tathāgata is called the noble one' (SN 5.1098).

Sappurisāti ettha pana paccekabuddhā tathāgatasāvakā ca sappurisāti veditabbā. Te hi lokuttaraguṇayogena sobhanā purisāti sappurisā. Sabbeva [P 0.0350] vā ete dvedhāpi vuttā. Buddhāpi hi ariyā ca sappurisā ca paccekabuddhā buddhasāvakāpi. Yathāha –

Here, however, 'good persons' (sappurisā) should be understood as the paccekabuddhas and the Tathāgata's disciples. For they are 'good persons' (sappurisā) because they are excellent persons (sobhanā purisā) due to their connection with supramundane qualities. Or indeed, all these may be spoken of in both ways. For Buddhas, too, are noble ones and good persons, and so are paccekabuddhas and the Buddha's disciples. As it is said:

“Yo ve kataññū katavedi dhīro,

Kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca hoti;

Dukhitassa sakkacca karoti kiccaṃ,

Tathāvidhaṃ sappurisaṃ vadantī”ti. (jā. 2.17.78);

'One who is grateful, who acknowledges what is done, is wise,

a good friend, and firm in devotion;

who earnestly does what needs to be done for one in distress—

such a one they call a good person' (Ja 2.17.78).

‘Kalyāṇamitto [M 0.0385] daḷhabhatti ca hotī’ti ettāvatā hi buddhasāvako vutto. Kataññutādīhi [V 0.0380] paccekabuddhā buddhāti. Idāni yo tesaṃ ariyānaṃ adassanasīlo, na ca dassane sādhukārī, so ariyānaṃ adassāvīti veditabbo. So cakkhunā adassāvī ñāṇena adassāvīti duvidho. Tesu ñāṇena adassāvī idha adhippeto. Maṃsacakkhunā hi dibbacakkhunā vā ariyā diṭṭhāpi adiṭṭhāva honti, tesaṃ cakkhūnaṃ vaṇṇamattaggahaṇato, na ariyabhāvagocarato. Soṇasiṅgālādayopi cakkhunā ariye passanti, na ca te ariyānaṃ dassāvino.

Indeed, by the words, 'is a good friend and firm in devotion,' a disciple of the Buddha is spoken of. By gratitude and the other qualities, paccekabuddhas and Buddhas are spoken of. Now, one who is of a nature not to see those noble ones and who does not delight in seeing them should be understood as 'one who does not see the noble ones.' This is twofold: not seeing with the eye and not seeing with wisdom. Of these, the one who does not see with wisdom is intended here. For even when noble ones are seen with the fleshly eye or the divine eye, they are as if unseen, since those eyes grasp only their mere appearance and do not have the state of nobility as their domain. Dogs, jackals, and the like also see noble ones with their eyes, but they are not 'seers of the noble ones.'

Tatridaṃ vatthu – cittalapabbatavāsino kira khīṇāsavattherassa upaṭṭhāko vuḍḍhapabbajito ekadivasaṃ therena saddhiṃ piṇḍāya caritvā therassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā piṭṭhito āgacchanto theraṃ pucchi – ‘ariyā nāma bhante kīdisā’ti? Thero āha – ‘idhekacco mahallako ariyānaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vattapaṭipattiṃ katvā saha carantopi neva ariye jānāti, evaṃdujjānāvuso, ariyā’ti. Evaṃ vuttepi so neva aññāsi. Tasmā na cakkhunā dassanaṃ ‘dassanaṃ’, ñāṇadassanameva ‘dassanaṃ’. Yathāha – “kiṃ te vakkali iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena? Yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.87). Tasmā cakkhunā passantopi, ñāṇena ariyehi diṭṭhaṃ aniccādilakkhaṇaṃ apassanto, ariyādhigatañca dhammaṃ anadhigacchanto, ariyakaradhammānaṃ ariyabhāvassa ca adiṭṭhattā, ‘ariyānaṃ adassāvī’ti veditabbo.

Here is the story: It is said that the attendant of the Arahant-elder dwelling on Cittalapabbata, one who had gone forth in old age, one day went for alms with the elder. Carrying the elder’s bowl and robe and following behind him, he asked the elder, “Venerable sir, what are the noble ones like?” The elder replied, “Here, friend, some old man, having taken the bowl and robes of the noble ones and performed his duties, though walking along with them, does not know the noble ones. So hard to know, friend, are the noble ones.” Even when this was said, he still did not understand. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not ‘seeing’; it is only the vision of wisdom that is ‘seeing.’ As it is said: “What is it to you, Vakkali, to see this foul body? One who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.87). Therefore, one who, though seeing with the eye, does not see with wisdom the characteristics of impermanence and so on that are seen by the noble ones, and does not realize the Dhamma that has been realized by the noble ones, should be understood as ‘one who does not see the noble ones’ because of not having seen the qualities that make one noble and the state of nobility.

Ariyadhammassa [P 0.0351] akovidoti satipaṭṭhānādibhede ariyadhamme akusalo. Ariyadhamme avinītoti, ettha pana

Unskilled in the noble Dhamma means unskilled in the noble Dhamma in its divisions such as the establishments of mindfulness. Regarding 'untrained in the noble Dhamma,' here, however,

Duvidho vinayo nāma, ekamekettha pañcadhā;

Abhāvato tassa ayaṃ, avinītoti vuccati.

The discipline is said to be twofold, and each of these is fivefold; because of its absence, one is called 'undisciplined'.

Ayañhi saṃvaravinayo pahānavinayoti duvidho vinayo. Ettha ca duvidhepi vinaye ekameko vinayo pañcadhā bhijjati. Saṃvaravinayopi hi sīlasaṃvaro satisaṃvaro ñāṇasaṃvaro khantisaṃvaro vīriyasaṃvaroti pañcavidho. Pahānavinayopi tadaṅgapahānaṃ vikkhambhanapahānaṃ samucchedapahānaṃ paṭippassaddhipahānaṃ nissaraṇapahānanti pañcavidho.

Indeed, this discipline is twofold: the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandoning. And herein, in this twofold discipline, each one discipline is divided fivefold. Indeed, the discipline of restraint is fivefold: restraint of morality, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, restraint of patience, and restraint of energy. The discipline of abandoning is also fivefold: abandoning by the particular factor, abandoning by suppression, abandoning by eradication, abandoning by tranquillization, and abandoning by escape.

Tattha [M 0.0386][V 0.0381] “iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto”ti (vibha. 511) ayaṃ sīlasaṃvaro. “Rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.213; ma. ni. 1.295; saṃ. ni. 4.239; a. ni. 3.16) ayaṃ satisaṃvaro.

Therein, “He is endowed, well endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint” (Vibh. 511)—this is the restraint of morality. “He guards the eye faculty; he attains to restraint in the eye faculty” (Dī. Ni. 1.213; etc.)—this is the restraint of mindfulness.

“Yāni sotāni lokasmiṃ, (ajitāti bhagavā)

Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi,

Paññāyete pidhīyare”ti. (su. ni. 1041) –

“The streams that are in the world, Ajita,” said the Blessed One, “mindfulness is their checking. The restraint of the streams I proclaim; by wisdom they are shut off” (Su. Ni. 1041).

Ayaṃ ñāṇasaṃvaro nāma. “Khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassā”ti (ma. ni. 1.24; a. ni. 4.114; 6.58) ayaṃ khantisaṃvaro. “Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.114; 6.58) ayaṃ vīriyasaṃvaro. Sabbopi cāyaṃ saṃvaro yathāsakaṃ saṃvaritabbānaṃ vinetabbānañca kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, vinayanato vinayoti vuccati. Evaṃ tāva ‘saṃvaravinayo’ pañcadhā bhijjatīti veditabbo.

This is called the restraint of knowledge. “He is able to endure cold and heat” (Ma. Ni. 1.24; etc.)—this is the restraint of patience. “He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual pleasure” (Ma. Ni. 1.26; etc.)—this is the restraint of energy. And all this restraint is called ‘restraint’ (saṃvara) because of its restraining of bodily misconduct and so on, which are to be restrained and disciplined; and it is called ‘discipline’ (vinaya) because of its disciplining. Thus, for now, it should be understood that the ‘discipline of restraint’ is divided fivefold.

Tathā yaṃ nāmarūpaparicchedādīsu vipassanāñāṇesu paṭipakkhabhāvato, dīpālokeneva tamassa, tena tena vipassanāñāṇena tassa tassa anatthassa pahānaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – nāmarūpavavatthānena sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā, paccayapariggahena [P 0.0352] ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhīnaṃ, tasseva aparabhāgena kaṅkhāvitaraṇena kathaṃkathibhāvassa, kalāpasammasanena ‘ahaṃ mamā’ti gāhassa, maggāmaggavavatthānena amagge maggasaññāya, udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā, vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā, bhayadassanena sabhaye abhayasaññāya, ādīnavadassanena assādasaññāya, nibbidānupassanāya abhiratisaññāya, muccitukamyatāñāṇena amuccitukāmatāya, upekkhāñāṇena anupekkhāya, anulomena dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ nibbāne ca paṭilomabhāvassa, gotrabhunā saṅkhāranimittaggāhassa pahānaṃ, etaṃ ‘tadaṅgapahānaṃ’ nāma.

Furthermore, just as darkness is abandoned by the light of a lamp, so in the insight knowledges, beginning with the determination of mind-and-matter, because of being the opposite factor, there is the abandoning of each particular non-beneficial state by each respective insight knowledge. This is as follows: the abandoning of identity view by the determination of mind-and-matter; of the views of causelessness and dissimilar cause by the grasping of conditions; of the state of perplexity by the overcoming of doubt, which is its subsequent stage; of the grasp of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ by the comprehension of groups; of the perception of ‘path’ in what is not the path by the determination of path and not-path; of the annihilationist view by the knowledge of seeing arising; of the eternalist view by the knowledge of seeing passing away; of the perception of safety in what is fearful by the knowledge of seeing fear; of the perception of gratification by the knowledge of seeing danger; of the perception of delight by the contemplation of disenchantment; of the unwillingness to be liberated by the knowledge of the desire for deliverance; of non-equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity; of the state of being contrary to the stability of phenomena and to Nibbāna by conformity knowledge; of the grasping of the sign of formations by change-of-lineage knowledge. This is called ‘abandoning by the particular factor.’

Yaṃ pana upacārappanābhedena samādhinā pavattibhāvanivāraṇato, ghaṭappahāreneva udakapiṭṭhe sevālassa, tesaṃ tesaṃ nīvaraṇādidhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, etaṃ ‘vikkhambhanapahānaṃ’ nāma. “Yaṃ catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃtaṃmaggavato [M 0.0387] attano attano santāne diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādinā [V 0.0382] (dha. sa. 277) nayena vuttassa samudayapakkhikassa kilesagaṇassa accantaṃ appavattibhāvena pahānaṃ, idaṃ ‘samucchedapahānaṃ’ nāma. Yaṃ pana phalakkhaṇe paṭippassaddhattaṃ kilesānaṃ, etaṃ ‘paṭippassaddhipahānaṃ’ nāma. Yaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭattā pahīnasabbasaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ, etaṃ ‘nissaraṇapahānaṃ’ nāma. Sabbampi cetaṃ pahānaṃ yasmā cāgaṭṭhena pahānaṃ, vinayanaṭṭhena vinayo, tasmā ‘pahānavinayo’ti vuccati. Taṃtaṃpahānavato vā tassa tassa vinayassa sambhavatopetaṃ pahānavinayoti vuccati. Evaṃ pahānavinayopi pañcadhā bhijjatīti veditabbo.

Now, the abandoning of those various hindrances and other states by preventing their occurrence through concentration, distinguished as access and absorption—like the removal of moss from the surface of water by a blow with a pot—this is called ‘abandoning by suppression.’ The abandoning by way of utter non-arising of the mass of defilements pertaining to the side of the origin, spoken of in the way beginning, “due to the development of the four noble paths, for one who possesses the respective path, in one’s own continuum, for the abandoning of views…” (Dhs. §1003), this is called ‘abandoning by eradication.’ Now, the state of the defilements having been tranquillized at the moment of fruition, this is called ‘abandoning by tranquillization.’ Nibbāna, which is the escape from all conditioned things, having abandoned all conditioned things, this is called ‘abandoning by escape.’ And all this abandoning is called the ‘discipline of abandoning’ because it is ‘abandoning’ in the sense of relinquishing, and ‘discipline’ in the sense of removing. Or, it is called the ‘discipline of abandoning’ because for one who possesses that respective abandoning, that respective discipline can occur. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of abandoning is also divided fivefold.

Evamayaṃ saṅkhepato duvidho, bhedato ca dasavidho vinayo, bhinnasaṃvarattā, pahātabbassa ca appahīnattā, yasmā etassa assutavato puthujjanassa natthi, tasmā abhāvato tassa, ayaṃ ‘avinīto’ti vuccatīti. Esa [P 0.0353] nayo sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinītoti etthāpi. Ninnānākaraṇañhetaṃ atthato. Yathāha – “yeva te ariyā teva te sappurisā, yeva te sappurisā teva te ariyā. Yo eva so ariyānaṃ dhammo so eva so sappurisānaṃ dhammo, yo eva so sappurisānaṃ dhammo so eva so ariyānaṃ dhammo. Yeva te ariyavinayā teva te sappurisavinayā, yeva te sappurisavinayā teva te ariyavinayā. Ariyeti vā sappuriseti vā, ariyadhammeti vā sappurisadhammeti vā, ariyavinayeti vā sappurisavinayeti vā, esese eke ekaṭṭhe same samabhāge tajjāte taññevā”ti.

Thus, this discipline is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail. Because this is absent in an uninstructed worldling—due to his broken restraint and because what is to be abandoned has not been abandoned—therefore, due to its absence, he is called ‘undisciplined.’ This same method applies also to the phrases: ‘one who does not see good persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, and is undisciplined in the Dhamma of good persons.’ For in meaning, this is not different. As it is said: “Whosoever are the noble ones, they are the good persons; and whosoever are the good persons, they are the noble ones. Whatever is the Dhamma of the noble ones, that is the Dhamma of the good persons; and whatever is the Dhamma of the good persons, that is the Dhamma of the noble ones. Whatever are the disciplines of the noble ones, they are the disciplines of the good persons; and whatever are the disciplines of the good persons, they are the disciplines of the noble ones. Whether ‘noble one’ or ‘good person,’ or ‘Dhamma of the noble ones’ or ‘Dhamma of good persons,’ or ‘discipline of the noble ones’ or ‘discipline of the good persons’—this is that; they are one, of one meaning, the same, of the same portion, of that nature, that very same thing.”

Rūpaṃ attato samanupassatīti idhekacco rūpaṃ attato samanupassati – ‘yaṃ rūpaṃ so ahaṃ, yo ahaṃ taṃ rūpa’nti rūpañca attānañca advayaṃ samanupassati. “Seyyathāpi nāma telappadīpassa jhāyato yā acci so vaṇṇo, yo vaṇṇo sā accīti acciñca vaṇṇañca advayaṃ samanupassati,” evameva idhekacco rūpaṃ attato samanupassatīti evaṃ rūpaṃ attāti diṭṭhipassanāya passati. Rūpavantaṃ vā attānanti ‘arūpaṃ attā’ti gahetvā, chāyāvantaṃ rukkhaṃ viya, taṃ rūpavantaṃ samanupassati. Attani vā rūpanti ‘arūpameva attā’ti gahetvā, pupphamhi gandhaṃ viya, attani rūpaṃ samanupassati. Rūpasmiṃ [M 0.0388] vā attānanti ‘arūpameva attā’ti gahetvā, karaṇḍake maṇiṃ viya, attānaṃ rūpasmiṃ samanupassati. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘One regards form as self’: Here someone regards form as self, thinking: ‘What form is, that I am; what I am, that is form.’ Thus he regards form and self as non-dual. Just as, when an oil lamp is burning, one might regard the flame and the color as non-dual, thinking: ‘What the flame is, that is the color; what the color is, that is the flame’; in the same way, someone here regards form as self. Thus he sees form as self with the seeing that is a view. ‘Or he regards the self as possessing form’: having taken the formless as self, he regards it as possessing form, like a tree possessing a shadow. ‘Or he regards form as in the self’: having taken the formless itself as self, he regards form as in the self, like fragrance in a flower. ‘Or he regards the self as in form’: having taken the formless itself as self, he regards the self as in form, like a gem in a casket. The same method applies to feeling and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0383] ‘rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī’ti suddharūpameva attāti kathitaṃ. ‘Rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ, attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ; vedanaṃ attato samanupassati… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassatī’ti imesu sattasu ṭhānesu ‘arūpaṃ attā’ti kathitaṃ. Vedanāvantaṃ [P 0.0354] vā attānaṃ, attani vā vedanaṃ, vedanāya vā attānanti evaṃ catūsu khandhesu tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vasena dvādasasu ṭhānesu ‘rūpārūpamissako attā’ kathito. Tattha ‘rūpaṃ attato samanupassati vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassatī’ti imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu ucchedadiṭṭhi kathitā. Avasesesu sassatadiṭṭhi. Evamettha pannarasa bhavadiṭṭhiyo pañca vibhavadiṭṭhiyo honti. Tā sabbāpi maggāvaraṇā, na saggāvaraṇā, paṭhamamaggavajjhāti veditabbā.

Here, in the statement ‘one regards form as self,’ it is taught that pure form itself is self. In these seven cases—‘one regards the self as possessing form,’ ‘form as in the self,’ ‘the self as in form’; and ‘one regards feeling as self,’ ‘…perception…,’ ‘…formations…,’ ‘…consciousness as self’—it is taught that the formless is self. In the twelve cases comprising three modes for each of the four mental aggregates—such as ‘one regards the self as possessing feeling,’ ‘feeling as in the self,’ or ‘the self in feeling’—it is taught that the self is a mixture of form and the formless. Among these, in the five cases where one regards form as self, or feeling… perception… formations… or consciousness as self, the annihilationist view is taught. In the remaining cases, the eternalist view is taught. Thus there are here fifteen views of being and five views of non-being. It should be understood that all of these are obstructions to the path, not obstructions to heaven, and are to be destroyed by the first path.

1008. Satthari kaṅkhatīti satthu sarīre vā guṇe vā ubhayattha vā kaṅkhati. Sarīre kaṅkhamāno ‘dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nāma sarīraṃ atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhati. Guṇe kaṅkhamāno ‘atītānāgatapaccuppannajānanasamatthaṃ sabbaññutañāṇaṃ atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhati. Ubhayattha kaṅkhamāno ‘asītianubyañjanabyāmappabhānurañjitāya sarīranipphattiyā samannāgato sabbañeyyajānanasamatthaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito lokatārako buddho nāma atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhati. Ayañhissa attabhāve guṇe vā kaṅkhanato ubhayattha kaṅkhati nāma. Vicikicchatīti ārammaṇaṃ nicchetuṃ asakkonto kicchati kilamati. Nādhimuccatīti tattheva adhimokkhaṃ na labhati. Na sampasīdatīti cittaṃ anāvilaṃ katvā pasīdituṃ na sakkoti, guṇesu nappasīdati.

1008. ‘To doubt the Teacher’ is to doubt the Teacher’s body, or his qualities, or both. Doubting the body, one wonders: ‘Does a body adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks of a great man exist or not?’ Doubting the qualities, one wonders: ‘Does the knowledge of all-knowingness, capable of knowing the past, future, and present, exist or not?’ Doubting both, one wonders: ‘Does a Buddha exist or not—a liberator of the world, endowed with the accomplishment of a body embellished by the eighty minor characteristics and a fathom-long radiance, who abides having penetrated the knowledge of all-knowingness capable of knowing all that is knowable?’ Indeed, this one, due to doubting his personal existence or his qualities, is called one who doubts in both respects. ‘Is perplexed’ means that, being unable to decide about the object, one is troubled and wearied. ‘Is not resolved’ means one does not obtain conviction in that. ‘Is not confident’ means one is unable to make the mind limpid and become confident; one does not gain confidence in his qualities.

Dhamme kaṅkhatītiādīsu pana ‘kilese pajahantā cattāro ariyamaggā, paṭippassaddhakilesāni cattāri sāmaññaphalāni, maggaphalānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayabhūtaṃ amataṃ mahānibbānaṃ nāma atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhantopi ‘ayaṃ dhammo niyyāniko nu kho aniyyāniko’ti kaṅkhantopi dhamme kaṅkhati [M 0.0389] nāma. ‘Cattāro [P 0.0355] maggaṭṭhakā cattāro phalaṭṭhakāti idaṃ saṅgharatanaṃ atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhantopi, ‘ayaṃ saṅgho suppaṭipanno nu kho duppaṭipanno’ti kaṅkhantopi, ‘etasmiṃ saṅgharatane dinnassa vipākaphalaṃ atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhantopi saṅghe kaṅkhati nāma. ‘Tisso pana sikkhā atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhantopi, ‘tisso sikkhā sikkhitapaccayena ānisaṃso atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhantopi sikkhāya kaṅkhati nāma.

Further, in such phrases as ‘doubts the Dhamma,’ one who doubts whether ‘the four noble paths that abandon the defilements, the four fruits of recluseship in which defilements are allayed, and the deathless, great Nibbāna, which is the object-condition for the paths and fruits, exist or not,’ and one who doubts whether ‘this Dhamma is emancipating or not emancipating,’ is said to doubt the Dhamma. One who doubts whether ‘the four persons established in the path and the four persons established in the fruit—this jewel of the Sangha—exist or not,’ or whether ‘this Sangha is of good conduct or of bad conduct,’ or whether ‘there is a result-fruit from what is given to this jewel of the Sangha or not,’ is said to doubt the Sangha. One who doubts whether ‘the three trainings exist or not,’ or whether ‘there is a benefit because of having trained in the three trainings or not,’ is said to doubt the training.

Pubbanto [V 0.0384] vuccati atītāni khandhadhātāyatanāni. Aparanto anāgatāni. Tattha atītesu khandhādīsu ‘atītāni nu kho, na nu kho’ti kaṅkhanto pubbante kaṅkhati nāma. Anāgatesu ‘anāgatāni nu kho, na nu kho’ti kaṅkhanto aparante kaṅkhati nāma. Ubhayattha kaṅkhanto pubbantāparante kaṅkhati nāma. ‘Dvādasapadikaṃ paccayavaṭṭaṃ atthi nu kho natthī’ti kaṅkhanto idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu kaṅkhati nāma. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – imesaṃ jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paccayā ‘idappaccayā’. Idappaccayānaṃ bhāvo ‘idappaccayatā’. Idappaccayā eva vā ‘idappaccayatā’; jātiādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Jātiādīsu taṃ taṃ paṭicca āgamma samuppannāti ‘paṭiccasamuppannā’. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – idappaccayatāya ca paṭiccasamuppannesu ca dhammesu kaṅkhatīti.

The prior extremity is said to be the past aggregates, elements, and bases. The latter extremity is the future ones. Herein, one who doubts about the past aggregates, etc., thinking, ‘Were there past ones or not?’ is said to doubt the prior extremity. One who doubts about the future ones, thinking, ‘Will there be future ones or not?’ is said to doubt the latter extremity. One who doubts about both is said to doubt the prior and latter extremities. One who doubts, ‘Does the twelve-factored round of conditions exist or not?’ is said to doubt phenomena that are dependently arisen based on specific conditionality. Herein, this is the explanation of the term: the conditions for these things such as aging-and-death are ‘specific conditions.’ The state of these specific conditions is ‘specific conditionality.’ Or, ‘specific conditions’ itself is ‘specific conditionality’; this is a designation for birth and so on. Because they have arisen dependently, having come to be in reliance on this and that, such as birth, they are ‘dependently arisen.’ This is what is meant: one doubts about specific conditionality and about phenomena that are dependently arisen.

1009. Sīlenāti gosīlādinā. Vatenāti govatādināva. Sīlabbatenāti tadubhayena. Suddhīti kilesasuddhi; paramatthasuddhibhūtaṃ vā nibbānameva. Tadekaṭṭhāti idha pahānekaṭṭhaṃ dhuraṃ. Imissā ca pāḷiyā diṭṭhikileso vicikicchākilesoti dveyeva āgatā. Lobho doso moho māno thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime pana aṭṭha anāgatā. Āharitvā pana dīpetabbā. Ettha hi diṭṭhivicikicchāsu pahīyamānāsu apāyagamanīyo lobho doso moho māno thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti sabbepime pahānekaṭṭhā hutvā pahīyanti. Sahajekaṭṭhaṃ pana āharitvā dīpetabbaṃ. Sotāpattimaggena hi [P 0.0356] cattāri diṭṭhisahagatāni vicikicchāsahagatañcāti pañca cittāni pahīyanti. Tattha dvīsu asaṅkhārikadiṭṭhicittesu pahīyantesu tehi sahajāto lobho moho uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime kilesā sahajekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti. Sesadiṭṭhikileso ca vicikicchākileso ca pahānekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti. Diṭṭhigatasampayuttasasaṅkhārikacittesupi pahīyantesu tehi sahajāto lobho moho [M 0.0390] thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime kilesā sahajekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti. Sesadiṭṭhikileso ca vicikicchākileso ca pahānekaṭṭhavasena pahīyanti. Evaṃ pahānekaṭṭhasmiṃyeva sahajekaṭṭhaṃ labbhatīti idaṃ sahajekaṭṭhaṃ āharitvā dīpayiṃsu.

1009. ‘By virtue’ means by such as cow-virtue. ‘By observance’ means by such as the cow-observance. ‘By virtue and observance’ means by both of these. ‘Purity’ means purity from defilements, or Nibbāna itself, which is ultimate purity. ‘Having a single function’: here, that which has the single function of abandoning is primary. In this Pali passage, only two defilements have been mentioned: the defilement of views and the defilement of doubt. But these eight—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—have not been mentioned. They should, however, be brought in and explained. For here, when views and doubt are being abandoned, all these—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing that lead to the plane of misery—are abandoned, having the single function of being abandoned. However, that which has the single function of co-nascence should be brought in and explained. For by the path of stream-entry, five consciousnesses are abandoned: four accompanied by views and one accompanied by doubt. Therein, when the two unprompted consciousnesses accompanied by views are abandoned, these defilements co-nascent with them—greed, delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—are abandoned by way of the single function of co-nascence. The remaining defilement of views and the defilement of doubt are abandoned by way of the single function of abandoning. When the prompted consciousnesses connected with wrong view are also abandoned, these defilements co-nascent with them—greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—are abandoned by way of the single function of co-nascence. The remaining defilement of views and the defilement of doubt are abandoned by way of the single function of abandoning. Thus, that which has the single function of co-nascence is found even within that which has the single function of abandoning. This is how they explained, having introduced that which has the single function of co-nascence.

Taṃsampayuttoti tehi tadekaṭṭhehi aṭṭhahi kilesehi sampayutto. Vinibbhogaṃ vā katvā tena lobhena tena dosenāti evaṃ ekekena sampayuttatā dīpetabbā. Tattha lobhe gahite, moho māno thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ayaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhe kilesagaṇo lobhasampayutto nāma. Dose [V 0.0385] gahite, moho thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ayaṃ kilesagaṇo dosasampayutto nāma. Mohe gahite, lobho doso māno thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ayaṃ kilesagaṇo mohasampayutto nāma. Māne gahite, tena sahuppanno lobho moho thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ayaṃ kilesagaṇo mānasampayutto nāma. Iminā upāyena tena thinena tena uddhaccena tena ahirikena tena anottappena sampayutto taṃsampayuttoti yojanā kātabbā. Taṃsamuṭṭhānanti tena lobhena…pe… tena anottappena samuṭṭhitanti attho.

‘Associated with them’ means associated with those eight defilements that have a single function. Or, having made a division, the association with each one should be shown thus: ‘with that greed, with that hatred,’ and so on. Here, when greed is taken, this group of defilements in the aggregate of formations—delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—is called ‘associated with greed.’ When hatred is taken, this group of defilements—delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—is called ‘associated with hatred.’ When delusion is taken, this group of defilements—greed, hatred, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—is called ‘associated with delusion.’ When conceit is taken, this group of defilements that arise together with it—greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—is called ‘associated with conceit.’ By this method, the connection should be construed as: ‘associated with that sloth, with that restlessness, with that shamelessness, with that lack of fear of wrongdoing’—this is ‘associated with them.’ ‘Arisen from them’ means arisen from that greed… and so on… arisen from that lack of fear of wrongdoing.

Ime dhammā dassanena pahātabbāti ettha dassanaṃ nāma sotāpattimaggo; tena pahātabbāti attho. ‘Kasmā pana sotāpattimaggo dassanaṃ nāma jāto’ti? ‘Paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato’. ‘Nanu gotrabhu paṭhamataraṃ passatī’ti[P 0.0357]? ‘No na passati; disvāpi kattabbakiccaṃ pana na karoti, saṃyojanānaṃ appahānato. Tasmā passatī’ti na vattabbo. Yattha katthaci rājānaṃ disvāpi paṇṇākāraṃ datvā kiccanipphattiyā adiṭṭhattā ‘ajjāpi rājānaṃ na passāmī’ti vadanto cettha jānapadapuriso nidassanaṃ.

‘These states are to be abandoned by seeing’: here ‘seeing’ is the path of stream-entry; the meaning is that they are to be abandoned by it. ‘But why is the path of stream-entry called “seeing”?’ ‘Because it is the first to see Nibbāna.’ ‘But does not the change-of-lineage consciousness see it even earlier?’ ‘No, it does not see. For even having seen, it does not accomplish the task that should be done, since it does not abandon the fetters. Therefore, it cannot be said that it “sees.”’ An illustration here is a man from the countryside who, though he has seen the king somewhere and given a gift, says, ‘I still have not seen the king,’ because the accomplishment of his business has not been seen.

1011. Avaseso lobhoti dassanena pahīnāvaseso. Lobho dosamohesupi eseva nayo. Dassanena hi apāyagamanīyāva pahīnā. Tehi pana aññe dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Tadekaṭṭhā’ti tehi pāḷiyaṃ āgatehi tīhi kilesehi sampayogatopi pahānatopi ekaṭṭhā pañca kilesā. Neva dassanena na bhāvanāyāti idaṃ saṃyojanādīnaṃ viya [M 0.0391] tehi maggehi appahātabbataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana “sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena satta bhave ṭhapetvā anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe ye uppajjeyyuṃ, nāmañca rūpañca etthete nirujjhantī”tiādinā nayena kusalādīnampi pahānaṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ tesaṃ maggānaṃ abhāvitattā ye uppajjeyyuṃ, te upanissayapaccayānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahīnattā pahīnāti imaṃ pariyāyaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

1011. ‘Remaining greed’ is the greed remaining from what is abandoned by seeing. This same method applies to hatred and delusion. For by seeing, only those defilements leading to the plane of misery are abandoned. But this was said to show the others apart from them. ‘Having a single basis’: the five defilements have a single basis with the three defilements mentioned in the Pāḷi text, both in terms of association and in terms of abandoning. ‘Neither by seeing nor by development’: this is said with reference to their not being abandonable by those paths, like the fetters and so on. As for the abandoning of even wholesome states and so on, which is permitted by the method stated as: ‘By the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, with the cessation of formational consciousness, having set aside seven existences, whatever name-and-form would arise in the beginningless round of saṃsāra, these cease right here,’ this should be understood as stated with reference to this reason: those states that would arise because those paths have not been developed are said to be abandoned because the defilements that are their decisive support conditions have been abandoned.

1013. Dassanenapahātabbahetukattike ime dhammā dassanena pahātabbahetukāti niṭṭhapetvā, puna ‘tīṇi saṃyojanānī’tiādi pahātabbe dassetvā, tadekaṭṭhabhāvena hetū ceva sahetuke ca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha ‘kiñcāpi dassanena pahātabbesu hetūsu lobhasahagato moho lobhena sahetuko hoti, dosasahagato moho dosena, lobhadosā ca mohenāti pahātabbahetukapadepete saṅgahaṃ [V 0.0386] gacchanti, vicikicchāsahagato pana moho aññassa sampayuttahetuno abhāvena hetuyeva, na sahetukoti tassa pahānaṃ dassetuṃ ime dhammā dassanena pahātabbahetū’ti vuttaṃ.

1013. In the triad on states with roots to be abandoned by seeing, having concluded, ‘These states have roots to be abandoned by seeing,’ and then having shown the things to be abandoned with ‘three fetters,’ etc., it is stated in order to show both the roots and the states with roots by way of their having a single basis. Therein, although among the roots to be abandoned by seeing, delusion accompanied by greed becomes a state with a root by means of greed, delusion accompanied by hatred by means of hatred, and greed and hatred by means of delusion—thus these are included under the term ‘states with roots to be abandoned’—delusion accompanied by doubt, however, due to the absence of another associated root, is only a root, not a state with a root. Therefore, to show its abandonment, it is said, ‘These states are roots to be abandoned by seeing.’

1018. Dutiyapade [P 0.0358] uddhaccasahagatassa mohassa pahānaṃ dassetuṃ ime dhammā bhāvanāya pahātabbahetūti vuttaṃ. So hi attanā sampayuttadhamme sahetuke katvā piṭṭhivaṭṭako jāto, vicikicchāsahagato viya aññassa sampayuttahetuno abhāvā pahātabbahetukapadaṃ na bhajati. Tatiyapade avasesā akusalāti puna akusalaggahaṇaṃ vicikicchuddhaccasahagatānaṃ mohānaṃ saṅgahatthaṃ kataṃ. Te hi sampayuttahetuno abhāvā pahātabbahetukā nāma na honti.

1018. In the second term, to show the abandoning of delusion accompanied by restlessness, it is said: 'These states are roots to be abandoned by development.' For it, having made its associated states to be states with a root, has become one that turns back; like delusion accompanied by doubt, due to the absence of another associated root, it does not come under the term 'a state with a root to be abandoned.' In the third term, 'the remaining unwholesome states,' the word 'unwholesome' is taken up again for the sake of including the delusions accompanied by doubt and restlessness. For these, due to the absence of an associated root, are not called 'states with a root to be abandoned.'

1029. Parittārammaṇattike ārabbhāti ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Sayañhi parittā vā hontu mahaggatā vā, parittadhamme ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannā parittārammaṇā, mahaggate ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannā mahaggatārammaṇā, appamāṇe ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannā appamāṇārammaṇā. Te pana parittāpi honti mahaggatāpi appamāṇāpi.

1029. In the triad of limited-object states, the word `ārabbha` means 'having taken as object.' For whether the states themselves are limited or exalted, those that have arisen taking a limited state as object are 'of limited object'; those that have arisen taking an exalted state as object are 'of exalted object'; and those that have arisen taking an immeasurable state as object are 'of immeasurable object.' But those latter states can be limited, exalted, or immeasurable.

1035. Micchattattike [M 0.0392] ānantarikānīti anantarāyena phaladāyakāni; mātughātakakammādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tesu hi ekasmimpi kamme kate taṃ paṭibāhitvā aññaṃ kammaṃ attano vipākassa okāsaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Sineruppamāṇepi hi suvaṇṇathūpe katvā cakkavāḷamattaṃ vā ratanamayapākāraṃ vihāraṃ kāretvā taṃ pūretvā nisinnassa buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa yāvajīvaṃ cattāro paccaye dadatopi taṃ kammaṃ etesaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ paṭibāhetuṃ na sakkoti eva. Yā ca micchādiṭṭhi niyatāti ahetukavādaakiriyavādanatthikavādesu aññatarā. Tañhi gahetvā ṭhitaṃ puggalaṃ buddhasatampi buddhasahassampi bodhetuṃ na sakkoti.

1035. In the triad of wrongness, `ānantarika` means 'yielding fruit without interval'; this is a designation for such kamma as matricide and so on. For when even one of these kammas has been done, another kamma cannot obstruct it and create an opportunity for its own result. Even if one were to build a golden stupa the size of Mount Sineru, or have a monastery built with a jeweled wall the size of a world-sphere, and having filled it, were to give the four requisites for life to the Sangha headed by the Buddha seated therein, that kamma would be unable to obstruct the result of these kammas. And the wrong view that is 'fixed' is any one of the views of causelessness, inaction, or nihilism. For a person who has grasped and holds to such a view cannot be awakened even by a hundred Buddhas or a thousand Buddhas.

1038. Maggārammaṇattike ariyamaggaṃ ārabbhāti lokuttaramaggaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Te pana parittāpi honti mahaggatāpi.

1038. In the triad of path-object states, 'having the noble path as object' means having taken the supramundane path as object. But those states can be limited or exalted.

1039. Maggahetukaniddese [P 0.0359] paṭhamanayena paccayaṭṭhena hetunā maggasampayuttānaṃ khandhānaṃ sahetukabhāvo dassito. Dutiyanayena maggabhūtena sammādiṭṭhisaṅkhātena hetunā sesamaggaṅgānaṃ sahetukabhāvo [V 0.0387] dassito. Tatiyanayena magge uppannahetūhi sammādiṭṭhiyā sahetukabhāvo dassitoti veditabbo.

1039. In the exposition of 'path as root,' by the first method, the state of having a root for the aggregates associated with the path is shown by way of the root in the sense of a condition. By the second method, the state of having a root for the remaining path factors is shown by way of the root designated as right view, which constitutes the path. By the third method, it should be understood that the state of having a root for right view is shown by way of the roots that have arisen in the path.

1040. Adhipatiṃ karitvāti ārammaṇādhipatiṃ katvā. Te ca kho parittadhammāva honti. Ariyasāvakānañhi attano maggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhaṇakāle ārammaṇādhipati labbhati. Cetopariyañāṇena pana ariyasāvako parassa maggaṃ paccavekkhamāno garuṃ karontopi attanā paṭividdhamaggaṃ viya garuṃ na karoti. ‘Yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karontaṃ tathāgataṃ disvā tassa maggaṃ garuṃ karoti na karotī’ti? Karoti, na pana attano maggaṃ viya. Arahā na kiñci dhammaṃ garuṃ karoti ṭhapetvā maggaṃ phalaṃ nibbānanti. Etthāpi ayamevattho. Vīmaṃsādhipateyyanti idaṃ sahajātādhipatiṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Chandañhi jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā maggaṃ bhāventassa chando adhipati nāma hoti, na maggo. Sesadhammāpi chandādhipatino nāma honti, na maggādhipatino. Cittepi eseva nayo. Vīmaṃsaṃ pana jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā maggaṃ bhāventassa vīmaṃsādhipati ceva hoti maggo cāti. Sesadhammā maggādhipatino nāma honti. Vīriyepi eseva nayo.

1040. `Having made it the dominant factor` means having made it the object-dominant factor. And those states are only limited ones. For it is when noble disciples review their own path, giving it weight, that the object-dominant factor is obtained. But when a noble disciple reviews another's path with the knowledge of others' minds, even though he gives it weight, he does not give it weight in the same way as his own penetrated path. 'When one sees the Tathāgata performing the Twin Miracle, does one give weight to his path or not?' One does, but not in the same way as to one's own path. An arahant gives no weight to any state except the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Here, too, this is the meaning. The phrase 'dominance of investigation' is stated to show the conascence-dominant factor. For one who develops the path making zeal foremost, zeal is the dominant factor, not the path. The other states are called 'zeal-dominant,' not 'path-dominant.' The same principle applies to consciousness. But for one who develops the path making investigation foremost, investigation is the dominant factor, and the path is as well. The other states are called 'path-dominant.' The same principle applies to energy.

1041. Uppannattikaniddese [M 0.0393] jātāti nibbattā, paṭiladdhattabhāvā. Bhūtātiādīni tesaṃyeva vevacanāni. Jātā eva hi bhāvappattiyā bhūtā. Paccayasaṃyoge jātattā sañjātā. Nibbattilakkhaṇappattattā nibbattā. Upasaggena pana padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā abhinibbattāti vuttā. Pākaṭībhūtāti pātubhūtā. Pubbantato [P 0.0360] uddhaṃ pannāti uppannā. Upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā samuppannāti vuttā. Nibbattaṭṭheneva uddhaṃ ṭhitāti uṭṭhitā. Paccayasaṃyoge uṭṭhitāti samuṭṭhitā. Puna uppannātivacane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Uppannaṃsena saṅgahitāti uppannakoṭṭhāsena gaṇanaṃ gatā. Rūpaṃ vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇanti idaṃ nesaṃ sabhāvadassanaṃ. Dutiyapadaniddeso vuttapaṭisedhanayena veditabbo. Tatiyapadaniddeso uttānatthoyeva.

1041. In the exposition of the triad of the arisen: `Jāta` (born) means produced, having attained its own being. `Bhūta` (become) and so on are synonyms for this. For what is born is 'become' by having reached a state of being. It is `sañjāta` (conjoined) because it is born from a conjunction of conditions. It is `nibbatta` (produced) because it has attained the characteristic of production. By adding a prefix, the word is augmented to `abhinibbatta` (fully produced). `Pātubhūta` (appeared) means having become manifest. `Uppanna` (arisen) means arisen subsequent to a previous point. By adding a prefix, the word is augmented to `samuppanna` (co-arisen). `Uṭṭhita` (arisen) means 'stood up' in the sense of having been produced. `Samuṭṭhita` (arisen together) means 'stood up' from a conjunction of conditions. Furthermore, the reason for the term 'arisen' should be understood by the method explained below. 'Included in the arisen portion' means counted in the arisen category. 'Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness'—this is to show their intrinsic nature. The exposition of the second term should be understood by way of the stated negation. The exposition of the third term is plain in meaning.

Ayaṃ pana tiko dvinnaṃ addhānaṃ vasena pūretvā dassito. Laddhokāsassa hi kammassa vipāko duvidho – khaṇappatto, ca appatto ca. Tattha ‘khaṇappatto’ uppanno nāma. ‘Appatto’ cittānantare vā uppajjatu, kappasatasahassātikkame vā. Dhuvapaccayaṭṭhena natthi nāma na hoti, uppādino dhammā nāma jāto. Yathā hi – “tiṭṭhateva sāyaṃ, poṭṭhapāda, arūpī attā saññāmayo[V 0.0388]. Atha imassa purisassa aññā ca saññā uppajjanti aññā ca saññā nirujjhantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.419). Ettha āruppe kāmāvacarasaññāpavattikāle kiñcāpi mūlabhavaṅgasaññā niruddhā kāmāvacarasaññāya pana niruddhakāle avassaṃ sā uppajjissatīti arūpasaṅkhāto attā natthīti saṅkhyaṃ agantvā ‘tiṭṭhateva’ nāmāti jāto. Evameva laddhokāsassa kammassa vipāko duvidho…pe… dhuvapaccayaṭṭhena natthi nāma na hoti, uppādino dhammā nāma jāto.

This triad, however, is shown by fulfilling it with respect to two time periods. For the result of a kamma that has obtained its opportunity is twofold: that which has reached its moment and that which has not. Therein, that which 'has reached its moment' is called 'arisen.' That which 'has not reached' may arise in the next mind-moment or after the lapse of a hundred thousand eons. Because of its nature as a fixed condition, it is not that it is non-existent; it is called a state that has the nature of arising. Just as: 'Poṭṭhapāda, that formless self consisting of perception certainly persists. Then, for this person, other perceptions arise and other perceptions cease' (Dī. Ni. 1.419). Here, in the formless realm, at the time of the occurrence of sense-sphere perception, although the root life-continuum perception has ceased, since it will certainly arise when the sense-sphere perception has ceased, the self, so-called 'formless', not having gone to the reckoning of 'it does not exist', becomes known as 'it certainly persists.' In the same way, the result of a kamma that has obtained its opportunity is twofold... because of its nature as a fixed condition, it is not that it is non-existent; it is called a state that has the nature of arising.

Yadi pana āyūhitaṃ kusalākusalakammaṃ sabbaṃ vipākaṃ dadeyya, aññassa okāso na bhaveyya. Taṃ pana duvidhaṃ hoti – dhuvavipākaṃ, adhuvavipākañca. Tattha pañca ānantariyakammāni, aṭṭha samāpattiyo, cattāro ariyamaggāti etaṃ ‘dhuvavipākaṃ’ nāma. Taṃ [P 0.0361] pana khaṇappattampi atthi, appattampi. Tattha ‘khaṇappattaṃ’ uppannaṃ nāma. ‘Appattaṃ’ anuppannaṃ nāma. Tassa vipāko cittānantare vā uppajjatu kappasatasahassātikkame vā. Dhuvapaccayaṭṭhena anuppannaṃ nāma na hoti, uppādino dhammā nāma jātaṃ. Metteyyabodhisattassa maggo anuppanno nāma, phalaṃ uppādino dhammāyeva nāma jātaṃ.

If, however, all the accumulated wholesome and unwholesome kamma were to give its result, there would be no opportunity for any other. But that is twofold: of fixed result and of unfixed result. Therein, the five kammas with immediate consequence, the eight attainments, and the four noble paths—this is called 'of fixed result.' That, in turn, exists as that which has reached its moment and that which has not. Therein, 'that which has reached its moment' is called 'arisen.' 'That which has not reached' is called 'unarisen.' Its result may arise in the next mind-moment or after the passing of a hundred thousand eons. Because of its nature as a fixed condition, it is not that the 'unarisen' is non-existent; it is called a state that has the nature of arising. The path of the Bodhisatta Metteyya is called 'unarisen'; its fruit is indeed called a state that has the nature of arising.

1044. Atītattikaniddese [M 0.0394] atītāti khaṇattayaṃ atikkantā. Niruddhāti nirodhappattā. Vigatāti vibhavaṃ gatā, vigacchitā vā. Vipariṇatāti pakativijahanena vipariṇāmaṃ gatā. Nirodhasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ gatāti atthaṅgatā. Abbhatthaṅgatāti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Uppajjitvā vigatāti nibbattitvā vigacchitā. Puna atītavacane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Parato anāgatādīsupi eseva nayo. Atītaṃsena saṅgahitāti atītakoṭṭhāsena gaṇanaṃ gatā. Katame teti? Rūpaṃ vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ. Parato anāgatādīsupi eseva nayo.

1044. In the exposition of the triad of the past: `atītā` means having passed beyond the three moments. `Niruddhā` means having reached cessation. `Vigatā` means having gone to non-being, or having vanished. `Vipariṇatā` means having undergone transformation by abandoning its natural state. `Atthaṅgatā` means having gone to the setting called cessation. `Abbhatthaṅgatā` is the word augmented by a prefix. 'Having arisen and departed' means having been produced and then vanished. Furthermore, the reason for the term 'past' has already been stated below. The same method applies hereafter to the future and so on. 'Included in the past portion' means reckoned within the past division. What are they? Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The same method applies hereafter to the future and so on.

1047. Atītārammaṇattikaniddese atīte dhamme ārabbhātiādīsu parittamahaggatāva dhammā veditabbā. Te hi atītādīni ārabbha uppajjanti.

1047. In the exposition of the triad of past-object states, in the phrases such as 'having taken past states as object,' only limited and exalted states should be understood. For they arise having taken past states, etc., as object.

1050. Ajjhattattikaniddese tesaṃ tesanti padadvayena sabbasatte pariyādiyati. Ajjhattaṃ paccattanti ubhayaṃ niyakajjhattādhivacanaṃ. Niyatāti attani jātā. Pāṭipuggalikāti pāṭiyekkassa pāṭiyekkassa [V 0.0389] puggalassa santakā. Upādiṇṇāti sarīraṭṭhakā. Te hi kammanibbattā vā hontu mā vā, ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhavasena pana idha upādiṇṇāti vuttā.

1050. In the exposition of the internal triad, by the two words `tesaṃ tesaṃ` (of those beings), all beings are encompassed. `Ajjhattaṃ` (internal) and `paccattaṃ` (personal) are both designations for what is one's own and internal. `Niyaka` means arisen in oneself. `Pāṭipuggalika` (individual) means belonging to each particular person. `Upādiṇṇa` (appropriated) means states based in the body. For whether they are produced by kamma or not, they are here called 'appropriated' in the sense of being taken up, grasped, and wrongly viewed.

1051. Parasattānanti attānaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttasadisameva. Tadubhayanti taṃ ubhayaṃ.

1051. `Parasattānaṃ` (of other beings) means of the remaining beings, having excluded oneself. `Parapuggalānaṃ` (of other persons) is a synonym for that. The rest is just like what was stated previously. `Tadubhayaṃ` means 'that which is both.'

1053. Ajjhattārammaṇattikassa paṭhamapade parittamahaggatā dhammā veditabbā. Dutiye [P 0.0362] appamāṇāpi. Tatiye parittamahaggatāva. Appamāṇā pana kālena bahiddhā kālena ajjhattaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na karonti. Sanidassanattikaniddeso uttānoyevāti.

1053. In the first term of the triad of internal-object states, limited and exalted states should be understood. In the second, immeasurable states as well. In the third, only limited and exalted states. However, immeasurable states do not take as object something that is at one time external and at another time internal. The exposition of the triad of the visible is quite plain.

Dukanikkhepakathā

Discourse on the Exposition of the Dyads

1062. Dukesu adosaniddese mettāyanavasena metti. Mettākāro mettāyanā. Mettāya ayitassa mettāsamaṅgino cittassa bhāvo [M 0.0395] mettāyitattaṃ. Anudayatīti anuddā, rakkhatīti attho. Anuddākāro anuddāyanā. Anuddāyitassa bhāvo anuddāyitattaṃ. Hitassa esanavasena hitesitā. Anukampanavasena anukampā. Sabbehipi imehi padehi upacārappanāppattā mettāva vuttā. Sesapadehi lokiyalokuttaro adoso kathito.

1062. In the dyads, in the exposition of non-hatred, `metti` is so called by way of the application of loving-kindness (`mettāyana`). The mode of loving is `mettāyanā`. The state of a mind that has arisen through loving-kindness, one endowed with loving-kindness, is `mettāyitattaṃ`. Because it protects (`anudayati`), it is called `anuddā`; the meaning is 'it protects' (`rakkhati`). The mode of protecting is `anuddāyanā`. The state of a mind that has arisen through protecting is `anuddāyitattaṃ`. By way of seeking what is beneficial, it is `hitesitā`. By way of trembling accordingly, it is `anukampā`. By all these terms, it is only loving-kindness that has reached access and absorption that is spoken of. By the remaining terms, worldly and supramundane non-hatred is explained.

1063. Amohaniddese dukkhe ñāṇanti dukkhasacce paññā. Dukkhasamudayetiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca dukkhe ñāṇaṃ savanasammasanapaṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇāsu vattati. Tathā dukkhasamudaye. Nirodhe pana savanapaṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇāsu eva. Tathā paṭipadāya. Pubbanteti atītakoṭṭhāse. Aparanteti anāgatakoṭṭhāse. Pubbantāparanteti tadubhaye. Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu ñāṇanti ayaṃ paccayo, idaṃ paccayuppannaṃ, idaṃ paṭicca idaṃ nibbattanti, evaṃ paccayesu ca paccayuppannadhammesu ca ñāṇaṃ.

1063. In the exposition of non-delusion, 'knowledge in suffering' means wisdom in the truth of suffering. This same method applies to the terms beginning with 'the origin of suffering', and so on. And here, knowledge in the truth of suffering occurs in the modes of hearing, considering, penetrating, and reviewing. Similarly with the truth of the origin of suffering. In the case of the truth of cessation, however, it occurs only in the modes of hearing, penetrating, and reviewing. Similarly with the path leading to the cessation of suffering. 'In the past' means in the past portion. 'In the future' means in the future portion. 'In the past and future' means in both of them. 'Knowledge in phenomena that are dependently arisen through specific conditionality' means: 'This is the condition, this is the conditioned phenomenon; dependent on this, this has arisen'—thus it is knowledge in conditions and in phenomena arisen from conditions.

1065. Lobhaniddesepi heṭṭhā anāgatānaṃ padānaṃ ayamattho – rañjanavasena rāgo. Balavarañjanaṭṭhena sārāgo. Visayesu sattānaṃ anunayanato anunayo. Anurujjhatīti anurodho, kāmetīti attho. Yattha katthaci bhave sattā [P 0.0363] etāya nandanti, sayaṃ vā nandatīti nandī. Nandī [V 0.0390] ca sā rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo cāti nandīrāgo. Tattha ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe sakiṃ uppannā taṇhā ‘nandī’. Punappunaṃ uppajjamānā ‘nandīrāgo’ti vuccati. Cittassa sārāgoti yo heṭṭhā balavarañjanaṭṭhena sārāgoti vutto, so na sattassa, cittasseva sārāgoti attho.

1065. In the exposition of greed, for the terms that were not given below, this is the meaning: By way of delighting, it is lust (rāga). In the sense of strong delighting, it is intense lust (sārāga). From repeatedly leading beings towards sense objects, it is compliance (anunaya). Because it desires (anurujjhati), it is anurodha; the meaning is 'it desires' (kāmeti). That by which beings delight in any existence whatsoever, or that which itself delights, is delight (nandī). And that delight (nandī), in the sense of delighting, is also lust (rāga); hence it is delight-lust (nandīrāgo). Therein, craving that has arisen once in regard to a single object is 'delight'. Craving that arises again and again is called 'delight-lust'. As for 'intense lust of the mind', that which was stated below as 'intense lust' in the sense of strong delighting—the meaning is that this is the intense lust of the mind only, not of the being.

Icchanti etāya ārammaṇānīti icchā. Bahalakilesabhāvena mucchanti etāya pāṇinoti mucchā. Gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā gahaṇavasena ajjhosānaṃ. Iminā sattā gijjhanti, gedhaṃ āpajjantīti gedho; bahalaṭṭhena vā gedho. “Gedhaṃ vā pavanasaṇḍa”nti hi bahalaṭṭheneva vuttaṃ. Anantarapadaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Sabbatobhāgena vā gedhoti paligedho. Sañjanti etenāti saṅgo; lagganaṭṭhena vā saṅgo. Osīdanaṭṭhena paṅko. Ākaḍḍhanavasena ejā. “Ejā imaṃ purisaṃ parikaḍḍhati tassa tasseva bhavassa abhinibbattiyā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Vañcanaṭṭhena māyā. Vaṭṭasmiṃ sattānaṃ jananaṭṭhena [M 0.0396] janikā. “Taṇhā janeti purisaṃ cittamassa vidhāvatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.55-57) hi vuttaṃ. Vaṭṭasmiṃ satte dukkhena saṃyojayamānā janetīti sañjananī. Ghaṭanaṭṭhena sibbinī. Ayañhi vaṭṭasmiṃ satte cutipaṭisandhivasena sibbati ghaṭeti, tunnakāro viya pilotikāya pilotikaṃ; tasmā ghaṭanaṭṭhena sibbinīti vuttā. Anekappakāraṃ visayajālaṃ taṇhāvipphanditanivesasaṅkhātaṃ vā jālamassā atthīti jālinī.

It is 'wish' (icchā) because with it they wish for objects. It is 'infatuation' (mucchā) because with it beings are infatuated, due to the state of gross defilements. By way of grasping after having swallowed and finished, it is 'devouring' (ajjhosānaṃ). By this, beings are greedy (gijjhanti), they fall into greed (gedhaṃ); therefore, it is 'greed' (gedho); or 'greed' in the sense of thickness. For it is said, 'greed or a forest thicket', in the sense of thickness. The immediately following term is augmented by way of a prefix. Or, greed in every way is 'entanglement' (paligedho). It is 'attachment' (saṅgo) because by it they are attached; or 'attachment' in the sense of clinging. In the sense of sinking down, it is 'mire' (paṅko). By way of dragging, it is 'agitation' (ejā). For it is said: 'Agitation drags this person along for the production of this or that very existence.' In the sense of deceiving, it is 'deceit' (māyā). In the sense of generating beings in the round of existence, it is the 'progenitress' (janikā). For it is said: 'Craving generates a person, his mind runs about.' It is the 'generator' (sañjananī) because it generates, yoking beings to suffering in the round of existence. In the sense of stitching, it is the 'seamstress' (sibbinī). For this stitches and joins a being in the round of existence by way of death and rebirth-linking, like a tailor stitches one piece of cloth with another; therefore, it is called the 'seamstress' in the sense of stitching. It is 'she who possesses a net' (jālinī) because she has a net of sense objects of many kinds, or a net described as the agitation and settling of craving.

Ākaḍḍhanaṭṭhena sīghasotā saritā viyāti saritā. Allaṭṭhena vā saritā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “saritāni sinehitāni ca somanassāni bhavanti jantuno”ti (dha. pa. 341). Allāni ceva siniddhāni cāti ayañhettha attho. Visatāti [P 0.0364] visattikā. Visaṭāti visattikā. Visālāti visattikā. Visakkatīti visattikā. Visaṃvādikāti visattikā. Visaṃharatīti visattikā. Visamūlāti visattikā. Visaphalāti visattikā. Visaparibhogāti visattikā. Visatā vā pana sā taṇhā rūpe sadde gandhe rase phoṭṭhabbe dhamme kule gaṇe vitthatāti visattikā (mahāni. 3). Anayabyasanapāpanaṭṭhena kummānubandhasuttakaṃ viyāti suttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “suttakanti kho, bhikkhave, nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.159). Rūpādīsu vitthataṭṭhena visaṭā. Tassa tassa paṭilābhatthāya satte āyūhāpetīti āyūhinī. Ukkaṇṭhituṃ appadānato sahāyaṭṭhena dutiyā. Ayañhi sattānaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ ukkaṇṭhituṃ na deti, gatagataṭṭhāne piyasahāyo viya abhiramāpeti. Tena vuttaṃ –

In the sense of dragging along, it is the 'river' (saritā), like a river with a swift current. Or, in the sense of being moist, it is saritā. For this was said: 'For a creature, there are mental pleasures that are flowing and smooth.' The meaning here is 'moist and smooth'. Because it spreads (visatā), it is visattikā. Because it is scattered (visaṭā), it is visattikā. Because it is extensive (visālā), it is visattikā. Because it proceeds variously (visakkati), it is visattikā. Because it is deceptive (visaṃvādikā), it is visattikā. Because it withdraws the mind from turning towards renunciation (visaṃharati), it is visattikā. Because it has a root of suffering (visamūlā), it is visattikā. Because it has the fruit of suffering (visaphalā), it is visattikā. Because its enjoyment is suffering (visaparibhogā), it is visattikā. Or else, that craving, which is called visatā, is spread out over forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, mental phenomena, families, and groups; therefore, it is visattikā. In the sense of leading to calamity and disaster, it is the 'thread' (suttaṃ), like a small string that follows a turtle. For this was said: 'Bhikkhus, “thread” is a designation for delight-lust.' In the sense of being spread out over forms, etc., it is 'the diffuse' (visaṭā). It is the 'exerter' (āyūhinī) because it makes beings exert themselves for the sake of obtaining this or that. It is the 'companion' (dutiyā) in the sense of being a friend, because it gives no opportunity to become weary. For this does not allow beings to become weary in the round of existence; in every place they go, it makes them delight, like a dear companion. Therefore it was said:

“Taṇhādutiyo [V 0.0391] puriso, dīghamaddhāna saṃsaraṃ;

Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ, saṃsāraṃ nātivattatī”ti. (a. ni. 4.9; itivu. 15; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 107);

“A person with craving as a companion, wanders on for a long time; this state and that state, he does not pass beyond saṃsāra.”

Paṇidhānakavasena paṇidhi. Bhavanettīti bhavarajju. Etāya hi sattā, rajjuyā gīvāya baddhā goṇā viya, icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ niyyanti. Taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ vanati bhajati allīyatīti vanaṃ. Vanati yācatīti vā vanaṃ. Vanathoti byañjanena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Anatthadukkhānaṃ vā samuṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena gahanaṭṭhena ca vanaṃ [M 0.0397] viyāti ‘vanaṃ’; balavataṇhāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Gahanataraṭṭhena pana tato balavataro ‘vanatho’ nāma. Tena vuttaṃ –

By way of directing the mind, or by way of longing, it is 'aspiration' (paṇidhi). 'The guide to existence' (bhavanettī) means the rope of existence. For by this, beings are led to whatever place they desire, like oxen bound by a rope at the neck. It is a 'forest' (vanaṃ) because it resorts to (vanati), attends upon (bhajati), and clings to (allīyati) this or that object. Or, it is vanaṃ because it longs for (vanati) or begs for (yācati). The term vanatho is the word augmented by the consonant 'tha'. Or, because it is like a forest in the sense of giving rise to what is unbeneficial and to suffering, and in the sense of being tangled and dense, it is called 'forest' (vanaṃ); this is a name for strong craving. But in the sense of being even more tangled, that which is even stronger than that is named 'thicket' (vanatho). Therefore it was said:

“Vanaṃ chindatha mā rukkhaṃ, vanato jāyate bhayaṃ;

Chetvā vanañca vanathañca, nibbanā hotha bhikkhavo”ti. (dha. pa. 283);

“Cut down the forest of craving, not the tree; from the forest, fear is born. Having cut down the forest and the thicket, be free from the forest, O bhikkhus.”

Santhavanavasena santhavo; saṃsaggoti attho. So [P 0.0365] duvidho – taṇhāsanthavo mittasanthavo ca. Tesu idha taṇhāsanthavo adhippeto. Sinehavasena sineho. Ālayakaraṇavasena apekkhatīti apekkhā. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “imāni te deva caturāsītinagarasahassāni kusāvatīrājadhānīpamukhāni. Ettha deva chandaṃ janehi, jīvite apekkhaṃ karohī”ti (dī. ni. 2.266). Ālayaṃ karohīti ayañhettha attho. Pāṭiyekke pāṭiyekke ārammaṇe bandhatīti paṭibandhu. Ñātakaṭṭhena vā pāṭiyekko bandhūtipi paṭibandhu. Niccasannissitaṭṭhena hi sattānaṃ taṇhāsamo bandhu nāma natthi.

By way of association, it is ‘association’ (santhavo); the meaning is ‘communing.’ It is of two kinds: association through craving and association with friends. Of these, association through craving is intended here. By way of affection, it is ‘affection’ (sineho). It is ‘longing’ (apekkhā) because one regards something by way of making it a basis for clinging. This too has been said: ‘Your Majesty, these eighty-four thousand cities with Kusāvatī as the royal capital are yours. Here, Your Majesty, generate desire, create a longing for the kingdom.’ The meaning here is: ‘create a clinging.’ It is a ‘bond’ (paṭibandhu) because it binds one to each particular object. Or, in the sense of a kinsman, a particular kinsman (bandhu) is also a ‘bond’ (paṭibandhu). For in the sense of being constantly depended upon, there is indeed no kinsman for beings equal to craving.

Ārammaṇānaṃ asanato āsā. Ajjhottharaṇato ceva tittiṃ anupagantvāva paribhuñjanato cāti attho. Āsisanavasena āsisanā. Āsisitassa bhāvo āsisitattaṃ. Idāni tassā pavattiṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ rūpāsātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āsisanavasena āsāti āsāya atthaṃ gahetvā rūpe āsā rūpāsāti evaṃ navapi padāni veditabbāni. Ettha ca purimāni pañca pañcakāmaguṇavasena vuttāni. Parikkhāralobhavasena chaṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ visesato pabbajitānaṃ. Tato parāni [V 0.0392] tīṇi atittiyavatthuvasena gahaṭṭhānaṃ. Na hi tesaṃ dhanaputtajīvitehi aññaṃ piyataraṃ atthi. ‘Etaṃ mayhaṃ etaṃ mayha’nti vā ‘asukena me idaṃ dinnaṃ idaṃ dinna’nti vā evaṃ satte jappāpetīti jappā. Parato dve padāni upasaggena vaḍḍhitāni. Tato paraṃ aññenākārena vibhajituṃ āraddhattā puna jappāti vuttaṃ. Jappanākāro jappanā. Jappitassa bhāvo jappitattaṃ. Punappunaṃ visaye lumpati ākaḍḍhatīti lolupo. Lolupassa bhāvo loluppaṃ. Loluppākāro loluppāyanā. Loluppasamaṅgino bhāvo loluppāyitattaṃ.
