It is ‘yearning’ (āsā) from ‘pervading’ or ‘consuming’ objects; the meaning is from overwhelming them and consuming them without reaching satisfaction. By way of yearning, it is ‘yearning’ (āsisanā). The state of one who yearns is ‘yearningness’ (āsisitattaṃ). Now, to show its place of occurrence, ‘yearning for forms’ (rūpāsā), etc., is stated. Therein, taking the meaning of yearning (āsā) as ‘yearning,’ all nine terms should be understood thus: ‘yearning in regard to form is rūpāsā.’ Herein, the first five are stated in connection with the five cords of sensual pleasure. The sixth is by way of greed for requisites, especially for the ordained. The three after that pertain to householders, by way of things that are insatiable. For them, there is indeed nothing dearer than wealth, children, and life. It is ‘muttering’ (jappā) because it makes beings mutter, ‘This is mine, this is mine,’ or ‘This was given to me by so-and-so, this was given.’ The two terms after that are augmented by a prefix. After that, because the analysis was started in another mode, ‘muttering’ is stated again. The mode of muttering is jappanā. The state of one who mutters is jappitattaṃ. It is ‘covetous’ (lolupo) because it repeatedly seizes and drags at an object. The state of being covetous is loluppaṃ. The mode of covetousness is loluppāyanā. The state of one endowed with covetousness is loluppāyitattaṃ.

Pucchañjikatāti [M 0.0398] yāya taṇhāya lābhaṭṭhānesu, pucchaṃ cālayamānā sunakhā viya, kampamānā vicaranti, taṃ tassā kampanataṇhāya nāmaṃ. Sādhu manāpamanāpe visaye kāmetīti sādhukāmo. Tassa bhāvo sādhukamyatā. Mātā [P 0.0366] mātucchātiādike ayuttaṭṭhāne rāgoti adhammarāgo. Yuttaṭṭhānepi balavā hutvā uppannalobho visamalobho. “Rāgo visama”ntiādivacanato (vibha. 924) vā yuttaṭṭhāne vā ayuttaṭṭhāne vā uppanno chandarāgo adhammaṭṭhena ‘adhammarāgo’, visamaṭṭhena ‘visamalobho’ti veditabbo.

‘Tail-wagging’ (pucchañjikatā): that craving on account of which beings wander about in places of gain, trembling like dogs wagging their tails—this is a name for that craving which causes trembling. It is a ‘desirer of the good’ (sādhukāmo) because it desires good and very pleasing objects. The state of this is ‘desire for the good’ (sādhukamyatā). Lust in an improper situation, such as towards one’s mother or maternal aunt, is ‘unrighteous lust’ (adhammarāgo). Greed that has arisen strongly even in a proper situation is ‘uneven greed’ (visamalobho). Or, from the statement ‘Lust is uneven,’ etc., desire-lust that has arisen in either a proper or an improper situation should be understood as ‘unrighteous lust’ in the sense of being unrighteous, and as ‘uneven greed’ in the sense of being uneven.

Ārammaṇānaṃ nikāmanavasena nikanti. Nikāmanākāro nikāmanā. Patthanāvasena patthanā. Pihāyanavasena pihanā. Suṭṭhu patthanā sampatthanā. Pañcasu kāmaguṇesu taṇhā kāmataṇhā. Rūpārūpabhave taṇhā bhavataṇhā. Ucchedasaṅkhāte vibhave taṇhā vibhavataṇhā. Suddhe rūpabhavasmiṃyeva taṇhā rūpataṇhā. Arūpabhave taṇhā arūpataṇhā. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo diṭṭhirāgo. Nirodhe taṇhā nirodhataṇhā. Rūpe taṇhā rūpataṇhā. Sadde taṇhā saddataṇhā. Gandhataṇhādīsupi eseva nayo. Oghādayo vuttatthāva.

By way of liking objects, it is ‘liking’ (nikanti). The mode of liking is nikāmanā. By way of aspiring, it is ‘aspiration’ (patthanā). By way of yearning, it is ‘yearning’ (pihanā). Intense aspiration is ‘thorough aspiration’ (sampatthanā). Craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure is sensual craving (kāmataṇhā). Craving for existence in the form and formless realms is craving for existence (bhavataṇhā). Craving for non-existence, reckoned as annihilation, is craving for non-existence (vibhavataṇhā). Craving in the pure form-existence alone is craving for form (rūpataṇhā). Craving in the formless existence is craving for the formless (arūpataṇhā). Lust accompanied by the annihilationist view is lust associated with views (diṭṭhirāgo). Craving for cessation is craving for cessation (nirodhataṇhā). Craving for forms is craving for form (rūpataṇhā). Craving for sounds is craving for sound (saddataṇhā). The same principle applies to craving for smells (gandhataṇhā), and so on. The floods (ogha) and so on have the meanings already stated.

Kusaladhamme āvaratīti āvaraṇaṃ. Chādanavasena chādanaṃ. Satte vaṭṭasmiṃ bandhatīti bandhanaṃ. Cittaṃ upagantvā kilissati saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ karotīti upakkileso. Thāmagataṭṭhena anusetīti anusayo. Uppajjamānā cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhātīti pariyuṭṭhānaṃ; uppajjituṃ appadānena kusalacāraṃ gaṇhātīti attho. “Corā magge pariyuṭṭhiṃsu dhuttā magge pariyuṭṭhiṃsū”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 430) hi maggaṃ gaṇhiṃsūti attho. Evamidhāpi gahaṇaṭṭhena pariyuṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paliveṭhanaṭṭhena latā viyāti latā. “Latā ubbhijja tiṭṭhatī”ti (dha. pa. 340) āgataṭṭhānepi ayaṃ taṇhā latāti vuttā. Vividhāni vatthūni icchatīti vevicchaṃ. Vaṭṭadukkhassa mūlanti [V 0.0393] dukkhamūlaṃ. Tasseva dukkhassa nidānanti dukkhanidānaṃ. Taṃ dukkhaṃ ito pabhavatīti dukkhappabhavo. Bandhanaṭṭhena pāso viyāti pāso. Mārassa pāso mārapāso. Duruggilanaṭṭhena baḷisaṃ viyāti baḷisaṃ. Mārassa baḷisaṃ [M 0.0399] mārabaḷisaṃ. Taṇhābhibhūtā mārassa visayaṃ nātikkamanti, tesaṃ upari māro vasaṃ vattetīti iminā pariyāyena mārassa visayoti māravisayo[P 0.0367]. Sandanaṭṭhena taṇhāva nadī taṇhānadī. Ajjhottharaṇaṭṭhena taṇhāva jālaṃ taṇhājālaṃ. Yathā sunakhā gaddulabaddhā yadicchakaṃ nīyanti, evaṃ taṇhābaddhā sattāpīti daḷhabandhanaṭṭhena gaddulaṃ viyāti gaddulaṃ. Taṇhāva gaddulaṃ taṇhāgaddulaṃ. Duppūraṇaṭṭhena taṇhāva samuddo taṇhāsamuddo.

It obstructs wholesome states, thus it is an obstruction (āvaraṇa). By way of covering, it is a covering (chādana). It binds beings in the round of suffering, thus it is a bond (bandhana). Approaching the mind, it defiles it and makes it corrupted, thus it is a defilement (upakkileso). Because it has reached a state of strength, it lies latent, thus it is a latent tendency (anusayo). When arising, it assails the mind, thus it is an obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna); the meaning is that by not giving an opportunity for wholesome conduct to arise, it seizes it. For in such passages as, ‘Thieves beset the road, scoundrels beset the road,’ the meaning is that they seized the road. So too here, obsession should be understood in the sense of seizing. In the sense of entwining, it is like a creeper (latā), thus it is a creeper. In the passage where it is said, ‘The creeper springs up and stands,’ this craving is also called a creeper. It desires various things, thus it is acquisitiveness (veviccha). It is the root of the suffering of the round, thus it is the root of suffering (dukkhamūla). It is the cause of that same suffering, thus it is the cause of suffering (dukkhanidāna). That suffering originates from this, thus it is the origin of suffering (dukkhappabhavo). In the sense of binding, it is like a snare (pāso), thus it is a snare; the snare of Māra (mārapāso). In the sense of being hard to disgorge, it is like a fish-hook (baḷisa), thus it is a fish-hook; the fish-hook of Māra (mārabaḷisa). Beings overcome by craving do not transcend Māra’s domain; Māra exercises power over them. In this sense it is the domain of Māra (māravisayo). In the sense of flowing, craving itself is a river: the river of craving (taṇhānadī). In the sense of overwhelming, craving itself is a net: the net of craving (taṇhājālaṃ). Just as dogs tied with a leash are led about at will, so too are beings bound by craving. Thus, in the sense of being a strong bond, it is like a leash (gaddula); craving itself is a leash, the leash of craving (taṇhāgaddulaṃ). In the sense of being difficult to fill, craving itself is an ocean: the ocean of craving (taṇhāsamuddo).

1066. Dosaniddese anatthaṃ me acarīti avuḍḍhiṃ me akāsi. Iminā upāyena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Aṭṭhāne vā pana āghātoti akāraṇe kopo – ekacco hi ‘devo ativassatī’ti kuppati, ‘na vassatī’ti kuppati, ‘sūriyo tappatī’ti kuppati, ‘na tappatī’ti kuppati, vāte vāyantepi kuppati, avāyantepi kuppati, sammajjituṃ asakkonto bodhipaṇṇānaṃ kuppati, cīvaraṃ pārupituṃ asakkonto vātassa kuppati, upakkhalitvā khāṇukassa kuppati idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – aṭṭhāne vā pana āghāto jāyatīti. Tattha heṭṭhā navasu ṭhānesu satte ārabbha uppannattā kammapathabhedo hoti. Aṭṭhānāghāto pana saṅkhāresu uppanno kammapathabhedaṃ na karoti. Cittaṃ āghātento uppannoti cittassa āghāto. Tato balavataro paṭighāto. Paṭihaññanavasena paṭighaṃ. Paṭivirujjhatīti paṭivirodho. Kuppanavasena kopo. Pakopo sampakopoti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Dussanavasena doso. Padoso sampadosoti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Cittassa byāpattīti cittassa vipannatā, viparivattanākāro. Manaṃ padūsayamāno uppajjatīti manopadoso. Kujjhanavasena kodho. Kujjhanākāro kujjhanā. Kujjhitassa bhāvo kujjhitattaṃ.

1066. In the exposition of hatred, ‘He has done me harm’ means he has caused my non-thriving. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances. Or again, there is groundless aversion, that is, anger without cause. For a certain person becomes angry thinking, ‘It is raining too much,’ or becomes angry thinking, ‘It is not raining’; becomes angry thinking, ‘The sun is too hot,’ or becomes angry thinking, ‘It is not hot.’ He becomes angry when the wind blows and when it does not blow. Unable to sweep, he becomes angry at the Bodhi leaves. Unable to put on his robe, he becomes angry at the wind. Having stumbled, he becomes angry at a tree stump. It is with reference to this that it is said: ‘Or again, groundless aversion arises.’ Therein, in the nine grounds below, since the aversion arises in regard to beings, it constitutes a breach of the course of action. But groundless aversion, having arisen in regard to formations, does not constitute a breach of the course of action. It arises while striking at the mind, thus it is aversion of mind. Stronger than that is repugnance. Repugnance is in the sense of striking against. It opposes, thus it is opposition. Anger is in the sense of being agitated. Fierce anger and vehement anger are the word intensified by a prefix. Hatred is in the sense of corruption. Malice and vehement malice are the word intensified by a prefix. Ill will of mind is the mind’s ruination, a state of perversion. It arises while corrupting the mind, thus it is corruption of mind. Wrath is in the sense of being angry. The state of being angry is anger. The state of one who is angry is angerfulness.

Idāni akusalaniddese vuttanayaṃ dassetuṃ doso dussanātiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmā “yo evarūpo cittassa āghāto…pe… kujjhitatta”nti ca idha vutto, “doso dussanā”tiādinā nayena heṭṭhā vutto, ayaṃ vuccati dosoti. Evamettha yojanā kātabbā. Evañhi sati punaruttidoso paṭisedhito hoti. Mohaniddeso [P 0.0368] amohaniddese vuttapaṭipakkhanayena [M 0.0400] veditabbo. Sabbākārena panesa vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āvi bhavissati.

Now, to show the method stated in the exposition of the unwholesome, it is said, ‘hatred, corruption,’ and so on. Therefore, what is stated here as ‘whatever kind of aversion of mind… angerfulness,’ and what is stated below by the method beginning ‘hatred, corruption,’ this is called hatred. The connection should be made here in this way. For when this is so, the fault of repetition is refuted. The exposition of delusion should be understood by the method of its counterpart stated in the exposition of non-delusion. This, however, will become clear in all its aspects in the Vibhaṅga Commentary.

1079. Tehi [V 0.0394] dhammehi ye dhammā sahetukāti tehi hetudhammehi ye aññe hetudhammā vā nahetudhammā vā te sahetukā. Ahetukapadepi eseva nayo. Ettha ca hetu hetuyeva ca hoti, tiṇṇaṃ vā dvinnaṃ vā ekato uppattiyaṃ sahetuko ca. Vicikicchuddhaccasahagato pana moho hetu ahetuko. Hetusampayuttadukaniddesepi eseva nayo.

1079. Regarding ‘those states that are with a root’: with reference to those root-states, whatever other states there are, whether they are root-states or non-root-states, they are ‘with a root.’ The same principle applies to the term ‘rootless.’ And here, a root is just a root; but when it arises together with two others or one other, it is also ‘with a root.’ However, delusion accompanied by doubt and restlessness, though a root, is rootless. The same principle applies in the exposition of the dyad ‘associated with a root’.

1091. Saṅkhatadukaniddese purimaduke vuttaṃ asaṅkhatadhātuṃ sandhāya yo eva so dhammoti ekavacananiddeso kato. Purimaduke pana bahuvacanavasena pucchāya uddhaṭattā ime dhammā appaccayāti pucchānusandhinayena bahuvacanaṃ kataṃ. Ime dhammā sanidassanātiādīsupi eseva nayo.

1091. In the exposition of the dyad of the conditioned, with reference to the unconditioned element mentioned in the previous dyad, the exposition is made in the singular: ‘that very state.’ But in the previous dyad, since the question was posed in the plural, the plural was used in conformity with the question: ‘these states are unconditioned.’ The same principle applies in such cases as ‘these states are with manifestation,’ and so on.

1101. Kenaci viññeyyadukaniddese cakkhuviññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇena vijānitabbā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca kenaci viññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇādīsu kenaci ekena cakkhuviññāṇena vā sotaviññāṇena vā vijānitabbā. Kenaci na viññeyyāti teneva cakkhuviññāṇena vā sotaviññāṇena vā na vijānitabbā. ‘Evaṃ sante dvinnampi padānaṃ atthanānattato duko hotī’ti heṭṭhā vuttattā ‘ye te dhammā cakkhuviññeyyā na te dhammā sotaviññeyyā’ti ayaṃ duko na hoti. Rūpaṃ pana cakkhuviññeyyaṃ saddo na cakkhuviññeyyoti imamatthaṃ gahetvā ‘ye te dhammā cakkhuviññeyyā na te dhammā sotaviññeyyā, ye vā pana te dhammā sotaviññeyyā na te dhammā cakkhuviññeyyā’ti ayameko dukoti veditabbo. Evaṃ ekekaindriyamūlake cattāro cattāro katvā vīsati dukā vibhattāti veditabbā.

1101. In the exposition of the dyad ‘cognizable by something,’ ‘cognizable by the eye’ means cognizable by eye-consciousness. The same principle applies to the other terms. And here, ‘cognizable by something’ means cognizable by any one of the consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. ‘Not cognizable by something’ means not cognizable by that same eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. Since it was stated below, ‘This being so, it is a dyad because of the difference in meaning of the two terms,’ the formulation ‘those states that are cognizable by the eye are not cognizable by the ear’ is not a dyad. However, taking the meaning that ‘form is cognizable by the eye, but sound is not cognizable by the eye,’ it should be understood that this is one dyad: ‘those states that are cognizable by the eye are not cognizable by the ear; or again, those states that are cognizable by the ear are not cognizable by the eye.’ Thus it should be understood that twenty dyads are analyzed by taking each sense faculty as a basis and forming four for each.

Kiṃ [P 0.0369] pana ‘manoviññāṇena kenaci viññeyyā kenaci na viññeyyā’ natthi? Tenettha dukā na vuttāti? No natthi, vavatthānābhāvato pana na vuttā. Na hi, yathā cakkhuviññāṇena aviññeyyā evāti vavatthānaṃ atthi, evaṃ manoviññāṇenāpīti vavatthānābhāvato ettha dukā na vuttā. Manoviññāṇena [M 0.0401] pana kenaci viññeyyā ceva aviññeyyā cāti ayamattho atthi. Tasmā so avuttopi yathālābhavasena veditabbo. Manoviññāṇanti hi saṅkhyaṃ gatehi kāmāvacaradhammehi kāmāvacaradhammā eva tāva kehici viññeyyā kehici aviññeyyā. Tehiyeva rūpāvacarādidhammāpi kehici viññeyyā kehici aviññeyyā. Rūpāvacarehipi kāmāvacarā kehici viññeyyā kehici aviññeyyā. Teheva rūpāvacarādayopi [V 0.0395] kehici viññeyyā kehici aviññeyyā. Arūpāvacarehi pana kāmāvacarā rūpāvacarā apariyāpannā ca neva viññeyyā. Arūpāvacarā pana kehici viññeyyā kehici aviññeyyā. Tepi ca kecideva viññeyyā keci aviññeyyā. Apariyāpannehi kāmāvacarādayo neva viññeyyā. Apariyāpannā pana nibbānena aviññeyyattā kehici viññeyyā kehici aviññeyyā. Tepi ca maggaphalānaṃ aviññeyyattā kecideva viññeyyā keci aviññeyyāti.

But is there not the case of states ‘cognizable by some mind-consciousness and not cognizable by some’? Is it for that reason that the dyads are not stated here? It is not that this is not the case; rather, they are not stated because there is no delimitation. For, just as there is the delimitation ‘only uncognizable by eye-consciousness,’ there is no such delimitation for mind-consciousness. Because of this lack of delimitation, the dyads are not stated here. However, the meaning that some states are cognizable by mind-consciousness and some are uncognizable does exist. Therefore, though unstated, it should be understood as it is obtainable. For, by sense-sphere states that are counted as ‘mind-consciousness,’ some sense-sphere states themselves are cognizable by some and uncognizable by others. By those same consciousnesses, some form-sphere and other states are also cognizable by some and uncognizable by others. By form-sphere consciousnesses also, some sense-sphere states are cognizable by some and uncognizable by others. By those same consciousnesses, some form-sphere and other states are also cognizable by some and uncognizable by others. By formless-sphere consciousnesses, however, sense-sphere, form-sphere, and unincluded states are never cognizable. But some formless-sphere states are cognizable by some of them and uncognizable by others; and even then, only some are cognizable and some are uncognizable. By unincluded consciousnesses, sense-sphere and other states are never cognizable. But unincluded states, because Nibbāna is uncognizable, are cognizable by some and uncognizable by others; and even those, because paths and fruits are uncognizable, only some are cognizable while others are uncognizable.

1102. Āsavaniddese pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo kāmāsavo nāma. Rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo jhānanikanti sassatadiṭṭhisahajāto rāgo bhavavasena patthanā bhavāsavo nāma. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhāsavo nāma. Aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu aññāṇaṃ avijjāsavo nāma. Tattha tattha āgatesu pana āsavesu asammohatthaṃ ekavidhādibhedo veditabbo. Atthato hete cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena āsavāti evaṃ ekavidhāva honti. Vinaye pana “diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti (pārā. 39) duvidhena āgatā. Suttante saḷāyatane tāva “tayome, āvuso, āsavā – kāmāsavo bhavāsavo avijjāsavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.321) tividhena āgatā. Nibbedhikapariyāye “atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā nirayagamanīyā[P 0.0370], atthi āsavā tiracchānayonigamanīyā, atthi āsavā pettivisayagamanīyā, atthi āsavā manussalokagamanīyā, atthi āsavā devalokagamanīyā”ti (a. ni. 6.63) pañcavidhena āgatā. Chakkanipāte āhuneyyasutte – “atthi āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā adhivāsanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā parivajjanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā [M 0.0402] vinodanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā bhāvanā pahātabbā”ti (a. ni. 6.58) chabbidhena āgatā. Sabbāsavapariyāye (ma. ni. 1.14 ādayo) ‘dassanapahātabbehi’ saddhiṃ sattavidhena āgatā. Idha panete kāmāsavādibhedato catubbidhena āgatā. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhāte kāme āsavo ‘kāmāsavo’. Rūpārūpasaṅkhāte kammato ca upapattito ca duvidhepi bhave āsavo ‘bhavāsavo’. Diṭṭhi eva āsavo ‘diṭṭhāsavo’. Avijjāva āsavo ‘avijjāsavo’.

1102. In the exposition of the taints, lust associated with the five strands of sensual pleasure is called the taint of sensual desire. Desire-lust for form and formless existences, delight in jhāna, lust that arises together with an eternalist view, and aspiration by way of existence, is called the taint of existence. The sixty-two views are called the taint of views. Ignorance regarding the eight bases is called the taint of ignorance. Furthermore, to avoid confusion regarding the taints that are mentioned in various contexts, their classification as single, and so on, should be understood. In terms of meaning, these are called 'taints' (āsavas) because they have long been steeped in; thus they are of a single kind. In the Vinaya, however, they are presented as twofold: 'for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life and for the destruction of taints pertaining to future lives.' In the Suttas, first in the Saḷāyatana section, they are presented as threefold: 'There are, friends, these three taints—the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.' In the Nibbedhika discourse: 'There are, bhikkhus, taints leading to hell, taints leading to the animal realm, taints leading to the sphere of afflicted spirits, taints leading to the human world, and taints leading to the deva world,' they are presented as fivefold. In the Āhuneyyasutta in the Book of the Sixes: 'There are taints to be abandoned by restraint, taints to be abandoned by use, taints to be abandoned by endurance, taints to be abandoned by avoidance, taints to be abandoned by removal, and taints to be abandoned by development,' they are presented as sixfold. In the Discourse on All the Taints, along with those 'to be abandoned by seeing,' they are presented as sevenfold. Here, however, they are presented as fourfold, classified as the taint of sensual desire and so on. Therein, this is the meaning of the words: The taint in relation to the five strands of sensual pleasure is the 'taint of sensual desire.' The taint in relation to form and formless existences, whether arising from kamma or from rebirth, is the 'taint of existence.' Views themselves are the 'taint of views.' Ignorance itself is the 'taint of ignorance.'

1103. Kāmesūti pañcasu kāmaguṇesu. Kāmacchandoti kāmasaṅkhāto chando, na kattukamyatāchando, na dhammacchando. Kāmanavasena rajjanavasena ca kāmoyeva rāgo kāmarāgo. Kāmanavasena [V 0.0396] nandanavasena ca kāmova nandīti kāmanandī. Evaṃ sabbattha kāmatthaṃ viditvā taṇhāyanaṭṭhena kāmataṇhā, sinehanaṭṭhena kāmasineho, pariḍayhanaṭṭhena kāmapariḷāho, mucchanaṭṭhena kāmamucchā, gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena kāmajjhosānanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ aṭṭhahi padehi vibhatto kāmāsavo nāma vuccati.

1103. ‘Kāmesu’ refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Kāmacchando’ means desire reckoned as sensual pleasure, not the desire to act, nor desire for the Dhamma. In the sense of desiring and in the sense of lusting, sensual pleasure itself is lust; thus it is ‘sensual lust.’ In the sense of desiring and in the sense of delighting, sensual pleasure itself is delight; thus it is ‘sensual delight.’ Thus, having understood the meaning of sensuality in all these ways, sensual craving is to be known as craving in the sense of thirsting, sensual affection as affection in the sense of attachment, sensual burning as burning in the sense of torment, sensual infatuation as infatuation in the sense of delusion, and sensual obsession as obsession in the sense of swallowing and consuming. This is what is meant: this taint of sensual desire, analyzed into these eight terms, is so called.

1104. Bhavesu bhavachandoti rūpārūpabhavesu bhavapatthanāvaseneva pavatto chando ‘bhavachando’. Sesapadānipi imināva nayena veditabbāni.

1104. Regarding ‘desire for existence in existences’ (bhavesu bhavachando): in the form and formless existences, the desire that arises solely by way of the aspiration for existence is called ‘desire for existence’ (bhavachando). The remaining terms should also be understood in this same way.

1105. Sassato lokoti vātiādīhi dasahākārehi diṭṭhippabhedova vutto. Tattha sassato lokoti ettha khandhapañcakaṃ lokoti gahetvā ‘ayaṃ loko nicco dhuvo sabbakāliko’ti gaṇhantassa ‘sassata’nti gahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Asassatoti [P 0.0371] tameva lokaṃ ‘ucchijjati vinassatī’ti gaṇhantassa ucchedagahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Antavāti parittakasiṇalābhino ‘suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā’ kasiṇe samāpannassa antosamāpattiyaṃ pavattitarūpārūpadhamme lokoti ca kasiṇaparicchedantena ca ‘antavā’ti gaṇhantassa ‘antavā loko’ti gahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Sā sassatadiṭṭhipi hoti ucchedadiṭṭhipi. Vipulakasiṇalābhino pana tasmiṃ kasiṇe samāpannassa antosamāpattiyaṃ pavattitarūpārūpadhamme lokoti ca kasiṇaparicchedantena [M 0.0403] ca ‘ananto’ti gaṇhantassa ‘anantavā loko’ti gahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Sā sassatadiṭṭhipi hoti, ucchedadiṭṭhipi.

1105. By ‘the world is eternal,’ and so on, the varieties of views are stated in ten ways. Here, with ‘the world is eternal,’ taking the five aggregates as the world and grasping that ‘this world is eternal, permanent, everlasting,’ the view arises, taking the form of grasping as ‘eternal.’ With ‘the world is not eternal,’ grasping that same world as ‘cut off, destroyed,’ the view arises, taking the form of grasping as annihilation. ‘The world is finite’—for one who has obtained a limited kasiṇa, having attained concentration on a kasiṇa ‘as small as a winnowing basket or a saucer,’ and grasping the form and formless phenomena occurring within that attainment as the world, and also grasping, by the limit of the kasiṇa's demarcation, that it is ‘finite,’ the view arises, taking the form of grasping as ‘the world is finite.’ That can be either an eternalist view or an annihilationist view. But for one who has obtained an extensive kasiṇa, having attained concentration on that kasiṇa, and grasping the form and formless phenomena occurring within that attainment as the world, and also grasping, by the limit of the kasiṇa's demarcation, that it is ‘infinite,’ the view arises, taking the form of grasping as ‘the world is infinite.’ That can be either an eternalist view or an annihilationist view.

Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti bhedanadhammassa sarīrasseva ‘jīva’nti gahitattā sarīre ucchijjamāne ‘jīvampi ucchijjatī’ti ucchedagahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Dutiyapade sarīrato aññassa jīvassa gahitattā sarīre ucchijjamānepi ‘jīvaṃ na ucchijjatī’ti sassatagahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi. Hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇātiādīsu satto tathāgato nāma. So paraṃ maraṇā hotīti gaṇhato paṭhamā sassatadiṭṭhi. Na hotīti gaṇhato dutiyā ucchedadiṭṭhi. Hoti ca na ca hotīti gaṇhato tatiyā ekaccasassatadiṭṭhi. Neva hoti na nahotīti gaṇhato catutthā amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhi. Ime dhammā āsavāti ime kāmāsavañca bhavāsavañca rāgavasena ekato katvā, saṅkhepato tayo, vitthārato cattāro dhammā āsavā nāma.

‘That the life-principle is the same as the body’—since the ‘life-principle’ is grasped as being identical with the body, which is subject to dissolution, the view arises in the manner of grasping annihilation, thinking ‘when the body is destroyed, the life-principle is also destroyed.’ In the second statement, since the life-principle is grasped as being different from the body, the view arises in the manner of grasping permanence, thinking ‘even when the body is destroyed, the life-principle is not destroyed.’ ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ and so on—here, a being is called the Tathāgata. For one who grasps that ‘the Tathāgata exists after death,’ the first is the eternalist view. For one who grasps that ‘he does not exist,’ the second is the annihilationist view. For one who grasps that ‘he both exists and does not exist,’ the third is the partial eternalist view. For one who grasps that ‘he neither exists nor does not exist,’ the fourth is the view of the evasive wrigglers. ‘These phenomena are taints’—here, combining the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence by way of lust, concisely there are three, but in detail, these four phenomena are called taints.

Yo [V 0.0397] pana brahmānaṃ vimānakapparukkhaābharaṇesu chandarāgo uppajjati, so kāmāsavo hoti na hotīti? Na hoti. Kasmā? Pañcakāmaguṇikassa rāgassa idheva pahīnattā. Hetugocchakaṃ pana patvā lobho hetu nāma hoti. Ganthagocchakaṃ patvā abhijjhākāyagantho nāma. Kilesagocchakaṃ patvā lobho kileso nāma hoti. Diṭṭhisahajāto pana rāgo kāmāsavo hoti na hotīti? Na hoti; diṭṭhirāgo nāma hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ “diṭṭhirāgaratte purisapuggale dinnadānaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti, na mahānisaṃsa”nti [P 0.0372] (paṭi. ma. 1.129).

Now, as for the desire and lust that arises for brahmās regarding celestial mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, or ornaments, is that the taint of sensual desire or not? It is not. Why? Because lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure has been abandoned in this very human realm. However, having reached the section on roots, greed is called a root. Having reached the section on ties, it is called the bodily tie of covetousness. Having reached the section on defilements, greed is called a defilement. Now, is lust that arises together with a view the taint of sensual desire or not? It is not; it is called lust associated with a view. For this has been said: 'A gift given to a person infatuated with lust for views is not of great fruit or great benefit' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.129).

Ime pana āsave kilesapaṭipāṭiyāpi āharituṃ vaṭṭati, maggapaṭipāṭiyāpi. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā kāmāsavo anāgāmimaggena pahīyati, bhavāsavo arahattamaggena, diṭṭhāsavo sotāpattimaggena, avijjāsavo arahattamaggena. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā sotāpattimaggena diṭṭhāsavo pahīyati, anāgāmimaggena kāmāsavo, arahattamaggena bhavāsavo avijjāsavo cāti.

Now, it is proper to present these taints both in the sequence of the defilements and in the sequence of the paths. In the sequence of the defilements: the taint of sensual desire is abandoned by the path of non-returning; the taint of existence by the path of arahantship; the taint of views by the path of stream-entry; and the taint of ignorance by the path of arahantship. In the sequence of the paths: by the path of stream-entry, the taint of views is abandoned; by the path of non-returning, the taint of sensual desire; and by the path of arahantship, both the taint of existence and the taint of ignorance.

1121. Saṃyojanesu mānaniddese seyyohamasmīti mānoti uttamaṭṭhena ‘ahaṃ seyyo’ti evaṃ uppannamāno. Sadisohamasmīti mānoti [M 0.0404] samasamaṭṭhena ‘ahaṃ sadiso’ti evaṃ uppannamāno. Hīnohamasmīti mānoti lāmakaṭṭhena ‘ahaṃ hīno’ti evaṃ uppannamāno. Evaṃ seyyamāno sadisamāno hīnamānoti ime tayo mānā tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ uppajjanti. Seyyassāpi hi ‘ahaṃ seyyo sadiso hīno’ti tayo mānā uppajjanti. Sadisassāpi, hīnassāpi. Tattha seyyassa seyyamānova yāthāvamāno, itare dve ayāthāvamānā. Sadisassa sadisamānova…pe… hīnassa hīnamānova yāthāvamāno, itare dve ayāthāvamānā. Iminā kiṃ kathitaṃ? Ekassa tayo mānā uppajjantīti kathitaṃ. Khuddakavatthuke pana paṭhamakamānabhājanīye eko māno tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ uppajjatīti kathito.

1121. In the exposition of conceit among the fetters, the conceit 'I am superior' is the conceit that arises in the sense of being supreme, thus: 'I am superior.' The conceit 'I am equal' is the conceit that arises in the sense of being exactly equal, thus: 'I am equal.' The conceit 'I am inferior' is the conceit that arises in the sense of being lowly, thus: 'I am inferior.' Thus, these three conceits—of superiority, equality, and inferiority—arise for three kinds of people. For even for a superior person, the three conceits 'I am superior,' 'I am equal,' and 'I am inferior' arise. The same is true for an equal person and for an inferior person. Therein, for a superior person, only the conceit of superiority is an accurate conceit; the other two are inaccurate conceits. For an equal person, only the conceit of equality is an accurate conceit… For an inferior person, only the conceit of inferiority is an accurate conceit; the other two are inaccurate conceits. What is stated by this? It is stated that three conceits arise for one person. But in the Khuddakavatthu, in the first analysis of conceit, it is stated that one conceit arises for three kinds of people.

Mānakaraṇavasena māno. Maññanā maññitattanti ākārabhāvaniddesā. Ussitaṭṭhena unnati. Yassuppajjati taṃ puggalaṃ unnāmeti, ukkhipitvā ṭhapetīti unnamo. Samussitaṭṭhena dhajo. Ukkhipanaṭṭhena cittaṃ sampaggaṇhātīti sampaggāho. Ketu vuccati bahūsu dhajesu accuggatadhajo. Mānopi punappunaṃ uppajjamāno aparāpare upādāya accuggataṭṭhena ketu viyāti ‘ketu’. Ketuṃ icchatīti ketukamyaṃ, tassa bhāvo ketukamyatā. Sā pana cittassa, na attano. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘ketukamyatā [V 0.0398] cittassā’ti. Mānasampayuttañhi cittaṃ ketuṃ icchati. Tassa ca bhāvo ketukamyatā; ketusaṅkhāto mānoti.

It is conceit (māna) by way of the act of conceiving. 'Conceiving' (maññanā) and 'the state of having conceived' (maññitattaṃ) are designations of aspect and state. It is 'elevation' (unnati) in the sense of being raised up. It makes the person in whom it arises lofty; having lifted them up, it places them, hence it is 'uplifting' (unnamo). It is a 'banner' (dhajo) in the sense of being highly raised. In the sense of lifting up, it takes hold of the mind, hence it is 'firm grasping' (sampaggāho). A 'standard' (ketu) is said to be the most highly raised banner among many banners. Conceit, too, arising again and again, is like a standard (ketu) in the sense of being exceedingly elevated by grasping at one thing after another; thus it is 'ketu'. It desires a standard, thus it is 'desire for a standard' (ketukamyaṃ); its state is 'the state of desiring a standard' (ketukamyatā). But that belongs to the mind, not to the self. Therefore it is said: 'The state of desiring a standard belongs to the mind.' For the mind associated with conceit desires a standard, and its state is 'the state of desiring a standard'; that is, conceit is reckoned as a standard.

1126. Issāniddese [P 0.0373] yā paralābhasakkāragarukāramānanavandanapūjanāsu issāti yā etesu paresaṃ lābhādīsu ‘kiṃ iminā imesa’nti parasampattikhiyyanalakkhaṇā issā. Tattha lābhoti cīvarādīnaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ paṭilābho. Issukī hi puggalo parassa taṃ lābhaṃ khiyyati, ‘kiṃ imassa iminā’ti na icchati. Sakkāroti tesaṃyeva paccayānaṃ sukatānaṃ sundarānaṃ paṭilābho. Garukāroti garukiriyā, bhāriyakaraṇaṃ. Mānananti manena piyakaraṇaṃ. Vandananti pañcapatiṭṭhitena vandanaṃ. Pūjanāti gandhamālādīhi pūjanā. Issāyanavasena issā. Issākāro issāyanā. Issāyitabhāvo issāyitattaṃ. Usūyādīni issādivevacanāni.

1126. In the exposition of envy, the phrase 'envy regarding others' gain, honour, respect, reverence, veneration, and worship' refers to that envy which has the characteristic of disparaging others' good fortune, thinking, 'What is this to them?' Therein, 'gain' is the acquisition of the four requisites, such as robes. For an envious person disparages another's gain, thinking, 'What is this to him?' and does not wish it for him. 'Honour' is the acquisition of those same requisites when they are well-made and fine. 'Respect' is the act of treating with respect, of making much of someone. 'Reverence' is making someone dear with the mind. 'Veneration' is venerating with the five-point prostration. 'Worship' is worshipping with perfumes, garlands, and so on. Envy (issā) is so called by way of being envious. The mode of envy is issāyanā. The state of having been envious is issāyitattaṃ. Terms like usūyā are synonyms for envy.

Imissā [M 0.0405] pana issāya khiyyanalakkhaṇaṃ āgārikenāpi anāgārikenāpi dīpetabbaṃ. Āgāriko hi ekacco kasivaṇijjādīsu aññatarena ājīvena attano purisakāraṃ nissāya bhaddakaṃ yānaṃ vā vāhanaṃ vā ratanaṃ vā labhati. Aparo tassa alābhatthiko tena lābhena na tussati. ‘Kadā nu kho esa imāya sampattiyā parihāyitvā kapaṇo hutvā carissatī’ti cintetvā ekena kāraṇena tasmiṃ tāya sampattiyā parihīne attamano hoti. Anāgārikopi eko issāmanako aññaṃ attano sutapariyattiādīni nissāya uppannalābhādisampattiṃ disvā ‘kadā nu kho eso imehi lābhādīhi parihāyissatī’ti cintetvā, yadā taṃ ekena kāraṇena parihīnaṃ passati, tadā attamano hoti. Evaṃ parasampattikhiyyanalakkhaṇā ‘issā’ti veditabbā.

Now, the characteristic of disparagement in this envy should be illustrated by the cases of both a householder and one who has gone forth. For a certain householder, by his own manly effort, through some livelihood such as farming or trade, might acquire a fine vehicle, a mount, or a jewel. Another person, wishing him not to have that gain, is not pleased with it. He thinks, 'When will this person lose this good fortune and go about as a wretch?' and when for some reason that person does lose that good fortune, he is gratified. Similarly, a certain monastic with an envious mind sees another's good fortune—gain, etc., that has arisen based on his own learning, mastery of the scriptures, and so on. He thinks, 'When will this person lose these gains, etc.?' and when he sees him lose them for some reason, he is gratified. Thus envy should be understood as having the characteristic of disparaging others' good fortune.

1127. Macchariyaniddese vatthuto macchariyadassanatthaṃ ‘pañca macchariyāni āvāsamacchariya’ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āvāse macchariyaṃ āvāsamacchariyaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

1127. In the exposition of stinginess, in order to show stinginess with respect to its objects, it is said: 'There are five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings,' and so on. Therein, stinginess regarding a dwelling is dwelling-stinginess. This same method applies to the remaining terms.

Āvāso nāma sakalārāmopi pariveṇampi ekovarakopi rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīnipi. Tesu vasantā sukhaṃ vasanti paccaye labhanti. Eko bhikkhu vattasampannasseva pesalassa bhikkhuno tattha āgamanaṃ na icchati. Āgatopi ‘khippaṃ [P 0.0374] gacchatū’ti cinteti. Idaṃ ‘āvāsamacchariyaṃ’ [V 0.0399] nāma. Bhaṇḍanakārakādīnaṃ pana tattha vāsaṃ anicchato āvāsamacchariyaṃ nāma na hoti.

A 'dwelling' can be an entire monastery, a monastic compound, a single cell, or places for spending the night or the day, and so on. Those who dwell in them live in comfort and obtain requisites. When one bhikkhu does not wish for the arrival there of another bhikkhu who is accomplished in the observances and amiable, or if one does arrive, thinks, 'May he go away quickly!'—this is called 'dwelling-stinginess.' However, if one does not wish for quarrel-makers and the like to reside there, it is not dwelling-stinginess.

Kulanti upaṭṭhākakulampi ñātikulampi. Tattha aññassa upasaṅkamanaṃ anicchato kulamacchariyaṃ hoti. Pāpapuggalassa pana upasaṅkamanaṃ anicchantopi maccharī nāma na hoti. So hi tesaṃ pasādabhedāya paṭipajjati. Pasādaṃ rakkhituṃ samatthasseva pana bhikkhuno tattha upasaṅkamanaṃ anicchanto maccharī nāma hoti.

'Family' means a family of supporters or a family of relatives. Not wishing another to approach them is stinginess regarding family. However, one who does not wish an evil person to approach them is not called stingy, for that person acts for the destruction of their confidence. But one who does not wish for the approach of a bhikkhu who is capable of protecting their confidence is called stingy.

Lābhoti catupaccayalābhova. Taṃ aññasmiṃ sīlavanteyeva labhante ‘mā labhatū’ti cintentassa lābhamacchariyaṃ hoti. Yo pana saddhādeyyaṃ vinipāteti, aparibhogadupparibhogādivasena vināseti, pūtibhāvaṃ gacchantampi aññassa na deti, taṃ disvā ‘sace imaṃ esa na labheyya[M 0.0406], añño sīlavā labheyya, paribhogaṃ gaccheyyā’ti cintentassa macchariyaṃ nāma natthi.

'Gain' is the gain of the four requisites. When another virtuous one is obtaining it, for one to think, 'May he not obtain it!' is stinginess regarding gain. But suppose someone squanders an offering of faith, wastes it through non-use or wrong use, and does not give it to another even when it is going rotten. If, on seeing that person, one thinks, 'If this person did not receive this, another virtuous one would receive it and it would be properly used,' this is not called stinginess.

Vaṇṇo nāma sarīravaṇṇopi guṇavaṇṇopi. Tattha sarīravaṇṇe maccharipuggalo ‘paro pāsādiko rūpavā’ti vutte taṃ na kathetukāmo hoti. Guṇavaṇṇamaccharī sīlena dhutaṅgena paṭipadāya ācārena vaṇṇaṃ na kathetukāmo hoti.

'Praise' is of two kinds: praise of physical appearance and praise of virtue. In that regard, concerning praise of physical appearance, when it is said, 'Another is pleasing and handsome,' a stingy person is unwilling to speak of it. One who is stingy about praise of virtue is unwilling to speak of the praise due to another's morality, ascetic practices, mode of practice, or conduct.

Dhammoti pariyattidhammo ca paṭivedhadhammo ca. Tattha ariyasāvakā paṭivedhadhammaṃ na maccharāyanti, attanā paṭividdhadhamme sadevakassa lokassa paṭivedhaṃ icchanti. Taṃ pana paṭivedhaṃ ‘pare jānantū’ti icchanti. Tantidhammeyeva pana dhammamacchariyaṃ nāma hoti. Tena samannāgato puggalo yaṃ guḷhaṃ ganthaṃ vā kathāmaggaṃ vā jānāti taṃ aññaṃ na jānāpetukāmo hoti. Yo pana puggalaṃ upaparikkhitvā dhammānuggahena, dhammaṃ vā upaparikkhitvā puggalānuggahena na deti, ayaṃ dhammamaccharī nāma na hoti.

'The Dhamma' is of two kinds: the Dhamma of the scriptures and the Dhamma of penetration. In this regard, noble disciples are not stingy with the Dhamma of penetration. Having penetrated the Dhamma themselves, they wish for its penetration by the world with its devas. They desire that others know that penetration. However, what is called 'stinginess regarding the Dhamma' pertains only to the Dhamma of the scriptures. A person possessed of this does not wish to make known to another a profound text or path of discourse that he knows. But if someone, after examining a person, does not give the Dhamma out of concern for the Dhamma, or, after examining the Dhamma, does not give it out of concern for the person, this is not called a person who is stingy regarding the Dhamma.

Tattha ekacco puggalo lolo hoti, kālena samaṇo hoti, kālena brāhmaṇo, kālena [P 0.0375] nigaṇṭho. Yo hi bhikkhu ‘ayaṃ puggalo paveṇiāgataṃ tantiṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ dhammantaraṃ bhinditvā āluḷissatī’ti na deti, ayaṃ puggalaṃ upaparikkhitvā dhammānuggahena na deti nāma[V 0.0400]. Yo pana ‘ayaṃ dhammo saṇho sukhumo, sacāyaṃ puggalo gaṇhissati aññaṃ byākaritvā attānaṃ āvikatvā nassissatī’ti na deti, ayaṃ dhammaṃ upaparikkhitvā puggalānuggahena na deti nāma. Yo pana ‘sacāyaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ gaṇhissati, amhākaṃ samayaṃ bhindituṃ samattho bhavissatī’ti na deti, ayaṃ dhammamaccharī nāma hoti.

Here, a certain person is fickle: at one time he is an ascetic, at another a brahmin, at another a Nigaṇṭha. If a bhikkhu, thinking, 'This person will break up and confuse the traditional textual lineage, this subtle and profound distinction in the Dhamma,' does not give it, this is called 'not giving after examining the person out of concern for the Dhamma.' If one, thinking, 'This Dhamma is subtle and profound; if this person learns it, he will declare the highest attainment, reveal himself, and be ruined,' does not give it, this is called 'not giving after examining the Dhamma out of concern for the person.' But if one, thinking, 'If this person learns this Dhamma, he will be capable of breaking up our doctrine,' does not give it, this is called a person who is stingy regarding the Dhamma.

Imesu pañcasu macchariyesu āvāsamacchariyena tāva yakkho vā peto vā hutvā tasseva āvāsassa saṅkāraṃ sīsena ukkhipitvā vicarati. Kulamacchariyena tasmiṃ kule aññesaṃ dānamānanādīni karonte disvā ‘bhinnaṃ vatidaṃ kulaṃ mamā’ti cintayato lohitampi mukhato uggacchati, kucchivirecanampi hoti, antānipi khaṇḍākhaṇḍāni hutvā nikkhamanti. Lābhamacchariyena saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā santake lābhe maccharāyitvā puggalikaparibhogaṃ viya paribhuñjitvā yakkho vā peto vā mahāajagaro vā hutvā nibbattati. Sarīravaṇṇaguṇavaṇṇamaccharena pariyattidhammamacchariyena ca attanova [M 0.0407] vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇeti, paresaṃ vaṇṇe ‘kiṃ vaṇṇo eso’ti taṃ taṃ dosaṃ vadanto pariyattidhammañca kassaci kiñci adento dubbaṇṇo ceva eḷamūgo ca hoti.

Among these five kinds of stinginess, first, due to stinginess regarding a dwelling, one becomes a yakkha or a peta and wanders about carrying the rubbish of that very dwelling on one's head. Due to stinginess regarding a family, on seeing others making offerings and showing respect in that family, one thinks, 'Alas, this family of mine is broken!' and blood gushes from one's mouth, one suffers a stomach purge, and one's intestines come out in pieces. Due to stinginess regarding gain, being stingy with gains belonging to the Sangha or a group and enjoying them as if they were for personal use, one is reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great python. Due to stinginess about praise of physical appearance and praise of virtue, and stinginess about the Dhamma of the scriptures, one praises one's own praise, and when it comes to the praise of others, one speaks of this or that fault, saying, 'What kind of praise is that?'; and by not giving even a little of the Dhamma of the scriptures to anyone, one becomes ugly and a slobbering mute.

Apica āvāsamacchariyena lohagehe paccati. Kulamacchariyena appalābho hoti. Lābhamacchariyena gūthaniraye nibbattati. Vaṇṇamacchariyena bhave bhave nibbattassa vaṇṇo nāma na hoti. Dhammamacchariyena kukkuḷaniraye nibbattatīti.

Furthermore, due to stinginess regarding a dwelling, one is cooked in an iron house. Due to stinginess regarding a family, one has little gain. Due to stinginess regarding gain, one is reborn in the dung hell. Due to stinginess regarding praise, in existence after existence, one who is reborn has no praise. Due to stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one is reborn in the hot-ember hell.

Maccharāyanavasena maccheraṃ. Maccharāyanākāro maccharāyanā. Maccharena ayitassa maccherasamaṅgino bhāvo maccharāyitattaṃ. ‘Mayhameva hontu mā aññassā’ti sabbāpi attano sampattiyo byāpetuṃ na icchatīti viviccho. Vivicchassa bhāvo vevicchaṃ, mudumacchariyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Kadariyo [P 0.0376] vuccati anādaro. Tassa bhāvo kadariyaṃ. Thaddhamacchariyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tena hi samannāgato puggalo parampi paresaṃ dadamānaṃ nivāreti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Stinginess (maccheraṃ) is so called on account of being stingy. The act of being stingy is maccharāyanā. The state of one affected by stinginess, of one possessing stinginess, is maccharāyitattaṃ. One who thinks, 'Let them be for me alone, not for another,' and does not wish to share any of his own possessions, is called viviccha (one who wants to be separate). The state of such a one is vevicchaṃ; this is a name for mild stinginess. One who is disrespectful is called kadariya (mean). His state is kadariyaṃ (meanness); this is a name for hard stinginess. Indeed, a person endowed with this prevents another from giving to others. And this was said:

Kadariyo pāpasaṅkappo, micchādiṭṭhi anādaro;

Dadamānaṃ nivāreti, yācamānāna bhojananti. (saṃ. ni. 1.132);

"A mean person of evil intention,

of wrong view, disrespectful;

prevents another from giving

food to those who beg for it."

Yācake [V 0.0401] disvā kaṭukabhāvena cittaṃ añcati saṅkocetīti kaṭukañcuko. Tassa bhāvo kaṭukañcukatā. Aparo nayo – kaṭukañcukatā vuccati kaṭacchuggāho. Samatittikapuṇṇāya hi ukkhaliyā bhattaṃ gaṇhanto sabbatobhāgena saṅkuṭitena aggakaṭacchunā gaṇhāti, pūretvā gahetuṃ na sakkoti; evaṃ maccharipuggalassa cittaṃ saṅkucati. Tasmiṃ saṅkucite kāyopi tatheva saṅkucati, paṭikuṭati, paṭinivattati, na sampasāriyatīti maccheraṃ ‘kaṭukañcukatā’ti vuttaṃ.

On seeing beggars, one's mind bends and contracts with bitterness; this is a kaṭukañcuka (one with a bitter contraction). The state of that is kaṭukañcukatā. Another method: kaṭukañcukatā is said to be 'grasping with a ladle.' For when one is taking rice from a pot filled to the brim, one takes it with the tip of a ladle that is contracted on all sides; one is not able to take a full scoop. So too the mind of a stingy person contracts. When the mind has contracted, the body too contracts in the same way: it recoils, turns back, and does not stretch out. Thus stinginess is called kaṭukañcukatā.

Aggahitattaṃ cittassāti paresaṃ upakārakaraṇe dānādinā ākārena yathā na sampasāriyati, evaṃ āvaritvā gahitabhāvo cittassa. Yasmā pana maccharipuggalo attano santakaṃ paresaṃ adātukāmo hoti parasantakaṃ gaṇhitukāmo, tasmā ‘idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayhameva hotu, mā aññassā’ti pavattivasenassa attasampattinigūhanalakkhaṇatā attasampattiggahaṇalakkhaṇatā [M 0.0408] vā veditabbā. Sesaṃ imasmiṃ gocchake uttānatthameva.

The mind’s state of being ungenerous is its state of grasping, being closed off, such that it is not extended in the manner of giving and so on for the benefit of others. Since a stingy person is unwilling to give their own possessions to others and desires to take what belongs to others, this should be understood as having the characteristic of concealing or grasping one’s own good fortune, proceeding with the thought: ‘Let this excellent thing be for me alone, not for another!’ The rest in this section is clear in meaning.

Imāni pana saṃyojanāni kilesapaṭipāṭiyāpi āharituṃ vaṭṭati maggapaṭipāṭiyāpi. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojanāni anāgāmimaggena pahīyanti, mānasaṃyojanaṃ arahattamaggena, diṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsā sotāpattimaggena, bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ arahattamaggena, issāmacchariyāni sotāpattimaggena, avijjā arahattamaggena. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā diṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsaissāmacchariyāni sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti, kāmarāgapaṭighā [P 0.0377] anāgāmimaggena, mānabhavarāgaavijjā arahattamaggenāti.

These fetters can also be taken up according to the order of the defilements and according to the order of the path. According to the order of the defilements: the fetters of sensual lust and aversion are abandoned by the path of the non-returner; the fetter of conceit by the path of arahantship; the fetters of views, doubt, and adherence to rites and rituals by the path of stream-entry; the fetter of craving for existence by the path of arahantship; the fetters of envy and avarice by the path of stream-entry; and the fetter of ignorance by the path of arahantship. According to the order of the path: the fetters of views, doubt, adherence to rites and rituals, envy, and avarice are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; the fetters of sensual lust and aversion by the path of the non-returner; and the fetters of conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance by the path of arahantship.

1140. Ganthagocchake nāmakāyaṃ gantheti, cutipaṭisandhivasena vaṭṭasmiṃ ghaṭetīti kāyagantho. Sabbaññubhāsitampi paṭikkhipitvā sassato loko idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti iminā ākārena abhinivisatīti idaṃsaccābhiniveso. Yasmā pana abhijjhākāmarāgānaṃ viseso atthi, tasmā abhijjhākāyaganthassa padabhājane “yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmarāgo”ti avatvā yo rāgo sārāgotiādi vuttaṃ. Iminā yaṃ heṭṭhā vuttaṃ ‘brahmānaṃ vimānādīsu chandarāgo kāmāsavo na hoti, ganthagocchakaṃ patvā abhijjhākāyagantho hotī’ti taṃ suvuttanti veditabbaṃ. Parato kilesagocchakepi eseva nayo. Ṭhapetvā sīlabbataparāmāsanti idaṃ yasmā sīlabbataparāmāso ‘idameva sacca’ntiādinā ākārena nābhinivisati, ‘sīlena suddhī’tiādinā [V 0.0402] eva pana abhinivisati, tasmā micchādiṭṭhibhūtampi taṃ paṭikkhipanto ‘ṭhapetvā’ti āha.

1140. In the section on knots, it is the ‘bodily knot’ because it ties the mental body, connecting it to the round of existence by way of death and rebirth-linking. ‘Adherence to this as the truth’ is to adhere in this way: having rejected even what was spoken by the Omniscient One, one insists, ‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, the rest is foolish.’ Since there is a difference between covetousness and sensual lust, in the analysis of terms for the bodily knot of covetousness, instead of saying, ‘whatever sensual desire, sensual lust there is for sensual pleasures,’ it is said, ‘whatever lust, strong lust,’ and so on. By this it should be understood that what was said previously is well-said, namely: ‘For the brahmās, desire and lust for their celestial mansions, etc., is not a sensual taint, but when it comes to the section on knots, it becomes the bodily knot of covetousness.’ Further on, in the section on defilements, the method is the same. ‘Excluding adherence to rites and rituals’: this is because adherence to rites and rituals does not involve adhering in the manner, ‘This alone is true,’ etc., but rather one adheres with the view, ‘Purity comes through moral rules,’ etc. Therefore, although it is a form of wrong view, he rejected it, saying ‘excluding.’

1162. Nīvaraṇagocchakassa thinamiddhaniddese cittassa akallatāti cittassa gilānabhāvo. Gilāno hi akallakoti vuccati. Vinayepi vuttaṃ – “nāhaṃ, bhante, akallako”ti (pārā. 151). Akammaññatāti cittagelaññasaṅkhātova akammaññatākāro. Olīyanāti olīyanākāro. Iriyāpathikacittañhi iriyāpathaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontaṃ, rukkhe vagguli viya, khīle laggitaphāṇitavārako viya ca, olīyati. Tassa taṃ ākāraṃ [M 0.0409] sandhāya olīyanāti vuttaṃ. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggavasena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Līnanti avipphārikatāya paṭikuṭitaṃ. Itare dve ākārabhāvaniddesā. Thinanti sappipiṇḍo viya avipphārikatāya ghanabhāvena ṭhitaṃ. Thiyanāti ākāraniddeso. Thiyitabhāvo thiyitattaṃ, avipphāravaseneva thaddhatāti attho.

1162. In the section on hindrances, in the explanation of sloth and torpor, ‘unwieldiness of mind’ means the sickness of the mind. For a sick person is indeed called ‘unwieldy.’ It is also said in the Vinaya: ‘Venerable sir, I am not unwell.’ ‘Unworkability’ is the characteristic of unworkability, which is known as the mind’s sickness. ‘Sinking’ is the characteristic of drooping. For a mind that supports the postures, being unable to sustain a posture, droops like a bat on a tree or like a pot of molasses hung on a peg. With reference to that characteristic of it, it is called ‘sinking.’ The second term is intensified by means of a prefix. ‘Shrunken’ means contracted or recoiled due to lack of expansion. The other two are descriptions of the characteristic and the state. ‘Sloth’ is like a lump of ghee, remaining in a dense state due to lack of expansion. ‘Slothfulness’ (thiyanā) is a description of the characteristic. The state of being dense is slothfulness (thiyitattaṃ); the meaning is stiffness due to lack of expansion.

1163. Kāyassāti [P 0.0378] khandhattayasaṅkhātassa nāmakāyassa. Akallatā akammaññatāti heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Megho viya ākāsaṃ kāyaṃ onayhatīti onāho. Sabbatobhāgena onāho pariyonāho. Abbhantare samorundhatīti antosamorodho. Yathā hi nagare rundhitvā gahite manussā bahi nikkhamituṃ na labhanti, evampi middhena samoruddhā dhammā vipphāravasena nikkhamituṃ na labhanti. Tasmā antosamorodhoti vuttaṃ. Medhatīti middhaṃ; akammaññabhāvena vihiṃsatīti attho. Supanti tenāti soppaṃ. Akkhidalādīnaṃ pacalabhāvaṃ karotīti pacalāyikā. Supanā supitattanti ākārabhāvaniddesā. Yaṃ pana tesaṃ purato soppapadaṃ tassa punavacane kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Idaṃ vuccati thinamiddhanīvaraṇanti idaṃ thinañca middhañca ekato katvā āvaraṇaṭṭhena thinamiddhanīvaraṇanti vuccati. Yaṃ yebhuyyena sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ niddāya pubbabhāgaaparabhāgesu uppajjati taṃ arahattamaggena samucchijjati. Khīṇāsavānaṃ pana karajakāyassa dubbalabhāvena bhavaṅgotaraṇaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ asammisse vattamāne te supanti, sā nesaṃ niddā nāma hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, aggivessana, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno niddaṃ okkamitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.387). Evarūpo panāyaṃ karajakāyassa dubbalabhāvo na maggavajjho, upādinnakepi anupādinnakepi labbhati. Upādinnake labbhamāno yadā khīṇāsavo dīghamaggaṃ [V 0.0403] gato hoti, aññataraṃ vā pana kammaṃ katvā kilanto, evarūpe kāle labbhati. Anupādinnake labbhamāno paṇṇapupphesu labbhati. Ekaccānañhi rukkhānaṃ paṇṇāni sūriyātapena pasāriyanti rattiṃ paṭikuṭanti, padumapupphādīni sūriyātapena pupphanti, rattiṃ puna paṭikuṭanti[P 0.0379]. Idaṃ pana middhaṃ akusalattā khīṇāsavānaṃ na hotīti.

1163. ‘Of the body’ means of the mental body comprised of the three aggregates. ‘Unwieldiness’ and ‘unworkability’ are in the way stated above. ‘Covering’ is so called because it covers the body like a cloud covers the sky. A ‘complete covering’ is a covering in every respect. ‘Internal obstruction’ is so called because it obstructs internally. For just as people besieged in a city cannot get out, so the mental states obstructed by torpor cannot get out by way of expansion. Therefore it is called ‘internal obstruction.’ ‘Torpor’ is so called because ‘it harms’; the meaning is, it afflicts through unworkability. ‘Sleepiness’ is so called because ‘one sleeps’ on account of it. ‘Nodding’ is so called because it causes the nodding state of the eyelids, etc. ‘Sleeping’ and ‘the state of being asleep’ are descriptions of the characteristic and the state. The reason for repeating the word ‘sleepiness’ before these has already been stated. ‘This is called the hindrance of sloth and torpor’: this sloth and this torpor, taken together, are called the hindrance of sloth and torpor because they are an obstruction. That which arises mostly in trainees and worldlings in the periods before and after sleep is eradicated by the path of arahantship. For the arahants, however, there is a lapsing into the life-continuum due to the weakness of the physical body. When this occurs, continuing unmixed, they sleep; this is what is called their sleep. Thus the Blessed One said: ‘I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after spreading out my four-fold outer robe, lying down on my right side, entering upon sleep mindful and clearly comprehending.’ This kind of weakness of the physical body is not to be abandoned by the path; it is found in both what is clung to and what is not clung to. When found in what is clung to, it occurs at such times when an arahant has gone on a long journey or is tired after doing some work. When found in what is not clung to, it occurs in leaves and flowers. For the leaves of some trees spread out in the sun’s heat and contract at night; lotuses and other flowers bloom in the sun’s heat and contract again at night. But this torpor, being unwholesome, does not occur for the arahants.

Tattha [M 0.0410] siyā – “na middhaṃ akusalaṃ. Kasmā? Rūpattā. Rūpañhi abyākataṃ. Idañca rūpaṃ. Tenevettha ‘kāyassa akallatā akammaññatā’ti kāyaggahaṇaṃ kata”nti. Yadi ‘kāyassā’ti vuttamattenevetaṃ rūpaṃ, kāyapassaddhādayopi dhammā rūpameva bhaveyyuṃ. ‘Sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti’ (dha. sa. 163; dī. ni. 1.230) ‘kāyena ceva paramasaccaṃ sacchikarotī’ti (ma. ni. 2.183; a. ni. 4.113) sukhapaṭisaṃvedanaparamatthasaccasacchikaraṇānipi rūpakāyeneva siyuṃ. Tasmā na vattabbametaṃ ‘rūpaṃ middha’nti. Nāmakāyo hettha kāyo nāma. Yadi nāmakāyo, atha kasmā ‘soppaṃ pacalāyikā’ti vuttaṃ? Na hi nāmakāyo supati, na ca pacalāyatīti. ‘Liṅgādīni viya indriyassa, tassa phalattā. Yathā hi ‘itthiliṅgaṃ itthinimittaṃ itthikuttaṃ itthākappo’ti imāni liṅgādīni itthindriyassa phalattā vuttāni, evaṃ imassāpi nāmakāyagelaññasaṅkhātassa middhassa phalattā soppādīni vuttāni. Middhe hi sati tāni hontīti. Phalūpacārena, middhaṃ arūpampi samānaṃ ‘soppaṃ pacalāyikā supanā supitatta’nti vuttaṃ.

Here it might be said: ‘Torpor is not unwholesome. Why? Because it is material form. For material form is indeterminate, and this is material form. For that reason, the term ‘body’ is used here in the phrase “the unhealthiness and unworkability of the body.”’ If this were material form simply because it is said ‘of the body,’ then such states as tranquility of body would also be material form. And in the passages, ‘He feels pleasure with the body’ and ‘he realizes the ultimate truth with the body,’ the experiencing of pleasure and the realization of the ultimate truth would have to be done by the physical body. Therefore, it should not be said, ‘Torpor is material form.’ Here ‘body’ means the mental body. If it is the mental body, then why is it said ‘drowsiness, nodding’? For the mental body does not sleep, nor does it nod. It is because they are its result, like the characteristics, etc., of a faculty. For just as these characteristics, etc.—‘the female feature, the female sign, female coquetry, the female deportment’—are said to be so because they are the result of the femininity faculty, so too drowsiness, etc., are said to be so because they are the result of this torpor, which is designated as the sickness of the mental body. For when torpor is present, these occur. By a figurative expression based on the effect, torpor, though it is non-material, is called ‘drowsiness, nodding, sleeping, the state of being asleep.’

‘Akkhidalādīnaṃ pacalabhāvaṃ karotīti pacalāyikā’ti vacanatthenāpi cāyamattho sādhitoyevāti na rūpaṃ middhaṃ. Onāhādīhipi cassa arūpabhāvo dīpitoyeva. Na hi rūpaṃ nāmakāyassa ‘onāho pariyonāho antosamorodho’ hotīti. ‘Nanu ca imināva kāraṇenetaṃ rūpaṃ? Na hi arūpaṃ kassaci onāho, na pariyonāho, na antosamorodho hotī’ti. Yadi evaṃ, āvaraṇampi na bhaveyya. Tasmā. Yathā kāmacchandādayo arūpadhammā āvaraṇaṭṭhena nīvaraṇā, evaṃ imassāpi onāhanādiatthena onāhāditā veditabbā. Apica “pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe”ti (dī. ni. 2.146; saṃ. ni. 5.233) vacanatopetaṃ arūpaṃ. Na hi [P 0.0380] rūpaṃ cittupakkileso, na paññāya dubbalīkaraṇaṃ hotīti.

This point is also established by the meaning of the statement, ‘“Nodding” (pacalāyikā) is so called because it causes the nodding state of the eyelids, etc.’; thus, torpor is not material form. And its non-material nature is also shown by such terms as ‘covering.’ For material form is not a ‘covering,’ ‘complete covering,’ or ‘internal obstruction’ of the mental body. ‘But is it not for this very reason that it is material form? For a non-material state is not a covering for anything, nor a complete covering, nor an internal obstruction.’ If so, it could not be an obstruction (āvaraṇa) either. Therefore, just as sensual desire and other non-material states are hindrances (nīvaraṇā) in the sense that they obstruct (āvaraṇaṭṭhena), so this too should be understood as ‘covering,’ etc., in the sense that it covers. Moreover, from the statement, ‘having abandoned the five hindrances, imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom,’ it is also non-material. For material form is not an imperfection of the mind, nor does it weaken wisdom.

Kasmā [V 0.0404] na hoti? Nanu vuttaṃ –

Why is it not so? Has it not been said:

“Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā suraṃ pivanti merayaṃ, surāmerayapānā appaṭiviratā, ayaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamo samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ upakkileso”ti (a. ni. 4.50).

‘Bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who drink liquor and spirits, who do not abstain from drinking liquor and spirits. This, bhikkhus, is the first imperfection of ascetics and brahmins.’

Aparampi [M 0.0411] vuttaṃ “cha khome, gahapatiputta, ādīnavā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānānuyoge – sandiṭṭhikā dhanajāni, kalahappavaḍḍhanī, rogānaṃ āyatanaṃ, akittisañjananī, kopīnanidaṃsanī, paññāya dubbalīkaraṇītveva chaṭṭhaṃ padaṃ bhavatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.248). Paccakkhatopi cetaṃ siddhameva. Yathā majje udaragate, cittaṃ saṃkilissati, paññā dubbalā hoti, tasmā majjaṃ viya middhampi cittasaṃkileso ceva paññāya dubbalīkaraṇañca siyāti. Na, paccayaniddesato. Yadi hi majjaṃ saṃkileso bhaveyya, so “ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese”ti (ma. ni. 1.297) vā, “evameva kho, bhikkhave, pañcime cittassa upakkilesā, yehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhaṃ cittaṃ na ceva mudu hoti, na ca kammaniyaṃ, na ca pabhassaraṃ, pabhaṅgu ca, na ca sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya. Katame pañca? Kāmacchando, bhikkhave, cittassa upakkileso”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.214) vā, “katame ca, bhikkhave, cittassa upakkilesā? Abhijjhā visamalobho cittassa upakkileso”ti (ma. ni. 1.71) vā – evamādīsu upakkilesaniddesesu niddesaṃ āgaccheyya. Yasmā pana tasmiṃ pīte upakkilesā uppajjanti ye cittasaṃkilesā ceva paññāya ca dubbalīkaraṇā honti, tasmā taṃ tesaṃ paccayattā paccayaniddesato evaṃ vuttaṃ. Middhaṃ pana sayameva cittassa saṃkileso ceva paññāya dubbalīkaraṇañcāti arūpameva middhaṃ.

Furthermore, it is said: ‘Son of a householder, there are these six dangers in indulging in liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, which are a cause for heedlessness: immediate loss of wealth, increased quarrels, a breeding ground for illness, engendering disrepute, indecent exposure, and sixth, it is a cause for the weakening of wisdom.’ This is also established by direct experience. Just as when liquor enters the stomach, the mind becomes defiled and wisdom weakens, so too, it might be said, torpor is a defilement of the mind and a weakener of wisdom. No, because of its designation as a condition. For if liquor were a defilement, it would be included in expositions of defilements, such as: ‘having abandoned these five hindrances, the mind’s defilements’; or ‘So too, bhikkhus, there are these five defilements of the mind, corrupted by which the mind is neither malleable nor wieldy nor radiant, but is brittle and not rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, bhikkhus, is a defilement of the mind’; or ‘And what, bhikkhus, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’—and similar passages. But since, when it is drunk, defilements arise that are both defilements of the mind and weakeners of wisdom, it is so described because it is a condition for them, by way of designating the condition. Torpor, however, is itself a defilement of the mind and a weakener of wisdom; therefore, torpor is only non-material.

Kiñca bhiyyo? Sampayogavacanato. “Thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇena nīvaraṇañceva nīvaraṇasampayuttañcā”ti (dha. sa. 1176) hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā sampayogavacanato nayidaṃ rūpaṃ. Na hi rūpaṃ sampayuttasaṅkhyaṃ labhatīti. Athāpi siyā – ‘yathālābhavasenetaṃ [P 0.0381] vuttaṃ. Yathā hi “sippisambukampi sakkharakathalampi macchagumbampi carantampi tiṭṭhantampī”ti (dī. ni. 1.249; ma. ni. 1.433) evaṃ ekato katvā yathālābhavasena vuttaṃ. Sakkharakathalañhi tiṭṭhati yeva na carati, itaradvayaṃ tiṭṭhatipi caratipi. Evamidhāpi middhaṃ nīvaraṇameva, na sampayuttaṃ[V 0.0405], thinaṃ nīvaraṇampi sampayuttampīti sabbaṃ ekato katvā yathālābhavasena “nīvaraṇañceva nīvaraṇasampayuttañcā”ti vuttaṃ. Middhaṃ pana yathā sakkharakathalaṃ tiṭṭhateva na carati, evaṃ nīvaraṇameva, na sampayuttaṃ. Tasmā rūpameva middhanti. Na, rūpabhāvāsiddhito. Sakkharakathalañhi na caratīti vināpi suttena siddhaṃ. Tasmā tattha yathālābhavasenattho hotu[M 0.0412]. Middhaṃ pana rūpanti asiddhametaṃ. Na sakkā tassa iminā suttena rūpabhāvo sādhetunti middhassa rūpabhāvāsiddhito na idaṃ yathālābhavasena vuttanti arūpameva middhaṃ.

What more? Because of the statement about association. For it is said: 'The hindrance of sloth and torpor, by way of the hindrance of ignorance, is both a hindrance and associated with a hindrance.' Therefore, because of this statement about association, this is not material form. For material form does not attain the count of 'associated.' But it might be said: 'This is stated according to what is obtainable. Just as "oysters and conch shells, gravel and potsherds, and shoals of fish, both moving and stationary" are grouped together and stated according to what is obtainable—for gravel and potsherds are only stationary and do not move, while the other two are both stationary and moving—so here also, torpor is merely a hindrance, not associated, while sloth is both a hindrance and associated. Thus, all are grouped together and stated according to what is obtainable: "both a hindrance and associated with a hindrance." But torpor, just as gravel and potsherds are only stationary, is merely a hindrance, not associated. Therefore, torpor is simply material form.' No, because its being material form is not established. For the fact that gravel and potsherds do not move is established even without a scriptural text. Therefore, let the meaning there be 'according to what is obtainable.' But that torpor is material form—this is unestablished. It is not possible to establish its being material form by this scriptural text. Since the material nature of torpor is unestablished, this was not stated 'according to what is obtainable.' Thus, torpor is only immaterial.

Kiñca bhiyyo? ‘Cattattā’tiādivacanato. Vibhaṅgasmiñhi “vigatathinamiddhoti tassa thinamiddhassa cattattā vantattā muttattā pahīnattā paṭinissaṭṭhattā, tena vuccati vigatathinamiddho”ti (vibha. 547) ca, “idaṃ cittaṃ imamhā thinamiddhā sodheti visodheti parisodheti moceti vimoceti parimoceti, tena vuccati thinamiddhā cittaṃ parisodheti” cāti (vibha. 551) – evaṃ ‘cattattā’tiādi vuttaṃ. Na ca ‘rūpaṃ’ evaṃ vuccati, tasmāpi arūpameva middhanti. Na, cittajassāsambhavavacanato. Tividhañhi middhaṃ – cittajaṃ utujaṃ āhārajañca. Tasmā yaṃ tattha cittajaṃ tassa vibhaṅge jhānacittehi asambhavo vutto, na arūpabhāvo sādhitoti rūpameva middhanti. Na, rūpabhāvāsiddhitova. Middhassa hi rūpabhāve siddhe sakkā etaṃ laddhuṃ. Tattha cittajassāsambhavo vutto. So eva ca na sijjhatīti arūpameva middhaṃ.

What more? Because of statements such as 'because it is abandoned.' For in the Vibhaṅga it is said: '"Free from sloth and torpor": because that sloth and torpor has been abandoned, given up, released, discarded, and relinquished, one is called "free from sloth and torpor"'; and: 'One cleanses, purifies, and clarifies this mind of this sloth and torpor; one releases, liberates, and fully liberates it; therefore it is said, "one purifies the mind of sloth and torpor"'. Thus it is stated 'because it is abandoned,' etc. But material form is not spoken of in this way; therefore, too, torpor is only immaterial. No, because of the statement about the non-arising of that which is born of consciousness. For torpor is threefold: born of consciousness, born of temperature, and born of nutriment. Therefore, in the Vibhaṅga, the non-arising of that which is born of consciousness is stated in relation to the jhānic consciousnesses; its immaterial nature is not established. Thus torpor is only material form. No, precisely because its being material form is unestablished. For if the material nature of torpor were established, this could be granted, that therein, the non-arising of the mind-born is stated. But that very material nature is not established. Therefore torpor is only immaterial.

Kiñca bhiyyo? Pahānavacanato. Bhagavatā hi “cha, bhikkhave, dhamme pahāya bhabbo paṭhamajjhānaṃ [P 0.0382] upasampajja viharituṃ; katame cha? Kāmacchandaṃ, byāpādaṃ, thinamiddhaṃ, uddhaccaṃ, kakkuccaṃ, vicikicchaṃ; kāmesu kho panassa ādīnavo sammapaññāya sudiṭṭho hotī”ti (a. ni. 6.73) ca, “ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya balavatiyā paññāya attatthaṃ vā paratthaṃ vā ñassatī”ti (a. ni. 5.51) ca ādīsu middhassāpi pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Na ca rūpaṃ pahātabbaṃ. Yathāha – “rūpakkhandho abhiññeyyo, pariññeyyo, na pahātabbo, na bhāvetabbo na sacchikātabbo”ti (vibha. 1031) imassāpi pahānavacanato arūpameva middhanti. Na, rūpassāpi pahānavacanato. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahathā”ti (ma. ni. 1.247; saṃ. ni. 3.33). Ettha hi rūpassāpi pahānaṃ vuttameva. Tasmā akāraṇametanti. Na, aññathā vuttattā. Tasmiñhi sutte “yo, bhikkhave, rūpe chandarāgavinayo [V 0.0406] taṃ tattha pahāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.25) evaṃ chandarāgappahānavasena rūpassa pahānaṃ vuttaṃ, na yathā “cha dhamme pahāya pañca nīvaraṇe pahāyā”ti evaṃ pahātabbameva vuttanti, aññathā vuttattā, na rūpaṃ middhaṃ. Tasmā yānetāni “so ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso [M 0.0413] upakkilese”tiādīni suttāni vuttāni, etehi ceva aññehi ca suttehi arūpameva middhanti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi –

What more? Because of the statement about abandoning. For the Blessed One has said: 'Bhikkhus, by abandoning six things one is able to enter and abide in the first jhāna. What six? Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness, remorse, and doubt; and for that person the danger in sensual pleasures is well seen with right wisdom'; and: 'Having abandoned these five hindrances, with powerful wisdom one will know what is for one's own good and for the good of others'. In these and other passages, the abandoning of torpor is also mentioned. But material form is not to be abandoned. As it is said: 'The aggregate of material form is to be directly known, to be fully understood; it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realized.' Because of this statement about its abandoning, too, torpor is only immaterial. No, because of the statement about abandoning material form: 'Bhikkhus, material form is not yours. Abandon it.' Here the abandoning of material form is indeed stated. Therefore this is not a reason. No, because it is stated in another way. For in that sutta it is said: 'Bhikkhus, the removal of desire and lust for material form—that is the abandoning there.' Thus the abandoning of material form is stated by way of abandoning desire and lust, not in the same way as 'by abandoning six things' and 'by abandoning the five hindrances,' where what is itself to be abandoned is stated. Because it is stated in another way, torpor is not material form. Therefore, from those suttas that have been cited, such as 'Having abandoned these five hindrances, the mind's defilements,' and from other suttas, it should be understood that torpor is only immaterial. For thus it is said:

“Pañcime, bhikkhave, āvaraṇā nīvaraṇā cetaso ajjhāruhā paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā. Katame pañca? Kāmacchando, bhikkhave, āvaraṇo nīvaraṇo…pe… thinamiddhaṃ, bhikkhave, āvaraṇaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ cetaso ajjhāruhaṃ paññāya dubbalīkaraṇa”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.220) ca, “thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, andhakaraṇaṃ acakkhukaraṇaṃ aññāṇakaraṇaṃ paññānirodhikaṃ vighātapakkhikaṃ anibbānasaṃvattanika”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.221) ca, “evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati thinamiddhaparetenā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.236) ca, “ayoniso, bhikkhave, manasikaroto anuppanno ceva kāmacchando uppajjati…pe… anuppannañceva [P 0.0383] thinamiddhaṃ uppajjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.216) ca, “kevalohāyaṃ, bhikkhave, akusalarāsi yadidaṃ pañca nīvaraṇā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.371) ca –

'Bhikkhus, these five are obstructions, hindrances, that overwhelm the mind, weakeners of wisdom. What five? Sensual desire, bhikkhus, is an obstruction, a hindrance… Sloth and torpor, bhikkhus, is an obstruction, a hindrance, that overwhelms the mind, a weakener of wisdom.' And: 'The hindrance of sloth and torpor, bhikkhus, is blinding, causing non-vision, causing non-knowledge, destructive to wisdom, siding with vexation, not conducive to Nibbāna.' And: 'So too, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind assailed by sloth and torpor, overcome by sloth and torpor…' And: 'Bhikkhus, when one attends unwisely, unarisen sensual desire arises… unarisen sloth and torpor arises.' And: 'This is a sheer mass of the unwholesome, bhikkhus, that is, the five hindrances.'

Evamādīni ca anekāni etassa arūpabhāvajotakāneva suttāni vuttāni. Yasmā cetaṃ arūpaṃ tasmā āruppepi uppajjati. Vuttañhetaṃ mahāpakaraṇe paṭṭhāne – “nīvaraṇaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca nīvaraṇo dhammo uppajjati, na purejātapaccayā”ti etassa vibhaṅge “āruppe kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca thinamiddhaṃ… uddhaccaṃ avijjānīvaraṇa”nti (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Tasmā sanniṭṭhānamettha gantabbaṃ arūpameva middhanti.

And many such suttas have been spoken that illuminate its immaterial nature. Because it is immaterial, it also arises in the immaterial sphere. As it is said in the Great Treatise, the Paṭṭhāna: 'A hindrance-state arises in dependence on a hindrance-state, not by way of prenascent condition.' In its analysis: 'In the immaterial sphere, in dependence on the hindrance of sensual desire, arise sloth and torpor… restlessness, the hindrance of ignorance.' The whole should be elaborated. Therefore, the conclusion should be reached here that torpor is only immaterial.

1166. Kukkuccaniddese akappiye kappiyasaññitātiādīni mūlato kukkuccadassanatthaṃ vuttāni. Evaṃsaññitāya hi kate vītikamme, niṭṭhite vatthujjhācāre, puna sañjātasatinopi ‘duṭṭhu mayā kata’nti evaṃ anutappamānassa pacchānutāpavasenetaṃ uppajjati. Tena taṃ mūlato dassetuṃ ‘akappiye kappiyasaññitā’tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha akappiyabhojanaṃ kappiyasaññī hutvā paribhuñjati, akappiyamaṃsaṃ kappiyamaṃsasaññī hutvā, acchamaṃsaṃ sūkaramaṃsanti, dīpimaṃsaṃ vā migamaṃsanti [V 0.0407] khādati; kāle vītivatte kālasaññāya, pavāretvā appavāritasaññāya, pattasmiṃ raje patite paṭiggahitasaññāya bhuñjati – evaṃ ‘akappiye kappiyasaññāya’ vītikkamaṃ [M 0.0414] karoti nāma. Sūkaramaṃsaṃ pana acchamaṃsasaññāya khādamāno, kāle ca vikālasaññāya bhuñjamāno ‘kappiye akappiyasaññitāya’ vītikkamaṃ karoti nāma. Anavajjaṃ pana kiñcideva vajjasaññitāya, vajjañca anavajjasaññitāya karonto ‘anavajje vajjasaññāya vajje ca anavajjasaññāya’ vītikkamaṃ karoti nāma. Yasmā panetaṃ “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇaṃ, akataṃ kusalaṃ, akataṃ bhīruttāṇaṃ, kataṃ pāpaṃ, kataṃ luddaṃ, kataṃ kibbisa”nti evaṃ anavajje vajjasaññitāyapi kate vītikkame uppajjati, tasmāssa aññampi vatthuṃ anujānanto yaṃ evarūpantiādimāha.

1166. In the exposition of remorse, the phrases beginning with 'perceiving the unallowable as allowable' are stated to show remorse from its root. For when a transgression is committed based on such a perception, and when the offense regarding the object is concluded, this remorse arises by way of subsequent regret in one who, even upon mindfulness having arisen again, laments, 'I have done wrong.' Therefore, to show this from its root, it is said, 'perceiving the unallowable as allowable,' and so on. Here, one consumes unallowable food perceiving it as allowable; one eats unallowable meat perceiving it as allowable meat—for instance, eating bear meat thinking it is pork, or leopard meat thinking it is deer meat; one eats after the proper time has passed with the perception that it is the proper time; having been formally satisfied, one eats with the perception that one has not been satisfied; when dust has fallen into the bowl, one eats with the perception that it has been properly received—thus one is said to commit a transgression by 'perceiving the unallowable as allowable.' On the other hand, one who eats pork with the perception that it is bear meat, or eats at the proper time with the perception that it is the wrong time, is said to commit a transgression by 'perceiving the allowable as unallowable.' Further, one who does something blameless with the perception that it is blameworthy, or something blameworthy with the perception that it is blameless, is said to commit a transgression by 'perceiving the blameless as blameworthy and the blameworthy as blameless.' Since this remorse arises even when a transgression is committed by perceiving the blameless as blameworthy—thinking, 'Alas, I have not done what is beautiful, not done what is wholesome, not made a protection from what is fearful; I have done what is evil, what is cruel, what is wicked'—therefore, allowing for another basis for it, the Blessed One said, 'whatever is of such a kind,' and so on.

Tattha [P 0.0384] kukkuccapadaṃ vuttatthameva. Kukkuccāyanākāro kukkuccāyanā. Kukkuccena ayitassa bhāvo kukkuccāyitattaṃ. Cetaso vippaṭisāroti ettha katākatassa sāvajjānavajjassa vā abhimukhagamanaṃ ‘vippaṭisāro’ nāma. Yasmā pana so kataṃ vā pāpaṃ akataṃ na karoti, akataṃ vā kalyāṇaṃ kataṃ na karoti, tasmā virūpo kucchito vā paṭisāroti ‘vippaṭisāro’. So pana cetaso, na sattassāti ñāpanatthaṃ ‘cetaso’ vippaṭisāroti vuttaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāvaniddeso. Uppajjamānaṃ pana kukkuccaṃ āraggamiva kaṃsapattaṃ manaṃ vilikhamānameva uppajjati, tasmā manovilekhoti vuttaṃ. Ayamassa kiccaniddeso. Yaṃ pana vinaye “atha kho āyasmā sāriputto bhagavatā paṭikkhittaṃ anuvasitvā anuvasitvā āvasathapiṇḍaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti kukkuccāyanto na paṭiggahesīti (pāci. 204) kukkuccaṃ āgataṃ, na taṃ nīvaraṇaṃ. Na hi arahato ‘duṭṭhu mayā idaṃ kata’nti evaṃ anutāpo atthi. Nīvaraṇapatirūpakaṃ panetaṃ ‘kappati na kappatī’ti vīmaṃsanasaṅkhātaṃ vinayakukkuccaṃ nāma.

Here, the term 'remorse' has the meaning already stated. The mode of remorsing is 'remorse.' The state of one affected by remorse is 'remorsefulness.' In the phrase 'remorse of mind,' 'remorse' (vippaṭisāra) refers to the facing of what has been done and not done, or what is blameworthy and blameless. And since it does not make an evil deed that has been done undone, nor a good deed that has not been done done, it is a 'deformed' or 'contemptible' regret; thus it is 'remorse.' To make it known that this belongs to the mind, not to a being, it is called 'remorse of mind.' This is its exposition in terms of its nature. When remorse arises, it arises scratching the mind just as an awl's tip scratches a bronze plate; therefore it is called 'a mental scratch.' This is its exposition in terms of its function.
