However, the remorse mentioned in the Vinaya—'Then the Venerable Sāriputta, feeling remorse, did not accept the almsfood from the lodging, thinking, "The Blessed One has rejected consuming it day after day"'—is not a hindrance. For an arahant has no subsequent regret thinking, 'I have done this wrongly.' Rather, this is a counterfeit of the hindrance; it is called 'Vinaya-remorse,' which is reckoned as the investigation, 'Is this allowable or not?'

1176. “Katame dhammā nīvaraṇā ceva nīvaraṇasampayuttā cā”ti padassa niddese yasmā thinamiddhaṃ aññamaññaṃ na vijahati, tasmā thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇena nīvaraṇañceva nīvaraṇasampayuttañcāti abhinditvā vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana uddhacce satipi kukkuccassa abhāvā kukkuccena vināpi uddhaccaṃ uppajjati, tasmā taṃ bhinditvā vuttaṃ. Yañca yena sampayogaṃ na gacchati, taṃ na yojitanti veditabbaṃ.

1176. In the exposition of the phrase, 'Which states are both hindrances and associated with hindrances?': since sloth and torpor do not abandon one another, the hindrance of sloth and torpor is spoken of without division as being 'both a hindrance and associated with a hindrance.' But since restlessness can arise even without remorse, due to the absence of remorse when restlessness is present, this is spoken of with division. And it should be understood that whatever does not enter into association with something is not conjoined with it.

Ime [M 0.0415][V 0.0408] pana nīvaraṇe kilesapaṭipāṭiyāpi āharituṃ vaṭṭati maggapaṭipāṭiyāpi. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā kāmacchandabyāpādā anāgāmimaggena pahīyanti, thinamiddhuddhaccāni arahattamaggena, kukkuccavicikicchā sotāpattimaggena, avijjā arahattamaggena. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā sotāpattimaggena kukkuccavicikicchā pahīyanti, anāgāmimaggena kāmacchandabyāpādā, arahattamaggena thinamiddhuddhaccāvijjāti.

These hindrances can be taken up according to the order of the defilements and also according to the order of the path. According to the order of the defilements: sensual desire and ill will are abandoned by the path of non-returning; sloth, torpor, and restlessness by the path of arahantship; remorse and doubt by the path of stream-entry; and ignorance by the path of arahantship. According to the order of the path: by the path of stream-entry, remorse and doubt are abandoned; by the path of non-returning, sensual desire and ill will; by the path of arahantship, sloth, torpor, restlessness, and ignorance.

1182. Parāmāsagocchake [P 0.0385] te dhamme ṭhapetvāti pucchāsabhāgena bahuvacanaṃ kataṃ.

1182. In the section on adherence, regarding the phrase 'setting aside those states,' the plural is used in conformity with the question.

1219. Upādānaniddese vatthusaṅkhātaṃ kāmaṃ upādiyatīti kāmupādānaṃ kāmo ca so upādānañcātipi kāmupādānaṃ. Upādānanti daḷhaggahaṇaṃ. Daḷhattho hi ettha upasaddo upāyāsaupakaṭṭhādīsu viya. Tathā diṭṭhi ca sā upādānañcāti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Diṭṭhiṃ upādiyatīti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. ‘Sassato attā ca loko cā’tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.31) hi purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi upādiyahi. Tathā sīlabbataṃ upādiyatīti sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Sīlabbatañca taṃ upādānañcātipi sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Gosīlagovatādīni hi ‘evaṃ suddhī’ti abhinivesato sayameva upādānāni. Tathā, vadanti etenāti ‘vādo’; upādiyanti etenāti ‘upādānaṃ’. Kiṃ vadanti, upādiyanti vā? Attānaṃ. Attano vādupādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ; ‘attavādamattameva vā attā’ti upādiyanti etenāti attavādupādānaṃ.

1219. In the exposition of clinging: (1) 'Clinging to sensual pleasure' (kāmupādāna) is so called because one clings to sensual pleasure, which is reckoned as an object; or it is sensual pleasure and it is clinging, thus it is 'clinging to sensual pleasure.' 'Clinging' (upādāna) means firm grasping; for here the prefix upa- has the sense of 'firm,' as in words like upāyāsa (trouble) and upakaṭṭha (drawn near). (2) Similarly, 'clinging to views' (diṭṭhupādāna) is so called because it is a view and it is clinging; or because one clings to a view. For in such cases as 'the self and the world are eternal,' a subsequent view clings to a preceding one. (3) Similarly, 'clinging to rites and rituals' (sīlabbatupādāna) is so called because one clings to rites and rituals; or because it is a rite or ritual and it is clinging. For such things as the cow-practice and the cow-vow, through adherence to the idea 'purification comes about in this way,' are themselves clingings. (4) Similarly, 'that by which they speak' is a 'doctrine' (vāda); 'that by which they cling' is 'clinging' (upādāna). What do they speak of or cling to? The self. The doctrine and clinging related to the self is 'clinging to the doctrine of self' (attavādupādāna); or, 'that by which they cling to the mere doctrine of self as "self"' is 'clinging to the doctrine of self.'

1220. Yo kāmesu kāmacchandoti etthāpi vatthukāmāva anavasesato kāmāti adhippetā. Tasmā vatthukāmesu kāmacchando idha kāmupādānanti anāgāminopi taṃ siddhaṃ hoti. Pañcakāmaguṇavatthuko panassa kāmarāgova natthīti.

1220. Here, in the phrase 'whatever desire is for sensual pleasures,' it is sensual pleasures as objects that are intended without remainder by the term 'sensual pleasures.' Therefore, since desire for sensual pleasures as objects is here 'clinging to sensual pleasure,' this is established even for a non-returner. For him, however, there is no sensual lust at all that is grounded in the objects of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

1221. Diṭṭhupādānaniddese natthi dinnanti. Dinnaṃ nāma atthi, sakkā kassaci kiñci dātunti jānāti; dinnassa pana phalaṃ vipāko natthīti gaṇhāti. Natthi yiṭṭhanti. Yiṭṭhaṃ vuccati mahāyāgo. Taṃ yajituṃ sakkāti jānāti; yiṭṭhassa pana phalaṃ vipāko natthīti gaṇhāti. Natthi hutanti āhunapāhunamaṅgalakiriyā. Taṃ kātuṃ sakkāti jānāti; tassa pana phalaṃ vipāko natthīti [M 0.0416] gaṇhāti. Natthi, sukatadukkaṭānanti ettha dasa kusalakammapathā sukatakammāni nāma. Dasa akusalakammapathā dukkaṭakammāni [P 0.0386] nāma. Tesaṃ atthibhāvaṃ [V 0.0409] jānāti phalaṃ vipāko pana natthīti gaṇhāti. Natthi ayaṃ lokoti paraloke ṭhito imaṃ lokaṃ natthīti gaṇhāti. Natthi paralokoti idha loke ṭhito paralokaṃ natthīti gaṇhāti. Natthi mātā natthi pitāti mātāpitūnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ jānāti, tesu katapaccayena koci phalaṃ vipāko natthīti gaṇhāti. Natthi sattā opapātikāti cavanakaupapajjanakā sattā natthīti gaṇhāti. Sammaggatā sammā paṭipannāti anulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇā lokasmiṃ natthīti gaṇhāti. Ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentīti imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ attanāva abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena ñatvā pavedanasamattho sabbaññū buddho nāma natthīti gaṇhāti.

1221. In the exposition of clinging to views: 'There is nothing given' means: one knows that giving exists—that it is possible for someone to give something—but one holds that there is no fruit or result of what is given. 'There is nothing sacrificed' means: 'sacrificed' refers to a great sacrifice; one knows it is possible to perform a sacrifice, but one holds that there is no fruit or result of what is sacrificed. 'There is no oblation' means: this refers to offerings for guests, hospitality, and auspicious rites; one knows it is possible to perform them, but one holds that there is no fruit or result. 'There is no fruit or result of good and bad actions' means: here, the ten wholesome courses of action are called good actions, and the ten unwholesome courses of action are called bad actions; one knows of their existence but holds that they have no fruit or result. 'There is no this world' means: standing in the other world, one holds that this world does not exist. 'There is no other world' means: standing in this world, one holds that the other world does not exist. 'There is no mother, there is no father' means: one knows of the existence of mother and father but holds that there is no fruit or result from any action done in relation to them. 'There are no spontaneously arisen beings' means: one holds that there are no beings who pass away and are reborn. 'There are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are well-gone, well-practiced, who, having realized this world and the next for themselves by direct knowledge, make it known' means: one holds that there are no righteous ascetics and brahmins in the world who have entered upon the concordant path; and one holds that there is no omniscient Buddha capable of making known this world and the next, having known them himself through his own superior knowledge.

Imāni pana upādānāni kilesapaṭipāṭiyāpi āharituṃ vaṭṭati maggapaṭipāṭiyāpi. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā kāmupādānaṃ catūhi maggehi pahīyati, sesāni tīṇi sotāpattimaggena. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā sotāpattimaggena diṭṭhupādānādīni pahīyanti, catūhi maggehi kāmupādānanti.

These clingings can be taken up according to the order of the defilements and also according to the order of the path. According to the order of the defilements: clinging to sensual pleasure is abandoned by the four paths, while the remaining three are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. According to the order of the path: by the path of stream-entry, clinging to views and the others are abandoned; by the four paths, clinging to sensual pleasure is abandoned.

1235. Kilesagocchake kilesā eva kilesavatthūni. Vasanti vā ettha akhīṇāsavā sattā lobhādīsu patiṭṭhitattāti ‘vatthūni’. Kilesā ca te tappatiṭṭhānaṃ sattānaṃ vatthūni cāti ‘kilesavatthūni’. Yasmā cettha anantarapaccayādibhāvena uppajjamānā kilesāpi vasanti eva nāma, tasmā kilesānaṃ vatthūnītipi ‘kilesavatthūni’.

1235. In the section on defilements, the defilements themselves are the 'bases of defilements.' Or, they are 'bases' (vatthūni) because beings with unexhausted taints dwell (vasanti) in them, being established in greed and so on. They are defilements, and they are bases for the beings established in them; thus they are 'bases of defilements.' And since defilements also dwell here, arising by way of conditions such as the proximity condition, they are also 'bases of defilements' in the sense of being bases for subsequent defilements.

1236. Tattha katamo lobho? Yo rāgo sārāgoti ayaṃ pana lobho hetugocchake ganthagocchake imasmiṃ kilesagocchaketi tīsu ṭhānesu atirekapadasatena niddiṭṭho. Āsavasaṃyojanaoghayoganīvaraṇaupādānagocchakesu aṭṭhahi aṭṭhahi padehi niddiṭṭho. Svāyaṃ atirekapadasatena niddiṭṭhaṭṭhānepi aṭṭhahi aṭṭhahi padehi niddiṭṭhaṭṭhānepi nippadesatova gahitoti veditabbo. Tesu [P 0.0387] hetuganthanīvaraṇaupādānakilesagocchakesu catumaggavajjhā taṇhā ekeneva [M 0.0417] koṭṭhāsena ṭhitā. Āsavasaṃyojanaoghayogesu catumaggavajjhāpi dve koṭṭhāsā hutvā ṭhitā. Kathaṃ? Āsavesu kāmāsavo bhavāsavoti, saṃyojanesu kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ bhavarāgasaṃyojananti, oghesu kāmogho bhavoghoti, yogesu kāmayogo bhavayogoti.

1236. Herein, what is greed? It is lust, intense lust. This greed has been indicated in three places—in the section on roots, the section on bodily ties, and this section on defilements—with more than a hundred terms. In the sections on taints, fetters, floods, yokes, hindrances, and clingings, it has been indicated with eight terms each. It should be understood that although it is indicated in some places with more than a hundred terms and in other places with eight terms each, it is included without remainder. Among these, in the sections on roots, bodily ties, hindrances, clingings, and defilements, the craving to be abandoned by the four paths stands as a single part. But in the sections on taints, fetters, floods, and yokes, even the craving to be abandoned by the four paths stands as two parts. How? In the taints, as the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence; in the fetters, as the fetter of sensual lust and the fetter of lust for existence; in the floods, as the flood of sensual desire and the flood of existence; in the yokes, as the yoke of sensual desire and the yoke of existence.

Imāni pana kilesavatthūni kilesapaṭipāṭiyāpi āharituṃ vaṭṭati maggapaṭipāṭiyāpi. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā [V 0.0410] lobho catūhi maggehi pahīyati, doso anāgāmimaggena, mohamānā arahattamaggena, diṭṭhivicikicchā sotāpattimaggena, thinādīni arahattamaggena. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā sotāpattimaggena diṭṭhivicikicchā pahīyanti, anāgāmimaggena doso, arahattamaggena sesā sattāti.

These items of defilement can be presented according to the order of the defilements and according to the order of the paths. According to the order of the defilements: greed is abandoned by the four paths; hatred by the path of non-returning; delusion and conceit by the path of arahantship; wrong view and doubt by the path of stream-entry; and sloth and so on by the path of arahantship. According to the order of the paths: wrong view and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; hatred by the path of non-returning; and the remaining seven by the path of arahantship.

1287. Kāmāvacaraniddese heṭṭhatoti heṭṭhābhāgena. Avīcinirayanti vā aggijālānaṃ vā sattānaṃ vā dukkhavedanāya vīci, antaraṃ, chiddaṃ ettha natthīti avīci. Sukhasaṅkhāto ayo ettha natthīti nirayo. Niratiatthenapi nirassādatthenapi nirayo. Pariyantaṃ karitvāti taṃ avīcisaṅkhātaṃ nirayaṃ antaṃ katvā. Uparitoti uparibhāgena. Paranimmitavasavattideveti paranimmitesu kāmesu vasaṃ vattanato evaṃladdhavohāre deve. Anto karitvāti anto pakkhipitvā. Yaṃ etasmiṃ antareti ye etasmiṃ okāse. Etthāvacarāti iminā yasmā etasmiṃ antare aññepi caranti kadāci katthaci sambhavato, tasmā tesaṃ asaṅgaṇhanatthaṃ ‘avacarā’ti vuttaṃ. Tena ye etasmiṃ antare ogāḷhā hutvā caranti sabbattha sadā ca sambhavato, adhobhāge caranti avīcinirayassa heṭṭhā bhūtupādāyapavattibhāvena, tesaṃ saṅgaho kato hoti. Te hi avagāḷhāva caranti, adhobhāgeva carantīti avacarā. Ettha pariyāpannāti iminā pana yasmā ete etthāvacarā aññatthāpi avacaranti, na pana tattha pariyāpannā honti, tasmā tesaṃ aññatthāpi avacarantānaṃ pariggaho kato hoti. Idāni te ettha pariyāpannadhamme rāsisuññatapaccayabhāvato [P 0.0388] ceva sabhāvato ca dassento khandhātiādimāha.

1287. In the exposition of the sense-sphere, 'below' means by the lower part. 'Avīci hell': because there is no interval (vīci), no gap, herein for the flames, or for the beings, or for the painful feeling, it is called Avīci. Because happiness, called sukha, is not herein, it is called nirayo. It is also a nirayo in the sense of being without delight (nirati) and without taste (nirassāda). 'Having made it the limit' means having made that hell called Avīci the boundary. 'Above' means by the upper part. 'The devas who wield power over others’ creations' refers to the devas who have acquired this designation because they exercise power over sensual pleasures created by others. 'Having included' means having placed within. 'Whatever is in this interval' refers to whatever aggregates, elements, and bases are in this space. By this term 'etthāvacarā': since in this interval other dhammas—exalted and supramundane—also occur, arising occasionally somewhere, therefore, to not include them, 'avacarā' is stated. By that, the inclusion is made of those dhammas which, having become immersed, occur in this interval—arising always and everywhere—and which occur in the lower part, below the Avīci hell, due to the existence of primary and derived matter. For they occur only as immersed, and they occur in the lower part; therefore, they are 'avacarā'. But by this 'included herein': since these dhammas that occur here also occur elsewhere, yet are not included there, their inclusion is thus made, even though they occur elsewhere. Now, wishing to show those dhammas included herein by way of their nature as an aggregate, as voidness of self, and as a condition, and also by their intrinsic nature, the Blessed One said, 'aggregates,' etc.

1289. Rūpāvacaraniddese [M 0.0418] brahmalokanti paṭhamajjhānabhūmisaṅkhātaṃ brahmaṭṭhānaṃ. Sesamettha kāmāvacaraniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Samāpannassa vātiādīsu paṭhamapadena kusalajjhānaṃ vuttaṃ, dutiyena vipākajjhānaṃ, vuttaṃ tatiyena kiriyajjhānaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

1289. In the exposition of the form-sphere, 'the Brahmā world' means the Brahmā-abode designated as the first-jhāna plane. The rest here should be understood by the same method as was stated in the exposition of the sense-sphere. In the passage beginning with 'samāpannassa vā,' by the first term, wholesome jhāna is stated; by the second, resultant jhāna is stated; by the third, functional jhāna is stated. Thus it should be understood.

1291. Arūpāvacaraniddese ākāsānañcāyatanūpageti ākāsānañcāyatanasaṅkhātaṃ bhavaṃ upagate. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

1291. In the exposition of the formless-sphere, 'gone to the base of the infinity of space' means those who have gone to the existence designated as the base of the infinity of space. This same method applies to the second term as well. The rest should be understood by the same method as was explained above.

1301. Saraṇadukaniddese yvāyaṃ tīsu akusalamūlesu moho, so lobhasampayutto ca lobhena [V 0.0411] saraṇo, dosasampayutto ca dosena saraṇo. Vicikicchuddhaccasampayutto pana moho diṭṭhisampayuttena ceva rūparāgaarūparāgasaṅkhātena ca rāgaraṇena pahānekaṭṭhabhāvato saraṇo sarajoti veditabbo.

1301. In the exposition of the dyad on defiled states, that delusion which is among the three unwholesome roots, when associated with greed, is defiled by greed, and when associated with hatred, is defiled by hatred. But delusion associated with doubt and restlessness should be understood as being defiled and impure because it is defiled by the defilement of lust—that is, lust associated with wrong view and lust designated as lust for form and lust for the formless—on account of their having the same quality of being abandoned together.

Suttantikadukanikkhepakathā

The Discussion on the Exposition of the Suttanta Dyads

1303. Suttantikadukesu mātikākathāyaṃ atthato vivecitattā yāni ca nesaṃ niddesapadāni tesampi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva suviññeyyattā yebhuyyena uttānatthāni eva. Idaṃ panettha visesamattaṃ – vijjūpamaduke tāva cakkhumā kira puriso meghandhakāre rattiṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tassa andhakāratāya maggo na paññāyi. Vijju niccharitvā andhakāraṃ viddhaṃsesi. Athassa andhakāravigamā maggo pākaṭo ahosi. So dutiyampi gamanaṃ abhinīhari. Dutiyampi andhakāro otthari. Maggo na paññāyi. Vijju niccharitvā taṃ viddhaṃsesi. Vigate andhakāre maggo pākaṭo ahosi. Tatiyampi gamanaṃ abhinīhari. Andhakāro otthari. Maggo na paññāyi. Vijju niccharitvā andhakāraṃ viddhaṃsesi.

1303. In the Suttanta Dyads, since their meaning has been analyzed in the discussion on the mātikā, and since their expository terms are easily understood in the way stated above, they are for the most part of manifest meaning. Here, however, is a specific point. In the dyad of the lightning simile, a man with eyesight, it seems, set out on a path at night in the darkness of the clouds. Because of the darkness, the path was not apparent. A flash of lightning shot forth and destroyed the darkness. Then, with the departure of the darkness, the path became manifest to him. He proceeded on his journey a second time. Again darkness descended, and the path was not apparent. A flash of lightning shot forth and destroyed it. When the darkness had departed, the path became manifest. He proceeded on his journey a third time. Darkness descended, and the path was not apparent. A flash of lightning shot forth and destroyed the darkness.

Tattha cakkhumato purisassa andhakāre maggapaṭipajjanaṃ viya ariyasāvakassa sotāpattimaggatthāya vipassanārambho. Andhakāre maggassa apaññāyanakālo viya saccacchādakatamaṃ. Vijjuyā niccharitvā andhakārassa viddhaṃsitakālo viya sotāpattimaggobhāsena uppajjitvā saccacchādakatamassa [M 0.0419] vinoditakālo. Vigate andhakāre maggassa pākaṭakālo viya [P 0.0389] sotāpattimaggassa catunnaṃ saccānaṃ pākaṭakālo. Maggassa pākaṭaṃ pana maggasamaṅgipuggalassa pākaṭameva. Dutiyagamanābhinīhāro viya sakadāgāmimaggatthāya vipassanārambho. Andhakāre maggassa apaññāyanakālo viya saccacchādakatamaṃ. Dutiyaṃ vijjuyā niccharitvā andhakārassa viddhaṃsitakālo viya sakadāgāmimaggobhāsena uppajjitvā saccacchādakatamassa vinoditakālo. Vigate andhakāre maggassa pākaṭakālo viya sakadāgāmimaggassa catunnaṃ saccānaṃ pākaṭakālo. Maggassa pākaṭaṃ pana maggasamaṅgipuggalassa pākaṭameva. Tatiyagamanābhinīhāro viya anāgāmimaggatthāya vipassanārambho. Andhakāre maggassa apaññāyanakālo viya saccacchādakatamaṃ. Tatiyaṃ vijjuyā niccharitvā andhakārassa viddhaṃsitakālo viya anāgāmimaggobhāsena uppajjitvā saccacchādakatamassa vinoditakālo. Vigate [V 0.0412] andhakāre maggassa pākaṭakālo viya anāgāmimaggassa catunnaṃ saccānaṃ pākaṭakālo. Maggassa pākaṭaṃ pana maggasamaṅgipuggalassa pākaṭameva.

Herein, the noble disciple’s undertaking of insight for the sake of the path of stream-entry is like the man with eyesight setting out on the path in the darkness. The time when the path is not apparent in the darkness is like the darkness that conceals the truths. The time when the darkness is destroyed by the lightning flashing forth is like the time when the darkness that conceals the truths is dispelled by the arising of the light of the path of stream-entry. The time when the path becomes manifest after the darkness has departed is like the time when the four truths become manifest to the path of stream-entry. But that which is made manifest by the path is manifest only to the person endowed with the path. The undertaking of the second journey is like the undertaking of insight for the sake of the path of once-returning. The time when the path is not apparent in the darkness is like the darkness that conceals the truths. The time when the darkness is destroyed by the second flash of lightning is like the time when the darkness that conceals the truths is dispelled by the arising of the light of the path of once-returning. The time when the path becomes manifest after the darkness has departed is like the time when the four truths become manifest to the path of once-returning. But that which is made manifest by the path is manifest only to the person endowed with the path. The undertaking of the third journey is like the undertaking of insight for the sake of the path of non-returning. The time when the path is not apparent in the darkness is like the darkness that conceals the truths. The time when the darkness is destroyed by the third flash of lightning is like the time when the darkness that conceals the truths is dispelled by the arising of the light of the path of non-returning. The time when the path becomes manifest after the darkness has departed is like the time when the four truths become manifest to the path of non-returning. But that which is made manifest by the path is manifest only to the person endowed with the path.

Vajirassa pana pāsāṇo vā maṇi vā abhejjo nāma natthi. Yattha patati taṃ vinividdhameva hoti. Vajiraṃ khepentaṃ asesetvā khepeti. Vajirena gatamaggo nāma puna pākatiko na hoti. Evameva arahattamaggassa avajjhakileso nāma natthi. Sabbakilese vinivijjhati vajiraṃ viya. Arahattamaggopi kilese khepento asesetvā khepeti. Vajirena gatamaggassa puna pākatikattābhāvo viya arahattamaggena pahīnakilesānaṃ puna paccudāvattanaṃ nāma natthīti.

But for a diamond, there is no so-called unbreakable stone or gem. Wherever it falls, that place is pierced right through. A diamond, in destroying, destroys without remainder. A path that a diamond has gone along does not become normal again. So too, for the path of arahantship there is no so-called invulnerable defilement. It pierces all defilements like a diamond. The path of arahantship, too, in destroying defilements, destroys them without remainder. Just as there is no return to a normal condition for a path that a diamond has gone along, so there is no so-called returning again for the defilements abandoned by the path of arahantship.

1307. Bāladukaniddese bālesu ahirikānottappāni pākaṭāni, mūlāni ca sesānaṃ bāladhammānaṃ. Ahiriko hi anottappī ca na kiñci akusalaṃ na karoti nāmāti. Etāni dve paṭhamaṃyeva visuṃ vuttāni. Sukkapakkhepi ayameva nayo. Tathā kaṇhaduke.

1307. In the exposition of the dyad on fools, among the qualities of a fool, shamelessness and lack of moral dread are manifest, and they are the roots of the other qualities of a fool. For a shameless person and one who lacks moral dread, there is no unwholesome deed whatsoever that they will not do. Therefore, these two have been stated separately at the very beginning. This same method applies also to the bright side. Likewise in the dark dyad.

1311. Tapanīyadukaniddese katattā ca akatattā ca tapanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kāyaduccaritādīni [P 0.0390] hi katattā tapanti, kāyasucaritādīni akatattā. Tathā hi puggalo ‘kataṃ me kāyaduccarita’nti tappati, ‘akataṃ me kāyasucarita’nti tappati. ‘Kataṃ me vacīduccarita’nti tappati…pe… ‘akataṃ me [M 0.0420] manosucarita’nti tappati. Atapanīyepi eseva nayo. Kalyāṇakārī hi puggalo ‘kataṃ me kāyasucarita’nti na tappati, ‘akataṃ me kāyaduccarita’nti na tappati…pe… ‘akataṃ me manoduccarita’nti na tappatīti (a. ni. 2.3).

1311. In the exposition of the dyad on what causes remorse, remorse should be understood as arising on account of what has been done and what has not been done. For bodily misconduct and so on cause remorse because they have been done, while bodily good conduct and so on cause remorse because they have not been done. Thus, a person feels remorse, thinking: 'I have committed bodily misconduct,' and feels remorse, thinking: 'I have not performed bodily good conduct.' One feels remorse, thinking: 'I have committed verbal misconduct' …and so on… 'I have not performed mental good conduct.' This same method applies to what does not cause remorse. For a person who does what is good does not feel remorse, thinking: 'I have performed bodily good conduct,' and does not feel remorse, thinking: 'I have not committed bodily misconduct' …and so on… 'I have not committed mental misconduct.'

1313. Adhivacanadukaniddese yā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānanti sabbadhammaggahaṇaṃ. Saṅkhāyatīti saṅkhā, saṃkathiyatīti attho. Kinti saṃkathiyati? Ahanti mamanti paroti parassāti sattoti bhāvoti posoti puggaloti naroti māṇavoti tissoti dattoti, ‘mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bimbohanaṃ’ ‘vihāro pariveṇaṃ dvāraṃ vātapāna’nti evaṃ anekehi ākārehi saṃkathiyatīti ‘saṅkhā’. Samaññāyatīti samaññā. Kinti samaññāyati? ‘Ahanti…pe… vātapāna’nti samaññāyatīti [V 0.0413] ‘samaññā’. Paññāpiyatīti paññatti. Vohariyatīti vohāro. Kinti vohariyati? ‘Aha’nti…pe… ‘vātapāna’nti vohariyatīti vohāro.

1313. In the exposition of the dyad on designation, the phrase 'of those various phenomena' is for the inclusion of all phenomena. 'It is reckoned' is reckoning; the meaning is, 'it is spoken of.' How is it spoken of? As 'I,' 'mine,' 'another,' 'another's,' 'a being,' 'a state,' 'a person,' 'an individual,' 'a man,' 'a youth,' 'Tissa,' 'Datta'; as 'a bed, a chair, a mat, a pillow'; as 'a monastery, a monastic cell, a door, a window'—since it is spoken of in these many ways, it is 'reckoning.' 'It is designated' is designation. How is it designated? As 'I' …and so on… 'a window,' it is designated; thus it is 'designation.' 'It is made known' is concept. 'It is used' is conventional usage. How is it used? As 'I' …and so on… 'a window,' it is used; thus it is 'conventional usage.'

Nāmanti catubbidhaṃ nāmaṃ – sāmaññanāmaṃ guṇanāmaṃ kittimanāmaṃ opapātikanāmanti. Tattha paṭhamakappikesu mahājanena sammannitvā ṭhapitattā mahāsammatoti rañño nāmaṃ ‘sāmaññanāmaṃ’ nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “mahājanasammatoti kho, vāseṭṭha, mahāsammato tveva paṭhamaṃ akkharaṃ upanibbatta”nti (dī. ni. 3.131). Dhammakathiko [P 0.0391] paṃsukūliko vinayadharo tepiṭako saddho pasannoti evarūpaṃ guṇato āgatanāmaṃ ‘guṇanāmaṃ’ nāma. Bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddhotiādīnipi tathāgatassa anekāni nāmasatāni guṇanāmāneva. Tena vuttaṃ –

Regarding 'name,' a name is fourfold: common name, quality-based name, created name, and spontaneously arisen name. Therein, among those in the first aeon, because it was established by the consensus of the great populace, the king's name 'Mahāsammata' is called a 'common name.' This is referred to when it was said: '“Because he was approved by the great mass of people, Vāseṭṭha, the designation ‘Mahāsammata’ first arose.”' A name that comes from a quality, such as 'Dhamma-preacher,' 'rag-robe-wearer,' 'expert in the discipline,' 'master of the Tipiṭaka,' 'one with faith,' or 'one with devotion,' is called a 'quality-based name.' The many hundreds of names of the Tathāgata, such as 'the Blessed One,' 'the Arahant,' and 'the Perfectly Enlightened One,' are also indeed quality-based names. Therefore, it was said:

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti.

“Innumerable are the names of the great sage that come by way of his qualities; by a quality, a name may be discerned, even from a thousand names.”

Yaṃ pana jātassa kumārakassa nāmaggahaṇadivase dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā samīpe ṭhitā ñātakā kappetvā pakappetvā ‘ayaṃ asukonāmā’ti nāmaṃ karonti, idaṃ ‘kittimanāma’ nāma. Yā pana purimapaññatti pacchimapaññattiyaṃ patati, purimavohāro pacchimavohāre patati, seyyathidaṃ – purimakappepi cando candoyeva nāma, etarahipi candova. Atīte sūriyo… samuddo… pathavī… pabbato pabbatoyeva, nāma, etarahipi [M 0.0421] pabbatoyevāti idaṃ ‘opapātikanāmaṃ’ nāma. Idaṃ catubbidhampi nāmaṃ ettha nāmameva hoti.

But the name that relatives standing nearby, having made offerings to those worthy of offerings on the name-taking day of a newborn boy, create by devising and devising in detail, saying, 'This one is named so-and-so'—this is called a 'created name.' Furthermore, that former designation which falls into a later designation, that former usage which falls into a later usage—namely, just as in a former aeon the moon was named 'moon,' and now also it is 'moon'; in the past the sun… the ocean… the earth… a mountain was named 'mountain,' and now also it is 'mountain'—this is called a 'spontaneously arisen name.' This fourfold name is, in this context, just a single name.

Nāmakammanti nāmakaraṇaṃ. Nāmadheyyanti nāmaṭṭhapanaṃ. Niruttīti nāmanirutti. Byañjananti nāmabyañjanaṃ. Yasmā panetaṃ atthaṃ byañjeti tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Abhilāpoti nāmābhilāpova. Sabbeva dhammā adhivacanapathāti adhivacanassa nopathadhammo nāma natthi. Ekadhammo sabbadhammesu nipatati, sabbadhammā ekadhammasmiṃ nipatanti. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi nāmapaññatti ekadhammo, so sabbesu catubhūmakadhammesu nipatati. Sattopi saṅkhāropi nāmato muttako nāma natthi.

'Act of naming' is the making of a name. 'Appellation' is the establishing of a name. 'Expression' is the name that expresses the meaning. 'Articulation' is the name that makes the meaning manifest. And because this makes the meaning manifest, it is so called. 'Utterance' is just the name uttered towards the meaning. 'All phenomena are the path of designation' means there is no such thing as a phenomenon that is not a basis for designation. One phenomenon falls upon all phenomena, and all phenomena fall upon one phenomenon. How so? For this name-designation is one phenomenon, and it falls upon all phenomena of the four planes. There is no such thing as a being or a formation that is free from a name.

Aṭavīpabbatādīsu rukkhopi jānapadānaṃ bhāro. Te hi ‘ayaṃ kiṃ rukkho nāmā’ti puṭṭhā ‘khadiro’ ‘palāso’ti attanā jānanakanāmaṃ kathenti. Yassa nāmaṃ na jānanti tampi ‘anāmako’ [V 0.0414] nāmāti vadanti. Tampi tassa nāmadheyyameva hutvā tiṭṭhati. Samudde macchakacchapādīsupi eseva nayo. Itare dve dukā iminā samānatthā eva.

In places such as forests and mountains, even a tree is the responsibility of the country-folk. For when they are asked, 'What is this tree named?' they state the name known to them: 'It is a khadira,' 'It is a palāsa.' Even that of which they do not know the name, they call 'the nameless one.' And that too stands as its appellation. In the ocean, for fish, turtles, and so on, this is the very same method. The other two dyads have the same meaning as this one.

1316. Nāmarūpaduke [P 0.0392] nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena ca namanaṭṭhena ca nāmanaṭṭhena ca nāmaṃ. Tattha cattāro khandhā tāva nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena ‘nāmaṃ’. Yathā hi mahājanasammatattā mahāsammatassa mahāsammatoti nāmaṃ ahosi, yathā vā mātāpitaro ‘ayaṃ tisso nāma hotu, phusso nāma hotū’ti evaṃ puttassa kittimanāmaṃ karonti, yathā vā ‘dhammakathiko’ ‘vinayadharo’ti guṇato nāmaṃ āgacchati, na evaṃ vedanādīnaṃ. Vedanādayo hi mahāpathavīādayo viya attano nāmaṃ karontāva uppajjanti. Tesu uppannesu tesaṃ nāmaṃ uppannameva hoti. Na hi vedanaṃ uppannaṃ ‘tvaṃ vedanā nāma hohī’ti koci bhaṇati. Na ca tassā nāmaggahaṇakiccaṃ atthi. Yathā pathaviyā uppannāya ‘tvaṃ pathavī nāma hohī’ti nāmaggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi, cakkavāḷasinerucandimasūriyanakkhattesu uppannesu ‘tvaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ nāma hohi tvaṃ nakkhattaṃ nāma hohī’ti nāmaggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi, nāmaṃ uppannameva hoti, opapātikapaññattiyaṃ nipatati, evaṃ vedanāya uppannāya ‘tvaṃ vedanā nāma hohī’ti nāmaggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Tāya [M 0.0422] uppannāya vedanāti nāmaṃ uppannameva hoti. Opapātikapaññattiyaṃ nipatati. Saññādīsupi eseva nayo. Atītepi hi vedanā vedanāyeva, saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ viññāṇameva. Anāgatepi, paccuppannepi. Nibbānaṃ pana sadāpi nibbānamevāti. ‘Nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena’ nāmaṃ.

1316. In the dyad on name-and-form, 'name' is so called in the sense of making a name, in the sense of bending, and in the sense of causing to bend. Therein, the four aggregates are first 'name' in the sense of making a name. For it is not in the way that the name 'Mahāsammata' arose for Mahāsammata because he was approved by the great populace, or in the way parents create a 'created name' for a son, saying, 'Let him be named Tissa, let him be named Phussa,' or in the way a name such as 'Dhamma-preacher' or 'expert in the discipline' comes from a quality, that the names of feeling and so on come to be. For feeling and so on, like the great earth and so on, arise while making their own name. When they have arisen, their name has already arisen. For no one says to a feeling that has arisen, 'You shall be named feeling,' nor is there any task of taking a name for it. Just as when the earth has arisen there is no task of taking its name, saying, 'You shall be named earth'; and just as when the Cakkavāḷa, Sineru, the moon, the sun, and the constellations have arisen there is no task of taking their names, saying, 'You shall be named Cakkavāḷa... you shall be named constellation'—the name has already arisen, it falls under spontaneously arisen designation—so too, when feeling has arisen, there is no task of taking its name, saying, 'You shall be named feeling.' When it has arisen, the name 'feeling' has already arisen. It falls under spontaneously arisen designation. This is the same method for perception and so on. For in the past also, feeling was just feeling; perception... formations... consciousness was just consciousness. So too in the future and in the present. But Nibbāna is always just Nibbāna. Thus, 'name' is in the sense of making a name.

‘Namanaṭṭhenā’pi cettha cattāro khandhā nāmaṃ. Te hi ārammaṇābhimukhā namanti. ‘Nāmanaṭṭhena’ sabbampi nāmaṃ. Cattāro hi khandhā ārammaṇe aññamaññaṃ nāmenti. Nibbānaṃ ārammaṇādhipatipaccayatāya attani anavajjadhamme nāmeti.

Also, in the sense of inclining, the four aggregates here are 'name'. For they incline towards an object. In the sense of causing to incline, all that is mental is 'name'. For the four aggregates cause one another to incline towards an object. Nibbāna, due to being a condition of object-predominance, causes the faultless states to incline towards itself.

1318. Avijjābhavataṇhā vaṭṭamūlasamudācāradassanatthaṃ gahitā.

1318. Ignorance and craving for existence are taken in order to show the root and origin of the round of existence.

1320. Bhavissati attā ca loko cāti khandhapañcakaṃ attā ca loko cāti gahetvā ‘taṃ bhavissatī’ti gahaṇākārena niviṭṭhā sassatadiṭṭhi. Dutiyā ‘na bhavissatī’ti ākārena niviṭṭhā ucchedadiṭṭhi.

1320. Regarding 'the self and the world will exist': the eternalist view is the view established in the mode of grasping 'it will exist,' having taken the five aggregates as 'self' and 'world.' The second, the annihilationist view, is the one established in the mode of 'it will not exist.'

1326. Pubbantaṃ [P 0.0393][V 0.0415] ārabbhāti atītakoṭṭhāsaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karitvā. Iminā brahmajāle āgatā aṭṭhārasa pubbantānudiṭṭhiyo gahitā. Aparantaṃ ārabbhāti anāgatakoṭṭhāsaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karitvā. Iminā tattheva āgatā catucattālīsa aparantānudiṭṭhiyo gahitā.

1326. 'With respect to the past' means having taken the past portion as an object. By this, the eighteen views concerning the past that come in the Brahmajāla Sutta are included. 'With respect to the future' means having taken the future portion as an object. By this, the forty-four views concerning the future that come in that same sutta are included.

1332. Dovacassatāniddese sahadhammike vuccamāneti sahadhammikaṃ nāma yaṃ bhagavatā paññattaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ, tasmiṃ vatthuṃ dassetvā āpattiṃ āropetvā ‘idaṃ nāma tvaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, iṅgha desehi vuṭṭhāhi paṭikarohī’ti vuccamāne. Dovacassāyantiādīsu evaṃ codiyamānassa paṭicodanāya vā appadakkhiṇagāhitāya vā dubbacassa kammaṃ dovacassāyaṃ. Tadeva dovacassantipi vuccati. Tassa bhāvo dovacassiyaṃ. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Vippaṭikūlagāhitāti vilomagāhitā. Vilomagahaṇasaṅkhātena vipaccanīkena sātaṃ assāti vipaccanīkasāto. ‘Paṭāṇikagahaṇaṃ gahetvā ekapadeneva taṃ nissaddamakāsi’nti sukhaṃ paṭilabhantassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tassa bhāvo vipaccanīkasātatā. Ovādaṃ anādiyanavasena anādarassa bhāvo anādariyaṃ. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Anādiyanākāro vā anādaratā. Garuvāsaṃ avasanavasena uppanno agāravabhāvo agāravatā. Sajeṭṭhakavāsaṃ avasanavasena uppanno appaṭissavabhāvo appaṭissavatā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ [M 0.0423] evarūpā dovacassatā nāma vuccati. Atthato panesā tenākārena pavattā cattāro khandhā, saṅkhārakkhandhoyeva vāti. Pāpamittatādīsupi eseva nayo. Dovacassatā pāpamittatādayo hi visuṃ cetasikadhammā nāma natthi.

1332. In the exposition of being difficult to correct: 'When being admonished in accordance with the Dhamma': here 'in accordance with the Dhamma' refers to a training rule laid down by the Blessed One. When, after the matter has been pointed out and the offense charged, one is told, 'You have committed such-and-such an offense; come, you should confess it, rise from it, and make amends for it.' 'Being difficult to correct,' etc.: in such cases, when one is being reproached, the action of a person who is difficult to correct, by way of counter-reproach or by taking it ungraciously, is 'difficulty in being corrected' (dovacassāyaṃ). This is also called dovacassa. The state of this is dovacassiyaṃ. The other term (dovacassatā) is a synonym for this. 'Adopting an opposing stance' (vippaṭikūlagāhitā) is adopting a perverse stance. 'One who delights in opposition' (vipaccanīkasāto) is one for whom there is delight in what is contrary, which is characterized by adopting an opposing stance. This is a designation for one who finds pleasure in this, as in 'Having adopted a contrary position, he silenced him with a single word.' The state of this is 'delight in opposition' (vipaccanīkasātatā). The state of disrespect (anādariyaṃ) is due to not heeding advice. The other term (anādaratā) is a synonym for this. Or, the manner of not heeding is 'disrespectfulness' (anādaratā). The state of irreverence (agāravatā) arises from not dwelling with respect for one's teacher. The state of disobedience (appaṭissavatā) arises from not dwelling with deference to one's seniors. This quality of being difficult to correct is so called. In terms of ultimate reality, however, this is the four aggregates occurring in such a manner, or it is just the aggregate of formations. The same principle applies to having bad friends and so on. For being difficult to correct, having bad friends, and the like are not separate mental factors.

1333. Natthi [P 0.0394] etesaṃ saddhāti assaddhā; buddhādīni vatthūni na saddahantīti attho. Dussīlāti sīlassa dunnāmaṃ natthi, nissīlāti attho. Appassutāti sutarahitā. Pañca macchariyāni etesaṃ atthīti maccharino. Duppaññāti nippaññā. Sevanakavasena sevanā. Balavasevanā nisevanā. Sabbatobhāgena sevanā saṃsevanā. Upasaggavasena vā padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Tīhipi sevanāva kathitā. Bhajanāti upasaṅkamanā. Sambhajanāti sabbatobhāgena bhajanā. Upasaggavasena vā padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Bhattīti daḷhabhatti. Sambhattīti sabbatobhāgena bhatti. Upasaggavasena vā padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Dvīhipi daḷhabhatti eva kathitā. Taṃsampavaṅkatāti tesu puggalesu kāyena ceva cittena ca sampavaṅkabhāvo; tanninnatā tappoṇatā tappabbhāratāti attho.

1333. They have no faith, thus they are 'faithless' (assaddhā); that is, they do not place faith in the Buddha and so on. 'Unvirtuous' (dussīla): there is no 'bad name' for virtue; the meaning is they are without virtue (nissīla). 'Of little learning' (appassuta) means devoid of learning. They possess the five kinds of stinginess, thus they are 'stingy' (maccharino). 'Of little wisdom' (duppaññā) means lacking wisdom. 'Association' (sevanā) is by way of associating. 'Intimate association' (nisevanā) is strong associating. 'Thorough association' (saṃsevanā) is associating in every way. Or the word is augmented by a prefix. All three terms speak of associating. 'Resorting to' (bhajanā) is approaching. 'Thoroughly resorting to' (sambhajanā) is resorting to in every way. Or the word is augmented by a prefix. 'Devotion' (bhatti) is firm devotion. 'Complete devotion' (sambhatti) is devotion in every way. Or the word is augmented by a prefix. Both terms speak of firm devotion. 'Inclination towards them' (taṃsampavaṅkatā) means being inclined to those persons both physically and mentally; that is, being sloped towards them, bent on them, biased towards them.

1334. Sovacassatādukaniddesopi vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo.

1334. The exposition of the dyad on amenability to admonition should also be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.

1336. Pañcapi [V 0.0416] āpattikkhandhāti mātikāniddesena ‘pārājikaṃ saṅghādisesaṃ pācittiyaṃ pāṭidesanīyaṃ dukkaṭa’nti imā pañca āpattiyo. Sattapi āpattikkhandhāti vinayaniddesena ‘pārājikaṃ saṅghādisesaṃ thullaccayaṃ pācittiyaṃ pāṭidesanīyaṃ dukkaṭaṃ dubbhāsita’nti imā satta āpattiyo. Tattha saha vatthunā tāsaṃ āpattīnaṃ paricchedajānanakapaññā āpattikusalatā nāma. Saha kammavācāya āpattivuṭṭhānaparicchedajānanakapaññā pana āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā nāma.

1336. The five categories of offenses, according to the exposition in the Mātikā, are these five offenses: pārājika, saṅghādisesa, pācittiya, pāṭidesanīya, and dukkaṭa. The seven categories of offenses, according to the exposition in the Vinaya, are these seven offenses: pārājika, saṅghādisesa, thullaccaya, pācittiya, pāṭidesanīya, dukkaṭa, and dubbhāsita. Therein, the wisdom that knows the delimitation of those offenses together with their basis is called skill in offenses. But the wisdom that knows the delimitation of emerging from offenses together with the formal act is called skill in emerging from offenses.

1338. Samāpajjitabbato samāpatti. Saha parikammena appanāparicchedajānanakapaññā pana samāpattikusalatā nāma. ‘Cande vā sūriye vā nakkhatte vā ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ gate vuṭṭhahissāmī’ti avirajjhitvā tasmiṃyeva samaye vuṭṭhānakapaññāya atthitāya samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā nāma.

1338. It is an 'attainment' (samāpatti) because it is to be attained (samāpajjitabba). But the wisdom that knows the delimitation of absorption together with the preliminary work is called skill in attainment. The existence of the wisdom for emerging at that very time without failing in one's resolve—'I will emerge when the moon or the sun or a constellation has reached such and such a position'—is called skill in emerging from attainment.

1340. Aṭṭhārasannaṃ [M 0.0424][P 0.0395] dhātūnaṃ uggahamanasikārasavanadhāraṇaparicchedajānanakapaññā dhātukusalatā nāma. Tāsaṃyeva uggahamanasikārajānanakapaññā manasikārakusalatā nāma.

1340. The wisdom that knows the eighteen elements by way of learning, attention, hearing, retention, and delimitation is called skill in the elements. The wisdom that knows these same elements by way of learning and attention is called skill in attention.

1342. Dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ uggahamanasikārasavanadhāraṇaparicchedajānanakapaññā latā nāma. Tīsupi vā etāsu kusalatāsu uggaho manasikāro savanaṃ sammasanaṃ paṭivedho paccavekkhaṇāti sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha savanauggahapaccavekkhaṇā lokiyā, paṭivedho lokuttaro. Sammasanamanasikārā lokiyalokuttaramissakā. ‘Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā’tiādīni (vibha. aṭṭha. 225) paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅge āvibhavissanti. ‘Iminā pana paccayena idaṃ hotī’ti jānanakapaññā paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā nāma.

1342. The wisdom that knows the twelve bases by way of learning, attention, hearing, retention, and delimitation is called skill in the bases. Or, in these three skills, all the following are applicable: learning, attention, hearing, comprehension, penetration, and reviewing. Therein, hearing, learning, and reviewing are mundane; penetration is supramundane. Comprehension and attention are mixed, mundane and supramundane. The passage beginning 'With ignorance as condition, formations come to be' will become clear in the analysis of dependent origination. But the wisdom that knows, 'This comes to be from this as condition,' is called skill in dependent origination.

1344. Ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalatādukaniddese hetū paccayāti ubhayampetaṃ aññamaññavevacanaṃ. Cakkhupasādo hi rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjanakassa cakkhuviññāṇassa hetu ceva paccayo ca. Tathā sotapasādādayo sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ, ambabījādīni ca ambaphalādīnaṃ. Dutiyanaye ye ye dhammāti visabhāgapaccayadhammānaṃ nidassanaṃ. Yesaṃ yesanti visabhāgapaccayasamuppannadhammanidassanaṃ. Na hetū na paccayāti cakkhupasādo saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjanakassa sotaviññāṇassa na hetu na paccayo. Tathā sotapasādādayo avasesaviññāṇādīnaṃ. Ambādayo ca tālādīnaṃ uppattiyāti evamattho veditabbo.

1344. In the exposition of the pair on skill in what is possible and impossible, 'cause' and 'condition' are both synonymous terms. For the eye-sensitivity, taking a form as object, is both a cause and a condition for the arising of eye-consciousness. Similarly, ear-sensitivity and so on are for ear-consciousness and so forth, and mango seeds and so on are for mango fruits and so forth. In the second method, 'whatever phenomena' is an indication of phenomena that are dissimilar conditions. 'For whatever phenomena' is an indication of phenomena that have arisen from dissimilar conditions. 'Neither cause nor condition' means that eye-sensitivity, taking a sound as object, is neither a cause nor a condition for the arising of ear-consciousness. Similarly, ear-sensitivity and so on are not for the remaining consciousnesses and so forth, and mango seeds and so on are not for the arising of palmyra palms and so forth. This is how the meaning should be understood.

1346. Ajjavamaddavaniddese [V 0.0417] nīcacittatāti padamattameva viseso. Tassattho – mānābhāvena nīcaṃ cittaṃ assāti nīcacitto. Nīcacittassa bhāvo nīcacittatā. Sesaṃ cittujukatācittamudutānaṃ padabhājanīye āgatameva.

1346. In the exposition of uprightness and gentleness, the term 'humility of mind' is merely a specific term. Its meaning is: one whose mind is humble due to the absence of conceit is called 'humble-minded.' The state of being humble-minded is 'humility of mind.' The rest—straightness of mind and softness of mind—has already come up in the verbal analysis of the respective terms.

1348. Khantiniddese khamanakavasena khanti. Khamanākāro khamanatā. Adhivāsenti etāya, attano upari āropetvā vāsenti, na paṭibāhanti, na paccanīkatāya tiṭṭhantīti adhivāsanatā[P 0.0396]. Acaṇḍikassa bhāvo acaṇḍikkaṃ. Anasuropoti asuropo vuccati na sammāropitattā duruttavacanaṃ. Tappaṭipakkhato anasuropo suruttavācāti attho. Evamettha phalūpacārena [M 0.0425] kāraṇaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ. Attamanatā cittassāti somanassavasena cittassa sakamanatā, attano cittasabhāvoyeva, na byāpannacittatāti attho.

1348. In the exposition of patience: 'patience' (khanti) is by the power of enduring. The mode of enduring is 'endurance' (khamanatā). 'Forbearance' (adhivāsanatā) is that by which they forbear; having placed it upon themselves, they let it dwell; they do not ward it off, they do not stand in opposition. The state of being non-irascible is 'non-irascibility' (acaṇḍikkaṃ). Regarding 'non-harshness' (anasuropo): 'harshness' (asuropo) is called ill-spoken words because of not being well-composed. In opposition to that, 'non-harshness' means well-spoken words. Thus here the cause is indicated by a figurative use of the effect. 'Contentment of mind' (attamanatā cittassa) is the mind's own satisfaction by the power of gladness; it is the mind's own natural state, not a mind afflicted by ill will—this is the meaning.

1349. Soraccaniddese kāyiko avītikkamoti tividhaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ. Vācasiko avītikkamoti catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritaṃ. Kāyikavācasikoti iminā kāyavacīdvārasamuṭṭhitaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ pariyādiyati. Idaṃ vuccati soraccanti idaṃ pāpato suṭṭhu oratattā soraccaṃ nāma vuccati. Sabbopi sīlasaṃvaroti idaṃ yasmā na kevalaṃ kāyavācāheva anācāraṃ ācarati manasāpi ācarati eva, tasmā mānasikasīlaṃ pariyādāya dassetuṃ vuttaṃ.

1349. In the exposition of gentleness: 'bodily non-transgression' is the threefold good bodily conduct. 'Verbal non-transgression' is the fourfold good verbal conduct. By 'bodily and verbal,' the virtue with right livelihood as the eighth factor, which arises through the doors of body and speech, is encompassed. 'This is called gentleness': this non-transgression is called 'gentleness' (soracca) because of being well restrained from evil. 'All restraint by virtue': this was said to show the inclusion of mental virtue, since one commits misconduct not only with body and speech but also with the mind.

1350. Sākhalyaniddese aṇḍakāti yathā sadose rukkhe aṇḍakāni uṭṭhahanti, evaṃ sadosatāya khuṃsanavambhanādivacanehi aṇḍakā jātā. Kakkasāti pūtikā sā yathā nāma pūtirukkho kakkaso hoti paggharitacuṇṇo evaṃ kakkasā hoti. Sotaṃ ghaṃsayamānā viya pavisati. Tena vuttaṃ ‘kakkasā’ti. Parakaṭukāti paresaṃ kaṭukā amanāpā dosajananī. Parābhisajjanīti kuṭilakaṇṭakasākhā viya cammesu vijjhitvā paresaṃ abhisajjanī, gantukāmānampi gantuṃ adatvā lagganakārī. Kodhasāmantāti kodhassa āsannā. Asamādhisaṃvattanikāti appanāsamādhissa vā upacārasamādhissa vā asaṃvattanikā. Iti sabbānevetāni sadosavācāya vevacanāni. Tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ pahāyāti idaṃ pharusavācaṃ appajahitvā [P 0.0397] ṭhitassa antarantare pavattāpi saṇhavācā asaṇhavācā eva nāmāti dīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

1350. In the exposition of affability: 'Knotty words' (aṇḍakā) are so called because just as knots appear on a diseased tree, so knots are born from words of disparagement and contempt due to a faulty state. 'Harsh' (kakkasā): it is putrid; just as a putrid tree is harsh and flakes off powder, so too is this speech harsh. It enters the ear as if grating it. Therefore, it was said, 'harsh.' 'Caustic to others' (parakaṭukā) means it is caustic and unpleasant to others, generating aversion. 'Intensely clinging to others' (parābhisajjanī): just as a crooked, thorny branch, having repeatedly pierced the skin, clings intensely, so too this speech, having pierced, clings intensely in the minds of others; not allowing even those who wish to leave to go, it tends to snag them. 'Bordering on anger' (kodhasāmantā) means near to anger. 'Not conducive to concentration' (asamādhisaṃvattanikā) means it is not conducive to either absorption concentration or access concentration. Thus all these are synonyms for faulty speech. 'Having abandoned such speech': this was said to clarify that for one who stands without having abandoned harsh speech, even gentle speech that occurs intermittently is indeed not named gentle speech.

Neḷāti [V 0.0418] eḷaṃ vuccati doso. Nāssā eḷanti neḷā; niddosāti attho. “Neḷaṅgo setapacchādo”ti (udā. 65; saṃ. ni. 4.347; peṭako. 25) ettha vuttaneḷaṃ viya. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā, sūcivijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. Atthamadhuratāya sarīre kopaṃ ajanetvā pemaṃ janetīti pemanīyā. Hadayaṃ gacchati, appaṭihaññamānā sukhena cittaṃ pavisatīti hadayaṅgamā. Guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavāti porī. Pure saṃvaḍḍhanārī viya sukumārātipi porī. Purassa esātipi porī; nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Nagaravāsino hi [M 0.0426] yuttakathā honti. Pitimattaṃ pitāti bhātimattaṃ bhātāti vadanti. Evarūpī kathā bahuno janassa kantā hotīti bahujanakantā. Kantabhāveneva bahuno janassa manāpā cittavuḍḍhikarāti bahujanamanāpā. Yā tatthāti yā tasmiṃ puggale. Saṇhavācatāti maṭṭhavācatā. Sakhilavācatāti muduvācatā. Apharusavācatāti akakkhaḷavācatā.

'Faultless' (neḷā): a fault is called eḷa. Since it has no fault, it is neḷā; the meaning is 'flawless.' It is like the word neḷa used in the passage 'with flawless limbs and a white canopy.' 'Pleasing to the ear' (kaṇṇasukhā) means it is pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of its phrasing; it does not cause an earache like the piercing of a needle. 'Affectionate' (pemanīyā) means that due to the sweetness of its meaning it does not generate anger in the body but generates affection. 'Going to the heart' (hadayaṅgamā) means it goes to the heart; it enters the mind with ease, without being obstructed. 'Urbane' (porī): because it is full of good qualities, it is 'foremost' (pure bhavā). It is also 'urbane' because it is very refined, like a woman well-bred in the city (pure). It is also 'urbane' because it is 'of the city' (purassa esā); that is, it is the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers are speakers of what is proper. They speak of someone as 'father' out of affection, and as 'brother' out of fondness. Such speech is dear to many people, thus it is 'dear to the many' (bahujanakantā). Because it is dear, it is pleasing to many people and enhances their minds, thus it is 'pleasing to the many' (bahujanamanāpā). 'That which is there' means that which is in that person. 'Smoothness of speech' (saṇhavācatā) is polished speech. 'Friendliness of speech' (sakhilavācatā) is gentle speech. 'Non-harshness of speech' (apharusavācatā) is non-rough speech.

1351. Paṭisanthāraniddese āmisapaṭisanthāroti āmisaalābhena attanā saha paresaṃ chiddaṃ yathā pihitaṃ hoti paṭicchannaṃ evaṃ āmisena paṭisantharaṇaṃ. Dhammapaṭisanthāroti dhammassa appaṭilābhena attanā saha paresaṃ chiddaṃ yathā pihitaṃ hoti paṭicchannaṃ, evaṃ dhammena paṭisantharaṇaṃ. Paṭisanthārako hotīti dveyeva hi lokasannivāsassa chiddāni, tesaṃ paṭisanthārako hoti. Āmisapaṭisanthārena vā dhammapaṭisanthārena vāti iminā duvidhena paṭisanthārena paṭisanthārako hoti, paṭisantharati, nirantaraṃ karoti.

1351. In the exposition of hospitality: 'material hospitality' is the mending with material things in such a way that the deficiency for oneself and others, due to not receiving material things, is closed and covered. 'Dhamma hospitality' is the mending with the Dhamma in such a way that the deficiency for oneself and others, due to not receiving the Dhamma, is closed and covered. 'One becomes hospitable': indeed, there are just these two deficiencies in worldly co-existence, and one becomes a mender of them. 'By material hospitality or by Dhamma hospitality': by means of these two kinds of hospitality, one becomes a mender, one mends, one does so without interval.

Tatrāyaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya kathā – paṭisanthārakena hi bhikkhunā āgantukaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvāva paccuggantvā pattacīvaraṃ [P 0.0398] gahetabbaṃ, āsanaṃ dātabbaṃ, tālavaṇṭena bījitabbaṃ, pādā dhovitvā makkhetabbā, sappiphāṇite sati bhesajjaṃ dātabbaṃ, pānīyena pucchitabbo, āvāso paṭijaggitabbo. Evaṃ ekadesena āmisapaṭisanthāro kato nāma hoti.

Here is the traditional account from the beginning: A hospitable bhikkhu, upon seeing an incoming visitor, should go out to meet him and take his bowl and robe. A seat should be given, he should be fanned with a palm-leaf fan, his feet should be washed and anointed with oil, and if there is ghee and molasses, a tonic should be given. He should be asked about drinking water, and his dwelling place should be prepared. In this way, material hospitality is considered to have been performed in part.

Sāyaṃ pana navakatarepi attano upaṭṭhānaṃ anāgateyeva, tassa santikaṃ gantvā nisīditvā avisaye apucchitvā tassa visaye pañho pucchitabbo. ‘Tumhe katarabhāṇakā’ti apucchitvā tumhākaṃ ‘ācariyupajjhāyā kataraṃ ganthaṃ vaḷañjentī’ti pucchitvā pahonakaṭṭhāne pañho pucchitabbo. Sace kathetuṃ sakkoti iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce sakkoti sayaṃ kathetvā dātabbaṃ. Evaṃ ekadesena dhammapaṭisanthāro kato nāma hoti.

Further, in the evening, even if the more junior visitor has not yet come to one's place of attendance, one should go to him, sit down, and without asking about what is not his subject, ask a question concerning his subject. Without asking, ‘Of which reciter tradition are you?’ one should ask, ‘Which text do your teachers and preceptors use?’ and then ask a question on a point where he is capable of answering. If he is able to speak on it, that is good. If he is not able, one should speak on it oneself and give the explanation. In this way, hospitality in the Dhamma is considered to have been performed in part.

Sace [V 0.0419] attano santike vasati taṃ ādāya nibaddhaṃ piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ. Sace gantukāmo hoti punadivase gamanasabhāgena taṃ ādāya ekasmiṃ gāme piṇḍāya caritvā uyyojetabbo. Sace aññasmiṃ disābhāge bhikkhū nimantitā honti taṃ bhikkhuṃ icchamānaṃ ādāya gantabbaṃ. ‘Na [M 0.0427] mayhaṃ esā disā sabhāgā’ti gantuṃ anicchante sesabhikkhū pesetvā taṃ ādāya piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ. Attanā laddhāmisaṃ tassa dātabbaṃ. Evaṃ ‘āmisapaṭisanthāro’ kato nāma hoti.

If he is staying in one's presence, one should regularly take him along when going for alms. If he wishes to leave, on the next day one should take him along in a direction suitable for his journey, go for alms in one village, and then send him off. If bhikkhus are invited in another direction, one should take that bhikkhu along if he wishes to go. If he does not wish to go, saying, 'This direction is not suitable for me,' one should send the other bhikkhus and, taking him, go for alms. One should give him the material requisites one has obtained. In this way, 'material hospitality' is considered to have been performed in full.

Āmisapaṭisanthārakena pana attanā laddhaṃ kassa dātabbanti? Āgantukassa tāva dātabbaṃ. Sace gilāno vā avassiko vā atthi, tesampi dātabbaṃ. Ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ dātabbaṃ. Bhaṇḍagāhakassa dātabbaṃ. Sārāṇīyadhammapūrakena pana satavārampi sahassavārampi āgatāgatānaṃ therāsanato paṭṭhāya dātabbaṃ. Paṭisanthārakena pana yena yena na laddhaṃ, tassa tassa dātabbaṃ. Bahigāmaṃ nikkhamitvā jiṇṇakaṃ vā anāthaṃ bhikkhuṃ vā bhikkhuniṃ vā disvā tesampi dātabbaṃ.

But to whom should one who provides material hospitality give what one has obtained? First, it should be given to the visitor. If there is a sick person or a monk without a rains-residence, it should be given to them too. It should be given to one’s teachers and preceptors. It should be given to the keeper of the requisites. One who is fulfilling the states of cordiality, however, should give to all who come, again and again, a hundred or a thousand times, starting from the elder's seat. But the one providing hospitality should give to each and every one who has not received anything. Having gone outside the village, upon seeing an old or helpless bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, it should be given to them too.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – corehi kira guttasālagāme pahate taṅkhaṇaññeva ekā nirodhato vuṭṭhitā khīṇāsavattherī daharabhikkhuniyā bhaṇḍakaṃ gāhāpetvā mahājanena saddhiṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā ṭhitamajjhanhike nakulanagaragāmadvāraṃ [P 0.0399] patvā rukkhamūle nisīdi. Tasmiṃ samaye kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero nakulanagaragāme piṇḍāya caritvā nikkhanto theriṃ disvā bhattena āpucchi. Sā ‘patto me natthī’ti āha. Thero ‘imināva bhuñjathā’ti saha pattena adāsi. Therī bhattakiccaṃ katvā pattaṃ dhovitvā therassa datvā āha – ‘ajja tāva bhikkhācārena kilamissatha, ito paṭṭhāya pana vo bhikkhācāraparittāso nāma na bhavissati, tātā’ti. Tato paṭṭhāya therassa ūnakahāpaṇagghanako piṇḍapāto nāma na uppannapubbo. Ayaṃ ‘āmisapaṭisanthāro’ nāma.

Herein is the story. It is said that when the village of Guttasāla was attacked by robbers, at that very moment a certain elder bhikkhunī who was an arahant, having just arisen from the attainment of cessation, had a young bhikkhunī take her requisites and set out on the road with a great crowd of people. At high noon, she reached the gate of the village of Nakulanagara and sat down at the foot of a tree. At that time, the Elder Mahānāga, a resident of the Kāḷavalli Pavilion, was leaving after having gone for alms in the village of Nakulanagara. Seeing the elder bhikkhunī, he invited her with food. She said, 'I have no bowl.' The elder said, 'Please eat from this very one,' and gave it to her with the bowl. After she had finished her meal, the elder bhikkhunī washed the bowl, gave it back to the elder, and said: 'For today you will be wearied by the alms round, but from this day on, you, dear sirs, will have no such thing as anxiety about the alms round.' From that day on, alms food worth less than a kahāpaṇa never arose for the elder. This is called 'material hospitality.'

Imaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā bhikkhunā saṅgahapakkhe ṭhatvā tassa bhikkhuno kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetabbaṃ, dhammo vācetabbo, kukkuccaṃ vinodetabbaṃ, uppannaṃ kiccaṃ karaṇīyaṃ kātabbaṃ, abbhānavuṭṭhānamānattaparivāsā dātabbā. Pabbajjāraho pabbājetabbo upasampadāraho upasampādetabbo. Bhikkhuniyāpi attano santike upasampadaṃ ākaṅkhamānāya kammavācaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Ayaṃ ‘dhammapaṭisanthāro’ nāma.

Having performed this hospitality, a bhikkhu, standing on the side of helpfulness, should explain a meditation subject to that bhikkhu, recite the Dhamma, dispel his remorse, and do any arisen duty or task that should be done. Rehabilitation, emergence from an offense, penance, and probation should be given. One fit for the going forth should be given the going forth; one fit for higher ordination should be given higher ordination. It is also proper for a bhikkhunī to perform the formal act for a probationer in her presence who desires higher ordination. This is called 'hospitality in the Dhamma.'

Imehi [M 0.0428][V 0.0420] dvīhi paṭisanthārehi paṭisanthārako bhikkhu anuppannaṃ lābhaṃ uppādeti, uppannaṃ thāvaraṃ karoti, sabhayaṭṭhāne attano jīvitaṃ rakkhati coranāgarañño pattaggahaṇahattheneva aggaṃ gahetvā patteneva bhattaṃ ākiranto thero viya. Aladdhalābhuppādane pana ito palāyitvā paratīraṃ gatena mahānāgaraññā ekassa therassa santike saṅgahaṃ labhitvā puna āgantvā rajje patiṭṭhitena setambaṅgaṇe yāvajīvaṃ pavattitaṃ mahābhesajjadānavatthu kathetabbaṃ. Uppannalābhathāvarakaraṇe dīghabhāṇakaabhayattherassa hatthato paṭisanthāraṃ labhitvā cetiyapabbate corehi bhaṇḍakassa aviluttabhāve vatthu kathetabbaṃ.

By means of these two kinds of hospitality, a hospitable bhikkhu generates unarisen gain, makes arisen gain stable, and protects his own life in a place of danger, like the elder who, taking the best portion for the robber Nāga king with the very hand that accepts the bowl, scattered food with that very bowl. Regarding the generation of unobtained gain, the story should be told of King Mahānāga who, having fled from here and gone to the further shore, received support from a certain elder, and upon returning and being reestablished in his kingdom, instituted at Setambaṅgaṇa a great life-long donation of medicines. Regarding making arisen gain stable, the story should be told of how, after receiving hospitality from the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, his requisites were not plundered by robbers on Cetiyapabbata.

1352. Indriyesu aguttadvāratāniddese cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti kāraṇavasena cakkhūti laddhavohārena rūpadassanasamatthena [P 0.0400] cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvā. Porāṇā panāhu – “cakkhu rūpaṃ na passati, acittakattā; cittaṃ na passati, acakkhukattā; dvārārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭanena pana pasādavatthukena cittena passati. Īdisī panesā ‘dhanunā vijjatī’tiādīsu viya sasambhārakathā nāma hoti. Tasmā cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvā”ti ayamevettha atthoti. Nimittaggāhīti itthipurisanimittaṃ vā subhanimittādikaṃ vā kilesavatthubhūtaṃ nimittaṃ chandarāgavasena gaṇhāti, diṭṭhamatteyeva na saṇṭhāti. Anubyañjanaggāhīti kilesānaṃ anubyañjanato pākaṭabhāvakaraṇato anubyañjananti laddhavohāraṃ hatthapādasitahasitakathitaālokitavilokitādibhedaṃ ākāraṃ gaṇhāti. Yatvādhikaraṇamenantiādimhi yaṃkāraṇā yassa cakkhundriyāsaṃvarassa hetu, etaṃ puggalaṃ satikavāṭena cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ apihitacakkhudvāraṃ hutvā viharantaṃ ete abhijjhādayo dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ anubandheyyuṃ ajjhotthareyyuṃ. Tassa saṃvarāya na paṭipajjatīti tassa cakkhundriyassa satikavāṭena pidahanatthāya na paṭipajjati. Evaṃbhūtoyeva ca na rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, na cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatīti vuccati.

1352. In the exposition of unguardedness in the sense faculties, 'having seen a form with the eye' means having seen a form with eye-consciousness, which is capable of seeing a form and has acquired the designation 'eye' by way of cause. But the ancients say: 'The eye does not see a form, as it is non-mental; the mind does not see, as it lacks an eye. But one sees with the mind that is based on the sensitive matter through the impact of the sense door and its object.' This is a statement that includes the accessories, like such expressions as 'one shoots with a bow.' Therefore, the meaning here is just this: 'having seen a form with eye-consciousness.' 'He grasps the sign' means he grasps with sensual desire a sign that is a basis for the defilements, such as the sign of a woman or a man or a beautiful sign; he does not stop at what is merely seen. 'He grasps the details' means he grasps the particular features—which are called 'details' because they make the defilements manifest—such as the various modes of hands and feet, smiling, laughter, speech, glancing, and looking about. Regarding 'owing to which...': that is, for which reason, as a cause for non-restraint in the eye faculty, these states of covetousness and so on would flow in upon, pursue, and overwhelm a person who dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, with the eye-door unclosed by the gate of mindfulness. 'He does not practice for its restraint' means he does not practice for the purpose of closing the eye faculty with the gate of mindfulness. And it is just such a person who is said to 'not guard the eye faculty, not achieve restraint in the eye faculty.'

Tattha kiñcāpi cakkhundriye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā natthi, na hi cakkhupasādaṃ nissāya sati vā muṭṭhassaccaṃ vā uppajjati. Apica yadā rūpārammaṇaṃ [M 0.0429] cakkhussa āpāthamāgacchati tadā bhavaṅge dvikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā niruddhe kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ, tato vipākamanodhātu [V 0.0421] sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ, tato vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ, tato kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu [P 0.0401] voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tadanantaraṃ javanaṃ javati. Tatrāpi neva bhavaṅgasamaye na āvajjanādīnaṃ aññatarasamaye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā atthi. Javanakkhaṇe pana dussīlyaṃ vā muṭṭhassaccaṃ vā aññāṇaṃ vā akkhanti vā kosajjaṃ vā uppajjati, asaṃvaro hoti.

Herein, although in the eye faculty itself there is no restraint or non-restraint—for neither mindfulness nor a lapse of mindfulness arises dependent on the eye-sensitivity—yet, when a form-object comes into the focus of the eye, then, after the life-continuum has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element arises and ceases, accomplishing the function of adverting. Thereafter, eye-consciousness accomplishes the function of seeing; thereafter, the resultant mind-element, the function of receiving; thereafter, the resultant, rootless mind-consciousness-element, the function of investigating; thereafter, the functional, rootless mind-consciousness-element, accomplishing the function of determining, arises and ceases. Immediately after that, impulsion runs. In this process, there is no restraint or non-restraint either at the time of the life-continuum or at the time of any of the others, beginning with adverting. But at the moment of impulsion, if immorality, a lapse of mindfulness, ignorance, intolerance, or laziness arises, that is non-restraint.

Evaṃ honto pana so ‘cakkhundriye asaṃvaro’ti vuccati. Kasmā? Yasmā tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi, āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nagare catūsu dvāresu asaṃvutesu kiñcāpi antogharadvārakoṭṭhakagabbhādayo susaṃvutā, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ arakkhitaṃ agopitameva hoti. Nagaradvārena hi pavisitvā corā yadicchakaṃ kareyyuṃ. Evameva javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi, āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittānīti.

However, when it is so, that non-restraint is called 'non-restraint in the eye faculty.' Why? Because when that non-restraint is present, the door is also unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting. What is this like? It is as if, in a city with its four gates unguarded, even though the houses, gate-towers, chambers, and so on within are well-guarded, all the goods inside the city are still unprotected and unguarded. For, having entered through the city gates, robbers can do as they please. In the very same way, when immorality and other such states arise at the impulsion stage, with that non-restraint being present, the door is also unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting.

Sotena saddaṃ sutvātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Yā imesanti evaṃ saṃvaraṃ anāpajjantassa imesaṃ channaṃ indriyānaṃ yā agutti yā agopanā yo anārakkho yo asaṃvaro, athakanaṃ, apidahananti attho.

In the phrases beginning with 'having heard a sound with the ear,' this is the same method. As for 'Whatever of these': it is whatever non-guarding, whatever non-protection, whatever non-watchfulness, whatever non-restraint there is regarding these six faculties of one who does not attain restraint in this way; the meaning is non-closing, non-covering.

1353. Bhojane amattaññutāniddese idhekaccoti imasmiṃ sattaloke ekacco. Appaṭisaṅkhāti paṭisaṅkhānapaññāya ajānitvā anupadhāretvā. Ayonisoti anupāyena. Āhāranti asitapītādiajjhoharaṇīyaṃ. Āhāretīti paribhuñjati ajjhoharati. Davāyātiādi anupāyadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Anupāyena hi āhārento davatthāya madatthāya maṇḍanatthāya vibhūsanatthāya vā āhāreti, no idamatthitaṃ paṭicca. Yā tattha asantuṭṭhitāti yā tasmiṃ ayoniso āhāraparibhoge asantussanā [P 0.0402] asantuṭṭhibhāvo. Amattaññutāti amattaññubhāvo, pamāṇasaṅkhātāya mattāya ajānanaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ apaccavekkhitaparibhogavasena pavattā bhojane amattaññutā nāma vuccati.

1353. In the exposition on immoderation in eating, 'some individual here' means some individual in this world of beings. 'Without reflection' means not knowing or not considering with the wisdom of reflection. 'Unwisely' means by an improper means. 'Food' means what is to be swallowed, such as things eaten and drunk. 'He eats' means he consumes or ingests. The phrase beginning with 'for indulgence' is said to show the improper means. For one who eats by an improper means eats for the sake of indulgence, for the sake of intoxication, for the sake of adornment, or for the sake of embellishment, not with reference to this purpose. 'Whatever dissatisfaction there is' means whatever non-contentment or state of being not content there is in that unwise consumption of food. 'Immoderation' means the state of not knowing the measure, the not knowing of the measure known as the proper amount. 'This is called' means this, which occurs by way of unreflective consumption, is called 'immoderation in eating.'

1354. Indriyesu [M 0.0430] guttadvāratāniddese cakkhunātiādi vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Na nimittaggāhī hotīti chandarāgavasena vuttappakāraṃ nimittaṃ na gaṇhāti. Evaṃ sesapadānipi vuttapaṭipakkhanayeneva [V 0.0422] veditabbāni. Yathā ca heṭṭhā ‘javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati, dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi, āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittānī’ti vuttaṃ, evamidha tasmiṃ sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi guttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi, āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nagaradvāresu susaṃvutesu, kiñcāpi antogharādayo asaṃvutā honti, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ surakkhitaṃ sugopitameva hoti – nagaradvāresu pihitesu corānaṃ paveso natthi – evameva javane sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi guttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi, āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Tasmā javanakkhaṇe uppajjamānopi ‘cakkhundriye saṃvaro’ti vutto. Sotena saddaṃ sutvātiādīsupi eseva nayo.

1354. In the exposition on having guarded doors in the faculties, the phrase beginning with 'with the eye' should be understood only by the method already stated. 'He is not a grasper of signs' means he does not grasp a sign of the kind previously stated through sensual desire. Thus the remaining terms should also be understood only by the method that is the opposite of the one already stated. And just as it was stated previously, 'When immorality and other such states arise at the impulsion stage, with that non-restraint being present, the door is also unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting,' so too here, when virtue and so forth arise in that impulsion, the door is also guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting. What is this like? Just as when the city gates are well-guarded, even if the houses and so on within are unguarded, all goods within the city are well-protected and well-guarded—for when the city gates are closed, there is no entry for thieves. In the very same way, when virtue and so forth arise at the impulsion stage, the door is also guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting. Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of impulsion, this restraint is called 'restraint in the eye faculty.' In the phrases beginning with 'having heard a sound with the ear,' this is the same method.

1355. Bhojane mattaññutāniddese paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāretīti paṭisaṅkhānapaññāya jānitvā upāyena āhāraṃ paribhuñjati. Idāni taṃ upāyaṃ dassetuṃ neva davāyātiādi vuttaṃ.

1355. In the exposition on moderation in eating, the phrase 'he eats food reflectively and wisely' means: he consumes food, knowing with the wisdom of reflection and by a proper means. Now, to show that proper means, the phrase beginning with 'not for indulgence' was said.

Tattha ‘neva davāyā’ti davatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha naṭalaṅghakādayo davatthāya āhārenti nāma. Yañhi bhojanaṃ bhuttassa naccagītakabyasilokasaṅkhāto davo atirekatarena paṭibhāti, taṃ bhojanaṃ adhammena visamena pariyesitvā te āhārenti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu evaṃ na āhāreti.

Herein, 'not for indulgence' means one does not eat for the sake of indulgence. In this regard, dancers, acrobats, and the like are ones who eat for the sake of indulgence. For they, having sought unrighteously and improperly that food which, when eaten, causes indulgence—described as dancing, singing, composing poetry, and reciting verses—to appear more exceedingly, then eat it. But this monk does not eat in this way.

Na [P 0.0403] madāyāti mānamadapurisamadānaṃ vaḍḍhanatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha rājarājamahāmattā madatthāya āhārenti nāma. Te hi attano mānamadapurisamadānaṃ vaḍḍhanatthāya piṇḍarasabhojanādīni paṇītabhojanāni bhuñjanti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu evaṃ na āhāreti.

'Not for intoxication' means one does not eat for the purpose of increasing pride-intoxication and male arrogance. In this regard, kings and great ministers of kings are ones who eat for the sake of intoxication. For they consume choice foods, such as meals of rich flavor, for the purpose of increasing their own pride-intoxication and male arrogance. But this monk does not eat in this way.

Na maṇḍanāyāti sarīramaṇḍanatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha rūpūpajīviniyo mātugāmā antepurikādayo ca sappiphāṇitaṃ nāma pivanti, te hi siniddhaṃ muduṃ mandaṃ bhojanaṃ āhārenti ‘evaṃ no aṅgalaṭṭhi susaṇṭhitā [M 0.0431] bhavissati, sarīre chavivaṇṇo pasanno bhavissatī’ti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu evaṃ na āhāreti.

'Not for adornment' means one does not eat for the purpose of adorning the body. In this regard, women who live by means of their beauty, and ladies of the inner palace and the like, drink ghee and molasses. For they eat rich, soft food in small quantity, thinking, 'In this way our limb-bones will be well-formed, and the complexion of our skin will be clear.' But this monk does not eat in this way.

Na vibhūsanāyāti sarīre maṃsavibhūsanatthāya na āhāreti. Tattha nibbuddhamallamuṭṭhikamallādayo [V 0.0423] susiniddhehi macchamaṃsādīhi sarīramaṃsaṃ pīṇenti ‘evaṃ no maṃsaṃ ussadaṃ bhavissati pahārasahanatthāyā’ti. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu evaṃ sarīre maṃsavibhūsanatthāya na āhāreti.

'Not for embellishment' means: one does not eat for the sake of embellishing the body with flesh. In this regard, wrestlers, boxers, and the like fatten the flesh of their bodies with very rich fish, meat, and so on, thinking, 'Thus our flesh will become abundant for the purpose of withstanding blows.' But this monk does not eat in this way for the sake of embellishing the body with flesh.

Yāvadevāti āhārāharaṇe payojanassa paricchedaniyamadassanaṃ. Imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyāti imassa catumahābhūtikakarajakāyassa ṭhapanatthāya āhāreti. Idamassa āhārāharaṇe payojananti attho. Yāpanāyāti jīvitindriyayāpanatthāya āhāreti. Vihiṃsūparatiyāti vihiṃsā nāma abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakā khuddā. Tassā uparatiyā vūpasamanatthāya āhāreti. Brahmacariyānuggahāyāti brahmacariyaṃ nāma tisso sikkhā, sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ, tassa anuggaṇhanatthāya āhāreti.

'Just for...' indicates the definite demarcation of the purpose in taking food. 'For the maintenance of this body' means: one eats for the purpose of maintaining this body born of parents and composed of the four great elements. This is the meaning: this is one's purpose in taking food. 'For sustenance' means: one eats for the purpose of sustaining the life faculty. 'For the cessation of affliction' means: 'affliction' (vihiṃsā) is the hunger that arises from the condition of not having eaten. One eats for its cessation, for its pacification. 'For the support of the holy life' means: the 'holy life' (brahmacariya) is the three trainings and the entire Dispensation. One eats for the purpose of supporting it.

Itīti upāyanidassanaṃ; iminā upāyenāti attho. Purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmīti purāṇavedanā nāma abhuttappaccayā uppajjanakavedanā. Taṃ paṭihanissāmīti āhāreti. Navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti navavedanā nāma atibhuttappaccayena uppajjanakavedanā. Taṃ na uppādessāmīti āhāreti. Atha vā, ‘navavedanā’ nāma bhuttappaccayā [P 0.0404] nauppajjanakavedanā. Tassā anuppannāya anuppajjanatthameva āhāreti. Yātrā ca me bhavissatīti yāpanā ca me bhavissati. Anavajjatā cāti ettha atthi sāvajjaṃ atthi anavajjaṃ. Tattha adhammikapariyesanā adhammikapaṭiggahaṇaṃ adhammena paribhogoti idaṃ ‘sāvajjaṃ’ nāma. Dhammena pariyesitvā dhammena paṭiggahetvā paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanaṃ ‘anavajjaṃ’ nāma. Ekacco anavajjeyeva sāvajjaṃ karoti, ‘laddhaṃ me’ti katvā pamāṇātikkantaṃ bhuñjati. Taṃ jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi kilamati. Sakalavihāre bhikkhū tassa sarīrapaṭijagganabhesajjapariyesanādīsu ussukkaṃ āpajjanti. ‘Kiṃ ida’nti vutte ‘asukassa [M 0.0432] nāma udaraṃ uddhumāta’ntiādīni vadanti. ‘Esa niccakālampi evaṃpakatikoyeva, attano kucchipamāṇaṃ nāma na jānātī’ti nindanti garahanti. Ayaṃ anavajjeyeva sāvajjaṃ karoti nāma. Evaṃ akatvā ‘anavajjatā ca bhavissatī’ti āhāreti.

The word 'iti' indicates the means; the meaning is 'by this means.' 'And I shall ward off old feeling': 'old feeling' is the feeling that arises from the condition of not having eaten.
