One eats thinking, 'I shall ward it off.' 'And I shall not give rise to a new feeling': 'new feeling' is the feeling that arises from the condition of overeating. One eats thinking, 'I shall not give rise to it.' Alternatively, 'new feeling' is the feeling that does not arise from the condition of having eaten. One eats precisely so that this feeling, not having yet arisen, will not arise. 'And there will be sustenance for me' means: there will be continuance for me. 'And blamelessness': here, there is the blameworthy and the blameless. Among these, unrighteous seeking, unrighteous acceptance, and unrighteous consumption—this is called 'blameworthy.' To consume after seeking righteously, accepting righteously, and reflecting—this is called 'blameless.' A certain person makes what is blameless into something blameworthy. Thinking, 'I have received this,' he eats beyond the proper measure. Unable to digest it, he becomes afflicted by means of emetics, purgatives, and so on. The monks in the entire monastery become anxious in attending to his body, searching for medicine, and so on. When asked, 'What is this?' they say things like, 'So-and-so's stomach is bloated.' They censure and rebuke him, saying, 'He is always like this by nature; he does not know the measure of his own stomach.' This one is said to make what is blameless into something blameworthy. Without doing so, one eats thinking, 'And there will be blamelessness.'

Phāsuvihāro cāti etthāpi atthi phāsuvihāro atthi na phāsuvihāro. Tattha ‘āharahatthako alaṃsāṭako tatthavaṭṭako kākamāsako bhuttavamitako’ti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ bhojanaṃ na phāsuvihāro nāma. Etesu hi ‘āharahatthako’ nāma bahuṃ bhuñjitvā attano [V 0.0424] dhammatāya uṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto ‘āhara hattha’nti vadati. ‘Alaṃsāṭako’ nāma accuddhumātakucchitāya uṭṭhitopi sāṭakaṃ nivāsetuṃ na sakkoti. ‘Tatthavaṭṭako’ nāma uṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto tattheva parivaṭṭati. ‘Kākamāsako’ nāma yathā kākehi āmasituṃ sakkā hoti, evaṃ yāva mukhadvārā āhāreti. ‘Bhuttavamitako’ nāma mukhena sandhāretuṃ asakkonto tattheva vamati. Evaṃ akatvā ‘phāsuvihāro ca me bhavissatī’ti āhāreti. Phāsuvihāro nāma catūhi pañcahi ālopehi ūnūdaratā. Ettakañhi bhuñjitvā pānīyaṃ pivato cattāro iriyāpathā sukhena pavattanti. Tasmā dhammasenāpati evamāha –

'And a comfortable abiding': here too, there is a comfortable abiding and there is not a comfortable abiding. In this regard, the eating of these five brahmins—the 'Bring-Hand,' the 'Enough-Cloth,' the 'Rolls-There,' the 'Crow's-Morsel,' and the 'Eats-and-Vomits'—is called 'not a comfortable abiding.' For among them, the one called 'Bring-Hand' is one who, having eaten much and being unable to get up by himself, says, 'Bring your hand.' The 'Enough-Cloth' is one who, though he gets up, cannot put on his lower garment due to an excessively bloated stomach. The 'Rolls-There' is one who, unable to get up, just rolls around right there. The 'Crow's-Morsel' is one who eats up to the opening of his mouth, in such a way that crows could peck at the food. The 'Eats-and-Vomits' is one who, unable to hold it in his mouth, vomits right there. Without acting in this way, one eats thinking, 'And there will be a comfortable abiding for me.' A comfortable abiding is having a stomach that is four or five mouthfuls less than full. For one who eats this much and then drinks water, the four postures proceed with ease. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma said:

“Cattāro [P 0.0405] pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

Having left four or five mouthfuls uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the comfortable abiding of a resolute monk.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne aṅgāni samodhānetabbāni. ‘Neva davāyā’tihi ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, ‘na madāyā’ti ekaṃ, ‘na maṇḍanāyā’ti ekaṃ, ‘na vibhūsanāyā’ti ekaṃ, ‘yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāyā’ti ekaṃ, ‘vihiṃsūparatiyā brahmacariyānuggahāyā’ti ekaṃ, ‘iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmī’ti ekaṃ, ‘yātrā ca me bhavissatī’ti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ. Anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cāti ayamettha bhojanānisaṃso. Mahāsīvatthero panāha – heṭṭhā cattāri aṅgāni paṭikkhepo nāma. Upari pana aṭṭhaṅgāni samodhānetabbānīti – tattha ‘yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā’ti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, ‘yāpanāyā’ti ekaṃ, ‘vihiṃsūparatiyāti’ ekaṃ, ‘brahmacariyānuggahāyā’ti ekaṃ, ‘iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmī’ti ekaṃ, ‘navañca [M 0.0433] vedanaṃ na uppādessāmī’ti ekaṃ, ‘yātrā ca me bhavissatī’ti ekaṃ, ‘anavajjatā’ cāti ekaṃ. Phāsuvihāro pana bhojanānisaṃsoti. Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhārento bhojane mattaññū nāma hoti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogesu yuttappamāṇajānanavasena pavatto paccavekkhitaparibhogo bhojane mattaññutā nāma vuccati.

Furthermore, in this place, the factors should be combined. ‘Not for sport’ is one factor; ‘not for intoxication’ is one; ‘not for adornment’ is one; ‘not for embellishment’ is one; ‘just for the maintenance and continuance of this body’ is one; ‘for the cessation of discomfort and for the support of the holy life’ is one; ‘thus I shall ward off old feelings and not produce new feelings’ is one; ‘and my journey will proceed’ is one factor. Blamelessness and comfortable abiding—this is the benefit of food here. But the Great Elder Sīva said: The first four factors are called rejection. The following eight factors, however, should be combined. Here, ‘just for the maintenance of this body’ is one factor; ‘for continuance’ is one; ‘for the cessation of discomfort’ is one; ‘for supporting the holy life’ is one; ‘thus I shall ward off old feelings’ is one; ‘and not produce new feelings’ is one; ‘and my journey will proceed’ is one; and ‘blamelessness’ is one. Comfortable abiding, however, is the benefit of food. Thus, one who partakes of food endowed with these eight factors is called one who is moderate in eating. This is said to be moderation in eating: namely, this consumption with reflection that proceeds by way of knowing the suitable and proper measure in seeking, receiving, and consuming.

1356. Muṭṭhassaccaniddese asatīti sativirahitā cattāro khandhā. Ananussati appaṭissatīti upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Asaraṇatāti asaraṇākāro. Adhāraṇatāti dhāretuṃ asamatthatā. Tāya hi samannāgato puggalo ādhānappatto nidhānakkhamo na hoti. Udake alābukaṭāhaṃ [V 0.0425] viya ārammaṇe pilavatīti pilāpanatā. Saṃmusanatāti naṭṭhamuṭṭhassatitā. Tāya hi samannāgato puggalo nikkhittabhatto viya kāko, nikkhittamaṃso viya ca siṅgālo hoti.

1356. In the exposition of forgetfulness, 'lack of mindfulness' means the four aggregates devoid of mindfulness. 'Non-recollection, non-remembrance': the word is expanded by way of prefixes. 'The state of not remembering' means the mode of not remembering. 'Inability to retain' means the inability to hold. For a person endowed with this is not capable of receiving and storing. 'Floating' is so called because one floats on the object like a gourd bowl on water. 'Lapsing of memory' means the state of lost and forgotten mindfulness. For a person endowed with this is like a crow with its eyes fixed on a meal that has been set down, or like a jackal with its eyes fixed on meat that has been set down.

1361. Bhāvanābalaniddese kusalānaṃ dhammānanti [P 0.0406] bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ āsevanāti ādisevanā. Bhāvanāti vaḍḍhanā. Bahulīkammanti punappunaṃ karaṇaṃ.

1361. In the exposition of the power of development, 'of wholesome states' means of the factors of enlightenment. 'Cultivation' is initial practice. 'Development' is increasing. 'Making much of' is doing again and again.

1368. Sīlavipattiniddeso sīlasampadāniddesapaṭipakkhato veditabbo. Diṭṭhivipattiniddeso ca diṭṭhisampadāniddesapaṭipakkhato diṭṭhisampadāniddeso ca diṭṭhupādānaniddesapaṭipakkhato. Sīlavisuddhiniddeso kiñcāpi sīlasampadāniddesena samāno, tattha pana visuddhisampāpakaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha visuddhippattaṃ sīlaṃ. Sati ca sampajaññañca, paṭisaṅkhānabalañca bhāvanābalañca, samatho ca vipassanā ca, samathanimittañca paggahanimittañca, paggāho ca avikkhepo ca, sīlasampadā ca diṭṭhisampadā cāti imehi pana chahi dukehi catubhūmakāpi lokiyalokuttaradhammāva kathitā.

1368. The exposition of failure in virtue should be understood as the opposite of the exposition of accomplishment in virtue. And the exposition of failure in view as the opposite of the exposition of accomplishment in view; and the exposition of accomplishment in view as the opposite of the exposition of clinging to views. Although the exposition of purification of virtue is similar to the exposition of accomplishment in virtue, in that exposition of purification of virtue the virtue that leads to purification—the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha—is discussed, whereas here in the exposition of accomplishment in virtue it is the virtue that has attained purification. By these six dyads—mindfulness and clear comprehension; the power of reflection and the power of development; serenity and insight; the sign of serenity and the sign of exertion; exertion and non-distraction; and accomplishment in virtue and accomplishment in view—only mundane and supramundane phenomena of the four planes are explained.

1373. Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddese kammassakataññāṇanti ‘idaṃ kammaṃ sakaṃ, idaṃ no saka’nti jānanapaññā. Tattha attanā vā kataṃ hotu parena vā sabbampi akusalakammaṃ no sakaṃ. Kasmā? Atthabhañjanato anatthajananato ca. Kusalakammaṃ pana anatthabhañjanato atthajananato ca ‘sakaṃ’ nāma. Tattha yathā [M 0.0434] nāma sadhano sabhogo puriso addhānamaggaṃ paṭipajjitvā antarāmagge gāmanigamādīsu nakkhatte saṅghuṭṭhe ‘ahaṃ āgantuko, kaṃ nu kho nissāya nakkhattaṃ kīḷeyya’nti acintetvā yathā yathā icchati tena tena nīhārena nakkhattaṃ kīḷanto sukhena kantāraṃ atikkamati, evameva imasmiṃ kammassakataññāṇe ṭhatvā ime sattā bahuṃ vaṭṭagāmikammaṃ āyūhitvā sukhena sukhaṃ anubhavantā arahattaṃ pattā gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā. Saccānulomikañāṇanti [P 0.0407] catunnaṃ saccānaṃ anulomaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇaṃ phalasamaṅgissa ñāṇanti maggañāṇaphalañāṇāniyeva.

1373. In the exposition of the purification of view, the knowledge of ownership of kamma is the wisdom that knows, “This kamma is my own; this is not my own.” Here, any unwholesome kamma, whether done by oneself or by another, is not one’s own. Why? Because it destroys what is beneficial and generates what is unbeneficial. Wholesome kamma, however, is called “one’s own” because it destroys what is unbeneficial and generates what is beneficial. For just as a man with wealth and possessions, having set out on a long road, when a festival is proclaimed in a village or town on the way, without thinking, “I am a newcomer; on whom should I depend to enjoy the festival?” enjoys the festival in whatever way he wishes and happily crosses the wilderness; so too, standing firm in this knowledge of ownership of kamma, beings who have accumulated much kamma leading to the round, experiencing happiness from happiness, have attained arahantship and passed beyond the range of reckoning. Knowledge in conformity with the truths is the insight knowledge that is in conformity with the four truths. The knowledge of one endowed with the path and the knowledge of one endowed with the fruit are just the path knowledge and the fruit knowledge.

1374. ‘Diṭṭhivisuddhi kho panā’tipadassa niddese yā paññā pajānanātiādīhi padehi heṭṭhā vuttāni kammassakataññāṇādīneva cattāri ñāṇāni vibhattāni.

1374. In the exposition of the phrase, “Now, purification of view,” the four knowledges mentioned above—the knowledge of ownership of kamma and so on—are analyzed by the terms “wisdom, understanding,” and so on.

1375. ‘Yathādiṭṭhissa [V 0.0426] ca padhāna’nti padassa niddese yo cetasiko vīriyārambhotiādīhi padehi niddiṭṭhaṃ vīriyaṃ paññāgatikameva; paññāya hi lokiyaṭṭhāne lokiyaṃ lokuttaraṭṭhāne lokuttaranti veditabbaṃ.

1375. In the exposition of the phrase, “and the striving of one who sees thus,” the energy indicated by such terms as “the mental arousal of energy” is of the same nature as the associated wisdom; for it should be understood that wisdom is mundane in a mundane context and supramundane in a supramundane context.

1376. Saṃvegadukaniddese jātibhayanti jātiṃ bhayato disvā ṭhitañāṇaṃ. Jarāmaraṇabhayādīsupi eseva nayo.

1376. In the exposition of the dyad on spiritual urgency, fear of birth is the knowledge established by seeing birth as a danger. The same method applies to the fear of aging, death, and so on.

1377. Anuppannānaṃ pāpakānantiādīhi jātiādīni bhayato disvā jātijarābyādhimaraṇehi muccitukāmassa upāyapadhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Padabhājanīyassa panattho vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 367 bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā) āvi bhavissati.

1377. By such phrases as “of unarisen evil states,” the striving that is the means is explained for one who, seeing birth and so on as fearful, desires to be released from birth, aging, sickness, and death. The meaning of the verbal analysis, however, will become clear in the commentary to the Vibhaṅga.

1378. ‘Asantuṭṭhitā ca kusalesu dhammesū’ti padaniddese bhiyyokamyatāti visesakāmatā. Idhekacco hi āditova pakkhikabhattaṃ vā salākabhattaṃ vā uposathikaṃ vā pāṭipadikaṃ vā deti, so tena asantuṭṭho hutvā puna dhurabhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ vassāvāsikaṃ deti, āvāsaṃ kāreti, cattāropi paccaye deti. Tatrāpi asantuṭṭho hutvā saraṇāni gaṇhāti, pañca sīlāni samādiyati. Tatrāpi asantuṭṭho hutvā pabbajati. Pabbajitvā ekaṃ nikāyaṃ dve nikāyeti tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ gaṇhāti, aṭṭha samāpattiyo bhāveti, vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhāti[M 0.0435]. Arahattappattito paṭṭhāya mahāsantuṭṭho nāma hoti. Evaṃ yāva arahattā visesakāmatā ‘bhiyyokamyatā’ nāma.

1378. In the exposition of the phrase, “and discontent with wholesome states,” desire for more means the desire for distinction. Here, someone at first gives a fortnightly meal, or a ticket-meal, or an Uposatha-day meal, or a first-day-of-the-fortnight meal. Being discontent with that, he then gives a regular meal, a meal for the Sangha, or a rains-residence robe; he has a dwelling built; he provides the four requisites. Still being discontent, he goes for refuge and undertakes the five precepts. Still being discontent, he goes forth. Having gone forth, he masters one Nikāya, two Nikāyas, and then the entire Tipiṭaka, the Word of the Buddha. He develops the eight attainments, cultivates insight, and attains arahantship. From the attainment of arahantship onwards, he is called one who is greatly content. Thus, the desire for distinction up to arahantship is called “desire for more.”

1379. ‘Appaṭivānitā ca padhānasmi’nti padassa niddese yasmā pantasenāsanesu adhikusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya ukkaṇṭhamāno padhānaṃ paṭivāseti nāma[P 0.0408], anukkaṇṭhamāno no paṭivāseti nāma, tasmā taṃ nayaṃ dassetuṃ yā kusalānaṃ dhammānantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sakkaccakiriyatāti kusalānaṃ karaṇe sakkaccakāritā. Sātaccakiriyatāti satatameva karaṇaṃ. Aṭṭhitakiriyatāti khaṇḍaṃ akatvā aṭṭhapetvā karaṇaṃ. Anolīnavuttitāti alīnajīvitā, alīnapavattitā vā. Anikkhittachandatāti kusalacchandassa anikkhipanaṃ. Anikkhittadhuratāti kusalakaraṇe vīriyadhurassa anikkhipanaṃ.

1379. In the exposition of the phrase, “and unremittingness in striving”: since one who is weary when developing highly wholesome states in remote lodgings recoils from striving, while one who is not weary does not recoil, therefore, to show this method, the passage beginning “of wholesome states” was stated. Therein, acting respectfully means acting with respect when doing wholesome deeds. Acting continuously means doing them constantly. Acting without interruption means doing them without a break, without setting them aside. Unyielding conduct means a non-sluggish life, or non-sluggish behavior. Not casting off desire means not abandoning wholesome desire. Not casting off the yoke means not abandoning the yoke of energy in doing what is wholesome.

1380. ‘Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ [V 0.0427] vijjā’ti ettha pubbenivāsoti pubbe nivutthakkhandhā ca khandhapaṭibaddhañca. Pubbenivāsassa anussati pubbenivāsānussati. Tāya sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ. Tayidaṃ pubbe nivutthakkhandhapaṭicchādakaṃ tamaṃ vijjhatīti vijjā. Taṃ tamaṃ vijjhitvā te khandhe vidite pākaṭe karotīti viditakaraṇaṭṭhenāpi vijjā.

1380. In the phrase ‘the knowledge of the recollection of past abodes is a true knowledge’: Herein, ‘past abodes’ means the aggregates previously lived in and what is connected with the aggregates. The recollection of past abodes is ‘pubbenivāsānussati.’ The knowledge associated with that is the ‘knowledge of the recollection of past abodes.’ This pierces (vijjhati) the darkness that conceals the aggregates previously lived in; therefore, it is a true knowledge (vijjā). Having pierced that darkness, it makes those aggregates known (vidita) and manifest; hence, it is also a true knowledge in the sense of making known.

Cutūpapāte ñāṇanti cutiyañca upapāte ca ñāṇaṃ. Idampi sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhicchādakaṃ tamaṃ vijjhatīti vijjā. Taṃ tamaṃ vijjhitvā sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhiyo viditā pākaṭā karotīti viditakaraṇaṭṭhenāpi vijjā. Āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇanti sabbakilesānaṃ khayasamaye ñāṇaṃ. Tayidaṃ catusaccacchādakatamaṃ vijjhatīti vijjā. Taṃ tamaṃ vijjhitvā cattāri saccāni viditāni pākaṭāni karotīti viditakaraṇaṭṭhenāpi vijjā.

Knowledge of passing away and reappearance is knowledge of passing away and of reappearance. This too pierces (vijjhati) the darkness that conceals the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings; therefore, it is a true knowledge (vijjā). Having pierced that darkness, it makes the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings known (vidita) and manifest; hence, it is also a true knowledge in the sense of making known. Knowledge of the destruction of the taints is the knowledge at the moment of the destruction of all defilements. This pierces (vijjhati) the darkness that conceals the four truths; therefore, it is a true knowledge (vijjā). Having pierced that darkness, it makes the four truths known (vidita) and manifest; hence, it is also a true knowledge in the sense of making known.

1381. ‘Cittassa [P 0.0409] ca adhimutti nibbānañcā’ti ettha ārammaṇe adhimuccanaṭṭhena, paccanīkadhammehi ca suṭṭhumuttaṭṭhena aṭṭha samāpattiyo cittassa adhimutti nāma. Itaraṃ pana ‘natthi ettha taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ vānaṃ’, ‘niggataṃ vā tasmā vānā’ti nibbānaṃ. Tattha aṭṭha samāpattiyo sayaṃ vikkhambhitakilesehi vimuttattā vimuttīti vuttā, nibbānaṃ pana sabbakilesehi accantaṃ vimuttattā vimuttīti.

1381. In the phrase ‘the mind’s resolution and Nibbāna’: here, the eight attainments are called the mind’s resolution because they are resolved upon their object and because they are well freed from opposing states. The other, however, is Nibbāna because “there is no `vāna` called craving here,” or because “it has departed from that `vāna`.” Therein, the eight attainments are called liberation (`vimutti`) because they are liberated from the defilements they have suppressed, but Nibbāna is called liberation because it is utterly liberated from all defilements.

1382. Maggasamaṅgissa [M 0.0436] ñāṇanti cattāri maggañāṇāni. Phalasamaṅgissa ñāṇanti cattāri phalañāṇāni. Tattha paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ pañca kilese khepentaṃ nirodhentaṃ vūpasamentaṃ paṭippassambhentaṃ uppajjatīti khaye ñāṇaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Dutiyamaggañāṇaṃ cattāro kilese. Tathā tatiyamaggañāṇaṃ. Catutthamaggañāṇaṃ pana aṭṭha kilese khepentaṃ nirodhentaṃ vūpasamentaṃ paṭippassambhentaṃ uppajjatīti ‘khaye ñāṇaṃ’ nāma jātaṃ. Taṃ taṃ maggaphalañāṇaṃ pana tesaṃ tesaṃ kilesānaṃ khīṇante niruddhante vūpasamante paṭippassambhante anuppādante appavattante uppannanti anuppāde ñāṇaṃ nāma jātanti.

1382. The knowledge of one endowed with the path means the four path knowledges. The knowledge of one endowed with fruition means the four fruition knowledges. Therein, the first path knowledge arises destroying, bringing to an end, pacifying, and tranquillizing five defilements—thus, what is called the ‘knowledge of destruction’ has arisen. The second path knowledge destroys four defilements. Likewise, the third path knowledge. But the fourth path knowledge arises destroying, bringing to an end, pacifying, and tranquillizing eight defilements—thus, what is called the ‘knowledge of destruction’ has arisen. But each respective fruition knowledge arises when those respective defilements have been destroyed, have ceased, have been pacified, have been tranquillized, are unarisen, and do not occur—thus, what is called the ‘knowledge of non-arising’ has arisen.

Aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaaṭṭhakathāya

In the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī

Nikkhepakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nikkhepakaṇḍa is finished.

4. Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍo

4. The Commentary Section

Tikaatthuddhāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Extraction of Meaning of the Triads

1384. Idāni [M 0.0437][V 0.0428] nikkhepakaṇḍānantaraṃ ṭhapitassa aṭṭhakathākaṇḍassa vaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto. Kasmā panetaṃ aṭṭhakathākaṇḍaṃ nāma jātanti? Tepiṭakassa buddhavacanassa atthaṃ uddharitvā ṭhapitattā. Tīsupi hi piṭakesu dhammantaraṃ āgataṃ aṭṭhakathākaṇḍeneva paricchinditvā vinicchitaṃ suvinicchitaṃ nāma hoti. Sakale abhidhammapiṭake nayamaggaṃ mahāpakaraṇe pañhuddhāraṃ gaṇanacāraṃ asallakkhentenāpi aṭṭhakathākaṇḍatoyeva samānetuṃ vaṭṭati.

1384. Now the turn for the explanation of the Commentary Section, which was established after the Section on Deposition, has arrived. But why has this come to be called the Commentary Section? Because the meaning of the Buddha's word in the Tipiṭaka has been extracted and established. For in the three Piṭakas, any different point of Dhamma that has come up is delimited by the Commentary Section alone and becomes decided, well-decided. Even one who does not discern the path of method in the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the extraction of questions in the Mahāpakaraṇa, and the course of enumeration, can still reconcile them from the Commentary Section alone.

Kuto [P 0.0410] pabhavaṃ pana etanti? Sāriputtattherappabhavaṃ. Sāriputtatthero hi ekassa attano saddhivihārikassa nikkhepakaṇḍe atthuddhāraṃ sallakkhetuṃ asakkontassa aṭṭhakathākaṇḍaṃ kathetvā adāsi. Idaṃ pana mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhipitvā idaṃ vuttaṃ – abhidhammo nāma na sāvakavisayo, na sāvakagocaro; buddhavisayo esa, buddhagocaro. Dhammasenāpati pana saddhivihārikena pucchito taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā sammāsambuddhassa kathesi. Sammāsambuddho tassa bhikkhuno aṭṭhakathākaṇḍaṃ kathetvā adāsi. Kathaṃ? Bhagavā hi ‘katame dhammā kusalā’ti pucchi. ‘Kusalā dhammā nāma katame’ti sallakkhesīti attho. Athassa tuṇhībhūtassa ‘nanu yaṃ mayā katame dhammā kusalā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotītiādinā nayena bhūmibhedato kusalaṃ dassitaṃ, sabbampi taṃ catūsu bhūmīsu kusalaṃ, ime dhammā kusalā’ti iminā nayena kaṇṇikaṃ kaṇṇikaṃ ghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ gocchakaṃ gocchakaṃ katvā atthuddhāravasena kusalādidhamme dassento kathetvā adāsi.

But what is the origin of this? It originates from the Elder Sāriputta. For the Elder Sāriputta taught and gave the Commentary Section to one of his own co-resident pupils who was unable to discern the extraction of meaning in the Section on Deposition. This, however, was rejected in the Great Commentary, where it was said: 'The Abhidhamma is not the domain of disciples, nor their sphere; it is the domain of the Buddha, the sphere of the Buddha.' The General of the Dhamma, however, when questioned by his co-resident pupil, took him to the Teacher's presence and related it to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One then taught and gave the Commentary Section to that monk. How? For the Blessed One asked, 'Which phenomena are wholesome?' The meaning is: 'He should consider which phenomena are wholesome.' Then, to him who remained silent: 'Is it not so that I have shown what is wholesome by the method beginning, “Which phenomena are wholesome? At the time when a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense-sphere arises…,” according to the divisions of the planes? All of that wholesome in the four planes—these phenomena are wholesome.' By this method, making it into portions, groups, and clusters, pointing out wholesome and other phenomena by way of extracting the meaning, he taught and gave it.

Tattha [V 0.0429] catūsūti kāmāvacararūpāvacarārūpāvacaraapariyāpannāsu. Kusalanti phassādibhedaṃ kusalaṃ. Ime dhammā kusalāti ime sabbepi tāsu tāsu bhūmīsu vuttā phassādayo dhammā kusalā nāma.

Therein, 'in the four' refers to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the supramundane. The term 'wholesome' refers to that which is differentiated as contact and so on. 'These phenomena are wholesome' means: all these phenomena, such as contact and others, mentioned in their respective planes, are called 'wholesome'.

1385. Akusalānaṃ pana bhūmivasena bhedābhāvato dvādasa akusalacittuppādāti āha. Tattha uppajjatīti uppādo. Cittameva uppādo [M 0.0438] cittuppādo. Desanāsīsameva cetaṃ. Yathā pana ‘rājā āgato’ti vutte amaccādīnampi āgamanaṃ vuttameva hoti, evaṃ ‘cittuppādā’ti vutte tehi sampayuttadhammāpi vuttāva hontīti. Sabbattha cittuppādaggahaṇena sasampayuttadhammaṃ cittaṃ gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Ito paraṃ catūsu bhūmīsu vipākotiādīnaṃ sabbesampi tikadukabhājanīyapadānaṃ attho, vedanāttikādīsu ca sukhādīnaṃ navattabbatā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva pāḷiyatthaṃ [P 0.0411] vīmaṃsitvā veditabbā. Visesamattameva pana vakkhāma.

1385. But because there is no division by way of planes for unwholesome states, he said, 'twelve unwholesome consciousness-arisings.' Therein, 'it arises' (uppajjati), thus it is an 'arising' (uppādo). Consciousness (citta) itself is an arising (uppādo), hence 'consciousness-arising' (cittuppādo). And this is just a heading of the teaching. Just as when it is said, 'The king has arrived,' the arrival of his ministers and so on is also said to have happened, so too when 'consciousness-arisings' is said, the phenomena associated with them are also said to have been mentioned. In all cases, it should be understood that by the term 'consciousness-arising,' the consciousness together with its associated phenomena is included. From here onward, the meaning of all terms for classifying the triads and dyads—such as 'resultant in the four planes,' etc.—and in the Feeling Triad and the like, the 'not-to-be-stated' nature of terms such as 'pleasure,' etc., should be understood by investigating the meaning of the Pāḷi text in the way explained before. We will, however, speak only of the special points.

1420. Tattha parittārammaṇattike tāva sabbo kāmāvacarassa vipākoti ettha dvipañcaviññāṇāni cakkhupasādādayo nissāya niyameneva iṭṭhāniṭṭhādibhede rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbadhamme ārabbha pavattantīti parittārammaṇāni. Kusalākusalavipākā pana dve manodhātuyo hadayavatthuṃ nissāya cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ anantarā niyamato rūpādīneva ārabbha pavattantīti parittārammaṇā. Kusalavipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu somanassasahagatā pañcadvāre santīraṇavasena chasu dvāresu tadārammaṇavasenāti niyamato rūpādīni cha parittārammaṇāneva ārabbha pavattatīti parittārammaṇā. Kusalākusalavipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātudvayaṃ pañcadvāre santīraṇavasena chasu dvāresu tadārammaṇavasena niyamato rūpādīni cha parittārammaṇāneva ārabbha pavattati. Paṭisandhivasena pavattamānampi parittaṃ kammaṃ kammanimittaṃ gatinimittaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ karoti, pavattiyaṃ bhavaṅgavasena, pariyosāne cutivasena pavattamānampi tadeva ārammaṇaṃ karotīti parittārammaṇaṃ. Aṭṭha pana sahetukavipākacittuppādā ettha vuttanayeneva tadārammaṇavasena paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena ca parittadhammeyeva ārabbha pavattanti. Kiriyamanodhātu pañcadvāre rūpādīni ārabbha pavattati. Somanassasahagatāhetukakiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu chasu dvāresu paccuppanne manodvāre atītānāgatepi paritte rūpādidhammeyeva ārabbha khīṇāsavānaṃ pahaṭṭhākāraṃ kurumānā pavattatīti parittārammaṇā. Evamime pañcavīsati cittuppādā ekanteneva parittārammaṇāti veditabbā.

1420. Therein, first, in the triad of limited objects, concerning the statement 'all are sense-sphere resultants': here, the two sets of fivefold consciousness, dependent on the eye-sensitivity, etc., invariably arise taking as their object phenomena such as visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects, which are distinguished as desirable, undesirable, etc.; thus they have limited objects. The two mind-elements that are wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant, dependent on the heart-base, arise immediately after eye-consciousness, etc., invariably taking as their object only visible forms, etc.; thus they have limited objects. The wholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy, functioning as investigating in the five sense-doors and as registration in the six doors, invariably arises taking as its object only the six limited objects, visible forms, etc.; thus it has a limited object. The pair of wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness-elements, functioning as investigating in the five sense-doors and as registration in the six doors, invariably arises taking as its object only the six limited objects, visible forms, etc. When arising by way of rebirth-linking, it takes as object a limited kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign; during the course of life, when arising by way of the life-continuum, and at the end, when arising by way of death, it takes that same object; thus it has a limited object. The eight resultant consciousness-arisings with roots, in the way stated here, arise taking only limited phenomena as their object, whether functioning by way of registration, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, or death. The functional mind-element arises in the five sense-doors taking visible forms, etc., as its object. The rootless functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy arises taking as its object only limited phenomena such as visible form, etc.—present in the six doors, or past and future in the mind-door—and produces a pleased expression for the arahants; thus it has a limited object. In this way, these twenty-five consciousness-arisings should be understood as invariably having limited objects.

1421. Viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanadhammā [V 0.0430] attano attano heṭṭhimaṃ samāpattiṃ ārabbha pavattanato [P 0.0412] mahaggatārammaṇā. Eva maggaphaladhammā nibbānārammaṇattā appamāṇārammaṇā.

1421. The phenomena of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have exalted objects because they arise taking their own respective lower meditative attainments as object. Similarly, the path and fruition phenomena have immeasurable objects because they have Nibbāna as their object.

Kusalato [M 0.0439] cattāro kiriyato cattāroti aṭṭha ñāṇavippayuttacittuppādā sekkhaputhujjanakhīṇāsavānaṃ asakkaccadānapaccavekkhaṇadhammasavanādīsu kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha pavattikāle parittārammaṇā. Atipaguṇānaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle mahaggatārammaṇā. Kasiṇanimittādipaññattipaccavekkhaṇakāle navattabbārammaṇā. Akusalato cattāro diṭṭhigatasampayuttacittuppādā pañcapaṇṇāsāya kāmāvacaradhammānaṃ ‘satto satto’ti parāmasanaassādanābhinandanakāle parittārammaṇā. Tenevākārena sattavīsati mahaggatadhamme ārabbha pavattikāle mahaggatārammaṇā. Paṇṇattidhamme ārabbha pavattanakāle siyā navattabbārammaṇā. Diṭṭhivippayuttānaṃ teyeva dhamme ārabbha kevalaṃ assādanābhinandanavasena, pavattiyaṃ paṭighasampayuttānaṃ domanassavasena, vicikicchāsampayuttacittuppādassa aniṭṭhaṅgatavasena, uddhaccasahagatassa vikkhepavasena avūpasamavasena ca pavattiyaṃ parittamahaggatanavattabbārammaṇatā veditabbā. Etesu pana ekadhammopi appamāṇe ārabbha pavattituṃ na sakkoti, tasmā na appamāṇārammaṇā.

Four wholesome and four functional, thus eight consciousness-arisings dissociated from knowledge, for trainees, worldlings, and arahants, have limited objects when they arise taking sense-sphere phenomena as object in such cases as giving disrespectfully, reviewing, listening to the Dhamma, etc. For those who are very skilled, at the time of reviewing the first jhānas, etc., they have exalted objects. At the time of reviewing concepts such as kasiṇa-signs, they have 'not-to-be-stated' objects. Four unwholesome consciousness-arisings associated with wrong view have limited objects at the time of misapprehending, savoring, and delighting in the fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena with the notion 'a being, a being.' In the same way, they have exalted objects when they arise taking the twenty-seven exalted phenomena as object. When they arise taking conceptual phenomena as object, they may have 'not-to-be-stated' objects. For those consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view, when they arise taking those same phenomena as object merely by way of savoring and delighting; for those associated with aversion, by way of displeasure; for the consciousness-arising associated with doubt, by way of indecisiveness; and for that accompanied by restlessness, by way of distraction and non-pacification—in these cases it should be understood that they have limited, exalted, or 'not-to-be-stated' objects. However, not even one of these phenomena can arise taking an immeasurable object. Therefore, they do not have immeasurable objects.

Kusalato cattāro kiriyato cattāroti aṭṭha ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādā sekkhaputhujjanakhīṇāsavānaṃ sakkaccadānapaccavekkhaṇadhammasavanādīsu yathāvuttappakāre dhamme ārabbha pavattikāle parittamahaggatanavattabbārammaṇā honti. Gotrabhukāle lokuttaradhamme paccavekkhaṇakāle ca nesaṃ appamāṇārammaṇatā veditabbā.

Four wholesome and four functional, thus eight consciousness-arisings associated with knowledge, for trainees, worldlings, and arahants, have limited, exalted, or 'not-to-be-stated' objects when they arise taking as object phenomena of the kind already mentioned in such cases as giving respectfully, reviewing, listening to the Dhamma, etc. At the time of change-of-lineage and when reviewing supramundane phenomena, it should be understood that they have immeasurable objects.

Yaṃ panetaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ taṃ sabbatthapādakacatutthaṃ ākāsakasiṇacatutthaṃ ālokakasiṇacatutthaṃ brahmavihāracatutthaṃ ānāpānacatutthaṃ [P 0.0413] iddhividhacatutthaṃ dibbasotacatutthaṃ cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ yathākammupagañāṇacatutthaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇacatutthaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇacatutthaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthanti kusalatopi kiriyatopi dvādasavidhaṃ hoti.

Now, that fourth jhāna of the form realm is twelvefold, both as wholesome and as functional: the fourth jhāna that is a foundation everywhere, the fourth of the space kasiṇa, the fourth of the light kasiṇa, the fourth of the divine abidings, the fourth of mindfulness of breathing, the fourth of the modes of supernormal power, the fourth of the divine ear, the fourth of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, the fourth of the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their kamma, the fourth of the divine eye, the fourth of the knowledge of past lives, and the fourth of the knowledge of the future.

Tattha ‘sabbatthapādakacatutthaṃ’ nāma aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu catutthajjhānaṃ. Tañhi vipassanāyapi pādakaṃ [V 0.0431] hoti, abhiññānampi, nirodhassāpi, vaṭṭassāpi pādakaṃ hotiyevāti sabbatthapādakanti vuttaṃ. ‘Ākāsakasiṇaālokakasiṇacatutthāni’ pana vipassanāyapi abhiññānampi vaṭṭassāpi pādakāni [M 0.0440] honti, nirodhapādakāneva na honti. ‘Brahmavihāraānāpānacatutthāni’ vipassanāya ceva vaṭṭassa ca pādakāni honti, abhiññānaṃ pana nirodhassa ca pādakāni na honti. Tattha dasavidhampi kasiṇajjhānaṃ kasiṇapaṇṇattiṃ ārabbha pavattattā, brahmavihāracatutthaṃ sattapaṇṇattiṃ ārabbha pavattattā, ānāpānacatutthaṃ nimittaṃ ārabbha pavattattā parittādivasena navattabbadhammārammaṇato navattabbārammaṇaṃ nāma hoti.

Here, ‘the fourth jhāna that is a foundation everywhere’ refers to the fourth jhāna in the eight kasiṇas. For it serves as a foundation for insight, for the higher knowledges, for cessation, and also for the round of existence—hence it is called a 'foundation everywhere.' The ‘fourth jhānas of the space kasiṇa and light kasiṇa,’ however, serve as foundations for insight, for the higher knowledges, and for the round of existence, but they do not serve as foundations for cessation. The ‘fourth jhānas of the divine abidings and mindfulness of breathing’ serve as foundations for insight and for the round of existence, but not for the higher knowledges and for cessation. Among these, since all ten kinds of kasiṇa jhāna arise taking a kasiṇa concept as object, the fourth jhāna of the divine abidings arises taking a being concept as object, and the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing arises taking the sign as object, they are called 'having a not-to-be-stated object' because their object is a phenomenon that is not-to-be-stated by way of being limited, etc.

‘Iddhividhacatutthaṃ’ parittamahaggatārammaṇaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Tañhi yadā kāyaṃ cittasannissitaṃ katvā adissamānena kāyena gantukāmo cittavasena kāyaṃ pariṇāmeti, mahaggatacitte samodahati, samāropeti, tadā upayogaladdhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hotīti katvā rūpakāyārammaṇato parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Yadā cittaṃ kāyasannissitaṃ katvā dissamānena kāyena gantukāmo kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmeti, pādakajjhānacittaṃ rūpakāye samodahati, samāropeti, tadā upayogaladdhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hotīti katvā mahaggatacittārammaṇato mahaggatārammaṇaṃ hoti.

The fourth jhāna of the modes of supernormal power has a limited or exalted object. How? For when one, wishing to go with an invisible body, makes the body dependent on the mind, transforms the body by means of the mind, and places and establishes it in an exalted consciousness, at that time the body obtained through application becomes the object. Thus, because its object is the material body, it has a limited object. When one, wishing to go with a visible body, makes the mind dependent on the body, transforms the mind by means of the body, and places and establishes the foundational jhāna-consciousness in the material body, at that time the mind obtained through application becomes the object. Thus, because its object is the exalted consciousness, it has an exalted object.

‘Dibbasotacatutthaṃ’ saddaṃ ārabbha pavattattā ekantaparittārammaṇameva. ‘Cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ’ parittamahaggataappamāṇārammaṇaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Tañhi [P 0.0414] paresaṃ kāmāvacaracittajānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti, rūpāvacarārūpāvacaracittajānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ, maggaphalajānanakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ hoti. Ettha ca puthujjano sotāpannassa cittaṃ na jānāti, sotāpanno vā sakadāgāmissāti evaṃ yāva arahato netabbaṃ. Arahā pana sabbesaṃ cittaṃ jānāti. Aññopi ca uparimo heṭṭhimassāti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo. ‘Yathākammupagañāṇacatutthaṃ’ kāmāvacarakammajānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti, rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakammajānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ.

The fourth jhāna of the divine ear, because it arises taking sound as its object, has exclusively a limited object. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds has limited, exalted, and immeasurable objects. How? For when knowing the sense-sphere minds of others, it has a limited object; when knowing their form-sphere or formless-sphere minds, it has an exalted object; when knowing path and fruition minds, it has an immeasurable object. And here, a worldling does not know the mind of a stream-enterer; a stream-enterer, in turn, does not know the mind of a once-returner; and so it should be understood up to the Arahant. An Arahant, however, knows the minds of all. Furthermore, this distinction should be understood: any higher person knows the mind of a lower person. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of beings' faring according to their kamma has a limited object when knowing sense-sphere kamma, and an exalted object when knowing form-sphere or formless-sphere kamma.

‘Dibbacakkhuñāṇacatutthaṃ’ rūpārammaṇattā ekantaparittārammaṇameva. ‘Pubbenivāsañāṇacatutthaṃ’ parittamahaggataappamāṇanavattabbārammaṇaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Tañhi kāmāvacarakkhandhānussaraṇakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakkhandhānussaraṇakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ. Atīte attanā vā parehi vā bhāvitamaggaṃ sacchikataphalañca anussaraṇakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Atīte buddhā maggaṃ [V 0.0432] bhāvayiṃsu, phalaṃ sacchākaṃsu, nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyiṃsūti [M 0.0441] chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇavasena maggaphalanibbānapaccavekkhaṇatopi appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Atīte ‘vipassī nāma bhagavā’ ahosi[P 0.0415]. Tassa ‘bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, bandhumā nāma rājā pitā, bandhumatī nāma mātā’tiādinā nayena nāmagottapathavīnimittādianussaraṇakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ hoti.

The fourth jhāna of the divine eye, because it has form as its object, has exclusively a limited object. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of past lives has limited, exalted, immeasurable, and ineffable objects. How? For at the time of recollecting the aggregates of the sense-sphere, it has a limited object. At the time of recollecting the aggregates of the form-sphere or formless-sphere, it has an exalted object. In the past, at the time of recollecting the path developed by oneself or by others and the fruition realized, it has an immeasurable object. In the past, by way of recollecting those whose round of existence is cut off—thinking, 'The Buddhas developed the path, realized the fruition, and attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element'—and also by way of reviewing the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, it has an immeasurable object. In the past, at the time of recollecting name, clan, the earth-kasiṇa sign, and so on, by the method beginning with, 'There was a Blessed One named Vipassī. His city was named Bandhumatī, the king named Bandhumā was his father, and Bandhumatī was his mother,' it has an ineffable object.

‘Anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthe’pi eseva nayo. Tampi ayaṃ anāgate ‘kāmāvacare nibbattissatī’ti jānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. ‘Rūpāvacare vā arūpāvacare vā nibbattissatī’ti jānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ. ‘Maggaṃ bhāvessati phalaṃ sacchikarissati’ ‘nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyissatī’ti jānanakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Anāgate “metteyyo nāma bhagavā uppajjissati, subrahmā nāmassa brāhmaṇo pitā bhavissati, brahmavatī nāma brāhmaṇī mātā bhavissatī”tiādinā nayena nāmagottajānanakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ hoti.

For the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future, this same method applies. For that jhāna too, at the time of knowing, 'In the future, this person will be reborn in the sense-sphere,' has a limited object. At the time of knowing, 'He will be reborn in the form-sphere,' or, 'He will be reborn in the formless-sphere,' it has an exalted object. At the time of knowing, 'He will develop the path, he will realize the fruition, he will attain final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element,' it has an immeasurable object. In the future, at the time of knowing the name and clan by the method beginning with, 'A Blessed One named Metteyya will arise. The brahmin named Subrahmā will be his father, the brahmin woman named Brahmavatī will be his mother,' it has an ineffable object.

Arūpāvacaracatutthaṃ pana āsavānaṃ khayacatutthañca pāḷiyaṃ āgataṭṭhāneyeva kathessāmi. Kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu upekkhāsahagatā sabbesampi etesaṃ kusalākusalakiriyacittānaṃ purecārikā. Tassā tesu vuttanayeneva ārammaṇabhedo veditabbo. Pañcadvāre pana voṭṭhabbanavasena pavattiyaṃ ekantaparittārammaṇāva hoti. Rūpāvacaratikacatukkajjhānādīni parittādibhāvena navattabbadhammaṃ ārabbha pavattito navattabbārammaṇāni. Ettha hi rūpāvacarāni pathavīkasiṇādīsu pavattanti, ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ugghāṭimākāse, ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ viññāṇāpagameti.

Now, I will speak of the fourth jhāna of the formless-sphere and the fourth jhāna of the destruction of the taints only in the place where they appear in the Pāḷi. The functional, rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity is the forerunner of all these wholesome, unwholesome, and functional cittas. The distinction of its object in relation to them should be understood by the method already stated. However, in the five doors, when it occurs by way of determining, it has exclusively a limited object. The form-sphere jhānas of the triad and tetrad systems, etc., have ineffable objects because they arise taking as object a dhamma that is ineffable in terms of being limited, etc. Indeed, herein, the form-sphere jhānas occur in relation to concepts such as the earth-kasiṇa; the base of infinite space occurs in relation to the space-concept obtained by the removal of the kasiṇa; the base of nothingness occurs in relation to the absence of the consciousness of the base of infinite space.

1429. Maggārammaṇattike ādimhi vuttā aṭṭha ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādā sekkhāsekkhānaṃ attanā paṭividdhamaggānaṃ paccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇā, maggena pana asahajātattā na maggahetukā, attanā paṭividdhamaggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhaṇakāle ārammaṇādhipativasena maggādhipatino, aññadhammārammaṇakāle na vattabbā maggārammaṇātipi maggādhipatinotipi. Cattāro ariyamaggā maggasaṅkhātassa maggasampayuttassa vā hetuno atthitāya ekantato maggahetukāva. Vīriyaṃ pana vīmaṃsaṃ vā [P 0.0416] jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā maggabhāvanākāle [M 0.0442] sahajātādhipatinā siyā maggādhipatino, chandacittānaṃ aññatarajeṭṭhakakāle siyā na vattabbā maggādhipatinoti.

1429. In the triad on path-object, the eight occurrences of consciousness associated with knowledge mentioned at the beginning, for trainees and non-trainees at the time of reviewing the paths they have penetrated, have the path as object. However, because they are not co-nascent with the path, they are not path-rooted. At the time of reviewing the path they have penetrated, having made it weighty, by way of object-predominance, they have the path as predominant factor. At the time of taking another dhamma as object, they are not to be called 'having the path as object' nor 'having the path as predominant factor'. The four noble paths, because of the existence of a root that is designated as 'path' or is associated with the path, are exclusively path-rooted. However, at the time of developing the path, having made either energy or investigation pre-eminent, through co-nascent predominance, they may have the path as predominant factor; at the time when either desire or consciousness is pre-eminent, it may be that they are not to be called 'having the path as predominant factor'.

Dvādasavidhe [V 0.0433] rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāne sabbatthapādakacatutthādīni nava jhānāni neva maggārammaṇāni na maggahetukāni na maggādhipatīni. Cetopariyañāṇapubbenivāsañāṇaanāgataṃsañāṇacatutthāni pana ariyānaṃ maggacittajānanakāle maggārammaṇāni honti, maggena pana asahajātattā na maggahetukāni, maggaṃ garuṃ katvā appavattito na maggādhipatīni. Kasmā panetāni na maggaṃ garuṃ karontīti? Attano mahaggatatāya. Yathā hi rājānaṃ sabbo loko garuṃ karoti, mātāpitaro pana na karonti. Na hi te rājānaṃ disvā āsanā vuṭṭhahanti, na añjalikammādīni karonti, daharakāle voharitanayeneva voharanti. Evametānipi attano mahaggatatāya na maggaṃ garuṃ karonti.

In the twelvefold fourth jhāna of the form sphere, the nine jhānas beginning with the fourth jhāna that is the basis for everything are neither path-object, nor path-rooted, nor path-predominant. However, the fourth jhānas of the knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, and knowledge of the future, for noble ones at the time of knowing the path-consciousness, have the path as object. However, because they are not co-nascent with the path, they are not path-rooted. Because they do not occur having made the path weighty, they do not have the path as predominant factor. But why do these not make the path weighty? Because of their own exalted nature. For just as the whole world makes the king weighty, his parents do not. Indeed, upon seeing the king, they do not rise from their seats, nor do they perform gestures of reverence such as the añjali; they speak in the same way they spoke when he was a child. So too, these jhānas, because of their own exalted nature, do not make the path weighty.

Kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātupi ariyānaṃ maggapaccavekkhaṇakāle paccavekkhaṇapurecārikattā maggārammaṇā hoti, maggena asahajātattā pana na maggahetukā, maggaṃ garuṃ katvā appavattito na maggādhipati. Kasmā garuṃ na karotīti? Attano ahetukatāya hīnatāya jaḷatāya. Yathā hi rājānaṃ sabbo loko garuṃ karoti, attano parijanā pana khujjavāmanakaceṭakādayo attano aññāṇatāya paṇḍitamanussā viya nātigaruṃ karonti, evameva idampi cittaṃ attano ahetukatāya hīnatāya jaḷatāya maggaṃ garuṃ na karoti.

The functional, rootless mind-consciousness-element also, for noble ones at the time of reviewing the path, because it is the forerunner of the reviewing-knowledge, has the path as object. However, because it is not co-nascent with the path, it is not path-rooted. Because it does not occur having made the path weighty, it does not have the path as predominant factor. Why does it not make the path weighty? Because of its own rootless, inferior, and dull nature. For just as the whole world makes the king weighty, his own attendants—hunchbacks, dwarfs, servants, and the like—due to their own ignorance, do not make him as weighty as wise people do. In the same way, this consciousness, because of its own rootless, inferior, and dull nature, does not make the path weighty.

Ñāṇavippayuttakusalādīni ñāṇābhāvena ceva lokiyadhammārammaṇatāya ca maggārammaṇādibhāvaṃ na labhanti, navattabbārammaṇāneva hontīti veditabbānīti.

Wholesome states dissociated from knowledge, and so on, both because of the absence of knowledge and because they have a mundane dhamma as object, do not attain the state of being path-object, etc. They are simply not to be designated in these terms. Thus it should be understood.

1432. Atītārammaṇattike [P 0.0417] viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanadhammā heṭṭhā atītasamāpattiṃ ārabbha pavattitā ekantena atītārammaṇāva.

1432. In the triad on past-object, the dhammas of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, because they arise taking as object a past attainment below them, exclusively have a past object.

1433. Niyogā anāgatārammaṇā natthīti niyamena pāṭiyekkaṃ cittaṃ anāgatārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Nanu ca anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ ekantena anāgatārammaṇaṃ, cetopariyañāṇampi anāgataṃ ārabbha pavattatīti? No [M 0.0443] na pavattati. Pāṭiyekkaṃ pana etaṃ ekaṃ cittaṃ nāma natthi. Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānena saṅgahitattā aññehi mahaggatacittehi missakaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘niyogā anāgatārammaṇā natthī’ti.

1433. By necessity, there are no future objects—that is, there is no individual consciousness that takes a future object by rule. But is it not so that knowledge of the future exclusively has a future object, and that the knowledge of others’ minds also arises concerning the future? It is not that it does not arise. However, there is no single, separate consciousness of this kind. Because it is included in the fourth jhāna of the form sphere, it is mixed with other exalted consciousnesses. Therefore it is said, 'By necessity, there are no future objects.'

1434. Dvipañcaviññāṇāni[V 0.0434], tisso manodhātuyo ca paccuppannesu rūpādīsu pavattito paccuppannārammaṇā nāma. Dasa cittuppādāti ettha aṭṭha tāva sahetukā devamanussānaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle kammaṃ vā kammanimittaṃ vā ārabbha pavattiyaṃ atītārammaṇā. Bhavaṅgacutikālesupi eseva nayo. Gatinimittaṃ pana ārabbha paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle tato paraṃ bhavaṅgakāle ca paccuppannārammaṇā. Tathā pañcadvāre tadārammaṇavasena pavattiyaṃ. Manodvāre pana atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇānaṃ javanānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā pavattito atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇā. ‘Kusalavipākāhetukaupekkhāsahagatamanoviññāṇadhātuya’mpi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi sā manussesu jaccandhādīnaṃ paṭisandhi hoti. Pañcadvāre ca santīraṇavasenāpi paccuppannārammaṇā hotīti ayamettha viseso. ‘Somanassasahagatā’ pana pañcadvāre santīraṇavasena tadārammaṇavasena ca paccuppannārammaṇā hoti. Manodvāre tadārammaṇavasena sahetukavipākā viya atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇāti veditabbā.

1434. The two sets of fivefold consciousnesses and the three mind-elements, arising concerning present forms, etc., are called 'having present objects'. Here, among the ten types of consciousness-arisings, eight rooted resultant consciousnesses, at the time of the rebirth-linking of devas and humans, arise taking kamma or a kamma-sign as their object, and thus have past objects. The same principle applies also at the times of life-continuum and death. However, when arising at the time of rebirth-linking taking a destiny-sign as its object, and subsequently at the time of the life-continuum, they have a present object. Likewise, when they occur in the five doors by way of retention. In the mind-door, however, because they arise taking as object the objects of impulsions which have past, future, or present objects, they have past, future, or present objects. The same principle applies also to the 'wholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity'. For this occurs only as the rebirth-linking of those born blind, etc., among humans. And in the five doors, by way of investigation, it also has a present object—this is the distinction here. The one 'accompanied by joy', however, in the five doors, by way of investigation and by way of retention, has a present object. In the mind-door, by way of retention, like the rooted resultants, it should be understood as having past, future, or present objects.

‘Akusalavipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu’ pana kusalavipākāya upekkhāsahagatāhetukāya samānagatikā eva. Kevalañhi [P 0.0418] sā āpāyikānaṃ paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena pavattatīti ayamettha viseso. ‘Kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu’ somanassasahagatā khīṇāsavānaṃ pañcadvāre pahaṭṭhākāraṃ kurumānā paccuppannārammaṇā hoti. Manodvāre atītādibhede dhamme ārabbha hasituppādavasena pavattiyaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇā hoti.

The 'unwholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element', however, is of the same nature as the wholesome-resultant rootless one accompanied by equanimity. For it only occurs by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death for beings of the woeful states; this is the distinction here. The 'functional rootless mind-consciousness-element' accompanied by joy, for those whose cankers are destroyed, occurs in the five doors producing an expression of delight, and has a present object. In the mind-door, when it arises by way of smile-production, taking as object phenomena of past, etc., kinds, it has past, future, or present objects.

Kāmāvacarakusalantiādīsu kusalato tāva cattāro ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādā. Sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ atītādibhedāni khandhadhātuāyatanāni sammasantānaṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇā honti. Paṇṇattinibbānapaccavekkhaṇe navattabbārammaṇā. Ñāṇavippayuttesupi eseva nayo[M 0.0444]. Kevalañhi tehi maggaphalanibbānapaccavekkhaṇā natthi. Ayamevettha viseso.

Regarding 'sense-sphere wholesome', and so on, firstly from the wholesome side, there are four consciousness-arisings associated with knowledge. For trainees and worldlings, when they are contemplating and reviewing the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of past, etc., kinds, these have past, future, or present objects. When reviewing concepts or Nibbāna, their objects are unspecifiable. The same principle applies also to those consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge. Only, with them, there is no reviewing of path, fruition, and Nibbāna. This alone is the distinction here.

Akusalato cattāro diṭṭhisampayuttacittuppādā atītādibhedānaṃ khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ assādanābhinandanaparāmāsakāle atītādiārammaṇā honti. Paṇṇattiṃ ārabbha assādentassa abhinandantassa ‘satto satto’ti parāmasitvā gaṇhantassa navattabbārammaṇā honti. Diṭṭhivippayuttesupi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi tehi parāmāsaggahaṇaṃ natthi. Dve paṭighasampayuttacittuppādā [V 0.0435] atītādibhede dhamme ārabbha domanassitānaṃ atītādiārammaṇā, paṇṇattiṃ ārabbha domanassitānaṃ navattabbārammaṇā. Vicikicchuddhaccasampayuttā tesu eva dhammesu aniṭṭhaṅgatabhāvena ceva uddhatabhāvena ca pavattiyaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannanavattabbārammaṇā. Kiriyato aṭṭha sahetukacittuppādā kusalacittuppādagatikā eva. Kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu upekkhāsahagatā pañcadvāre voṭṭhabbanavasena pavattiyaṃ paccuppannārammaṇāva[P 0.0419]. Manodvāre atītānāgatapaccuppannārammaṇānañceva paṇṇattinibbānārammaṇānañca javanānaṃ purecārikakāle atītānāgatapaccuppannanavattabbārammaṇā.

Among the unwholesome, the four consciousness-arisings associated with wrong view, at the time of savoring, delighting in, and misapprehending the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of past and other kinds, have past and other such objects. When taking a concept as object, for one who savors, delights in, and grasps it by misapprehending it as 'a being, a being,' they have unspecifiable objects. This same principle applies also to those dissociated from wrong view. It is only that with them, there is no grasping through misapprehension. The two consciousness-arisings associated with aversion, for those afflicted with displeasure towards phenomena of past and other kinds, have past and other such objects; for those afflicted with displeasure towards a concept, they have unspecifiable objects. Those associated with doubt and restlessness, in their occurrence concerning those same phenomena, due to their state of indecisiveness and agitation, have past, future, present, or unspecifiable objects. Among the functional, the eight rooted consciousness-arisings are of the same nature as the wholesome consciousness-arisings. The functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, when occurring in the five doors by way of determining, has only a present object. In the mind-door, at the time of preceding the impulsions that have past, future, or present objects, as well as concepts and Nibbāna as objects, it has past, future, present, or unspecifiable objects.

Yathāvuttappabhede rūpāvacarajjhāne sabbatthapādakacatutthaṃ ākāsakasiṇacatutthaṃ ālokakasiṇacatutthaṃ brahmavihāracatutthaṃ ānāpānacatutthanti imāni pañca navattabbārammaṇāneva. ‘Iddhividhacatutthaṃ’ kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmentassa atītapādakajjhānacittaṃ ārabbha pavattanato atītārammaṇaṃ. Mahādhātunidhāne mahākassapattherādīnaṃ viya anāgataṃ adhiṭṭhahantānaṃ anāgatārammaṇaṃ hoti. Mahākassapatthero kira mahādhātunidhānaṃ karonto anāgate aṭṭhārasavassādhikāni dve vassasatāni ime gandhā mā sussiṃsu, pupphāni mā milāyiṃsu, dīpā mā nibbāyiṃsūti adhiṭṭhahi. Sabbaṃ tatheva ahosi. Assaguttatthero vattaniyasenāsane bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sukkhabhattaṃ bhuñjamānaṃ disvā ‘udakasoṇḍi divase divase, purebhattaṃ dadhirasā hotū’ti adhiṭṭhahi. Purebhattaṃ gahitaṃ dadhirasaṃ hoti pacchābhatte pākatikameva. Kāyaṃ pana cittasannissitaṃ katvā adissamānena kāyena gamanakāle, aññassa vā pāṭihāriyassa [M 0.0445] karaṇakāle, kāyaṃ ārabbha pavattattā paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti.

Among the form-sphere jhānas with their aforementioned divisions, the fourth jhāna that is the basis for all, the fourth jhāna on the space kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna on the light kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna of the divine abodes, and the fourth jhāna on mindfulness of breathing—these five have only unspecifiable objects. The 'fourth jhāna of the modes of psychic power,' for one who transforms the mind by means of the body, arises by taking a past base-jhāna consciousness as its object; thus, it has a past object. As in the case of the Elder Mahākassapa and others at the great relic enshrinement, for those who make a determination regarding the future, it has a future object. It is said that the Elder Mahākassapa, while conducting the great relic enshrinement, made a determination concerning the future: 'For two hundred and eighteen years, may these fragrances not dry up, may these flowers not wither, may these lamps not be extinguished.' And everything happened just so. The Elder Assagutta, seeing the community of monks eating dry food at the Vattaniya monastery, made a determination: 'May the water pond, day after day, in the forenoon, have the taste of curd.' Water taken in the forenoon had the taste of curd; in the afternoon, it was just as it is naturally. However, having made the body dependent on the mind, at the time of traveling with an invisible body or at the time of performing another miracle, because it arises taking the body as object, it has a present object.

‘Dibbasotacatutthaṃ’ vijjamānasaddameva ārabbha pavattito paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti. Cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ atīte sattadivasabbhantare anāgate sattadivasabbhantare paresaṃ cittaṃ jānantassa atītārammaṇaṃ anāgatārammaṇañca hoti. Sattadivasātikkame pana taṃ jānituṃ na sakkoti. Atītānāgataṃsañāṇānañhi esa visayo. Na etassa paccuppannajānanakāle pana paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti.

The 'fourth jhāna of the divine ear,' because it arises by taking only an existing sound as its object, has a present object. The 'fourth jhāna of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds,' for one who knows the minds of others within seven days in the past and within seven days in the future, has a past object and a future object. However, one cannot know it beyond seven days, for that is the domain of the knowledges of the past and future, not of this one. At the time of knowing the present, however, it has a present object.

Paccuppannañca [P 0.0420] nāmetaṃ tividhaṃ – khaṇapaccuppannaṃ santatipaccuppannaṃ addhāpaccuppannañca. Tattha uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgappattaṃ ‘khaṇapaccuppannaṃ’. Ekadvisantativārapariyāpannaṃ ‘santatipaccuppannaṃ’. Tattha andhakāre [V 0.0436] nisīditvā ālokaṭṭhānaṃ gatassa na tāva ārammaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti; yāva pana taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, etthantare ekadvisantativārā veditabbā. Ālokaṭṭhāne vicaritvā ovarakaṃ paviṭṭhassāpi na tāva sahasā rūpaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti; yāva taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, etthantare ekadvisantativārā veditabbā. Dūre ṭhatvā pana rajakānaṃ hatthavikāraṃ ghaṇḍibherīādiākoṭanavikārañca disvāpi na tāva saddaṃ suṇāti; yāva pana taṃ suṇāti, etasmimpi antare ekadvisantativārā veditabbā. Evaṃ tāva majjhimabhāṇakā. Saṃyuttabhāṇakā pana ‘rūpasantati arūpasantatī’ti dve santatiyo vatvā, ‘udakaṃ akkamitvā gatassa yāva tīre akkantaudakalekhā na vippasīdati, addhānato āgatassa yāva kāye usumabhāvo na vūpasammati, ātapā āgantvā gabbhaṃ paviṭṭhassa yāva andhakārabhāvo na vigacchati, antogabbhe kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaritvā divā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā olokentassa yāva akkhīnaṃ phandanabhāvo na vūpasammati, ayaṃ rūpasantati nāma; dve tayo javanavārā arūpasantati nāmā’ti vatvā ‘tadubhayampi santatipaccuppannaṃ nāmā’ti vadanti.

This which is called 'the present' is threefold: the momentary present, the continuity present, and the duration present. Therein, that which has reached arising, presence, and dissolution is the 'momentary present.' That which is included within one or two turns of continuity is the 'continuity present.' In this regard, for one who, having sat in darkness, goes to a place of light, the object is not yet apparent; until it becomes apparent, it should be understood that one or two turns of continuity have passed in the interval. For one who, having moved about in a lighted place, enters a chamber, form is not yet immediately apparent; until it becomes apparent, it should be understood that one or two turns of continuity have passed in the interval. Furthermore, standing at a distance, even after seeing the particular hand movements of washermen or the particular movements of striking a bell, drum, and so on, one does not yet hear the sound; until one hears it, it should be understood that one or two turns of continuity have passed in this interval. Thus far is the view of the Majjhima reciters. The Saṃyutta reciters, however, speak of two continuities, 'material continuity and immaterial continuity,' and having done so, they explain: 'For one who has walked through water, as long as the mark of the trodden water on the bank has not settled; for one who has come from a long journey, as long as the heat in the body has not subsided; for one who has come from the sun's heat and entered an inner chamber, as long as the state of darkness has not departed; for one who, having attended to a meditation subject in an inner chamber, opens a window during the day and looks out, as long as the trembling of the eyes has not subsided—this is called material continuity. Two or three turns of impulsion are called immaterial continuity.' Having stated this, they say, 'Both of these are called the continuity present.'

Ekabhavaparicchinnaṃ pana addhāpaccuppannaṃ nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya bhaddekarattasutte “yo cāvuso, mano ye ca dhammā ubhayametaṃ paccuppannaṃ. Tasmiṃ ce paccuppanne chandarāgapaṭibaddhaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ, chandarāgapaṭibaddhattā viññāṇassa tadabhinandati, tadabhinandanto paccuppannesu dhammesu saṃhīratī”ti (ma. ni. 3.284) vuttaṃ. Santatipaccuppannañcettha [P 0.0421] aṭṭhakathāsu āgataṃ. Addhāpaccuppannaṃ sutte.

That which is defined by a single existence, however, is called the 'duration present.' It is with reference to this that it is said in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta: 'Friends, whatever mind and whatever mental objects there are, both these are the present. If, in that present, consciousness is bound by desire and lust, then because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in that. Delighting in that, one is carried away by present phenomena' (M. Ni. 3.284). Herein, the continuity present is found in the commentaries, and the duration present is found in the Suttas.

Tattha [M 0.0446] keci ‘khaṇapaccuppannaṃ cittaṃ cetopariyañāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ hotī’ti vadanti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Yasmā iddhimassa ca parassa ca ekakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppajjatīti. Idañca nesaṃ opammaṃ – yathā ākāse khitte pupphamuṭṭhimhi avassaṃ ekaṃ pupphaṃ ekassa vaṇṭaṃ paṭivijjhati vaṇṭena vaṇṭaṃ paṭivijjhati, evaṃ parassa cittaṃ jānissāmīti rāsivasena mahājanassa citte āvajjite avassaṃ ekassa cittaṃ ekena cittena uppādakkhaṇe vā ṭhitikkhaṇe vā bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā paṭivijjhatīti. Taṃ pana vassasatampi vassasahassampi āvajjanto yena cittena āvajjeti, yena ca jānāti tesaṃ dvinnaṃ sahaṭṭhānābhāvato āvajjanajavanānañca aniṭṭhe ṭhāne nānārammaṇabhāvappattidosato ayuttanti aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhittaṃ. Santatipaccuppannaṃ pana addhāpaccuppannañca ārammaṇaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, some say: 'The momentary-present mind is the object of the knowledge of others' minds.' For what reason? Because the mind of the one with psychic power and that of another person arise in a single moment. And this is their simile: just as when a handful of flowers is thrown into the air, one flower will inevitably pierce another's stalk with its stalk, so too, when adverting to the minds of a great crowd of people by way of a mass with the thought, 'I will know another's mind,' the mind of one person is inevitably pierced by one mind at the moment of arising, the moment of presence, or the moment of dissolution. But this is rejected in the commentaries as incorrect, because, even if one were to advert for a hundred or a thousand years, the mind with which one adverts and the mind with which one knows do not have a co-existent state; and because of the fault of the adverting and javana minds arriving at a state of having different objects in an undesirable sphere. Rather, it should be understood that the continuity-present and the duration-present are its object.

Tattha [V 0.0437] yaṃ vattamānajavanavīthito atītānāgatavasena dvitijavanavīthiparimāṇakāle parassa cittaṃ, taṃ sabbampi santatipaccuppannaṃ nāma. Addhāpaccuppannaṃ pana javanavārena dīpetabbanti yaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ taṃ suvuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ dīpanā – iddhimā parassa cittaṃ jānitukāmo āvajjeti. Āvajjanaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā teneva saha nirujjhati. Tato cattāri pañca javanāni yesaṃ pacchimaṃ iddhicittaṃ, sesāni kāmāvacarāni. Tesaṃ sabbesampi tadeva niruddhaṃ cittamārammaṇaṃ hoti. Na ca tāni nānārammaṇāni honti. Addhāpaccuppannavasena paccuppannārammaṇattā ekārammaṇāni. Ekārammaṇattepi ca iddhicittameva parassa cittaṃ pajānāti, na itarāni; yathā cakkhudvāre cakkhuviññāṇameva rūpaṃ passati, na itarānīti. Iti idaṃ santatipaccuppannassa ceva addhāpaccuppannassa ca vasena paccuppannārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0422] hoti. Yasmā vā santatipaccuppannampi addhāpaccuppanneyeva patati, tasmā addhāpaccuppannavasenetaṃ paccuppannārammaṇanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, whatever mind of another there is in the time measuring two or three javana-processes, by way of past and future from the present javana-process, all that is called the 'continuity-present'. As for the 'duration-present', that it should be explained by the javana-turn—what is said in the commentary on this is well said. Herein, this is the explanation: one with psychic power, wishing to know another's mind, adverts. The adverting, having taken a momentary-present mind as its object, ceases together with that very object. Following that, four or five javanas arise, of which the last is the psychic-power mind, and the rest are sense-sphere. For all of these, that very same ceased mind is the object. And they do not have different objects. Because they have a present object by way of the 'duration-present', they have a single object. And even when they have a single object, only the psychic-power mind distinctly knows the other's mind, not the others; just as at the eye-door, only eye-consciousness sees a form, not the others. Thus, this has a present object by way of the continuity-present and the duration-present. Or, since the continuity-present also falls within the duration-present, it should be understood that this has a present object by way of the 'duration-present'.

‘Pubbenivāsañāṇacatutthaṃ’ nāmagottānussaraṇe nibbānanimittapaccavekkhaṇe ca navattabbārammaṇaṃ, sesakāle atītārammaṇameva. Yathākammupagañāṇacatutthampi atītārammaṇameva. Tattha kiñcāpi pubbenivāsacetopariyañāṇānipi atītārammaṇāni honti, atha kho tesaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇassa atītakkhandhā khandhapaṭibaddhañca kiñci anārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Tañhi atītakkhandhakhandhapaṭibaddhesu dhammesu sabbaññutaññāṇasamagatikaṃ hoti. Cetopariyañāṇassa ca sattadivasabbhantarātītaṃ cittameva ārammaṇaṃ. Tañhi aññaṃ [M 0.0447] khandhaṃ vā khandhapaṭibaddhaṃ vā na jānāti, maggasampayuttacittārammaṇattā pana pariyāyato maggārammaṇanti vuttaṃ. Yathākammupagañāṇassa ca atītacetanāmattamevārammaṇanti. Ayaṃ viseso veditabbo. Ayamettha aṭṭhakathānayo. Yasmā pana “kusalā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa yathākammupagañāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.404) paṭṭhāne vuttaṃ, tasmā cattāropi khandhā cetopariyañāṇayathākammupagañāṇānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ honti. Tatrāpi yathākammupagañāṇassa kusalākusalā evāti.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of past lives, in the recollection of names and clans and in the reflection on the sign of Nibbāna, has an inexpressible object; at other times, it has only a past object. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma also has only a past object. Herein, although the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of others' minds also have past objects, yet for the knowledge of past lives, there is nothing whatsoever among the past aggregates or what is connected to the aggregates that is not its object. For it is similar in nature to the knowledge of omniscience regarding phenomena which are the past aggregates and what is connected to them. For the knowledge of others' minds, only the mind that has passed within seven days is its object. For it does not know another aggregate or what is connected to an aggregate; however, because it has as its object the mind associated with the path, it is said figuratively to have the path as its object. For the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, only past volition is its object. This distinction should be understood. This is the method of the commentaries here. However, since it is said in the Paṭṭhāna: 'Wholesome aggregates are a condition by way of object-condition for the knowledge of psychic powers, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, and the knowledge of the future,' therefore, all four aggregates are the object for the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma. Even there, for the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, only wholesome and unwholesome aggregates are its object.

‘Dibbacakkhuñāṇacatutthaṃ’ vijjamānavaṇṇārammaṇattā paccuppannārammaṇameva. Anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthaṃ anāgatārammaṇameva. Tañhi anāgatakkhandhakhandhapaṭibaddhesu dhammesu pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ viya sabbaññutaññāṇasamagatikaṃ [V 0.0438] hoti. Tattha kiñcāpi cetopariyañāṇampi anāgatārammaṇaṃ hoti, taṃ pana sattadivasabbhantare uppajjanakacittameva ārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0423] karoti. Idaṃ anāgate kappasatasahasse uppajjanakacittampi khandhepi khandhapaṭibaddhampi. Rūpāvacaratikacatukkajjhānādīni atītānāgatapaccuppannesu ekadhammampi ārabbha appavattito ekantanavattabbārammaṇānevāti veditabbāni.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the divine eye, because it has presently existing visible form as its object, has only a present object. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future has only a future object. For it, like the knowledge of past lives, is similar in nature to the knowledge of omniscience with respect to phenomena which are the future aggregates and what is connected to them. Herein, although the knowledge of others' minds also has a future object, it, however, takes as its object only the mind that is to arise within seven days. This knowledge of the future, however, takes as its object even the mind that is to arise in a hundred thousand kappas in the future, and the aggregates, and what is connected to the aggregates. The fine-material sphere jhānas of the triad and tetrad systems, and so on, because they do not arise taking even one phenomenon among past, future, and present as object, should be known as having exclusively inexpressible objects.

1435. Ajjhattattike anindriyabaddharūpañca nibbānañca bahiddhāti idaṃ yathā indriyabaddhaṃ parapuggalasantāne bahiddhāti vuccamānampi tassa attano santānapariyāpannattā niyakajjhattaṃ hoti, evaṃ na kenaci pariyāyena ajjhattaṃ hotīti niyakajjhattapariyāyassa abhāvena bahiddhāti vuttaṃ, na niyakajjhattamattassa asambhavato. Niyakajjhattamattassa pana asambhavamattaṃ sandhāya ajjhattārammaṇattike bahiddhārammaṇatā vuttā. Ajjhattadhammāpagamamattatova ākiñcaññāyatanārammaṇassa ajjhattabhāvampi bahiddhābhāvampi ajjhattabahiddhābhāvampi ananujānitvā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ na vattabbaṃ ajjhattārammaṇantipītiādi vuttaṃ.

1435. In the internal triad, form not bound by faculties and Nibbāna are 'external'. Just as form bound by faculties, though called 'external' when in another individual's continuum, is personally internal for that individual because it is included in their own continuum, so too form not bound by faculties and Nibbāna are not internal in any way whatsoever. Therefore, they are called 'external' due to the absence of any mode of being personally internal, not because of the impossibility of being merely personally internal. However, with reference to the mere impossibility of being personally internal, the state of having an external object is stated in the triad of internal objects. And precisely because of the mere absence of an internal phenomenon, without permitting the internal nature, the external nature, or the internal-and-external nature of the object of the base of nothingness, it is said, 'The base of nothingness should not be called "having an internal object,"' and so on.

Tattha na kevalaṃ tadeva navattabbārammaṇaṃ, tassa pana āvajjanampi, upacāracittānipi, tassārammaṇassa paccavekkhaṇacittānipi, tasseva assādanādivasena pavattāni akusalacittānipi navattabbārammaṇānevāti. Tāni [M 0.0448] pana tasmiṃ vutte vuttāneva hontīti visuṃ na vuttāni. Kathaṃ vuttāneva hontīti? Etañhi ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, yañca tassa purecārikaṃ āvajjanaupacārādivasena pavattaṃ, tena saha ekārammaṇaṃ bhaveyya. Taṃ sabbaṃ atītārammaṇattike ‘kāmāvacarakusalaṃ, akusalaṃ, kiriyato nava cittuppādā, rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāna’nti evaṃ vuttānaṃ etesaṃ cittuppādānaṃ ‘siyā na vattabbā atītārammaṇātipī’tiādinā nayena navattabbārammaṇabhāvassa anuññātattā, ākiñcaññāyatanassa ca ‘ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, cattāro maggā apariyāpannā, cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni, ime dhammā na vattabbā atītārammaṇātipī’ti evaṃ ekantena navattabbārammaṇattavacanato navattabbārammaṇanti vuttaṃ. Idāni [P 0.0424] taṃ ajjhattārammaṇattike ekampi vuccamānaṃ yasmā heṭṭhā tena saha ekārammaṇabhāvampi sandhāya kāmāvacarakusalādīnaṃ navattabbārammaṇatā vuttā, tasmā idhāpi tesaṃ navattabbārammaṇabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Ko hi tena saha ekārammaṇānaṃ navattabbārammaṇabhāve antarāyoti[V 0.0439]? Evaṃ tasmiṃ vutte ‘vuttāneva hontī’ti veditabbāni. Sesamettha ajjhattārammaṇattike pāḷito uttānameva.

Herein, not only does that base of nothingness itself have an inexpressible object, but also its adverting consciousness, its access consciousnesses, the consciousnesses that review that object, and even the unwholesome consciousnesses that arise by way of relishing, etc., that very object—these too have inexpressible objects. However, since they are already stated when that base of nothingness is stated, they are not stated separately. How is it that they are already stated? For this base of nothingness, and whatever consciousness precedes it arising by way of adverting, access, etc., would have the same object as it. All of this is stated to have an inexpressible object because, in the triad of past objects, for those states of consciousness mentioned as 'sense-sphere wholesome...,' etc., the state of having an inexpressible object has been permitted by the method beginning 'it may be... not to be called "having a past object,"' and also because for the base of nothingness itself, the state of having an inexpressible object is stated definitively thus: 'The base of nothingness... these phenomena are not to be called "having a past object."' Now, although it is stated alone in the triad of internal objects, because previously the state of having an inexpressible object was stated for the sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, etc., with reference to their having the same object as it, therefore, here too, it indicates their state of having an inexpressible object. For what obstacle is there for those that have the same object as it to have an inexpressible object? Thus, when that is stated, it should be understood that 'they are already stated.' The rest here in the triad of internal objects is clear from the Pāḷi itself.

Ārammaṇavibhāge pana viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti imesaṃ tāva kusalavipākakiriyavasena channaṃ cittuppādānaṃ attano santānasambandhaṃ heṭṭhimasamāpattiṃ ārabbha pavattito ajjhattārammaṇatā veditabbā. Ettha ca kiriyaākāsānañcāyatanaṃ kiriyaviññāṇañcāyatanasseva ārammaṇaṃ hoti, na itarassa. Kasmā? Ākāsānañcāyatanakiriyasamaṅgino kusalassa vā vipākassa vā viññāṇañcāyatanassa abhāvato. Kusalaṃ pana kusalavipākakiriyānaṃ tiṇṇampi ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Ākāsānañcāyatanakusalaṃ nibbattetvā ṭhitassa tato uddhaṃ tividhassapi viññāṇañcāyatanassa uppattisambhavato. Vipākaṃ pana na kassaci ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Vipākato vuṭṭhahitvā cittassa abhinīhārāsambhavato. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassa ārammaṇakaraṇepi eseva nayo. Rūpāvacarattikacatukkajjhānādīnaṃ sabbesampi niyakajjhattato bahiddhābhāvena bahiddhābhūtāni pathavīkasiṇādīni ārabbha pavattito bahiddhārammaṇatā veditabbā.

Further, in the classification of objects, regarding the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, for these six types of consciousness—by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional—the state of having an internal object should be understood, because they arise by taking as object the lower attainment connected with one's own continuity. And here, the functional base of infinite space is the object of only the functional base of infinite consciousness, not of the others. Why?
