Because for one endowed with the functional base of infinite space, there is an absence of the wholesome or resultant base of infinite consciousness. The wholesome, however, is the object of all three: wholesome, resultant, and functional. Why? Because for one who stands having produced the wholesome base of infinite space, there is the possibility of the arising of the threefold base of infinite consciousness above that. The resultant, however, is not the object of any. Why? Because after emerging from the resultant, it is impossible to direct the mind. This is the same method also in making the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception an object. For all of the form-sphere jhānas of the triad and tetrad, and so on, the state of having an external object should be understood, because they arise by taking as object external things such as the earth kasiṇa, etc., due to their being external to one's own internal state.

Sabbeva kāmāvacarā kusalākusalābyākatā dhammā, rūpāvacaraṃ catutthaṃ jhānanti ettha kusalato tāva cattāro ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādā attano [M 0.0449] khandhādīni paccavekkhantassa ajjhattārammaṇā. Paresaṃ khandhādipaccavekkhaṇe paṇṇattinibbānapaccavekkhaṇe ca bahiddhārammaṇā. Tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Ñāṇavippayuttesupi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi tesaṃ nibbānapaccavekkhaṇaṃ [P 0.0425] natthi. Akusalato cattāro diṭṭhisampayuttacittuppādā attano khandhādīnaṃ assādanābhinandanaparāmāsagahaṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇā, parassa khandhādīsu ceva anindriyabaddharūpakasiṇādīsu ca tatheva pavattikāle bahiddhārammaṇā, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Diṭṭhivippayuttesupi eseva nayo. Kevalañhi tesaṃ parāmāsagahaṇaṃ natthi. Dvepi paṭighasampayuttā attano khandhādīsu domanassitassa ajjhattārammaṇā, parassa khandhādīsu ceva anindriyabaddharūpapaṇṇattīsu ca bahiddhārammaṇā, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Vicikicchuddhaccasampayuttānampi vuttapakāresu dhammesu vicikicchanaphandanabhāvavasena pavattiyaṃ ajjhattādiārammaṇatā veditabbā.

Regarding 'All sense-sphere phenomena—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and the fourth form-sphere jhāna': here, first, from the wholesome, the four consciousnesses associated with knowledge have internal objects for one who is reviewing their own aggregates, etc. When reviewing the aggregates, etc., of others, and when reviewing concepts and Nibbāna, they have external objects. By way of both, they have internal-and-external objects. For those dissociated from knowledge, this is the same method. It is just that for them, there is no reviewing of Nibbāna. From the unwholesome, the four consciousnesses associated with wrong view have internal objects at the time of grasping one's own aggregates, etc., by way of savoring, delighting, and misapprehending. When they occur in the same way with regard to the aggregates, etc., of another, and to non-faculty-bound form, kasiṇas, etc., they have external objects. By way of both, they have internal-and-external objects. For those dissociated from wrong view, this is the same method. It is just that for them, there is no grasping by way of misapprehension. The two consciousnesses associated with aversion have internal objects for one who is afflicted with displeasure regarding their own aggregates, etc. When occurring with regard to the aggregates, etc., of another, and to non-faculty-bound form and concepts, they have external objects. By way of both, they have internal-and-external objects. For those associated with doubt and restlessness as well, the state of having internal, etc., objects should be understood according to their occurrence in the aforementioned types of phenomena by way of the state of doubting and agitation.

Dvipañcaviññāṇāni[V 0.0440], tisso ca manodhātuyoti, ime terasa cittuppādā attano rūpādīni ārabbha pavattiyaṃ ajjhattārammaṇā, parassa rūpādīsu pavattā bahiddhārammaṇā, tadubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Somanassasahagataahetukavipākamanoviññāṇadhātu pañcadvāre santīraṇatadārammaṇavasena attano pañca rūpādidhamme, manodvāre tadārammaṇavaseneva aññepi ajjhattike kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha pavattiyaṃ ajjhattārammaṇā, paresaṃ dhammesu pavattamānā bahiddhārammaṇā, ubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Upekkhāsahagatavipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātudvayepi eseva nayo. Kevalaṃ panetā sugatiyaṃ duggatiyañca paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasenāpi ajjhattādibhedesu kammādīsu pavattanti.

The two sets of five consciousnesses and the three mind-elements—these thirteen consciousnesses have internal objects during their occurrence when taking one's own form, etc., as object. When they occur with regard to the form, etc., of another, they have external objects. By way of both, they have internal-and-external objects. The rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy has an internal object when it occurs in the five doors by way of investigating and registering, taking as object one's own five phenomena of form, etc., and when it occurs in the mind door only by way of registering, taking as object other internal sense-sphere phenomena. When occurring with regard to the phenomena of others, it has an external object. By way of both, it has an internal-and-external object. For the pair of rootless resultant mind-consciousness-elements accompanied by equanimity, this is the same method. It is just that these also occur in happy and unhappy destinations by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, with regard to objects such as kamma, etc., which are distinguished as internal, etc.

Aṭṭha mahāvipākacittānipi tāsaṃyeva dvinnaṃ samānagatikāni. Kevalaṃ panetāni santīraṇavasena na pavattanti. Paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivaseneva etāni sugatiyaṃyeva pavattanti. Somanassasahagatāhetukakiriyā pañcadvāre attano rūpādīni ārabbha pahaṭṭhākārakaraṇavasena pavattiyaṃ ajjhattārammaṇā, parassa [P 0.0426] rūpādīsu pavattā bahiddhārammaṇā. Manodvāre tathāgatassa jotipālamāṇavamaghadevarājakaṇhatāpasādikālesu attanā katakiriyaṃ paccavekkhantassa hasituppādavasena pavattā ajjhattārammaṇā[M 0.0450].

The eight great resultant consciousnesses also have the same course as those two. It is just that these do not occur by way of investigating. These occur only in a happy destination, only by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. The rootless functional consciousness accompanied by joy has an internal object when it occurs in the five doors, taking as object one's own form, etc., by way of producing a joyful appearance. When it occurs with regard to the form, etc., of another, it has an external object. In the mind door, when it occurs by way of producing a smile for the Tathāgata as he reviews an action done by himself at the times of the young man Jotipāla, King Maghadeva, the ascetic Kaṇha, and so on, it has an internal object.

Mallikāya deviyā santatimahāmattassa sumanamālākārassāti evamādīnaṃ kiriyākaraṇaṃ ārabbha pavattikāle bahiddhārammaṇā. Ubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā. Upekkhāsahagatakiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu pañcadvāre voṭṭhabbanavasena manodvāre ca āvajjanavasena pavattiyaṃ ajjhattādiārammaṇā. Aṭṭha mahākiriyā kusalacittagatikā eva. Kevalañhi tā khīṇāsavānaṃ uppajjanti, kusalāni sekkhaputhujjanānanti ettakamevettha nānākaraṇaṃ.

At the time of its occurrence taking as object the action done by Queen Mallikā, the great minister Santati, the garland-maker Sumana, and so on, it has an external object. In both ways, it has an internal-and-external object. The rootless functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, during its occurrence in the five doors by way of determining and in the mind door by way of adverting, has internal, etc., objects. The eight great functional consciousnesses are indeed of the same nature as the wholesome consciousnesses. It is just that those functional consciousnesses arise for Arahants, while the wholesome consciousnesses arise for trainees and worldlings—this much is the difference here.

Vuttappakāre rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāne sabbatthapādakacatutthādīni pañca jhānāni imasmiṃ tike okāsaṃ labhanti. Etāni hi kasiṇapaṇṇattinimittārammaṇattā bahiddhārammaṇāni.

Among the aforementioned types of form-sphere fourth jhāna, the five jhānas—beginning with the fourth which is the basis for all—find a place in this triad. For these have external objects because their object is a kasiṇa concept.

‘Iddhividhacatutthaṃ’ kāyavasena cittaṃ, cittavasena vā kāyaṃ pariṇāmanakāle attano kumārakavaṇṇādinimmānakāle ca sakāyacittānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇato ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, bahiddhā hatthiassādidassanakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, kālena ajjhattaṃ kālena bahiddhā, pavattiyaṃ ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

Regarding the fourth jhāna for the kinds of psychic power: at the time of transforming the mind by means of the body, or the body by means of the mind, and at the time of creating one's own appearance of a boy, etc., it has an internal object because it makes one's own body and mind its object. At the time of displaying external elephants, horses, etc., it has an external object. At times internal, at times external; during its occurrence, it has an internal-and-external object.

‘Dibbasotacatutthaṃ’ [V 0.0441] attano kucchisaddasavanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, paresaṃ saddasavanakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ. ‘Cetopariyañāṇacatutthaṃ’ paresaṃ cittārammaṇato bahiddhārammaṇameva. Attano cittajānane pana tena payojanaṃ natthi. ‘Pubbenivāsacatutthaṃ’ attano khandhānussaraṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa khandhe, anidriyabaddharūpaṃ, tisso ca paṇṇattiyo anussaraṇato bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ.

‘The divine ear as the fourth’—at the time of hearing sounds within one’s own belly, it has an internal object; at the time of hearing the sounds of others, it has an external object; in both ways, it has an internal-and-external object. ‘The knowledge of others' minds as the fourth’—because it has the minds of others as its object, it has only an external object. However, in knowing one's own mind, there is no purpose for it. ‘The recollection of past lives as the fourth’—at the time of recollecting one’s own aggregates, it has an internal object; due to recollecting another’s aggregates, form not bound by faculties, and the three concepts, it has an external object; in both ways, it has an internal-and-external object.

‘Dibbacakkhucatutthaṃ’ [P 0.0427] attano kucchigatādirūpadassanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, avasesarūpadassanakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ. ‘Anāgataṃsañāṇacatutthaṃ’ attano anāgatakkhandhānussaraṇakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ, parassa anāgatakkhandhānaṃ vā anindriyabaddhassa vā rūpassa anussaraṇakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, ubhayavasena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ. Ākiñcaññāyatanassa navattabbārammaṇatāya kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

‘The divine eye as the fourth’ has an internal object at the time of seeing forms, etc., located within one's own belly; it has an external object at the time of seeing the remaining forms; in both ways, it has an internal-and-external object. ‘The knowledge of the future as the fourth’ has an internal object at the time of recollecting one's own future aggregates; it has an external object at the time of recollecting another’s future aggregates or form not bound by faculties; in both ways, it has an internal-and-external object. The reason for the base of nothingness having an unspecifiable object has indeed been stated previously.

Dukaatthuddhāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Elucidation of the Meaning of the Dyads

1441. Hetugocchakaniddese [M 0.0451] tayo kusalahetūtiādinā nayena hetū dassetvā puna teyeva uppattiṭṭhānato dassetuṃ catūsu bhūmīsu kusalesu uppajjantītiādi vuttaṃ. Iminā upāyena sesagocchakesupi desanānayo veditabbo.

1441. In the exposition of the root-cluster, after having shown the roots by the method beginning with “the three wholesome roots,” the passage beginning “they arise in the wholesome states in the four planes…” was spoken in order to show those very roots by way of their place of origin. By this method, the way of teaching in the remaining clusters should also be understood.

1473. Yattha dve tayo āsavā ekato uppajjantīti ettha tividhena āsavānaṃ ekato uppatti veditabbā. Tattha catūsu diṭṭhivippayuttesu avijjāsavena, diṭṭhisampayuttesu diṭṭhāsavaavijjāsavehi saddhinti kāmāsavo duvidhena ekato uppajjati. Bhavāsavo catūsu diṭṭhivippayuttesu avijjāsavena saddhinti ekadhāva ekato uppajjati. Yathā cettha evaṃ yattha dve tīṇi saṃyojanāni ekato uppajjantīti etthāpi saṃyojanānaṃ uppatti ekato dasadhā bhave. Tattha kāmarāgo catudhā ekato uppajjati, paṭigho tidhā, māno ekadhā. Tathā vicikicchā ceva bhavarāgo ca. Kathaṃ? Kāmarāgo tāva mānasaṃyojanaavijjāsaṃyojanehi ceva, diṭṭhisaṃyojanaavijjāsaṃyojanehi ca, sīlabbataparāmāsaavijjāsaṃyojanehi ca, avijjāsaṃyojanamatteneva ca saddhinti evaṃ catudhā ekato uppajjati. Paṭigho pana issāsaṃyojanaavijjāsaṃyojanehi ceva, macchariyasaṃyojanaavijjāsaṃyojanehi ca, avijjāsaṃyojanamatteneva [V 0.0442] ca saddhinti evaṃ tidhā ekato uppajjati. Māno bhavarāgāvijjāsaṃyojanehi saddhiṃ ekadhāva ekato uppajjati[P 0.0428]. Tathā vicikicchā. Sā hi avijjāsaṃyojanena saddhiṃ ekadhā uppajjati. Bhavarāgepi eseva nayoti. Evamettha dve tīṇi saṃyojanāni ekato uppajjanti.

1473. Where it is said, “two or three taints arise together,” the arising together of the taints should be understood in three ways. Therein, the taint of sensual desire arises together in two ways: with the taint of ignorance in the four consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view, and with the taints of wrong view and ignorance in those associated with wrong view. The taint of existence arises together in one way only: with the taint of ignorance in the four consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view. Just as here, so too where it is said, “two or three fetters arise together,” the arising together of the fetters would occur in ten ways. Therein, sensual lust arises together in four ways, aversion in three, and conceit in one. Similarly for doubt and attachment to existence. How? Sensual lust arises together in four ways: with the fetters of conceit and ignorance; with the fetters of wrong view and ignorance; with the fetters of adherence to rules and observances and ignorance; and with the fetter of ignorance alone. Aversion, however, arises together in three ways: with the fetters of envy and ignorance; with the fetters of stinginess and ignorance; and with the fetter of ignorance alone. Conceit arises together in one way only, with the fetters of attachment to existence and ignorance. Similarly for doubt, for it arises in one way with the fetter of ignorance. In the case of attachment to existence, this is the same method. Thus, in this way, two or three fetters arise together.

1511. Yaṃ panetaṃ nīvaraṇagocchake yattha dve tīṇi nīvaraṇāni ekato uppajjantīti vuttaṃ, tatthāpi aṭṭhadhā nīvaraṇānaṃ ekato uppatti veditabbā. Etesu hi kāmacchando duvidhā ekato uppajjati, byāpādo catudhā, uddhaccaṃ ekadhā. Tathā vicikicchā. Kathaṃ? Kāmacchando tāva asaṅkhārikacittesu uddhaccanīvaraṇaavijjānīvaraṇehi, sasaṅkhārikesu thinamiddhauddhaccaavijjānīvaraṇehi saddhiṃ duvidhā ekato uppajjati. Yaṃ panetaṃ dve tīṇīti vuttaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedavasena vuttaṃ. Tasmā catunnampi ekato uppajjatīti [M 0.0452] vacanaṃ yujjati eva. Byāpādo pana asaṅkhārikacitte uddhaccaavijjānīvaraṇehi, sasaṅkhārike thinamiddhauddhaccaavijjānīvaraṇehi, asaṅkhārikeyeva uddhaccakukkuccaavijjānīvaraṇehi, sasaṅkhārikeyeva thinamiddhauddhaccakukkuccaavijjānīvaraṇehi saddhinti catudhā ekato uppajjati. Uddhaccaṃ pana avijjānīvaraṇamattena saddhiṃ ekadhāva ekato uppajjati. Vicikicchuddhaccaavijjānīvaraṇehi saddhiṃ ekadhāva ekato uppajjati.

1511. Regarding what was said in the hindrance-cluster, “where two or three hindrances arise together,” there too the arising together of hindrances should be understood in eight ways. For among these, sensual desire arises together in two ways, ill will in four ways, restlessness in one way, and similarly doubt. How? Sensual desire, for instance, arises together in two ways: with the hindrances of restlessness and ignorance in unprompted consciousnesses, and with the hindrances of sloth, torpor, restlessness, and ignorance in prompted consciousnesses. As for the statement “two or three,” it was said with reference to the lower limit. Therefore, the statement that even four can arise together is indeed appropriate. Ill will, however, arises together in four ways: with the hindrances of restlessness and ignorance in an unprompted consciousness; with the hindrances of sloth, torpor, restlessness, and ignorance in a prompted consciousness; with the hindrances of restlessness, remorse, and ignorance in an unprompted consciousness itself; and with the hindrances of sloth, torpor, restlessness, remorse, and ignorance in a prompted consciousness itself. Restlessness, however, arises together in one way only, with the hindrance of ignorance alone. Doubt arises together in one way only, with the hindrances of restlessness and ignorance.

1577. Yampidaṃ kilesagocchake yattha dve tayo kilesā ekato uppajjantīti vuttaṃ, tattha ‘dve kilesā aññehi, tayo vā kilesā aññehi kilesehi saddhiṃ uppajjantī’ti evamattho veditabbo. Kasmā? Dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃyeva vā ekato uppattiyā asambhavato.

1577. Regarding what was said in the defilement-cluster, “where two or three defilements arise together,” the meaning should be understood thus: ‘two defilements arise together with other defilements, or three defilements arise together with other defilements.’ Why? Because of the impossibility of the arising together of only two or only three.

Tattha dasadhā kilesānaṃ ekato uppatti hoti. Ettha hi lobho chadhā ekato uppajjati. Paṭigho dvidhā. Tathā mohoti veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Lobho tāva asaṅkhārike diṭṭhivippayutte mohauddhaccaahirikānottappehi, sasaṅkhārike mohathinauddhaccaahirikānottappehi, asaṅkhārikeyeva mohamānuddhaccāhirikānottappehi[P 0.0429], sasaṅkhārikeyeva mohamānathinauddhaccaahirikānottappehi, diṭṭhisampayutte pana asaṅkhārike mohauddhaccadiṭṭhiahirikānottappehi, sasaṅkhārike mohadiṭṭhithinauddhaccaahirikānottappehi saddhinti chadhā ekato uppajjati.

Therein, the arising together of the defilements occurs in ten ways. For herein, greed arises together in six ways, aversion in two ways, and delusion should be understood similarly. How? Greed, for instance, arises together in six ways: in an unprompted state dissociated from wrong view, with the defilements of delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness; in a prompted state, with the defilements of delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness; in an unprompted state itself, with the defilements of delusion, conceit, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness; in a prompted state itself, with the defilements of delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness; in an unprompted state associated with wrong view, with the defilements of delusion, restlessness, wrong view, shamelessness, and recklessness; and in a prompted state, with the defilements of delusion, wrong view, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness.

Paṭigho [V 0.0443] pana asaṅkhārike mohauddhaccaahirikānottappehi, sasaṅkhārike mohathinauddhaccaahirikānottappehi saddhinti evaṃ dvidhā ekato uppajjati. Moho pana vicikicchāsampayutte vicikicchuddhaccaahirikānottappehi, uddhaccasampayutte uddhaccaahirikānottappehi saddhinti evaṃ dvidhā ekato uppajjati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Aversion, however, arises together in two ways: in unprompted states, with delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness; and in prompted states, with delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness. Delusion, however, arises together in two ways: when associated with doubt, with doubt, restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness; and when associated with restlessness, with restlessness, shamelessness, and recklessness. The remainder everywhere else is of clear meaning.

Aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaaṭṭhakathāya

In the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī:

Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Commentary Section is Concluded.

Nigamanakathā

The Concluding Words

Ettāvatā ca –

And thus far:

Cittaṃ [M 0.0453] rūpañca nikkhepaṃ, atthuddhāraṃ manoramaṃ;

Yaṃ lokanātho bhājento, desesi dhammasaṅgaṇiṃ.

Which delightful Dhammasaṅgaṇī—comprising the sections on Mind, Matter, the Summary, and the Elucidation of Meaning—the Lord of the World taught while analyzing it.

Abhidhammassa saṅgayha, dhamme anavasesato;

Ṭhitāya tassā āraddhā, yā mayā atthavaṇṇanā.

The exposition of the meaning of that Dhammasaṅgaṇī, which stands having compiled the phenomena of the Abhidhamma in their entirety, is that which has been undertaken by me.

Anākulānamatthānaṃ, sambhavā aṭṭhasālinī;

Iti nāmena sā esā, sanniṭṭhānamupāgatā.

Because it is the source of lucid meanings, it is named Aṭṭhasālinī; this very commentary has reached its conclusion.

Ekūnacattālīsāya, pāḷiyā bhāṇavārato;

Ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ dhammassa, niṭṭhāpentena taṃ mayā.

By me, completing it, which consists of thirty-nine recitation sections of the Pāḷi, for the long endurance of the Dhamma.

Yaṃ [P 0.0430] pattaṃ kusalaṃ tassa, ānubhāvena pāṇino;

Sabbe saddhammarājassa, ñatvā dhammaṃ sukhāvahaṃ.

By the power of whatever merit has been attained by me, may all beings, having known the happiness-bringing Dhamma of the King of the True Dhamma,

Pāpuṇantu [V 0.0444] visuddhāya, sukhāya paṭipattiyā;

Asokamanupāyāsaṃ, nibbānasukhamuttamaṃ.

through the pure and pleasant practice, attain the supreme bliss of Nibbāna, which is free from sorrow and distress.

Ciraṃ tiṭṭhatu saddhammo, dhamme hontu sagāravā;

Sabbepi sattā kālena, sammā devo pavassatu.

May the True Dhamma long endure! May all beings be respectful towards the Dhamma! May the heavens rain rightly in due season!

Yathā rakkhiṃsu porāṇā, surājāno tathevimaṃ;

Rājā rakkhatu dhammena, attanova pajaṃ pajanti.

Just as the good kings of old protected their subjects, so too may the king righteously protect these people as his own offspring.

Paramavisuddhasaddhābuddhivīriyapaṭimaṇḍitena sīlācārajjavamaddavādiguṇasamudayasamuditena sakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhaṇasamatthena paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatena tipiṭakapariyattippabhede sāṭṭhakathe satthusāsane appaṭihatañāṇappabhāvena mahāveyyākaraṇena karaṇasampattijanitasukhaviniggatamadhurodāravacanalāvaṇṇayuttena yuttamuttavādinā vādīvarena mahākavinā pabhinnapaṭisambhidāparivāre chaḷabhiññādippabhedaguṇapaṭimaṇḍite uttarimanussadhamme suppatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ therānaṃ mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vaṃsālaṅkārabhūtena vipulavisuddhabuddhinā buddhaghosoti garūhi [M 0.0454] gahitanāmadheyyena therena katā ayaṃ aṭṭhasālinī nāma dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathā.

This commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, called the Aṭṭhasālinī, was composed by the Elder whose name, Buddhaghosa, was given by his preceptors—he who was adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a wealth of virtues such as good conduct, uprightness, and gentleness; capable of penetrating the profound doctrines of his own and other schools; possessed of mature wisdom; versed in the three divisions of the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries; whose unobstructed knowledge shone forth in the Teacher’s Dispensation; a great grammarian; whose speech was sweet and majestic, flowing from the ease born of perfected vocal organs; a speaker of what is suitable and desirable; foremost among speakers; a great poet; possessed of vast and purified wisdom; and who was an ornament to the lineage of the Elders residing at the Great Monastery, those lamps unto the lineage of the Theras, whose wisdom was well-established in the super-human states that are attended by the distinct analytical knowledges and adorned with qualities such as the six supernormal knowledges.

Tāva tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, lokanittharaṇesinaṃ;

Dassentī kulaputtānaṃ, nayaṃ paññāvisuddhiyā.

May it endure in the world for as long, showing the path to the purification of wisdom to the sons of good family who seek to cross over the world.

Yāva ‘buddho’ti nāmampi, suddhacittassa tādino;

Lokamhi lokajeṭṭhassa, pavattati mahesinoti.

As long as even the name 'Buddha'—of the pure-minded Such One, the eldest in the world, the great sage—endures in the world.

Aṭṭhasālinī nāma

Named the Aṭṭhasālinī,

Dhammasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī is completed.
